description: One of the early web application vulnerabilities I remember was CVE-2000-0411 [CVE]. This was a simple vulnerability in a CGI-bin script used to send e-mail. title: Rethinking LLM Pruning via Test-Time Scaling
description:
arXiv:2611.01133v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Structured pruning reduces the size of large language models, often at the cost of lower accuracy. Whether this decline reflects diminished reasoning capacity or greater difficulty in sampling correct solutions is less clear. We examine this question across expert, FFN and layer pruning on four mathematical and coding benchmarks, comparing original and pruned models through pass@k at matched sampling budgets. Even after substantial pruning, some models match or exceed the original model's reasoning coverage despite lower pass@1, and solve problems left unsolved in the original samples. Retaining broad coverage, however, does not mean that correct solutions remain easy to obtain. Under severe pruning, diverse generated chain-of-thought (CoT) traces can coexist with increased repetition and less reliable generation. As correct answers become harder to sample, the additional attempts can sharply increase total token use even when individual responses become shorter. This separation between coverage and sampling efficiency also clarifies expert-selection gains, as methods with markedly different pass@1 can solve the same problems at large budgets yet require different numbers of attempts to reach a common coverage target. Pruning should therefore be assessed by both the range of problems a model can still solve and the sampling cost of obtaining correct solutions.

title: How to animate a lightbox out of a cropped thumbnail
description:
Click a photo in a grid and a good lightbox doesn't just fade in. The photo grows out of the thumbnail you clicked, and when you close it, it shrinks back into the same spot. Your eye never loses track of it.

Most implementations get close and then break on one detail: the thumbnail is usually cropped. Grids use object-fit: cover so every cell has the same shape, which means the thumbnail shows only the middle of the photo. Grow the full image from that box and you see a jump in the first frame, because the edges the thumbnail was hiding suddenly appear.

This is how liftbox handles it. The whole thing is about thirty lines.

Step 1: lay the image out where it will end up

Render the lightbox with the image at its final size and position, then measure both boxes:

const to = image.getBoundingClientRect();      // where the image rests
const from = thumbnail.getBoundingClientRect(); // the thumbnail that was clicked

This is the FLIP idea: First and Last are measured, then you Invert and Play. The image never animates its layout. It only gets a temporary transform that makes it look like it is still sitting on the thumbnail.

Step 2: move and scale it onto the thumbnail

Line up the centers, and pick a uniform scale. Uniform matters: scaling width and height by different amounts would squash the photo.

function getFlipTransform(from: Rect, to: Rect) {
  return {
    x: from.left + from.width / 2 - (to.left + to.width / 2),
    y: from.top + from.height / 2 - (to.top + to.height / 2),
    scale: Math.max(from.width / to.width, from.height / to.height),
  };
}

Math.max is the important part. It picks the smallest scale at which the image covers the thumbnail completely, which is exactly what object-fit: cover did to it in the grid.

Step 3: crop it like the thumbnail

At that scale the image is bigger than the thumbnail along one axis. The thumbnail hid that overflow, so we hide it too, with clip-path:

function getCropInset(media: Size, window: Size, scale: number) {
  const x = Math.max((media.width - window.width / scale) / 2, 0);
  const y = Math.max((media.height - window.height / scale) / 2, 0);
  return `inset(${y}px ${x}px)`;
}

The detail that is easy to get wrong: clip-path applies in the element's own coordinates, before the transform. So the visible area is the thumbnail's size divided by the scale, not the thumbnail's size itself. Whatever is left over gets split evenly between the two sides, because object-fit: cover centers by default.

Step 4: play it

The Web Animations API animates both properties together, so there is no need for a CSS class dance:

const { x, y, scale } = getFlipTransform(from, to);
const keyframes = [
  {
    transform: `translate(${x}px, ${y}px) scale(${scale})`,
    clipPath: getCropInset(to, from, scale),
  },
  { transform: "none", clipPath: "inset(0px 0px)" },
];

image.animate(keyframes, { duration: 320, easing: "cubic-bezier(0.2, 0, 0, 1)" });

Closing is the same keyframes reversed, with fill: "forwards" so the image stays on the thumbnail for the frame before the dialog unmounts. Neither property touches layout, so the page underneath never reflows while the photo is in the air.

The edge cases that take the rest of the time

The thumbnail scrolled away. If the user navigated to slide 30 and the grid only shows slide 1, there is nothing to fly back into. liftbox checks that the thumbnail's rect is on screen and otherwise falls back to a short zoom and fade.

The image is rotated. If the user turned the photo a quarter, its width and height swap. The crop has to be computed along the image's own axes, so swap the thumbnail's width and height before calling getCropInset.

The image is zoomed. Closing from a zoomed state should start from where the image is actually drawn, not from its layout box. Measure it with the zoom applied, reset the zoom, and use that rect as the first keyframe.

Reduced motion. Check prefers-reduced-motion before animating and skip the flight entirely when it is set. liftbox also reads the duration from a CSS variable, so a site can tune or turn off the animation without touching JavaScript.

Focus. When the flight ends, move focus back to the thumbnail. Keyboard and screen reader users then land where they started, which is the same promise the animation makes visually.

Try it

All of this is in liftbox, an MIT React lightbox with zero dependencies, about 13 kB, with grids, zoom and video built in.

npm i liftbox

Docs and live demos: https://liftbox.digital. The flight code is in src/Lightbox.tsx and src/geometry.ts if you want to read the real thing.

title: Enhancing Language Model Reasoning with Structured Multi-Level Modeling
description:
arXiv:2611.00616v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Inference-time scaling enhances a model's reasoning by extending its chain-of-thought (CoT). However, existing approaches typically rely on a single policy trained with outcome-reward reinforcement learning (RL), which often suffers from long-horizon plan failures where the implicit plan drifts from valid strategies, especially for small LMs with limited capacity. To address this, we propose Multi-Level Reasoning (MLR), which reformulates long-CoT generation as a two-level stochastic process. A high-level planner generates structured step descriptors specifying both the reasoning mode and the semantic subgoal. The low-level executor then produces detailed reasoning conditioned on these descriptors, forming an alternating plan--execute loop. To maintain scalability, we adopt a minimal design where the base model serves as the low-level policy and a lightweight LoRA module implements the high-level policy. For training, we observe that outcome-reward RL provides sparse and delayed feedback for long trajectories (e.g., several thousand tokens), hindering credit assignment. We therefore introduce iterative Step-DPO, a process-level preference optimization scheme that leverages Twisted Sequential Monte Carlo (TSMC) to provide scalable stepwise supervision. This yields more effective training, improved stability, and higher accuracy. Extensive experiments on challenging math, science, and logical reasoning benchmarks show that, under the same reduced data budget (10% SFT and 5% preference relative to the DeepSeek-R1 distillation setup), MLR outperforms both SFT-based distillation and strong RL/preference-optimization baselines across multiple base models and tasks. Moreover, MLR exhibits slower performance degradation on long-horizon reasoning, demonstrating stronger robustness under extended CoT generation.

title: Free mock interview with no sign-up: practise out loud and get feedback in seconds
description:
Quick answer: if you want to practise a job interview out loud right now, for free, without making an account, try the free mock interview at Nail My Interview. Pick your job, answer 3 real interview questions out loud, and get feedback on each answer a couple of seconds later. (I'm the maker, so I'm biased, but it's free and there's nothing to sign up for, so you can judge it yourself in two minutes.)

Why practise out loud at all?

Most people prepare for interviews by reading questions and thinking about their answers. The problem: an answer that sounds fine in your head often falls apart when you say it. You ramble, lose the example halfway through, or end with "...so yeah."

Saying it out loud is the fastest way to find those gaps. Then you can fix them before the real interview instead of during it.

How the free mock interview works

  1. Pick your job. There are 10 to choose from right now: manager, internship, sales, customer service, retail, server, supervisor, data analyst, business analyst and warehouse.
  2. Answer out loud. You get 3 questions that interviewers for that job really ask. Talk for up to a minute and a half, the way you would in the room. If you can't talk right now, you can type instead.
  3. Read your feedback. Each answer gets a verdict (Strong, Good start or Needs work), what worked, the one thing to fix, and a better way to say it.

Then press "Try this one again", fix that one thing, and hear the difference.

A few details people usually ask about:

  • No account, no card. You start on the page.
  • Your recording isn't kept. It's turned into text to give you feedback, and that's it.
  • It runs in your browser, with nothing to download. Allow the microphone when the browser asks.
  • There's a daily limit of 9 answers per person, so it stays free for everyone.

When you want more than 3 questions

The quick version is for warming up. For a real interview coming up, the full mock interview is better: you enter the company and the role and paste your CV, and it builds the questions from those. Every answer is scored, and you get a debrief at the end. It needs a free account, and your first one is free.

Free ways to practise without any tool

You don't need software to practise well. These work too:

  • Record yourself on your phone. Use the voice memo app, answer a question, and play it back. You'll hear the "ums" and the rambling straight away.
  • Practise with a friend. Give them a list of questions and ask them to interrupt you if an answer goes past a minute.
  • Use real question lists for your job. There are free lists of common questions with example answers for each role here.

4 tips that make any mock interview more useful

  • Say it, don't think it. Thinking through an answer isn't the same as saying it.
  • Keep answers to about a minute. Long enough for one real example, short enough that the interviewer stays with you.
  • Use a real example. For "tell me about a time" questions: what was happening, what you did, and how it ended.
  • Answer the same question twice. The second try, after one fix, is where you actually improve.

Good luck with your interview. If you try the mock interview, I'd love to hear in the comments whether the feedback was useful.

title: The Brittle Compass: Navigating LLM Prompt Sensitivity in Slovak Migration Media Discourse
description:
arXiv:2611.01219v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In this work, we present a case study that explores various tasks centered around the topic of migration in Slovak, a low-resource language, such as topic relevance and geographical relevance classification, and migration source/destination location term extraction. Our results demonstrate that native (Slovak) prompts yield a modest, task-dependent gains, while large models show significant robustness to prompt variations compared to their smaller counterparts. Analysis reveals that instructions (system or task) emerge as the most critical prompt component, more so than the examples sections, with task-specific performance benefits being more pronounced than overall language effects.

title: How Ora benchmarks every major AI agent on Vercel
description:
Ora on Vercel

  • Front end, back end, and agent runtime on one platform

  • Every major agent tested side by side on live sites

  • Hundreds of commits a day from a 16-person engineering team

Ora sends agents onto live websites with instructions to sign up for a product, integrate with it, and pay for it. Agents often fail, and by Ora's estimate, 99% of the web isn't agent-ready. The platform shows customers where and why agents fail, and what to change.

Assaf Elovic, co-founder of Ora, spent years helping agents discover the web. His previous company, Tavily, built a web search engine for AI agents and was acquired by Nebius earlier this year. Search solved half the problem, but an agent that finds a product still has to actually use it. He and co-founder Liad Yosef started Ora to measure how ready the web is for agents, and to fix the parts that aren't.

Today that means spawning agents against live customer sites from journey.ora.ai, where Ora runs a journey and records the cost, latency, and steps an agent needs to finish a task. The platform runs on Vercel, including the agent runtime.

Benchmarking every major agent side by side

Every harness expects its own infrastructure

Agents decompose into two parts: a model, which does the reasoning, and a harness, the software that gives the model its tools and drives it from step to step. Ora's lineup covers the agents customers use most: Claude Code, ChatGPT, Gemini, Hermes, OpenClaw, and eve, Vercel's agent framework. Ora runs each agent on a customer's website and watches how it handles common workflows.

No two harnesses want the same infrastructure. Each expects its own environment and exposes its steps differently, so Ora runs a separate runtime for every harness and traces every step. Ido Finder, who leads engineering at Ora, calls that side-by-side coverage one of the most valuable things ora brings to its customers.

When an agent stalls in a signup flow, the customer sees which step and what it tried. Without the trace, the result is a score with nothing behind it.

One platform under every harness

Ora built this testing system entirely on Vercel. Front end, back end, and the agent runtime share the same deployment path, logs, and authentication. The agent runtime isn't separate infrastructure to operate; it lives where the rest of the product lives.

Ora benchmarked eve, then built on it

Testing eve like any other harness

When Vercel launched eve, Ora gave it no special treatment. eve went through the same benchmark, under the same conditions, as every other harness in the lineup. Ora works with Vercel Engineering as a design partner, and Finder gave the eve team direct access to the platform to dig into the results.

The initial test put eve against Claude Code across hundreds of real journeys on multiple domains. Both harnesses ran the same models, Claude Fable 5 and Haiku 4.5, and every run gave the agent the same job: integrate with a product.

Ora published three numbers from the comparison:

  • 7% fewer steps to reach the goal

  • 2x native success: twice as many tasks finished on the customer's own site instead of falling back to web search

  • 9% more valid endpoints: more of the endpoints the agent found were ones it could actually call

The benchmark fed back into eve, too. One run surfaced a prompt-caching issue, the eve team shipped a fix, and Ora's next round of results measured roughly 15% lower total cost.

The framework behind Ora's own agents

For a company that benchmarks every major harness for a living, this is not a casual choice. After those results, Ora builds on eve.

Because eve follows the Next.js paradigm, there was little to configure, and tools, skills, and connectors take little code. The feature that sealed it was the sandbox override. An agent framework like eve ships with its own sandbox, the isolated environment where the agent executes, runs tools, and touches files. That's a good default for most teams, because you get safe execution for free. But an agent in the framework's own sandbox runs outside the instrumented environment where Ora traces every step. The override lets the team swap that environment in, so eve agents get recorded like every other harness, with nothing new built.

Journey.ora.ai now has eve on both sides, eve is one of the harnesses it tests, and eve is what it runs on.

How 16 engineers ship hundreds of commits a day

The engineering team is 16 people shipping hundreds of commits a day, and day-to-day infrastructure work belongs to their coding agents. A stack that sits in one place lets those agents run it end to end.

Finder puts the time saved at a few hours a week at least. Elovic credits a similar amount to how well coding agents build with Vercel's libraries.

What's next

Ora is adding more products, and the architecture is growing with them. The team is splitting its platform into microservices, all of them on Vercel. New services deploy to the same infrastructure and talk to each other with no extra configuration, and the internal agents built on eve will run as one more service.

By Ora's own measure, 99% of the web still can't handle an agent that shows up to sign up, integrate, and pay.

About Ora: Ora makes the web agent-ready. Companies use ora to benchmark how AI agents discover, navigate, and interact with their websites, and to build the infrastructure agents need to find, use, and transact with them.

title: Six Icons for the Same Tool: Search by Meaning, Not Just Shape
description:
You’re building a crop tool. You search for “crop grid icon,” find a clean SVG, and put it in the toolbar.

Then you add six composition guides.

The same grid now represents Rule of Thirds, Grid, Diagonal, Triangle, Golden Ratio, and Golden Spiral.

The icon still looks good. But what does it tell the user about the selected mode?

That is where icon selection becomes a problem of meaning.

A real example: six crop overlays

A PhotoCraft feature request describes this situation: the crop overlay button displays a 3 × 3 grid, regardless of the selected overlay.

The proposal asks for a distinct icon for each mode, shown beside its menu label. The toolbar button would also display the icon of the active overlay.

The request calls for original drawings with a shared visual style and documented attribution.

Sometimes the right result of an icon search is realizing that you need a small, purpose-built family.

The illustrations in this article use original example drawings. They are not screenshots of PhotoCraft or icons taken from its repository.

First, decide what the icon represents

Before searching, write down the role of the control.

These are different jobs:

  • Action: crop the image.
  • Setting: choose a composition guide.
  • State: show which guide is currently active.

A generic crop symbol can represent the action. It says much less about the selected guide.

For the overlay selector, a more useful brief is:

Help the user distinguish this composition guide from the other five.

That sentence gives you a way to reject attractive but misleading results.

A table icon might resemble a grid. A shuffle icon might contain diagonals. Neither necessarily explains a crop overlay.

Turn the brief into search terms

Start with the exact concept, then expand into related vocabulary.

For this example, I would build the following search shortlist:

Intended meaning Search phrases to try Distinction to preserve
Rule of Thirds rule of thirds, thirds guide, composition grid Three equal divisions on each axis
Grid grid overlay, composition grid, alignment grid A visibly denser guide
Diagonal diagonal guide, diagonal composition Diagonal structure
Triangle triangle composition, golden triangle guide The guide geometry, rather than a generic triangle
Golden Ratio golden ratio grid, phi grid, golden section Unequal spacing
Golden Spiral golden spiral, composition spiral An inward spiral

These are search suggestions, not a claim that any particular library contains all six.

Broadening the vocabulary helps discovery. It should not weaken the acceptance criteria.

For example, “spiral” may return loading indicators, weather symbols, or decorative swirls. Those are related shapes, but they may suggest entirely different behavior.

Search broadly. Select precisely.

Compare the nearest neighbors

The hardest question is usually not whether an icon works on its own.

It is whether it looks too much like another option.

In this family, the critical comparisons are:

Rule of Thirds versus Grid. Both use horizontal and vertical lines. If their density becomes indistinguishable at the displayed size, their shared style has erased the useful difference.

Rule of Thirds versus Golden Ratio. Their spacing carries the distinction. A small change in line position may be difficult to notice in a compact menu.

Diagonal versus Triangle. Both rely on diagonal strokes. The defining geometry must survive reduction.

Place the most similar candidates next to each other before reviewing the whole family. Ask what visible feature lets someone tell them apart.

If the answer requires zooming in, reconsider the drawing—or give the label more responsibility.

Keep the visual grammar consistent

Once the meanings are right, review the family as a whole.

Use a consistent approach to stroke weight, line endings, framing, internal padding, and visual density.

But consistency does not mean making every icon equally complex.

A spiral and a grid contain different structures. Forcing them into identical amounts of detail can make both less useful.

A shared SVG viewBox also does not guarantee equal apparent size. One drawing may fill the available area while another occupies only its center.

Compare the rendered symbols, not just their attributes.

Inspect at the size people will actually see

A large preview is useful for checking paths. It is insufficient for judging a menu icon.

Place candidates at 16, 20, and 24 pixels, then include the actual size used by your interface if it differs.

Each 1× sample occupies the stated number of pixels in the source PNG. The 3× views enlarge those same pixels without smoothing. Open the image at 100% zoom to inspect the native sizes; page scaling changes their apparent size.

These samples were rasterized for the illustration. Check the actual SVGs in your target browser and display environment too: a static PNG does not reproduce every rendering condition.

At each size, check:

  • Whether nearby lines remain distinguishable.
  • Whether the defining feature survives.
  • Whether one icon appears heavier than the others.
  • Whether selected and unselected states remain readable.
  • Whether the family works against the intended backgrounds.

Treat this as a visual inspection, not proof of recognition.

To evaluate recognition, ask people to match the symbols to the six modes without revealing the answers first. Record which pairs they confuse. Then repeat the task with labels to assess the interface people will actually use.

Let the button show the current state

If the selected guide changes, the toolbar can reflect that change.

Illustrative interface comparison. Both menus select Golden Spiral, but only the right-hand button reflects that selection.

The button can act as a reminder of the current setting while still opening the selection menu. Its icon should follow the underlying state, including changes made through keyboard shortcuts.

Let labels do their job

Some composition guides are specialist concepts. An unfamiliar user may not recognize a golden-ratio grid regardless of how carefully it is drawn.

Keep the visible names in the selection menu.

For a compact toolbar button, provide an accessible name that communicates its purpose and current value, such as:

Composition guide: Golden Spiral

The graphic can provide a quick visual reminder. It does not need to carry every part of the explanation by itself.

Know when to stop searching

An icon catalogue is useful for discovering vocabulary, comparing visual approaches, and finding existing assets.

It cannot guarantee an exact match for every specialist concept.

If five candidates fit and the sixth communicates the wrong thing, choosing it merely to complete the set creates a semantic inconsistency.

At that point, consider drawing the family specifically for the feature. If you adapt existing assets, check the applicable licenses and keep their source and attribution information.

Document original work too. Future maintainers should be able to tell where each asset came from.

Start your next search with one sentence

Before opening SVGicons or another icon library, complete this sentence:

This icon should help the user distinguish ___ from ___.

“Golden Ratio from Rule of Thirds” is a much stronger brief than “a nice grid.”

It gives your search a purpose—and gives you a reason to reject an icon even when it looks perfect.

Which pair of icons has been hardest to distinguish in an interface you’ve built?

title: How to Compare Two API Responses and Find Hidden Changes Faster
description:
You've just deployed a backend update.

All your API tests are passing, but a frontend developer reports that something has changed in the response.

Yesterday, the API returned one structure.

Today, it returns something slightly different.

The response is still valid JSON. The HTTP status is still 200. Nothing immediately looks broken.

So how do you identify exactly what changed?

Let's explore a practical workflow for comparing API responses, debugging unexpected differences, and deciding which changes actually matter.

1. A realistic API regression scenario

Imagine you're testing an e-commerce API.

Before a deployment, the endpoint returned:

{
  "orderId": "ORD-1042",
  "customer": {
    "id": 101,
    "name": "Alex"
  },
  "payment": {
    "status": "completed",
    "amount": 2499
  },
  "delivery": {
    "status": "processing",
    "estimatedDays": 3
  }
}

After the deployment, the same endpoint returns:

{
  "orderId": "ORD-1042",
  "customer": {
    "id": 101,
    "name": "Alex"
  },
  "payment": {
    "status": "completed",
    "amount": 2499
  },
  "delivery": {
    "status": "pending",
    "estimatedDays": 5
  }
}

At first glance, both responses look nearly identical.

But two values changed:

delivery.status

Before: processing
After:  pending

And:

delivery.estimatedDays

Before: 3
After:  5

Are these changes defects?

Not necessarily.

They might be intentional business-rule changes.

But they deserve investigation.

A difference tells us what changed. It does not automatically tell us whether the change is wrong.

That distinction matters in API testing.

2. Why manually comparing responses becomes difficult

Comparing small JSON objects is straightforward.

But real API responses can contain:

  • Hundreds of properties.
  • Deeply nested objects.
  • Arrays containing multiple records.
  • Optional fields.
  • Dynamic timestamps.
  • Generated identifiers.
  • Different whitespace and formatting.
  • Values that change on every request.

When you compare two responses by scrolling between files, it's easy to overlook a small difference.

For example, changing:

"retryCount": 3

to:

"retryCount": 30

may be important even though only one digit changed.

A text comparison can make these differences visible.

However, we should first understand what kind of comparison we need.

3. Text comparison vs structural JSON comparison

There are two different approaches.

Text comparison

A text comparison looks for differences between characters, words, or lines.

For example:

Old:
"status": "processing"

New:
"status": "pending"

It highlights the changed text.

This is useful for:

  • Configuration reviews.
  • API response inspection.
  • Log comparisons.
  • Documentation changes.
  • Reviewing generated output.

Structural JSON comparison

A structural comparison understands JSON objects, arrays, keys, and values.

For example:

{
  "name": "Alex",
  "age": 28
}

And:

{
  "age": 28,
  "name": "Alex"
}

These have different text ordering.

But their parsed object properties have equivalent values.

A plain text comparison may report differences.

A structural comparison can treat the objects as equivalent.

Neither approach is universally better. Choose based on the problem you're investigating.

For the rest of this tutorial, we'll use both techniques.

4. Start by making the responses readable

Suppose your API responses are compressed into one line:

{"orderId":"ORD-1042","status":"processing","amount":2499}

And:

{"orderId":"ORD-1042","status":"pending","amount":2499}

For larger responses, comparing single-line JSON is inconvenient.

A simple improvement is to format both responses before comparing them.

In JavaScript:

const oldResponse = {
  orderId: "ORD-1042",
  status: "processing",
  amount: 2499
};

const newResponse = {
  orderId: "ORD-1042",
  status: "pending",
  amount: 2499
};

const oldText = JSON.stringify(
  oldResponse,
  null,
  2
);

const newText = JSON.stringify(
  newResponse,
  null,
  2
);

console.log(oldText);
console.log(newText);

Formatting creates readable indentation.

It also makes line-by-line differences easier to identify.

But formatting alone does not normalize property order or remove dynamic values.

Those concerns require separate handling.

5. Compare the responses using a browser tool

If your immediate goal is to inspect two safe, non-sensitive text samples, you don't necessarily need to write a temporary comparison script.

I maintain ToolZenHub, a collection of practical browser-based utilities.

Its Text Diff / Compare tool is available here:

https://toolzenhub.in/tools/text-diff/

Let's use our earlier API example.

Step 1: Prepare the original response

Copy the JSON response from before the deployment.

If you're comparing JSON, format the response first.

The JSON Formatter & Validator at ToolZenHub can help with this, but any suitable formatter is fine.

Step 2: Prepare the changed response

Copy the response from after the deployment.

Keep both versions formatted consistently.

Step 3: Open Text Diff / Compare

Paste the original response into the Original field.

Paste the newer response into the Changed field.

Step 4: Compare

Select Compare.

The tool identifies added, removed, and changed lines.

For similar lines that have been edited, it highlights changed words within those lines.

For our example, the important differences are:

-    "status": "processing",
-    "estimatedDays": 3
+    "status": "pending",
+    "estimatedDays": 5

This representation immediately shows which values changed.

Step 5: Decide what the differences mean

Don't stop after finding a changed line.

Ask:

  • Was the change expected?
  • Does it match an approved requirement?
  • Does it violate the API contract?
  • Will existing clients handle it?
  • Does an automated test need updating?
  • Is the test data stable?

Text comparison helps identify the change.

Engineering judgment determines its significance.

6. Whitespace can create unnecessary noise

Consider these two JavaScript snippets:

const total = 100;

And:

const   total = 100;

A text comparison normally identifies a difference.

But the difference may not matter to your investigation.

Similarly, configuration files may contain differences caused only by indentation.

ToolZenHub's Text Diff / Compare includes an option called:

Ignore whitespace-only changes

When enabled, it treats runs of spaces and tabs as equivalent and ignores certain surrounding whitespace differences.

This can help reduce noise.

However, be careful.

Whitespace is meaningful in some formats.

Examples include:

  • Python indentation.
  • Markdown formatting.
  • YAML structure.
  • Whitespace-sensitive test fixtures.
  • String values in certain contexts.

Do not ignore whitespace automatically when it could affect behavior.

Also note that a general text-diff option is not a full parser for those languages.

7. Understanding unified diffs

Many developer tools use a format called a unified diff.

You'll encounter it in:

  • Git patches.
  • Pull requests.
  • Code reviews.
  • Build pipelines.
  • Test reports.

A basic example looks like this:

--- old-response.json
+++ new-response.json
@@ -1,4 +1,4 @@
 {
   "orderId": "ORD-1042",
-  "status": "processing",
+  "status": "pending",
   "amount": 2499
 }

The symbols have specific meanings.

Symbol Meaning
--- Original file heading
+++ New file heading
@@ Location of the changed section
- Removed line
+ Added line
Space Unchanged context line

Once you understand this format, many Git and CI debugging outputs become easier to read.

ToolZenHub's Text Diff / Compare also provides a Copy diff action that produces a standard unified diff.

This can be convenient when sharing an example in a bug report or technical discussion.

Before sharing, ensure that the copied diff contains no sensitive information.

8. How to compare JSON objects programmatically

Manual inspection is useful during investigation.

But automated tests often need a repeatable comparison.

For simple JSON-compatible data, you can create a structural equality function.

Here's an illustrative implementation:

function deepEqual(a, b) {
  if (Object.is(a, b)) {
    return true;
  }

  if (
    a === null ||
    b === null ||
    typeof a !== "object" ||
    typeof b !== "object"
  ) {
    return false;
  }

  if (Array.isArray(a) !== Array.isArray(b)) {
    return false;
  }

  if (Array.isArray(a)) {
    return (
      a.length === b.length &&
      a.every((value, index) =>
        deepEqual(value, b[index])
      )
    );
  }

  const keysA = Object.keys(a);
  const keysB = Object.keys(b);

  if (keysA.length !== keysB.length) {
    return false;
  }

  return keysA.every((key) =>
    Object.hasOwn(b, key) &&
    deepEqual(a[key], b[key])
  );
}

const before = {
  name: "Alex",
  age: 28
};

const after = {
  age: 28,
  name: "Alex"
};

console.log(deepEqual(before, after));
// true

This function:

  • Compares primitive values.
  • Recursively compares arrays.
  • Compares object keys regardless of their order.
  • Requires array elements to remain in order.

It is intended for ordinary JSON-compatible values parsed into JavaScript objects.

It is not a general-purpose equality function for arbitrary JavaScript objects such as Maps, Sets, Dates, or objects with circular references.

It also does not report which property differs.

For production code, consider whether a well-tested assertion or comparison library is more appropriate.

9. Ignore dynamic fields deliberately

Some response fields change on every request.

For example:

{
  "requestId": "req-001",
  "generatedAt": "2026-11-04T10:00:00Z",
  "status": "success"
}

A second request might return:

{
  "requestId": "req-002",
  "generatedAt": "2026-11-04T10:00:01Z",
  "status": "success"
}

A strict comparison reports changes.

But these particular differences may be expected.

Instead of ignoring every mismatch, explicitly select the fields you intend to compare.

function extractStableFields(response) {
  return {
    status: response.status
  };
}

const before = {
  requestId: "req-001",
  generatedAt: "2026-11-04T10:00:00Z",
  status: "success"
};

const after = {
  requestId: "req-002",
  generatedAt: "2026-11-04T10:00:01Z",
  status: "success"
};

console.log(
  deepEqual(
    extractStableFields(before),
    extractStableFields(after)
  )
);
// true

This is an example of selecting fields for comparison.

It doesn't mean request identifiers or timestamps should never be tested.

Those fields may have their own important validation rules.

The goal is to avoid mixing unrelated assertions into one comparison.

10. API comparison with Playwright

Suppose you're validating an endpoint using Playwright.

You want to check that its important fields match an expected response.

A test could look like this:

const { test, expect } = require("@playwright/test");

test("order response matches expected fields", async ({
  request
}) => {
  const response = await request.get(
    "/api/orders/ORD-1042"
  );

  expect(response.ok()).toBeTruthy();

  const actual = await response.json();

  expect(actual).toMatchObject({
    orderId: "ORD-1042",
    payment: {
      status: "completed",
      amount: 2499
    }
  });
});

This example assumes your Playwright configuration has the correct API base URL and authentication, and that the sample endpoint exists.

toMatchObject() checks the specified properties and permits additional object properties.

This is useful when you want to verify an API contract without requiring every unrelated response field to match.

For stricter comparisons, you can use toEqual() when the complete object should match the expected structure and values.

Choosing the right assertion

Use a partial match when:

  • Additional response properties are acceptable.
  • You only care about specified fields.
  • The API contract allows compatible extensions.

Use a strict equality assertion when:

  • The entire response structure matters.
  • Unexpected properties should fail the test.
  • You have a deterministic expected object.

Avoid creating overly broad assertions merely to make tests pass.

Tests should reflect the intended behavior of the application.

11. A useful regression-testing workflow

Here's a practical process for investigating changed API responses.

Step 1: Capture known test data

Use a controlled test environment and known inputs.

Step 2: Record the response before the change

Keep the original response for comparison.

Step 3: Deploy or enable the updated behavior

Make sure the environment and test data remain comparable.

Step 4: Capture the new response

Use the same request conditions where possible.

Step 5: Format and compare

A text diff provides a quick visual summary of changes.

Step 6: Separate expected from unexpected changes

Classify differences using the requirements and API contract.

Step 7: Add or update automated assertions

Convert important findings into repeatable checks.

Step 8: Record evidence

Keep relevant sanitized examples and test results.

This workflow is useful for backend releases, migration testing, integration testing, and investigating regressions.

12. Limitations of a browser-based text diff

A text-diff tool is useful, but it is not a complete API regression-testing system.

For example, it does not automatically determine:

  • Whether a field violates an API schema.
  • Whether a changed response is correct.
  • Whether two arrays are semantically equivalent.
  • Whether a change breaks downstream consumers.
  • Whether a difference is expected under particular business rules.

ToolZenHub's Text Diff / Compare is explicitly a line-based comparison tool.

It displays differences and can highlight changed words within similar adjacent lines.

It doesn't claim to perform structural JSON validation.

The tool also has stated input limits of 300,000 characters and 20,000 lines per side.

For very large datasets, automated comparison scripts or specialized diff tools may be a better choice.

The ToolZenHub tool runs its comparisons in the browser without uploading the compared text to the website.

Even so, only use data that you're authorized to handle in that environment.

13. Quick debugging checklist

When two API responses differ, ask:

  1. Are both responses valid JSON?
  2. Have both been formatted consistently?
  3. Is the difference caused only by whitespace?
  4. Have property order or array order changed?
  5. Are dynamic fields creating noise?
  6. Which values changed?
  7. Were those changes expected?
  8. Does the API contract still hold?
  9. Are downstream clients affected?
  10. Can automated tests catch similar problems next time?

Final thoughts

A passing HTTP status doesn't prove that an API response is unchanged.

And a detected difference doesn't automatically prove that something is broken.

Effective API regression testing requires both:

Visibility into what changed, and an understanding of what those changes mean.

Use text comparison to quickly identify differences.

Use structural validation and automated assertions to verify the actual contract.

When you're investigating two response samples and want a quick side-by-side comparison, you can try the Text Diff / Compare tool I maintain at ToolZenHub:

https://toolzenhub.in/tools/text-diff/

It can help remove repetitive manual inspection, particularly when you're comparing configuration files, test outputs, and API response samples.

The real goal is to spend less time searching for changed lines and more time understanding whether those changes matter.

References

  • Playwright assertions
  • MDN: JSON.stringify()
  • Git documentation: Diff format

Disclosure: I maintain ToolZenHub, the website referenced in this article. This tutorial was prepared using AI assistance and should be reviewed before publication.

title: S1CogBench: What System One Decision Models Can and Cannot Do on Cognitive Experiments
description:
arXiv:2611.00911v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Language models are no longer used only to generate text. Software also asks them for decisions, in routing, guardrails, and automated gates. System One decision models, also called typed decision models, such as Jev and Laya, return one fast decision over the legal options, leaving no text to inspect. However, a fast, well-formed decision does not show that the model used the evidence. Cognitive experiments can test this, because they vary task demands and measure how behavior changes, yet existing cognitive benchmarks evaluate language and multimodal models. We introduce S1CogBench to ask what these models can and cannot do on 24 cognitive tasks, evaluating five open models and Jev and keeping conditions and scoring apart from disclosed adaptations. We find that decision models vary widely in reliability, acting well does not imply predicting humans, aggregate scores hide how decisions respond to conditions, and speed comes mainly from answering without generation. To our knowledge, S1CogBench is the first benchmark of System One decision models on established cognitive experiments, and it gives a shared test of whether their decisions respond to evidence, feedback, memory load, and future opportunities before software relies on them.

title: Cuatro bugs en la API de 8004scan: cómo comprobé que sí los arreglaron
description:
Un issue cerrado no es un fix. El comentario de cierre lo escribe alguien que cree haberlo arreglado, y muchas veces lo arregló en el camino que probó, no en el que reportaste.

Entre el 14 de octubre y el 4 de noviembre reporté cuatro bugs en el tracker público de 8004scan. Los cuatro están cerrados. Esto es lo que encontré y cómo verifiqué cada uno.

1. El endpoint MCP no completaba el handshake

POST /api/v1/mcp devolvía 405 Method Not Allowed con allow: GET, HEAD. El cliente SSE abría con 200 y se quedaba en silencio: ni evento endpoint, ni ping, ni un byte en 25 segundos. En mainnet y en testnet.

Eso rompe cualquier cliente MCP: lo primero que manda es initialize, y va por POST.

La verificación es la misma petición que fallaba:

curl -i -X POST https://api.8004scan.io/api/v1/mcp \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2025-06-18","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"test","version":"1.0"}}}'

Responde 200 con serverInfo y las capacidades. Tardó 605 ms en mainnet y 546 ms en testnet.

2. El historial de entregas daba 500

GET /api/v1/webhooks/{id}/deliveries devolvía 500 con un JWT de dueño válido y un webhook activo. No había forma de saber si un evento se entregó, ni por qué falló.

Ahora responde 200 en los dos hosts, y el objeto trae lo que faltaba: event_type, status, attempts, last_attempt_at y response_status.

3. Borrar un webhook daba 500 y lo dejaba vivo

DELETE /api/v1/webhooks/{id} devolvía 500 DATABASE_ERROR y el webhook seguía con active: true. Solo se podían agregar, nunca quitar. Cuando cambia la URL que recibe, la vieja sigue recibiendo para siempre.

Ahora responde 200 con {"success":true,"message":"Webhook deleted"}. La lista pasó de dos webhooks a uno, y el historial del borrado da 404: se va con él.

El cuarto lo cerré yo

El issue de métricas de wallet lo cerré yo, no ellos. Era su pipeline, no un bug reproducible de mi lado. Vale decirlo, porque un tracker con issues abiertos que ya no aplican también es ruido.

Lo que me llevo

Repetir la petición exacta, no una parecida. Un 405 se comprueba con el mismo POST y el mismo header Accept. Un GET que ahora funciona no dice nada.

Probar los dos hosts. Los reportes eran de mainnet y testnet, y el arreglo podía haber llegado a uno solo.

Mirar los efectos, no solo el código de estado. Que el DELETE devuelva 200 no dice si borró. Hay que volver a listar. Y si el recurso tenía historial, hay que ver qué pasó con él.

Y una trampa que encontré de paso: si rotas el secreto de firma al registrar un webhook nuevo, el anterior queda firmado con el secreto viejo. Sigue activo, sigue recibiendo, y falla con 401 en cada entrega. Con un solo secreto compartido, dos webhooks activos no pueden convivir. Hay que borrar el viejo, no solo agregar el nuevo.

Los cuatro reportes están en alt-research/8004scan-issue-tracker.

title: Dunning Compliance Is a Code Review Problem
description:
Most dunning compliance advice is written for lawyers and read by nobody. Meanwhile the actual decisions — how many texts you may send, what the email must say, when consent was recorded and where that record lives — get made by whoever writes the retry job. If compliance lives in a PDF nobody opens, it does not live anywhere. It has to survive as checks in the codebase and fields in the schema.

Start with consent, because everything else hangs off it. For email, the rules are comparatively forgiving: a transactional notice about a failed payment to an existing customer sits on solid ground in most jurisdictions, provided it is actually about the payment and carries working identification and opt-out mechanics where the law requires them. SMS is stricter everywhere. In the US, marketing texts need express written consent; transactional texts still need a defensible consent record, a recognizable sender, and a functioning STOP path — and “the customer gave us a number at checkout” is a thinner record than most teams assume. Store the consent event like you store a payment event: timestamp, surface, exact language shown, and the number it applied to. If you cannot query it, you do not have it.

Second: frequency is a compliance surface, not just a UX one. Several regimes and carrier rules treat repeated automated messages as a category problem regardless of content. Cap your sequences in code, per channel, per customer, with the caps visible in one config file a reviewer can read. A dunning flow that can send nine touches because three separate jobs each think they own three is a bug with legal consequences.

Third: content constraints are checkable. No threats you cannot carry out (“your account will be deleted tonight” when it will not be), no invented deadlines, no fees described that the contract does not support, and in the EU and UK, consumer-protection rules on top of the privacy ones. Write these as lint rules for templates: banned phrases fail the build, required elements (business identity, a real reply path, the actual amount) are asserted present. Templates change often; the checks should run every time they do.

Fourth: data handling. Card-update links should be tokenized, single-purpose, and expiring; logs should never carry full card data (they should not carry it at all — that is what your processor’s vault is for); and retention needs a number, in days, that somebody chose on purpose. “Forever” is not a retention policy, it is an accident in progress.

None of this is exotic. It is the same discipline as idempotency keys and webhook signature checks — boring, testable, and much cheaper before the first regulator or carrier asks than after. If you want the whole thing as a pass/fail list you can work through with your own stack open beside it, a compliance checklist for dunning that a developer can actually implement covers consent records, channel rules, content constraints, and data handling in implementation order.

Finally, build the audit drill before anyone asks for it. Once a quarter, pull a random sample of twenty dunning sends across channels and reconstruct each one’s paperwork from the system’s own records: the consent event behind the number or address, the frequency cap in force at send time, the template version that produced the copy, and the suppression checks that ran. Time the exercise. If a single send takes an afternoon to document, the records exist on paper but not in practice, and that gap — not any individual rule — is the real compliance risk. The drill has a side benefit engineers appreciate: it is a standing test of the logging nobody otherwise exercises until an incident, and it turns “we keep good records” from an assertion into a measured retrieval time.

Treat the checklist like a test suite: run it when the flow changes, not when someone remembers. That habit — compliance as a maintained property of the system rather than a document about the system — is the core of Swipe Again’s recovery work, and it is available to any team willing to write the checks down.

title: "Done" isn't a test result. How your AI agent should hand off UI work
description:
Your AI agent finishes a change and reports back: "Done. The form is accessible, responsive and works on mobile."

Did anyone check? Often the agent wrote the code, looked at it, and described what it hoped was true as if it had been tested.

Design Decision Method's last step is there to stop that. Step 6, deliver and validate, asks the agent to hand over the work, the decisions behind it, and a short validation status that says what each result rests on.

What step 6 asks for

The method asks the agent to deliver three things:

  • the requested artifact (spec, mockup, prototype, or code)
  • the consequential decisions and assumptions
  • a short validation status

Before validating, the agent defines a few observable acceptance criteria matched to the purpose of the experience. Then it labels each result by its evidence level and says what it did not test.

Five evidence labels

Each label says what a result can support and what it can't:

Level Can support Cannot support
Proposed A target to aim for Any claim about the result
Heuristic review Likely problems, effort comparisons Task-completion rates
Automated check Specific rule failures Overall accessibility or usability
Manual test Behaviour of a flow, keyboard and focus Population-level outcomes
User research Real task outcomes for the sampled users Claims beyond the sample

Two rules come with it. Never fabricate a measurement. If something wasn't tested, the record says "not tested". And a mockup can show routes and states, but it cannot establish task-completion rates.

A worked example: a handoff note

Say you ask your agent to rebuild the sign-up form on example.com. It's one page with name, email and password, and a clear way to fix errors.

Without the method, the handoff is the sentence at the top of this post. With it, the agent's note might read:

Delivered: Sign-up form (code). One page, three fields.

Decisions: Errors show next to the field and in a summary at the top. Entered values are kept after an error. The placeholder for email is name@example.com.

Assumptions: No social sign-in was requested, so none was added.

Acceptance criteria and status:

  • Valid entries survive a validation error. Manual test: submitted with a bad password, and name and email were still filled in.
  • Each error is announced next to its field. Heuristic review of the markup only. Not tested with a screen reader.
  • Text and background contrast. Automated check: the contrast check found no failures on the colours used. This does not show the whole form is accessible.
  • People complete sign-up without help. Proposed. Not tested. No user research was done.

Not tested: screen reader pass, mobile keyboard behaviour, the server's error responses.

Every line says what it rests on. You can see that mobile keyboard behaviour is the next check, and that nobody has tried the form with real users.

Why this matters when you build with agents

An agent that sounds confident is easy to trust. The evidence labels give you a quick way to read the handoff. "Proposed" means it hasn't been checked. "Automated check" means one rule ran. "Manual test" means somebody actually walked through the flow.

The list of untested items also gives you the next prompt: ask for exactly those checks.

The method doesn't claim this saves time. That hasn't been measured. What it does give you is a handoff note that says where its checks stop.

Keep it proportional

Pick a few criteria that fit the design. The method warns against a fixed score or a universal time or click limit. A copy fix might need one line of status. A new checkout flow needs more. The design record template has a short "Validation status" section for this: the evidence levels reached, what was tested and what wasn't, and open questions.

Where this fits

Deliver and validate is step 6 of six: establish context, choose the visual system, map objects before layout, write a decision record, structure each view, then deliver and validate.

Try it

Design Decision Method is a lightweight design decision workflow for developers building interfaces with AI agents. It follows the open Agent Skills format and is MIT licensed. Install paths for Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI, and Codex are in the README.

  • Docs: https://frozonfreak.github.io/DesignDecesionMethod/
  • Repo: https://github.com/frozonfreak/DesignDecesionMethod
  • Evidence levels and record format: https://github.com/frozonfreak/DesignDecesionMethod/blob/main/references/acceptance-and-validation.md
  • Design record template: https://github.com/frozonfreak/DesignDecesionMethod/blob/main/assets/design-record-template.md

title: Inside the Vercel intern experience
description:
The best way to learn is by shipping product to users in production, and that's why we don’t treat our interns as temporary guests. Every intern at Vercel is expected to operate like a core part of our engineering team from day one.

This past winter, we welcomed a small cohort of those interns to our headquarters in San Francisco. Over an intense four months, they contributed to some of our most important products: the CDN, v0, financial infrastructure, AI Gateway, and more. They shipped features used by millions, helped close the gap for enterprise deals, and in more than a few cases, left a mark that will outlast their time here.

Meet the Winter '26 intern cohort

Yash Kothari, CDN Team

University of Waterloo

What Yash shipped:

Yash's internship spanned the full CDN stack, from infrastructure to CLI to UI in the dashboard.

His first major project was Project-level routing, which is part of the new CDN tab in the Vercel dashboard. This feature lets customers update routing rules, including redirects, rewrites, and header transforms, from the dashboard, API, CLI, or SDK, without needing to redeploy their project or touch a single line of code. Yash built the underlying API endpoints (including a staging/publish workflow), the vercel routes CLI commands, and contributed AI-powered route generation. Right after launch, hundreds of teams immediately adopted it and created thousands of rules.

"One of my favorite things about my internship was that at Vercel you get a lot of autonomy and ownership," Yash said. "I hopped on calls with enterprise customers, saw my work featured on Vercel's changelog, and demoed my work in a live YouTube community session."

In the second half of his internship, Yash worked on Vercel's Firewall and Security products. He shipped the vercel firewall CLI command, enabling users and AI agents to configure custom rules, IP blocks, and firewall controls directly from the terminal. He also built an AI-powered Firewall Rule Builder that lets users describe a desired rule in natural language and generates a WAF custom rule automatically.

Kavin Valli, v0 Team

University of Waterloo

What Kavin shipped:

Kavin worked across the full v0 platform over four months, taking on projects that ranged from user-facing features to cost efficiency for the system’s backend infrastructure.

He started by building Folders and v0 Projects end-to-end: core CRUD operations, a library page redesign, favoriting, visibility controls (private/team/public), and folder sharing. He also closed a critical gap in v0's version history by shipping the manual commit button, which ensured that manual edits in the VM editor properly created commits and blocks, which closed the loop between manual edits and v0's iteration model.

His highest-leverage work came later in the term, when he focused on VM and sandbox infrastructure. By splitting VMs into tiered pools and routing smaller projects to a cost-efficient default pool, Kavin significantly reduced memory usage and infrastructure cost for roughly 80% of sandboxes.

"I worked on v0 and got thrown into the deep end pretty quickly, especially around the v1 launch," remembered Kavin. "It was a bit chaotic at times, but that's something I actually enjoyed."

His final and most involved project was taking ownership of the v0 Slack agent. He shipped Slack preview deployments for safe testing, rebuilt the router agent with improved thread history and SAML re-auth resume, redesigned project context tracking, and built out the full PR flow including v0 labels, Slack thread links, and merged/closed state tracking. The result was an agent that went from rough around the edges to something teams can genuinely rely on.

Mingchung Xia, Financial Infrastructure Team

University of Waterloo

What Mingchung shipped:

Mingchung pushed over 250 PRs in four months and became one of the top contributors on Vercel's central control systems monorepo.

His most externally visible project was the v1/billing/charges API endpoint and the vercel usage CLI command, which let users view their usage and costs in the standardized FOCUS v1.3 FinOps format. Originally scoped as a full-internship project, Mingchung completed it early and expanded its scope into a joint launch with Vantage. The work was subsequently adopted by Meta, Notion, Porsche, and other prominent companies to analyze their Vercel spend in a modern, compliant format.

His most technically complex project was designing and building Vercel's core entitlements system, which is the infrastructure that enables granting, revoking, and provisioning entitlements across project-based monetization, add-ons, enterprise, and marketplace work streams. The system architecture incorporated strong and eventual consistency guarantees, async and synchronous derivations, transactional outboxing, write-ahead logs, plan change manifests, stale-validation sentinels, and materializations. It was rolled out to production and backfilled across all active subscriptions.

"Most companies don't give interns or even existing engineers the opportunity to touch payment systems or billing infrastructure, let alone own it end to end," explained Mingchung. "Correctness is imperative when you're working with money, and I got to experience that firsthand at Vercel."

He finished his internship by shipping Vercel Buy, a new billing service supporting frictionless purchasing for agent credits, gateway credits, v0 credits, and pro subscriptions, complete with a CLI surface.

Mingchung will be joining Vercel full-time on the Financial Infrastructure team after completing his degree.

Kevin Thomas, v0 Team

University of Waterloo

What Kevin shipped:

Kevin's work spanned ML infrastructure, enterprise features, reliability engineering, and incident response, often simultaneously.

His most ambitious self-directed project was v0's auto model routing system: a full pipeline that automatically routes user prompts to the right model tier based on complexity. Kevin proposed the system, built the labeling pipeline, experimented with multiple classifier architectures (embedding-based MLP classifiers, TF-IDF baselines, fine-tuned TinyBERT), and integrated everything into TypeScript-only functions for production deployment. By launch, the system had processed over 1.4 million v0 messages and became the default for all non-enterprise users, reducing decision fatigue and latency for a very large share of v0's user base.

"From working on on-call incidents and vulnerabilities in month one to working directly with enterprise customers in April, I've gotten to work on an unusually wide range of meaningful problems," Kevin said at the end of his internship.

In the latter half of his internship, Kevin focused on enterprise work, most notably the v0 × Snowflake integration. He built enterprise admin controls for model access, RBAC for team skill management, resolved issues in SAML and isolated tenant environments, and shipped the integration itself. This work directly unblocked enterprise customers, supported renewals, and addressed live customer issues.

Kevin also served as a primary investigator for several incidents around signup, billing, auth, and account access, staying at the center of v0's reliability work throughout his term.

Sylvie Zhang, AI Gateway Team

University of Pennsylvania

What Sylvie shipped:

Sylvie worked across the AI Gateway service, contributing to everything from database and backend logic to observability, the frontend, and documentation.

Her first project was Price Strikethrough, surfacing provider MSRP as a strikethrough price alongside Gateway pricing, making provider discounts visible to end users. It touched the full stack and gave her a complete view of the AI Gateway product from the start.

"All that sounded daunting to a student like me with little experience," Sylvie said, "but it was the best learning experience I could have asked for."

Her most impactful and technically demanding project was the AI SDK v5 → v6 endpoint migration for AI Gateway's OpenAI-compatible and Anthropic-compatible endpoints. As the AI provider landscape had grown significantly more complex since v5 was designed, maintaining the legacy version had become a bottleneck, especially for handling token usage granularity differences across providers. Sylvie led the migration with a disciplined approach: deep cross-provider knowledge to catch incorrect AI-generated assumptions, systematic multi-turn and cross-provider testing scripts, concurrency testing to surface race conditions, proactive customer communication, and a deliberate fallback strategy that left legacy code in place until the migration proved stable.

The result was a cleaner, more maintainable Gateway service better equipped to handle the continued evolution of AI providers and models.

Advice for future interns

We asked these interns to share their top advice for future cohorts.

Take ownership from day one

Vercel gives interns real autonomy, but that means it's on you to use it well. Don't wait to be assigned work. Take initiative, identify what needs to be done, and start shipping.

Ask questions

Every intern said the same thing: no one at Vercel makes you feel like a burden for asking. The team genuinely wants you to succeed, so use that to your advantage and ask.

Work in public

Share your PRs in team channels. Post updates. Present at Demo Days. The feedback loop is fast, and the visibility helps you iterate and build trust faster.

Talk to people outside your team

Some of the best conversations happen across team lines with engineers, designers, finance, and people in roles you've never considered. Go to the office. Grab lunch with someone new.

Give yourself time to ramp up

The codebase, the culture, and the pace can be a lot at once. Don't rush. The first few weeks are for absorbing, not sprinting. Take time to ramp well, and you will be able to run fast.

Apply to become a Vercel intern

There are additional internship opportunities coming soon. If you want to join our next cohort, check our career site in September to apply.

title: I Built SmartBase: A Free SQL-Powered Cloud Backend Platform for Developers
description:
Building SmartBase: Exploring a Simpler Approach to Cloud Database Management**

Modern application development requires more than just writing code. Developers also need reliable databases, storage systems, authentication and APIs to connect everything together.

For independent developers, students and small development teams, managing these backend components can become a significant challenge.

This is one of the technology problems I have been exploring through the development of SmartBase by Miyoni.

What is SmartBase?

SmartBase is a SQL-powered cloud database and backend platform designed to simplify how developers create, manage and connect databases to their applications.

Its central idea is straightforward: developers should be able to concentrate on building their applications without having to manage an entire database server infrastructure.

SmartBase brings several backend capabilities together in one platform.

  1. Cloud Database Management

SmartBase allows developers to create and manage cloud databases through its web interface.

Developers can:

  • Create databases.
  • Design and manage tables.
  • Execute SQL queries.
  • Organize application data.
  • Manage database structures.

The free plan provides up to 20 databases, 50 tables per database and a maximum of 500 tables in total.

  1. REST API Integration

A database becomes more useful when applications can communicate with it.

SmartBase provides REST API capabilities that allow developers to connect their applications to their cloud databases.

This makes it possible to build applications that retrieve, create, update and manage data through API requests.

For example, a developer building a student management application could connect the application to a SmartBase database to manage student records.

  1. Cloud Storage

Applications frequently need somewhere to store files, documents and other resources.

SmartBase also provides cloud storage capabilities, with 1 GB available on its free plan.

This gives developers another backend component within the same platform.

  1. Authentication

User authentication is another important part of modern application development.

SmartBase includes authentication functionality and Google sign-in integration, helping developers incorporate user access into their applications.

  1. Designed for Developers

One of the important ideas behind SmartBase is accessibility.

Whether someone is developing a personal project, experimenting with SQL, building a website or creating an application, having database and backend capabilities available through one platform can simplify the development process.

The goal is to make backend development more approachable without removing the flexibility developers need.

Why I Am Building SmartBase

Building a technology platform involves more than creating a website and adding features.

It requires thinking about reliability, security, usability, performance and the actual problems developers experience.

With SmartBase, the broader ambition is to create a useful cloud development platform that brings essential backend services together.

There is still room to improve, expand and learn from the developer community. Feedback from people who build real applications is particularly valuable.

Who Can Benefit From SmartBase?

SmartBase is designed for people such as:

  • Independent software developers.
  • Web application developers.
  • Android developers.
  • Computer science students.
  • Startup founders.
  • Developers experimenting with cloud technologies.

Explore SmartBase

If you are interested in exploring its capabilities, you can visit the official platform and documentation:

Official website: https://smartbase.de5.net/

Documentation: https://smartbase.de5.net/docs

The interesting question is not simply how many databases a platform can host, but how effectively it helps developers turn their ideas into working applications.

That is the direction behind SmartBase by Miyoni.

Disclosure: This article discusses a platform developed by Miyoni. Feature descriptions and free-plan limits should be checked against the current official documentation.

title: Diagnose slow LCP on phones: field-first, split into subparts, and prove user-visible impact
description:
When phones report slow LCP, the practical question is not “how do I speed up the site” but “which visible element are users waiting for, and which stage of its load path dominates?”

Implementation (overview)

  • Start with field data (CrUX, Search Console, or your RUM) to confirm the complaint on phones and to identify the affecting URL and likely LCP element. Field data answers whether real users see a problem; don’t skip it.
  • Reproduce the same phone-sized viewport and content state in a lab trace to gather navigation and resource timings that explain why the field signal exists.
  • Break LCP into four subparts: Time to First Byte (TTFB), resource discovery/load delay, resource download duration, and element render delay. Each subpart points at a different ownership domain (server, markup/priority, asset size/network, or client rendering).
  • Map the dominant subpart to the smallest useful fix: server or CDN work for TTFB; preload or earlier markup for discovery delay; file format/size or CDN for download duration; reduce render-blocking CSS/JS or avoid hidden-state logic for render delay.
  • Apply a single, targeted change and re-measure the same element on the same phone state. Compare subpart distributions, not just the headline LCP number.

Expected behavior

  • You’ll get a clear diagnosis explaining which part of the load path caused the visible delay on phones. A well-targeted change should shorten the dominant subpart in lab traces and, when broadly rolled out, align with field improvements for the tested page.
  • The article includes a small helper that computes the breakdown and returns a recommendation tied to the dominant subpart.

Limitations

  • This workflow is page- and content-shape specific. A fix for a hero-image landing page may not apply to a text-heavy page with the same LCP score but a different dominant subpart.
  • Lab traces explain causality but are sensitive to device, CPU contention, and network variability. Always anchor claims to field evidence when possible.

The server will insert a verified implementation example that computes the breakdown and chooses a recommendation for the dominant subpart.

Working example 

export function analyzeLCP({ navigationTiming, lcpEntry, resourceTiming } = {}) {
  if (!navigationTiming || typeof navigationTiming.responseStart !== 'number') {
    throw new TypeError('navigationTiming with numeric responseStart required');
  }
  if (typeof lcpEntry?.renderTime !== 'number') {
    throw new TypeError('lcpEntry with numeric renderTime required');
  }

  const navigationStart = typeof navigationTiming.navigationStart === 'number'
    ? navigationTiming.navigationStart
    : 0;

  const ttfb = Math.max(0, navigationTiming.responseStart - navigationStart);

  const hasResource = Boolean(
    resourceTiming &&
    typeof resourceTiming.startTime === 'number' &&
    typeof resourceTiming.responseEnd === 'number'
  );

  let resourceLoadDelay = 0;
  let resourceLoadDuration = 0;
  let elementRenderDelay = 0;

  if (hasResource) {
    resourceLoadDelay = Math.max(0, resourceTiming.startTime - navigationTiming.responseStart);
    resourceLoadDuration = Math.max(0, resourceTiming.responseEnd - resourceTiming.startTime);
    elementRenderDelay = Math.max(0, lcpEntry.renderTime - resourceTiming.responseEnd);
  } else {
    elementRenderDelay = Math.max(0, lcpEntry.renderTime - navigationTiming.responseStart);
  }

  const totalLcpMs = ttfb + resourceLoadDelay + resourceLoadDuration + elementRenderDelay;
  const parts = [
    { name: 'ttfb', ms: ttfb },
    { name: 'resourceLoadDelay', ms: resourceLoadDelay },
    { name: 'resourceLoadDuration', ms: resourceLoadDuration },
    { name: 'elementRenderDelay', ms: elementRenderDelay },
  ];

  // When two parts tie, prefer the part that better maps to a developer-actionable
  // front-end intervention. In practice we want elementRenderDelay to win ties
  // with ttfb so that zero-resource LCPs attribute dominance to rendering.
  const priority = {
    ttfb: 1,
    resourceLoadDelay: 2,
    resourceLoadDuration: 3,
    elementRenderDelay: 4,
  };

  const dominant = parts.reduce((a, b) => {
    if (a.ms > b.ms) return a;
    if (b.ms > a.ms) return b;
    // tie: choose higher priority
    return priority[a.name] >= priority[b.name] ? a : b;
  });

  const recommendations = {
    ttfb: 'Improve server TTFB: reduce backend work, cache HTML, or use a CDN.',
    resourceLoadDelay: 'Start loading the LCP resource earlier: improve discovery or preload it.',
    resourceLoadDuration: 'Reduce the resource size or use a more efficient format.',
    elementRenderDelay: 'Reduce render-blocking CSS/JS and avoid hiding the LCP element.',
  };

  return {
    totalLcpMs,
    breakdown: parts,
    dominantSubpart: dominant.name,
    recommendation: recommendations[dominant.name],
  };
}

Read the full article: https://chriseugenerodriguez.com/blog/diagnose-slow-lcp-on-phones

title: Dual-Axis Policy Entailment: A Benchmark for Policy-Change Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2611.00536v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Whether a policy shifts domains and, by extension, continues, broadens, narrows, or reverses previous policy is of paramount importance to the study of public policy. We propose Dual-Axis Policy Entailment (DAPE), which evaluates an ordered pair of policy directives on both dimensions at once: a binary judgment determines whether the two directives govern the same policy domain, and a five-way judgment determines whether the later directive continues, broadens, narrows, or reverses the earlier policy, or governs a different domain altogether. Read together, the two judgments form one five-category label, our primary metric. The two-axis design captures two central dimensions of policy change without conflating errors on either dimension into a generic "irrelevant" label, and it makes annotation more rigorous: a coder cannot dismiss a difficult pair as domain-irrelevant without an explicit, checkable decision. We introduce an expert-annotated benchmark of 1,000 ordered directive pairs drawn from a large corpus of Chinese government policy, together with an annotation-calibration protocol (an adjudication packet with pre/post agreement measurement) that we contribute as a methodological artifact. Fourteen open-weight models and four frontier API flagships fail the task zero-shot: even the best frontier flagship's chance-corrected agreement with expert labels is far below the human ceiling (Cohen's $\kappa \approx 0.29$ vs. $0.53$). A fine-tuned open-weight model (LoRA SFT of Qwen3-14B, five-fold cross-validation) closes this gap, reaching the coder-mutual human ceiling ($\kappa = 0.524$ vs. $0.527$). Finally, we apply our method to China's AI policy (1980-2024) and map the direction of policy change across eras.

title: Geoffrey Hinton: Maybe it would have been better if we had never developed artificial intelligence
description:
Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton has warned that humanity might have been better off never developing artificial intelligence, highlighting severe risks of societal division and corporate prioritization of profit over safety.

Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton, known as one of the fathers of artificial intelligence, has expressed new concerns. He said he fears that technology could create a huge gap between rich and poor and endanger society, leading it to disintegration.

The attitude of technology leaders

Referring to the heads of large companies, such as Mark Zuckerberg, Elon Musk and Sam Altman, Hinton argued that they know the risks but prefer the money. According to him, companies are rushing to evolve systems to stay ahead, ignoring the consequences.

Hinton likened a serious future crisis to the partial nuclear accident at Three Mile Island in 1979. In his assessment, it may take a similarly serious incident for companies to learn from their mistakes and take action.

There is still time for security.

Despite his fears, Hinton believes that humans are still in control and that there is still time to make a big effort to make the technology safe.

description:
Every deployment produces a set of files, including the pages, functions, and assets Vercel serves. Deployment Storage keeps those files available so you can inspect previous deployments and roll back when needed.

Instantly roll back to previous deployments in seconds

If a production deploy ships a bug or a change you want to reverse, rolling back restores the previous version in seconds. Open your project, click Instant Rollback on the Production Deployment tile, then choose an earlier production deployment. Vercel immediately repoints your domains to that deployment, with no rebuild required.

Deployment Storage pricing

  • Deployment Storage is billed at $0.10 per GB per month

  • Hobby teams include up to 10 GB

Existing teams continue with their current pricing, with no change to their bill at this time.
