title: Building RTL (Arabic) Interfaces: Layout, Type, Tone, and Testing for Saudi Users
description:
Saudi Arabia is one of the most exciting digital markets right now. Fintech, e-commerce, healthtech, logistics, and SaaS products are launching fast. But many of them still make the same mistake: they design in English, translate to Arabic, and hope it works.
If you do a simple translation for local Arabic users, it’ll never work. It can even break your site. Here's what Arabic-first really means, broken into four parts: layout, type, tone, and testing.

Why translation alone isn't enough

Saudi users are used to polished Arabic experiences. The banking apps, delivery apps, and government services they use every day are built properly for Arabic. When a new product shows up with an English layout and translated text, they notice right away.
We often get this type of issue from our clients at Wavespace. It’s that the bounce rate is high for their local users.
They usually won't say, "This has a UX problem." They'll just feel the product isn't made for them, and they'll leave.
So, all your site’s misaligned buttons, menus on the wrong side, send the same message: this company didn't take Arabic users seriously.
Arabic-first design fixes that by building the product around Arabic speakers from the first screen, not adding Arabic at the end. It's the approach a good UI/UX design agency in Riyadh takes from day one.

Part 1: Layout

Mirror the structure, don't just flip the screen

Right-to-left design means the whole reading flow moves from right to left. Navigation anchors on the right. Form labels sit on the right. Content hierarchy starts on the right.
But flipping every element blindly creates a mess. Good RTL design rebuilds the layout so it still feels balanced and the most important content stays easy to find.

Know what to mirror and what to leave alone

Should mirror:

Navigation and menus
Back and forward arrows, chevrons
Progress bars and step indicators
Carousels and swipe direction
Icons that point a direction

Should stay the same:

Logos and brand marks
Play, pause, and media controls
Checkmarks and most universal icons
Phone numbers, emails, codes, and URLs
Agree on this list early. It saves weeks of back-and-forth later.

Plan for mixed content

Saudi products are full of English inside Arabic: brand names, product codes, prices, and emails. If these aren't handled properly, sentences jump around and become hard to read. Your design and dev teams should decide how mixed text behaves before the first screen is built.

Keep it the same everywhere

A great Arabic mobile app doesn't help if the web dashboard or emails switch back to left-to-right. Users move between phone, laptop, and inbox. The experience should feel the same for everyone.

Part 2: Type

Use fonts built for Arabic UI

Not every Arabic font works on screens. Some look elegant in print but fall apart at small sizes. Popular UI choices include Cairo, Almarai, IBM Plex Sans Arabic, and Noto Sans Arabic. Pick one that pairs well with your Latin font, so both languages feel like the same brand.

Give Arabic room to breathe

Arabic letters have taller shapes above and below the line. Text that looks fine in English can feel cramped in Arabic. Increase line height, test real paragraphs, and leave space in buttons and labels.
This matters most in mobile app design, where small screens leave little room for error and most Saudi users meet your brand first.

Avoid English-only styles

No letter-spacing. Arabic letters connect. Spacing them out breaks words.
No uppercase tricks. Arabic has no capital letters, so styles that rely on caps don't carry over. Careful with italics. Fake slanted Arabic often looks broken.

Decide on numbers and currency

Arabic can use Western digits (123) or Eastern Arabic digits (١٢٣). Many Saudi products use Western digits in the interface, but it depends on your audience. Pick one rule and apply it to prices, dates, and stats everywhere. Saudi Arabia also introduced an official riyal symbol in 2025. Check that your fonts and design system support it before you use it in pricing.

Part 3: Tone

Rewrite, don't just translate

Word-for-word translation often sounds stiff or strange. Arabic communication tends to be more formal, and some English phrases simply don't carry the same meaning. You have to write all the headlines, buttons, error messages, and onboarding copy in Arabic.
And, you can take help from someone local who understands both the language and your product.

Choose your voice: formal or friendly

Modern Standard Arabic feels professional and works well for banking, government, and enterprise tools. A lighter, more conversational tone can work for consumer apps and younger audiences. Decide early, document it, and stay consistent.

Watch for gendered language

Arabic grammar is gendered. A button or message written only for one gender can feel off to half your users. Good Arabic UX writing finds neutral phrasing or adapts based on what users have shared.

Respect local context

Small details build trust:

Support both Hijri and Gregorian dates where users expect them.
Remember the Saudi work week runs Sunday to Thursday. Schedules, support hours, and delivery estimates should reflect that.
Use local sign-in and payment options your users already trust.
Make privacy and consent screens clear, especially with Saudi Arabia's Personal Data Protection Law (PDPL) now in force.

Part 4: Testing

Test with real Saudi users

Automated checkers and design reviews catch layout bugs. They don't catch the moments where a user in Riyadh or Jeddah feels confused, unsure, or put off by the tone.
Run short usability sessions with real Saudi users from your target audience. Five people per key segment usually surface the biggest problems.

Test both languages, not just one

Switch the full product to Arabic and walk through every core flow: sign-up, onboarding, checkout, payments, and support. Then do the same in English. Many bugs only show up when users switch languages mid-session.

Use real Arabic content

Placeholder text hides problems. So, when you use long names, real addresses, and actual product descriptions, it reveals broken layouts that lorem ipsum never will.

What this looks like in real projects

At Wavespace, we've worked with 550+ companies since 2019 and hold a 4.9 average rating across 250+ reviews on Clutch, Upwork, and Fiverr. Our Gulf work is Arabic-first from day one:

Cerebra: we designed and built a bilingual Arabic-English platform for a Saudi cybersecurity company serving banks, government, and enterprise teams. Keeping design and development in one team kept both languages aligned from the first screen.

Akshab: for a Saudi luxury oud and fragrance brand, we designed an e-commerce experience with premium storytelling, delivering 45% faster product discovery.
If you're planning a product for Saudi users, use the checklist below as a starting point before your first design review.

title: How I Saved Cloud Costs by Ditching Kubernetes for WebAssembly and Rust
description:
Hey Dev.to family! Let’s be real: defaulting to Kubernetes for every single microservice is starting to feel like massive architectural overkill. If your AI model server has to wait on heavy Linux containers to boot just to handle a quick inference task, you are probably burning cash on idle compute and killing user experience with slow cold starts. Today, let’s look at how I’m swapping out legacy container orchestration for WebAssembly (Wasm) and Rust to get microsecond starts at the absolute edge.

The era of defaulting to Kubernetes for every microservice is officially over. In 2026, orchestrating heavy Docker containers for high speed AI inference is a massive architectural bottleneck. Containers carry the baggage of an entire operating system, resulting in cold starts that destroy user experience. US cloud engineering teams at FAANG companies are actively deprecating legacy Kubernetes clusters in favor of WebAssembly (Wasm) and Rust.

If you are architecting cloud native backends for a Next.js application, pushing your logic into distributed Wasm modules is no longer optional. It is the baseline standard for performance, memory safety, and infrastructure cost reduction.

How do you deploy cloud native AI without Kubernetes?

Modern US tech stacks rely on the WebAssembly Component Model rather than Linux containers. A Wasm module contains only your compiled business logic, meaning it can achieve cold start times under 5 milliseconds. This is critical when deploying AI models to the edge.

Instead of routing traffic through a heavy Kubernetes ingress controller, modern cloud architects use Next.js Edge Middleware to intercept requests globally. The middleware authenticates the payload and instantly routes it to a serverless Rust Wasm function running on a distributed CDN node. This eliminates the need for complex pod scaling, node pools, and excessive AWS EC2 billing.

  • Microsecond Cold Starts: V8 isolates spin up Wasm modules instantly, allowing AI inference requests to execute without the typical container boot delay.
  • Absolute Sandboxing: WebAssembly executes in a deny by default sandbox. Unlike Docker containers which share the host kernel, Wasm modules cannot access the filesystem or network without explicit capability grants.
  • Infrastructure Reduction: Replacing idle K8s nodes with event driven Wasm functions drastically reduces cloud provider compute costs.

How do you write a serverless WebAssembly handler in Rust?

To replace a traditional Python or Node.js microservice, US engineering teams write serverless handlers in Rust. Rust guarantees memory safety and compiles flawlessly to the wasm32-wasi target.

Below is a production ready architectural concept using the Spin framework to handle an HTTP request, process a payload securely, and return a response without ever touching a Linux container.

use spin_sdk::http::{IntoResponse, Request, Response};
use spin_sdk::http_component;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct InferencePayload {
    data_vector: Vec<f32>,
}

#[derive(Serialize)]
struct InferenceResult {
    processed_value: f32,
    status: String,
}

// 2026 FAANG Standard: Serverless Wasm HTTP handler in Rust
#[http_component]
fn handle_ai_inference(req: Request) -> anyhow::Result<impl IntoResponse> {
    println!("Handling edge inference request via WebAssembly...");

    // Parse the incoming JSON payload safely
    let payload: InferencePayload = serde_json::from_slice(req.body())?;

    // Simulate high speed memory safe computation
    let mut sum = 0.0;
    for val in payload.data_vector.iter() {
        sum += val * 1.5;
    }

    let result = InferenceResult {
        processed_value: sum,
        status: "Success".to_string(),
    };

    // Return a strict JSON response directly from the edge node
    let response_body = serde_json::to_string(&result)?;

    Ok(Response::builder()
        .status(200)
        .header("content-type", "application/json")
        .body(response_body)
        .build())
}

This module compiles to a binary of less than 2 megabytes, deploys globally in seconds, and executes securely alongside your Next.js frontend.

How does WebAssembly impact US cloud engineering salaries?

Generalist DevOps engineers who only know how to write YAML files for Kubernetes are experiencing a severe market contraction. The 2026 US job market demands Cloud Systems Engineers who can write the actual memory safe logic that runs on the edge.

This architectural shift is exactly why intensive programs like Coding Macaw have redesigned their curriculum to focus entirely on Rust, Next.js, and WebAssembly rather than legacy container orchestration. Hiring managers are sourcing candidates with verified Course Report backgrounds who can prove they understand low level systems programming. If you can migrate a bloated AWS Kubernetes cluster to a hyper efficient Wasm edge network, you can easily command a total compensation package exceeding $350k.

FAQs:

1. Why are companies moving away from Kubernetes for edge computing?
Kubernetes relies on Docker containers which contain entire operating systems. This causes slow cold starts and high memory overhead, making it inefficient for global edge deployments and high speed AI inference compared to WebAssembly.

2. What makes WebAssembly better than Docker containers?
WebAssembly modules are incredibly lightweight, often under a few megabytes, and execute in microsecond cold starts using V8 isolates. They also provide superior security through strict, deny by default sandboxing.

3. Where can I learn to build WebAssembly cloud architectures?
You can master these specific systems engineering architectures through advanced curriculums like Coding Macaw, which specifically targets the intersection of Rust, Next.js, and Wasm for the modern US job market.

What do you all think?

Have you started experimenting with WebAssembly in your backends yet, or are you firmly Team Kubernetes? Have you tried moving any container workloads to edge modules? Let’s talk about it in the comments, and do not forget to follow for more US tech market insights!

title: $1 million hacker challenge for Vercel Sandbox
description:
Agents need to run untrusted code, and the microVM has become the standard way to do it: a dedicated guest kernel per workload, isolated from the host and from every other workload on the same machine.

But recent security research and real-world incidents have revealed that agents running untrusted code do not need to cross a VM boundary to escape containment; they only need one network path the security model failed to account for, which we explained in our post A sandbox without a network boundary is only half a sandbox.

Isolation only holds if both sides of it hold: the Firecracker microVM and the host-side network controls. Recently our CTO pointed an open-weight model with no safeguards at Vercel Sandbox. It did not escape, but it mapped the guest kernel, built a VM to reproduce its ideas, and wrote a fuzzer.

Defenders have first-mover advantage, but it won't last forever, and the choice is when to test the boundaries (we strongly encourage building a scanning program, which you can do on any budget with an open-source tool like deepsec and AI Gateway).

We are proactively choosing to test Vercel Sandbox on our own schedule, not an attacker's, and we are doing it in the open, with the best researchers in the world.

So for two weeks, we are paying up to $1,000,000 USD to the researchers who can escape a Vercel Sandbox.

The challenge

Starting today, Vercel is running a two-week public HackerOne program focused on Vercel Sandbox isolation.

  • Program: Public HackerOne program, open to all eligible researchers

  • Window: Tuesday, August 18 to Tuesday, September 1, 2026, or earlier if the reward pool is exhausted

  • Max per report: $50,000 USD, for a vulnerability that lets a threat actor read or modify another Vercel tenant's data

  • Total pool: Up to $1,000,000 USD in total payouts

Bounties are paid per report, scoped to a single root cause, and assigned by Vercel triage based on the maximum demonstrable impact. The full bounty table, detailed scope, and the list of known-duplicate classes are on the HackerOne program page.

How Vercel Sandbox is built

Vercel Sandbox runs on bare-metal EC2 hosts. Each sandbox gets its own Firecracker microVM with a dedicated guest kernel, and inside that microVM a Linux container runs the operator's code. The microVM, not the container, is the security boundary, so operator-supplied code runs two layers removed from the host. We assume that code is fully hostile: root inside the container, full kernel access inside the microVM, and motivated to reach the host or another tenant.

The network side of the boundary is enforced on the host, outside the microVM, where code inside the sandbox cannot modify or disable it. The sandbox firewall intercepts outbound TCP and DNS, checks each connection against the operator's domain and CIDR policies, and can inject credentials at the boundary so they never enter the microVM.

What we're looking for

In short: anything that breaks the sandbox boundary.

  • Compute boundary: Escaping the Firecracker microVM to the EC2 host, or reaching another tenant's sandbox through the compute layer (reading, modifying, or executing code in it), or crashing another tenant's sandbox from within another sandbox

  • Network boundary: Defeating the sandbox firewall without crossing the microVM: reaching destinations the operator did not authorize, exfiltrating data, or retrieving brokered credentials

Container namespace escapes that only reach the Firecracker guest OS are not in scope. Namespaces are a developer-experience feature, not the security boundary.

Bounties

Severity

Bounty

Critical

$25,000 – $50,000

High

$10,000 – $25,000

Medium

$5,000 – $10,000

Low

$1,000 – $5,000

The full bounty table, with example vulnerability classes for each tier, is on the HackerOne program page.

How to participate

The program is open now and closes on Tuesday, September 1, 2026, or earlier if the $1,000,000 USD reward pool is exhausted. Reports go through the HackerOne program page.

To reproduce a finding, boot a sandbox with the @vercel/sandbox SDK and demonstrate the impact with a live proof of concept. The default sandbox OS is enough for most reports; bring a custom image from the Vercel Container Registry only if your PoC needs extra tooling. We will not reward static-analysis-only findings; to issue a payout, we need to see the boundary break.

Full rules, eligibility, the complete scope and bounty table, and the submission process are on the HackerOne program page.

Results and payouts

We will triage reports from the day the program opens through one month after it closes. As findings are confirmed, we will pay bounties, ship fixes, and credit every researcher whose report holds up. The techniques discovered during this program will become permanent additions to the sandbox boundary, protecting every workload on Vercel long after the challenge ends. After the program closes, we will publish a follow-up writeup of the techniques and the fixes we shipped.

Thanks to HackerOne for standing up the program, and to the researchers who will spend the next two weeks trying to break what we built.

title: React: useEffect()
description:
1. What is useEffect?
useEffect() is used to perform side effects in a React component.

A side effect is an operation that happens outside the normal rendering process.

Examples:

  • Fetching API data
  • Setting a timer
  • Adding an event listener
  • Updating the browser tab title
  • Subscribing to an event

Basic syntax

useEffect(() => {
    // Your code
}, [dependencies]);

There are two important parts:
() => {} -Effect function
[] -Dependency array

Let's learn what the dependency array does.

2. Three types of useEffect

Type 1: Run only once — []

useEffect(() => {
    console.log("Component Mounted");
}, []);

Output:

Component Mounted
  • Runs after the component initially mounts.
  • Does not run again on ordinary re-renders.
  • Useful for fetching API data on mount.

Type 2: Run when state changes — [count]

useEffect(() => {
    console.log("Count changed:", count);
}, [count]);

Output when count increases from 0 to 3:

Count changed: 0
Count changed: 1
Count changed: 2
Count changed: 3
  • Runs after initial mount.
  • Runs again whenever count changes.

Type 3: Run on every render — no dependency array

useEffect(() => {
    console.log("Rendered");
});

Output:

Rendered
Rendered
Rendered
Rendered

It runs after every render.

3. Complete React example
This example demonstrates useState + useEffect.

import { useState, useEffect } from "react";

function App() {
    const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

    useEffect(() => {
        console.log("Count changed:", count);
    }, [count]);

    return (
        <div>
            <h1>Count: {count}</h1>

            <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>
                Increment
            </button>
        </div>
    );
}

export default App;

title: How Vercel Agent accesses production safely
description:
An agent working on production systems needs permission to act. A request like “fix this deployment” doesn’t tell you upfront which actions it will take or what access it will need. Grant agents broad access and a mistake can affect unrelated resources. Ask for approval at every step and the user has to approve individual actions before they know how the agent intends to solve the problem. Repeated prompts can turn that review into a habit of clicking approve.

Vercel Agent starts by investigating the problem, then proposes a plan showing what it would do and what access it would need. Approving that plan grants the additional permissions to carry it out, so the user can review the proposed fix before authorizing any changes.

The plan determines the permissions

For a broken production deployment, Vercel Agent might inspect recent deployments and build logs, then compare the failed deployment with the last known-good one. Read-only access lets that investigation run automatically. If it leads to a proposed redeploy, Vercel Agent requests the additional access in a plan the user can review and approve in one decision.

Access is defined by scopes, the named capabilities recognized by the Vercel authorization system. Any plan requesting access beyond the read-only baseline waits for approval as a whole, including any read-only tasks it contains. In this example, the investigation runs under a separate read-only plan before Vercel Agent proposes the redeploy:

Plan

Work

Requested scope

Investigate the failure

Inspect recent deployments and build logs, then compare the failed deployment with the last successful one

read:deployment

Redeploy the last known-good build

Create a deployment

read-write:deployment

A short read-only lookup can run without a plan. For longer investigations, Vercel Agent creates a read-only plan so the user can follow its tasks and progress while it runs automatically.

The plan connects what the user wants done to what Vercel Agent is allowed to do:

  • Intent: The outcome the user asks for.

  • Work: The tasks Vercel Agent proposes to achieve it.

  • Access: The scopes those tasks require.

  • Enforcement: The credentials and API checks that enforce access limits.

Each stored plan records its tasks and progress, with requested scopes attached to each task. The task descriptions explain why access is needed, and the scopes are combined across the plan.

The read-only baseline currently includes every registered scope beginning with read:. Plans need approval when they request access beyond that baseline or include supported external actions, such as opening a GitHub pull request. Read-only operations can still expose sensitive information, so automatic approval does not mean the work is harmless.

Vercel Agent can only use permissions the user already has

Vercel Agent runs as a Vercel App, which the user authorizes to act on their behalf within a team. That authorization is limited by the user’s existing permissions, so approving a plan cannot grant access the user does not have.

The Vercel OAuth service exchanges that authorization for shorter-lived tokens with specific scopes. These scopes define which capabilities the token permits, such as reading deployments or changing project settings. Vercel APIs check the token on each request to enforce those limits.

A user may authorize Vercel Agent for a team with dozens of projects. A redeploy plan requests deployment write access. Editing environment variables, changing domains, and managing team membership each require their own permissions.

Deployment write access is broader than a single redeploy. Naming deployment X in a plan does not, by itself, restrict the token to that deployment. The runtime, the software that coordinates Vercel Agent’s execution, checks that the plan is active before selecting its approved credential. Vercel APIs check each request against that credential’s permissions.

Approval determines which permissions Vercel Agent can use

When a user approves a plan that needs additional Vercel access, its requested scopes are checked again and a token is prepared containing the read-only baseline plus the approved permissions. The runtime, the software that coordinates Vercel Agent’s execution, checks that the plan is active before selecting its approved credential. That credential remains subject to its scopes, team, the user’s permissions, and expiry.

The credential used depends on the work:

Work

Credential

Read-only investigation

A baseline token with read-only scopes

Approved Vercel changes

A token with baseline scopes plus the approved additional scopes

External actions

Credentials and permissions specific to that provider

The model’s instructions tell it when to propose a plan and request approval. If it attempts an operation outside the token’s permissions, Vercel APIs reject the request, even if the model considers the action necessary to complete the task.

A single plan can include Vercel changes and a GitHub pull request. The user reviews both in one plan, while each provider uses separate permissions and credentials. GitHub pull-request access is tied to an owner and repository, so approval to open a pull request in acme/storefront applies to that repository even if the user also has access to acme/payments. Opening a pull request there requires its own approval.

Plans and tokens use the same permission definitions

A proposed plan can request a permission that has been renamed or removed. We initially maintained a separate permission list for Vercel Agent, which could fall out of sync with the OAuth service that issues its tokens. We moved to the same scope definitions so those mismatches could be caught during planning.

At session setup, Vercel Agent loads those definitions from the Vercel scope registry into an in-memory catalog. Fetching the registry requires authorization for the team, while the scope definitions themselves are shared across teams. The catalog supplies the definitions used at three stages:

  • Plan validation: Requested scopes are normalized, and unknown or malformed names are rejected before the plan is stored or presented for approval.

  • Approval: The requested scopes determine whether the plan fits within the read-only baseline or needs additional access.

  • Token preparation: Valid scopes define the credentials for approved work.

For example, a task to update firewall rules might request an outdated scope. The system rejects the proposed plan and returns valid scopes so Vercel Agent can correct it before requesting approval. This catches the mismatch during planning and requires an explicit correction instead of a fallback to broader access.

Fetching the registry adds latency and a service dependency, so Vercel Agent caches the catalog and uses that copy to check stored plans when they are loaded. Those checks reflect the cached definitions until the catalog is refreshed with changes from the registry.

Resuming work requires an active, approved plan

Vercel Agent may receive approval after the original chat request has ended, or lose its connection before carrying out an approved redeploy. The stored plan includes its state, who approved it, and when, alongside its tasks and requested permissions. That record connects the proposed work to the access the user authorized and allows the approval to be checked when work resumes.

Before resuming, the runtime reloads the plan and checks that it is active before selecting a credential with its approved permissions. A stopped plan fails that check, even if its token has time remaining before expiry.

If approval and a request to stop arrive together, the plan can move from waiting for approval to active only if the stop has not already changed its status. The runtime then checks again that the plan is active before using the approved credential.

If the investigation reveals that the current plan needs replacing, Vercel Agent can propose another. A replacement requesting elevated access needs its own approval, giving the user a chance to review the revised work and permissions together.

Where permissions need more precision

As Vercel Agent reached more of the platform, we had to correct access rules for actions that involve multiple resources or have different consequences. Attaching a domain can require both domain and project permissions, while staging a firewall rule and publishing it need different levels of access. Scopes need to capture these distinctions while keeping each plan’s access request manageable.

Matching those scopes to a proposed fix requires care throughout planning:

  • Choosing scopes: Vercel Agent chooses scopes with incomplete information, so it can request too little access and leave a task blocked, or too much and grant more authority than the work needs. Task-level guidance helps it choose, while validation catches invalid scope names. Even a valid scope can grant broader access than necessary.

  • Describing the work: “Redeploy the last successful build” gives the user a concrete action to assess, while scope names alone leave them to work out the consequences. The plan needs to explain the intended change and make clear which limits the token actually enforces.

  • Understanding denials: A denied operation could indicate a missing scope, an incorrect resource, or an operation that should remain blocked. Vercel Agent needs to distinguish those cases before requesting additional permissions.

Even with the right permissions, a redeploy requires judgment about whether the selected commit is safe to ship. That depends on the application, the failure, and the proposed fix. The user needs enough information to assess the choice, and Vercel Agent still has to execute it correctly.

Read-only investigation also needs controls for the information it retrieves, including sensitive project configuration and operational details. We chose a read-only baseline so Vercel Agent can investigate before asking for approval, and that choice needs continued review as scopes and the information they expose change. Other systems may need a narrower baseline. Separate controls must govern how retrieved information is handled and where it can go.

Vercel Agent can make a wrong decision or encounter malicious instructions in content it reads, such as build logs. Scoped credentials limit which operations it can perform in either case, but permitted operations can still cause harm. Plans therefore work alongside sandbox isolation, network policy, secret handling, rate limits, audit logs, and service authorization. Our work on security boundaries in agentic architectures explains the separation between an agent, its credentials, and the code it executes.

From investigation to approved action

Authority stays attached to the work that required it. The runtime selects the approved credential for an active plan, and its scopes define the operations Vercel Agent can perform. With the investigation already done, the user can assess a proposed fix and its requested access together.

Try Vercel Agent to investigate an issue in your project. Review what it finds and, if it proposes a change, assess the plan and requested access before approving it.

title: I Replaced Docker Desktop on Windows (It’s Faster, and It Doesn’t Need WSL)
description:
Here's a confession: I don't use WSL.

I don't open an Ubuntu shell. I don't run Linux tools on Windows.
The only reason WSL was on my laptop was Docker.

And yet it was the heaviest thing on my machine.

I'd stop every container. docker ps was empty.
vmmem was still sitting on 2 GB of my RAM.

I'd delete 5 GB of images to make room.
My disk got none of it back.

Bind-mounted projects were slow.
And Docker Desktop had a steady supply of small bugs:
the kind you fix by restarting it, then restarting it again.

None of it was a bug I could report and wait out.
Docker Desktop runs on WSL 2, and WSL 2 is a whole
general-purpose Linux VM. I was paying for all of it
to use one thing.

So I asked a dumb question:
what if the VM only had to run Docker?

The problem

If you run Linux containers on Windows, you know the drill:

  • vmmem keeps a gigabyte or two long after your containers stop
  • you delete images and the VHDX never shrinks
  • a project bind-mounted from C:\ is slow
  • at a company with 250+ people, Docker Desktop needs a paid plan

I didn't want a better Docker Desktop.
I wanted something smaller.

What I built

hyperbutler: a Docker engine for Windows 11. No WSL.

It boots a tiny Linux VM directly through the Windows
Host Compute Service (the same API WSL 2 uses underneath),
runs dockerd inside it, and gives you the normal Docker API
on a named pipe.

hyperbutler start
docker run --rm hello-world
docker compose up -d
hyperbutler stop

You keep the stock docker CLI and Compose. That's the whole point.

Same laptop, both with default settings:

hyperbutler Docker Desktop (WSL 2)
Start until a container runs 2.5 s 5.6 s
Bind mount from C:\: read 2000 small files 0.4 s 3.4 s
Idle memory, VM running ~320 MiB 1.7–2.7 GB
Disk after deleting ~5 GB of images 1.5 GiB, given back 6.8 GiB, kept
Installed size 179 MB ~6.7 GB
Needs WSL no yes

One machine, one build of each. Not a general result.
The full method and raw CSVs are in the repo.

How it works

Three pieces, and each gets only the privilege its job needs:

 docker CLI / Compose
        |  named pipe
        v
 hyperbutler engine         <- runs as you, no admin
   Docker API relay, network, file sharing
        |                          |
        | start / stop             | Hyper-V sockets
        v                          |
 hyperbutler broker         <- tiny Windows service,
   the only part that talks to HCS |  the only privileged piece
        |                          |
        v                          v
 Linux VM on Hyper-V (no WSL)
   dockerd + containerd
   read-only, hash-pinned system disk
   data disk that gives freed space back
  • The engine is a normal process running as you. It relays the Docker API into the VM, runs the VM's network in user mode (no virtual switch, no vEthernet adapter), and serves your C:\ folders to containers.
  • The VM is a minimal Alpine userland that boots in about a second. Its system disk is read-only and checked by hash. Its data disk hands deleted blocks back to Windows, which is why the disk row above says 1.5 GiB, not 6.8.
  • The broker is the only part with privileges. More on that below, because it's the part I worried about most.

Written in Go, end to end: the engine, the broker and the agent inside the VM.

The 2 MiB holes

The memory number didn't come for free.

My first version had the same problem as everyone else:
after a workload, the VM wouldn't give memory back.
Not all of it. Just a little more every run.

Linux said the memory was free.
Windows said the VM was still using it.
Both were right.

The Hyper-V balloon driver only reports free memory back
to the host in 2 MiB chunks. After a workload, about
70 MiB was free in smaller pieces. Free to Linux.
Invisible to Windows. Growing with every run.

Think of a parking lot where the attendant only counts
a space as free if ten in a row are empty. Scatter a few
empty spaces around, and the lot looks full forever.

One kernel parameter fixed it:

page_reporting.page_reporting_order=0

After that, the VM went back to idle after every fill
(+84 MiB down to about 0).

If you've ever wondered why vmmem never quite comes
back down, this is one of the reasons.

The phone call that was 20x faster

The second surprise was the network.

All container traffic crosses one Hyper-V socket between
Windows and the VM. Downloads into a container topped out
at 2.7 Gbit/s, and the profiler said everything was idle.

It turns out Windows sends slowly on a Hyper-V socket it
accepted: about 1 ms per ~600 KB.
On one it dialed: about 50 µs.

Same socket type. Same data. Different caller.
I couldn't find this documented anywhere.

So I flipped it: the VM listens, Windows dials.
Plus segmentation offload. 2.7 → 10.2 Gbit/s.

The part I'm most careful about

Windows only lets administrators touch HCS.
The easy fix is "add yourself to Hyper-V Administrators."

I didn't want that. That group has unrestricted control
over Hyper-V, and every program you run inherits it.

So the installer adds one tiny Windows service instead.
It's the only privileged piece, and it was designed
backwards from the bugs that broke similar tools before:

  • no paths, no command lines, no JSON: seven typed requests
  • it learns who you are from the pipe, not from the message
  • it only boots an image whose hash is compiled into it
  • when your connection closes, your VM dies with it

Files, ports and the Docker API never run there.
They stay in your own unprivileged process.

Where it stands, honestly

  • Preview. v0.1.0-preview.2 is out. v0.1.0 stable waits on a 24-hour soak.
  • Windows 11 only, x64. Home, Pro, Enterprise.
  • Unsigned for now. SmartScreen will complain. Check the SHA256SUMS.
  • Linux containers + CLI + Compose. That's it. No Kubernetes, no Windows containers.
  • Side by side is fine. Docker Desktop can stay installed.

Try it

Download the MSI from
Releases, then:

hyperbutler start
docker run --rm hello-world

If something breaks, hyperbutler doctor tells you what
your PC is missing.

GitHub: https://github.com/Higangssh/hyperbutler

What I need most is machines that aren't mine.

Genuine question: what's the most RAM you've caught
vmmem holding with nothing running? I'd love to compare.

title: Validate Telegram Mini App Raw initData in Express to Stop Front-End Identity Spoofing in React
description:
Imagine you are building an order checkout system inside a Telegram Mini App using React. When a user opens your application inside their mobile client, Telegram injects an embedded WebView context exposing the global window.Telegram.WebApp object. React developers often jump straight into building UI components by pulling user profile details directly from window.Telegram.WebApp.initDataUnsafe.user.

If you send this initDataUnsafe user ID directly to your API to look up accounts, process orders, or issue rewards, your application is completely vulnerable to identity spoofing. Because Mini Apps are standard web applications running inside an embedded browser frame, anyone can open your Mini App's URL in a standard desktop browser, open Developer Tools, and mutate window.Telegram.WebApp.initDataUnsafe to contain any target user ID. An attacker can easily impersonate administrators or drain balances belonging to other users.

To secure your React Mini App, you must ignore initDataUnsafe for authorization and treat the raw window.Telegram.WebApp.initData query string as an unverified credential. In this walkthrough, we will cover how to structure your React application lifecycle, perform server-side HMAC-SHA256 validation in Express, and safely control Telegram's native MainButton without exposing unauthorized actions.

Decoding the WebApp Context and Front-End Initialization

When integrating Telegram with React, developers often struggle between using the official script tag or installing third-party wrapper packages like @twa-dev/sdk. While wrapper packages offer TypeScript interfaces, third-party libraries frequently fall behind official Telegram Bot API feature releases. The most reliable approach is referencing the official script in your index.html file while declaring type definitions for window.Telegram.WebApp in your codebase.

Add the official Telegram WebApp script inside your public HTML entry point:

<!-- index.html -->
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8" />
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0" />
    <title>Mini App</title>
    <script src="https://telegram.org/js/telegram-web-app.js"></script>
  </head>
  <body>
    <div id="root"></div>
  </body>
</html>

Telegram provides two distinct properties on window.Telegram.WebApp:

  1. initDataUnsafe: An unverified JavaScript object parsed directly by the client browser. It contains fields like user, auth_date, query_id, and hash. Because this object exists in mutable client memory, it provides zero security.
  2. initData: A raw, URL-encoded string of parameters sent by Telegram's launch context. It contains key-value pairs representing the exact payload before client-side parsing.

An example initData raw string looks like this:

query_id=AAG...&user=%7B%22id%22%3A987654321%2C%22first_name%22%3A%22Alice%22%7D&auth_date=1710000000&hash=a1b2c3d4...

The hash inside this string is an HMAC-SHA256 signature calculated by Telegram using a secret key derived from your Telegram Bot Token. The front-end cannot alter any value inside initData without breaking the hash. Your React application must pass this raw string to your API server inside an HTTP header (such as Authorization: Bearer <initData>) on every initial load.

// src/services/api.ts
export async function verifyAndFetchUserSession(rawInitData: string) {
  const response = await fetch('/api/auth/verify', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: {
      'Content-Type': 'application/json',
      'Authorization': `TelegramInitData ${rawInitData}`
    }
  });

  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error('Authentication failed: Invalid Telegram signature');
  }

  return response.json();
}

Implementing Server-Side HMAC SHA-256 Validation in Express

To verify that the payload originated from Telegram and was not altered by a proxy or client console script, your backend must perform the cryptographic verification procedure specified in the Telegram Bot API documentation.

The algorithm requires these steps:

  1. Parse the raw URL-encoded initData string into key-value pairs.
  2. Extract and remove the hash key from the key-value pairs.
  3. Sort all remaining key-value pairs alphabetically by their keys.
  4. Format the sorted key-value pairs into a newline-separated string in the format key=value\nkey=value. Telegram designates this string as the data_check_string.
  5. Compute a secret key by taking the HMAC-SHA256 hash of your Bot Token string, using the constant string "WebAppData" as the HMAC key.
  6. Compute the HMAC-SHA256 hash of the data_check_string using the generated secret key.
  7. Compare the resulting hex digest against the client's hash parameter using a constant-time string comparison function to prevent timing attacks.
  8. Verify the auth_date parameter to reject stale initialization strings. If auth_date is older than your expiration threshold (e.g., 86,400 seconds or 24 hours), reject the request to prevent replay attacks.

Here is a complete Express authentication middleware implementing raw string verification using Node.js's built-in crypto module:

// server/middleware/verifyTelegram.js
const crypto = require('crypto');

function validateTelegramInitData(req, res, next) {
  const authHeader = req.headers['authorization'];
  if (!authHeader || !authHeader.startsWith('TelegramInitData ')) {
    return res.status(401).json({ error: 'Missing or malformed Authorization header' });
  }

  const rawInitData = authHeader.substring('TelegramInitData '.length);
  const urlParams = new URLSearchParams(rawInitData);
  const receivedHash = urlParams.get('hash');

  if (!receivedHash) {
    return res.status(400).json({ error: 'Missing hash parameter in initData' });
  }

  // Remove hash parameter before sorting
  urlParams.delete('hash');

  // Sort keys alphabetically and format into data_check_string
  const paramsArray = Array.from(urlParams.entries());
  paramsArray.sort(([aKey], [bKey]) => aKey.localeCompare(bKey));
  const dataCheckString = paramsArray.map(([key, value]) => `${key}=${value}`).join('\n');

  const botToken = process.env.BOT_TOKEN;
  if (!botToken) {
    throw new Error('BOT_TOKEN environment variable is not defined');
  }

  // Compute HMAC secret key derived from Bot Token using constant seed "WebAppData"
  const secretKey = crypto
    .createHmac('sha256', 'WebAppData')
    .update(botToken)
    .digest();

  // Compute HMAC hash of data_check_string
  const calculatedHash = crypto
    .createHmac('sha256', secretKey)
    .update(dataCheckString)
    .digest('hex');

  // Perform constant-time equality check
  const hashBuffer = Buffer.from(receivedHash, 'utf-8');
  const calculatedBuffer = Buffer.from(calculatedHash, 'utf-8');

  if (hashBuffer.length !== calculatedBuffer.length || !crypto.timingSafeEqual(hashBuffer, calculatedBuffer)) {
    return res.status(403).json({ error: 'Invalid cryptographic signature' });
  }

  // Check auth_date for replay attack prevention (max age: 24 hours)
  const authDate = parseInt(urlParams.get('auth_date') || '0', 10);
  const currentTime = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000);
  const maxAge = 86400;

  if (!authDate || (currentTime - authDate) > maxAge) {
    return res.status(403).json({ error: 'InitData payload has expired' });
  }

  // Parse verified user payload and attach to request
  const userJson = urlParams.get('user');
  req.telegramUser = userJson ? JSON.parse(userJson) : null;

  return next();
}

module.exports = { validateTelegramInitData };

Safe React Lifecycle and MainButton Integration

Telegram's native MainButton renders inside the mobile client container outside your React DOM tree. Because MainButton is controlled imperatively via global WebApp methods (window.Telegram.WebApp.MainButton), improperly managing its state inside React components leads to broken event handlers and double-click actions.

Two critical implementation mistakes often break React Mini Apps:

  1. Showing or enabling the MainButton before backend initialization finishes.
  2. Attaching MainButton.onClick event listeners without clearing them in React's useEffect cleanup return function, causing handlers to accumulate on every component re-render.

The proper architecture requires synchronizing backend authentication status with React state, initializing Telegram.WebApp.ready(), and safely handling MainButton click registration.

Here is a complete checkout component demonstrating safe backend authentication and MainButton binding:

// src/components/CheckoutApp.tsx
import React, { useEffect, useState, useCallback } from 'react';
import { verifyAndFetchUserSession } from '../services/api';

interface UserProfile {
  id: number;
  first_name: string;
  username?: string;
}

export const CheckoutApp: React.FC = () => {
  const [user, setUser] = useState<UserProfile | null>(null);
  const [isLoading, setIsLoading] = useState<boolean>(true);
  const [error, setError] = useState<string | null>(null);
  const [orderProcessed, setOrderProcessed] = useState<boolean>(false);

  const handleMainButtonClick = useCallback(async () => {
    const webApp = window.Telegram?.WebApp;
    if (!webApp) return;

    webApp.MainButton.showProgress(false);
    try {
      const response = await fetch('/api/orders/checkout', {
        method: 'POST',
        headers: {
          'Content-Type': 'application/json',
          'Authorization': `TelegramInitData ${webApp.initData}`
        },
        body: JSON.stringify({ itemSKU: 'PREMIUM_SUBSCRIPTION' })
      });

      if (!response.ok) throw new Error('Order creation failed');

      setOrderProcessed(true);
      webApp.MainButton.setText('ORDER COMPLETE');
      webApp.MainButton.disable();
    } catch (err) {
      webApp.showAlert('Failed to process order. Please try again.');
    } finally {
      webApp.MainButton.hideProgress();
    }
  }, []);

  useEffect(() => {
    const webApp = window.Telegram?.WebApp;
    if (!webApp) {
      setError('Telegram WebApp context not found');
      setIsLoading(false);
      return;
    }

    // Signal to Telegram container that interface is ready to render
    webApp.ready();
    webApp.expand();

    const rawInitData = webApp.initData;
    if (!rawInitData) {
      setError('No initialization data provided');
      setIsLoading(false);
      return;
    }

    // Validate raw initData against Express backend before unlocking UI
    verifyAndFetchUserSession(rawInitData)
      .then((data) => {
        setUser(data.user);
        setIsLoading(false);
      })
      .catch((err) => {
        setError(err.message);
        setIsLoading(false);
      });
  }, []);

  useEffect(() => {
    const webApp = window.Telegram?.WebApp;
    if (!webApp || isLoading || error || !user || orderProcessed) return;

    const mainButton = webApp.MainButton;
    mainButton.setText('CONFIRM AND PAY');
    mainButton.enable();
    mainButton.show();

    // Register click event handler
    mainButton.onClick(handleMainButtonClick);

    // Clean up event handler on component unmount or state update
    return () => {
      mainButton.offClick(handleMainButtonClick);
      mainButton.hide();
    };
  }, [isLoading, error, user, orderProcessed, handleMainButtonClick]);

  if (isLoading) {
    return <div style={{ padding: '20px', textAlign: 'center' }}>Authenticating with Telegram...</div>;
  }

  if (error) {
    return <div style={{ padding: '20px', color: 'red' }}>Error: {error}</div>;
  }

  return (
    <div style={{ padding: '16px', fontFamily: 'sans-serif' }}>
      <h2>Welcome, {user?.first_name}</h2>
      {orderProcessed ? (
        <p>Your order has been confirmed successfully!</p>
      ) : (
        <p>Item: Premium Subscription — Click the button below to purchase.</p>
      )}
    </div>
  );
};

Production Notes and Edge Cases

Deploying Telegram Mini Apps in production requires strict operational safeguards around WebApp execution:

  1. Never Bundle Bot Tokens: Never expose your BOT_TOKEN in React client-side environment variables (REACT_APP_BOT_TOKEN or VITE_BOT_TOKEN). HMAC generation must solely occur inside server memory.
  2. Handling Replay Protection Windows: Keep your auth_date validation window strictly bounded. A standard expiration limit of 86,400 seconds (24 hours) protects against stale links being reused while allowing reasonable session lifetime for returning users.
  3. Managing Viewport Heights: Mobile web view containers vary between iOS and Android Telegram clients. Call Telegram.WebApp.expand() immediately upon component mounting to prevent unexpected vertical scrolling and clipping inside bottom navigation bars.
  4. Clean Up MainButton Callbacks: Neglecting to invoke MainButton.offClick(handler) inside React unmount hooks causes registered listeners to stack in client memory. If a user triggers a route transition inside React, subsequent button presses will invoke unmounted component callbacks simultaneously.

Building high-performance Telegram Mini Apps requires careful separation between client UI components and backend signature validation. If you are launching complex Mini Apps, high-volume payment flows, or custom client integrations, consider working with BotCreator — a specialized development studio that ships production-ready Telegram bots and Mini App platforms.

title: Service-worker interviews punish unconditional skipWaiting and wipe-all caches — you need a waiting + compatibility card
description:
TL;DR: When a PWA ship leaves users with ChunkLoadError (deployed worker update + asset consistency—not SSR hydration, WS reconnect, optimistic fold, a11y, bug-bash, or teammate PR), the round scores update-policy ownership, not a lucky skipWaiting(). Durable habit: live-listen hashed assets / open-tab unsaved state / API dual-version tolerance → pin a speakable four-box card on a desktop live overlay (lifecycle wait · asset compatibility · adoption · rollback+observe) → own update policy and spoken verify matrix. Optional Application→Service Workers / ChunkLoadError shot only to anchor evidence. LIVE desktop overlay only when BYOE is allowed—ask the recruiter first.

Why a newly installed worker waits — and what unconditional skipWaiting breaks

A service-worker update interview is not a “force the new worker now” trivia quiz. Interviewers watch whether you keep waiting until it is safe to adopt, name which assets stay compatible, and prove rollback—while unconditional skipWaiting(), wipe-all-caches on activate, renaming the worker URL to force update, or testing only a fresh tab only “works” for one quiet ship.

Official guidance agrees. web.dev’s service worker lifecycle explains why a newly installed worker waits while old clients stay open, and warns that skipWaiting() is not a free refresh. Chrome Workbox — handling service worker updates centers a waiting prompt, messageSkipWaiting, and a controlling reload. PracHub (2026-09-15) covers the two-tab timeline, skipWaiting ≠ page reload, and cache retention. InterviewLane is secondary PWA/SW intro.

What still needs a person after “I’ll just skipWaiting() and delete every cache”?

  • Lifecycle wait — installed / waiting / activating / controlling; which clients still hold the old worker.
  • Asset compatibility — content-hashed chunks; which previous assets stay fetchable while old tabs live.
  • Adoption — default wait · prompt · controlled skipWaiting · single controllerchange reload.
  • Rollback + observe — worker version, asset 404, ChunkLoadError, no-op worker, retain previous assets.

Unconditional skipWaiting while an old page holds unsaved state—or still expects hashed chunks you just wiped—is the process fail SW-update rounds punish.

Concrete beat: unconditional skipWaiting / wipe caches / rename URL / fresh-tab-only → process fail

Suppose the interviewer shares a PWA sandbox:

“After yesterday’s ship, users hit ChunkLoadError on long-lived tabs. Design a safe service-worker update. Show waiting, adoption, and rollback.”

Without an update-policy beat, openings score differently:

Opening move What it optimizes for How it silently fails the round
Unconditional skipWaiting + clients.claim Looks “always fresh” early Old tabs lose unsaved state; page may still expect deleted hashed chunks
Wipe every cache on activate / rename worker URL Feels decisive under pressure Breaks open-tab asset continuity; rename-to-force skips the waiting contract
Speak lifecycle wait → asset compatibility → adoption → rollback+observe Shows deployed-worker + asset ownership Matches web.dev / Workbox / PracHub

Why force-update openings score worse: a lucky fresh tab while another holds draft state, or a wipe that 404s hashed chunks the old controller still requests, ships a “knows skipWaiting, skips compatibility” signal. Paraphrasing product-truth anti-patterns only (not reprinting any encyclopedia body): unconditional skipWaiting, wipe-all-caches on activate, rename-worker-URL to force update, and fresh-tab-only tests break once long-lived tabs or dual-version APIs appear. Naming “content-hashed? Unsaved open tabs? API dual-version? Safe refresh prompt?” beats a force-update dump. Paste-ready teleprompter / pass-the-round-for-you products pull candidates off that path. Narrow X heat ~0/7d; do not invent virality.

OfferCC’s SW-update question (safely update a service worker, 2026-07-21 / updated 2026-09-01) is product-truth foil—not an encyclopedia to paste. The differential here is LIVE listen + four-box speakable card the candidate owns.

Four-box speakable SW-update card + ~20–30s speak-aloud

When policy allows a desktop live overlay, the useful surface is a four-box speakable SW-update card, not a paste-ready “always skipWaiting + wipe caches” dump.

Box One-line prompt Example after “ChunkLoadError on long-lived tabs after ship”
1. Lifecycle wait Who waits; which clients still control? “New worker installed and waiting; Tab A still controlled by v12; do not activate until safe.”
2. Asset compatibility What stays fetchable across versions? “Content-hashed chunks; keep previous asset set until old tabs close or reload; no wipe-all on activate.”
3. Adoption Wait, prompt, or controlled skipWaiting? “Default wait; prompt ‘Refresh to update’; on accept → controlled skipWaiting + one controllerchange reload.”
4. Rollback + observe How do you prove and reverse a bad ship? “Watch worker version, asset 404, ChunkLoadError; ship no-op worker; retain previous assets for rollback window.”

Leave off the card: a teleprompter essay the candidate never owns. Scope: deployed worker update + asset consistency—not Canva, mid-pad progressive, SQL grain, virtualized list, feature-flag, payment idempotency, offline-first sync, drag-drop a11y, image LCP, progressive-delivery, incident, or SD ledger.

Speak (~20–30s):

“Wait: v13 installed, waiting; open tabs still on v12. Compat: retain previous hashed chunks while old clients live; never wipe-all on activate. Adoption: default wait; prompt refresh; on accept, controlled skipWaiting + one controllerchange reload. Rollback+observe: monitor worker version, asset 404, ChunkLoadError; retain previous assets; no-op worker if needed. Verify: two-tab timeline, unsaved form survives wait, dual-version API, skip only after prompt.”

Ritual: hear hash / open-tab / unsaved / API-compat → pin → adoption → optional shot → speak rollback+observe

Use this when external / BYOE tools are in scope, or with voice and a notepad alone.

  1. Hear hash / open-tab / unsaved / API-compat (≈10–20s) — Live-listen: content-hashed? Long-lived tabs with unsaved state? API dual-version? Safe refresh prompt allowed?
  2. Pin the card (≈20–30s) — On the desktop live overlay, fill lifecycle wait · asset compatibility · adoption · rollback+observe—one speakable line each.
  3. Name asset compatibility, then adoption — What previous assets must stay fetchable; then default wait · prompt · controlled skipWaiting · single controllerchange reload.
  4. Optional Application→Service Workers / ChunkLoadError screenshot — Capture only when needed to anchor evidence. Skip when live-listen already names the boundary.
  5. Speak rollback + observe the candidate owns — Worker version; asset 404; ChunkLoadError; no-op worker; retain previous assets. Overlay = checklist, not teleprompter.

When screenshot helps vs live-listen alone: Prefer live-listen when clarifying questions already lock hashed assets, open tabs, unsaved state, API dual-version, or a safe refresh prompt. Prefer a bounded shot when evidence is visual—Application→Service Workers waiting worker, ChunkLoadError, or Network 404 on a hashed chunk. The shot anchors evidence; it does not replace the four boxes.

Closing: six contrasts, hard policy gate, OfferCC allow-list, checklist

Contrast vs JUST PASS’d SSR hydration (do not merge the essays): Hydration Soft scores mismatch class · evidence stage · repair hatch · verify matrix—SSR first-render contract. This piece is different: deployed worker update + asset consistency—lifecycle wait · asset compatibility · adoption · rollback+observe. Do not swap hydration evidence stages for waiting-worker + hashed-chunk ownership.

Contrast vs JUST PASS’d WS reconnect (do not merge the essays): WebSocket Soft scores connection · backoff + jitter · resume cursor · stop/UX—transport recovery. This piece is different: worker lifecycle waiting, open-tab asset continuity, and controlled adoption after a ship. Do not swap socket generation for SW update-policy ownership.

Contrast vs JUST PASS’d optimistic reconcile (do not merge the essays): Optimistic Soft scores confirmed · pending · conflict · reconcile—an asynchronous mutation fold. title: I found a bug in Tauri's universal macOS builds (and my CI lied to me)
description:
TL;DR 🧵 A Tauri app with two [[bin]] targets can't be bundled as a universal macOS app: only the main binary gets merged with lipo. And tauri-action will happily finish green after uploading nothing. Below: why it happens, workarounds for both, and the issue I filed.

I maintain StackerPulse, a small open-source desktop app built with Rust and Tauri v2. It ships for Windows, Linux and macOS from a single GitHub Actions workflow.

Getting the macOS release out took two surprises:

Symptom Cause Fix
🍎 #1 Failed to copy binary … does not exist universal build merges only the main binary make extra bins opt-in with required-features
✅ #2 CI is green, release has no installers tauri-action silently skips uploads without a release id pass tagName, verify the assets

🍎 Surprise 1: "file does not exist" in a universal build

The app crate has two binaries: the app itself and a small command-line scanner.

[[bin]]
name = "stacker-pulse"
path = "src/main.rs"

[[bin]]
name = "seedscan-cli"
path = "src/seedscan_cli.rs"

Windows and Linux bundled fine. The universal macOS build (--target universal-apple-darwin) compiled for both architectures and then died at bundling:

Built application at: .../target/universal-apple-darwin/release/stacker-pulse
failed to bundle project: Failed to copy binary from
".../target/universal-apple-darwin/release/seedscan-cli": does not exist

🔍 What's going on

I read the tauri-cli source (2.12.4). Two things don't line up:

  • 🧩 In crates/tauri-cli/src/interface/rust/desktop.rs, the universal branch of build() builds both architectures, then runs one lipo -create command, for the main binary only.
  • 📦 The bundler takes its list from get_binaries() in crates/tauri-cli/src/interface/rust.rs, which returns every [[bin]] whose required-features are enabled.

The extra binary is compiled for each architecture but never merged into target/universal-apple-darwin/release/, so the bundler goes looking for a file that was never created.

🛠️ Workaround

get_binaries() skips binaries whose required-features aren't enabled. Make the extra binary opt-in:

[[bin]]
name = "seedscan-cli"
path = "src/seedscan_cli.rs"
required-features = ["cli"]

[features]
cli = []

tauri build enables no features, so the app bundles cleanly on every OS. The CLI is built separately, once per architecture on macOS, and merged by hand:

cargo build --release --features cli --bin seedscan-cli --target aarch64-apple-darwin
cargo build --release --features cli --bin seedscan-cli --target x86_64-apple-darwin
lipo -create -output seedscan-cli \
  target/aarch64-apple-darwin/release/seedscan-cli \
  target/x86_64-apple-darwin/release/seedscan-cli

⚠️ Pass --features cli to cargo test and cargo clippy too, or the CLI's tests silently stop running. This workaround relies on tauri-cli respecting required-features, which is reliable since 2.11.3.

📮 Reported upstream

There was no existing report for this case: older issues are about externalBin sidecars, a different mechanism. So I filed tauri-apps/tauri#16460 with a minimal reproduction and a suggested fix: run lipo for every binary returned by get_binaries(), not just the main one.

At the time of writing, the issue is open and waiting for triage.

✅ Surprise 2: green CI, empty release

With bundling fixed, the release workflow finished green. The draft release had the CLI archives and checksums, and no installers at all. 🙃

The workflow creates a draft release first and passes its id to tauri-apps/tauri-action. My step that looked up the id returned an empty string. Given no release id and no tag name, tauri-action builds everything, logs this, and exits successfully:

No releaseId or tagName provided, skipping all uploads...

🛠️ Two fixes

1. Give tauri-action the tag as a fallback, so it can find the draft on its own, and make the id lookup fail loudly:

- uses: tauri-apps/tauri-action@<pinned-sha>
  with:
    releaseId: ${{ needs.create-release.outputs.release_id }}
    tagName: ${{ github.ref_name }}
    releaseDraft: true

2. Check the result, not the exit code:

- name: The installers really are on the draft
  shell: bash
  env:
    GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
  run: |
    case "$RUNNER_OS" in
      Windows) want='\.msi$' ;;
      macOS)   want='\.dmg$' ;;
      *)       want='\.AppImage$' ;;
    esac
    gh release view "$TAG" --json assets --jq '.assets[].name' > assets.txt
    grep -Eq "$want" assets.txt || { echo "::error::No installer was attached"; exit 1; }

The next run attached every installer, and a missing one now turns the build red instead of quietly shipping an empty release. 🎉

💡 Takeaways

  1. 📖 When a tool fails strangely, read its source. The answer to surprise 1 was in about ten lines of tauri-cli.
  2. 🟢 A green check means "the steps ran", not "the job is done". Add a step that verifies what you actually care about.
  3. 📮 Report it upstream, even with a workaround in hand. A minimal reproduction and a pointer to the code takes an hour and saves the next person a day.

The project, the workflow and the full changelog are on GitHub. If you've hit something similar with Tauri or tauri-action, I'd love to hear about it in the comments 👇
