title: I default to Next.js for a reason that has almost nothing to do with performance
description:
Framework choice is usually developer preference dressed up as strategy, and I say that as someone whose default has been Next.js for years. The reasons I would give another developer are not the reasons that matter to the person paying for the project, and the gap between those two lists is worth writing down, because the second list is the one that survives contact with a budget.

The problem it solves is a rendering problem, not a framework problem

A plain React application renders in the browser. The visitor downloads a JavaScript bundle, the bundle runs, and only then does content appear. Behind a login that is completely fine and often the right architecture. For anything that needs to be found, it is bad, because the first thing a crawler or a three-year-old phone receives is an empty document with a script tag in it.

The standard answer is to bolt server rendering onto React by hand. That is not a weekend. It is a genuine engineering project with its own maintenance bill, its own subtle hydration bugs and its own bus factor, and it competes for time with the actual product.

Next.js ships that as the default posture rather than as an achievement. Pages render on the server, the browser receives real HTML immediately, and JavaScript takes over only for the parts that genuinely need it. You get app-grade interactivity where you want it and document-grade indexability everywhere else, and you are not the one maintaining the seam between them.

The features that pay for themselves are the boring ones

Images are the largest thing on most pages, and they are handled properly without a plugin: modern formats, correct sizes per device, lazy loading below the fold, and reserved space so nothing jumps while loading. On a typical marketing site that single feature is worth more to a Core Web Vitals score than anything else on the optimisation list, and it arrives for free.

Alongside it, route-level code splitting so a visitor to the contact page does not download the checkout logic. Font subsetting so text renders without a flash. Metadata handled as data rather than as tags somebody remembers to update when a page gets duplicated.

None of that is exotic. Every one of those is something a competent team does by hand when there is time and skips when there is not, and there is never time in month four. The argument for the framework is not that it can do these things. It is that they are the path of least resistance rather than the path of most discipline.

SEO controls as code, which matters more now than it did

Per-page titles, canonical URLs, hreflang across multiple language deployments, structured data, sitemaps generated from real content, redirects when a slug changes. All of it is code, versioned alongside everything else, reviewable in the same place as the rest of the application. On a hosted platform, several of those are whatever the vendor decided to expose this year, and that list changes without asking you.

This got more consequential rather than less when answer engines started reading the same signals. Clean server-rendered HTML with correct schema is what a classic crawler needs and what a retrieval system needs, for the same underlying reason: both have to work out what the page says and decide whether to trust it. The technical work behind ranking and the technical work behind being cited are, at the level where you actually do them, the same work.

Being on the mainstream path is a hiring decision

Here is the part that is genuinely commercial, and that developers tend to skip because it feels unambitious.

Stack Overflow's 2025 developer survey puts Next.js at the top of the web frameworks and technologies section across respondent segments, at roughly 21 to 24 per cent, consistently ahead of Express and ASP.NET Core. That number is not a quality claim and I am not presenting it as one. It is a supply claim. It means the documentation is thorough, security patches are frequent, most problems have already been solved publicly by somebody else, and when the client eventually replaces me they will not struggle to find a person who recognises the conventions in the codebase.

A niche framework can be technically lovely and still hand the client a hiring problem three years after the people who chose it have moved on. I would rather build on something with a large maintained ecosystem than on the most elegant option with four contributors and a Discord.

Where I talk people out of it

If a marketing team needs to edit content daily without a developer in the loop, WordPress and its editor ecosystem is frequently the better answer, and saying so has never cost me a project I wanted.

If the site is a handful of static pages that will barely change, Next.js is more machinery than the job needs. Hand-written HTML or a static generator is cheaper to build, cheaper to host, and will still work untouched in five years.

If the hosting is locked to shared PHP with no Node runtime, that is a real constraint and not one to argue with from a slide.

And if an in-house team maintains everything and knows a different stack well, that settles it. Handing a team a framework nobody there can maintain is a worse outcome than a technically inferior stack they can. That failure is not loud. It shows up as a slow accumulation of things nobody wants to touch.

The lock-in question, which clients ask and developers dismiss

"Will we be tied to you if you build it in this?" is a reasonable question and it deserves a better answer than a reassuring noise.

The honest version has three parts. It is an open-source framework with a very large developer pool, so the supply argument above cuts in the client's favour rather than mine. The code is theirs. And it runs on any host with a Node runtime, which is most hosts — it does not require a specific platform-as-a-service, whatever the deployment tutorials imply by only ever demonstrating one.

That last part is worth saying out loud because the ecosystem's documentation creates a strong impression otherwise. This site runs on ordinary shared hosting with Node support. That is not a clever trick; it is the default capability, obscured by the fact that nobody writes tutorials about boring hosting.

Where genuine lock-in does creep in is one level up from the framework: platform-specific middleware behaviour, image optimisation that assumes a particular CDN, storage and auth SDKs that only exist on one vendor. Those are choices made inside the project rather than consequences of the framework, and they are worth being deliberate about at the start, when avoiding them is free.

The thing that actually goes wrong on these projects

Not performance. Not SEO. The bundle.

Server Components ship no JavaScript to the client, which is the entire mechanism behind the payload difference, and it is easy to lose without noticing. One "use client" at the wrong level of the tree pulls everything beneath it into the client bundle, and nothing in the development experience tells you that happened. The page still works. It is just heavier than it was last month, and then heavier again, and six months later somebody runs an audit and finds the marketing site shipping half a megabyte of JavaScript for three interactive elements.

The discipline is unglamorous and it is the whole game: push client boundaries as far down the tree as they will go, check what the build actually emitted rather than what you assumed, and treat a growing first-load figure as a bug rather than as weather.

A framework that makes the right thing the default still lets you opt out of it accidentally, and on a long-lived project that is where the performance goes.

The one question that decides it

Does the thing need to be both discoverable and interactive?

Product configurators, multilingual catalogues, portals, booking flows, anything with a real front end that also has to rank. That is where server rendering plus a real component model earns its cost, and where doing it by hand costs more than the framework does.

A brochure that needs to exist, load fast and be found does not need any of it, and I would rather say so than sell the harder build. The uncomfortable version of the framework argument is that a lot of sites are the second thing, which means the honest default for an agency is not one framework but a short list with a written rule for choosing between them.

Read the full version

This is the condensed version. The full article covers the WordPress comparison in more detail, what happens to portability and lock-in, the hosting requirements in practice, and where the line falls in package terms.

Why We Build with Next.js, and When We Don't

This copy is a snapshot from the day it was posted, and it will not be updated here. The original on our site is the version we keep current: when a study publishes new figures, a price changes or a tool is renamed, that is where the correction lands. If you want the up-to-date version, follow the link above.

Sources

The framework capabilities described above are documented in the Next.js documentation, and the rendering model underneath the App Router is the React team's own Server Components reference. The adoption figure is from the Stack Overflow 2025 Developer Survey, technology section. The metrics that the image handling, code splitting and font work are optimising for are defined on web.dev. Which projects it suits, and which it does not, is my own judgement.

If you have moved a content-editing team from WordPress onto a headless Next.js front end, I would like to know how the editing experience landed six months later, because that is the part I find hardest to predict in advance.

title: The timeout that ate the database pool: how Inngest lost every connection twice in one afternoon
description:
At 14:00 UTC on October 10, 2026, both of Inngest's database connection poolers lost every connection to the primary database. Not most of them. All of them. And then, at 15:30, it happened again.

Inngest runs background jobs for other companies. When you trigger a function there, a scheduler has to look up your account and your function before any work can start. Those lookups go through the database. With no usable connections, run scheduling stalled and queue processing stopped for most accounts.

The team restarted the poolers. That did not reliably fix it. They raised the pool size. That did not help either. The pool was not too small. It was being emptied faster than it could be refilled, by the very timeouts meant to protect it.

This is a story about a timeout doing exactly what it was told to do, in exactly the wrong place.

The pooler in the middle

First, the pieces, plainly.

A database connection is expensive to open. So most services do not open a fresh one for every request. They keep a pool of open connections and hand them out as needed.

A pooler sits between your service and the database. PgBouncer is one such pooler. Your service connects to PgBouncer, PgBouncer connects to the database, and PgBouncer decides which real database connection serves each query. It lets many application connections share a smaller number of database connections.

A database driver is the library your code uses to talk to the database. Inngest's report points to pgx, the Go driver for Postgres, and to how it interacts with PgBouncer. You do not need to know pgx to follow this story. You only need to know that the driver is the part that sends your query, waits for an answer, and gives up when a deadline passes.

A deadline, in Go, is usually a context with a timeout. You say: this lookup has 200 milliseconds, and if it is not done by then, stop waiting. That sounds safe. It usually is.

The loop that ate the pool

Here is the sequence Inngest describes, slowed down.

Several frequently used lookups had short deadlines. Under normal load, a lookup waits briefly in PgBouncer for a free database connection, gets one, runs, and returns. The deadline never fires.

But suppose the lookup is still waiting in PgBouncer when its deadline expires. The driver cancels the query and closes its connection to PgBouncer. That is the normal, polite thing to do when you have given up.

The problem is that PgBouncer had nothing running to cancel. The query had not started yet. It was still queued, waiting for a connection.

So PgBouncer later ran the abandoned query on a database connection anyway. Then, instead of returning that connection to the pool for reuse, it closed the connection entirely. One cancelled wait, one dead connection.

Now repeat that at scale. Each pooler opens new database connections one at a time. That is a slow refill. If cancellations are destroying connections faster than the pooler can open replacements, the pool drains toward zero. Thousands of clients queue behind the empty pool. Their deadlines expire too. More cancellations. More dead connections. The timeout meant to shed load becomes the thing that keeps the load going.

Inngest reproduced this behaviour in a test environment, so this is not a guess about what might have happened. It is the mechanism the report names.

Two details made October 10 worse. Both collapses started at the top and bottom of the hour, when cron scheduled work roughly triples the query rate. Cron work is work on a schedule, like a job that runs every hour on the hour, and a lot of it lands at once. At the same moments, a new set of lookups that had been rolled out to all accounts before the weekend began failing in large numbers, adding to the cancellations. A spike plus a fresh source of failures, feeding the same loop.

That is also why the obvious fixes failed. Restarting the poolers did not reliably recover them, because the loop restarted with them. Raising the pool size did not help, because opening connections, not the pool limit, was the bottleneck. If you can only refill one connection at a time, a bigger bucket does not help when the bucket has a hole in it.

What actually stopped it

The second collapse ended when Inngest moved all services to connection poolers run alongside the database by its database provider. Processing recovered between 16:10 and 16:25.

That move introduced a new problem, and it is worth naming because it shows how incident fixes trade one risk for another. The new route reached the database through network address translation gateways, and some connections through those gateways were silently dropped. Queries on a dropped connection hung for up to 16 minutes before failing, which intermittently stalled processing, most visibly for cron functions. Inngest moved the affected service back to the original poolers at 04:17 on October 11, and improved the gateways' routing on October 12.

The lasting fix for the pool collapse itself was different, and it is the part you can take home. Inngest changed the lookups involved so that a deadline now ends the caller's wait without cancelling the underlying query. The caller stops waiting. The query is allowed to finish, and its connection goes back to the pool instead of being destroyed. That removes the trigger for this collapse on those lookups. Inngest says it is reviewing the remaining database calls on the execution path and their timeouts, which is the honest version of this fix: it is not done everywhere yet.

The guard you can steal this week

The pattern below is a simplified illustration, not Inngest's code. It shows the split that matters: one deadline for how long the caller waits, and a separate life for the query itself.

The dangerous shape is one deadline doing two jobs:

ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 200*time.Millisecond)
defer cancel()

// If this is still waiting in the pooler when the deadline fires,
// the cancellation can destroy the very connection you were waiting for.
row := pool.QueryRow(ctx, "SELECT name FROM accounts WHERE id = $1", accountID)

The safer shape separates the two:

result := make(chan lookupResult, 1)

go func() {
    // queryCtx is deliberately not tied to the caller's deadline.
    // The query runs to completion and its connection returns to the pool.
    row := pool.QueryRow(queryCtx, "SELECT name FROM accounts WHERE id = $1", accountID)
    var name string
    err := row.Scan(&name)
    result <- lookupResult{name: name, err: err}
}()

select {
case r := <-result:
    return r.name, r.err
case <-time.After(200 * time.Millisecond):
    // The caller stops waiting. It does not cancel the query.
    return "", errors.New("lookup timed out")
}

Use this only where it is safe, which is the part people skip. This shape makes sense for a read-only lookup that can safely run to completion even after the caller has given up. It does not make sense as a blanket rule for writes, where a query finishing late could do something the caller already assumed had failed. Check that before you copy it.

Then add three checks around it, because code alone will not save you from the next spike:

  1. Separate your timeouts in your head before you separate them in code. Ask, for each database call: is this deadline for waiting in the queue, for running the query, or for both? If you cannot answer, you have found a candidate for this bug.
  2. Alert on pool health, not just on slow queries. A pool draining toward zero usable connections, and a rising count of cancelled waits, is the early signal. Slow queries alone will mislead you, because in this incident the queries were not slow. They never started.
  3. Load test at the spike, not at the average. Test with the top-of-hour burst, and with a newly deployed lookup failing at the same time. A pool that survives average load can still collapse in the first minute of a burst, and that minute is when everyone is watching.

The wider lesson from the same weekend

October 10 was the second incident in two days, and the first one explains why the second hurt so much. On October 9, from 21:05 to 21:49, one data center provider lost connectivity between its data center and Inngest's other data centers, plus outbound internet access. Inngest runs across three data centers, and function execution depends on all three. Accounts processed in the cut-off data center could not reach the primary database. Accounts elsewhere with run state stored there could not make progress. And accounts with no dependency on that data center were still delayed, because they shared an event-processing pipeline with the affected accounts, and failing work built a backlog there.

Inngest's structural answer is to consolidate onto a single data center that acts as a single cell, which removes this whole class of cross-data-center failure. That is a bigger bet than a timeout fix, and it is still under way. But the two incidents share one lesson: a dependency you treat as background, a shared pipeline or a pooler queue, can become the whole incident when it fails in a way your timeouts and retries were not designed for.

In both cases, the internal failures also counted against functions' configured retries, and a step that failed permanently on an internal error left its run stuck in a Running state instead of marking it failed, so failure handlers were not notified. Inngest has since changed that, so such runs are now marked failed. A stuck state that looks alive is its own kind of outage, quieter than a pool collapse and harder to notice.

So check your own code this week. Find one database lookup with a short deadline that goes through a pooler. Ask what happens if that deadline fires while the query is still waiting, not running. If the answer is "I am not sure", you have found your next test.

What is the shortest deadline in your codebase, and do you know whether it cancels a waiting query or just stops the wait?

title: Designing for Cognitive Accessibility & Neurodiversity
description:
• Make Content Understandable with Plain Language and Structure
  • Design Patterns That Reduce Cognitive Load and Increase Predictability
  • Progressive Disclosure That Respects Working Memory and Accessibility
  • Testing with Neurodiverse Users and Meaningful Success Metrics
  • Practical Application: Checklists, Protocols, and Code Patterns
  • Sources

Cognitive accessibility is product quality: when people with attention, memory, language, or learning differences can’t use your features, you lose customers, increase support volume, and build brittle software. Treating cognitive accessibility as an engineering and content discipline — not a one-off UX tweak — yields measurable reductions in errors and abandonment.

The product symptoms are familiar: high drop-off during multi-step tasks, support tickets for "I can't find X," low comprehension scores on content pages, and failed onboarding metrics on top of accessibility compliance gaps. These are not abstract UX problems — they represent real friction for people with ADHD, dyslexia, dementia, or other cognitive differences, and they map directly to the WCAG objectives around readable, predictable, and navigable content.

Make Content Understandable with Plain Language and Structure

Clear content is the fastest, highest-leverage accessibility win you can ship.

  • Use plain language as your baseline: short sentences, active voice, and one idea per sentence. The federal Plain Writing Act and government content teams codify this because it improves comprehension for broad audiences.
  • Structure for scanning: front-load headings, provide a one-sentence summary at the top, use bulleted steps for actions, and add a short tl;dr or checklist for long pages. WebAIM and other accessibility practitioners recommend these patterns to help readers with limited working memory or attention regulation.
  • Replace jargon with defined terms; expand acronyms on first use. Wherever you must keep technical language, provide a short definition or an optional “learn more” footnote that doesn’t interrupt the main path.

Practical copy example (before → after):

Before (dense, long) After (plain, scannable)
If the asynchronous provisioning process fails due to an improperly configured token, the operation may abort and require re-initiation. If provisioning fails because the token is invalid, the operation will stop. Fix the token and try again.
Complex transaction histories are stored in a paginated view under the Reports tab. See Transaction history → Reports. The list is paginated; use filters to narrow results.

Why this matters: Readable content reduces extraneous cognitive load (the processing your interface forces on people that does not help them reach their goal). Short, scannable content reduces time-to-decision and decreases support calls.

Design Patterns That Reduce Cognitive Load and Increase Predictability

Design choices are cognitive choices. Make them predictable and minimal.

  • Chunk information: group related controls and content so users can rely on short-term memory less. Use clear labels and consistent placement. This reduces the need to hold context in memory.
  • Minimize choices where possible — apply defaults and progressive defaults for advanced options. Hick’s law shows selection time grows with the number of choices; fewer visible options = faster decisions.
  • Make interactions consistent across the product: identical icons, labels, and flows build mental models so users learn once and reuse that model. WCAG explicitly calls out predictability and readable content as success criteria.
  • Avoid disruptive interactions: popovers, unexpected modals, and auto-playing visuals increase extraneous load — prefer inline, contextual feedback instead.

Table: patterns vs cognitive benefit

Pattern Cognitive problem it addresses Implementation note
Chunking (clear headings & shorter lists) Overwhelm / scanning difficulty Headings = navigation anchors; keep 3–5 items per list
Defaults & smart suggestions Decision paralysis Pre-fill or suggest values based on past data
Visible focus + large targets Motor & attention friction 44x44px targets, strong focus outlines, outline-offset for clarity
Inline validation with helpful error copy Memory + recovery Show exactly which field failed and why; don't only show an error code

A contrarian point: displaying every feature on the first screen can feel honest, but it usually weaponizes cognitive load. Instead, design a fast-path for the top 80% of goals and surface advanced controls when they become relevant.

Progressive Disclosure That Respects Working Memory and Accessibility

Progressive disclosure works when it respects discoverability and assistive tech.

  • Principle: show only what users need now; keep the rest discoverable and reachable. The W3C supplemental cognitive guidance recommends design patterns (including progressive disclosure) as a way to make content usable.
  • Use semantic HTML first: the native <details> / <summary> pair provides a keyboard and screen-reader-friendly disclosure pattern with minimal JavaScript. MDN documents the element behavior and keyboard affordances. details has built-in toggle semantics and emits a toggle event you can hook for analytics or lazy loading.

Example: native, accessible disclosure (preferred)

<details>
  <summary>Why your payment failed</summary>
  <p>Common reasons: expired card, insufficient funds, or a blocked merchant. Try these steps:</p>
  <ol>
    <li>Check your card expiry date.</li>
    <li>Contact your bank to confirm the transaction.</li>
  </ol>
</details>

When you need custom accordion behavior (visual design or grouping), prefer a pattern built from semantic controls (button), with explicit aria state and keyboard handling. Minimal accessible accordion pattern:

<!-- Accordion header -->
<button aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="panel-1" id="accordion-1">
  More details
</button>

<!-- Associated region -->
<div id="panel-1" role="region" aria-labelledby="accordion-1" hidden>
  <p>Details shown here.</p>
</div>

// Minimal toggle handler
document.querySelectorAll('button[aria-controls]').forEach(btn => {
  btn.addEventListener('click', () => {
    const region = document.getElementById(btn.getAttribute('aria-controls'));
    const expanded = btn.getAttribute('aria-expanded') === 'true';
    btn.setAttribute('aria-expanded', String(!expanded));
    if (!expanded) region.removeAttribute('hidden'); else region.setAttribute('hidden', '');
  });
});

Key rules for progressive disclosure:

  • Ensure keyboard users can reach and toggle every control (no hover-only reveals). Keyboard-first equals accessibility-first.
  • Make hidden content reachable in the accessibility tree (role="region" + aria-labelledby) and avoid removing content from DOM if it should be discovered by assistive tech.
  • Avoid hiding critical warnings or error states behind a disclosure. If something is required for task success, surface it.

Testing with Neurodiverse Users and Meaningful Success Metrics

Testing is the only reliable way to validate cognitive accessibility assumptions.

Recruitment and representation:

  • Recruit participants who identify across the neurodiversity spectrum (ADHD, autism, dyslexia, intellectual disabilities, age-related cognitive decline). Specialist recruiters (e.g., AbilityNet, Fable) or local advocacy organizations accelerate finding participants and advising on accommodations.
  • Compensate fairly and schedule sessions with flexibility, breaks, and the option for alternative communication formats. AbilityNet documentation covers practical planning and recruitment approaches for inclusive testing.

Study design and protocol:

  1. Define clear, goal-based tasks that match real-world use. Convert goals into scenarios, not abstract test steps.
  2. Use moderated sessions where you need qualitative insight or have accessibility-specific probes. Observe, record, and collect think-aloud notes, but avoid interrupting the user during task attempts.
  3. Combine metrics: task success rate, time-on-task, error rate, and subjective workload (NASA‑TLX). NASA‑TLX provides a validated measure of perceived mental workload across six dimensions and is widely used in HCI studies.

Quantitative and qualitative metrics that matter:

  • Task success (complete / partial / fail) — primary signal for functional accessibility.
  • Time-on-task (median + IQR) — watch for long tails where neurodiverse participants may need more time.
  • Error taxonomies (where they stalled and why).
  • NASA‑TLX or an abbreviated workload measure to quantify perceived cognitive effort.
  • Comprehension checks: 2–3 short questions after a content page to measure retention.
  • Support funnel changes: reduction in "how do I..." tickets after fixes.

Sample size guidance: iterative testing of 4–6 users per round uncovers major issues quickly; for accessibility and edge cases, run multiple rounds with different neurodiverse profiles. Jakob Nielsen’s discount-usability guidance remains useful for iterative discovery, but accessibility testing benefits from slightly broader representation across conditions than a single generic usability cohort.

Practical Application: Checklists, Protocols, and Code Patterns

Shipable, prioritized actions you can run in the next sprint.

Content clarity checklist (low friction)

  • Use a one-line summary at the top of every page. Bold the action word.
  • Keep sentences under 20 words where possible. Flesch-Kincaid grade 7–9 target for general audiences.
  • Headings: H1 for page purpose, H2 for top sections, H3 for step-level subheads. Each heading should be usable as a quick summary.
  • Replace “click here” links with descriptive anchors.

UI / interaction checklist

  • Keyboard: all interactive controls reachable and operable without tabindex hacks. (Remember: summary in <details> is inherently focusable.)
  • Focus visible and high contrast (2:1 visible offset).
  • Reduce simultaneity: avoid auto‑playing media; allow users to pause/stop.
  • Error messaging: show what happened, why, and the next actionable step.

Progressive disclosure patterns (three-tier)

  1. Summary (one line) — for scan & quick decisions (use <summary> or button).
  2. Inline expand — for contextual help and short details (use accessible accordion).
  3. Off-page deep dive — link to full documentation or printable guide when the user wants complete instructions.

Testing protocol (30–60 minute moderated session)

  1. Pre-study: consent, an intake form with accessibility preferences, and baseline context.
  2. Warm-up (5 min): an easy task to orient the participant.
  3. Core tasks (20–30 min): 3–5 goal-directed tasks that reflect realistic scenarios. Collect task success, time, and errors.
  4. Subjective measures: NASA‑TLX (short mode) + Single Ease Question (SEQ) for each task.
  5. Debrief (5–10 min): open-ended feedback, what confused them, and what helped.

Quick engineering fixes to prioritize (48–72 hours)

  • Add meaningful heading summaries and a short page TL;DR.
  • Replace ambiguous icons with labelled buttons.
  • Convert long blocks of text to bulleted steps.
  • Implement simple details/summary where extra explanation is optional.

Code pattern to include in your component library (accordion example shown earlier) — standardize aria-expanded, aria-controls, role="region", and keyboard handling. Add unit tests that assert aria-expanded toggles and that the region becomes visible and focusable.

Important: Put cognitive accessibility checks into your Definition of Done. Automated checks (axe, Lighthouse) catch many issues, but only real user testing with neurodiverse participants reveals the cognitive friction your metrics will miss.

Treat the practices above as instruments, not one-time fixes: measure, iterate, and prioritize by impact on task success and workload scores.

Sources

Cognitive Accessibility at W3C WAI - Definitions, WCAG connections (Readable, Predictable, Navigable), and the COGA task force guidance on design patterns and supplemental guidance.

PlainLanguage.gov - Federal plain language guidance and checklist for writing clear, usable content; practical rules that reduce misunderstanding.

WebAIM — Writing Clearly and Simply - Practical, web-oriented plain-language techniques focused on accessibility and cognitive readability.

MDN Web Docs —

element - Browser behavior, keyboard support, and examples for the native disclosure widget.

AbilityNet — A Step-by-Step Guide to User Testing - Practical guidance for recruiting, running, and reporting inclusive user tests with people with disabilities.

NASA Task Load Index (NASA‑TLX) - Overview of the validated subjective workload instrument used to quantify perceived cognitive workload.

Nielsen Norman Group — Why You Only Need to Test with 5 Users - Rationale for small, iterative usability studies and how to run efficient test cycles.

GOV.UK — Writing for GOV.UK (Content Design) - Strong, research-backed advice on front-loading content, scannability, and plain English practices used at scale.

Microsoft Accessibility — Inclusive Design resources - Inclusive design training, toolkits, and research that highlight cognition and mental-health considerations in product design.

title: Amazon ECS Gateway Arrives with Generated Hostnames and No Custom Domain Support
description:
AWS has released Amazon ECS Gateway, an account-level ingress resource letting platform teams define networking once and application teams opt services in with a connector. title: 库存与缺货监控：轮询商品详情 API 监测库存状态，及时补货或通知用户到货
description:
​
摘要：本文从工程实现角度拆解一个比价与返利平台的核心链路：如何用关键词搜索聚合同款商品、如何做商品归一化与同款判定、如何通过详情 API 拉取价格与优惠信息、如何计算返利并保证数据一致性。文中给出可运行的 Java 示例代码、接口设计、缓存与限流策略，以及上线后常见的坑与优化方向。

一、需求拆解：比价与返利平台到底要解决什么问题
用户的核心诉求只有一句话：同一个商品，在哪买最便宜、还能返多少。但落到工程上，这句话会被拆成一条很长的链路：

搜索聚合：用户输入关键词，平台需要同时向多个电商渠道（自营商城、第三方联盟、开放平台）发起搜索，把结果合并成一个列表。
同款归一：不同渠道对同一商品的标题、SKU、图片、规格描述都不一样，需要判定“这是不是同一个东西”。
详情补全：搜索结果通常只有标题和主图，价格、券后价、库存、促销规则需要再调详情 API 获取。
优惠计算：满减、优惠券、平台补贴、会员价叠加后，才是用户真正关心的到手价。
返利计算：按渠道佣金比例、平台抽成、用户等级计算预估返利，并明确“预估”与“结算”的差异。
结果展示：按到手价升序、返利降序或综合排序，给出清晰的对比表格。
下面这张图是整体链路，后续章节会逐段展开。

flowchart TD
A[用户输入关键词] --> B[搜索聚合服务]
B --> C1[渠道A 搜索API]
B --> C2[渠道B 搜索API]
B --> C3[渠道C 搜索API]
C1 --> D[结果合并与去重]
C2 --> D
C3 --> D
D --> E[同款归一 / 商品聚类]
E --> F[详情API批量补全]
F --> G[优惠与到手价计算]
G --> H[返利计算]
H --> I[排序与分页返回]
I --> J[前端比价列表]

二、整体架构设计
推荐把系统拆成四层，避免搜索、详情、计算逻辑互相耦合：

层次 职责 关键设计
接入层 接收关键词、分页、排序参数，做参数校验与鉴权 统一响应结构，错误码可枚举
聚合层 并发调用多渠道搜索，合并、去重、同款聚类 线程池隔离 + 超时降级，单渠道失败不影响整体
详情层 按商品 ID 批量拉取价格、优惠、库存 批量接口 + 本地缓存 + 异步刷新
计算层 到手价、返利、排序 纯函数计算，便于单测与规则调整
一个重要的原则是：搜索接口要快，详情接口要准。搜索阶段允许返回不完整数据（比如只有标题和主图），详情阶段再补齐；这样首屏响应时间可以控制在几百毫秒内。

三、关键词搜索聚合：并发、超时与降级
3.1 统一渠道适配接口
不同渠道的搜索 API 参数和返回结构差异很大，先抽象出统一接口，后续新增渠道只需要实现适配器。

public interface SearchProvider {
/** 渠道标识，如 taobao、jd、pdd /
String channel();
/* 按关键词搜索，返回统一结构的商品摘要 */
List<ItemBrief> search(SearchRequest request) throws ProviderException;
}
public class SearchRequest {
private String keyword;
private int page = 1;
private int pageSize = 20;
private String sort; // price_asc / sales_desc / default
private long timeoutMs = 800;
// getter / setter 省略
}
public class ItemBrief {
private String channel;
private String itemId; // 渠道内商品ID
private String title;
private String mainImage;
private BigDecimal price; // 展示价，可能不含优惠
private String shopName;
private String detailUrl;
// getter / setter 省略
}

3.2 并发聚合与超时控制
多渠道搜索必须并发执行，并且给每个渠道设置独立超时。任何一个渠道超时或报错，都只记录日志并跳过，不能拖垮整个请求。

@Service
public class SearchAggregator {
private final List<SearchProvider> providers;
private final ExecutorService pool;
public SearchAggregator(List<SearchProvider> providers) {
this.providers = providers;
// 每个渠道一个线程，避免相互阻塞
this.pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(
Math.max(providers.size(), 4),
r -> {
Thread t = new Thread(r, "search-pool");
t.setDaemon(true);
return t;
});
}
public List<ItemBrief> aggregate(SearchRequest request) {
List<Future<List<ItemBrief>>> futures = new ArrayList<>();
for (SearchProvider provider : providers) {
futures.add(pool.submit(() -> provider.search(request)));
}
List<ItemBrief> result = new ArrayList<>();
long deadline = System.currentTimeMillis() + request.getTimeoutMs();
for (int i = 0; i < futures.size(); i++) {
long remain = deadline - System.currentTimeMillis();
if (remain <= 0) {
break;
}
try {
result.addAll(futures.get(i).get(remain, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS));
} catch (TimeoutException e) {
futures.get(i).cancel(true);
log.warn("渠道 {} 搜索超时，已降级", providers.get(i).channel());
} catch (Exception e) {
log.warn("渠道 {} 搜索失败", providers.get(i).channel(), e);
}
}
return result;
}
}

3.3 结果合并与去重
合并阶段先做粗粒度去重：同一渠道内 itemId 相同直接去重；跨渠道则保留全部，交给下一步同款归一处理。

public List dedup(List items) {
Map map = new LinkedHashMap<>();
for (ItemBrief item : items) {
String key = item.getChannel() + ":" + item.getItemId();
map.putIfAbsent(key, item);
}
return new ArrayList<>(map.values());
}

四、同款商品归一：从标题到 SKU 的判定策略
同款判定是比价平台最难也最有价值的部分。纯靠标题字符串匹配误判率很高，建议采用“多信号加权 + 阈值”的方案。

4.1 可用的判定信号
品牌 + 型号：最可靠的信号，例如“iPhone 15 Pro 256G”。
标准化标题：去掉促销词（包邮、正品、秒杀、官方旗舰店）后做分词与相似度计算。
关键规格：容量、颜色、尺码、版本等，从标题或详情属性中抽取。
图片指纹：主图感知哈希（pHash）相似度，作为辅助信号。
条码 / GTIN：如果渠道返回了条码，直接作为强匹配依据。
4.2 加权打分实现
public class SameItemScorer {
private static final Set<String> NOISE_WORDS = Set.of(
"包邮", "正品", "秒杀", "官方", "旗舰店", "新品", "限时", "特价");
/** 返回 0~1 的相似度分数 /
public double score(ItemBrief a, ItemBrief b) {
double titleSim = titleSimilarity(normalize(a.getTitle()), normalize(b.getTitle()));
double brandSim = Objects.equals(extractBrand(a.getTitle()), extractBrand(b.getTitle())) ? 1.0 : 0.0;
double specSim = specSimilarity(a.getTitle(), b.getTitle());
// 权重可按业务数据回归调整
return 0.5 * titleSim + 0.3 * brandSim + 0.2 * specSim;
}
private String normalize(String title) {
if (title == null) {
return "";
}
String t = title.toLowerCase();
for (String noise : NOISE_WORDS) {
t = t.replace(noise, "");
}
return t.replaceAll("[\s\p{Punct}]+", "");
}
private double titleSimilarity(String a, String b) {
if (a.isEmpty() || b.isEmpty()) {
return 0;
}
// 简化示例：用 Jaccard 相似度，生产环境可换成分词 + 余弦相似度
Set<String> sa = new HashSet<>(Arrays.asList(a.split("")));
Set<String> sb = new HashSet<>(Arrays.asList(b.split("")));
Set<String> inter = new HashSet<>(sa);
inter.retainAll(sb);
Set<String> union = new HashSet<>(sa);
union.addAll(sb);
return union.isEmpty() ? 0 : (double) inter.size() / union.size();
}
private String extractBrand(String title) {
// 生产环境建议维护品牌词典或用 NER 模型
return title == null ? "" : title.split(" ")[0];
}
private double specSimilarity(String a, String b) {
// 抽取 256G / 8+128G / XL 等规格片段做比对
return Objects.equals(extractSpec(a), extractSpec(b)) ? 1.0 : 0.0;
}
private String extractSpec(String title) {
if (title == null) {
return "";
}
Matcher m = Pattern.compile("(\d+\s[gGtTmM][bB]?|\d++\d+[gG])").matcher(title);
return m.find() ? m.group() : "";
}
}

当分数超过阈值（例如 0.75）时归为同款，聚合成一个“商品组”，组内每个渠道的报价作为一条比价记录。

五、详情 API：批量拉取价格、优惠与库存
5.1 详情接口设计
详情接口一定要支持批量，否则 20 个商品就是 20 次 RPC，延迟不可接受。

public interface DetailProvider {
String channel();
/** 批量查询详情，单次建议不超过 20 个 */
Map<String, ItemDetail> batchDetail(List<String> itemIds) throws ProviderException;
}
public class ItemDetail {
private String channel;
private String itemId;
private BigDecimal price; // 当前售价
private BigDecimal originalPrice; // 划线价
private List coupons; // 可用优惠券
private List promotions;// 满减、限时折扣
private Integer stock;
private String skuInfo;
// getter / setter 省略
}

5.2 缓存策略
价格是高频变化数据，但也不是每次都要实时拉取。推荐分层缓存：

数据类型 缓存位置 TTL 说明
商品基础信息（标题、主图） Redis 24 小时 变化慢，可长缓存
价格与库存 Redis 60~120 秒 短缓存 + 异步刷新
优惠券信息 Redis 5 分钟 券有有效期，需校验时间
返利比例 本地缓存 + Redis 10 分钟 变更频率低
@Service
public class DetailService {
private final Map<String, DetailProvider> providerMap;
private final StringRedisTemplate redis;
private final ObjectMapper mapper = new ObjectMapper();
public ItemDetail getDetail(String channel, String itemId) {
String key = "detail:" + channel + ":" + itemId;
String cached = redis.opsForValue().get(key);
if (cached != null) {
try {
return mapper.readValue(cached, ItemDetail.class);
} catch (Exception ignored) {
// 反序列化失败则回源
}
}
DetailProvider provider = providerMap.get(channel);
if (provider == null) {
throw new IllegalArgumentException("未知渠道: " + channel);
}
Map<String, ItemDetail> map = provider.batchDetail(List.of(itemId));
ItemDetail detail = map.get(itemId);
if (detail != null) {
try {
redis.opsForValue().set(key, mapper.writeValueAsString(detail), Duration.ofSeconds(90));
} catch (Exception e) {
log.warn("详情缓存写入失败", e);
}
}
return detail;
}
}

六、到手价计算：优惠叠加的正确姿势
到手价不是简单的“售价减券”，要按渠道规则顺序计算，并且每一步都要校验可用性。

public class PriceCalculator {
/**

  • 计算到手价
  • 顺序：售价 -> 满减 -> 优惠券 -> 平台补贴 */ public BigDecimal finalPrice(ItemDetail detail) { BigDecimal price = detail.getPrice(); // 1. 满减：取满足门槛的最大优惠 BigDecimal bestFullReduce = BigDecimal.ZERO; for (Promotion p : detail.getPromotions()) { if ("FULL_REDUCE".equals(p.getType()) && price.compareTo(p.getThreshold()) >= 0 && p.getDiscount().compareTo(bestFullReduce) > 0) { bestFullReduce = p.getDiscount(); } } price = price.subtract(bestFullReduce); // 2. 优惠券：只取一张最优券 BigDecimal bestCoupon = BigDecimal.ZERO; for (Coupon c : detail.getCoupons()) { if (price.compareTo(c.getThreshold()) >= 0 && c.getAmount().compareTo(bestCoupon) > 0) { bestCoupon = c.getAmount(); } } price = price.subtract(bestCoupon); // 3. 兜底，不允许出现负数 return price.max(BigDecimal.ZERO).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP); } }

七、返利计算：预估与结算要分开
返利是平台的核心卖点，也是最容易产生客诉的地方。关键是把“预估返利”和“实际结算返利”明确区分。

public class RebateCalculator {
/** 渠道佣金比例，例如 0.05 表示 5% /
private final BigDecimal commissionRate;
/* 平台抽成比例 /
private final BigDecimal platformRate;
/* 用户等级加成，例如 1.0 / 1.2 /
private final BigDecimal userLevelFactor;
public RebateCalculator(BigDecimal commissionRate,
BigDecimal platformRate,
BigDecimal userLevelFactor) {
this.commissionRate = commissionRate;
this.platformRate = platformRate;
this.userLevelFactor = userLevelFactor;
}
/* 预估返利 = 实付金额 * 佣金比例 * (1 - 平台抽成) * 用户等级系数 */
public BigDecimal estimate(BigDecimal paidAmount) {
return paidAmount
.multiply(commissionRate)
.multiply(BigDecimal.ONE.subtract(platformRate))
.multiply(userLevelFactor)
.setScale(2, RoundingMode.DOWN);
}
}

展示时建议同时给出三个数字：到手价、预估返利、返利后实际成本，让用户一眼看懂。

渠道 售价 优惠 到手价 预估返利 返利后成本
渠道 A 2999.00 满 2000 减 200 2799.00 83.97 2715.03
渠道 B 2899.00 券 100 2799.00 55.98 2743.02
渠道 C 3050.00 无 3050.00 122.00 2928.00
八、接口设计与返回结构
对外提供一个聚合比价接口，内部完成搜索、归一、详情、计算全流程。

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/compare")
public class CompareController {
private final CompareService compareService;
public CompareController(CompareService compareService) {
this.compareService = compareService;
}
@GetMapping("/search")
public Result<PageResult<CompareGroup>> search(
@RequestParam String keyword,
@RequestParam(defaultValue = "1") int page,
@RequestParam(defaultValue = "20") int pageSize,
@RequestParam(defaultValue = "final_price_asc") String sort) {
if (keyword == null || keyword.trim().isEmpty()) {
return Result.fail("关键词不能为空");
}
return Result.ok(compareService.compare(keyword.trim(), page, pageSize, sort));
}
}

返回结构建议按“商品组”组织，组内是各渠道报价，前端可以直接渲染成对比卡片：

{
"code": 0,
"data": {
"total": 128,
"list": [
{
"groupId": "g_10086",
"title": "iPhone 15 Pro 256G 原色钛金属",
"mainImage": "https://cdn.example.com/1.jpg",
"offers": [
{
"channel": "A",
"shopName": "官方旗舰店",
"price": 2999.00,
"finalPrice": 2799.00,
"couponText": "满2000减200",
"rebate": 83.97,
"stock": 12,
"detailUrl": "https://example.com/item/1"
}
]
}
]
}
}

九、性能与稳定性优化
并行化：搜索与详情都走线程池，按渠道隔离，避免慢渠道拖垮全局。
批量接口：详情必须批量，单次 20 个以内，减少 RPC 次数。
多级缓存：本地缓存挡热点，Redis 挡中频，回源只处理冷数据。
限流熔断：对每个渠道单独限流，失败率超阈值自动熔断，恢复后逐步放量。
异步刷新：缓存过期时先返回旧值，后台异步刷新，避免缓存击穿。
降级兜底：详情拉取失败时，用搜索返回的展示价兜底，并标注“价格可能有变动”。
// 缓存击穿保护示例：只允许一个线程回源
public ItemDetail getWithLock(String channel, String itemId) {
String key = "detail:" + channel + ":" + itemId;
String lockKey = "lock:" + key;
Boolean locked = redis.opsForValue().setIfAbsent(lockKey, "1", Duration.ofSeconds(5));
if (Boolean.TRUE.equals(locked)) {
try {
return loadFromRemote(channel, itemId);
} finally {
redis.delete(lockKey);
}
}
// 未抢到锁，短暂等待后读缓存
sleepQuietly(50);
return getDetail(channel, itemId);
}

十、常见坑与经验总结
同款误判：标题相似不代表同款，尤其是配件和套装。务必引入规格与品牌信号，并保留人工纠错入口。
价格不一致：搜索价与详情价经常不同，展示时以详情价为准，并注明更新时间。
优惠券失效：券有库存和有效期，计算前必须校验，否则用户下单时价格对不上。
返利口径不清：预估返利要写清计算依据和结算周期，避免客诉。
渠道规则变更：把渠道规则做成配置，不要硬编码在代码里。
合规问题：只使用官方开放平台或授权联盟接口，遵守各渠道的数据使用协议。
整体来看，比价与返利平台的技术难点不在单个接口，而在于聚合链路的稳定性和同款判定的准确性。先把搜索聚合和详情补全做稳，再逐步优化同款算法和返利规则，是比较务实的落地路径。如有任何疑问，欢迎留言探讨！

title: How to Build an IT Asset Lifecycle Management System with Node.js and PostgreSQL
description:
Managing company equipment sounds simple until you have dozens of laptops, monitors, phones, and other devices moving between employees, departments, and locations.

A spreadsheet might tell you which laptop belongs to whom today. But can it tell you who previously held that laptop, when it went for repair, whether its warranty has expired, or why it was retired?

Those questions become important as an organization grows.

In this tutorial, we'll build the foundation of an IT asset lifecycle management system using Node.js, Express, and PostgreSQL. Rather than creating another basic CRUD application, we'll focus on asset states, controlled transitions, transaction safety, and historical records.

By the end, you'll understand how to structure a backend that keeps track of equipment throughout its lifecycle.

1. Understanding the IT Asset Lifecycle

An IT asset lifecycle describes the stages an asset passes through, from acquisition to final disposal.

A typical lifecycle looks like this:

Stage Description
Procurement Equipment is purchased or ordered
Registration Asset information is recorded
Available Equipment is ready for assignment
Assigned Equipment is issued to an employee
Maintenance Equipment is being inspected or repaired
Returned Equipment is received back and assessed
Retired Equipment is permanently removed from active use

There is an important distinction here: not every business event needs to become a permanent asset status.

For example, returned is often better modeled as an event. Once a laptop is returned and inspected, its current state might become available or maintenance.

This avoids building an unnecessarily complicated state machine.

For our implementation, we'll use four operational states:

  • available
  • assigned
  • maintenance
  • retired

We'll record procurement and registration details separately, while assignment, return, repair, and retirement actions will create historical events.

2. Choosing the Technology Stack

We'll use three main technologies:

Technology Responsibility
Node.js JavaScript runtime
Express HTTP API and routing
PostgreSQL Relational database and transaction management

PostgreSQL is particularly useful here because equipment records have relationships, constraints, and consistency requirements.

Consider a laptop assignment. We need to update its current holder and record the assignment event. Either both operations should succeed or neither should be committed.

That's where database transactions become essential.

Project Setup

Create a project:

mkdir asset-lifecycle-api
cd asset-lifecycle-api

npm init -y

npm install express pg dotenv

Enable ES modules in package.json:

{
  "type": "module",
  "scripts": {
    "start": "node server.js"
  },
  "dependencies": {
    "dotenv": "^17.0.0",
    "express": "^5.0.0",
    "pg": "^8.0.0"
  }
}

The version ranges above are illustrative; use currently maintained compatible releases and commit your generated lockfile.

Create a .env file:

DATABASE_URL=postgresql://postgres:password@localhost:5432/asset_db
PORT=3000

Replace the example credentials with your local database credentials. Never commit .env files or real secrets to source control.

Create the database:

CREATE DATABASE asset_db;

We'll run our schema against that database next.

3. Designing the PostgreSQL Database

A common mistake in asset tracking applications is storing everything in one table.

That approach makes the current inventory easy to display, but historical information becomes difficult to reconstruct.

For this example, we'll use two tables:

  1. assets — the current state of each asset.
  2. asset_events — the history of lifecycle actions.

This gives us a practical separation between current state and historical events.

Create the Assets Table 

CREATE TABLE assets (
    id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,

    asset_tag TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    serial_number TEXT UNIQUE,
    name TEXT NOT NULL,

    status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'available'
        CHECK (status IN (
            'available',
            'assigned',
            'maintenance',
            'retired'
        )),

    assigned_to TEXT,

    purchased_on DATE,
    warranty_expires_on DATE,

    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
    updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),

    CONSTRAINT valid_assignment CHECK (
        (status = 'assigned' AND assigned_to IS NOT NULL)
        OR
        (status <> 'assigned' AND assigned_to IS NULL)
    )
);

The valid_assignment constraint prevents an asset from remaining assigned to someone while its status says available, maintenance, or retired.

This is useful because database constraints protect data even when an application bug bypasses expected validation.

In a larger system, assigned_to should normally reference an employee or user record through a foreign key. We're using text here to keep the example focused.

Create the Asset Events Table 

CREATE TABLE asset_events (
    id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,

    asset_id BIGINT NOT NULL
        REFERENCES assets(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,

    event_type TEXT NOT NULL
        CHECK (event_type IN (
            'registered',
            'assigned',
            'returned',
            'sent_to_maintenance',
            'maintenance_completed',
            'retired'
        )),

    from_status TEXT,
    to_status TEXT NOT NULL,

    performed_by TEXT NOT NULL,
    details JSONB NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'::jsonb,

    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);

CREATE INDEX idx_asset_events_history
ON asset_events (asset_id, created_at DESC, id DESC);

The event table records what happened, when it happened, and which application identity performed the action.

For example:

Event Previous State New State
Registered — Available
Assigned Available Assigned
Returned Assigned Available
Sent for repair Available Maintenance
Repair completed Maintenance Available
Retired Available Retired

An event history is useful for troubleshooting, compliance evidence, and understanding equipment movement.

However, an ordinary database table is not automatically a tamper-proof audit log. Stronger audit requirements may need restricted permissions, append-only enforcement, external log retention, or additional integrity controls.

4. Connecting Node.js to PostgreSQL

Create db.js:

import 'dotenv/config';
import pg from 'pg';

const { Pool } = pg;

export const pool = new Pool({
  connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL,
  max: 10,
  connectionTimeoutMillis: 5000,
  idleTimeoutMillis: 30000,
});

A connection pool lets your application reuse database connections instead of opening a new connection for every request.

For ordinary independent queries, pool.query() is convenient.

For transactions, we'll acquire a dedicated client from the pool.

This distinction matters because all statements in a PostgreSQL transaction must run through the same database connection.

5. Implementing Controlled Lifecycle Transitions

Instead of allowing arbitrary status updates, we'll define which changes are permitted.

Our state-transition rules are:

const transitions = {
  available: {
    assign: 'assigned',
    send_to_maintenance: 'maintenance',
    retire: 'retired',
  },

  assigned: {
    return: 'available',
  },

  maintenance: {
    complete_maintenance: 'available',
    retire: 'retired',
  },

  retired: {},
};

An assigned laptop cannot be directly assigned to somebody else using this simplified workflow. It must first be returned.

Similarly, a retired asset cannot be reactivated accidentally.

Different organizations may need additional rules, such as direct reassignments, lost equipment, quarantine, or disposal approval.

For now, we want a small state machine with predictable behavior.

6. Building the Lifecycle REST API

Create server.js:

import express from 'express';
import { pool } from './db.js';

const app = express();
app.use(express.json({ limit: '100kb' }));

const transitions = {
  available: {
    assign: 'assigned',
    send_to_maintenance: 'maintenance',
    retire: 'retired',
  },
  assigned: {
    return: 'available',
  },
  maintenance: {
    complete_maintenance: 'available',
    retire: 'retired',
  },
  retired: {},
};

const eventNames = {
  assign: 'assigned',
  return: 'returned',
  send_to_maintenance: 'sent_to_maintenance',
  complete_maintenance: 'maintenance_completed',
  retire: 'retired',
};

function getAssetId(value) {
  if (!/^[1-9]\d*$/.test(value)) return null;

  const id = Number(value);

  return Number.isSafeInteger(id) ? id : null;
}

// Demo identity only. Replace with authenticated
// authorization context before production.
function getActor() {
  return 'demo-operator';
}

app.post('/assets', async (req, res) => {
  const { assetTag, name } = req.body ?? {};

  if (
    typeof assetTag !== 'string' ||
    !assetTag.trim() ||
    typeof name !== 'string' ||
    !name.trim()
  ) {
    return res.status(400).json({
      error: 'Valid assetTag and name are required',
    });
  }

  const client = await pool.connect();

  try {
    await client.query('BEGIN');

    const result = await client.query(
      `INSERT INTO assets (asset_tag, name)
       VALUES ($1, $2)
       RETURNING *`,
      [assetTag.trim(), name.trim()]
    );

    const asset = result.rows[0];

    await client.query(
      `INSERT INTO asset_events
       (asset_id, event_type, to_status, performed_by)
       VALUES ($1, 'registered', 'available', $2)`,
      [asset.id, getActor()]
    );

    await client.query('COMMIT');

    return res.status(201).json(asset);
  } catch (error) {
    await client.query('ROLLBACK');

    if (error.code === '23505') {
      return res.status(409).json({
        error: 'Asset tag already exists',
      });
    }

    throw error;
  } finally {
    client.release();
  }
});

app.post('/assets/:id/transition', async (req, res) => {
  const id = getAssetId(req.params.id);
  const { action, assignedTo } = req.body ?? {};

  if (!id || typeof action !== 'string') {
    return res.status(400).json({
      error: 'Invalid asset ID or action',
    });
  }

  if (
    action === 'assign' &&
    (typeof assignedTo !== 'string' ||
      !assignedTo.trim())
  ) {
    return res.status(400).json({
      error: 'assignedTo is required',
    });
  }

  const client = await pool.connect();

  try {
    await client.query('BEGIN');

    const result = await client.query(
      'SELECT * FROM assets WHERE id = $1 FOR UPDATE',
      [id]
    );

    const asset = result.rows[0];

    if (!asset) {
      await client.query('ROLLBACK');
      return res.status(404).json({
        error: 'Asset not found',
      });
    }

    const nextStatus = transitions[asset.status]?.[action];

    if (!nextStatus) {
      await client.query('ROLLBACK');

      return res.status(409).json({
        error: 'Invalid lifecycle transition',
      });
    }

    const holder =
      action === 'assign' ? assignedTo.trim() : null;

    const updated = await client.query(
      `UPDATE assets
       SET status = $1,
           assigned_to = $2,
           updated_at = NOW()
       WHERE id = $3
       RETURNING *`,
      [nextStatus, holder, id]
    );

    await client.query(
      `INSERT INTO asset_events
       (asset_id, event_type, from_status,
        to_status, performed_by, details)
       VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4, $5, $6::jsonb)`,
      [
        id,
        eventNames[action],
        asset.status,
        nextStatus,
        getActor(),
        JSON.stringify(
          action === 'assign'
            ? { assignedTo: holder }
            : {}
        ),
      ]
    );

    await client.query('COMMIT');

    return res.json(updated.rows[0]);
  } catch (error) {
    await client.query('ROLLBACK');
    throw error;
  } finally {
    client.release();
  }
});

app.get('/assets/:id/history', async (req, res) => {
  const id = getAssetId(req.params.id);

  if (!id) {
    return res.status(400).json({
      error: 'Invalid asset ID',
    });
  }

  const result = await pool.query(
    `SELECT event_type, from_status, to_status,
            performed_by, details, created_at
     FROM asset_events
     WHERE asset_id = $1
     ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC`,
    [id]
  );

  res.json(result.rows);
});

app.use((error, req, res, next) => {
  console.error(error);

  res.status(500).json({
    error: 'Internal server error',
  });
});

app.listen(process.env.PORT || 3000, () => {
  console.log('Asset lifecycle API is running');
});

This example demonstrates the core workflow. It is not a complete production authentication or authorization implementation.

Why Use SELECT ... FOR UPDATE?

Imagine two IT administrators trying to assign the same available laptop at almost the same time.

Without proper concurrency control, both requests might read the asset as available before either update completes.

PostgreSQL's FOR UPDATE acquires a row-level lock inside the transaction.

The second transaction must wait for the first to finish. It then reads the updated status and can reject an invalid transition.

This is one way to prevent conflicting changes to an asset's current state.

Why Keep Updates and Events in One Transaction?

Suppose the application successfully changes an asset to assigned but fails to write the assignment event.

Now the system shows a current holder without a corresponding historical record.

By wrapping both operations in a transaction, we ensure they are committed together or rolled back together.

That is essential when the asset history needs to remain consistent with operational changes.

7. Testing the Asset Lifecycle API

Start the server:

npm start

Register an Asset 

curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/assets \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "assetTag": "LAP-001",
    "name": "Dell Latitude Laptop"
  }'

The response will contain the newly registered asset, initially marked as available.

Assign the Asset

Replace 1 with the ID returned during registration if necessary.

curl -X POST \
  http://localhost:3000/assets/1/transition \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "action": "assign",
    "assignedTo": "employee-101"
  }'

The asset now moves from available to assigned.

The assignment also creates a historical event.

Return the Asset 

curl -X POST \
  http://localhost:3000/assets/1/transition \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "action": "return"
  }'

After a valid return, its current status becomes available, and the previous holder is cleared.

View Lifecycle History 

curl http://localhost:3000/assets/1/history

A typical response includes:

[
  {
    "event_type": "returned",
    "from_status": "assigned",
    "to_status": "available",
    "performed_by": "demo-operator",
    "details": {},
    "created_at": "..."
  },
  {
    "event_type": "assigned",
    "from_status": "available",
    "to_status": "assigned",
    "performed_by": "demo-operator",
    "details": {
      "assignedTo": "employee-101"
    },
    "created_at": "..."
  }
]

This is much more useful than knowing only the asset's latest status.

It gives the IT team a chronological record of important activities.

8. Adding Warranty Tracking

Asset lifecycle management is not just about assignment and return.

IT departments also need visibility into warranty expiry, service contracts, and maintenance schedules.

Our assets table already includes warranty_expires_on.

We can query warranties expiring within the next 30 calendar days:

SELECT
    id,
    asset_tag,
    name,
    warranty_expires_on
FROM assets
WHERE status <> 'retired'
  AND warranty_expires_on >= CURRENT_DATE
  AND warranty_expires_on <= CURRENT_DATE + 30
ORDER BY warranty_expires_on ASC;

A scheduled job could run this query daily and notify the responsible team.

For production, the notification system should also keep delivery records to avoid repeatedly sending identical alerts.

A simple notification_log table with an appropriate uniqueness rule can help prevent duplicate reminders.

You should also distinguish between equipment warranties and software subscription renewals. They may involve different records, owners, and renewal policies.

9. Preparing the System for Production

The API we've created demonstrates state management and transaction safety, but several additional controls are necessary before using it with real company data.

Authentication and Authorization

Our example uses a fixed demo-operator identity.

A production system must replace that with verified identity information from its authentication layer.

Permissions should distinguish between users who can view equipment, assign assets, approve transfers, manage maintenance, and retire equipment.

Do not trust an identity or permission value simply because it appears in an incoming HTTP request.

Input Validation

Validate request bodies with a schema validation library such as Zod or another maintained solution.

Examples include:

  • Enforcing valid asset identifiers
  • Limiting string lengths
  • Rejecting unsupported actions
  • Validating dates and serial numbers
  • Applying consistent error responses

Tenant Isolation

If multiple organizations use the same application, add organization ownership to relevant tables.

Every operation must then enforce organization-level access controls. For stronger isolation, consider PostgreSQL row-level security with correctly scoped database roles and policies.

Transaction Safety

Always release database clients, even when an operation fails.

Use parameterized SQL queries to separate untrusted values from query text.

For higher availability and resilience, consider connection limits, transaction timeouts, retry strategies for appropriate transient failures, and graceful shutdown.

Auditing

A useful audit record should capture:

  • Who performed the action
  • What changed
  • When it changed
  • Which asset was affected
  • Relevant business context

For stronger accountability, preserve the previous assignee, current assignee, approved request, and reason for each handover.

Other Production Requirements

A complete implementation should also include:

  • Database migrations
  • Automated tests for valid and invalid transitions
  • Pagination for event history
  • Backup and recovery procedures
  • Error monitoring and structured logging
  • Idempotency for retried commands
  • Asset reconciliation and periodic audits
  • Secure equipment disposal procedures
  • Protection of historical events from unauthorized changes

An important test case is sending two simultaneous assignment requests for the same device and confirming that only one succeeds.

10. Build Your Own or Use an Existing Platform?

Building an asset management backend is a useful engineering project.

But maintaining a complete IT asset management platform involves more than storing equipment records.

Real organizations often need QR code scanning, signed handovers, employee offboarding, maintenance workflows, location tracking, reports, and role-based access.

If your goal is to learn backend architecture, building the system yourself is an excellent exercise.

If your goal is operational asset management, it may be more practical to evaluate an existing solution.

For example, Stackroom's IT asset management platform provides equipment assignment, custody records, and lifecycle visibility as part of a broader asset management workflow.

The right choice depends on whether you're solving a software engineering problem or an equipment management problem.

11. Final Thoughts

An effective IT asset lifecycle management system needs more than an assets table and a few CRUD endpoints.

The most important architectural decisions are often the less visible ones:

  • Keeping current state separate from historical activity
  • Defining valid lifecycle transitions
  • Using database transactions for consistent updates
  • Preventing conflicting assignments
  • Enforcing constraints at the database level
  • Preserving meaningful operational history

Node.js and PostgreSQL provide a solid foundation for implementing these patterns.

The same principles also apply to equipment checkout systems, inventory services, rental platforms, and other applications where resources move between people or operational states.

Start with a small, reliable lifecycle model. Add workflows as your actual business requirements become clear.

A system that accurately answers "Who has this asset, and how did it get here?" is already solving one of the most important problems in equipment management.

References and Further Reading

  • PostgreSQL Documentation — Constraints
  • node-postgres — Transactions
  • node-postgres — Parameterized Queries
  • Express — Production Security Best Practices

title: Product Listing using JavaScript API
description:
This mini project is developed using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. It fetches product details from the DummyJSON API (https://dummyjson.com/products?limit=200) using the Fetch API.

The project dynamically displays up to 200 products on the webpage, including their product images, brand names, descriptions, and prices. Each product is displayed in a separate card with an Add to Cart button.

Key Features:

  • Fetches product data from an external API.

  • Uses JavaScript DOM manipulation to create product cards dynamically.

  • Displays product images, brand names, descriptions, and prices.

  • Provides an Add to Cart button for each product.

Objective: The main objective of this project is to understand API integration, asynchronous JavaScript, Fetch API, and DOM manipulation in a real-world application.

Code :

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
    <title>Document</title>

    <style>
        * {
            padding: 0;
            margin: 0;
            box-sizing: border-box;
        }

        span {
            font-size: 26px;
            font-weight: 600;
        }

        div {
            box-shadow: rgba(100, 100, 111, 0.2) 0px 7px 29px 0px;
            width: 450px;
            display: flex;
            flex-direction: column;
            justify-content: center;
            align-items: center;
            padding: 20px ;
            gap: 30px;

        }
        div:hover {
            transform: scale(1.1);
        }

        img {
            width: 300px;
        }

        .price {
            text-decoration: line-through;

        }

        body {
            display: grid;
            grid-template-columns: /*repeat(3, minmax(0, 1fr));*/ repeat(auto-fit, minmax(350px, 1fr));
            gap: 40px;
        }

        button {
            padding: 15px 20px;
            font-weight: 700;
            background-color: rgb(8, 98, 216);
            color: white;
            border: none;
            border-radius: 10px;
            cursor: pointer;
        }
        button:hover {
            background-color: rgb(17, 59, 199);
        }
    </style>

</head>
<body>
    <script>
        fetch("https://dummyjson.com/products?limit=200")
            .then((res) => res.json())
            .then((data) => {
        const productList = data.products;

        for (let i = 0; i < productList.length; i++) {

             const card = document.createElement("div");

                    const elem = document.createElement("img");
                    elem.src = productList[i].images[0];
                    card.appendChild(elem);

                    const brandTag = document.createElement("h3");
                    brandTag.innerText = `Brand : ${productList[i].brand}`;
                    card.appendChild(brandTag);

                    const para = document.createElement("p");
                    para.innerHTML = `<span>Description :</span> ${productList[i].description}`;
                    card.appendChild(para);

                    const priceTag = document.createElement("h3");
                    priceTag.className = "price";
                    priceTag.innerText = `Price :  ${productList[i].price}`;
                    card.appendChild(priceTag);

                    const btn = document.createElement("button");
                    btn.innerText = "Add to cart";
                    card.appendChild(btn);

                    document.body.appendChild(card);

                }
            })
    </script>

</body>
</html>
