title: Satechi's Four-Display Dock: A Practical Shopify Guide to Clearer ChatGPT Product Information
description:
Official manufacturer image, used for product-information teaching; not a WESWOO client project.

Visit the product page for Satechi's Thunderbolt 4 Multimedia Pro Dock and one of its main selling points is immediately apparent: support for up to four displays. But expand the Compatibility section and the picture becomes more specific. Base M1 and M2 MacBooks are limited to one external display, while base M3 MacBooks need to operate in clamshell mode to support two external displays.

The dock itself hasn't changed. What changes is whether it can deliver the experience a particular buyer expects, based on the computer they're using.

That's an important distinction for merchants. Someone asking ChatGPT to recommend a dock isn't necessarily interested in its documented maximum display capability. They want to know whether it will work with their own setup. A product description that only highlights the headline specification doesn't answer that question.

This guide uses a real Satechi product to walk through a practical Shopify workflow: organize product information, check what Shopify Catalog receives, distinguish purchasable variants from compatibility requirements, and test whether the selected version remains consistent across the storefront.

The information comes from Satechi's public product page and support documentation. The Shopify Partner Directory also lists a Shopify website project for the brand. The admin workflows discussed below are implementation recommendations, not descriptions of Satechi's private fields, apps, or theme code. We have not verified the brand's current ChatGPT listings. Project reference.

1. Start with the product itself: plug options don't change display capability

On the Satechi product page, the purchase option is labeled Plug. During our visit, it offered US, EU, and UK versions, with the following published SKUs:

Purchase option Published SKU What the choice identifies
US ST-DT4PMM-US US plug version
EU ST-DT4PMM-EU EU plug version
UK ST-DT4PMM-UK UK plug version

These aren't different performance tiers, such as a single-display version and a four-display version. Selecting another plug changes the physical power-plug version, not the display capabilities of the host computer.

Power specifications need the same careful distinction. Satechi lists an approximately 0.8 m Thunderbolt 4 cable and a 135W power supply as included items. Host PD charging, however, is limited to 96W. The 135W rating describes the supplied power adapter; it does not mean the laptop receives 135W of charging power. Package and power details.

For the merchant, these details belong in three different places:

  • Plug options belong in the purchasable variants.
  • Display restrictions belong in compatibility information.
  • Included accessories belong in the package contents.

Keeping those categories separate makes the product easier to maintain and reduces the chance of a buyer misunderstanding what a variant actually changes.

2. Describe capabilities together with the conditions behind them

A useful first step is to review the product record for statements that describe an outcome without explaining when it applies.

This dock is a good example. Base M1 and M2 MacBooks are limited to one external display. Base M3 MacBook Air and MacBook Pro models require clamshell mode to support two external displays. Satechi also states that this model neither requires nor supports DisplayLink or SiliconMotion software.

One detail matters here: restrictions documented for base chips should not be generalized to every Pro- or Max-chip configuration. Compatibility needs to be tied to the specific host models and conditions in the official documentation. Compatibility; software requirements.

A practical content review can use the following table:

Information to examine What the record needs Maintenance location
Maximum display capability Supported host, operating conditions, and limits Description and compatibility content
Power figures Included supply rating versus host charging limit Package list and power specifications
US, EU, UK A clear plug option, not a performance tier Variant option name and values
Software Requirements and exclusions for this exact model Product explanation and FAQ

In Shopify, open Products → the product. Review the description, then inspect the relevant Variants row for its options, SKU, price, inventory, and media.

Shopify is rolling out a redesigned product editing experience, so some stores may manage variants directly on the same page rather than through separate detail screens. Editing variants.

Have the content owner identify what each statement applies to, and the product specialist check the technical conditions. The developer can then decide how to display the approved information.

Ideally, a developer should be working from a verified compatibility matrix, not trying to reconstruct one from a headline that says the dock supports four displays.

Give shared specifications a clear place to live

When the same compatibility information appears in the product description, FAQ, and theme components, each copy becomes another place that someone has to remember to update.

For a custom storefront, it's better to decide where approved product information belongs before adding more display components.

A suggested Shopify workflow:

  1. Go to Settings → Metafields and metaobjects and check whether an existing standard product definition already covers the information. If it doesn't, create suitable multi-line text definitions for compatibility restrictions and package contents. These are suggested fields for this workflow, not a disclosure of Satechi's actual admin structure.
  2. Open Products → the product → Metafields, enter the verified conditions and included items, and save. Keep prices and inventory in their native Shopify records rather than duplicating them in text fields.
  3. In the theme editor, open the product template and connect supported text or collapsible blocks to the relevant dynamic sources. Preview another product to make sure its own information appears correctly, then save.

The sequence matters: create the definition, enter its value, and connect it to the storefront.

Creating a metafield definition doesn't automatically display anything on the product page. Likewise, displaying a metafield in the theme doesn't automatically make it the description source used by Shopify Catalog.

Shopify documents each part separately: Definitions, values, and theme connections.

3. Check which description Shopify Catalog actually receives

A custom product page might display detailed compatibility information from a metafield, while the original Description field still contains an older introduction.

In that situation, fixing the visible page alone doesn't resolve the separate data source that Catalog may be using.

Open Sales channels → Agentic → Shopify Catalog in Sources → Review product data mapping. Under Product fields, check the source currently mapped to the description.

If the approved description lives somewhere else, select the appropriate source, preview the product, and save the change. Shopify notes that an empty mapped source falls back to the default field, so it's important to check field coverage across products rather than relying on one fully completed example. Catalog mapping.

The following checks help identify where a correction is actually needed:

Check What to look for in the data preview Corrective action
Description Host conditions alongside display claims Fix the actual exported source, not just the theme component
Purchase option Plug still means plug Correct the product option if its meaning is unclear
Price Current selling price versus reference price Check variant pricing and List price separately
Package and power Supply rating separated from host PD limit Correct the source and align the page with it

One pricing detail is easy to overlook. Catalog's List price can use either Price or an eligible Compare-at price. That setting doesn't determine which merchant's price ChatGPT displays in its initial shopping results.

OpenAI explains that initial prices typically come from the first listed merchant, may not be the lowest available, and can take time to update. ChatGPT pricing explanation.

If an exported description is missing a compatibility restriction, correct the source that feeds the export.

If the exported data looks right but an external AI summary leaves out the restriction, preserve the original query, complete result, landing link, and timestamp before reporting the discrepancy.

These are two different problems and shouldn't be treated as the same synchronization issue.

4. Group actual product versions, not an entire category

It's reasonable to treat different plug configurations of the same dock as product options. It's not reasonable to group every related docking product into the same model.

For example, the Thunderbolt 5 CubeDock and Thunderbolt 4 Slim Hub Pro appear in Satechi's related-products area. They are separate products. Sharing the same general dock category doesn't make them plug variants of the Thunderbolt 4 Multimedia Pro Dock.

When reviewing your own catalog, start by checking the product relationships under Products. Only consider Custom variant grouping when versions of the same product are maintained as separate product records and grouping them for the channel makes sense.

Shopify Catalog supports grouping by title delimiter, product metafield, or tag prefix.

There is one important consequence: enabling custom grouping overrides Catalog's use of Combined Listings settings. Before saving, inspect Products in group to make sure the right records are included.

If a need review result appears, investigate whether there are duplicate option combinations. Don't solve the problem by inventing an arbitrary model suffix that doesn't reflect a real product distinction. Grouping and review results.

The aim is a clear purchasing decision. Buyers shouldn't be led to believe that choosing a different plug gives them capabilities that belong to another device.

5. Put compatibility information where buyers make their decision

Satechi already provides expandable sections for technical specifications, compatibility, and important information. That makes the details available, but merchants should also consider whether the most important restrictions are visible when someone is ready to purchase.

Observed during this visit: base M1/M2 and M3 restrictions in Compatibility, with Plug: US in the purchase bar. US$349.99 and Sold Out describe this session only.

The following is a design recommendation, not a feature we claim Satechi has implemented.

Consider adding a short host-compatibility check near the purchase area. It could identify the buyer's chip, ask how many external displays they need, and check for clamshell use when the base M3 condition applies.

Confirmed condition Expected page response
Base M1/M2 MacBook, requesting two independent external displays Explain the product's single-external-display restriction
Base M3 MacBook, requesting two external displays Ask about clamshell operation before presenting a positive result
Only “MacBook Pro” is known Ask for the chip from About This Mac; do not infer it
The requirement relies on DisplayLink Show that this model does not support that software solution

The development team should work from a verified rule set. If a model or configuration hasn't been covered, its compatibility should remain unconfirmed rather than being presented as a definite yes.

The compatibility interaction and the Plug selector serve different purposes. One checks whether the product suits the buyer's intended setup; the other identifies which physical version they're purchasing.

For a small number of fixed notices, existing theme blocks may be enough. If the guidance needs to change according to several inputs, a custom selector may be more appropriate.

During acceptance testing, check how the explanation changes with the confirmed inputs. Simply confirming that a new AI button appears isn't enough.

6. Make sure the selected version survives when the link is shared

During this session, opening variant=40223722471512 selected the EU version. After clicking US, the main image and Plug text changed to US, but the address retained the original parameter.

This is a single-session observation, not a conclusion about every device, region, or browser.

It does, however, point to a useful storefront test: after changing a variant and copying the address, does reopening that address preserve the version the buyer selected?

Shopify documents variant deep links using actual variant IDs and explains that variant-specific product information should follow the selected variant. Theme variant support.

A practical test sequence:

  1. Open a real deep link for EU. Check the selected option, image, price, and purchase state.
  2. Switch to US, copy the current address, and open it in another tab. If it still selects EU, document the mismatch between the selected state and the shared link for the theme developer to investigate.
  3. If inventory and test authorization allow it, add one unit to the cart. Check the model, plug, quantity, and amount shown in the cart. This verifies the actual add-to-cart result; a highlighted option by itself doesn't.

The page displayed Sold Out during this visit, so we didn't test the cart or checkout.

For your own preview theme and authorized test conditions, cover available, unavailable, and return-to-page states. An unavailable version should never silently become another in-stock version in the cart.

7. Check the package contents before recommending accessories

The actual Related Products area included checkboxes for other expansion devices. But a related product isn't necessarily something a buyer needs in order to use the selected dock.

This is particularly relevant here because the dock already includes a power supply and host cable. Before recommending additional purchases, check whether they duplicate something in the package.

A longer cable, for example, introduces its own length and protocol requirements. If the buyer needs a different display configuration, recommending another dock as a substitute may make more sense than suggesting two docks as a presumed bundle.

To manage recommendations in Shopify, open Apps → Search & Discovery → Product recommendations → Add recommendations.

Select the product, assign additional-use items to Complementary products, and use Related products for substitutes. Save the changes, then add a supported recommendation block to the product template.

Complementary products also need to be in stock and have Active status to appear. Recommendation configuration.

These are product-level recommendations. Selecting items conditionally according to the buyer's host computer, package contents, and chosen variant requires defined business rules and appropriate storefront logic.

A recommendation should never be treated as proof of compatibility.

Keep the purpose of each part clear:

  • Plug changes the purchasable version.
  • Compatibility guidance checks the intended use.
  • Alternative models address different requirements.

8. Keep evidence that shows exactly what changed

After updating the product information, open Sales channels → Agentic, run a relevant search, and expand Listing insights.

Review the available signals for description, images, reviews, variants/options, and policies. The preview represents Catalog search, while an external AI channel may rank results differently. Search preview and listing signals.

For each change, keep the original query, source information, preview, timestamp, and a record of what was updated.

A quality indicator alone doesn't explain what was wrong or how it was fixed.

The following two prompts can help audit an external answer about this specific product:

Using Satechi's official documentation, explain whether the Thunderbolt 4 Multimedia Pro Dock can provide two independent external displays for a base M2 MacBook Air. Cite the restriction and source rather than substituting the maximum four-display claim.

What do the dock's 135W supply and 96W PD figures each refer to? Does the package already include power and a host cable? Distinguish included items from purchases that are necessary separately.

The first prompt checks whether host-specific display conditions are preserved. The second checks whether power specifications and package contents are being described correctly.

These are audit prompts, not test results we obtained or evidence of a completed recommendation experiment.

A useful evidence record can look like this:

Evidence to retain What it establishes
Description source and product preview Restrictions are present in exported information
Product records, package list, and page Model, plug, and power meanings are consistent
Before/after links and reopened selection The intended version survives the link
Actual cart lines, where testing was performed The added version matches the choice
Query and complete AI answer Whether that answer preserved the critical conditions

Shopify also documents automatic /agents.md, /llms.txt, and /llms-full.txt discovery endpoints.

These files provide store-discovery information, but they don't replace Catalog product data. For the issue discussed in this guide, checking the product description, variants, and field mapping is a more direct starting point than buying a separate file-generation tool. Discovery files versus product information.

From WESWOO's perspective on custom store design and development, this is part of delivering a maintainable storefront: product information that can be updated, options buyers can understand, usage restrictions that are easy to find, and an order that still reflects the version they selected.

For this dock, the final checks come down to three straightforward questions:

  • Can the buyer's computer use the dock as intended?
  • Which plug version are they actually purchasing?
  • Does the cart still contain that same selected version?

Sources and storefront observations checked on November 4, 2026. No access to the brand's admin, hardware test, checkout test, or verification of its actual ChatGPT recommendations was performed.

title: Parsing Run Times in a Calculator: mm:ss, Seconds, and the Ties That Cost Points
description:
Any calculator that scores a timed event has the same quiet problem: people type times in five different ways. One person types 14:30. Another types 870. A third types 14.30 and means fourteen minutes and thirty seconds. If your parser guesses wrong, the score is wrong, and the user usually cannot tell.

This post walks through a small, boring approach that has held up well for me when building fitness-test calculators: accept a few clearly defined formats, reject everything else with a helpful message, and compare times as whole seconds.

Decide what you accept, and write it down

Before writing code, list the formats you will accept. Mine are:

  • mm:ss such as 14:30 or 9:05
  • m:ss with a single-digit minute
  • h:mm:ss for very long events, such as 1:02:15
  • plain seconds such as 870, only when the field is labelled as seconds

Everything else is an error. That includes 14.30, 14,30, and 14m30s. It is tempting to be generous, but a decimal point in a time field is genuinely ambiguous, because it can mean 14.3 minutes or 14 minutes 30 seconds. When a wrong guess changes someone's score, asking again is the kinder choice.

A parser that returns seconds or an error 

// Returns total seconds, or null if the text is not a valid time.
export function parseTime(text) {
  const t = String(text).trim();

  // Plain seconds: digits only
  if (/^\d+$/.test(t)) return Number(t);

  // mm:ss or h:mm:ss
  const parts = t.split(":");
  if (parts.length < 2 || parts.length > 3) return null;
  if (!parts.every(p => /^\d+$/.test(p))) return null;

  const nums = parts.map(Number);
  const seconds = nums[nums.length - 1];
  const minutes = nums[nums.length - 2];
  const hours = nums.length === 3 ? nums[0] : 0;

  if (seconds > 59) return null;
  if (nums.length === 3 && minutes > 59) return null;

  return hours * 3600 + minutes * 60 + seconds;
}

Three details matter here.

Seconds above 59 are rejected. 14:75 is not "fifteen fifteen". It is a typo, and silently accepting it moves the score by a full minute.

Minutes are only capped when hours are present. 75:00 is a valid way to type a very slow walk, but 1:75:00 is not valid.

The function returns null, not zero. A zero would flow through the scoring code as a fantastic time. Returning null forces the caller to handle the failure.

Compare in integers, display in strings

Once everything is whole seconds, scoring becomes simple integer comparison against a table. This avoids a class of bugs where "9:05" < "10:00" is evaluated as a string comparison and returns the wrong answer, because "9" sorts after "1".

// Rows are sorted from fastest to slowest.
// maxSeconds is the slowest time that still earns the points.
export function scoreRun(seconds, table) {
  for (const row of table) {
    if (seconds <= row.maxSeconds) return row.points;
  }
  return 0;
}

Only convert back to mm:ss when you show a value to the user:

export function formatTime(totalSeconds) {
  const m = Math.floor(totalSeconds / 60);
  const s = totalSeconds % 60;
  return `${m}:${String(s).padStart(2, "0")}`;
}

Ties and boundaries

Scoring tables usually say something like "14:00 or faster". That means the boundary belongs to the better row. If the table's slowest time for 70 points is 14:00, then exactly 840 seconds should earn 70 points, and 841 seconds should earn the next row down.

I write boundary tests for every row, three of them each:

  1. One second faster than the boundary
  2. Exactly the boundary
  3. One second slower than the boundary 
import { test } from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert";

test("boundary is inclusive", () => {
  const table = [
    { maxSeconds: 840, points: 70 },
    { maxSeconds: 900, points: 60 },
  ];
  assert.equal(scoreRun(839, table), 70);
  assert.equal(scoreRun(840, table), 70);
  assert.equal(scoreRun(841, table), 60);
});

The numbers above are illustrative. When you build a real calculator, copy the thresholds from the governing document for the test you are scoring, and cite that document on the page.

Be kind in the error messages

A good error message names the field, shows an example, and does not blame the user:

  • "Enter your run time as minutes and seconds, like 14:30."
  • "Seconds must be between 00 and 59."

I also keep the raw text in the field when validation fails. Clearing the input makes people retype everything, and they notice.

Input masks: use sparingly

Auto-inserting a colon as people type looks polished, but it breaks on mobile keyboards and with paste. If you add a mask, make sure pasting 14:30 and typing 1430 both work, and that backspace behaves. In my experience a plain text input with clear validation beats a clever mask.

Accessibility notes

  • Use a visible label, not placeholder text alone.
  • Set inputmode="numeric" only if you also accept the colon on that keyboard. Otherwise a numeric keypad can make mm:ss impossible to type on some phones.
  • Announce validation errors with aria-live="polite" so screen readers pick them up.

What I would test first

If you only have time for a few tests, write these:

  • parseTime("14:30") equals 870
  • parseTime("870") equals 870
  • parseTime("14:75") is null
  • parseTime("14.30") is null
  • parseTime("") is null
  • Every boundary in the table, three ways

I applied this approach in AFTPTCalc, a free set of military fitness test calculators I maintain: https://aftptcalc.com/ . The scoring tables there are kept as data and checked row by row against the published source documents.

Disclosure: I used an AI writing assistant to help draft and edit this post. The code and examples are my own and the numbers are illustrative.

title: Chart Types for Analyzing Flow and Process
description:
Most dashboards describe quantities that sit still: how much is in each region, each team, each stage. Flow analysis asks where things go instead: which route carries the most, who keeps handing work back to whom, which team everything passes through. Five charts do this work, and two questions tell you which one to start with.

The same table of from-to pairs can feed a Sankey, a dependency wheel, or an arc diagram, and each shows it differently, so the choice depends on what you know about the nodes and what you need to read from them. Below, the two questions come first, then the five charts, then a worked example that runs one data set through three of them.

Two Questions, Five Answers

Start with two questions: does the position of the nodes matter, and do you need to see how much moves or what connects to what?

Does the position of the nodes matter? How much moves What connects to what
Yes, stages or a sequence Sankey diagram Arc diagram
Yes, places on a map Flow map Flow map
No, or they have none Dependency wheel Network graph

The position matters when the question depends on where the nodes sit: in stages the flow passes through, in a sequence such as steps or time, or on a map. Countries always have a place on a map, but if the question is only who trades with whom, and how much, the map adds distances that the eye mistakes for volume, and a dependency wheel is often the better start. Stages also mean the flow moves one way. If it loops back, the stages no longer hold, and the first question needs a new answer.

The second question is about what you need to read. All five charts can size their links by volume, but the Sankey and the dependency wheel are built around amounts, and the arc diagram and the network graph around the pattern of links. When the geography matters, a flow map does both. The network graph is also where you land when you are still exploring.

Shortlist: Which Chart Answers Which Question

Chart Type Question
Sankey diagram Which paths carry the most, and where does the flow narrow?
Flow map Where does the volume move geographically?
Arc diagram Which nodes connect to which, when their order is fixed?
Dependency wheel Which pairs exchange the most with each other?
Network graph What is the shape of the whole connection structure?

Five Charts, Five Questions

Sankey Diagram: Which paths carry the most, and where does the flow narrow?

A Sankey diagram draws flows between stages, with link width sized to volume.

Best for a process with several routes through it, where the question is which route dominates. It is the default for a reason: it is the only one of the five with direction, volume, and sequence all built into its layout.

Watch out: Too many nodes and it turns to spaghetti. Best with a clear direction and a few stages.

Cousins: A funnel chart is the linear, single-path case of the same idea.

Flow Map: Where does the volume move geographically?

Mexico’s flow is more than twice China’s, yet its line is the shortest on the map.

A flow map shows lines drawn between locations on a map, weighted by the volume moving along them.

Best for movement between places: shipments, migration, traffic, trade. When the nodes are locations, the map does the layout work for free: an arrangement you invent will rarely place them better than the one people already have in their heads.

Watch out: Long lines look important because they are long. Distance is not volume, and the eye keeps confusing the two.

Cousins: A choropleth map shows what sits in each place; a flow map shows what travels between them. A connector map draws the same kind of lines to show which places are connected; size them by volume and add direction, and it becomes a flow map.

Arc Diagram: Which nodes connect to which, when their order is fixed?

An arc diagram has nodes placed along a single line, with connections drawn as arcs above it.

Best for sequences where position already means something and you also need to see the links: text, code, timelines. It is the chart for when you cannot move the nodes because their order is the data. Nodes with no order of their own can be given one: sort them by group, and clusters show up as nested arcs. The arcs above are also sized by weight, so the diagram shows volume too. But a long arc stands out for its height whatever it carries, which makes the diagram easier to read for what connects than for how much moves.

Watch out: The layout is only as good as the node order. Sort them badly and every arc crosses every other one.

Cousins: A network graph drops the fixed order and lets a layout algorithm find the structure instead.

Dependency Wheel: Which pairs exchange the most with each other?

Color shows direction: each ribbon takes the color of the league the players leave.

A dependency wheel, also known as a chord diagram, has nodes arranged around a circle, with ribbons between them sized to the volume exchanged.

Best for a closed set of players where the traffic between them, rather than through them, is the story. A circle has no beginning, which is exactly right when nothing about your nodes suggests a first or a last.

Watch out: A ribbon has no arrowhead. Unless its color shows where it starts, A to B reads the same as B to A.

Cousins: A Sankey with origins on the left and destinations on the right shows the same volumes with an unambiguous direction, giving up the circular overview.

Network Graph: What is the shape of the whole connection structure?

A network graph has nodes and edges positioned by a layout algorithm rather than by data values.

Best for finding hubs, clusters, and isolated pockets when you do not yet know what you are looking for. It is the only one of the five that imposes no order on the nodes, which is both why it can surprise you and why it is so hard to read precisely.

Watch out: Position comes from the layout, not from any data value. The same graph re-laid out looks like a different network, and neither picture is a measurement.

Cousins: An arc diagram fixes the node order, trading the free layout for readability.

How They Chain: A Worked Example

The interesting thing about this set is that each chart is limited by exactly the assumption that makes it readable. Drop the assumption and you see the next thing.

Take work items moving between teams: intake, then whoever handles it, then an outcome.

One set of handoffs through three charts, and what each one adds.

Start with the Sankey. Left to right, sized by volume. Suppose most items go in through one channel, land with one team, and resolve. A visible slice peels off into a node called reassigned.

That node is an artifact. A Sankey needs a direction and stages, so work that goes back where it came from has nowhere to live, and it ends up in a catch-all node. The chart is not wrong. Its stages run one way, so the loop has to go somewhere. Repeating each team at every step can show it, but after a round trip or two the diagram turns to spaghetti.

Drop the stages and keep the volumes: a dependency wheel of team-to-team handoffs. Suppose most of that reassigned volume turns out to be two teams passing the same work back and forth between each other. On the Sankey that was one gray ribbon into a generic node. On the wheel it is a nameable, fixable relationship between two specific teams.

Now drop the volumes too: a network graph. No stages, no circle, no imposed order. Suppose one team turns out to be connected to almost every other. It is not the largest by volume, and both previous charts size a node by its volume, so it never stood out on either. Nearly every path in the organization passes through it.

Three charts, two assumptions dropped, and each drop revealed something the previous layout had no room for. That is the argument for treating the two questions at the top as a starting point instead of a verdict. The chart that answers your question best is often the one you reach for second.

What Is Not Here

You won’t find a bar chart of volume per node, a flowchart, or a table of from-to pairs.

A bar chart of volume per node describes quantities that sit still, and flow is about what moves between things. A flowchart draws the steps and decisions of a process, not how much actually moves through them. The from-to table is a different case: it is complete, precise, and unreadable past about twenty rows. Every chart above trades some of that precision for a structure you can actually see.

The table is worth dwelling on because it is usually where flow data starts, and it is frequently where it stops. Two hundred rows of origin, destination, and volume contain every fact that a Sankey contains, plus the exact numbers that a Sankey turns into widths. What it does not contain is the shape. Nobody reads two hundred rows and notices that two of the entries form a loop, or that one node appears in a third of them. The chart’s whole value is that it loses the decimals and surfaces the structure, and the table’s whole value is the reverse. Keep both, and know which one you are asking.

What to Do With This

If you have a from-to table sitting in a warehouse somewhere and no chart built on it, the two questions at the top of this page will point you to a first chart in about a minute. Position first, then volume or connections.

Many teams have that table and have never drawn it, because the table looks like it already answers the question.

These five answer how much moves and what connects to what. Why a flow changed is a question for root cause analysis charts. When the process is a schedule with deadlines and dependencies, start with project and resource planning charts.

title: Designing a React Native app for field reps: cheap Android phones, direct sunlight, weak signal
description:
Most mobile design advice assumes a new iPhone, indoors, on Wi-Fi. The people using our field sales app have mid- and low-end Android phones, stand in car parks and dealer shopfronts at midday, and often have one bar of signal.

We still borrowed heavily from Apple's Human Interface Guidelines, because grouped lists, large titles and calm hierarchy make dense data readable. But a lot of Apple's defaults fail outdoors on Android. Here's what we kept, what we changed, and why.

Contrast: Apple blue is too faint in sunlight

iOS system blue, #007AFF, is about 4.0:1 contrast on white. That just passes WCAG AA for large text, and it becomes invisible in direct sun.

We use a darker accent (#0369A1, about 6:1) as the tint for every action, link and selected state. Secondary text is grey at 72% instead of the usual lighter grey, giving roughly 5.4:1. If a rep has to tilt the phone to read a label, the label is wrong.

Icon tiles can still use bright iOS-style hues (indigo, green, orange), because the glyph on top is white and the tile is large.

Touch targets: 52px minimum

Android's guideline is 48dp. We use 52px minimum row height. Reps tap with gloves, with a pen in the other hand, or while walking. The extra 4px measurably reduced mis-taps on the payments screen.

There's one primary button per screen: filled, 52px tall, radius 12.

No hidden gestures

Swipe-to-delete is elegant and nobody in our user base discovers it. Every action has a visible control: a red ✕ to remove, a button to add. We have a SwipeRow component, and the rule is that it's never the only way to do something.

Back navigation must work with Android's back button and gesture on every screen. We never rely on the iOS swipe-from-left-edge.

Fonts: Android ignores fontWeight with custom fonts

We use Inter (the open-licence face closest to SF Pro, which may only be used on Apple platforms). On Android, fontWeight: '600' on a custom font family silently does nothing. You get regular weight.

The fix is to load each weight as its own font face and reference it by name:

// theme
export const font = {
  regular:  'Inter_400Regular',
  medium:   'Inter_500Medium',
  semibold: 'Inter_600SemiBold',
  bold:     'Inter_700Bold',
};

// usage: never fontWeight
<Text style={{ fontFamily: font.semibold, fontSize: 17 }}>Choose dealer</Text>

We load exactly four weights to keep startup fast on slow phones.

No blur

Real-time blur (iOS "materials", Liquid Glass) is slow on low-end Android and hard to read in sunlight. Translucent bars use a near-opaque fill instead. It looks 90% as good and scrolls smoothly on a budget phone.

Native pickers, not iOS wheels

Date and time pickers use Android's own components on Android. Reps already know how they work. An iOS-style wheel on Android looks polished in a screenshot and confuses the person who has to use it.

Words: the team's vocabulary, not the designer's

The biggest gains weren't visual. "Choose dealer" beats "Who paid?". "Policy" beats "Scheme" when the team says "policy". If a field is required, the label says "required". An optional-looking label gets skipped.

For teams that work in two languages, we show an optional second line under the English on section headers, the main button and error messages. English stays first, and the second language never replaces it.

Choices become shortcuts

When a field is free text with common answers (like a payment policy name), the text box comes first and looks like a box. Common values sit underneath as one-tap shortcuts labelled "Or tap a common one". People don't feel forced into a list, and most still tap a shortcut.

Motion

It's short, ease-out and purposeful, with light haptics on selection and a success haptic plus sound when a payment is saved. Everything goes instant when the OS "Reduce motion" setting is on.

These rules come from the design guide of Beatplan field sales app (disclosure: this is the product I work on), an Expo and Supabase field sales system that's used daily and now sold as full source code. The payments screen is the reference implementation, and you can try it in the live demo. It's interesting to compare on a cheap Android phone outdoors.

This article was written with AI assistance.

title: Step-dLLM: Adaptive Step-aware Sparse Attention for Efficient Diffusion LLM Inference
description:
arXiv:2611.01320v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) generate tokens in parallel via iterative denoising, but their bidirectional attention prevents the KV caching used by autoregressive models and recomputes the full attention map at every step, incurring quadratic per-step cost. Existing sparse attention methods for dLLMs construct a sparse mask after an initial full-attention warm-up and reuse it for the remaining steps, while allocating the sparsity budget uniformly across heads. We argue both choices ignore key structural properties of attention in dLLMs: empirically, attention patterns are only locally consistent across steps and shift abruptly at certain transitions, and different heads concentrate their attention mass to very different extents. To this end, we design Step-dLLM, which periodically refreshes a block-sparse mask at anchor steps along the denoising trajectory and reuses it within each locally consistent interval, while employing a head-adaptive global budget that more aggressively compresses heads with concentrated attention. Backed by a fused IO-aware Triton kernel for block-sparse attention, Step-dLLM applies to pre-trained LLaDA-1.5 and Dream-7B-Instruct without retraining, achieving a 2.78x end-to-end speedup over dense FlashAttention on LLaDA-1.5 at 8K context with 256 denoising steps and 90% sparsity, while improving the accuracy-latency trade-off over prior sparse-attention methods.

title: Managed MySQL hosting compared: prices and backups in 2026
description:
TL;DR

  • What you get: one table with the smallest useful managed MySQL plan on five platforms, what it costs per month, and what happens to your data if something breaks.
  • Who it's for: anyone running Laravel, WordPress, Rails or any app that needs MySQL and doesn't want to babysit a server.
  • Time needed: 10 minutes to read, 5 minutes to create a database.
  • Short answer: for a hobby app or staging, Hubfly space ($3.92/mo for 0.5 vCPU / 1 GiB) or Aiven Developer ($5) are cheapest. For production data you can't lose, pay for daily backups and point-in-time restore: DigitalOcean ($15.15) is the cheapest fixed plan with both built in; Railway can cost less if you turn on backups and point-in-time restore yourself. PlanetScale ($39) is the pick when you need high availability from day one.

You need MySQL. Your app is a Laravel shop, a WordPress site or an old Rails monolith, and the framework expects it. Most "managed database" comparisons only talk about Postgres, and the MySQL ones list prices without saying the most important thing: what you get back when someone runs DROP TABLE on a Friday.

This guide fixes that. You'll see what the smallest MySQL plan costs on five platforms, what backups each one includes, and where each one wins. Then you'll create a MySQL database on Hubfly space.

Try it on Hubfly space: new accounts start free, no card needed.

The price table

Prices are each vendor's official monthly list price for the smallest plan that runs MySQL with about 1 GB of memory, read on 4 November 2026. Prices change; follow the links before you buy.

Provider Smallest MySQL plan Monthly price Backups included Point-in-time restore High availability
Hubfly space 0.5 vCPU, 1 GiB RAM, 10 GiB storage $3.92 (docs) Not yet: automatic backups are "coming soon" No No (single instance)
Aiven Developer 1 CPU, 1 GB RAM, 8 GB storage $5 (pricing) A single backup, for disaster recovery only No No
Railway Usage-based MySQL template on a volume ≈ $7.68 at light use (see math below) (pricing) Optional volume backups: daily kept 6 days, weekly 27, monthly 89 (docs) Optional, you turn it on (docs) Optional Group Replication cluster (docs)
DigitalOcean 1 vCPU, 1 GiB RAM, single node $15.15 (pricing) Daily full backups (docs) Any point in the last 7 days Not on the 1 GiB plan; HA from $60/mo (2 GiB primary + standby, existing accounts) or Advanced Edition
Aiven Hobbyist 1 CPU, 1 GB RAM, 8 GB storage from $19 (pricing) A single backup, for disaster recovery only No No
PlanetScale PS-10 (Vitess) 1/8 vCPU, 1 GB RAM per node, 3 nodes, 10 GB storage $39 (pricing, AWS us-east-1) Automatic backups every 12 hours, included (docs) Not listed in the backups docs Yes: 1 primary + 2 replicas in 3 availability zones

Two providers you might expect are missing on purpose:

  • Render has no managed MySQL. Its docs show you how to run MySQL yourself as a private service with a disk. You get daily disk snapshots, but Render itself says relying on a snapshot to restore a database "is not recommended" and points you to mysqldump.
  • AWS RDS for MySQL is the default in big companies, but its price depends on instance class, region, storage type and backup size. Use the AWS pricing page with your real numbers; a one-line price here would mislead you.

Free options exist too. Aiven lists a free MySQL plan (1 CPU, 1 GB RAM, 1 GB disk, 76 connections) and says it may power off idle free services. Aiven also says its free tier "is not aimed at production workloads". Fine for learning, not for customer data.

How the Hubfly space price adds up

Hubfly space bills a managed database by the hour for the CPU and memory you pick, plus storage, plus a 30% management fee on compute while the instance runs. There's no seat or project fee. The math for the default MySQL size (0.5 vCPU, 1 GiB, 10 GiB storage), at 730 hours a month:

Item Formula Per month
CPU 0.5 vCPU × $0.004 × 730 h $1.46
Memory 1 GiB × $0.002 × 730 h $1.46
System disk 1 GiB × $0.00001536 × 730 h $0.01
Compute $2.93
Management 30% × ($1.46 + $1.46) $0.88
Storage 10 GiB × $0.00001536 × 730 h $0.11
Total $3.92

The Create a database form with MySQL selected. The panel on the right shows each line of the monthly estimate.

If you only need 1 GiB of storage, the same size costs $3.82, the "From $3.82/mo" price on the MySQL card. MySQL needs at least 1 GiB of memory, so the smaller Nano size ($2.02) is only for PostgreSQL and SQLite (libSQL).

Bigger sizes follow the same formula: Medium (1 vCPU, 2 GiB) is $7.72, Large (2 vCPU, 4 GiB) is $15.31. Storage stays cheap at about $0.011 per GiB-month, so 100 GiB adds roughly $1.12. Storage is billed even while the instance is stopped; compute and management are not.

How the Railway estimate adds up

Railway doesn't sell database plans. MySQL is a template that runs as a normal service on a volume, and you pay per second for what it actually uses (rates):

  • Memory: $0.00000386 per GB-second = $10.14 per GB-month
  • CPU: $0.00000772 per vCPU-second = $20.29 per vCPU-month
  • Volume: $0.00000006 per GB-second = $0.16 per GB-month

A quiet MySQL that averages 0.5 GB of memory and 0.05 vCPU, with 10 GB of data: 0.5 × $10.14 + 0.05 × $20.29 + 10 × $0.16 = $7.68 a month. The Hobby plan's $5 minimum covers the first $5 of that. A busier database that holds 1 GB of memory and uses 0.25 vCPU lands near $17. The upside: you pay for real use. The catch: your bill moves with your traffic, and backups are billed as extra volume storage.

What "backups" really means on each platform

Part of the price gap between $4 and $15 is a bigger CPU; the rest is backups. Here's what you can do after a bad migration deletes a table:

  • Point-in-time restore (DigitalOcean, Railway if you turn it on): you pick a timestamp, say two minutes before the bad query, and get a copy of the database from that moment. DigitalOcean keeps this for 7 days. This is what you want for production.
  • Scheduled snapshots (PlanetScale every 12 hours, Railway volume backups): you can go back to the last snapshot. You lose everything written since then.
  • One disaster-recovery backup (Aiven Developer and Hobbyist): Aiven keeps a single backup to recover the service if its hardware fails. It's not a history you can browse.
  • Nothing automatic yet (Hubfly space): automatic backups are listed as "coming soon" on the create form. Until they ship, run your own mysqldump on a schedule and store the file somewhere else (see below).

Where each one wins

Hubfly space wins on price for small databases. $3.92 a month for a dedicated 0.5 vCPU and 1 GiB, billed hourly, with MySQL 8.4 LTS or 9.7 LTS, TLS, an IP allowlist and credentials built in. It also runs your app, so a Laravel or WordPress container and its database live in one account with one bill. It loses on backups (none automatic yet) and placement: you can't pick a region for a managed database, so check latency from where your app runs.

Aiven wins if you want a big-name managed service for $5. The Developer plan is cheap and simple. Backups are thin until you reach the $75 Startup plan, which adds 2 days of point-in-time restore.

Railway wins if your database is idle most of the time and you already deploy there. Usage pricing can beat any fixed plan for a quiet app. You opt in to backups, point-in-time restore and HA yourself.

DigitalOcean wins on production basics for the money. $15.15 gets you daily backups and restore to any point in the last 7 days, with no extra setup. For failover you need a 2 GiB+ plan with a standby node, or Advanced Edition for new accounts. Note that from 15 October 2026 for new accounts (30 November 2026 for all accounts), new Standard Edition clusters can't add standby or read-only nodes or go above 4 GiB RAM; those move to the pricier Advanced Edition.

PlanetScale wins when downtime costs real money. Even the $39 PS-10 runs three nodes across three availability zones, on Vitess, the system PlanetScale built its MySQL product on. It's overkill for a side project and the right tool for a growing product.

Which one should you pick?

Your situation Pick
Side project, staging or a learning app Hubfly space ($3.92) or Aiven Developer ($5)
App you deploy on Railway already, light traffic Railway MySQL template
Production data, small budget, need point-in-time restore DigitalOcean ($15.15)
Production, can't afford downtime PlanetScale ($39+)
You also want the app, storage and email in one place Hubfly space, plus your own backup job

Create a MySQL database on Hubfly space

  1. Open the dashboard and click Create Project. Give it a name like shop-data, choose Managed service, and click Create Project.
  2. On Add your first managed service, click Create a database.
  3. Under Engine & version, choose MySQL. Keep MySQL 8.4 LTS unless your app needs 9.7.
  4. Under Size, choose Small (0.5 vCPU, 1 GiB). Nano is greyed out for MySQL because it needs at least 1 GiB.
  5. Set Storage to what you need. You can grow it later but never shrink it, so start small.
  6. Under IP allowlist, click Add my IP, then add the address range your app connects from. Do this before you create the database. The default is open to all IPs, and anyone with the password could connect.
  7. Name the instance, for example shop-mysql, check the price panel, and click Create database. Wait until the instance shows as running; this usually takes a few minutes.

Why the allowlist matters: a database open to the whole internet invites password-guessing. Credentials stop most attempts, but an allowlist means strangers can't even open a connection.

Set up your own nightly backup

Until automatic backups ship, run mysqldump from a scheduled job and keep the file outside the database. Put host, port, user and password under a [client] section in ~/.shop-mysql.cnf and run chmod 600 ~/.shop-mysql.cnf, so the job never stops to ask for a password. Use the MySQL 8.x client (mysql-client from Oracle's MySQL repository or Homebrew); the MariaDB client that some Linux distributions install doesn't accept --ssl-mode. Save this as backup.sh, make it executable, and schedule it with cron:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -o pipefail
mysqldump --defaults-extra-file=$HOME/.shop-mysql.cnf \
  --single-transaction --no-tablespaces --routines --triggers \
  --ssl-mode=REQUIRED <your-database> | gzip > shop-$(date +%F).sql.gz

set -o pipefail makes the job fail loudly if the dump fails, instead of leaving an empty file that looks like a backup. --no-tablespaces avoids the "PROCESS privilege" error that managed database users usually hit. --single-transaction takes a consistent copy without locking InnoDB tables, so your app keeps working while the dump runs.

Upload the file to an S3-compatible bucket such as Hubfly space Storage (about $0.011 per GB-month) and delete files older than 14 days. Then restore one into a scratch database once, so you know it works before you need it:

gunzip -c shop-<date>.sql.gz | mysql --defaults-extra-file=$HOME/.shop-mysql.cnf --ssl-mode=REQUIRED <scratch-database>

What can go wrong

  1. A timeout or "Can't connect to MySQL server" when your app connects. The allowlist doesn't include your app's address. Add your app's outbound IP or range to the database's IP allowlist and try again. ("Access denied" is different: it means a wrong user or password.)
  2. Connection fails with an SSL error. The database is served over TLS. Add --ssl-mode=REQUIRED to the mysql client, and turn on TLS in your driver's connection settings.
  3. The bill is higher than the table. Check storage: it's billed while the instance exists, even when stopped, and on DigitalOcean extra storage costs $0.215 per GiB-month. On Railway, check memory: a MySQL that caches more data uses more RAM, and you pay for it by the second.

Takeaway

For a small MySQL database, the cheapest managed option is now under $4 a month. What you pay more for elsewhere is mostly backups and failover. Decide how much data you can afford to lose, then pick the cheapest plan that covers it. If that answer is "a day's worth is fine and I'll run my own dump", Hubfly space is the cheapest place to start.

Read next: How to move your app from Railway to Hubfly space · Docker health checks that catch real problems · Managed databases on Hubfly space

Go further on Hubfly space

  • Run the app next to the database: deploy your Laravel or WordPress container on Hubfly space Cell and connect it with the credentials from the database's Connect page. (Databases docs)
  • Store backups and uploads: keep nightly dumps and user files in Hubfly space Storage, S3-compatible. (Storage docs)
  • Moving from another host? Follow the Railway migration guide for the app side, then load your mysqldump file into the new database.

Create your MySQL database on Hubfly space: from $3.82 a month, billed by the hour. New accounts get 360 free container hours a month for the app side.

title: CheXPoT: Post-Hoc Visual Verification and Correction of VLM-Generated Radiology Reports
description:
arXiv:2611.00785v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have shown promise for chest radiograph report generation, but adoption remains limited because of hallucinated findings that are not grounded in the image. Correcting these hallucinations and improving overall report quality remains a significant challenge. Prior work has addressed this problem by refining models with reinforcement learning, preference optimization, or chain-of-thought supervision, often at substantial compute cost. To address this gap, we introduce CheXPoT, a program-of-thought (PoT) framework that verifies each generated finding against image features and removes those it cannot ground. CheXPoT decomposes generated reports into predicates with RadGraph and an LLM, grounds these predicates against a DenseNet-121 and Grad-CAM visual evidence table, executes PoT verification code, and rewrites reports after removing unsupported predicates. On a 4,145-image held-out split, CheXPoT yields statistically significant precision gains on 8 of 14 CheXpert classes and F1 gains on 5, with no significant decreases in either metric. CheXPoT lifts micro-average precision from 19.2% (MedGemma-4B) to 46.8% (MedGemma-4B + CheXPoT) and micro-average F1 from 23.0% to 49.4%, absolute gains of 27.6% and 26.4% respectively. We also tested CheXPoT on other VLM report generators. On LLaVA-Med, CheXPoT lifts micro-average precision from 4.5% to 17.7% and micro-average F1 from 6.3% to 19.4%. On MAIRA-2, CheXPoT lifts micro-average precision from 15.6% to 42.1% and micro-average F1 from 21.0% to 45.3%. Our results suggest that inexpensive post-hoc visual verification may improve VLM trustworthiness by correcting unsupported findings from generated reports. CheXPoT lays a foundation for tools that help validate VLM-generated radiology reports and reduce unsupported findings. These innovations may subsequently help increase trust and adoption of VLM tools in Medicine.

title: 2,000 TripAdvisor reviews in 62 seconds for one cent: what one Times Square hotel's guests actually complain about
description:
TripAdvisor shows a hotel's all-time score at the top of the page. For an old hotel with 18,000 reviews, that number mostly describes stays from years ago. If you want to know what guests say now, you need the recent reviews themselves, in a table.

So we pulled them. One run of our TripAdvisor Reviews Scraper on Apify, pointed at the Hotel Edison Times Square, asking for 2,000 reviews:

  • Time: 62 seconds.
  • Cost: $0.0096 of compute on our side. A user pays $0.50 per 1,000 reviews on the Starter tier, so this run is $1.00 for anyone else.
  • Coverage: 2,000 reviews from 12 Dec 2024 to 3 Nov 2026, plus one row for the hotel itself.

Every number below comes from that one run. Reviews are written by members of the public, so this post shows counts only: no reviewer names and no quotes from reviews.

The input 

{
  "startUrls": [
    { "url": "https://www.tripadvisor.com/Hotel_Review-g60763-d93437-Reviews-Hotel_Edison_Times_Square-New_York_City_New_York.html" }
  ],
  "maxReviewsPerPlace": 2000
}

Any TripAdvisor review page works the same way: hotels, restaurants and attractions, on any TripAdvisor country site. Filters are optional: ratings (for example only 1 and 2 stars), reviewsSince, languages, tripTypes (family, couples, solo, business, friends), reviewsContaining and sortBy.

From Python:

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN")
run = client.actor("locaihost/tripadvisor-reviews").call(run_input={
    "startUrls": [{"url": "https://www.tripadvisor.com/Hotel_Review-g60763-d93437-Reviews-Hotel_Edison_Times_Square-New_York_City_New_York.html"}],
    "maxReviewsPerPlace": 2000,
})
rows = list(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items())
reviews = [r for r in rows if r["type"] == "review"]

Each review row has the rating, title, full text, language (and whether TripAdvisor machine-translated it), published date, travel month, trip type, sub-ratings when given, helpful votes, photo count and the hotel's reply. Reviewer names are off by default. The place row carries the address, coordinates, all-time rating and histogram, sub-scores, the "#169 of 529 hotels" ranking, amenities, and three numbers computed from the reviews you collected: owner reply rate, average reply lag and the rating over the last 90 days.

Finding 1: the all-time score hides two good years

Reviews Average 5 stars
All time (TripAdvisor's own histogram) 18,836 3.9 40%
Latest 2,000 (Dec 2024 to Nov 2026) 2,000 4.43 71%

The headline 3.9 is dragged down by older stays: 2,482 of the hotel's one and two-star reviews are in the all-time histogram, and only 176 of them are in the last two years. Month by month, the recent average sits between 4.18 (September 2026) and 4.67 (April 2025), with no trend down.

If you compare hotels by their all-time score, an older property that has improved looks worse than it is. A 90-day or 12-month average from the raw reviews is fairer, and it's one column in the output (ratingLast90d: 4.35 over 250 reviews here).

Finding 2: who is happiest

Trip type Reviews Average
Solo 93 4.78
Friends 256 4.68
Family 620 4.58
Couples 262 4.47
Business 124 4.34
Not given 645 4.14

Business travellers rate it lowest of the groups that say why they came. Reviewers who don't pick a trip type are the least happy of all, which is common: an angry reviewer fills in fewer optional fields.

Finding 3: what the bad reviews are about

We split the reviews into 176 low (1 or 2 stars) and 1,701 high (4 or 5 stars) and counted how many in each group mention a word at least once (whole words only):

Mentioned Low reviews High reviews
noise / noisy 23% 7%
bathroom 26% 8%
old / dated / outdated 20% 5%
check-in 17% 8%
window 16% 1%
price / expensive / overpriced 18% 6%
rude 12% 0%
fee / fees 11% 1%
air conditioning / AC 11% 2%
dirty 9% 0%
staff 44% 54%
location 34% 54%
clean 15% 33%

The pattern is clear even with simple word counts. Happy guests talk about the staff and the location. Unhappy guests talk about the room itself (bathroom, noise through the windows, an old building, the air conditioning) and about the front desk (check-in, rude, fees). "Staff" shows up in both groups, because staff are the reason for both the best and the worst reviews.

This is the cheapest version of the analysis. With the full text in a dataframe, the next step is an embedding or topic model over the 176 low reviews, which takes a few seconds on a laptop.

Finding 4: the hotel answers almost everything

1,991 of the 2,000 reviews have a reply from the hotel (99.6%), including 175 of the 176 low ones, and the average reply comes 4.6 days after the review. That's a well-run reply process. For a competitor analysis, reply rate and reply lag are two of the most telling columns: they show which hotels have someone watching their reviews.

What it doesn't do

  • It reads what a logged-out visitor can see. A list stops at about 10,000 reviews; for bigger places, run it per star rating to go deeper.
  • Machine-translated reviews are marked (machineTranslated). 161 of these 2,000 were translations; filter them out with languages if you only want originals.
  • It doesn't name staff. Names in the hotel's replies are replaced with [name removed].

Try it

The Actor is locaihost/tripadvisor-reviews on the Apify Store: $0.50 per 1,000 reviews and $1 per 1,000 places on the Starter tier, cheaper on the higher tiers, and links that aren't a TripAdvisor place are never charged. It also works from AI agents through Apify's MCP server, so "pull the last 500 reviews of these 10 hotels and tell me what the one-star ones have in common" is one tool call away.

If you run it and something looks wrong, open an issue on the Actor page and we'll fix it the same day.

title: Multi-Estimate Elicitation Does Not Uniformly Debias Language Model Judgments
description:
arXiv:2611.00597v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Does eliciting five weighted estimates within a single response change how a language model responds to information? Across anchoring, hindsight, base-rate, conjunction, and status-quo/default tasks, we compare direct numerical answers with a multi-estimate response format, contrasting source framings, explicitly random cues, and probability-consistency constraints. We evaluate three completed configurations--gpt-6.1-sol, claude-sonnet-5.5, and Qwen3-8B (reasoning disabled, analyzed descriptively). In the first two configurations, direct elicitation yielded near-zero irrelevant-anchor indices and status-quo effects, while remaining responsive to informative sources and informed advice. Of 23 preregistered confirmatory tests, six rejected after Holm adjustment; however, all six absolute point estimates fell below their prespecified smallest effect sizes of interest without establishing equivalence. Moreover, while separate versus joint elicitation shifted conjunction judgments, interpretation is constrained by between-call noise. Ultimately, multi-estimate elicitation failed to produce uniform debiasing or response attenuation across tasks and models, though post hoc correlations between candidate spread and anchoring error motivate independent predictive validation. Materials: https://github.com/asj252/llm-judgment-studies
