title: Agents struggle with the same bad UX we do
description:
Computer-use agents can’t guess, improvise, or ask a coworker. That makes them the most honest usability testers we’ve ever had.

The first time I watched an agent fail on a vendor portal, I recognized the failure immediately. Not because I understood the model. Because I’d failed in exactly the same place myself.

For example, I watched a run where an agent reached a form that had two buttons labeled “Continue” and “Submit”, chose the wrong one, and the run stalled. This wasn’t the agent’s fault, it was bad UX.

I design products at Deck, where we build infrastructure for computer-use agents: software that logs into websites and operates them the way a person would, clicking, typing, and navigating. Most of the portals our agents work in were never designed to be automated. They’re utility accounts, vendor payment pages, and back-office tools with no API, built for humans and often barely built for those.

Watching thousands of agent runs across these portals has taught me something I didn’t expect. The places agents get stuck are almost never exotic. They’re the same places people get stuck. The difference is that people hide it.

Humans glance over bad design. Agents can’t.

Steve Krug observed years ago in Don’t Make Me Think that people rarely figure out how a website works. They muddle through: guessing, backtracking, and moving on once something seems to work. That muddling is a kind of invisible labor, and it hides an enormous amount of design debt.

When a button label is ambiguous, a person tries one and sees what happens. When a menu only appears on hover, a person waves the mouse around until it shows up. When a session expires halfway through a form, a person sighs, logs back in, and starts again. When they truly can’t work something out, they ask a coworker who learned the trick last month. None of this shows up in analytics as failure. It shows up as “time on task,” or not at all.

An agent can’t do most of that. It doesn’t remember the trick from last month. It can’t lean over and ask someone. It can retry, but it can’t intuit which of two identically labeled buttons the designer meant. So the debt that humans quietly absorb becomes visible, run after run, as a step that broke.

That’s what makes agents unusually honest testers. They don’t experience frustration, but they surface every place where a design depends on someone guessing right.

Where agents get stuck

The failures cluster into a handful of patterns. None of them will surprise a designer. That’s the point.

1. Labels that only make sense if you already know. “Manage,” “Edit,” and “Settings” all on one page. Icon-only buttons with no text. Two buttons that both say “Continue.” Don Norman’s idea of signifiers, the cues that tell you what an action will do, is the whole game here. When the signifier is missing, a person relies on memory or experimentation. An agent has neither.

2. State that hides. Menus that exist only on hover. Buttons that are disabled with no explanation of why. Status communicated purely by color. Jakob Nielsen’s first usability heuristic, visibility of system status, was written for people. It turns out to be the first requirement for agents too. If the interface doesn’t say what state it’s in, nothing operating it can know.

3. Interruptions. The cookie banner, the “rate your experience” modal, the promotional interstitial that appears on the third visit, the chat widget that slides over the submit button. Every one of these is a small tax on human attention. For an agent, an unexpected overlay can be the end of the run. It’s a useful mirror: if an interruption is disruptive enough to stop a machine cold, it’s worth asking what it costs your users.

4. Time. Sessions that expire mid-task. One-time codes that time out before they arrive. Pages that log you out “for your security” during a multi-step process. People tolerate these grudgingly. For any automated or delegated work, they’re often the single largest source of failure, and they’re a sign that the system was designed around a single short visit, not around real work.

5. Success that doesn’t announce itself. This is the one I care about most, because it’s the one I spent years on in payments. You submit a payment and land back on the dashboard with no confirmation. Did it go through? A person checks their email, or refreshes, or calls someone. An agent has to decide whether the task is done, and if the interface doesn’t say so clearly, it can’t. In my last piece for UX Collective I argued that trust in financial products lives in moments like this. Agents make the same argument from the other side: a task isn’t complete until the interface tells you it is.

We’ve seen this before: the curb-cut effect

None of this is new territory. It’s accessibility.

Many of the fixes that help agents are the same ones that help people using screen readers, keyboard navigation, or magnification: real text labels instead of icon-only buttons, states that are announced instead of implied, predictable structure, no content that only exists on hover. The WebAIM Million report has documented year after year how common these basic gaps are across the web’s most visited homepages.

Angela Glover Blackwell called this pattern the curb-cut effect: design for people with specific constraints, and you end up improving things for everyone. Curb cuts were built for wheelchairs and are used by every parent with a stroller. Clear labels and visible state were required for assistive technology, and they help every user who’s tired, rushed, or new.

Agents are, in a sense, the newest constrained user. They push in the same direction accessibility advocates have been pushing for decades, which is a welcome thing. The work that makes a portal legible to an agent is largely the work we should have done for people already.

Where the analogy breaks

It would be too clean to say “design for agents and humans benefit.” Three places it gets complicated:

Some friction is supposed to be there. I’ve written before about graduated ceremony: matching the weight of a confirmation to the consequence of the action. Some steps exist precisely to slow things down. A confirmation before moving money, a second check before deleting an account. Making those steps “agent-friendly” by removing them would be a mistake. The better answer is to design for delegation explicitly: let a person grant an agent specific, limited authority up front, so the ceremony happens at the moment of handoff rather than disappearing altogether.

Not every site wants agents. CAPTCHAs and bot detection exist for real reasons: fraud, scraping, abuse. Some services have a legitimate interest in knowing whether a human is present. “Agent-legible” and “agent-permitted” are different questions, and designers will increasingly have to answer the second one deliberately rather than by accident.

Agents also fail where people don’t. They can misread a visually dense layout a person would parse instantly, or miss context a human gets from the surrounding page. So agent failures aren’t a perfect proxy for human failures. They’re a strong signal, not a verdict. When an agent and a person both struggle in the same place, that overlap is where I’d look first.

Using agents as a usability lens

You don’t need to build for agents to learn from them. A few questions I now ask in every design review, whether or not an agent will ever touch the screen:

  • Could someone who can’t guess complete this? If the path depends on trying both buttons, it’s a labeling problem.
  • Is every state visible without hovering, remembering, or color alone?
  • Does success announce itself? If the only proof a task finished is that nothing went wrong, it hasn’t been designed yet.
  • Does each interruption earn its place? If it would stop a machine, it’s costing your users more than you think.
  • Does this flow survive a real task’s length? Timeouts designed for a single quick visit break every longer process, human or not.

For years, usability testing meant recruiting people and watching them muddle through. That’s still irreplaceable. But there’s now a second kind of tester showing up on our interfaces, one that never muddles, never guesses, and never quietly absorbs our mistakes. The places it gets stuck are a map of the design debt we’ve been asking people to carry.

Trust has always lived in the details. Agents just stopped letting us get away with skipping them.

References and further reading

  • Steve Krug, Don’t Make Me Think
  • Don Norman on signifiers, The Design of Everyday Things
  • Jakob Nielsen, “10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design”
  • WebAIM Million annual accessibility report
  • Angela Glover Blackwell, “The Curb-Cut Effect,” Stanford Social Innovation Review
  • “The hidden UX of payments” in the UX Collective

Agents struggle with the same bad UX we do was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: ISC Stormcast For Wednesday, November 4th, 2026 https://isc.sans.edu/podcastdetail/10164, (Wed, Nov 4th)
Using Flying Saucer 10.7.0: Grid, @font-face and Java 21
description:
A dashboard template with a two-column CSS grid and a net total that a script writes after load prints as one column with no total when Flying Saucer renders it. The renderer ships for Java as org.xhtmlrenderer:flying-saucer-pdf, and 10.7.0, released 24 October 2026, is its current version. We ran into that grid while testing the library for this post, so it comes first, and later sections draw on more 10.7.0 runs, the R8 user's guide, the code and what NVD, GHSA and OSV record.

We work at Iron Software, and the end of this article covers our library, IronPDF.

What Does Flying Saucer Do With CSS Grid and a Script-Written Total?

It lays the grid items out as ordinary blocks and drops the script. The engine targets CSS 2.1, extended with its own -fs- print properties and some later CSS. A set in the code, CSSName.UNSUPPORTED_CSS3_PROPERTIES, names 52 CSS3 properties that layout passes over, grid and flexbox among them, and the R8 user's guide says script tags are ignored.

import org.xhtmlrenderer.pdf.ITextRenderer;

import java.io.FileOutputStream;
import java.io.OutputStream;

public class GridScriptCards {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        // A two-column grid with a total that a script writes after load, as many dashboards do.
        String xhtml = "<html><head><style>"
                + ".grid { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; gap: 16px; }"
                + ".tile { padding: 10px; border: 1px solid #999; }"
                + "</style></head><body>"
                + "<div class='grid'><div class='tile'>Orders 412</div><div class='tile'>Returns 9</div></div>"
                + "<p id='total'></p>"
                + "<script>document.getElementById('total').textContent = 'Net orders 403';</script>"
                + "</body></html>";

        ITextRenderer renderer = new ITextRenderer();
        renderer.setDocumentFromString(xhtml);
        renderer.layout();
        try (OutputStream out = new FileOutputStream("grid-script-cards.pdf")) {
            renderer.createPDF(out);
        }
    }
}

grid-script-cards.pdf is a single US Letter page with Orders 412 above Returns 9 at the same left margin, and the text layer has no Net orders 403. During the run the Html5Support logger printed one warning naming display: grid, grid-template-columns and gap as unsupported, then the PDF was written as normal. That warning, first logged in 10.2.0, is the only sign of the problem. Any template a front-end team designs in a browser is affected, and the routes around it are a float and table layout or the project's separate Chrome module, covered below.

Does @font-face Embed the Font in the PDF?

Not with the CSS a browser accepts. A plain @font-face rule resolves the font for layout, but the PDF only names it, so the reader's viewer has to supply the face.

import org.xhtmlrenderer.pdf.ITextRenderer;

import java.io.FileOutputStream;
import java.io.OutputStream;
import java.nio.file.Path;

public class FontFaceCss {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        // The same @font-face rule a browser would use, with the TTF resolved against the base URL.
        String xhtml = "<html><head><style>"
                + "@font-face { font-family: 'Brand'; src: url('georgia.ttf'); }"
                + "h1 { font-family: 'Brand'; }"
                + "</style></head><body><h1>Quarterly summary</h1></body></html>";

        ITextRenderer renderer = new ITextRenderer();
        renderer.setDocumentFromString(xhtml, Path.of("fonts").toUri().toString());
        renderer.layout();
        try (OutputStream out = new FileOutputStream("font-face.pdf")) {
            renderer.createPDF(out);
        }
    }
}

The heading in font-face.pdf references a TrueType font called Georgia with no font file in its descriptor, so on a machine without Georgia the viewer substitutes another face. Adding the vendor property -fs-pdf-font-embed: embed to the rule, which the user's guide documents, produced an embedded Georgia subset in a second run. Brand fonts depend on embedding. So does the PDF/A archive format, an ISO preservation standard whose rule 6.2.11.4.1 requires all fonts embedded, and it has a second font catch. With a font registered as BaseFont.IDENTITY_H and PDF/A-3b requested, veraPDF 1.30.3 failed the output on the CIDSet rule 6.2.11.4.2, while BaseFont.CP1252 passed for Western European text.

Can CMS HTML Go Straight Into setDocumentFromString?

No. The parser is XML, and the user's guide says most HTML found in the wild can't be rendered and should go through TagSoup, JTidy or a similar cleaner first.

import org.xhtmlrenderer.pdf.ITextRenderer;

import java.io.FileOutputStream;
import java.io.OutputStream;

public class RawCmsFragment {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        // Valid HTML5 as a browser reads it, with an unclosed <p> and <li> and a bare <br>.
        String html = "<h1>Release notes</h1>"
                + "<p>Version 3.2 ships today.<br>Highlights:"
                + "<ul><li>Faster search<li>New export menu</ul>";

        ITextRenderer renderer = new ITextRenderer();
        // The XML parser rejects the string here, before layout starts.
        renderer.setDocumentFromString(html);
        renderer.layout();
        try (OutputStream out = new FileOutputStream("release-notes.pdf")) {
            renderer.createPDF(out);
        }
    }
}

The run stopped in setDocumentFromString with XRRuntimeException wrapping a SAX error at line 1, column 24, saying the markup following the root element must be well-formed, and no file was written. Parsing with jsoup and passing its W3CDom result to setDocument rendered this fragment in a test run, and it adds a dependency and a step to every render.

Which Advisories Show Up in a Dependency Scan?

Mostly history rather than the current release, with one recent batch in a dependency.

  • Builds through 9.3.2: A default flying-saucer-pdf build resolves com.lowagie:itext 2.1.7, and GitHub's GHSA-86p9-x5pw-94qx flags that artifact for CVE-2017-9096 at every version up to 4.2.2, with no fixed version.
  • CVE-2017-9096 scores 8.8 High under CVSS 3.0 (NIST): An XXE weakness in iText's XML parsing, which NIST also scores 6.8 on CVSS 2 and NVD doesn't tag as disputed.
  • OpenPDF from 9.4.0: It took over the PDF layer at that release, which came out at the end of December 2023.
  • XXE changes with no CVE: Two hardening changes, one to XMLResource in 9.12.1 (June 2025) and one to DocumentBuilderFactory in 10.4.0 (July 2026), shipped with no CVE identifier, which leaves scanners blind to builds that lack them.
  • Advisories on the current tree: Neither OSV nor GHSA lists any advisory for a Flying Saucer artifact, and OSV, queried for the libraries 10.7.0 pulls in on 3 November 2026, had nothing for them either. The exception is Apache's Batik page, which names seven medium-rated CVEs in 1.19, the version 10.7.0 pulls in, and everything older, all patched by the 1.20 release of 20 October 2026.

Teams still on 9.3.2 or earlier carry the iText finding. Moving to 10.4.0 or later picks up the iText and XXE changes, while the Batik fixes need a release that moves off 1.19, and none had reached Maven Central on 3 November 2026.

What Changes With the Chrome Module and the Java 21 Floor?

The Chrome module trades the CSS gap for a browser to manage, and the 10.x line needs a recent JVM.

The module, flying-saucer-chrome-pdf, first shipped with 10.3.0 in June 2026 and hands each page to chrome-headless-shell. Unless told otherwise it asks Google's chrome-for-testing feed for the current Stable build and refreshes that answer daily, so the browser doing the printing changes underneath the application, and on 3 November 2026 that answer was build 156.0.8078.80. Calling setChromeVersion pins it. Two more details in the 10.7.0 source matter in production. The print call fires on Page.loadEventFired with no dedicated delay setting in ChromiumPdfOptions (a desktop Chrome run needed addExtraArg("--virtual-time-budget=5000") in one-shot mode to print a late script's text), and on Linux arm64 the platform check throws even though the chrome-for-testing JSON offers linux-arm64 downloads for Stable. The exception suggests setBinaryPath, yet the check runs before that path is read, and a test with os.name Linux and os.arch aarch64 still threw with a path supplied.

Java is the other constraint. Since 10.0.0 in September 2025, every 10.x jar targets Java 21 (class file 65), and compiling against 10.7.0 with the JDK 17 javac failed with a wrong-version error in the test run. Java 17 projects are held to 9.x, where 9.13.4 is the newest build. Separately, the parent POM leaves slf4j-api to the application as a provided dependency, and without it constructing the first renderer threw NoClassDefFoundError.

Where Does IronPDF for Java Fit These Checks?

If the trade-offs above don't fit a project, IronPDF for Java is a commercial library that prints HTML through Chromium. On 2026.11.3, our run of the grid above put Orders 412 and Returns 9 in two columns and printed Net orders 403 from the script. Scripts run by default, since ChromePdfRenderOptions starts with setEnableJavaScript on, a WaitFor can pause the capture for a fixed delay, network idle or a named element, raw CMS HTML needs no jsoup pass, and PDF/A-3b output is one saveAsPdfA call.

The library itself is com.ironsoftware:ironpdf on Maven Central, built as Java 8 bytecode, with eleven 2026 builds by 3 November 2026, numbered by month, the newest published that day. The engine it bundles or downloads is pinned by each IronPDF release, so a Chromium update arrives only as an IronPDF version bump. A free trial is available for testing it against your own templates.

Summing Up the Flying Saucer Checklist

Grid and script missing from the PDF, unembedded @font-face fonts, an XML-only parser, a Chrome module that follows the Stable channel and a Java 21 floor are the checks this post ran on Flying Saucer 10.7.0, and the iText 2.1.7 dependency behind CVE-2017-9096 belongs to pre-9.4.0 builds. For pages built for a browser, IronPDF for Java renders them in Chromium from a single dependency, and our HTML file example shows the call.

Flying Saucer, OpenPDF, iText, Apache Batik, Georgia, Chrome and veraPDF are trademarks of their respective owners, we have no affiliation with any of them, and the details above come from each project's source, documentation, release notes and the NVD, GHSA and OSV databases.

Drafted with AI. Flying Saucer code run and claims checked by the Iron Software DevRel team on 3 November 2026, with IronPDF APIs checked against com.ironsoftware:ironpdf 2026.11.3.

title: How v0 authenticates to Snowflake without exposing the user's OAuth token
description:
AI-generated applications often need to authenticate to external services on behalf of their users. That creates a problem: generated code shouldn't have access to the user's credentials.

We faced that decision when building the v0 Snowflake integration. It lets users connect Snowflake, inspect schemas, query data, and generate applications that run against their warehouses. That generated code has to authenticate to Snowflake, but it is written by a model and runs without human review, and prompt injection can steer it into exfiltrating whatever it can read, so the user's OAuth token should never enter the environment the code runs in.

We solved this with a Snowflake request proxy for v0 sandboxes, built on the Vercel Sandbox firewall. The sandbox can run normal Snowflake clients, but the real credential is resolved at request time in a server proxy outside the sandbox runtime. This lets existing Snowflake clients work inside the sandbox without exposing the user's credential to generated code.

The harder problem was deciding where the proxy could safely inject the credential. The obvious implementation, replacing a placeholder token wherever it appears, introduces another credential leak.

Isolation doesn't protect secrets

v0 runs generated applications in isolated sandboxes. Isolation protects the rest of the system from untrusted code, but it doesn't protect secrets inside the sandbox.

If a generated app can read a token from the filesystem, that token can be copied into logs, returned in an API response, embedded into generated client code, or sent to another host. Sandbox isolation limits what the application can access, but it does not help once the credential itself is available inside the sandbox.

For Snowflake, the credential represents the Snowflake role the user connected with. v0 should be able to help the user explore and build with data they are authorized to access, but generated code should not receive raw provider credentials just because it needs one.

Every Snowflake request goes through the proxy

The sandbox cannot talk to Snowflake directly. When code inside it sends a request to the user's Snowflake account host, the sandbox firewall forwards that request to the v0 Snowflake proxy:

The firewall terminates TLS with a certificate authority unique to each sandbox, which lets the proxy read and rewrite traffic that would otherwise be encrypted. The sandbox trusts that certificate authority automatically, so the Snowflake SDK and CLI run with their default certificate validation, OCSP included. The proxy then verifies the sandbox's OIDC token, looks up the v0 chat the sandbox belongs to, restores the user session bound to that chat, and retrieves a fresh Snowflake credential for that user.

The sandbox does not choose where a token-bearing request is sent. The proxy derives the Snowflake account host from the server-side credential and rejects invalid account URLs, keeping the credential scoped to the connected Snowflake account rather than trusting host information supplied by generated code.

Compatibility without credential exposure

As a stopgap, the first version of the integration wrote the user's real token into the sandbox's Snowflake token files. The proxy replaced that approach. Ideally, we would remove token files from the sandbox entirely, but Snowflake clients expect credentials in different locations depending on the authentication flow.

Some requests, such as Snowflake SQL API calls, authenticate with an Authorization: Bearer header. Other client flows read local token files and send the token as part of a login request. Once the client has authenticated, subsequent requests use Snowflake-issued session tokens, and the proxy passes those requests through untouched.

To preserve compatibility, v0 still writes a token-shaped placeholder into the sandbox. The placeholder is a fixed, public, 72-byte string that grants no access, and its only job is to let existing Snowflake SDK and CLI flows behave as if a token exists. The proxy never authorizes a request based on the placeholder itself. Instead, the proxy authorizes the request using the sandbox's server-side identity and its binding to the user's chat.

The real OAuth token, the reusable credential that represents the user, is never written into the sandbox. Snowflake does issue session tokens that live inside the sandbox after login, but each of those belongs to a single authenticated session.

Those sessions are short-lived in practice. The Snowflake helper in generated apps destroys its connection after each query, which ends the session right away. Closing the chat does not end a session on its own, but tearing down the sandbox takes the token with it, and Snowflake expires the session server-side after four hours of inactivity by default. When a request reaches the proxy, it decides whether and where to attach the credential.

Why blind replacement fails

The first version of the proxy searched each request for the placeholder and swapped in the real token wherever it appeared:

The problem is that generated code controls parts of the request, including where the placeholder can appear. A SQL statement, for example, is caller-controlled data. If a query contains the placeholder as a string literal, blind replacement turns that query into one containing the real OAuth token. If the database then returns that string, the real token comes back into the sandbox as query output, and the proxy would have leaked the token it was built to keep out.

Stricter matching does not close the hole. The proxy shouldn't inject a credential based on attacker-controlled text. Instead, it needs to know which field in each Snowflake request carries authentication.

Injecting credentials only into authentication fields

Snowflake requests reach the proxy in three shapes, and each shape puts authentication in a different place.

For Snowflake SQL API requests, the proxy sets the OAuth token on the Authorization: Bearer header. The body remains caller-controlled SQL and is not rewritten. If the placeholder appears in the SQL payload, the proxy rejects the request before it reaches Snowflake and logs it as placeholder misuse.

For Snowflake login requests, the proxy parses the JSON request body, sets the token structurally at the login token field, and serializes the body again. If the placeholder remains anywhere else in the request body, the proxy fails closed.

Post-login session requests authenticate with Snowflake-managed session tokens, so the proxy has nothing to inject.

Failing closed

The proxy rejects any request where:

  • The sandbox is not bound to a chat

  • No user-scoped credential can be obtained

  • The Snowflake account host cannot be derived

  • The placeholder appears outside an approved authentication field

  • A structured login body cannot be parsed safely

Requests are also bounded before inspection so that compressed or oversized bodies cannot turn the proxy into an unbounded parser. Every proxied request emits an observability event with the upstream outcome, status, duration, and injection location. This surfaces misuse and integration failures without exposing secrets.

Handling refresh and deploy

Token refresh cannot depend on an ambient browser cookie, because proxy requests originate from the sandbox, not from the user's browser session. v0 binds the user session to the sandbox instead, and the proxy mints and refreshes OAuth credentials from that binding.

The publish path uses Snowflake CLI flows with the same credential boundary. Deploy can write the placeholder into credential files, but never the real token.

After deployment, the application runs in Snowpark Container Services and authenticates as its own service user, with a token that Snowflake manages and rotates automatically, mounted at /snowflake/session/token. The user's OAuth token and the v0 proxy are no longer involved.

The resulting security boundary

For users, none of this is visible. Connect Snowflake, ask v0 to inspect schemas or build an app, preview the result, and deploy when it's ready.

The security model rests on five rules:

  • Credential injection happens only at each endpoint's authentication fields

  • Requests that use the placeholder outside an authentication field are rejected and logged

  • Token-bearing requests go only to the connected Snowflake account host

  • Credentials are minted and refreshed server-side

  • Generated code uses Snowflake without ever reading the user's OAuth token

In its first 15 days in production, the proxy attached credentials server-side for roughly 13,000 requests and recorded zero placeholder-misuse rejections.

Although we built this proxy for Snowflake, the same problem applies to other integrations: generated code often needs to authenticate without receiving the user's long-lived credential. The important part is to inject credentials only into protocol-defined authentication fields, rather than rewriting arbitrary request data.

The v0 Snowflake integration is now available in beta. Get started by reading the integration docs.

title: What I Learned Evaluating AI Image, Video and Audio Models
description:
Part of my week is spent as a freelance AI evaluator. I review output from AI models that generate images, video, audio and user interfaces, and score each one against a structured rubric. It is detailed work, and it has changed how I think about building software.

The first lesson: following instructions matters more than looking good. An image can be beautiful, but if the prompt asked for three people and the model drew four, it failed the task. A plainer result that does exactly what was asked is the better answer. That rule applies to almost everything I build now. Do what the user asked first, then make it pretty.

The second lesson: false positives are worse than misses. When you flag a problem that is not really there, you send the people training the model in the wrong direction. I would rather be precise and miss a small issue than be loud and wrong. In my own projects, that means I test carefully before I call something broken or fixed.

The third lesson: short, clear feedback beats long explanations. A tight verdict that names the exact issue is more useful than a paragraph of opinion. I bring the same habit to code reviews and client conversations.

Working on the evaluation side also makes it clear how much human judgment still sits behind these systems. Models improve because people check their work, carefully and consistently. For anyone moving into AI or software, I recommend trying evaluation work. You learn quickly what good output looks like, and you start to see the gap between a demo and something people can rely on.

Originally published at tonycantave.com by Tony Sterlin Cantave, a Connecticut software developer and AI model evaluator.

title: eBay Best Offer Accepted Price API: Get What Buyers Actually Paid (2026)
description:
An eBay Best Offer accepted price API answers a question eBay itself won't: what did the buyer actually pay?

When a listing sells through an accepted Best Offer, eBay's sold page shows the original asking price, struck through. The negotiated price stays hidden. If you build comps, price inventory or run a valuation tool, those asking prices quietly push every number you calculate upward.

Here is a real example from last week. A PSA 10 Charizard VMAX 074/073 (Champion's Path) sold on October 25, 2026:

What eBay shows What the buyer paid
$349.00 (asking price) $307.00 (accepted offer)

That's $42, or 12%, off the price you'd have recorded. In the same search, 11 of 60 recent sales closed on a Best Offer. Average those in at the asking price and your "market value" is fiction.

This post shows how to get the real number with one request.

The short version 

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $COMPSNIPER_API_KEY" \
  "https://api.compsniper.com/v1/scrape?keyword=psa+10+charizard+vmax+074&count=100&bestOfferPrice=true"

Add bestOfferPrice=true to a sold search and every sale that closed on an accepted offer gains two fields:

{
  "title": "2020 Pokemon SWSH FA Charizard Vmax 074/073 Champion's Path Secret PSA 10",
  "bestOfferAccepted": true,
  "soldPrice": "349.00",
  "acceptedOfferPrice": "307.00",
  "acceptedOfferPriceStatus": "found",
  "endedAt": "2026-10-25"
}
  • soldPrice is untouched: it's still the listed price, so you can see the discount.
  • acceptedOfferPrice is what the buyer paid.
  • acceptedOfferPriceStatus tells you where that price stands: found, pending (still being looked up, check back shortly) or not_available.

No eBay developer account, no seller access to the transaction, no scraping on your side. The free plan includes 100 requests a month, and the accepted price costs nothing extra.

Why the official eBay APIs don't help here

If you've tried to solve this with eBay's own tools, you've hit these walls:

  • Trading API GetBestOffers only returns offers on your own listings. Useless for market comps.
  • Browse API returns active listings only. No sold prices at all.
  • Finding API findCompletedItems was decommissioned in February 2025.
  • Marketplace Insights API is a limited release for approved partners, and it isn't taking most new developers.

So the accepted price on other sellers' sales is simply not available from eBay to a regular developer. That's the gap this fills.

Python: comps with the real accepted prices 

import os
import statistics
import requests

def sold_comps(keyword, count=100):
    r = requests.get(
        "https://api.compsniper.com/v1/scrape",
        headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['COMPSNIPER_API_KEY']}"},
        params={"keyword": keyword, "count": count, "bestOfferPrice": "true"},
        timeout=90,
    )
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()["items"]

def real_price(item):
    """Use the accepted offer when we have it, otherwise the sold price."""
    if item.get("bestOfferAccepted") and item.get("acceptedOfferPriceStatus") == "found":
        return float(item["acceptedOfferPrice"])
    return float(item["soldPrice"])

items = sold_comps("psa 10 charizard vmax 074")
asking = [float(i["soldPrice"]) for i in items]
paid = [real_price(i) for i in items]

print(f"median from eBay's displayed prices: ${statistics.median(asking):,.2f}")
print(f"median from what buyers paid:        ${statistics.median(paid):,.2f}")

for i in items:
    if i.get("acceptedOfferPriceStatus") == "found":
        print(f"{i['endedAt']}  asked ${i['soldPrice']}  paid ${i['acceptedOfferPrice']}  {i['title'][:60]}")

Prefer a package? pip install compsniper wraps the same calls with retries built in.

JavaScript (Node 18+, no dependencies) 

const params = new URLSearchParams({
  keyword: "psa 10 charizard vmax 074",
  count: "100",
  bestOfferPrice: "true",
});

const res = await fetch(`https://api.compsniper.com/v1/scrape?${params}`, {
  headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.COMPSNIPER_API_KEY}` },
});
if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`API error ${res.status}`);

const { items } = await res.json();
const realPrice = (i) =>
  i.bestOfferAccepted && i.acceptedOfferPriceStatus === "found"
    ? Number(i.acceptedOfferPrice)
    : Number(i.soldPrice);

for (const i of items.filter((x) => x.bestOfferAccepted)) {
  console.log(i.endedAt, "asked", i.soldPrice, "paid", i.acceptedOfferPrice ?? "(pending)", i.title);
}

What to do with pending

Accepted prices aren't always ready the moment a sale appears. A row marked pending is still being looked up. Two simple strategies:

  1. For a live price check, use the accepted price where it's found and fall back to the sold price elsewhere (the real_price helper above).
  2. For a database, store the item ID and re-check later. GET /v1/best-offer-prices?itemIds=... returns the latest status for up to 100 sales at once, so you can fill in the gaps on a schedule.

One more detail: accepted prices are returned for sales in US dollars on ebay.com. On other eBay sites, accepted-offer rows come back as not_available.

Where this matters most

  • Graded cards and collectibles: offers are everywhere, and a 10 to 15% gap on a $300 card is the difference between profit and loss.
  • Resale pricing tools: your users trust your "sold for" number. Asking prices make it wrong in the direction that hurts them.
  • Inventory valuation: one inflated comp per category compounds across thousands of SKUs.
  • Arbitrage bots: buying at the "market price" when the market really clears 12% lower is how bots lose money.

Try it

  1. Create a free account at compsniper.com and copy your API key.
  2. Run the curl above with your own search.
  3. Compare the two medians.

Full reference: Accepted Best Offer prices docs. Runnable examples: ebay-best-offer-price-api on GitHub.

Over to you: when you price items from eBay sold listings today, are you counting Best Offer sales at the asking price, or throwing them out entirely?
