title: Adding a Database Server Doubled Capacity. One Index Multiplied It by 2,600.
description:
Measure first, then climb the ladder.

The API is slow.

The dashboard takes two seconds to load. Someone opens the database graph and sees CPU at 100%.

Then the meeting starts.

"We need a read replica."
"Should we add Redis?"
"Maybe it's time to shard."

All three sound like serious engineering. All three cost money, add moving parts, and stay with you for years.

But nobody in that meeting has asked the first question: what is the database actually doing?

Nikki Siapno's recent Level Up Coding piece on scaling databases lays out a sensible order: measure the bottleneck, reduce the work, optimize queries, then add replicas, and shard last.

So this article puts that order to the test. One table, one slow query, one load test, and real measurements at each step.

The Test

The setup is a small PostgreSQL lab that you can run yourself. The full script is at the end of this article.

  • PostgreSQL 16.15 on a 2-core Linux cloud machine
  • An orders table with 5 million rows and 100,000 customers
  • One common query: the 20 latest orders for a customer
  • 8 clients sending that query as fast as they can for 30 seconds
  • Each step repeated 3 times, reporting the median

Here is the query:

SELECT id, status, amount, created_at
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 4242
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 20;

It looks harmless. You probably have one like it in your code right now.

To keep the comparison fair, the primary database was pinned to one CPU core. The second core ran the load generator, or the replica in the replica test.

The Results

Read that table twice.

The replica worked. Capacity went up about 2.2 times, which is close to what a second core should give.

But one CREATE INDEX on the original server handled about 2,600 times the traffic. It beat the two-server setup by about 1,180 times.

The index took 4.8 seconds to build and used 150 MB of disk.

Step 1: Measure the Bottleneck

Before touching anything, ask PostgreSQL where the time goes.

The pg_stat_statements extension records every query shape, how often it runs, and how long it takes. It must be added to shared_preload_libraries, which needs a restart.

SELECT calls,
       round(mean_exec_time::numeric, 1) AS avg_ms,
       round(total_exec_time::numeric / 1000, 1) AS total_seconds,
       left(query, 70) AS query
FROM pg_stat_statements
ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC
LIMIT 10;

Sort by total time, not average time. A 5 ms query that runs a million times hurts more than a 2 second report that runs once a day.

Next, look at the plan of your worst query:

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, status, amount, created_at
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 4242
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 20;

This is the real output from the test, shortened:

Limit (actual time=224.516..224.520 rows=20)
  Buffers: shared hit=66670
  -> Sort
       -> Seq Scan on orders
            Filter: (customer_id = 4242)
            Rows Removed by Filter: 4999944
Execution Time: 245.630 ms

Here is the whole problem in one line: Rows Removed by Filter: 4999944.

To find 56 rows for one customer, PostgreSQL read all 5 million. Think of a librarian who walks past every book in the building each time someone asks for one author.

No amount of extra hardware changes what this query is doing.

Different symptoms point to different problems:

What you see Look at first
High CPU, slow queries Query plans, missing indexes
Many rows read, few returned Indexes
Same query running repeatedly N+1 queries, caching
Too many connections Connection pooling
Slow only at peak, plans are ok Hardware or replicas
Fast database, slow API The app or another service
Slow writes, heavy disk use Write volume, too many indexes

These two queries help with the first pass:

-- Tables being read the hard way
SELECT relname, seq_scan, seq_tup_read, idx_scan,
       seq_tup_read / NULLIF(seq_scan, 0) AS rows_per_scan
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
ORDER BY seq_tup_read DESC
LIMIT 10;

-- Connection pressure
SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE state = 'active') AS active,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE state = 'idle in transaction') AS idle_in_txn,
       count(*) AS total,
       current_setting('max_connections') AS max
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE backend_type = 'client backend';

Step 2: The Replica Added Capacity, Not Speed

This is the step many teams take first, so it deserves a fair look.

With a replica, the same 8 clients were split between two servers. Throughput doubled and average latency fell from 2,020 ms to 926 ms.

That looks like a fix. It isn't.

With no load, the query took 246 ms on the primary and 304 ms on the replica. The plan on the replica was identical: same sequential scan, same 4,999,944 rows thrown away.

So where did the latency gain come from?

Queueing. With 8 clients on one core, each request spent most of its time waiting behind other requests. A second server shortened the line. The checkout was just as slow.

A replica shortens the queue. It does not make the work smaller.

The replica also brings bills of its own: another server to pay for and monitor, and one more problem that the next section measures.

Step 3: The Replica Problem Nobody Sees in Testing

A read replica copies changes from the primary a moment after they commit. That moment is called replication lag.

Here is the test. Insert a row on the primary, wait for the commit, then read it from the replica straight away. Do that 2,000 times.

This was the best possible case: both servers on the same machine, no network between them, and almost no load.

Idle Under write load
Writes tested 2,000 2,000
Row missing on first read 1,973 1,473
Median catch-up 0.33 ms 0.53 ms
Worst catch-up 18.44 ms 41.12 ms

98.65% of immediate reads missed the row on an idle system.

The replica was only 0.33 ms behind. That was still slower than the next read.

Don't read too much into the idle and load numbers being in that order. The point is that "very low lag" and "no stale reads" are different things. Across a real network, lag will be higher.

Your users meet this as a strange bug:

  1. A user updates their profile.
  2. The app redirects to the profile page.
  3. The page shows the old name.
  4. The user refreshes, and now it's correct.

The fix is to read from the primary right after a write. Here is a simple Django router that does this for the rest of a request:

import threading

_state = threading.local()

class PrimaryAfterWriteRouter:
    def db_for_read(self, model, **hints):
        return "default" if getattr(_state, "wrote", False) else "replica"

    def db_for_write(self, model, **hints):
        _state.wrote = True
        return "default"

    def allow_relation(self, obj1, obj2, **hints):
        return True

    def allow_migrate(self, db, app_label, **hints):
        return db == "default"

def primary_after_write_middleware(get_response):
    def middleware(request):
        _state.wrote = False
        try:
            return get_response(request)
        finally:
            _state.wrote = False
    return middleware

Add the class to DATABASE_ROUTERS and the middleware to MIDDLEWARE.

This covers one request. In the profile example, the redirect is a second request, so you also need something that carries over, such as a short-lived cookie or session flag that keeps that user on the primary for a few seconds.

Also keep money reads on the primary: balances, stock counts, permissions, and anything a decision depends on.

The Failure This Lab Hit by Accident

The first run of this test never finished.

During the write-heavy stage, the replica fell behind. PostgreSQL's primary keeps only a limited amount of old WAL (its change log), and it recycled the segment the replica still needed. The replica could never catch up, and the primary's log filled with this line every few seconds:

ERROR: requested WAL segment 00000001000000000000004C has already been removed

Nothing crashed. The replica stayed up and kept answering queries, while its data froze in the past. The test sat waiting for a row that would never arrive until it was stopped.

This is the scariest kind of failure: a healthy-looking server serving old data.

The fix was a replication slot, which makes the primary keep WAL until the replica has received it:

pg_basebackup -h primary -D /data/replica -R -X stream -c fast -C -S lab_slot

Slots have their own danger. If a replica dies and the slot stays, the primary keeps WAL forever and can fill its disk. Set max_slot_wal_keep_size as a limit, and watch both of these:

SELECT slot_name, active,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)) AS wal_held
FROM pg_replication_slots;

SELECT application_name, state,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), replay_lsn)) AS behind,
       replay_lag
FROM pg_stat_replication;

If a replica is missing from the second query, it has stopped replicating. Alert on that.

Step 4: Cache Only What Repeats

Redis is the next suggestion in most of these meetings, so the lab tested it on the slow, unindexed query.

The code is the standard cache-aside pattern: check Redis, and on a miss, query PostgreSQL and store the result for 5 minutes. One client ran for 60 seconds with three traffic patterns:

Traffic pattern Hit rate Average Median
All customers equally 0.4% 218 ms 210 ms
90% from 1,000 customers 9.8% 197 ms 209 ms
90% from 100 customers 84.7% 33 ms 0.08 ms

The third row is what people imagine when they say "add a cache." The first two rows are what can happen instead.

The cache did not fail. The traffic did not repeat enough. With 100,000 customers and about 5 slow queries a second, most keys were requested once and never seen again before the test ended.

Even in the best case, the misses stayed painful. The 95th percentile was still 219 ms, because every miss ran the same full table scan.

Compare that with the plain index: under 1 ms on average, even with 8 clients at full speed, with no hit rate to worry about and no invalidation to get wrong.

A cache makes a good query cheaper. It is a poor way to hide a bad one.

So before you add one, ask these questions:

  • Do the same keys get read again and again?
  • How stale can this data be?
  • Who invalidates it when the data changes?
  • What happens to the database if Redis restarts and every request misses?

That last one is a real risk. OpenAI's write-up, covered below, describes using cache locking and leasing so that only one reader fetches a missed key from PostgreSQL.

Step 5: The Index, and Its Bill

Here is the plan after one index:

CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_customer_created
ON orders (customer_id, created_at DESC);

Limit (actual time=0.034..0.205 rows=20)
  Buffers: shared hit=23
  -> Index Scan using orders_customer_created on orders
       Index Cond: (customer_id = 4242)
Execution Time: 0.228 ms

From 66,670 buffers to 23. From 245.6 ms to 0.23 ms.

The column order matters. customer_id narrows down to one customer, and created_at DESC means the rows are already sorted, so PostgreSQL can stop after 20. The sort step disappears.

Use CONCURRENTLY on a live table. A plain CREATE INDEX blocks writes while it builds. In Django, the safe version looks like this:

from django.contrib.postgres.operations import AddIndexConcurrently
from django.db import migrations, models

class Migration(migrations.Migration):
    atomic = False

    dependencies = [("orders", "0041_previous")]

    operations = [
        AddIndexConcurrently(
            model_name="order",
            index=models.Index(
                fields=["customer_id", "-created_at"],
                name="orders_customer_created",
            ),
        ),
    ]

If a concurrent build fails, it leaves an invalid index behind. Drop it and try again.

Indexes are not free, though. The lab measured insert speed on a 1 million row table with no indexes, 1 index, and 5 indexes:

Indexes Inserts/sec Index size
0 6,524 0 MB
1 5,879 17 MB
5 5,178 131 MB

Five indexes cost about 21% of write speed on this test. These runs were noisy, and the ranges for 0 and 1 index overlapped, so treat the trend as the finding, not the exact percentage.

The cost grows with every index you never use. This query finds the candidates:

SELECT s.relname, s.indexrelname, s.idx_scan,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(s.indexrelid)) AS size
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes s
JOIN pg_index i ON i.indexrelid = s.indexrelid
WHERE s.idx_scan = 0
  AND NOT i.indisunique
  AND NOT i.indisprimary
ORDER BY pg_relation_size(s.indexrelid) DESC;

Before you drop one, remember these counts are per server. An index with no scans on the primary may be busy on a replica.

Step 6: Shard Last, and Mean It

This lab did not test sharding. It would need several machines to say anything honest. So here are two real teams that lived at the top of the ladder.

Case study: Figma

Figma's database team describes a stack that grew almost 100x since 2020.

They climbed in order. In 2020 they ran a single Postgres database on AWS's largest physical instance. By the end of 2022 they had caching, read replicas, and about a dozen vertically partitioned databases, with related tables split into their own groups.

Only then did they hit real limits. Some tables reached several terabytes and billions of rows, and the highest-write tables neared the IOPS limit on RDS.

Horizontal sharding started in late 2022. The first table took roughly nine months and shipped in September 2023. Figma called the work "an order of magnitude more complex" than their earlier scaling, and listed what it gave up: cross-shard transactions, foreign keys, and globally unique indexes.

Case study: OpenAI

OpenAI's January 2026 post describes serving 800 million ChatGPT users on PostgreSQL, with one primary handling writes and nearly 50 read replicas.

They did not shard their PostgreSQL deployment. Their reasons: sharding would mean changing hundreds of endpoints and could take months or years, and the workload is mainly reads.

But they were not doing nothing. They optimized queries, reviewed ORM-generated SQL, used PgBouncer, put a cache in front, and moved shardable, write-heavy workloads to systems such as Azure Cosmos DB.

Note what both stories share. Neither team reached for the biggest tool first, and both moved based on a specific limit they had measured.

Signs you might really need sharding

  • A write bottleneck on the primary that remains after query and index work
  • A single table so large that maintenance like vacuum causes reliability problems
  • Storage or IOPS limits on the largest machine you can buy
  • Isolating noisy tables into their own database has already been done

Replicas will not help with any of these writes, because every replica has to apply every write too.

And there is a smaller step that people skip. PostgreSQL partitioning splits a big table into pieces on the same server, which helps with time-based data and deleting old rows, with no routing layer at all.

The Ladder

Here is the order, with the question that earns each step:

Step Question that earns it
1. Measure What exactly is slow?
2. Do less Do we need this query at all?
3. Fix queries Is it reading more rows than it returns?
4. Pool Are connections the limit?
5. Cache Do the same reads repeat, and can they be stale?
6. Scale up Is a healthy query simply short of hardware?
7. Replicas Are reads the limit, and can they lag?
8. Partition Is one table too big to manage?
9. Shard Are writes or data size beyond one primary?

You can stop at any step. Most systems should.

What This Test Does Not Prove

  • 2,600x is not a promise. This query was chosen because it had no index on a big table. It is a best case for indexing. If your query already uses a good index, you will see nothing like this.
  • The replica test was a clean case. One extra core, no network, and only reads. Real replicas also have to replay writes.
  • One query is not a workload. Real systems have many query shapes competing for the same resources.
  • The numbers depend on the machine. This was a small shared cloud machine, and baseline runs ranged from 3.7 to 5.5 requests per second. Trust the size of the gaps, not the decimals.
  • Cold caches matter. The replica's 304 ms included reading pages into memory for the first time, while the primary's data was already cached.

What To Do on Monday

  1. Turn on pg_stat_statements if it's off, and find your top 10 queries by total time.
  2. Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on each one. Look for a high Rows Removed by Filter.
  3. Check for N+1 queries. In Django, select_related and prefetch_related can remove whole groups of queries.
  4. Add indexes from real query patterns, using CONCURRENTLY.
  5. Drop indexes nobody uses, after checking every replica.
  6. Before any new infrastructure, write down the number it should change. "Replica will take p95 from X to Y." If nobody can fill in that sentence, the measuring isn't finished.
  7. If you already have replicas, alert on lag and on a replica going missing, and list which reads must stay on the primary.

Common Questions

Should I add an index for every slow query?
No. Start with queries that run often. An index for a report that runs once a month may cost more in write overhead than it saves.

Is high CPU always a reason to scale up?
No. High CPU tells you the database is working hard. The query plan tells you whether that work is necessary. In this test, a missing index was creating almost all of it.

Can a replica ever beat an index?
Yes, when queries are already efficient and you simply have too many of them. That is exactly when replicas earn their cost.

When should I cache instead of optimizing?
When a query is already good but runs constantly on data that rarely changes. A homepage product list is a classic example.

Do managed databases solve this?
They help with backups, replicas and failover. They will not fix a sequential scan on 5 million rows.

Are ORMs the problem?
Not by themselves. But they make it easy to run queries you never see. OpenAI's post specifically calls out reviewing ORM-generated SQL.

Run It Yourself

Run this on a throwaway machine or container with at least 2 cores, and allow about 15 minutes. It creates and deletes its own data in /tmp/scaling-lab.

docker run -it --rm --cpus=2 ubuntu:24.04 bash

# inside the container
apt-get update
apt-get install -y postgresql redis-server python3-psycopg2 python3-redis util-linux

Save the script below as /tmp/scaling_lab.py, then run it as the postgres user:

chmod a+r /tmp/scaling_lab.py
su postgres -s /bin/bash -c \
  'cd /tmp && PATH=/usr/lib/postgresql/16/bin:$PATH python3 /tmp/scaling_lab.py'

The results are saved to lab_results.json. Change one thing at a time: try 20 million rows, a hotter or colder cache pattern, or a real replica on a second machine.

Click to expand the full lab script (scaling_lab.py)

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Database scaling lab: test each step of the scaling ladder on one workload.

Stages: measure, read replica, cache, index, index write cost, stale reads.
Needs PostgreSQL 16 with contrib, Redis, psycopg2, redis-py and 2 CPU cores.
Run as a non-root user with the PostgreSQL bin directory on PATH.
Use a throwaway machine. It creates and deletes its own data in BASE.
"""
import json, os, random, re, shutil, statistics as st, subprocess as sp, time
import psycopg2, redis

BASE = "/tmp/scaling-lab"
P, R, RP = 55432, 55433, 56379
ROWS, CUSTOMERS, RUN_S, REPEATS = 5_000_000, 100_000, 30, 3
READ = ("SELECT id, status, amount, created_at FROM orders "
        "WHERE customer_id = %s ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20")
out = {}

def sh(cmd, core=None, check=True):
    if core is not None:
        cmd = f"taskset -c {core} {cmd}"
    r = sp.run(cmd, shell=True, capture_output=True, text=True)
    if check and r.returncode:
        raise RuntimeError(cmd + "\n" + r.stdout + r.stderr)
    return r.stdout

def conn(port=P):
    c = psycopg2.connect(host=BASE, port=port, dbname="postgres")
    c.autocommit = True
    return c

def q(sql, port=P):
    c = conn(port); cur = c.cursor(); cur.execute(sql)
    rows = cur.fetchall() if cur.description else []
    c.close()
    return rows

def plan(port=P):
    rows = q("EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) " + READ.replace("%s", "4242"), port)
    return [r[0] for r in rows]

def pgbench(port, script, clients, core, seconds=RUN_S):
    cmd = (f"pgbench -n -h {BASE} -p {port} -f {script} -c {clients} -j 1 "
           f"-T {seconds} postgres")
    return sp.Popen(f"taskset -c {core} {cmd}", shell=True, stdout=sp.PIPE,
                    stderr=sp.STDOUT, text=True)

def parse(text):
    tps = float(re.search(r"tps = ([\d.]+)", text).group(1))
    lat = float(re.search(r"latency average = ([\d.]+) ms", text).group(1))
    return tps, lat

def setup():
    shutil.rmtree(BASE, ignore_errors=True); os.makedirs(BASE)
    sh(f"initdb -D {BASE}/p -A trust")
    with open(f"{BASE}/p/postgresql.conf", "a") as f:
        f.write(f"port={P}\nunix_socket_directories='{BASE}'\nlisten_addresses=''\n"
                "shared_buffers=1GB\nmax_parallel_workers_per_gather=0\n"
                "shared_preload_libraries='pg_stat_statements'\nwal_level=replica\n"
                "max_wal_senders=5\nhot_standby=on\nmax_connections=50\n")
    with open(f"{BASE}/p/pg_hba.conf", "a") as f:
        f.write("local replication all trust\n")
    sh(f"pg_ctl -D {BASE}/p -l {BASE}/p.log -w start", core=0)
    q("CREATE EXTENSION pg_stat_statements")
    q(f"""CREATE TABLE orders(id bigserial PRIMARY KEY, customer_id int NOT NULL,
          status text NOT NULL, amount int NOT NULL,
          created_at timestamptz NOT NULL, note text NOT NULL)""")
    q(f"""INSERT INTO orders(customer_id, status, amount, created_at, note)
          SELECT (random()*{CUSTOMERS-1})::int + 1,
                 (ARRAY['new','paid','shipped','done'])[1+(random()*3)::int],
                 (random()*50000)::int,
                 now() - random() * interval '365 days', repeat('x', 40)
          FROM generate_series(1, {ROWS})""")
    q("ANALYZE orders")
    with open(f"{BASE}/read.sql", "w") as f:
        f.write(f"\\set cid random(1, {CUSTOMERS})\n" + READ.replace("%s", ":cid") + ";\n")
    with open(f"{BASE}/write.sql", "w") as f:
        f.write(f"\\set cid random(1, {CUSTOMERS})\n\\set amt random(1, 50000)\n"
                "INSERT INTO orders_w(customer_id,status,amount,created_at,note) "
                "VALUES (:cid,'new',:amt,now(),repeat('x',40));\n")
    with open(f"{BASE}/load.sql", "w") as f:
        f.write(f"\\set cid random(1, {CUSTOMERS})\n\\set amt random(1, 50000)\n"
                "INSERT INTO orders(customer_id,status,amount,created_at,note) "
                "VALUES (:cid,'new',:amt,now(),repeat('x',40));\n")
    q("SELECT count(*) FROM orders")
    out["table_mb"] = q("SELECT pg_total_relation_size('orders')/1048576")[0][0]

def start_replica():
    sh(f"pg_basebackup -h {BASE} -p {P} -D {BASE}/r -R -X stream -c fast -C -S lab_slot")
    with open(f"{BASE}/r/postgresql.conf", "a") as f:
        f.write(f"port={R}\nmax_connections=50\n")
    sh(f"pg_ctl -D {BASE}/r -l {BASE}/r.log -w start", core=1)
    for _ in range(100):
        if q("SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_replication")[0][0]:
            break
        time.sleep(0.2)
    q("SELECT count(*) FROM orders", R)

def stage_baseline():
    results = []
    q("SELECT pg_stat_statements_reset()")
    for _ in range(REPEATS):
        p = pgbench(P, f"{BASE}/read.sql", 8, 1)
        results.append(parse(p.communicate()[0]))
    out["baseline"] = results
    out["top_query"] = q("""SELECT calls, round(mean_exec_time::numeric,1),
        round(total_exec_time::numeric/1000,1), shared_blks_hit+shared_blks_read,
        left(query,70) FROM pg_stat_statements ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC LIMIT 1""")
    q(READ.replace("%s", "4242"))
    out["plan_noindex"] = plan()

def stage_replica():
    results = []
    for _ in range(REPEATS):
        a = pgbench(P, f"{BASE}/read.sql", 4, 1)
        b = pgbench(R, f"{BASE}/read.sql", 4, 0)
        ra, rb = parse(a.communicate()[0]), parse(b.communicate()[0])
        results.append((ra[0] + rb[0], (ra[1] + rb[1]) / 2))
    out["replica"] = results
    out["plan_replica"] = plan(R)

def stage_cache():
    os.sched_setaffinity(0, {1})
    r = redis.Redis(unix_socket_path=f"{BASE}/redis.sock")
    pg = conn(); cur = pg.cursor()
    def get_orders(cid):
        key = f"orders:{cid}"
        hit = r.get(key)
        if hit is not None:
            return True
        cur.execute(READ, (cid,))
        r.set(key, json.dumps(cur.fetchall(), default=str), ex=300)
        return False
    def run(pick, seconds=60):
        r.flushall()
        times, hits, end = [], 0, time.monotonic() + seconds
        while time.monotonic() < end:
            t = time.perf_counter(); hits += get_orders(pick())
            times.append((time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000)
        times.sort()
        return dict(requests=len(times), hit_rate=round(hits / len(times), 3),
                    mean_ms=round(st.mean(times), 2), p50_ms=round(times[len(times)//2], 2),
                    p95_ms=round(times[int(len(times)*.95)], 2))
    out["cache_uniform"] = run(lambda: random.randint(1, CUSTOMERS))
    def hot(size):
        return lambda: (random.randint(1, size) if random.random() < .9
                        else random.randint(1, CUSTOMERS))
    out["cache_hot_1000"] = run(hot(1000))
    out["cache_hot_100"] = run(hot(100))
    pg.close(); os.sched_setaffinity(0, {0, 1})

def stage_index():
    t = time.monotonic()
    q("CREATE INDEX orders_customer_created ON orders (customer_id, created_at DESC)")
    out["index_build_s"] = round(time.monotonic() - t, 1)
    out["index_mb"] = q("SELECT pg_relation_size('orders_customer_created')/1048576")[0][0]
    q(READ.replace("%s", "4242"))
    out["plan_index"] = plan()
    results = []
    for _ in range(REPEATS):
        p = pgbench(P, f"{BASE}/read.sql", 8, 1)
        results.append(parse(p.communicate()[0]))
    out["indexed"] = results

def stage_writes():
    extra = ["customer_id", "created_at", "status", "amount", "(customer_id, created_at DESC)"]
    res = {}
    for n in (0, 1, 5):
        q("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS orders_w")
        q("CREATE TABLE orders_w (LIKE orders INCLUDING DEFAULTS)")
        q("ALTER TABLE orders_w ALTER id SET DEFAULT nextval('orders_id_seq')")
        q("INSERT INTO orders_w SELECT * FROM orders LIMIT 1000000")
        for i, col in enumerate(extra[:n]):
            q(f"CREATE INDEX w{i} ON orders_w ({col.strip('()')})")
        q("CHECKPOINT")
        tps = []
        for _ in range(REPEATS):
            p = pgbench(P, f"{BASE}/write.sql", 4, 1, 20)
            tps.append(parse(p.communicate()[0])[0])
        res[n] = dict(tps=tps, index_mb=q("SELECT pg_indexes_size('orders_w')/1048576")[0][0])
    out["writes"] = res
    q("DROP TABLE orders_w")

def stale(n=2000, limit_s=35, give_up_s=5):
    wr, rd = conn(P), conn(R)
    w, c = wr.cursor(), rd.cursor()
    miss, lag, gave_up, end = 0, [], 0, time.monotonic() + limit_s
    for _ in range(n):
        if time.monotonic() > end:
            break
        w.execute("INSERT INTO orders(customer_id,status,amount,created_at,note) "
                  "VALUES (1,'new',1,now(),'x') RETURNING id")
        i = w.fetchone()[0]; t = time.perf_counter(); first = True
        while True:
            c.execute("SELECT 1 FROM orders WHERE id = %s", (i,))
            if c.fetchone():
                break
            if first:
                miss += 1; first = False
            if time.perf_counter() - t > give_up_s:
                gave_up += 1
                break
        lag.append((time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000)
    wr.close(); rd.close(); lag.sort()
    return dict(reads=len(lag), stale_first_read=miss, gave_up=gave_up,
                p50_ms=round(lag[len(lag)//2], 3), p99_ms=round(lag[int(len(lag)*.99)], 2),
                max_ms=round(lag[-1], 2))

def stage_stale():
    out["stale_idle"] = stale()
    p = pgbench(P, f"{BASE}/load.sql", 8, 1, 45)
    time.sleep(3)
    out["stale_load"] = stale()
    out["lag_under_load"] = q("""SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(
        pg_current_wal_lsn(), replay_lsn)), replay_lag::text
        FROM pg_stat_replication""")
    p.wait()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(sh("postgres --version").strip(), flush=True)
    setup()
    sh(f"redis-server --port 0 --unixsocket {BASE}/redis.sock --save '' --daemonize yes --dir {BASE}")
    for name, fn in [("baseline", stage_baseline), ("replica_start", start_replica),
                     ("replica", stage_replica), ("cache", stage_cache),
                     ("index", stage_index), ("writes", stage_writes), ("stale", stage_stale)]:
        t = time.monotonic(); fn()
        print(name, "done in", round(time.monotonic() - t), "s", flush=True)
        json.dump(out, open("lab_results.json", "w"), indent=1, default=str)
    sh(f"pg_ctl -D {BASE}/r -m fast -w stop", check=False)
    sh(f"pg_ctl -D {BASE}/p -m fast -w stop", check=False)
    sh(f"redis-cli -s {BASE}/redis.sock shutdown nosave", check=False)

Back to That Meeting

"We need a read replica."

Maybe you do. In this test, the replica did what it promised: it doubled capacity.

But it also cost a second server, introduced stale reads, and left a 5-million-row scan behind every request. One line of SQL did far more.

Here is the short version:

  • Measure first. One EXPLAIN showed 4,999,944 wasted rows.
  • Replicas add capacity. They don't make a bad query good.
  • Replicas lag. Even at 0.33 ms, 98.65% of immediate reads missed the row.
  • Caches need repetition. Hit rate ranged from 0.4% to 84.7% on the same code.
  • Indexes have a bill. Five of them cost about 21% of insert speed here.
  • Sharding is real work. Teams like Figma did it only after hitting measured limits.

So the next time someone says "we need to scale," ask one question first:

Which number is the bottleneck, and how do we know?

Over to You

What was the most expensive scaling step your team took that one index could have avoided? Tell me in the comments 👇

Test details: PostgreSQL 16.15 and Redis on a 2-core Linux cloud machine. 5 million rows, 8 clients, 3 repeats per step with medians reported. Numbers will vary on other machines. The scaling order in this piece follows Nikki Siapno's article on database scaling in the Level Up Coding System Design Newsletter (October 2026).

If this was useful, follow me here for more stories from the backend trenches, and subscribe to The Backend Tech Lead on Substack for weekly blueprints.

title: Introducing Run SDK: secure eval for your agents
description:
Agents increasingly write TypeScript programs to coordinate tools and process their results. Once those programs touch real applications, some steps require authentication, while others need human approval.

Executing that code with eval gives it the same access as the application around it, including its secrets and internal services, and leaves no durable way to pause at those boundaries.

Today, we're releasing the Run SDK, a package for executing untrusted JavaScript and TypeScript without giving it direct access to your application or system. Applications expose narrow host functions and can interrupt execution for authentication or human-in-the-loop approval. The program resumes after a decision without repeating completed work.

A small interface to the host

The Run SDK evaluates JavaScript or type-stripped TypeScript in a fresh QuickJS context inside a worker thread, with no direct route to Node.js or the network.

The application exposes selected operations through hostFunctions. These are regular functions that become callable globals inside the sandbox:

Here, the generated program knows about store.listOrders(). The database client and its credentials remain in the application.

Calls cross the sandbox boundary through serialization. A host function may return a promise, so existing service clients can sit behind this interface without being passed into the sandbox.

You can try this in the playground. Code you run there can only reach the host functions on the page.

Code mode in practice

The Run SDK is the internal module powering code mode tool execution in the AI SDK. Giving an agent a program changes the unit of work. One model response can describe the calls and the logic connecting them:

The two requests happen concurrently, and invoice filtering stays local to the program. Only the useful result returns to the application.

This is a good fit for agents that work across several internal services. A research agent can combine search results before answering. A support agent can inspect an account without putting an entire billing response back into its context.

The same package can power a code interpreter or a product feature that accepts customer-defined transformations. In both cases, the application chooses the available data and operations.

Host functions work best when they map to actions in your product, like refunding an order. Exposing orders.refund(id) gives the application a clear place to check the user and the order. A generic request function would make that authority much harder to reason about.

Native support for human-in-the-loop and auth

Reading invoices is different from issuing a refund. When generated code reaches a sensitive operation, the host function can interrupt execution:

When the run is interrupted, the result includes a signed token the application can save with an approval request and use to resume the run when a decision arrives.

Resuming replays the program, but settled host function calls use their recorded results. Host function work completed before the interruption does not run again. The interrupted function receives the approval and continues from there.

This mechanism also works when a workflow must wait for authentication. The application owns the waiting period; the worker does not need to remain alive.

Running within limits

A sandbox still needs to account for code that loops forever or produces an oversized result. createRunner() sets shared limits:

Limits can also be set per run. The defaults cover the QuickJS heap and the values crossing the host boundary; applications can tighten them for their workload.

Each invocation receives a new QuickJS context. Dynamic evaluation is disabled and built-in prototypes are hardened. This boundary applies to the generated program, while host functions remain trusted application code and must perform their normal authorization checks.

The Run SDK is intended for JavaScript computation inside an application. Workloads that require an operating system, package installation, or process-level isolation should use Vercel Sandbox instead.

Extracting the execution layer

The first version of this runtime lived inside just-bash as js-exec, backed by QuickJS. It let agents write TypeScript against the shell's virtual filesystem and command set.

We extracted that layer into the Run SDK and replaced the Node-shaped environment with application-defined host functions. We tested the underlying mechanism in eve, using it to run agent-generated TypeScript against real tools. It now powers code mode in the AI SDK where existing AI SDK tools are mapped to host functions, while the Run SDK handles their sandboxed execution.

Getting started

The Run SDK supports Node.js 22.13+ and Bun. You will need pnpm or another package manager installed on your local development machine.

Check out the documentation and API reference.

Read more

title: The A2A CLI and Rust: The Same Code, Three Ways to Serve It
description:
This article provides a step by step guide to the A2A CLI, driven against Rust agents that speak A2A Protocol v1.0. The same Rust code, a Lucas-Lehmer test over the first N Mersenne prime exponents, is served three ways: on the official A2A Rust SDK, as a plain stdin/stdout program wrapped by a2a server --exec, and behind an ADK coordinator on Gemini started with the ADK CLI. Each one is timed from the A2A CLI and from a Rust client.

https://github.com/xbill9/rust-dev/tree/main/a2a-benchmark-rust

The A2A CLI talks to all three with the same commands, and a2a server --exec turns a 30-line program with no A2A code into an agent that ADK can call. One a2a send from a shell takes a median 20.74 ms against the SDK agent, of which 7.62 ms is starting the CLI. From a Rust client the SDK agent adds 0.55 to 1.40 ms per call, the wrapped program 3.33 to 5.05 ms, and the ADK coordinator a median 1328 ms on gemini-3.5-flash and 2283 ms on gemini-3.8-flash. Every call through N=26 returned the right count of primes.

What Is Being Built?

Agent Port How it speaks A2A
mersenne-agent 8104 Official Rust SDK, JSON-RPC at /jsonrpc and HTTP+JSON at /rest
mersenne-exec 8105 A stdin/stdout Rust program served by a2a server --exec
rust_bench 8106 ADK LlmAgent on Gemini, served by adk api_server --a2a
echo 8108 a2a server --echo, for the first command 
a2a CLI ──► adk api_server --a2a (:8106) ──Gemini──► RemoteA2aAgent ──► mersenne-agent (:8104)
                    rust_bench                                     └──► a2a server --exec (:8105) ──► mersenne-exec
                        └── run_benchmark tool ──► mersenne-bench ──► both Rust agents

Versions, read from the machine on 2026-11-03:

Component Version
A2A protocol 1.0
A2A CLI (a2a) v0.3.1
a2a-lf / a2a-server-lf / a2a-client-lf 0.4.2 / 0.5.3 / 0.2.9
Rust 1.99.1, edition 2024
google-adk / a2a-sdk / google-genai 2.13.0 / 1.3.0 / 2.34.0
Model gemini-3.8-flash on Vertex AI

The a2a-*-lf crates are the official SDK from a2aproject/a2a-rs. Agent cards carry the protocol as Major.Minor, so they read 1.0.

Step 1 — Install the A2A CLI

The CLI is one Go binary. Homebrew, WinGet and release binaries work; from source:

go install github.com/a2aproject/a2a-cli@latest
mv "$(command -v a2a-cli)" "$(dirname "$(command -v a2a-cli)")/a2a"
a2a version

a2a v0.3.1
commit:  none
built:   unknown
go:      go1.26.3
os/arch: linux/amd64

go install names the binary a2a-cli; the docs and the CLI's own skill call it a2a.

Step 2 — Talk to an Echo Server

a2a server --echo starts an agent that sends back what it receives, so the client can be checked before any agent code exists:

a2a server --echo --port 8108 &
a2a send -a http://localhost:8108 "hello world from A2A"

Task:     01a1a35f-2b2b-7f3a-92a2-e3dc6c69e359
Context:  01a1a35f-2b2c-7120-ac45-a74adab9d1d2
Status:   completed (2026-11-03T16:44:45-05:00)
Artifacts:
  [01a1a35f-2b2c-71ba-8e6c-22c4b7c210df] hello world from A2A
History:
  [user] hello world from A2A

Every send creates a task with an id, a context, a final status and its artifacts. The Go servers started by the CLI stamp local time; the Rust SDK agent stamps UTC.

Step 3 — Build and Start the Rust Agents

The rig is one Cargo project with four binaries: the SDK agent, the stdin/stdout program, the benchmark client, and a shared library holding the Lucas-Lehmer code.

git clone https://github.com/xbill9/rust-dev
cd rust-dev/a2a-benchmark-rust
cargo build --release
scripts/start-all.sh

agents up: 8104 native, 8105 exec

start-all.sh rebuilds, stops any running copy, starts the SDK agent on 8104 and a2a server --exec on 8105 with logs in logs/, and waits until both cards answer. scripts/test-cli.sh runs the CLI commands below against them and checks each reply.

Step 4 — Read an Agent Card

card get fetches /.well-known/agent-card.json and prints what the agent offers:

a2a card get -a http://localhost:8104

Name:         Mersenne Prime Agent Rust
Description:  A Rust A2A v1.0 agent (official a2a-rs SDK) that confirms the first n Mersenne primes with the Lucas-Lehmer test and reports the elapsed time.
Version:      0.1.0
Interfaces:
  JSONRPC (A2A v1.0)     http://localhost:8104/jsonrpc
  HTTP+JSON (A2A v1.0)   http://localhost:8104/rest
Streaming:    true
Skills:
  find-mersenne-rust   Find Mersenne Primes in Rust

The card lists two interfaces. The CLI picks one, and --transport chooses.

Step 5 — Send, Stream, Switch Transport, Send Data

A plain message:

a2a send -a http://localhost:8104 "Calculate the first 12 Mersenne primes"

Status:   completed (2026-11-03T21:44:45Z)
  Found first 12 Mersenne primes in 0.0902ms.
Artifacts:
  [mersenne-report] Found first 12 Mersenne primes in 0.0902ms. {"elapsed_ms":0.090239,"exponents":[2,3,5,7,13,17,19,31,61,89,107,127],"found":12,"requested":12}

The mersenne-report artifact carries two parts: the summary as text, and the same result as a data part, so a client reads the timing from a field.

--stream prints each event as it arrives, here the working status before the result:

a2a send -a http://localhost:8104 --stream "first 8"

[status] working
Task:     01a1a35f-2b64-77b5-9417-18b1f425b17d
Context:  01a1a35f-2b64-77b5-9417-18b24253b719
Status:   completed (2026-11-03T21:44:45Z)
  Found first 8 Mersenne primes in 0.0164ms.

--transport rest sends the same request over HTTP+JSON, and --data-part sends structured input:

a2a send -a http://localhost:8104 --transport rest "first 4"
a2a send -a http://localhost:8104 --data-part '{"count": 6}'

  Found first 4 Mersenne primes in 0.0080ms.
  Found first 6 Mersenne primes in 0.0108ms.

🔎 Tip: Data Parts Arrive as Floats

A2A v1.0 carries data parts as a protobuf Struct, whose only number type is a double. {"count": 6} sent by the CLI reaches the agent as 6.0, so a strict integer field fails to deserialise. Read numbers with as_f64 and check for a whole value:

if let PartContent::Data(v) = &part.content
    && let Some(n) = v.get("count").and_then(|n| n.as_f64())
    && n >= 1.0
    && n.fract() == 0.0
{
    return n as usize;
}

Step 6 — Script It With JSON Output

-o json prints the whole task, which pipes into anything:

a2a send -a http://localhost:8104 -o json 'first 3' | python3 -c 'import sys,json; t=json.load(sys.stdin)["task"]; print(t["status"]["state"], [p for a in t["artifacts"] for p in a["parts"] if "data" in p][0]["data"])'

TASK_STATE_COMPLETED {'elapsed_ms': 0.007166, 'exponents': [2, 3, 5], 'found': 3, 'requested': 3}

Step 7 — Tasks: List, Start in the Background, Wait

The SDK agent keeps its tasks in memory, and the CLI reads them back:

a2a task list -a http://localhost:8104

ID                                    STATUS     CONTEXT
01a1a35f-2b4f-7190-b6df-81bb7b76c2cc  completed  01a1a35f-2b4f-7190-b6df-81bca35e8b6d
01a1a35f-2b64-77b5-9417-18b1f425b17d  completed  01a1a35f-2b64-77b5-9417-18b24253b719
01a1a35f-2bab-7012-b094-1022dce75f36  completed  01a1a35f-2bab-7012-b094-1023824b35eb

--async returns as soon as the task exists. N=25 takes over a second, long enough to catch it running:

a2a send -a http://localhost:8104 --async "first 25"

Task:     01a1a3f5-9da1-746b-abae-84307e4e1735
Context:  01a1a3f5-9da1-746b-abae-8431b422e72e
Status:   working (2026-11-04T00:29:05Z)
History:
  [user] first 25

task get --wait polls until the task finishes:

a2a task get -a http://localhost:8104 01a1a3f5-9da1-746b-abae-84307e4e1735 --wait --poll-interval 500ms

Task:     01a1a3f5-9da1-746b-abae-84307e4e1735
Context:  01a1a3f5-9da1-746b-abae-8431b422e72e
Status:   completed (2026-11-04T00:29:06Z)
  Found first 25 Mersenne primes in 1509.7683ms.

Step 8 — The Native Rust Agent

The SDK agent is one AgentExecutor. It emits a working status, runs the big-integer work on a blocking thread, then returns the finished task:

let done = async move {
    // Big-integer work is CPU-bound; keep it off the async workers.
    let report = tokio::task::spawn_blocking(move || find_mersenne_primes(count))
        .await
        .map_err(|e| A2AError::internal(format!("worker panicked: {e}")))?;
    let summary = report.summary();
    let data = serde_json::to_value(&report)
        .map_err(|e| A2AError::internal(format!("serialise report: {e}")))?;
    // ... Task { status: Completed, artifacts: [Part::text(summary), Part::data(data)] }
};
Box::pin(stream::once(async { Ok(working) }).chain(stream::once(done)))

The server wires the SDK's routers into axum, one per transport plus the card:

let handler = Arc::new(DefaultRequestHandler::new(MersenneExecutor, InMemoryTaskStore::new()));
let card = Arc::new(StaticAgentCard::new(agent_card(&base)));

let app = axum::Router::new()
    .nest("/jsonrpc", a2a_server::jsonrpc::jsonrpc_router(handler.clone()))
    .nest("/rest", a2a_server::rest::rest_router(handler))
    .merge(a2a_server::agent_card::agent_card_router(card));

The Lucas-Lehmer test runs on num-bigint with the reduction mod 2^p − 1 done by folding the high bits onto the low ones. The timed region holds only the tests, on a monotonic clock, and no prime is ever turned into a decimal string. Two slow tests check the arithmetic: one runs the test on every prime exponent up to 9941 and asserts it accepts exactly the first 22 known ones, the other confirms all 26:

cargo test --release --lib -- --ignored

test tests::all_26_exponents_prime ... ok
test tests::exhaustive_through_n22 ... ok

test result: ok. 2 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 5 filtered out; finished in 25.70s

Step 9 — Serve a Plain Program With a2a server --exec

mersenne-exec knows nothing about A2A. It reads the message on stdin and prints two lines:

echo 'first 5' | target/release/mersenne-exec

{"requested":5,"found":5,"elapsed_ms":0.007023000000000001,"exponents":[2,3,5,7,13]}
Found first 5 Mersenne primes in 0.0070ms.

The A2A CLI makes it an agent:

a2a server --exec "$PWD/target/release/mersenne-exec" --chunk=$'\n' \
  --name "Mersenne Prime Exec Rust" \
  --advertise-address "http://localhost:8105" --port 8105

The same client commands work against it:

a2a send -a http://localhost:8105 --stream "first 8"

Status:   submitted
History:
  [user] first 8
[status] working
[artifact] {"requested":8,"found":8,"elapsed_ms":0.01543,"exponents":[2,3,5,7,13,17,19,31]}Found first 8 Mersenne primes in 0.0154ms.
[status] completed

The exec server starts the program once per message, hands it the text, and returns stdout as the artifact.

🔎 Tip: Two --exec Flags ADK Needs

  • --advertise-address http://localhost:8105. The exec server's card names 127.0.0.1 by default, and ADK's RemoteA2aAgent refuses a card whose RPC URL has a different origin from the one the card came from.
  • --chunk=$'\n'. With it, each output line streams as its own chunk. Without it, stream requests get UNSUPPORTED_OPERATION: the Go CLI falls back to polling and ADK's Python client fails. ADK keeps only the last chunk, so mersenne-exec prints the JSON line first and the summary last.

Step 10 — Put ADK in Front

ADK needs its Python package and Gemini on Vertex AI, signed in with application-default credentials:

pip install -U "google-adk[a2a]"
gcloud auth application-default login
source scripts/adk-env.sh

adk-env.sh sets GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_VERTEXAI=TRUE, GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION=global, the project, and MODEL_NAME, which defaults to gemini-3.8-flash.

adk/rust_bench/agent.py is an ADK LlmAgent with both Rust agents as RemoteA2aAgent sub-agents and one tool:

native_agent = RemoteA2aAgent(
    name="native_rust_agent",
    description="Rust A2A v1.0 agent on the official a2a-rs SDK. ...",
    agent_card=f"{NATIVE_URL}{AGENT_CARD_WELL_KNOWN_PATH}",
)

root_agent = LlmAgent(
    name="rust_bench",
    model=os.getenv("MODEL_NAME", "gemini-3.8-flash"),
    tools=[run_benchmark],
    sub_agents=[native_agent, exec_agent],
)

The ADK CLI runs it three ways:

adk run rust_bench                                # terminal
adk web --port 8107                               # dev UI
adk api_server --a2a --port 8106 adk              # A2A server, from the rig root

adk api_server --a2a serves each agent folder that holds an agent.json card, at /a2a/<name>; scripts/start-adk.sh starts it in the background. The A2A CLI then treats the coordinator like any other agent:

a2a send -a http://localhost:8106/a2a/rust_bench/.well-known/agent-card.json \
  --timeout 120s "Find the first 9 Mersenne primes with the exec agent"

Status:   completed (2026-11-03T21:44:51Z)
Artifacts:
  [f2d2f27d-24ce-4120-8368-d966c99617a9] Found first 9 Mersenne primes in 0.0236ms.
History:
  [user] Find the first 9 Mersenne primes with the exec agent
  [agent] {"args":{"agent_name":"exec_rust_agent"},"id":"call_1332004","name":"transfer_to_agent"}
  [agent] {"id":"call_1332004","name":"transfer_to_agent","response":{"result":null}}
  [agent] {"requested":9,"found":9,"elapsed_ms":0.023635,"exponents":[2,3,5,7,13,17,19,31,61]}
  [agent] Found first 9 Mersenne primes in 0.0236ms.

The history shows the hand-off: Gemini calls transfer_to_agent, the Rust agent answers, and its JSON report comes back through two A2A hops.

Step 11 — Keep the Model Away From the Numbers

A benchmark through an LLM can time the model writing a number. Two rules keep the timing in code:

  • The benchmark client checks every reply. mersenne-bench reads the timing from the agent's data part or JSON line, rejects a report where requested differs from N or found differs from min(N, 26), and rejects an LLM-path reply with no transfer_to_agent to a Rust agent. Each row records where its report came from and who it was routed to.
  • ADK benchmarks go through a tool. run_benchmark runs mersenne-bench and returns medians already computed and rounded. The instruction tells Gemini to quote them, and scripts/check-adk-reply.py verifies a reply: one run_benchmark call, with the arguments asked for, and every number in the answer a value the tool returned.

A benchmark request sent from the CLI, saved with -o json. The tool call and the head of the answer:

a2a send -a $CARD --timeout 300s -o json "Benchmark both agents for N=3 to 6 with 2 reps" > reply.json

[tool call] {"max_n": 6, "min_n": 3, "reps": 2}
### Arguments Used
- `min_n`: 3
- `max_n`: 6
- `reps`: 2

The answer goes on with a summary per agent and a row per N. The check:

scripts/check-adk-reply.py reply.json 3 6 2

state: TASK_STATE_COMPLETED
run_benchmark calls: 1
args sent: {'max_n': 6, 'min_n': 3, 'reps': 2}  requested: {'min_n': 3, 'max_n': 6, 'reps': 2}
numbers in reply: 57  not from the tool: 0
PASS

scripts/adk-reliability.sh sends ten benchmark requests with varied ranges and ten requests that name no agent. On gemini-3.8-flash, 10 of 10 benchmark replies passed the checker and 10 of 10 unnamed requests went to native_rust_agent.

The sweep covers the whole exponent table, N=1 to 26. Exponent 23209 is a 6,987-digit number, and the arithmetic stays in BigUint throughout.

Step 12 — Benchmark From a Rust Client 

REPS=20 scripts/bench.sh          # native + exec, N=1..26
ADK=1 REPS=3 scripts/bench.sh     # adds the ADK series

mersenne-bench is built on the SDK's client crate, a2a-client-lf. Each call records the agent's own compute time and the client's round trip; overhead is the round trip minus compute, per call. Direct calls, medians of 20 reps:

N native compute ms native overhead ms exec compute ms exec overhead ms
1 0.001039 0.731 0.0004555 4.046
10 0.04249 0.793 0.04200 4.391
20 26.33 0.970 60.21 4.374
22 181.1 1.255 264.6 3.558
24 781.1 1.073 868.9 3.335
26 2484 1.396 2619 3.588

Through ADK, medians of 3 reps, one run per model. All 26 rows in each run went to native_rust_agent and read its data part:

N 3.5-flash compute ms 3.5-flash round trip ms 3.8-flash compute ms 3.8-flash round trip ms
1 0.002051 1665.053 0.002615 2073.666
10 0.04513 1394.245 0.04390 2458.155
20 72.95 1332.994 68.52 2336.569
22 279.8 1868.178 287.3 2679.324
26 2226 3455.492 2241 4123.353

The slowest single call on gemini-3.8-flash took 29.0 s, at N=9.

Step 13 — Time the A2A CLI Itself

scripts/cli-bench.py runs one a2a send -o json process per call, the way a shell script would, and applies the same checks to each reply. Wall time covers starting the CLI, fetching the card, sending, and exiting. Two reference commands, 20 runs each:

Command Median ms Min ms Max ms
a2a version 7.17 5.57 9.62
a2a card get (native) 9.18 8.30 11.17

The full sweep, N=1 to 26, 5 reps direct and 3 through ADK:

Agent Calls Overhead per call, per-N medians Median of the per-N medians
native 130 10.92 to 21.82 ms 20.28 ms
exec 130 9.43 to 20.81 ms 17.51 ms
ADK, 3.8-flash 78 1825.22 to 3017.92 ms 2217.55 ms

Every ADK call went to native_rust_agent; the slowest took 22693.6 ms. The sweep times each agent in its own block, so native and exec ran minutes apart. Run in alternating order, N=1, 30 runs each (scripts/cli-transport.py):

native, default (JSON-RPC): median 20.74 ms, min 18.60, max 26.51
native, --transport rest: median 21.49 ms, min 19.63, max 26.15
exec (HTTP+JSON only): median 20.81 ms, min 18.67, max 28.07
a2a version: median 7.62 ms, min 6.07, max 10.71

From a shell, the transport and the serving path make no difference to the CLI's cost: about 21 ms per call, about a third of it starting the process. Against the Rust client's 0.55 to 1.40 ms, the CLI fits scripts and checks, and the Rust client fits a benchmark.

The CLI's overhead in the sweep drops to about 11 ms for both agents once compute passes 100 ms (N=21 and up). Why is untested.

🔎 Tip: Compare Compute Only Between Runs Paced Alike

The same native process at N=20 takes 26.07 ms when calls arrive back to back and 68.09 ms when each call follows a 1.3 s idle gap (mersenne-bench --gap-ms 1300). ADK's model round trip spaces calls out too, and its mid-range compute times sit close to the gap series: 68.52 ms at N=20 on gemini-3.8-flash. The CPU-level cause, clock scaling or core placement on a hybrid laptop CPU, is untested.

Compare and Contrast

Serving path Code the agent needs Overhead from a Rust client a2a send from a shell, N=1
Official Rust SDK 🥇 an AgentExecutor and three routers 0.55 to 1.40 ms 20.74 ms
a2a server --exec 🥈 none: stdin in, stdout out 3.33 to 5.05 ms 20.81 ms
ADK coordinator 🥉 an agent.py, an agent.json card 1328 ms on 3.5-flash, 2283 ms on 3.8-flash 2664.00 ms on 3.8-flash

Rust-client ranges are the smallest and largest per-N medians; the ADK figures are the medians of its per-N medians. The exec figure includes starting a process for every message; how it splits between process start and the HTTP hop was not measured. At N=26 the work itself dominates every path: 2484 ms native and 2619 ms exec, direct.

So, Which One?

For an agent built to be one, use the SDK: about a millisecond of protocol cost, both transports, tasks the CLI can list and wait on.

For a program that already exists, a2a server --exec makes it an agent with no code change. A few milliseconds per call buys that, and ADK can call it once the two flags are set.

For routing by natural language, put ADK in front and keep the timing out of the model: a tool for anything computed, and a check that the model sent the arguments asked for.

For talking to any of them, the A2A CLI is the one client: card get, send, --stream, task get --wait, and -o json for scripts. Each call costs about 21 ms, so time agents from a long-lived client.

Summary

The goal of this article was to drive the A2A CLI against Rust agents on A2A v1.0, and to measure what each way of serving the same Rust code costs per call. The key to the solution was one benchmark client that reads timing from a structured report and checks that every reply answers the question asked. The results on one laptop were:

  • 🟢 The A2A CLI drove all three agents with the same commands: card, send, stream, REST, data parts, JSON output, task list, --async and task get --wait
  • 🟢 Every call through N=26, from the Rust client and from the CLI, reported found = min(N, 26)
  • 🟢 The SDK agent added 0.55 to 1.40 ms per call from a Rust client
  • 🟢 a2a server --exec served an A2A-unaware program to the CLI and to ADK
  • 🟢 On gemini-3.8-flash, 10 of 10 benchmark replies quoted only tool values, and 10 of 10 unnamed requests went to the native agent
  • ⚠️ One a2a send from a shell costs about 21 ms whatever the agent, 7.62 ms of it starting the CLI
  • ⚠️ The wrapped program added 3.33 to 5.05 ms per call from a Rust client
  • ⚠️ ADK added a median 1328 ms per call on gemini-3.5-flash and 2283 ms on gemini-3.8-flash, with one call at 29.0 s
  • ❌ Compute times from calls spaced by idle gaps run slower and do not compare with back-to-back runs

Scope: one 13th Gen Intel Core i7-1360P laptop on Linux, release build, every agent and client on the same machine, 2026-11-03 and 2026-11-04. Rust-client series have 20 reps per N direct and 3 through ADK, with one run per model on Vertex AI's shared global endpoint, so the difference between the two Gemini models is a single sample. The CLI series has 5 reps per N direct and 3 through ADK, on gemini-3.8-flash only, and reliability was checked on that model only, ten requests of each kind. The gRPC transport, task cancel, task subscribe, push notifications and authentication were not exercised.

The strategy for serving and benchmarking Rust A2A agents with the A2A CLI was validated with an incremental step by step approach.

References

  • The rig: https://github.com/xbill9/rust-dev/tree/main/a2a-benchmark-rust
  • CLI tour transcripts: https://github.com/xbill9/rust-dev/blob/main/a2a-benchmark-rust/results/cli-tour-20261103T214445Z.md and https://github.com/xbill9/rust-dev/blob/main/a2a-benchmark-rust/results/cli-tour-20261104T002904Z.md
  • CLI timing: https://github.com/xbill9/rust-dev/blob/main/a2a-benchmark-rust/results/cli-bench-20261104T002328Z.md
  • Introducing the A2A CLI: https://a2a-protocol.org/latest/blog/2026/10/01/introducing-a2a-cli/
  • A2A CLI: https://github.com/a2aproject/a2a-cli
  • A2A Rust SDK: https://github.com/a2aproject/a2a-rs
  • Agent Development Kit: https://google.github.io/adk-docs/
  • Why Did My Benchmark Stop at N=22?: https://dev.to/gde/why-did-my-benchmark-stop-at-n22-a-debugging-story-in-nine-bugs-3m2l

title: Build parametric 3D CAD parts from Claude Code with SolidCraft MCP
description:
If you have tried to get an AI agent to make a real, editable 3D part, you have probably hit the same wall: it writes an STL or a pile of OpenSCAD, and the moment you want to change one dimension you start over. A parametric CAD tool with a feature timeline fixes that, and SolidCraft is one that ships with its own MCP server.

tangency-labs/solidcraft is an open-source parametric 3D CAD application written in pure Rust. Per the README you sketch, constrain and build solids on a parametric feature timeline, change a dimension and watch the model rebuild, and run it on desktop, in the browser, or let AI agents model through the built-in MCP server. This post walks through the setup for Claude Code and what to expect.

What SolidCraft can do today

The README calls it "early but usable for simple parts" and backs that with a number: 75 of 76 public reference parts match their analytic or FreeCAD-computed volume, area, centre of mass and bounding box. The one miss is a tracked bug.

The feature list is already broad:

  • Sketches and constraints: lines, arcs, splines and text, solved by its own constraint solver, with parameter-driven dimensions.
  • Features: extrude, revolve, sweep, loft, fillet, chamfer, shell, draft, holes, threads, patterns, mirror, split and combine, all on an editable timeline.
  • Parameters and configurations with unit-aware expressions.
  • Assemblies with joints, motion studies, interference checks and mass properties.
  • Sheet metal with flanges, hems, fold and unfold, and flat patterns.
  • Files: STEP, IGES, 3MF, STL, OBJ and glTF in and out where supported, plus URDF export and its own .sc designs.

The important line for agent users is the last one in that list: the desktop app, browser app, headless CLI and MCP server all run the same commands. Whatever the agent does, you can open and edit by hand.

Step 1: install SolidCraft

Pick the build for your machine from the README:

  • Windows: the MSI installer from the latest release. The Windows downloads are not signed yet, so SmartScreen asks you to choose More info, then Run anyway.
  • macOS: the disk image (Apple silicon and Intel), signed and notarized.
  • Linux: the AppImage, or the Snap: 
sudo snap install solidcraft
  • Browser: solidcraft.io/app, no install. Good for a first look, but the MCP server needs the CLI.

If you prefer to build from source with Rust:

cargo run --release -p solidcraft -- --sample      # desktop app with a sample part
cargo run --release -p solidcraft-cli -- commands  # the command registry

Step 2: add the MCP server to Claude Code

solidcraft-cli mcp is a Model Context Protocol server. One line registers it with Claude Code:

claude mcp add solidcraft -- solidcraft-cli mcp

Two modes are worth knowing. Run headless, the server keeps its own design session. Started with --connect, it drives the running desktop app so you can watch every feature appear on the timeline. For a first session, the connected mode is far easier to trust.

On older Windows installers the CLI is not on PATH. The README says to give the full path instead, which by default is C:\Program Files\SolidCraft\solidcraft-cli.exe.

Step 3: ask for a part with real parameters

The README's own demo is a good template for a prompt: a Raspberry Pi 4 case built from an empty design, with a sketch dimensioned from the board's parameters, extrude, fillet and shell, M2.5 standoffs patterned on the 58 by 49 mm hole rectangle, port cut-outs, vent slots and engraved text. Then the case height goes from 24 to 32 mm in Parameters and everything rebuilds.

So ask for parameters, not just a shape:

Create a box enclosure 90 x 60 mm with a height parameter of 30 mm,
2 mm walls (shell), 1 mm fillets on the outer edges, and four M3 standoffs
patterned on a 70 x 40 mm rectangle. Name every dimension as a parameter.

When it is done, change height in the Parameters panel yourself. If the model rebuilds cleanly, the agent built it the right way. Export STEP for a machinist or STL or 3MF for a printer.

Step 4: script it when you need repeatability

A SolidCraft script is a JSON list of the same commands the UI runs. You can run one headless and write a file:

cargo run --release -p solidcraft-cli -- run examples/bracket.json --out bracket.step

This is handy once the agent has produced a part you like: keep the command list in the repo and regenerate the STEP in CI instead of trusting a binary file.

What people are building with it

The builds we track on the SolidCraft page show where it fits:

  • A skeptical CAD user designed and delivered a custom part for a paying client with no crash, citing the editable feature timeline, constrained sketches and clean STEP and STL exports.
  • One user hit a "wire not closed" error on a simple sketch in FreeCAD, redid it in SolidCraft and had it working in two minutes.
  • A hobbyist replicated a Telecaster body from PDFs with SolidCraft connected to desktop ChatGPT, then had it add bindings and a kill switch. The first run missed the wire holes between the pickup pockets, so check the model.
  • Another builder made a bot that models in SolidCraft and used it to design printable armor that snaps onto 6-inch poseable figures.

Related tools

If you want text-to-CAD as a skill set for agents rather than a full CAD app, text-to-cad generates 3D CAD models from text and runs related manufacturing and drawing workflows locally. For organic shapes, scenes and renders instead of engineering parts, MCP for Blender connects Blender to an LLM the same way.

Caveats

  • The project describes itself as early. Use it for simple parts first and check volumes and dimensions before you send anything to a shop.
  • Agents still miss details, as the guitar body example shows. The parametric timeline makes fixes cheap, but you are the reviewer.
  • This walkthrough follows the README and has not been run end to end by us.

Source repo: tangency-labs/solidcraft. License: MIT or Apache-2.0.
