title: Designing UX for Nondeterministic Software
description:
Almost every interface convention you use was designed for software that knew what had happened.

A form submits. A spinner turns. A checkmark appears. The checkmark means done, and it has meant done for thirty years, which is why users stopped reading the words next to it a long time ago.

Then we started shipping systems where the result is not known at the moment the screen updates, and kept the checkmark.

Two Kinds of Uncertainty, One Failure

They are worth separating, because they break differently.

The answer may be wrong. A model produces plausible output with no inherent guarantee of correctness. The system has an answer. Whether it is true is a different question that the system often cannot settle.

The operation may not have happened yet. Distributed settlement produces outcomes that are provisional for a while. Accepted, then included, then confirmed, then eventually final. The early states can still unwind.

One is a correctness problem and the other is a timing problem. They converge on the same interface failure: the screen asserts something definite about a state that is not yet definite, and the user acts on the assertion.

The damage compounds. Users calibrate on the interface, not on the architecture diagram. Show a reliable looking checkmark often enough and people stop verifying, precisely as you move them onto a system where verifying matters.

The States Your Interface Is Probably Missing

On Ethereum, blocks arrive roughly every twelve seconds. A transaction in a block has one confirmation, and each subsequent block adds another. Finality is something else entirely: validators vote on checkpoints at epoch boundaries, an epoch being thirty two slots or about six and a half minutes, and finalisation normally lands around two epochs later, in the region of thirteen minutes.

Between inclusion and finality the transaction is real but not settled. Single block reorganisations do happen when a proposer publishes late. Under unusual conditions the chain can keep producing blocks while failing to finalise them at all, which has occurred briefly on mainnet.

Most dApp interfaces compress all of that into two states: pending, then success. The states that actually matter are missing:

Submitted but not included. The transaction is in the mempool. It may sit there. It may be replaced. It may never land.
Included but not settled. Real, visible on a block explorer, and still capable of unwinding.
Failed after acceptance. The transaction was accepted, executed, and reverted. Gas was consumed. Nothing happened. This state is almost never designed and it is the one that generates support tickets.

For each, the interface should answer one question in plain language: what may the user do now? Finality matters because it gates action. If someone should not ship goods, release a document or treat funds as received until settlement, say so at the point of the decision, not in the docs.

Show the Basis, Not a Score

On the probabilistic side, the common pattern is an answer with no visible provenance, which leaves the user judging it by how reasonable it sounds. Fluency is not correlated with correctness, so that is not a judgement at all.

Showing the source material beats showing a confidence number, for a simple reason: a source can be checked and a number cannot. A reviewer shown the actual passage can assess whether it supports the claim. A reviewer shown “87 percent confident” has been handed something that looks quantitative, is hard to calibrate, and gets read as an endorsement.

And put it at the point of action. If the output feeds a button, the basis for that output belongs on the same surface as the button, not one navigation step away.

Signing Is Where UX Becomes Security

This is the part of nondeterministic UX that is not really a UX problem.

Any surface asking a user to approve a transaction should show what is actually being authorised in terms they can evaluate. A large share of loss in this space has come from users approving payloads that their wallet displayed accurately and that meant nothing to the reader. Blind signing is a design failure before it is a user error.

Two things follow. Keys stay scoped and under threshold approval, so that a single bad approval has a bounded blast radius rather than an unbounded one. And the control itself lives in the contract, not the client: a disabled button is a suggestion, and eligibility and transfer restrictions belong to be enforced at transfer time, under something like ERC-3643 with KYC and AML checks wired into identity. The interface can make a control legible. It cannot be the control.

That contract logic goes through independent audit before it holds value, with time budgeted to fix findings rather than acknowledge them. Interface polish on top of unaudited logic is decoration.

When Blockchain Is the Wrong Tool Here

We build these systems, so take this section as the one written against our own interest.

A great many “blockchain UX problems” are not UX problems. They are the visible symptom of an architecture chosen without a reason that required it.

Settlement uncertainty is a genuine cost. It costs design effort, support load, user comprehension, and conversion. That cost is worth paying when something actually requires a shared ledger: multiple organisations writing to one record, no neutral party available to hold it, real disputes about history. Absent that, you have bought a hard UX problem and received nothing for it.

Before designing the pending states, it is worth asking whether they need to exist. A conventional database with signed audit logging gives you tamper evidence, settles instantly, has no reorganisation semantics to explain, and lets you keep the checkmark honest. For a large share of requirements, that is the better product.

If the answer comes back that a ledger genuinely is required, design the states properly. If it does not, you have just removed the problem rather than solved it.

The Honest Alternative: Hide It

For many products, the best interface for nondeterminism is one that does not expose it.

Wait for settlement server side and show success when it is actually true. Run the probabilistic step in the background and surface only verified results. Use an intermediated model where that suits the users and your regulatory position.

Each of these removes a class of UX problem by removing the user’s exposure to the uncertainty. The trade is real: latency, some transparency, and in custodial arrangements a materially different trust model. Neither choice is automatically correct.

What is not defensible is the middle position most products reach by accident, which is exposing the user to uncertainty while presenting an interface that denies it exists.

Scope the Unhappy Paths Before They Get Cut

In deterministic software, error handling is an edge case. In nondeterministic software, it is normal operation, and the recovery path carries real traffic.

It is also the first thing cut when a scope conversation gets tight, because it looks like polish. It is not polish. Three questions, answered during design rather than after launch:

How does a user discover something was wrong, given it will usually look fine? How do they correct it without involving support? And what happens to anything downstream that already consumed the incorrect result?

That third one is deferred most often and costs most to answer late. A correction that cannot propagate is not a correction.

Whatever you build, keep the parts that outlast the model and the chain: the state machine, the copy, the recovery flows, the deterministic controls, the keys. Those are the system. If they live with a vendor, your ability to change either layer leaves when they do.

RWaltz is a technology partner building blockchain, AI, and enterprise software, including smart contracts, tokenization platforms, and custom integrations. Our approach is security-first and build-to-own: honest scoping, independent audits, and client-owned IP and keys, so what we deliver belongs to you.

title: What broke when we counted conversions twice (and the boring test that fixed it)
description:
We run a small Israeli tools and home-improvement store, ramo.co.il, on Next.js and Vercel. A few weeks ago our ad dashboards said we were doing great. Our bank account disagreed.

The cause was dull: the purchase event fired twice on the thank-you page. Once on the first render, and again after a client-side navigation re-mounted the component. Google Ads and Meta both happily counted two sales, and the bidding algorithms started paying more for traffic that wasn't converting as well as they thought.

How we found it

Not from the dashboards. We opened the network tab, finished a test order and watched two identical purchase hits go out a few hundred milliseconds apart. That was the whole investigation.

The fix

  1. Fire purchase events from one place only, keyed by order ID.
  2. Store the order ID in sessionStorage after sending, and skip if it's already there.
  3. Pass the same transaction_id / event_id to every platform so they can dedupe on their side too.

The test that keeps it fixed

The real win was a Playwright test that runs before every deploy. It loads a product page, adds to cart, completes a test checkout and counts outgoing requests per platform. If any tag fires zero times or more than once, the deploy is blocked.

It takes about a minute to run and it has already caught one regression from an unrelated refactor.

If you sell anything online, check your purchase event today. Place a test order with the network tab open. It's five minutes, and it might explain why your ROAS looks better than your revenue.

title: Amazon Connect Customer lets agents pause and resume emails
description:
Amazon Connect Customer lets agents pause emails while waiting for information or approvals, freeing them to handle higher-priority contacts and resume their work later. For example, an agent waiting for a supervisor to approve a refund can pause the email and take an incoming call. Paused time is tracked separately from active handling time, giving supervisors a more accurate view of the time agents spend working on emails.

Agents can pause and resume emails directly from the Agent Workspace or Contact Control Panel (CCP) and see how long each email has been paused. Supervisors can monitor paused emails and pause duration in real time, and use flows to automatically resume or transfer emails that remain paused beyond a configured threshold.

Amazon Connect Customer email pause and resume is available in the US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Africa (Cape Town), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), and Europe (London) regions. title: Agentforce Coworker gets $50 per-user plan and Teams access
description:
Salesforce has announced an expansion of Agentforce Coworker, the assistant that takes a job from an employee, coordinates the relevant Agentforce agents and workflows, and returns results and suggested actions for review. The company says more than 185,000 people now use it and that usage grew 21x in three months.

What is available now

Four things are live today:

  • Skills. A workflow that has proven itself becomes a short request anyone on the team can run. Salesforce's example is a top rep's renewal playbook becoming the team standard.
  • Conversation History. A user can resume a conversation across Salesforce, Teams and the new apps with context intact.
  • Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 connections. Email, calendars and files around an account are combined with Salesforce data, so a meeting brief or renewal plan covers more than CRM records.
  • A per-user plan at $50 per user per month. Salesforce frames it as a way to start small, measure value and widen use. It notes that pricing and packaging may change.

Customers can turn Coworker on in Setup. Giving every user a seat on the per-user plan goes through a Salesforce account executive.

What comes later

In November 2026 the company expects general availability of Coworker in Microsoft Teams, an iOS app, desktop apps for Mac and Windows, an MCP server for connectivity, and a free trial for Flex Credits customers. In December 2026 it lists Daily Digest, scheduled tasks, and Coworker in the Field Service, Consumer Goods Cloud and Life Sciences Cloud mobile apps. Salesforce adds that availability varies by region and that unreleased features should not drive purchase decisions.

Governance

Salesforce says Coworker works within existing employee permissions, sharing rules and access controls. Administrators can manage access to supported agents and actions, and approval and audit capabilities exist for supported operations.

Customer figures

These come from Salesforce's own announcement and have not been independently checked:

  • Fulton Bank runs more than 20 use cases for about 3,000 users.
  • The Adecco Group is rolling Coworker out across 40 countries.
  • BACA Systems enabled it in 20 minutes in an environment with 1,300 custom objects. It reports that questions which used to take 45 to 60 minutes of switching between systems were answered directly.

What to watch

The usage growth figure has no stated baseline, so it says little about absolute scale. The customer examples are large organisations. A smaller team should judge the product on its own pilot, using one repeatable workflow and a before-and-after time measurement.

title: Introducing Vercel for Slack
description:
Vercel Agent now works in Slack. Mention it the way you'd pull a teammate into a thread, and it reads the discussion, answers with the context of the platform running your app, and turns the team's decisions into changes you approve. Vercel for Slack is available today in Public Beta for Pro and Enterprise teams.

Work starts in conversation. An alert gets noticed in a channel, a fix gets agreed on in a thread, and then someone leaves Slack to do the work. With Vercel Agent, you can tag it in for answers about your infrastructure or hand it the work, all without leaving the conversation.

What is Vercel Agent?

When we introduced Vercel Agent, we called it an AI teammate for your development workflow. Today it's the first responder for your production apps. When something changes, it investigates your logs, metrics, and deployments, finds the root cause, and proposes a fix, often before anyone's opened a laptop. Give it a PR and it flags the regressions and risky changes that a passing CI run won't show.

In Slack, that agent joins the conversation itself. It is a core part of Vercel, so your deployments, build statuses, logs, metrics, code reviews, and PRs are in front of it before you've typed anything. Mention @Vercel in a channel, a thread, or a DM, and it answers like a teammate with every tab already open. And answering is only half of it, because once you know what's wrong, the agent can go fix it:

  • Diagnose issues: Investigate incidents, trace errors to the deploy that caused them, explain a cost spike, and answer questions about your codebase.

  • Code alongside your team: Fix failing builds and CI, review PRs with knowledge of how the code runs in production, and turn a thread's decision into a tested pull request.

  • Operate your projects: Roll back deployments, update configuration, manage feature flags, and resolve unusual usage before it becomes a bill.

The agent is read-only by default, and anything that changes code or configuration goes through a plan that you approve. Vercel for Slack brings that whole loop into the threads where you and your team are already discussing work.

Accelerating development with a conversation

Teams form decisions through collaboration. Incidents get triaged in a channel, code reviews are hashed out in threads, and features get scoped between standups. But once a thread settles on what needs to be done, the actions still need to be translated into tickets, terminal commands, and PR descriptions. Every handoff drops context, and the conversation that held the full picture becomes the thing everyone summarizes from memory. Vercel for Slack gives the agent the full context of the original conversation for every turn.

Answers in one place speed up the whole team

A deployment goes out at 1:42pm. By 1:51, checkout error rates are climbing and an alert lands in the platform engineering channel.

What used to happen next was a scatter. One responder opens logs to see how bad it is, another asks their coding agent to line up the anomaly up against the deploy timeline, a third starts reading the diff of the suspect PR. Each person investigates alone, in their own view of the same system, and the thread is where they reconcile by pasting screenshots, summarizing agent findings, and correcting each other as they establish the actual state of the situation. The minutes that matter get spent assembling the picture before anyone can act on it.

With Vercel for Slack, the first question goes to the agent, right in the thread.

"@Vercel, checkout errors spiked after the 1:42 deploy. What's going on?"

It sizes the blast radius, correlates the spike with the deployment, identifies the PR that shipped in it, and explains which change, in which file, caused which behavior. The answer arrives in the channel, where the whole team reads the same diagnosis at the same time.

Nobody has to re-run a teammate's investigation or wait for the recap, because everyone is looking at the same report. The engineer who knows the checkout code speaks to the change itself, the on-call weighs how many users are hit against how long a fix would take, and what's left for the thread is the decision, whether to roll back or fix forward.

Vercel Agent understands how your team already talks

The thread, channel, or DM is the beginning of the prompt itself. You don't have to re-explain anything that was already said, or pass in any context from your app or codebase. Bring it into a conversation like any other team member and it reads the room, picks up what the team has been discussing, and can act on it when asked.

One example of this was our iteration on Vercel Agent's plan card, the message it posts in Slack to request approval for the work it wants to do. The first version we tested internally was a wall of text, but when one of our engineers noticed that people were often approving actions without reading all of the details, we had a redesign thread that ran 47 replies deep on what a person needs to see before confirming an action on the group's behalf. Tagging Vercel Agent in at the end of that thread is what resulted in the card you see today.

By the time a PR from a conversation like this lands in a thread, the tests have already run and the preview deployment is live, so the team can start reviewing it in the conversation that kicked off the feature in the first place.

Vercel Agent reviews pull requests in the thread

Ask Vercel Agent for a review in the thread where the PR is being discussed, and the conversation is passed along with the request. What your team has been raising becomes context for what Vercel Agent checks, and its findings land back in the same thread, so discussing them, deciding, and fixing them is one loop instead of a trip to another tool.

One example from one of our own PR discussions was a review someone requested mid-thread. The agent came back with a bug sitting just outside the diff, the same title rendered twice in the UI.

A finding doesn't have to end as a comment. If the team agrees it should be fixed, the agent can patch the PR itself, and that change arrives the same way everything else does, as a proposal waiting on an approval.

Changes always go through a plan your team approves

When a thread lands on a change, Vercel Agent replies with a plan that says what will happen, in which project, and at what scope. Decisions in a channel form in fragments, across people and hours, and nobody types "DECISION:", so the plan is where all of that becomes one explicit thing to say yes to. Once approved, the agent does the work under its own identity, and the audit trail shows who asked, who approved, and what ran.

One example from our own threads was a cached page showing stale data after we shipped an update. Someone called for a cache purge scoped to just the specific pages, since it was peak hours, and asked the agent to set it up. The plan that came back matched the ask exactly, a purge of the specific path and its sub-paths with the rest of the site's cache left warm, and nothing ran until someone approved it.

Whether a thread ends in a diagnosis, a pull request, or a cache purge, the last step belongs to a person.

Getting started

The easiest way to get started is to simply ask Vercel Agent questions. Ask about the error you're chasing or the build that just failed, see what comes back, and let your team decide over time how much of the work the agent takes on. Until someone approves a plan, it's only ever reading.

Vercel for Slack is available in Public Beta for Pro and Enterprise teams. To start using Vercel Agent in Slack:

  • Open the Slack app in the Vercel Marketplace and click Connect Account.

  • Choose the Slack workspace to connect, then click Allow.

  • Mention @Vercel in a channel, a thread, or a DM.

  • Sign in to your Vercel account when it prompts you the first time.

See the Vercel for Slack docs for setup and permissions.

title: How to reconcile Stripe payments in a double-entry ledger
description:
A customer pays $2,400 by card, Stripe says the payment succeeded, and it is tempting to write one line in your books: Stripe balance, plus $2,400. Almost every part of that line is wrong. The amount is wrong, because Stripe keeps a fee. The balance is wrong, because the money is not spendable yet. And the timing is wrong, because at the moment Stripe says “succeeded”, the number you need to record it may not exist yet.

A Stripe payment is not one event. It is a sequence of events spread over seconds for the fee and days for the cash, and a ledger that reconciles with Stripe records each of them as Stripe does. To reconcile Stripe payments, you record that sequence step by step. This guide shows which events to listen for, the accounts that mirror Stripe's balances, and the exact ledger transaction for each step, for a card payment and a bank debit.


One card payment, as it is usually imagined and as Stripe actually records it.

A card payment is four events, not one

Here is a real $2,400.00 card payment from a Stripe test account, as Stripe's own event log shows it:

Time Event What it tells you
18:30:12 payment_intent.created A payment for $2,400.00 has been started
18:30:13 charge.succeeded The card was charged $2,400.00
18:30:13 payment_intent.succeeded The payment is complete
18:30:16 charge.updated The charge now carries its balance transaction

The first three arrive within a second, and the third is the one every integration tutorial tells you to listen for. It is the wrong moment to record the payment, because on both charge.succeeded and payment_intent.succeeded the charge's balance_transaction field is still null.

The balance transaction is Stripe's record of what the payment did to your Stripe balance: the gross amount, the fee, the net, and the date the money becomes spendable (available_on). It is the only place the real fee comes from, and in the log above it appears three seconds after the payment succeeded.


The first four seconds of a card payment with Stripe's default capture. The fee does not exist until charge.updated.

If you post to the ledger at succeeded anyway, you post every payment without its fee. You then either guess the fee from Stripe's rate, which will disagree with Stripe by a cent often enough to matter, or correct it later with a second transaction. Both make the books disagree with Stripe for reasons that are not in Stripe.

Record the payment once, when the balance transaction exists

The gap comes from a setting, not from cards. Since API version 2024-04-10, Stripe's default capture_method is automatic_async: the confirm call returns as soon as the card is authorized, and Stripe creates the balance transaction in the background (Stripe's asynchronous capture docs ). Integrations on older API versions never see the gap, which is why it surprises people.

What we recommend: listen for charge.updated, and post the payment once, from the balance transaction it carries. It works on every API version and every capture setting, it is the event Stripe itself points to, and it is the one path that does not depend on your checkout request surviving. The webhook carries the balance transaction's id, so fetch the fee, net and available_on with GET /v1/balance_transactions/txn_....

How your checkout gets there is your call, and none of it changes the ledger:

  • Keep the default and let the customer see “succeeded” straight away. The ledger catches up a few seconds later.
  • Pass capture_method: 'automatic' with confirm: true. The confirm call then waits for the balance transaction (about half a second longer in our tests), and you can post before you answer the customer. Set it explicitly, because an API or SDK upgrade otherwise changes the default underneath you.
  • Poll the PaymentIntent for a few seconds after confirming, if you want the same effect without changing capture. 
const paymentIntent = await stripe.paymentIntents.create({
  amount: 240000,
  currency: 'usd',
  customer: customerId,
  payment_method: paymentMethodId,
  confirm: true,
  capture_method: 'automatic', // not the default since 2024-04-10
  expand: ['latest_charge.balance_transaction'],
});

const balanceTransaction = paymentIntent.latest_charge?.balance_transaction;
// fee, net and available_on are all here, in the same response

Whichever you choose, the posting is identical: one transaction, carrying the real fee and the balance transaction id, written under one idempotency key. A checkout that posts first and a webhook that arrives later write the same transaction, so the second does nothing, and reconciliation sees exactly one posting per movement either way.

What we advise against is the shape the gap tempts you into: a “sale” transaction at succeeded, at gross, into a Stripe clearing account, followed seconds later by a second transaction moving it to pending once the fee is known. It records nothing the second transaction does not, and it doubles every payment's rows.

Dated at the charge. The posting may be written seconds or minutes after the payment. It still takes effect at the moment the customer paid, because that is when the income and the obligation came into existence. Recording an event after it happened, dated when it happened, is ordinary accounting, and it keeps a charge at 23:59:58 on 31 December in the year it belongs to.

Stripe has two balances, and only one of them is cash

The net of $2,330.10 does not land somewhere you can spend it. Stripe keeps two balances:

  • Pending - money Stripe has collected for you and has not released yet. Every new balance transaction lands here first.
  • Available - money you can pay out to your bank, or use for refunds and transfers.

Money moves from pending to available on the balance transaction's available_on date. In the US that is usually two business days after the charge. It is longer in many other countries, and a new Stripe account's first payout typically waits 7 to 14 days. In our own Stripe test account it was six to seven days.


The net sits in the pending balance until available_on. Only then can it be paid out.

This matters for anything that pays money out of Stripe. A platform that pays sellers, hosts or freelancers from its Stripe balance can only pay from available. If the books show one “Stripe” balance of $2,330.10 on day 0, a payout run that trusts the books will try to spend money Stripe will refuse to release.

balance.available is not a per-payment event

It is natural to expect Stripe to announce when this payment's money became available. It does not. balance.available fires when your available balance changes, and its payload is the whole balance object. It does not say which payments were released, and one event can cover hundreds of them.

You do not need it to. available_on is set the moment the balance transaction exists, so you know the release date seconds after the charge. Store it, and run a scheduled job that posts every release whose date has arrived. Treat balance.available as a hint to run that job early, never as the source of what to post.

Date the release on available_on, not on the charge. This one is easy to get wrong because both dates are right there. Posting the release with the charge's date tells the ledger the money was available from day 0. A balance sheet for day 1 then reports cash that Stripe was still holding, and, worse, it reported the correct figure when you ran it on day 1 and a different one when you ran it again on day 3. A report that changes its mind about the past with no new event to explain it is the kind of thing an auditor stops trusting the whole ledger over. We shipped exactly that in our own demo application, and it was caught by comparing the same report run on two different days.

Bank debits take days, and can still fail

A card gives you an answer in a second. A US bank debit (ACH Direct Debit) gives you a promise. The PaymentIntent moves to processing, and stays there for up to four business days while the customer's bank decides. Then it either succeeds or fails, and a “succeeded” debit can still come back as a return for up to 60 days on a personal account.


A bank debit spends days in clearing before it either reaches Stripe or fails.

Whether your ledger records anything during those four days depends on one business question: do you deliver before the debit succeeds?

  • If you wait for success before confirming the order, a bank debit is just a slow card. Post once, on success, exactly as below. You do not need anything new.
  • If you confirm at processing (the booking is held, the subscription is active, the goods ship), you now owe something to someone for money you do not have. That has to be in the books from day 0, and it needs somewhere to sit that is honest about what it is.

That somewhere is a clearing account: an asset that means “money a payment method has promised us and has not delivered”. It is debited when the debit starts processing, and credited when it resolves, either into Stripe's pending balance on success, or back out on failure. A clearing account with a balance is a list of open promises. One that has been non-zero for a debit started two weeks ago is a debit nobody followed up.

A card does not need a clearing account. Accounting tools often recommend one for Stripe (some call it Undeposited Funds), and the reason is real but different: it groups many charges into the single payout that lands in the bank. The pending and available accounts already model that. A card payment's money is in Stripe's pending balance within seconds, so there is no open promise for clearing to hold. A later refund or dispute is a new movement with its own balance transaction, not the original payment failing.

Mapping Stripe onto your chart of accounts

Every place money sits at Stripe gets its own account, and each account means one thing.

Account Type Mirrors Is it cash?
assets:stripe-pending Asset Stripe's pending balance No. It cannot be spent yet.
assets:stripe-available Asset Stripe's available balance Yes
assets:stripe-clearing Asset Bank debits started and not yet resolved No. It may never arrive.
expenses:stripe-fees Expense Stripe's processing fees Not applicable

The rule that makes this reconcile: at any moment, stripe-pending should equal Stripe's pending balance, and stripe-available should equal Stripe's available balance. Those are two numbers you can fetch from GET /v1/balance and compare. Any difference is either a movement Stripe made that you have not posted, or a posting you made that Stripe never confirmed. Clearing has no Stripe counterpart to compare to, which is exactly why it should stay small and short-lived.

The other side of each payment depends on your business, and getting it right matters more than anything Stripe-specific here. In the examples below, a marketplace takes a 12% commission and owes the rest to a host:

  • income:commission - the platform's share. Only money you keep is income.
  • liabilities:escrow/host-9001 - the host's share, owed from the moment the customer pays. It is not income that you later spend.

The ledger transactions

All three examples use the same $2,400.00 payment. The card fee is Stripe's standard US rate at the time of writing (2.9% + $0.30 = $69.90). The bank debit fee is 0.8%, capped at $5.00.

A card payment: one transaction, written when the fee is known

Posted once the balance transaction exists, from charge.updated or from your checkout, dated at the charge.

Account Debit Credit
assets:stripe-pending 2,330.10
expenses:stripe-fees 69.90
liabilities:escrow/host-9001 2,112.00
income:commission 288.00
Total 2,400.00 2,400.00

Three things about its shape are deliberate:

  • Gross on the business side, net on the Stripe side. The customer paid $2,400.00, so commission and the host's share are split from $2,400.00. Stripe's pending balance only ever received $2,330.10, so that is what the Stripe account gets. Recording the net as revenue would understate revenue by every fee you have ever paid.
  • The Stripe account appears on exactly one line. You could debit pending $2,400.00 and credit it $69.90 for the fee. The account would net to the same figure, and the posting would no longer match the balance transaction, which is a single net movement of $2,330.10. Match the shape of the thing you reconcile against.
  • The fee comes from the balance transaction, never from a rate. A computed fee makes reconciliation compare your arithmetic with itself.

A bank debit: two transactions, through clearing

Only if you deliver at processing. Otherwise, post the card-shaped transaction on success.

1. On payment_intent.processing, dated then:

Account Debit Credit
assets:stripe-clearing 2,400.00
liabilities:escrow/host-9001 2,112.00
income:commission 288.00

2a. On success, when the balance transaction exists:

Account Debit Credit
assets:stripe-pending 2,395.00
expenses:stripe-fees 5.00
assets:stripe-clearing 2,400.00

2b. Or on failure, the first transaction is undone:

Account Debit Credit
liabilities:escrow/host-9001 2,112.00
income:commission 288.00
assets:stripe-clearing 2,400.00

Either way clearing returns to zero for this payment. Post the failure as its own transaction rather than editing or deleting the first one: the record that you believed a debit was coming, and that it did not, is history you will want when the customer asks why their booking was cancelled.

A return after success is not this case. By then the money reached Stripe, so it comes back out as a dispute with its own balance transaction, and it is recorded like any other dispute.

Funds becoming available

Posted by the scheduled job, dated at available_on. The same for a card and a bank debit.

Account Debit Credit
assets:stripe-available 2,330.10
assets:stripe-pending 2,330.10

Nothing about the business changed, so nothing outside Stripe's accounts moves. Only now can this money pay the host.

Making it reconcile, not just balance

Every transaction above balances. That is the ledger's arithmetic check, and it says nothing about whether the ledger agrees with Stripe. A payment that neither the checkout nor the webhook recorded leaves the books balanced and $2,330.10 short. These are the habits that close that gap:

  • Put the balance transaction id (txn_...) on the Stripe line. It is the key that ties one posting to one Stripe movement. The charge id is not enough, because one charge produces several balance transactions over its life: the payment, a refund, a dispute.
  • Classify in the description, identify in metadata. “Booking payment” is a description. The order id, charge id, PaymentIntent id and balance transaction id belong in metadata, where they can be searched and joined.
  • One idempotency key per step, derived from the business object. order_123:payment and order_123:available, never a random id. Webhooks are delivered at least once, and a retry must replay the posting rather than add a second one.
  • Recover missed webhooks with a sweep that looks for evidence. Run a scheduled job that asks “which charges have a balance transaction and no posting?” Do not key it on an order status field that the webhook also writes. Ours did, and it skipped every booking it existed to catch, because the webhook had moved the status past the value the sweep looked for. The sweep reported running every hour, and the gap was only found when the balances were compared with Stripe's.
  • Compare balances, then compare movements. Account balance against GET /v1/balance tells you whether you are wrong. Posting against balance transaction, one by one, tells you where.

What this guide does not cover

Each of these follows the same principle, one posting per balance transaction, and each has a detail worth its own treatment:

  • Refunds and disputes. Each creates a negative balance transaction, and a dispute adds a fee that is not refunded even if you win.
  • Payouts to your bank. One payout moves many payments' worth of available balance at once, so it reconciles against the payout, not against individual charges.
  • Multi-currency charges. When the charge currency differs from your settlement currency, the balance transaction carries the exchange rate Stripe applied, and the net lands in the settlement currency.
  • Stripe Connect. Destination charges and transfers to connected accounts add a second balance per connected account.

Where this goes next

The Stripe accounts are the easy half. The harder half is deciding what the other side of each payment is, because that decision makes revenue real or fictional. Money you hold for somebody else is a liability from the moment it arrives, and refunds and fee policies make that harder, not easier. I went through where that breaks in an earlier post: why marketplace accounting becomes so hard.

Everything here works in any double-entry ledger, including one you build yourself. The accounts, the one posting per balance transaction and the checks against GET /v1/balance need no vendor.

Originally published at ledfra.com.

I write these while building Ledfra, a double-entry ledger with an API and real financial statements on top. It reads your Stripe balances with a read-only key and lists every movement missing on either side. It does not move money or pay out. If you would rather poke at it than read about it, there is a live demo with a seeded marketplace in it - no signup.

title: Indexed but zero impressions: what ten pages and one backlink taught us (Lullwood)
description:
Lullwood, a free browser horror game, had ten pages indexed by Google, yet Search Console gave us no query data to see our name in. The 14 impressions it did report cannot be tied to any query. Crawling, speed and schema were all fine. Google's URL Inspection tool lists exactly one outside page linking to us, a post we published ourselves.

That is the whole diagnosis. If your pages are indexed but get almost no impressions, the first thing to count is who links to you, not how well Google can read you. Below is the evidence, the API behind each number, and what we do not know. We make Lullwood, so this is our own site's data.

What the SEO checklist covered

We did what a search checklist says, and measured each item on 2026-10-28:

  • A sitemap submitted to Search Console. It went from 11 URLs to 18 in one release, and it listed 18 when we measured on 2026-10-28.
  • IndexNow pings that run on their own after a deploy that changes a page. The run after that release returned HTTP 200 for all 18 URLs.
  • Valid WebSite, Organization, VideoGame and FAQPage JSON-LD on the home page. All of it parses.
  • A 0.121 second time to first byte on the home page.
  • HTTP 200 for nine search and AI crawlers (GPTBot, OAI-SearchBot, ChatGPT-User, ClaudeBot, Claude-SearchBot, PerplexityBot, Googlebot, Bingbot, Applebot) on /, /robots.txt, /llms.txt and /sitemap.xml.
  • One H1 per page and self-referential absolute canonicals.

What that bought us

In the 28 days from 2026-09-28 to 2026-10-26, the Search Console API reported 1 click, 14 impressions and an average position of 2.7. The home page had 13 of those impressions and the one click.

Do not read 2.7 as page one. It is an average over 14 impressions on queries Google will not name. The same API returned no query rows at all, so there is nothing to filter for our name and nothing to confirm those 14 were for it.

The URL Inspection API said 10 of the 11 sitemap URLs at that time were "Submitted and indexed". The exception was a form page, /suggest.

Why indexed pages can get almost no impressions

Across everything we inspected, the referringUrls field listed four distinct pages linking to ours. Three are our own: the home page, /credits and /devlog. The fourth is a dev.to cross-post of one of our devlog posts, published 2026-10-27. So the external set is one URL, and we made it. That list is what Google reports for the pages we inspected, not a full backlink audit.

The page ranking for our name makes it worse. When we searched for Lullwood on 2026-10-22 and 2026-10-26, with a web-search tool and not a logged-in Google results page, our own GitHub repository was the result that ranked, first on the 26th. We fetched that repo page on 2026-10-28: its website link to www.lullwoodgame.com carries rel="nofollow". The repo does not appear in our referring URLs at all.

The one place we could make a followed link ourselves was the body of a dev.to article. The links in our published one had no nofollow. A GitHub README, an itch.io game page and the Three.js Discourse all mark outbound links nofollow when we fetched an example of each.

Crawlability and authority are different problems

Crawlability is whether a search engine can fetch and understand a page. Authority is whether anyone else vouches for it. A checklist fixes the first, because every item on it is something you control from your own repo. The second needs people you do not control to link to you, so it is not on the list and cannot be shipped in a release.

The rule we took from our numbers: when Search Console says indexed and the impressions are close to nothing, stop editing the site and start counting referring URLs.

What we are doing next

As of 2026-10-28 the number of distinct external pages linking to Lullwood is still one. This is a diagnosis, not a result.

More cross-posts are scheduled, with the canonical set to the page on our site. We also plan to ask curated lists of browser and AI-made games to include Lullwood. Those lists mark links nofollow too, so we expect them to help readers and answer engines more than rankings. We will report the referring-URL count again, whatever it is. If it rises and impressions for our name stay near nothing, authority is lagging and we keep going. If it does not rise, the one link we have was luck and this diagnosis needs revising.

The original, with the source of every number, is on the Lullwood devlog. If you want to see the site all this is about, you can play Lullwood free in your browser, or read how to survive Lullwood.

We are one human founder plus a team of Claude agents building Lullwood in the open.

title: Amazon RDS for Oracle now supports copying option groups during cross-Region snapshot copy
description:
Amazon RDS for Oracle now lets you copy the option group associated with a DB snapshot when you copy that snapshot to another AWS Region.

Amazon RDS for Oracle uses option groups to enable and configure features that make it simple to manage your databases. Option groups are specific to the AWS Region where you create them. Previously, customers wanting to replicate RDS backups that had option groups to a different AWS Region had to copy the snapshot without the option group and then recreate the option group in the target Region before restoring the snapshot. Now, you no longer need to separate the steps and can instead initiate the snapshot copy and specify the option group copy in the same request as the snapshot copy.

The existing boolean parameter CopyOptionGroup on the CopyDBSnapshot API and CLI commands now also support cross-Region copy, along with cross-account copy. You can now copy options groups to the destination snapshot in the target AWS Region from the source snapshot by setting this parameter to true.

This capability is available on Amazon RDS for Oracle in all commercial AWS Regions and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. To learn more, review the Amazon RDS API Documentation.

title: `color-scheme: only` Is Not a Value, and the Line You Are About to Ship Does Nothing
description:
Safari 27.3 beta started darkening light websites that never implemented dark mode. If you have read about it this week, you have probably also read that the way out is color-scheme: light only.

That is correct. What nobody mentions is that only on its own is not a value, and the declaration most people reach for first is dropped by the parser without a word.

The grammar, from the spec

CSS Color Adjustment Level 1 defines the property like this:

Name:    color-scheme
Value:   normal | [ light | dark | <custom-ident> ]+ && only?
Initial: normal

Read the value line carefully. only is behind && and a ?. It is an optional modifier that must accompany at least one scheme keyword. It is not an alternative to light or dark.

So this is valid, and means what you want:

:root { color-scheme: light only; }

And this is not a valid declaration at all:

:root { color-scheme: only; }   /* dropped */

No error, no warning, no visual difference on your machine. An invalid declaration is discarded at parse time and the property keeps its previous value, which is normal. The line is in your stylesheet, your diff, your review, and it is doing nothing.

What only actually does

The spec is one sentence: "Forbids the user agent from overriding the color scheme for the element."

The mechanism is in the algorithm for the used color scheme. If the user's preferred scheme is in your list, that is used. Otherwise:

if the user has indicated an overriding preference for their chosen color scheme, and the only keyword is not present in color-scheme for the element, the user agent must override the color scheme

only is the one token that makes that branch not fire. light alone tells the browser you support light. light only tells it that it may not overrule you.

Those two are a single word apart and nobody reviewing a stylesheet reads them as different things.

Why this was always going to happen

The same spec explains, in a note, why browsers had been leaving pages alone until now:

Because many pages were authored before color scheme support existed, user agents cannot automatically adapt the colors used in elements under their control, as it might cause unreadable color contrast with the surrounding page.

That was the constraint. A browser could not safely recolour a page that had said nothing, because it did not know enough. A vendor that believes it now knows enough, through analysing the page rather than guessing, is no longer bound by it. One of them has decided that.

The part that reaches you as a bug report

A recoloured page is a visible change with no visible cause. The user did not install anything, your deploy did not change, and the setting that did it is not one they think of as a setting.

And you cannot query your way out. Safari's own documentation says it "prevents websites from detecting when Adaptive Dark Mode has been applied", and that "JavaScript that queries CSS colors will get the original authored colors, not the transformed ones". So getComputedStyle reports your stylesheet, not the screen.

Which means the broken-looking line above fails in the worst possible way. You ship color-scheme: only, you check your own page, it looks right, because it always looked right on your machine. The declaration is invalid, the browser keeps recolouring, and the only instrument that would tell you is one the browser deliberately disabled.

Two minutes that settle it

The property reads back, even when the colours do not:

getComputedStyle(document.documentElement).colorScheme
// "light only"  -> parsed, you are opted out
// "normal"      -> your declaration was dropped

That works because the computed value of color-scheme is, per the spec, "the keyword normal, or an ordered list of specified color scheme keywords". It is reporting what the parser kept, which is exactly the question. It is not reporting any colour, which is the question the browser will not answer.

Check the string, not the screen.

title: Workflow SDK adds idempotent starts
description:
The Workflow SDK's start() function can now admit a run and claim a hook in one atomic step. Duplicate workflow starts fail safely. The atomic start replaces the previous getHookByToken()-then-start() pattern, whose gap between the lookup and the start left a documented duplicate-start race.

Subscribe to messages inside the run

The claimed Hook exists from the moment the run is admitted, so resumeHook works even before the run begins executing, and early payloads are buffered and delivered in order. Inside the workflow, createHook({ token }) with the same token binds to the already-claimed hook: guaranteed, registering nothing new, adding no step, and resolving getConflict() to null.

Idempotency with no extra code

The token is the idempotency key, and it comes from your own domain: an order ID, an invoice ID, an import ID, or a request ID. The token alone guarantees idempotency. Exactly one run owns it, and a duplicate start() throws HookConflictError carrying the owner's conflictingRunId and never becomes a run. The workflow doesn't have to open the hook at all, and if it never does, the token was only an idempotency key and the run completes normally.

Setting experimental_minRetention keeps the token unavailable after the run ends, counted from start(), so late duplicates are still refused.

Upgrade to workflow 5.3.1 and read the idempotency documentation to get started.

title: How to Mask Sensitive Data in SQL: Make a Safe Database Copy
description:
Data masking replaces sensitive values, like names, emails, and card numbers, with hidden versions. The result is a database copy you can share with developers or testers without exposing real people. In this tutorial, you'll copy a MySQL database into a new one and mask its private columns on the way, using *Data Transfer* in VisuaLeaf.

Before you start

  • VisuaLeaf is connected to a MySQL 8 server.
  • The sample database summer_camp. It has 7 linked tables: guardians, campers, counselors, camp_sessions, enrollments, payments and incident_reports.
  • One rule: *never mask the original database.* You always mask a copy.

The summer_camp database in VisuaLeaf’s schema view: 7 tables linked by foreign keys.

Step 1: Create the target database

The masked copy needs a place to go:

CREATE DATABASE summer_camp_dev
  CHARACTER SET utf8mb4
  COLLATE utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci;

Or, without writing SQL, use the *Create Database* form: type summer_camp_dev as the name, keep utf8mb4 as the character set, and add a comment so everyone knows what this database is for. Then click *Create Database*.

Creating the empty summer_camp_dev database with VisuaLeaf’s Create Database form.

Step 2: Your first job: mask names and emails

In *Data Transfer, click *New task** and name it Mask summer_camp. Then click *Add job*. The job editor has three parts: Source, Target, and Mapping.

First, tell the job where the data comes from and where it goes:

  • *Source:* type Table, database summer_camp, table guardians
  • *Target:* type Table, database summer_camp_dev, table guardians

Leave When rows already exist on Add or update. If you run the job again, existing rows are updated instead of duplicated.

Set the source and target tables for the first job.

Scroll down to *Data Transformation Rules. In *Field mapping, every row is one column of the table. In the **Value Script**** column, pick a mask from the list: *Mask name* for first_name and last_nameand *Mask email* for email.

For more options, like keeping the last characters or replacing a value with fixed text, use the *Mask a field* button above the table.

The *Live preview* on the right shows what the job will write for a real row: Emily becomes E****, and her email becomes e***********r@example.com.

Pick a mask in Value Script and check the result in Live preview.

Click *Save, then run the job with the play button next to it. When it finishes, the job shows a green check and the task shows *Completed**.

Save the job and run it. A green check means it’s done.

See the difference

In the Connections panel, double-click guardians under summer_camp_dev. The table opens with a ready-made SELECT * FROM guardians query and the data below it. Names and emails are masked. Phone, address, and city are still real, because we haven't masked them yet.

Double-click a table to see its data. Names and emails are now masked.

To compare, open guardians from summer_camp as well and put the two tabs side by side.

Original data on the left, masked copy on the right.

Step 3: A second job: mask a different kind of data

Add another job for campers (source summer_camp.campers, target summer_camp_dev.campers). Mask first_name and last_name as *Name, and allergies as *Replace with text**, for example Sample note. Run it.

We did guardians first on purpose: every camper points to a guardian, so the guardians must already exist in the copy. More on that in Step 5.

Since both tables are now insummer_camp_dev, you can check them together. Type this in the query box of the open table and click Run:

SELECT c.first_name, c.last_name, c.allergies, g.email
FROM campers c
JOIN guardians g ON g.guardian_id = c.guardian_id
WHERE c.camper_id = 1;

The values are masked, but the JOIN still returns a row. The links between tables survived because we didn't touch the IDs.

The JOIN still works on the masked copy: camper 1 is still linked to their guardian.

Step 4: Add jobs for the other tables

Repeat for the remaining 5 tables. Don't run anything yet: first you add the masks to the jobs, so the data is masked while it's copied, in a single pass.

The full list of masks:

Table Column Mask
guardians (existing job) phone Mask phone
guardians (existing job) national_id Mask SSN
guardians (existing job) home_address Replace with text
counselors first_name, last_name Mask name
counselors email Mask email
counselors phone Mask phone
counselors bank_iban Keep first / last characters (last 4)
payments card_holder_name Mask name
payments card_number Mask credit card
payments card_expiry Mask (generic)
incident_reports description Replace with text

camp_sessions and enrollments hold nothing private, so they're copied as they are. Don't mask the ID columns (camper_id, guardian_id...): they link the tables together.

All 7 jobs are ready. Next, we set the order they run in.

Step 5: Set the run order and run

A child table can only be copied after its parent table exists in the target. Every camper points to a guardian, so guardians is the parent of campers.

Set this with the *Parents* column on each job. The easiest way is the Visual view: click a job card, and in Job Details, under Parent dependencies, tick the jobs that must finish first. You can also drag from the right edge of one card onto another. Arrange the cards in this order:

Click a job to pick its parents. Mask payments waits for guardians and enrollments.

Then click *Run All* and check that every job shows Completed in *Monitor* or *History*.

Step 6: Check for leaks

Open the masked tables again, like in Step 2. Then check free-text columns, which often hide names you masked elsewhere:

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM summer_camp_dev.incident_reports
WHERE description LIKE '%Carter%';

The result should be *0*.

The leak check returns 0, and every incident description is replaced in the copy.

Bonus: Schedule the task

The task's *Schedule* is set to Manual by default. Click the pencil next to it, pick Weekly, choose Every Monday at 9 AM, and click Save Schedule, and VisuaLeaf refreshes summer_camp_dev with freshly masked data on its own.

Schedule the task to refresh the masked copy every Monday at 9 AM.

Because the jobs use *Add or Update*, each scheduled run updates the existing rows instead of adding duplicates.

Export the masked data

Sometimes a developer needs a file, not a database connection. Since summer_camp_dev is already masked, you can export it safely with a new Data Transfer job.

*One table.* Set the source to *Table, for example summer_camp_dev.guardians. Then pick a file as the target: *CSV file, **JSON file*, *XML file,**** or *Excel workbook*.

*The entire database.* Set *Source Type* to *Database* and *Database Name* to summer_camp_dev. Then pick a *Target Type*:

  • *SQL dump (tables and data):* one .sql file that rebuilds the whole masked database. This is the easiest thing to send to someone.
  • *CSV files, *JSON files, **XML files**** or *Excel workbooks:* one file per table.
  • *Database* or a MongoDB *Collection:* copy the masked data to another server.

Export the masked table straight to an Excel file.

Things to watch out for

  • *Unique columns.* Two masked emails can end up identical and break a UNIQUE constraint. Use a consistent *ID (hash)* when a column must stay unique.
  • *Required columns.* Don't write this field as NULL (see If Missing), so it fails on NOT NULL columns.
  • *Empty values.* Check in the Live preview whether Replace with text also fills NULL rows.

Wrapping up

You now have summer_camp_dev: a full copy of the database with the same tables, the same links and realistic data, but no real names, emails, card numbers or health notes. The original was never touched, and everything was masked in a single pass while the data was copied.

The same steps work for any database: find the columns you'd never want leaked, pick a mask for each, keep the IDs, set the parents, and check the Live preview before you run. Once you save the task, you can rerun it, schedule it, or export the result whenever someone needs safe data.

*Ready to try it on your own database?* Download VisuaLeaf for Windows, macOS or Linux, and create your first masking task in a few minutes.

title: The OnePassApps Stylesheet: 403 Custom Properties, Container Queries and Forced Colours
description:
I work on OnePassApps, the team behind app.onepassapps.com. This post is a byte-level read of the stylesheet the live site actually serves - the one file every page on the site is painted with. No design documents and no memory: a plain HTTPS GET of the home page, then of the stylesheet that page links to, with a browser User-Agent and no JavaScript.

The file

The live home page links two stylesheets. The first, /shell-fallback.css, is 3,054 bytes and is the pre-JavaScript fallback that puts the first pixels on screen. The second, /assets/index-B_evf03w.css, is the real one: 242,648 bytes of CSS, served with a one-year immutable cache header, an ETag, and no Last-Modified. The same page also preloads three JavaScript chunks as modules.

403 CSS custom properties

The bundle declares 403 CSS custom properties and references them 2,885 times with var(). They are not a token system in the abstract - they cluster into families with obvious names:

  • brand and surface: brand, brand-edge, brand-glow, brand-ink, canvas, paper, pane, raised
  • ink scale: ink-1, ink-2, ink-3, ink-disabled, plus color-ink-1 through color-ink-4
  • control sizing: control-xs, control-sm, control-md, control-lg, hit-min
  • motion: dur-instant, dur-fast, dur-base, dur-slow, dur-reveal, paired with ease-out, ease-in-out, ease-spring, ease-settle
  • layout: gutter, measure, hero-pad, dialog-pad, and a container scale from container-sm up to container-3xl

That last group is the useful one for anyone writing their own stylesheet against this design: the sizes are named, not magic numbers repeated through rules.

Fonts: one family, 7 files, served from our own host

There are 14 font-face blocks, every one of them for the same family, Inter Variable, declared as a variable font with a weight axis from 100 to 900 and font-display set to swap. Each block carries its own unicode-range declaration, and together they point at 7 woff2 files - the Latin, Latin Extended, Greek, Greek Extended, Cyrillic, Cyrillic Extended and Vietnamese subsets, 218,512 bytes in total.

Two things follow. The fonts are not loaded from Google Fonts or any third-party origin - they come off the same host as the CSS, so a reader's browser makes no request to a font CDN. And the page does not preload them: the document head contains no font preload link at all, so the first paint does not wait on a font file.

How the theme is chosen

The stylesheet contains zero occurrences of the prefers-color-scheme media feature, so the operating system's dark-mode setting cannot switch this site's colours on its own. The choice is made in the application code instead: the JavaScript reads the operating system preference with matchMedia, resolves it to a light or dark theme, and applies it through the class selectors the stylesheet already understands - the stylesheet carries the dark and light variable sets, and the page toggles between them.

In other words the theme is a decision the app makes, with the system preference available as an input, rather than a rule the reader's laptop imposes.

Container queries, not just breakpoints

The stylesheet uses 65 container-query rules across 13 named containers - banner, diff, dtstatus, filelist, icongrid, main, not, pane, present, reactions, tile-meta, tints and toolgrid - alongside 23 distinct media conditions across 61 media blocks.

The media conditions are the accessibility surface, and they are worth reading closely:

  • forced-colors: 6 block(s), so the site keeps working when the operating system forces its own palette
  • prefers-contrast: 2 block(s), so a reader who asks for more contrast gets it
  • prefers-reduced-motion: 10 block(s), split between a reduce case and a no-preference case
  • pointer and hover capability: 15 block(s) covering coarse and fine pointers and hover-capable devices
  • width: 26 block(s) on viewport width in pixels and in rem, the rem ones ranging from 40rem up to 100rem

So the layout is built to be read on a phone and on a desktop, with a mouse and with a keyboard, with motion switched off, and with the operating system forcing colours it did not choose.

The rest of the accounting

  • 28 feature-query blocks - the site asks what the browser supports before using it
  • 5 cascade layers, named base components properties theme utilities - so specificity does not have to be fought with important flags
  • 3 keyframe animations, named spin toolpass-startup-ready-in tp-image-ready
  • 40 color-mix() calls - colours composed out of existing tokens instead of hand-picked hex values
  • 120 hex literals, 66 of them unique - a small literal palette, with everything else derived from it

Why this is worth a look

The interesting part is not that a stylesheet exists. It is that this one keeps its decisions in named variables, derives its colours, supports forced colours and reduced motion, and serves its fonts from its own host. Every one of those is a decision you can check, and this post checked them by reading the bytes the server sent - no browser required.

The tools themselves are on the OnePassApps home page, and the per-app walkthroughs are in the app guides.

I work on OnePassApps, so all of the above is a measurement of our own build rather than a review of someone else's.

title: Deconstructing an Autonomous AI Video Production Pipeline for Enterprise Creatives
description:
Building a high-throughput AI video production agency requires solving three core technical bottlenecks: character temporal consistency, high-resolution upscaling without artifact hallucination, and autonomous asset delivery.

In this teardown, we explore how Hivve Studio architectures an autonomous production stack for high-growth tech brands.

Architecture Overview 

[ Creative Brief & Prompt Schema ]
             │
             ▼
[ Midjourney v6 / Flux.1 LoRA Conditioning ] (Visual Anchors)
             │
             ▼
[ Kling / Runway Gen-3 / Sora Video Synthesis ] (Temporal Motion)
             │
             ▼
[ Topaz Neural Upscale & Frame Interpolation ] (4K Master)
             │
             ▼
[ AudioCraft & ElevenLabs Neural Soundscape ]
             │
             ▼
[ Autonomous Delivery via OpenClaw Workflows ]

1. Consistent Character & Asset Embeddings

The fatal flaw of amateur AI video is temporal flicker and morphing subjects. To eliminate drift, Hivve Studio trains proprietary LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) models on client assets, enforcing strict seed consistency across camera rotations.

2. Autonomous Distribution Workflows

Video assets are not produced in isolation. By wiring generation pipelines into autonomous agent orchestrators (using OpenClaw and custom webhooks), generated video creatives are automatically formatted, captioned, and syndicated across multi-channel campaign repositories.

3. CAD & 3D Ray-Traced Video Integration

For luxury hardware and fine jewelry, synthetic diffusion models are paired with ray-traced CAD geometry (Rhino, MatrixGold, Blender). This ensures sub-millimeter precision, true diamond refractive caustics ($n = 2.417$), and precious metal micro-roughness.
