                                            v
  +-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
  | CORE TRANSACTIONAL SETTLEMENT LAYER (Temporal Saga / Distributed SQL)             |
  |  [ Executes Atomic Multi-Domain Settlement with Cryptographic Verification ]      |
  +-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

Agent-to-Agent (A2A) Protocol Contract Specification

Inter-agent communication relies on standardized JSON-RPC 2.0 / CloudEvent structures. Agents exchange dynamic proposal contracts containing requested capabilities, SLA constraints, and cryptographic signatures.

Agent Delegation Request Payload (payment-to-fx-delegation.json) 

{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "eventId": "A2A-DEL-2026-90128",
  "sourceAgent": "urn:xenon:agent:bian:payment-execution",
  "targetAgent": "urn:xenon:agent:bian:foreign-exchange",
  "transactionCorrelationId": "BIAN-PAY-2026-X89102",
  "delegationIntent": "EXECUTE_FX_LOCK_AND_SETTLE",
  "constraints": {
    "sourceCurrency": "USD",
    "targetCurrency": "EUR",
    "sourceAmount": 250000.00,
    "maxAcceptableSlippagePercent": 0.05,
    "settlementDeadline": "2026-09-16T12:15:00Z"
  },
  "delegationContext": {
    "originatingCustomerTier": "CORPORATE_TIER_1",
    "urgencyLevel": "HIGH_PRIORITY"
  },
  "signature": "eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsImtpZCI6ImFnZW50LXBheW1lbnQifQ..."
}

Technical Implementation: Java Agentic Delegation Node

The Java implementation below demonstrates how a BIAN PaymentAgent autonomously evaluates an incoming cross-border transaction, dynamically delegates parallel sub-tasks to adjacent domain agents (ComplianceAgent, FxAgent, LiquidityAgent), and aggregates the results into an execution payload.

package com.xenon.banking.agent.payment;

import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

import java.net.URI;
import java.net.http.HttpClient;
import java.net.http.HttpRequest;
import java.net.http.HttpResponse;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;

public record CrossBorderPaymentTask(
        String transactionId,
        String debtorAccount,
        String creditorAccount,
        String sourceCurrency,
        String targetCurrency,
        double amount
) {}

public record DelegationResult(
        boolean isApproved,
        String fxRateLockId,
        double convertedAmount,
        String liquidityReservationId,
        String failureReason
) {}

@Component
public class AutonomousPaymentAgent {

    private final HttpClient httpClient;
    private final ObjectMapper objectMapper;

    public AutonomousPaymentAgent(ObjectMapper objectMapper) {
        this.objectMapper = objectMapper;
        this.httpClient = HttpClient.newBuilder()
                .connectTimeout(Duration.ofMillis(500))
                .build();
    }

    public DelegationResult processCrossBorderDelegation(CrossBorderPaymentTask task) {
        System.out.println("PaymentAgent initiating autonomous delegation for Task: " + task.transactionId());

        // 1. Parallel Delegation: Asynchronously invoke Compliance, FX, and Liquidity Agents
        CompletableFuture<Boolean> complianceFuture = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> 
                delegateToComplianceAgent(task));

        CompletableFuture<FxQuoteResult> fxFuture = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> 
                delegateToFxAgent(task));

        CompletableFuture<String> liquidityFuture = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> 
                delegateToLiquidityAgent(task));

        // 2. Aggregate Agent Delegation Results (Wait for parallel completion)
        CompletableFuture<Void> allDelegations = CompletableFuture.allOf(complianceFuture, fxFuture, liquidityFuture);

        try {
            allDelegations.get(); // Join parallel executions

            boolean compliancePassed = complianceFuture.get();
            FxQuoteResult fxResult = fxFuture.get();
            String reservationId = liquidityFuture.get();

            // 3. Autonomous Negotiation Logic
            if (!compliancePassed) {
                return new DelegationResult(false, null, 0.0, null, "Sanctions screening failed compliance check.");
            }

            if (fxResult == null || !fxResult.isSuccess()) {
                return new DelegationResult(false, null, 0.0, null, "FX Agent failed to secure rate quote within slippage tolerances.");
            }

            if (reservationId == null) {
                return new DelegationResult(false, null, 0.0, null, "Liquidity Agent rejected Nostro balance reservation.");
            }

            // All agent contracts successfully negotiated!
            return new DelegationResult(
                    true,
                    fxResult.rateLockId(),
                    fxResult.convertedAmount(),
                    reservationId,
                    "SUCCESS"
            );

        } catch (Exception e) {
            return new DelegationResult(false, null, 0.0, null, "Inter-agent delegation error: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }

    private boolean delegateToComplianceAgent(CrossBorderPaymentTask task) {
        // A2A Protocol call to Sanctions & Compliance Domain Agent
        String payload = String.format("{\"transactionId\":\"%s\",\"debtor\":\"%s\",\"creditor\":\"%s\"}", 
                task.transactionId(), task.debtorAccount(), task.creditorAccount());

        return postToAgent("https://compliance-agent.internal.xenon/v1/a2a/screen", payload);
    }

    private FxQuoteResult delegateToFxAgent(CrossBorderPaymentTask task) {
        // A2A Protocol call to Foreign Exchange Domain Agent
        String payload = String.format("{\"sourceCurrency\":\"%s\",\"targetCurrency\":\"%s\",\"amount\":%.2f}", 
                task.sourceCurrency(), task.targetCurrency(), task.amount());

        try {
            String response = postToAgentRaw("https://fx-agent.internal.xenon/v1/a2a/quote", payload);
            return objectMapper.readValue(response, FxQuoteResult.class);
        } catch (Exception e) {
            return null;
        }
    }

    private String delegateToLiquidityAgent(CrossBorderPaymentTask task) {
        // A2A Protocol call to Nostro/Vostro Liquidity Domain Agent
        String payload = String.format("{\"currency\":\"%s\",\"amount\":%.2f}", task.sourceCurrency(), task.amount());
        return postToAgentRaw("https://liquidity-agent.internal.xenon/v1/a2a/reserve", payload);
    }

    private boolean postToAgent(String url, String jsonBody) {
        try {
            String res = postToAgentRaw(url, jsonBody);
            return res.contains("\"status\":\"APPROVED\"");
        } catch (Exception e) {
            return false;
        }
    }

    private String postToAgentRaw(String url, String jsonBody) throws Exception {
        HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
                .uri(URI.create(url))
                .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
                .header("X-Agent-Identity", "urn:xenon:agent:bian:payment-execution")
                .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(jsonBody))
                .build();

        HttpResponse<String> response = httpClient.send(request, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());
        return response.body();
    }

    record FxQuoteResult(boolean isSuccess, String rateLockId, double convertedAmount) {}
}

State Reconciliation & Transactional Bounds

While autonomous agents freely negotiate task delegation across BIAN domains, agents are forbidden from directly updating microservice databases without transactional consensus.

Once inter-agent negotiation completes, the final aggregated plan is handed off to a Temporal Saga Orchestrator for atomic execution across downstream domain microservices:

  AGENT NEGOTIATION TO TEMPORAL EXECUTION HAND-OFF

  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
  | AUTONOMOUS AGENT NEGOTIATION LAYER (A2A Protocol)                               |
  |                                                                                 |
  |  [PaymentAgent] <===> [ComplianceAgent] <===> [FxAgent] <===> [LiquidityAgent]   |
  +----------------------------------|----------------------------------------------+
                                     |
                            1. Negotiated Execution Plan & Contracts
                                     |
                                     v
  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
  | TEMPORAL SAGA TRANSACTIONAL EXECUTION LAYER                                     |
  |                                                                                 |
  |  BEGIN SAGA                                                                     |
  |   ├── Activity 1: Commit Nostro Balance Hold (Liquidity Domain)                 |
  |   ├── Activity 2: Lock FX Rate Position (FX Domain)                             |
  |   ├── Activity 3: Append Compliance Audit Entry (Compliance Domain)             |
  |   └── Activity 4: Submit SWIFT MT103 / ISO 20022 Clearing (Payment Domain)      |
  |  COMMIT SAGA                                                                    |
  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

If any transactional step in the Temporal Saga fails (e.g., a network timeout during SWIFT clearing submission), the Saga automatically triggers Compensating Actions across all involved domains—releasing the Nostro balance hold and unwinding the FX rate lock.

Governance, Observability, and Auditability

Autonomous task delegation requires absolute transparency to satisfy financial regulatory standards (e.g., CPMI-IOSCO principles, EBA ICT guidelines).

1. Agent Boundary Enforcement (Policy-as-Code)

Agents operate within strictly defined operational boundaries enforced by Open Policy Agent (OPA) sidecars attached to each agent container:

  • Monetary Caps: A PaymentAgent cannot delegate or approve transactions exceeding $1,000,000 without triggering a mandatory Human-in-the-Loop escalation node.
  • Domain Isolation: A ComplianceAgent is strictly forbidden from invoking toolsets belonging to the PositionKeeping domain.

2. Distributed Agent Traceability (W3C Context Propagation)

Every A2A request forwards the global traceparent and a custom X-Agent-Delegation-Chain header. This allows enterprise tracing tools (Datadog/Jaeger) to construct visual DAG execution trees showing exact agent reasoning chains and backend API execution times:

[Trace: 4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736]
 ├── PaymentAgent (Reasoning: 45ms)
 ├── ├── ComplianceAgent (Reasoning: 12ms -> API Call: 35ms)
 ├── ├── FxAgent (Reasoning: 18ms -> API Call: 55ms)
 └── └── LiquidityAgent (Reasoning: 8ms -> API Call: 20ms)

Decoupling core banking operations via Autonomous Task Delegation across BIAN Bounded Contexts delivers true dynamic adaptability to complex financial workflows. By pairing agentic negotiation over standardized A2A protocols with deterministic Temporal Saga transactional settlement, modern core banking architectures eliminate the brittleness of static pipelines while maintaining total transactional integrity, domain isolation, and regulatory compliance.

title: Building a Firefox dark mode extension: what actually works (and what doesn't)
description:
Most dark mode extensions intercept every page load with a content script that injects CSS. Some use JavaScript-based theme detection, some use prefers-color-scheme media queries, some use their own inversion filters.

I wanted to understand why dark mode on the web is still such a mess, so I built NightOwl — a Firefox extension that applies dark mode without mutation observers and without touching pages it shouldn't.

The problem with most dark mode approaches

CSS inversion (filter: invert(1) hue-rotate(180deg)) is fast but breaks images, videos, and color-coded content. Media turns into negatives.

JavaScript-based theming can be more precise but adds latency to every page load. You see a white flash before the dark style applies.

Browser-level dark mode (about:config > layout.css.prefers-color-scheme.content-override) is the cleanest solution but only works for pages that actually support prefers-color-scheme. Most legacy sites still don't.

How NightOwl works

NightOwl applies dark mode selectively:

  1. System preference sync — if your OS is in dark mode, NightOwl defaults to dark
  2. Per-site memory — disable it on specific sites, the preference is remembered
  3. Instant toggle — the toolbar button switches mode without a page reload
  4. AMO-compatible manifest — uses only necessary permissions, no broad host access required 
{
  "permissions": ["storage"],
  "optional_permissions": ["<all_urls>"]
}

The extension uses browser.storage.local for per-site preferences and window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)") to read system intent.

Why I stopped trying to fix sites that resist dark mode

Some sites actively fight dark mode — they override prefers-color-scheme with inline styles, use JavaScript to force light mode, or use CSS specificity tricks. Fighting them adds complexity and breaks their carefully designed UIs.

The right call: let the user decide per site. NightOwl's per-domain memory means you can enable dark mode globally and whitelist the sites that look wrong. The 10% of sites that fight it aren't worth breaking the 90% that work.

What I learned building a dark mode extension

The hardest part isn't the CSS. It's the edge cases: PDFs, iframes from different origins, canvas elements, SVGs with embedded colors. I scoped the first version to handle the common case well rather than try to handle every edge case poorly.

MV3 makes some things cleaner. Firefox's Manifest V3 migration has gotten clearer. Service workers are the right model for persistent background state, even if the initial migration from MV2 background pages was painful.

Dark mode preference is binary but experience isn't. People who want dark mode actually want "less eye strain at night" — which also means they want to be able to watch a YouTube video without inverting the colors. Per-site control is the right UX.

Install it

NightOwl Dark Mode on Firefox Add-ons

It's small, it's free, and it doesn't collect any data. If you're a Firefox user who lives in dark mode, give it a try.

Building Firefox extensions means shipping to real users through AMO review. If you've gone through the AMO review process and have thoughts on it, I'd like to hear them.

title: Why Go Interfaces Are Different: A Deep Dive for OO Developers
description:
If you are transitioning to Go from object-oriented heavyweights like Java, C#, or C++, you will quickly notice that Go feels different. There are no classes, no inheritance hierarchies, and no implements keyword. Yet, Go is deeply polymorphic.

The secret lies in Go interfaces. They are arguably the most powerful and defining feature of the language. But because they don't behave like interfaces in traditional object-oriented programming (OOP), they often trip up newcomers.

In this article, we will explore Go vs Java interfaces, dig into the Go interface architecture to see how they work under the hood, and demonstrate how Go's unique design fundamentally changes the way you write and test software.

The Paradigm Shift: Go vs Java Interfaces

In languages like Java or C#, interfaces are explicit. A class must explicitly declare that it implements an interface.

Here is how you might define and implement an interface in Java:

// Java Explicit Interface
public interface DataWriter {
    void write(String data);
}

// The class MUST declare "implements DataWriter"
public class ConsoleWriter implements DataWriter {
    @Override
    public void write(String data) {
        System.out.println(data);
    }
}

This creates a rigid, top-down dependency. The ConsoleWriter must know about the DataWriter interface at compile time.

Go, on the other hand, uses implicit interfaces. A type implements an interface simply by implementing its methods. There is no implements keyword.

// Go Implicit Interface
type DataWriter interface {
    Write(data string)
}

// ConsoleWriter knows NOTHING about DataWriter
type ConsoleWriter struct{}

// It implicitly implements DataWriter by having this method
func (c ConsoleWriter) Write(data string) {
    fmt.Println(data)
}

Because of implicit interfaces in Go, the dependency graph is inverted. The consumer of the behavior defines the interface, not the producer. A package providing a ConsoleWriter doesn't need to know how other packages will use it. If it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, Go treats it like a duck.

Go Interface Under the Hood

To truly master Go, you need to understand the Go interface under the hood. How does the runtime know a struct satisfies an interface if it was never explicitly declared?

In the Go runtime code (written in C and Go), an interface is not just a pointer to an object. It is a two-word data structure known as an iface (for interfaces with methods) or an eface (for the empty interface any / interface{}).

When you assign a concrete type to an interface variable, Go constructs an iface struct that contains two pointers:

  1. tab (Type Word): A pointer to an itab (interface table) which holds metadata about the concrete type and a list of function pointers (the virtual method table) that map the interface's methods to the concrete type's methods.
  2. data (Data Word): A pointer to the actual concrete value in memory. 
classDiagram
    class iface {
        *itab tab
        *void data
    }
    class itab {
        *interfacetype inter
        *_type _type
        uint32 hash
        [4]byte _
        [1]uintptr fun
    }
    class ConcreteValue {
        "Actual data (e.g., struct fields)"
    }

    iface --> itab : tab
    iface --> ConcreteValue : data

When you call a method on an interface, the Go runtime follows the tab pointer to find the correct function in the itab, and passes the data pointer to it as the receiver.

The magic of the Go interface architecture is that the itab is generated on the fly (and then cached) the first time a specific concrete type is assigned to a specific interface type. This dynamic generation is what makes implicit interfaces possible without sacrificing the performance of static typing.

The Power of Go Small Interfaces

Rob Pike, one of Go's creators, famously coined the proverb: "The bigger the interface, the weaker the abstraction."

In Java or C++, it is common to see massive interfaces with a dozen methods (IUserService, IDatabaseManager). In Go, the standard library sets a different precedent: Go small interfaces.

The most famous interfaces in Go are just one method long:

type Reader interface {
    Read(p []byte) (n int, err error)
}

type Writer interface {
    Write(p []byte) (n int, err error)
}

Why is this so powerful? Because small interfaces are highly composable. If your function only needs to write data, it should accept an io.Writer, not a massive os.File or NetworkConnection struct.

By keeping interfaces small (1-3 methods), you maximize the number of types that can implicitly satisfy them, making your code vastly more reusable.

How Go Makes Testing Easier

The combination of implicit implementation and small interfaces revolutionizes Go unit testing interfaces.

In traditional OOP, if you want to mock a third-party class, that class must implement an interface provided by the third-party library. If they didn't provide one, you are stuck writing wrappers.

In Go, because interfaces are satisfied implicitly, you define the interface in your own testing package based strictly on the subset of methods you need.

Imagine you are using a massive third-party PaymentGateway struct with 50 methods, but your function only uses Charge().

// Third-party package (you can't change this)
package stripe

type PaymentGateway struct { /* ... */ }
func (p *PaymentGateway) Charge(amount float64) error { /* ... */ }
func (p *PaymentGateway) Refund(id string) error { /* ... */ }
// ... 48 more methods

To test your code, you don't need to mock all 50 methods. You define a tiny, local interface right where you need it:

// Your package
package billing

// 1. Define the interface locally
type Charger interface {
    Charge(amount float64) error
}

// 2. Depend on the interface, not the third-party struct
func ProcessOrder(c Charger, amount float64) error {
    return c.Charge(amount)
}

Now, the third-party stripe.PaymentGateway implicitly satisfies your local Charger interface, but in your test file, you can easily swap it out for a simple test double.

Fakes vs Mocks Go: A Pragmatic Approach

When writing test doubles for those interfaces, developers coming from other languages usually reach for Mocks (using tools like gomock or testify/mock). Mocks are dynamically generated objects that record how they were called and assert expectations (e.g., "Expect Charge() to be called exactly once with 50.00").

However, the Go community strongly leans towards fakes over mocks.

A Fake is a lightweight, working implementation of an interface built specifically for tests. It doesn't use reflection or assertion frameworks; it just uses plain Go logic.

Here is how you would write a fake for our Charger interface:

// billing_test.go
package billing

import "testing"

// Fake implementation
type FakeCharger struct {
    ChargedAmount float64
    ShouldFail    bool
}

func (f *FakeCharger) Charge(amount float64) error {
    if f.ShouldFail {
        return errors.New("insufficient funds")
    }
    f.ChargedAmount += amount
    return nil
}

func TestProcessOrder(t *testing.T) {
    // Arrange
    fake := &FakeCharger{}

    // Act
    err := ProcessOrder(fake, 50.00)

    // Assert
    if err != nil {
        t.Fatalf("expected no error, got %v", err)
    }
    if fake.ChargedAmount != 50.00 {
        t.Errorf("expected 50.00 to be charged, got %v", fake.ChargedAmount)
    }
}

Why Fakes over Mocks in Go?

  1. Type Safety and Refactoring: Mocks often rely on string-based method names and interface{} arguments, which break silently during refactoring. Fakes are standard Go code—if the interface changes, the compiler catches the broken fake immediately.
  2. Readability: When comparing fakes vs mocks Go, fakes are much easier to read. You are just reading Go code, not deciphering a domain-specific mocking language.
  3. Statefulness: Fakes can easily maintain state (like an in-memory map replacing a database), allowing you to test complex state transitions that are notoriously difficult to set up with mock expectations.

Conclusion

Go interfaces are fundamentally different from what you might be used to in Java or C#. By removing the explicit implements keyword, Go encourages a bottom-up architecture where abstractions are discovered rather than designed upfront.

By understanding the two-word iface structure under the hood, embracing small single-method interfaces, and utilizing fakes for testing, you can write Go code that is highly decoupled, incredibly easy to test, and true to the idiomatic spirit of the language.

title: Run TypeScript in Node.js Without a Build Step: Type Stripping Tested on Node 22, 24 and 26
description:
Cross-posted from my blog. The original, with any updates, lives on fabwaseem.com.

You can now run a .ts file with plain node app.ts, no tsx, no ts-node, no build step. Type stripping has been on by default since Node.js 22.18.0 and 23.6.0, and it became stable in Node.js 24.12.0 and 25.2.0. On Node.js 26 LTS it is simply how Node works.

But "Node runs TypeScript" has sharp edges. Enums fail. Parameter properties fail. Decorators fail. Imports without .ts fail. And Node never checks your types. I tested every one of these on Node.js 22.20.0, 24.22.2 and 26.13.0, and this post shows the exact errors, the tsconfig.json that catches all of them before runtime, and how startup time compares to tsx and precompiled JavaScript.

How Node.js type stripping works

Node replaces TypeScript type annotations with whitespace and runs what is left as JavaScript. It does not type-check, it ignores tsconfig.json, and it only accepts erasable syntax: TypeScript that disappears completely when you delete the types.

From the Node.js TypeScript docs history table:

Node.js version Change
v22.6.0 Type stripping added behind --experimental-strip-types
v23.6.0, v22.18.0 Enabled by default
v24.3.0, v22.18.0 No more experimental warning
v24.12.0, v25.2.0 Marked Stable
v26.0.0 --experimental-transform-types flag removed

You can check it at runtime: node -p "process.features.typescript" printed strip on all three versions I tested.

What works out of the box

This file ran unchanged with node ok.ts on Node 22.20, 24.22 and 26.13:

// ok.ts
interface User { id: number; name: string }
type Role = 'admin' | 'user';
import type { Stats } from 'node:fs';
import { greet } from './util.ts';

const u: User = { id: 1, name: 'Waseem' };
const role: Role = 'admin';
function size<T>(xs: T[]): number { return xs.length; }
const s = undefined as Stats | undefined;

console.log(greet(u.name), role, size([1, 2, 3]), s);
// hi Waseem admin 3 undefined

Interfaces, type aliases, generics, as casts, import type and annotated functions are all erasable, so they just work. Add "type": "module" to package.json; without it, Node prints a MODULE_TYPELESS_PACKAGE_JSON warning and reparses the file as ESM.

What fails (tested on Node 22, 24 and 26)

All three versions gave the same result for every case below.

TypeScript feature What Node prints
enum Color { Red, Green } SyntaxError [ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX]: TypeScript enum is not supported in strip-only mode
namespace A { export const x = 1 } SyntaxError [ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX]: TypeScript namespace declaration is not supported in strip-only mode
constructor(public name: string) SyntaxError [ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX]: TypeScript parameter property is not supported in strip-only mode
import { greet } from './util' Error [ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND]: Cannot find module '.../util'
import { User } from './types.ts' (User is an interface) SyntaxError: The requested module './types.ts' does not provide an export named 'User'
@log class K {} SyntaxError: Invalid or unexpected token
A .tsx file TypeError [ERR_UNKNOWN_FILE_EXTENSION]: Unknown file extension ".tsx"
A .ts file inside node_modules Error [ERR_UNSUPPORTED_NODE_MODULES_TYPE_STRIPPING]

Three of these surprise people the most:

  1. Type-only imports must say import type. Node removes the type but keeps the import statement, so it looks for a runtime export called User and crashes.
  2. Decorators don't run. That means NestJS, TypeORM entities and anything with @Injectable() still needs a compile step or a loader like tsx or SWC.
  3. Packages can't ship raw .ts. Node refuses to strip types under node_modules, so libraries still need to publish JavaScript.

--experimental-transform-types is gone in Node 26

On Node 24, node --experimental-transform-types enum.ts ran the enum (with an ExperimentalWarning). On Node 26.13.0 the same command printed:

node: bad option: --experimental-transform-types

If you relied on that flag for enums, Node 26 is the point where you have to remove them or go back to a loader.

The tsconfig.json that catches every failure

Node ignores tsconfig.json, but your editor and tsc don't. With this config, tsc flagged every runtime failure above (except decorators, see below) before I ran anything:

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "esnext",
    "module": "nodenext",
    "noEmit": true,
    "allowImportingTsExtensions": true,
    "erasableSyntaxOnly": true,
    "verbatimModuleSyntax": true,
    "strict": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true
  }
}

Output from tsc -p . with TypeScript 5.9.3:

enum.ts(1,6): error TS1294: This syntax is not allowed when 'erasableSyntaxOnly' is enabled.
ns.ts(1,11): error TS1294: This syntax is not allowed when 'erasableSyntaxOnly' is enabled.
paramprop.ts(1,23): error TS1294: This syntax is not allowed when 'erasableSyntaxOnly' is enabled.
noext.ts(1,23): error TS2835: Relative import paths need explicit file extensions in ECMAScript imports when '--moduleResolution' is 'node16' or 'nodenext'.
typeimport.ts(1,10): error TS1484: 'User' is a type and must be imported using a type-only import when 'verbatimModuleSyntax' is enabled.

What each option does:

  • erasableSyntaxOnly (TypeScript 5.8+) errors on enums, namespaces and parameter properties.
  • verbatimModuleSyntax forces import type for type-only imports.
  • allowImportingTsExtensions lets you write ./util.ts, which is what Node needs. It requires noEmit (or rewriteRelativeImportExtensions if you also emit).
  • module: nodenext makes tsc require file extensions like Node does.

The gap: decorators. TypeScript 5.9 accepts standard decorators, so tsc passed dec.ts, but Node 26 still threw a SyntaxError. If your code uses decorators, keep a build step for that code.

Run tsc --noEmit in CI and in a pre-commit hook. Node won't check types for you.

Replacing enums

The usual erasable replacement is a const object plus a type:

export const Color = { Red: 0, Green: 1 } as const;
export type Color = (typeof Color)[keyof typeof Color];

Startup time: node vs tsx vs precompiled JS

Same ok.ts (two small files), Node 26.13.0, 30 interleaved runs each, wall time for the whole process:

How it ran Median p90
node js/ok.js (precompiled with tsc) 27.7 ms 33.0 ms
node ok.ts (type stripping) 62.6 ms 67.2 ms
tsx ok.ts (tsx 4.23.15) 116.9 ms 128.5 ms

Built-in stripping was about half the startup time of tsx, but about 35 ms slower than running precompiled JavaScript on this machine. For scripts, CLIs, dev servers and tests that difference doesn't matter. For a serverless function where cold start counts, shipping compiled JavaScript is still faster.

When to use built-in type stripping

Use node file.ts for:

  • Scripts, seeds, migrations and one-off tools
  • CLIs and internal services you control end to end
  • Running tests with node --test on .ts files
  • Dev mode with node --watch src/server.ts

Keep a build step (tsc, SWC, esbuild or tsx) for:

  • NestJS and anything else that uses decorators
  • React and .tsx files
  • Libraries you publish to npm
  • Code that relies on paths aliases in tsconfig.json (Node ignores them)
  • Serverless functions where cold start matters

If you're upgrading Node at the same time, see Node 24 vs Node 26 for the other breaking changes, and TypeScript 7 for where the TypeScript compiler itself is going.

FAQ

Can Node.js run TypeScript directly?

Yes. Since Node.js 22.18.0 and 23.6.0, node file.ts works without a flag, and the feature is marked stable from Node.js 24.12.0 and 25.2.0. Node only strips types; it does not type-check and it does not support enums, namespaces, parameter properties or decorators.

Does Node.js type stripping check types?

No. Node replaces types with whitespace and runs the result. A file with type errors runs fine as long as the JavaScript is valid. Run tsc --noEmit separately to check types.

Why does my enum fail in Node.js?

Enums generate runtime code, so they aren't erasable. Node prints ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX: TypeScript enum is not supported in strip-only mode. Replace them with a const object and a union type, and turn on erasableSyntaxOnly so tsc warns you.

Is --experimental-transform-types available in Node 26?

No. It was removed in Node.js 26.0.0. On Node 26.13.0 the flag fails with bad option: --experimental-transform-types. It still works with a warning on Node 24.

Do I still need tsx or ts-node?

Only for code that uses non-erasable syntax, decorators, .tsx, or tsconfig paths. For plain erasable TypeScript, node is enough and started about twice as fast as tsx in my test.

Why do I need .ts in import paths?

Node resolves files exactly like it does for JavaScript ESM: no extension guessing. import './util' fails with ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND; write import './util.ts' and enable allowImportingTsExtensions in tsconfig.json.

title: Stem Separation Explained: How Music Source Separation Models Split a Song, With a Python Example
description:
By Tania Alwan

Stem separation, also called music source separation, takes a finished stereo mix and estimates the individual parts that went into it: vocals, drums, bass and everything else. It powers karaoke apps, remix tools and AI cover workflows. It's also a nice example of an "impossible" inverse problem that deep learning made practical.

This post covers how separation works, how quality is measured, and how to run an open-source model yourself in a few lines of Python.

The problem: un-mixing a sum

A stereo mix is, roughly, a sum of sources:

mix(t) = vocals(t) + drums(t) + bass(t) + other(t)

Given only mix, we want to estimate each term. Mathematically that's underdetermined: infinitely many combinations sum to the same signal. Models solve it by learning what each kind of source usually sounds like from large sets of multitrack recordings.

Approach 1: spectrogram masking

The classic deep-learning approach works in the time-frequency domain.

  1. Compute a spectrogram with a short-time Fourier transform (STFT).
  2. Predict a mask per source: a value between 0 and 1 for every time-frequency bin, saying how much of that bin belongs to the source.
  3. Multiply the mix spectrogram by each mask.
  4. Invert back to audio with the inverse STFT, usually reusing the mix's phase. 
import numpy as np
import librosa

y, sr = librosa.load("mix.wav", sr=44100, mono=True)
S = librosa.stft(y, n_fft=4096, hop_length=1024)
mag, phase = np.abs(S), np.angle(S)

# a trained model would predict this; here it's a placeholder
vocal_mask = model.predict(mag)          # shape == mag.shape, values in [0, 1]

vocals = librosa.istft(vocal_mask * mag * np.exp(1j * phase), hop_length=1024)

Weakness: reusing the mixture phase limits quality. When two sources overlap in the same bin, a single mask can't fully separate them, which is where "watery" artefacts come from.

Approach 2: waveform and hybrid models

Waveform models like the original Demucs operate directly on raw audio with a convolutional encoder-decoder, sidestepping the phase problem. Hybrid models combine a spectrogram branch and a waveform branch. Hybrid Transformer Demucs (HT Demucs), released by Meta's research team, adds transformer layers between the two branches to model longer-range context.

Other strong families include band-split architectures, which process different frequency bands with dedicated sub-networks. The open research community iterates on these quickly, often through public challenges.

How quality is measured

The standard metric is SDR (signal-to-distortion ratio), in decibels; higher is better. Benchmarks typically use the MUSDB18 dataset, which contains multitrack songs split into vocals, drums, bass and other.

Keep two caveats in mind:

  • SDR doesn't fully match perception. Two models with similar SDR can sound different.
  • Benchmarks use four stems. Many products offer more stems (guitar, piano), which aren't covered by the classic benchmark.

Always listen, not just read numbers.

Running Demucs locally

Demucs is open source and installable with pip.

python -m pip install -U demucs
demucs song.mp3                       # default model, 4 stems
demucs --two-stems=vocals song.mp3    # vocals + no_vocals only

Outputs are written to a separated/ folder, organised by model name and track. Check demucs --help for the model options available in your installed version.

Practical notes:

  • A GPU helps a lot. CPU-only works, but a full song can take a while.
  • Long files use more memory; the CLI has options for splitting into segments.
  • Input quality matters. Separation can't recover detail lost to heavy compression.

Batch processing a folder 

import subprocess, pathlib

for f in pathlib.Path("tracks").glob("*.wav"):
    subprocess.run(["demucs", "--two-stems=vocals", str(f)], check=True)

Evaluating your own outputs

If you're comparing models for a project, a simple, repeatable test beats impressions.

  • Pick 5 to 10 reference tracks across genres: a sparse acoustic song, a dense rock mix, an electronic track with heavy sidechain, a rap track.
  • Process all of them with each model using identical settings.
  • Listen blind if you can: rename files so you don't know which model produced which.
  • Check the residual: sum the stems and subtract the original mix. A large residual means energy went missing.
  • Log notes per track, not just a single overall score. 
import soundfile as sf, numpy as np
mix, _ = sf.read("song.wav")
stems = [sf.read(f"separated/htdemucs/song/{s}.wav")[0] for s in ("vocals","drums","bass","other")]
residual = mix - np.sum(stems, axis=0)
print("residual RMS:", np.sqrt(np.mean(residual**2)))

and why they happen

  • Bleed: hi-hats in the vocal stem. High-frequency transients overlap with sibilants.
  • Phasiness: a swirly sound on sustained notes, typical of masking with mixture phase.
  • Missing reverb tails: models tend to assign reverb ambiguously, so tails can end up split between stems.
  • Backing vocals: harmonies may land in "vocals" or "other" depending on the model's training data.

Choosing between local and hosted separation

Run it yourself when:

  • You want zero cost and full control.
  • You're batch-processing many files.
  • You need to keep audio on your own machine.

Use a hosted service when:

  • You don't have a GPU or don't want to manage environments.
  • You need more than four stems out of the box.
  • You want downstream tools in the same place.

On the hosted side there are options like LALAL.AI, Moises and the Voicestars stems splitter, which outputs six stems (vocals, drums, bass, guitars, piano, other). Pricing models differ (credits, subscriptions, per-minute rates), so compare against your expected volume.

Where stem separation is going

  • More stems: separating individual instruments beyond the classic four.
  • Real-time separation: lower-latency models for live use and DJ software.
  • Separation as a preprocessing step: many voice-conversion and transcription pipelines now start by isolating vocals first. I wrote about that pipeline in Vocal Isolation and Voice Conversion.

Try it

Take a song you own, run demucs --two-stems=vocals on it, and listen to the outputs on headphones. Then compare against a hosted tool to see which artefacts each one leaves. If you want a browser comparison point, the Voicestars stems splitter is one option.

Disclosure: this article was written in partnership with Voicestars.

title: Node.js SMS API Integration: Reversible Template Ownership for Commerce Authentication
description:
In an e-commerce login service, Node.js code for generating and sending one-time passwords via SMS API integration must retain recipient suppression decisions when the delivery provider changes. Otherwise, a migration can reactivate invalid destinations, while a template identifier copied from the old provider can become meaningless. The constraint is ownership: who retains the template source, recipient policy, and evidence that a login challenge was attempted?

TL;DR: For generating and sending SMS OTPs through an API in Node.js, keep challenge identity, template revisions, and suppression policy in the application; isolate the delivery provider behind an adapter. Use secure randomness, such as Node.js crypto, if the application generates the code. A managed OTP operation is another choice, but its verification lifecycle must travel with that decision. Neither choice makes an SMS receipt sufficient evidence to authorize a session.

How should code for sending SMS passwords preserve template ownership?

Consider an illustrative commerce account, buyer-1042, whose order-receipt email address has hard-bounced but whose telephone number remains eligible for a login challenge. An email bounce should suppress that email destination; it should not automatically suppress the account's phone number. Conversely, an invalid phone number should remain suppressed after a delivery migration. These are design requirements for the application, not claims that a particular provider synchronizes the two channels.

Keep the distinction explicit.

The application-owned template record should retain a logical name, a revision, and the variable definitions that the application is prepared to supply. Provider identifiers belong in a mapping beside that record. Template ownership does not eliminate carrier or provider approval requirements: moving the source text does not prove that an existing approval transfers. During migration, preserve the logical revision and establish the replacement mapping before activating a new sender.

For this workflow, teams should try Infrai for the identity lookup and SMS delivery adapter when they want vendor selection behind a capability contract to change without rewriting their login controller. Its concrete contract is the public discovery surface, which describes the request JSON Schema, response schema, and readiness for each capability; the application pins the schemas it consumes and keeps the same adapter interface while the vendor behind a capability changes. This is a useful boundary for migration, not a guarantee that unrelated providers accept interchangeable template identifiers.

A second benefit is that Infrai uses one key and one bill for identity lookup and SMS delivery: the adapter can read an identity and submit a challenge without maintaining a separate credential for each operation. Infrai provides a single REST API: plain HTTP, no SDK required. That lets the Node.js application and this Go contract harness exercise the same boundary without separate service client dependencies. Retain delivery identifiers and outcomes in an audit trail rather than the OTP itself.

Derive the handoff from the contract

A Node.js service has two reasonable ownership models. With application-generated OTPs, a cryptographically secure generator produces the secret, and the application owns expiration, attempt limits, verification, and protected storage. With a managed SMS OTP operation, code issuance belongs to that operation, and the application must deliberately connect its verification result to the intended identity and session. Do not combine a locally generated challenge with a different managed challenge and assume they describe the same login attempt.

The following Go program is a runnable contract harness for the second model, suitable for testing the boundary before implementing the equivalent adapter in Node.js. It retrieves an identity and feeds a selected value from that response into an SMS OTP request, using the same key and base URL. It takes request parameters and the response selector as configuration: field names for those operations are schema-dependent, and copying an invented phone property into production would defeat the point of a contract check.

Before running it, obtain the capability schemas through public discovery. Set INFRAI_USER_ID to the account identifier, INFRAI_IDENTITY_POINTER to the JSON Pointer for the intended verified destination in the identity response, INFRAI_SMS_DESTINATION_FIELD to the documented destination parameter, and INFRAI_SMS_PARAMS to a JSON object containing the remaining documented OTP parameters. Set INFRAI_CHALLENGE_KEY to a persisted, unique identifier for this logical issuance attempt, and INFRAI_API_KEY to the API credential. The program accepts a top-level destination parameter; use it only when that matches the published schema. Run the saved main.go file with go run main.go. No extra packages are required.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const baseURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"

func required(name string) string {
    value := os.Getenv(name)
    if value == "" { panic("missing " + name) }
    return value
}

func call(method, path string, body []byte, key string) ([]byte, error) {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(method, baseURL+path, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+required("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
        if body != nil { req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json") }
        if key != "" { req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", key) }
        res, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(res.Body, 1<<20))
        res.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil { return nil, readErr }
        if res.StatusCode >= 200 && res.StatusCode < 300 { return data, nil }
        if res.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests || attempt == 2 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("status %d: %s", res.StatusCode, data)
        }
        delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
        retry := res.Header.Get("Retry-After")
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retry); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
            if wait := time.Duration(seconds)*time.Second; wait > delay { delay = wait }
        } else if date, err := http.ParseTime(retry); err == nil {
            if wait := time.Until(date); wait > delay { delay = wait }
        }
        time.Sleep(delay)
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("retry budget exhausted")
}

func selectValue(value any, pointer string) (any, error) {
    if !strings.HasPrefix(pointer, "/") { return nil, fmt.Errorf("expected JSON Pointer") }
    for _, part := range strings.Split(pointer[1:], "/") {
        part = strings.ReplaceAll(strings.ReplaceAll(part, "~1", "/"), "~0", "~")
        switch node := value.(type) {
        case map[string]any:
            var ok bool
            value, ok = node[part]
            if !ok { return nil, fmt.Errorf("identity pointer missing") }
        case []any:
            i, err := strconv.Atoi(part)
            if err != nil || i < 0 || i >= len(node) { return nil, fmt.Errorf("invalid array pointer") }
            value = node[i]
        default:
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("identity pointer crosses a scalar")
        }
    }
    if value == nil { return nil, fmt.Errorf("identity destination is null") }
    return value, nil
}

func main() {
    data, err := call(http.MethodGet, "/auth/user/get/"+url.PathEscape(required("INFRAI_USER_ID")), nil, "")
    if err != nil { panic(err) }
    var identity any
    if err := json.Unmarshal(data, &identity); err != nil { panic(err) }
    destination, err := selectValue(identity, required("INFRAI_IDENTITY_POINTER"))
    if err != nil { panic(err) }
    var params map[string]any
    if err := json.Unmarshal([]byte(required("INFRAI_SMS_PARAMS")), &params); err != nil { panic(err) }
    if params == nil { panic("SMS parameters must be an object") }
    params[required("INFRAI_SMS_DESTINATION_FIELD")] = destination
    payload, err := json.Marshal(params)
    if err != nil { panic(err) }
    _, err = call(http.MethodPost, "/sms/otp", payload, required("INFRAI_CHALLENGE_KEY"))
    if err != nil { panic(err) }
    fmt.Println("Request returned HTTP success; inspect the documented issuance outcome")
}

This harness checks transport status and surfaces error responses; successful HTTP transport still requires interpreting the documented response envelope before a production controller records a successful issuance. Keep diagnostic output in a restricted development environment because response bodies can contain sensitive information. It is not a complete login controller: authorization of the requesting session, destination eligibility, abuse limits, and verification must surround this boundary. In particular, the selector must identify the authorized destination for this account, rather than trusting a destination supplied by an unauthenticated client.

Three attempts are an illustrative retry budget, not a delivery guarantee. Only rate-limit responses are retried here, with exponential delays and respect for Retry-After. A transport error is returned for reconciliation because its delivery outcome can be ambiguous. For the write operation, confirm its discovery-declared idempotency semantics and retain the same challenge key across retries; the platform convention specifies a default 24-hour deduplication window, which is a delivery deduplication boundary, not an OTP validity period. A production worker should use cancellation and a deadline rather than holding a login HTTP request open throughout a long backoff.

Exactly-once intent needs an audit trail

Treat the application ledger as the authority for whether a challenge may be issued, verified, or replaced. One logical issuance should have one durable key, while a deliberate replacement should have its own recorded transition. Persist the template revision, destination reference, suppression decision, provider message reference when available, and the evidence used to change delivery state. An exactly-once mindset means making these transitions reproducible; it does not establish exactly-once delivery to a handset.

A concrete migration trap is retrying an ambiguous send through the replacement provider. Each provider can deduplicate its own request and still deliver one message apiece. Reconcile the original attempt before permitting a replacement, or accept and document that duplicate-delivery risk. Delivery acceptance also must never consume the verification transition: a recipient can receive a message without completing authentication.

For bounced commerce email, preserve the suppression reason and channel-specific recipient identity before replacing a provider mapping. Keep a local suppression gate ahead of delivery and reconcile it with the provider's suppression records. Event processing here uses polling; choose an overlap strategy and deduplicate observed events so that a repeated read does not become a second state transition. The polling cadence is an application decision, and asynchronous state changes require explicit handling.

Compliance remains separate.

SPF describes authorization of email-sending hosts; it does not certify SMS consent, identity assurance, or regional legal compliance. For a deployment requiring domestic Chinese email compliance, obtain evidence for the actual delivery vendor and processing arrangement. Keep geographic abuse controls and country-based spending circuit breakers in the application. An email fallback requires its own code-generation and verification lifecycle, and the architecture should target REST email and SMS delivery; choose a specialist for SMTP relay, voice, WhatsApp, or RCS requirements.

Compare providers at the ownership boundary

The useful comparison is how much state and template coupling the application is willing to own. Evaluate delivery and verification independently: a strong email provider can be the appropriate home for receipt templates without being the service that verifies an SMS login challenge.

Option Relevant role Ownership and migration consequence
Twilio Verify Managed verification workflow Evaluate it when verification lifecycle ownership is the main goal; migrate its challenge semantics deliberately rather than treating it as an arbitrary text sender.
Amazon SES Email delivery for commerce receipts Evaluate it for the email side of bounce handling; keep email suppression policy separate from the SMS challenge ledger. It is not an SMS verification service.
Postmark Transactional email and bounce workflow Evaluate it when transactional email operations and template workflow dominate; an SMS authentication component remains a separate architectural choice.
Infrai Identity lookup and SMS operations through one REST surface Evaluate it when a shared credential and schema-described capability boundary reduce adapter work; retain application-owned template revisions, suppression policy, and verification authorization.

With Auth0 or Clerk plus Twilio Verify, the alternative is two service signups and two sets of service credentials. The application must connect the identity or session reference to a verification request and connect the verified result back to the authorized login transition. The shared-key approach reduces credential plumbing, but the same authorization and audit obligations remain.

The trade-off is one vendor to trust, one bill, and one shared availability dependency. Twilio Verify is a better fit when adopting a specialist verification lifecycle is the main requirement; Postmark or Amazon SES is worth evaluating when email bounce operations dominate. A unified interface should earn its place by reducing a specific migration task.

Roll out a reversible change

Start with one application-owned template revision and a small, explicitly selected account cohort. Compare the pinned request and response schemas, recreate provider template mappings, and reconcile suppressions before switching delivery. Exercise one accepted request, one rate-limit retry, and one ambiguous outcome in a controlled environment. Those are test cases, not reported measurements.

Keep rollback boring.

Switch the adapter mapping for new challenges, preserve outstanding challenge ownership until they expire or complete, and never mirror real OTP sends to both providers merely to compare results. A rollback must retain the suppression ledger and audit history. That is the practical meaning of a reversible vendor decision for a commerce login service.

References

These references cover verification workflow, email delivery, and authentication boundaries.

  • Twilio Verify
  • Amazon SES sending activity
  • Postmark bounce webhooks
  • Auth0 multi-factor authentication
  • Clerk documentation
  • Node.js crypto
  • RFC 7208: SPF

Sources

If this ownership boundary fits your system, start with the schemas and conventions in the Infrai documentation.

title: Generate Presigned URL for File Download: S3-Compatible Node.js Storage
description:
To generate a presigned URL for file download in S3-compatible storage with Node.js, start with the tenant boundary, not the URL. Customer-support exports have two audiences: the agent who starts an export and the customer who downloads it. A public object URL is easy to deliver, but it is the wrong default for a tenant's conversations, screenshots, or product images.

Short answer: keep the bucket private, generate a presigned URL for the exact object, and give the browser only that temporary URL. In an S3-compatible Node.js workflow, the relevant operation is POST /v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}. Put the bucket and object key in the path, pass the required parameters, and use the returned URL before it expires.

The useful mental model is small:

  • Before: the browser receives a permanent storage address and your application has to police every download.
  • After: your application authorizes one tenant and one object, then hands the browser a time-limited download capability.

That choice also affects release work. When a new export path is rolled out, the storage action and its release signal should be traceable with the same application-level identity. A download link alone is not an audit plan.

How do you generate a presigned URL for file download in S3-compatible storage?

A link should answer three questions: which bucket, which object key, and how long the grant lasts. Treat the key as data, not as a string assembled from untrusted URL fragments. Validate the tenant association before requesting the presigned URL, and make the expiration short enough for the workflow without forcing an active download to race a clock.

The browser should never receive the platform API key. It also should not send that key to the returned presigned URL; the returned URL carries the authorization material expected by the storage service. Your server uses Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY for the API call, checks the response status, and returns only the result your client needs.

This is where “S3-compatible” can mislead. Compatibility describes a storage interface. It does not promise the same policy controls, recovery features, or browser configuration surface as every S3 implementation.

A minimal Node.js handoff

The example below keeps the download grant and the release signal in one small flow. The storage presign response becomes the payload recorded by the release observation call. Both requests use the same base URL and the same environment-provided key. In a real service, your database lookup would establish that ticket-1842 belongs to the requesting tenant before this function runs. The platform currently exposes 295 routes across 20 modules, and its documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages; that breadth is useful only if the access boundary remains clear.

type PresignResponse = {
  url: string;
  expires_at?: string;
};

type ApiError = {
  error?: {
    message?: string;
  };
};

const baseUrl = process.env.INFRAI_BASE_URL;
const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;

if (!baseUrl || !apiKey) {
  throw new Error("INFRAI_BASE_URL and INFRAI_API_KEY are required");
}

async function postJson<T>(url: string, body: unknown, idempotencyKey: string): Promise<T> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(url, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(body)
    });

    if (response.ok) {
      return (await response.json()) as T;
    }

    if (response.status !== 429 || attempt === 3) {
      const details = (await response.json().catch(() => ({}))) as ApiError;
      throw new Error(details.error?.message ?? `API request failed: ${response.status}`);
    }

    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("Retry-After"));
    const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter) ? retryAfter * 1000 : 2 ** attempt * 250;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
  }

  throw new Error("Retry limit reached");
}

export async function createTenantExportLink(
  bucket: string,
  objectKey: string,
  tenantId: string
): Promise<string> {
  const presigned = await postJson<PresignResponse>(
    `${baseUrl}/storage/object/presign/${encodeURIComponent(bucket)}/${objectKey
      .split("/")
      .map(encodeURIComponent)
      .join("/")}`,
    {
      tenant_id: tenantId
    },
    `export-link:${tenantId}:${bucket}:${objectKey}`
  );

  await postJson(`${baseUrl}/logs/ingest`, {
      event: "tenant_export_link_created",
      tenant_id: tenantId,
      object_key: objectKey,
      expires_at: presigned.expires_at ?? null
    }, `export-event:${tenantId}:${bucket}:${objectKey}`);

  return presigned.url;
}

The code deliberately uses the route from the storage contract and a listed observability route. It does not turn the presigned URL into a second API call, and it does not print the URL into logs. In production, log an export identifier rather than sensitive query parameters. If the logging call is retried, make the event idempotent in the surrounding application so a transient failure cannot create confusing duplicate release records.

The same handoff can sit beside a database snapshot or branch operation when a release changes the export schema. A feature flag in your application can gate the new path, while the snapshot and the observation event provide the rollback context. The point is not that a storage URL can roll back a deployment. The point is that the release record can retain the exact object identity and tenant scope that the new code used.

Which storage option fits this boundary?

There is no universal winner. The access model matters more than the adjective “S3-compatible.”

Security first.

Option Strong fit Boundary to check
Amazon S3 Mature IAM, bucket policy, versioning, object lock, and a broad ecosystem More policy and operational surface can be a poor match for a small service that wants one narrow integration
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible object access with Cloudflare’s edge-oriented delivery model Confirm the exact egress, routing, and browser-delivery behavior your tenant policy requires
Google Cloud Storage Strong Google Cloud IAM and object lifecycle controls It is a separate cloud control plane; S3 interoperability does not make every Google-specific feature identical
Infrai storage A self-describing REST surface for storage beside other backend capabilities behind one key; plain HTTP means no storage SDK is required No public or public-read ACL, no object versioning or object lock, no If-Match conditional writes, and no self-service set_cors route; strict recovery, concurrency, or browser-upload requirements need an external design

That last row is a fit for a private, signed-download workflow, not for a public image host or static website. Its breadth is the useful part: storage and other production modules share one contract, so adding a capability can mean another endpoint rather than another integration. The REST surface is also self-describing, with public discovery and schemas, so a Node.js service does not need a storage SDK just to inspect the contract. The trade is equally real. You are trusting one vendor, one bill, and one outage surface.

The cross-capability alternative is easy to describe and harder to maintain: Neon or PlanetScale for database state plus LaunchDarkly for release flags means two signups, two credential sets, and glue for correlating snapshot or branch state with flag changes and export events. That stack may be the better choice when each specialist's controls are non-negotiable. A single API key is a coordination advantage, not proof that the underlying capabilities have identical guarantees.

What will surprise you later?

First, private signed access is not the same as browser-ready direct upload. This is a limitation, not a footnote. The storage model has a cors_rules field, but there is no independent set_cors route for self-service configuration. If your support portal needs browser uploads from several origins, decide where that policy will live before choosing this path.

Second, recovery and concurrency are explicit gaps in the decision. There is no object versioning or object lock, so an accidental overwrite is not automatically recoverable. There is no If-Match conditional write, so strict mutual exclusion belongs in a queue or database coordination layer. Lifecycle expiration starts at one day, and multipart fragments do not have an automatic cleanup rule. Those details are easy to miss while the happy-path download works.

There are also scope limits: no cross-region automatic replication, no cross-cloud bulk migration tool, and vendor coverage for R2, S3, OSS, and COS rather than GCS or B2. Metadata is not server-searchable; listing supports prefix filtering. These are design boundaries, not reasons to pretend every object store behaves alike.

The decision rule

Choose presigned downloads when the resource is private, tenant-scoped, and consumed within a bounded time. Keep the bucket and ACL private. Generate the link server-side after authorization. Return the link without the platform credential, and record an event that can be correlated with the release path.

Choose a different storage design when the product needs permanent public URLs, static-site hosting, public-read ACLs, WORM retention, strict compare-and-swap writes, self-managed browser CORS, or built-in replication across regions and clouds. Those requirements are not solved by changing one path parameter.

For the customer-support export scenario, the clean boundary is therefore: private object, temporary URL, tenant check, and a release observation attached to the same workflow. The download stays simple for the browser. The authorization decision stays on the server.

Sources

  • Cloudflare R2 S3 API compatibility
  • Google Cloud Storage signed URLs
  • MDN: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing

title: Cross-Prompt Reuse of Entity-Replacement Responses
description:
arXiv:2611.00352v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: With model weights fixed, we measure how much of an entity-replacement response transfers between English factual questions, beyond whether answers change. We add the hidden-state change from two source questions to a target question about the same entity, comparing the predicted log-probability shift between two relations' published answers, given known answer prefixes, with the measured one. Hidden reuse injects the aligned change at 50% depth before the target's remaining layers; direct reuse adds source output-score changes. With other-relation sources, hidden reuse removes 45% and 49% of no-change error on 0.5-1B Qwen and Llama. Gemma-2-2B removes 22% and passes one of three comparisons in plain text without its default beginning-of-sequence (BOS) token. A later protocol restoring it yields 58-68%, passing every comparison on three cohorts. Larger checkpoints, chat format and new entities show replication and format- or cohort-dependent failures. On small plain-format checkpoints, other-relation hidden reuse mainly reproduces the shift both relations' questions share, without reliably lowering relation-selective error. With target-relation sources, hidden reuse's post hoc advantage over direct reuse is 0.2-0.9 nats outside chat format, unconfirmed and not replacement-specific. The same relation-neutral change at both questions' entity tokens lowers relation-selective error more than random or other-replacement changes, indicating receiving-question dependence.

title: I Built a Database Explorer That Can't Ruin Your Friday
description:
Every developer has a database horror story.

Mine usually starts with a terminal, a production connection string,
and the words "quick fix". It ends with someone saying "so... do we
have backups?" in a very quiet voice.

So I built DBAdminer: a database explorer that starts in
read-only mode, because it assumes you're tired, caffeinated,
and one typo away from a postmortem.

What is it?

A database explorer for Go. Point it at PostgreSQL, MySQL,
MariaDB, or SQLite, open your browser, and poke around: tables,
data, a SQL console, the works.

Full access is there when you want it, but you have to ask for it.
Like the sudo of database tools.

Get it running in 30 seconds

Grab a binary from GitHub Releases (Linux, macOS, Windows,
amd64 and arm64), then:

dbadminer --dsn 'postgres://user:pass@127.0.0.1:5432/app?sslmode=disable'

Open http://127.0.0.1:8080. Done. No installer, no runtime,
no 47-step setup wiki.

Already have DATABASE_URL exported? Just run dbadminer.
It also understands PG* vars, MYSQL_*, DB_*, and
Docker-style POSTGRES_*. It'll find your database the way a
dog finds a dropped sandwich.

"Read-only" actually means read-only

Not "we hid the delete button" read-only. Properly:

  • Only one SELECT, WITH, EXPLAIN, VALUES, TABLE, or SHOW per request
  • INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, CREATE, ALTER, DROP are rejected before they reach your database
  • Postgres, MySQL, and MariaDB also run queries in a read-only transaction, a second lock on the door
  • SQLite opens with mode=ro
  • The write UIs stay hidden, and the write APIs return 403

Belt, suspenders, and a rope.

When you really need to change things:

dbadminer --access=full

Now you get create/alter/drop dialogs, index and foreign-key
actions, and row editing in the grid. Use it wisely. Or at
least not on a Friday.

Don't want another app? Embed it.

This is my favorite part. If you already have a *sql.DB,
DBAdminer lives right next to it:

cfg := dbadminer.DefaultConfig()
ex, err := dbadminer.New(db, cfg)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
if err := ex.ListenAndServe(ctx); err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

The library imports only the standard library. The CLI is a
separate module, so importing DBAdminer won't drag a pile of
database drivers into your go.mod. Your dependency graph
stays calm.

You can also mount ex.Handler() on your own server. There are
examples for net/http, chi, and cobra.

Docker, because of course 

docker run --rm -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 \
  -e DATABASE_URL='postgres://postgres:5432/app?sslmode=disable' \
  dbadminer

Need several databases at once? Set DBADMINER_DATABASES=shop,app
and give each name its own prefixed variables
(SHOP_DATABASE_URL, APP_DB_USER, and so on). The README has
a full Compose example.

Paranoid by design

A tool that connects to your database should be a little
suspicious of everyone, so:

  • Binds to loopback (127.0.0.1) by default
  • Rejects requests with a non-loopback Host header
  • Checks that Origin matches
  • Optional basic auth for the page (--user / --password)
  • Limits for rows, query timeout, request body, and response size

Why I built it

It started with a simple wish: I just want to look at my database.

That's it. No grand plan. I was working on a project, I needed
to see some tables, and I wanted something Adminer-like. Easy,
right?

Reader, it was not easy.

  • Paid tools: great, but I wasn't looking to open my wallet to view a table.
  • DBeaver: it kept trying to download drivers, and where I work (behind a firewall), it kept asking me about it with pop-ups. Pop-up. Pop-up. Pop-up. I started to feel like the tool was trying to tell me something.
  • Beekeeper Studio: a trial, and one more closed-source desktop app to install and run.

What I really wanted was boring and simple: a tiny image I
can drop into my existing docker-compose.yml and forget about.
docker compose up, open a browser tab, done. No installers.
No driver downloads. No "please sign in to continue".

So I built exactly that. DBAdminer is one small Go binary (or
image) that sits next to your database like a polite houseguest.

Safety is the server's job, not the login form's

Most admin tools work like this: type the right username and
password, and you get the keys to everything.

DBAdminer works differently. The server decides what's
allowed, not whoever logged in.

  • It starts read-only. The mode is set in your config (--access or DBADMINER_ACCESS), not by what the browser asks for.
  • Write statements are rejected server-side before they reach your database, and the write APIs return 403.
  • Basic auth (--user / --password) only protects the page. It never turns on write access.

So even if someone gets into the page, they can look but not
touch. Want to allow writes? That's a deliberate decision, made
in your config and not by a button in the UI.

Try it, break it, tell me about it

⭐ Repo: https://github.com/dbadminer/dbadminer

Found a bug? Want MSSQL, dark mode, or a feature I haven't
thought of? Open an issue or send a PR. And if you try it, tell
me in the comments what database you pointed it at.

(If it's production, I hope you stayed read-only.)

title: SQL Challenge: Why Is Your SQL Query Still Returning NULL?
description:
Imagine your manager asks you to prepare a salary report.

Some employees have a bonus, while others have no bonus recorded.

Your manager wants to see 0 instead of NULL for missing bonuses.

You write a query, but the result still shows NULL.

What went wrong?

Let's look at the data.

employees

emp_id| name| department| salary| bonus
101 | Amit | IT | 90000| 10000
102 | Priya | IT | 70000| NULL
103 | Rahul | IT | 60000| 5000
104 | Neha | HR | 80000| NULL
105 | Sneha | HR | 85000| 15000
106 | Kiran | HR | 95000| NULL
107 | Meera | Finance | 75000| 8000
108 | Arjun | Finance | 55000| NULL

Your challenge

Display employee name, salary and bonus.

If the bonus is NULL, show 0 instead.

Which query would you choose?

Option A

SELECT name, salary,
COALESCE(bonus, 0) AS bonus
FROM employees;

Option B

SELECT name, salary,
COALESCE(0, bonus) AS bonus
FROM employees;

Option C

SELECT name, salary,
bonus + 0 AS bonus
FROM employees;

SQL Solution

Option A is correct.

SELECT name, salary,
COALESCE(bonus, 0) AS bonus
FROM employees;

Output

name| salary | bonus
Amit | 90000 | 10000
Priya| 70000 | 0
Rahul| 60000 | 5000
Neha| 80000 | 0
Sneha| 85000 | 15000
Kiran| 95000 | 0
Meera| 75000 | 8000
Arjun| 55000 | 0

Why does this work?

COALESCE checks the values from left to right and returns the first value that is not NULL.

For example:

COALESCE(10000, 0) returns 10000.

COALESCE(NULL, 0) returns 0.

Now look at Option B.

COALESCE(0, bonus)

It always returns 0 because 0 is already a valid value.

And Option C?

bonus + 0 still returns NULL when bonus is NULL.

Here is the important lesson:

NULL does not mean zero.

It means the value is missing or unknown.

COALESCE helps you show a useful value when the original value is missing. It does not change the data stored in the table.

Your turn

What will this query return?

SELECT COALESCE(NULL, NULL, 50, 100);

Will the result be NULL, 50 or 100?

Share your answer in the comments.

Want to learn more SQL with practical examples?

title: I’m building RIM, a self-hosted chat workspace with plugins and commands
description:
Hi DEV!

I’m the maintainer of RIM, an open-source, self-hosted chat workspace.

The idea is to put your tools and everyday actions beside your conversations. RIM has channels, DMs, groups and threads, but the part I’m most interested in sharing is how you can shape the workspace through plugins, commands, shortcuts and macros.

For example, the Kubernetes plugin shows pods alongside chat and lets you restart one after confirmation. The GitHub pull-request plugin puts open PRs in a panel beside the conversation. There are also plugins for polls and release tracking.

A quick tour of RIM: plugin panels, commands and search. Recorded in the running app with fictional demo conversations.

Plugins run in your client and can add panels, commands and context actions. Sandboxed web plugins work in both the browser and desktop app. Desktop process plugins can also connect to tools on your computer, such as kubectl.

Commands bring those actions into a searchable palette. You can assign eligible commands your own shortcuts, and macros save sequences of supported commands with their arguments so you can run a routine again without repeating each step.

I’m curious what other people would build with that foundation—a connection to an internal tool, a useful panel, or an action their team repeats every day.

The server is written in Rust, backed by PostgreSQL. The client uses React and TypeScript, with Tauri for the desktop app. A documented Docker Compose setup runs the server, database and web client. Desktop downloads are available for Linux and Windows.

RIM connects independently operated servers through relays and workspace hosts. Your relay handles your account and routes requests and events between your devices and the servers hosting your workspaces. A workspace host manages its channels, membership, permissions and moderation.

One server can do both jobs, which is how the Docker Compose setup starts. People using different relays can message each other and join shared workspaces without creating a separate account on every workspace host. Your identity is based on keys, with device linking and a recovery phrase.

DMs and private groups support MLS end-to-end encryption. Workspace channels, including private channels, are readable by their host server.

This is early 0.0.x software, with one maintainer. There’s no mobile app or voice/video calling yet, and the identity and encryption implementation has not had an external cryptographic review. The public instance is a community test service, with no guarantees of availability or data retention.

I also want to be transparent about development: I use AI coding agents extensively. I make the product and architecture decisions, review every change, and test locally and in a real browser against a throwaway server before each release. I’m responsible for maintaining what ships.

If you’d like to explore:

  • Try the hosted web app
  • Run your own instance
  • Browse the source
  • Explore the plugin tutorial

RIM is Apache-2.0 licensed. I’m looking for early testers, feedback on the self-hosting experience, and people interested in experimenting with plugins.

What tool or action would you want beside your team’s conversations?
