  • The Record: FBI blames TraderTraitor for Binance hack
  • AP: Binance security hack, North Korea
  • Blockaid: Binance hack analysis
  • Chainalysis: Binance exploit latest findings and response
  • Reuters via Investing.com: Binance says hackers used fake job interview
  • CoinDesk, Nov 3: Binance's $6.3 billion hack began with a fake job interview
  • CoinDesk, Oct 30: How one Ethereum permission let an attacker drain Binance
  • Cointelegraph: EIP-7702's role in the Binance hack
  • CNBC: Circle and Tether freeze funds

title: Halt, name and business, or how a greeting read as a refusal
description:
Development covered 25 Sep 2026 to 26 Sep 2026 (commit dates).

Here is a small interaction that went wrong in a way I find instructive. In Myriad Immortal Sect, the halls in a sect compound have people stationed at their doors. Click the Main Hall and its keeper greets you first; close the greeting and the hall's screen opens. That is the design, and it gives every building a voice.

The Main Hall's keeper is a gate guard whose first line is "Halt. Name and business." Two separate blind play-tests of the itch.io build reached that line, read it, pressed the button under it, and concluded they had been refused entry.

The button was the sentence that mattered

The button under every greeting said "Close". After "Halt. Name and business.", "Close" reads as "you are dismissed". Nothing on the screen told the player that closing the greeting was the way in.

The guard's line was fine. It is in character and it is the kind of thing a gate guard says. The problem was the label of the action, which is really a short sentence about what happens next. When closing a greeting opens a screen, the button now says "Go in". Buildings with nothing behind them keep "Close". One word, and a building nobody could enter became a building with a gruff doorman.

If you want to see which halls have someone stationed at the door, the codex entry for the Medicine King Valley main hall is a typical example.

My first theory was wrong

Before I found the label, I had a different explanation, and I shipped a fix for it.

On that build a player four steps from the Main Hall clicked it and got the guard's line, although they could not see a guard. The guard stands inside the doorway, so the hall is drawn over him. I concluded that the click was landing on a hidden sprite underneath, and changed click selection to pick whatever is drawn on top.

Then I tried to reproduce it on purpose, with a different building, and it behaved exactly as designed: click the library, the librarian speaks, close, the library opens. No hidden sprite had taken the click. The guard answered because he is the hall's keeper. So the change came back out, and the real problem turned out to be the word "Close".

The lesson I keep relearning: reproduce the failure deliberately before you fix it, in a second place if you can. A fix built on the first plausible story can easily pass its own test while changing behaviour nobody asked to change.

Two more ways a greeting arrived wrong

While I was looking at doorways, two related issues turned up.

When you click a hall that sits behind a corner, the walk bends around it. On the exact frame the walk turned a corner the character was briefly not moving, and the game read "not moving and near an NPC" as "arrived". So the keeper's line opened four or five steps short of the door, and a second click was needed. A corner is not a stop, and now it is not treated as one.

The doorstep prompt, which previews a keeper's first line as you approach, also showed "Halt. Name and business..." floating over an empty step with no speaker, because the keepers had no name set in the layout. It now names the speaker exactly as the greeting panel does. A line of dialogue without a speaker reads as the game itself talking to you, which in this case made it sound even more like a refusal.

The same restraint, applied to the inbox

A different kind of greeting changed in this window too: email. Players who link an address can now get a reminder when a sign-in streak is about to lapse, alongside the comeback note for players who have been away.

The design question was not how to send more, it was how to send less. Any mail the game sends on its own initiative is now limited to one per player per day, and a mail that would exceed that is deferred to a later day rather than dropped. Mail you caused yourself, like a sign-up confirmation, is never held back. A game that greets you twice a day by email is a game you unsubscribe from. The streak pays out in the currencies listed in the codex of currencies, which is what those reminders are protecting.

What to check in your own game

Read every button label as the second half of the sentence above it. "Halt. Name and business." plus "Close" is a dismissal. The same line plus "Go in" is a welcome. Players read the pair, not the parts.

The guard is still gruff, but now he lets you in: walk up to his hall, free in the browser.

title: How Website Reliability Affects the Customer Journey
description:
A website is often the first place where people learn about a business, explore its services, or decide whether to become a customer. But attracting visitors is only one part of the process. The website also needs to work properly when people visit it.

Slow pages, unexpected errors, or broken forms can make visitors leave before they take action. This is why website reliability plays an important role in creating a smooth customer journey and building trust.

What Does Website Reliability Mean?

Website reliability means that a website works properly whenever someone needs to use it. It should load without unnecessary delays, remain available, protect visitor information, and work smoothly across different devices.

There are four important parts of website reliability:

Speed: Pages should load quickly so visitors do not have to wait.

Availability: The website should remain accessible without frequent downtime.

Security: Visitors should feel safe while sharing information or making transactions.

Consistent performance: The website should work properly on mobile phones, tablets, and desktop computers.

These areas may seem technical, but they directly affect how people experience a business online.

How Website Reliability Affects Different Stages of the Customer Journey

A customer journey includes several steps, from discovering a business to making a purchase or contacting its team. Website performance can influence every one of these stages.

1. First Impressions During Website Discovery

When someone hears about a business, they often visit its website to learn more. They may find it through a Google search, a social media post, an advertisement, or a recommendation.

At this stage, the website creates an important first impression. If the homepage takes too long to load or displays an error, visitors may leave without exploring further.

For example, imagine someone searching for a software development company. They click on a website that looks relevant, but the page takes several seconds to open. Instead of waiting, they may return to the search results and visit another company.

A fast and accessible website makes it easier for visitors to continue exploring.

2. Building Trust While Visitors Explore

After landing on a website, people usually look for information about the business, its services, experience, and previous work.

If pages open properly, menus work, and information is easy to access, visitors can explore with confidence. However, broken links, missing images, or repeated loading problems can create doubt.

Website security also matters here. Visitors may hesitate to share their details if a website appears unsafe or does not use a secure connection.

A reliable website helps create a professional impression and gives potential customers more confidence in the business.

3. Helping Customers Take Action

The next step may be filling out a contact form, requesting a quotation, booking a service, or making a purchase.

These actions depend on different website features working correctly. For example, a contact form may look fine but fail to send information to the business team. In that case, a potential lead could be lost without either side noticing.

Businesses should regularly test their forms, buttons, payment steps, and other important features. They should also check whether submitted information reaches the right system, such as a customer management tool.

Even a small technical issue can prevent someone from completing an action.

4. Creating a Better Experience on Every Device

Many people browse websites using mobile phones, while others use laptops or desktop computers. A website should provide a smooth experience across all these devices.

If text is difficult to read, buttons are hard to click, or pages do not fit smaller screens, visitors may struggle to find what they need.

Businesses should test their most important pages on different screen sizes and internet connections. This helps identify problems that may not appear during regular desktop testing.

5. Encouraging Customers to Return

The customer journey does not always end after someone makes a purchase or sends an enquiry. People may return to check updates, explore other services, or contact the business again.

A website that works consistently makes these visits easier. On the other hand, repeated downtime or slow performance can affect the customer's overall experience and reduce their willingness to return.

Maintaining website reliability is therefore important not only for attracting new visitors but also for keeping existing customers satisfied.

What Can Businesses Do to Improve Website Reliability?

Improving website reliability does not always require rebuilding the entire website. Businesses can start with a few practical steps.

1. Check website speed: Review important landing pages and identify images, scripts, or other elements that make them slow.

2. Monitor website uptime: Use monitoring tools to receive alerts when the website becomes unavailable.

3. Test important forms: Submit test enquiries and confirm that the information reaches the correct team or system.

4. Review mobile performance: Open important pages on different mobile devices and check whether everything works properly.

5. Keep software updated: Regularly update website platforms, plugins, and other components to address known issues and security risks.

6. Run regular security checks: Review access permissions, use secure connections, and make sure sensitive information is handled properly.

These checks can help businesses identify problems before they affect too many visitors.

Why Marketing and Development Teams Should Work Together

Website reliability is not only the responsibility of developers. Marketing teams also depend on the website to support campaigns, generate leads, and communicate with potential customers.

For example, a marketing team may spend time and money bringing visitors to a landing page. But if that page loads slowly or its enquiry form does not work, the campaign may not deliver the expected results.

When marketing and development teams work together, they can identify these issues more easily. Both teams can review website performance, test important pages, and focus on improving the visitor experience.

Final Thoughts

Website reliability has a direct connection with how customers discover, explore, and interact with a business online. A slow page, broken form, or unexpected outage can interrupt the customer journey and create a poor impression.

Businesses should treat website performance, availability, security, and mobile usability as ongoing priorities rather than one-time tasks. Regular testing and monitoring can help keep the website working as expected.

A good customer experience starts when someone visits a website, but a reliable website helps make sure that experience continues smoothly.

Read more: Explore how website reliability influences the customer journey for further insights into website performance and its role in customer experience.

title: GPT-6.1 Terra now available on AI Gateway
description:
GPT-6.1 Terra from OpenAI is now available on AI Gateway.

GPT-6.1 Terra is a fast model for visual reasoning, computer use, and writing, and it improves on the previous Terra model in visual reasoning, factual accuracy, and coding. It suits high-volume work in documents and desktop apps, such as filling out forms, interpreting technical drawings, or entering invoice details into accounting software. OpenAI still recommends its larger GPT-6 models for the most complex coding tasks.

The model accepts text and images and returns text, with a context window of more than 1M tokens. It supports configurable reasoning effort, structured outputs, tool calling, and implicit and explicit prompt caching. For latency-sensitive work, fast mode is available as openai/gpt-6.1-terra-fast.

GPT-6.1 Terra works with the AI SDK, the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API, the Responses API, and coding agents connected to AI Gateway. Use openai/gpt-6.1-terra as the model name:

To use it in Codex, Cursor, and more, install the latest Vercel CLI and run setup:

Then select openai/gpt-6.1-terra in the agent. See the coding agents guide for details.

Try GPT-6.1 Terra in the model playground.

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.

AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and does not charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests.

title: Native edges: principles for native apps with a shared core
description:
For a long time, building a client for every platform you cared about was expensive. You wrote every screen twice, fixed every bug twice, and either staffed a team per platform or decided which platforms your users would have to live without. So the industry did what it usually does and found ways to make that cost bearable.

Electron, React Native, and more recently Tauri came out of that. They gave teams a dynamic runtime, hot reloading, and the whole ecosystem of web libraries, so one team could ship to several platforms at once. And it worked: Slack, Linear, Discord, Notion, and Visual Studio Code run on a web stack, and many of us have them open all day. Raycast went the same way to get to Windows. Raycast 2.0 shares a React and TypeScript frontend between macOS and Windows and loads it in each platform's web view, and the team was open about why: hiring, the UI components the web already has, consistent extensions, and iteration speed. Those are good reasons.

Coding agents changed part of that math. Writing a SwiftUI view and then its Jetpack Compose twin used to be the expensive part, and today an agent writes most of it while you review. What's still expensive is compiling it, and if you've ever sat waiting on Xcode or Gradle, you know how much of a day goes into that. At Tuist we've spent years chipping away at that problem, with caching, selective testing, runners to run the builds on, and now Once, with remote execution coming next.

Once native builds are fast too, iteration speed becomes a much weaker argument for a web runtime. The other reasons, like the ecosystem or hiring, may still apply to you, and I don't expect anyone to rewrite a large codebase because the economics moved. But it got us thinking about how we'd build a multi-platform app if we started one today, so we wrote down the principles we'd follow and built a small sample app to see whether they hold up.

None of this is entirely new to us. Almost ten years ago we were exploring modular architectures for iOS apps and came up with microfeatures, which many teams adopted and which we later renamed The Modular Architecture. Tuist itself grew out of that work. This post takes the same ideas about boundaries and build graphs and stretches them across platforms.

We call this set of principles native edges. An app has two layers, and both ship inside it. The headless core holds the business logic and has no UI at all, and the native edges are what users see and touch, one per platform, each connecting the core to its platform. We stayed away from frontend and backend on purpose, because most people hear those words and think UI and server.

The principles are:

  1. Keep business logic in a headless core.
  2. Choose a core language that runs everywhere you ship.
  3. Connect the edges to the core through a small, typed API.
  4. Make every screen reachable by an address.
  5. Model the whole app in one build graph.

You don't have to take all of them. Some projects will have good reasons to keep a piece of logic in Swift, to share less, or to use different tools than we do, and that's fine.

The sample app

To see whether the principles hold up end to end, we built Native Edges, a client-side agent. You sign in with your ChatGPT account and talk to an agent whose loop, tools, and conversation history live on your device, while the model runs in the cloud. There's an iOS app in SwiftUI, an Android app in Kotlin and Jetpack Compose, and a command-line tool in Rust, and all three sit on one headless core, also written in Rust. The core handles the device-code sign-in and token refresh, runs the agent loop and its requests to the model, provides the tools the agent uses to read earlier conversations, and stores the history in SQLite through Diesel.

Here's the iOS app, built and launched on a simulator with once run. It signs in with a device code, lists the stored conversations, and asks the agent something that makes it go back to earlier ones. Then the CLI lists the app's routes and builds the URL for one conversation, and the simulator opens it:

▶️ Watch the demo on the original post

We'll keep coming back to the sample throughout the post. Here are its three edges, plus two more that the same core could support but the sample doesn't include:

  • Native edges: iOS (SwiftUI + Swift), Android (Jetpack Compose + Kotlin), CLI (terminal), plus Linux and Windows (GPUI) and Web (HTML + JavaScript), which aren't in the sample.
  • Headless core in Rust: route catalog and deep links, sign-in and sessions, agent loop and model API, conversation history.
  • Bridges: iOS calls the core through UniFFI Swift bindings, Android through UniFFI Kotlin bindings + JNA, the CLI and desktop through plain Rust calls, and the web through WebAssembly.

(See the diagram on the original post)

1. Keep business logic in a headless core

The rule we follow is simple to say: put in the edge whatever only the platform can do, and put everything else in the core.

The edge is the layer users touch. For apps, that means a UI written in a framework that compiles for the platform and follows its conventions, which today is SwiftUI on Apple platforms and Jetpack Compose on Android. Anything you can only reach through the platform's frameworks belongs there too: the Keychain or the Android Keystore, presenting a browser for an OAuth flow, registering for push notifications, Live Activities, share extensions, or on-device speech recognition. These are the details users notice when an app gets them wrong, so we'd rather each platform own them.

A command-line tool is an edge too, one whose platform happens to be the terminal, and so is a web app, with the core compiled to WebAssembly and the browser as its platform.

The core is the logic that's the same everywhere: which fields of a record can be edited, how a list is paginated, how an OAuth token is refreshed, how history is reconciled after a reconnect, or making sure a late response from a cancelled request doesn't overwrite newer results. Because the core has no UI and doesn't depend on any platform framework, you can cover most of the app's behavior with unit tests that run in seconds, without a simulator, an emulator, or UI automation, and those tests cover every platform at once. Each edge still needs some tests for rendering and platform integration, but far fewer than before.

Ghostty, the terminal emulator by Mitchell Hashimoto, is one of my favorite examples of this split. Its core, libghostty, is written in Zig, exposes a C API, and handles terminal emulation, fonts, and rendering. On top of it sit a macOS app written in Swift with AppKit and SwiftUI and a Linux app that uses GTK. Ghostty's core does more than ours, since it includes rendering, but the idea is the same: one shared engine, and on each platform an app that feels like it belongs there.

2. Choose a core language that runs everywhere you ship

Look for a language with good toolchains and a good standard library on every platform you support, so you don't find out halfway through a feature that the API you need doesn't exist on one of them. Rust does well here. It compiles to iOS, Android, macOS, Linux, Windows, and WebAssembly, and its crates cover almost everything a client needs. The browser is a bit of a special case: the core runs there as WebAssembly, but on wasm32-unknown-unknown parts of the standard library, like the file system and threads, don't work, so a web edge needs crates that go through the browser's APIs instead, like fetch for networking or IndexedDB for storage. Zig is another good option, with explicit allocators and cross-compilation built into its toolchain, and Go can work too, although it brings a garbage collector with it.

Memory is one of the main reasons we lean towards Rust and Zig. Neither has a garbage collector, so you decide when memory is allocated and freed, which matters in places with strict limits, like watches, embedded devices, or the app extensions and widgets the system kills when they use too much. It also means your app doesn't run a second garbage collector next to Swift's reference counting or the Android runtime's own collector. You still have to respect ownership rules at the boundary and measure memory on constrained targets, but you're the one in control.

A question we get a lot is why we don't use Kotlin Multiplatform on Apple platforms, or Swift on Android. Both work, and teams ship real apps with them. Our concern is that a language built for one platform brings its runtime and memory model along to the others, and its standard library and tooling tend to be most complete on the platform where it started. Rust and Zig don't have a home platform in that sense, and for a shared core that's what we want.

I also think the choice of language will matter less and less. As models write more of the code, the questions that remain are whether the language fits the job and whether agents are good at writing and reasoning about it. Rust does well on both: its compiler is strict and its error messages are detailed, so when an agent gets something wrong, it finds out right away and knows why.

If we picked a stack today, it would look like this:

Platform Native edge: UI Native edge: platform services Headless core
iOS, iPadOS, macOS SwiftUI Swift Rust
Android Jetpack Compose Kotlin Rust
Linux, Windows GPUI Rust Rust
Command line Terminal Rust Rust
Web HTML and JavaScript Browser APIs Rust compiled to WebAssembly

For desktop outside macOS, we'd go with GPUI, the UI framework the Zed team built for their editor. GPUI draws its own UI on the GPU instead of using the operating system's toolkit, compiles to a native binary, and integrates with each platform, and there are component libraries for it, like GPUI Component, for building desktop apps in the spirit of Zed. Since GPUI is Rust too, on Linux and Windows the edge and the core share a language and need no bridge at all.

The command line is in the table because the terminal is a platform too, and developers can tell right away when a CLI starts fast, follows the terminal's conventions, and plays well with pipes and scripts. With a headless core, a CLI is a thin edge over logic you already have, so building one in Rust is cheap. Agents use a lot of software through CLIs, and I expect this edge to matter more and more as they do.

3. Connect the edges to the core through a small, typed API

The sample uses UniFFI, a tool from Mozilla that generates Swift and Kotlin bindings from annotations in the Rust code. The core marks what it exports, and the edges call typed functions and get typed values back, with no C headers or JSON in between:

#[derive(uniffi::Record)]
pub struct Destination {
    pub route: String,
    pub params: Params,
    pub url: String,
}

#[derive(Debug, uniffi::Error)]
#[uniffi(flat_error)]
pub enum CoreError {
    /// No session, or it expired: show the sign-in screen.
    Unauthorized { message: String },
    Failed { kind: String, message: String },
}

/// Resolves a deep link into its destination and parents.
#[uniffi::export]
pub fn open(url: String) -> Result<Vec<Destination>, CoreError> {
    // ...
}

/// Sends a message and waits for the agent's answer.
#[uniffi::export]
pub fn send(
    id: Option<String>,
    text: String,
) -> Result<Conversation, CoreError> {
    // ...
}

In Swift, these are ordinary functions, and the Rust error becomes a Swift error you can catch. send blocks while the agent works, so the sample runs it off the main actor with a small background helper of its own:

let stack = try EdgesCore.open(url: link)
let reply = try await background {
    try EdgesCore.send(id: id, text: text)
}

Kotlin gets the same API, with CoreException.Unauthorized in place of the Swift error case, and the CLI calls the Rust functions directly. Adding a capability means exporting a function in Rust, and the apps get it with compiler-checked types. The core returns plain values, like a conversation and the URLs it links to, and leaves it to each edge to decide how to present them: a pushed view on iOS, a back-stack entry on Android, or printed output in the terminal.

Sometimes the core needs something only the platform provides, so the API has to work in the other direction too. A token refresh rotates the session, and the new session has to land in the Keychain on iOS and in Keystore-backed encrypted storage on Android. For that we use the delegate pattern: the core declares what it needs as an interface, and each edge provides an implementation. In UniFFI, that's a Rust trait marked with_foreign, which Swift and Kotlin can implement:

/// Provided by the edge: the Keychain on iOS, the Keystore
/// on Android, and a private file in the terminal.
#[uniffi::export(with_foreign)]
pub trait SecureStorage: Send + Sync {
    fn read(&self, key: String) -> Option<String>;
    fn write(&self, key: String, value: String);
    fn delete(&self, key: String);
}

On iOS, the implementation is a small class over the Keychain, and the app hands it to the core at launch, along with a directory where the core keeps its SQLite database:

final class Keychain: SecureStorage {
    func read(key: String) -> String? { /* SecItemCopyMatching */ }
    func write(key: String, value: String) { /* SecItemAdd */ }
    func delete(key: String) { /* SecItemDelete */ }
}

let directory = URL.applicationSupportDirectory.path
_ = try launch(dataDir: directory, storage: Keychain())

Android passes a Keystore class that encrypts the value with an Android Keystore key, and the CLI passes one that writes files only you can read. The split of responsibilities is what we like here: the core decides what to store and when, such as a renewed session after a refresh, and the edge decides how the operating system protects it. The core's tests pass an in-memory implementation, so they don't need a Keychain or a simulator. We kept the trait simple for the sample, but in a production app write and delete should report failures so the core can handle them.

4. Make every screen reachable by an address

Core tests cover the shared rules, but sometimes you want to test how an edge and the core work together, like whether a screen renders the data the core returns or whether a tap triggers the right call. Whether you or an agent runs that test, you want to get to the screen in one step, not ten.

A CLI makes this easy, because every operation is a named command with options and arguments you can find in the code and run. Web apps are close, since every page has a URL that an agent can read from the route definitions and open. Mobile and desktop apps usually have neither, so getting to a screen means launching the app and tapping through every step in between, which is slow and breaks every time the UI changes. We think native apps deserve a declarative navigation system that does two things:

  1. Makes routes discoverable. The app declares destinations as data, like an enum or a list of types, so someone reading the code, or an agent, can find every place the app can go.
  2. Lets you open any route directly. A single entry point takes a route, usually as a URL, and builds the navigation state for it, so you can jump straight to a specific screen or record.

Navigation itself belongs to the platform. Each one has strong conventions for stacks, tabs, sheets, transitions, and Back behavior, and users expect them. What the core can own is the route catalog and URL parsing, so every edge agrees on which destinations exist and what a link means. In the sample, each route has an identifier, a URL pattern, and a parent, so a deep link opens on top of the screens you'd normally pass through, and Back works as if you had tapped your way there:

// Simplified from core/src/routes.rs.
pub static ROUTES: &[Route] = &[
    Route {
        id: "conversations",
        path: "conversations",
        parent: None,
    },
    Route {
        id: "new",
        path: "conversations/new",
        parent: Some("conversations"),
    },
    Route {
        id: "conversation",
        path: "conversations/{id}",
        parent: Some("conversations"),
    },
];

Every edge asks the core what a URL means, and tapping a row opens that row's URL, so taps and deep links go through the same code. That's what makes this useful for agents: one can list the routes with the CLI and then open a specific conversation on a simulator or an emulator with a single command:

edges routes
xcrun simctl openurl booted edges://conversations/011d032b115d6baa
adb shell am start -a android.intent.action.VIEW \
  -d edges://conversations/011d032b115d6baa

In the sample, each edge keeps its own database, so a link only opens a conversation that exists in that app. The same URLs can also arrive from notifications and shared links, so treat them as untrusted input: opening a route picks a screen, and the core and the server still check what the user can see.

Each platform already has tools for the edge side:

  • iOS and macOS: model destinations as a Codable enum and drive a NavigationStack from a NavigationPath, then turn incoming URLs into that path in onOpenURL. Point-Free's swift-navigation models every destination, including sheets and alerts, as state, so opening a screen means constructing a value. On macOS, open <url> does what simctl openurl does on a simulator.
  • Android: Navigation Compose supports type-safe routes declared as @Serializable classes, with deep links mapped to them. In Navigation 3, the back stack is a list of keys that you own, and deep link matchers turn a URL into the initial back stack.
  • Desktop with GPUI: GPUI declares actions with names and dispatches them by name, which is how Zed's command palette lists everything the editor can do. Routes can follow the same pattern, with a command-line flag like --open <route> as the entry point.

5. Model the whole app in one build graph

You can build all of this with the tools you already have, but we'd recommend a build system that can model the entire graph: the Rust core compiled for each platform, the Swift and Kotlin bindings generated from it, the apps that link them, and the tests for each of them.

Xcode and Gradle work well inside their own ecosystems, and they treat everything outside as foreign. Rust usually gets in as a script phase or a custom task that runs Cargo, or as a prebuilt binary checked into the repository, and the outer build system sees one opaque step. Gradle can cache a custom task if you declare every input and output, but neither tool can schedule or cache the individual crates inside it, so the Rust side ends up rebuilding more than it should.

Bazel and Buck2 can model all of this, which is why many teams use them. They also ask you to learn their rules and configure toolchains, and a lot of teams find the developer experience hard to live with. For the sample we used Once, the build system we're building at Tuist, which models the same kind of typed graph with remote caching and keeps the configuration in a single TOML file. It's early and still in canary, so expect rough edges. Here's an excerpt of the sample's once.toml:

# The headless core, built once per edge.
[[target]]
name = "CoreIOS"
kind = "rust_library"
srcs = ["core/src/**/*.rs"]
deps = ["./CoreIOSDependencies"]

[target.attrs]
crate_name = "edges_core"
crate_root = "core/src/lib.rs"
target = "aarch64-apple-ios-sim"
crate_type = "staticlib"

# The terminal edge.
[[target]]
name = "CLI"
kind = "rust_binary"
srcs = ["cli/src/**/*.rs"]
deps = ["./Core", "./CoreDependencies"]

# The SwiftUI edge, and the Swift bindings it calls.
[[target]]
name = "SwiftBindings"
kind = "uniffi_bindings"
deps = ["bindgen/Bindgen", "./CoreIOS"]

[target.attrs]
language = "swift"

[[target]]
name = "IOS"
kind = "apple_application"
srcs = ["ios/Sources/**/*.swift"]
deps = ["./CoreIOS", "./SwiftBindings", "./SimulatorSDK"]

[target.attrs]
platform = "ios"
bundle_id = "dev.tuist.edges"
sdk_frameworks = ["Security"]

# The Jetpack Compose edge.
[[target]]
name = "Android"
kind = "android_binary"
srcs = ["android/src/**/*.kt"]
deps = ["./CoreAndroid", "./KotlinBindings", "./Compose"]

[target.attrs]
application_id = "dev.tuist.edges"
min_sdk_version = 26

Rust libraries, Apple applications, Android binaries, the bindings between them, and their tests all live in the same graph. Once resolves third-party crates from Cargo.lock into per-platform dependency targets, so each crate compiles separately with its own cache key, instead of one cargo build compiling everything at once.

The graph generates the bindings too, so nobody has to check them into the repository. Once doesn't have a built-in rule for UniFFI yet, so the sample adds one in a small Starlark module that builds uniffi-bindgen from source, runs it against the compiled core, and compiles the generated code into a Swift module for iOS and a Kotlin library for Android. Once caches that step like any other, keyed on the generator, its configuration, and the compiled core.

This graph is also what caching relies on. Each step gets a key computed from its inputs, so a change to a SwiftUI view doesn't recompile the Rust core, and you can share the results between your machine, your teammates', CI, and agents working in other worktrees. When the work a build does grows with the size of your change and not the size of your app, native iteration starts to feel close to the hot reloading that made web runtimes so attractive. Linking, installing, and launching still take time, but you stop paying for a full rebuild on top.

Keep the graph fast

The shape of the graph matters as much as the build system. A build can only run in parallel what the graph lets it run in parallel, and Apple's WWDC talk on build parallelization calls the longest chain of dependencies the critical path: no extra cores or remote workers make the build shorter than that. So we keep the graph shallow and wide. We only add a dependency when we need it, put interfaces in their own modules so implementations compile side by side (Bruno Rocha explains the technique in Reducing iOS Build Times by using Interface Modules), and keep shared foundations small, because everything downstream rebuilds when they change. Spotify's account of moving its iOS app to Bazel shows what that buys you: with remote caching and the module isolation they did during the migration, their CI feedback loop went from 80 minutes to 20.

The same goes for deciding what each edge includes. A widget doesn't need the agent, and a web build pays for every kilobyte it ships, but if each edge builds the core with its own Cargo features, the cache sees a different core per edge, and you end up building and keeping warm one graph per edge. Bazel's documentation on configurations warns about the same growth. We'd rather split the core into crates, like storage, networking, and the agent, and let each edge depend on the ones it needs, the way Mozilla's megazords link only the components an app uses. A crate's hash doesn't depend on who uses it, so adding or removing an edge doesn't invalidate anything shared. For dropping unused code from a binary, the linker's dead-code stripping does the job after the core is compiled and cached.

Try both approaches below. Each edge links the crates it picks through a small umbrella crate, drawn dashed. Turn edges on and off or edit a file in storage, and watch which nodes get a new hash:

🧪 Try the interactive graph on the original post

The sample's graph is small, but it has this shape: each edge depends only on its build of the core and its own platform libraries, and no edge depends on another.

Adopting native edges

Starting with one platform

We like to start with one platform and move logic into the core as soon as it looks reusable, without trying to design the core up front. A few signs that something belongs there: it doesn't import any platform framework, another platform would need the same behavior, or you'd want to test it without launching the app. Some typical candidates:

  • The API client: routes, request and response types, validation, and error mapping.
  • Authentication: building the sign-in URL, exchanging codes for tokens, and refreshing them.
  • Pagination, search, and filtering rules for lists.
  • Form validation, like which fields are required and what a valid date range looks like.
  • The route catalog and deep-link parsing.
  • Local caching and reconciling data after a reconnect.

When the second platform comes along, most of the work is building a new edge on top of a core that's already built and tested. And keep doing it as features change: when a Swift or Kotlin model starts making business decisions, that's your cue to move the logic into the core.

If you already have clients

Most teams won't start from scratch, and that's the more interesting case. If you already have clients on several platforms, each in its own language and built with its own tools, I'd start by modeling them in one build graph connected to a remote cache. That makes builds faster before any code moves, and it makes adding a Rust core affordable later. Then pick one piece that's duplicated across your clients, like the API client, authentication, or validation rules, and move it into the core, and while you're at it, think about what your app would look like as a CLI or a set of commands an agent can run. You keep shipping your clients the whole time, and over time you'll notice the edges getting thinner and thinner until they're mostly UI and calls to platform APIs.

What we're doing at Tuist

We're doing this ourselves. The native clients of Atlas, our internal operations platform, follow these principles: an iOS and macOS app in SwiftUI, an Android app in Kotlin, and a CLI, all on one Rust core. We've also started moving Tuist's own clients to the same model. When we looked across them, we found a lot of duplicated logic, most of it in Swift and some of it rewritten in Kotlin and other languages, and we're now moving that layer into a shared Rust core with the CLI and the apps as its edges. We'll write about it as the work progresses.

It would be a dream for us to see more apps built natively again, apps that use less memory, feel at home on their platform, and run faster. This is early work, and we kept the sample small on purpose. The sample app and Once are on GitHub if you want to try the principles, and if you build something with them, we'd love to hear about it.

title: Documenso discovery and the team-scoped signing API boundary
description:
Documenso discovery and the team-scoped signing API boundary

Documenso is an open-source document-signing platform that can be self-hosted. A deployment handles signed documents, recipient details, templates, team settings, API tokens, and webhooks. The public signing page may be intentionally reachable, but the API token that creates envelopes or retrieves documents is a team-scoped credential with significant authority.

On 2026-11-04 at 19:38 UTC, a bounded ZoomEye SDK probe used sub_type=all, page 1, and page size one. app="Documenso" returned 0 matches and title="Documenso" returned 422. The title result is a discovery lead that can include a signing page, a login page, documentation, or an instance that is no longer active. It does not prove that a token is exposed or that a signing flow is unprotected.

Token authority follows the team

Documenso's API documentation says API tokens are scoped to a specific team. The token inherits permissions from the creating user's team role: an administrator has full team access, a manager can create and edit documents and templates, and a member manages their own documents. This is more precise than a generic user token, but the resulting authority still needs review.

Use separate tokens for separate integrations. Name the token for the service that owns it, set an expiration where available, and store it outside public source code. When an integration is retired, revoke the token and verify that requests fail. A token can be valid even if the human who created it changes roles, so review token ownership when team membership changes.

Document signing also involves recipients. A token may create envelopes, add fields, and request signatures, but the documentation states that the API cannot sign on behalf of recipients. That boundary is important: an API credential can drive the workflow without becoming the recipient's signing identity. Preserve the recipient verification and signing evidence separately from the integration's ability to create the document.

Webhooks and outbound network risk

Documenso can send webhooks when documents are created, opened, signed, completed, rejected, cancelled, or updated. A webhook can carry document identifiers, recipient state, and signing status. The receiving system should authenticate the sender according to the integration, reject unexpected event formats, and avoid treating a webhook as the only evidence of legal completion.

Self-hosting documentation states that outbound request checks are best-effort and not a complete SSRF mitigation, and that they can fail open. That makes network egress a deployment responsibility. Restrict the self-hosted instance from internal management services, metadata endpoints, and unrelated private networks unless a specific integration requires them. If webhooks must reach an internal system, use a dedicated egress path and an approved destination allowlist.

Review the webhook destination list as part of the administrative inventory. A team administrator who can set an arbitrary URL may create a request from the Documenso host to another service. The target should authorize the request using a shared secret or signature, and the sender should have a bounded retry policy. Do not assume the application's URL validation replaces firewall policy.

Public signing surfaces

A document-signing link is designed to be used by a recipient, possibly without a Documenso account. The token or link in that URL can be a bearer capability. Review its expiration, recipient binding, and behavior after cancellation or completion. Do not post real signing links in public documentation or send them through link-preview systems that may fetch the URL.

The self-hosted deployment requires a signing certificate; the documentation notes that document signing fails without one. Inventory the certificate, its trust chain, renewal process, and failure behavior. A public title match is not proof that a signing certificate is valid or that the instance is accepting documents. Validate only owned instances through the product's normal workflow.

A bounded discovery plan

Keep the title and app observations separate and record sub_type=all, time, page, and size. Confirm a candidate host with the owner, then check the public page, signing link behavior, team settings, API tokens, webhook endpoints, and egress restrictions. Run a test envelope through the full lifecycle with non-sensitive data.

The security outcome is not a count of 422 title matches. It is a short inventory of owned signing services whose team roles, API tokens, webhook destinations, signing certificates, and outbound network paths have been verified. ZoomEye provides the external discovery context; the document owner and platform administrator provide the authority evidence.

References

  • ZoomEye query for title="Documenso"
  • Documenso: authentication
  • Documenso: team-scoped API access
  • Documenso: webhook setup
  • Documenso: self-hosting

title: AWS SysOps Is Now CloudOps Engineer: SOA-C03 Explained
description:
AWS Certified SysOps Administrator – Associate now has a new name: AWS Certified CloudOps Engineer – Associate. The exam code moved from SOA-C02 to SOA-C03. Here is what changed, what stayed the same, how the exam works today and how it leads on to DevOps Engineer – Professional, all taken from AWS’s official pages and exam guides.

What happened to SysOps Administrator

AWS renamed the certification as part of the SOA-C03 exam update. AWS says the new name reflects the evolving nature of cloud operations and a shift in industry terminology. The key dates were:

  • 9 September 2025: registration for SOA-C03 opened, along with the new exam guide.
  • 29 September 2025: the last day to take SOA-C02.
  • 30 September 2025: the first day to take SOA-C03.

The new name only applies to people who pass SOA-C03. It is not changed retroactively. If you already hold SysOps Administrator – Associate, you do not need to take the new exam. Your certification stays valid for 3 years from the date you earned it, and you can keep showing its badge until it expires. If you later pass SOA-C03 as well, you get a separate CloudOps Engineer badge.

What changed in the content

AWS’s announcement names three main shifts. Containers are now in scope. There is more emphasis on multi-account and multi-Region architectures. And there is more on automation and infrastructure as code. AWS also says no task statements were removed, but the outline is more detailed and some tasks were reorganised.

The exam guide’s comparison page shows how the domains moved:

SOA-C02 domain SOA-C02 SOA-C03
Monitoring, Logging, and Remediation (now Monitoring, Logging, Analysis, Remediation, and Performance Optimization) 20% 22%
Reliability and Business Continuity 16% 22%
Deployment, Provisioning, and Automation 18% 22%
Security and Compliance 16% 16%
Networking and Content Delivery 18% 18%
Cost and Performance Optimization 12% merged into Domain 1

The comparison page also lists the specific changes:

  • Moved: SOA-C02 Tasks 6.1 and 6.2 (cost and performance) now sit in Task 1.3. VPNs moved from Task 4.2 to Task 5.1.
  • Added: the CloudWatch agent for EC2 instances, Amazon ECS clusters and Amazon EKS clusters; stacks with CloudFormation and the AWS CDK; enforcing compliance requirements such as Region and service selection; and CloudWatch network monitoring services.
  • Removed: configuring S3 static website hosting.

The June 2026 exam guide update

AWS published version 1.1 of the SOA-C03 exam guide on 1 June 2026. It changed the wording or examples of ten skills. It also added five services to the in-scope list: Amazon Bedrock, AWS DevOps Agent, AWS Health Dashboard, Kiro and AWS Security Agent. The revision history lists no change to the domains or their weights. If your study notes date from before June 2026, check the in-scope services list again. The revision history now also lists a version 1.2, published on 29 October 2026, so check the revisions page for any later changes.

Exam labs

The SOA-C02 exam guide originally included exam labs: tasks performed in the AWS Management Console or AWS CLI. AWS removed them from 28 March 2023 “until further notice”. After that, SOA-C02 was 50 scored and 15 unscored multiple-choice and multiple-response questions in 130 minutes.

The SOA-C03 exam guide lists only two question types, multiple choice and multiple response. It does not list exam labs. So if you remember SysOps as the exam with labs, that no longer matches the current guide.

SOA-C03 at a glance

Detail SOA-C03
Level Associate
Questions 65: 50 scored and 15 unscored
Time 130 minutes
Question types Multiple choice and multiple response
Passing score 720 on a scaled score of 100–1,000
Cost 150 USD
Delivery Pearson VUE test centre or online proctored
Languages English, Japanese, Korean and Simplified Chinese
Valid for 3 years

AWS will retire the Korean and Simplified Chinese versions of SOA-C03 after 19 November 2026. English and Japanese continue.

Unscored questions are not identified on the exam. Unanswered questions are marked wrong and there is no penalty for guessing. The exam uses a compensatory scoring model, so you need to pass the exam as a whole, not each section.

The exam guide describes a target candidate with 1 year of experience with deployment, management, troubleshooting, networking and security on AWS. It also asks for at least 1 year in a related operations role, such as system administrator. If you have no IT work experience, AWS suggests earning Cloud Practitioner first.

The five domains

Domain Weight
Monitoring, Logging, Analysis, Remediation, and Performance Optimization 22%
Reliability and Business Continuity 22%
Deployment, Provisioning, and Automation 22%
Security and Compliance 16%
Networking and Content Delivery 18%

In short: CloudWatch, CloudTrail, EventBridge and Systems Manager for monitoring and remediation; scaling, health checks, Multi-AZ, AWS Backup and disaster recovery for reliability; CloudFormation, the AWS CDK, StackSets and event-driven automation for deployment; IAM, Organizations, AWS Config, KMS and GuardDuty for security; and VPCs, Route 53, CloudFront and flow logs for networking.

The path to DevOps Engineer – Professional

AWS’s exam page names DevOps Engineer – Professional (DOP-C02) and Security – Specialty as certifications that people go on to earn after CloudOps Engineer. DOP-C02 is a bigger exam:

Detail SOA-C03 DOP-C02
Level Associate Professional
Questions 65 (50 scored) 75 (65 scored)
Time 130 minutes 180 minutes
Passing score 720 750
Cost 150 USD 300 USD
Target experience 1 year on AWS 2 or more years on AWS

DOP-C02 has six domains: SDLC Automation (22%), Configuration Management and IaC (17%), Resilient Cloud Solutions (15%), Monitoring and Logging (15%), Incident and Event Response (14%), and Security and Compliance (17%). Its target candidate also needs experience with the software development lifecycle and with programming or scripting.

The link between the two matters for recertification. Earning DOP-C02 automatically recertifies CloudOps Engineer – Associate. It also works for older SysOps Administrator – Associate holders, who can recertify by upgrading to DevOps Engineer – Professional. People who hold both DevOps Engineer – Professional and SysOps Administrator – Associate can keep both current by passing the latest DOP-C02 exam. AWS also gives you a 50% discount voucher for your next exam once you earn a certification.

Our suggestions

This is our advice, not AWS’s. It is based on the official content above.

  • Studying from SOA-C02 material: start with the comparison page. Put extra time into containers with the CloudWatch agent, the AWS CDK, multi-account tools such as StackSets and AWS RAM, and CloudWatch network monitoring. Skip S3 static website hosting.
  • Planning your time: three domains carry 22% each, so 66% of the exam is monitoring, reliability and deployment. Give them most of your study hours.
  • Thinking about DOP-C02 next: the overlap is strongest in monitoring, IaC, resilience and security. The biggest new area is CI/CD. SOA-C03 lists designing CI/CD pipelines as out of scope, while SDLC Automation is the largest DOP-C02 domain.
  • Holding SysOps Administrator already: you do not have to sit SOA-C03. If DevOps Engineer – Professional is your goal anyway, passing it before your SysOps certification expires also recertifies it.

To check your readiness, ExamCrest has free SOA-C03 practice questions you can try first.

Confirm the latest details on AWS’s CloudOps Engineer – Associate page, the DevOps Engineer – Professional page and the recertification page before you book.

I run ExamCrest, where this post first appeared. Try free SOA-C03 practice questions: https://examcrest.com/exam/aws-soa-c03/free-questions?utm_source=devto&utm_campaign=soa-c03-blog-copy

title: Your Shopify Hero Image Is Probably Lazy-Loaded. Here's the Liquid Fix.
description:
On a lot of Shopify stores I audit, the biggest image on the homepage is also the last one the browser bothers to fetch.

It's the hero banner. It's almost always the Largest Contentful Paint element on mobile. And somewhere in a custom section, someone has written loading: 'lazy' on it, so the browser waits until layout is done before it even starts the download.

Here's how to check for it and fix it in Liquid, without an app.

How it happens

Shopify's image_tag filter already does the sensible thing. Per the docs, loading is set to lazy automatically for images in sections further down the page, and images near the top are left alone. If you just write:

{{ section.settings.image | image_url: width: 2400 | image_tag }}

you get a good default.

The trouble starts when a theme or a freelancer "optimises" every image by hand:

{{ section.settings.image | image_url: width: 2400 | image_tag: loading: 'lazy' }}

Passing loading yourself overrides the default. Now the hero is lazy too, wherever the merchant puts that section, including first on the page. I've also seen the same thing come from old themes that used a lazy-loading JavaScript library with data-src attributes, which is even worse, because the real URL isn't in the HTML at all.

How to check in two minutes

  1. Run the homepage through PageSpeed Insights on mobile.
  2. Open the "LCP request discovery" insight. If it says lazy load is applied to the LCP image, or that fetchpriority=high should be applied, you've found it.
  3. Confirm in the HTML: view source, search for the hero's file name, and look at its <img> tag for loading="lazy".

Do the check on the live storefront, not inside the theme editor. That matters for the fix below.

The fix: decide by section position

Every section has section.index, its 1-based position within its location (the template, or a section group like the header). That's exactly what you need: the first section on the page gets priority, everything below is lazy.

Dawn does this in sections/image-banner.liquid. Simplified (Dawn works out sizes and widths from the section settings; I've left those out):

{%- liquid
  assign fetch_priority = 'auto'
  if section.index == 1
    assign fetch_priority = 'high'
  endif
-%}

{{
  section.settings.image
  | image_url: width: 3840
  | image_tag:
    sizes: '100vw',
    fetchpriority: fetch_priority
}}

Two things to notice. Dawn doesn't pass loading at all, it lets image_tag decide. And it uses fetchpriority, which isn't a named option of the filter; image_tag passes through any HTML attribute you give it as a parameter, so fetchpriority: 'high' ends up on the <img>.

If your section has to set loading explicitly (say, a custom slideshow where only the first slide should load early), make it conditional instead of hardcoded:

{%- liquid
  if section.index == 1 and forloop.first
    assign img_loading = 'eager'
    assign img_priority = 'high'
  else
    assign img_loading = 'lazy'
    assign img_priority = 'auto'
  endif
-%}

{{ block.settings.image | image_url: width: 2400 | image_tag: loading: img_loading, fetchpriority: img_priority, sizes: '100vw' }}

Only the first slide of the first section gets priority. Slides two and three can wait.

The catch: section.index is sometimes nil

The docs list three cases where section.index returns nil:

  • static sections (rendered with {% section 'name' %})
  • while rendering in the online store editor
  • when the section comes back through the Section Rendering API

With the code above, nil == 1 is false, so you fall back to lazy and auto. That's the safe direction, but it explains two things that confuse people. First, the editor preview will never show fetchpriority="high", so test on the live store. Second, if your hero is a static section in theme.liquid, the check never passes, and you need to set it explicitly for that one section.

What about preload: true?

image_tag also takes preload: true, which makes Shopify send a preload resource hint as a Link HTTP header. It doesn't change the <img> tag itself, and Shopify's own docs say to use it sparingly.

In practice, fetchpriority: 'high' on an <img> that's already in the HTML is usually enough. I'd only add preload when the LCP image is a CSS background or sits deep in the markup where the browser finds it late. Preloading two or three images just means they fight each other for bandwidth.

Don't forget sizes

One more thing I fix in the same pass. Without a sizes attribute the browser assumes the image is full viewport width, which is right for a full-bleed banner but wrong for a half-width image next to text. On a phone, that can mean downloading a much bigger file than the slot needs. Set sizes to match the layout, like Dawn does with (min-width: 750px) 50vw, 100vw for split banners.

Quick checklist

  • Search your theme for loading: 'lazy' and loading="lazy". Anything in a section that can sit at the top of the page needs a condition, not a hardcoded value.
  • Give the first image of the first section fetchpriority: 'high'.
  • Leave everything else to image_tag's default.
  • Test on the live storefront, then rerun PageSpeed Insights and check the LCP request discovery insight again.

It's a ten-minute change that rarely needs an app. If you'd rather someone else went through a custom theme for this kind of thing, it's part of what we do in our Shopify theme development work.

title: Saidzoda-Tajik-E5-Large: Fine-Tuning a 560M Embedder for Tajik Retrieval
description:
arXiv:2611.00592v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Finding the passage that answers a question is the first step of most practical systems built on documents, and for Tajik we found no openly described model for it. We present Saidzoda-Tajik-E5-Large, a Tajik text embedder built from multilingual-e5-large-instruct (560M parameters). We asked our own Tajik language model to write questions for passages from Tajik laws, tax documents, Wikipedia and web text, and trained on 235,140 question and passage pairs for one epoch, with hard negatives chosen by another embedder and English and Russian pairs mixed in so the model would not forget those languages. On laws the model had never seen, the right passage is among the top ten results for 93.6% of questions, up from 80.2%; on tax documents, 94.5% against 82.6%. On Belebele, the one test we have that was written by people, the gain is smaller and not confirmed (92.2% to 95.2%, with touching intervals), and Russian and English do not change. On law and tax questions written in the same style as its training questions, it is tied with Giga-Embeddings-3B, a model five times its size; on Belebele the 3B and 8B models score slightly higher, and only after we fine-tuned them on our data are they clearly ahead. We also report what failed: training in bfloat16 broke the model, and replacing Tajik letters with similar Russian ones did not help. Our law, tax and Wikipedia test questions come from the same model that wrote the training questions, so we treat those scores as an upper limit until questions written by Tajik speakers are available.

title: How to Keep Secrets in Python Without Pushing Them to GitHub
description:
How to Keep Secrets in Python Without Pushing Them to GitHub

In Python application development it’s common to work with API keys, access tokens, or database credentials. Accidentally publishing these values in a public repository can compromise your project’s security and generate unexpected costs. Below is a practical, straightforward method to keep your secrets out of the code and prevent them from ending up on GitHub.

1. Understanding the Risk of Storing Secrets in the Repository

Git records every change permanently. Even if you delete a secret in a later commit, the value remains in the history and anyone who clones the repository can retrieve it. This situation is described in the best‑practice guide for secret management in development teams, which recommends preventing sensitive values from entering the source tree from the start【3】. Moreover, public repositories are indexed by search engines and can be automatically scanned by bots looking for exposed keys.

2. Using .env Files and the python‑dotenv Library

The simplest and most widely adopted solution is to store the values in a plain‑text file called .env. Each line contains an environment variable in the form NAME=value. For example:

API_KEY=12345abcde
DB_PASSWORD=mi_contraseña_secreta

The file is never committed to the repository; it lives locally or in the deployment environment. When your application starts, the python‑dotenv library reads the .env file and loads those variables into the process environment, so you can access them with os.getenv():

import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv

load_dotenv()               # Load .env into the environment
api_key = os.getenv("API_KEY")
db_pass = os.getenv("DB_PASSWORD")

This practice is outlined in the guide on secret and API‑key management in Python, which advises keeping secrets out of the code and loading them only when needed【1】.

3. Protecting the .env File with .gitignore and Best Practices

To make sure the file never gets included in commits, add it to the project’s .gitignore:

# .gitignore
.env

It’s good practice to create a .env.example file that contains only the variable names without values. This way, any collaborator knows which variables need to be defined without exposing real data.

# .env.example
API_KEY=
DB_PASSWORD=

When the project is initialized, each developer copies this file to .env and fills in the local values. If you accidentally commit the file, you can purge it from history with tools like git filter-branch or git filter-repo, although preventing the inclusion in the first place is the ideal approach【3】.

4. Advanced Alternatives for Production Environments

4.1 GitHub Secrets

GitHub provides a mechanism called Secrets that allows you to store encrypted values at the repository or organization level. These secrets can be consumed by GitHub Actions during CI/CD pipelines without appearing in logs. The official GitHub documentation explains how to create and use these secrets securely【2】.

In a workflow, a secret is accessed with the syntax ${{ secrets.NAME }} and passed to the container or script that runs the application. This option is ideal when deployment is performed entirely on GitHub’s infrastructure.

4.2 External Secret Managers

For more complex projects, you can integrate specialized services such as HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, or Azure Key Vault. These systems offer automatic credential rotation, auditing, and policy‑based access control. Although their setup is more involved, they provide an additional security layer that goes beyond a simple .env file.

5. Quick Checklist to Avoid Exposing Secrets

Action ✅ Yes ❌ No
Add .env to .gitignore
Keep a .env.example without values
Review history with git log --stat before publishing
Use python-dotenv to load variables
Configure GitHub Secrets for CI/CD
Avoid printing sensitive variables in logs
Rotate credentials regularly

Following this checklist on every new project significantly reduces the risk of leaks.

Conclusion

Keeping secrets out of source code is an essential practice for any Python developer publishing to GitHub. By using a .env file together with python-dotenv, protecting it with .gitignore, and supplementing with GitHub Secrets or external managers, you can ensure that your keys and passwords remain confidential in both development and production.

Ready to secure your next project?

Create a .env.example file right now, add .env to your .gitignore, and test variable loading with python-dotenv. If you use GitHub Actions, configure at least one secret and watch your pipeline run without revealing sensitive information. Protect your code and sleep easy!

Sources and references

  • Gestión de Secretos y API Keys en Python: Guía de .env
  • Almacenamiento de los secretos de forma segura - GitHub Docs
  • Gestión de secretos: del .env a Vault sin dejar claves en Git
  • Secretos - Documentación de GitHub
  • How to hide sensitive credentials using Python - GeeksforGeeks

title: Never Let a Display Toggle Write to the Database
description:
A support ticket arrives. Two users are looking at the same record and reading different numbers. Nothing in the logs. No exception, no failed request, no alert. The row is simply wrong, and nobody can say when it became wrong.

Trace it far enough and you often land on the same small piece of UI: a dropdown that lets the user change the unit a quantity is displayed in. Kilograms or pounds. Therms or MMBtu. Minutes or hours. Someone built it as a convenience, wired it straight to the field, and it writes back.

That control is not a formatting feature. It is a write path into your data, and it is almost never treated like one.

The shape of the bug

Here is the version that gets shipped. It looks harmless in review.

// The user picks a unit from the dropdown.
function onUnitChange(next: Unit) {
  const converted = convert(form.quantity, form.unit, next);
  form.quantity = converted;   // <- the display just wrote to the model
  form.unit = next;
}

Switch to the other unit and back again, and you have round-tripped the value through two divisions. With a non-terminating ratio you do not get your original number back. Do it four times and the drift is visible. Do it once on a record nobody looks at for a month and it is invisible, permanent, and indistinguishable from a legitimate edit.

The second failure is worse, because it needs no arithmetic error at all. A user switches the dropdown to read a value in a different unit, does not change anything, and hits save out of habit. The form submits the converted number against the original unit. The record is now off by whatever the conversion factor is.

Both of these are the same mistake: the presentation layer was given permission to write.

Rule 1: one canonical unit in storage

Pick a canonical unit per quantity type and store only that. The database does not know about user preferences, locales, or dropdowns.

CREATE TABLE measurement (
  id            bigint PRIMARY KEY,
  -- always stored in grams; the column name says so
  mass_g        numeric(20, 6) NOT NULL,
  recorded_at   timestamptz    NOT NULL
);

Put the unit in the column name. mass_g, duration_ms, volume_ml. A column called quantity with a sibling called unit invites every consumer to do its own conversion, and they will not all agree. A column called mass_g cannot be misread by the next person, and it cannot be misread by a reporting query written by someone who never read your code.

Conversion happens on the way out and on the way in at the edge, and nowhere else.

Rule 2: the converted value never travels back

Make display units a view concern that physically cannot reach the write path. The simplest way is to keep the canonical value in the model and derive the displayed one:

type Measurement = { massG: number };     // canonical, the only thing persisted

function display(m: Measurement, unit: Unit): string {
  return format(fromGrams(m.massG, unit), unit);
}

function onUnitChange(next: Unit) {
  viewState.unit = next;                  // view state only
  // model untouched
}

function onUserEdit(raw: string, unit: Unit) {
  model.massG = toGrams(parseDecimal(raw), unit);   // convert in, once
}

Two functions, toGrams and fromGrams, and a model that has no unit field at all. If the model cannot express "quantity in pounds", nothing downstream can accidentally persist one.

When the stored unit genuinely has to vary - because the source system sends mixed units and you need the original for audit - store both: the canonical value you compute with, and the as-received value and unit you never compute with. Never one field that means different things on different rows.

Rule 3: inexact types are the other half of the same bug

Unit conversion multiplies and divides. If the column is a binary floating point type, every one of those operations is an opportunity to lose the exact value, and the loss compounds silently.

The PostgreSQL documentation is blunt about this. real and double precision are listed as variable-precision, inexact, with 6 and 15 decimal digits of precision respectively. numeric is exact, with user-specified precision, and the docs say it "is especially recommended for storing monetary amounts and other quantities where exactness is required", with calculations yielding exact results where possible for addition, subtraction and multiplication. The same docs note that numeric calculations are slower than the floating point types - that is the trade, and for a quantity somebody will reconcile later it is an easy one.

-- wrong for anything that gets reconciled
volume double precision

-- right
volume_m3 numeric(20, 6)

The application side matters just as much. A JavaScript number is a double. If your API serialises a numeric column into JSON and the client parses it as a number, you have just thrown away the exactness you paid for in the database. Carry it as a string to the edge and parse it with a decimal library, or do the arithmetic server-side and send the client a formatted result it only displays.

And define rounding once, in one module, with the rounding mode written down. Two services that round differently will produce two totals, and the argument about which one is correct will cost more than the feature did.

Rule 4: a quantity is not always a single number

This is the modelling mistake that is cheap on day one and brutal to retrofit.

Sometimes the thing a user calls "the quantity" is a shape spread across a window, not a scalar. A monthly figure that is really a daily rate across a delivery period. A subscription allowance that resets. A forecast with a curve.

// day one, and it leaks into every report before anyone notices
type Line = { quantityG: number };

// what it actually is
type Line = {
  from: PlainDate;
  to: PlainDate;
  dailyQuantityG: number;     // or an explicit per-day profile
};

If you model it as a scalar, the first question that asks for a daily breakdown forces a migration through every report, export and integration that has already consumed the scalar. Aggregation over a shape is a different operation from summing a column, and you want to discover that before the data is in production.

Rule 5: one concept, three structures

The same trap in a different costume. You have a field that can be set three ways - a fixed value, a value derived from an index, or an offset against a reference. The tempting schema is one table, a type column, and a handful of nullable columns.

-- the shortcut
CREATE TABLE price (
  kind              text NOT NULL,      -- 'fixed' | 'indexed' | 'differential'
  fixed_amount      numeric,            -- null unless kind = 'fixed'
  index_code        text,               -- null unless kind = 'indexed'
  index_multiplier  numeric,            -- null unless ...
  base_reference    text,
  offset_amount     numeric
);

It works until the first reconciliation. After that, every query that has to understand the field carries a branch, the branches get copied, and two of them disagree. Nothing enforces that fixed_amount is present exactly when kind = 'fixed'.

Model each variant as its own structure and put the branching in one mapping layer:

type Price =
  | { kind: 'fixed'; amount: Decimal }
  | { kind: 'indexed'; indexCode: string; multiplier: Decimal }
  | { kind: 'differential'; baseRef: string; offset: Decimal };

A discriminated union makes the illegal states unrepresentable in the code, and the exhaustiveness check in your compiler tells you every place that needs updating when a fourth variant arrives. In the database, either use separate tables with a shared parent or add check constraints that make the nullability rules explicit:

ALTER TABLE price ADD CONSTRAINT price_shape CHECK (
  (kind = 'fixed'        AND fixed_amount IS NOT NULL AND index_code IS NULL)
  OR (kind = 'indexed'   AND index_code  IS NOT NULL AND fixed_amount IS NULL)
  OR (kind = 'differential' AND base_reference IS NOT NULL)
);

Rule 6: amend, do not overwrite

Once a record has been acted on by somebody else, an in-place UPDATE destroys the only evidence of what they acted on. "What did this say on the 14th" is a question that gets asked eventually, and the honest answer should not be "we cannot tell you".

Append amendments instead, and derive the current state:

CREATE TABLE measurement_amendment (
  id              bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  measurement_id  bigint      NOT NULL REFERENCES measurement(id),
  before          jsonb       NOT NULL,
  after           jsonb       NOT NULL,
  amended_by      text        NOT NULL,
  amended_at      timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

Three rules keep this honest. Every amendment carries who and when, not just what. Deletions are reversals - a new row that negates the previous state - not DELETE statements, because a deleted row and a row that was never written look identical afterwards. And the reconstruction path gets a test, because an audit trail nobody has ever replayed is a hope, not a guarantee.

Rule 7: concurrency, surfaced rather than swallowed

Two people editing the same record is normal, not an edge case. The default behaviour of a naive update is last-write-wins, and it is silent.

UPDATE measurement
   SET mass_g = $1, version = version + 1
 WHERE id = $2
   AND version = $3;         -- the version the editor loaded
-- 0 rows affected means somebody else got there first

Check the affected row count and tell the user. A conflict dialog is annoying. A silently discarded edit is a support ticket three weeks later with no evidence attached.

Approach What the user sees What you can prove later
Last write wins Nothing Nothing
Version column, error surfaced A conflict they resolve Who overwrote what, and when
Amendment log + version column A conflict they resolve Full state at any past moment

Rule 8: bulk import bypasses your form

Every system that reaches a certain size grows a spreadsheet importer, and the importer does not go through your UI. Validation that lives only in the form is not validation.

Three things make an importer safe. The rules live in the domain layer, so the form and the importer call the same code. There is a preview stage that shows exactly what will be created, changed and skipped, before anything is written. And the commit is all-or-nothing, in one transaction, because a half-applied import of a thousand rows is worse than a rejected one - a rejection is obvious, a partial apply looks like success.

One calculation, two readers

The last one is not really about data types at all.

If the total on the screen and the total in the export disagree by a rounding step, users stop trusting the whole system. Downtime is forgivable because it is understood. A number that changes depending on where you read it is not.

So the aggregate is computed in one place, called by both the screen and the export, with the rounding rules defined once. Not two implementations that are "basically the same". One.

Ship checklist

  1. Every quantity column names its unit (mass_g, not quantity plus a unit column).
  2. The write model has no display-unit field at all.
  3. Conversion happens exactly twice: parse in at the edge, format out at the edge.
  4. Money and reconciled quantities use an exact decimal type, never float or double precision.
  5. Decimal values cross the API as strings, not JSON numbers.
  6. Rounding mode and precision are defined in one module and imported everywhere.
  7. Quantities that are really shapes over a window are modelled as shapes from day one.
  8. Variant concepts are discriminated unions in code and check constraints in the schema.
  9. Edits append amendments with actor and timestamp; deletes are reversals.
  10. Updates carry a version and surface conflicts to the user instead of resolving them.
  11. The importer shares the domain validation, previews its effect, and commits atomically.

Most of these cost a morning at the start of a project. All of them cost a migration and a trust problem if you add them after the data is live.

We build and maintain data-entry and data-management systems where the numbers have to reconcile afterwards. The patterns above are the ones we have found worth enforcing from the first screen rather than the first incident.

title: CuriousTogether: Implications of Curiosity and Cultural Grounding in Multi-Agent LLM Interactions
description:
arXiv:2611.01301v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-agent settings, exhibiting emergent collective behaviors, yet the role of curiosity as a driver of such dynamics remains understudied. We introduce CuriousTogether, a framework evaluating curiosity-driven multi-agent LLM interactions across three complementary dimensions: novelty-seeking, epistemic and social curiosity. Across eight tasks spanning reasoning, creative generation, and social bias mitigation, curiosity-guided multi-agent settings yield improvements over non-curious ones on seven out of eight tasks, with gains of up to 20.6% in story generation (semantic diversity) and a 14.9 pp reduction in stereotype rates. Furthermore, country-conditioned cultural grounding show benefits for story generation and social tasks, but can hurt precision-oriented reasoning. Finally, we show that inference-time multi-agent curiosity-based approach offers favorable quality-token trade-offs, compared with single-agent baselines. Together, these findings support curiosity-guided interaction as a practical mechanism for improving multi-agent collaboration, with downstream benefits for reasoning, creative, and societal tasks.
