title: 8 Ways to Test Applications Across Multiple Devices and Operating Systems
description:
Your users don't all run the same phone, OS version or browser. One person opens your app on a flagship iPhone with the latest iOS, another on a budget Android phone two OS versions behind, and a third on a tablet in landscape mode over a patchy 4G connection. Each combination can expose a different bug.

Testing every possible device isn't realistic, but testing too few is risky. A layout that looks perfect on a Pixel can overlap on a Samsung, and a feature that runs smoothly on iOS 18 can crash on an older release.

The answer is a deliberate strategy that combines the right device mix, automation, cloud testing and non functional testing. Here are eight practical ways to test applications across multiple devices and operating systems without slowing down your releases.

8 ways to test across devices and operating systems

1. Build a data-driven device matrix
Start with your own analytics, not a generic list of popular phones. Look at which devices, OS versions, screen sizes and browsers your users actually have, and rank them by traffic and revenue.

Group them into tiers. Tier 1 covers the devices most of your users rely on and gets tested on every build. Tier 2 covers older OS versions and less common screen sizes and gets tested before each release. Tier 3 covers long-tail devices and gets spot checks. Review the matrix every quarter, because new phones and OS updates shift the picture quickly.

2. Use cloud testing to access real devices at scale
Buying and maintaining hundreds of phones and tablets is expensive, and devices go out of date fast. Cloud testing platforms solve this by giving your team remote access to real devices and browsers hosted in data centers.

With cloud testing, you can open a specific model and OS version in seconds, run manual checks, or point your automated suite at dozens of devices at once. Platforms such as HeadSpin, BrowserStack, Sauce Labs and Firebase Test Lab also handle device updates, cleanup and maintenance, so your team focuses on testing instead of hardware.

3. Balance emulators, simulators and real devices
Emulators and simulators are fast, free and easy to spin up, which makes them ideal for early development and quick feedback in CI. But they don't fully reproduce real hardware: battery behavior, sensors, camera, GPU rendering, memory limits and manufacturer customizations all differ.

Use virtual devices for frequent, early checks and real devices for pre-release validation and anything hardware-dependent. Combining both keeps feedback fast without letting device-specific bugs slip through.

4. Automate cross-platform tests and run them in parallel
Manually repeating the same test on 20 devices doesn't scale. Automate your core user journeys with frameworks like Appium for cross-platform coverage, or Espresso and XCUITest for native apps. Flutter and React Native teams can use their own integration testing tools.

The real speed gain comes from parallel execution. Instead of running one device after another, run your suite across many devices simultaneously on a cloud testing grid. A suite that takes three hours sequentially can finish in minutes.

5. Design responsive layouts and test every screen size
Screen fragmentation goes beyond phone models. You also need to account for tablets, foldables, notches, punch-hole cameras, split-screen mode, landscape orientation and user font-size settings.

Test how each key screen adapts at different sizes and orientations. Visual regression tools can compare screenshots across devices and flag layout shifts, cut-off text or overlapping elements automatically, catching problems that functional checks miss.

6. Make non functional testing part of every release
An app can pass every functional test and still deliver a poor experience. Non functional testing checks how well the app works, not just whether it works, and results often vary dramatically by device and OS.

Cover these areas across your device matrix:

  • Performance: app launch time, screen load time, frame rate and memory use, especially on low-end devices.
  • Battery and resource use: background activity and CPU drain that may only show up on certain hardware.
  • Compatibility: behavior after OS upgrades and on manufacturer-customized Android versions.
  • Accessibility: screen reader support on both TalkBack and VoiceOver, color contrast and touch target sizes.
  • Security: permission handling and data storage differences between OS versions.

Many cloud testing platforms include performance metrics, so you can run non functional testing on the same real devices as your functional suite instead of maintaining a separate setup.

7. Test under real-world network conditions
Users move between Wi-Fi, 5G, 4G and weak signals, and some live in regions with high latency. An app that feels instant on office Wi-Fi can time out on a congested mobile network.

Simulate slow, lossy and offline connections to check loading states, timeouts, retries and offline behavior. For apps with a global audience, test on devices in different regions and carrier networks, which some cloud testing providers support through SIM-enabled devices in multiple countries.

8. Integrate cross-device testing into CI/CD
Cross-device testing works best when it runs automatically. Connect your device tests to your CI/CD pipeline so every pull request triggers a quick run on Tier 1 devices, and nightly or pre-release builds run the full matrix, including non functional testing.

Feed results back to developers with screenshots, videos and logs from each device, and track pass rates and performance trends over time. This turns device coverage from a last-minute scramble into a steady, predictable part of how you ship.

Conclusion

You can't test every device on the market, but you can test the ones that matter in a smart, repeatable way. Start with a device matrix built from real user data, use cloud testing to reach real devices without owning them, and automate your key journeys so they run in parallel on every build.

Then go beyond pass and fail. Non functional testing for performance, network behavior, accessibility and compatibility shows how your app actually feels on each device. Teams that combine these eight practices catch device-specific issues early, release with confidence, and give every user a consistent experience, whatever phone or OS they use.

title: Youssef Saoud: A Practical Spring Boot Backend Checklist for 2027
description:
For a Spring Boot backend heading into 2027, my review checklist starts with authorization, transaction boundaries, concurrent requests, and recovery after partial failure.

I'm Youssef Saoud, a Java backend developer building Orqestra, a project and vendor management application using Spring Boot, Angular, and PostgreSQL. These are the questions I would bring to a backend review as I plan further work on the project.

The year is a planning horizon. The engineering problems already exist today.

1. Can a request change its own privileges?

Consider an employee accepting an invitation. The request should provide the password needed to finish registration. It should not be trusted to choose the account's role or replace the invited email address.

In Orqestra, acceptance constructs the account from the invitation's stored identity and role. Administrative invitation operations have an administrator permission check.

Review question: Which values come from an authenticated identity or trusted database record, and which come from the caller?

The integration tests include an acceptance payload that attempts to supply an administrator role and a different email. The resulting account must still use the invitation's stored values.

2. What happens when two requests arrive together?

Checking that an invitation is pending is insufficient if two requests can both observe that state before either updates it.

Orqestra's acceptance transaction obtains a pessimistic write lock on the invitation row. It then validates the invitation, creates the account, and marks the invitation accepted within the transaction.

Review question: What coordinates competing attempts to perform the same state transition?

@Transactional defines the unit of work, but the concurrency strategy still needs to be explicit. Locking also has costs: this implementation performs password hashing while the transaction is open, which deserves measurement as traffic grows.

3. Where does the database transaction stop?

An SMTP server does not participate in the application's PostgreSQL transaction. Saving an invitation and submitting an email are separate operations with separate failure modes.

Orqestra commits the invitation before submitting the email, then records the delivery outcome separately. Failed submission leaves an invitation that an administrator can resend.

Review question: If the external call fails after the database commits, what state remains, and who can recover it?

A successful SMTP submission also does not establish inbox delivery.

4. Can an old result overwrite newer state?

Resending an invitation rotates its token. An earlier email attempt might finish after a newer resend.

The delivery result is associated with the token hash for that attempt. Orqestra applies the result only when that hash still matches the invitation's current hash.

Review question: Does an asynchronous result identify the version of the work it belongs to?

This check protects the current delivery status from a superseded attempt. It does not cancel an email already submitted to a provider.

5. What does the test actually prove?

The invitation tests cover expiry, revocation, reuse, role preservation, token rotation, and failed-delivery retries. A focused concurrency test starts two acceptance attempts and checks that one succeeds and one account exists.

Email delivery is mocked. These tests exercise application behavior around delivery outcomes, rather than real provider delivery or production load.

Review question: Which guarantee is tested, and which assumption still needs operational evidence?

My next improvement

There is still a crash window between committing an invitation and submitting its email. A transactional outbox is a candidate improvement: persist a delivery job alongside the invitation change, then let a worker handle delivery and retries.

That work would need its own rules for duplicate attempts, superseded tokens, and worker failures. It is a proposed improvement, not an implemented guarantee.

For my 2027 work, these questions give each feature a concrete review standard: permissions, competing requests, external failures, stale results, and evidence.

You can inspect the invitation implementation and tests and follow my work on GitHub or LinkedIn.

More technical writing and projects: Youssef Saoud.

title: I built a free, offline replacement for TORA that explains every simplex step
description:
For our Operations Research course at NMIMS Shirpur, my teammates and I wanted a tool that shows why each simplex step happens, not only the final answer. So I built OR/Studio: a free, open-source Operations Research workbench that runs in the browser and works offline.

What it does

There are 13 solver modules: simplex (including Big-M, two-phase and dual), integer programming, nonlinear programming, transportation, assignment, network models, project planning, queuing, inventory, game theory, Markov chains, simulation and job sequencing.

Every tableau and ratio test comes with a plain-language reason and the rule that was applied. In tutor mode you pick the entering variable and leaving row yourself and get told what went wrong if you're off. In diff mode you type your own working and it finds the first step where you diverged.

Exact arithmetic

Fractions are exact, so the numbers in a tableau match what you'd get by hand. Big-M and prohibited routes use a symbolic M, never a large number.

How I tested it

The solvers are pure TypeScript with no UI dependency, and I tested them against independent checks, not against themselves:

  • Linear programs against vertex enumeration and strong-duality checks on random instances.
  • Integer programs and assignment against brute force.
  • Transportation, max flow and games re-formulated as LPs and compared.
  • Shortest-path and spanning-tree algorithms that must agree with each other.

The repo has 452 tests. The hardest part wasn't the algorithms. It was the edge cases: unbounded problems, cycling, degenerate pivots and negative cycles.

What it doesn't do yet

Separable programming isn't implemented, "Save as PDF" goes through the browser's print dialog, and the nonlinear module works in floating point. I've opened these as issues.

Try it

  • Live: https://or-studio.antideploy.app
  • Code (MIT): https://github.com/Jay-Naik2526/or-studio

I'd like feedback from anyone taking or teaching an OR course, especially bugs and missing methods.

title: Zoho Integration Services in Node.js: Upsert Without Duplicates
description:
A webhook retries, and your Node.js worker creates a second Account in Zoho CRM for the same customer. Sales now has two half-histories, and finance invoices the wrong one. This failure appears in how Zoho integration services handle retries and identity in production, usually after a timeout or a duplicate event from the source system. Teams hit it first in order-to-cash flows, where a duplicate Account later reaches invoicing. The cause is rarely the API call. It is a missing identity rule: nothing tells Zoho which record is which. This article shows how to fix that with an idempotent upsert client, bounded retries, and a review queue.

Context and Setup

Zoho integration services connect Zoho apps to outside systems, and the hard part is consistency when messages repeat. In the scenario below, a source system sends events to a Node.js service that writes Accounts into Zoho CRM.

Prerequisites: Node.js 18 or later (for global fetch), a Zoho OAuth client with a refresh token, and a custom Account field named Organization_Number holding a legal identifier. The scale of the problem is well documented. According to MuleSoft’s 2025 Connectivity Benchmark Report, the average enterprise runs 897 applications and integrates only 29 percent of them.

Building Zoho Integration Services with Idempotent Upserts
An idempotent write gives the same result whether it runs once or five times. Zoho CRM’s upsert endpoint provides that when you pick the right match field.

Step 1: Pick the match key
Match on an identifier the business already enforces, such as an organization number. Names and emails drift, so they make weak keys.

Add a custom field for the legal identifier to the Accounts module.
Normalize it before sending (strip spaces and punctuation).
Pass it as duplicate_check_fields so Zoho decides between insert and update.

Step 2: Write the upsert client for Zoho integration services
js
// Node 18+: global fetch, no dependencies
const ZOHO_API = "https://www.zohoapis.com/crm/v6"; // Why: region specific (.eu, .in elsewhere)

async function upsertAccount(record, token, attempt = 1) {
const res = await fetch(${ZOHO_API}/Accounts/upsert, {
method: "POST",
headers: {
Authorization: Zoho-oauthtoken ${token},
"Content-Type": "application/json",
},
body: JSON.stringify({
data: [record],
// Why: a retry updates the existing record instead of creating a duplicate
duplicate_check_fields: ["Organization_Number"],
}),
});

// Why: only transient errors deserve a retry; a 4xx means the payload is wrong
if ((res.status === 429 || res.status >= 500) && attempt <= 3) {
const delay = 2 ** attempt * 500; // exponential backoff: 1s, 2s, 4s
await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, delay));
return upsertAccount(record, token, attempt + 1);
}

const body = await res.json();
const item = body.data?.[0];
if (res.ok && item?.code === "SUCCESS") {
return { id: item.details.id, action: item.action }; // "insert" or "update"
}
// Why: fail loudly so the caller can route the record to a review queue
throw new Error(Zoho rejected record: ${JSON.stringify(item ?? body)});
}
Step 3: Weigh the trade-offs
We retry a fixed number of times, then send the record to a queue with a named owner. This costs reviewer time, so the queue stays short only if the match rule is strict.

Batching is the other lever. Zoho’s CRM API limits documentation (reviewed November 2026) allows up to 100 records per insert, update, or upsert call and caps the deduction for such a call at 10 credits. Credits run on a rolling 24-hour window, so batch non-urgent syncs.

Real-World Application

In one of our Zoho integration projects at Oodles, Devinco AS, a Norwegian provider of integrated mobile solutions, needed its course platform connected to Zoho CRM. The goal was tracking sales, accounts, and contacts without manual entry.

We built a trigger that creates a Won Deal on each sale, with separate pipeline stages for paid and free courses. Account matching uses organization numbers, and a new account is created only when no match exists. Contact lookup runs on email with duplicate prevention, and Deal Contact Roles separate course orderers from attendees.

Key Takeaways

An upsert keyed on a business identifier makes retries safe, because repeats update instead of clone.
Retry only 429 and 5xx responses, with exponential backoff, since 4xx errors fail identically every time.
Batch up to 100 records per call to cut credit use, and keep single-record calls for time-sensitive events.
Route rejected records to an owned review queue so failures are visible, not silent.

Questions about your own sync design? Share them in the comments, or talk with us about Zoho integration services.

What are Zoho integration services?
Zoho integration services connect Zoho apps to each other and to external systems such as ERP, billing, and e-commerce platforms. The work includes data mapping, trigger design, retry and error handling, and monitoring so records stay consistent.

How do you avoid duplicate records in Zoho CRM from Node.js?
Use the Upsert Records endpoint with duplicate_check_fields set to a stable identifier, such as an organization number. Zoho then updates the matching record instead of inserting a second one, which makes webhook retries safe.

How do you authenticate to the Zoho CRM API?
Register a server-based client in the Zoho API Console, complete the OAuth 2.0 grant once for a refresh token, then exchange it for short-lived access tokens sent in an Authorization: Zoho-oauthtoken header.

What happens when Zoho API credits run out?
Zoho rejects further calls until credits free up on the rolling 24-hour window, and admins can add credits. Batch records and queue non-urgent syncs so real-time flows keep their credits.

Should Zoho integration services use webhooks or polling?
Use webhooks for event-driven flows such as a closed deal, because they avoid spending credits on empty polls. Reserve scheduled reads for backfills and daily reconciliation, where comparing record counts catches silent mismatches.

title: From Lookups to Lessons: Turning Retrieved Knowledge into Parametric Memory
description:
arXiv:2611.00450v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) helps large language models (LLMs) answer factual questions beyond their training data, but it adds storage and inference costs. Distilling previously retrieved information into parametric memories enables reuse without online retrieval. However, training the memory to mimic a retriever rewards accurate independent predictions, which do not necessarily improve the final output quality when combined with the LLM's existing predictions. To address this, we introduce ResMem, in which the LLM reads retrieved text offline to generate teacher targets. This design avoids storing massive token representations, unlike existing parametric memory approaches such as MLP Memory, which relies on k-nearest neighbor (kNN) datastores. Furthermore, by using the LLM as an offline teacher that reads privileged retrieved evidence alongside the input, we train a parametric memory to learn an additive logit residual. This residual aligns the predictions of a student sharing the same backbone with the teacher distribution, while self-distillation updates remain confined to the parametric memory. On a Wikipedia subset, ResMem reduces the storage retained for teacher construction by 94.7% compared with the evaluated kNN pipeline. Across five question answering datasets, ResMem raises mean token F1 from 32.83% for the frozen LLM to 34.48%. It also breaks 21% fewer of the LLM's correct answers than a kNN-trained memory. These findings validate our motivation of treating retrieval as a learning resource, with parametric memory shaped by how retrieved knowledge is used to inform the model's future predictions. Code and model weights are available at https://github.com/SSRand/From-Lookups-to-Lessons and https://huggingface.co/RandHan/ResMem-Mistral-7B-v0.3.

title: npm 12 Blocks Install Scripts by Default. Node 26 LTS, Out Oct 28, Still Ships npm 11.
description:
On October 8, tensorlake@0.5.144 was on npm for about 1 hour 40 minutes. It was not a real release. Someone with access to the maintainer's GitHub account committed a payload and ran the project's own release workflow, so the package even carried valid npm provenance. A preinstall hook ran the payload the moment it was installed on a developer machine.

The payload went after GitHub and npm tokens, AWS and GCP credentials, SSH keys, .env files and browser passwords, then used those tokens to republish itself into other packages. It also installed a small service called gh-token-monitor that deletes your home directory if the stolen GitHub token gets revoked (SafeDep found it only arms for tokens on accounts with no organizations). That's all in the maintainers' own GitHub advisory (GHSA-8g63-53c9-65j2), and it's part of the Mini Shai-Hulud campaign that has been hitting npm since April.

npm already has a fix for the "runs on install" part. npm 12, out since July 8, doesn't run dependency preinstall, install or postinstall scripts unless your project allows them.

Here's the catch. Node 26 became LTS on October 28, and the npm it ships is 11.20.0. That's not npm 12. I checked the bundled npm version for every current LTS line in the Node release index today:

Node release Date npm it ships
26.13.0 (LTS "Lithium") Oct 28, 2026 11.20.0
24.22.2 (LTS "Krypton") Oct 27, 2026 11.19.1
22.23.4 (LTS "Jod") Oct 20, 2026 10.9.9

The only Node line with npm 12 bundled right now is the 27 alpha. So if you install Node the normal way and never run npm install -g npm, you're on a version that still runs every install script in your tree.

What each package manager actually did

I wanted to see this rather than trust release notes, so on a scratch box I made a tiny local package whose preinstall writes a marker file to the temp dir. I installed it next to esbuild (a normal, harmless package that has a postinstall) with each tool, then checked whether the marker file existed.

Tool Script ran? What it printed
npm 10.9.9 (what Node 22 ships) yes nothing at all
npm 11.21.1 yes a warning listing both packages
npm 12.2.1 no "2 packages had install scripts blocked"
pnpm 10.34.6 no "Ignored build scripts: esbuild@0.25.11, harmless-preinstall@file:..."
bun 1.4.2 no "Blocked 1 postinstall"

Two things stood out. On npm 10 there's no hint anything ran. On npm 11 the warning reads like a heads-up about the future, but the marker file was there, so the script had already run. The script also had a console.log, and that line never showed up in the install output on npm 10 or 11. You don't see install scripts run.

pnpm and bun already block by default. If you're on either, most of this post is about your CI and your teammates, not you.

Check a project in 10 seconds

This prints your npm version, whether install scripts are on, which packages in your lockfile actually have install scripts (npm records hasInstallScript in package-lock.json), and whether any of the tensorlake persistence files exist on the machine.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# install-scripts-check.sh: who gets to run code when you type npm install?
# usage: bash install-scripts-check.sh [project-dir]   (needs jq)
cd "${1:-.}" || exit 1
v=$(npm -v); major=${v%%.*}; ign=$(npm config get ignore-scripts)
allow=$(jq -c '.allowScripts // empty' package.json 2>/dev/null)
echo "node $(node -v), npm $v, ignore-scripts=$ign"
if [ "$major" -ge 12 ]; then echo "OK   npm 12+: dependency install scripts blocked unless allowed"
elif [ "$ign" = "true" ]; then echo "OK   ignore-scripts=true: install scripts off"
else echo "WARN npm $major runs every dependency install script (it only warns)"; fi
[ "$ign" = "true" ] && [ -n "$allow" ] && echo "WARN ignore-scripts=true silently overrides allowScripts"
echo "allowScripts: ${allow:-none}"
if [ -f package-lock.json ]; then
  n=$(jq '[.packages | keys[] | select(. != "")] | length' package-lock.json)
  echo "lockfile: $n packages; these have install scripts:"
  jq -r '.packages | to_entries[] | select(.value.hasInstallScript == true)
    | "  \(.key | sub("^.*node_modules/"; ""))@\(.value.version)"' package-lock.json
fi
echo "tensorlake worm persistence (all should be missing):"
for f in ~/.config/gh-token-monitor ~/.local/bin/gh-token-monitor.sh \
         ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.user.gh-token-monitor.plist; do
  if [ -e "$f" ]; then echo "  FOUND $f  <- remove BEFORE revoking GitHub tokens"
  else echo "  missing $f"; fi
done
systemctl --user list-unit-files 2>/dev/null | grep -q gh-token-monitor \
  && echo "  FOUND gh-token-monitor systemd user service <- stop it first"
for f in .claude/settings.json .vscode/tasks.json; do
  grep -qE 'SessionStart|folderOpen' "$f" 2>/dev/null && echo "  CHECK $f runs a command on open. Did you write it?"
done
exit 0

I ran it on a fresh lockfile for a pretty normal small-SaaS stack (next, react, react-dom, prisma 7, @prisma/client 7, stripe, tailwindcss, sharp) with the npm that was on the box:

node v24.22.1, npm 11.21.1, ignore-scripts=false
WARN npm 11 runs every dependency install script (it only warns)
allowScripts: {"prisma@7.10.1":true,"@prisma/engines@7.10.1":true}
lockfile: 191 packages; these have install scripts:
  @prisma/engines@7.10.1
  prisma@7.10.1
tensorlake worm persistence (all should be missing):
  missing /home/box/.config/gh-token-monitor
  missing /home/box/.local/bin/gh-token-monitor.sh
  missing /home/box/Library/LaunchAgents/com.user.gh-token-monitor.plist

That allowScripts list is already there because I approved Prisma with npm 12 first (next section). The script still says WARN on npm 11, and that's fair. On 11.21.1 a package you explicitly deny does get skipped (I tested that), but anything new that isn't on the list still runs. Only npm 12 flips the default. With npm 12.2.1 first on the PATH, the same project gives OK npm 12+: dependency install scripts blocked unless allowed.

The number worth noticing: 191 packages in the lockfile, 2 with install scripts. Your allowlist will probably be short. Short enough to read every entry.

Moving to npm 12 without breaking your build 

npm install -g npm@12
npm install                      # blocked scripts get listed at the end
npm install-scripts ls           # same list, read-only
npm install-scripts approve prisma @prisma/engines
npm install-scripts deny some-package-you-dont-trust
npm rebuild                      # runs the scripts you just approved
git add package.json && git commit -m "allowScripts for npm 12"

On the starter project above, npm 12 listed @prisma/engines@7.10.1 (postinstall: node scripts/postinstall.js) and prisma@7.10.1 (preinstall: node scripts/preinstall-entry.js). After the approve step, package.json had:

"allowScripts": {
  "prisma@7.10.1": true,
  "@prisma/engines@7.10.1": true
}

Approvals are pinned to the version you reviewed by default. When Prisma bumps, the new version is blocked again until you look at it. That's a little annoying and it's exactly the point. A hijacked patch release of a package you trust is how these worms spread. npm install-scripts prune cleans out entries for versions you no longer have.

GitHub's npm v12 breaking-changes note covers two other defaults that changed at the same time: git dependencies and remote tarball URLs are no longer resolved unless you allow them. If your install breaks on a github: dependency after upgrading, that's why.

Three gotchas

ignore-scripts=true beats your allowlist. Setting it in .npmrc was a common hardening tip after the first Shai-Hulud wave in September 2025. On npm 12 it silently wins over allowScripts. I approved my test package, ran npm install --ignore-scripts, and the marker file never appeared. Same install without the flag, it did. Pick one setup and remove the other.

CI has its own npm. Upgrading on your laptop does nothing for the build server. Cloudflare's Oct 23 changelog says their Workers Builds and Pages images now ship Node 22.23.4 and 24.22.1, and per the Node release index those come with npm 10.9.9 and 11.19.1. If your CI sets up Node with something like actions/setup-node, you get that Node's bundled npm unless you upgrade it. Add an npm install -g npm@12 step before npm ci, or check what your builder uses.

Your laptop is the real target. SafeDep's teardown of the tensorlake payload shows the loader checks CI, GITHUB_ACTIONS, GITLAB_CI and RUNNER_ENVIRONMENT and simply exits on CI. It wants the machine where your SSH keys, .env files and logged-in browser live. That's also where AI coding agents type npm install for you without you reading the package name. I wrote down some rules for keeping coding agents from installing junk or reading your secrets on a side project, and they matter more once you know worms skip CI on purpose.

If you think you installed something bad

The order matters here, and it's the opposite of what your instincts say.

  1. Take the machine off the network.
  2. Remove gh-token-monitor before you revoke anything. The advisory gives the commands: on Linux systemctl --user disable --now gh-token-monitor.service and delete ~/.config/gh-token-monitor/ and ~/.local/bin/gh-token-monitor.sh; on macOS launchctl bootout the com.user.gh-token-monitor LaunchAgent and delete the plist.
  3. Rotate tokens from a different, clean machine.
  4. Look through the repos and packages your tokens could write to. The tensorlake advisory says to look for unexpected releases, commits authored claude, and a branch named dependabot/github_actions/format/setup-formatter. Sonatype and Socket also flag changed .claude/settings.json and .vscode/tasks.json files, which is why the script greps them.
  5. Rebuild the machine from a clean image.

What npm 12 doesn't fix

Blocking install scripts closes one door. Code that runs when you import the package is untouched. A GitHub advisory from October 9 for an npm package called testrrrd describes exactly that: it fires the same beacon from postinstall and again from its main file at import time, so --ignore-scripts alone doesn't stop it. If a bad version lands in your lockfile, you'll run it the first time your app starts.

So the lockfile still matters. Commit it, use npm ci in CI, and don't auto-merge dependency bumps the same hour they're published. It's the same lesson as the trivy-action tags that got repointed in one night: a name you trust is not the same as the code you get.

For most small projects the whole fix is upgrading npm, one install, approving two or three packages and committing package.json.

If you've already moved to npm 12: how many packages ended up in your allowScripts, and which one broke first when you upgraded?

title: Reverting Git Won’t Undo Your Database Migration
description:
A release introduces an application bug. You revert the deployment configuration, and the previous container image starts successfully.

But requests still fail.

The application has returned to its previous version. The database has not.

For stateful applications, a deployment rollback and a recovery plan cover different things.

A simple column rename can break rollback

Consider an application that reads this column:

SELECT customer_name FROM orders;

A new release renames it:

ALTER TABLE orders
RENAME COLUMN customer_name TO billing_name;

The new application expects billing_name. The previous application expects customer_name.

If the release fails after the migration, deploying the previous image leaves it querying a column that no longer exists.

The same compatibility problem can appear during a rolling deployment, while old and new application instances run together.

This is an illustrative example. The locking and operational impact of schema changes depend on the database engine and workload.

Separate schema evolution into stages

The expand, migrate, contract pattern spreads a breaking change across compatible steps. GitLab documents this approach for changes that must work across application versions. GitLab's compatibility guide

For this example, a staged approach could look like:

1. Expand

Introduce the new column while keeping the existing one.

Old application instances can continue using the original schema.

Adding a column still needs operational review: defaults, constraints, table size and database behavior can affect deployment safety.

2. Migrate

Introduce application behavior that supports the transition.

Define how both representations stay consistent while older instances remain active. A one-time backfill is insufficient if ongoing writes can immediately make the columns disagree.

Backfill existing records in controlled batches where appropriate. Make progress observable and retries safe.

Check completeness and consistency before switching reads.

3. Contract

Remove the old representation only after its consumers have stopped using it and the intended rollback window has closed.

Consumers may include background workers, reports, integrations and scheduled jobs—not just web application instances.

Once the old column is removed, an older application version may no longer be a valid recovery target.

Keep GitOps reconciliation in the recovery plan

A manual change to a running Deployment can conflict with the desired state maintained by a GitOps controller.

Decide how recovery changes the authoritative configuration, and how reconciliation behaves during the incident.

Also distinguish a Git revert from the deployment tool's rollback operation. They are separate mechanisms with their own behavior and constraints. Check the documentation for your deployed version, such as Argo CD's automated sync policy.

Neither operation inherently reverses database writes or external side effects.

Test the previous application against the migrated database

A useful compatibility test is:

Create representative starting data
    → Apply the proposed migration
    → Run the previous application version
    → Exercise important reads and writes
    → Run the new application version
    → Verify transition behavior

For a rolling release, also test the period when both versions operate concurrently.

A successful migration command proves that the database accepted the change. It does not prove application compatibility.

Write down where rollback stops being safe

Before release, answer:

  • Which application versions support the resulting schema?
  • Can migration jobs resume safely after interruption?
  • What happens to writes made during the transition?
  • At what step does recovery require a forward fix?
  • If restoration is necessary, what happens to data written since the backup?

The recovery target is a compatible application-and-data state.

How does your team define the rollback window for releases that change the database?

title: OpenPDF in Java: Encryption Setup, CSS Support, Footers
description:
Give OpenPDF's HTML module a two-column grid ledger whose total an inline script writes, and the PDF comes back with Hosting120.00Support80.00 on one line, a bold Total, and no figure after it. That run used 3.0.5, released on 22 May 2026 by the LibrePDF project, whose library began as a fork of iText 4.2.0. The ledger leads this post and five more problems follow, each one run against those jars or traced to the source that documents it.

We work at Iron Software, and the end of this article covers our library, IronPDF.

What Happens to Flexbox, Grid and Script in openpdf-html?

They are ignored. The core library's HTMLWorker parser has been deprecated since 2.1.0, and the openpdf-html module built for HTML is a Flying Saucer fork from June 2025 whose README says Flying Saucer set out to render XHTML with CSS 2.1 in plain Java, simpler than a browser engine. That README still marks HTML5 as in progress and lists JavaScript as a roadmap item. In the 3.0.5 jar, the CSSName property table holds 127 names, display, float and border-collapse among them, with none for flexbox, grid or gap.

import org.openpdf.pdf.ITextRenderer;

import java.io.FileOutputStream;
import java.io.OutputStream;

public class FlexGridScript {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        // A flex row, a two-column grid and a script that writes the total, as a browser template would have them.
        String html = "<html><head><style>"
                + ".row { display: flex; gap: 16px; }"
                + ".card { flex: 1; border: 1px solid #999; padding: 8px; }"
                + ".ledger { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 3fr 1fr; }"
                + "</style></head><body>"
                + "<div class='row'><div class='card'>North</div><div class='card'>South</div>"
                + "<div class='card' id='east'></div></div>"
                + "<div class='ledger'><span>Hosting</span><span>120.00</span>"
                + "<span>Support</span><span>80.00</span><b>Total</b><b id='sum'></b></div>"
                + "<script>document.getElementById('east').textContent = 'East';"
                + "document.getElementById('sum').textContent = (120 + 80).toFixed(2);</script>"
                + "</body></html>";

        try (OutputStream out = new FileOutputStream("flex-grid-script.pdf")) {
            ITextRenderer renderer = new ITextRenderer();
            renderer.setDocumentFromString(html);
            renderer.layout();
            renderer.createPDF(out);
        }
    }
}

Opened in a viewer, the 1,233-byte page shows two boxes stacked down the left edge, North over South, with their text starting at x = 48.8 and their borders spanning the full text width, so the flex row never formed. Below them sits an empty bordered strip where East belonged, since no script ran, and the ledger reads as the single line quoted at the top. Browser-built templates and script-drawn charts end up the same way. The module's layout model stays CSS 2.1, so columns come from tables or floats and every total is computed in Java first.

Why Does Encryption Throw NoClassDefFoundError?

Because Bouncy Castle is optional in the POM and required at run time. The 3.0.5 core pulls in exactly one runtime library, Brotli4j at version 1.23.0, and leaves bcprov-jdk18on to the application as optional. The class below reads an existing two-page statement, sets AES-128 encryption on a PdfStamper and stamps every page.

import org.openpdf.text.Element;
import org.openpdf.text.Font;
import org.openpdf.text.FontFactory;
import org.openpdf.text.Phrase;
import org.openpdf.text.Rectangle;
import org.openpdf.text.pdf.ColumnText;
import org.openpdf.text.pdf.PdfContentByte;
import org.openpdf.text.pdf.PdfGState;
import org.openpdf.text.pdf.PdfReader;
import org.openpdf.text.pdf.PdfStamper;
import org.openpdf.text.pdf.PdfWriter;

import java.awt.Color;
import java.io.FileOutputStream;

public class StampAndEncrypt {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        PdfReader reader = new PdfReader("statement-table.pdf");
        PdfStamper stamper = new PdfStamper(reader, new FileOutputStream("statement-copy.pdf"));

        // The user password opens the file, and the owner password lifts the permission flags.
        stamper.setEncryption("view-2026".getBytes(), "owner-2026".getBytes(),
                PdfWriter.ALLOW_PRINTING, PdfWriter.ENCRYPTION_AES_128);

        Font font = FontFactory.getFont(FontFactory.HELVETICA_BOLD, 60, Font.NORMAL, new Color(200, 0, 0));
        PdfGState translucent = new PdfGState();
        translucent.setFillOpacity(0.25f);

        // getOverContent draws above the existing page, so the stamp lands on top of the table.
        for (int page = 1; page <= reader.getNumberOfPages(); page++) {
            Rectangle size = reader.getPageSize(page);
            PdfContentByte over = stamper.getOverContent(page);
            over.saveState();
            over.setGState(translucent);
            ColumnText.showTextAligned(over, Element.ALIGN_CENTER, new Phrase("COPY", font),
                    size.getWidth() / 2, size.getHeight() / 2, 45);
            over.restoreState();
        }
        stamper.close();
        reader.close();
    }
}

On the declared dependencies alone, setEncryption threw NoClassDefFoundError for a Bouncy Castle ASN.1 class, ASN1OctetString on some runs and ASN1Encodable on others, from inside the PdfEncryption constructor, and a 0-byte statement-copy.pdf was left on disk. With bcprov-jdk18on 1.84 added, the same class produced a copy of about 4.5 KB, encrypted at revision 4 with the AESV2 filter, opening with view-2026, with a translucent COPY across both pages. Because the error only appears when the code path runs, a test suite that never encrypts will not catch it. The fix is an explicit Maven dependency on Bouncy Castle, and the next section explains why 1.84 is not the version to pick.

Which Advisories Touch an OpenPDF Build?

A query to OSV on 3 November 2026 found no record for either OpenPDF artifact at version 3.0.5, the core or the HTML module. The records that do come up sit one step away.

  • CVE-2026-8763 scores 9.1 Critical under CVSS 3.1 (NIST): A Name Constraints bypass in Bouncy Castle 1.84, the version the OpenPDF 3.0.5 build declares.
  • CVE-2026-13506 scores 7.5 High under CVSS 3.1 (NIST): Forcing a lazy ASN.1 sequence resets the nesting-depth guard, again in 1.84. Both records are fixed in bcprov-jdk18on 1.85, released on 12 July 2026, and the master branch of OpenPDF still pins 1.84 on 3 November 2026. Bouncy Castle's October records, such as CVE-2026-18036, also list 1.85 and are fixed in 1.86.
  • CVE-2017-9096 scores 8.8 High under CVSS 3.0 (NIST): XML external entities in iText before 5.5.12, and GHSA-86p9-x5pw-94qx widens it to the com.lowagie:itext artifact up to 4.2.2, whose 4.2.0 tag is where OpenPDF started. The com.github.librepdf coordinates are not listed, and the 3.0.5 XmlParser disables external entities.

The rest of the exposure comes from intended behavior. OpenPDF's security policy calls the library neither sandboxed nor hardened, and the project leaves every check on HTML, fonts, image locations and paths to whoever calls it, naming local file access, server-side request forgery and path traversal among the cases it does not block. In a test run, an <img> whose src was a file: URI pulled a PNG off the local disk into the PDF. Because the project asks that no CVEs be filed for such behavior, an advisory scan will not list it, and the remedy it gives is jsoup sanitizing, whitelisted src and href values and generation inside a container or sandbox. Licensing is MPL-2.0 OR LGPL-2.1+ for the core and the LGPL 2.1 or later for openpdf-html.

Who Is Affected by the Java 21 Floor?

Any team whose services run on Java 17 or below. The README sets Java 21 as the minimum for the 2.1.x line and later, and javac from JDK 17 stops on the first OpenPDF import of a 3.0.5 example.

error: cannot access Document
  bad class file: openpdf-3.0.5.jar(/org/openpdf/text/Document.class)
    class file has wrong version 65.0, should be 61.0

The Java 17 option is the 2.0.x branch, last released as 2.0.5 on 26 May 2025, which is older than openpdf-html itself (first shipped as 2.1.0 in June 2025) and than the move to the org.openpdf packages in 3.0.

How Much Layout Code Does a Simple Invoice Need?

Every placed element is a coordinate in points from the bottom-left corner of the page. A one-page US Letter invoice with a logo, a right-aligned title and a rule under the letterhead takes the class below.

import org.openpdf.text.Document;
import org.openpdf.text.Element;
import org.openpdf.text.Font;
import org.openpdf.text.Image;
import org.openpdf.text.PageSize;
import org.openpdf.text.Paragraph;
import org.openpdf.text.pdf.BaseFont;
import org.openpdf.text.pdf.PdfContentByte;
import org.openpdf.text.pdf.PdfWriter;

import java.io.FileOutputStream;

public class InvoiceLayout {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        // US Letter is 612 x 792 points, and the 120-point top margin leaves room for the letterhead.
        Document document = new Document(PageSize.LETTER, 36, 36, 120, 36);
        PdfWriter writer = PdfWriter.getInstance(document, new FileOutputStream("invoice-layout.pdf"));
        document.open();

        BaseFont sans = BaseFont.createFont("fonts/LiberationSans-Regular.ttf", BaseFont.IDENTITY_H, BaseFont.EMBEDDED);
        BaseFont sansBold = BaseFont.createFont("fonts/LiberationSans-Bold.ttf", BaseFont.IDENTITY_H, BaseFont.EMBEDDED);

        // Absolute positions count from the bottom-left corner, so y = 792 is the top edge.
        Image logo = Image.getInstance("img/logo.png");
        logo.scaleToFit(150, 60);
        logo.setAbsolutePosition(36, 792 - 36 - logo.getScaledHeight());
        document.add(logo);

        PdfContentByte canvas = writer.getDirectContent();
        canvas.beginText();
        canvas.setFontAndSize(sansBold, 20);
        canvas.showTextAligned(Element.ALIGN_RIGHT, "Invoice 4471", 576, 730, 0);
        canvas.endText();
        canvas.setLineWidth(0.75f);
        canvas.moveTo(36, 684);
        canvas.lineTo(576, 684);
        canvas.stroke();

        // Flowing elements start at the top margin and wrap between the side margins.
        Font body = new Font(sans, 11);
        document.add(new Paragraph("Bill to: Ève Lefèvre, Rue du Rhône 12, Genève", body));
        document.add(new Paragraph("Consulting, October 2026: CHF 3,200.00", body));
        document.close();
    }
}

The run produced a 25,786-byte Letter page with the logo scaled to 150 by 60 points at y = 696, Invoice 4471 ending at x = 576 and the rule at y = 684. Each of those numbers was chosen by hand, so a switch to A4, a taller logo or a new margin means recalculating them. Developers coming from HTML and CSS templates feel this most.

Why Does a Page X of Y Footer Take an Event Class?

OpenPDF's HeaderFooter class can print the current page number but not the total, so a footer reading Page 2 of 3 takes a PdfPageEventHelper, a PdfTemplate placed empty on each page and a write in onCloseDocument, once the total is known. In the test run, getPageNumber() returned 4 inside onCloseDocument for a three-page file, so the count written into the template has to subtract one. The three pages then shared a single 30 by 12 point form object for the total, and each read Page 1 of 3 through Page 3 of 3. Any report with running footers needs this class or the library's other route, stamping the numbers afterwards through PdfStamper when the total is already fixed.

Moving the Ledger to IronPDF for Java

For teams that would rather keep that ledger in HTML, IronPDF for Java is a commercial option that renders with Chromium, through an engine it downloads on first run or takes from a platform ironpdf-engine artifact. Our 2026.11.3 run of the first section's page laid the three cards out side by side, kept the ledger in two columns and printed the script's 200.00. It is added from Maven Central as one dependency, com.ironsoftware:ironpdf, that runs on Java 8 and later, and the 2026 line there has reached 2026.11.3, published on 3 November.

With IronPDF for Java, page numbers become a TextHeaderFooter passed to addTextFooter with Page {page} of {total-pages}, and a SecurityOptions object sets the user and owner passwords before saveAs writes the file. Markup from users still needs sanitizing before any renderer sees it.

To run your own templates through IronPDF for Java, there is a free trial.

Five Checks Before Shipping OpenPDF

OpenPDF 3.0.5 needs Java 21, an explicit and current Bouncy Castle, sanitized input, CSS 2.1 templates and hand-placed layout, and IronPDF for Java answers the HTML rendering, layout and Java-version items with a Chromium renderer on Java 8 and later.

OpenPDF, Flying Saucer, iText and Bouncy Castle are trademarks of their respective owners, we have no affiliation with any of them, and the facts above are drawn from their public repositories, Maven Central records and advisory databases.

Drafted with AI. OpenPDF code run and claims checked by the Iron Software DevRel team against com.github.librepdf:openpdf 3.0.5 and com.ironsoftware:ironpdf 2026.11.3 on 3 November 2026.

title: Fidelity Collapses with Table Size, Not Turn Count: Delivery Architecture in a Deployed Tool-Using Agent
description:
arXiv:2611.00442v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When a multi-turn agent delivers a tool's structured records into the model's context and re-emits them each turn, every turn can corrupt data the tool computed correctly. We measure this in a production award-travel agent: two architectures over identical frozen payloads, lineage-matched prompts and sampling, differing only in delivery architecture. SYNTHESIS feeds full record sets into the planner's context and answers follow-ups in-head; BYPASS, the deployed system, keeps records in session state, translates follow-ups into arguments for a deterministic filter, and delivers rows over a typed side channel. Across 24 dialogues (339 scored turns per condition), BYPASS scores 92.3% of turns fully correct, SYNTHESIS 45.7% (paired gap +46.6pp [+35.7, +57.1]). Varying delivered-table size by capture date, SYNTHESIS collapses from near-perfect at 10 rows or fewer to 8% or less beyond about 74 rows. On a content-controlled prefix ladder the collapse threshold orders by model capability, from under 10 rows (GPT-4o-mini) to about 198 or more (Gemini 2.5 Pro), while BYPASS stays size-flat for all four models. The collapse is expensive: beyond 100 rows, where almost no SYNTHESIS answer is correct, each correct one costs roughly 200x BYPASS's flat \$0.012. Practitioners converged on typed side-channel delivery for rendering, not correctness; we show it was, unknowingly, also a correctness decision.

title: A Supabase row-level security checklist for multi-role apps (from a 163-policy production schema)
description:
I run a production app on Supabase with eight user roles: field reps, team leads, business leads, key account managers, admins, directors, accounts and logistics. Each sees a different slice of the same tables. The schema has 64 tables and 163 row-level security policies, and the client is never trusted with any of it.

This is the checklist I now apply to every table and function. It's ordered by how badly things break if you skip it.

1. RLS on every table. No exceptions, no "internal" tables 

alter table public.vehicle_inspections enable row level security;

A table without RLS is readable by any signed-in user through the auto-generated API. "Nobody queries that table from the app" doesn't matter, because anybody can call the API directly.

Add a check to your migrations or CI that fails if any table in public has RLS disabled:

select tablename from pg_tables
where schemaname = 'public' and not rowsecurity;
-- must return zero rows

2. Policies target authenticated. Nothing is granted to anon

If your app has no public pages, anon should have no policies at all. Write policies to authenticated explicitly rather than relying on the default public role, which includes anon.

Also turn off public sign-ups in Supabase Auth if accounts are created by admins. Otherwise anyone can create an authenticated user and inherit every policy written for "any signed-in user."

3. Role checks live in the policy, not in the app 

create policy "accounts validate payments"
on public.payments for update to authenticated
using (
  exists (select 1 from public.users u
          where u.id = auth.uid() and u.role in ('ACCOUNTS','ADMIN'))
);

Hiding the "Validate" button from field reps is good UX. It isn't security. The policy is.

4. Users must not be able to change their own scope

This is the most common hole I see. If your policies read users.role or users.region_label, and users can update their own row, a rep can promote themselves to director with one API call.

Lock it down with column grants:

revoke update on public.users from authenticated;
grant update (full_name, phone) on public.users to authenticated;

Then role and scope changes go through an admin-only function.

5. SECURITY DEFINER functions do their own authorisation

Definer functions run with the owner's rights and bypass RLS. That's why you use them (aggregates across regions, dashboards), and also why they're dangerous.

create or replace function public.region_summary(p_region text)
returns table (...)
language plpgsql
security definer
set search_path = public          -- stops search_path hijacking
as $$
begin
  if not exists (select 1 from users where id = auth.uid()
                 and role in ('TL','BL','ADMIN','DIRECTOR')) then
    raise exception 'not allowed';
  end if;
  ...
end $$;

Two rules apply every time: pin search_path, and check the caller's role inside the function body.

6. Keep secrets out of tables users can read

Our push-notification webhook shares a secret with an Edge Function. It sits in an app_settings table, but the policy for that table excludes the secret row from normal users. Assume any row a user can select will eventually be selected.

7. Never put the service_role key in the client

That one key bypasses every policy above. It belongs in Edge Function secrets and nowhere else: not in .env files that ship with the app, not in a config file "just for testing."

8. Test permissions as each role, in SQL, on every change

The checklist only works if it stays true. I keep a SQL test file that impersonates each role and tries the forbidden things:

-- as a field rep, try to read another region's payments
set local role authenticated;
set local request.jwt.claims = '{"sub": "<rep-uuid>"}';
select count(*) from payments where region_label <> 'North';
-- expect 0

A script spins up a temporary Postgres, applies the full schema, runs a functional smoke test and the security suite (33 checks today), and prints ALL SECURITY CHECKS PASSED. Any migration that adds a permission rule adds a test in the same commit.

The short version

Check Why
RLS enabled on every table Missing RLS = readable by any signed-in user
Policies to authenticated, nothing to anon Default role includes anonymous users
Public sign-ups off when admins create accounts Otherwise anyone becomes authenticated
Role checks inside policies UI hiding is cosmetic
Column grants on users Stops self-promotion
Definer functions pin search_path and check role They bypass RLS
Secrets excluded from readable rows Readable means read
service_role never in the client It bypasses everything
SQL tests per role, every change Permissions decay silently

This schema is part of Beatplan field sales app, a field sales system I now license as full source code. Buyers get the migrations, all 163 policies and the security test suite, so they can verify everything above themselves before they trust it with their team's data.

title: Designing search for 56,000 games: what actually helps players find a game
description:
Running a portal with 56,000 browser games sounds like a search problem, and it is, but not the kind most search advice covers. Players do not arrive with a precise query. They arrive with a mood, ten free minutes, and a vague idea like something relaxing or something with cars. Search that only matches exact titles fails them, because they do not know the titles yet.

The first lesson was that categories matter more than keywords. A player who clicks puzzle games is not searching, they are browsing with intent, and the category page is the search result. We rebuilt category pages to load instantly, show the most played games first, and keep the filters visible, so a player can narrow from puzzle to word puzzle to crossword in two clicks without typing anything.

The second lesson was about spelling and synonyms. Players type car game, cars, racing, and driving for the same thing, and a search that treats those as different queries returns different results for the same intent. We added a small synonym map for the most common terms, built from our own search logs, not from a generic thesaurus. It is boring work and it made the biggest difference: the share of searches that returned zero useful results fell sharply once synonyms were handled.

The third lesson was speed over cleverness. A search box that suggests results as you type feels modern, but on a low-end phone on a slow connection it feels broken, because suggestions arrive after the player has already pressed enter. We made search server-rendered and fast first, then added suggestions only where they did not slow the first result. Players forgive a plain search box. They do not forgive a slow one.

The fourth lesson was that recency is a trap. Sorting by newest fills the page with games nobody has played, while sorting by most played fills it with the same ten games forever. We settled on a blend: proven games at the top, a rotating set of less-played games below, so discovery keeps happening without the page turning into a graveyard of untested titles.

None of this required machine learning or a search vendor. It required watching real searches, fixing the top twenty failed queries, and repeating that every month. The full catalogue is at GameZiko, where you can play free browser games with no download and no sign-up, and the search box is the simplest thing on the page, which is exactly how it should be.
