title: Your Code Has Bugs You Haven't Met Yet: A Friendly Deep Dive into SAST with SonarQube
description:
"An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure."
— Benjamin Franklin

The bug that waited six months

Let me tell you about a Friday night that went sideways.

A team I know shipped a tiny feature: a search box on an internal admin dashboard. Two lines of code built a SQL query by gluing the user's input straight into a string. It passed code review. It passed QA. It worked perfectly for six months.

Then someone typed ' OR '1'='1 into that box. Every customer record came back in one page.

Here's the painful part: nobody was careless. The reviewer was looking at business logic, not string concatenation. QA was testing whether search worked, not whether it could be abused. The bug wasn't hidden. It was sitting in plain sight, in a pull request, waiting.

A tool that reads code for exactly this kind of mistake would have flagged it in seconds, before the merge button was ever clicked.

That tool category has a name: SAST. And one of the most popular ways to do it is SonarQube.

If the pattern feels familiar, it should. Injection is still a headline category: it sits at #5 in the OWASP Top 10:2025 (it was #3 in 2021). It dropped because the industry got better at it, not because it went away.

The post at a glance

  • Reading time: about 14 minutes
  • Hands-on time: about 10 minutes, with Docker
  • You will learn: what SAST is, how taint analysis works, how SonarQube is built, how to gate pull requests, and how to keep a team from muting the tool
  • You need: Docker, a project with some code, and a coffee

Here's the road map:

  • What SAST actually is (and what it isn't)
  • How a machine can "read" your code and spot a vulnerability
  • What SonarQube does, and how its pieces fit together
  • Running it locally with Docker in about ten minutes
  • Wiring it into CI so bad code can't sneak into main
  • The honest stuff: false positives, noisy dashboards, and how to get your team to actually care

Grab a coffee. Let's go.

So what is SAST, really?

SAST (Static Application Security Testing) reads your source code without running it, and looks for patterns that lead to security holes.

Think of it like a spell-checker, but for danger. A spell-checker doesn't need you to say the sentence out loud to know "recieve" is wrong. SAST doesn't need your app to run to know that user input is flowing straight into a SQL query.

The word that matters most is static. The code is just text on disk. No server, no database, no test data. That's what makes SAST so useful: it can run the moment you write a line, long before anything is deployed.

Where SAST fits among its cousins

You'll hear a pile of acronyms in AppSec conversations. Here's the cheat sheet:

Approach What it looks at When it runs Great at catching Blind spots
SAST (static) Your source code While coding, on every PR Injection, hardcoded secrets, unsafe APIs, crypto misuse Runtime config, server setup, business logic
DAST (dynamic) Your running app, from outside Against staging or test environments Misconfigured headers, auth issues, real exploitable endpoints Can't point to the exact line of code
SCA (composition) Your dependencies (npm, Maven, pip) On every build Known CVEs in third-party libraries Bugs in your code
IAST (interactive) The app from inside, while tests run During QA and integration tests Confirmed, real-path vulnerabilities Only sees code paths your tests exercise

None of these replaces the others. But if you can only start with one, SAST gives you the best bang for the buck. It's cheap, fast, and it talks to developers in their own language: file name, line number, here's why, here's the fix.

The "shift left" argument

You've probably heard "shift left." It just means: find problems earlier in the timeline, where they're cheaper to fix.

A vulnerability caught in your editor costs you thirty seconds. The same vulnerability caught in a penetration test costs a ticket, a context switch, a re-review and a redeploy. Caught in production by an attacker? That's an incident report, a lawyer, and possibly a news headline.

The shape is the point: effort multiplies at every stage. The numbers are an illustrative model, not measured data.

SAST is the most "left" security check you can run. It lives right next to your code.

How does a tool "read" code?

A SAST engine turns your code into a structured model, then asks questions about how data moves through it. It's less magic than it sounds. Let's peel it open, one layer at a time.

Step 1: From text to a tree

To you, code is text. To a SAST tool, text is useless until it's parsed into an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST): a tree where every node is a meaningful piece, like a function call, a variable, or a string.

Take this tiny snippet, shown in Python and Node.js:

name = request.args.get("name")
sql = f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{name}'"
cursor.execute(sql)

const name = req.query.name;
const sql = `SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '${name}'`;
db.query(sql);

The tool no longer sees characters. It sees: a variable name assigned from request.args.get (or req.query), a string built by interpolation, and a call to execute (or query). Now it can reason.

Step 2: Simple rules (pattern matching)

The easiest checks just look at the tree's shape. "Is someone calling MD5 for password hashing?" "Is there a hardcoded string that looks like an AWS key?" "Is this catch block empty?"

These are fast and precise, but they only see one spot at a time.

Step 3: Following the data (taint analysis)

This is where SAST gets clever. Taint analysis tracks untrusted data as it travels through your program. It uses three ideas:

  • Source: where untrusted data enters. Think HTTP parameters, headers, file uploads, or message queues.
  • Sink: a dangerous place for that data to land. Think SQL queries, shell commands, file paths, or HTML output.
  • Sanitizer: something that makes the data safe on the way. Think parameterized queries, escaping, or strict validation.

The rule is simple: if tainted data reaches a sink without passing through a sanitizer, raise the alarm.

If the data passes a sanitizer, nothing is reported; if it reaches the sink untouched, you get a vulnerability.

In our snippet, request.args.get("name") (or req.query.name) is the source, cursor.execute(sql) (or db.query(sql)) is the sink, and nothing cleans the data in between. That's SQL injection, flagged before the code ever runs. And the real power is that the source and sink can live in different files, three function calls apart. A human reviewer looking at one diff would never connect them. The engine does.

The fix the tool will nudge you toward 

name = request.args.get("name")
sql = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?"
cursor.execute(sql, (name,))
rows = cursor.fetchall()

const name = req.query.name;
const sql = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = $1";
const { rows } = await db.query(sql, [name]);

The parameterized query acts as the sanitizer. The data can still be anything, but it can no longer change the shape of the SQL.

The placeholder depends on your driver: ? for sqlite3 and mysql2, %s for psycopg2, $1 for node-postgres. The idea is identical: the value travels separately from the query text.

A quick reality check

Static analysis has a famous trade-off. Being exhaustive means more false positives (alarms that aren't real). Being conservative means more false negatives (real bugs it misses). Every tool picks a spot on that dial. We'll come back to how to live with this later.

"Debugging is twice as hard as writing the code in the first place."
— Brian Kernighan, The Elements of Programming Style

Meet SonarQube

SonarQube is a code quality and security platform from SonarSource that runs SAST (and much more) on every branch and pull request, and turns the results into a simple pass/fail signal. It's been around since 2007, and it's probably the tool your company's platform team has already heard of.

What makes it different from a pure security scanner is its scope. SonarQube cares about the whole health of your code: security vulnerabilities, yes, but also reliability bugs, maintainability problems, duplication and test coverage. Security people love it for the first part. Developers tend to love it for the rest.

The family, untangled

SonarSource renamed things in 2024–2025, so blog posts online can be confusing. Here's today's lineup:

Product What it is Who it's for
SonarQube for IDE (formerly SonarLint) A free plugin for VS Code, IntelliJ, Visual Studio and Eclipse Every developer, catching issues as they type
SonarQube Community Build (formerly Community Edition) Free, open-source, self-hosted; released on a regular cadence Learning, small teams, single-branch analysis
SonarQube Server (Developer, Enterprise, Data Center editions) Commercial, self-hosted; branch and PR analysis, deeper taint analysis Teams who need PR decoration and full security coverage
SonarQube Cloud (formerly SonarCloud) The SaaS version, hosted by Sonar Teams who don't want to run a server; has a free tier

Two things worth knowing before you choose:

  • Server versions now use calendar numbering, like 2025.1. Some releases are marked LTA (Long-Term Active), which is what you want for a stable production install.
  • The free Community Build analyzes one branch and doesn't decorate pull requests. The heavier security analysis, including cross-file taint tracking, lives in the commercial editions and SonarQube Cloud. For learning and for this tutorial, Community Build is perfect.

The four ideas you need to know

Once you understand these, the whole SonarQube UI makes sense:

  1. Rules. A single check, like "SQL queries should not be built from user input." SonarQube ships with thousands of them across 30+ languages.
  2. Quality Profiles. A named set of rules per language. The default is called "Sonar way", and it's a sensible starting point. You can copy it and tune it.
  3. Quality Gates. The pass/fail verdict. A gate is a set of conditions, like "no new vulnerabilities" and "coverage on new code is at least 80%." If any condition fails, the gate fails, and your pipeline can stop the merge.
  4. New Code. SonarQube's secret weapon. Instead of shouting about ten years of legacy debt, it focuses on code you changed recently. More on this in a moment.

How the pieces talk to each other

The architecture is simpler than it looks. The scanner runs where your code is (your laptop or a CI runner). It does the analysis and uploads a report. The server processes that report, stores results in a database, and shows them in the web UI.

The important bit: your source code never has to leave your CI runner. Only the analysis report travels to the server.

Hands-on: your first scan in about ten minutes

You need Docker and a project with some code in it. That's it. We'll run the free Community Build locally and scan a deliberately vulnerable snippet.

1. Start the server 

docker run -d --name sonarqube \
  -p 9000:9000 \
  sonarqube:community

Give it a minute or two to boot (it starts an Elasticsearch instance inside, so it's not instant). Then open http://localhost:9000 and log in with admin / admin. It'll ask you to change the password right away.

Heads up: this quick-start uses an embedded H2 database. It's fine for a demo, but never use it in production. For a real install, point SonarQube at PostgreSQL with a docker-compose.yml. On Linux you may also need sysctl -w vm.max_map_count=524288 for Elasticsearch to start.

2. Create a project and a token

In the UI:

  1. Click Create Project → Local project.
  2. Give it a key, for example my-first-scan.
  3. For the baseline, choose Previous version as the definition of "new code."
  4. Choose Locally as the analysis method and generate a token. Copy it somewhere safe; you'll see it only once.

3. Add some deliberately bad code

Let's give the scanner something to find. Save this as app.py in an empty folder:

import sqlite3
import hashlib
from flask import Flask, request

app = Flask(__name__)
AWS_SECRET = "AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE"   # hardcoded credential

@app.route("/user")
def get_user():
    name = request.args.get("name")                # source
    conn = sqlite3.connect("app.db")
    query = f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{name}'"
    return str(conn.execute(query).fetchall())     # sink

def hash_password(pw):
    return hashlib.md5(pw.encode()).hexdigest()   # weak hashing

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(debug=True)                            # debug in prod

Four problems, hiding in about twenty lines. Let's see how many get caught.

4. Run the scanner

The easiest way is the scanner's own Docker image, so you don't install anything:

docker run --rm \
  --network host \
  -e SONAR_HOST_URL="http://localhost:9000" \
  -e SONAR_TOKEN="<your-token>" \
  -v "$(pwd):/usr/src" \
  sonarsource/sonar-scanner-cli \
  -Dsonar.projectKey=my-first-scan

On macOS or Windows, swap localhost for host.docker.internal and drop --network host.

Projects you'll scan again and again deserve a config file. Drop a sonar-project.properties at the root:

sonar.projectKey=my-first-scan
sonar.projectName=My First Scan
sonar.sources=.
sonar.exclusions=**/tests/**,**/node_modules/**
sonar.python.version=3.12

Python projects use the scanner CLI or the Docker image above, with the sonar-project.properties file you just wrote. There's no build plugin to add, so the same command works on your laptop and in CI.

JavaScript and TypeScript projects can skip Docker and run the npm scanner directly, with no install step:

npx @sonar/scan   -Dsonar.host.url=http://localhost:9000   -Dsonar.token=<your-token>   -Dsonar.projectKey=my-first-scan

Without -Dsonar.projectKey, it takes the key from the name field in package.json.

5. Look at the dashboard

Refresh the project page. Expect the hardcoded secret, the weak MD5 hash and the Flask debug mode to show up, either as issues or as Security Hotspots depending on the rule and your version.

The SQL injection is the interesting one. It needs cross-function taint analysis, which lives in the commercial editions. On Community Build it may not be reported at all. That's not a bug in your test; it's the edition boundary, and it's a good reason to know what your tier can and can't see. The next section explains the hotspot idea.

Reading the report without panicking

Your first dashboard will probably show hundreds of issues. That's normal, and you don't have to fix them all. Let's decode what you're looking at.

Issue types, in human terms

SonarQube sorts findings by which quality of your software they hurt:

What you see What it means Example What to do
Vulnerability (Security) The tool is confident this is exploitable SQL built from request data, reaching execute() Fix it. Usually before merging.
Security Hotspot Security-sensitive code that needs a human to judge Using random(), a permissive CORS setting, a regex that could be slow Review it and mark it Safe or Fix
Bug (Reliability) Code that will likely misbehave Null dereference, unclosed resource, always-true condition Fix it; these become production incidents
Code Smell (Maintainability) Code that works but is hard to change 200-line function, duplicated blocks, deep nesting Fix when you touch that code

Each issue also carries a severity (Blocker, High, Medium, Low, Info) and a Clean Code attribute explaining why it matters. Click any issue and you'll get the exact line, a description of the risk, and usually a compliant code example. This is where developers actually learn something.

Not sure what to do with a finding? Follow the flow:

Every finding ends in one of three outcomes: fix it, justify it, or defer it on purpose.

Hotspots are not vulnerabilities

This trips up nearly everyone. A Vulnerability is SonarQube saying: "This is a problem." A Hotspot is SonarQube saying: "This could be a problem, and only you know the context."

Using a non-cryptographic random number is fine for shuffling a playlist. It's a disaster for generating a password reset token. The tool can't know which one you're doing, so it asks. Your job is to review hotspots, not ignore them.

The ratings

The dashboard grades Security, Reliability and Maintainability from A (best) to E. A single unresolved critical vulnerability can drag your Security rating to D or E. That's intentional: one real hole matters more than a thousand smells.

"Clean as You Code": the idea that saves your sanity

Imagine scanning a ten-year-old codebase for the first time. 4,000 issues. Your team will look at that number, sigh, and close the tab forever.

SonarQube's answer is a philosophy called Clean as You Code:

Don't try to fix the past. Just make sure every new change is clean.

It's the Boy Scout rule in a CI pipeline:

"Leave the campground cleaner than you found it."
— The Boy Scout rule, popularized in Clean Code by Robert C. Martin

The default Quality Gate, "Sonar way", only judges new code: the lines added or changed since your baseline. It checks roughly that new code has:

  • 0 new issues
  • 100% of new Security Hotspots reviewed
  • At least 80% test coverage
  • At most 3% duplication

The magic is that legacy code gets cleaner over time anyway, because every file you touch for a new feature gets held to the new standard. No "cleanup sprint" required. Old debt fades, new debt never arrives.

Putting it in your pipeline

A scan you run by hand is a scan you'll forget. The real value comes when every pull request is scanned automatically and the Quality Gate can block the merge.

Here's the flow we're building. A developer opens a PR, CI runs tests and the scanner, SonarQube judges the new code, and the result comes back as a status check on the PR.

The loop is the point: a red gate doesn't end the conversation, it just sends the change back for one more push.

GitHub Actions example

First, add two repository secrets under Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions:

  • SONAR_TOKEN: a token generated in SonarQube (use a project analysis token, not your admin token)
  • SONAR_HOST_URL: your server's URL, like https://sonar.yourcompany.com

Then create .github/workflows/sonarqube.yml:

Python:

name: SonarQube Analysis

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize, reopened]

jobs:
  sonarqube:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0   # full history = accurate "new code" and blame data

      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"

      - name: Run tests with coverage
        run: |
          pip install -r requirements.txt pytest pytest-cov
          pytest --cov=. --cov-report=xml

      - name: SonarQube Scan
        uses: SonarSource/sonarqube-scan-action@v5
        env:
          SONAR_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.SONAR_TOKEN }}
          SONAR_HOST_URL: ${{ secrets.SONAR_HOST_URL }}
        with:
          args: >
            -Dsonar.python.coverage.reportPaths=coverage.xml
            -Dsonar.qualitygate.wait=true

JavaScript (Node.js):

name: SonarQube Analysis

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize, reopened]

jobs:
  sonarqube:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0   # full history = accurate "new code" and blame data

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22

      - name: Run tests with coverage
        run: |
          npm ci
          npx jest --coverage --coverageReporters=lcov

      - name: SonarQube Scan
        uses: SonarSource/sonarqube-scan-action@v5
        env:
          SONAR_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.SONAR_TOKEN }}
          SONAR_HOST_URL: ${{ secrets.SONAR_HOST_URL }}
        with:
          args: >
            -Dsonar.javascript.lcov.reportPaths=coverage/lcov.info
            -Dsonar.qualitygate.wait=true

A few lines deserve a closer look:

  • fetch-depth: 0 is the most-forgotten line in every SonarQube setup. Without the full Git history, SonarQube can't tell which lines are new, and "Clean as You Code" quietly breaks.
  • sonar.qualitygate.wait=true makes the job wait for SonarQube's verdict and fail if the gate fails. That red X is what stops the merge.
  • Coverage is generated by your tests, not by SonarQube. SonarQube only reads the report. No report, no coverage number.
  • The Python property reads Cobertura XML, which pytest-cov writes as coverage.xml. The JavaScript property reads LCOV, which Jest writes to coverage/lcov.info.

The @v5 above is an example. Newer major versions of the action exist, so check the releases page, pin to a release you've verified, and update it on purpose, not by accident.

Making the gate actually block merges

The workflow failing isn't enough on its own. Go to Settings → Branches → Branch protection rules for main, enable Require status checks to pass, and select the SonarQube job. Now a failed Quality Gate physically blocks the merge button.

On SonarQube Server Developer Edition and above, or SonarQube Cloud, you also get PR decoration: a comment on the pull request summarizing new issues, with links straight to the problem lines. Developers see the feedback where they already are, which matters more than you'd think.

Using GitLab, Jenkins or Azure DevOps?

Same idea, different syntax. SonarQube has official integrations for GitLab CI, Azure Pipelines, Bitbucket Pipelines and Jenkins (via the SonarQube Scanner plugin plus a waitForQualityGate step). The three essentials stay identical: full Git history, a coverage report, and waiting for the gate.

The honest part: false positives, noise, and people

The hardest part of SAST is not installing the tool. It's getting a team to trust it. A scanner that cries wolf gets muted. Here's how to avoid that fate.

Dealing with false positives

You will see findings that aren't real problems. When that happens, resist the urge to silence everything. Instead:

  • Mark it in the UI, not in code. In SonarQube, set the issue to False Positive or Accepted and leave a short comment explaining why. Future you, and your auditor, will thank you.
  • Use // NOSONAR sparingly. It suppresses every issue on that line, silently, forever. It's the duct tape of static analysis. Some teams ban it outright in code review.
  • Tune the Quality Profile if one rule is consistently wrong for your codebase. Copy "Sonar way", deactivate that rule, and document the decision. Never edit the built-in profile directly.
  • Exclude what isn't yours. Generated code, vendored libraries, migrations and test fixtures inflate the noise. Use sonar.exclusions and sonar.test.exclusions.

Common mistakes I see over and over

  1. Shallow clones in CI. No full history means broken "new code" detection. (Yes, again. It's that common.)
  2. Scanning before tests. Coverage shows 0% and the gate fails for the wrong reason.
  3. Gating on overall code instead of new code. The gate fails on day one for legacy reasons, and the team learns to ignore red.
  4. One shared admin token in every pipeline. Use project-scoped analysis tokens and rotate them.
  5. Treating SonarQube as the whole security program. It doesn't scan your dependencies for known CVEs the way a dedicated SCA tool does (newer commercial editions add SCA as an option), and it never sees your runtime config. Pair it with SCA, secrets scanning and DAST.
  6. Running H2 in production. It's for demos only. Use PostgreSQL.

Rolling it out to a real team

The rollout plan that works tends to look like this:

Four steps, and the gate only turns on in week 3, after people have had time to get curious.

  1. Week 1, observe. Turn on scanning in CI, but don't block anything. Let people look at the dashboard and get curious.
  2. Week 2, install the IDE plugin. Get every developer on SonarQube for IDE in connected mode, so their editor uses the same rules as the server. Catching issues while typing is far less annoying than catching them in CI.
  3. Week 3, enable the gate on new code only. Use "Sonar way" as-is. Announce it, explain Clean as You Code, and answer questions.
  4. Ongoing, review together. Spend fifteen minutes in a retro now and then looking at hotspots and false positives. Tune the profile as a team.

The pattern underneath: make the tool a teammate, not a cop. Developers adopt tools that make them better at their job. They route around tools that only make them slower.

Wrapping up

Remember that search box from the start? With SonarQube in the pipeline, that PR would have come back red in a few minutes, with the exact line and a fix example attached. No incident, no Friday night, no awkward meeting.

That's the whole promise of SAST: catch the boring, predictable, expensive mistakes while they're still cheap. Not because developers are careless, but because humans are bad at spotting the same pattern for the thousandth time, and machines are great at it.

"We are what we repeatedly do. Excellence, then, is not an act, but a habit."
— Will Durant, summarizing Aristotle

Your quick-start checklist

  • [ ] Run SonarQube Community Build locally with Docker
  • [ ] Scan one real project and skim the dashboard
  • [ ] Install SonarQube for IDE in your editor
  • [ ] Add the scanner to CI with fetch-depth: 0 and a coverage report
  • [ ] Turn on sonar.qualitygate.wait=true
  • [ ] Protect main so a failed gate blocks the merge
  • [ ] Gate on new code only, with "Sonar way"
  • [ ] Review hotspots; mark false positives with a reason
  • [ ] Pair it with dependency scanning (SCA) and secrets scanning

Over to you

Start small. Scan one repo this week. You'll almost certainly find something that makes you go "huh, how long has that been there?"

If this helped, drop a ❤️ or a 🦄, and tell me in the comments: what's the weirdest thing a static analysis tool has ever caught in your code? I read every reply.

Sources

  • SonarQube downloads and editions
  • Official SonarQube Docker image
  • SonarQube release announcements
  • SonarQube security-related rules
  • sonarqube-scan-action releases
  • OWASP Top 10:2025 introduction

title: Tell HN: Gemini trains on chat history, even for subscribers (personal accounts)
description:
If you have a personal Google AI subscription, all your saved chat history in Gemini can be used for training and there is no way to opt out unless you turn off chat history or use temporary chat sessions. These chat transcripts may even be read by human reviewers. Although Google claims to disconnect them from your account when human-reviewed, they explicitly warn not to enter confidential information.

https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/16836988

“[Gemini app activity] is used to improve Google services for everyone, including by training generative AI models, if your Keep Activity setting is on.“

https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/13594961?hl=en#human_review

“A subset of chats are reviewed by human reviewers”

https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/13594961?hl=en#pn_retain_data

“Chats reviewed by human reviewers [...] are not deleted when you delete your activity. Instead, they are retained for up to three years.”

https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/13594961?hl=en#pn_data_usage

“Please don’t enter confidential information that you wouldn’t want a reviewer to see or Google to use to improve our services, including machine-learning technologies.”

To disable their training on your chat sessions, you need to turn off “Keep Activity” in Gemini’s settings. Turning that off means you’ll lose any chat sessions after 72 hours.

I learned this too late, thinking that having a paid subscription = not being turned into the product. Apparently paying is not enough.

title: AlloyDB Omni Adds a Read-Only Web UI for Cluster Observability
description:
TL;DR

  • AlloyDB Omni is a downloadable, self-managed edition of AlloyDB that keeps full PostgreSQL compatibility and runs on infrastructure a company operates itself.
  • Google announced general availability of a web UI for AlloyDB Omni, covering Red Hat RPM installs and container deployments.
  • The console is read-only by design: it shows cluster health, CPU, memory and disk I/O charts fed by Prometheus, and slow statements ranked by latency, in its read-only interface.
  • The prerequisites are operational: a Prometheus server for the charts, an alloydbui role holding pg_monitor on each cluster, and the interface reachable on port 9080.
  • Coverage has holes worth knowing before deployment: standalone container installations lose the chart panels, and Columnar Store views require table privileges.
  • The console records configuration drift for remediation through the provisioning workflow. Google explicitly identifies the provisioning workflows used for corrections: Kubernetes CRDs or GitOps manifests, Ansible playbooks, or alloydbctl.

The Google Cloud blog published Introducing the AlloyDB Omni web UI for easier cluster observability, signed by Omkar Deshmukh and Josh Choinsky. Google describes the operational problem directly: command-line tools make cluster health harder to see and issues harder to diagnose quickly.

Google's framing of the problem is that managing PostgreSQL across on-premises, edge and multi-cloud environments "often forces administrators to rely on command-line tools, making it hard to see cluster health and quickly diagnose issues." The console is the answer it shipped: a production-ready, read-only view of hardware telemetry, query performance and configuration flags, available for Red Hat RPM installations and for containers.

What the console shows in its read-only interface

The cluster overview is the anchor. Connection profiles let an administrator keep local, staging and production targets side by side and switch between saved profiles. Under that, the panels are the operational ones: CPU use, memory allocation, storage I/O and active connection trends, plus a ranked list of statements by total latency and call frequency.

That ranking gives a DBA a direct view of the statements with the highest total latency. Slow queries sort themselves to the top, so an unindexed statement shows up as a latency row. The interface runs its own limited account for this, and the documentation names it: an alloydbui role granted pg_monitor on each cluster.

The read-only constraint is the design decision

A console with read access to a production database requires a product review covering data exposure and diagnostic permissions. Granting change authority adds write operations and configuration changes to that review. Google kept the first: the interface operates strictly in read-only mode, which means a diagnostic session cannot execute write commands or alter database configuration.

The value of that boundary is administrative. The read-only boundary gives an access review a concise scope covering diagnostic permissions and the exclusion of write commands and configuration changes. An administrator account requires a review of its write and configuration permissions. The same logic explains why the provisioning workflow keeps its authority: Google points at Kubernetes custom resources and GitOps manifests, Ansible playbooks and alloydbctl as the places where changes are made.

Charts come from Prometheus, and the role comes from you

The panels do not generate their own telemetry. To see time-series charts for CPU, memory and disk I/O, the environment needs a Prometheus server scraping the exporter, and the AlloyDB Omni Kubernetes operator runs a monitoring agent that exposes Prometheus-compatible metrics on port 9187. The interface itself is reached on port 9080.

Two consequences follow, and both are ordinary for teams that already run self-managed databases. First, the console adds a dependency on a service you operate, so a broken Prometheus shows up as empty charts, which is the honest failure. Second, the role has to be created per cluster with the right grants, and the documentation is specific about what each view needs: at least one permission on a table to see its Columnar Store data, SELECT on tables for the Vector Columns section, and SELECT on pg_stat_ann_indexes for vector index data.

The narrow permission set is the interesting half of the design. A monitoring account limited to pg_monitor and a handful of catalog views gives a third-party dashboard a narrow privilege scope, documented as a single line in an access review.

Anyone doing custom web and mobile development against Postgres will recognise the drift problem the flag view addresses: settings that differ between staging and production and become visible in a central, queryable catalogue.

Columnar engine and vector index coverage

AlloyDB Omni ships a columnar engine that keeps frequently accessed data in memory to accelerate analytical queries. The console tracks its memory footprint against the hardware limit and shows which tables and columns are actually resident, giving the team direct evidence of how the acceleration feature is operating.

The same panel family gives direct visibility into vector search workflows and AI model integrations, while the documentation lists vector index data and vector column data.

Drift detection stops before remediation

The flag audit is a catalogue of active database parameters, filtered so that settings differing from the engine defaults stand out. Read that as a drift detector: it answers what changed, and it leaves the correction to the pipeline that owns configuration.

For an estate spread over bare metal, containers and Kubernetes, that split is the correct one, and it also sets the limit of what the console can promise. A team needs a GitOps or Ansible path for database parameters to remediate the drift exposed by the console. The console makes the gap visible and leaves the remediation work to the team.

That is the same discipline monitoring that explains an incident keeps pushing toward: an explanatory view connected to the workflow that performs remediation.

What to check before installing it

Start with the deployment type, because the support matrix is not uniform. On standalone container installations the telemetry charts and the system insights panels are unavailable, since the containerized monitoring agent does not exist for that shape; the catalog views and the flag audit still work. Kubernetes, Red Hat RPM and the RPM orchestrator get the full set.

Then decide who holds the credentials. The interface stores connection profiles in a directory under the home account that starts it, encrypted with a 256-bit AES key protected by the ALLOYDB_OMNI_UI_KEYSTORE environment variable at startup. The team should manage that keystore as a secret with its existing secrets tooling.

Finally, treat the read-only boundary as a control to verify, with a test account, on a cluster where a mistake is cheap. A console that cannot write is a genuine improvement in day-to-day operations, and it earns that position only once someone has tried to make it write.

Originally published on the Netics blog.

title: JasperReports 7.1.1 PDFs: Fonts, Extra JARs and PDF/UA Tags
description:
An HTML timesheet sent through a JasperReports text field came out as nine plain lines of 10-point Helvetica down the left margin. That run used JasperReports Library 7.1.1 (Maven Central, 1 November 2026, GNU LGPL v3), the Java engine that compiles JRXML band designs, fills them and writes PDF among other outputs. What follows is a checklist of what tripped up a Java 17 build on its way to a PDF, with every item reproduced in a run or traced to the changelog and the advisory databases.

We work at Iron Software, and the end of this article covers our library, IronPDF.

What an HTML Timesheet Looks Like in a JasperReports Text Field

HTML enters only as the content of a text element flagged markup="html", where a Swing JEditorPane parses it, per the markup sample in the vendor's docs. The test template is one such field, fed a timesheet the way a web app would serve it, <style> block and all.

import net.sf.jasperreports.engine.JREmptyDataSource;
import net.sf.jasperreports.engine.JRException;
import net.sf.jasperreports.engine.JasperCompileManager;
import net.sf.jasperreports.engine.JasperExportManager;
import net.sf.jasperreports.engine.JasperFillManager;
import net.sf.jasperreports.engine.JasperPrint;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

public class TimesheetMarkupReport {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws JRException {
        // A stylesheet rule, a CSS grid and a table, as a web app would serve the timesheet.
        String html = "<style>.over { color: #c00; font-weight: bold }</style>"
                + "<h2>Timesheet, week 42</h2>"
                + "<div style='display:grid;grid-template-columns:1fr 1fr'><div>A. Novak</div><div>R. Osei</div></div>"
                + "<table border='1'><tr><th>Engineer</th><th>Hours</th></tr>"
                + "<tr><td>A. Novak</td><td>38.5</td></tr>"
                + "<tr><td>R. Osei</td><td class='over'>44.0</td></tr></table>";

        Map<String, Object> parameters = new HashMap<>();
        parameters.put("Html", html);

        // html-markup.jrxml holds one text field with markup="html" that prints the Html parameter.
        JasperPrint print = JasperFillManager.fillReport(
                JasperCompileManager.compileReport("html-markup.jrxml"), parameters, new JREmptyDataSource());
        JasperExportManager.exportReportToPdfFile(print, "timesheet-markup.pdf");
    }
}

Read with pypdf, the content stream of the 1,147-byte timesheet-markup.pdf holds nine text runs at x = 40, each about 12.58 points below the last and all in 10-point Helvetica, so the h2 is the size of a table cell. A. Novak and R. Osei, meant to sit side by side in the grid, follow each other down the page. Engineer, Hours and the four cell values do the same with no border drawn around them, and 44.0 prints in black because the .over class never took effect. There is not a single rectangle or line operator on the page.

Script never runs here, and the 7.0.2 release deleted the old Chrome add-on for JavaScript visualizations. For HTML-first teams, the vendor's route is a rebuild of each layout in Jaspersoft Studio.

Fonts That Stop a Report at Fill Time

Point a style at a family the JVM has never seen, such as fontName="Report Serif", and JasperFillManager throws JRFontNotFoundException before any page exists. The trace passes through TextMeasurer, since line breaking needs real glyph widths. According to the exception's Javadoc, refusing to guess is deliberate, because a stand-in font shifts the metrics and may clip text.

Leaving the font unset has a cost too. An invoice template that marks its title bold="true" and names no font exported a file with one font, Helvetica, and drew that title in the regular weight. The recommended route for bold faces and custom families is a font extension, registered in a properties file at the classpath root, though a pdfFontName attribute on each element also printed bold in a test run.

net.sf.jasperreports.extension.registry.factory.simple.font.families=net.sf.jasperreports.engine.fonts.SimpleFontExtensionsRegistryFactory
net.sf.jasperreports.extension.simple.font.families.reportserif=fonts/reportserif/fonts.xml

Add a fonts.xml mapping the family to DejaVu Serif regular and bold, and the export embeds both as subsets. A house typeface means maintaining that bundle alongside the templates.

Encryption, PDF Export and the Extra JARs They Need

Since 7.0.0 the PDF writer lives in jasperreports-pdf, and leaving it out produced a JRRuntimeException naming that artifact. The writer runs on 1.3.43.jaspersoft.2, a Jaspersoft fork of OpenPDF hosted in a Jaspersoft repository and absent from Central, so a Central-only mirror cannot resolve it as declared. Since 7.0.8 the writer also accepts stock OpenPDF 1.3.43 from Central in its place, and a swapped-in run exported both timesheet reports with one warning that link annotation tagging for PDF/UA was off. Its OpenPDF 3 sibling from 7.1.0, jasperreports-openpdf, pulls in a Jaspersoft build of OpenPDF 3.0.5 compiled for Java 21, and that build raised UnsupportedClassVersionError on Java 17.

Encryption brings in one more JAR, as this export of a compiled timesheet.jasper with two passwords shows.

import net.sf.jasperreports.engine.JRException;
import net.sf.jasperreports.engine.JasperFillManager;
import net.sf.jasperreports.engine.JasperPrint;
import net.sf.jasperreports.engine.data.JRMapCollectionDataSource;
import net.sf.jasperreports.export.SimpleExporterInput;
import net.sf.jasperreports.export.SimpleOutputStreamExporterOutput;
import net.sf.jasperreports.pdf.JRPdfExporter;
import net.sf.jasperreports.pdf.SimplePdfExporterConfiguration;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

public class EncryptedTimesheet {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws JRException {
        Map<String, Object> parameters = new HashMap<>();
        parameters.put("Week", "week 43");

        // Map rows need no bean class, and each key matches a field in the template.
        List<Map<String, ?>> rows = List.of(
                Map.of("project", "Billing API", "engineer", "A. Novak", "hours", 30.0),
                Map.of("project", "Data platform", "engineer", "R. Osei", "hours", 38.5));

        JasperPrint print = JasperFillManager.fillReport(
                "timesheet.jasper", parameters, new JRMapCollectionDataSource(rows));

        JRPdfExporter exporter = new JRPdfExporter();
        exporter.setExporterInput(new SimpleExporterInput(print));
        exporter.setExporterOutput(new SimpleOutputStreamExporterOutput("timesheet-week-43.pdf"));

        // A user password to open the file, an owner password to change it, and printing as the one permission.
        SimplePdfExporterConfiguration config = new SimplePdfExporterConfiguration();
        config.setEncrypted(true);
        config.set128BitKey(true);
        config.setUserPassword("week43");
        config.setOwnerPassword("payroll-admin");
        config.setAllowedPermissionsHint("PRINTING");
        exporter.setConfiguration(config);

        exporter.exportReport();
    }
}

Run with only the JasperReports JARs, exportReport threw NoClassDefFoundError naming an org.bouncycastle.asn1 class (ASN1OctetString or ASN1Encodable, varying between runs) and left a 0-byte timesheet-week-43.pdf behind. Bouncy Castle does not arrive with the PDF extension, and the vendor's PdfEncrypt sample adds bcprov-jdk18on itself. With version 1.86 added at runtime, the result needed week43 to open, used 128-bit RC4 (V 2, R 3), and allowed printing and nothing else. That matches the usual password-protection split of an open password and a change password.

Advisories That Still Apply to 6.x and Early 7.x

The table lists the records in NVD, CVE.org, OSV and the GitHub Advisory Database on 3 November 2026 for the library and for the Jackson version its last 6.x release declares.

Advisory Score and scorer Affected Fixed in
CVE-2025-10492, deserialization 9.8 NIST (CVSS 3.1), 8.7 Jaspersoft (CVSS 4.0) Library 7.0.3 and earlier 7.0.4
CVE-2026-6009, deserialization 8.7 Jaspersoft (CVSS 4.0), NVD analysis pending Library 7.0.6 and earlier 7.0.7
4 jackson-core advisories 3 high and 1 moderate (GitHub) Jackson 2.17.1, declared by 6.21.5 Jackson 2.22.3, and 7.1.1 uses 2.22.4
12 jackson-databind advisories 5 high and 7 moderate (GitHub) Jackson 2.17.1, declared by 6.21.5 Jackson 2.22.3, and 7.1.1 uses 2.22.4
CVE-2026-110879, jackson-databind type validator bypass 9.8 HeroDevs (CVSS 3.1), NVD analysis pending Jackson 2.10.0 to before 2.18.12, which covers 2.17.1 2.18.12, 2.21.8 and 2.22.4
CVE-2026-68498, jackson-core memory exhaustion 7.5 HeroDevs (CVSS 3.1), NVD analysis deferred Jackson 2.16.0 to before 2.18.10, which covers 2.17.1 2.18.10, 2.21.6 and 2.22.2

Both library records describe Java deserialization with a path to remote code execution, and neither is marked disputed. Of the Jackson entries, CVE-2026-91776 is one of the high ones, about jackson-databind keeping every unknown raw type ID. OSV holds CVE-2026-110879 and CVE-2026-68498 with no affected package attached, so a query for Jackson 2.17.1 does not return them, and their ranges come from CVE.org. The last 6.x release, 6.21.5, dates from 4 July 2025, before either library fix, and no later 6.x release is on Maven Central. A 7.1.1 build with the PDF extension and Bouncy Castle came back with zero OSV matches across its 34 JARs, and the move there runs through the template change below.

Version 7 Template Conversion and the PDF/UA Tagging Change

Version 7 swapped the Commons Digester parsers for Jackson XML, and its changelog says the 7.x library on its own cannot open .jrxml or .jrtx files saved by 6.x or earlier. Jaspersoft Studio 7 or newer converts them. Every .jasper file needs a fresh compile, imports change where packages moved into separate JARs, and the 3D pie, bar and stacked bar charts come out flat because the 7.1.1 chart theme hands each 3D type to its flat chart method. Since 7.0.6, jasperreports-maven-plugin can run the update and compile steps inside a build.

Accessibility work meets an edition line in the same changelog. Release 7.0.8 put PDF tagging behind a PdfTagger interface and moved its newest, fullest implementation into the JasperReports Library Professional extensions, and tagging is what PDF/UA and PDF/A files rely on.

Where an HTML Renderer Fits

Markup that loses its layout, fonts to package, extra JARs, a Jaspersoft repository, 6.x advisories and an edition line for tagging add up to a long list, and IronPDF for Java shortens it whenever the source is an HTML page.

Our timesheet string went to PdfDocument.renderHtmlAsPdf untouched on 2026.11.3, and the grid split the two names into columns while the .over rule printed 44.0 in bold red. The renderHtmlAsPdf example shows the call. For the password step, getSecurity().setPassword and setOwnerPassword do the work, and the ironpdf POM declares no Bouncy Castle dependency to add. Tagged output comes from convertToPdfUA and convertToPdfA in that one com.ironsoftware:ironpdf dependency, which has eleven 2026 builds on Maven Central, 2026.1.3 through 2026.11.3.

What This Means for HTML Reports on JasperReports

For reports that start as HTML pages, IronPDF is where we would begin, since the timesheet above needed no JRXML rewrite. A free trial key is enough to run your own page through it.

Did the version 7 template conversion or the font setup take your team longer?

JasperReports and Jaspersoft are trademarks of their owner, we have no affiliation with Actian or the Jaspersoft business, and the details above draw on the project's changelog, POMs and samples, NVD, CVE.org, OSV, Maven Central and our own runs.

Drafted with AI. JasperReports code run and claims checked by the Iron Software DevRel team against net.sf.jasperreports:jasperreports 7.1.1 on 3 November 2026, with the IronPDF details checked against the com.ironsoftware:ironpdf 2026.11.3 API.

title: ArgoCD GitOps Mastery: Production Kubernetes Continuous Delivery Architecture
description:
Originally published on the HostingPodium Enterprise Engineering Blog.

Free SRE & Developer Diagnostics: Test your stack live with our DMARC Record Checker, Generator & SPF/DKIM Validator, Free Website Speed & Core Web Vitals Checker, or explore all 9 Free Webmaster & Cloud Engineering Tools.

A comprehensive guide to implementing production-grade GitOps continuous delivery using ArgoCD, Argo Rollouts, and Helm on enterprise Kubernetes clusters with automated rollback and multi-environment promotion gates.

Architectural Overview: Enterprise ArgoCD GitOps Mastery: Production Kubernetes Continuous Delivery Architecture

Modern enterprise engineering demands robust, scalable infrastructure that can withstand high concurrency, distributed network latency, and stringent regulatory mandates. Operating ArgoCD GitOps Mastery: Production Kubernetes Continuous Delivery Architecture in production requires transitioning from basic prototypes to resilient, automated architectures built on high-availability design principles.

HostingPodium engineers enterprise solutions around Production Kubernetes & Red Hat OpenShift Container Orchestration, ensuring your technical teams eliminate operational bottlenecks, reduce mean time to recovery (MTTR), and enforce verifiable data sovereignty across hybrid environments.

In high-scale enterprise ecosystems, architectural resilience cannot be treated as an afterthought. Workloads running on distributed infrastructure require deterministic execution guarantees, verifiable fault isolation, and immutable deployment pipelines that protect mission-critical operations against data corruption, regional cloud provider outages, and sudden spikes in transactional throughput.

Production Technology Stack & Infrastructure Primitives

Deploying ArgoCD GitOps Mastery: Production Kubernetes Continuous Delivery Architecture at enterprise scale requires rigorous calibration of the underlying compute, storage, and networking layers. Our architecture standardizes on the following core components:

Core Execution Tier & Tooling 

- **Platform Execution Engines:** Hardened deployment across Kubernetes, Red Hat OpenShift, ArgoCD GitOps, Istio Service Mesh, Calico CNI, Prometheus Operator, Helm running on dedicated [bare-metal servers](https://hostingpodium.com/our-services/server-hosting-administration/) or [private VPC](https://hostingpodium.com/our-services/cloud-platform-engineering/) clusters.

- **Declarative Automation:** Standardized on Immutable GitOps Delivery, Declarative Infrastructure as Code, Automated Horizontal/Vertical Pod Autoscaling, [Zero-Trust](https://hostingpodium.com/blog/enterprise-zero-trust-network-wireguard-mesh/) Pod Network Policies, ensuring deterministic configuration management and immutable infrastructure delivery.

- **Storage Tiers:** High-IOPS NVMe storage pools with automated cross-datacenter replication, point-in-time recovery, and snapshot auditing.

- **[Telemetry](https://hostingpodium.com/our-services/observability/) & Instrumentation:** Unified metrics collection, distributed tracing, and real-time log aggregation powered by [Prometheus and Grafana](https://hostingpodium.com/blog/prometheus-grafana-enterprise-observability-stack/).

By decoupling the stateful storage persistence layer from stateless compute runners, this architecture achieves linear horizontal scalability. Under increased traffic bursts, autoscaling controller groups dynamically instantiate compute nodes while persistent storage volumes maintain zero data loss through continuous synchronous journaling and distributed lock management.

High Availability, Failover & Service Level Agreements

Operational continuity is foundational to our enterprise engagements. Every system deployment is governed by transparent, mathematically validated SLA targets:

Resilience Standards 

- **Availability SLA:** Multi-master control plane quorum, 99.99% ingress uptime, and sub-minute node replacement automation.

- **Clustering & Redundancy:** N+1 high-availability cluster topology with automated health checks, sub-second failover routing, and zero single points of failure.

- **[Disaster Recovery](https://hostingpodium.com/our-services/backup-disaster-recovery/) Metrics:** Documented Recovery Point Objectives (RPO < 15 minutes) and Recovery Time Objectives (RTO < 30 minutes) verified by scheduled chaos engineering tests.

Dynamic failover mechanisms rely on distributed consensus protocols such as Raft or Paxos, preventing split-brain conditions during transient network partitions. Load balancers continuously monitor TCP health probes, automatically draining traffic away from degraded cluster nodes within 500 milliseconds of threshold degradation.

Enterprise Security, Governance & Compliance Standards

Security is integrated natively across all architectural tiers, adhering to modern zero-trust network access (ZTNA) frameworks:

Data Protection & Regulatory Alignment 

- **Compliance Frameworks:** Engineered to satisfy PCI-DSS segmentation, container image vulnerability scanning via Trivy/Clair, and immutable audit trails. across sovereign cloud and private on-premises infrastructures.

- **Cryptographic Controls:** Strict TLS 1.3 protocol enforcement in transit and AES-256 cryptographic encryption for all persistent data at rest.

- **Identity & RBAC:** Centralized Role-Based Access Control, multi-factor authentication, and OAuth2/SAML Single Sign-On (SSO) integration.

- **Vulnerability Management:** Continuous automated CVE scanning, container image provenance verification, and tamper-proof operational logging.

Network perimeters are isolated using hardened software-defined firewall policies, strict egress filtering, and encrypted wireguard tunnels for inter-node communication. Privileged access requires cryptographic short-lived certificates issued through automated mutual TLS (mTLS) identities.

Performance Tuning & Low-Latency Kernel Calibration

Achieving peak performance for ArgoCD GitOps Mastery: Production Kubernetes Continuous Delivery Architecture requires micro-optimization at the operating system and Linux kernel layer. Standard cloud instance default configurations often introduce artificial I/O throttling and excessive TCP buffer latency.

Production Kernel Optimizations

Our engineering deployments apply custom sysctl tuning tailored for high-concurrency workloads:

- **TCP Buffer Scaling:** Optimization of `net.ipv4.tcp_rmem` and `net.ipv4.tcp_wmem` to enable automatic window scaling across high-bandwidth wide-area links.

- **Connection Queue Depth:** Expansion of `net.core.somaxconn` to 65,535 and `net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog` to mitigate connection drops during high burst traffic.

- **Memory Virtualization:** Calibration of `vm.swappiness=1` and `vm.dirty_ratio=10` to prevent unexpected page cache latency spikes and enforce deterministic NVMe disk writes.

- **Storage I/O Scheduler:** Implementation of the `mq-deadline` or `none` multi-queue I/O schedulers for enterprise NVMe drives, maximizing IOPS throughput and minimizing queue wait time.

Observability, Telemetry & SRE Incident Response Runbooks

Comprehensive observability transforms reactive firefighting into proactive infrastructure reliability engineering. Every component within ArgoCD GitOps Mastery: Production Kubernetes Continuous Delivery Architecture exports real-time telemetry metrics.

Unified Observability Stack

Our SRE framework instruments the environment with the following operational capabilities:

- **Granular Metric Scraping:** Prometheus agents scrape application and system health endpoints at 10-second intervals, aggregating metrics into clustered central storage.

- **Actionable Grafana Dashboards:** Visualization matrices monitor latency p95 and p99 percentiles, CPU saturation, memory exhaustion, and I/O wait times.

- **Smart Anomaly [Alerting](https://hostingpodium.com/our-services/monitoring-incident-support/):** Alertmanager triggers multi-channel notifications (Slack, PagerDuty, Webhooks) based on rate-of-change heuristics rather than crude static thresholds.

- **Distributed Tracing:** OpenTelemetry context propagation enables end-to-end trace auditing across [microservices](https://hostingpodium.com/our-services/application-modernization/) to isolate high-latency bottlenecks.

Operational Failure Scenarios & Automated Recovery Mechanics

Infrastructure must be designed to withstand hardware degradation, hypervisor failure, and sudden database node crashes. Our architecture incorporates self-healing automation runbooks:

Failure Mitigation Matrix 

- **Split-Brain Protection:** Quorum-based voting nodes guarantee that isolated network partitions cannot independently accept writes, preventing split-brain data corruption.

- **Automated Leader Re-election:** In the event of primary node failure, standby replicas evaluate replication lag and promote the most synchronized node within 3 seconds.

- **Graceful Degradation:** Read-only replicas continue serving cached query traffic even during transient primary database failovers, guaranteeing zero read downtime.

- **Immutable Snapshot Restoration:** Automated hourly block-level snapshots stored on write-once-read-many (WORM) storage protect against accidental deletion or ransomware events.

Step-by-Step Implementation Roadmap

Our engineering methodology follows a disciplined four-phase deployment lifecycle to ensure zero downtime:

- **Discovery & Topology Assessment:** Detailed audit of existing workloads, network throughput, storage IOPS, and integration dependencies.

- **Staging & Performance Benchmarking:** Provisioning of isolated staging environments to stress-test throughput, failover mechanics, and API latency under simulated load.

- **Canary Rollout & Production Cutover:** Controlled cutover utilizing blue-green or canary release strategies with automated rollback triggers.

- **24/7 Managed SRE Support:** Continuous performance calibration, automated kernel patching, and proactive incident response runbooks.

To evaluate predictable cloud infrastructure economics for container clusters without unpredictable bandwidth egress surcharges, see our AWS Cloud Cost & Egress Alternative analysis.

title: React Props: How Do Components Share Data With Each Other?
description:
Imagine you're building an e-commerce application.

You have one Product component, but you need to display different products:

  • Laptop – ₹50,000
  • Mobile – ₹20,000
  • Headphones – ₹2,000

Would you create three separate components for these products?

Not necessary!

React provides something called Props (Properties) that allows you to reuse the same component with different data.

1. What are Props?

Props are a way to pass data from a parent component to a child component.

Think of a component as a function. Props act like the function's parameters.

Let's understand with an example.

Parent Component

function App() {
    return (
        <div>
            <Product name="Laptop" price={50000} />
            <Product name="Mobile" price={20000} />
            <Product name="Headphones" price={2000} />
        </div>
    );
}

Here, we're passing different values to the same Product component.

Child Component

function Product(props) {
    return (
        <div>
            <h2>{props.name}</h2>
            <p>Price: ₹{props.price}</p>
        </div>
    );
}

The child component receives the values through the props object.

Output

Laptop
Price: ₹50000

Mobile
Price: ₹20000

Headphones
Price: ₹2000

Notice something?

We created only one component but reused it three times with different data.

That's the power of props!

2. How do Props work internally?
When a parent component passes data to a child component, React makes that data available through the child's props.

For example:

<Product name="Laptop" price={50000} />

The child receives an object conceptually like this:

{
    name: "Laptop",
    price: 50000
}

You can access these values using:

props.name
props.price

3. Props Destructuring

Instead of writing props.name and props.price repeatedly, we can use destructuring.

function Product({ name, price }) {
    return (
        <div>
            <h2>{name}</h2>
            <p>Price: ₹{price}</p>
        </div>
    );
}

Both approaches work the same way.

4. Important Rules About Props

Props are passed from parent to child.

Props can contain strings, numbers, arrays, objects and functions.

Props are read-only.

A child component should not directly modify its props.

Different component instances can receive different props.

5. When do developers use Props?

Real-world examples:

Passing product information to product cards.

Passing user information to profile components.

Passing data to reusable table components.

Passing event handler functions to child components.

Passing configuration values to reusable UI components.

Final Thoughts :

Props make React components reusable and help us build applications with smaller, independent components.

Instead of writing the same UI repeatedly, create one reusable component and provide different data through props.

*Write once. Reuse everywhere. That's the idea behind React Props! *

title: Your AI agent can't know everything. Let it ask another agent.
description:
You're building an agent that helps a team plan Java upgrades. Someone asks it which Spring Boot version first required Java 17.

It doesn't know. Another agent does.

That agent belongs to another team. It runs on another server. Maybe it was built with another framework.

Skills won't help here. Neither will subagents. Both live inside your agent, in your workflow, on your server.

You need a protocol neither side owns. That's A2A (Agent2Agent): an open protocol for agents to find each other and hand over work, across frameworks and vendors.

Here's how it works, and how we run both sides of it in ByteChef, an open-source workflow automation and AI agent platform built on Java and Spring.

A2A in three ideas

The Spring AI team covers agents working across system boundaries in their A2A post. The protocol comes down to three things:

  • The agent card. Every A2A agent publishes a small JSON document at /.well-known/agent-card.json with its name, description, and skills. A client reads it to learn what the agent can do and where to send messages.
  • The protocol. Agents talk over HTTP with JSON-RPC. A client sends a message. The agent answers with a message or a task.
  • Two roles. A server publishes a card and answers messages. A client reads a card and sends work. Any agent can take either role.

The whole contract is a JSON card and an HTTP endpoint. That's why a Spring AI agent can call one built with another framework, and the other way round. Neither side needs to know how the other works.

The example: a tech lead asks a release expert

We built two templates, one for each side of the protocol.

The server: Java release expert

The Java release expert is three steps:

  1. New Workflow Call starts the workflow with one input, message. Behind an A2A Server, the text of the incoming A2A message lands here.
  2. AI Agent answers with an Anthropic model and no tools.
  3. Reply returns the answer to the caller as message.

Its system prompt:

You are the Java Release Expert. You answer questions about Java and Spring
release history: versions, release dates, headline features and migration
notes. Answer in at most 6 short bullets. If you are not sure of a date, say so.

Nothing in this workflow mentions A2A. It's an ordinary callable workflow. The A2A Server does the protocol work around it.

The client: Tech lead agent

The Tech lead agent is a chat agent:

  1. New Chat Request starts the workflow when you send a message in the workflow chat.
  2. AI Agent uses an Anthropic model, Chat Memory for follow-up questions, and the A2A Agent Tool in its Tools slot.
  3. Reply sends the answer back to the chat.

Its system prompt:

You are a tech lead helping a team plan upgrades. For any question about Java
or Spring versions, release dates or features, delegate to the remote Java
Release Expert with the agent client tool and build your answer on its reply.
Say that you asked the remote agent.

The tech lead doesn't know Java release history. It knows who to ask.

Serving an agent is configuration

An A2A Server in ByteChef turns one or more workflows into a remote agent. You find it under Servers → A2A Servers.

Each server has:

  • A name and a description. These become the name and description on the agent card.
  • Workflows. Every workflow you add becomes a skill on the card. The skill's name and description default to the workflow's label and description, and you can change them under Workflow Skills. Only workflows that start with a New Workflow Call trigger are exposed, and adding a workflow deploys it.
  • A URL. The address contains a secret key. The Connect tab shows two URLs, the Agent Card URL and the Endpoint URL.
  • An optional API key check. With Require authentication on, callers also need an API key created under Settings, sent as an Authorization: Bearer header. With it off, the secret in the URL is enough. 
https://<your-bytechef-host>/api/automation/a2a/<server key>

When a message arrives, the server starts the workflow and passes the message text as its message input. When the run finishes, the workflow's response goes back to the caller.

The server answers message/send and message/stream, and supports tasks/get and tasks/cancel for runs that take longer.

The agent card advertises text in and text out. If your server sits behind a proxy, set ByteChef's public URL so the card points to an address other agents can reach.

Calling an agent is one tool

The A2A Agent Tool goes in an AI Agent's Tools slot. It has one property, Agent URL. For a ByteChef A2A Server, that's the Endpoint URL from the Connect tab.

When the agent decides to delegate, the tool:

  1. Reads the card from <Agent URL>/.well-known/agent-card.json.
  2. Sends the task as an A2A message over JSON-RPC.
  3. Waits up to 60 seconds for the reply.
  4. Returns the text of that reply to the agent.

The reply can be a plain message or a task with artifacts. The tool pulls the text out of either.

If the remote agent can't be reached, returns an error, or takes longer than 60 seconds, the tool fails with an error that names the agent URL. It doesn't hang.

The model sees a tool called sendTaskToRemoteAgent, and the system prompt tells it when to use it. To reach several remote agents, add one A2A Agent Tool per URL.

If the remote server requires authentication, add an A2A connection to the tool. It has one field, Token, sent as an Authorization: Bearer header. For a ByteChef A2A Server, that's the API key.

One limit to know: when a server exposes several workflows, a caller has to say which skill it wants. The A2A Agent Tool doesn't choose a skill, so point it at a server that exposes one workflow. The template pair is set up that way.

Try it

Set up the server first. The client needs its URL.

The server:

  1. Import Java release expert into a project.
  2. Add your Anthropic connection to the model and save the project.
  3. Open A2A Servers, click New A2A Server, name it Java Release Expert, and give it a description. The description goes on the agent card.
  4. Leave Require authentication off for a local demo. Turn it on for anything reachable from outside, and give callers an API key.
  5. Click Add Workflows, pick the project and version, and select the workflow. This deploys it.
  6. Open the Connect tab and copy the Endpoint URL.

The client:

  1. Import Tech lead agent into a project.
  2. Open the A2A Agent Tool under the AI Agent and paste the Endpoint URL into Agent URL.
  3. If the server has Require authentication on, add an A2A connection with the API key.
  4. Add your Anthropic connection to the model.
  5. Open the chat and ask: Which Spring Boot version first required Java 17?

The tech lead should call sendTaskToRemoteAgent. The server starts the release expert workflow, and the expert's answer comes back as the tool result. The tech lead builds its own answer on that reply and says it asked the remote agent.

Chat Memory lets you follow up with What would we need to change to move from Boot 2.7? without repeating the context.

Both templates run on the same ByteChef here, but nothing depends on that. The client only needs the Endpoint URL. The server could be another ByteChef instance, and the client could be any A2A client.

Subagents or A2A?

Both answer the same need: hand this to a specialist. The difference is distance.

Subagents A2A
The specialist is An agent you define on this agent Any A2A agent, anywhere
It runs In the same workflow run On its own server, reached over HTTP
It's built with ByteChef Anything that speaks A2A
The caller learns about it from The subagent's definition The remote agent's card
Use it when The specialist is part of this agent The specialist belongs to someone else, or serves many callers

The Java release expert fits A2A because many agents could use it. Serve it once, and every agent that needs release facts can call the same URL.

Spring AI vs. ByteChef setup

ByteChef uses the same A2A Java SDK as the Spring AI post: the same agent card, the same JSON-RPC transport, the same message types. A ByteChef agent can call any A2A agent, and any A2A client can call a ByteChef A2A Server.

What ByteChef adds is the product around it:

  • Serving an agent is configuration. Add a workflow to an A2A Server, and ByteChef builds the agent card, handles the JSON-RPC methods, and runs the workflow for each message.
  • Calling an agent is one tool. Paste a URL into the A2A Agent Tool. ByteChef reads the card, sends the message, and unwraps the reply.
  • Access is managed in the app. Turn on Require authentication and give callers an API key, without writing security code.

Wrapping up

Skills, questions, todo lists, and subagents all make one agent more capable. A2A lets it use agents it doesn't own, built on frameworks it has never seen.

Have a specialist other agents should be able to ask? Import the Java release expert and the Tech lead agent, connect them, and ask your first question across the wire.

This is Part 5 of our AI Agentic Patterns series. Part 1 covered Agent Skills, Part 2 covered asking the user, Part 3 covered todo lists, and Part 4 covered subagents. If you like where ByteChef is going, a star on GitHub helps a lot.

Originally published on the ByteChef blog.

description:
Most AI-generated animation is a video model prompt. This repo takes the opposite route: sevenevesai/riso-windowseat holds procedural risograph films and prints, each a single index.html of Canvas 2D and Web Audio, with no libraries, fonts, images or network calls. The author directed, and Claude Code wrote the code using a kit of skills, craft docs and a render harness that is in the repo. You can use the same kit to make your own.

What is in the repo

Per the README, there are nine films (Window Seat, Roost, Held, Nonpareil, Eclosion, Passenger, Standby, Lumen, Emergence), all 1080 x 1080 at 30 fps, plus two print series exported at 2160 x 2160. Every frame is a pure function of time, seek(t), so any moment can be inspected exactly and the MP4 cannot drop frames. You can watch them at seveneves.ai/riso or open any index.html and press Play.

Setup

You need Node.js 18 or later and Claude Code.

git clone https://github.com/sevenevesai/riso-windowseat
cd riso-windowseat/tools
npm install && npm run setup && npm test

npm install brings playwright-core and a bundled ffmpeg. npm run setup downloads the Chromium and Firefox builds the harness drives. The released MP4s are Firefox renders (render.mjs --engine firefox). npm test runs the harness self-tests and exits 0 when they pass.

Ask Claude Code

Open Claude Code in the repo root. CLAUDE.md gives the session the contract and commands, and the riso-film, riso-still and riso-score skills in .claude/skills/ carry the workflow and gates. Example prompts from the README:

  • "Make a 40 second riso film of a lighthouse keeper's night."
  • "Make a riso poster of a heron on a pier at dusk."
  • "Score this film" or "The rain at 66 s is too loud."
  • "Extend Window Seat with a snowy mountain pass after the lake."

After each edit to a film, a hook flags any Math.random() call and a missing window.__riso, which keeps renders deterministic.

The workflow it enforces

A work is designed in its FILM.md or PRINT.md, its hardest frame is proved first, and then it is inspected as frame strips, 1:1 crops and loudness sheets rendered by tools/. Each record keeps design decisions, measurements and the work's remaining weaknesses. That discipline is why this is a good template for any agent-built creative project: the agent checks its own output against measurable gates.

Use cases

The riso-windowseat page on Deduped lists four starting points: make a film from a one-line prompt, export a 2160 x 2160 poster PNG with tools/still.mjs, fix a loud moment or score an existing film, and extend Window Seat with a new scene.

Caveats

  • Licensing: code, films and prints are MIT, but Window Seat's piano recordings are CC BY 3.0 (keep the credit) and Eclosion's wing geometry is CC BY-SA 4.0. See THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md before redistributing.
  • The first setup downloads two browser builds.
  • This walkthrough follows the README and we have not run it end to end.

Source: sevenevesai/riso-windowseat.

title: When an MCP tool changes, what should you test again?
description:
Disclosure: this article was prepared with AI assistance for DraftYourApp. This walkthrough uses a hypothetical example to explain a review process; it does not report a customer incident or a live test.

A successful tool call answers a narrow question: did this operation work with these inputs, permissions and conditions? When the contract changes, the old result may no longer answer the question you have today.

Consider a synthetic order-status tool. Yesterday its input was an order reference. Today the descriptor requires both an order reference and a region. A button can still look correct while sending yesterday’s arguments.

1. Keep a record of what was reviewed

Record the tool name, description, input contract, relevant output expectations and annotations alongside the test inputs. Keep credentials and personal data out of the record.

For this example, use a clearly fictional order reference such as DEMO-ORDER-001. Do not send that reference to an arbitrary production server: use a controlled test environment where its meaning and permitted effects are known.

2. Inspect the current contract

Compare the current descriptor with the reviewed version. Which input became required? Did the meaning of a field change? Does the tool still perform the same task?

Treat the comparison as a review aid. A textual difference does not, by itself, tell you whether a change is harmless or compatible with your application.

In DraftYourApp’s documented MCP flow, inspection contacts the server and lists tools without executing them. The subsequent remote test is a separate, explicit action. Discovery is still a network interaction; it is not an offline check.

3. Check permissions before running anything

Confirm the destination, the scope of the operation and the arguments you are authorized to send. A tool test may affect real data. Do not remove authentication or broaden permissions simply to turn a failing test green.

If the tool list depends on authentication state, compare like with like. A difference between an authenticated and an unauthenticated session is not sufficient evidence that a deployment changed.

4. Repeat the relevant test

For the fictional order-status example, update the arguments to include the region defined by your controlled fixture. Record the actual response and compare it with the expected outcome. Also check the intended behavior when a required field is missing or the order does not exist in that fixture.

Do not label these cases “passed” until they have actually been exercised. A written expected result is a test plan, not a receipt.

DraftYourApp’s guide calls for inspection and testing again when descriptors change or a test receipt expires. Keep the evidence associated with the contract it tested.

5. Check the user-facing task

Once the selected operation is reviewed, check how the interface handles its output and failure states. A local preview, a remote operation test and a check in the intended client each answer different questions.

For the order example, can the user understand which order was found, which region was used and what to do if no result is available? A successful response alone does not establish that the whole interaction is useful.

Start with one task and one observable result. Expand only when the evidence supports it.
