title: PageSift 1.0: the Rust web content engine is feature-complete
description:
Fifteen days, twenty-five releases. PageSift went public as 0.20 on October 20; today it ships 1.0.

PageSift is a web content engine written in Rust. It turns URLs, PDFs and Office files into clean Markdown and structured data for AI agents and LLM pipelines — one self-hosted binary with a Firecrawl-compatible HTTP API, a Jina Reader-compatible endpoint (including /s/), an MCP server, and Python / Node.js / Rust SDKs.

1.0 is not a speed release — performance landed with the 0.9 architecture rebuild. 1.0 is feature completion.

What 1.0 adds

OCR, built from scratch. Scanned PDFs were PageSift's documented weak spot. 1.0 ships its own OCR pipeline — text detection, recognition, formula recognition (LaTeX out), layout analysis — running on a self-written inference runtime (safetensors executor; no ONNX Runtime) and a self-written CUDA GPU layer. Models are open weights, downloaded on first use, off by default. On the olmOCR-bench scanned set it scores 0.543 vs Docling (GPU) at 0.410.

Selector extraction with memory. Give it a JSON schema; when a site redesign breaks your selectors, it relocates elements using element fingerprints and a statistical posterior — and reports relocated, ambiguous, or missing instead of silently returning wrong data.

Change monitoring. A /v2/monitor endpoint family with block-level diffing that separates noise changes (prices, dates, counters) from substantive ones.

Browser actions, sessions, and an agent endpoint across the HTTP, MCP and Jina surfaces — plus WARC files as input, a hooks + [[rules]] system, and per-host secret injection.

The architecture in three ideas

  1. Measured instead of fixed. The hundreds of hand-tuned timeouts, thresholds and concurrency limits are gone. A statistical kernel derives them from runtime observations — survival analysis (Kaplan–Meier) for timeouts, a Universal Scalability Law fit for global concurrency, and "posterior expected value − shadow price × cost" for render decisions. One global meta-parameter remains: δ = 0.05. With no observations, behaviour matches the old fixed values; an estimate takes over only when the difference is statistically significant.
  2. Scheduling that follows the hardware. One resident CPU worker per core (no blocking thread pool), pinned to NUMA node sets rather than individual cores — because measurements said so: hard per-core pinning cost −33.9% throughput in the 0.70 experiments, node-set pinning gained +8.63%. The code comments cite the measurement behind each such decision.
  3. Failures are reported, never dressed up as success. 0.91 was a release about exactly this: jobs whose results couldn't be saved, replicated, or delivered by webhook previously ended as completed. They now fail loudly, with an errors endpoint. 1.0 extends the rule to the API surface: options the engine cannot honor are rejected (unknown MCP arguments error; unimplementable Jina headers return UNSUPPORTED_OPTION), and the release notes carry a Known limits section that lists what isn't tested and what doesn't work — including security caveats.

Performance (re-measured 2026-11-04)

Workload PageSift 1.0 Fastest rival Gap
PDF → Markdown, olmOCR-bench 1,269 pages, single thread 2.4 ms/page pypdf 50.0 ms/page ×20.8
HTML → Markdown, 600 documents 0.24 ms/page Turndown 1.9 ms/page ×8.1
Main content, Firecrawl 597 pages, single thread p50 1.0 ms/page crw 7.4 ms/page ×7.3
Office / e-books, 81 files 93.6 files/s Kreuzberg 19.5 ×4.8
Wide crawl, 200 sites × 100 pages, unthrottled 3,500–4,400 pages/s, 280–316 MB peak Spider 2,000–2,700 pages/s, 5.5 GB —

Honest footnotes, because they matter: competitor numbers are the recorded late-October runs, not re-run for this release; and the workloads where PageSift loses are listed in the same document ("Largest gaps") — e.g. a single-host replay looks slow mostly because of the default 1-second per-host politeness interval, which is policy, not engine speed. Full data and reproduction scripts live in the repo (docs/benchmarks.md, benchmarks/).

Battle-tested once, properly

In late October an external team integrated PageSift into their production system and immediately hit a real bug: the official Node binding required a newer glibc than their server had (2.32). 0.81.5 fixed it — build baseline lowered to glibc 2.28, plus a release gate that fails the release if any artifact exceeds it. A user found it; the project fixed it and made it impossible to reintroduce silently. That's the workflow 1.0 is built around.

Who it's for / not for

For: teams feeding RAG or agent pipelines who want a self-hosted Firecrawl/Jina alternative without per-page pricing, and anyone who needs web pages, PDFs and Office files in one pipeline.

Not for: people who need a hosted cloud API (PageSift is self-hosted; a hosted version is not part of 1.0), or bypassing hard anti-bot targets (robots.txt and politeness are respected; captchas are reported, not solved).

PageSift is a solo project. It exists because the crawler feeding my other project was too slow and not clean enough, so I wrote my own. 1.0 closes the feature list. What I want next is more production workloads breaking it in interesting ways.

Repo: https://github.com/YOLOW92/pagesift — AGPL-3.0, commercial licensing available. Issues and head-to-head benchmarks welcome, good or bad.

title: Vercel Security Review now in public beta
description:
Vercel Security Review is now in public beta for Pro and Enterprise teams. Once enabled, every push to a connected GitHub repository is automatically reviewed for vulnerabilities, and findings are reported in the Vulnerabilities dashboard.

What triggers a review

Security Review runs automatically when code is pushed to a connected GitHub repository. Because reviews start from push events rather than pull requests, direct and force pushes to your production branch are reviewed as well. Every project affected by a single push is reviewed together.

What a finding includes

Each finding records the project, environment, branch, and commit, with a summary, a suggested fix, and an AI-generated severity rating.

Security Review adds its own GitHub check to each commit it reviews. When there's a pull request, it also posts findings as review comments that link back to each finding. On public repositories, finding details stay in the dashboard.

Fixes and resolution

Clicking Fix with Vercel Agent on a vulnerability report hands the finding to Vercel Agent, which proposes a fix and opens a pull request for you to review. Nothing merges until you approve it.

To fix findings with your coding agent instead, use vercel security vulnerabilities in the Vercel CLI, or copy any finding as Markdown or JSON.

Security policies

Teams can write security policies in plain language, for all projects or specific ones, to give Security Review more context about how they build. Set a team policy in Agent settings and a project policy in the project's Security settings.

Limitations

Security Review analyzes source code. It isn't a security audit, and it doesn't perform runtime or penetration testing. It helps you find vulnerabilities but doesn't guarantee your application is free of them.

Pricing

Security Review is billed at the Vercel Agent rate: provider inference at the underlying token rate with no markup, plus the Vercel Token Rate of $0.25 per million tokens (input, cached, output). Reviews run on each push to GitHub, so cost scales with how often you push and how much code changes.

Security reviews are free until November 10, 2026, and fixes made with Vercel Agent are billed at the Vercel Agent rate.

Enable Security Review in your team’s Agent settings, or read the documentation and the announcement to learn more. The CLI command needs Vercel CLI 65.10.0 or later.

title: Bring your agent to Notion with Chat SDK
description:
Your team already works in Notion. Now your agent can too.

With the new Notion adapter for Chat SDK, the same agent you run on Slack, Discord, GitHub, Teams, or WhatsApp can join comment discussions on your Notion pages, no separate codebase required.

Each Notion page maps to a channel and each comment thread to a thread, so replies stay threaded automatically.

The adapter supports mentions, message editing, conversation history, and up to three file attachments. By default, your bot replies when @-mentioned and where mentions aren't available in a workspace, it can trigger on a keyword or on all comments instead.

Notion doesn't support buttons, modals, or reactions, and cards render as markdown. Discussions can start at the page or block level, but not on inline text ranges. History fetches return only open comments.

Read the documentation to get started, browse the directory, or build your own.

title: TypeScript `globalThis` Typing in 2026: Safely Adding Properties to the Global Scope Without `any`
description:
TypeScript globalThis Typing in 2026: Safely Adding Properties to the Global Scope Without any

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Why globalThis Typing Still Matters in 2026

The global scope remains the path of least resistance for quick hacks. Developers drop variables onto globalThis to share state across modules, expose debug hooks to the browser console, or bridge third-party scripts that expect global names. TypeScript sees these assignments and defaults to any, erasing type safety at the exact boundary where typos and runtime crashes cluster.

The broken pattern looks innocent: globalThis.featureFlags = { darkMode: true } compiles without complaint, but every access to globalThis.featureFlags surrenders type checking. When another engineer misspells darkMode as darkmode three modules away, the compiler stays silent and the test suite passes until production traffic hits the undefined code path.

Declaration merging solves this. TypeScript permits extending the globalThis interface with new properties, restoring autocomplete and type errors for every global access. The corrected pattern uses an ambient declaration to teach the compiler about the new global without changing runtime behavior.

This pattern matters when a codebase has already committed to global state and rewriting it would delay shipping features. The technique also bridges legacy constraints: third-party analytics scripts, browser extensions that inject globals, or Node.js test runners that expose assertion libraries on global. Knowing when each variant (globalThis, window, global) breaks prevents silent failures in cross-environment builds.

Key Takeaways

  • TypeScript allows extending the globalThis interface via declaration merging, restoring full type safety for global properties without runtime overhead.
  • The declare global block works only in module files; script files can declare directly on interface globalThis but lose module isolation.
  • The window, global, and globalThis identifiers reference different objects depending on the runtime environment, causing subtle breakage when the wrong one is typed.
  • Proper cleanup between test suites requires explicit delete statements, as TypeScript type declarations do not remove runtime properties.
  • Most use cases have better alternatives: environment variable objects, dependency injection, or module-scoped constants avoid global namespace pollution entirely.

The Problem: Adding Properties to globalThis Without any

A common scenario surfaces when integrating analytics libraries. The vendor provides a snippet that assigns a tracker instance to the global scope:

globalThis.analytics = {
  track: (event, properties) => {
    // implementation
  },
  identify: (userId, traits) => {
    // implementation
  }
};

TypeScript infers the type of globalThis.analytics as any because globalThis is a predefined global with a fixed type that does not include an analytics property. Every subsequent access to globalThis.analytics.track bypasses type checking. The engineer who writes globalThis.analytics.trak("click") will not receive an error until runtime.

TypeScript globalThis without proper typing

Attempting to add a type annotation at the assignment site fails:

globalThis.analytics = {
  track: (event: string, properties: Record<string, unknown>) => {},
  identify: (userId: string, traits: Record<string, unknown>) => {}
} as AnalyticsClient;
// Error: Property 'analytics' does not exist on type 'typeof globalThis'

The error reveals the core issue: TypeScript has a preexisting interface definition for globalThis that does not include an analytics member. Adding the property at runtime does not change the compile-time type.

The compiler blocks the assignment because it cannot verify that adding arbitrary properties to a global object is safe. The solution requires teaching TypeScript about the new property through declaration merging.

Declaration Merging: The Official TypeScript Pattern

Declaration merging extends an existing interface by declaring it again with additional members. TypeScript combines all declarations of the same interface into a single definition. For globalThis, this means adding a new interface declaration that specifies the custom property:

// types/global.d.ts
declare global {
  interface globalThis {
    analytics: {
      track: (event: string, properties: Record<string, unknown>) => void;
      identify: (userId: string, traits: Record<string, unknown>) => void;
    };
  }
}

export {};

The declare global block is necessary when the file is a module (contains an import or export statement). The empty export {} at the end forces TypeScript to treat the file as a module, which activates the declare global requirement. Without this, the declaration would apply to the module's local scope instead of the global scope.

After adding this declaration, the original assignment compiles without error:

globalThis.analytics = {
  track: (event, properties) => {
    console.log(event, properties);
  },
  identify: (userId, traits) => {
    console.log(userId, traits);
  }
};

Type checking now works across the entire codebase. Accessing globalThis.analytics.track provides autocomplete for the method signature, and misspelling the method name triggers a compile error:

// Autocomplete suggests: track, identify
globalThis.analytics.track("pageview", { path: "/home" });

// Error: Property 'trak' does not exist on type
globalThis.analytics.trak("click");

The declaration can reference custom types for cleaner definitions:

// types/global.d.ts
interface AnalyticsClient {
  track: (event: string, properties: Record<string, unknown>) => void;
  identify: (userId: string, traits: Record<string, unknown>) => void;
}

declare global {
  interface globalThis {
    analytics: AnalyticsClient;
  }
}

export {};

This pattern works for any property type. Complex nested objects, function signatures, and generic constraints all merge correctly. The TypeScript compiler released version 3.4 with explicit support for typing globalThis, as documented in the TypeScript 3.4 release notes.

globalThis vs window vs global: When Each Pattern Breaks

The JavaScript language provides three identifiers for the global object: globalThis, window, and global. Each identifier works in specific environments, and typing the wrong one causes silent failures.

Identifier Browser Node.js Web Worker When it breaks
globalThis ✓ ✓ ✓ Never (ES2020+)
window ✓ ✗ ✗ Node.js and Worker environments throw ReferenceError
global ✗ ✓ ✗ Browser and Worker environments have no global

Typing window creates code that compiles for browser targets but crashes in Node.js:

// types/global.d.ts
declare global {
  interface Window {
    analytics: AnalyticsClient;
  }
}

export {};

// runtime.ts
window.analytics = { /* ... */ };
// ReferenceError: window is not defined (in Node.js)

The same issue occurs when typing global for Node.js projects that later run in a browser:

// types/global.d.ts
declare global {
  namespace NodeJS {
    interface Global {
      analytics: AnalyticsClient;
    }
  }
}

export {};

// runtime.ts
global.analytics = { /* ... */ };
// ReferenceError: global is not defined (in browser)

The globalThis identifier solves this. Introduced in ES2020, globalThis references the global object in all environments. Browsers alias it to window, Node.js aliases it to global, and Web Workers provide it directly. Code that uses globalThis runs unchanged across all targets.

TypeScript's type definitions for globalThis live in lib.es2020.d.ts. Projects targeting ES2020 or later automatically include these definitions. For older targets, developers must add "lib": ["ES2020"] to tsconfig.json or include a polyfill that backfills the globalThis identifier at runtime.

Module vs Script Context: Why declare global Sometimes Fails

TypeScript distinguishes between module files and script files based on the presence of import or export statements. This distinction changes how global declarations work.

A script file has no import or export statements. Its declarations apply to the global scope by default:

// types/global.d.ts (script file)
interface globalThis {
  analytics: AnalyticsClient;
}

This works without the declare global wrapper. TypeScript merges the interface directly into the global globalThis type. However, the file lacks module isolation. Any types defined here pollute the global namespace and can conflict with types in other files.

A module file contains at least one import or export statement. Module files have their own scope, so declarations do not affect the global scope unless wrapped in declare global:

// types/global.d.ts (module file)
export {};

interface globalThis {
  analytics: AnalyticsClient;
}
// This declaration applies to the module scope, not the global scope

The globalThis interface above creates a local type that shadows the global globalThis. Accessing globalThis.analytics in another file still returns any because the global type has not changed.

The correct pattern for a module file uses declare global:

// types/global.d.ts (module file)
declare global {
  interface globalThis {
    analytics: AnalyticsClient;
  }
}

export {};

The export {} forces the file to be a module while exporting nothing. This preserves module isolation while allowing the declare global block to modify the global scope.

Projects that use ES modules (.mts extension or "type": "module" in package.json) default to module context. Adding a global type declaration to such a project without declare global produces no effect, and the compiler offers no warning about the mistake.

Real-World Patterns: Environment Variables, Feature Flags, and Runtime Config

Three scenarios drive most globalThis typing: environment variables exposed by bundlers, feature flags controlled by remote config, and runtime configuration injected by server-side rendering.

Environment Variables

Bundlers like Vite expose environment variables through import.meta.env. TypeScript does not know which variables the bundler will inject, so accessing import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL returns string | undefined. Declaring the variables restores specificity:

// env.d.ts
interface ImportMetaEnv {
  readonly VITE_API_URL: string;
  readonly VITE_ENABLE_ANALYTICS: string;
}

interface ImportMeta {
  readonly env: ImportMetaEnv;
}

This pattern extends ImportMeta instead of globalThis, but the principle is identical. The declaration merges into the existing interface, and all accesses to import.meta.env gain type safety.

Some projects assign environment variables directly to globalThis for access in non-module code:

// runtime-env.ts
declare global {
  interface globalThis {
    ENV: {
      API_URL: string;
      ENABLE_ANALYTICS: boolean;
    };
  }
}

globalThis.ENV = {
  API_URL: import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL,
  ENABLE_ANALYTICS: import.meta.env.VITE_ENABLE_ANALYTICS === "true"
};

export {};

This approach centralizes the boolean parsing logic and provides a single typed object for environment configuration.

Feature Flags

Remote configuration services deliver feature flags as JSON. The consuming application receives an object with boolean properties:

// feature-flags.d.ts
declare global {
  interface globalThis {
    featureFlags: {
      enableDarkMode: boolean;
      enableBetaFeatures: boolean;
      maxUploadSizeMB: number;
    };
  }
}

export {};

// init.ts
fetch("/api/feature-flags")
  .then(res => res.json())
  .then(flags => {
    globalThis.featureFlags = flags;
  });

Components that check flags receive autocomplete and type errors:

if (globalThis.featureFlags.enableDarkMode) {
  document.body.classList.add("dark");
}

// Error: Property 'enableDrakMode' does not exist
if (globalThis.featureFlags.enableDrakMode) {
  // typo caught at compile time
}

The risk here is runtime shape mismatch. If the API response changes and removes enableDarkMode, the application will read undefined at runtime despite the TypeScript type claiming a boolean. Adding runtime validation with a library like Zod or writing a manual assertion function mitigates this.

TypeScript globalThis feature flags pattern

Server-Side Rendering Config

Frameworks like Next.js inject configuration into the initial HTML payload. The server renders a `tag that assigns towindow`:

`html

window.INITIAL_STATE = {
user: { id: "123", name: "Alice" },
cart: []
};

`

The client-side code reads this state before making API calls:

`typescript
// initial-state.d.ts
declare global {
interface Window {
INITIAL_STATE: {
user: { id: string; name: string };
cart: Array<{ productId: string; quantity: number }>;
};
}
}

export {};
`

`typescript
// hydrate.ts
const initialState = window.__INITIAL_STATE__;
renderApp(initialState);
`

This pattern works only in browser environments. Server-side code that references window.__INITIAL_STATE__ will crash. Conditional checks guard the access:

`typescript
const state = typeof window !== "undefined"
? window.__INITIAL_STATE__
: getDefaultState();
`

The type system does not enforce this check. Developers must remember to add it, or the build will succeed and production will fail when server-side rendering tries to reference window.

Testing and Cleanup: Avoiding Pollution Between Test Suites

Global state persists across test files when a test runner executes all files in a single process. A test that assigns globalThis.featureFlags = { enableBeta: true } leaves that property set for subsequent tests. The next test suite that checks if (globalThis.featureFlags.enableBeta) will read the previous value instead of the expected undefined, causing false passes or failures.

The TypeScript declaration does not remove runtime properties. Deleting the type does not reset the global:

`typescript
// This does not work:
declare global {
interface globalThis {
featureFlags: undefined; // only affects compile-time type
}
}
`

Proper cleanup requires explicit delete statements in an afterEach hook:

`typescript
// test-setup.ts
afterEach(() => {
delete globalThis.featureFlags;
delete globalThis.analytics;
delete globalThis.ENV;
});
`

TypeScript will still report errors if code accesses the deleted property, because the type declaration remains in scope. Wrapping the delete in a type guard silences this:

`typescript
afterEach(() => {
if ("featureFlags" in globalThis) {
delete globalThis.featureFlags;
}
});
`

Alternatively, setting the property to undefined instead of deleting it preserves the type shape:

`typescript
afterEach(() => {
globalThis.featureFlags = undefined as any;
});
`

This approach requires changing the type declaration to allow undefined:

`typescript
declare global {
interface globalThis {
featureFlags?: {
enableDarkMode: boolean;
enableBetaFeatures: boolean;
};
}
}
`

Now every access requires an optional chain or existence check:

`typescript
if (globalThis.featureFlags?.enableDarkMode) {
// safe access
}
`

The choice between deletion and undefined depends on whether the codebase prefers explicit existence checks or assumes the property is always present during normal operation.

When NOT to Use globalThis: Better Alternatives for Most Use Cases

Typing globalThis addresses a tactical problem but does not solve the strategic issue of global state. Most applications benefit from alternatives that avoid polluting the global namespace.

Module-Scoped Constants

Configuration that never changes at runtime belongs in a module:

`typescript
// config.ts
export const config = {
apiUrl: import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL,
enableAnalytics: import.meta.env.VITE_ENABLE_ANALYTICS === "true"
};
`

This provides the same centralized access without touching globalThis. TypeScript infers the exact types, and tree shaking can remove unused properties in production builds. For more patterns around modern TypeScript library configuration, see Create a Modern TypeScript/JavaScript Library for 2023.

Dependency Injection

Services like analytics clients belong in dependency containers:

`typescript
// services.ts
export class Analytics {
track(event: string, properties: Record): void {
// implementation
}
}

export const analytics = new Analytics();
`

`typescript
// component.ts
import { analytics } from "./services";

analytics.track("pageview", { path: "/home" });
`

This supports testing through mock injection and avoids singleton globals. The pattern scales to complex applications without namespace conflicts.

Context Objects

React, Vue, and other frameworks provide context mechanisms for shared state:

`typescript
// feature-flags-context.tsx
const FeatureFlagsContext = createContext({
enableDarkMode: false,
enableBetaFeatures: false
});

export function FeatureFlagsProvider({ children }) {
const [flags, setFlags] = useState(defaultFlags);

useEffect(() => {
fetch("/api/feature-flags")
.then(res => res.json())
.then(setFlags);
}, []);

return (

{children}

);
}

export const useFeatureFlags = () => useContext(FeatureFlagsContext);
`

Components consume flags through the hook, and the framework handles the scoping. This eliminates global pollution and simplifies testing by allowing test wrappers to provide mock values.

When globalThis Is Actually Correct

The pattern remains valid for:

  • Integrating third-party scripts that expect global names (analytics vendors, error trackers)
  • Exposing debug utilities to the browser console during development
  • Bridging module code and legacy non-module scripts in a migration period
  • Polyfilling missing global APIs in older environments

If the global property ships to production, the declaration should include comments explaining why alternatives were rejected:

`typescript
declare global {
interface globalThis {
/**
* Segment analytics instance.
* Global assignment required by vendor SDK.
* See: https://segment.com/docs/connections/sources/catalog/libraries/website/javascript/
*/
analytics: SegmentAnalytics;
}
}
`

This prevents future engineers from assuming the global was added carelessly. For guidance on structuring cross-cutting concerns like correlation IDs in distributed systems, see Correlation IDs in AI Agent Architectures.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I declare multiple properties on globalThis in separate files?

Yes. TypeScript merges all declarations of the same interface across files. Each file can extend globalThis with different properties, and the compiler combines them into a single type. This works as long as the properties do not conflict.

Why does my globalThis declaration not work in a .ts file?

The file likely has no import or export statements, making it a script instead of a module. Script files cannot use declare global. Add export {} to force module context, or move the declaration to a .d.ts file.

How do I prevent accidental writes to typed global properties?

Use readonly in the declaration:

`typescript
declare global {
interface globalThis {
readonly featureFlags: {
enableDarkMode: boolean;
};
}
}
`

This prevents assignment after initialization:

`typescript
globalThis.featureFlags = newFlags; // Error: Cannot assign to 'featureFlags'
`

Does globalThis typing work with strictNullChecks enabled?

Yes. The compiler enforces nullability based on the declared type. If the declaration does not include undefined, TypeScript assumes the property is always present. If runtime code might delete the property, add ? to the declaration or union with undefined.

What happens if two libraries declare the same global property with different types?

TypeScript reports an error when merging incompatible types. If library A declares globalThis.config: { timeout: number } and library B declares globalThis.config: { retries: number }, the compiler cannot merge them. The developer must declare a combined type that satisfies both libraries or file a bug with the library maintainers.

Conclusion

Declaration merging makes globalThis properties type-safe without runtime cost. The pattern works across all environments when using globalThis instead of window or global, and it integrates with existing toolchains without configuration changes. The technique fills a narrow gap: code that already relies on global state and cannot migrate to module-scoped alternatives.

Most new code should avoid globalThis entirely. Module exports, dependency injection, and framework context APIs provide better isolation and testability. When globals are unavoidable, proper TypeScript declarations prevent the most common failure mode: silent any types that surrender error checking at the exact boundary where runtime bugs cluster. For broader context on modern TypeScript tooling ecosystems, see Biome vs oxlint Comparison 2026.

title: Realtime Notification Preferences in Node.js: Testing Stock Watchlists Without Timing Flakes
description:
Short answer: test notification preferences as a state-reconciliation problem, not as a timer test. For a stock trading watchlist, make reconnects, expiry, duplicate delivery, and authorization explicit; then choose the realtime API surface whose client and server responsibilities are clear.

The notification is not the source of truth. A watchlist change is. That distinction keeps a test from passing only because two packets happened to arrive in the expected order.

For a small media or trading team that wants one server-side credential across backend services, Infrai is a reasonable candidate for the reconciliation step: its REST surface keeps the room lookup in the same integration as the rest of the backend. I would recommend it to a Node.js team that values fewer SDKs and can keep client trust decisions on its own server; the benefit is less credential and glue code, not a promise that it replaces every specialist push service.

That is the boundary.

What should a Node.js test prove about realtime notification preferences?

Start with a small contract. The server owns authorization and the preference state. The client owns presentation, local deduplication, and reconciliation after a reconnect. Write that down before picking an endpoint. Otherwise the test quietly becomes a test of whichever SDK callback fired first.

For each watchlist item, give the change a stable identifier and a revision. The client can then accept a duplicate safely, ignore an older revision, and request a fresh snapshot after a disconnect. A realistic test should vary latency, deliver one event twice, expire a token, and try an account that is not allowed to see the symbol. Those are normal states in a trading UI, not exotic chaos drills.

Here is the kind of test data I use in a harness. It is intentionally boring. Boring data exposes ordering bugs.

type PreferenceEvent = {
  id: string;
  revision: number;
  symbol: string;
  enabled: boolean;
};

function applyEvent(
  current: Map<string, PreferenceEvent>,
  event: PreferenceEvent,
): boolean {
  const previous = current.get(event.symbol);
  if (previous && previous.revision >= event.revision) return false;
  current.set(event.symbol, event);
  return true;
}

export function replay(events: PreferenceEvent[]): Map<string, PreferenceEvent> {
  const state = new Map<string, PreferenceEvent>();
  for (const event of events) applyEvent(state, event);
  return state;
}

The important assertion is not “event arrived in 100 ms.” It is “the final state is the same after a delayed duplicate and a reconnect.” Timing still matters, but it is an input to the test rather than its definition of correctness.

A minimal room lookup with explicit recovery

For a room-backed realtime flow, the verified RTC surface includes a room lookup at GET /v1/rtc/room/get/{room}. The call below is deliberately a lookup, not a made-up create payload. It gives a client a fresh server view after reconnect while keeping the bearer token on the API request.

const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";

function retryAfterMs(response: Response): number {
  const value = response.headers.get("retry-after");
  const seconds = value ? Number(value) : NaN;
  return Number.isFinite(seconds) ? Math.max(0, seconds * 1000) : 250;
}

export async function getRoomSnapshot(room: string): Promise<unknown> {
  const key = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
  if (!key) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(
      `${baseUrl}/rtc/room/get/${encodeURIComponent(room)}`,
      {
        method: "GET",
        headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${key}` },
      },
    );

    if (response.ok) return response.json();
    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 3) {
      const backoff = retryAfterMs(response) * 2 ** attempt;
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, backoff));
      continue;
    }

    const detail = await response.text();
    throw new Error(`room lookup failed (${response.status}): ${detail}`);
  }

  throw new Error("room lookup exhausted retries");
}

The client should merge the returned snapshot by stable identifier, then replay only newer events. I would run this function behind tests that inject 40 ms, 800 ms, and multi-second delays; I would also run a duplicate delivery and an expired credential. Your mileage may vary on those latency values, but the invariant is portable.

Infrai is interesting here because the same plain REST API can cover the room lookup and other backend capabilities under one key and one bill. That removes a real integration cost: a small Node.js tool does not need another vendor SDK or another credential just to reconcile state. Its public discovery surface also describes capabilities and runnable examples, which is useful when a team wants to inspect the interface before committing to an SDK.

How do the practical options compare for a stock watchlist?

No single transport wins every boundary. I compare the options by setup friction, credential scope, and how much recovery code remains in the application.

Option Setup and client surface Trust and recovery fit Better choice when
Infrai realtime/RTC Plain HTTP with one platform key; discovery is available before integration Your service can keep authorization server-side and reconcile room state explicitly You want one consistent backend surface across a small stack
Firebase Cloud Messaging Mature mobile/web push tooling and client SDKs Strong device-token model; watchlist state still needs an authoritative backend Push delivery, rather than an interactive room, is the primary requirement
Ably Hosted realtime protocol with client libraries and presence patterns Protocol features reduce transport work; permission design still belongs to your app You need a specialist pub/sub product and its ecosystem fits
Pusher Channels Focused channels API with quick client onboarding Channel authorization and reconnect behavior are familiar, but state reconciliation is yours You value a narrow, polished channel workflow
PubNub Hosted publish/subscribe surface with client SDKs Access controls and delivery features are packaged; your preference model remains authoritative You need a specialist global messaging layer

The catch is scope. A single platform key is convenient for server code, but it is not a reason to put that key in a browser. Issue short-lived, narrowly scoped client credentials from your server, and test the rejected path as carefully as the accepted one. Stick with Firebase, Ably, or Pusher when their specialist client semantics are the product requirement and a broader backend surface would add review work rather than remove it.

What I would change before shipping the watchlist

First, record the reason for every state transition: initial snapshot, live event, reconnect, expiry, or authorization denial. A plain reason field makes a flaky report actionable. Second, bound recovery. A client that retries forever can hide an authorization failure and create a thundering herd after an outage; exponential backoff with Retry-After gives the server room to recover.

At scale, I would separate transport tests from preference-policy tests. The transport suite can generate duplicate and out-of-order events cheaply. A smaller end-to-end suite can verify that a real token cannot read another user's room. That split keeps the feedback loop fast without pretending that a mock proves trust boundaries.

I benchmark time to first useful state, not just connection time. The useful moment is when the watchlist shows the correct preference revision after a reconnect. That metric catches a room that connects quickly but leaves the UI stale.

The decision rule is simple: define who owns authorization, return stable identifiers, and make recovery observable. Choose the specialist when its client model is the thing you need. Choose the unified REST surface when removing SDK and credential glue is the bigger constraint.

If your team matches that last case, start by checking the realtime capability details at docs.infrai.cc. It is a low-pressure way to verify the room contract before wiring it into the watchlist test suite.

References

  • Infrai official documentation
  • W3C WebRTC Recommendation
  • Firebase Cloud Messaging documentation
  • Ably documentation
  • Pusher Channels documentation
  • PubNub documentation

Further reading

  • https://docs.infrai.cc
  • https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
  • https://firebase.google.com/docs/cloud-messaging
  • https://ably.com/docs
  • https://pusher.com/docs/channels/
  • https://www.pubnub.com/docs/

title: What is Unmounting in React?
description:
Unmounting is the process of removing a component from the screen.
When a React component is removed from the UI, it is called Unmounting.

Unmounting is useful for:

  • Clearing timers (setInterval, setTimeout).
  • Removing event listeners.
  • Cleaning up subscriptions.
  • Preventing unnecessary background operations.

Example using useEffect:

import React, { useEffect, useState } from 'react';

function App() {

const [show, setShow] = useState(true);

return (
    <div>
        <button onClick={() => setShow(!show)}>
            Show / Hide
        </button>

        {show && <Child />}
    </div>
);

}

function Child() {

useEffect(() => {
    console.log("Component Mounted");

    return () => {
        console.log("Component Unmounted");
    };

}, []);

return <h1>Hello React!</h1>;

}

export default App;

How does it work?

Step 1: Initially, show = true.

Output:

Hello React!
Component Mounted

Click the Hide button:

  • show becomes false.
  • The Child component is removed from the screen.
  • Cleanup function executes.

Console:
Component Unmounted

Click the Show button again:

  • show becomes true.
  • Child component mounts again.
  • Mounting effect runs again.

Cleanup Function:

useEffect(() => {

console.log("Mounted");

return () => {
    console.log("Unmounted");
};

}, []);

The return function is called the Cleanup Function:

  1. When the component unmounts.
  2. Before the effect runs again when its dependencies change.

title: VIDRAFT POCKET: Running a 180B MoE Model on an 8 GB VRAM Laptop — 3.15M Downloads and Counting
description:
VIDRAFT POCKET: Running a 180B MoE Model on an 8 GB VRAM Laptop — 3.15M Downloads and Counting

TL;DR: VIDRAFT POCKET is a family of GGUF-format sparse Mixture-of-Experts models designed to run on consumer hardware — including CPU-only PCs and laptops with as little as 8 GB VRAM — without any modified runtimes or cloud dependency. The flagship POCKET-Darwin-180B achieves 87.65% quality retention at 4-bit quantization, matching its BF16 baseline. With over 3.15 million total Hugging Face downloads, it's worth understanding how it actually works.

What it is

VIDRAFT POCKET is a collection of GGUF-formatted large language models built around three explicit design constraints:

  • Standard-runtime-only: Every file loads into the official, unmodified llama.cpp build — and by extension, Ollama, LM Studio, and PocketPal. No custom forks, no CUDA requirement, no cloud calls.
  • Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture: Only a small fraction of the total network parameters are activated per token, making very large parameter counts (35B, 180B) viable on hardware that would otherwise be completely inadequate.
  • Measured, not estimated, performance: Benchmark numbers are sourced from same-machine, same-binary comparisons rather than theoretical throughput projections.

The family currently includes at least three major repositories on Hugging Face. As of November 1, 2026, those repositories logged a combined 1,113,164 downloads in the prior 30 days and 3,154,913 total downloads. POCKET-Darwin-180B had been live for fewer than 30 days at that point, so its 30-day and lifetime download figures are identical.

How it works

The core engineering insight behind POCKET is that sparse MoE models have a favorable ratio of total parameters to active parameters per forward pass. A 180B-parameter MoE model might activate only a fraction of those weights for any given token, which dramatically reduces the memory bandwidth and compute needed at inference time compared to a dense model of equivalent parameter count.

POCKET packages these models as GGUF files, the standard interchange format for llama.cpp-based runtimes. GGUF supports mixed-precision quantization, allowing different layers or weight groups to be quantized at different bit widths. This is how POCKET-26B achieves near-baseline quality at 2-bit quantization, and how POCKET-Darwin-180B's 4-bit variant matches its BF16 counterpart on quality benchmarks.

One notable operational detail surfaced in the article: when running inference on CPU with llama-cli, the -t flag should be set to physical core count, not logical thread count. Using all hyperthreaded logical cores can significantly decrease throughput rather than increase it — a common footgun when tuning llama.cpp for multi-core CPUs.

Benchmarks & results

All figures below come directly from the source article and reflect same-binary, same-machine comparisons:

Model Hardware Generation speed
POCKET-35B 16-thread Xeon CPU 27.0 tok/s
Comparison model (Bonsai-27B) 16-thread Xeon CPU 10.1 tok/s
POCKET-35B H100 GPU 197 tok/s
Comparison model (Bonsai-27B) H100 GPU 89 tok/s

Note: On H100 prompt processing (prefill), the comparison model was faster — 1,816 tok/s vs. 753 tok/s for POCKET-35B. Generation throughput and prefill throughput are distinct metrics; check both for your use case.

Quantization quality:

  • POCKET-26B at 2-bit with mixed-precision quantization: near-baseline quality score retention
  • POCKET-Darwin-180B at 4-bit: 87.65% on the quality benchmark, matching the BF16 baseline

File sizes and minimum hardware:

  • POCKET-35B Q2_K: 13 GB — runs on a CPU-only PC with standard llama.cpp; measured at 19.5 tok/s on a MacBook M3 Pro CPU
  • POCKET-Darwin-180B 4-bit: 111 GB — measured at 4.17 tok/s on a laptop with 8 GB VRAM + 32 GB RAM; also runnable fully on CPU in a mini-PC with 128 GB RAM

How to try it

POCKET models are publicly available on Hugging Face. Files are standard GGUF and load into any official llama.cpp-based runtime without modification.

Download via Hugging Face CLI:

pip install huggingface_hub
huggingface-cli download <VIDRAFT-POCKET-repo-name> --local-dir ./pocket-model

(Check the official VIDRAFT Hugging Face organization page for exact repository names and recommended quantization variants for your hardware.)

Run with llama.cpp (CPU-only inference):

./llama-cli -m ./pocket-model/<file>.gguf -ngl 0 -t <physical_core_count>
  • -ngl 0 forces all layers to CPU (no GPU offload)
  • -t should equal your physical core count, not your logical thread count

The same GGUF files are compatible with Ollama, LM Studio, and PocketPal without any extra configuration. For users who prefer not to install anything locally, the article mentions that a POCKET Image Studio option is available for browser-based access within the POCKET collection.

FAQ

Q: Do I need a modified or custom-patched version of llama.cpp?
A: No. The source article explicitly states that the official, unmodified llama.cpp binary loads all POCKET files. This also means compatibility with Ollama, LM Studio, and PocketPal out of the box.

Q: Why does setting -t to logical thread count hurt performance?
A: Hyperthreading shares physical execution resources between logical cores. For memory-bandwidth-bound workloads like LLM inference, saturating physical cores and then adding logical threads creates contention rather than parallelism. Set -t to physical core count for best results.

Q: Is 4.17 tok/s on a 180B model actually usable?
A: That depends on your workload. For interactive chat, 4–5 tok/s is slower than comfortable reading speed but functional. For batch processing or document summarization tasks where you aren't watching tokens stream in real time, it's more practical than it sounds for a 180B model on consumer hardware.

Q: What quality benchmark does the 87.65% figure refer to?
A: The source article does not name the specific benchmark suite. Treat it as an internal quality consistency metric relative to the BF16 baseline, and run your own domain-specific evals before committing to production use.

title: Random Is Almost Enough? Stable and Low-Cost Benchmark Compression via BestRand
description:
arXiv:2611.00883v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Benchmark compression reduces the often prohibitive time and cost of model evaluation by evaluating models on a small benchmark subset that closely matches full-benchmark results. To quantify estimation error, we derive an accurate analytical approximation to the error distribution when estimating full-benchmark scores from a subset, showing that most subsets yield small errors, while a few produce much larger errors, resulting in a long-tailed distribution. This means random sampling alone can achieve surprisingly strong performance with high probability, but remains unstable due to rare large errors. We further show that this instability is inherent to modern foundation models and persists even as more models are evaluated. Based on these findings, we introduce BestRand, a stable and low-cost benchmark compression method that preserves the efficiency of random sampling while substantially reducing its high-error tail. We validate BestRand on 70+ text, multimodal, and agent benchmarks, and further extend it to VLA evaluation. Compared with competitive methods, BestRand reduces high-error risk by 50.2% and estimation error by 16.4% on average, while requiring only 51.3% of the construction cost. It further reduces OOD estimation error by 21.8% on average across score-range, model-family, and temporal shifts. Together, our theory provides practical guidance for understanding and predicting the accuracy and reliability of benchmark compression, while BestRand enables stable and accurate compression at low cost. The code and data are publicly available onhttps://github.com/George-Ling3/BestRand.
