title: Free AWS Security Assessment Toolkit: 42 Checks, a Local GUI, and Client-Ready HTML Reports
description:
An engineering walkthrough of a lightweight read-only AWS security assessment toolkit with 42 controls, CLI, local dashboard, baseline diff, suppressions, and self-contained HTML reporting

There is a classic trap in cloud security: looking at a green dashboard and deciding that "AWS is secure."

I do not work that way. When I start an AWS security assessment, I first want fast, boring answers to boring questions:

**- Is MFA enabled for the root user?

  • Do root access keys exist?
  • Are there IAM users without MFA?
  • Have access keys been living forever?
  • Is SSH or RDP open to the internet?
  • Are S3 buckets public?
  • Is encryption enabled where I expect it?
  • Are CloudTrail and AWS Config configured?
  • Are GuardDuty, Security Hub, and Inspector actually enabled?
  • Do EC2 instances require IMDSv2?
  • Do RDS and DynamoDB have reasonable recovery controls?
  • Is an EKS API endpoint accepting 0.0.0.0/0?
  • Has ordinary cloud hygiene debt started piling up?**

This is not sexy zero-day research. It is plumbing. But a surprising amount of real-world security posture is built from exactly this plumbing.

That is why I built an AWS Security Assessment Toolkit, a small read-only tool for the first technical pass over an AWS account.

It grew out of consulting work I was doing through Bulwark Advisory, but this article is not a services pitch. It is an engineering walkthrough: what I wanted to automate, why I did not try to build another giant CSPM, where automation helps, and where a human still has to think.

At the time of writing, this article describes toolkit v2.0.0.

TL;DR

If you are short on time, here is the whole idea.

The toolkit performs a point-in-time AWS posture assessment through read-only APIs.
The current release includes:

  • 42 controls;
  • one assessment engine shared by CLI and local GUI;
  • cross-account scanning through STS AssumeRole;
  • baseline/diff support;
  • suppressions and waivers with reasons and expiration;
  • Console, JSON, Markdown, HTML, CSV, SARIF, and JUnit outputs;
  • a self-contained client-facing HTML report;
  • scheduled-run support for drift detection;
  • no automatic remediation of target resources.

And the most important caveat:

42 PASS results do not mean "AWS is secure." They mean that 42 specific checks, in a specific scope, returned those results at a specific point in time.

That principle shaped most of the design.

New to cloud security? Five terms in sixty seconds

A little vocabulary before we go deeper.

Security posture

The current state of security-relevant configuration. Is a Security Group open? Is encryption enabled? Is an audit trail present?
Control

One concrete rule we evaluate. For example: "The root user should have MFA."
Finding

The result of evaluating a control. A finding contains status, severity, resource context, evidence, and remediation guidance.
Baseline

A saved result from an earlier assessment. It gives us something stable to compare against.
Drift

A configuration change relative to that baseline. Drift can be good, bad, or neutral.
CSPM

Cloud Security Posture Management, the category of products and services that continuously or periodically evaluate cloud configuration, standards, and misconfigurations.

In plain English, this toolkit is closer to a building inspection than a break-in attempt.

A pentest asks:

"Can I get through the window?"

A posture assessment first asks:

"Is the window even closed?"

Where the project started

I liked the core idea: understandable read-only boto3 checks, very little magic, and a fast point-in-time result.

For my own workflow, I wanted more:

  • a modular architecture;
  • a control registry;
  • one normalized finding model;
  • broader AWS coverage;
  • cross-account assessment;
  • baseline and diff support;
  • documented suppressions;
  • CI-friendly outputs;
  • a local GUI;
  • client-ready HTML;
  • and a hard read-only boundary.

Over time, the seed became a separate toolkit.

The problem I actually wanted to solve

The AWS Shared Responsibility Model separates security of the cloud from security in the cloud.

The "in the cloud" part gets interesting fast. AWS can secure the physical infrastructure perfectly while the customer still has:

  • overly permissive IAM;
  • public buckets;
  • Security Groups open to 0.0.0.0/0;
  • weak logging coverage;
  • missing recovery controls;
  • long-lived credentials;
  • unused keys;
  • poorly scoped public endpoints.

The AWS Well-Architected Security Pillar emphasizes a strong identity foundation, traceability, defense in depth, automation of security best practices, and protection of data.

This is exactly where configuration assessment is useful as a first filter. AWS Security Hub CSPM already evaluates environments against standards such as AWS Foundational Security Best Practices and CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark. I treat those as important reference points for control design, not as competitors that my tool needs to "beat."

My requirement was narrower:

I wanted a portable first-pass scanner that I understand end to end, can adapt to an assessment workflow, can run under a read-only role, and can turn into a useful deliverable.

What the toolkit checks today

Version 2.0.0 registers 42 controls across ten categories:

Area Examples
Identity root MFA, root keys, console MFA, access-key age, Access Analyzer
Data Protection S3/EBS/RDS/SQS encryption, S3 public access
Network SSH/RDP exposure, risky ports, default SGs, VPC Flow Logs, CloudFront HTTPS
Compute IMDSv2, EBS encryption by default, SSM coverage
Database RDS posture
Containers EKS endpoint exposure and logging
Serverless Lambda-related posture
Logging & Detection CloudTrail, Config, GuardDuty, Security Hub, Inspector, Macie
Resilience backups, PITR, versioning, deletion protection, Multi-AZ
Cost & Hygiene unattached EBS, unused Elastic IPs

These are not 42 vulnerability signatures and they are not 42 proofs of exploitability.

They are 42 deterministic posture checks.

For example, EC2-002 answers a narrow question:

Does this instance require IMDSv2?

It does not answer:

Could an attacker actually steal workload credentials through SSRF?

That requires application context and separate testing.

Why status semantics matter more than a red circle

I use five primary statuses:

Status Meaning
PASS The check ran and the control condition is satisfied
FAIL The check ran and the control condition is violated
WARN An advisory condition needs context
ERROR The state could not be verified reliably
SKIP The finding was intentionally waived/suppressed by policy

For both engineers and auditors, ERROR matters a lot.

If the scanner gets AccessDenied, that is not PASS.

If a service API is unavailable, that is not PASS.

If a Region was not assessed, that is not PASS.

Unknown should not magically become green.

Otherwise we get security theater with a really nice color palette.

Severity is not business risk

Another design rule I care about:

CRITICAL, HIGH, MEDIUM, and LOW are technical triage priorities in the toolkit.

They are not CVSS scores.

They are not final business-risk decisions.

Consider the same finding twice:

Security Group exposes TCP/22 to 0.0.0.0/0

Resource A:

Disposable training instance
No sensitive data
Automatically destroyed tonight

Resource B:

Production jump host
Privileged network path
Customer data environment

Same technical control.

Very different business risk.

So the workflow becomes:

Scanner severity
      |
      v
Technical validation
      |
      v
Asset / data / exposure context
      |
      v
Compensating controls
      |
      v
Likelihood + impact
      |
      v
Business priority

The scanner helps sort the queue. It does not replace the risk owner.

Scope: a green result without scope is almost useless

Before an assessment, I want to know at least:

  • which AWS account is in scope;
  • which principal performs the scan;
  • which Regions are covered;
  • which services are actually used;
  • which controls are enabled;
  • which controls are excluded;
  • which suppressions are applied;
  • when the scan runs.

Regions are especially important.

Some AWS resources are global, others are Regional. Some Regions are opt-in. Service availability also differs.

So the sentence:

"We scanned AWS."

does not tell me very much.

This is better:

"We ran toolkit v2.0.0 against account X, across all enabled/opted-in Regions, using this control set and this read-only role."

Now we have a reproducible technical statement.

Architecture: one engine, two interfaces

I did not want to build two scanners, one for a terminal and one for a pretty UI. The architecture looks roughly like this:

             AWS credential chain / optional AssumeRole
                              |
                              v
                    Assessment Context
                 account / regions / policy
                              |
                              v
                       Control Registry
                              |
                              v
                     Assessment Engine
                              |
                              v
                    Normalized Findings
                              |
                    Suppression Policy
                              |
                              v
                     AssessmentReport
                              |
        +---------+-----------+-----------+
        |         |           |           |
        v         v           v           v
       CLI       GUI         HTML      JSON/CSV/
                                      SARIF/JUnit

The CLI and GUI call the same Assessment Engine.

That gives me one source of truth for:

  • collection;
  • control logic;
  • statuses;
  • severity;
  • suppressions;
  • evidence;
  • reports.

Consistency in security tooling is boring. That is a compliment.

Read-only is a design constraint, not a marketing phrase

The toolkit is for assessment, not remediation. In the target account I expect inspection operations such as:

Get*
List*
Describe*

not:

Create*
Delete*
Modify*
Put*
Enable*
Disable*

There is one obvious exception: sts:AssumeRole. For cross-account consulting, temporary credentials are much cleaner than asking a customer for long-lived access keys.

The AWS managed SecurityAudit policy is explicitly described as useful for software that audits security configuration metadata, so it is a reasonable starting point for an assessment role.

I still do not treat a managed policy as magic. Optional services and a particular scope can require additional read permissions.

I test the read-only boundary at release time

The repository includes a release check that:

  • statically collects boto3 operations;
  • validates operations and paginators against the installed botocore model;
  • looks for obvious mutating API prefixes;
  • explicitly allows only the expected sts:AssumeRole exception.

This is not a mathematical proof. It is a practical regression guard. If somebody accidentally adds modify_* to the assessment path tomorrow, I would rather learn about it in CI than in a customer account.

Cross-account access and why External ID matters

A typical setup looks like this:

Assessor account / workstation
           |
           | sts:AssumeRole
           v
Customer SecurityAudit role
           |
           v
Customer AWS account

For example:

aws-sec-audit \
  --profile assessor \
  --role-arn arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/SecurityAudit \
  --external-id customer-123 \
  --all-regions

AWS recommends an External ID for third-party role access as a way to mitigate the confused deputy problem.

One detail that is easy to miss: the External ID is not a secret. Its purpose is different. It helps the target account constrain when the third party is allowed to assume that role on a particular customer's behalf. It is a small detail with a big impact on a clean consulting access model.

The CLI stayed

I like GUIs when I need to configure scope quickly or show results to somebody else. But automation without a CLI gets painful fast. A simple run still looks like:

aws-sec-audit --profile security-audit --all-regions

Focused controls:

aws-sec-audit \
  --include IAM-001,IAM-002,S3-001 \
  --regions eu-west-1,eu-central-1

Tag-based selection:

aws-sec-audit --tag encryption
aws-sec-audit --tag cis --tag public-access
aws-sec-audit --exclude-tag cost

That matters for CI, repeatability, and boring shell automation. Boring shell automation is underrated.

Then I built a GUI anyway

At some point I noticed that every customized run ended with me reopening the README:

Right, --all-regions, then --role-arn, then --tag, then baseline... what did I call that flag again?

That usually means the interface can be better.

So I built a Local Dashboard Edition.

Install and run:

python -m pip install ".[ui]"
aws-sec-audit-ui

By default it listens on:

http://127.0.0.1:8765

The browser does not ask for an AWS access key or secret key.

boto3 uses the normal credential provider chain:

  • AWS profiles;
  • AWS SSO-backed profiles;
  • environment/workload credentials;
  • optional AssumeRole.

A small security warning

127.0.0.1 is not a cosmetic default.

The dashboard can display:

  • account metadata;
  • resource names and ARNs;
  • evidence;
  • configuration details.

I do not treat the local UI as a ready-made multi-user web service. If it is ever exposed on a shared network, that becomes a different product requirement: authentication, TLS, authorization, tenant isolation, session/CSRF protection, and encrypted persistence.

Binding a local admin tool to 0.0.0.0 does not magically turn it into an enterprise portal. Unfortunately.

The dashboard is for triage, not dashboard-driven security

After a scan I want to understand quickly:

  • how many FAIL findings exist;
  • how many ERROR results indicate coverage gaps;
  • whether any CRITICAL/HIGH items are open;
  • which categories dominate;
  • which findings are new relative to the baseline;
  • which items deserve a human review first.

But the dashboard should never become a source of false confidence.
Green is a signal, not a magic amulet.

If the scope is incomplete, credentials are insufficient, or a relevant control does not exist, the color of the card will not save you.

A finding has to answer "what exactly?"

A weak scanner says:

FAIL: S3 is insecure

Okay. Now what?

A normalized finding in the toolkit contains:

control ID
title
status
severity
account
region
affected resources
evidence
remediation
references

At minimum, a finding should answer four questions:

  1. What is wrong?
  2. Where exactly is it?
  3. Why did the scanner reach that conclusion?
  4. What is a reasonable next action?

Evidence matters to me a lot. Without evidence, a finding turns into an opinion very quickly.

Suppressions: accepted risk should not disappear

Real environments always have exceptions. For example:

  • a public endpoint is public by design;
  • a resource is temporarily excluded;
  • a legacy workload is already being retired;
  • a compensating control changes the risk;
  • the risk was formally accepted;
  • remediation is already scheduled for the next sprint.

The bad implementation is to delete the finding. The slightly less bad implementation is to hide it so well that nobody remembers why.

I prefer a waiver that records:

  • control;
  • Region;
  • resource pattern;
  • reason;
  • optional expiration date.

A suppressed finding remains visible as SKIP, and the original evidence is retained. That helps different people in different ways.

A team lead asks:

"Who made this decision, and why?"

An auditor asks:

"Is there a traceable exception?"

Future you asks:

"Why on earth did we allow this three months ago?"

All three deserve an answer.

Baseline and diff: the second scan is more useful than the first

The first scan tells you:

What violates our controls right now?

The second tells you:

What changed?

For example:

Previous assessment
18 open findings

Current assessment
6 open findings

Resolved: 14
New:       2
Unchanged: 4

Now remediation conversations get much more concrete.

You can separate:

  • fixed;
  • new regression;
  • accepted;
  • still open.

Scheduled runs through cron, systemd, or CI can provide lightweight drift detection. But I do not call that real-time detection.

Polling every few hours answers:

"Has the posture changed since the last run?"

It does not answer:

"What happened twelve seconds ago, and who did it?"

For that, I want CloudTrail, EventBridge, GuardDuty, AWS Config, Security Hub, and an event-driven detection workflow. Do not make a posture scanner cosplay as a SIEM.

Point-in-time evidence is not operating effectiveness

This is one of the most important points from an auditor's perspective.

Suppose the toolkit reports:

CloudTrail enabled: PASS

What does that prove?

It proves that the observed configuration satisfied the control when the scan ran.

What does it not prove?

That CloudTrail was correctly enabled:

  • yesterday;
  • for the last 90 days;
  • through the entire audit period;
  • in every previously used Region;
  • without interruption.

That is the difference between point-in-time configuration evidence and evidence of operating effectiveness over time.

For historical evidence I would add sources such as:

  • AWS Config configuration history;
  • Security Hub finding history;
  • CloudTrail;
  • change tickets;
  • IaC history;
  • operational procedures.

AWS Config is specifically designed to retain configuration history after recording begins. Security Hub updates control findings through periodic or change-triggered checks.
So in a serious assessment I would never write:

"This scan proves that the control operated effectively all quarter."

It does not.

The HTML report is client-ready, not consultant-free

Raw JSON is wonderful. Especially if your client is also jq. Most clients are still human. That is why the toolkit can generate a self-contained HTML report:

aws-sec-audit \
  --all-regions \
  --format html \
  --output reports/aws-security-assessment.html

It includes:

  • executive summary;
  • scan metadata;
  • color-coded severity;
  • status counters;
  • category breakdown;
  • filters;
  • search;
  • affected resources;
  • evidence;
  • remediation;
  • references;
  • print-friendly styling.

The exported HTML is standalone. It does not need the dashboard afterward.

I still do not consider the generated report a final consulting opinion.
The scanner knows configuration.
It does not know:

  • why the workload exists;
  • what data it processes;
  • what the blast radius is;
  • which compensating controls are effective;
  • how much downtime is acceptable;
  • which "easy fix" will break production.

That is where the human part of an assessment begins.

Turning a finding into an action plan

A team lead does not need thirty red lines. They need a queue of work.
For example:

Finding Decision Owner Priority Target
Root without MFA Fix now Platform P0 Today
Public SSH to bastion Restrict CIDR / replace access model Cloud P1 3 days
S3 versioning disabled on dev bucket Accept temporarily App Team P3 Review next quarter
GuardDuty disabled Enable and integrate findings Security P1 This sprint

The flow looks more like:

Automated finding
       |
       v
Engineer validates
       |
       v
Business / architecture context
       |
       v
Remediation option
       |
       v
Owner + priority + target date
       |
       v
Re-scan / evidence of closure

Automation removes repetitive work. Ownership closes risk.

Those are different jobs.

Multiple reports from one scan

I deliberately separated collection from presentation.

One scan can produce multiple representations:

aws-sec-audit --all-regions \
  --export json=reports/report.json \
  --export html=reports/report.html \
  --export csv=reports/report.csv \
  --export junit=reports/junit.xml \
  --export sarif=reports/report.sarif

The toolkit currently supports:

  1. Console
  2. JSON
  3. Markdown
  4. HTML
  5. CSV
  6. SARIF
  7. JUnit XML

In practice, it means fewer repeated AWS API calls and less chance that two reports accidentally describe slightly different points in time.

What does "fast assessment" actually mean?

I can sometimes get a useful first picture within a couple of hours.

That does not mean:

"We fully proved AWS security in two hours."

It means something closer to:

  1. agree scope and credentials;
  2. run the automated posture pass;
  3. investigate ERROR results and coverage gaps;
  4. triage high-priority findings;
  5. manually validate the most important items;
  6. define the first remediation priorities.

It is a first pass.

It can tell you quickly whether the environment looks disciplined, has a handful of isolated gaps, or smells strongly of configuration debt.

The actual depth depends on:

  • number of accounts;
  • Regions;
  • resource volume;
  • architecture;
  • service mix;
  • permissions;
  • compliance requirements;
  • manual-validation needs.

Garbage in, garbage out applies to cloud security too. Give the scanner a half-blind role and you should expect a half-blind report.

Why not just Security Hub?

Security Hub CSPM is already an AWS-native service for ongoing posture management, standards, and control findings.

I am not trying to replace it. For continuous AWS governance, Security Hub is often a natural part of the architecture.

My toolkit solves a different problem:

  • portable assessment;
  • independent first pass;
  • local execution;
  • my normalized finding model;
  • custom scope;
  • client artifact;
  • fast re-scan after remediation.

Sometimes I compare both views.

If Security Hub says one thing and a direct API check says another, that is not a reason to pick your favorite dashboard. It is a reason to investigate scope, evaluation schedule, AWS Config recording coverage, and control semantics.

Why not just Prowler?

Prowler is a mature open-source cloud security platform with hundreds of AWS checks, multiple cloud providers, compliance frameworks, UI/API/CLI, and a large community.

If your requirement is a broad open-source CSPM, it absolutely belongs on the evaluation list. I built something different.

I wanted a tool that is:

  • small enough that I can understand the code path;
  • easy to modify for a specific assessment workflow;
  • local;
  • read-only;
  • infrastructure-light;
  • intentionally limited to an explainable control set;
  • aligned with my reporting flow.

This is not a "who has more checks" competition. Sometimes you need hundreds of controls. Sometimes you need the right forty, an architecture diagram, and an engineer willing to ask uncomfortable questions.

What a green dashboard does NOT mean

I would happily print this section next to every CSPM dashboard.
A PASS result does not prove that:

  • the application has no SQL injection;
  • no IAM attack path exists;
  • secrets have never leaked;
  • CloudTrail was not disabled yesterday;
  • Kubernetes workloads are secure;
  • the source code is vulnerability-free;
  • incident response is ready;
  • backups can actually be restored;
  • every relevant resource was in scope;
  • compensating controls operate exactly as described.

A posture scanner answers its controls. It does not answer every question in the security universe.

Where the toolkit sits in my assessment workflow

My AWS assessment looks more like this:

Scope / architecture
        |
        +--> AWS posture scan
        |
        +--> IAM / privilege review
        |
        +--> Network exposure
        |
        +--> Logging / detection
        |
        +--> Data protection
        |
        +--> Backup / recovery
        |
        +--> Application / API layer
        |
        +--> Manual validation
        |
        v
Risk prioritization
        |
        v
Action plan
        |
        v
Re-test

The toolkit covers part of posture and discovery.

It does not replace:

  • threat modeling;
  • penetration testing;
  • source-code review;
  • IAM privilege and attack-path analysis;
  • architecture review;
  • API/AppSec testing;
  • incident-readiness assessment;
  • backup restore testing;
  • interviews with engineering and security teams.

That is fine. A good tool does not need to pretend to be an entire security program.

What I intentionally did NOT add

Every security side project eventually starts whispering:

"Add an LLM. Add a database. Add auto-remediation. Add multi-tenancy. Add a Slack bot. And maybe blockchain?"

I stopped earlier.

The current design does not include:

  • automatic remediation;
  • hosted credential storage;
  • a cloud database;
  • multi-user authentication;
  • a real-time detection engine;
  • a "magic" security score;
  • an LLM deciding whether a configuration is risky.

I like this model:

Deterministic check
        |
        v
Finding + evidence
        |
        v
Human judgment

If I add AI later, I would put it after the evidence:

Finding
   |
   +--> explanation
   +--> correlation
   +--> remediation draft
   +--> executive summary

Root MFA is still better evaluated by a boolean. It does not hallucinate.

What comes next

Natural directions include:

  • deeper IAM controls;
  • AWS Organizations and multi-account orchestration;
  • more framework mappings;
  • historical trends;
  • WAF/API efficacy testing as a separate module;
  • ticketing/SIEM integrations;
  • signed reports;
  • additional services.

But I want to keep the main principle:

Tooling should remove repetitive work, not hide security judgment behind charts.

Final thoughts

The AWS Security Assessment Toolkit came from a simple need: get a fast, reproducible first technical view of AWS security posture.

TODAY IT INCLUDES: 42 controls + CLI + local GUI + AssumeRole + suppressions + baseline/diff + 7 report formats + a self-contained HTML report.

For me, that is a useful level of lightweight assessment tooling.
Not a full CSPM.
Not a pentest.
Not an audit-opinion generator.
Not a "Make AWS Secure" button.

Just an engineering lever that saves time where automation makes sense and leaves humans responsible for the parts that require context. Those are usually the security tools I enjoy using the most.

References

AWS

  • AWS Shared Responsibility Model
  • AWS Well-Architected Framework: Security Pillar
  • AWS IAM security best practices
  • AWS Security Hub CSPM introduction
  • AWS Foundational Security Best Practices
  • CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark in Security Hub CSPM
  • AWS Security Hub control reference
  • AWS managed policy: SecurityAudit
  • Third-party access and External IDs
  • How AWS Config records configuration history
  • Security Hub security-check schedules

Open source

  • Prowler
  • AWS Security Assessment Toolkit repository by Bulwark Advisory

title: Cross-Lingual Persona Effects in LLM Negotiation
description:
arXiv:2611.00300v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Tell an LLM negotiator to be "headstrong" and it should hold firm on price, but does that instruction retain the same behavior in every language? To test this, we use identical buyer and seller instances of Gemini 3.6 Flash to negotiate the same 12 CraigslistBargain scenarios in English and Korean. The pilot-scale 2 x 2 x 3 design crosses interaction language, seller urgency (none or strong), and buyer persona (cooperative, neutral, or headstrong), yielding 432 attempted negotiations. We call this property cross-lingual social-policy fidelity: whether a prompt-defined social policy produces the same behavioral effect regardless of interaction language. It often does not. Korean negotiations reached agreement far more often than English (77.3% vs. 52.5%, a 24.8-point gap, Holm-adjusted p = .0039), but only for neutral and headstrong buyers; cooperative buyers were already near-ceiling in both languages. Buyers' opening offers barely differed by language; the gap instead emerged later, through larger seller concessions and a smaller final gap in Korean, and agreed prices were also lower in Korean. Repeating the full design with Qwen3.7 Flash as both agents gives directional support: agreement was again higher in Korean (+13.9 points vs. Gemini's +24.8, with an interval whose lower bound is near zero), and sellers again conceded more. Pragmatic analysis reveals why: while both languages frequently featured face-threatening acts like rejections and counter-offers, Korean dialogue softened these threats with substantially more politeness mitigation, especially among sellers (11.7% vs. 3.6%). These results show that such a policy can produce different simulated negotiation behavior, not just different wording, when only the interaction language changes.

title: Your Best Dunning Email Is Worthless in the Spam Folder
description:
Developers who work on billing recovery will debug everything: retry intervals, decline-code mapping, webhook idempotency, the card-update page's mobile layout. Then the recovery email — the artifact the whole system exists to deliver — goes out from a subdomain nobody warmed, with a subject line that reads like a phishing attempt, and lands in spam. The retry logic was perfect. The customer never saw it.

Dunning email has a deliverability problem that ordinary product email does not. It talks about money, failed payments, and updating card details, which is precisely the vocabulary spam filters and cautious humans are trained to distrust. It is also sent disproportionately to your least-engaged customers — the ones who have not opened anything in months — which is exactly the sending pattern that drags a domain's reputation down. Every unopened dunning email makes the next one more likely to be filtered. The failure compounds in the worst direction.

The fixes are mostly unglamorous infrastructure, and they are checkable. Send billing mail from a dedicated subdomain so its reputation is not hostage to your marketing sends, and authenticate it properly: SPF, DKIM, and a DMARC policy that is actually enforced rather than parked at monitor-only. Keep the from-name and from-address boringly consistent with what the customer saw at signup; a payment email from a name they do not recognize is a delete, or worse, a spam report. Put the card-update link on your real domain, never a shortener. And write subject lines that a bank would write — "Your payment didn't go through" survives filters and humans; "URGENT: action required on your account!!" survives neither.

Then instrument it like the revenue surface it is. Track delivery, bounces, and spam complaints per send, not per month. A hard bounce on a dunning email is diagnostic gold: it often means the account's contact email is dead, which means the subscription behind it is unrecoverable by email and should route to another channel immediately instead of burning four more sends. A complaint spike after a copy change is a rollback signal, not a rounding error.

For the full working list — authentication setup, subdomain strategy, copy patterns that stay out of the filter, and the per-send metrics worth alerting on — a deliverability checklist for dunning email that lands in the inbox lays it out in implementation order, written for the person who owns the sending pipeline rather than the person who owns the brand book.

Bounce policy deserves its own paragraph because billing teams routinely get it backwards. A hard bounce — the address does not exist — should end email attempts to that address immediately and reroute the account to whatever second channel exists, even if that channel is only a banner the customer sees at next login. Soft bounces, the full mailbox and the temporary server refusal, earn a short, bounded retry of the message itself, and then the same rerouting. What neither should trigger is the marketing team's usual reflex, suppressing the contact entirely: a suppressed billing contact is an account you have decided to let die silently. Keep the billing suppression list separate from the marketing one, review it like a failure queue in its own right, and treat every address on it as a small mystery worth one human look — a mistyped domain at signup accounts for more of them than anyone expects, and it is fixable in a single apologetic email to the corrected address.

Recovery systems are usually judged on retry intelligence. Fair enough. But a retry the customer never learns about is only half a recovery, and the other half lives or dies in the inbox. That is why Swipe Again's recovery work treats the email itself — its authentication, its timing, its plain-spoken copy — as part of the retry, not as the notification stapled to it.

title: Let your AI assistant draft customer replies (with a human in the loop): elozi-mcp
description:
I build Elozi, a customer-service workspace. I wanted AI assistants to help with support without giving them free rein, so I published elozi-mcp (MIT, v0.1.1).

It is a small stdio bridge that connects desktop agents (Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor, Codex or any MCP stdio client) to Elozi's hosted endpoint. It stores no data locally, adds no telemetry and does not retry tool calls automatically.

Permissions come from the token. In the Elozi panel you create an agent of type "Agent via MCP" and a service identity with channels, departments, capabilities, validity and daily quotas. The assistant only sees tools your token allows. A good start is conversation.read plus reply.submit: it reads and drafts, a person approves. Add reply.send or conversation.manage only when you want it to act alone.

Requirements: Node.js 22+ and an ELOZI_API_TOKEN (starts with elozi_svc_, shown once).

Install / run:

npx -y elozi-mcp

Cursor example (~/.cursor/mcp.json):

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "elozi": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "elozi-mcp"],
      "env": { "ELOZI_API_TOKEN": "elozi_svc_YOUR_TOKEN" }
    }
  }
}

Claude Code users can also connect over HTTP directly:

claude mcp add --transport http elozi https://elozi.je4ndev.com/api/agent/mcp --header "Authorization: Bearer ${ELOZI_API_TOKEN}"

Keep the token in private config only, never in chats or URLs.

npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/elozi-mcp
Repo: https://github.com/JE4NVRG/elozi

title: Conclusiones sobre Go: ¿un C++ ligero?
description:
Después de evaluar Go, durante las últimas semanas, debo admitir que... me gusta. Debe ser entendido como un C extendido, más que como una variante de C++, pero que soporta ciertos características de POO (programación orientada a objetos).

Es decir, uno podría pasarse a Go sin echar de menos, necesariamente, características de objetos. Se aprecia desde el principo que la idea es simplificar, siguiendo las conclusiones más actuales sobre POO, dejando de poner tanto énfasis en clases y herencia (aunque se soporta de alguna forma), y sobre todo, poniendo el énfasis en el polimorfismo.

Así que... definitivamente, un programador de C se sentirá muy cómodo en Go, probablemente notando que está utilizando un C mejorado con algunas extensiones de POO. Un programador de C++, Java o C# puede también sentirse cómodo, sintiendo que tiene que adaptarse, en cierto sentido, a algunas restricciones.

Por supuesto, no todo es mágico en Go. Ya he dicho que me gusta, pero tengo las siguientes espinitas.

  1. El sistema de paquetes. Si pones package x, tienes que tener ese archivo x.go en su propio subdirectorio x. Es decir, si decides reorganizar la estructura de tu aplicación, te encontrarás que tienes que rehacer la estructura de directorios, y también renombrar los package dentro de los archivos Go.

  2. Compilación de paquetes. Afortunadamente, un package se compila solo una vez (al contrario que en C, donde es necesario crear las famosas guards). Pero... no se permiten relaciones circulares. Es decir, la estructura Punto de un paquete A puede hacer uso de la estructura Lector un paquete B. Pero en ningún caso desde el paquete B se puede hacer referencia a Punto del paquete A. Para superar esto, será probablemente necesario crear una interface para la estructura Lector. Quizás pueda ser posible refactorizar ambos paquetes para eliminar el mayor número de dependencias. Esto está lejos del soporte de Java o C#, que automáticamente crean lo que sería equivalente a las interfaces de las clases, con el esqueleto de las firmas de los miembros públicos. Aunque es verdad que esto puede crear módulos excesivamente interdependientes (esto es bueno), también limita ciertas prácticas, como por ejemplo tener todos los métodos que leen una determninada estructura todos juntos en un package, si no se es cuidadoso.

  3. La implementación de la herencia. Si pones una estructura A dentro de una estructura B, en la práctica, estás haciendo que B derive de A. De hecho, B podrá hacer uso de los métodos definidos para A. Por un lado, colocar la estructura A dentro de B parece indicar que tendrás que apañártelas tú mismo con la herencia, cuando es obvio que el compilador va a ofrecer cierto soporte automático del que, al principio, puedes no ser consciente. Personalmente, me gustaría una sintaxis del tipo type B struct: A o algo parecido, lo que ya sugiere que el compilador va a ofrecer un soporte de la herencia explícito.

¿Y tú? ¿Has probado Go?

title: HALO: Hierarchical Evidence Selection and Reinforcement Learning for Allocating Budgeted Label Optimization from Longitudinal Clinical Records
description:
arXiv:2611.00986v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Learning from extensive longitudinal clinical records--spanning repeated encounters, evolving conditions, and heterogeneous documentation--under a finite labeling budget requires solving two coupled problems: deciding what evidence to keep and deciding which patients deserve higher-fidelity labels. Prior work on active learning and multi-fidelity label acquisition mainly addresses the second problem, while treating the evidence presented to the acquisition policy as fixed. We present HALO, a Hierarchical Evidence Selection and Reinforcement Learning pipeline for Allocating Budgeted Label Optimization from Longitudinal Clinical Records. This framework jointly learns what to read and what label source to acquire under budget. HALO first selects informative evidence from longitudinal records and then uses a budget-aware policy to allocate free-, silver-, and gold-fidelity label sources. For frozen policies, our theory characterizes asymmetric acquired-label channels and gives a budget-constrained finite-sample gold-risk bound for a common downstream logistic model. In a heart-failure case study, HALO attained the highest MedAlign acquired-label F1 at six of eight target budgets. A downstream classifier trained on HALO-acquired labels attained the highest external MGB F1 at budgets 15-60 and remained within 0.01 of the best comparator at budgets 75-120.

title: I gave AI agents a video downloader: building a remote MCP server in Python
description:
AI assistants can write code and summarise articles, but when I asked one to "download this video" it had no way to do it. I had already built SaveDock, a free video and audio downloader on Django, yt-dlp and Celery, so I gave agents a way to use it: an MCP server.

What is MCP?

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard that lets an AI client, such as Claude or Cursor, call tools that live on a server. The client lists the tools, reads their descriptions, and decides when to use them. You don't write a plugin for each assistant. You write one server.

The design: a thin adapter, not a second app

My first idea was to put yt-dlp inside the MCP server. I dropped it. The download logic, rate limits and storage already existed behind a REST API, so the MCP server only talks to that API:

agent --MCP--> mcp_server --REST--> /api/v1 --> Celery worker --> storage

The MCP process has no Django, no yt-dlp and no database. Rate limits, quotas and error handling stay in one place, so the website, the API and MCP cannot drift apart.

Four tools

Tool Purpose
get_video_info(url) Title, duration and available qualities (read-only)
download_video(url, quality, audio_only) Starts a download and waits briefly
get_download_status(job_id) Checks a running job
cancel_download(job_id) Stops a job

Downloads can take longer than an agent wants to wait, so download_video waits up to 25 seconds and then returns a job id. The agent can poll with get_download_status. The result is a temporary link: the file itself is never put into the conversation.

Errors an agent can act on

A failure returns isError: true with a stable code and a retryable flag:

{"error": {"code": "...", "message": "...", "retryable": false}}

That way the model can decide whether to retry, wait, or tell the user what went wrong instead of guessing from a stack trace.

Free access without opening the door

There is no signup, but there is a limit: 10 downloads per hour per IP. The catch is that all MCP callers arrive from the MCP server's own address. So the server forwards each caller's IP to the API (only when a trusted proxy sits in front), and the limit applies per user, not per server. A caller who passes a wrong API key gets a 401, not a silent downgrade.

Try it 

claude mcp add --transport http video-downloader https://mcp.savedock.pro/mcp

Then ask your assistant: "What qualities are available for this video?" or "Save the audio of this video as MP3."

Docs and a hosted endpoint: https://savedock.pro/mcp-server/

What I learned

  • Keep the MCP layer thin. Put business logic behind one API.
  • Return structured errors, not just text.
  • Design tools for waiting: agents time out sooner than downloads finish.
  • Anonymous access needs a per-user limit, or one heavy user blocks everyone.

Only use it on content you have the right to download. Feedback is welcome in the comments, especially from people building MCP servers.

title: GitHub Octoverse 2026: What 7.38 Billion Monthly Commits Reveal About Agent-Generated Code Infrastructure
description:
GitHub's Octoverse 2026 report shows merged pull requests tripled to 220 million per month in less than a year. Commits more than tripled to 7.38 billion per month, with most growth in H2 2026. New repository creation doubled to 30.3 million per month. These numbers represent the first platform-scale measurement of agentic engineering impact, and the methodology behind them exposes interesting infrastructure choices for measuring agent activity at scale.

The report introduces LLM-based classification for both repository taxonomy and geolocation correction. GitHub used a fine-tuned multilingual embedding model to sort repositories into NAICS sectors and applied LLM classification to extract country codes from user profiles to correct VPN bias. This is not just measurement. It is a blueprint for how platforms handle automated activity when traditional signals break down.

The Measurement Stack

GitHub's approach to classifying 30 million new repositories per month relies on three layers:

Repository industry classification:

  • Fine-tuned multilingual embedding model
  • Input features: name, description, topics, README
  • Output: NAICS sector assignment
  • Sampling strategy: random samples per year from 2022 to 2026

Geolocation correction:

  • LLM classification extracts ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 codes from user profiles
  • Adjusts for VPN usage bias in push data
  • Aggregates pushes by country across the Octoverse year

Interoperability tracking:

  • Keyword matching on name, description, topics, README
  • Target terms: interoperability, reverse engineering, clean room implementation, drop-in replacement, protocol re-implementation
  • Counts public repositories created each year

This stack matters because traditional heuristics (commit message patterns, file types, contributor counts) do not scale when agent-generated code floods the platform. Embedding models and LLM classification provide a semantic layer that can handle volume and variety.

Infrastructure Implications of Tripling Merge Rates

When merged PRs triple in six months, every part of the platform feels pressure:

CI/CD pipelines:

  • Webhook delivery systems must handle 3x event volume
  • Build queue depth increases unless runner pools scale proportionally
  • Artifact storage grows faster than linear with merge count (branches, tags, intermediate builds)

Code review tooling:

  • Diff rendering services see 3x load
  • Comment threading and notification systems scale with PR volume
  • Review assignment algorithms need to distinguish human-reviewed from auto-merged PRs

Repository storage:

  • Git object databases grow with commit count, not just code size
  • Packfile generation and repack operations become bottlenecks
  • Ref advertisement during clone/fetch operations slow down with more branches

Search and indexing:

  • Code search indexes must ingest 7.38 billion commits per month
  • Blame view generation scales poorly with commit density
  • Repository graph queries (contributors, forks, dependencies) become more expensive

The platform must decide which operations to optimize for agent-generated patterns and which to throttle. GitHub's infrastructure choices here are not public, but the numbers suggest significant investment in horizontal scaling and caching layers.

LLM-Based Classification Trade-offs

Using LLMs to classify repositories and correct geolocation data introduces new failure modes:

Classification Task Benefit Risk
Repository industry Handles multilingual repos, semantic understanding of purpose Embedding drift over time, misclassification of novel project types
VPN-adjusted location Corrects for privacy tool usage, improves country-level accuracy Relies on profile text quality, fails for empty or misleading profiles
Interoperability detection Finds clean room implementations, protocol re-implementations Keyword matching misses implicit interop, false positives on unrelated terms

The embedding model approach for industry classification is interesting because it avoids brittle rule-based systems. A fine-tuned model can learn that a repo named "rust-postgres" with a README about database drivers belongs in the information sector, even if the description is sparse. But this requires ongoing retraining as new frameworks and terminology emerge.

The VPN correction using LLM profile parsing is a pragmatic hack. GitHub knows that IP-based geolocation is increasingly unreliable, so they extract location from user-provided text. This works when users fill out profiles honestly but breaks down for privacy-conscious developers or automated accounts.

Agent Activity Signals

The report does not explicitly label which commits are agent-generated, but the growth curve suggests a methodology for inferring agent activity:

Commit velocity patterns:

  • Sudden spikes in commit frequency per repository
  • Consistent commit timing (hourly, on the hour) suggesting scheduled jobs
  • Commit messages with templated structure or AI tool signatures

PR merge patterns:

  • Auto-merge without human review comments
  • Merge within seconds or minutes of PR creation
  • Batch merges of similar changes across multiple repos

Repository creation patterns:

  • Repos created with full project structure in initial commit
  • Immediate CI/CD configuration files
  • README and documentation generated in consistent style

These signals are not definitive. A human developer using Copilot or Cursor heavily will exhibit some of these patterns. But at platform scale, the aggregate shift is clear.

Observability Gaps

GitHub's report highlights what platforms can measure but also exposes gaps:

What is visible:

  • Commit count, PR merge rate, repository creation rate
  • Geographic distribution (with VPN correction)
  • Industry classification (with embedding model)

What remains hidden:

  • Which commits were generated by AI tools vs. human-written
  • How much human review happened before merge
  • Whether agent-generated code introduced bugs or security issues
  • Cost per commit (compute, storage, network)

The lack of explicit agent attribution is a design choice. GitHub does not require developers to label AI-generated code, so the platform must infer activity from behavioral signals. This works for aggregate reporting but makes it hard to reason about individual repository health.

Deployment Shape for Classification Services

A system that classifies 30 million repositories per month needs careful architecture:

# Conceptual classification pipeline
class RepoClassifier:
    def __init__(self, embedding_model, llm_client):
        self.embedding_model = embedding_model
        self.llm_client = llm_client
        self.batch_size = 1000

    async def classify_batch(self, repos):
        # Extract features
        features = [
            {
                "name": r.name,
                "description": r.description,
                "topics": r.topics,
                "readme_sample": r.readme[:2000]  # Truncate
            }
            for r in repos
        ]

        # Generate embeddings
        embeddings = await self.embedding_model.embed_batch(features)

        # Classify using nearest neighbor or fine-tuned head
        sectors = self.classify_embeddings(embeddings)

        return sectors

    def classify_embeddings(self, embeddings):
        # Could be k-NN against labeled examples
        # or a fine-tuned classification head
        pass

The pipeline must handle:

  • Rate limiting to avoid overwhelming the embedding model
  • Retry logic for transient failures
  • Caching for repositories that have not changed
  • Fallback to keyword-based classification when embeddings fail

For VPN correction, the LLM classification step is simpler but still needs guardrails:

async def extract_country_code(profile_text):
    prompt = f"""
    Extract the ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country code from this profile.
    Return only the two-letter code or "UNKNOWN".

    Profile: {profile_text}
    """

    response = await llm_client.complete(prompt, max_tokens=10)
    code = response.strip().upper()

    if len(code) == 2 and code.isalpha():
        return code
    return "UNKNOWN"

This approach is cheap (short prompts, short completions) but requires validation. GitHub likely runs this classification in batch mode on historical data rather than real-time.

Security Boundaries

Measuring agent activity at scale introduces new attack surfaces:

Classification poisoning:

  • Adversaries could craft repo names and READMEs to manipulate industry classification
  • Embedding models can be fooled by adversarial text
  • VPN correction relies on user-provided profile text, which is trivially spoofed

Resource exhaustion:

  • Automated repo creation at scale could overwhelm classification pipelines
  • Embedding generation is compute-intensive
  • LLM calls for geolocation correction add latency and cost

Privacy leakage:

  • Aggregated data might reveal which organizations are using AI tools heavily
  • Geolocation correction could expose users trying to hide their location
  • Interoperability tracking might identify clean room implementations before public announcement

GitHub's methodology section does not address these risks, but any platform implementing similar classification must consider them.

Failure Modes

The system breaks down in predictable ways:

Embedding model drift:

  • New programming languages and frameworks not in training data
  • Multilingual repos with mixed language content
  • Repos with minimal or misleading metadata

LLM hallucination:

  • Extracting country codes from ambiguous profile text
  • Misinterpreting location references (e.g., "I work remotely from everywhere")
  • Generating plausible but incorrect codes

Keyword matching brittleness:

  • Interoperability detection misses repos that implement protocols without mentioning it
  • False positives on unrelated uses of terms like "drop-in replacement"
  • Language-specific terminology not captured by English keywords

The report does not quantify error rates, but these failure modes are inherent to the approach.

What This Means for Platform Design

GitHub's methodology reveals three principles for measuring agent activity at scale:

  1. Semantic classification beats heuristics. Embedding models and LLMs can handle the variety and volume of agent-generated content better than rule-based systems.

  2. Correction layers are necessary. Traditional signals (IP geolocation, commit patterns) break down when agents and privacy tools are widespread. Platforms need secondary classification to adjust for bias.

  3. Aggregate metrics hide individual behavior. Platform-wide numbers show trends but do not attribute activity to specific tools or developers. This is a feature, not a bug, for privacy reasons.

Other platforms (GitLab, Bitbucket, internal enterprise Git servers) will need similar measurement stacks as agent-generated code becomes the norm.

Technical Verdict

Use this approach when:

  • You operate a platform with millions of repositories and need aggregate metrics
  • Traditional heuristics (commit patterns, file types) are too noisy or brittle
  • You have access to embedding models and LLM APIs for classification
  • Privacy concerns prevent explicit labeling of agent-generated content

Avoid this approach when:

  • You need precise attribution of individual commits to AI tools
  • Your platform is small enough that manual review or rule-based systems work
  • You cannot afford the compute cost of embedding generation and LLM classification
  • You need real-time classification (batch processing is inherent to this design)

GitHub's Octoverse 2026 methodology is not a blueprint for detecting AI-generated code in your CI pipeline. It is a blueprint for measuring platform-wide trends when agent activity dominates. The infrastructure choices (embedding models, LLM-based correction, keyword matching) are pragmatic responses to scale, not optimal solutions for precision.

Source Links

  • GitHub Octoverse 2026 (Simon Willison)

title: How to auto-reframe a video to 9:16 with ffmpeg and frame differencing
description:
Auto reframe in video editors is usually sold as AI subject tracking. For the most common case, a person moving in front of a background that stays still, a much simpler method finds the same framing: compare each frame with the one before and see where the picture changed. The reframe tool in the osFoundry desktop app works this way, in Rust and ffmpeg. Below is the same method in about 60 lines of Python, run on a 7.5-second 1920×1080 clip of three shots. It lands on the same crops as the app, to the pixel.

1. Shrink the video to 64×36 grey frames

There is no need to look at full-size frames to find where something moved. ffmpeg can hand over the video as raw bytes, four frames a second, scaled down to 64×36 and converted to one grey byte per pixel:

import math, re, subprocess, sys

FFMPEG, SRC = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
W, H, FPS = 64, 36, 4

raw = subprocess.run(
    [FFMPEG, "-loglevel", "error", "-i", SRC,
     "-vf", f"fps={FPS},scale={W}:{H}", "-pix_fmt", "gray", "-f", "rawvideo", "-"],
    capture_output=True, check=True).stdout
frames = [raw[i:i + W * H] for i in range(0, len(raw) - W * H + 1, W * H)]

Each frame is 2,304 bytes. The 7.5-second clip gives 30 frames and so 29 pairs to compare. Scaling down also averages away most of the grain, which matters for the next step.

2. Find the centre of what changed

For each pair of frames, take the difference of every cell, ignore small differences, and compute the centre of mass of the rest, weighted by how much each cell changed:

def centroid(prev, curr, floor=12):
    total = sx = sy = 0
    for i, (a, b) in enumerate(zip(prev, curr)):
        d = abs(b - a)
        if d < floor:
            continue
        total += d
        sx += d * (i % W)
        sy += d * (i // W)
    if total < W * H * 0.5:
        return None
    return sx / total / W, sy / total / H

samples = [centroid(a, b) for a, b in zip(frames, frames[1:])]

The two constants are what make this usable. The noise floor of 12 (out of 255) drops changes that come from the sensor and the compression. On this clip, with the floor at 12 an average of 381 of the 2,304 cells count as changed. With the floor at 1, 1,855 do, which is most of the frame, and the centre gets pulled toward the middle of the picture: the first sample lands at 0.44 of the width instead of 0.40.

The second check returns None when the total change is tiny. When nothing moved, the "centre of the change" is the centre of noise, and following it makes the frame drift for no reason. None means "keep the previous position".

3. Limit how fast the frame may move

A raw centroid jumps whenever a second person enters the shot. Capping the step at 5% of the frame per sample keeps it from whipping across:

def smooth(samples, step=0.05):
    cur = next((s for s in samples if s), (0.5, 0.5))
    out = []
    for s in samples:
        if s:
            cur = tuple(min(1, max(0, c + max(-step, min(step, t - c))))
                        for c, t in zip(cur, s))
        out.append(cur)
    return out

track = smooth(samples)

It starts from the first real observation, so a clip that opens on a still frame doesn't pan in from the centre.

4. Find the cuts with ffmpeg's scene score

ffmpeg's select filter gives every frame a scene score between 0 and 1, and showinfo prints the frames that pass. The timestamps go to stderr, not stdout:

log = subprocess.run(
    [FFMPEG, "-hide_banner", "-i", SRC,
     "-filter_complex", "select='gt(scene,0.35)',showinfo", "-f", "null", "-"],
    capture_output=True, text=True).stderr
cuts = [round(float(t) * 1000) for t in re.findall(r"pts_time:([\d.]+)", log)]

On this clip that finds cuts at 1,767 ms and 4,733 ms. Printing the score of every frame (select='gte(scene,0)',metadata=print) shows how wide the margin is: the two cuts score 0.616 and 0.432, and no other frame of the 225 scores more than 0.068.

5. One crop per shot

Finally, average the track inside each shot and put a 9:16 window around that point. 1080 × 9/16 is 607.5; the width is rounded down to an even 606 because H.264 needs even dimensions.

duration = len(frames) * 1000 // FPS
per = duration / len(track)
bounds = [0] + [c for c in cuts if 0 < c < duration] + [duration]
cw = int(1080 * 9 / 16) // 2 * 2
for start, end in zip(bounds, bounds[1:]):
    a = int(start // per)
    part = track[a:max(a + 1, math.ceil(end / per))]
    bx = sum(p[0] for p in part) / len(part)
    x = min(max(round(1920 * bx - cw / 2), 0), 1920 - cw)
    print(f"{start / 1000:.2f}-{end / 1000:.2f}s  crop={cw}:1080:{x}:0")

0.00-1.77s  crop=606:1080:369:0
1.77-4.73s  crop=606:1080:668:0
4.73-7.50s  crop=606:1080:932:0

These are the same three crops the app produced for this clip. The whole script took 3.5 seconds on this Mac, most of it in the pure-Python loop.

The cuts matter more than they look. Averaged over the whole clip, the subject sits at x = 707, just 50 pixels from a plain center crop (657), because she walks on the left in one shot and on the right in another. Only per shot does the average mean anything.

Putting the shots back together

The crops become one filter_complex: trim each shot, crop it, and join the parts. This is the form the app builds:

[0:v]trim=start=0.000:end=1.767,setpts=PTS-STARTPTS,crop=606:1080:369:0[v0];
[0:v]trim=start=1.767:end=4.733,setpts=PTS-STARTPTS,crop=606:1080:668:0[v1];
[0:v]trim=start=4.733:end=7.500,setpts=PTS-STARTPTS,crop=606:1080:932:0[v2];
[v0][v1][v2]concat=n=3:v=1:a=0[out]

(Drop the line breaks when you pass it to -filter_complex.) The output is 606×1080 and the same length as the input.

The app's Rust explains why it doesn't animate the crop inside a shot, even though ffmpeg could:

/// 🔴 Per scene, not per frame. ffmpeg can animate a crop, but a crop that moves continuously is
/// a pan the editor never asked for; cutting between fixed framings is what an editor would
/// actually do, and it is also what stays honest when the tracking is wrong — a bad framing
/// lasts one scene rather than smearing across the whole clip.
pub fn reframe_segments(
    cuts: &[i64],
    duration_ms: i64,
    track: &[(f64, f64)],
    width: u32,
    height: u32,
    target: f64,
) -> Vec<ReframeSegment> {

Where frame differencing fails

The method finds what moves, not who matters. It works when the subject is the main thing moving and the camera stays still. It goes wrong when:

  • the camera pans, so every cell changes and the centre lands near the middle;
  • the background is busy, such as traffic or a crowd;
  • two people move on opposite sides, and the average ends up between them.

Reflections are a milder case. In the first shot of this clip the woman's reflection in a window moves too, but it stays close to her, so the frame still finds her. A face or person detector handles the hard cases better, at the price of a model. The app's answer for those cases is a manual override: the user drags a point onto the subject, and the analysis is skipped.

The desktop app used here is free from the osFoundry download page.

title: GAVAGAI: Referential Alignment for Infant-Scale Vision-Language Models via Balanced Optimal Transport
description:
arXiv:2611.00319v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A child learns which words name which things from roughly 100 million words of input. Vision-language models trained at a comparable scale bind words to referents far less reliably, and we argue that part of the gap is structural: the usual next-token captioning objective has no variable standing for "this word refers to that region," so training applies no direct pressure to ground words. We add such a variable by treating each scene as a small assignment problem between the content words heard and the regions seen, solved as entropic optimal transport under two constraints. First, a word may be assigned to a special NOTHING column instead of any region, which matters because most content words in caregiver speech do not name anything visible. Second, no region may receive more than a bounded share of the assignment mass, a capacity constraint that encodes mutual exclusivity. The alignment step costs about eight Sinkhorn iterations, small next to the vision encoder. In controlled simulation, the naive version of the idea, a row-wise softmax that forces every word onto some region, collapses to 0.000 word-to-picture accuracy under realistic non-reference rates, below the 0.058 of captioning alone, while our two constraints reach 0.075 in that regime and 0.700 on clean input. A one-parameter version of the model reproduces adult cross-situational learning accuracy across three ambiguity conditions (RMSE 0.024). On the SAYCam infant video corpus, adding the alignment loss to a next-token captioning model raises word-to-picture accuracy from 32.4% to 48.7% and localization IoU from 0.18 to 0.38. A contrastive model trained on the same child's data remains stronger on its own benchmark, so our claim is that the loss improves a captioning objective under high non-reference rates, not that it sets a new best.

title: What Is Web Design? A Complete Guide for Businesses
description:
Why Does Web Design Matter?

Your website is often the first place potential customers learn about your business. If it looks outdated, loads slowly, or makes information difficult to find, visitors may leave without exploring your services.

Understanding what web design is helps businesses create websites that look professional, communicate value, and guide visitors toward meaningful actions.

Web design is not just about choosing attractive colors or adding images. It combines visual appearance, navigation, usability, accessibility, and responsive layouts to create a better experience for visitors.

What Is Web Design?
Web design is the process of planning and creating a website’s layout, visual appearance, structure, and user experience. It includes colors, typography, images, navigation, page organization, and interactive elements.

The goal is to make a website attractive, easy to use, and aligned with business objectives.

For example, a service-based business may need clear service pages, customer testimonials, and a contact form. An online store may require product categories, product images, filters, and a simple checkout process.

In simple terms, good web design helps visitors understand your business, find relevant information, and take the next step.

Why Is Web Design Important for Businesses?

  1. Creates a Professional First Impression
    A consistent layout, readable typography, and relevant images help communicate credibility. A cluttered or outdated website can make it harder for visitors to understand your business and its offerings.

  2. Improves Navigation
    Visitors should be able to find services, product details, and contact information without unnecessary effort. Clear menus, descriptive headings, and organized pages make browsing easier.

  3. Supports Conversions
    An effective website guides visitors toward actions such as requesting a quote, booking a consultation, or purchasing a product.

Clear calls to action, such as “Contact Us” or “Request a Quote,” help visitors understand what to do next.

  1. Improves Mobile Usability
    Responsive web design allows a website’s layout to adapt to different screen sizes. Readable text, easy-to-tap buttons, and mobile-friendly navigation help visitors use the website on smartphones and tablets.

  2. Supports SEO and Performance
    Organized content, logical navigation, and mobile usability contribute to a better website experience. Loading speed and visual stability also matter.

Google’s Core Web Vitals documentation explains how to assess loading performance, responsiveness, and visual stability.

Design alone cannot guarantee higher search rankings, but usability and performance should be considered throughout the design process.

What Are the Main Elements of Web Design?
Effective web design combines several elements to create a consistent and useful website.

Element Purpose
Layout Organizes content and creates a clear visual hierarchy
Colors Supports brand identity and consistency
Typography Makes content readable and highlights important information
Images and graphics Communicates ideas and supports the brand message
Navigation Helps visitors find relevant pages
User interface (UI) Makes buttons, menus, and forms understandable
User experience (UX) Helps visitors complete tasks more easily
Responsive design Adapts layouts to different screen sizes
Accessibility Helps more people use the website effectively
Visual Design and Readability
A well-designed website makes important information easy to notice. Clear headings, appropriate spacing, consistent fonts, and a focused color palette help visitors scan content quickly.

Avoid using too many fonts, excessive animations, or competing colors that distract from the main message.

Accessibility Matters
Accessible design considers visitors with different abilities. Useful practices include maintaining sufficient text contrast, using descriptive link labels, and ensuring interactive elements can be navigated using a keyboard.

The W3C Web Accessibility Initiative’s design tips provide practical guidance for improving website accessibility.

What Are the Different Types of Web Design?
The right approach depends on your website’s purpose, audience, and technical requirements.

Type Description Common Use
Responsive design Adapts layouts to available screen space Business websites and online stores
Adaptive design Uses predefined layouts for selected screen sizes Projects with specific device requirements
Static website design Displays content that remains largely consistent until manually updated Simple informational websites
Dynamic website design Displays content that can change based on data or user interaction Portals and membership websites
eCommerce design Organizes products, shopping carts, and checkout journeys Online stores
These approaches can overlap. For example, an online store can use responsive design and dynamically managed product information.

Choose an approach based on your audience’s needs and your business goals.

What Is the Web Design Process?
A structured process helps businesses create websites that are useful, consistent, and aligned with their objectives.

Step 1: Define Your Goals
Identify what your website should achieve, such as generating leads, explaining services, selling products, or providing customer support. Understanding your audience helps determine what information visitors need and which actions matter most.

Step 2: Plan the Website Structure
Organize pages into a logical structure, such as Home, About, Services, Portfolio, Blog, and Contact.

Create a sitemap and wireframes to plan the placement of headings, text, images, and calls to action before finalizing the visual design.

Step 3: Create the Visual Design
Select colors, fonts, imagery, and spacing that reflect your brand. Keep design elements consistent across pages so visitors can recognize your brand and navigate comfortably.

Step 4: Review Usability and Mobile Design
Check that the website works on mobile, tablet, and desktop screens. Review navigation, text readability, button sizes, accessibility, and the clarity of calls to action.

Step 5: Develop and Test
Web designers plan the visual experience, while developers implement the design and functionality.

Test important features such as forms, navigation, links, and checkout processes where relevant. Review performance and use Google’s Core Web Vitals guidance to identify possible user experience issues.

Step 6: Launch and Improve
After launch, review user feedback, website analytics, and conversion data. Use these insights to improve content, navigation, performance, and calls to action.

What Is the Difference Between Web Design and Web Development?
Web design and web development work together, but they have different responsibilities.

Web Design Web Development
Focuses on appearance, layout, and user experience Focuses on technical implementation and functionality
Defines colors, typography, navigation, and page structure Builds interactive features, integrations, and page components
Uses wireframes, mockups, and prototypes Uses programming languages, frameworks, and other technologies
For example, a designer may create a contact form’s appearance, while a developer ensures that the form submits information correctly.

Both disciplines are important for creating a website that looks professional and works reliably.

Common Web Design Mistakes to Avoid
Even an attractive website can create problems when usability is overlooked. Avoid these common mistakes:

Cluttered layouts: Too many competing elements make information harder to scan.
Confusing navigation: Unclear menu labels make pages difficult to find.
Poor mobile usability: Small buttons and overflowing content frustrate mobile visitors.
Weak calls to action: Visitors may not know what step to take next.
Unreadable text: Small fonts and insufficient contrast reduce readability.
Unoptimized images: Large media files can contribute to slow loading.
Ignoring accessibility: Some visitors may struggle to navigate or understand the website.
Neglecting updates: Outdated content and broken links can damage the user experience.
Quick Website Design Checklist
Use this checklist to review your website:

The homepage clearly explains what the business offers.
Navigation is simple and consistent.
Services and products are easy to find.
Text is readable and well organized.
The website works across different screen sizes.
Calls to action clearly explain the next step.
Contact forms and important features work correctly.
Images are relevant and optimized.
Accessibility and website performance have been reviewed.
Internal links lead to the correct pages.
Use the results to prioritize improvements based on visitor needs and business goals.

Frequently Asked Questions About Web Design
What is web design in simple words?
Web design is the process of planning how a website looks, organizes information, and helps visitors interact with its content.

Does web design require coding?
Not always. Designers can create layouts and prototypes without writing production code. Building a functional website may require developers, website builders, content management systems, or a combination of these options.

Does web design affect SEO?
Yes. Mobile usability, clear content structure, navigation, and website performance can support SEO. However, design alone does not guarantee higher rankings.

What makes a web design effective?
An effective website communicates value clearly, organizes information logically, works across devices, considers accessibility, and makes the next step easy to understand.

Conclusion: Build a Website That Supports Your Business Goals
Understanding what web design is helps businesses focus on more than appearance. Clear messaging, thoughtful layouts, intuitive navigation, responsive behavior, and performance-conscious design can improve the visitor experience.

By understanding your audience and following a structured design process, you can create a website that communicates your value and supports your business objectives.

title: ArSciKids: Arabic Curriculum-Aligned Datasets for Scientific Experiment and Multiple-Choice Question Generation in Primary Education
description:
arXiv:2611.01191v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Despite growing interest in Arabic natural language processing, curriculum-aligned educational resources remain scarce compared with English, and few public datasets for Arabic curriculum content with structured, generation-ready annotations are available, particularly for primary-school science. We introduce ArSciKids, a collection of two Arabic datasets designed for curriculum-aligned educational content generation: (1) a scientific-experiments dataset containing 999 manually curated records from official primary-school science textbooks in Saudi Arabia, Syria, and Jordan, and (2) an assessment-question dataset containing 2,167 multiple-choice questions collected from the Saudi Manhaji educational platform. The experiment records are structured with titles, objectives, tools, procedures, observations, conclusions, keywords, and grade levels, while the assessment records contain lesson references, questions, four answer options, correct answers, and explanations. Both datasets cover grades 1-6 and consist of real-life Arabic educational content rather than machine-translated or synthetically generated material. We assess the usefulness of these resources for generation by fine-tuning ten open models spanning sub-billion to several-billion parameter scales using LoRA. Models are evaluated using automatic metrics, including ROUGE and BLEU, and answer accuracy for multiple-choice generation. Moreover, we evaluate the results using a five-criterion human evaluation protocol. The results show substantial differences across model scales and tasks. ArSciKids will be publicly available, and we hope that it provides a manually curated, structured foundation for research on Arabic educational NLP, curriculum-aware generation, and low-resource language modeling.
