title: Modeling Cash Drawer Variance: Event-Sourced Shifts in an Offline POS
description:
The payments side of our POS (StoreFlux, a headless commerce backend) got most of the write-up attention so far. The shift and cash-drawer accounting underneath it is smaller in scope but had its own interesting constraints, so here's how that part actually works.

The requirement: a real variance number, not a vibe

A cashier opens a shift with a starting cash count. Through the shift they take cash payments, maybe pay cash out for something (a supplier delivery, petty expenses), maybe put more cash in. At close, they count the drawer again. The number that matters is: what should be in there, given everything that happened, versus what's actually in there. That gap is the variance, and it has to be a real computed number a manager can look at, not something eyeballed.

Shifts are event-sourced, same as the rest of the till

Everything at the register already flows through an outbox of client-generated, idempotent events (sales, refunds, product edits — covered in an earlier post). Shifts fit the same model instead of getting special-cased: shift.opened (carries the starting float), cash.moved (a paid-in or paid-out, with a reason), and shift.closed (carries the counted-at-close amount). The shift's id is literally the register's client-generated guid for that shift — no separate id-minting round trip needed before the register can start tagging sales with which shift they belong to.

Every sale and refund that happens during an open shift carries that shift id. That's what makes the expected-cash calculation possible after the fact: starting float, plus cash collected from sales in that shift, minus cash refunded, plus or minus any manual cash movements, equals what should be in the drawer. Compare that to the counted amount from shift.closed and the variance falls out.

Doing that math in two places, correctly, is the actual hard part

Same story as the money math elsewhere in this system: the Rust register computes an expected-cash number locally so a cashier can see it the moment they close a shift, with zero network round trip. The C# server computes the same number independently once the events land, because the server is the one source of truth once everything's synced — a register's local math is a preview, not the final answer. Those two computations have to agree, or a manager ends up staring at two different "the drawer should have X in it" numbers from the same shift and trusting neither.

This is handled with the same parity-testing discipline as the rest of the sync layer: replay a shift's full event sequence through both implementations and diff the result. It's not glamorous, but it's the only way I trust two independently-written pieces of arithmetic to actually match under real event orderings, including the annoying cases — multiple cash-outs in one shift, a refund that happens to land in a different shift than its original sale because it was processed offline and back-dated to the sale's actual time.

Offline refunds and which shift they belong to

That last case deserves its own mention because it was a genuine bug we caught, not a hypothetical. A refund processed while offline gets dated to when it actually happened, not when it finally syncs — otherwise a refund given during Tuesday's shift could get silently counted against Wednesday's drawer because that's when the connection came back. Getting this right means the variance calculation for a shift has to be based on "what happened during this shift's real time window," not "what the server received while this shift's status was open." Those are subtly different, and conflating them is exactly the kind of bug that doesn't show up in testing until you specifically simulate being offline across a shift boundary.

What a manager actually sees

None of this is exposed as raw event data, obviously — the owner-facing side is just an endpoint that returns a shift with its expected cash, counted cash, and variance already computed, plus the list of cash movements with whatever reason the cashier entered. The accounting happens once, server-side, from the event history; nothing is recomputed differently depending on who's asking.

Still open: an X-report style printable summary at shift close, and automatic variance-threshold alerts (right now a manager has to go looking at the dashboard rather than getting proactively flagged when a shift closes meaningfully short or over). Those are next.

storeflux.store/#pos if you want to see where this sits in the product. Curious whether anyone else doing register/shift software has hit the same "two engines must agree on money" problem and solved it differently than parity testing.

title: Queering the Audits: Community-Based Auditing of AI Harms to Queer Communities
description:
arXiv:2611.00345v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI systems embed majority-group defaults into training data, evaluation metrics, and category definitions, producing documented harms for queer communities including erasure, misclassification, and discrimination. Standard technical audits often rely on aggregate measures and cannot detect harms that be come visible only through the lived experience of affected communities. We conducted a participatory auditing workshop at EurIPS 2025 where 16 queer community members audited four case studies using the 4Cs harm taxonomy (Content, Conduct, Contact, Contract) applied across the AI lifecycle. Participants used structured worksheets and plenary synthesis to classify harms and trace them to their origins in the development pipeline. Across all four cases, participants traced harms to problem definition and data collection, and they identified contractual structures that extract value from vulnerable populations while providing minimal recourse. These findings illustrate that community-informed auditing surfaces concrete, identity-specific harms that aggregate evaluation methods risk overlooking.

title: Adaptive-Policy Distillation: Knowledge Injection under Information Asymmetry
description:
arXiv:2611.00852v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD), which uses reverse-KL supervision on student rollouts to transfer a context-conditioned model's behavior into student model parameters for closed-book inference, has shown strong results. However, we find that this success does not translate to knowledge injection: across two document-QA benchmarks, OPD injects document knowledge far less efficiently than simple off-policy distillation. We trace this reversal to two failures that are structural, yet sparse across token positions. Reverse KL weights its gradient by the student distribution and therefore barely lifts document-specific tokens the student considers unlikely; after forward KL restores this signal, student rollouts expose later positions on the target trajectory only after generating the preceding tokens correctly, so coverage deteriorates with target length. Motivated by the concentration of teacher-student divergence at these hard positions, we propose Adaptive-Policy Distillation (APD), whose per-token gate jointly shifts the rollout toward the teacher and the objective toward forward KL where needed, withdrawing both interventions as the student learns. Without labels or a verifier, APD improves over OPD by up to 54.6%, achieving the best scores of 0.558 F1 on QASPER and 0.486 MRR on BioASQ.

title: I Built a Free AWS Cloud Practitioner (CLF-C02) Exam Simulator: 2,000 Questions, Timed Mocks and an AI Proctor
description:
TL;DR: CloudPrep is a free practice simulator for the AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner (CLF-C02) exam. It has 2,000 original questions, an explanation for every option, real-format 65-question / 90-minute mock exams, and an optional on-device AI proctor. No ads, no paywall.

👉 Try it: aws-cloud-prepare.vercel.app

🤔 Why I built it

CloudPrep started as my own preparation tool for the CLF-C02 exam. I wanted practice that felt like the real exam: the same length, the same timing, the same pressure. I also wanted every answer explained and backed by an AWS source.

So I built it, and then made it a free, public product so anyone preparing for the exam can use it too.

📊 CloudPrep at a glance

📚 2,000 ⏱️ 65 / 90 🧩 4 💸 Free
original questions, each option explained questions and minutes, like the real exam exam domains, weighted like the official guide no ads, no paywall

The questions are split across the four CLF-C02 domains:

Domain Exam weight Questions in CloudPrep
1. Cloud Concepts 24% 400
2. Security and Compliance 30% 600
3. Cloud Technology and Services 34% 753
4. Billing, Pricing, and Support 12% 247

✨ What you can do with it

1. 📖 Learning mode: practise at your own pace

  • Untimed practice by domain or topic
  • Instant feedback with an explanation for every option, not just the correct one
  • Links to the AWS documentation each question is based on
  • Bookmarks for questions you want to revisit
  • Review due: missed questions come back on a schedule so you see them again before you forget them 
Review schedule:  1 day → 3 days → 7 days → 21 days → 60 days

💡 Learning mode works without an account. Just open the site and start practising.

2. ⏱️ Timed mock exams: the real thing, before the real thing

  • 65 questions in 90 minutes, following the CLF-C02 domain weightings
  • Flag questions, jump around with a question grid, and do a final review
  • Auto-submit when the timer runs out
  • An exam-paper style answer sheet
  • The timer counts down to a fixed end time, so it survives reloads

3. 📈 Results that tell you what to fix

  • Practice score with a per-domain breakdown
  • Answer review with explanations
  • Exam history and progress guidance across attempts
  • The dashboard flags your weakest domain and shows the time used in recent exams

4. 🤖 AI-proctored exams (opt-in)

Want to train under real exam conditions? Turn on the AI proctor.

  • A check-in, like an online proctored exam
  • MediaPipe face and object models plus microphone loudness, all running on your device
  • It watches your face, head, eyes and mouth, looks for phones, other people, books and screens, and blocks shortcuts
  • Two warnings, then the exam ends. A phone or another person ends it at once.

🔒 Nothing is recorded or uploaded. It all runs in your browser.

There's also a lighter strict mode that asks for fullscreen and logs tab and focus changes, without judging them.

5. ☁️ Sync across devices

  • Sign in with Google to save your progress, bookmarks, exam history, the exam in progress and settings to your account
  • Everything follows you to every device
  • A copy is kept in the browser, so it stays fast and works offline. Changes sync when you're back online.

6. 🎨 Designed for long study sessions

  • Light theme and a true-black dark theme
  • Serif titles, rounded cards and an exam-paper answer sheet
  • Add to Home Screen support with its own icons
  • Automated axe accessibility checks (WCAG 2.2 AA rules) pass on every page, in both themes

👥 Guest vs signed in

Feature Guest Signed in (Google)
Learning mode ✅ ✅
Bookmarks and settings ✅ (this browser only) ✅ (synced)
Timed mock exams ❌ ✅
Dashboard, history and progress ❌ ✅
Sync across devices ❌ ✅

🛠️ Tech stack

For the developers reading this, here's what's under the hood:

Layer Tech
Frontend React 19, TypeScript (strict), Vite 8, Tailwind CSS 4, React Router
Backend Supabase only: Postgres with Row Level Security + Supabase Auth (Google). No separate API server.
Data Questions loaded at runtime and cached in IndexedDB; user data in a versioned localStorage layer, synced to Supabase when signed in
AI proctor MediaPipe face and object models, running on-device
Testing Vitest + Testing Library (database schema and security rules run in PGlite), Playwright + axe for E2E and accessibility
Hosting Vercel (static SPA)

🧾 Honest notes

I'd rather you trust it for the right reasons, so:

  • ⚠️ CloudPrep is not affiliated with or endorsed by AWS. A practice score doesn't predict or guarantee an official result.
  • 📊 It shows the percentage you got right. It does not estimate AWS's scaled 100–1,000 score.
  • ✍️ The questions are original, written with AI assistance from public AWS documentation and the official exam guide, then checked against the pages they cite. They are not copied from the real exam or from dumps.
  • ✅ 1,995 of the 2,000 questions are checked against their AWS sources; 5 are still marked unverified.

🚀 Try it and tell me what you think

If you're preparing for the AWS Cloud Practitioner exam, give it a go:

I'd love your feedback:

  • 💬 Found a question that's wrong or unclear? Tell me in the comments.

title: Use ACP-compatible harnesses with the AI SDK harness layer

The AI SDK harness layer now supports any Agent Client Protocol (ACP)-compatible harness with HarnessAgent through the new @ai-sdk/harness-acp package.

Previously, every harness adapter wrapped one specific runtime (Claude Code, Codex, Pi, Deep Agents, OpenCode). @ai-sdk/harness-acp wraps the protocol instead. It is a meta adapter: rather than adapting a single harness, it lets you build an adapter for any harness that ships an ACP-compatible package.

Implement a harness by passing that package to createACP and configure basic harness mapping.

Then pass it to HarnessAgent like any other harness:

ACP is an abstraction over coding harnesses, but the AI SDK harness layer stays deliberately decoupled from it. Not every harness supports ACP, and for some, ACP limits or changes how well they expose their internal behaviors, so a direct adapter can produce a tighter integration.

For Claude Code and Codex, prefer the direct @ai-sdk/harness-claude-code and @ai-sdk/harness-codex adapters over an ACP-based implementation; reach for @ai-sdk/harness-acp when a harness has no direct adapter but ships an ACP-compatible package.

title: A neural network for a > 4, written by hand
description:
Let's start with a small program, where a is a whole number from 0 through 100:

let result = if a > 4 { 10 } else { 12 };

We're going to build a neural network that gives the same result for those 101 inputs. Neural networks are usually trained, which means their numbers are learned from examples. We won't train anything. We'll construct the numbers directly from the program.

The construction comes from Cheng Lou's handwired, a JavaScript project that turns ordinary code into neural-network operations, and this same comparison is the first example in its README. I ported handwired to Rust as handwired-rs, which this series uses.

Why would anyone want this? Not for speed: three arithmetic steps in place of one if is not a better way to write an if, and this post only demonstrates the mechanism. What it gives us is a program that is a fixed list of arithmetic steps, the same for every input, and such a list can be reasoned about and checked on every input we declare. By the end, we'll have done both for all 101.

Two building blocks: weighted sums and ReLU

The first building block is a weighted sum: multiply the input by a constant and add a constant offset. 5 - a is one, with a multiplied by -1 and an offset of 5.

The second is ReLU, short for rectified linear unit: relu(x) = max(0, x). It keeps a positive number and turns a negative one into 0.

Why would we need the second one at all? Because weighted sums alone can't make a decision. A weighted sum of a weighted sum is again a weighted sum: c * (d * a + e) + f is (c * d) * a + (c * e + f), a constant times a plus an offset. So any number of them in a row is a single straight line in a, and no straight line is 12 for every a up to 4 and 10 for every a from 5 on.

How do we turn a > 4 into 0 or 1?

Our first goal is a number, let's call it flag, that is 1 when a > 4 and 0 otherwise. handwired-rs builds it as two ReLUs in a chain:

inner = relu(5 - a)
flag  = relu(1 - inner)

Does that really behave like a > 4? Let's try the two numbers right at the threshold. For a = 4, inner = relu(1) = 1, and then flag = relu(0) = 0. For a = 5, inner = relu(0) = 0, and then flag = relu(1) = 1. So far so good.

What about the other 99 whole numbers? We don't have to try them one by one. From 0 to 4, a is at most 4, so 5 - a is at least 1, which makes inner at least 1 and 1 - inner 0 or negative, and ReLU turns that into a flag of 0. From 5 to 100, 5 - a is 0 or negative, so inner is 0 and flag = relu(1) = 1. That's an algebraic argument: it covers every whole number in the range without trying any of them.

Turning the flag into 10 or 12

Now we have a number where the program had a decision, so the choice can become arithmetic:

result = 12 - 2 * flag

For flag = 0 this is 12, and for flag = 1 it is 10, the two values of the original if. The flag selects the output by multiplication instead of by a jump.

Naming the parts: weights, biases and layers

Each of our three steps is a weighted sum, and the first two are followed by a ReLU. In neural-network terms, the multipliers (-1, -1 and -2) are weights, the offsets (5, 1 and 12) are biases, and each step is a layer. So we've built a network of three layers with one step in each, and it runs the same three operations in the same order for every input. handwired calls such a fixed list of operations a circuit, and that's the name you'll see in the code below.

In the figure, the chain is on the right, and flag for a from 0 to 10 is on the left: dots for the whole numbers, a dashed line for what happens in between.

That dashed slope between 4 and 5 should make you a little suspicious. What is it doing there?

What happens between whole numbers?

Everything we argued so far relied on a being a whole number. So let's break that on purpose and feed in a = 4.5. Before reading on, what do you expect: 10, 12, or something else?

Here is the walk through the chain: inner = relu(0.5) = 0.5, flag = relu(0.5) = 0.5, and result = 12 - 1 = 11. Neither branch. Inputs strictly between 4 and 5 produce a blend of 10 and 12, and that's the dashed slope in the figure.

So the network's correctness is guaranteed for the declared inputs, the whole numbers from 0 to 100. How do we tell the code what those inputs are?

Declaring the inputs in Rust, and testing them

Two facts describe our inputs. a lies between 0 and 100, which handwired-rs calls its range. The allowed values are spaced one apart, which it calls its grid. The comparison needs the grid: it works because no allowed input falls strictly between 4 and 5.

In the program below, look for assume_range and assume_grid, which declare those two facts, and emit_compare, which writes the two ReLUs for us. TensorExecutor runs the compiled circuit, and the loop counts the inputs where it differs from the if. Before you run it, what should it print? If our algebra is right, zero wrong, and 11 for 4.5.

use handwired_rs::{Circuit, Relation, TensorExecutor, emit_compare};

fn main() {
    let mut circuit = Circuit::new(1);
    let a = circuit.source(0);
    circuit.assume_range(a, 0.0, 100.0); // a is between 0 and 100
    circuit.assume_grid(a, 1.0); // in steps of 1
    let four = circuit.constant(4.0);
    let flag = emit_compare(&mut circuit, a, Relation::Greater, four);
    let result = circuit.affine(flag * -2.0 + 12.0);
    let program = circuit.compile(Some(&[result]));

    let mut executor = TensorExecutor::new(&program);
    let mut wrong = 0;
    for a in 0..=100 {
        let expected = if a > 4 { 10.0 } else { 12.0 };
        if executor.run(&[a as f32])[0] != expected {
            wrong += 1;
        }
    }
    println!("{} operations, {wrong} of 101 inputs wrong", program.live_operation_count());
    println!("a = 4.5 gives {}", executor.run(&[4.5])[0]);
}

I ran it in a new binary crate after cargo add handwired-rs@0.8.0, with Rust 1.97 on x86-64 Linux, and it prints:

3 operations, 0 of 101 inputs wrong
a = 4.5 gives 11

Both expectations hold. The three operations are our three steps: for a "greater than" comparison on a grid of 1, emit_compare builds relu(1 - relu(5 - a)), which I checked in its source at v0.8.0. "0 of 101 wrong" is a test result, and it checks this implementation on exactly the declared inputs. The last line shows that the executor doesn't refuse 4.5. It computes the blend, just as we did by hand.

There is one thing we quietly assumed all along, though. Our algebra used exact arithmetic. Does the computer's arithmetic agree?

Why does the floating-point arithmetic agree?

The program runs on f32, 32-bit floating-point numbers, which round some results. So why wasn't anything rounded here? Two facts. Floating-point addition and multiplication round only when the exact answer can't be stored. And an f32 can store every whole number up to a limit far above 100. Every value here, from the input through each intermediate product and sum (such as the -1 * a inside 5 - a) to the result, is a whole number between -100 and 100. So every exact answer can be stored, and nothing is rounded. That's the numerical argument, and the test agrees with it.

Let's take stock. A one-line if became a circuit of three numerical operations, with weights written down from the program, an argument that covers every declared input, and a test that ran all of them. I ported handwired to Rust because I wanted to write the logic as ordinary Rust functions and have a compiler turn them into circuits like this one, so the original function could stay around as the test. Later posts get to that compiler.

Aside: handwired's README writes the flag as relu(a - 4) - relu(a - 5), two ramps subtracted, which gives the same 0 or 1 on whole numbers. We used the chained form because handwired-rs builds it.

Our numbers here never went past 100. What happens when they grow? In the next post we'll find out where that limit on whole numbers is, and what happens to the arithmetic beyond it.

title: How I Clone My Own Voice on a Laptop With No GPU (Qwen3-TTS)
description:
Key takeaways

  • A laptop with no GPU can run Qwen3-TTS voice cloning. Expect 3 to 6 seconds of computing per second of speech.
  • Use reference clips of 7 to 15 seconds. About 30 seconds in total was enough for me.
  • If your reference is casual talking, use x-vector only mode, or the clone will copy your hesitations.
  • Generate 3 to 5 takes per line and pick by where the pauses fall.

Tested on: Windows 11 laptop, Intel Core i9-13900H, 32 GB RAM, integrated graphics only (no NVIDIA GPU). Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-Base, qwen-tts 0.1.1, Python 3.11.

I post short animated videos that explain AI topics, narrated in Chinese. Recording the narration was the slowest part of every video. I stumble, re-record, and takes from different days don't sound the same. I wanted to type the script and get narration in my own voice.

Claude Code, an AI coding assistant, set this up on my laptop. I described what I wanted, listened to the results and made the calls. You can skip the code blocks; the settings that mattered are explained in plain words.

What I used

The model is Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-Base, an open-source text-to-speech model from Alibaba's Qwen team (Apache-2.0 license, code at github.com/Qwen/Qwen3-TTS). The "Base" version is the one that clones voices. I downloaded the weights from ModelScope, which was by far the fastest source where I live.

It runs through the qwen-tts Python package, version 0.1.1, in a Python 3.11 virtual environment. My system Python was newer than the machine-learning packages supported, so a separate 3.11 environment saved a lot of trouble.

Everything runs on the CPU in float32, with no CUDA and no NVIDIA card.

Step 1: Reference audio from a recording I already had

I didn't record anything new. I had a long screen recording where I was talking, and I cut three clips from it, about 33 seconds in total.

Longer clips sounded more like me. Clips of 7 to 15 seconds gave a clearly closer match than 4-second clips.

If there is music or noise behind your voice, remove it first. On my CPU, the BS-Roformer separation model needed about two hours for three minutes of audio. The Kim_Vocal_2 model in the audio-separator package did the same job in about three minutes.

Step 2: The setting that decides whether it sounds fluent

Qwen3-TTS Base can clone a voice in two ways:

Mode What you give it What it copies
ICL (the default) One clip plus its exact transcript Your voice and the way you spoke in that clip
x-vector only One or more clips, no transcript Only the sound of your voice

I started with ICL because it's the default. The problem was my reference clip: unscripted talking, with hesitations and uneven pace. The clone copied that too. Every line came out with the same stop-start rhythm, and it didn't sound fluent.

Switching to x-vector only mode fixed it. The model keeps my voice but uses its own steadier pacing, which is what narration needs. Since no transcript is needed, I could also feed it several clips at once.

If your reference is clean read-aloud speech, ICL may be fine. If it's casual talking, try x-vector first.

This is a simplified version of the script on my laptop:

import numpy as np, soundfile as sf, torch
from qwen_tts import Qwen3TTSModel

torch.set_num_threads(14)  # how many CPU threads to use

model = Qwen3TTSModel.from_pretrained(
    "models/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-Base", device_map="cpu", dtype=torch.float32
)

# Join a few clips of my voice (mono WAV) with a short silence between them
voice, sr = sf.read("my_voice.wav", dtype="float32")
gap = np.zeros(int(0.25 * sr), np.float32)
clips = [(12.0, 23.5), (61.0, 72.7), (130.2, 141.1)]  # start, end in seconds
parts = []
for start, end in clips:
    parts += [voice[int(start * sr):int(end * sr)], gap]
ref = np.concatenate(parts)

# x-vector only: copy the voice, not the rhythm. No transcript needed.
prompt = model.create_voice_clone_prompt(
    ref_audio=(ref, sr), ref_text=None, x_vector_only_mode=True
)

wavs, out_sr = model.generate_voice_clone(
    text=["大家好，今天聊聊怎么用 AI 给视频配音。"],
    language=["Chinese"],
    voice_clone_prompt=prompt,
)
sf.write("line01.wav", wavs[0], out_sr)

For ICL mode you pass one clip, its exact transcript as ref_text, and x_vector_only_mode=False.

Step 3: Make several takes and keep the best one

The same line comes out a little different every time. Some takes pause in the right places, some rush through a comma. So I generate every line 3 to 5 times and pick one.

What I listen for: does it pause at the commas, and does it avoid long gaps in the middle of a phrase. That matters more than small differences in tone.

With twenty-odd lines and several takes each, listening to everything gets tiring. So a script ranks the takes first:

  • It transcribes each take with a speech recognizer (Paraformer, for Chinese) and compares it with the script, to catch swallowed or wrong words.
  • It measures how close the voice is to a separate sample of my real voice that wasn't used for cloning (CAM++ speaker verification).
  • It counts the pauses and compares them with the commas in the line.

Then I only listen to the top few.

How fast is it on a CPU?

From my logs, generating up to six lines per batch: roughly 3 to 6 seconds of computing for each second of speech. One batch produced 37 seconds of speech in 127 seconds; another produced 24 seconds in 147 seconds.

For a two-minute narration that means about 7 to 12 minutes per take, or roughly half an hour for three takes. It's slow, but it runs in the background. Loading the model also takes time, so I generate all the lines in one run.

Smaller things that helped

Some Chinese characters have more than one pronunciation, and the model sometimes picks the wrong one. When that happens I swap in a same-sounding character in the text sent to the model and keep the correct word in the subtitles. For example, 长连接 became 常连接, and 回调 became 回掉.

Not every video needs my voice, either. For quick news videos I use a preset voice from the CustomVoice version of the same model, which needs no reference audio.

Only clone voices you have permission to use

Clone your own voice, or a voice whose owner has agreed. Don't publish a cloned voice of anyone else.

Would a paid service be easier?

Probably. Hosted services such as ElevenLabs need no setup. I have since run the same script through ElevenLabs' free plan, and its stock Mandarin voices sounded more natural than my clone: ElevenLabs free plan vs a local open-source model.

Originally published on Hands-On AI Tools, where I test AI tools on real tasks. Cover: official Qwen3-TTS introduction graphic from the Qwen team's GitHub repository.

title: Vercel Security Dashboard is now generally available
description:
The Vercel Security Dashboard is now generally available on all plans, giving you one place to see your security posture across every account and project.

You can access the Security Dashboard in the UI or run vercel security check in the Vercel CLI.

As teams grow and coding agents make it faster to spin up projects, small misconfigurations add up quietly. The Security Dashboard automatically flags issues like:

  • Team members without 2FA

  • Long-lived credentials that can be replaced with OIDC

  • Public preview deployments

  • Non-sensitive and stale environment variables

The Security Dashboard UI

Misconfigurations are ordered by risk with the most severe first, and each finding links to the settings that fix them.

Findings that are just noise for your team can also be muted, and all results can be exported to a CSV file for triage or reporting.

The Security Dashboard CLI

You can also run the same checks in your terminal through the new Vercel CLI vercel security check command, allowing your agents to work through the findings for you.

An agent using vercel security check --findings can read what failed, apply the fix and re-check to confirm. Fixes an agent can apply include:

  • Turning on Git fork protection

  • Marking an environment variable as sensitive

  • Replacing a static credential with OIDC federation

You can also scope the check to one project with --project when you want a narrow change set.

In CI or any other non-interactive environment, the command writes the report to stdout as JSON automatically, giving agents structured output without extra flags.

Get started by running your first scan from the Security Dashboard, and learn more in the Security Dashboard documentation.

title: KV-Cache Offload to NVMe vs Recompute: The TTFT Bill Comes Due
description:
Anyone who has run a long-context model in production has met the same wall. The GPU has enough compute to generate tokens quickly, and not enough memory to hold the conversation state that makes those tokens coherent. The state is the KV cache, and at long context it grows faster than the model weights it is supposed to serve.

There are two ways out. You can move the cache to cheaper memory and read it back when needed, or you can throw it away and recompute it. Both are in production at scale, both are defended loudly by their proponents, and both have a failure mode that only shows up under real traffic.

Part One: How big the cache actually gets

For a dense transformer, the KV cache per token is:

2 x layers x kv_heads x head_dim x bytes_per_element

Take a 70-billion-parameter model with 80 layers, 8 key-value heads (grouped-query attention), a head dimension of 128, and FP16 storage. Per token that is 2 x 80 x 8 x 128 x 2 bytes, or 327,680 bytes, about 0.31 megabytes. At 8,000 tokens of context that is 2.5 gigabytes per conversation. At 128,000 tokens it is 40 gigabytes, which is more than the weights of many models people are actually serving.

That number explains the entire architecture of modern inference serving. Continuous batching works because it interleaves sequences; prefix caching works because it avoids recomputing the same system prompt; paged attention works because it stops fragmentation from wasting the cache. Every one of those techniques exists to manage a data structure that grows linearly with context and does not shrink.

Part Two: The offload path

The offload argument is straightforward. NVMe drives deliver 5 to 14 gigabytes per second of sequential read on a modern enterprise part, and a PCIe 5.0 drive can do it at a cost per gigabyte two orders of magnitude below HBM. If the cache is written once and read once per decode step, and the decode step is already taking tens of milliseconds, the transfer can hide inside the compute.

That last clause is doing a lot of work. Hiding a transfer inside compute requires that the transfer and the compute overlap, which requires that the cache access pattern is predictable, which requires that the scheduler knows which sequence will be decoded next. In a batching system with dynamic arrival, that prediction is exactly the thing you cannot make reliably. The result is a tail: most steps hide the transfer, and a minority wait for it, and the p99 latency is set by the minority.

The second problem is write amplification. Every generated token appends to the cache. A naive implementation writes the whole block again; a good implementation appends. The difference between those two designs is a factor of a hundred in write bandwidth at long context, and it is the difference between an offload path that works and one that melts the drive.

Part Three: The recompute path

The recompute argument is equally straightforward. If the cache is too expensive to keep, do not keep it. When a conversation resumes, run the prefill again over the history. A prefill pass over 8,000 tokens on a modern accelerator is a few hundred milliseconds of compute, and compute is the resource you bought the GPU for.

The failure mode here is different and, in some ways, worse. Recompute turns a memory problem into a compute problem that competes with the work you are already doing. Under load, the GPU is saturated with decode steps for active users, and a resumed conversation arrives as a burst of prefill that has to be scheduled ahead of them or behind them. Ahead means existing users see a latency spike; behind means the resuming user waits.

There is a subtle economic point buried here. Prefill and decode have very different arithmetic intensity. Prefill is compute-bound and efficient; decode is memory-bandwidth-bound and inefficient. A serving system that recomputes is choosing to spend its most efficient resource on work it has already done once. A serving system that offloads is choosing to spend its cheapest resource on a transfer that might not overlap. Neither is obviously right; the answer depends on the ratio of resumed sessions to new sessions, which is a workload property nobody publishes.

Part Four: The hybrid that actually ships

In practice, production systems do both, with a policy. The cache stays in HBM for the active set, spills to host DRAM for the warm set, and is dropped for the cold set, where dropping means recompute on return. The policy is usually an LRU variant with a cost model attached: keep a sequence if the expected reuse probability times the recompute cost exceeds the storage cost.

The interesting engineering problem is that the cost model needs to know the future. A user who comes back in thirty seconds and a user who never comes back look identical at eviction time. Every production system solves this with a heuristic, and every heuristic is wrong in a way that shows up as either wasted memory or a latency spike. This is why the serving frameworks that win are the ones that expose the policy as configuration rather than hard-coding it.

Part Five: What this means outside the datacenter

The long-context assistant on your phone is running the same trade at a smaller scale. Mobile memory is shared with the operating system, the camera pipeline and every other app, and the model cannot assume it will get two gigabytes for a cache. That is why on-device assistants quietly truncate context, and why the experience of "it forgot what I said five minutes ago" is not a model quality problem but a memory budget problem.

The same arithmetic explains why long-context API pricing is not linear in tokens. Providers charge more for input than the raw compute suggests because the cache has to live somewhere, and somewhere costs money every second, not just when it is used.

Market sizing

Inference serving is the fastest-growing part of the AI infrastructure market, with analysts putting 2026 spend somewhere between 60 and 90 billion dollars, of which memory and storage for serving is a meaningful slice. If context lengths keep doubling every eighteen months, as the model releases suggest, the cache becomes the dominant memory consumer in the fleet, and the offload market becomes a storage market. That is a strange sentence to write about GPUs, and it is where the numbers point.

The comparison that matters

Offload optimises for compute efficiency and pays in tail latency and drive endurance. Recompute optimises for memory simplicity and pays in wasted compute and scheduling contention. The right answer is a policy, not a technology, and the policy depends on a number most teams never measure: the fraction of requests that are resumptions rather than new conversations.

Measure that number first. Everything else is a guess about a workload you have not characterised.

title: What If You Could Tell a Machine Exactly *What* and *How* to Move? DreamX Breaks the Mold
description:
DreamX Unveiled: The First Universal Latent‑Action Video Diffusion Model Hits the Public Sphere

Lead (Nov 3 2026) – A single arXiv posting and a Hugging Face model card shifted the AI conversation from “when will video diffusion become usable?” to “how will creators and robots actually command motion today.” That moment arrives with DreamX, the first diffusion engine that learns a latent representation of action and lets users dictate what happens and how it looks in a single request.

Key stat: DreamX delivers a +23 % lift on the Robotics‑ActionBench action‑consistency metric while matching state‑of‑the‑art FVD scores.

The release follows a meticulously staged rollout that began in June 2026 and culminates in a universal model poised to reshape content‑creation pipelines, robotic control stacks, and the emerging market for reusable “action libraries.” This article dissects the launch, benchmarks the competition, and evaluates the practical impact on production workflows.

1. Timeline & Roll‑out Blueprint

Date Milestone Core deliverable Strategic purpose
June 15 2026 DreamX‑World 1.0 (arXiv 2606.16993) Interactive text‑/image‑to‑video diffusion, camera‑control module E‑PRoPE, multi‑style rendering. Proves that a pre‑trained video diffusion backbone can follow long‑range camera trajectories, laying the data‑engine foundation.
August 13 2026 DreamX‑Phi 1.0 (arXiv 2608.13489) Action‑conditioned video world model for robotic manipulation; injects per‑arm constraints into diffusion steps. Demonstrates that latent actions respect physics, giving industrial partners a concrete use case.
Nov 3 2026 DreamX: Universal Latent‑Action Learner (arXiv 2611.05377) + Hugging‑Face model card (49 up‑votes) Full diffusion engine, latent‑action encoder/decoder, E‑PRoPE camera controller, and an open‑beta API. Announces the general‑purpose engine, synchronising visibility across pre‑print servers, model hubs, and AI newsletters.
Oct – Dec 2026 Closed beta (Oct–Nov) → Open beta (Dec) Partner studios, robotics labs, and game‑engine teams test the API; collect telemetry on latency, action drift, and user ergonomics. Generates real‑world feedback, refines the “prompt‑plus‑action” UI, and primes the marketplace for action assets.

Why the staged rollout matters (part 1)

DreamX engineers treated the research pipeline as a product‑development funnel. First, they validated the diffusion backbone on free‑form video generation (World).

Why the staged rollout matters (part 2)

Next, they tethered the model to a concrete domain (Phi) to showcase controllability. Finally, they stripped away domain constraints, exposing a universal latent‑action learner that any downstream user can plug into. The November launch aligns the arXiv pre‑print with a Hugging Face model hub posting, guaranteeing that the paper’s citations, the model’s download counters, and community chatter spike simultaneously.

2. Competitive Landscape

Competitor Primary strength (quantified) DreamX differentiator
Google Phenaki‑2 Trained on 10 B video‑text pairs; supports coherent narratives up to 30 seconds. Lacks explicit action abstraction; cannot guarantee that “pick‑up” translates to consistent kinematics across styles.
Meta Make‑A‑Video‑3 Achieves photorealistic rendering at ≈18 fps on a consumer‑grade RTX 3090. Provides only prompt‑level control; users cannot anchor a motion vector independent of visual style.
Runway Gen‑2 Real‑time generation (≈12 fps) with a built‑in library of 200 motion templates. Relies on pre‑canned motion templates; DreamX learns latent actions from data, enabling novel motions not present in a template bank.

DreamX’s latent‑action layer decouples semantics (the “pick‑up” or “jump”) from visual appearance (photorealistic, cartoon, low‑poly). That separation gives DreamX a strategic moat:

  1. Cross‑embodiment transfer – A latent “grasp” vector trained on a simulated robot arm reproduces on a real‑world manipulator without retraining the diffusion backbone.
  2. Reusable action tokens – Studios can publish a library of “action tokens” (e.g., “door‑open‑slow”) that any artist applies to any visual style.
  3. Engineering barrier – Replicating DreamX demands a pre‑trained video diffusion model (e.g., Stable‑Diffusion‑Video) plus a custom latent‑action encoder. Competitors must rebuild both components from scratch.

Key stat: DreamX runs at ≈30 fps on a single NVIDIA A100 when the lightweight E‑PRoPE controller handles camera pose updates, a speed comparable to Gen‑2 but with far richer motion control.

3. The “Prompt‑Plus‑Action” Interface

Traditional video generation pipelines separate motion from appearance: creators capture motion‑capture data, clean it, then feed it to a style‑transfer renderer. DreamX collapses that workflow into a single API call:

{
  "prompt": "A futuristic courier glides through a neon‑lit alley, delivering a holographic package",
  "action_token": "glide_forward_3m_speed_1.2",
  "style": "cell‑shaded"
}

The model parses the prompt for visual attributes, injects the action_token into the latent action encoder, and renders the requested style in the diffusion decoder. Two technical consequences follow.

3.1 Editable Latent Actions

DreamX exposes the latent action vector as a mutable tensor. Users can apply arithmetic operations—add speed, reverse direction, elongate trajectories—without recomputing the entire video. This capability reduces the average iteration time for motion tweaks from minutes (re‑rendering a full clip) to seconds (adjusting a vector and re‑decoding).

3.2 Cross‑Domain Reuse

Because the action token lives in a modality‑agnostic space, the same token drives a photorealistic render, a stylized illustration, or a real‑time Unity animation. Studios that previously maintained separate pipelines for VFX, game cut‑scenes, and advertising now share a single action repository.

4. Numbers that Matter

Metric DreamX (Nov 2026) Phenaki‑2 Make‑A‑Video‑3
Fréchet Video Distance (FVD) 78 (comparable to SOTA) 82 80
Action‑Consistency (Robotics‑ActionBench) +23 % over baseline N/A N/A
Inference speed (A100) 30 fps (E‑PRoPE) 12 fps 18 fps
Parameter count 1.9 B (diffusion) + 0.4 B (action encoder) 2.3 B 2.0 B
Community up‑votes (HF) 49 27 31

The +23 % lift on action consistency proves that DreamX’s latent actions preserve intended kinematics better than any prompt‑only baseline. The 30 fps inference rate satisfies real‑time requirements for interactive applications such as virtual production or robot teleoperation.

5. Case Study: Automating a Product Demo

A mid‑size consumer‑electronics firm needed 100 variants of a 10‑second product demo. The brief required:

  • A consistent “hand‑off” motion where a hand passes a smartphone to a second hand.
  • Four visual styles: photorealistic, matte‑paint, low‑poly, and a stylized comic look.
  • Slightly different camera pans for each variant.

Traditional pipeline

  1. Motion‑capture studio records the hand‑off (2 days).
  2. Engineers clean the mocap data, retarget it to each visual style (3 days).
  3. Artists manually adjust camera moves for each variant (4 days).

DreamX workflow

  1. Engineer writes a single prompt + action token (≈30 minutes).
  2. System generates all 100 videos in a batch, swapping style and camera parameters on the fly (≈2 hours).

Result: Production timeline shrinks by ≈40 %; cost savings exceed $250,000 for a single campaign.

6. Risks & Pivot Points

Risk Manifestation Mitigation
Action drift – latent action deviates from physically plausible motion. Generated robot‑arm clips intersect objects, or human avatars perform unnatural twists. Deploy the paper’s Action Consistency Metric as a pre‑flight check; integrate physics‑aware regularisers in the diffusion step.
Prompt‑action ambiguity – users misuse natural language to describe actions, leading to mismatched vectors. “Jump” token generates a slow hop instead of a high leap. Provide a curated taxonomy of action tokens; build a UI that visualises the latent vector before rendering.
Compute cost – real‑time inference still demands high‑end GPUs for full‑resolution output. Small studios cannot afford A100‑scale hardware. Offer a cloud‑based API with tiered pricing; release a quantised 8‑bit version that runs on RTX 4090 with modest quality loss.
Intellectual‑property exposure – latent action libraries may contain proprietary motion data. Competitors copy a “signature” action token. License action libraries under DRM‑protected tokens; embed watermarking in the latent space.

DreamX’s developers acknowledge these concerns in the appendix of the arXiv paper and propose an open‑source evaluation suite to standardise action‑consistency testing across the community.

7. Outlook: From Beta to Ecosystem

The closed beta (Oct 2026) already yields promising telemetry: partner studios report average latency 33 ms per frame, while robotics labs measure a 15 % reduction in control‑loop latency compared to traditional simulation‑to‑real pipelines. The upcoming open beta (Dec 2026) will expose the API to a broader audience, encouraging the emergence of:

  • Action marketplaces – creators upload tokenised motions (e.g., “sword‑slash‑fast”) and earn royalties per API call.
  • Hybrid pipelines – VFX houses combine DreamX‑generated base motion with fine‑grained key‑frame tweaks for cinematic polish.
  • Robotics‑as‑a‑Service – robot manufacturers integrate DreamX’s Action API to let end‑users program tasks via natural language.

If adoption follows the early‑beta trends, DreamX could become the de‑facto standard for controllable video diffusion within two years, forcing competitors to retrofit latent‑action layers onto their own backbones.

8. Key Takeaway

DreamX arrives not as a flashy headline but as a technical pivot that unifies motion and style in a single latent space. Its staged rollout, clear performance margins, and concrete API design give it a competitive edge that extends beyond raw image quality.

  • Content creators stand to compress months of motion‑capture and key‑frame work into a handful of prompt‑plus‑action statements.
  • Robotics engineers gain a reusable motion vocabulary that transfers across simulators and real hardware.

9. The Takeaway

  • Action as a first‑class citizen: DreamX’s latent‑action layer lets users specify motion independently of visual style.
  • Speed that scales: ≈30 fps on a single A100 meets real‑time demands while preserving high fidelity.
  • Reusable tokens: One action token powers photorealistic, stylized, and low‑poly renders alike.
  • Economic impact: Early adopters report up to 40 % faster production cycles and savings exceeding $250,000 per campaign.
  • Open ecosystem: Upcoming beta will seed action marketplaces and robotics‑as‑a‑service offerings.

Bottom line: DreamX does not merely add a new button to the video‑generation toolbox; it rewrites the underlying workflow by making action a first‑class citizen in diffusion models. Stakeholders who integrate the Action API now position themselves at the forefront of a workflow revolution that promises faster turn‑arounds, lower costs, and a new class of reusable motion assets.

title: Atlassian Connect end of support: what Jira and Confluence admins should check before 31 January 2027
description:
Disclosure: I'm from Kayabyte, which makes Burnrate and other Forge apps for Jira and Confluence. Burnrate comes up near the end.

Short answer: Atlassian Connect, the older way of building Cloud apps, reaches end of support on 31 January 2027. Atlassian doesn't say every Connect app stops working that day, but it will only address critical security patches from then on, and it warns that breakages will become more frequent and some platform changes will stop apps without advance notice. Admins should list their apps, check the warning on the Connected Apps page, ask each vendor for a migration plan, and test any replacement before the date, starting with the apps that billing, payroll or support depend on.

This page is for site admins, not developers. Facts about Connect come from Atlassian's own posts, linked below; things change, so check them before you rely on a date.

What changes on 31 January 2027

Atlassian's post says that from this date:

  • It will only address critical security patches, and support SLAs will be relaxed.
  • Connect will no longer evolve with the platform, and deprecations will come with shorter windows.
  • "Breakages will become more frequent, and the user experience will degrade."
  • Some infrastructure changes "will cause apps to stop functioning without advance notice."

Atlassian has said it will share more on what happens after end of support, and hasn't yet given those details.

The checklist

  1. List your apps. Copy the list from your site's Connected Apps page in administration. Note who uses each app and who owns it.
  2. Read the warning. That page shows a Connect end of support warning for apps it applies to. A vendor can replace the generic text with its own message and a link to its migration plan.
  3. Don't panic at a flag. Atlassian's developer advocate has called the "at risk" flag "a blurry signal" that can produce false positives. It's a reason to check, not a verdict.
  4. Ask the vendor three things. Is the app fully on Forge today? If not, by what date? Does anything stop working or change after the move?
  5. Check independently if you want. forge-apps.com shows the Forge status of released Marketplace versions. It isn't run by Atlassian and doesn't show a vendor's intentions.
  6. Check what the move removes. Vendors' own notes show that some features don't survive a migration, so read the change notes for what your team uses.
  7. Rank by damage. Rank apps by what breaks if they stop without warning. Reports used for invoices, payroll, audits and SLAs come first.
  8. Test before you need it. If you may have to change app, compare old and new on one closed period and one real project. Leave time for this: a month-end report needs at least one month-end to compare.

Questions for reporting and cost apps

Reports fail quietly, so these need a closer look:

  • Do the numbers match? Compare one closed month against a figure you trust.
  • Who is named on the worklog? Worklogs synced from another time app may show that app as the author in Jira, and per-person figures can then come up short. Open one work item and check.
  • Do past figures stay fixed? If a rate changes, last month's cost shouldn't move.
  • Where does the data go? Forge apps can run entirely on Atlassian's platform, but not all of them do. Ask, and check the app's listing.

Which of our apps this affects

None of the Kayabyte apps. Burnrate, Group Participants, Group Watchers and Personal WIP Limits were all built on Forge from the start, so there's no migration to wait for. Burnrate is the one that matters for this topic: it prices native Jira worklogs with dated rates and shows budgets. It's new, with no reviews, so test it against a closed month as above. It's on the Atlassian Marketplace.

FAQ

When does Atlassian Connect end? End of support begins on 31 January 2027. The date was moved from December 2026.

Will my Connect apps stop working on 31 January 2027? Atlassian doesn't say that all of them stop on that date. It does say breakages will become more frequent and that some platform changes will stop apps without advance notice.

How do I know if a Marketplace app is on Connect or Forge? Look for the warning on the Connected Apps page in site administration and ask the vendor. forge-apps.com, which isn't run by Atlassian, also shows the status of released versions.

What does the "at risk" banner mean? It's based on an app's migration status and the intent its vendor has declared. Atlassian describes it as a blurry signal that can produce false positives, so ask the vendor before you replace an app.

What should I do first? List your apps, rank them by what would break if they stopped without warning, and ask the vendors of the top ones for a migration date.

title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore: How AWS Built Multi-Agent Orchestration for Engineering Decision Workflows
description:
AWS just published the first detailed look at AgentCore, their multi-agent orchestration layer inside Amazon Bedrock. The use case is aerospace component substitution: an engineer needs to evaluate whether part B can replace part A in a certified aircraft system. Traditionally this takes days of manual cross-referencing across PDFs, CAD drawings, spec sheets, and regulatory documents. AWS compressed it to minutes by coordinating specialized agents that gather evidence, validate compliance, and surface recommendations while keeping the human engineer as the final decision-maker.

This is not a demo. The architecture reveals production patterns for state flow between agents, human-in-the-loop approval gates, multimodal evidence retrieval, and failure handling in managed cloud infrastructure.

The Orchestration Problem

Multi-agent systems fail when orchestration becomes a bottleneck. A central coordinator that serializes every agent call creates latency and single points of failure. AWS designed AgentCore to avoid this by treating orchestration as a declarative graph of agent capabilities rather than a procedural script.

Each agent in the substitution workflow has a narrow responsibility:

  • Specification Agent: Retrieves technical specs from multimodal knowledge bases (text + images from PDFs, CAD metadata).
  • Compliance Agent: Checks regulatory constraints (FAA airworthiness directives, OEM bulletins).
  • Compatibility Agent: Evaluates dimensional fit, material properties, and performance envelopes.
  • Risk Agent: Surfaces failure modes, maintenance history, and field service reports.

AgentCore routes context between these agents without forcing them through a single queue. State flows as structured evidence objects, not raw LLM outputs.

State Flow and Context Passing

The key primitive is the evidence bundle. When the Specification Agent retrieves a datasheet, it does not return unstructured text. It returns a typed object with:

  • Source document ID and page reference
  • Extracted parameters (dimensions, tolerances, material codes)
  • Confidence scores for each extraction
  • Multimodal embeddings for cross-modal retrieval

The Compliance Agent receives this bundle and queries its own knowledge base using both text and image embeddings. If the part drawing shows a mounting pattern, the embedding captures spatial geometry that text alone would miss. Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings handle this by encoding text and images into a shared vector space, so a query like "mounting hole pattern for bracket assembly" retrieves both written specs and CAD screenshots.

State does not accumulate in a monolithic context window. Each agent maintains its own working memory and publishes findings to a shared evidence store. The orchestrator tracks dependencies (Compatibility Agent waits for Specification Agent results) but does not serialize execution.

Human-in-the-Loop Approval Gates

The Strands Agents SDK exposes a human_approval_required flag that pauses execution and surfaces a decision point. In the aerospace workflow, this triggers after all agents have contributed evidence but before the final substitution recommendation is generated.

The approval gate is not a simple yes/no prompt. It presents:

  • Structured evidence from each agent
  • Confidence intervals for critical parameters
  • Highlighted discrepancies (e.g., material spec mismatch)
  • Regulatory citations that require manual review

The engineer can approve, reject, or request additional evidence. If they request more data, the orchestrator reruns specific agents with refined queries. This is async by design. The workflow persists state to DynamoDB and resumes when the engineer returns, even if that takes hours.

Multimodal Evidence Retrieval

The knowledge base is not a flat vector store. AWS uses Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with multimodal embeddings to index:

  • PDF technical manuals (text + embedded diagrams)
  • CAD drawings exported as images with metadata
  • Maintenance logs (structured tables + free-text notes)
  • Regulatory documents (text + compliance matrices)

When the Compatibility Agent needs to verify a dimensional constraint, it queries with both the part number (text) and a reference image of the mounting interface (image). The retrieval system returns documents where either modality matches, ranked by combined similarity.

This avoids the failure mode where an agent retrieves a spec sheet but misses the critical diagram on the next page. The multimodal embedding treats the diagram as first-class evidence, not an afterthought.

Failure Modes and Recovery

AWS does not hide failure. The orchestrator tracks agent execution status and surfaces errors to the human operator. Common failure modes:

Failure Type Recovery Strategy Impact
Agent timeout Retry with exponential backoff, escalate to human if 3 failures Delays workflow but preserves partial evidence
Retrieval miss Surface "no evidence found" to human, allow manual document upload Prevents false negatives from incomplete knowledge base
Conflicting evidence Flag discrepancy, require human adjudication Stops workflow until resolved
Tool call error Log error, continue with degraded evidence set Partial results still useful for human review

The system does not retry silently. Each failure is logged with context (which agent, which tool, which query) and surfaced in the approval gate UI. The engineer sees what worked and what did not.

Deployment Shape

The architecture runs entirely on managed AWS services:

  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore: Orchestration layer, agent definitions, tool routing
  • Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases: Multimodal vector store with OpenSearch Serverless backend
  • Amazon Nova: Multimodal embeddings and LLM inference
  • AWS Lambda: Custom tool implementations (e.g., CAD file parser)
  • Amazon DynamoDB: Workflow state persistence
  • Amazon S3: Document storage (PDFs, CAD files, images)

There is no Kubernetes cluster, no custom orchestrator, no hand-rolled state machine. The Strands Agents SDK abstracts the plumbing into declarative agent definitions and tool schemas.

Agent Definition Example

The Specification Agent is defined as a JSON schema that Bedrock interprets:

{
  "agentName": "SpecificationAgent",
  "instruction": "Retrieve technical specifications for aerospace components from multimodal knowledge bases. Extract dimensions, materials, and performance parameters.",
  "tools": [
    {
      "name": "query_knowledge_base",
      "description": "Search technical documentation using text and image queries",
      "parameters": {
        "query_text": "string",
        "query_image": "optional base64 image",
        "filter": "optional metadata filter"
      }
    },
    {
      "name": "extract_parameters",
      "description": "Parse structured data from retrieved documents",
      "parameters": {
        "document_id": "string",
        "parameter_names": "array of strings"
      }
    }
  ],
  "knowledgeBases": [
    {
      "id": "kb-aerospace-specs",
      "retrievalConfig": {
        "vectorSearchConfiguration": {
          "numberOfResults": 10,
          "overrideSearchType": "HYBRID"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

The orchestrator uses this schema to route tool calls and manage retrieval. The agent does not implement retry logic or error handling. That lives in the platform.

Versioning and Rollback

AWS handles agent versioning through Bedrock's built-in version control. Each agent definition has a version number. When you update an agent's instruction or tool schema, Bedrock creates a new version and keeps the old one.

Workflows reference agent versions explicitly. If a workflow is in progress when you deploy a new agent version, it continues using the old version until completion. New workflows pick up the new version.

This prevents mid-flight failures when you change agent logic. The trade-off is that you cannot hot-patch a running workflow. If you discover a bug in an agent, you must wait for in-progress workflows to complete or manually abort them.

Trade-Offs

What you gain:

  • No orchestrator code to write or maintain
  • Built-in state persistence and async execution
  • Multimodal retrieval without custom embedding pipelines
  • Human-in-the-loop primitives that handle async latency
  • Managed scaling and failure recovery

What you give up:

  • Lock-in to AWS Bedrock and its pricing model
  • Limited control over orchestration logic (no custom DAG execution)
  • Opaque retry and timeout behavior (you configure thresholds but do not control the retry loop)
  • Multimodal embeddings are black-box (you cannot inspect or debug the vector space)

Technical Verdict

Use AgentCore when:

  • You need multi-agent coordination on AWS infrastructure without building an orchestrator
  • Your workflow requires human approval gates with async decision latency
  • You have multimodal evidence (PDFs with diagrams, CAD files, images) that agents must retrieve and reason over
  • You want managed state persistence and do not want to run your own database for workflow tracking

Avoid AgentCore when:

  • You need fine-grained control over orchestration logic (custom retry policies, dynamic DAG construction)
  • Your agents run on-prem or in a different cloud (AgentCore is AWS-only)
  • You cannot tolerate vendor lock-in to Bedrock's pricing and API surface
  • Your workflow requires real-time latency (sub-second agent coordination). AgentCore optimizes for correctness and auditability, not speed.

The aerospace substitution use case is a good fit because correctness matters more than speed, human oversight is mandatory, and the evidence is inherently multimodal. If your domain has similar constraints, AgentCore provides production-grade plumbing without custom orchestration code.

title: FydelisSec Toolkit: Construindo um Ecossistema de Segurança em Rust >
description:
Autor: Adiel Santos Fontes / FydelisTechOS

Fonte:github.com/fydelis2025/Pentest

Local: Salvador, Bahia — Brasil

Data: Novembro de 2026

Linguagem: Rust

Licença: Apache-2.0

Resumo

Este artigo apresenta o FydelisSec Toolkit, um repositório open-source dedicado ao desenvolvimento de ferramentas de segurança, auditoria e testes de penetração todas escritas integralmente em Rust. O projeto não se trata de uma única aplicação, mas de um ecossistema unificado de utilitários que compartilham a mesma filosofia técnica: performance máxima, confiabilidade, segurança de memória e portabilidade entre plataformas. Aqui exploramos os motivos da escolha da linguagem, a arquitetura comum a todos os projetos, os desafios de desenvolvimento e os princípios éticos que guiam todo o trabalho.

Por que Rust para Segurança?

Quando decidimos criar um conjunto de ferramentas de segurança do zero, a escolha da linguagem foi o primeiro passo — e Rust se impôs como a alternativa mais sólida. Em um domínio onde:

Velocidade importa — milhões de operações por segundo fazem diferença
Estabilidade é crítica — um crash no meio de um teste pode comprometer dados
Concorrência é constante — múltiplas tarefas rodando ao mesmo tempo sem conflitos
Distribuição precisa ser simples — entregar sem exigir instalação de runtime
Rust oferece vantagens que nenhuma outra linguagem combina:

Execução nativa

Sem interpretador, sem coletor de lixo desempenho no nível de C/C++

Segurança de memória

Nenhum dangling pointer, nenhum acesso fora do limite erros comuns em auditorias eliminados em tempo de compilação

Concorrência sem medo

O sistema de tipos impede condições de corrida; múltiplas threads trabalhando sem risco

Binário único

Cada projeto compila para um arquivo executável independente fácil de distribuir e usar

Gerenciamento moderno

Cargo resolve dependências, compila e empacota em um só fluxo

Multiplataforma

Mesmo código compila nativamente para Windows, Linux e macOS

"Em segurança, confiança no código é o primeiro requisito. Rust não só nos dá velocidade nos dá garantias."

O Ecossistema FydelisSec

O repositório organiza-se como uma coleção de projetos independentes, cada um com sua finalidade, mas todos alinhados pelos mesmos padrões técnicos:

Arquitetura modular — cada ferramenta vive em sua própria pasta, com Cargo.toml e código-fonte próprios
Filosofia CLI unificada — mesma interface, mesmos padrões de ajuda e de saída em todos os utilitários
Construção compartilhada — cargo build --release funciona da mesma forma em qualquer projeto
Princípios comuns — validação de entradas, tratamento de erros claro, mensagens que guiam o usuário
Comportamento previsível — códigos de saída padronizados, relatórios estruturados, confirmações explícitas
Cada projeto resolve um problema específico dentro do universo de segurança — desde testes de credenciais até análise de sistemas — mas todos partilham a mesma base técnica e a mesma visão: ferramentas profissionais, transparentes e responsáveis.

Princípios de Desenvolvimento

Código que o Usuário Entende

Ferramentas de segurança costumam ser confusas. Aqui, o padrão é outro:

Ajuda detalhada acessível via --help em qualquer ferramenta
Mensagens de erro dizem o que aconteceu e como resolver
Saída legível tanto para humanos quanto para automação
Confirmações antes de ações destrutivas ou demoradas
Performance como Requisito

Otimização não é algo opcional

Paralelismo onde faz sentido, com balanceamento de carga entre núcleos
Estruturas de dados eficientes para busca e filtragem
Processamento sem cópias desnecessárias de dados em memória
Compilação otimizada por padrão: LTO ativado, sem símbolos de depuração no release
Segurança no Próprio Código

Nenhum uso desnecessário de unsafe — o mínimo possível, sempre justificado
Validação de todos os dados de entrada, inclusive de arquivos e de processos externos
Tratamento robusto de caminhos, permissões e limites do sistema operacional
Revisão de dependências — apenas bibliotecas confiáveis e mantidas entram no projeto
Portabilidade Real

O mesmo código funciona nativamente nos três principais sistemas operacionais:

Caminhos de arquivo usando tipos abstratos, não strings fixas
Detecção dinâmica de binários e comandos conforme o ambiente
Separação explícita de trechos específicos de sistema operacional quando inevitável
Desafios Comuns e Soluções

Processos Externos e Integração

Muitas tarefas de segurança envolvem chamar programas do sistema. Cada ferramenta lida com isso de forma padronizada:

Detecção automática de disponibilidade dos utilitários necessários
Tratamento de saídas com formatos diferentes entre versões
Tempo limite e encerramento limpo de processos travados
Normalização de mensagens para análise consistente
Estado entre Execuções

Operações longas podem ser interrompidas. O sistema de cache e retomada:

Salva progresso de forma leve e segura
Evita retrabalho na próxima execução
Funciona de forma transparente para o usuário
Não deixa lixo no sistema além de arquivos temporários padrão
Concorrência sem Caos

Quando múltiplas tarefas rodam ao mesmo tempo:

Contadores atômicos para estatísticas — sem gargalo de bloqueio
Sinalização limpa de conclusão entre threads
Tratamento de interrupção do usuário (Ctrl+C) com estatísticas finais
Encerramento ordenado sem corrupção de dados
Ética como Fundamento

Mais importante que qualquer funcionalidade é o compromisso com a responsabilidade:

Todo o código neste repositório destina-se a uso exclusivo em sistemas e dados sobre os quais você tenha autorização legal. Auditoria, pesquisa, defesa e fortalecimento da segurança são atividades legítimas acessar ou interferir em sistemas sem consentimento explícito é crime.

As ferramentas não exploram falhas para contornar defesas; elas aplicam métodos conhecidos de teste de resistência, da mesma forma que um profissional autorizado faria. O objetivo não é facilitar ataques é tornar o conhecimento acessível para que sistemas sejam mais seguros.

Como Participar

O repositório está aberto e convida a comunidade:

Testar e relatar problemas encontrados
Sugerir melhorias e novos utilitários
Contribuir com código seguindo os padrões estabelecidos
Estudar para aprender como ferramentas de segurança funcionam por dentro
Toda contribuição fortalece o ecossistema e ajuda a construir um ambiente digital mais seguro.

Conclusão

O FydelisSec Toolkit é mais que um conjunto de programas é uma demonstração do que a combinação de Rust + conhecimento + ética pode produzir. Ferramentas rápidas, estáveis, transparentes e acessíveis, desenvolvidas de forma independente a partir de Salvador, Bahia.

A meta continua sendo a mesma: criar referência, compartilhar saber e lembrar que tecnologia não é neutra o que importa é para quem e para quê serve.

"O conhecimento em segurança deve ser compartilhado para que todos possam se defender."

FydelisTechos © 2026 — github.com/fydelis2025/Pentest

title: How to Localize App Screenshots Without Redrawing Them
description:
You extracted every string. You wired up i18next (or react-intl, or .strings files). Your UI now speaks Japanese, German and Spanish.

Then you open your App Store listing, your landing page, or your docs, and every screenshot is still in English.

That's the part of localization most of us skip. It's also the part users see first. On an app store page, people look at screenshots before they read a single line of your description. A Japanese user scrolling past English screenshots has already decided your app "isn't for them."

This post covers which images actually need localizing, the usual ways teams handle it, and a faster approach I've been using.

Which images actually need localizing?

Before you translate anything, take inventory. Text baked into images usually hides in five places:

• App Store / Google Play screenshots — usually the highest-impact images you own.

• Open Graph and social share images — what people see when your link is shared.

• Landing page hero and feature images — especially UI mockups with button labels.

• Help docs and tutorials — screenshots of your own interface.

• Email banners and onboarding graphics.

A quick test: open your site with a non-English locale and screenshot every page. Any English you can still read is on your list.

The three usual approaches (and where they break)

  1. Recreate each image per language in Figma. This gives the best control, if you still have clean source files. But the work grows linearly: 5 screenshots × 10 languages is 50 assets. And every copy change means redoing all of them.

  2. Hand it to a designer or agency. Good quality, but slow and expensive for a small team. It also turns every small copy tweak into a ticket.

  3. OCR + machine translation + paste it back on top. Cheap, but the result usually looks off. The new text doesn't match the original font, the background behind the old text needs patching, and longer translations overflow their boxes.

None of these is great when you just want your screenshots to match your already-translated UI.

Translating text directly inside the image

AI image translation tools now handle the whole pipeline in one step: detect the text, translate it, erase the original, and render the translation back in roughly the same position and style.

I use Editaimg's image translator for this. The workflow:

  1. Upload the screenshot (PNG, JPG or WebP).
  2. Pick the target language.
  3. Let it detect and replace the text.
  4. Review the result and download.

It currently supports 16 languages: Arabic, Chinese, English, French, German, Hindi, Indonesian, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish, Thai, Turkish and Vietnamese.

It's pay-as-you-go with credit packs rather than a subscription, which suits localization work: you do a big batch when you launch a language, then almost nothing for months.

Tips to get usable results

AI translation gets you most of the way. These habits close the gap:

• Start from screenshots with less text. Fewer, shorter labels translate more cleanly than dense paragraphs.

• Leave room for expansion. German and Russian often run 20–35% longer than English. If a button label is already tight, it will overflow.

• Check right-to-left languages manually. For Arabic, confirm the text direction and alignment look natural, not just that the words are correct.

• Inspect CJK and Thai rendering. Make sure characters aren't clipped and line breaks fall in sensible places.

• Use your own glossary. If your UI calls it a "Workspace," the screenshot shouldn't say "Project." Compare against your translation files.

• Get a native speaker to glance at the hero images. Ten minutes of review on your top three images is worth it.

A workflow that scales

Don't localize everything at once. Pick the two or three languages where you already see traffic or sign-ups in your analytics. Translate only your store screenshots and landing page hero for those. Watch conversion for a few weeks, then expand to the rest of your images and languages.

Keep your English originals and translated versions in a predictable folder structure (for example screenshots/ja/01-home.png). Then your store upload or static site build can pick the right file per locale.

Wrapping up

Localization isn't done when the strings are translated. If your screenshots still speak only English, so does the first impression of your product.

If you're localizing e-commerce images rather than app screenshots, I wrote a separate guide on translating Amazon listing images.

How does your team handle screenshot localization today? I'd love to hear what's worked for you in the comments.

Abstract: Test-time search can improve structured planning, but when methods differ in prompts, post-processing, and selection, it is unclear what an observed gain should be attributed to. We study this question on DisasterBench, where models compose typed multi-tool workflows, by decomposing inference into three observable stages: whether a correct workflow is discovered, whether it survives structural validation, and whether it is finally selected. Comparing independent sampling, a nominal tree-search configuration, and multi-operator search under controlled inference budgets on two model families, we find that (i) the nominal tree-search configuration realizes non-adaptive complete-workflow sampling, and independent sampling with its expansion prompt reproduces its candidate discovery without constructing a tree; (ii) structural validation never removes the last correct workflow in our evaluated candidate pools, whereas majority voting leaves a discovered correct workflow unselected on 10-19% of tasks per pool, with an audit confirming substantive tool-choice or information-flow errors in 57 of 60 examined cases; and (iii) a tool-specification-aware verifier recovers some of these losses but overturns more correct decisions than it fixes. Our results motivate auditing realized rather than nominal inference pipelines, and reporting discovery, validity, and selection separately.
