title: Your AI agent forgets why. Give it a decision record
description:
You spend a session getting an order form right. One page, not three steps. A review summary before submit. Delivery date where people actually look for it. Then a new prompt regenerates the form, and the agent goes back to a three-step wizard, because nothing told it why you chose otherwise.

The agent kept the code. It did not keep the reasons.

Design Decision Method handles this with step 4 of its workflow: the decision record.

What a decision record captures

For a choice that would be costly to undo, the method asks you (or your agent) to record:

  • task frequency
  • user familiarity
  • the cost of a mistake
  • the device
  • the pattern chosen, and why

It also asks you to judge effort in a specific way: compare the effort to read, remember, enter, navigate, and recover, rather than counting clicks or visible elements. A three-step flow has fewer fields per screen. That does not make it less effort if people have to go back to check what they entered on step one.

Two more rules keep the record honest:

  • Cite a source only when it resolves an actual design problem. No decorative references.
  • Mark departures. When the design departs from a cited source's rule, add one adaptation line: source rule / what this design does instead / why the frequency, familiarity, or error cost requires it. Never present an adaptation as upstream guidance.

A worked example

Say you run a small print shop at example.com, and you ask your agent to build the order form. This is an illustration of how the procedure applies, not a case study or a measured result.

The decision row looks like this:

Decision Frequency Familiarity Error cost Device Pattern chosen Reason
Order form layout Occasional, once per order Mostly first-time customers Medium: a wrong size or quantity means a reprint Phone first One page, grouped sections, review summary before submit Customers need to see size, quantity, and price together to catch mistakes. Splitting them across steps adds recall effort at the point of decision.

If a source you cite recommends a different pattern for this form, that is where an adaptation line goes, in the same three-part form.

The record also carries a short validation status, because step 6 of the method asks for an honest evidence label on each result: proposed, heuristic review, automated check, manual test, or user research. For this form it might read:

  • Valid entries survive a validation error: not tested (manual test planned).
  • Size, quantity, and price visible together before submit: heuristic review.

Untested stays untested. The record says so instead of implying the form works.

What the next prompt does with it

Next week you ask the agent to add a "rush delivery" option. The following prompt starts from that record. The agent can see the form is one page for a reason, and that the reason is error cost, not taste. It adds the option inside the existing structure instead of reinventing the flow.

A person still checks the result. The method does not measure how many prompts that removes, and whether it saves time has not been measured.

Keep it small

The decision record is proportional. A small change gets a few lines. The repo's design record template is a scaffold, not mandatory overhead. Save the record with the work (as docs/design/<slug>.md) when your project keeps design records, or deliver a compact record inline with the change when it does not.

You do not need a record for every edit either. The method is a shared procedure, not mandatory for every small edit. Record the choices you would be annoyed to re-argue.

Where this fits

The decision record is step 4 of six: establish context, choose the visual system, map objects before layout, write a decision record, structure each view, then deliver and validate.

Try it

Design Decision Method is a lightweight design decision workflow for developers building interfaces with AI agents. It follows the open Agent Skills format and is MIT licensed. Install paths for Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI, and Codex are in the README.

  • Docs: https://frozonfreak.github.io/DesignDecesionMethod/
  • Repo: https://github.com/frozonfreak/DesignDecesionMethod
  • Design record template: https://github.com/frozonfreak/DesignDecesionMethod/blob/main/assets/design-record-template.md

title: Sam Altman's Hardware Gaslighting: Why Local Inference Terrifies Cloud AI Monopolies
description:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman stirred up significant controversy across the developer and local AI community when he remarked:

"Running inference on local hardware is a terrible allocation of scarce resources. Compute should be concentrated in massive hyperscale data centers where efficiency is maximized."

Let's call this what it actually is: Hardware Gaslighting.

The Economic Threat of Local Silicon

Why does the CEO of the world's most heavily funded AI startup care whether an engineer runs a model on their own MacBook Pro or RTX 4090?

Because software sovereignty destroys subscription monopoly rents.

When an engineer or enterprise runs a quantized 8B or 70B open-weights model locally:

  1. Recurring API Revenue Becomes $0: No monthly token invoice, no rate limit throttling, no credit card lock-in.
  2. Data Privacy is Absolute: Zero proprietary source code or customer logs leave the perimeter.
  3. Silicon Belongs to the Builder: A one-time capital expense for a 128GB Unified Memory Mac Studio or local multi-GPU rig amortizes to zero within months.

The Silicon Valley playbook has always relied on the "You will own nothing and be happy" cloud rentier model. When developers started running production-grade inference on commodity hardware, the panic began.

The Hypocrisy of the "Efficiency" Argument

The argument that centralized 5-gigawatt data centers in the desert are "environmentally more efficient" than running a model on idle edge silicon is computationally absurd.

  • Per-Token Network Latency: Transmitting prompt contexts across transatlantic fiber lines burns gigawatt-hours of networking infrastructure.
  • Cooling Overhead (PUE Penalty): Cooling hundreds of thousands of GPUs in concentrated hyperscale centers requires massive industrial chilling plants.
  • Idle Capacity: Millions of personal laptops, workstations, and local servers sit with billions of unused TOPS of compute every single second.

Claiming that putting a 70B model on your local machine is "wasteful" is equivalent to an airline telling you that owning a bicycle is an inefficient allocation of transportation assets.

Software Sovereignty Is Non-Negotiable

The future of engineering doesn't belong to developers waiting in line for API rate limits to reset. It belongs to builders who own their compute, run their own weights, and refuse to pay rent on their own intelligence.

Don't surrender your silicon.

Originally published on Kürşat Yılmaz Technical Blog

title: Financial Crime Mitigation with MongoDB / Part IV: Agentic AI for Case Management
description:
Welcome back to the last part of our series on Building a Financial Crime Mitigation Platform. We have shown how MongoDB ideally supports the technical capabilities of modern digital financial operations as a unified data platform. In case you missed it, be sure to check out the series overview.

In today’s world, fraud management systems need to react in the moment. Immediacy has become a must-have characteristic of control systems. Real-time monitoring is required not only to block potential fraudulent activities, but also to fulfill customers’ expectations. Modern financial services, like instant payments, demand straight-through screening processing that executes all the corresponding checks instantaneously. Therefore, the challenge is to ensure comprehensive checks are executed without creating bottlenecks in the customer experience.

This blog explains how to operationalize enhanced due diligence with an agentic SAR investigation pipeline built with LangGraph and MongoDB. Rather than stopping at alert generation, the solution uses specialized agents to triage suspicious activity, gather evidence in parallel across entities, transaction, network, and watchlist data, analyze investigative leads, draft compliance-ready SAR narratives, and route cases through durable human-in-the-loop review.

To begin, we must put in perspective the end-to-end process for fraud management, which consists of the following stages:

Figure 1. Fraud management end-to-end process.

Fraud reaction’s due diligence

Previously, we learned how to build a dynamic profile for the fraud prevention stage. Then, we analyzed how fraud detection can be enhanced by conducting a behavioural analysis and transaction monitoring. Now, if an activity has been flagged as suspicious, then we have arrived at the last stage, fraud reaction: here we need to combine information from the customer profile, the anti-money laundering policies, with the transaction’s contextual information, along with the Suspicious Activity Report generated in the previous step. This last process is known as due diligence.

Enhanced due diligence

Historically, digitized anti-money laundering (AML) solutions focused on dashboarding and rule-based automation. While these improved service level agreements (SLAs), they introduced a "fragmentation tax" risk. Analysts must manually stitch together disparate data points, leading to high false-positive rates and significant operational latency.

Agentic AI introduces a paradigm shift: rather than relying on brittle, hard-coded rules, financial services institutions can deploy autonomous, specialized agents that synthesize disparate data points in real-time. However, for these agents to be effective in an enterprise setting, they require more than just a large language model (LLM); they require a durable, high-performance data backbone.

Digitized solutions came to the rescue to support risk analysts in their jobs. Mainly, by enabling reporting dashboards, powered by fast search engines, and automating some tasks with rule-based logic. Even though digitized solutions drastically improved SLAs, it was still error-prone. Several studies have shown that not only the rate of false positives remains high, but they are increasingly running on a costly operation with little to no return on investment (ROI).

(Agentic AI) Enhanced due diligence

Agentic AI capabilities make the perfect fit for this scenario: Having smart agents that can automate manual checks more accurately, being able to easily combine several data points, or better yet generate synthetic data for evaluating potential scenarios, and lastly bringing natural language interactive ability, makes the perfect co-pilot to risk analyst for providing precise recommendations in complex cases, or to have the full autonomy to approve or reject evident cases that won’t require a human escalation.

Putting into practice agentic AI-enhanced due diligence (EDD)

Coming back to the demo prototype we’ve explored in the series, we have a team of agents specialized in completing specific tasks:

Figure 2. Specialized agents created for enhanced due diligence operations.

When operationalizing Agentic AI for “fraud reaction”, the architectural focus must be on state management. A common pitfall is assuming the agent itself holds the "truth." In enterprise AML, the agent is merely the processor; the state must reside in a durable, persistent store.

MongoDB and LangGraph provide an ideal architectural fit: LangGraph provides the orchestration and dynamic routing, and MongoDB serves as the single source of truth. Its flexible document model handles the polymorphic nature of AML data (SARs, alerts, and entity metadata) without the need for destructive schema migrations. Leveraging MongoDB Atlas Vector Search allows financial institutions to consolidate transactional data and vector embeddings into a single store, eliminating the "database sprawl" associated with maintaining separate vector databases and operational stores.

For CTOs, "agentic" does not imply "unsupervised." The true power of this architecture lies in the Human-in-the-loop (HITL) pattern as an explicit Audit Design Pattern. Using MongoDB to store the complete provenance of an agent’s decision-making process supports auditability by making every step traceable. Risk analysts do not just see a final decision; they see the chain of thought and the data sources that led to that decision, allowing for faster, more confident sign-offs.

Figure 3. Stages for automating having a Human-in-the-loop as “analyst review” step.

Agentic process workflow

After building and configuring the specialized agents comes the agentic process workflow:

Figure 4. Agentic workflow for enhanced due diligence operations.

  1. The process begins with a notification to the triage agent that a new Suspicious Activity Report (SAR) has been registered. It proceeds to launch a few sub-agents for fetching actions: gathering information from the entity, transactions, watchlists, and network.
  2. Next, it derives all the consolidated information to a case analyst agent, which in turn orchestrates the analysis done by sub-agents. It sends all the generated output to a SAR author agent, an expert in Due Diligence terminology, which ensures that the case is documented using the organization's terminology.
  3. The SAR is handed over to a compliance QA agent that ensures that it is following the policies, rules, and standards defined by the risk management organization. Using its natural language capabilities, it can adjust accordingly.
  4. Lastly, the case is handed over to the risk analyst for the final human review in order to be dispatched for the corresponding compliance enforcement action.

Takeaways

Implementing agentic AI shifts your fraud mitigation strategy from "manual effort" to "autonomous scale." To successfully scale this architecture, keep these foundational principles in mind:

  • Design for specialization: Do not build "general purpose" agents. Design specialized agents with narrow scopes to simplify monitoring, governance, and model optimization.
  • Centralize state, distribute logic: Maintain a single contextual data layer (MongoDB) as your source of truth. Allow your orchestration framework (LangGraph) to handle the logic, but offload the persistence of state to the data platform.
  • Prioritize auditability: Ensure your agentic workflow captures not just the output, but the context and references used for each decision. This transforms "AI recommendations" into "compliance-ready logs."

This is the last article in this series. We would like to thank you for joining us in this journey. Feel free to revisit the series to have a full picture of building a Financial Crime Mitigation platform powered by a modern data platform like MongoDB. We also invite you to check out our prototype (demo repo) and share any feedback or suggestions. Thank you!

1  Global Financial and Economic Crime Outlook 2025

title: AI-Generated Mascots vs Developer-Controlled Rive Characters
description:
Stop Treating Your App Mascot Like a Video: Build an Interactive Character With Rive

AI-generated animation clips are great for demos. But what happens when your app needs skins, levels, emotions, eye tracking, and real-time control?

AI-generated mascot animations are everywhere.

You can generate a character, create a few animation clips, and integrate them into your React app, mobile application, or SaaS dashboard.

For a simple experience, that works.

But imagine your product grows.

Your mascot now needs to:

  • React to different application states.
  • Change skins without restarting its animation.
  • Display user progression and level-up effects.
  • Control eye direction and facial expressions independently.
  • Respond to taps, achievements, and real-time events.
  • Evolve into different character forms.

Suddenly, your mascot isn't just an animation anymore.

It's an interactive component of your application's UI.

And that's where the architecture matters.

1. The Problem With Clip-Based Mascots

Let's start with a common implementation.

You have five animation files:

mascot/
├── idle.webm
├── happy.webm
├── sad.webm
├── sleeping.webm
└── celebrating.webm

Your application switches between them based on user activity.

A simplified React implementation might look like this:

const animations = {
  idle: "/mascot/idle.webm",
  happy: "/mascot/happy.webm",
  sad: "/mascot/sad.webm",
  celebrating: "/mascot/celebrating.webm",
};

function Mascot({ state = "idle" }) {
  return (
    <video
      key={state}
      src={animations[state]}
      autoPlay
      muted
      playsInline
    />
  );
}

This example is intentionally minimal. Production code would also need to handle looping, animation completion, loading, and transitions.

But the general pattern is familiar:

Idle
  ↓
Happy
  ↓
Idle
  ↓
Celebrate
  ↓
Idle

For a simple decorative mascot, this may be completely sufficient.

However, things get more complicated when the character needs multiple simultaneous properties.

What if the mascot should be celebrating while wearing Skin 3, looking left, and displaying Level 7 energy?

You either need more prepared assets or a more sophisticated runtime composition system.

The limitation isn't necessarily AI generation. It's relying on fixed, pre-rendered clips for interactive product behavior.

2. The Combinatorial Explosion

Consider a gamified learning application with the following requirements:

Feature Variations
Emotional states 8
Character skins 5
Progression levels 10
Facial variations 3

If you render every combination as a separate animation:

const emotions = 8;
const skins = 5;
const levels = 10;
const faces = 3;

const combinations =
  emotions * skins * levels * faces;

console.log(combinations); // 1200

That's potentially 1,200 animation combinations.

Not necessarily 1,200 files in every implementation, of course. Layered rendering and reusable assets can reduce the number significantly.

But if your architecture depends on unique pre-rendered clips, customization becomes increasingly expensive to maintain.

Every new skin, level, or expression may require additional animation work.

And now imagine adding:

  • Eye tracking
  • Mouth controls
  • Accessories
  • Different character forms
  • Contextual reactions
  • Voice assistant interactions

This is why character architecture should be considered early in product development.

3. A Different Approach: Rive State Machines

Rive is a real-time animation tool and runtime that supports interactive vector graphics, reusable animation rigs, and state machines.

Instead of exporting every character variation as a separate video, you can build a reusable character system.

For example:

                 APP LOGIC
                     │
                     ▼
              RIVE CONTROLLER
                     │
       ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
       │             │             │
       ▼             ▼             ▼
   EMOTIONS       APPEARANCE    PROGRESSION
       │             │             │
   Idle/Happy      Skin 0–4      Level 1–10
   Thinking        Outfit        Energy 0–100
   Celebrate       Character     Evolution
       │             │             │
       └─────────────┼─────────────┘
                     ▼
               CHARACTER RIG
                     │
                     ▼
              REAL-TIME OUTPUT

The character can respond to multiple independent controls.

For example, a custom Rive state machine might expose:

Input Type Purpose
emotion Number Current emotional state
skin Number Selected character skin
level Number User progression level
energy Number Energy or visual intensity
eyes Number Eye expression
isTalking Boolean Talking mode
Celebrate Trigger One-shot celebration

These are custom inputs designed by the animator, not built-in Rive input names.

Your development team receives a documented contract describing what each input does.

That's the important difference.

The mascot's behavior becomes part of the application's logic.

4. React Integration: Controlling a Rive Mascot

Let's look at a simplified React example using @rive-app/react-canvas.

Install the package:

npm install @rive-app/react-canvas

Then load your Rive file and state machine.

import { useEffect } from "react";
import {
  useRive,
  useStateMachineInput,
} from "@rive-app/react-canvas";

const MACHINE = "MascotController";

export default function Mascot({
  emotion = 0,
  skin = 0,
  level = 1,
}) {
  const { RiveComponent, rive } = useRive({
    src: "/mascot.riv",
    stateMachines: MACHINE,
    autoplay: true,
  });

  const emotionInput = useStateMachineInput(
    rive,
    MACHINE,
    "emotion"
  );

  const skinInput = useStateMachineInput(
    rive,
    MACHINE,
    "skin"
  );

  const levelInput = useStateMachineInput(
    rive,
    MACHINE,
    "level"
  );

  useEffect(() => {
    if (emotionInput) {
      emotionInput.value = emotion;
    }
  }, [emotion, emotionInput]);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (skinInput) {
      skinInput.value = skin;
    }
  }, [skin, skinInput]);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (levelInput) {
      levelInput.value = level;
    }
  }, [level, levelInput]);

  return (
    <RiveComponent
      style={{
        width: 240,
        height: 240,
      }}
    />
  );
}

This assumes your .riv file already contains the named state machine and numeric inputs.

Now the parent application can control the character:

<Mascot
  emotion={3}
  skin={2}
  level={7}
/>

The Rive file decides how those values affect the visual character.

The React application decides when and why those values change.

The developer controls the behavior. The animator defines how that behavior looks.

That separation makes collaboration much easier.

5. One-Shot Animations and Completion Events

Not every animation should loop.

Some actions should play once:

  • Celebrate
  • Eat
  • Drink
  • Level Up
  • Wave
  • React to Tap

A Rive state machine can expose triggers for these actions.

For example, a Celebrate trigger can play a celebration and return to the appropriate ongoing state.

Rive also supports runtime events, allowing the character to communicate information back to the application.

A useful event contract might include:

CelebrateComplete
EatComplete
DrinkComplete
LevelUpComplete

This becomes especially useful in gamified applications.

Imagine a character drinking from an energy container.

Your application triggers the animation.

The character finishes drinking.

A completion event notifies the application.

The app updates its interface or continues the workflow.

The animation is no longer just visual feedback.

It becomes part of an event-driven interaction.

For reliable behavior, the state machine should also define what happens when users trigger multiple actions quickly, switch modes mid-animation, or repeat the same input.

6. Skins, Levels, and Character Evolution

This is where a reusable character rig becomes particularly valuable.

Imagine a fitness app mascot with four visual forms:

Unlit
  ↓
Kindling
  ↓
Steady
  ↓
Radiant

Each form represents a different stage of user progression.

The app also controls:

level: 1–10
energy: 0–100
emotion: 0–7
skin: 0–4

A properly designed character system can separate these concerns.

For example:

  • level controls prepared progression visuals.
  • energy adjusts glow intensity.
  • emotion controls facial expressions.
  • skin changes prepared appearance variations.
  • Celebrate triggers a one-shot reaction.

These controls can coexist.

You don't necessarily need a separate celebration video for every level, energy value, and skin combination.

You need reusable animations and a rig that supports those variations.

There are still practical limitations. A completely different outfit, silhouette, or character form may require additional artwork and rigging.

But reusable components help avoid unnecessary duplication.

7. Think in Layers, Not Just States

One of the biggest architectural improvements is separating character behavior into independent systems.

Instead of thinking only about:

Idle → Happy → Idle

Think about:

Character
│
├── Base Motion
│   ├── Idle
│   ├── Breathing
│   └── Body Movement
│
├── Facial Controls
│   ├── Eyes
│   ├── Eyebrows
│   └── Mouth
│
├── Emotions
│   ├── Happy
│   ├── Thinking
│   └── Sad
│
├── Appearance
│   ├── Skin
│   ├── Accessories
│   └── Character Form
│
├── Progression
│   ├── Level
│   ├── Energy
│   └── Evolution
│
└── One-Shot Actions
    ├── Celebrate
    ├── Wave
    └── Level Up

Not every Rive project needs this entire structure.

But planning around independent controls gives your character more flexibility as the product evolves.

The exact implementation may use state machines, nested artboards, data binding, reusable components, or a combination of supported Rive features.

The goal is to make the character predictable and controllable for developers.

8. What About Performance?

A common question is whether Rive is always faster or smaller than video animations.

The answer is no.

Performance depends on the actual assets and implementation.

A simple compressed video may be more efficient for certain visual effects.

A poorly optimized Rive file can also become expensive to render, particularly with complex vector geometry, effects, or excessive animation work.

However, Rive offers an important architectural advantage for interactive characters:

You can reuse character artwork and animations rather than exporting every variation as a separate pre-rendered clip.

For production apps, consider:

  • Reusing character geometry and animations.
  • Avoiding unnecessary state-machine complexity.
  • Testing on lower-end mobile devices.
  • Keeping visual effects appropriate for the target runtime.
  • Supporting reduced-motion preferences.
  • Measuring actual runtime performance and memory usage.

Choose the rendering approach based on your product's needs, not just the file format.

9. When Should You Use AI Animation vs Rive?

Requirement Fixed AI-generated clips Custom Rive mascot
Simple idle animation Great fit Great fit
Marketing animation Great fit Possible
Fixed celebration clip Great fit Great fit
Independent eye controls Requires extra architecture Supported with custom rig
Real-time facial expressions Limited in a fixed clip Supported with custom rig
Multiple skins Additional assets/compositing Reusable prepared variations
Level-based evolution Additional assets/logic State-driven progression
Developer-controlled behavior Clip selection Runtime inputs and events
Complex interactive mascot Requires custom systems Designed for this use case

AI-generated clips aren't inherently wrong.

They solve a different problem.

If your mascot is primarily decorative, a few animations may be all you need.

But if your mascot is part of the user experience, progression system, or AI assistant interface, a real-time interactive architecture is worth considering.

10. Build a Character System, Not an Animation Gallery

Before integrating a mascot into your application, ask:

Will this character need new functionality six months from now?

If your roadmap includes skins, progression, emotions, AI interactions, or personalization, consider building a reusable interactive mascot from the beginning.

At Mascot Engine, we create custom Rive mascots for:

  • React and web applications
  • Mobile apps
  • SaaS products
  • AI companions and assistants
  • Gamified learning and fitness experiences

Our work focuses on reusable character rigs, custom state machines, real-time developer controls, and integration-ready animation systems.

The goal isn't simply to make a character move.

It's to give developers a character they can actually control.

Final Thoughts

AI can help you create a beautiful mascot animation quickly.

But a beautiful animation isn't automatically an interactive character.

For simple experiences, pre-rendered clips are often enough.

For products that require real-time reactions, customization, progression, and developer-controlled behavior, think beyond the animation file.

Don't build a gallery of mascot animations. Build a mascot system that can grow with your app.

If you're building a product that needs this kind of interaction, explore Mascot Engine.

What approach are you currently using for animated characters in your apps: video clips, sprite sheets, Rive, or something else? I'd love to hear how you're handling interactive mascot behavior.

title: Appwrite Hackaton: MoviePlay
description:
Well, I recently quit my job so I got free time and this hackathon between Hashnode and Appwrite is announced. This is clearly a sign. So I decided to build MoviePlay. Before we get into the trials and tribulations of this project, let's get all the technical stuff out of the way.

The Idea

Have you ever had a debate with someone as to what is the correct order to watch Star Wars? There's the chronological order, the release order, the machete order

Team

  • Me

Tech Stack

  • ReactJS & Typescript (ViteJS)

  • TailwindCSS & DaisyUI

  • Appwrite Cloud

    • Database
    • Account
    • Functions
    • NodeJS

  • Vercel

  • The-Movie-Wrapper (I made this one, but still...)

Look at the code

You can see the code here and see it live here

Demo

Watch the video

On the using of Appwrite

I had already used a self-hosted version of Appwrite and have been tinkering with the closed cloud beta for a bit, so I was already familiar with the tool and will not really talk about onboarding.

Database

I was a bit disappointed relationships (as of 06/04/2023) are not yet supported on Cloud, so you still need to do all the foreign key constraints by hand, which makes fetching client-side a bit of a hassle.

Account

I really like how accounts are handled, especially oauth2 stuff; the fact that you can connect multiple providers for the same account seamlessly is pretty cool

Functions

I needed to use functions to store the number of views a playlist could get. I would have loved a trigger on database read operations, but I can see it would probably be too much performance overhead; the way I solved this is when navigating to a page, the page loader function triggers the function to increment the views number.

title: How to deploy a Go app with Docker using a tiny image
description:
You wrote a small Go web service and now you want it online. Go makes this easier than almost any other language: it compiles to one file that needs nothing else to run. So your Docker image doesn't need an operating system, a package manager or a shell, only your binary. This guide shows how to deploy a Go app with Docker: build that tiny image with a two-stage Dockerfile, put it online with an HTTPS address, and avoid the seven errors that break most first attempts.

Try it on Hubfly space →

What you'll build

  • A Go HTTP server with a /healthz endpoint, a built-in health check command and graceful shutdown.
  • A two-stage Dockerfile: stage 1 compiles with the full Go toolchain, stage 2 copies only the binary into a distroless image that runs as a non-root user.
  • A live deployment on Hubfly space with an HTTPS address.

The compiled server is about 6 MB. While idle, the Metrics tab shows about 1 MB of memory. On the free Shared tier (0.3 vCPU, 256 MB RAM) that leaves plenty of room.

You need Go 1.22 or newer installed locally (this guide uses Go 1.27.3), Docker if you want to test the image locally, and your code in a Git repository.

Step 1: Write a server that's ready for containers

Create a folder called shop-api and add main.go:

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "os/signal"
    "syscall"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    port := os.Getenv("PORT")
    if port == "" {
        port = "8080"
    }

    // "app healthcheck" lets a distroless image check itself (it has no curl).
    if len(os.Args) > 1 && os.Args[1] == "healthcheck" {
        c := http.Client{Timeout: 2 * time.Second}
        resp, err := c.Get("http://127.0.0.1:" + port + "/healthz")
        if err != nil || resp.StatusCode != http.StatusOK {
            os.Exit(1)
        }
        os.Exit(0)
    }

    mux := http.NewServeMux()
    mux.HandleFunc("GET /healthz", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        w.Write([]byte("ok"))
    })
    mux.HandleFunc("GET /", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        fmt.Fprintf(w, "Hello from Go! Server time: %s\n", time.Now().UTC().Format(time.RFC3339))
    })

    srv := &http.Server{
        Addr:              "0.0.0.0:" + port, // not localhost: the platform's proxy must reach it
        Handler:           mux,
        ReadHeaderTimeout: 5 * time.Second,
    }

    go func() {
        log.Printf("serving http://%s", srv.Addr)
        if err := srv.ListenAndServe(); err != nil && err != http.ErrServerClosed {
            log.Fatal(err)
        }
    }()

    // Finish in-flight requests when the platform stops or redeploys the container.
    stop, cancel := signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(), syscall.SIGINT, syscall.SIGTERM)
    defer cancel()
    <-stop.Done()

    ctx, done := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 10*time.Second)
    defer done()
    log.Println("shutting down")
    srv.Shutdown(ctx)
}

Then create the module:

go mod init shop-api
go run .

Open http://localhost:8080 and you'll see the greeting. curl localhost:8080/healthz returns ok.

Why each part matters:

  • 0.0.0.0, not localhost. Inside a container, localhost means "only this container". The platform's proxy connects from outside, so a server on 127.0.0.1 gives you a 502. More on that in 502 Bad Gateway in Docker? Bind to 0.0.0.0.
  • PORT from the environment lets you change the port without rebuilding.
  • The healthcheck argument matters because the final image has no curl or shell. The binary checks itself instead.
  • Graceful shutdown means a redeploy doesn't cut off requests halfway through.

The GET /healthz style of route needs Go 1.22 or newer and a go line of 1.22 or higher in go.mod. go mod init writes your current version, so you're fine. See "What can go wrong" if you're updating an older project.

Step 2: Write the two-stage Dockerfile

Add a Dockerfile next to main.go:

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1

# Stage 1: build a static binary
FROM golang:1.27 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.* ./
RUN go mod download
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o /out/app .

# Stage 2: copy only the binary into a tiny runtime image
FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian13:nonroot
COPY --from=build /out/app /app
USER nonroot:nonroot
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["/app"]

And a .dockerignore so local junk doesn't end up in the build:

.git
*.md
bin/
tmp/

What each line does:

  • COPY go.* ./ then go mod download copies go.mod (and go.sum if you have one) first. Docker caches the downloaded modules, so changing your code doesn't re-download them. Use go.* rather than go.mod go.sum: a module with no dependencies has no go.sum, and some builders fail on a file that doesn't exist.
  • CGO_ENABLED=0 is the important one. It produces a fully static binary. Without it, Go links against the system C library, and the binary can't start in an image that doesn't have one.
  • -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" removes local file paths and debug symbols. In this example the binary goes from about 8.9 MB to about 6 MB.
  • distroless/static-debian13:nonroot contains CA certificates, time zone data and a non-root user, and almost nothing else. HTTPS calls to other APIs work, and there's no shell for an attacker to use.

If you have Docker locally, check it before deploying:

docker build -t shop-api .
docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 shop-api

Step 3: Deploy the Go app's Docker image on Hubfly space

Push the code (with the Dockerfile at the repository root) to GitHub, GitLab or any Git server, then:

  1. In the dashboard, click Create Project, name it, pick a region and click Create Project.
  2. Click Create → Create Container. Name the container shop-api and choose Git repository.
  3. Connect the repository: GitHub App for your own repos, or Self-hosted Git with any public HTTPS URL (an access token is only needed for private repos). Pick the branch. If the app lives in a subfolder of a monorepo, put that folder in Repository directory.
  4. Leave Automatically detect the build on. A Dockerfile at the root of the build folder is used automatically. (If you'd rather not commit one, untick it and paste the Dockerfile into Custom Dockerfile. The form then also asks for a run command; enter /app. It's ignored when a Dockerfile is used.)
  5. Choose Shared Tier (free) or Dedicated Tier, click Continue through the remaining steps and click Start Build.

The build log shows each Dockerfile step. For this app the whole build, including pulling golang:1.27, compiling and deploying, took under 2 minutes. The compile step alone took about 26 seconds on the builder.

Why a build platform rather than pushing an image yourself: you skip the registry step entirely, and the build runs on linux/amd64 servers, so you won't accidentally ship an ARM image built on an Apple Silicon laptop.

Step 4: Give it an HTTPS address

  1. Open the container, go to Network and click Add Domain.
  2. Keep Auto Endpoint. Under Suggested ports the dashboard scans the running container. Your app shows up as 8080 · Open now. Click it.
  3. Leave TLS / SSL and Force HTTPS on and click Create Subdomain.

You get an address like https://shop-api.eu2.hubfly.app with a certificate already in place. Open /healthz and you should see ok.

If port 8080 doesn't appear under Suggested ports, your app isn't listening on 0.0.0.0. Fix that before going further.

To use your own domain later, see How to use your root domain as a custom domain.

Step 5: Check it's the build you expect

Go embeds build information in every binary. go version -m reads it from a file:

go build -o app . && go version -m app

To see the same thing from the deployed app, add a temporary route (import runtime/debug):

mux.HandleFunc("GET /version", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    bi, _ := debug.ReadBuildInfo()
    fmt.Fprint(w, bi)
})

Remove it after checking: it exposes your dependency versions. The output looks like this:

Look for CGO_ENABLED=0, GOOS=linux and GOARCH=amd64. Then open the container's Logs tab:

The startup line is marked ERR. Nothing is wrong: Go's log package writes to stderr by default, and the log viewer labels stderr lines that way. If you'd rather see them as normal output, add log.SetOutput(os.Stdout) at the top of main.

The Metrics tab confirms how light the app is:

What it costs

On the Shared Tier the container costs nothing within the free 360 compute hours a month, and it sleeps after 15 minutes without traffic. An always-on container uses 730 hours a month, so the free hours suit services that sleep. Creating resources needs a $5 prepaid credit, which your usage is drawn from.

For an always-on service, a Dedicated container with 0.5 vCPU, 512 MB RAM and 1 GB of disk costs:

Item Math Per month
CPU 0.5 vCPU × $0.004 × 730 h $1.46
RAM 0.5 GB × $0.002 × 730 h $0.73
Storage 1 GB × $0.00001536 × 730 h $0.01
Total $2.20

If you already run Kubernetes or another container platform, the same image runs there unchanged.

What can go wrong

COPY cache key: source "go.sum*" not found in build context

The Hubfly space builder doesn't accept a wildcard that matches no files. This happens with COPY go.mod go.sum* ./ when your module has no dependencies (so no go.sum). Use COPY go.* ./, which always matches go.mod.

exec /app: no such file or directory when the container starts

The file exists. What's missing is the C library it was linked against. You built without CGO_ENABLED=0 on the full golang image, which has a C compiler, so Go produced a dynamically linked binary. Run file app locally: it should say statically linked. Add CGO_ENABLED=0 to the build line. If you really need cgo (SQLite through mattn/go-sqlite3, for example), use gcr.io/distroless/base-debian13 as the runtime image instead.

exec format error

The image was built for ARM (an Apple Silicon Mac, for example) and the server runs x86. Build on the platform, as in step 3, or build locally with docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64.

502 Bad Gateway, or no port under Suggested ports

The server listens on localhost or 127.0.0.1. Bind to 0.0.0.0 as in step 1. Some example servers default to localhost:8080 and take an address flag; pass it in the Dockerfile, for example CMD ["-addr", "0.0.0.0:8080"].

Every route returns 404 page not found, even though the code looks right

Routes like "GET /healthz" need the Go 1.22 router. If your go.mod says go 1.21 or lower, Go keeps the old router for compatibility, and it treats "GET /healthz" as a literal path. Change the line to go 1.22 or higher (or run go mod edit -go=1.22) and rebuild.

Calls to other HTTPS APIs fail with x509: certificate signed by unknown authority

You're on FROM scratch, which has no CA certificates. Use distroless/static (it includes them), or copy /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt from the build stage.

A health check like curl -f http://localhost/ always fails

Distroless has no curl and no shell, so CMD-SHELL checks can't run. Use the binary itself in exec form: in a Dockerfile, HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s CMD ["/app", "healthcheck"]; in Compose, test: ["CMD", "/app", "healthcheck"]. The Docker health checks guide explains intervals and retries.

FAQ

How do I deploy a Go app with Docker?

Build it in a golang stage with CGO_ENABLED=0, copy the binary into a minimal runtime image (distroless/static or scratch), push the code to Git and let a build platform build and run it. Then add an HTTPS endpoint on the port the app listens on.

Should I use scratch or distroless for Go?

Distroless static for most apps. It's only slightly bigger than scratch but includes CA certificates, time zone data and a non-root user, which you'd otherwise copy in by hand. Pick scratch only if you want the absolute minimum and don't call HTTPS APIs or use time zones.

Why is my Go Docker image so big?

You're probably shipping the build stage. The golang image contains the whole toolchain. Use two stages and copy only the binary into the final one.

Do I need CGO_ENABLED=0?

For a static binary on scratch or distroless/static, yes. The golang:*-alpine images have no C compiler, so cgo is already off there, but setting it explicitly makes the Dockerfile safe on any base.

What does -ldflags="-s -w" do?

It strips the symbol table and debug information. The binary gets smaller (here from about 8.9 MB to 6 MB). Stack traces from panics still work.

How do I run database migrations before my Go app starts?

Run them as a separate one-off job that must finish before the app starts, rather than inside main. In Docker Compose that's a migrate service plus depends_on with condition: service_completed_successfully on your app.

Can I deploy a Go app for free?

On Hubfly space the Shared tier is free within 360 compute hours a month (you add $5 of prepaid credit before creating resources). It sleeps when idle and wakes on the next request, which suits side projects and staging.

Go further on Hubfly space

  • Deploy on every push: trigger a new build from GitHub Actions after your tests pass. How to deploy on every push with GitHub Actions.
  • Add a database: a managed PostgreSQL database for about $2 a month, reachable from your container over the private network.
  • Release safely: run two versions behind a load balancer and send 10% of traffic to the new one first. Canary releases with a weighted load balancer.

description:
Agent Platform Workbench

Change

Change

Security

Security

Feature

Custom organization policies for Agent Platform Workbench instances

You can now use custom organization policies to allow or deny the creation and update of Agent Platform Workbench instances based on their configuration. Custom constraints for the notebooks.googleapis.com/Instance resource are enforced when you create or update an instance, and support dry-run mode. This feature is now generally available (GA). For more information, see Create custom organization policy constraints.

Apigee X

Feature

Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool arguments are sent to the location their OpenAPI parameter declares

This change applies to Apigee X in all supported regions.

An MCP tool argument whose OpenAPI parameter declares in: header is now sent to your backend as a request header, and one that declares in: cookie is sent in the Cookie header. Previously both were appended to the query string. in: query and in: path parameters are unchanged, and every parameter still appears in the tool's inputSchema, so MCP clients supply arguments exactly as before. If a backend reads one of these values from the query string, declare the parameter in: query or read it from its declared location.

On a tool call that supplies at least one cookie argument, the Cookie header is replaced with only the declared cookie parameters, omitting any others. Any cookie your backend relies on must be declared as an in: cookie parameter.

An MCP proxy that was already deployed continues to use the previous query-string behavior until its configuration is next regenerated. To adopt the new routing on an existing MCP proxy, deploy a new revision of it.

For the full mapping, see Tool argument placement on the backend request.

Security

On October 24, 2026, we published a security bulletin for Apigee.

Two vulnerabilities in PHP core (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, "PHP2Shell") allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code remotely on a server running a vulnerable PHP version. The impact is limited to Drupal-based Apigee developer portals, which customers deploy and operate. Apigee, Apigee Hybrid, and the Apigee integrated portal don't use PHP and aren't affected.

Security bulletin published: GCP-2026-072

BigQuery

Feature

Conversation logging for Conversational analytics in BigQuery is now generally available (GA). You can log data agent conversations to a BigQuery table in the agent's project. For more information, see Conversation logging overview and Configure settings.

Feature

Python user-defined functions now support volume mounts, which let you access dependency files from Cloud Storage directly from your Python UDF code. This feature is in Preview.

Feature

The REGEXP_EXTRACT_GROUPS function produces substrings that match multiple capturing groups in a regular expression.

This function is in Preview.

Capacity Planner

Feature

Preview: You can use the Capacity Planner remote Model Context Protocol (MCP) server (capacityplanner.googleapis.com) to connect AI applications and agents to your Capacity Planner data (Preview). You can use the Capacity Planner MCP tools to query historical resource usage, usage forecasts, and reservation data across your projects, folders, and organizations.

For more information, see the Capacity Planner MCP reference and Google Cloud MCP servers overview.

Cloud Database Migration Service

Feature

You can now create heterogeneous conversion workspaces by importing database schema metadata files from a Cloud Storage bucket without requiring direct network connectivity between Database Migration Service and your source database during the schema conversion phase. For more information, see the following pages:

  • Create a conversion workspace for Oracle to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL
  • Create a conversion workspace for Oracle to AlloyDB for PostgreSQL
  • Create a conversion workspace for SQL Server to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL
  • Create a conversion workspace for SQL Server to AlloyDB for PostgreSQL

Compute Engine

Security

A vulnerability (CVE-2026-85299) about incorrect authorization in Compute Engine was discovered and has been addressed. For more information, see the GCP-2026-073 security bulletin.

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Feature

Control user intent matching for semantic governance policies

You can now turn user intent matching on or off for semantic governance policies by setting the sgpUserIntentMatching key on the authorization extension metadata. User intent matching is on by default; set the key to DISABLED to turn it off. Turning it off reduces protection against indirect prompt injection. When the key is set, policy evaluation logs report the mode each evaluation used in the sgpUserIntentMatchingMode field.

For more information, see Control user intent matching.

Feature

Cloud Storage output support for Gemini image generation models

Direct Cloud Storage output persistence is generally available (GA) for Gemini Nano Banana 2.1 (gemini-nano-banana-2.1), Gemini 3.1 Flash Image (gemini-3.1-flash-image), Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite Image (gemini-3.1-flash-lite-image), and Gemini 3 Pro Image (gemini-3-pro-image). You can set outputConfig.outputUriPrefix and generationConfig.responseFormat[].image.delivery to "URI" in generateContent and streamGenerateContent requests to write generated and edited images directly to a Cloud Storage bucket and receive the object URI in fileData.fileUri instead of inline bytes. For more information, see Save generated images to Cloud Storage.

Feature

Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS and Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite TTS are Generally Available (GA)

Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS and Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite TTS are available in General Availability (GA) in the global location and the us and eu multi-regions. The models support structured speaker and style metadata, inline vocal tags, multi-speaker dialogue, and streaming. Voice design and voice replication capabilities remain available in Preview.

For more information, see Generate speech with Gemini TTS.

Feature

Semantic governance policies support more model providers

Semantic governance policies now evaluate tool calls from agents that use models from providers other than Gemini. The policy engine reads each provider's request and response format, so the same policies apply whichever model your agent uses. Supported APIs include the Gemini Developer API and Gemini models on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, the Anthropic Messages API, Claude models on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, the OpenAI Chat Completions API, the Mistral AI API, the OpenAI-compatible endpoint on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (including Llama models), and self-hosted OpenAI-compatible servers such as vLLM. Streamed model responses aren't supported.

To govern these providers, update the when condition of your authorization policy to match each provider's request path. The updated condition also matches requests that include a query string.

For more information, see Supported model providers and Connect the policy engine to Agent Gateway.

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for bare metal

title: Usestate in Reactjs
description:
Usestate

UseState is one of the React Hooks used to manage state in a component.

Normally, when we use a local variable, changing its value does not trigger a re-render of the component.

But useState allows us to store a value and update the UI whenever that value changes.

Using a normal variable doesn't trigger a re-render the UI still doesn't show anything about your process by using a normal variable.

To overcome this using usestate updates changes in UI everytime when the component gets re-rendered.

const [stateVariable, stateFunction] = useState(0);

Statevariable -It stored the current state value.

StateFunction - It is a setterfunction used to update the current state value. When called, it tells React to re-render the component so the UI can reflect the updated state.

title: Introducing KryptoCore: Building an Open Security Foundation Together
description:
Open Security. Built Together. Free for Everyone.

Hey DEV Community! 👋

Today, I'd like to introduce KryptoCore, the first open-source project from KryptoCoreLabs.

It's still early. We're just getting started, and there's a lot of work ahead.

But that's exactly why I want to share it now.

Because the idea behind KryptoCore isn't simply to release another software library.

It's to build something useful, transparent, and secure together with the open-source community.

💡 Why KryptoCore?

There are already excellent cryptographic libraries available today.

And that's a good thing.

We're not trying to invent new encryption algorithms or replace well-established cryptographic implementations.

Instead, we're asking a different question:

Can we build a small, consistent, and reusable security foundation on top of established libraries, while keeping its design transparent and open to community review?

Modern applications often need similar security capabilities.

Rather than repeatedly integrating different cryptographic libraries, handling their interfaces, and making security-sensitive design decisions independently, we want to explore an approach that brings commonly needed functionality together behind clear, carefully designed interfaces.

That's where KryptoCore comes in.

🔐 What Is KryptoCore?

KryptoCore is an MIT-licensed, open-source cryptographic foundation currently under active development.

Our focus is on:

Established cryptography: Building on existing cryptographic libraries rather than inventing new primitives.

Consistent interfaces: Making security functionality easier to integrate and maintain.

Interoperability: Developing components across Python and Rust.

Clear security boundaries: Documenting assumptions, limitations, and responsibilities.

Testing: Improving reliability through automated tests and security checks.

Transparency: Keeping the source code available for inspection, criticism, and contributions.

The repository currently includes Python and Rust components, tests, documentation, and development tooling.

Explore the source code:

👉 https://github.com/kryptocorelabs/kryptocore

🦀 Why Python and Rust?

Python provides an accessible environment for application development and integration.

Rust offers strong memory-safety guarantees and useful tools for building security-sensitive components.

We're exploring how these ecosystems can work together while keeping the security model understandable.

Of course, using Rust doesn't automatically make software secure.

And wrapping an existing cryptographic library doesn't automatically make it safer.

Security depends on architecture, implementation, correct usage, testing, and independent review.

Those are exactly the areas where we want to invite outside perspectives.

🌍 The Bigger Vision: Community-Driven Security

Here's what matters most to us.

KryptoCore isn't supposed to become a closed product controlled by a single company.

We want it to remain an open foundation that anyone can inspect, use, modify, and improve under its open-source license.

Our long-term vision is a project where:

Developers contribute improvements and new ideas.

Security researchers challenge assumptions and identify weaknesses.

Contributors help maintain documentation and tests.

Architectural decisions are discussed openly.

Applications can build on a shared, reusable foundation.

The project should grow because people find it useful, not because we claim to have all the answers.

And that's why we're introducing it so early.

🛠️ Where We Are Today

KryptoCore is currently a development preview.

We've published the initial source code, documentation, tests, and development infrastructure.

But there are important limitations.

KryptoCore has not undergone an independent security audit and should not currently be treated as a production-ready cryptographic solution.

We're not claiming that the project is more secure than the established libraries it builds upon.

In fact, one of the most important questions we want to explore is whether our abstraction provides enough practical value to justify the additional complexity.

We believe that's a question worth discussing openly.

🤝 We Need Your Feedback

This is where you come in.

Whether you're an experienced security engineer, a Rust developer, a Python developer, or simply interested in open-source software, we'd appreciate your perspective.

Some questions we're particularly interested in:

  1. Architecture

Does a shared cryptographic foundation make sense, or would developers benefit more from using existing libraries directly?

  1. Security

Which security boundaries, assumptions, and failure modes should we pay particular attention to?

  1. Interoperability

What would make a Python/Rust security foundation genuinely useful?

  1. Testing and verification

What additional tests, verification methods, or review processes would help establish trust in the project?

  1. Community development

How can we make the project approachable for new contributors while maintaining a high standard for security-sensitive changes?

We're especially interested in constructive criticism.

If you think something in the architecture is unnecessary, risky, or could be done better, we'd genuinely like to hear it.

🚀 What's Next?

Our next steps are focused on strengthening the foundation rather than rapidly expanding its feature set.

That includes improving documentation, reviewing security assumptions, expanding test coverage, and making it easier for developers to evaluate and contribute to the project.

We're also exploring applications that use KryptoCore, including an encrypted vault, so the foundation can evolve around practical requirements rather than hypothetical features.

But we don't want to decide the project's entire future alone.

We want the community to help shape it.

❤️ Open Security. Built Together. Free for Everyone.

Security shouldn't depend on whether someone can afford a commercial product.

We believe useful security tools and foundations should be accessible, transparent, and open to improvement.

KryptoCore is just getting started.

And we'd love for you to be part of that journey.

GitHub: https://github.com/kryptocorelabs/kryptocore

License: MIT

Thanks for reading!

If you have suggestions, questions, or criticism, feel free to leave a comment or open an issue on GitHub.

Let's build something useful together. 🔐

title: What Logistics and Manufacturing Taught Me About Building Software
description:
People sometimes assume that moving into software and AI means starting over. For me it felt more like changing tools. I spent more than 15 years in logistics and manufacturing systems: running regional delivery routes for time sensitive shipments, managing production with ERP and SAP integration, working as a cleanroom equipment technician, handling fleet operations and shipping. Today I write Python and JavaScript, evaluate AI output for training, and build the screen management software behind Local Flyer Ads. Almost every habit I rely on as a developer started on a loading dock, a production floor or a delivery route.

Here are the lessons that carried over most directly.

Every system is a flow, and the bottleneck decides the speed

In a production plant you learn quickly that the line moves only as fast as its slowest station. Adding people to a station that is already keeping up changes nothing. Software works the same way. When a script or an app feels slow, the instinct is to optimize whatever code you happen to be looking at. The better move is to measure first and find the one step that is actually holding everything up. Sometimes it is a database query. Sometimes it is a network call that runs once per item when it could run once per batch. Production management trained me to look for the constraint before touching anything else.

Write the procedure before you trust the process

Cleanroom work runs on written procedures. You do not improvise when you are servicing equipment in a controlled environment, because small mistakes are expensive and hard to undo. That habit made me a better programmer. Before I build something, I write down in plain language what it should do, what inputs it expects and what should happen when something goes wrong. That short document becomes the checklist I test against. It also makes the code easier for someone else to pick up later, including future me.

The handoff is where things break

On a delivery route, the drive is rarely the problem. The trouble shows up at handoffs: a package that was scanned at one stop but not the next, a label that does not match the manifest, a pickup window that changed without anyone updating the schedule. Software fails at handoffs too. Most bugs I see live at the boundary between two pieces: one function returns a date as text and the next expects a date object, or an API changes a field name and the code downstream keeps running with empty values. Now I put my checks at the boundaries. Validate what comes in, confirm what goes out, and log both.

Data entry is a design problem

ERP and SAP integration taught me that bad data rarely comes from bad people. It comes from forms that make the wrong thing easy. If a field accepts any text, someone will type a date three different ways. If a dropdown is missing the right option, people will pick the closest wrong one. When I design screens and tools now, including the scheduling side of the Local Flyer Ads software, I try to make the correct input the easiest input. Clear choices, sensible defaults and validation that explains what it wants are worth more than any cleanup script.

Rubrics beat gut feelings

In logistics, performance is measured: on time rates, accuracy, turnaround. You cannot manage what you only feel. My AI evaluation work through Handshake AI is built on the same idea. I score image, video, audio and interface output against written rubrics rather than personal taste, because a rubric makes judgments consistent and explainable. I bring that into my own projects too. Before I call a feature done, I decide what done means and check it against that list.

Reliability is the whole job

A time sensitive delivery route does not get partial credit. The shipment arrives on time and intact, or the route failed. That standard stays with you. In software it shows up as caring about the unglamorous parts: error handling, retries, clear logs and alerts that tell you something broke before a customer does. For a screen network running inside local shops, a display that silently stops updating is the equivalent of a missed delivery, so a lot of my effort goes into making failures visible and recoverable.

If you are making a similar move

If you work in operations, logistics or manufacturing and you are curious about software, you are not starting from zero. You already understand flows, constraints, procedures and accountability. What you need to add is the language to express them in code. Pick one real problem from your own work, something repetitive or error prone, and automate a small piece of it with Python. Certifications helped me build structure around the fundamentals; CompTIA A+, Network+, Security+, Cloud+ and CySA+ each filled in a layer I had only seen from the outside. I am continuing my computer science degree for the same reason.

The tools changed. The way of thinking did not.

Originally published at tonycantave.com by Tony Sterlin Cantave, a Connecticut software developer and founder of Local Flyer Ads.

title: "Unable to verify the first certificate": when Node's --use-system-ca hint won't help
description:
TL;DR. Node's "unable to verify the first certificate" error now ends with a hint to try --use-system-ca. The flag helps when a root CA is missing and installed in the system store. It cannot help when the server leaves out an intermediate: I tested a host with a missing intermediate and it failed the same way with the flag on, hint included. Check what the server sends first.

To fix “unable to verify the first certificate” in Node.js, inspect the chain the remote server sends and the CA certificates trusted by the failing process. A public server may be missing an intermediate; an internal service or inspecting proxy may require an approved private CA. Keep TLS verification enabled while fixing that chain or trust configuration.

The certificate chain guide explains the leaf, intermediate and root roles. This walkthrough focuses on identifying which part Node.js cannot verify.

Capture the error code from the failing process

The message alone can hide useful detail. Reproduce the connection inside the same container, VM or runtime environment that fails, with the same destination and proxy configuration.

For a direct HTTPS request using Node's standard library:

import https from "node:https";

https.get("https://api.example.com/health", response => {
  console.log("status:", response.statusCode);
  response.resume();
}).on("error", error => {
  console.error("code:", error.code);
  console.error("message:", error.message);
  process.exitCode = 1;
});

Replace the example URL with your endpoint. This small script isolates a direct Node HTTPS connection; it does not automatically reproduce an application library's custom agent or proxy. Compare those settings if the script succeeds while your application fails.

Node's certificate error reference distinguishes these failures:

Error What to investigate
UNABLE_TO_VERIFY_LEAF_SIGNATURE A lone, non-self-signed leaf with no verifiable issuer in the presented chain
UNABLE_TO_GET_ISSUER_CERT_LOCALLY An issuer that the verifier cannot find locally
DEPTH_ZERO_SELF_SIGNED_CERT A self-signed leaf that this client does not trust
ERR_TLS_CERT_ALTNAME_INVALID A name mismatch, a separate problem from building the chain

For the last case, use the hostname mismatch checklist. Installing extra CA certificates does not make a certificate cover an unrelated hostname.

When Node suggests --use-system-ca

Since Node 23.11, some of these errors end with a hint:

unable to verify the first certificate; if the root CA is installed locally, try running Node.js with --use-system-ca

Node trusts its bundled CA list by default, not the certificates installed on the machine. The --use-system-ca flag adds the system store. If the missing root CA is installed there, that is the fix:

node --use-system-ca app.mjs

From Node 24.6 and 22.19, NODE_USE_SYSTEM_CA=1 does the same job where you can set an environment variable but not the command.

The hint does not mean the flag applies. A lone leaf gives the same error whether the missing piece is the root or an intermediate, so Node suggests the flag either way. The flag only changes which roots Node trusts. It cannot supply an intermediate the server left out. On Node 26.10, incomplete-chain.badssl.com, a public test host with a missing intermediate, still fails with UNABLE_TO_VERIFY_LEAF_SIGNATURE when the flag is set, and the message still suggests the flag.

Check what the server sends before changing how the process starts.

Inspect the certificates the server actually sends

Run this from the failing environment if OpenSSL is available:

openssl s_client -connect api.example.com:443 \
  -servername api.example.com -showcerts </dev/null

Read the certificate list and verification output separately. OpenSSL's s_client documentation describes -showcerts as the list sent by the server. It is not a reconstructed, verified chain.

Copy only the BEGIN CERTIFICATE through END CERTIFICATE blocks into the certificate decoder. It shows each supplied certificate's subject, issuer and dates, in pasted order. Check whether the leaf's issuer corresponds to the next certificate's subject. Matching those names is a useful clue, but it does not verify the signature or prove trust.

The public SSL checker offers another view of what a public host serves. It cannot reproduce a private network or your company's HTTPS inspection path.

If you control the public server, send its intermediates

For a public certificate, the usual deployment is the leaf first, followed by the required intermediate certificates. The client supplies a trusted root. Sending a root certificate from the server does not make the client trust it.

On an Nginx deployment using Certbot's standard file layout, the certificate directive normally points to the full chain:

ssl_certificate     /etc/letsencrypt/live/api.example.com/fullchain.pem;
ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/api.example.com/privkey.pem;

Use your actual paths. Nginx's certificate-chain documentation describes the combined certificate file and its order. A load balancer or managed certificate service has a different configuration surface; fix the certificate at the place that terminates TLS.

After validating the configuration and deploying it through your normal process, repeat the request from the failing Node environment. Also inspect the public endpoint again. Reading a corrected file on disk does not establish that the running listener loaded it.

If the service uses a private CA, configure deliberate trust

An internal CA may be absent from Node's default roots. An HTTPS inspection proxy can also present certificates signed by your organization's CA. Compare the observed issuer with the expected infrastructure, and obtain the approved CA certificate from the people who administer it.

Node supports extending its roots at startup:

NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS=/etc/company/approved-root-ca.pem node app.mjs

The NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS documentation specifies that the file contains trusted PEM certificates, is read when Node starts, and does not update when you change process.env later. Restart the actual application process with that setting.

Also inspect any explicitly configured ca option in your HTTPS agent or TLS connection. Node documents that an explicit ca replaces the normal and extra CA certificates for that connection. Adding an environment variable or --use-system-ca will not override it.

Do not use a random certificate copied from the failed connection as a new trust anchor. Establish the issuer you intend to trust and fix the server's intermediate chain independently.

Compare browsers and Node without assuming either is wrong

A browser success does not prove that every client can build the same path. Your browser and Node process may use different root stores, cached intermediates, network routes or proxy certificates.

Compare four things: the actual hostname, the leaf fingerprint, the sent intermediate list and the configured trust roots. If the fingerprint or issuer differs between your laptop and the container, investigate the path before rewriting certificate validation code.

Keep rejectUnauthorized enabled. Setting it to false, or disabling verification process-wide, removes the check whose failure you are investigating and can accept an unintended peer.

Verify the fix from the environment that failed

Repeat the original application request after the server or trust configuration changes. Confirm that the error disappears with normal verification settings.

Then follow the certificate monitoring walkthrough. An expiry check gives advance notice of dates. An HTTPS check with TLS verification enabled catches validation failures from its own network and trust context. A private CA path still needs a check that can reach and trust that environment.

Where Uptimepage fits

I build Uptimepage, an uptime monitor that checks your services from several regions and alerts you when one fails. Its HTTP checks verify TLS unless you turn that off, and a separate TLS certificate check warns you before a certificate expires. The certificate decoder and SSL checker linked above are free tools on the same site. It is open source under AGPL, so it can also run on your own server.

Whatever you use, run the openssl s_client command above against your own API today and count the certificates it sends.

Now the question for the comments: the last time you hit this error, was it a missing intermediate, a private CA or a proxy? I would like to hear what it turned out to be, and how long it took to find.

title: Spotting the Artificial: Dialogic Humor Improvisation in Humans and LLMs
description:
arXiv:2611.00492v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We propose a methodology for investigating the differences between natural and synthetic language in a challenging setting: humorous improvisational dialogue. Our experimental setting compares human-produced comedy improvisations with the dialogues generated by LLMs in a multi-agent environment that we designed. The analysis combines automated linguistic measures with manual annotation grounded in Systemic Functional Linguistics (SFL).
  The results show that, although LLMs can create coherent and creative scenes, they often fail to reproduce key characteristics of spontaneous spoken interaction. In addition, LLM-generated interactions display a strong tendency toward politeness and positive evaluations, contrasting with the broader range of attitudes found in human humorous improvisation. Our evidence highlights both the strengths and limitations of current LLMs in modeling dialogic humor and demonstrate the value of integrating linguistic theory with NLP methods for the analysis of machine-generated language
