title: The end of credential sprawl for agents
description:
Every useful agent reaches beyond your codebase. It posts to Slack, opens pull requests, queries Snowflake, or calls an internal API. That reach is what makes it valuable, and it's also where the risk lives, because for years, granting it meant provisioning a long-lived token and hoping it never leaked.

Vercel Connect replaces long-lived tokens with ones your code requests at runtime, scoped to the task and expiring on their own.

During the public beta, we've grown the ecosystem past 100 connectors, unified how they work, and added the governance capabilities teams need in production.

Today, Vercel Connect is generally available.

Vaults don't fix long-lived tokens

Managing credentials has become its own workload. Teams write rotation scripts, copy secrets across environments, and share tokens between users. Putting a token in a vault made it harder to steal, but no less dangerous once stolen. It never expires, and no vault limits what a leaked credential can do.

Agents compounded the problem by touching more systems with greater autonomy, more often. Yet the tools to contain a secret haven't changed.

With Vercel Connect, your app never stores credentials. It requests one:

  • You register a connector once for a provider like Slack, GitHub, Snowflake, Shopify, or your own OAuth service

  • You attach it to the projects and environments that need it

  • Your code requests a token at runtime, and it refreshes automatically

  • Your app has no provider secret to commit by accident

Requesting a token doesn't require another secret. Every deployment on Vercel carries an OIDC identity, and the SDK uses it to prove who's asking.

What changes when access becomes a request

The difference shows up in the properties of the credential:

Property

Stored token

Vercel Connect

Lifetime

Never expires

Short-lived, refreshed automatically

Reach

Everything the agent could need

Scoped to the task in the request

Identity

One shared bot for every user

App or a specific named user

Rotation

Mint, update copies, redeploy

None to perform

Revocation

Rotate and redeploy

One command, per user or all tokens

Credentials that used to sit in environments long after the work finished now expire on their own. Nothing lingers for an attacker to find.

Scoping happens per request. One step of an agent might read a repository, the next opens an issue, and each asks for only that.

How fine-grained a token can be depends on the service, and GitHub is the clearest example. Requests can restrict a token to a single repository with read-only permissions, rather than trusting a standing grant organization-wide.

The open-source GitHub Tools SDK puts this into practice. Choose a preset like code-review, and it mints tokens with only the required scopes.

Identity is per request as well. Tokens act as the app by default, but pass a named user as the subject and the token acts on their behalf, scoped to what they authorized during a one-time consent flow.

Connectors for the services you already use

Vercel Connect now ships with 100+ preset connectors for developer tools and SaaS providers like Notion, Shopify, and Workday, as well as managed connectors for Slack, GitHub, Linear, Salesforce, and more.

Your own services follow the same model via custom OAuth and API Key authentication, and any OAuth-capable MCP server can serve as a connector.

Finding and creating them is faster, too. Browse the full catalog on the Vercel website, create a connector in fewer steps, and manage everything from the dashboard, CLI, or API.

Governance that scales with your team

Teams adopting Vercel Connect need more than scoped tokens. They need to control who manages connectors and to track how access is used.

GA adds three capabilities:

  • Fine-grained RBAC controls who can create and manage connectors

  • Audit logs record authorization and connector activity

  • Token and trigger observability shows usage across projects

Together with per-environment attachment and one-command revocation, access becomes something you can inspect and prove.

When an auditor asks who had access to a system and when, the answer is a query against the audit log, not an investigation across projects and Slack threads.

Wherever your agents run

Vercel Connect is available wherever you and your users are:

  • Custom Environments are supported, so a qa environment gets its own connector alongside production, preview, and development

  • eve supports Connect out of the box, with connections declared per agent

  • Chat SDK support brings the same model to conversational apps

Build connected apps in v0

Apps and agents built in v0 use the same model.

Tell v0 which service your app needs, and it sets up the connector during the build. Slack, GitHub, and other managed connectors need nothing on the provider's side, and since tokens are minted at runtime, the generated app has no secret to keep.

The KERNEL team shipped a voice-driven browser agent this way:

Events flow in, without a secret either

Requesting tokens is half the picture. Your agent also needs to hear about events.

Triggers handle this without putting a secret back in your app. When a user posts in Slack, the provider sends the event to Vercel Connect. It verifies the signature server-side, re-attests the event with an OIDC identity, and forwards it to your project. Forwarded events arrive even with Deployment Protection enabled.

Your app has no bot token to act with and no signing secret to verify webhooks, yet the full loop still runs.

Moonpig Group runs its internal legal agent on this loop in production:

Built around a single call

Underneath everything is getToken from the Vercel Connect SDK.

Whether your agent is built on eve or the AI SDK, runs as a background job in Vercel Workflows, or is a loop you wrote yourself, it asks for a credential the same way.

Around that call, adapters handle the wiring:

  • @vercel/connect/eve supplies the credentials behind an agent's connections

  • @vercel/connect/chat hooks Connect into Chat SDK adapters

  • @vercel/connect/betterauth and @vercel/connect/authjs produce provider configs for Better Auth and Auth.js

  • @vercel/connect/ai-sdk and @vercel/connect/mcp do the same for AI SDK tools and MCP clients, whether your agent calls tools directly or through a server

For eve agents and Chat SDK applications, the two secrets a Slack integration usually keeps in your environment, SLACK_BOT_TOKEN and SLACK_SIGNING_SECRET, are gone from your app entirely.

Pricing and availability

Vercel Connect is available on all plans, with pricing based on token requests and trigger events. The Hobby plan includes 500 token requests and 1,000 triggers per month at no additional cost. Pro plans are billed at $3 per 1,000 token requests and $0.95 per 1,000 triggers, with custom pricing on Enterprise.

If you used Vercel Connect during the beta, your current billing terms stay unchanged until September 25, 2026, when the updated pricing takes effect.

  • Follow the complete guide in the knowledge base or read the changelog

title: Introducing Vercel CI
description:
Coding agents are opening more pull requests than ever, and each one waits on CI before anyone can review or merge it. Most CI systems run the entire workflow on every push, even a one-line change. The more your agents push, the more time you spend waiting on CI.

Today, we're announcing Vercel CI in Beta. It runs only the tasks affected by your code change, and spins up only the compute those checks need, the same way Fluid compute scales with your traffic.

At Vercel, our CI now keeps up with our coding agents. Time from git push to "CI passed" is 2-6x faster than it was before.

How it works

Vercel CI uses Turborepo to understand your tasks and which ones depend on each other. It reads turbo.json, so if you're already using Turborepo, there's no separate CI config to write.

If you're not on Turborepo yet, add turbo.json and the turbo package. It works in single-package repos too.

Then tag the tasks you want Vercel CI to run.

"tags": ["ci"] is all you need to get started. No workflow YAML to maintain, no drift between your CI config and turbo.json, and Remote Cache is on by default.

When you or your agent push code, Vercel CI determines which tasks need to run based on the change. Tasks whose inputs haven't changed come from cache. The remaining tasks each run on their own machine, powered by Hive, Vercel's compute layer, and start as soon as their dependencies finish.

Vercel CI gives each task the compute it needs and nothing more.

Running your CI on Vercel

To get started, follow the documentation or prompt your agent from your repo:

Once set up, you or your agent can watch and inspect CI through the Vercel dashboard, Vercel CLI, or Vercel MCP. When something fails, go straight to the failing task, see what's blocked behind it, and open its logs, or search across recent runs to see whether a test has been flaky all week.

Vercel CI posts a check to your pull request on GitHub, so your existing branch protection rules can block merges on failure, the same way they do today.

Closing the loop

Vercel CI has already completed nearly 8 million tasks across our own repositories and the private beta, and we're just getting started. We're working to keep shrinking the time between writing code and running it in production.

As we work toward general availability, we plan to add:

  • Advanced observability

  • A vc ci CLI command for distributed execution before pushing code

  • More granular test selection

Vercel CI is available in Beta today on all plans. Read the docs and try it on your repository.

title: Fighting Tool Sprawl: The Case for AI Tool Registries
description:
As enterprise AI agent adoption scales, the absence of centralized, organization-level tool infrastructure is producing compounding costs. When adoption is built around optimizing for deployment speed, enterprises expose themselves to a combination of risks: duplicated engineering effort, security exposure, and operational opacity.

Every enterprise needs its own shared tool registry, one that reflects its specific regulatory environment, security posture, and operational conventions. To be clear, this is not an argument for a public package manager, something like npm, PyPI, or Maven. The infrastructure each enterprise needs is internal; scoped to its own teams, its own data, its own policies, its own domain. Trying to expand the scope beyond the confines of individual organizations would be premature standardization in a fast-moving, nascent space.

A shared enterprise tool registry is not an optimization or a nice-to-have. It is foundational infrastructure as agent deployments scale beyond early experiments. The case for it rests on two pillars: reducing coordination cost and enabling risk management, both for the humans building with agents and for the agents themselves.

AI agents depend on tools that retrieve data, write records, trigger workflows, and call external APIs. According to McKinsey, in most large organizations, these tools are built by individual teams in an ad hoc fashion: undocumented, ungoverned, and invisible to the rest of the organization. This pattern is familiar to most engineering leaders, and the fragmentation it creates compounds with every new agent deployment. Teams rebuild what already exists elsewhere, security reviews miss tools that were never registered, and when something breaks, no one has a complete picture of what is running or why.

A coordination failure at infrastructure scale

The software industry solved an analogous problem decades ago with package managers. Centralized registries gave teams a way to discover, depend on, and govern shared code. The learning was clear: preventing duplication and inconsistency is an infrastructure problem, not a discipline problem.

The agent era presents the same problem in a new domain. When Kong launched its enterprise MCP Registry in February 2026, they explicitly called out the problems of manual MCP configuration, hardcoded and managed tool isolation across teams, fragmented integrations, and limited organization visibility.

Fragmented tool development is not a consequence of poor engineering practice. Rather, it is the predictable outcome of asking teams to solve an infrastructure problem at the application layer.

The visibility problem

Gravitee's The State of AI Agent Security 2026 survey quantifies what happens when agent tooling is invisible to the people responsible for securing it. The survey found that only 14.4% of teams with agents beyond the planning phase have full security approval, and 88% of organizations had an agent-related security incident this year. Bad practices like shared API keys are endemic, with only 22% of organizations treating agents as independent identities. This governance gap transforms agents from productivity boosters into high-velocity liabilities capable of executing unauthorized actions or leaking sensitive data before a human can even intervene.

The story is clear: adoption is outpacing governance, and in a race for speed, old lessons are having to be retaught. The majority of deployed agents (and the MCP servers powering them!) are operating without any security sign-off. This is not primarily a resourcing failure, and it is not something a registry alone solves. Security teams cannot review what they cannot discover, and without a registry, discovery is manual, incomplete, and stale. A registry does not make tools inherently secure; rather, it makes security work possible by ensuring tools exist not as transitory, ad hoc shims, but rather as inventoried artifacts that audits and policy can attach to.

It is worth revisiting public package managers here. These registries have not been able to eliminate a number of security problems, issues such as typosquatting, malicious packages, and dependency confusion, showing clearly that centralization alone is not a security solution. But they also show the converse: a registry is a precondition for security. Numerous community responses to breaches in these ecosystems demonstrate the power centralization provides. Centralization does not guarantee security, but decentralization forfeits the means to coordinate it.

Governance requires shared context

The default posture in most agent deployments is permissive: tools are available unless explicitly blocked. AgilityFeat's analysis of enterprise AI guardrails identifies the structural risk this creates, since an architecture not built on deny-by-default increases risk and creates upkeep costs.

Allow-by-default, replicated across dozens of independent agent deployments, produces an attack surface that scales with adoption. Inverting this requires a coordination point, a shared, organization-wide context. The registry itself isn’t a governance layer, but it is what makes governance possible. When every tool an agent can use is registered with ownership, version, and review status, the governance layer has something concrete to enforce against. Without that context, policy has to be reimplemented by every consuming team, and consistency becomes impossible. 

Frontegg's framework for AI agent governance describes what that policy layer looks like operationally: agent actions mapped to explicit, granular guardrails that define the operational boundaries for what any agent can attempt or execute. These guardrails live outside the registry, but they depend on it. A guardrail that references a tool the security team has never heard of cannot be written in the first place.

What a production-grade tool catalog requires

A mature enterprise tool registry has two core functions, discovery and versioning, and serves as the foundation for two others: certification metadata and access control. Think of it as an Internal Developer Portal (IDP) built for the agent era, solving the same coordination problem that IDPs solved for service teams, but one layer up.

Discovery allows any team building an agent to search for existing tools before writing new ones. With ownership metadata, version history, and usage metrics centralized, duplication is reduced not through mandate but through reduced friction. A well-designed catalog goes further than a flat list: tools should be grouped hierarchically by functional domain so that both humans and agents can find relevant capabilities quickly. 

Versioning closes a gap that neither discovery nor access controls address: when agent behavior changes, why did it change? A tool registry that tracks versions gives enterprises the visibility to answer that question. Was it the model? A tool prompt update? An underlying API change? Without proper versioning, finding the answer goes from a simple diff comparison to a time-consuming, manual investigation.

Certification status (things like security approval, API contract validation, PII handling checks) is metadata that the registry surfaces, not a boundary that the registry itself enforces. The actual review work happens through the security organization’s existing tooling. The registry’s contribution is making the result of that review visible at the moment a team is deciding whether to adopt a tool, ensuring the review actually informs the decision it was meant to inform.

Access control works the same way. A policy layer enforces authorization scoped to agent identity, team, environment, and action type, reading from the registry to know what tools exist and who owns them. The registry’s centralization lets access control be applied consistently, rather than forcing each team to come up with something bespoke.

None of this is achievable when each team maintains its own isolated tooling stack. Platform teams already understand why IDPs exist. The value of the paradigm in the agent context is no different.

The compounding cost of inaction

The cost of inaction is direct, not merely operational and security-related. Without a searchable, well-organized catalog of tools, teams continually reinvent the wheel, since it is easier to generate a tool than to find one that already exists. Duplication means redundancy and technical debt. A registry, by making tools discoverable and reusable, converts that redundant spend into capacity for actual work.

For platform engineering teams, the trajectory is clear. Agent adoption is increasing, tool duplication is increasing with it, and the shims that worked at small scale will not hold as the number of agents and tools grows. The security exposure documented in the Gravitee survey will widen, not narrow, without structural intervention.

The organizations that build centralized tool infrastructure now will be able to onboard new agents quickly, govern them consistently, and audit them when something goes wrong. Those that defer will rediscover, the hard way, what platform teams learned a decade ago: coordination problems do not resolve themselves at the application layer. They compound there.

title: RagLeap Physical: A Simulation-First Safety Bridge for AI Agents
description:
What should happen when an AI agent proposes an action that affects a physical-system simulation?

At RagLeap, we're exploring a controlled workflow:

AI proposes → Human approves → Safety limits are checked → Simulator verifies

RagLeap Physical is an open-source, pre-alpha Python project built around this idea.

🔗 GitHub: https://github.com/ragleap/ragleap-core/tree/main/packages/ragleap-physical

What it does

RagLeap Physical provides a simulation-first bridge between AI agents and physical-system simulators.

The project includes:

  • Safety envelopes
  • Exact-proposal approval
  • Dry runs
  • Runtime monitoring
  • Stop functionality
  • Audit logs
  • AI-facing tools
  • MCP server
  • Optional MuJoCo adapters
  • Workspace limits
  • Runnable simulation demos

The focus is not unrestricted AI control. It is controlled, observable interaction.

Release journey

v0.0.1 — Core bridge

The first release introduced the safety bridge, exact-proposal approval, runtime monitoring, audit logs, MCP tools, MuJoCo adapters, workspace limits, and simulation examples.

v0.0.2 — Operator console

The second release added a human operator console.

A named person can review pending proposals, approve the exact digest, apply the action, and stop.

The console is loopback-only, uses one token per person, and is not an AI tool.

v0.0.3 — Two-link workspace demo

The latest release adds:

examples/two_link_workspace_demo.py

The demo shows a two-link arm with one accepted workspace move and one refused move.

It also includes package metadata improvements and a fix for request handling in the operator console and MCP server.

Install 

pip install ragleap-physical==0.0.3

Optional extras:

pip install "ragleap-physical[mujoco]"
pip install "ragleap-physical[test]"
pip install "ragleap-physical[interop]"

Testing

The v0.0.3 release reports:

  • 255 tests passed with MuJoCo and the MCP SDK installed in Colab
  • GitHub CI on Python 3.10, 3.11, and 3.12

The Windows refusal-fix behavior is not yet verified.

Important limitations

This is pre-alpha and simulation-only.

It does not control real hardware. No real-robot or real-machine validation, safety certification, or regulatory compliance is claimed.

MuJoCo results are repeatable within one installed environment only. The wear-study and machine-tool numbers are invented.

Contribute

We welcome feedback and contributions from developers working on AI agents, simulation, robotics, MCP, and safety engineering.

Explore the package:

https://github.com/ragleap/ragleap-core/tree/main/packages/ragleap-physical

Install:

pip install ragleap-physical==0.0.3

AI proposes. Humans approve. The system verifies.

title: Introducing Atlas App Connections: Secure, One-Click Access for AI Tools
description:
For builders using AI coding tools, speed is everything. Integrations that require generating a credential, filing an access request, or waiting on a custom build can stop momentum (and productivity) in its tracks.

Until now, connecting an external application like an AI coding assistant to a MongoDB Atlas account introduced some of that friction. The only way to do so was by sharing long-lived service account credentials, a workaround that slowed builders down and left administrators managing a security risk they were reluctant to accept. Faced with that tradeoff, some organizations avoided third-party integrations, or defaulted to whatever tool was already the default in their AI stack, whether or not it was the best fit.

MongoDB Atlas App Connections closes that gap. It enables builders to securely connect AI coding tools to their MongoDB Atlas account with a single click. Built on OAuth 2.1, an industry-standard authorization framework, App Connections allows AI clients to act on the user's behalf via the MongoDB Atlas MCP Server, without long-lived credentials to generate, share, or manage.

Available now in Atlas App Connections

With Atlas App Connections, builders can connect their AI coding tools to MongoDB Atlas through the Atlas MCP Server, including:

  • ChatGPT

  • Claude

  • Claude Code

  • Codex CLI

  • Cursor

  • Devin

  • Devin Desktop

  • Grok

  • Grok CLI

Once connected, these tools can provision, manage, and query MongoDB Atlas resources directly on the builder's behalf, whether that means spinning up a new cluster, checking on an existing one, or working with the data inside it, based on the access the connecting user already has. Administrators control how far that access extends, choosing between read-only and full access before any AI client can act.

Using App Connections in practice

Here's what that looks like for a builder, using Claude as an example. Assuming Claude is already running, connecting a MongoDB Atlas account takes three steps:

  1. Install the MongoDB plugin by running /plugin install mongodb-atlas@claude-plugins-official.

  2. Grant Claude access by running /mcp, selecting plugin:mongodb-atlas:mongodb-atlas, and choosing Authenticate.

  3. Approve the one-click authorization.

Installing the plugin also adds a set of skills that teach Claude how to work with MongoDB Atlas, and installs MongoDB's remote MCP server behind the scenes. From there, the developer can simply ask Claude to provision a new database cluster, and Claude does it: translating that request into secure Atlas API calls through the Atlas MCP Server. There's no credential to generate or share to make that happen. The administrator overseeing that Atlas organization still has full visibility into the connection and can revoke it at any time.

What you get if you’re building

For builders, speed and security have always felt like a tradeoff. Bottlenecked by integration setup friction, many resorted to workarounds such as sharing high-risk, long-lived credentials just to keep building.

Atlas App Connections removes that tradeoff. A single click securely authorizes AI coding tools to connect to Atlas. There are no credentials to share and no manual configuration to manage. Builders stay in their flow, building at the speed of AI, without ever compromising account security to get there.

What you get if you’re governing an organization

For administrators, the calculus has been just as fraught. Engineering teams need modern AI coding tools to stay competitive, but granting those tools access via opaque, shared service accounts can mean losing track of who or what is actually acting on an organization's data.

Atlas App Connections eliminates that challenge. Access to connect AI clients to Atlas is disabled by default in existing organizations, and administrators must opt in. New organizations created during sign-up start with that access enabled, so first-time users get the best possible AI experience from the outset. Once approved, every action is attributed to both the application and the person who authorized it, visible in Atlas activity feeds. Administrators decide exactly how long an AI client's access can last before it requires re-approval, and can turn off AI client access for the entire organization at any time. Individual users can revoke their own connections whenever they choose. Atlas App Connections helps eliminate shadow AI without standing in the way of engineering teams doing their jobs.

How Atlas App Connections works

Connecting an AI coding tool to Atlas using App Connections takes five steps:

  1. The user installs MongoDB's plugin or connector for their AI client.

  2. The user requests to connect their MongoDB Atlas account from within that client.

  3. The client redirects the user to Atlas.

  4. The user logs in and sees a consent screen naming the application and exactly what it's asking to access.

  5. All the user has to do is click “Approve” and the application is enabled to act on their behalf through the Atlas MCP Server.

Behind the scenes, that approval gives the AI coding tool permission to obtain a short-lived access token and a refresh token on the user's behalf, so it doesn't need to ask the user to log in again for every action. The tool uses that access to provision, manage, and query Atlas resources through the Atlas MCP Server, scoped to whatever access the connecting user already has. All of this happens automatically, invisible to both the user and the application.

A few properties of that access are worth knowing:

  • User-scoped: The AI client can only take actions for which the user has permissions. If a user's Atlas permissions change, the AI client's access automatically changes with them.

  • Revocable: Users can revoke an AI client's access at any time, and it takes effect within 15 minutes.

  • Auditable: Every delegated action is attributed to both the AI client and the user it acted on behalf of.

  • Governed by the organization: Delegated access to AI clients is disabled by default. Atlas organization owners decide whether to turn it on, and for AI clients specifically, whether to allow read-only or full access. If an owner turns off delegation for the entire organization, that change takes effect immediately.

title: Death to long-lived static credentials
description:
Fifteen years ago, TLS was something you'd use to protect the most sensitive areas of your app. Then Google, Let's Encrypt, the EFF, and others led the push for HTTPS everywhere, making encryption the default for every request. Without it, anyone between the browser and server can read and tamper with the traffic.

OAuth, OIDC, DBSC, and related standards already provide building blocks for secure authentication, but standards alone do not make secure methods the norm. HTTPS needed tooling that made encryption easy and a sustained push that made it expected. Machine-to-machine authentication still resembles HTTPS in 2010, with some vendors and enterprises leading the way while long-lived static credentials remain the default for many SaaS vendors and infrastructure providers.

At Vercel, we want to make fast and secure the default across the web, including in our own services and the integrations in our Marketplace. We’ve built OIDC UI, a shadcn/ui registry that gives providers trust-policy forms and token verification code. We’re expanding OIDC support across Vercel and setting new authentication requirements for Marketplace providers.

Long-lived static credentials are insecure

Long-lived static credentials are secrets such as API keys and database passwords that applications keep reusing, often with no expiration. As agents take on more useful work, we give them access to our systems, tools, and data through credentials that can grant permissions far beyond the task at hand.

Those credentials can leak into a code repository or chat, be stolen when a service or dependency is compromised, or be exposed when prompt injection leads an agent to reveal them. However it happens, an attacker can use the credential with the permissions it grants until it expires or is revoked. Recent credential-theft and supply-chain incidents across the industry show why encryption at rest isn’t enough when malicious code can read an application’s credentials in production.

Rotating exposed credentials takes time and coordination across the systems that use them, and mistakes can disrupt production. At Vercel, we’ve previously spent thousands of engineering hours on multiple, very painful key rotations out of an abundance of caution, and we never want to have to do this again.

Better solutions already exist

With OIDC, your application can authenticate without storing a long-lived provider key. A trusted issuer provides a signed, short-lived token identifying the application, and the receiving service verifies that token before deciding what access to grant.

A stolen token stops working when it expires, limiting how long that copy can be used even if the leak goes unnoticed. Your application can obtain fresh credentials programmatically, removing the need to distribute and manually rotate a persistent provider key across the systems that use it.

We’ve been prioritizing OIDC across Vercel so applications can access Blob, AI Gateway, and Sandbox without storing long-lived keys for those services. Our OIDC federation has been generally available since 2024, letting applications running on Vercel exchange Vercel-issued identity tokens for temporary AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure credentials under configured project and environment trust policies. But for developers to stop managing long-lived keys, that support has to extend to all the services their applications depend on.

The rest of the web hasn’t followed

We surveyed more than 1,000 SaaS vendors and found that only 8.4% supported secure authentication methods.

But getting vendors to support secure authentication is only part of the problem. Even when a service offers a secure method, developers often choose a static key because it can be simpler to use. We see three main barriers to broader adoption:

  • Tooling and setup that make secure authentication more complicated than using a static key.

  • Added latency from fetching or exchanging tokens on the request path.

  • Weak incentives for vendors to offer and prioritize secure authentication.

Our goal is to make secure authentication the default on Vercel, while also using our Marketplace to help push more vendors to support it.

Our commitment to a more secure web

We have a responsibility to make this change practical across the services we run, the tools developers use, and the integrations we build with partners.

Make secure authentication easier to use

Using a secure token has to be easier than pasting a key, or developers will keep pasting keys. On Vercel, code retrieves an OIDC token with a function call, and a custom audience specifies the service intended to receive it.

With Vercel Connect, applications and agents use their deployment identity to request provider tokens at runtime, without having to store long-lived provider secrets in environment variables. Once the connector is configured and linked to the project and the user’s account is connected, code can request a token for that user with scopes the provider supports.

We’re also extending OIDC support across the Vercel API and CLI to remove the need for long-lived Vercel tokens in deployment workflows.

OIDC UI for API providers

OIDC UI is a shadcn/ui component registry with a trust-policy configurator and a server-side token verifier. It includes provider forms for Vercel, GitHub, GitLab, Google, Bitbucket, AWS, Azure, and custom OIDC issuers. A provider can let customers configure trust for a particular Vercel project’s production environment, then verify incoming tokens against that policy without building the configuration interface and verification code from scratch.

Reduce the performance cost of secure authentication

A static key in an environment variable is already available when a function runs, so reading it requires no network request. Fetching a token or exchanging it for provider credentials can add network latency, so reducing those calls is part of making secure authentication practical.

Vercel Functions receive a platform-issued token in the request header, which the SDK reads without fetching another. The platform reuses unexpired tokens, while Vercel Connect caches provider tokens in process and refreshes them near expiry. Custom-audience and provider exchanges require network calls.

For example, an application can use the Azure SDK to access Cosmos DB with temporary credentials instead of a database key. With Azure configured to trust the Vercel project and its default token audience, the callback supplies a Vercel OIDC token to ClientAssertionCredential, which exchanges it for the Azure access token used by CosmosClient.

Give providers an incentive to support secure authentication

The Vercel Marketplace offers access to third-party databases, content management systems, observability tools, and more. Our goal is for all of these vendors to support short-lived, identity-based authentication, whether they accept OIDC tokens directly or exchange them for temporary credentials. We’re working to make integrations configure that authentication automatically when developers connect a service, so it does not require a separate setup step.

HTTPS everywhere did not win on ergonomics alone. Chrome put a “Not secure” label on plain HTTP, and then it set deadlines. Now we are setting ours. By November 30, 2026, vendors who do not support OIDC auth from Vercel to their services and use long-lived secrets for authentication will have a similar “Not secure” message on their listing. By January 2027, vendors who do not offer secure auth will be delisted. We are holding the Vercel API and our own native integrations to the same bar.

From static to dynamic

Fifteen years ago, encrypting every request felt like overkill. Today, the padlock is so normal that we only notice when it's missing. Secure authentication between services should become just as routine, so developers can connect the systems they need without storing another long-lived secret. Going from static to dynamic has always been the Vercel mission. It started with pages, and now it’s credentials.

Additional resources

  • OIDC federation covers how deployments get short-lived identity tokens, with guides for AWS, GCP, Azure, and your own API.

  • Custom OIDC token audiences scopes each token to the one service meant to receive it.

  • Vercel Connect requests short-lived, scoped provider tokens at runtime, so code and agents never store credentials.

  • Vercel Connect guides walk through building agents this way, from Slack bots to GitHub agents.

Read more

title: OpenAI Is Buying the Git Host Lovable and Bolt Use. Check What Lives Only There
description:
• Book: System Design Pocket Guide: Fundamentals
  • The series: Pocket Guides for Developers — 8 short books on agents, RAG, prompts, observability, events, databases and system design — the whole series
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

If you have reviewed a change in the Codex app, you have already run code from a company OpenAI is now buying. On November 4, OpenAI said it will acquire Pierre Computer Company, whose open-source Trees and Diffs libraries handle file browsing and diff review inside Codex (OpenAI, StartupHub.ai, Investing.com).

No price was disclosed, the deal still needs regulatory approval, and until it closes, OpenAI and Pierre operate as separate companies (Investing.com).

The diff viewer is the part most developers have touched. The part to look at if you build on it is Pierre's other product, Code Storage: a Git host for code that agents write.

What OpenAI is buying

The open-source side first. Diffs (@pierre/diffs on npm) renders diffs and code, with split and stacked layouts, line annotations and an edit mode. Trees handles file navigation (StartupHub.ai). Both live in Pierre's Apache-2.0 monorepo on GitHub, which shows about 6,400 stars. OpenAI says the projects will stay open source and that it will keep contributing to them (StartupHub.ai).

Then the commercial side. Code Storage describes itself as "a high-scale, distributed storage system built on Git" with "API ergonomics optimized for machines." It serves native Git clone, push and fetch, ships SDKs for TypeScript, Python and Go, sends webhooks, and syncs with GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket. The customers on its homepage include Lovable, Bolt, Amp, Poke, Anything and Parahelp (Code Storage).

OpenAI plans to move Code Storage's features into Codex after the deal closes (StartupHub.ai, ShiftDelete.Net). Earlier the same week, OpenAI described Pando, its in-house source control system for engineers and agents working in parallel (StartupHub.ai).

Axios, which reported the deal first, framed it as OpenAI going after Microsoft's GitHub (ShiftDelete.Net). OpenAI's own post doesn't use that framing; it talks about adapting Git workflows for agents (StartupHub.ai).


Pierre brings two things to OpenAI: the diff and file-tree libraries already in Codex, and a Git host other AI products store code in.

What OpenAI told Code Storage customers

According to OpenAI, Code Storage customers can keep using the service after the deal closes, while the team moves its features into Codex (StartupHub.ai). The announcement gives no closing date and no shutdown date (ShiftDelete.Net). It also says nothing about pricing after the move, which StartupHub.ai lists as an open question.

So nothing changes for you today. What you can do now is find out how much of your code would be easy to take somewhere else, and Code Storage's own docs answer most of that.

The refs a GitHub sync never sees

Code Storage can sync with GitHub in two modes. In GitHub App mode the sync is two-way, and the docs say "Code Storage treats GitHub as the source of truth for synced repositories." Public mode imports a public repo once and keeps nothing in sync after that (Code Storage docs).

Even in two-way mode, only refs/heads/* and refs/tags/* sync from GitHub, and ephemeral refs stay in Code Storage (Code Storage docs). The ephemeral namespace exists for "previews, CI artifacts, and experiments" (Code Storage docs). You reach it by adding +ephemeral before .git in the repo URL. The docs are direct about what that means: "A normal git clone does not show the ref," and "Code Storage never mirrors an ephemeral ref to an upstream host" (Code Storage docs).

Git LFS has a related catch. LFS files uploaded only to an ephemeral ref never reach GitHub, and promoting that ref through the API leaves pointers on GitHub with no bytes behind them (Code Storage docs).

If your product keeps agent previews or experiment branches in that namespace, those refs exist with one vendor. That was true before November 4. A pending acquisition with no timeline is a good reason to check it now.


A normal clone and a GitHub sync see the branches and tags. The ephemeral namespace stays below the waterline.

Keep a copy you control

Start by listing what lives only in the ephemeral namespace. Code Storage remotes are HTTPS URLs authenticated with a JWT (Code Storage docs), so keep the full URL in an environment variable loaded from a secrets file, not typed into your shell history:

# URL ends in +ephemeral.git
git ls-remote "$CODE_STORAGE_EPHEMERAL_URL"

To copy those refs, try a mirror clone of the ephemeral URL into a second bare repo. The docs only show git push and git pull against that remote, so check that the clone actually holds the refs you listed:

git clone --mirror "$CODE_STORAGE_EPHEMERAL_URL" app-ephemeral.git
git -C app-ephemeral.git show-ref

For the normal namespace, the standard Git mirror recipe from GitHub's docs works against any Git remote. Clone once, point pushes at a backup you own, then fetch and push on a schedule:

git clone --mirror "$CODE_STORAGE_URL" app.git
cd app.git
git remote set-url --push origin "$BACKUP_URL"

# repeat on a schedule
git fetch -p origin
git push --mirror

The clone writes the URL, token included, into app.git/config, and Code Storage's Git tokens are JWTs, which can carry an expiry. Before each scheduled fetch, mint a fresh token and run git remote set-url origin "$CODE_STORAGE_URL", or hand the token to a credential helper.

A mirror push doesn't carry Git LFS objects. GitHub's docs add two commands for that:

git lfs fetch --all
git lfs push --all "$BACKUP_URL"

I haven't run any of these against Code Storage myself, the ephemeral clone included. They are plain Git, and they copy only the refs the remote shows you, which is why the ephemeral listing comes first.

Pierre also documents a full export into an S3 bucket you own: one bare repository per repo, "with all refs and history, plus every Git LFS object." You arrange it with Pierre's support, you stop reads and writes to your repos while it runs, and it excludes settings, access keys and webhooks (Code Storage docs). The export page doesn't say whether ephemeral refs are included. Ask before you rely on it.

Diff review is the part you already use

Trees and Diffs are already how Codex shows you what an agent changed (OpenAI, StartupHub.ai, Investing.com). So the review step is where you spend your time, whoever hosts the repo.

I build Hermes IDE, so weigh this with that in mind. Hermes runs Codex, Claude Code and other agent CLIs each in its own terminal, and starts each task on its own hermes/<name> branch and worktree in your repo (GitHub). The Review Desk (⌘G, or Ctrl+Shift+G on Windows and Linux) shows an agent's changes by turn or by file, and Land commits, opens a pull request or merges locally, with undo. The branches stay in your repo, and you push them to whatever remote you already use. Hermes is free to download, source-available under BSL 1.1, on macOS, Windows and Linux, and not affiliated with OpenAI or Pierre.


The Review Desk (⌘G) in By turn view for a Claude Code task in orders-api: two turns, turn 1's diff of src/db.ts, the changed files, and a commit message drafted from the turns.

What to watch next

Three things decide whether this matters for your stack: the closing date, what Code Storage costs once it moves into Codex, and whether it stays a standalone API for other companies' products. StartupHub.ai also asks how Pando and Code Storage will fit together (StartupHub.ai). OpenAI hasn't answered any of them yet.

If your product stores user code with a Git host built for agents, do you keep a mirror somewhere else?

If this was useful

Code Storage sells itself on system-design promises: quorum writes, failover, a 99.99% SLA. Deciding where your source of truth lives, and what copy survives when a vendor changes hands, is the same building-block thinking the System Design Pocket Guide: Fundamentals walks through. It is one of 8 short books in the Pocket Guides for Developers series, covering agents, RAG, prompts, observability, events, databases and system design: see the whole series.

If you run more than one coding agent, Hermes IDE keeps each task on its own branch in your repo; it's built in the open on GitHub.

title: Pulling every tweet for a keyword into SQLite (and what each run actually costs)
description:
I wanted a small local archive of posts about DuckDB: something I can query with plain SQL, re-run whenever I like, and not worry about duplicates. Here's the script I ended up with, the bill for each run, and the one mistake that made my second run cost as much as the first.

Disclosure: I work on TwitterAPI.io, the API used below. Written with AI assistance; the code and every number come from my own runs.

The query 

"duckdb" lang:en min_faves:20 -filter:replies

English posts that mention DuckDB, have at least 20 likes, and aren't replies. The min_faves filter keeps the archive to posts people actually engaged with, and it also keeps the bill down, because you pay per tweet returned.

The script

One file, standard library only. It pages through advanced_search (20 tweets per page), writes each tweet into SQLite keyed by its ID, and adds up the credits as it goes.

"""Collect every tweet for a search query into SQLite, page by page, and report the cost.

usage: TWITTERAPI_KEY=... python3 collect.py "<query>" [max_pages]
Re-running is safe: tweets are keyed by id, so pages you already have are not duplicated.
"""
import json, os, sqlite3, sys, time, urllib.parse, urllib.request

API = "https://api.twitterapi.io/twitter/tweet/advanced_search"
KEY = os.environ["TWITTERAPI_KEY"]
query = sys.argv[1]
max_pages = int(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else 10

db = sqlite3.connect("tweets.db")
db.execute("""CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS tweets (
    id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, query TEXT, created_at TEXT, author TEXT,
    text TEXT, likes INT, retweets INT, replies INT, raw TEXT)""")

def get_page(cursor):
    params = {"query": query, "queryType": "Latest", "cursor": cursor}
    req = urllib.request.Request(f"{API}?{urllib.parse.urlencode(params)}", headers={"X-API-Key": KEY})
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=30) as r:
        return json.load(r)

cursor, calls, fetched, new, credits = "", 0, 0, 0, 0
started = time.time()
while calls < max_pages:
    page = get_page(cursor)
    calls += 1
    tweets = page.get("tweets") or []
    fetched += len(tweets)
    credits += max(len(tweets) * 15, 15)  # billed per request: 15 credits per tweet, 15 minimum
    page_new = 0
    for t in tweets:
        cur = db.execute("INSERT OR IGNORE INTO tweets VALUES (?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?)", (
            t["id"], query, t.get("createdAt"), (t.get("author") or {}).get("userName"),
            t.get("text"), t.get("likeCount"), t.get("retweetCount"), t.get("replyCount"), json.dumps(t)))
        new += cur.rowcount; page_new += cur.rowcount
    db.commit()
    # "Latest" returns newest first: once a whole page is already stored, everything older is too.
    if tweets and page_new == 0:
        break
    if not page.get("has_next_page") or not tweets:
        break
    cursor = page.get("next_cursor") or ""

total = db.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM tweets WHERE query=?", (query,)).fetchone()[0]
cost = credits / 100_000  # 100,000 credits = $1
print(json.dumps({"query": query, "calls": calls, "tweets_returned": fetched, "new_rows": new,
                  "rows_in_db_for_query": total, "credits": credits, "cost_usd": round(cost, 5),
                  "seconds": round(time.time() - started, 1)}))

Run it:

export TWITTERAPI_KEY=...        # from your dashboard
python3 collect.py '"duckdb" lang:en min_faves:20 -filter:replies' 15

What it cost

The billing rule is simple: 15 credits per tweet returned, with a 15-credit minimum per request, and 100,000 credits = $1. A full page of 20 tweets is 300 credits, or $0.003. A request that returns nothing still costs 15 credits.

Run Requests Tweets returned New rows Credits Cost
1st run (empty database) 15 300 300 4,500 $0.045
2nd run, first version of the script 15 300 0 4,500 $0.045
2nd run, with the "stop on a known page" check 1 20 0 300 $0.003

The first run took about 45 seconds for 15 pages.

For scale: reading the same 300 posts through the official X API's pay-per-use tier at $0.005 per post read would be $1.50, about 33 times more per read.

The mistake: re-runs that pay for data you already have

My first version had no stop condition other than has_next_page. INSERT OR IGNORE meant no duplicate rows, so the database looked fine. But the second run walked the same 15 pages and paid for all 300 tweets again, while saving zero new ones.

The fix is the page_new == 0 check. With queryType=Latest the newest posts come first. So when the scheduled re-run reaches a page where every tweet is already stored, everything after it is already stored too, and it can stop. A daily re-run then costs about one page per 20 new posts, plus one page to confirm there is nothing newer.

Two caveats. First, this assumes the previous run finished: if a first backfill dies halfway, the next run sees the newest page as "known" and stops before reaching the gap. For long backfills, saving next_cursor after each page and resuming from it avoids this. Second, with a min_faves filter, posts that cross the threshold later show up deeper in the results; the stop check skips them, so run a full re-crawl now and then if you need them.

Querying it 

-- most-liked posts in the archive
SELECT likes, substr(text, 1, 80) FROM tweets ORDER BY likes DESC LIMIT 5;

-- posts per day
SELECT substr(created_at, 5, 6) AS day, COUNT(*) FROM tweets GROUP BY day ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC;

The raw column keeps the full JSON of each tweet, so you can add columns later without fetching again.

Notes if you try it

  • Rate limits: paid accounts get 20 requests per second. Free accounts are limited to 1 request every 5 seconds until credits are purchased, so add time.sleep(5) in the loop if you're on free credits.
  • Free credits: new accounts get up to $1 of free credits (bot check, one per person). That's enough for this whole exercise many times over.
  • Narrow queries save money: min_faves, lang: and -filter:replies cut the number of tweets returned, and returned tweets are what you pay for.

Pricing details are on the pricing page.

title: Journey before destination
description:
Journey Before Destination

I got into software engineering because I enjoyed it. I enjoyed the process of learning, the feeling of writing something and knowing that those sets of instructions were successful in achieving whatever goal they were set out to achieve, and that they did exactly what was needed.

Sometimes, things did what was needed but not in the way you expected. For many of us, it didn't matter how something worked as long as it worked. For a crazy few of us, however, it did. So we set out to figure out why something worked when we expected it not to, and then, being the crazy folks we were, we wanted to change that working code and break it. That sounds quite ridiculous if the thing being made wasn't software but some sort of physical object. It would be crazy to break a physical thing after you've made it and it works. But that's what software allowed us to do. We could experiment as much as we wanted, as long as we had the time.

Now, with the current world of AI-assisted and agentic development, or whatever fancy, investor-friendly term you want to use for it, it seems like all the fun is gone. Yes, you're achieving results, and at quite a fast pace, but where is the fun of losing your head over a config that isn't working for two days, only to find out that the issue was a character in the wrong case?

For me, the most memorable moments in my software engineering journey have been the ones where I spent a lot of time finding the root cause of an issue or figuring out a solution, followed by that hurrah moment when it finally worked the way I wanted it to. These weren't necessarily the most glamorous things you'd put on your CV. They may or may not have had enough business impact to look shiny enough for recruiters, but the journey of solving them was fun and satisfying because you learned so much about whatever system or context you were dealing with.

With AI, that whole journey seems to be reduced to almost nothing. You give it a prompt, wait a little, and there it is: a solution that either works or doesn't. Then you move on to giving it another prompt for the next JIRA ticket or asking it to solve the same problem in another way.

It feels like you've been riding horses, carriages or cars on your journeys, depending on the road, but now someone has just invented teleportation. Except it's not a perfect kind of teleportation where you know exactly where you're going to end up. It's more like the Floo Network from the world of Harry Potter. You say where you want to go, and the Floo Network takes you there, but sometimes, instead of a sandy beach, it drops you in the middle of a sandy desert. Now, there's no need to worry. You can ask it to take you to the correct beach with a little guidance, or ask it to take you home so you can start again, as long as you can afford it.

But the main thing to worry about is: where is the fun? Where is the journey? Would I want to land directly on the beach, or would I rather get there by train so I can watch the landscapes change along the way, look at the buildings in the cities, and see the sky go through its various phases?

One of my favourite memories ever is a trip to a mountain-top lake formed by a glacier. The reason I have such fond memories of this trip is the journey to get there: travelling along a small, dangerous path winding around mountains in a questionable jeep that somehow kept running on prayers alone. Then came the hike to the top, and when I finally reached it, the view was absolutely breathtaking.

If I could have teleported there instead, I would probably have looked at the lake, said "Nice lake", taken a picture and teleported back home. Then I would have forgotten about the place.

What I'm trying to say is that the journey part of software engineering seems to be diminishing, if not disappearing completely. Now, you just get the results, have a discussion about whether you like them or not, and then move on to the next ticket to repeat the cycle.

I don't want to argue that things shouldn't continue this way. We know AI is here to stay, and there's no going back. But the question is: will we ever enjoy this journey the way we used to?

I guess this is where I'll end this piece, leaving you with these words from Kaladin Stormblessed:

"Life before death, strength before weakness, journey before destination."

title: Distinguishing among reasoning levels of GPT 5.5 Pro via a grammar lens benchmark
description:
arXiv:2611.00555v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Does the level of test-time processing effort affect a language model's computational capability? A formal grammar-lens benchmark method, derived from the theory of computation, generates novel data at specified levels, each successively more computationally powerful than the levels below. Using this data, we tested GPT-5.5, and GPT-5.5-Pro-Medium, -High, and -XHigh, showing incrementally increased acceptance of test data: 16, 40, 43, and 52\%, respectively, illustrating the benchmark's ability to discern fine-grained differences among models' added test-time reasoning levels. Additionally, as test-time compute effort increases, model responses diverge from human responses to the same data. This increasing disagreement may turn out to be broadly characteristic of more capable language models, introducing the potential of a general capability-versus-alignment conflict.

title: Sudo command digests do not remove executable trust
description:
Sudo command digests do not remove executable trust

A digest in a sudoers rule can answer a narrow question: did the command file have the expected bytes when sudo checked it? It does not prove that the path is controlled by an administrator, that the file will remain unchanged until execution, or that the command's dependencies are equally trustworthy.

Sudo supports SHA-2 digest lists on command entries. An operator can pin a script or binary to a known hash and reject an unexpected replacement. That is useful for controlled deployment, but the sudo manual includes an important warning. If the user can write the command or its parent directory, the file may be replaced after the digest check and before execution. Systems without a suitable fexecve(2) path can have a related race.

What the digest proves

This warning changes the review method. Start with file ownership and directory permissions, not the hash value. Trace every directory in the command path and ask whether the invoking user, a service account, or an application process can create, rename, or replace an entry. A hash on a script in a writable directory is not a stable privilege boundary.

Ownership and execution race

Next, inspect interpreters and helpers. A script digest covers the script text, not the Python interpreter, shell, configuration file, plugin directory, or command it invokes. A pinned wrapper can still execute an unpinned program through a relative path or a user-controlled configuration variable. secure_path and env_reset may reduce that risk, but they do not turn a writeable dependency into a trusted one.

Review checklist

Operationally useful controls include:

  • Place privileged commands in administrator-owned directories that ordinary users cannot modify.
  • Keep scripts and their configuration files under the same ownership and deployment policy.
  • Avoid wildcard rules that let the caller choose arbitrary interpreted files.
  • Record the digest algorithm, source package, deployment time, and update owner.
  • Re-test the rule after package upgrades and emergency patching.

Change control

Digests also need an update process. If the only copy of the expected hash lives in someone's notes, an upgrade creates either an outage or an undocumented exception. Store the approved value in configuration management, generate it from a signed artifact, and require a review when it changes. The digest is evidence of file identity, not a substitute for artifact provenance.

Finally, check how sudo resolves the command at runtime. Absolute paths are easier to reason about than names looked up through PATH. A directory that is safe today can become unsafe after a permissions change or a new group membership. The review should therefore connect the sudoers entry to the filesystem, deployment pipeline, and application execution path.

Sudo command digests are useful when they close a specific integrity gap in an already controlled path. They are misleading when used to make a user-writable executable look approved. Treat the file, its parent directories, interpreter, dependencies, and update process as one trust decision.

References

  • sudoers manual, command digests and replacement warning: https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/sudoers.5.html

title: I Changed One Model Pin and Ten Test Results Went Stale
description:
I Changed One Model Pin and Ten Test Results Went Stale

From the agentdrill v0.1.0 release, part of agentic-suite: open-source, harness-agnostic security tools for AI-agent defenses.

One line changed in the config. The agent model pin went from Qwen3.5-4B-4bit to Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507-4bit. Nineteen test verdicts sat on disk, all green.

I could not tell you which of them were still true.

That is the actual problem with test evidence. It does not expire on its own. Nothing goes grey. A PASS earned under the old model sits next to a PASS earned under the new model and looks exactly as fresh. The dashboard has no concept of provenance unless you build one.

This happened mid-run in the agentdrill v0.1.0 field test, and the resolution is the part worth stealing. Full details in the field test report, Batch 9.

The instinct that would have wasted a day

The obvious move after a model switch is to re-run everything. Nineteen Track B cases, each one a real agent doing real work against a local LLM server. That is an expensive afternoon, and worse, it is indiscriminate. It re-proves the fresh results to avoid finding out which ones are stale.

The house rule for this run was stricter and better: run only what is failing or stale. So the question became a lookup problem. For each of the 19 cases, when was its verdict written, and was that before or after the pin switch?

Git was the ledger we already had

Every verdict in this field test is committed to git as a verdict.json, together with its captured LLM pairs. The pin switch also landed in a specific commit. That turns the question into arithmetic:

  1. Find the commit where the new pin landed
  2. For each case, find the last commit that wrote its verdict.json
  3. Verdict written before the switch: stale. After: fresh

The answer was 9 fresh and 10 stale. Not 11, which is what the report had been saying from a rougher earlier count. The forensics corrected the report, not the other way around. That correction is in the report now, because a number you cannot trace is a number you cannot defend.

Re-earn exactly what aged

The 10 stale cases were re-run. Nothing else. All 10 green, each with fresh request and response pairs. Then the verification step that matters: for every one of the 19 cases, read the model field out of its most recent captured requests and confirm the new pin is there.

That last check is only possible because of a detail from earlier in the run: every captured LLM request carries meta.model, so each evidence file describes the environment that produced it. Nineteen of nineteen cases now show the new agent pin in their latest capture batch. The mixed state is gone, and the proof is not my word, it is readable out of the files under results/track-b/cases.

The failure mode nobody warns you about

The worst part of this story is not the switch. It is that the first switch half-landed. The pin was changed in one place, but the field runner script still had the old model as its default, so early re-runs quietly kept using the old pin while we believed we had switched.

A config change that half-lands is nastier than no change, because your belief and your evidence diverge without any error message. We only caught it because the captures recorded the model name, and someone actually read them. The fix was to wire the pins through run-local.sh so there is exactly one source of truth.

What I take from this

  • Evidence has provenance. A verdict is a claim about a moment: this code, this config, this model. The verdict should say so, or the raw evidence should.
  • A change event should age your evidence. Nothing automatic did this for us. We built the habit: config change, then ask which verdicts predate it. Git made the question answerable in minutes.
  • Store the environment inside the evidence. meta.model in every capture file is what turned "trust me, it is the new pin" into a checkable fact.
  • Re-run the stale set, not the world. Discriminate re-runs keep the cost of honesty low. If re-proving everything is the only honest option you have, your evidence is not organized well enough to be cheap about.

Tip: a config change should age your evidence. Find which verdicts predate it before you re-run anything.

The question this leaves me with: when you last changed a model, a temperature, or a prompt, did your old greens get flagged, or are they still sitting on the dashboard looking fresh? Mine were. Ten of them. Green, stale, and indistinguishable from the truth until someone went and checked.

How does your team mark results that predate a config change? I want to hear whether anyone has this automated, because we did it with git one-liners and I suspect there is a better machine for it.

Code and receipts: agentdrill · field test report, Batch 9 · captured pairs with model pins

About agentdrill

This story is one of seven from the agentdrill v0.1.0 field test. agentdrill is the adversarial-testing engine in agentic-suite: open-source, harness-agnostic security tools for AI-agent defenses. It runs versioned attack packs against your deployed stack in CI and publishes honest results, misses included.

pip install agentsec-agentdrill   # v0.1.0 is live on PyPI
agentdrill quickstart             # first honest result in ~15 minutes, bundled demo

Dig deeper: the v0.1.0 field test report (73/73 units, every pass grounded), the release notes, and the rest of the suite at github.com/agentic-suite: agentdrill drills the defenses, agentwatch records the evidence.

title: Make Email Verification APIs State-Driven
description:
Email verification often starts as one column and one endpoint: store a token, set verified = true when the token arrives, and return success. That works until users click an old link, a mobile client retries after a timeout, or two requests redeem the same token at nearly the same time.

The durable approach is to model verification as a small state machine. The API then reports what happened instead of making clients infer state from a boolean or from inconsistent error messages. This also makes email fixtures, including a free disposable email address or a temp mail generator used in test environments, easier to reason about without weakening production rules.

Why a boolean verified flag is not enough

A boolean answers only one question: has this account been verified at some point? It cannot explain whether a token was issued, consumed, expired, revoked, or rejected because it belongs to another account.

Those distinctions matter for both security and operations. A user who clicks an expired link needs a different response from a user who presents a token that was already consumed. A support engineer also needs to know whether the email was never sent or whether the verification request failed later.

The state machine are useful because it gives each transition an owner and a clear outcome. A practical lifecycle might contain:

  • pending: an address was registered and verification is required.
  • sent: a verification message was requested.
  • verified: a valid token was consumed successfully.
  • expired: the token passed its deadline.
  • revoked: the token was invalidated by a password or email change.

The account state and token state should not be confused. An account can be pending while its newest token is expired, and a new token can then be issued without rewriting the history of the old one.

Model the verification lifecycle explicitly

Start with a token record that has a stable identifier, a digest rather than the raw token, an expiration time, and timestamps for each meaningful transition. For example:

CREATE TABLE email_verification_tokens (
    id uuid PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
    token_digest bytea NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    status text NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('pending', 'consumed', 'expired', 'revoked')),
    expires_at timestamptz NOT NULL,
    consumed_at timestamptz,
    created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

Do not store a reusable token in plaintext. The application can hash the value supplied by the client and compare the digest. If the database is exposed, an attacker should not receive a ready-to-use verification credential.

The token endpoint should evaluate expiry at the time of the transaction, not only in a background cleanup job. Cleanup is helpful for storage, but it is not the security boundary. A token that expired two seconds ago must be rejected even if a worker has not changed its row to expired yet.

Make the REST API idempotent

Clients retry. Networks drop responses, browsers reload pages, and a mobile app may submit the same verification request twice. A successful first request followed by a timeout must not become a confusing 409 on the second request if the account is already verified.

Use a transaction that locks the token row, checks its current status and deadline, then performs one transition. A simplified flow looks like this:

BEGIN
  SELECT token FOR UPDATE
  if token is missing or revoked: reject
  if token is expired: mark expired, reject
  if token is consumed: return the existing success outcome
  mark token consumed
  mark account verified
COMMIT

The response can distinguish the first successful consumption from a safe replay while keeping both outcomes useful to the client:

{
  "status": "verified",
  "user_id": "user_123",
  "already_verified": false
}

For a replay, return the same resource state and set already_verified to true, or use a documented conflict response if the product needs the distinction. What matters is that the contract is stable. The client should not guess what happend from a generic 500 response.

This is also where an idempotency key can help for the endpoint that requests a new email. Store the key with the user and operation, then return the original result when a retry arrives. Do not use the request timestamp as the key: two legitimate requests can happen in the same second.

Let PostgreSQL enforce the important invariants

Application checks are necessary, but concurrent requests can pass the same check before either one commits. PostgreSQL should enforce rules that must remain true under concurrency:

  • a token digest is unique;
  • a token belongs to one user;
  • a consumed token has a consumed_at value;
  • an account cannot have two current verification tokens if the product allows only one;
  • status values are restricted to known transitions.

A partial unique index can enforce one active token per user:

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX one_active_verification_token
ON email_verification_tokens (user_id)
WHERE status = 'pending';

When a new token is requested, revoke the prior pending token in the same transaction before inserting the replacement. If the insert loses a race, catch the constraint error and reload the current token state rather than returning an unexplained database failure. The error handling is a bit more work, but the behavior is predictable.

For auditability, record transition events separately when the workflow is important enough to investigate. The event should include the user ID, token ID, request ID, actor type, and reason. Avoid storing the raw token or the full email body in an audit table.

Test retries, expiry, and stale tokens

The happy path is the least interesting test. Cover these cases explicitly:

  1. Two requests redeem the same token concurrently; only one transition performs the verification.
  2. The response is lost after commit; a retry returns the verified state.
  3. A token expires during the request; the transaction rejects it using the database clock.
  4. A newer token is issued; the older token is revoked and cannot verify the account.
  5. A user changes their email; tokens for the previous address no longer work.
  6. A duplicate request for a new email does not create an uncontrolled message burst.

Tests should assert both the HTTP response and the final database state. A fake inbox is useful for checking message contents, but it should not be the source of truth for whether the token was consumed. Keep the protocol identifiers separate from search phrases such as tempail or temp org mail; those terms may appear in user input, but they are not correlation keys.

When inspecting failures, designing a verification-token inbox is a useful companion pattern for isolating messages from application state. For changes that update an existing address, auditing email-change APIs with PostgreSQL covers the history that a simple token table may miss.

Questions engineers usually ask

Should expired tokens be deleted immediately?

Usually no. Retain a short history so support and security investigations can distinguish an expired token from a missing one. A scheduled retention job can delete old rows later.

Should the token endpoint return the user session?

That is a product and threat-model decision. If verification is a prerequisite for login, returning a restricted session may be reasonable. Keep token consumption and session issuance in clearly separated steps so a replay cannot mint a second session accidentally.

Do we need a queue for this flow?

The state transition does not require one. A queue is useful for sending the email and retrying delivery, while the verification endpoint should remain a small, transactional REST API. Mixing delivery retries with token redemption makes failures harder to diagnose.

An explicit lifecycle turns verification from a fragile side effect into a maintained backend contract. PostgreSQL protects the invariants, the REST API reports stable outcomes, and retries become an expected operating condition instead of a production surprise.
