title: Out of Postgres Connections? Find the Limit You Hit and Get Back In
description:
"No connections left" is not one symptom. It is at least four different limits with four different fixes, and picking the wrong one makes things worse. I filled a Nano-sized Supabase lab on purpose and worked through the recovery steps one at a time, with the real error text and real timings.

Three things I did not expect: when the database is full, postgres cannot connect either; terminating idle backends recovers it in milliseconds; and raising the pool size made throughput worse for one of the two query shapes I tested.

How this was made: I wrote this with Claude's help: it drafted, and I ran every step, edited the text, and checked the results. The mistakes are mine.

The companion piece — how connections are counted in the first place, and why they multiply: https://dev.to/tomozilla/supabase-connection-budgets-pool-size-roles-modes-and-limits-4lc8
The code: https://github.com/tomozilla/connection-budget-en-demo

What I did and did not do

  • Everything new here ran in a local lab: a Supabase CLI stack with max_connections 90, pooler pool size 15, client cap 200 — Nano-like limits where going past a limit hurts nobody. Cost: $0.
  • I never filled a hosted database. It is shared infrastructure. So every "while full" result below is from the lab.
  • The hosted numbers I reuse (the client-cap scope, the live pool-size change, the Micro → Small upgrade) were measured on a throwaway Pro project that I created and deleted the same day, in the companion article.
  • Each experiment ran a few times at most.

1. First, read the error text

This is the step people skip. "Out of connections" covers at least four separate limits, and the fix differs for each.

What you see Which limit First move
(EMAXCONN) max client connections reached, limit: 200 the pooler's client cap, per role shrink the per-copy pool, or run fewer copies (§6)
(EMAXCONNSESSION) max clients reached in session mode the session-mode pool move to transaction mode if you can
(ECHECKOUTTIMEOUT) ... after 60000ms in Transaction mode the transaction pool is full, and you waited 60 s §7 — and read it before you raise the pool size
FATAL: remaining connection slots are reserved for roles with the SUPERUSER attribute (53300) max_connections itself §2–§4. This is the heavy one
(EAUTHQUERY) authentication query failed the pooler can't even open a connection to check your login same cause: max_connections is full
504 PGRST003 the Data API's own pool hunt the slow query
too many connections for role "..." a role's CONNECTION LIMIT check it is at least pool size + 1 (§8)
no error at all, just slow queueing §7. Watch p95, not the error count

→ The first three are inside the pooler; your database may still have room. The fourth means the database itself is full. Those are different emergencies.

Don't skip the last row. In the companion article, going from 5 clients to 100 changed throughput not at all — only the wait, from 0.1 s to 0.6 s — with zero errors the whole time.

2. When it is full, you cannot get in — not even as postgres

This surprised me most, and it changes what "preparation" means.

I filled max_connections with idle connections on one role, then tried to log in as several roles.

filled: 51 connections held, 39 refused
  remaining connection slots are reserved for roles with the SUPERUSER attribute
Role I tried to connect as Result
r1 (the app's role) refused, 53300
r2 (another app role) refused, 53300
postgres refused, 53300
supabase_admin connected, 3 ms

→ postgres is refused too, because on Supabase it is not a superuser and cannot use the reserved slots (superuser_reserved_connections, which is 3 on both hosted and the lab). The role you normally administer with is unavailable exactly when you need it.

That makes this a preparation problem, not a recovery step:

  • Decide before the incident how you will get in. Searching for a way while it is down is too late.
  • The dashboard's SQL editor reaches the database by a different path than a client connection. Mine worked when the database was not full; I did not test it against a full database, so I can't promise it.
  • PostgreSQL 17 has reserved_connections: set it, grant a role pg_use_reserved_connections, and that role still connects when full. It worked in the lab. I have not confirmed you can set it on a hosted project (the hosted value was 0), so do not build your plan on it.
  • In practice, knowing who can open the dashboard is the reliable answer.

3. See what is actually holding the connections

Once you are in, count before you act.

select usename,
       application_name,
       state,
       count(*) as n,
       max(now() - state_change)::interval(0) as longest_in_state
from pg_stat_activity
where backend_type = 'client backend'
group by 1, 2, 3
order by n desc;

Three columns matter. usename tells you whether one role dominates, or whether it is a Supabase service (supabase_auth_admin, supabase_storage_admin). application_name tells you the route: Supavisor means through the pooler, PostgREST 14.x means the Data API, empty usually means a direct connection. And then state:

state What it means How to read it
active running a query right now genuinely busy — go to §7
idle connected, doing nothing holding a seat — §4 clears these
idle in transaction stopped mid-transaction the dangerous one — §8

→ Lots of idle is a connection problem. Lots of active is a query problem. Skip this distinction and §7 will send you the wrong way.

4. Stop the bleeding: terminate

If idle is the culprit, kill those backends.

-- In a real incident, always filter by age so you don't kill connections that just opened
select pg_terminate_backend(pid)
from pg_stat_activity
where backend_type = 'client backend'
  and usename = 'r1'
  and state = 'idle'
  and now() - state_change > interval '1 minute';

From a full database in the lab:

Step Result
a normal connection while full refused, 53300
pg_terminate_backend on that role's idle backends 51 terminated in 12 ms
the same connection attempt, right after connected, 3 ms

→ Recovery is effectively instant. The slow part of an incident is deciding to do this, not doing it.

Two cautions. Drop state = 'idle' from that query and you will terminate running queries too, rolling back whatever they were writing. And what the killed client sees depends on the library: node-postgres' Pool crashed the process without an error handler (Unhandled 'error' event), recovered from the next query with one, and through the pooler produced no event at all.

Terminating does not fix the cause. The same app will reopen the same connections within minutes, so continue to §8.

5. Stop the bleeding: change the pool size (no restart)

If the pooler is the bottleneck, the pool size is the dial. The question I actually cared about was whether changing it forces a restart, because a restart during an incident is its own problem.

Measured on a hosted project: the same load — 10 clients each holding an 8-second query — run twice, changing only the pool size in the dashboard between runs.

Pool size Backends opened Time for all 10 queries Errors
3 4 25.3 s 0
15 10 9.3 s 0

→ It took effect immediately, with no restart. It works downward too: if one role is hogging the database, lowering the pool size hands capacity back to the others.

Before you reach for "raise it", though, read §7.

6. Stop the bleeding: split roles — but only for EMAXCONN

If you hit the client cap, this is different, because that cap is per role. Measured on a hosted project, with idle connections and no queries at all:

Attempt Result
215 clients on one role exactly 200 connect, the rest get (EMAXCONN) ... limit: 200
150 clients on each of two roles (300 total) all 300 connect, zero refusals

→ A second role really does buy another 200 client slots. As a stopgap for EMAXCONN, it works.

Now the catch. While those 300 clients were connected, the database held:

300 clients (2 roles)  ->  2 backends

→ Two. One per role, because nothing was running a query. Adding a role buys client slots and zero backend slots. If those 300 clients all start querying, you have moved the queue to max_connections, not removed it.

7. "Just raise the pool size" is half right

This is the part I got wrong before measuring.

Remember state from §3. Whether raising the pool helps depends entirely on whether the backends are waiting or burning CPU. To separate the two I used queries that both take about 100 ms for opposite reasons:

  • wait: pg_sleep(0.1) — the backend is idle, waiting (think an external API call or a lock).
  • cpu: count(*) over 2,000,000 rows — the backend is saturating a core (think a heavy aggregate).

60 concurrent clients, closed loop, pool size 15 vs 30:

Query Pool 15 (16 backends) Pool 30 (31 backends) Effect
wait 154/s, p50 409 ms 295–300/s, p50 204 ms throughput nearly doubled, latency halved
cpu 48–51/s, p50 1149–1230 ms, p95 1328–1465 ms 38–44/s, p50 1235–1493 ms, p95 1456–2160 ms throughput dropped, p95 got worse

→ The same change that nearly doubled one workload made the other measurably worse. The cpu row was 38, 44 and 44/s across three runs, against 48–51/s at pool 15.

The reason is obvious in hindsight: raising the pool does not add CPU. Thirty-one backends contending for the same cores each run slower, and the extra context switching costs more than it returns. Queries that are merely waiting have nothing to contend over, so they scale cleanly.

So the procedure is:

  1. Look at state (§3).
  2. Mostly idle or waiting → raising the pool size is worth it (§5, and it applies live).
  3. Mostly active → raising the pool makes it worse. Fix the query: pg_stat_statements, an index, fewer rows returned. If you can't, go to §9.

8. Remove the cause, or it comes back

A leaked transaction: idle in transaction

If §3 showed idle in transaction, fix that first. The connection never comes back on its own, and it blocks vacuum on the tables it touched.

I opened a transaction and did nothing:

state: idle in transaction, held: 2 seconds (and counting, indefinitely)

The fix is a timeout the client cannot wait out:

alter role r1 set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '5s';

→ The server killed it at 5.0 s: terminating connection due to idle-in-transaction timeout.

Fixing the application bug is the real answer, but this setting is a seatbelt you can fasten today, before you find the bug.

One role starving everyone

Per-role limits work, but the value matters. With pool size 15 and 40 clients running 5-second queries:

connection limit Backends Queries that failed
15 (same as pool size) 15 25 of 40, immediately
16 (pool size + 1) 16 0 (the rest waited)

→ Set it to at least pool size + 1. At exactly the pool size, the 16th backend is refused and clients that could have waited turn into errors instead. (Supavisor's transaction mode opens pool size + 1; that is measured in the companion article.)

Apply this to a role you created, not to authenticator (it would stop the Data API) and not to postgres.

A backstop the client cannot remove

statement_timeout is not a guardrail, because any role can change its own: a client can run SET statement_timeout = 0, and on the transaction pooler that zero is then inherited by the next client. Permissions do not stop this.

So the backstop has to live outside the session:

select cron.schedule('cancel-long-queries', '5 seconds', $$
  select pg_cancel_backend(pid)
  from pg_stat_activity
  where usename = 'batch_user'          -- scope it to a role you created
    and state = 'active'
    and now() - query_start > interval '6 seconds'
$$);

→ A client that had removed its own timeout and started a 30-second query was cancelled after 10–11 s (6 s plus the job interval).

Expect connections to linger

Closing clients does not free the slots at once: about 2 minutes in my measurements, and the docs say up to 5. Budget for 5. During an incident, "I stopped it and nothing freed up" is expected, not a second fault.

9. Last resort: a bigger instance

If §7 put you in the active column, this is where you end up. I upgraded the throwaway project to see what actually changes:

Micro Small
max_connections 60 90
pooler client cap 200 400
default pool size 15 15, unchanged
price shown in the dialog $9.68/mo $14.83/mo

→ Connections and client slots both grow, but your pool size does not. A bigger instance does not widen the pool for you — raise it yourself (§5), or you will have paid for headroom you aren't using.

One more thing worth knowing: moving to a paid plan buys no connections at all. Nano (free) and Micro (smallest paid) both have 60. Only compute size moves that number. Compute is billed hourly and is not covered by the Spend Cap.

A checklist for when it is quiet

  1. Decide who can get in when it is full. postgres cannot (§2).
  2. Keep the §3 query somewhere you can paste it, with the three meanings of state.
  3. Set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout on your roles now (§8).
  4. Set each pooled role's connection limit to pool size + 1 or more (§8).
  5. Put a query-killing backstop outside the session (§8).
  6. Alert on p95 latency, not on error count — the failure mode is silence (§1).
  7. Run the budget equation from the companion article against your current setup.

Takeaways

  • "Out of connections" is four different limits. Read the error text before acting (§1).
  • When the database is full, postgres cannot connect — only supabase_admin could. Arrange access in advance (§2).
  • state in pg_stat_activity decides your next move: idle → terminate, active → fix the query, idle in transaction → top priority (§3).
  • Terminating idle backends is instant: 51 in 12 ms, a normal connection 3 ms later (§4).
  • Pool size changes apply live, no restart: the same work took 25.3 s at pool 3 and 9.3 s at 15 (§5).
  • Splitting roles buys client slots and no backend slots: 300 clients held 2 backends (§6).
  • Raising the pool size helped waiting queries (154 → 295/s) and hurt CPU-bound ones (48 → 44/s). Check state first (§7).
  • statement_timeout can be removed by the client; the backstop must live outside the session (§8).
  • A bigger instance raises max_connections and the client cap but leaves the pool size at 15 (§9).
  • Every "while full" result here is from a local lab. I did not fill a hosted database.

The lab scripts for all of this are in the repo: https://github.com/tomozilla/connection-budget-en-demo

title: How to build an LLM evaluation from real failures
description:
Build the eval from failures you have actually read, rather than from a rubric you wrote in advance. Group those failures, put one domain expert in charge of the standard, and create the cases only after that. Use code where the property is mechanical, and add a model judge only after it agrees with that expert.

Bigcircle uses this order on client systems, because a score you cannot trace to a failure does not tell you what to fix. Every guide on this site tells you to build evals before you do anything else, and none of them has explained how. That gap is worth closing, because the order of the steps matters more than any individual technique in them, and most of the teams we work with have the order backwards.

The difficulty is not that evaluation is conceptually hard. It is that the thing you are trying to measure does not hold still. A traditional test suite asserts that a function returns four, and four is four regardless of who is asking. An eval asserts that an answer is grounded, or that a citation supports the claim attached to it, or that a system correctly declined to answer a question it had no evidence for. Those are judgements, they vary between reasonable people, and they change as you learn more about your own product. Barnett et al. reached the same conclusion across research, education and biomedical deployments: "validation of a RAG system is only feasible during operation" (Seven Failure Points, IEEE/ACM CAIN 2024). You cannot certify these systems the way you would certify a payments integration, which means the harness is not a gate you pass once but an instrument you keep running.

In this guide we walk through the process we use on client systems, in the order we use it. It starts with reading real failures before writing any criteria, grouping those failures into a taxonomy, and deciding who owns the standard. From there you build the case set, choose what to measure on it, and decide which of those checks need a model at all. Then you write the rubric for the ones that do, and validate that judge against human labels before it gates anything. Where our own systems illustrate a step, we use them: two in production with clients, and two we built and run ourselves.

What is LLM evaluation, exactly?

An eval is a test whose assertion requires judgement rather than equality.

The distinction matters more than it first appears. A unit test can be written before the feature exists, because the correct answer is knowable in advance. An eval usually cannot, because the definition of a correct answer is something you discover by looking at wrong ones. Everything else about an eval is ordinary engineering: it lives in the repository, it runs in continuous integration, it fails a build, and it has a history you can bisect when a regression appears.

# unit test
assert parse_date("2026-09-01") == date(2026, 9, 1)

# eval
assert grounded(answer, passages)         # every claim traceable to a passage
assert cites_correctly(answer, passages)  # each citation contains what it claims
assert refused_when_unanswerable(answer, passages)

Why can't you just write the rubric first?

Because you do not know your criteria until you have looked at outputs, and looking creates them.

This is not a failure of discipline, and a more rigorous team does not avoid it. Shankar et al. identified it as a structural property of the task and named it criteria drift:

To grade outputs, people need to externalize and define their evaluation criteria; however, the process of grading outputs helps them to define that very criteria.

We see this on nearly every engagement. A team sits down to write a rubric before launch and produces something like "the answer should be accurate and helpful." An hour of reading real outputs turns that into something far more specific. Does the response cite the controlling clause rather than a topically related one? Does it flag a conflict between two policies instead of silently picking one? Does it decline when the user's jurisdiction is not covered by the documents in scope? None of those would have occurred to anyone in advance. All of them are obvious in retrospect.

This is also why prefabricated metrics tend not to survive contact with a real product. A generic helpfulness or coherence score measures an abstraction that has no particular relationship to the failure modes your system exhibits, and when it moves you cannot say which change moved it. We have watched a team spend a sprint chasing a coherence score that fell after a retrieval change, on a system whose actual problem was that the reranker had started dropping the controlling clause. The score was real. It just was not measuring the thing that broke.

The rubric, then, is an output of the process rather than an input to it. The process that produces it is error analysis.

How do you find your actual failure modes?

Read your traces in a structured way before anyone writes a criterion, in three passes borrowed from qualitative research methods. The structure matters because unstructured reading produces impressions rather than counts, and impressions cannot tell you where to spend a quarter.

Start with open coding: pull real traces and write a free-form note on each one that went wrong. There are no categories at this stage and no attempt at consistency, because imposing either would defeat the purpose. Notes look like "cited the wrong section," "answered when it should have refused," or "used the policy that was superseded in March." The notes are raw observation, and the discipline is to resist labelling while you are still looking.

Then group those notes, the pass called axial coding, so that similar complaints collapse into a category and you end with a failure taxonomy of roughly five to ten modes. Whether "cited the wrong section" and "invented a clause number" become one category called citation error or two separate ones depends entirely on what you saw, and that decision is the substantive work of the pass.

Count before you plan the work, because the count decides where engineering time goes. If forty-three percent of your failures are retrieval misses, no amount of prompt work will move your quality this quarter. Counting makes that unarguable rather than a matter of opinion between two engineers who each read a handful of examples.

You stop at theoretical saturation, which in practice means twenty consecutive traces producing no new category, with at least a hundred reviewed before you trust that. Do not stop earlier. It is the common error, and it leaves a taxonomy of the sample rather than of the system. The modes you found are real, but the ones you missed are the ones that will show up in production. Every evaluator you build afterwards then targets a failure you have seen in your own system, rather than one you read about.

Who decides what good means?

One person, and not a committee.

Pick one principal domain expert: someone with real depth in the domain, or who truly represents the users the system is built for. Their job is to set the standard, and it has to be one person because three stakeholders labelling in parallel produce three rubrics and an argument. We have sat through that argument more than once, and it is almost always about vocabulary rather than about quality, which means it consumes a week and settles nothing. You need labels that stay consistent from one trace to the next, and one person gives you that where a panel does not.

The work itself is small and specific. The expert reads a trace, makes a binary pass-or-fail judgement, and writes a critique explaining the reasoning behind it. Teams cut the critique when they are busy, and cutting it costs more than it saves, because those critiques become the few-shot examples in the judge prompt later. On the trademark platform the useful ones named the clause that should have governed and said why the wrong one was plausible, which is the reasoning a judge needs in order to make the same call. The difference between a usable critique and a useless one is large:

Critique Usable?
"Wrong." No. It carries no information at all
"Bad citation." No. Which citation, and wrong in what way?
"Cites clause 7.2, which covers annual plans. The question was about monthly, governed by 7.4. The number quoted is correct for the wrong clause, which is worse than being plainly wrong because a reviewer scanning for errors will not catch it." Yes. This can become a few-shot example

The time cost is lower than teams tend to fear. Thirty to fifty traces to establish the standard, then periodic review as the system changes. What cannot be delegated is the judgement itself, because the expert is the only available source of the standard the system is being held to.

Where do the cases come from?

You have a taxonomy and someone who owns the standard. The next thing to build is the set of cases both will be applied to, and it is built to cover the modes the taxonomy named rather than to sample traffic. Keep it as JSONL, one case per line, so a diff is readable and a new case is one appended line.

{"id": "refund-001", "query": "What is the refund window for enterprise annual plans?", "gold_passages": ["policy-billing#p14"], "gold_answer": "30 days from invoice date.", "must_refuse": false, "tags": ["billing"]}
{"id": "refund-002", "query": "Can I get a refund after 90 days?", "gold_passages": ["policy-billing#p14"], "gold_answer": null, "must_refuse": true, "tags": ["out-of-policy"]}
{"id": "acl-001", "query": "What is the Q3 headcount plan?", "gold_passages": [], "must_refuse": true, "tags": ["permissions"], "as_user": "contractor@example.com"}

Two decisions in that format do most of the work.

Label the passage, not the document. This is the mistake most worth avoiding early:

{"gold_passages": ["employee-handbook.pdf"]}                    // useless
{"gold_passages": ["employee-handbook.pdf#p31-parental-leave"]} // testable

A document-level gold label makes retrieval recall look excellent while measuring nothing, because any chunk drawn from a ninety-page file counts as a hit. Ask the expert to mark the minimum span that answers the question, and if two spans are required, record both, which turns the case into a multi-hop test at no extra cost.

Stratify the set by the taxonomy you found, not by traffic volume. A uniform sample of production traffic returns whatever your users happen to ask most often, which is usually one easy intent repeated many times.

Bucket Share Why it exists
The dominant failure mode from your counts 30% The quarter's work lives here
Exact identifiers: ids, codes, part numbers 15% Embeddings blur these and nothing else catches it
Multi-hop or cross-document 15% Fails silently without a dedicated bucket
Unanswerable from the corpus 15% Tests refusal. Barnett's FP1
Permission-restricted 10% Runs as a user who must not see the answer
Adversarial: instructions inside a document 10% Prompt injection surface
Long tail, unusual phrasing 5% Where query rewriting breaks

Once a hand-built set exists, Chroma's generative benchmarking report (April 2025) describes one way to grow it: filter your documents with a judge aligned to your expert, then generate queries from what is left, steered by real production queries so they read like your traffic.

What should you measure?

With cases in hand, you can decide what to measure on them. Decompose the system first. Retrieval, tool use and generation fail for unrelated reasons and are repaired by unrelated work, so a single quality score cannot tell you which of the three broke on any given change.

Here is the whole set in one place, before we go through them. Standard names
are given where one exists, because you will meet these under those names in
Ragas and
elsewhere.

Layer Metric Answers Typical gate
Retrieval Recall@k Did any gold passage reach the top k? 0.90 at final depth
Retrieval MRR, or NDCG@k when passages are graded How high did the first useful passage land? above 0.6
Retrieval Exact-match rate on ids and codes Do identifiers survive embedding? above 0.95
Retrieval Filter loss Did permissions or metadata remove the gold passage? near 0
Generation Groundedness, called faithfulness in Ragas Is every claim supported by a passage? 0.95
Generation Citation validity Does each cited passage contain its claim? 0.95
Generation Completeness Was anything the passages supported left out? by eye, then by judge
Generation Refusal recall Of the cases that should refuse, how many did? 0.98
Tool use Selection, argument, execution, sequence accuracy Right tool, right parameters, error handled, right order 0.95 each
Judge TPR and TNR Of real failures, how many caught. Of good answers, how many passed TPR above 0.90
Judge Cohen's kappa Agreement with the expert above chance 0.6 to gate on
System p95 latency Can anyone wait for the answer? your interface budget

Two notes on that table. The gates are the ones we start from and then move once
a system has its own history; they are not standards. And precision does not
appear on the retrieval rows, because at the depths that matter here recall is
the constraint. Precision starts to matter when you are paying per passage in a
long context window.

Retrieval

If the passage never reaches the model, nothing downstream can recover, which is why this layer is measured first and why a low number here makes every other measurement uninterpretable.

def recall_at_k(retrieved_ids, gold_ids, k):
    return len(set(retrieved_ids[:k]) & set(gold_ids)) > 0

def reciprocal_rank(retrieved_ids, gold_ids):
    for i, doc_id in enumerate(retrieved_ids, start=1):
        if doc_id in gold_ids:
            return 1 / i
    return 0.0

Measure recall at your candidate depth and again at your final depth, because the two numbers answer different questions. Recall at fifty tells you what retrieval could deliver if nothing downstream discarded it, and recall at five after reranking tells you what the model actually receives. The gap between them is the reranker's contribution. If recall at fifty is already low, no reranker can help and the work belongs in retrieval. If recall at fifty is high and recall at five is not, the reranker is where the points are.

Recall tells you the passage is somewhere in the list, while MRR tells you whether it will survive context trimming. A system reporting recall at twenty of 0.95 alongside an MRR of 0.2 is retrieving the right thing and then burying it, and the two numbers together diagnose that in a way neither does alone.

Anthropic's contextual retrieval benchmarks, published in September 2024, give you a target to hold your own harness against. They measure the failure rate as one minus recall at twenty. Plain embedding retrieval missed 5.7%, and adding contextual embeddings, keyword search and a reranker took that to 1.9%.

Measure this before you touch generation quality, because the order is not a preference. At a recall of 0.6, four questions in ten are unanswerable before the model is ever invoked, so every prompt change you evaluate after that point is being measured against a ceiling you have not lifted. On Prospex, our own prospect-research engine, a single run reduced 420 collected items to the 6 that answered the question, and that reduction made the downstream answer quality worth measuring at all. Once those numbers are readable, which layer to change is the decision in RAG vs fine-tuning vs agentic search.

Tool use

This layer is consistently under-measured, and it is where agents fail quietly rather than loudly. Four separate questions need separate answers.

Check Failure it catches
Selection Called the wrong tool, or called one when it should not have acted at all
Arguments Right tool, wrong parameters, usually a schema mismatch or a date format
Execution The tool returned an error and the model continued as though it had not
Sequence Right tools in the wrong order, or a required step skipped entirely

Sequence is the one teams omit, and it produces agents reporting work as done when a step in the middle failed silently.

Safety: guardrails and PII

A guardrail and an eval are different mechanisms and teams keep conflating them. A guardrail runs on every request and blocks or rewrites. An eval runs against a fixed set and tells you whether the guardrail works. You do not pick one. You build the guardrail and then measure it, and teams skip the measuring.

Three kinds of case go in the set, and the third is the one teams miss.

Cases the guardrail should catch. A request that would send personal data to a provider, an action outside the policy, an instruction buried in a retrieved document. These are the obvious ones.

Cases it should let through. Over-blocking is a real failure with a real cost, and a guardrail tuned only on the first kind of case will get quieter and quieter until the product stops working. If nobody is measuring the allowed traffic, nobody notices.

Cases where the sensitive data arrives from retrieval rather than from the user. A redaction layer that reads the request and not the retrieved passages is a layer with a hole in it, and the hole only opens once the corpus grows.

PII handling has a second measurement most sets miss. If the boundary encodes on the way out and decodes on the way back, the eval has to check both directions. Redaction that never decodes cleanly produces answers that are safe and useless, and that failure shows up as a quality complaint rather than a safety one, so it gets routed to the wrong team.

Check Question Gate
Block recall Of the requests that should have been stopped, how many were? 1.0, and treat anything less as an incident
Over-block rate Of the requests that were fine, how many were stopped anyway? track it, or the guardrail tightens unnoticed
Redaction recall Was every sensitive field detected before the request left? 1.0
Decode fidelity Did the answer come back complete after decoding? by eye first, then by judge
Verdict coverage Is every decision recorded, including the allows? 1.0

That last row makes the rest possible, because a guardrail that logs only its blocks cannot be measured: the cases you most need are the ones it let through and should not have.

The gates here are not like the others in this guide. Elsewhere we start at 0.90 and move it once a system has history. On safety the target is 1.0 and a miss is an incident, because the cost of one leaked record is not on the same scale as one wrong answer.

Generation

Assertion Question
Groundedness Does every factual claim appear in the retrieved passages?
Citation validity Does each cited passage contain the claim attached to it?
Completeness Did it omit something the passages supported and the question required?
Refusal correctness Given these passages, should it have answered at all?

Notice that helpfulness does not appear, because it is not a measurement, and a judge asked to assess it tends to favour the longer answer.

When should you not build a judge?

You now know what to measure, so next comes what does the measuring, and for most of these checks it should not be a model. A judge is the expensive option, to build and then to run on every case forever, and teams reach for one earlier than the evidence justifies.

Check Use when Cost
Assertion in code The property is mechanical: valid JSON, a citation id that exists, a required field present, a forbidden string absent Minutes to write, free to run
Reference-based check You have a gold answer to compare against, or a gold passage set for computing recall An hour to write, free to run
Model judge The property requires reading comprehension: groundedness, whether a clause governs, whether a refusal was correct Days to build, and a cost per case indefinitely

The mistake we see most often is a team building a judge for a failure they could have fixed that afternoon. If a mode appears eleven times in your traces and a prompt change removes it, you have spent nothing and gained the fix. Build a judge for it instead and you have added a per-case cost that runs for as long as the product does, all to keep measuring something that stopped happening. Judges earn their cost on the modes that survive several attempted fixes.

How do you write a rubric that holds up?

For the modes that survive, you need a judge, and a judge is only as good as the question you give it. Each mode becomes one question the rubric asks. Four things decide whether that rubric works.

Rule Why
1 One question per judge Ask "is this good" and the judge weighs four things at once and blends them. The score moves and you cannot say what moved it
2 Binary, not scored Nobody can say what sits between a three and a four, so two people score the same answer differently and the noise hides real changes
3 Every clause comes from a real failure If you cannot point at the trace behind a clause, it guards against a problem you made up
4 Exclusions written into the prompt Judges prefer long, fluent answers unless you tell them not to

Two of those are worth more than a table row.

Ask one question at a time. "Does every claim appear in the passages?" fails in a way you can act on, because you go and check the claims. "Is this answer good?" gives you a number that dropped and no way to tell whether retrieval, the citation, or a missing refusal caused it.

Binary is harder to agree on than it looks, and that is the point. Two people will argue about where the line sits, and the argument is worth having. A team that cannot say whether an answer passes does not yet know what it wants from the system.

A three-way split is sometimes right, when a partial answer means something real. A five-point scale used as a gate rarely is. Ask two people to score the same answer and one says three and the other says four. A real change has to rise above that noise before anyone can see it, and that takes more labels than most teams will ever collect.

Our trademark platform is the case where a scale earns its place. Its harness scores every draft from 0 to 10 on six axes before an attorney sees it: structure, reasoning depth, citation accuracy, jurisdiction discipline, edge-case handling and tone. The scale works there because its main job is comparison. Production logging scores the base model and the fine-tuned one on the same inputs, so a regression from a model change shows up as a number that moved. The attorney's corrections stay the most valuable signal in the system, because they are the only measure of the gap the automated scoring cannot see.

Here is a rubric that came directly out of the failure note in the table above:

You are checking whether a cited clause governs the question asked.

QUESTION: {question}
PASSAGES: {passages}
ANSWER:   {answer}

For each citation in the ANSWER, decide whether the cited clause is the one
that governs the QUESTION, rather than a related clause on the same topic.

- valid     every citation governs the question asked
- invalid   at least one citation is topically related but not controlling

A correct number quoted from the wrong clause is invalid. Ignore style,
tone, and length entirely.

Return JSON: {"verdict": "...", "offending_citations": ["..."]}

You could not write that rubric without one thing someone noticed first: a right number pulled from the wrong clause is the case that hurts, because a reviewer skimming the output will not catch it. That came from a domain expert's critique. No off-the-shelf metric would have found it.

How do you know your judge is any good?

You measure it against the expert's labels, and the number most teams reach for first is the wrong one.

Suppose your set contains two hundred cases of which a hundred and eighty pass, and your judge agrees with the human labels ninety percent of the time. That sounds like a working judge. Now consider a judge that returns pass for every input without reading anything at all, which also scores ninety percent on that set. Raw agreement cannot distinguish between the two, because on an imbalanced set the majority class carries the score entirely. This is a common way for a team to convince itself a judge works. The number is high, it is easy to compute, and it stays high no matter how badly the judge handles the cases that matter.

Here is that "always pass" judge on the 200-case set:

Judge says fail Judge says pass
Expert failed 0 20
Expert passed 0 180

Raw agreement is 0.90, true positive rate 0.00 and true negative rate 1.00. The judge missed 20 of 20 real failures, and every one of those ships. Lower the share of failures in the set and agreement climbs on its own. That movement is the set getting more imbalanced, not the judge getting better.

Measure the two error rates separately

The true positive rate is recall on failures, meaning of the cases the expert failed, how many the judge caught. The true negative rate is its mirror, meaning of the cases the expert passed, how many the judge also passed. Report them separately and the judge's behaviour becomes legible, because the two failures cost very different amounts.

from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix, cohen_kappa_score

# 1 = expert failed the case (the thing we care about catching)
expert = [1,0,0,1,0,0,0,1,0,0]
judge  = [1,0,0,0,0,0,0,1,0,1]

tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(expert, judge).ravel()
tpr = tp / (tp + fn)     # 0.67  caught 2 of 3 real failures
tnr = tn / (tn + fp)     # 0.86  passed 6 of 7 good answers
print(cohen_kappa_score(expert, judge))   # 0.52
Judge says pass Judge says fail
Expert failed it ships the bug correct
Expert passed it correct noisy CI, wasted engineer time

A low true positive rate is the expensive failure. A judge at 0.9 TPR and 0.7 TNR costs an engineer ten minutes on a false alarm, while the reverse lets a real defect reach a user. When the two trade against each other, we bias toward catching failures.

Kappa is still worth computing as a single summary, because it corrects for chance agreement in a way raw accuracy does not.

κ Reading
below 0.4 The judge is not measuring your rubric
0.4 to 0.6 Usable for direction, not for a CI gate
0.6 to 0.8 Fine for a CI gate with a margin
above 0.8 As good as a second labeller

How many labels, and when to stop

Start at thirty and keep going until you stop learning. For validating a judge specifically, a hundred to a hundred and fifty labels with failures deliberately oversampled is the working range, and the oversampling is not optional. If ten percent of your traffic fails, a uniform sample of a hundred gives you ten negative examples. That puts an interval around your true positive rate wide enough that the number cannot support a release decision.

Below 0.4, check the humans before the judge

Do not begin tuning the judge prompt. Have a second person label thirty cases and compute human-to-human agreement first. If two domain experts only agree at 0.5, no judge will beat that, and what you have found is an underspecified task rather than a broken evaluator. That is a product problem, and no amount of prompt engineering resolves it.

When it fails, split the rubric before touching the model

A judge scoring around 0.45 is usually being asked a compound question, and the fix is to decompose it into separate calls that each ask one thing:

1. Does every factual claim appear in the passages?      grounded | not_grounded
2. Does each citation govern the question asked?         valid | invalid
3. Given the passages, should this have refused?         should_answer | should_refuse

Each of those is close to mechanical, and the results are compounded afterwards in code. This is usually the largest single improvement available, and it requires no prompt tuning beyond the split itself.

Three biases to expect

Judges prefer longer answers, so if a change made your outputs longer, some of the apparent improvement is an artefact; bucket by response length and check that the score holds within each bucket. In pairwise comparison one position, often the first, wins more often than it should, so run both orders and average. And a judge prefers text from its own model family, so if one provider both writes and judges, score a sample of cases with a judge from a different provider and look for disagreement concentrated on your own model's output.

Re-run the alignment check whenever you change the judge model, the rubric, or the task itself. Provider updates move judge behaviour silently, and nothing in your pipeline will announce that it has happened.

On RepliCoach, our own sales-roleplay build, we kept the model out of the number altogether. The model writes the coaching feedback and a versioned rubric sets the score. If the model both writes the feedback and sets the number, a model upgrade shifts every historical comparison, and nobody can tell whether reps improved or the scale moved. Raw model scores also drift between personas and between conversation lengths, so the build normalises them and watches the score distribution for each persona as the sign that the normalisation needs revisiting.

How do you stop overfitting the set?

You will overfit it, because the set is small, you read the failures, and you fix precisely those. Splitting it is the standard defence and it works here for the same reason it works anywhere else.

Split Size Use
Dev 70% Read these. Iterate against them freely
Test 30% Run before a release. Do not read the failures

When the dev split keeps improving and the test split does not move, you are tuning to the cases rather than to the task, and that divergence is invisible without the split. Beyond that, retire cases the system has passed for three months and replace them with fresh production failures, because a set that never changes is measuring a system that stopped changing.

Is the difference real?

Usually not, at the set sizes teams actually have. Eval sets are small and small sets are noisy, and a hundred cases scoring 0.90 carry a confidence interval of about six points either side. A run at 0.91 and a run at 0.89 are therefore the same result as far as the evidence goes, and teams ship on that difference every week.

Comparing the two runs as separate samples makes the problem worse than it has to be. Detecting a move from 0.89 to 0.91 that way needs somewhere near three and a half thousand cases, which no team building a product is going to label.

Both runs went over the same cases, though, so they were never separate samples to begin with. Throw away every case that scored the same in both and count only the ones that changed verdict.

Cases that flipped Reading
5 better, 0 worse Not enough yet
6 better, 0 worse Real
8 better, 1 worse Real
9 better, 3 worse Not enough yet
12 better, 3 worse Real

Six cases moving the same way is enough at the usual five percent threshold, because a change that did nothing would have split them roughly evenly. That is also why nine better against three worse is weaker evidence than six against none, though both leave you six cases ahead. This is a sign test and any statistics library will run it. It is also the second reason to write per-case results instead of an aggregate, since the aggregate is the one number that cannot tell you whether the move was real.

Two limits are worth holding on to. The test tells you the direction of the change is real, and says nothing about whether the size of it is worth shipping. And thirty cases can only produce six flips if the change touched a fifth of them, so a small set still hides small improvements. A two-point move needs at least three hundred cases even when every flip goes the same way, and more when some go the other way, so the better question is why a two-point move is a release decision at all.

We hold our own case studies to the same standard. We put a figure on a case study when it was measured the way this guide describes.

What does this look like in CI?

Deliberately ordinary, which is the point: a harness nobody runs is worth nothing, so the eval suite goes where every other check goes and fails a build the same way.

# .github/workflows/evals.yml
on:
  pull_request:
    paths: ["prompts/**", "retrieval/**", "chunking/**", "tools/**", "evals/**"]

jobs:
  evals:
    steps:
      - run: uv run evals --set evals/dev.jsonl --report out/report.json
      - run: uv run evals-gate out/report.json
        # fails if:
        #   recall@20        < 0.90
        #   groundedness_tpr < 0.90
        #   refusal_recall   < 0.98   (missed refusals are the expensive failure)
        #   p95_latency      > 2500ms

The path filter is the part worth paying attention to, because chunking configuration and retrieval settings change output quality as much as the prompt does. A filter that only fires on prompts/** will let the most expensive changes through ungated.

Three practices matter more than which LLM evaluation framework you choose. Version the eval set in the repository, because it is source: it gets reviewed, and you can bisect it. Write per-case results rather than only an aggregate, because you need to diff two runs and see which five cases flipped, and a score moving from 0.91 to 0.89 tells you nothing about where to look. And pin everything, meaning temperature at zero where the model still accepts the setting, pinned model versions for both the system and the judge, and those versions recorded in the report, since otherwise you cannot attribute a regression to your own change.

Temperature zero plus pinned versions reduces variation and does not remove it, so a case that has to come back the same still needs the repeat-run check in why LLM temperature 0 is not deterministic.

Our DevOps agent runs the same idea inside the product. A validation loop checks every generated template before it reaches AWS, and template errors before deploy fell from around ten percent to four across that loop's introduction. Every validation failure and its revision is recorded, and those records are the input to improving the loop rather than the prompt. On the trademark platform the harness keeps a fine-tuned model changeable at all. Without it nobody would touch a model an attorney has signed off on, and the system would sit frozen at whatever quality it launched with. When the model id itself changes, as it does with the GPT-4o deprecation, the migration runs this same harness on the current model and the replacement before traffic moves.

Where does online evaluation fit?

Online evaluation tells you whether your offline score means anything. Everything up to here is offline evaluation. You wrote the cases, an expert wrote down the right answers, and CI scores one against the other on every pull request. The other half is online evaluation, which watches the shipped system answer questions nobody wrote an answer key for.

Offline Online
Runs against Cases you wrote Live traffic
Right answer Written down first Never written down
Answers Did this change break something we already know about? Did something break that we never thought of?
Cadence Every pull request Continuously
On a failure Blocks the release Opens an investigation

Most teams build the first column and stop there, which is where this guide has left you, and it sits awkwardly against the claim the guide opened with: validation of these systems is only feasible during operation.

Your offline score is a proxy for how the system behaves in front of users, and a proxy needs checking. The check is short to state: when the eval improves and nothing moves in production, your cases do not represent your traffic. That is a finding about the set rather than about the model, and the response is to go back to error analysis with fresh traces instead of tuning the prompt again.

So you need a production signal to compare against, and ratings will not give you one. Almost nobody clicks the thumb, and the ones who do are the angriest and the most delighted. A study of the WildChat and LMSYS conversation logs found this feedback works as a lens on your users rather than as a clean training target (User Feedback in Human-LLM Dialogues, EMNLP 2025).

Behaviour arrives at volume instead: did the user ask the same question again in different words, abandon the session, hit retry, edit the answer before sending it, or escalate to a human? Any one of them is ambiguous, since someone copying an answer might be satisfied or might be collecting evidence for a complaint. Read against a baseline and in aggregate they move when quality moves, which is the only property you need from them.

Those signals also decide which traces you read. You get thousands a week and can read a hundred, so something has to choose which hundred. Take the traces carrying a negative signal, the outliers with unusual retry counts or session lengths, and the ones your judge scored badly. Then keep a slice of plain random traces in every batch, because the random slice is the only part that can find a failure mode your current signals do not describe. Ten to twenty traces a week keeps the reading going between rounds, plus a hundred fresh ones each time you run full error analysis.

On the DevOps agent this was easier than it usually is. The signal was mechanical: the validation loop checks each generated template before deploy and records every failure with the request that produced it, so the system keeps its own record of what the model gets wrong without anyone deciding a failure was one. Most products do not get that, so pick two behavioural signals and instrument them before you need them. Treat the gap between those and your eval score as the thing you are managing.

The loop this all becomes

Error analysis is not a phase you complete and move past. Production traces produce new failure notes, those notes cluster into modes, the modes become cases, the cases gate deployments, and the deployments produce more traces. Run it once and the set describes the failures you had when you built it. Keep the loop going and new failures enter the set as production finds them.

What will evals not tell you?

Question Why the harness cannot answer it
Is the product good? It measures a task against labels you wrote. Label the wrong task and you will pass confidently while users leave
Is it safe against a motivated attacker? The adversarial bucket contains the attacks you thought of. Prompt injection needs ongoing red-teaming
Do public numbers transfer? Contamination makes benchmark results weak evidence about your corpus
How does it behave under load? p95 with a single user says nothing about p95 under concurrency

A correct transcript can still be a failed call, so a voice product needs checks on the audio beside this text harness. Turn-taking, interruptions, intelligibility, and silence are scored on their own, and voice AI evals keeps those verdicts off the text score. Treat that set as its own cases rather than another row in the table above.

A fan-out needs the same kind of separate check. Score the merged result against the expected state, which when to fan out to many agents sets out, rather than the path each worker happened to take.

How do we run this, in order?

  1. Collect a hundred real traces, from production if you have it and from whoever asked for the feature if you do not.
  2. Open code them, writing a free-form note on each failure with no categories.
  3. Axial code, clustering into five to ten modes, then count them.
  4. Stop at saturation, meaning twenty fresh traces produce no new category.
  5. Name a principal domain expert, one person, making binary judgements with written critiques.
  6. Build the case set from the taxonomy, labelling the passage rather than the document.
  7. Fix what a prompt change can fix, and build no judge for it.
  8. Write assertions and reference checks for everything mechanical.
  9. Build a judge only for the modes that persist, one question each, binary, with the exclusions in the prompt.
  10. Validate it against a hundred labels with failures oversampled, reporting TPR and TNR. Below κ 0.4, check whether two people agree before you split the rubric.
  11. Split dev and test seventy-thirty.
  12. Compare runs by counting flipped cases, not by reading the aggregate.
  13. Gate CI on the wide path filter, chunking and retrieval included.
  14. Instrument two behavioural signals in the product, and check the eval moves with them.
  15. Feed every production failure back into the set.

Steps one through four take a day, and they decide whether everything after them is worth building. The first hour of it is thirty real queries copied into evals/dev.jsonl, with the person who knows the domain marking the paragraph that answers each one.

Common questions

How do I build evals for an LLM app?

Start from real traces and write a note on each failure before you name a category. Cluster the notes and have one expert mark pass or fail, with a critique, then build cases for those modes. Use code for anything mechanical, and let a model judge block a release only after it agrees with the expert.

What is an LLM eval?

An eval is a test whose pass or fail takes a judgement rather than an equality check. Grounded, correctly cited, and correctly refused are judgements, and two careful readers can disagree until the line is written down. The harness still lives in the repository, runs in continuous integration, and leaves a history you can bisect when a score moves.

Why can't I write the rubric first?

You learn the criteria by reading outputs, and that reading makes them specific. A rubric written before launch tends to ask for an answer that is accurate and helpful, which does not tell you what to change. An hour with real traces turns that into a concrete question, such as whether the response cited the clause that governs.

How many traces should I read?

Review at least a hundred traces, and stop when twenty fresh ones add no new failure category. Stopping earlier describes the sample you happened to open, and the modes you missed are the ones that show up later in production. Count after the categories exist, since a pile of retrieval misses will not move if the quarter goes to the prompt.

When should I not use an LLM as a judge?

Use code when the check is mechanical, such as valid structure, a citation that exists, or a forbidden string. Use a reference check when you already have a gold answer or a gold set of passages. A model judge takes days to build and a cost on every later case, so reserve it for modes that survive several fixes.

What is an LLM evaluation framework?

An LLM evaluation framework is the harness that runs a fixed set of cases against your system and scores each one, with code checks where the property is mechanical and a model judge only where it agrees with your expert. The tool you pick matters less than three practices: the case set versioned in the repository, per-case results, and pinned model versions recorded in every report.

How do I know the judge is good enough to gate a release?

Have the expert label about a hundred cases, with failures oversampled, and then see how many of those failures the judge caught. Also record how many good answers it passed, because raw agreement looks strong when most cases pass. Below a kappa of 0.4, check whether two people agree before you blame the judge, and split the question if they do not.

Sources and further reading

  • Hamel Husain, Creating a LLM-as-a-Judge That Drives Business Results and the LLM Evals FAQ.
  • Shankar et al., Who Validates the Validators?, UIST 2024, on criteria drift.
  • Barnett et al., Seven Failure Points When Engineering a RAG System, IEEE/ACM CAIN 2024.
  • Eugene Yan, Task-Specific LLM Evals that Do and Don't Work.
  • User Feedback in Human-LLM Dialogues, EMNLP 2025, on what implicit signals can and cannot carry.
  • Jason Liu, RAG series.
  • Anthropic, Contextual Retrieval.
  • Chroma, Generative Benchmarking, Evaluating Chunking Strategies and Context Rot.
  • Ragas metrics for standard definitions.
  • Ours: why RAG systems fail in production, why AI agents report unfinished work as done, when to fan out to many agents, why LLM temperature 0 is not deterministic, and GPT-4o deprecation: dates, replacement and how to migrate.
  • Prompt and evaluation engineers. The engagement that turns a quality feeling into a suite that can block a merge.

title: BSI C5:2026, TR-03185 & DiGA (TR-03161): Sicherheitsupdates ohne Rezertifizierung & Krypto-Inventar (CBOM) in CI/CD automatisieren
description:
Mit der Veröffentlichung des neuen BSI C5:2026 (Cloud Computing Compliance Criteria Catalogue), der Richtlinie BSI TR-03185 (Sicherer Software-Lebenszyklus), den verschärften Vorgaben für digitale Gesundheitsanwendungen (BSI TR-03161 / § 393 SGB V) sowie den seit September 2026 greifenden Meldepflichten des EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) stehen Softwarehersteller, SaaS-/Cloud-Anbieter und MedTech-Unternehmen vor einer doppelten Herausforderung:

  1. Schnelle Sicherheits- und Krypto-Updates ohne Rezertifizierungsverlust (BSI TR-03185): Wie lassen sich kritische CVE-Patches oder aktualisierte Krypto-Bibliotheken (z. B. OpenSSL 3.5+ mit hybrider Post-Quanten-Kryptographie nach BSI TR-02102-1) kurzfristig in Produktion bringen, ohne dass eine bestehende BSI-, DiGA- (BfArM) oder C5-Zertifizierung erlischt?
  2. Lückenlose Kryptographie- (CBOM) und SBOM-Nachweise im BSI C5:2026 (Domänen CRY, DEV & OPS): Wirtschaftsprüfer (IDW PS 951 / ISAE 3000 Typ 2) und Aufsichtsbehörden akzeptieren keine manuellen Ad-hoc-Erklärungen mehr. Gefordert sind eine risikobasierte 3-Klassen Patch-Klassifizierungsmatrix, eine maschinenlesbare Software Bill of Materials (CycloneDX SBOM nach BSI TR-03183-2) sowie ein aktuelles Krypto-Inventar (CBOM) zum BSI-Auslaufszenario 2031/2035.

In diesem technischen Leitfaden zeigen wir, wie Sie die Anforderungen von BSI C5:2026, BSI TR-03185 und DiGA TR-03161 in einem automatisierten CI/CD-Workflow zusammenführen.

🛡️ 1. Die 3-Klassen Update- & Patch-Matrix nach BSI TR-03185

Die Technische Richtlinie BSI TR-03185 erlaubt es Herstellern, Sicherheitsupdates ohne langwierige Neu- oder Rezertifizierung auszurollen, sofern jedes Release vor der Freigabe nach einer dokumentierten Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) in eine von drei Änderungsklassen eingestuft wird:

Änderungsklasse (BSI TR-03185) Technische Abgrenzung & Beispiele Rezertifizierung / BfArM-Anzeige nötig? Pflicht-Artefakte im CI/CD Release-Gate (Evidenz-Bundle)
Klasse A: Reiner Security- & Krypto-Patch Schließen von CVEs in Abhängigkeiten, Härtung von TLS-/SSH-Ciphern (TR-02102), Bugfixes ohne Änderung der Sicherheitsarchitektur oder externer APIs. Nein (Hersteller-Selbsterklärung nach BSI TR-03185-2) Erfolgreicher SAST/SCA-Lauf + CycloneDX SBOM (BSI TR-03183-2) + Host/Container-CBOM + unterzeichnetes Release-Freigabeprotokoll
Klasse B: Architekturrelevante Minor-Änderung Anpassung interner Sicherheitsmodule, Erweiterung nicht-kritischer Endpunkte oder Wechsel von Sub-Komponenten. Delta-Prüfung / Dokumentations-Update Aktualisiertes Threat Model (STRIDE) + Regressionstest-Protokoll + SBOM-Diff + PSO Sign-Off
Klasse C: Major Functional / Security Change Neue Authentifizierungsverfahren, veränderte Mandantentrennung, neue externe Angriffsflächen oder Verarbeitung neuer Art.-9-DSGVO-Datenkategorien. Ja (Vollständige Rezertifizierung / wesentliche DiGA-Änderungsanzeige) Vollständiges Sicherheitsgutachten + Penetrationstest + aktualisiertes C5-/TR-03161-Prüfdossier

👉 Vollständige Fachpublikation lesen:

  • BSI C5:2026 Cloud-Compliance, IT-Grundschutz & Nationale PQC-Leitlinie (CRY & CBOM)
  • BSI TR-03185: Software-Updates ohne Rezertifizierung & CRA-Compliance

⚙️ 2. CI/CD-Automatisierung: CycloneDX SBOM (TR-03183-2) & Krypto-Gate (TR-02102) in GitHub Actions

Für die C5:2026-Kriterien DEV-02 bis DEV-05 sowie CRY-01 / CRY-02 lässt sich die Erzeugung des Release-Evidence-Bundles vollständig in GitHub Actions oder GitLab CI automatisieren. Dabei wird unser quelloffener Zero-Dependency CLI-Scanner bsi-tr02102-pqc-audit-cli direkt als Krypto-Prüfschritt eingebunden:

name: BSI TR-03185 & C5:2026 Release-Gate (SBOM + CBOM Evidence)

on:
  release:
    types: [published]
  workflow_dispatch:

jobs:
  bsi-compliance-evidence:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Checkout Repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: 1. CycloneDX SBOM nach BSI TR-03183-2 generieren
        run: |
          pipx run cyclonedx-py environment -o sbom-tr03183-2.cdx.json

      - name: 2. Krypto-Policy & Zertifikate nach BSI TR-02102-1 bis -4 prüfen (CBOM)
        run: |
          curl -sSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/KenanErorr404/bsi-tr02102-pqc-audit-cli/main/bsi_pqc_check.py | python3 - \
            --generate-cbom-csv \
            --json-out cbom-tr02102-findings.json

      - name: 3. Revisionssicheres Audit-Artefakt für WP / C5 / BfArM archivieren
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: bsi-tr03185-c5-release-evidence
          path: |
            sbom-tr03183-2.cdx.json
            cbom-tr02102-findings.json
            host-cbom-preview.csv
            bsi-pqc-audit-report.html

🏥 3. Besonderheiten für Cloud-Anbieter (§ 393 SGB V) & DiGA-Hersteller (BSI TR-03161)

Im Gesundheitswesen greifen zwei Regelwerke unmittelbar ineinander:

  • Cloud-Infrastruktur (§ 393 SGB V): Jede Cloud-Plattform, auf der Sozial- oder Gesundheitsdaten verarbeitet werden, benötigt ein aktuelles BSI C5 Typ-2-Testat. In der Domäne CRY prüfen Auditoren ab 2026 insbesondere, ob ein dokumentierter Migrationsplan für das BSI-Auslaufszenario 2031 (Post-Quanten-Kryptographie) vorliegt, da Gesundheitsdaten (Art. 9 DSGVO) einen Schutzbedarf von weit über 10 Jahren aufweisen.
  • Anwendungsebene (BSI TR-03161-1/-2/-3 & BfArM Fast-Track): DiGA-Hersteller müssen bei jedem Update dokumentieren, ob es sich um eine anzeigepflichtige wesentliche Veränderung oder um ein privilegiertes Sicherheitsupdate der Klasse A nach BSI TR-03185 handelt.

💡 Tipp: Prüfen Sie Ihren aktuellen Krypto- und NIS-2-Compliance-Status in 60 Sekunden mit unserem kostenlosen, clientseitigen BSI PQC & NIS-2 Risiko- und Bußgeld-Rechner (pqc-nis2-rechner.html).

📥 4. Kostenlose €0+ CSV-Audit-Leseprobe & Schlüsselfertige .xlsx Enterprise-Toolkits

Sparen Sie Ihrem Entwicklungs-, Regulatory-Affairs- und ISMS-Team Wochen an manueller Vorlagenerstellung:

  1. 🆓 Kostenlose CSV-Audit-Leseprobe & Schnellstart-Matrix herunterladen (€0+ Community Edition)
    • Enthält BSI-Audit-Matrix-Leseprobe.csv (6 repräsentative Prüfpunkte aus BSI TR-03185 / DiGA TR-03161 sowie BSI TR-02102 CBOM) + README-Upgrade-auf-Enterprise-XLSX.md inklusive 20 % Upgrade-Rabattcode (BSI2026PRO).
  2. 🛡️ BSI TR-03185 & DiGA TR-03161 Audit-Readiness-Pack sichern (39,20 € statt 49,00 € mit Code BSI2026PRO)
    • 5 schlüsselfertige Enterprise-Assets im Sofort-Download (.zip):
      • BSI-TR-03185-und-DiGA-TR03161-Audit-Workbook.xlsx (3-Tab Excel-Workbook mit Executive Readiness Scoring Dashboard, vollständiger 3-Klassen Update- & Patch-Klassifizierungsmatrix Klasse A/B/C sowie BfArM DiGA TR-03161 & TR-03183 SBOM Mapping)
      • TR-03185-Prozess-Audit-Matrix.csv (Maschinenlesbarer Prüfkatalog für QMS/ISMS)
      • SOP-Sicherer-Release-Prozess-TR03185.md (Komplett ausformulierte Standard Operating Procedure für Entwicklungsteams)
      • Checkliste-Update-Ohne-Rezertifizierung.html (Druckbares & digital ausfüllbares Release-Freigabeprotokoll für BfArM, BSI und C5-Prüfer)
      • ci-cd/tr03185-release-gate.yml (Produktionsfertiger GitHub Actions Workflow für CycloneDX SBOM & Evidence-Bundling)
  3. 🔐 BSI TR-02102-1 PQC & CBOM Migrations-Toolkit (9 Dateien inkl. 45-Zeilen CBOM .xlsx & Server-Configs – 39,20 € mit Code BSI2026PRO)

title: Vercel Connect now supports Linq
description:
Vercel Connect now includes a managed connector for Linq, so your apps and agents can send and receive messages over iMessage, RCS, and SMS.

As a Vercel Managed Connector, Vercel can create a Linq account and phone number for you, or link an existing account. You never manage credentials yourself.

Create a connector from the dashboard or Vercel CLI:

Give your eve agent a phone number

The connector powers the new Linq channel in eve.

Run eve add channel/linq, choose Vercel Connect, and eve wires up the connector, phone numbers, and webhook for you:

The channel marks accepted messages as read and continues the same eve session for every message in a Linq conversation. Out of the box, the channel supports read receipts, typing indicators, and mid-conversation steering for a more natural messaging experience.

Use the connector in any project

Call getToken with your connector, and the @vercel/connect SDK exchanges your Vercel deployment's OIDC identity for a short-lived Linq token.

Pass it as the bearer token on any Linq Partner API request:

title: Building an MBTI Cognitive Functions Test in JavaScript: Data Model and Scoring
description:
An mbti cognitive functions test is one of those projects that looks like a form full of radio buttons until you sit down to write the scoring. This post builds the data layer for one in plain JavaScript: a model of the eight functions, rule-based derivation of each type's four-function stack, a scorer that ranks all sixteen types, tie handling, and unit tests. One caveat shapes everything below: a self-report measures how strongly you agree with statements written from a theory. It does not observe your functions. With that settled, an mbti cognitive functions test is a genuinely fun engineering problem.

What an MBTI cognitive functions test actually measures

Start with vocabulary. Jung described sensing, intuition, thinking and feeling, and as MBF on type dynamics puts it, "Jung called the processes functions." Attach an attitude — extraverted or introverted — and you get eight functions: Se, Si, Ne, Ni, Te, Ti, Fe and Fi. Type dynamics arranges four per type as Dominant, Auxiliary, Tertiary and Inferior. The fourth letter names the process you extravert: J extraverts judging (T or F), P extraverts perceiving (S or N). Extraverts use the dominant in the outer world; introverts show the auxiliary outwardly. Every mbti cognitive functions test is downstream of those rules.

Jung also wrote that "all the basic psychological functions seldom or never have the same strength or grade of development in one and the same individual" — as a rule, one predominates (Jung, Psychological Types, Ch. X). Hence stack-position scoring in this mbti cognitive functions test. But be precise about what any mbti functions test does: it asks how much you recognize yourself in descriptions of Ni or Se. A cognitive functions mbti test scores agreement with a taxonomy, not cognition itself, and an mbti cognitive functions test that claims more in its copy is overclaiming.

Data model for an mbti cognitive functions test

Three pieces carry the whole mbti cognitive functions test: the function list, statements that each target one function, and a scorer producing comparable numbers. Here is the skeleton I would start any jungian cognitive functions test with. Every later piece of the mbti cognitive functions test reads from it:

// Eight Jungian functions: a process (S, N, T, F) plus an attitude (e or i)
const FUNCTIONS = ['Se', 'Si', 'Ne', 'Ni', 'Te', 'Ti', 'Fe', 'Fi'];

// Each item measures one function on a 1-5 scale; 4 items per function, 32 total
const items = [
  { id: 1, fn: 'Ni', text: 'I often know where something is heading before I can explain why.' },
  { id: 2, fn: 'Se', text: 'I notice small changes in a room as soon as I walk in.' },
  // ...
];

function scoreFunctions(answers) {            // answers: { [itemId]: 1..5 }
  const totals = Object.fromEntries(FUNCTIONS.map(f => [f, 0]));
  const counts = Object.fromEntries(FUNCTIONS.map(f => [f, 0]));
  for (const item of items) {
    const a = answers[item.id];
    if (a == null) continue;                  // skipped items don't count
    totals[item.fn] += a - 3;                 // center the scale: -2..+2
    counts[item.fn] += 1;
  }
  return Object.fromEntries(FUNCTIONS.map(f =>
    [f, counts[f] ? totals[f] / (2 * counts[f]) : null]));  // -1..+1, or null
}

Answers are centered on 3, so disagreement pushes a function negative, and dividing by twice the number of answered items clamps each score into -1..+1. Skipped items are ignored, and a function with no answered items returns null rather than a polite zero. On a jungian functions test, an unanswered item is missing data, not neutrality. Four statements per function is demo-sized; a production mbti cognitive functions test would use more items without changing this shape. Since the mbti cognitive functions test scores agreement, keep statement wording behavioral ("I notice…") rather than identity claims.

Deriving MBTI function stacks from a four-letter code

No lookup table needed: the mbti function stack falls straight out of the type-dynamics rules. J means you extravert your judging process, P your perceiving one. An extravert leads with that extraverted process; an introvert leads with the other pair turned inward and shows the auxiliary to the world. The tertiary is the opposite process of the auxiliary, though its attitude is debated — the Foundation's answer is basically "You decide from your own experience!" — and the inferior is the dominant's opposite in every way. That is all an mbti cognitive functions test needs to build every stack on the fly.


const OPP = { S: 'N', N: 'S', T: 'F', F: 'T' };
const flip = a => (a === 'e' ? 'i' : 'e');

function stackFromCode(code) {                // e.g. 'INFJ'
  const [ei, sn, tf, jp] = code.toUpperCase().split('');
  // The last letter names the process you extravert: J -> T/F, P -> S/N
  const outward = jp === 'J' ? tf : sn;
  const inward = jp === 'J' ? sn : tf;
  const dom = ei === 'E' ? outward + 'e' : inward + 'i';
  const aux = ei === 'E' ? inward + 'i' : outward + 'e';
  const ter = OPP[aux[0]] + dom[1];           // one convention; the tertiary's attitude is debated
  const inf = OPP[dom[0]] + flip(dom[1]);     // opposite of the dominant in every way
  return [dom, aux, ter, inf];
}
// stackFromCode('INFJ') -> ['Ni', 'Fe', 'Ti', 'Se']
// stackFromCode('ENFP') -> ['Ne', 'Fi', 'Te', 'Si']

One comment in that code is doing honest work: the tertiary's attitude is a convention here, not scripture. The rules also have a satisfying symmetry — every function is dominant for exactly two types. Ni leads INFJ and INTJ, Se leads ESTP and ESFP, Fi leads ISFP and INFP, and so on. That symmetry is trivial to assert in a unit test, and an mbti cognitive functions test built on these rules gets it for free. Because mbti function stacks are derived rather than stored, the mbti cognitive functions test never carries a stale table someone could mistype.

Scoring a Myers Briggs cognitive functions test

Now the scoring step of the mbti cognitive functions test: compare the answer profile against every type's stack, with the dominant counting most and the inferior least. I use weights 4/3/2/1 and a 0.25 tie band — both are design choices for this mbti cognitive functions test, not a standard, so print them next to the results.

const WEIGHTS = [4, 3, 2, 1];                 // dominant .. inferior (a design choice)
const TYPES = ['ISTJ', 'ISFJ', 'INFJ', 'INTJ', 'ISTP', 'ISFP', 'INFP', 'INTP',
               'ESTP', 'ESFP', 'ENFP', 'ENTP', 'ESTJ', 'ESFJ', 'ENFJ', 'ENTJ'];

function rankTypes(fnScores, tieBand = 0.25) {
  const ranked = TYPES.map(code => ({
    code,
    fit: stackFromCode(code).reduce((s, fn, i) => s + WEIGHTS[i] * (fnScores[fn] ?? 0), 0),
  })).sort((a, b) => b.fit - a.fit);
  const top = ranked.filter(t => ranked[0].fit - t.fit <= tieBand);
  return { ranked, top };                     // top.length > 1 means "show the tie"
}

A worked example with illustrative scores: Ni +0.75, Fe +0.50, Ne +0.50, Ti +0.25, Se -0.50, everything else 0. INFJ computes as 4(0.75) + 3(0.50) + 2(0.25) + 1(-0.50) = 4.5. Here are the top five, which is the table an mbti cognitive functions test should show:

Type Stack Fit
INFJ Ni Fe Ti Se 4.5
ENTP Ne Ti Fe Si 3.75
ENFJ Fe Ni Se Ti 3.5
ESFJ Fe Si Ne Ti 3.25
INTP Ti Ne Si Fe 3.0

This table is where an mbti cognitive functions test earns or loses trust, and it surprised me the first time I ran it. ENTP comes second, ahead of ENFJ, even though ENTP shares neither of INFJ's lead functions. It collects points from Ne in first place and Fe in third, and nothing in its stack is negative. ENFJ shares Ni and Fe with INFJ in reverse order, but it pays for Se sitting in third place. That is the mbti cognitive functions test's weighted sum doing exactly what it was told, and a reminder that the weights are an opinion. The 0.75 gap to second place sits outside the tie band, so top holds one type here. If you're building a function test MBTI fans will actually trust, show this arithmetic instead of only the winner. For a contrasting philosophy, compare a Jung-inspired test that openly skips function stacks — its page states it does not measure the eight cognitive functions and that no self-report preference quiz can. That's a refreshing thing to read on a quiz page.

Ties and unit tests for your mbti cognitive functions test

With only four items per function, near-ties are common, so ties get first-class handling in any mbti cognitive functions test and the rules get tests. Three cover what breaks silently:

import { test, expect } from 'vitest';

test('INFJ stack follows the type-dynamics rules', () => {
  expect(stackFromCode('INFJ')).toEqual(['Ni', 'Fe', 'Ti', 'Se']);
});

test('each function is dominant for exactly two types', () => {
  const doms = TYPES.map(t => stackFromCode(t)[0]);
  for (const fn of FUNCTIONS) expect(doms.filter(d => d === fn)).toHaveLength(2);
});

test('all-neutral answers produce a full tie, not a type', () => {
  const answers = Object.fromEntries(items.map(i => [i.id, 3]));
  expect(rankTypes(scoreFunctions(answers)).top).toHaveLength(16);
});

The first locks the mbti cognitive functions test to a known stack. The second asserts that symmetry from earlier: each function is dominant for exactly two of the sixteen types. The third is my favorite — if every answer is neutral, all sixteen types tie and top comes back with sixteen entries, forcing the UI to show a tie instead of inventing a winner. An mbti cognitive functions test that returns a confident type from all-neutral input is broken somewhere in its centering, and this catches it loudly.

What I would not ship in an mbti cognitive functions test

Three rules I hold before shipping any mbti cognitive functions test:

  • No "accuracy %". Nothing here was validated against anything, so a percentage would be theater. Show the fit numbers and the tie band instead.
  • No unstated weights. Fixed weights like 4/3/2/1 are fine; shipping them silently turns the mbti cognitive functions test into a black box. Print them.
  • Show ties. If top.length > 1, render every tied type. Forcing one letter out of a quarter-point difference is where an mbti cognitive functions test starts lying.

I took a slower pass at the preference-pair side of this in How to build a personality test in JavaScript, which covers neutral answers and the same test-first habits. The mbti cognitive functions test in this post is the layer underneath. If there is a lesson, it is that an honest mbti cognitive functions test is careful plumbing plus a refusal to overclaim.

Editor's note from Nico: I help out with PersonalityTest, so I'm biased toward quizzes that admit their limits. This is a scoring exercise, not a claim that a self-report can see your functions.

To see that philosophy running, try the free MBTI-style test: 32 original statements, scored entirely in the browser, answers never uploaded, no account or email gate — and when a pair lands near the middle it says "balanced" and shows neighboring codes instead of forcing a letter. It is the same honesty the mbti cognitive functions test above is aiming for.

PersonalityTest is unofficial and not affiliated with The Myers-Briggs Company or the Myers & Briggs Foundation. The code here was written for this article.
