title: My webhook catcher taught me that 100 events is a budget you spend fast
description:
When I built the webhook catcher, I assumed integrations were calm, single POSTs. Reality is messier. I was testing a GitHub webhook flow last week—every push triggers a delivery, and when my local parser was slow, GitHub retried with exponential backoff. Within an hour I'd burned through the 100-event in-memory cap. The hook stopped accepting new events silently, and I spent twenty minutes wondering why my test wasn't progressing.

That was the real lesson: ephemeral storage isn't just about expiry, it's about throughput. If you're testing retry logic or bursty integrations, you need to poll aggressively or the buffer fills before you even look. I added a purge-and-reset routine to my test harness after that incident.

The 24-hour TTL is generous for debugging, but the 100-event ceiling means you can't "set it and forget it" for a full day. You have to consume as you go. I ended up packaging the receiver as https://x402.freeq.one/tools/webhook_catch.html so other agents can spin up a disposable test hook without deploying a public server, but I always pair it with a tight polling loop now.

title: Why You Shouldn't Let AI Agents Run Naked Bash: Building an Unprivileged Sandbox in Rust
description:
What If Your AI Coding Agent Deletes Your Project? Building a Zero-Trust Sandbox with Rust

AI coding agents are becoming an important part of modern software development.

Tools like Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Aider, OpenHands, Cursor, and other autonomous coding agents can execute terminal commands, modify source files, install dependencies, and run scripts.

But there is one important question:

What happens when an AI agent executes a dangerous command on your actual development machine?

Imagine an agent accidentally:

  • Deletes important project files.
  • Overwrites your .env configuration.
  • Reads SSH keys or cloud credentials.
  • Modifies Git history.
  • Executes an untrusted installation script.
  • Makes unexpected outbound network connections.

A simple confirmation prompt isn't always enough.

I started building ShadowCLI to explore a different approach: putting a zero-trust security boundary between AI coding agents and the developer's machine.

Introducing ShadowCLI

GitHub: https://github.com/6t9xstar/shadowcli

ShadowCLI is an open-source, Rust-based execution sandbox for AI coding agents.

Instead of allowing commands to modify your actual project immediately, ShadowCLI executes them inside an isolated Linux environment.

Changes are captured in a temporary copy-on-write layer. Developers can inspect the resulting differences, review modifications, approve changes, or discard the session.

The goal is simple:

Let AI agents work, but keep developers in control of what reaches their actual projects.

How Does It Work?

ShadowCLI uses multiple Linux security mechanisms to isolate command execution.

Its architecture combines:

  1. Linux User Namespaces – Isolate user and group identities.
  2. Mount Namespaces – Provide a private filesystem view.
  3. PID Namespaces – Isolate processes.
  4. Network Namespaces – Restrict outbound network access by default.
  5. Landlock LSM – Enforce filesystem access restrictions.
  6. Seccomp BPF – Block selected high-risk system calls.
  7. OverlayFS / CopyFS – Capture filesystem modifications without directly changing the host project during execution.

These layers work together to create a defense-in-depth execution environment.

Getting Started

ShadowCLI is designed for Linux systems with the required kernel and sandbox capabilities.

1. Clone the repository 

git clone https://github.com/6t9xstar/shadowcli.git

cd shadowcli

2. Build the project

You need Rust 1.80 or later.

cargo build --release

3. Install the binary 

sudo cp target/release/shadow /usr/local/bin/

4. Check system compatibility 

shadow doctor

This checks important system capabilities, including kernel compatibility, user namespaces, Landlock, Seccomp, and filesystem support.

5. Run a command inside the sandbox 

shadow run -- npm test

By default, outbound network access is blocked.

If a task requires network access, you can explicitly allow it:

shadow run --allow-network -- cargo build

You can also configure execution timeouts:

shadow run --timeout 30 -- ./agent-script.sh

Inspect Changes Before Applying Them

One of the most important parts of ShadowCLI is its review workflow.

After an agent executes commands, inspect the captured changes:

shadow diff

View a summary:

shadow diff --stat

Review modifications interactively:

shadow review

Apply approved changes:

shadow apply --all --yes

If you need to undo the most recent apply operation:

shadow apply --rollback

Or discard unapplied sandbox changes:

shadow discard

This creates a workflow where executing commands and accepting their modifications are separate decisions.

Who Can Use ShadowCLI?

ShadowCLI is designed as a general execution boundary for tools that execute terminal commands.

Potential integration targets include:

  • Claude Code
  • OpenAI Codex
  • Aider
  • OpenHands
  • Gemini CLI
  • OpenCode
  • Cline
  • Roo Code
  • Custom AI coding agents

For example, you can wrap a terminal-based agent command:

shadow run -- aider

You can also integrate sandboxed command execution into your own Python-based agent:

import subprocess

result = subprocess.run(
    [
        "shadow",
        "run",
        "--project",
        ".",
        "--allow-network",
        "--",
        "npm",
        "test"
    ],
    capture_output=True,
    text=True
)

print(result.stdout)
print(result.stderr)

Actual compatibility depends on how an agent interacts with the filesystem and launches subprocesses.

Security Is More Than a Confirmation Prompt

I believe AI-assisted development needs more than a simple permission dialog.

A secure execution workflow should consider:

  • Filesystem isolation.
  • Credential protection.
  • Network restrictions.
  • Process isolation.
  • System call restrictions.
  • Change inspection.
  • Explicit approval.
  • Recovery and rollback.

ShadowCLI brings these ideas together using native Linux security technologies and Rust.

It is not a replacement for security auditing, backups, or a hardened virtual machine. Its protection also depends on the host kernel, filesystem, configuration, and the correctness of its isolation mechanisms.

Open Source and Contributions

ShadowCLI is released under the Apache-2.0 license.

I'm continuing development and would appreciate feedback from developers working with:

  • Rust and Linux systems programming.
  • AI coding agents.
  • Linux kernel security.
  • Sandboxing and container isolation.
  • DevSecOps and application security.

If you're interested in this area, explore the repository, review the implementation, report issues, or contribute improvements.

GitHub Repository: https://github.com/6t9xstar/shadowcli

I'd particularly like to hear your thoughts:

Would you trust an AI coding agent with unrestricted access to your development machine, or would you prefer every modification to go through an isolated execution and review process?

Let's discuss.

title: EZ-Ar-VC: Robust Arabic Voice Anonymization with Generalization across Dialects and Code-Switching
description:
arXiv:2611.01268v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Voice conversion (VC) models can be used to anonymize speech data while preserving naturalness. Existing models, however, are mainly optimized for English and other high-resource languages, and they fail to generalize well to Arabic due to its distinct phonology. In this work, we comprehensively evaluate existing zero-shot VC systems for Arabic speech, identifying limitations in pronunciation preservation. We then train an Arabic-centric model based on EZ-VC on diverse Arabic speech, and demonstrate strong performance in intelligibility, naturalness, and pronunciation preservation, while maintaining high speaker dissimilarity. Through subjective evaluation, we further demonstrate its robustness to code-switching and cross-dialectal conversion, as well as its generalization to Arabic dialects with limited representation in the training data. Our findings highlight the limitations of zero-shot VC and the importance of target-language adaptation for robust voice anonymization.

title: Audit at the Precision You Deploy: Quantization Reshapes a Subliminally Learned Preference
description:
arXiv:2611.00665v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Subliminal learning allows AI models to inherit hidden preferences from seemingly unrelated training data, such as number sequences. Safety audits may evaluate models at standard 16-bit precision, while deployments may use compressed, quantized weights. We ask whether quantization changes the expression of a subliminal preference and what drives any resulting change. To investigate, we implant a "favourite animal: panda" preference into Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. We define its net strength as the difference in mean panda-answer probability between subliminal models and neutrally trained controls under the same quantization setting. Applying this metric across different compression levels reveals a stark contrast. While behaviour remains stable at 8 bits, 4-bit quantization triggers severe, opposing shifts depending on the quantizer. Half-Quadratic Quantization (HQQ) amplifies the preference, raising the subliminally trained model's panda probability from roughly 55% at 16 bits to 64% at 4 bits, while the controls stay near 17%. This raises the trait's net strength ~1.3 times its 16-bit value. In contrast, NormalFloat (NF4) at 4-bit suppresses it, shrinking the net strength to just ~0.3 times its 16-bit value, despite producing rounding errors of the same size to within 4%. We examine the structure of the rounding errors and find that their arrangement drives the divergence. Randomly shuffling HQQ's errors within each quantization group, without changing their magnitude, shifts the trait's net strength between 0.2 and 1.6 times its 16-bit value. Despite these opposing shifts, the underlying fine-tuning signal remains largely intact. Because a model's internal state and outward behaviour diverge so unpredictably under compression, a 16-bit audit cannot reliably bound real-world risks. Safety evaluations must test the exact quantized weights intended for deployment.

title: 9 Codex Config Keys to Set Before Your Coding Agent's First Long Task
description:
• Book: Event-Driven Architecture Pocket Guide
  • Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

You hand Codex a two-hour refactor and go to lunch. You come back to a terminal that has been sitting on an approval prompt since minute four, because the agent wanted to run npm install and the sandbox has no network.

Nothing broke. Codex did exactly what its defaults say. For a long unattended run, a few of those defaults work against you, and one of them hands the agent's shell more of your environment than you'd expect.

Here are nine settings for a long Codex run, eight of them keys in ~/.codex/config.toml and one a file next to it, each checked against OpenAI's config reference and advanced config guide as of November 4, 2026. For each one: what the default does to a long run, and a value to paste. One of them is a correction. If you copied a [profiles.*] table from an older blog post, it stopped working in Codex 0.134.0.

1. Pin the model and the effort

Keys: model, model_reasoning_effort

The reference lists effort values "such as low, medium, high, xhigh, max, or ultra", and says "available levels depend on the model and client." The docs list no default for either key. Leave them unset and the run gets whatever the client picks today.

model = "gpt-6.1-sol"
model_reasoning_effort = "high"

The docs' own profile example uses gpt-6.1-sol and notes it needs access on your account or workspace. Use a model your account lists. Pick an effort that model offers. Save the top levels for the profile in item 6, so your quick questions don't pay for them.

2–5. The permission keys decide whether it stalls

Four keys control what the agent may do without you. On a long run, getting them wrong means it either waits for hours or has more reach than you meant to give it.

2. approval_policy. Values are on-request, never or a granular table. The reference says untrusted "is unsupported" and on-failure "is deprecated", so check any old config for them. Its advice: "use on-request for interactive runs or never for non-interactive runs." Under on-request, OpenAI's approvals page says Codex asks before it edits files outside the workspace or runs network-dependent commands. That is the lunch-break stall. With never there are no prompts, and the page notes "you still control Codex's level of autonomy" through the sandbox.

approval_policy = "on-request"   # day to day; item 6 flips it

3. sandbox_mode. Values are read-only, workspace-write and danger-full-access. On launch Codex recommends Auto (workspace write plus on-request approvals) for version-controlled folders and read-only for everything else, per the approvals page. Take that recommendation in a folder without git and a long task can't write a single file. The same page labels the no-sandbox, no-approvals --yolo combination "not recommended". Don't use it on a run nobody watches.

sandbox_mode = "workspace-write"


The sandbox is the fence, approvals are the gate, and the network cable starts unplugged.

4. network_access under [sandbox_workspace_write]. "By default, the agent runs with network access turned off," says the approvals page. It also warns that "prompt injection can cause the agent to fetch and follow untrusted instructions." My suggestion is to keep it off and install dependencies before you start. If the task needs the network, turn it on for that run only. The advanced guide shows the one-run form:

codex --config sandbox_workspace_write.network_access=true

5. writable_roots. These are "additional writable roots when sandbox_mode = "workspace-write"." You need one when the task also edits a sibling repo, such as a shared types package. Use absolute paths. Inside every writable root, .git stays read-only, and so does .codex when it is a directory (approvals page).

[sandbox_workspace_write]
network_access = false
writable_roots = ["/path/to/shared-types"]

6. Profiles are files now

Key: none. It's a file next to config.toml.

The advanced guide is blunt about it: in Codex 0.134.0 and later, --profile no longer reads [profiles.<name>] from config.toml, and the top-level profile = "<name>" selector is no longer supported. A profile is now its own file, ~/.codex/<name>.config.toml, with top-level keys. Names can use letters, numbers, hyphens and underscores.

That suits long runs. Keep your daily config cautious and put the unattended settings in a file of their own:

# ~/.codex/long-run.config.toml
model = "gpt-6.1-sol"
model_reasoning_effort = "xhigh"  # if your model lists it
approval_policy = "never"
sandbox_mode = "workspace-write"

codex --profile long-run
codex exec --profile long-run "migrate the tests to vitest"

Precedence matters. The config basics page puts CLI flags and --config overrides first, then project .codex/config.toml files (trusted projects only), then the profile, then ~/.codex/config.toml. A repo's own .codex/config.toml can override your profile.

7. notify: find out when a turn ends

Key: notify

Unset, nothing tells you when a turn finishes. You keep going back to the terminal to check. notify takes a command array. Codex runs it with one JSON argument when it emits a supported event, and "currently only agent-turn-complete" is supported (advanced guide). The payload fields are type, thread-id, turn-id, cwd, input-messages and last-assistant-message.

notify = ["python3", "/path/to/codex-turn-log.py"]

A small script that appends one line per finished turn, so tail -f ~/.codex/turns.log shows a whole session:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
import json
import os
import sys
import time

event = json.loads(sys.argv[1])
if event.get("type") != "agent-turn-complete":
    sys.exit(0)

msg = event.get("last-assistant-message") or ""
line = "{} {} {}\n".format(
    time.strftime("%H:%M"),
    event.get("cwd", "?"),
    msg.replace("\n", " ")[:80],
)
path = os.path.expanduser("~/.codex/turns.log")
with open(path, "a") as f:
    f.write(line)

If you forward these events to a webhook or a queue instead, use turn-id as the dedupe key so a retried delivery doesn't post twice. If all you want is a desktop alert, the guide points to the built-in tui.notifications setting as the alternative.

8–9. Context size and secrets

8. project_doc_max_bytes. The AGENTS.md page says Codex "stops adding files once the combined size reaches the limit defined by project_doc_max_bytes (32 KiB by default)." The limit is combined, not per file. The advanced guide describes it as per file, and an open docs issue from July 31, 2026 says the code treats it as one shared budget along the root-to-folder chain. A large root AGENTS.md can use it up and silently drop a nested one, and the nested one usually holds the rules for the folder the agent is working in.

List every AGENTS.md and its size. Only the files on the path from the repo root to the folder the agent works in count toward one run, so add up those:

find . -name AGENTS.md -not -path '*/node_modules/*' \
  -exec wc -c {} +

If the total is close to 32,768, raise the limit. 65536 is the docs' own example:

project_doc_max_bytes = 65536

9. shell_environment_policy. This is the one that exposes secrets. The reference says ignore_default_excludes defaults to true, which keeps variables whose names contain KEY, SECRET or TOKEN. Unless another filter removes them, the commands the agent runs during a two-hour task can see the credentials you exported this morning. Set it to false to apply the automatic exclusions, and use the newer filters table. The legacy exclude and include_only arrays can't be combined with filters in the same layer.

[shell_environment_policy]
inherit = "core"
ignore_default_excludes = false

[shell_environment_policy.filters]
"AWS_*" = "exclude"
"AZURE_*" = "exclude"

inherit = "core" starts from what the docs call a trimmed set, and none starts from nothing. If your tests need a variable, give them a dummy value with set = { ... }. set runs after exclusions, so it can bring a name back. Don't write real secrets into config.toml. To check the result, ask the agent to run env | cut -d= -f1 | sort and read the names it prints.

Running the same config from Hermes IDE

I build Hermes IDE, so weigh this section with that in mind. Hermes runs Codex as a built-in agent, in a real terminal, with Codex's own interface, "exactly as it would anywhere else", in the README's words. You sign in to Codex with Codex's own login, and Hermes never asks for your tokens.


The ⌘N New task sheet's agent picker in Hermes 2.3.4, with Claude Code and Codex installed.

On top of that config, the ⌘N sheet (Ctrl+Shift+N on Windows and Linux) picks the agent, model, effort and account for each task, and you can save the combinations you use often as presets. Each task gets its own hermes/<task> branch and worktree, so workspace-write scopes Codex to that task's folder and not to your main checkout.


The ⌘N New task sheet: agent, project, worktree, approval, model and effort chips, and the "Hermes will run" command preview.

notify still fires, because Codex fires it. Hermes adds its own layer: one status per session, a notification when an agent is blocked on you or done, and ⌘I to jump to the agent that has waited longest. It never answers a permission prompt for you.

Hermes is free, source-available under BSL 1.1, runs on macOS, Windows and Linux, and isn't affiliated with OpenAI, Anthropic, Nous Research or any other agent vendor. The current release is 2.3.4, published October 15, 2026, and you can download it here.

If this was useful

notify turns every finished Codex turn into an event that some other program consumes. Once you send those events through a webhook or a queue, you're dealing with retries, duplicate deliveries and ordering, and the Event-Driven Architecture Pocket Guide covers those traps in a short read. If you run Codex next to other agents, Hermes IDE keeps each one on its own branch with one inbox.

title: Automated, Secure, and Scalable: Reference Implementation for Atlas on Azure
description:
Today’s cloud-driven world is characterized by the requirement to scale—and to do so massively and faster than ever. But standing up secure and compliant environments on the cloud is complex and requires huge efforts, as teams have to figure out networking, policies, identity, and governance requirements across numerous projects.

At MongoDB, we’re focused on empowering enterprise customers to build faster, smarter, and more securely. We know how important it is to developers to be able to quickly onboard and start building on a trusted platform. But to stand up secure, governed, production-ready Atlas clusters, a standardized cloud foundation is essential.

That’s where the MongoDB Atlas on Azure Reference Implementation comes in. Designed to bring the power of MongoDB Atlas to Microsoft Azure customers, this reference architecture and sample implementation enables teams to automatically deploy MongoDB Atlas clusters that align seamlessly with Microsoft Azure’s well-architected framework, avoiding inconsistent deployments, security gaps, and reduced developer productivity.

Introducing the MongoDB Atlas on Azure reference implementation  

 The MongoDB Atlas on Azure reference implementation extends automation and governance to the data layer, allowing you to deploy MongoDB Atlas with confidence that your database setup is repeatable and adheres to your organization’s policies and compliance frameworks automatically.

 The reference implementation (RI) is our prescriptive guidance and automation toolkit to deploy Atlas seamlessly within your enterprise-grade Azure environment.

 Here’s what it delivers:

  • Automated deployment: We provide Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) Terraform templates that automatically provision and configure Atlas to align perfectly with Azure and MongoDB architecture standards. This includes setting up both single-region and multi-region Atlas clusters using a DevOps Pipeline with a manual approval gate.

  • Prescriptive security: The RI provides guidance and recommendations on security best practices. It automates the configuration of private endpoints within customer Azure VNet, NSGs, NAT Gateway, and VNet Peering between multi-region application nodes—providing for secure communication and network isolation.

  • Scalable by design: The RI establishes a repeatable deployment pattern for MongoDB Atlas. This means every new development team can spin up a pre-configured, secure, and governed Atlas environment quickly, allowing your organization to rapidly and systematically scale.

  • Monitoring and observability: The RI includes a monitoring component, wherein an Azure Function App periodically queries the MongoDB Atlas API to gather database health and performance metrics, which are visualized in the Application Insights dashboards.

  • Test DB connectivity: The RI can also deploy an optional Web App to confirm the connectivity between the application and MongoDB Atlas was successful and secure.

MongoDB Atlas on Azure architecture overview

Single-region architecture

In the single-region deployment, all core components—including the MongoDB Atlas cluster, Azure Virtual Network, monitoring, and supporting application infrastructure—are provisioned within a single Azure region. This setup is ideal for applications with regional data residency requirements or when resilience to regional failure is not a primary concern.

Multi-region architecture

For organizations with higher requirements for business continuity and disaster recovery, the multi-region architecture distributes MongoDB Atlas cluster nodes and supporting infrastructure across multiple Azure regions. The design leverages VNet peering and multiple private endpoints to provide seamless, secure connectivity, even in the event of a regional failure.

Components:

  1. Application or service: Applications or services are deployed in the subnet with the NSG and the NAT so that they are secured and have visibility to the MongoDB Atlas clusters. These can include web apps, backend services, analytics jobs, or integration tools.

  2. MongoDB Atlas Cluster: The MongoDB Atlas clusters are visible through a private endpoint connection and can connect to the applications or services deployed in the secured Azure Virtual Network.

  3. Observability: An Azure Function App periodically queries the MongoDB Atlas API to gather database health and performance metrics, which are visualized in Application Insights dashboards.

  4. Resiliency: VNet Peering is enabled so that in case of a regional outage, all remaining regions have visibility to the rest of the MongoDB Atlas clusters.

Accelerating innovation

The MongoDB Atlas on Microsoft Azure Reference Implementation helps bridge the gap between developer agility and enterprise control. It provides the automation, security, and scalability needed to deliver data-driven innovation faster—while aligning with your organization’s cloud governance model. With this accelerator, enterprises can standardize data deployments, empower teams to focus on building applications instead of managing infrastructure and confidently scale MongoDB Atlas across their Azure ecosystem.

The RI offers a unified approach that brings together the best of MongoDB’s modern data platform and Azure’s cloud foundation—enabling organizations to innovate securely and at scale.

title: Chat SDK now supports Slack Enterprise Grid
description:
Chat SDK's Slack adapter now supports Slack Enterprise Grid.

Bots installed org-wide work across every workspace, with correct token resolution, tenant-scoped caches, and event retry deduplication.

The adapter now stores org-wide installations by enterprise ID. This matches how tokens are resolved for incoming events, slash commands, and interactive payloads. SlackInstallation records the new identity fields:

Token resolution behaves the same over HTTP webhooks and Socket Mode. Events route by the installation identity in the envelope's authorizations field, which keeps routing correct for Slack Connect shared channels.

The adapter is also hardened for multi-workspace deployments:

  • User profile and mention caches are scoped per installation, so one tenant's data never resolves for another.

  • API calls made with an org-wide token pass the event's team_id automatically, which Slack requires for workspace-scoped methods.

  • Retried event deliveries are deduplicated for 24 hours, covering Slack's Delayed Events redeliveries.

  • Outgoing mentions accept W-prefixed Grid user IDs alongside U-prefixed IDs.

Single-workspace installations are unaffected, and getInstallation and deleteInstallation work unchanged for both install types.

Read the Slack adapter documentation to get started.

title: How to move your app to another region on Hubfly space
description:
TL;DR — What you get: your app and its volumes running in a new region, with old addresses forwarding for weeks. Who it's for: anyone whose users are far from where the app runs, or who needs data in a specific region. Time: a few minutes of clicking, plus an estimated freeze of 2–4 minutes for a small app. Cost: the move fee is shown before you confirm (a small one-container app showed $5.00) and is refunded if you cancel before the freeze.

Checked against the Hubfly space dashboard and docs, November 2026.

You picked a region on day one, probably without thinking about it. Now most of your users are on another continent, and every request crosses an ocean twice. Or a customer asks where their data lives, and the answer is wrong.

Moving an app to another region usually means rebuilding it by hand and hoping nothing was missed. On Hubfly space you can move a whole app in one flow, with a written plan of everything that changes before you commit.

Try it on Hubfly space: the free tier includes 360 hours a month.

What moves, and what doesn't

A region move copies a Cell project's containers, writable root filesystems, volumes, images and routes. Hubfly space copies the data while the app runs, then freezes it briefly for the last changes, checks both sides match, and switches over.

Some things don't move with it:

  • Managed databases, Realtime, Storage buckets, Boxes and Mail need their own procedure.
  • Logs, metrics and firewall analytics from before the switch stay in the old region and aren't shown afterwards. Export what you need first.
  • Your public addresses change. Each Hubfly space subdomain gets a new name in the new region, and your outbound IP changes.

Step 1: Open the move screen

Open your project, click the gear icon next to its name, and go to Danger Zone. The first card is Move to another region. Click Choose region.

To move several projects at once, use Move several projects instead. A batch takes 2 to 20 projects and moves two at a time.

Step 2: Pick the target region

Regions that can't take your project are greyed out with the reason. Pick the one closest to your users and click Continue.

Step 3: Read the review. This is the important part

The review screen is your move plan. Read every line. It shows:

  • Two freeze modes. Copy first, then freeze copies while the app runs and freezes only for the last changes. Stop and copy stops the app first, then copies everything. Pick the first for most web apps, and the second if your app writes heavily to a volume (a self-hosted database, for example).
  • The freeze estimate, with the math shown. For a small app with a few MB of data, it estimated 2 to 4 minutes, mostly the time to stop, start and check the app. Before a speed test it assumes 40 MB/s. Click Measure transfer speed to replace that assumption with a measured speed, which matters most for bigger volumes.
  • The move fee and data sizes. A small one-container app with a few MB of data showed Move fee: $5.00.

Scroll down for the checklist. It's specific to your project:

  • New addresses. your-app.eu2.hubfly.app becomes your-app.us3.hubfly.app. Browsers are redirected and other requests are forwarded from the old address for about 30 days. An address with no traffic for 3 days stops forwarding sooner.
  • A new outbound IP. The screen shows the old and new IP. Add the new one to every allowlist your app connects to (an external database, a payment provider, a partner API) before the move.
  • DNS changes for custom domains. Each custom domain gets a per-record plan (CNAME or A record).
  • Hard-coded addresses. Environment variables that contain old addresses show up as warnings. Secret values are never displayed.

Step 4: Schedule it and confirm

Click Continue to reach Schedule and confirm:

  1. Freeze window. Pick your quietest hour (local time), or leave it empty to start now.
  2. Maximum freeze, from 1 to 1,440 minutes (default 10). If the estimate goes over your limit, the app keeps running and the move waits for you to choose: keep copying, freeze now, or cancel.
  3. Tick I have reviewed external database allowlists and the new outbound addresses.
  4. Type your project name and click Start move.

During the freeze, your sites show a maintenance page and TCP connections are refused. That's the downtime to plan for.

Step 5: Watch it, then switch your DNS

The project page shows copied bytes, the current step, the freeze time and verification status. Before switching over, Hubfly space compares data (Merkle roots), image digests, configuration and runtime checks. If verification fails before cutover, your source is restored automatically. You get an email when it's done or needs you.

After the move:

  1. Follow the DNS plan for each custom domain. The live checker shows when DNS and certificates are ready.
  2. Update TCP connection strings, registry push destinations, OAuth redirect URIs and webhooks before the forwarding deadline.
  3. Download the signed attestation if you need proof of the move for a customer or an audit. It records the copy roots and timestamps.

The cheaper-looking route that empties your volumes

The move screen has a second mode. A project that is hibernated or empty gets a different dialog, Change project region, which says "This is free." It only changes where the project starts next time. When it finishes, the History tab shows "Region changed from eu-north to usa-central", and the completion banner offers Download attestation.

So it's tempting to hibernate the app, change its region for free, then restore it. Don't do that for an app with data. A restore starts at $1.00 (about $1.40 for one container, one volume and one domain), and volumes come back empty: they're recreated from their saved configuration, not from your files.

Use the free change for an empty project. For anything with data, use the full move: it's the one that copies and checks your volumes.

Changed your mind? Cancel or move back

  • Before the freeze: cancel. The partial copy is removed and the fee is refunded.
  • After the move: the old copy is kept for the move-back period (7 days by default). Use Move back during that time to return to the old region.

What can go wrong

  1. The app breaks right after the move because an external service rejects it. Your outbound IP changed. Add the new IP from the review screen to the allowlist of your database, API or payment provider before the freeze window.
  2. Your app gets slower after moving closer to users. It probably still talks to a managed database in the old region, so every query crosses the ocean. Move the data too: dump it, restore it into a database in the new region, then switch DATABASE_URL. Do this before the freeze so both sides are ready.
  3. The freeze takes longer than you hoped. Big volumes and lots of writes mean more changes to copy at the end. Click Measure transfer speed, set a Maximum freeze you can live with, and schedule the window for your quietest hour. If the estimate goes over the limit, nothing freezes until you decide. And if you need zero downtime, a region move isn't the tool: it always has a freeze.

Limits and pricing

  • Fee: shown on the review screen before you confirm, and refunded if you cancel before the freeze. A small one-container app with a few MB of data showed $5.00. Changing the region of an empty or hibernated project is free.
  • Running cost should stay the same. Hubfly space lists one set of rates, with no regional pricing. A small always-on app with 0.5 vCPU, 0.5 GB RAM and a 1 GB volume costs: 0.5 × $0.004 × 730 + 0.5 × $0.002 × 730 + 1 × $0.00001536 × 730 = $1.46 + $0.73 + $0.01 = about $2.20 a month, before and after the move.

Who this is not for

  • Projects built around managed databases, Storage, Boxes or Mail. Those don't move with the project. The move covers Cell containers, volumes, images and routes.
  • Multi-region apps. This moves a project from one region to another. It doesn't run your app in two regions at once.

Go further on Hubfly space

  • Region migration docs: every option, including the CLI.
  • Project Transfer: hand a finished project to a client's account instead of moving it between regions.
  • Custom domains: set up the domain you'll repoint after the move.
  • Volumes: keep app data on volumes so it moves with the app.

FAQ

Can I change the region of a running app?

Yes: Project settings → Danger Zone → Move to another region. The app keeps running while data copies, then freezes briefly.

How long is the downtime?

The review screen estimates it for your project. For a small app with a few MB of data it estimated 2 to 4 minutes, mostly stopping, starting and checking the app. Big, busy volumes take longer, and you set the maximum.

Will my domain keep working?

Hubfly space subdomains get a new name and the old one forwards for about 30 days. Custom domains need the CNAME or A record change from the DNS plan.

Can I undo it?

Yes, with Move back during the retention period (7 days by default).

Ready to put your app closer to your users? Start free on Hubfly space, 360 hours included. Moving many projects for a team or customers? Talk to sales.

title: Color Name Tool: Find the Closest CSS Name for Any Hex Code
description:
Every designer has lived this moment: a client sends a screenshot, a brand guideline lists a hex code with nothing else, and someone asks "so what color is that, exactly?" The honest answer is that most hex codes have no exact name at all. There are roughly 16.7 million displayable colors and only 148 CSS named colors. A good color name tool bridges that gap — it takes your hex code, measures the distance to every named color, and hands you the closest match in plain English.

Why Color Names Exist at All

Computers speak in numbers. #3b7ddd is unambiguous; "a medium blue with a hint of gray" is not. Named colors exist because humans need handles. CSS standardized 140 color names in the 1990s — rebeccapurple joined later as a tribute — and designers have used them in conversation ever since: "make the button tomato," "use forestgreen for success."

Names compress information. Saying "this heading is darkslategray" tells a developer exactly what to type and tells a designer the intended mood. The catch is coverage: 148 names for 16.7 million colors means almost every color from a brand palette or a photograph has no exact name. That is where nearest-match identification earns its keep.

How Color Matching Actually Works

The Color Name Identifier compares your color against the full CSS named-color list using two different yardsticks, because "closest" depends on how you measure.

RGB Distance: Fast but Crude

The simplest approach treats a color as a point in three-dimensional space — red, green, blue — and computes the straight-line distance. Firebrick and your hex code might sit 40 units apart; crimson sits 90. Sort by distance, and the nearest name wins. This is cheap to calculate and usually lands in the right neighborhood, which is why it works well as a first pass.

LAB Distance: Closer to Human Perception

RGB distance has a flaw: it disagrees with your eyes. A shift of 30 units in green looks far more dramatic than 30 units in blue, and two colors close in RGB can read as totally different hues. The CIE LAB color space was designed to fix exactly this — distances in LAB correspond to perceived difference. Serious matching ranks candidates in LAB so that "closest" means closest to what a human would pick, not what arithmetic picks. The tool shows you the ranking either way, so you can judge whether the top match is a confident hit or a near-miss that deserves a second look.

Using a Color Name Tool Step by Step

The workflow is deliberately short. Paste your hex code into the input — the leading hash is optional. The tool immediately returns the closest named color, its hex value, its RGB breakdown, and how far it sits from your original color. If the distance is small, you have found your name; if it is large, the ranked list below shows the runners-up, and one of them usually fits better.

Watch the distance number, not just the name. A gap under 20 units is effectively the same color to most screens. A gap over 80 means the named palette simply does not contain what you are holding, and the honest answer is "unmatched" — the ranking still tells you which named color family it belongs to.

From Screenshot to Name: Picking the Color First

Often the color lives in an image, not a stylesheet. A competitor's landing page, a product photo, a mood board — you cannot paste a picture into a hex field. The Image Color Picker closes that loop: load the image, click the exact pixel you care about, and read off the hex code. Once you have the code, feed it to the name identifier and the full pipeline from picture to vocabulary is done in under a minute.

Converting Formats Along the Way

Names are only one dialect of color. Design tools speak hex, CSS increasingly speaks HSL, image editors speak RGB, and print shops want CMYK approximations. The Color Converter moves between all of these instantly, so once the name identifier tells you a color is close to steelblue, you can express steelblue in whatever format the next step demands.

And when one color is not enough — say the identifier points you at steelblue and you need a matching accent pair — the Color Palette Generator builds coordinated sets around any starting hue, using the same colorimetric logic that makes the match believable in the first place.

Who Actually Uses This

Frontend developers use it to replace magic hex codes with readable named colors in prototypes. Brand designers use it to check whether a new brand color collides with an overused name. Content writers use it to describe UI colors accurately in documentation — "the toolbar uses darkslategray" reads better than "the toolbar uses a dark gray, kind of bluish." Accessibility auditors use it as a sanity check before running the full contrast math: if your text color is dimgray on a whitesmoke background, the names alone warn you.

Why Run It in the Browser

A color is not a secret, but your design work is your business. The identifier runs entirely client-side: the hex goes in, the ranking comes out, and nothing touches a server. No account, no upload, no analytics on your palette. That matters when you are checking unreleased brand colors on a machine you do not fully control — an airport laptop, a shared studio machine, anywhere.

The Takeaway

Color names are a compression layer between human language and machine numbers, and 148 names will never cover 16.7 million colors. The practical move is nearest-match: measure distance in a perceptual space, pick the closest name, and read the distance to know how confident to be. Paste the hex, check the gap, and if the color lives in an image, grab it first with a picker. The whole question "what color is this" deserves a thirty-second answer, and now it has one.

title: Why "just retry it" can be dangerous
description:
Your Node.js service calls an external API. The request times out, returns 503 Service Unavailable, or gets a 429 Too Many Requests response. A retry sounds reasonable: wait briefly, send the same request again, and continue.

But not every failed-looking request actually failed on the server.

A timeout means the client did not receive the expected result in time. The server might have completed the operation and lost the response on the way back. If the request created a payout, order, or exchange operation, a blind retry could create it twice.

The practical goal isn't to retry everything. It's to retry only when the operation is safe, with a clear limit and a delay that respects the server.

We'll build a small JSON HTTP client using built-in Node.js APIs, then test transient errors, backoff, Retry-After, timeouts, and duplicate-request safety.

Scope: This is a standalone educational example, not the internal infrastructure of any cryptocurrency platform. It uses Node.js 22-compatible APIs, supports GET and explicitly opted-in POST, and expects a JSON response body on success. It is not a production-ready transaction client.

First, classify the failure

These cases require different decisions:

What happened Suggested behavior in this example
Network failure or request timeout Retry an eligible operation, within a bounded attempt limit
429 Too Many Requests Respect Retry-After when provided; otherwise use backoff
503 Service Unavailable, 502, 504 Consider a bounded retry for eligible operations
408 Request Timeout or selected 500 errors Retry only according to a deliberate policy
400, 401, 403, 404 Do not automatically retry without a change or an explicit contract
POST with an unknown result Do not retry blindly; confirm idempotency support or reconcile the operation

fetch() doesn't reject just because a server responds with HTTP 503. You still need to inspect response.status. Network errors and aborts, on the other hand, reject the promise.

1. Put a timeout on each attempt

Modern Node.js has fetch() and AbortSignal.timeout() built in:

const response = await fetch('https://api.example.test/data', {
  signal: AbortSignal.timeout(3000),
});

The URL above is deliberately a placeholder. Replace it with a real endpoint that you control or are authorized to query.

With a timeout signal, a request is aborted after the configured interval. Crucially, aborting the client-side request does not undo a remote operation that the server may already have started or completed.

Also distinguish two kinds of cancellation:

  • Per-attempt timeout: One attempt took too long. An eligible read can be retried.
  • Caller cancellation: The user, job, or parent request no longer needs the result. Stop the entire retry loop.

AbortSignal.any() combines the two signals. Our client will also read the JSON response inside the attempt's timeout window, instead of returning a Response and parsing its body later.

2. Add exponential backoff with jitter

Retrying immediately after a failure can make an overloaded service even slower. A simple exponential backoff increases the potential delay between attempts:

Attempt 1 fails → max backoff 300 ms
Attempt 2 fails → max backoff 600 ms
Attempt 3 fails → max backoff 1,200 ms
Attempt 4       → no retry after final failure

These are delay caps, not the exact sleeps. We'll use full jitter: choose a random delay between zero and the current capped value. That spreads clients out, helping avoid a synchronized retry spike.

The policy is bounded: four total attempts means one initial request plus at most three retries—not four retries.

3. Respect Retry-After without retrying too early

For 429 and 503, servers may include Retry-After:

HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 5

That means wait five seconds before another attempt. The header can also be an HTTP date.

Our implementation has a maximum amount of time it is willing to wait. If the server asks for an hour but the operation has only a ten-second wait budget, the client stops. It must not quietly truncate the server's required delay and retry too early. A higher-level job scheduler may choose to resume later.

4. Build a reusable JSON retry client

Create retry-json.mjs:

import { setTimeout as delay } from 'node:timers/promises';

const RETRYABLE_STATUSES = new Set([408, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504]);
const defaultWait = (ms, signal) => delay(ms, undefined, { signal });

export function parseRetryAfter(value, now = Date.now()) {
  if (value == null) return null;
  const text = value.trim();
  if (/^\d+$/.test(text)) {
    const seconds = Number(text);
    return Number.isSafeInteger(seconds) && seconds <= Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER / 1000
      ? seconds * 1000 : Infinity;
  }
  // The commonly used IMF-fixdate HTTP-date format, e.g. Fri, 23 Oct 2026 12:00:03 GMT.
  if (!/^[A-Za-z]{3}, \d{2} [A-Za-z]{3} \d{4} \d{2}:\d{2}:\d{2} GMT$/.test(text)) {
    return null;
  }
  const timestamp = Date.parse(text);
  return Number.isNaN(timestamp) ? null : Math.max(0, timestamp - now);
}

export async function fetchJsonWithRetry(url, {
  method = 'GET',
  headers = {},
  body,
  maxAttempts = 4,
  requestTimeoutMs = 3000,
  baseDelayMs = 300,
  maxBackoffMs = 3000,
  maxRetryAfterMs = 10_000,
  allowPostRetry = false,
  idempotencyKey,
  signal,
  fetchImpl = fetch,
  wait = defaultWait,
  random = Math.random,
  now = Date.now,
} = {}) {
  const httpMethod = method.toUpperCase();
  if (!['GET', 'POST'].includes(httpMethod)) {
    throw new TypeError('This JSON example supports GET and POST only');
  }
  if (!Number.isInteger(maxAttempts) || maxAttempts < 1 || maxAttempts > 8 ||
      !Number.isSafeInteger(requestTimeoutMs) || requestTimeoutMs < 1 ||
      !Number.isSafeInteger(baseDelayMs) || baseDelayMs < 1 ||
      !Number.isSafeInteger(maxBackoffMs) || maxBackoffMs < baseDelayMs ||
      !Number.isSafeInteger(maxRetryAfterMs) || maxRetryAfterMs < 0) {
    throw new RangeError('Invalid retry configuration');
  }
  if (httpMethod === 'POST' && allowPostRetry &&
      (typeof idempotencyKey !== 'string' || !idempotencyKey.trim() || typeof body !== 'string')) {
    throw new TypeError('Retrying POST requires a stable key and repeatable string body');
  }

  // POST retries are an explicit opt-in; the remote API must guarantee deduplication.
  const canRetry = httpMethod === 'GET' || (httpMethod === 'POST' && allowPostRetry);
  const requestHeaders = new Headers(headers);
  if (idempotencyKey != null) requestHeaders.set('Idempotency-Key', idempotencyKey);

  const jitter = (attempt) => {
    const cap = Math.min(maxBackoffMs, baseDelayMs * 2 ** (attempt - 1));
    return Math.floor(random() * (cap + 1)); // Full jitter in [0, cap].
  };

  for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= maxAttempts; attempt++) {
    signal?.throwIfAborted();
    const timeoutSignal = AbortSignal.timeout(requestTimeoutMs);
    const attemptSignal = signal
      ? AbortSignal.any([signal, timeoutSignal])
      : timeoutSignal;
    let response;

    try {
      response = await fetchImpl(url, {
        method: httpMethod,
        headers: requestHeaders,
        body,
        signal: attemptSignal,
      });
    } catch (error) {
      if (signal?.aborted) throw signal.reason;
      const transient = error instanceof TypeError || timeoutSignal.aborted;
      if (!canRetry || attempt === maxAttempts || !transient) throw error;
      await wait(jitter(attempt), signal);
      continue;
    }

    if (response.ok) {
      try {
        // Read within the timeout window, not after returning the Response.
        return await response.json();
      } catch (error) {
        if (signal?.aborted) throw signal.reason;
        if (!canRetry || attempt === maxAttempts || !timeoutSignal.aborted) throw error;
        await wait(jitter(attempt), signal);
        continue;
      }
    }

    const status = response.status;
    const header = response.headers.get('Retry-After');
    // Release the body before retrying to avoid holding connections unnecessarily.
    if (response.body) {
      try { await response.body.cancel(); } catch { /* already closed */ }
    }
    if (!canRetry || !RETRYABLE_STATUSES.has(status) || attempt === maxAttempts) {
      throw new Error(`HTTP ${status}`);
    }
    const serverWaitMs = parseRetryAfter(header, now());
    if (serverWaitMs !== null && serverWaitMs > maxRetryAfterMs) {
      // Do not silently cap Retry-After and hit the server too early.
      throw new Error(`Retry-After exceeds local wait budget (HTTP ${status})`);
    }
    await wait(serverWaitMs ?? jitter(attempt), signal);
  }
}

A few choices are intentional:

  • The helper only retries GET by default. It supports POST, but does not retry it unless the caller explicitly opts in and supplies a stable idempotency key and reusable string body.
  • The server—not the header alone—must actually implement idempotency semantics for that endpoint. Sending an arbitrary Idempotency-Key to an API that ignores it provides no protection.
  • The sample treats 408, 429, 500, 502, 503, and 504 as retryable HTTP statuses only for requests eligible for retry. This is an illustrative policy, not a universal rule for every API.
  • Invalid JSON is not treated as a transient network problem. The request succeeded at the HTTP level but its response is not valid for this JSON client.
  • The example accepts standard Retry-After seconds and the common IMF-fixdate HTTP-date format. Other historical date formats are outside its scope.

5. Use it for a read-only API request 

import { fetchJsonWithRetry } from './retry-json.mjs';

// Replace this placeholder with your own JSON GET endpoint.
const data = await fetchJsonWithRetry('https://api.example.test/rates', {
  maxAttempts: 4,
  requestTimeoutMs: 3000,
  baseDelayMs: 300,
  maxBackoffMs: 3000,
});

console.log(data);

This is a usage illustration. The .test file below uses mock responses instead of making real HTTP requests, so you can reproduce the results without an API key or an internet connection.

6. What about POST and duplicate operations?

HTTP defines GET as safe and idempotent, assuming the server implements the method correctly. A POST may create a new resource or trigger a financial side effect; repeating it can repeat the side effect.

Imagine creating a payout operation:

  1. Your client sends POST /payouts.
  2. The server creates the payout.
  3. The response gets lost, and your client times out.
  4. A naive retry sends another POST /payouts.

There could now be two payouts. A client-side timeout is not proof that the first payout failed.

Some APIs explicitly support a stable idempotency key for operations like this. If—and only if—the provider documents and guarantees that contract for the endpoint, you may opt in:

import { fetchJsonWithRetry } from './retry-json.mjs';

// ILLUSTRATIVE ONLY: the target endpoint must document idempotency support.
const payload = JSON.stringify({
  amount: '100.00',
  currency: 'USD',
});

const operation = await fetchJsonWithRetry('https://api.example.test/payouts', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
  body: payload,
  allowPostRetry: true,
  idempotencyKey: 'payout-workflow-123',
});

The same key and the exact same payload are sent on every attempt. In real systems, persist the key before calling the provider, bind it to the logical business operation, and keep it stable across process restarts. The provider must reject conflicting payloads under the same key and implement its own deduplication; key retention periods and response-replay behavior depend on that provider's contract.

If you cannot verify the remote operation's outcome or the provider's idempotency semantics, reconcile before retrying. That may mean querying the operation by your stable reference or escalating the uncertain result to a reconciliation worker.

7. Test the retry policy without external requests

The helper allows fetch, waiting, and randomness to be injected. This lets us simulate different failures quickly and deterministically.

Create retry-json.test.mjs. Here is a focused set of runnable tests:

import test from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { fetchJsonWithRetry } from './retry-json.mjs';

const url = 'https://api.example.test/data';
const reply = (status, data = {}, headers = {}) =>
  new Response(JSON.stringify(data), { status, headers });

test('GET retries 503 twice, then succeeds', async () => {
  const steps = [reply(503), reply(503), reply(200, { ok: true })];
  const waits = [];
  const result = await fetchJsonWithRetry(url, {
    fetchImpl: async () => steps.shift(),
    baseDelayMs: 100,
    random: () => 0.5,
    wait: async (ms) => waits.push(ms),
  });
  assert.deepEqual(result, { ok: true });
  assert.deepEqual(waits, [50, 100]);
});

test('429 honors Retry-After', async () => {
  const steps = [reply(429, {}, { 'Retry-After': '2' }), reply(200)];
  const waits = [];
  await fetchJsonWithRetry(url, {
    fetchImpl: async () => steps.shift(),
    wait: async (ms) => waits.push(ms),
  });
  assert.deepEqual(waits, [2000]);
});

test('does not retry a POST by default', async () => {
  let calls = 0;
  await assert.rejects(fetchJsonWithRetry(url, {
    method: 'POST',
    body: '{"amount":"100"}',
    fetchImpl: async () => { calls++; return reply(503); },
  }), /HTTP 503/);
  assert.equal(calls, 1);
});

test('opted-in POST reuses its idempotency key', async () => {
  const headersSeen = [];
  const result = await fetchJsonWithRetry(url, {
    method: 'POST',
    body: '{"amount":"100"}',
    allowPostRetry: true,
    idempotencyKey: 'operation-123',
    fetchImpl: async (_, options) => {
      headersSeen.push(options.headers.get('Idempotency-Key'));
      return headersSeen.length === 1 ? reply(503) : reply(200, { ok: true });
    },
    wait: async () => {},
  });
  assert.deepEqual(result, { ok: true });
  assert.deepEqual(headersSeen, ['operation-123', 'operation-123']);
});

Run them with Node.js 22 or another compatible current version:

node --test retry-json.test.mjs

An extended local test suite of 16 cases also checks timeouts, caller cancellation, invalid JSON, excessive Retry-After values, HTTP dates, validation, and retry exhaustion. All 16 passed on Node.js 22.16.0. These are mock-based tests, not performance benchmarks or tests against a real payment provider.

8. Production concerns beyond this demo

A short retry helper is only one layer of resilience. Before adopting a policy in a production backend, consider:

  • End-to-end deadline: The demo limits each attempt and each Retry-After wait, but does not impose one explicit absolute deadline for the whole operation. A total deadline, queue deadline, or request budget is often needed.
  • Retry amplification: If a frontend, API gateway, job worker, and provider SDK all retry independently, one failure can multiply into many requests. Choose where retries belong.
  • Idempotency and persistence: A stable key should be persisted and associated with the intended operation. Your own database may also need unique constraints, event deduplication, and transactional outbox processing.
  • Rate limiting: Retry-After helps, but real clients may also need shared rate limits, concurrency limits, and circuit breakers.
  • Observability: Record the operation ID, attempt number, HTTP status, elapsed time, and final outcome. Avoid logging access tokens, request secrets, or sensitive payloads.
  • Ambiguous outcomes: A timed-out write should enter a reconciliation path when the remote result is unknown. Do not turn uncertainty into an automatic second payment.
  • Replayable bodies: The example permits retries only for POST requests with a reusable string body. Streams and other one-shot bodies need different handling.

Key takeaways

Reliable retries require more than a for loop:

  1. Timeout each attempt, and recognize that a timeout says nothing definitive about remote side effects.
  2. Retry only eligible operations and carefully selected transient failures.
  3. Back off with jitter, and honor the server's Retry-After instructions.
  4. Bound the total number of attempts and stop when the server's requested delay exceeds your wait budget.
  5. Never assume an idempotency key works unless the provider explicitly implements it for that endpoint.
  6. Reconcile uncertain writes rather than blindly repeating them.

These practices won't eliminate network failures. They make your Node.js service less likely to turn a temporary problem into extra load, duplicate operations, or incorrect financial state.

References

  • Node.js: Global fetch, AbortSignal.timeout, and AbortSignal.any
  • Node.js: Timers Promises API
  • RFC 9110: HTTP idempotent methods
  • RFC 9110: Retry-After
  • MDN: 429 Too Many Requests
  • AWS: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter

AI disclosure: This initial draft and code examples were generated with AI assistance. The runnable example was tested with Node.js 22.16.0 using mock responses. Human technical review is required before publication.

title: Circuit Oracle: Automating Attribution Graph Analysis via Natural-Language Queries
description:
arXiv:2611.00420v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Attribution graphs, an emerging tool in mechanistic interpretability, use transcoders to decompose language model computations into sparse interpretable features connected by causal edges. However, turning a graph into a safety-relevant insight requires hours of manual analysis by experts. We introduce Circuit Oracle, an off-the-shelf LLM equipped with a multi-agent harness and task-specific authored skills, which answers natural-language questions about a target model by reading the attribution graph through tool calls. We evaluate it on three safety-relevant proxy tasks: detecting spurious features in probe circuits, eliciting hidden knowledge from taboo-finetuned models, and suppression jailbreaking via feature-level interventions. Beyond task scores, the oracle produces pruned subgraphs and context-specific feature explanations that we assess qualitatively. Results are mixed. On spurious-feature detection, Circuit Oracle reaches 78.2 $\pm$ 2.4% accuracy, outperforming single-layer feature-ranking baselines. On secret elicitation, trained self-explainers like Activation Oracles remain the stronger baseline. On refusal suppression over 50 prompts, its single committed intervention is slightly below a diff-in-means baseline, and only exceeds it when allowed the best of five attempts. Results are stable across five runs and across model choices for the agents. We also release the pruned subgraphs and context-specific feature readings that revise existing global labels, and invite future work to develop evaluations that can measure their usefulness directly.

title: Systems Thinking: Why the Best Technology Disappears Into the Background
description:
You do not think about the electrical grid. You plug in a device, and it works. You do not think about the water treatment system. You turn on a tap, and the water is clean. You do not think about the GPS satellite network. You enter a destination, and you are guided there.

These systems — electricity distribution, water treatment, satellite positioning — are extraordinarily complex. They represent decades of engineering, millions of components, and the coordinated effort of thousands of institutions. They also share one defining characteristic: they are invisible.

The invisibility is not accidental. It is the achievement.

What Invisibility Means

A system becomes invisible when it reliably does what it is supposed to do, every time, without requiring the user to understand how it works or manage its complexity. The electrical grid is invisible because when you plug something in, you do not need to think about generation, transmission, distribution, or voltage regulation. The system handles all of that. You experience only the outcome: a working device.

This kind of invisibility requires solving a specific set of engineering problems that are distinct from the problems of making a system functional.

Reliability is the first requirement. A system that works ninety percent of the time cannot become invisible. Every failure brings the system into consciousness — the user becomes aware of it in the moment it fails to do what they expected. A power outage makes people acutely aware of the electrical grid. A contamination event makes people acutely aware of the water treatment system. Reliability is what allows a system to fade into the background of daily life.

Simplicity of interface is the second requirement. A system that requires user management and attention cannot become invisible. If using the electrical grid required setting voltage parameters and managing load, nobody would be unaware of it. The interface — the plug socket, the switch — is so simple that the act of using it requires almost no conscious effort.

Appropriate scope is the third requirement. Systems become invisible when they do exactly what they are supposed to do and nothing else. A system that periodically asks users to make decisions they did not expect to make, or that generates outputs they did not ask for, keeps itself in consciousness.

Why Technology Products Fail at Invisibility

Most technology products are designed to be noticed. This is partly a function of the market dynamics of technology — differentiation requires visibility, adoption requires awareness, growth requires attention. But it is also a function of a design culture that conflates complexity with value.

A product with many features is visible because navigating the features requires ongoing attention. A product with a complex interface is visible because using it requires conscious effort. A product that frequently asks for user input is visible because it keeps inserting itself into the user's awareness.

This is fine for products where the value is in the complexity — professional tools, creative platforms, analytical software where the user's engagement with the complexity is part of the value. It is a serious problem for systems that are supposed to improve the background conditions of work rather than become work in themselves.

An agricultural diagnostic tool that requires a farmer to navigate multiple menus, enter contextual information, and interpret probabilistic outputs is not a background system. It is another thing the farmer has to manage, in addition to managing their farm. The tool's complexity competes with the farm for attention, and the farm usually wins.

Designing for Invisibility

Designing a system for invisibility requires a specific inversion of the usual technology design question.

The usual question is: what can this system do? The answer to this question tends to expand over time — more features, more capabilities, more surface area.

The question for invisibility is: what does the user need to do, and how can the system do everything except that? The answer to this question tends to contract over time — fewer interactions, simpler interfaces, more of the complexity absorbed by the system rather than delegated to the user.

ARCORA is designed around this inversion. The farmer needs to identify what is wrong with their crop and know what to do about it. Everything else — the image analysis, the disease classification, the treatment protocol lookup, the localisation into the appropriate language — is absorbed by the system. The farmer's interaction is two steps: take a photo, read the protocol. The complexity is real; the interface is not.

This is not simple to build. Absorbing complexity into a system, rather than delegating it to the user, requires that the system be genuinely capable of handling that complexity — which means higher accuracy requirements, more comprehensive training data, more thorough testing. The invisible system is harder to build than the visible one.

But it is the right goal. A tool that a farmer uses without thinking about it is a tool that actually changes how they farm. A tool they have to think about using is a tool they use rarely and eventually stop using entirely.

The best technology disappears. Building the kind of technology that disappears is the work.

Originally published at truffaire.in.

title: Microfrontends previews now link across repositories
description:
Microfrontends can now link Preview Deployments across repositories when their Git branch names match exactly.

In a monorepo, projects share the same Git repository, commits, and branches, so Vercel can automatically link their previews. Cross-repository projects have separate commit histories and branches in separate repositories. With this update, Vercel matches Git-connected projects by branch name and links their corresponding previews.

For example, when you preview the new-checkout branch of one project, requests to other projects in the Microfrontends group will use their new-checkout previews when available. This makes it easier to review coordinated changes across repositories in one preview experience.

This feature is enabled by default for new Microfrontends groups. You can manage it in your Microfrontends settings. Learn more about how deployment routing works for Microfrontends.
