title: Live video costs in 2026: Mux, Cloudflare, IVS, Hubfly space
description:
TL;DR

  • What you get: the monthly bill for one realistic live show (four 2-hour 1080p broadcasts a month) on four platforms, at 50, 500 and 2,000 viewers, with every formula shown.
  • Who it's for: developers adding live video to a course site, church, community, webinar series or SaaS product.
  • Time needed: 10 minutes to read, 5 more to plug in your own numbers.
  • Short answer: up to about 215 full-show viewers, Mux is free (100,000 free minutes plus a $20 credit). Between about 215 and 255 the two cost about the same, so pick on features. From about 255 to 500 concurrent viewers, Hubfly space Streams costs a fraction of the others. Above ~500 concurrent HD viewers, or if you need global edge delivery, captions or DRM, pick Mux, Cloudflare Stream or IVS.

You want to stream a weekly show to your own website. Every video API says "simple pricing". Then you open the pricing pages and find four different units: minutes encoded, minutes delivered, hours delivered by resolution and region, and gigabytes sent. You can't compare them in your head, and the wrong pick can cost you ten times more than it should.

This guide puts one show through all four price lists so you can see the real bill. It also shows where each platform beats the others, because none of them wins everywhere.

Try Hubfly space Streams free: the first 25 Mbps of speed, 20 processing Mbps-hours and 50 GB of bandwidth are free every month.

The show to price

Pick one concrete workload, or comparisons turn into vibes:

  • Four live shows a month, 2 hours each: 8 live hours, 480 minutes.
  • 1080p source with an adaptive ladder (1080p, 720p, 480p), so viewers on slow connections still get smooth playback.
  • Viewers watch the whole show. That's the worst case for your bill; real audiences drop off, so your bill will be lower.
  • Quality mix: half of viewers on 1080p, 30% on 720p, 20% on 480p. Per-minute vendors that price by resolution (Mux, IVS) and per-GB vendors (Hubfly space) both depend on this mix, so it's stated up front.
  • Keep the recordings for a month.
  • Viewers in North America or Europe (it matters for IVS, which prices by viewer region).

All prices are list prices from each vendor's official page on 4 November 2026, pay-as-you-go, before tax and before any negotiated discount.

How each platform charges for live video

Mux

Mux charges per minute. Live streams need the plus quality level (basic is on-demand only), and live is capped at 1080p.

  • Input (encoding): $0.03125 per minute at 1080p, $0.025 at 720p, for the first 5,000 minutes.
  • Delivery: first 100,000 minutes free every month, then $0.001 per minute at 1080p and $0.0008 at 720p and below.
  • Storage: Mux turns every live stream into an on-demand recording automatically. $0.003 per minute per month at 1080p.
  • Credit: the pay-as-you-go plan includes a $20 monthly usage credit.
  • Extras: live captions (6,000 minutes free, then $0.024/min), simulcasting at $0.02 per minute per target, DRM at $100/month plus $0.003 per license.

Cloudflare Stream

Cloudflare Stream bills two things only.

  • Delivery: $1 per 1,000 minutes delivered, any resolution. Ingest and encoding are free.
  • Storage: prepaid, $5 per month for each 1,000 minutes stored. Live recordings use it, and you can't start a new live stream if you run out.
  • Simulcast outputs count as delivered minutes. WebRTC (WHEP) playback is billed as delivery too.

Amazon IVS

Amazon IVS charges per hour, by channel type and by the resolution and region your viewers watch from.

  • Input: $2.00 per hour for a Standard channel (1080p with an adaptive ladder), $0.50 with Multitrack Video, $0.85 for Advanced HD (720p).
  • Output (North America and Europe, first 10,000 hours): $0.144 per viewer-hour at Full HD, $0.072 at HD, $0.036 at SD. Other regions cost more, up to $0.25 in South Korea.
  • New AWS accounts get a 12-month IVS free tier (basic-channel input, SD output) and up to $200 in AWS Free Tier credits (6-month free plan; use within 12 months), which would cover this show at 50 viewers for about three months.

Hubfly space Streams

Hubfly space Streams prices the network, not the minutes. Three meters:

  • Speed: the most the server may send at once. 41 µUSD per Mbps per hour (about $0.03 per Mbps a month). The first 25 Mbps of every hour is free. You can change it any time and the change applies live.
  • Processing: $0.004 per encoded Mbps-hour, only when Hubfly space re-encodes (a transcoding ladder, a mixer). Pass-through is free. 20 Mbps-hours free a month.
  • Bandwidth: $0.004 per GB sent to viewers and restream destinations. 50 GB free a month.
  • Ingest, previews, and moving recordings to Hubfly space Storage are free. A stopped server costs nothing.

The speed presets when creating a stream server. 2,500 Mbps is sized for about 500 HD viewers at once and costs $74.83 a month if left on all month, so raise it for the show and lower it after.

The default 1080p ladder re-encodes three renditions: 1080p at 6 Mbps, 720p at 3 Mbps and 480p at 1.2 Mbps. That's 10.2 Mbps of processing while you're live.

The Add a channel dialog with the 1080p adaptive ladder. Each rendition shows the processing it bills while live.

The bills, side by side

Prices read on 4 November 2026. Each price links to the vendor's official page.

Monthly cost (4 × 2-hour 1080p shows) 50 viewers 500 viewers 2,000 viewers
Mux (plus quality, PAYG) $0.00 $122.44 $754.24
Cloudflare Stream $29.00 $245.00 $965.00
Amazon IVS (Standard channel, NA/EU) $56.32 $419.20 $1,578.40
Hubfly space Streams $3.49 $32.32 Doesn't fit one server

Above 250 Mbps of speed (about 58 viewers in this scenario), Hubfly space needs a real deposit first.

Where the numbers come from

50 viewers: 50 × 480 = 24,000 viewer-minutes, or 400 viewer-hours.

  • Mux: input 480 min × $0.03125 = $15.00. Delivery is inside the free 100,000 minutes. Storage 480 min × $0.003 = $1.44. Total $16.44, fully covered by the $20 credit: $0.00.
  • Cloudflare: 24,000 / 1,000 × $1 = $24, plus one $5 storage block = $29.00.
  • IVS: input 8 h × $2 = $16. Output 400 h × (0.5 × $0.144 + 0.3 × $0.072 + 0.2 × $0.036 = $0.1008) = $40.32. Total $56.32.
  • Hubfly space: average viewer bitrate 0.5 × 6.16 + 0.3 × 3.128 + 0.2 × 1.296 = 4.28 Mbps (video plus audio), or 1.925 GB per viewer-hour. Bandwidth 400 × 1.925 = 770 GB − 50 free = 720 GB × $0.004 = $2.88. Processing 10.2 Mbps × 8 h = 81.6 − 20 free = 61.6 Mbps-hours × $0.004 = $0.25. Speed: 50 × 4.28 = 214 Mbps peak, so set 250 Mbps (no deposit needed) for 3 hours around each show: (250 − 25) × $0.000041 × 12 h = $0.11. Recording 22.2 GB × $0.0112 per GB-month = $0.25. Total $3.49.

Mux stays at $0 until about 215 viewers (208 viewers use up the free minutes, and the rest of the $20 credit covers a few more). Hubfly space becomes the cheaper option at about 255 viewers.

500 viewers: 240,000 viewer-minutes, 4,000 viewer-hours.

  • Mux: input $15.00. Delivery 240,000 − 100,000 free = 140,000 min × $0.0009 (half at the 1080p rate, half at 720p and below) = $126.00. Storage $1.44. Minus the $20 credit: $122.44.
  • Cloudflare: 240 × $1 + $5 = $245.00.
  • IVS: $16 + 4,000 × $0.1008 = $419.20.
  • Hubfly space: bandwidth 4,000 × 1.925 = 7,700 GB − 50 = 7,650 GB × $0.004 = $30.60. Processing $0.25. Speed: peak 500 × 4.28 = 2,139 Mbps, so set 2,500 Mbps for 3 hours per show: (2,500 − 25) × $0.000041 × 12 h = $1.22. Recording $0.25. Total $32.32.

2,000 viewers: 960,000 viewer-minutes, 16,000 viewer-hours.

  • Mux: $15 + (500,000 × $0.0009 + 360,000 × $0.000855) + $1.44 − $20 = $754.24 (Mux's second volume tier kicks in).
  • Cloudflare: 960 × $1 + $5 = $965.00.
  • IVS: $16 + 10,000 × $0.1008 + 6,000 × $0.0924 (second tier) = $1,578.40.
  • Hubfly space: 2,000 viewers at 4.28 Mbps need about 8,555 Mbps at once. A stream server tops out at 2,500 Mbps. This audience doesn't fit one server, so don't use Hubfly space Streams for it today.

The number that decides it: cost per viewer

Strip away the fixed costs and look at what one more full-show viewer adds each month (8 hours watched):

Platform Extra cost per viewer per month
Mux (after the free 100,000 minutes) 480 × $0.0009 = $0.43
Cloudflare Stream 480 × $0.001 = $0.48
Amazon IVS (NA/EU mix) 8 × $0.1008 = $0.81
Hubfly space Streams 8 × 1.925 GB × $0.004 = $0.06

Per-minute vendors don't care how many bits you send. Per-GB pricing does. So the useful question is: at what bitrate does per-GB stop being cheaper?

Mux's 1080p/720p mix works out to $0.054 per viewer-hour. At $0.004 per GB, that buys 13.5 GB an hour, which is a 30 Mbps stream. Against Cloudflare's $0.06 per viewer-hour, the break-even is 33 Mbps. Normal 1080p streams run at 4–8 Mbps, so per-GB pricing wins by a wide margin for typical video. If you stream at very high bitrates (4K, high-motion sports at 25+ Mbps), the gap closes.

Where each competitor wins

Pick on fit first, price second.

  • Mux wins for small audiences and analytics. The 100,000 free delivery minutes plus the $20 credit make a small weekly show free. You also get free Mux Data and Mux Player, live captions (6,000 free minutes) and optional DRM.
  • Cloudflare Stream wins on simplicity and reach. One price per minute, no bitrate math, free encoding, and delivery from Cloudflare's global network. If your viewers are spread across continents, that matters.
  • Amazon IVS wins for interactive and AWS-heavy apps. Real-Time stages for multi-host shows, built-in chat with free messages per input hour, and tight integration with the rest of AWS.
  • Hubfly space Streams wins on cost for mid-size audiences (about 255 to 500 concurrent viewers), and bundles things others charge for: restreaming to YouTube, Twitch and others (restream copies cost bandwidth only, about $0.09 per target per month here, versus $9.60 on Mux and $0.48 on Cloudflare), recording to Storage, and 24/7 playlists.

What Hubfly space Streams doesn't have yet, per its own docs: live captions, DRM, server-side ad insertion, a region picker and automatic failover between media nodes. Cloudflare, Mux and IVS deliver from large global networks; if your audience is spread across continents, weigh that before the price.

How to check these numbers yourself

Every figure above comes from a published price, so you can redo it in a spreadsheet:

  1. Viewer-minutes = viewers × minutes watched per month. Multiply by each per-minute price, after Mux's free 100,000 minutes.
  2. Viewer-hours by resolution for IVS: split viewers across Full HD, HD and SD, multiply by the regional rate.
  3. GB for Hubfly space = viewer-hours × average Mbps × 3,600 / 8 / 1,000. Subtract 50 GB, multiply by $0.004.
  4. Speed for Hubfly space = (cap − 25) × $0.000041 × hours at that cap. Size the cap at peak viewers × average Mbps, with headroom.
  5. Processing = sum of the ladder's billed Mbps × live hours, minus 20, × $0.004.

Swap in your own audience size, show length and quality mix. If most of your viewers watch on phones at 720p, every vendor except Cloudflare gets cheaper.

What can go wrong

  1. You leave speed at 2,500 Mbps all month. That's $74.08 a month instead of $1.22. Fix: raise speed an hour before the show and drop it back to 25 Mbps afterwards. The change applies live, and a server at 25 Mbps costs nothing for speed.
  2. Your audience outgrows the speed cap. When traffic hits the cap, Hubfly space slows delivery instead of dropping viewers, and raises a speed.throttled alert. Fix: size the cap at peak viewers × average bitrate, with headroom, up to the 2,500 Mbps maximum. Above 250 Mbps Hubfly space needs a real deposit first, so add it before the event, not during it.
  3. The 1080p ladder is rejected. The default ladder needs 10.2 Mbps of processing, and new servers start with an 8 Mbps processing cap. Outputs over the cap don't start (and aren't billed). Fix: set the processing cap to 12 or more when you create the server, or in its Settings. On Mux, a similar surprise is that live needs the plus quality level, not basic.

Takeaway

  • Up to about 215 viewers a show: Mux, because it's free.
  • About 215 to 255 viewers: Mux and Hubfly space cost about the same; pick on features.
  • About 255 to 500 concurrent viewers, mostly in one region: Hubfly space Streams, at roughly $0.06 per extra viewer per month versus $0.43–$0.81 elsewhere.
  • Larger, global, or needs captions or DRM: Mux or Cloudflare Stream. IVS if you're building interactive multi-host shows on AWS.

Go further on Hubfly space

  • Restream your show to YouTube, Twitch and Kick from the same server, for the cost of bandwidth.
  • Record every show to Hubfly space Storage and publish it as on-demand HLS video.
  • Run the website that embeds the player on Hubfly space Cell, next to your stream server, so your whole project lives in one place.

Moving from Mux, Cloudflare Stream or IVS? Point your encoder at a Hubfly space RTMPS or SRT ingest URL, swap the player's HLS link, and run your next show on the free tier first. Start free on Hubfly space and see the speed price before you confirm.

title: VR에서 AI를 누가 통제하는가 — VRChat 라벨 논란과 시각 훈련 앱의 다른 설계
description:
VR에서 AI를 누가 통제하는가 — VRChat 라벨 논란과 시각 훈련 앱의 다른 설계

VRChat의 'AI 라벨 거부' 논란, 왜 VR 사용자들이 화가 났을까

Road to VR 보도에 따르면 VRChat은 'AI 생성 콘텐츠' 라벨링 여부를 묻는 설문을 사용자에게 돌린 뒤, 결국 라벨을 붙이지 않기로 했습니다. 저품질 '슬롭' 확산을 걱정하던 커뮤니티는 강하게 반발했습니다.

저는 이 뉴스를 보면서 이상하게 마음이 쓰였습니다. 헤드셋을 쓴 사람에게 '무엇이 진짜인지'는 취향 문제가 아니라 신뢰 문제이기 때문입니다. 2016년, 첫 헤드셋을 쓰고 가상 공간에 들어갔던 밤이 떠올랐습니다. 코끝에 닿던 발포 패드 냄새, 렌즈에 맺힌 뿌연 김, 그리고 손을 뻗었을 때 아무것도 잡히지 않던 그 낯선 감각. 그때 저는 '이 공간이 나를 속이고 있지는 않은가'라는 생각을 처음 했습니다. 그리고 이 논쟁은 시각 훈련 영역에도 그대로 겹치는 질문을 던집니다. AI가 조용히 개입하는가, 아니면 사용자가 직접 조절하는가.

논쟁의 진짜 축은 기술이 아니라 통제권이다

사용자들이 분노한 지점은 AI의 존재 자체가 아니라 불투명성입니다. 무엇이 AI로 만들어졌는지 알 수 없고, 알 방법을 선택할 수도 없다는 것. VR처럼 몰입도가 높은 공간에서는 이 문제가 더 크게 느껴집니다. 헤드셋 안에서는 모든 시야가 시스템이 그린 그림이니까요. 2D 화면에서는 그냥 지나칠 라벨 하나가, VR에서는 '내가 보고 있는 세계 자체에 대한 고지'가 됩니다.

소프트웨어를 만드는 입장에서 보면 이건 설계 결정입니다. 어떤 기능을 자동으로 켤지, 어떤 기능을 사용자 손에 남길지. 기본값과 노출 방식이 곧 신뢰 정책이 됩니다. 이건 추상적인 윤리 담론이 아니라, 코드 레벨의 문제입니다. 토글 하나를 어디에 두느냐가 사용자와 제품 사이의 계약을 다시 씁니다.

같은 질문, 다른 설계: Amblyotube의 경우

약시(amblyopia)와 시각 협응 개선을 원하는 사람들에게도 같은 질문이 적용됩니다. Seven Sports의 Amblyotube는 Meta Quest에서 '사용자가 조절하는' 쪽을 택했습니다. 흐름을 정리하면 이렇습니다.

1. 먼저 사용자가 상태를 선언한다. 앱을 실행하면 약시안이 왼쪽인지 오른쪽인지 직접 지정합니다. 이 선택은 임의적이지 않습니다. 반대로 고르면 우세안을 훈련시켜 버리기 때문에, 개발팀도 이 단계를 '중요'하다고 명시합니다. 이어서 교정 안경을 쓴 상태에서 강도 프리셋(Mild/Moderate/Severe)을 고르거나, 내장된 LogMAR 시력 검사를 실행할 수 있습니다. 이 검사는 표준 Landolt C 시표를 가상 3미터 거리에서 눈별로 최대 30회 시행하고, 임상 계단식 알고리즘으로 logMAR 시력을 산출해 치료 프로필을 자동으로 맞춰 줍니다.

2. 우세안은 '디지털 타임아웃'에 들어간다. Dominant Eye Shader는 더 강한 눈에 블러·대비·밝기·감마·불투명도 필터를 겁니다. 불투명도 100%면 사실상 완전한 디지털 패칭이지만, 목표는 대개 부분 투명도입니다. 두 눈이 동시에 시각 정보를 처리하도록 훈련시키는 것이 핵심이기 때문입니다.

3. 약시안은 도구로 강조된다. AI Sharpener(MFBF 모드)는 영상 속 사람(얼굴·몸)을 감지해 약시안 쪽 화면에만 선택적으로 선명도를 올립니다. 여기에 붉은 외곽선(Outline)과 황록색 하이라이트(Highlight) 같은 시각 강조가 더해지고, 이 효과는 '숨쉬듯' 밝아졌다 어두워지는 펄스로 조절할 수 있습니다. Pulse Hz와 깊이도 사용자가 정합니다.

4. 두 눈이 하나로 합쳐지도록 유도한다. 움직이는 마젠타 초점 단서는 약시안에는 선명한 마젠타로, 우세안에는 옅은 회색으로 보입니다. 자연 영상 배경(피부톤·녹색·파랑)에서 마젠타가 도드라지며 약한 눈의 주의를 끌고, 뇌가 두 신호를 융합하도록 이끕니다. 선택적으로 Wedge Occlusion이 양쪽 시야 일부를 검은 쐐기로 가려 양안 경쟁(binocular rivalry)을 줄이고, 각 눈이 서로 다른 장면 일부를 보게 만듭니다.

여기서 눈여겨볼 점은 AI의 위치입니다. AI는 조용히 개입하는 블랙박스가 아니라, 강도를 사용자가 정하는 보조 엔진입니다. 심지어 Room View(AR 모드)를 켜면 가상 방 대신 실제 방 위에 영상이 겹쳐지고, 컨트롤 패널은 컨트롤러와 핸드 트래킹 어느 쪽으로도 조작할 수 있습니다.

YouTube를 시각 체조로 바꾸는 이유

기술적으로 가장 흥미로운 부분은 입력 콘텐츠입니다. VR 헤드셋은 독립된 두 개의 아이피스, 즉 눈마다 다른 화면을 보낼 수 있는 하드웨어입니다. Amblyotube는 이 구조를 그대로 활용해 양안 훈련(dichoptic training)을 구현합니다. 사용자는 YouTube 스타일 영상을 검색해 보거나, 오프라인에서도 재생되는 아동용 카탈로그를 이용합니다. 접착 패치도, 적청 안경의 색 왜곡도 필요 없습니다.

여기서 잠깐. 저는 이 부분을 읽고 한참을 멈춰 있었습니다. 제 조카가 어릴 적 안경 위에 패치를 붙이고 다니던 모습이 떠올랐거든요. 땀에 젖은 패치 테두리, 자꾸만 손으로 뜯어내던 그 손. 그 아이가 좋아하던 공룡 영상도 패치 때문에 절반은 색이 죽어 보였습니다. 기술이 그 시간을 조금 덜 외롭게 만들 수 있었다면, 하고 생각했습니다.

참고로 적청(anaglyph) 방식이 전체 화면 색을 왜곡하는 반면, 이 방식은 자연스러운 색을 유지합니다. 세션은 하루 30~40분, 최대 1시간을 권장합니다. VR 피로 관리 때문입니다.

누구에게 의미가 있을까

전통적인 패칭을 지루해하던 13세 이상 청소년에게 특히 잘 맞는다고 제품은 설명합니다. 다만 이건 진단도, 치료도, 완치도 아닙니다. 양안 협응과 깊이 지각을 위한 보조적 시각 훈련·교육용 소프트웨어이며, 전문 의료진의 지도를 대체하지 않습니다. 증상이 있다면 안과 전문의와 상담하세요.

VRChat의 논란은 결국 '누가 통제하는가'의 문제였습니다. 시각 훈련 앱도 같은 질문을 피할 수 없습니다. 기본값을 AI가 정하는가, 사용자가 정하는가. Amblyotube는 후자를 택한 구현 사례입니다.

저는 그 선택이 결국 신뢰의 문제라고 생각합니다. 라벨을 붙이든 안 붙이든, 사용자가 손잡이를 잡을 수 있게 두는 것. 그게 오래 가는 설계입니다.

Meta Quest 스토어에서 확인하세요: https://www.meta.com/en-gb/experiences/amblyotube/25906906972338493/

참고: https://roadtovr.com/vrchat-user-backlash-ai-content-label/

title: Hermetic CI/CD Pipeline Design for Game Studios
description:
• Why hermetic builds end the 'works on my machine' firefight
  • Essential components that make a pipeline truly hermetic
  • Practical patterns for hermetic CI/CD with Jenkins, Docker, and GitLab
  • How to cut build time: caching, distributed compilation, and artifact caching
  • Practical playbook: step-by-step implementation checklist

Hermetic CI/CD is the engineering move that converts random, environment-driven failures into repeatable, auditable processes: containerize the build environment, pin the toolchain by digest or lockfile, and treat every input as an explicit, versioned dependency. Making builds hermetic removes the single largest source of wasted time in shipping playable game builds.

Your nightly CI fails intermittently, console certification rejections arrive at random times, and QA validation drags because the build on CI is not the same as the one you run locally. Those are the symptoms of environment drift: SDK and compiler mismatches, asset import differences, non-deterministic build flags, and implicit network dependencies that change over time. The outcome is repeated firefighting: chasing which machine, which SDK, or which environment variable changed since "it worked yesterday".

Why hermetic builds end the 'works on my machine' firefight

A hermetic build treats a build as a function: defined inputs → deterministic process → reproducible outputs. When you make the inputs explicit (base image, SDK bundle, exact tool versions, lockfiles, asset manifests) you make the build verifiable and repeatable. That’s the practical goal behind the broader reproducible builds movement: guarantee that a given source and declared environment produce the same binaries and artifacts every time.

A contrarian, practical insight: hermeticity is not only about security or compliance — it’s about velocity. The upfront cost to lock and automate toolchains buys back hours per week across QA, artists, and engineers by eliminating debugging time spent investigating environment causes. The ROI scales with team size: the more people and platforms, the faster the payoff.

Important: Hermetic does not mean “slowly rigid.” It means declarative and versioned. Keep the runtime flexible, but the build inputs immutable.

: Reproducible Builds — definition and rationale. See Sources.

Essential components that make a pipeline truly hermetic

Every hermetic pipeline contains the same building blocks. Treat this as a checklist you enforce by automation and code:

  • Immutable base images and digest pinning — use image digests (sha256) not floating tags in FROM lines so the base is identical across runs. FROM myregistry/game-builder@sha256:<digest> ensures the same OS + SDK bundle every run.
  • Declarative toolchain bundles — embed or vend the platform SDKs and compiler toolchains into the CI image (or into an immutable Nix/Bazel environment). For consoles where redistribution is restricted, store signed SDK archives in an internal artifact repo and fetch them by checksum.
  • Deterministic build steps and flags — ensure compiler flags, environment variables, and timestamps are reproducible (strip or fix timestamps, sort inputs, use deterministic linkers where possible). Record the canonical build command and environment in ci/ scripts and in your CI job.
  • Build isolation — run builds in ephemeral containers or pod-based agents to remove leftover state and cross-run contamination. Use ephemeral workspaces so absolute paths are consistent across builders.
  • Content-addressed outputs and provenance — publish artifacts by content-hash (or signed versioned artifacts), store an SBOM or manifest containing checksums of inputs, and record the exact image digest, git SHA, and build commands used to produce the artifact. This becomes your audit trail.

Use the container build features that are designed for hermetic builds: pin images by digest and enable BuildKit cache mounts to keep dependency retrieval deterministic and fast. --mount=type=cache keeps package caches between builds without baking them into the image layers, which preserves reproducibility while improving network efficiency.

Example minimal Dockerfile pattern (use BuildKit syntax and pinned base):

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1.4
FROM ubuntu@sha256:... AS toolchain
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/var/cache/apt,sharing=locked \
    apt-get update && apt-get install -y build-essential clang=1:XX-YY

FROM ubuntu@sha256:... AS builder
COPY --from=toolchain /usr /usr
WORKDIR /workspace
COPY . /workspace
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip pip install -r ci/requirements.txt
RUN ./ci/build.sh

# produce a minimal runtime image or export artifacts

Caveat: always record the digest after build (e.g., docker buildx imagetools inspect) and keep that digest in your release metadata.

Practical patterns for hermetic CI/CD with Jenkins, Docker, and GitLab

This section gives battle-tested patterns you can drop into existing pipelines. Every snippet below assumes your build image is already built and pinned (game-builder@sha256:...).

Jenkins (Declarative Docker agent)

  • Use the docker agent or a Kubernetes pod template so each build runs in a pinned image. This avoids controller drift and lets you run the same container locally for reproduction. Example Jenkinsfile: 
pipeline {
  agent {
    docker {
      image 'registry.internal/game-builder@sha256:abcdef123456...'
      args  '--shm-size=1g'
    }
  }
  stages {
    stage('Checkout') { steps { checkout scm } }
    stage('Build') { steps { sh './ci/build.sh' } }
    stage('Archive') { steps { archiveArtifacts artifacts: 'build/artifacts/**', fingerprint: true } }
  }
}

The Jenkins declarative docker agent is a straightforward path to containerized builds for legacy Jenkins farms.

Kubernetes-based ephemeral agents (preferred at scale)

  • Use the Jenkins Kubernetes plugin to spin ephemeral pods where each pod’s container references an immutable image digest. This eliminates agent drift and keeps the controller light. podTemplate (YAML) lets you declare the exact container spec in the pipeline.

GitLab CI with pinned images and caches

  • For gitlab-runner with Docker executor, declare image: by digest, use cache: for intermediate caches, and publish artifacts: on success so downstream stages or QA can consume deterministic builds: 
image: registry.internal/game-builder@sha256:abcdef123456

stages:
  - build
  - test
  - publish

build:
  stage: build
  script:
    - ./ci/build.sh
  cache:
    key: ${CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG}
    paths: [.cache/]
  artifacts:
    paths: [build/artifacts/]
    expire_in: 7d

GitLab’s Docker executor runs builds in isolated containers and GitLab’s Dependency Proxy lets you cache upstream docker blobs to avoid external rate-limit failures.

Secrets, code signing and platform SDKs

  • Keep signing keys and restricted SDKs in an HSM or secret store (Vault / cloud KMS). Use short-lived credentials in CI via the runner/controller credentials mechanism; never bake SDK credentials into images. For console SDKs that cannot be redistributed, CI should retrieve signed SDK archives from an internal artifact repo and verify checksums before install.

Automation patterns you should adopt:

  • Make every build reproducible by script: ci/build.sh should accept --clean and --read-only-network modes.
  • Keep Dockerfile, build scripts, and lockfiles in the same repo as the code that uses them — treat the environment as code.

: Jenkins Pipeline examples for docker agent.

: Jenkins Kubernetes plugin and podTemplate ephemeral agents.

: GitLab Runner Docker executor docs.

: GitLab Dependency Proxy and caching features.

How to cut build time: caching, distributed compilation, and artifact caching

Hermetic builds and speed are not mutually exclusive. You can have both reproducibility and fast iteration by separating the immutable build environment from how you accelerate the build.

  • Compiler-level caching — For C/C++ builds (e.g., Unreal), use ccache, sccache, or engine-aware object caches. sccache supports remote S3/GCS backends and can serve cached object files across CI jobs and developer machines; set SCCACHE_BUCKET and related env vars during CI to share cache storage.
  • Distributed compilation — Use solutions that parallelize or distribute object compilation across a cluster (Incredibuild, FASTBuild, or distributed distcc setups). These tools let you maintain a hermetic toolchain while sharding CPU-bound work across many machines.
  • Remote build caches / action caches — Build systems like Bazel use a content-addressed remote cache (CAS) and action cache; when the action key matches, the output gets reused across machines and CI, providing hermeticity + speed. Use a remote cache server (or bazel-remote) with authentication to give CI exclusive write or read/write policies.
  • Asset import caches — For Unity teams, the Unity Accelerator (local cache server) stores imported assets so editors and CI instances don’t reimport the same FBX/PNG repeatedly; this dramatically reduces asset pipeline time. For Unreal, DDC (Derived Data Cache) and shared shader caches serve a similar role.
  • Dependency proxies and artifact repositories — Mirror and cache external dependencies locally (GitLab Dependency Proxy, Artifactory, Nexus). A local pull-through cache guarantees the same upstream blob is used, prevents outages, and reduces build-network jitter.

Example sccache snippet for CI (environment variables):

export SCCACHE_BUCKET=game-studio-sccache
export SCCACHE_REGION=us-west-2
export SCCACHE_S3_KEY_PREFIX=unreal
export RUSTC_WRAPPER=$(which sccache)
# For C/C++ wrappers, configure CC/CXX to use sccache as wrapper where supported.

sccache has multiple storage backends (S3, R2, Redis) which you can pick based on cost and latency.

When to use which acceleration:

  • Small teams: start with sccache/ccache + artifact repo + dependency proxy.
  • Medium-to-large studios: add distributed compilation (FASTBuild/Incredibuild) and shared DDC/Accelerator for assets.
  • If you use Bazel or similar action-based build systems, configure a remote cache (HTTP/gRPC) and restrict write access to CI workers to avoid cache poisoning.

Practical playbook: step-by-step implementation checklist

Treat this as your rollout plan. Each step ships value and keeps the build green.

  1. Audit and record current environment (2–3 days)
    • Lock git SHA for engine / submodules. Run gcc --version, clang --version, python --version. Produce a short env/ manifest of all tool versions and paths.
  2. Build a pinned base image (1 week)
    • Create a game-builder image that contains compilers, SDK installers, asset importers. Publish with a tag and capture the resulting digest: docker buildx build --push -t registry/internal/game-builder:1.2.3 . then docker inspect to get @sha256:.... Use that digest in CI.
  3. Make local reproducible build script (1 week)
    • Add ci/build.sh that runs the build using --read-only-network and emits an artifact-manifest.json (git_sha, image_digest, build_command, input_checksums).
  4. Convert CI jobs to use pinned images (2–4 days)
    • Update Jenkinsfile and .gitlab-ci.yml to use image: registry/internal/game-builder@sha256:.... Use cache and artifacts to save intermediate results.
  5. Add caching and distributed compilation (2–4 weeks, iterative)
    • Add sccache or ccache. Configure remote backend (S3 or internal object storage). Pilot FASTBuild or Incredibuild on a subset of targets to measure speedups.
  6. Add a dependency proxy and artifact repo (1 week)
    • Stand up GitLab Dependency Proxy, Nexus, or Artifactory and configure CI to prefer those endpoints.
  7. Automate tests in CI (1–2 weeks per engine)
    • Unity: run -runTests with Test Framework in batchmode and publish results as JUnit XML.
    • Unreal: use AutomationTool / Gauntlet to run functional and performance tests as part of CI and publish results artifact.
  8. Instrument and monitor CI (2 weeks)
    • Expose Jenkins/CI metrics to Prometheus or an OpenTelemetry pipeline; track build durations, success rates, cache hit rates, test flakiness. Create Grafana dashboards and alerts for sustained regressions (e.g., build success < 95% for 24h).
  9. Implement release gating and staged rollouts (ongoing)
    • Publish signed, versioned artifacts to a staging repo. Promote artifacts through channels (internal QA → external alpha → production) and use feature flags for progressive delivery (runtime toggles allow safe rollout).
  10. Enforce and educate (ongoing)
    • Make hermetic image build/rebuilds part of PR review. Provide a developer-quickstart.md showing how to run the container locally for reproducing CI builds.
  11. Measure and iterate (always)
    • Track build success rate, mean build time, cache hit ratio, and time-to-recover. Use these to prioritize further automation (more caching, indexed artifact directories, parallelized stages).
  12. Archive and attest
    • For each release, archive artifact-manifest.json, store the image digest, and sign the artifact. Store SBOMs and checksums in your release database for audits.

Runbook snippets (examples):

  • Get digest after pushing: 
docker buildx build --push -t registry.internal/game-builder:1.2.3 .
docker pull registry.internal/game-builder:1.2.3
docker inspect --format='{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' registry.internal/game-builder:1.2.3
# store the returned repo@sha256:...
  • Quick cache hit check for sccache: 
sccache --show-stats

Automated tests are not optional for hermetic flows. Unity’s Test Framework supports -runTests in batchmode and produces NUnit-compatible results; integrate this into your CI so each commit validates both code and asset import behavior. Unreal’s Automation tooling (AutomationTool / Gauntlet / RunUAT) supports running functional and performance suites in CI and reporting structured results.

Prometheus + OpenTelemetry are practical ways to monitor the build farm and CI controller. Instrument build duration, queue depth, cache hit ratios, and test flakiness; wire alerts to Slack or PagerDuty for sustained regressions so they get addressed before blocking production.

Sources:
Reproducible Builds - Explains the concept of reproducible and hermetic builds and why declaring inputs and deterministic builds matter.

Image digests | Docker Docs - How to pin images by digest and why digest pinning ensures immutable base images.

BuildKit | Docker Docs - BuildKit features such as cache mounts (--mount=type=cache) and reproducible build best-practices.

Creating your first Pipeline | Jenkins - Examples showing agent { docker { image ... } } and declarative pipeline patterns.

Kubernetes plugin | Jenkins plugin - Running ephemeral Jenkins agents in Kubernetes pods via podTemplate for agent isolation and reproducibility.

Docker executor | GitLab Runner Docs - How GitLab Runner runs jobs in isolated Docker containers and configuration for caches and images.

Dependency Proxy | GitLab Docs - GitLab's pull-through cache for container images and caching logic for manifests/blobs.

sccache (Mozilla) - GitHub - sccache features, backends (S3/R2/Redis), and configuration options for shared compilation caching.

FASTBuild - High-Performance Build System - FastBuild features for distributed, cached, high-performance builds used by many studios.

Unity Accelerator | Unity Manual - Unity's local cache server to speed up asset imports and reduce editor/CI re-import time.

Unity Test Framework — Command line arguments | Unity Docs - Running Unity automated tests in batch mode and CI-friendly flags.

Unreal Engine 5.1 Release Notes / Automation details - Notes and automation tooling references for UE Automation, Gauntlet, and test runners.

Remote Caching - Bazel Documentation - How Bazel uses action keys and a content-addressed remote cache to provide reproducible cached outputs.

Sonatype Nexus Repository - Artifact repository best-practices for hosting and proxying build artifacts and container images.

Incredibuild Supported Tools - Incredibuild support matrix and how it accelerates compilation and build tasks across large C++ codebases.

OpenTelemetry | Jenkins plugin - Observability and tracing integration for Jenkins, enabling metrics and traces to Prometheus/OpenTelemetry backends.

Prometheus — Overview | Prometheus Docs - Prometheus concepts and guidance for scraping and alerting for CI/CD targets.

Make the build environment a first-class artifact: version it, pin it, and monitor it — the engineering time you invest now becomes consistent velocity for the entire studio.

title: MEMENTO: Learning Context Management for Long Context Processing Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.00244v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM agents that operate over long inputs must perform context management: deciding what to retain in a fixed-size context window. A common approach is compaction, where the model replaces its history with a self-generated note. Yet off-the-shelf agentic models, including GPT-5.5 and GLM-5.3, often write ineffective notes, and reinforcement learning (RL) alone rarely discovers useful note-taking behavior. We present MEMENTO, a long-context agent built on Qwen3-8B and trained to manage its context through compaction. We first bootstrap note-taking by fine-tuning on synthetic trajectories annotated with notes generated in hindsight, then reinforce it with RL using a reward that combines answer correctness, note-quality heuristics, and confidence calibration. Although trained only to compact into a fresh window, MEMENTO extends at test time to strategies such as context folding and confidence-based backtracking. On book-level question answering across four benchmarks, with books of up to 2.5M tokens, MEMENTO raises Qwen3-8B's accuracy from 36.9% to 67.8% while never holding more than 20K tokens in context. It outperforms GPT-5.5 agent in the same harness (13.1%) and full book context (56.7%) at less than 1/50 the cost. It also nearly matches a ~100x larger GLM-5.3 agent (69.3%) at 1/9 the cost, and comes within 6.4 points of GLM-5.3 full context at 1/26 the cost.

title: How Destructuring Is Used in React
description:
1. What Is Destructuring?

Destructuring allows us to extract values from arrays and properties from objects and store them in separate variables.

React uses destructuring in many places, especially with:

  • useState
  • Props
  • Objects
  • API data

2. Destructuring with useState

One of the most common examples is the useState Hook.

import { useState } from "react";

function Counter() {

    const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

    return (
        <div>
            <h1>{count}</h1>

            <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>
                Increase
            </button>
        </div>
    );
}

export default Counter;

Here:

const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

useState() returns an array containing two values:

  1. The current state value.
  2. A function to update the state.

We use array destructuring to extract these two values.

  • count stores the current value.
  • setCount updates the value.

3. Destructuring Props

Props are used to pass data from a parent component to a child component.

Let's understand how destructuring makes working with props easier.

Without Destructuring 

function Student(props) {
    return (
        <div>
            <h2>{props.name}</h2>
            <p>{props.age}</p>
        </div>
    );
}

Here, we use props.name and props.age to access the values.

With Destructuring 

function Student({ name, age }) {
    return (
        <div>
            <h2>{name}</h2>
            <p>{age}</p>
        </div>
    );
}

Both examples produce the same result.

Instead of writing props.name and props.age, we directly extract the properties.

4. Destructuring Props in Parent Components

Let's see how a parent component passes data to a child component.

function Student({ name, course }) {
    return (
        <div>
            <h2>{name}</h2>
            <p>{course}</p>
        </div>
    );
}

function App() {
    return (
        <Student
            name="Lokesh"
            course="React"
        />
    );
}

export default App;

Output:

Lokesh
React

The Student component receives the props and extracts name and course using object destructuring.

5. Destructuring API Data

We can also use destructuring when working with API responses.

const user = {
    id: 1,
    name: "Lokesh",
    email: "lokesh@example.com"
};

const { name, email } = user;

console.log(name);
console.log(email);

Output:

Lokesh
lokesh@example.com

This is useful when an API returns an object containing many properties, but we only need a few of them.

6. Why Is Destructuring Useful in React?

Destructuring helps us:

  • Write cleaner component code.
  • Access props easily.
  • Extract values from useState.
  • Work with API response data.
  • Avoid repeatedly writing object property names.

yakshjethva / jvm-inside-out

JVM

title: How to read PostgreSQL EXPLAIN output
description:
TL;DR

  • Read the plan tree from leaves to root; cost, rows, and width are estimates, not measurements.
  • Start with plain EXPLAIN when execution consequences are unknown. EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement and adds observed time, rows, and loops.
  • Before diagnosing a row-count mismatch, check for early stops and loops. A substantial mismatch in a node that ran to completion warrants investigation.
  • One plan does not prove a cause: check statistics, parameters, and representative conditions. Rollback does not undo nextval sequence advances or resource consumption.

What does a PostgreSQL EXPLAIN plan show?

A PostgreSQL EXPLAIN plan shows the planner's chosen strategy as a tree of nodes, each representing one retrieval or processing step, along with estimated cost, row count, and row width for every node.

Scans sit at the leaves. Joins, sorts, and aggregates appear above them. In text output, the final result is at the top, indented -> lines mark child nodes, and Filter and Index Cond describe nodes rather than forming new ones. Follow rows from leaves to root, but execution order depends on the algorithm: a nested loop rescans its inner child for each outer row, while a hash join builds before probing.

Start with a plan that has just one node. The documented sequential scan of the regression-test table tenk1 in PostgreSQL 18 produces:

Seq Scan on tenk1 (cost=0.00..445.00 rows=10000 width=244)

Four fields appear: 0.00 startup cost, 445.00 total cost, 10,000 estimated rows, and 244 bytes average row width. These figures come from the documented PostgreSQL regression-test database example. They weren't measured in a separate run.

Run EXPLAIN (without ANALYZE) to inspect the tree and fields without executing the statement's planned operations.

What do cost, rows, and width actually mean?

Cost, rows, and width are the planner's predictions based on statistics and configurable cost parameters. They aren't measurements of elapsed time, actual I/O, or observed result size.

The two cost values use a configurable scale, with parameters including seq_page_cost (default 1.0) and random_page_cost (default 4.0). An upper node's cost includes its children's costs, so summing a branch double-counts modeled work. Costs compare modeled work under consistent assumptions. They're neither milliseconds nor portable benchmarks across servers, datasets, or PostgreSQL versions.

Row and width estimates depend on sampled statistics. The planner uses pg_class page and row counts and pg_statistic selectivity information. ANALYZE gathers these by sampling, so estimates remain approximate even after fresh analysis.

To move from predictions to observations, compare rows= with actual rows in an analyzed plan to find where estimates first diverge. Check completion and loops before concluding the estimate is wrong.

What does EXPLAIN ANALYZE add, and what should you watch out for?

EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement and reports actual time (startup and total, in milliseconds), actual rows, and loops alongside the original estimates.

When a node runs more than once (such as the inner side of a nested loop), the reported time and rows are per-execution averages. Multiply these averages by loops to estimate accumulated node time and rows, not the statement's elapsed time.

In the documented LIMIT 2 query against tenk1, the child Index Scan estimates 10 rows if run to completion, but the parent Limit stops after obtaining 2:

Limit (cost=0.29..14.33 rows=2 width=244) (actual time=0.051..0.071 rows=2.00 loops=1)

-> Index Scan using tenk1_unique2 on tenk1 (cost=0.29..70.50 rows=10 width=244) (actual time=0.051..0.070 rows=2.00 loops=1)

(Filter conditions and summary lines omitted from the documented excerpt.)

PostgreSQL explicitly says this isn't an estimation error. Before diagnosing a row-count mismatch, check whether a parent node such as Limit stopped the child early.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE performs INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE with ordinary side effects. The documentation recommends wrapping in a transaction and rolling back, but sequence values from nextval aren't reclaimed after rollback, and resource consumption persists. Use plain EXPLAIN first when execution consequences are unknown.

When does a row-count mismatch actually matter?

A substantial mismatch in a node that ran to completion warrants investigation, but one plan can't establish whether the mismatch changed the plan choice or caused the slow query.

Correlated predicates, skewed distributions, and insufficient distinct-value estimates can produce genuine errors that fresh ANALYZE alone may not fix.

A distinct-value estimate isn't itself an EXPLAIN node-row count. GoCardless reported (engineering blog, last edited September 2022) that PostgreSQL estimated approximately 25,000 distinct payout_id values, while the team's approximate data counts implied almost 3.5 million. The author reports that the distinct-value estimate became stable after the team raised a statistics target to 5,000. Server version, hardware, and hosting aren't established in the account. Check what the statistics represent. The value 5,000 isn't a universal target.

When investigating a mismatch in a node that ran to completion:

  1. Establish execution context: exact SQL, parameters, and PostgreSQL version.
  2. Find where estimated and actual rows first diverge.
  3. Inspect pg_stats for the relevant columns (most_common_vals, histogram_bounds, n_distinct).
  4. Test a targeted remedy and verify under representative conditions.

What are the limits of one EXPLAIN plan?

One plan shows what PostgreSQL chose and, with ANALYZE, what happened during that single execution. It doesn't establish why the plan was slow or that a fix generalizes.

A literal query investigated manually can produce a different plan from a prepared statement's generic plan. EXPLAIN EXECUTE can show the prepared statement's plan. PostgreSQL also warns against extrapolating small-dataset results to substantially different situations.

Treat the plan as a diagnostic starting point. Combine it with statistics inspection, representative data, and (for intermittent problems) auto_explain logging under controlled overhead.

Frequently asked questions about reading PostgreSQL EXPLAIN plans

Are EXPLAIN cost units milliseconds?

No. Costs use a configurable scale. EXPLAIN ANALYZE reports actual time in milliseconds. Don't treat cost comparisons across servers, datasets, or versions as timing measurements.

Does EXPLAIN ANALYZE change my data?

It executes the statement, so INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE can change data, and even SELECT can have side effects when it calls functions such as nextval. Rolling back a transaction doesn't reclaim nextval sequence advances or resource consumption. Use plain EXPLAIN when execution consequences are unknown.

Should I run ANALYZE whenever estimated rows differ from actual rows?

Not automatically. Check for early stops and loops first. If a node that ran to completion still shows a substantial mismatch, inspect relevant pg_stats. Fresh ANALYZE updates sampled statistics but may not resolve the mismatch.

title: OAuth Test Emails Need an Expiry Contract
description:
OAuth tests often fail in a place that does not look like an OAuth problem: the verification email. A test creates a disposable email account, starts a consent flow, waits for a message, and follows a link. If the inbox or link is reused carelessly, the suite can pass while hiding a real account-takeover path.

The useful question is not only “did the email arrive?” It is “what exactly was valid, for whom, and for how long?” I treat every OAuth email fixture as a short-lived security boundary. That makes failures easier to explain and keeps test conveniences from becoming production assumptions.

The hidden risk in OAuth email fixtures

A typical test has three moving parts:

  • an identity or account under test
  • a temporary inbox that receives a verification message
  • a one-time link or code that changes account state

Those parts have different lifetimes. The inbox may live for a test run, the message for a few minutes, and the verification token for only one successful redemption. When a helper uses “the newest email” without checking those boundaries, an old message can satisfy a new test.

That is how a harmless flaky test becomes a misleading security signal. The test may open a valid link from a previous run, or two parallel workers may consume the same message. The result looks green, but the assertion did not prove that the current flow owned the current evidence.

I found it useful to pair this approach with an email test signal pipeline. The pipeline answers what happened; the expiry contract answers whether that evidence was still allowed to matter.

Define the expiry contract

Before writing a helper, write down four limits:

  1. Fixture lifetime: when the inbox lease starts and when it ends.
  2. Message freshness: the earliest timestamp a message may have.
  3. Token lifetime: how long a verification link or code can be redeemed.
  4. Redemption count: whether the test expects one success and then rejection.

For example, a signup test might lease an inbox at 12:00:00, trigger the email at 12:00:03, accept messages received after 12:00:03, and require the link to fail on its second use. The exact values depend on the application, but the rules must be explicit. “Latest message” is not a rule.

The contract should also include a small clock-skew allowance. If the mail provider and application clocks differ by a few seconds, a strict comparison can create noise. Keep that allowance narrow and record it in the test output, so nobody quietly turns it into a ten-minute loophole later.

Separate inbox ownership from token validity

An inbox check proves that a message was delivered to the fixture. It does not prove that the token is valid for the account currently being tested. Those are separate assertions.

For inbox ownership, check the leased address, run identifier, or another non-secret marker in the message metadata. For token validity, check that the link belongs to the expected environment, has not expired, and cannot be redeemed twice. Never log the full token just to make a failure easier to debug.

This separation catches a few common mistakes:

  • a worker reads another worker’s inbox
  • a message from a prior run is accepted
  • a staging link is accidentally tested against production
  • a verification endpoint accepts a replayed token

If the test setup uses a dummy e mail or someone writes tempail in a manual note, keep those strings out of authentication assertions and reports. They are useful search terms for finding old helpers, not proof of ownership.

Record evidence without recording secrets

Every failed attempt should leave a compact evidence record. I normally keep:

type EmailFixtureEvidence = {
  runId: string;
  inboxId: string;
  triggeredAt: string;
  observedMessageIds: string[];
  acceptedMessageId?: string;
  tokenRedeemedAt?: string;
  rejectionReasons: string[];
};

Store message IDs, timestamps, subjects, and rejection reasons. Redact URLs, codes, and authorization values. A record such as “message-184 rejected: received before trigger” is much more useful than a raw email dump, and it is safer to keep in CI artifacts.

For larger suites, a failure ledger for email tests makes repeated timing or ownership failures visible. The ledger should group by reason, not just by test name. Otherwise one broken inbox lease can appear as dozens of unrelated OAuth failures.

A practical test fixture

The fixture can expose a narrow API:

const fixture = await emailFixtures.lease({
  runId,
  expiresInMs: 120_000,
});

const triggeredAt = new Date();
await app.startSignup({ email: fixture.address });

const message = await fixture.waitForMessage({
  since: triggeredAt,
  maxAgeMs: 60_000,
});

await expect(app.verify(message.link)).toSucceedOnce();
await expect(app.verify(message.link)).toFailWith("expired_or_used");

The important part is the shape, not this particular client. The helper owns cleanup, freshness filtering, redaction, and the one-use assertion. Individual tests should describe the account journey, not reimplement security policy every time. That makes the result more consistant across teams, even when the surrounding browser steps differ.

A security checklist for CI

Before trusting an OAuth email test, check:

  • Is every inbox leased to one worker and one run?
  • Is the message timestamp compared with the trigger timestamp?
  • Does the test reject a token after expiry and after first redemption?
  • Are redirect targets restricted to the intended environment?
  • Do logs avoid full links, codes, and authorization values?
  • Does cleanup happen when the browser test fails halfway through?
  • Can the evidence explain the failure without opening the inbox manually?

A little imperfect phrasing in a test description is fine; a more safer default is not. Keep the contract short enough that reviewers can actually verify it. If a helper becomes a mini identity provider, it is probably doing too much.

Final thoughts

Email fixtures are part of the OAuth threat model, even when they exist only in CI. Give the inbox, message, and token separate lifetimes; record useful evidence; and prove one-time redemption explicitly. This turns flaky verification steps into tests that say something meaningful about authentication.

The goal is not to make every test heavy. It is to make the trust boundary visible, so a green result means the current flow owned the current email and the token behaved as intended.

title: AStockArena: Beyond Returns, Can We Entrust Real Capital to the Decisions of Financial Agents?
description:
arXiv:2611.00515v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in dynamic financial trading, yet real-time trading benchmarks mainly evaluate agents by cumulative returns and risk-adjusted performance. Such outcome metrics cannot show whether trades are faithfully reported, supported by available evidence, and consistent with account states. We introduce AStockArena, a real-time decision-auditing benchmark for continuous trading in China's A-share market. Under shared market conditions and execution constraints, we evaluate 13 open- and closed-source models over 3,198 sequential decisions. AStockArena reconstructsthe actions actually posted to accounts by aligning reports, trade requests, execution responses, and account states, and audits them with eight checks spanning execution traceability (O), evidence sufficiency (RK), and financial meta-awareness (B), combining record verification with consensus expert annotation. Of 1,070 trading points, 72.99% exhibit at least one audit gap; model-level rates range from52.2% to 91.2%, with evidence gaps most prevalent. Historical trade-filtering replay further shows thatportfolio outcomes are sensitive to these flagged trades. Decision-process auditing thus offers a verifiable complement to return-based evaluation of financial agents.

title: What a Green Check on a Pull Request Should Promise
description:
Read this article on Signadot.

Most merge gates stop at build, unit tests and contracts. Coding agents clear those easily, so the check that matters most, behavior against the real system, has to run before merge.

Pick a merged pull request with a green check and ask the team what the check guarantees. You will hear which jobs ran. You will rarely hear what anyone downstream can now assume.

That matters because main is shared ground. Other teams cut branches from it, ship their own services against it and, when something breaks, start from the belief that what was already merged is correct. Every merge makes that promise to them, usually without anyone stating its terms.

Leaving the terms vague was cheap while people wrote each change and stuck around to support it. Coding agents undo both. They raise the number of PRs, and a growing share comes from sessions that keep no memory once the work is handed off. For teams verifying AI-generated code on Kubernetes, the merge gate is where that missing context shows up first.

The four questions a merge answers

Remove the tool names and a change has four questions to clear before others should depend on it.

  1. Does it build? The code compiles, clears linting and static analysis, and yields an artifact you can deploy.
  2. Does its logic hold? Unit tests show the code behaves as written, on its own, with its dependencies replaced by stubs.
  3. Does it keep its promises at the boundaries? The API shapes its callers rely on and the message formats it publishes stay compatible.
  4. Does it behave correctly in the running system? Through the real call paths, it returns correct results and stays within acceptable latency, error rate and resource use next to live versions of its neighbors.

Questions one through three are inexpensive. No environment is needed, they parallelize freely and they finish in minutes.

Question four needs a live system, and it alone catches the failure that does the most damage in microservices: code that is right in isolation and wrong in context. One consumer still reads a field that was renamed. A new retry loop triples traffic to a service two hops downstream. A query passes its test and then times out on data shaped like production’s.


Three questions run anywhere in minutes. The fourth needs a live system.

Why most gates stop at question three

Until recently, question four could not be answered before merge. It required an environment with every service up, and such environments were rare, slow to build and costly to run. A typical organization had one or two shared staging copies, always in demand and often broken.

The industry adapted. Changes merged once they cleared the first three questions, and system behavior got checked later, in a shared environment where untested work from every team accumulated. Release management, code freezes and on-call for pre-production grew up largely to handle that accumulation.

Nobody decided on principle that system behavior should be tested after merge. The gate was sized to the infrastructure. Because pre-merge environments were out of reach, the check that needed one moved to the other side of the merge.

The arrangement worked while people set the pace. Ten changes a day in staging could be untangled by reading the log and messaging a few authors, who still remembered their code and could ship a patch.

What coding agents do to a three-question gate

Agents increase the flow of changes. In GitLab’s 2026 research with the Harris Poll, 85% of respondents agreed that AI has shifted the bottleneck from writing code to reviewing and validating it. Nearly all of that extra output clears questions one through three, since those are the checks an agent can run and retry until they pass.

The agent has no view of the consumer three services away, because that consumer is not part of the feedback its loop receives. The cost of that blind spot is measurable. CodeRabbit’s analysis of 470 open-source pull requests found AI-generated PRs contained about 1.7 times as many issues as human-only ones, and logic and correctness issues were 75% more common. A three-question gate now waves through exactly the changes most likely to fail the fourth.

Catching those failures after merge gets harder with every additional change. Tracing a break across ten merged changes is an afternoon. Tracing it across fifty, many from agent sessions that have already ended, turns into a cross-team investigation, and each extra change in the window makes every failure slower to pin down. Release trains feel the same pressure, since batches grow as agents raise the merge rate.

So the old arrangement fails on both sides. More risky changes get through the gate, and the after-merge safety net is too overloaded to catch them.

Answering question four costs seconds now

The infrastructure limit behind that arrangement no longer applies. Giving a single change a realistic system no longer requires cloning the stack.

Here is the approach that replaced cloning. One set of stable services runs in the cluster, kept current by your existing deployment pipeline. For each pull request, only the service or two it modified get deployed beside that set.

The routing layer keeps changes apart. Test requests for a pull request carry a routing key in a header, passed from service to service by standard context propagation such as OpenTelemetry baggage. When a request with that key reaches a service the PR changed, it goes to the PR’s version. Everywhere else it goes to the shared stable version.

So each pull request gets a full, production-like system in which its own code is the only change, and dozens can run side by side on one cluster. Since only the modified services start, the lightweight ephemeral environment is up in seconds, and answering question four costs roughly what a unit test run does.


Question four moves to the left of the merge.

Writing the contract down

Without that limit, the pipeline can split its work cleanly.

CI speeds up once it drops every job that depends on a live system. The pull request takes on integration and end-to-end testing, whether a person or an agent wrote the code. The slow integration stage after merge becomes a quick smoke test or disappears.

What each stage is for changes too. After merge, the pipeline confirms there are no problems instead of hunting for them. The hunting is done before the promise to other teams is made.

Now the contract can be written in full, because each line is checked. The change builds. The logic passes its tests. The interfaces are compatible. The change ran correctly among the real services. A green check means proven, not likely.

The gate is a decision now

For a long time, a merge gated whatever the available environments allowed. That excuse is gone. Testing each change in a realistic system is no longer the costly step, and writing code is no longer what limits delivery. Verifying it is.

The teams getting the most from coding agents are not the ones with the highest output. They are the ones that test system behavior before merge, so extra output turns into shipped features rather than a backlog of unproven changes. Merging to test is the habit that change retires.

Signadot supplies the pull request stage in the table above: lightweight ephemeral environments on the Kubernetes cluster you already run, plus Jobs that execute integration and end-to-end suites inside them for every PR. Signadot for agentic development shows how that stage fits an agent-heavy pipeline. What stays with your team is deciding what a green check should guarantee, and writing that down.
