title: Building a software factory for AI SDK
description:
The AI SDK is one of the most popular open-source AI projects in the world. It serves over 20 million npm downloads a week and the repo has over 26,000 stars. Maintaining the codebase means tracking four moving targets at once:

  • Model providers: new providers, new capabilities, and new bugs

  • UI frameworks: bindings for React, Next.js, Svelte, Vue, and others

  • Sandboxes: the execution environments agents run code in

  • Harnesses: adapters for Codex, Claude Code, Pi, and others

After multiple years of growth, the repo was getting 100+ new issues every month, and when Anthropic's Opus 4.6 model was released, PRs hit an inflection point. By late June, that compounding had accumulated over 1,000 open issues and almost 800 pull requests.

That backlog is not a discipline problem. No maintainer, however good, can close that gap by working harder, and because generating code is cheap, it will only grow.

Instead of trying to scale ourselves, we built a software factory. Four weeks in, it authors between 25 and 35% of PRs we merge and closes 70-80% of issues.

Deciding what type of factory to build

Before we built anything, we had to answer three questions:

  • Why our existing approach using agents wasn't enough

  • What level of automation fit a project like the AI SDK

  • How to align automation and human effort to risk

Why not add more agents?

The best maintainers are already using agents aggressively. Mitchell Hashimoto runs Ghostty with the goal of an agent always working, and encodes every agent failure in AGENTS.md so it never repeats. Simon Willison runs four coding agents in parallel, and review bots like Vercel Agent and CodeRabbit sit on millions of repos. Other maintainers like Daniel Stenberg have opted to block AI-generated submissions to curl.

All of it helps, but none of it solves for the core constraint: every one of these solutions still routes every change through one human's attention. We believe that human accountability is still the core of trust in agentic engineering, so we knew our factory needed to solve for reviewer efficiency as a first principle.

What kind of automation fits AI SDK?

Software factories sit on a spectrum. At one end is full automation, where agents write, ship, and deploy without a human ever reading the code. In the middle are harnesses like Codex and Claude Code, where a person steers an agent or fleet of agents. At the far end is software you barely want to automate because the risk is too high, like firmware in a pacemaker or self-driving vehicle.

The AI SDK needs to operate closer to the careful end. It is foundational AI infrastructure with millions of applications built on top, so quality and security are non-negotiable, and a human needs to have control over what ships. We needed our factory to heavily automate the lifecycle around the human, without removing them.

How do we align automation and effort to risk?

For a given change, the depth of human review needed scales with risk.

Centralized roadmaps with detailed feature specs can define risk up front and directly shape the work going into a software factory. But open-source projects like AI SDK also get issues and pull requests from the community, and there is no guarantee they align with the goals of the project, or that changes are safe to make. Higher risk means human judgment is an even more critical part of the system.

To optimize our factory for that judgment, we knew agents had to go beyond generating code based on a request; they needed to evaluate full units of work in the context of the entire project.

Our goal was for the factory to generate a comprehensive assessment of each change for both fit and risk, including a full chain of documented evidence, making it easy for reviewers to apply the right amount of effort:

  • Docs fixes get a quick glance for verification

  • Well-defined provider changes get focused validation

  • A new public API gets deep review

What we built

ai-sdk-factory is a software factory that autonomously processes incoming issues and pull requests for AI SDK. Agents in the factory perform specific, reviewable tasks, like reproducing bugs, implementing features, and creating backports for older SDK versions. A human stays in control throughout the entire process, including merging every change.

We didn't ship the factory in one swing. We built it incrementally, starting at the beginning of the process with classification of issues as bugs, features, or documentation updates. That first step not only gave us more visibility into the shape of the backlog, but also passed helpful context to the other specialized agents we built later.

We prototyped multiple ways to build each new type of functionality, and in the process developed a set of guiding principles that shaped the architecture of the factory that went into production.

Build one agent per task

Once our classification agent reached a high level of accuracy, we focused on automating bug reproduction, fixes, and review of those fixes. We explored building a single agent equipped with skills for each step, but quickly realized that would come with a higher maintenance and troubleshooting burden over time.

Instead, we built a single agent for each specific task, making every new capability easier to reason about, test in isolation, and debug. Each one is scoped to a specific job, with its own prompts, context, and evals.

Today the factory has dedicated agents for every step in the flow:

  • Bug reproduction

  • Bug fixes

  • PR reviews

  • Backports

  • Documentation updates

  • Feature analysis

  • Feature implementation

Secure everything from the start

We implemented security with the second agent, because bug reproduction was the first step where the factory executed code based on content it didn't control.

A factory operating on a public repository has to assume attacker-controlled input: every issue, pull request, comment, and the links inside them are untrusted. Because successful open-source projects are high-value targets, threats range from malicious code changes and supply chain attacks to resource exhaustion, API key exfiltration, and prompt exfiltration.

Sandboxes are the foundation of our defense. Every agent in ai-sdk-factory runs inside an isolated Vercel Sandbox containing its code, its runtime, and only the secrets the agent's specific task needs. With those guardrails, untrusted content can shape what an agent proposes, but the damage any one task can do is contained to the sandbox.

We also built a shielding layer around the sandbox that controls what agents can reach over the network, blocking the paths an attacker would use to pull secrets out of the isolated environment.

The last line of defense is human review: nothing is merged without approval from a human on the AI SDK team.

Build value locally, then move to the cloud

The first several agents we built for the factory ran through a local CLI. That enabled our team to iterate quickly as we noticed inaccuracies, felt friction, and prototyped different ideas.

Once multiple steps were running reliably through the CLI, we were ready to move the system onto managed infrastructure. ai-sdk-factory uses:

  • Vercel Functions for the API, workers, and webhook ingress

  • Vercel Queues for task execution

  • Vercel Blob for logs

  • Vercel Sandbox for the agent workspaces

  • Neon Postgres for factory data

Today, GitHub webhooks feed the issue queue, and as soon as they arrive workers automatically pull them and kick off agent runs in sandboxes. We also built a monitoring UI that tracks every run in parallel, and visualizes the queue for the team of reviewers.

Shipping software through our factory

On July 24, a community member asked for blocked-domain support in OpenAI web search, and the request became issue #17898. The following section explains every step the software factory went through to process the issue, open a pull request with an implementation of the feature, and ultimately backport the merged feature to v5 and v6 of the SDK.

Classification

The first agent that runs in the factory classifies issues and pull requests. In this case, the ai-sdk-factory bot commented on the issue and applied a label, identifying the type as Feature with high confidence. The agent included its rationale for the classification in the comment.

Analysis

After classification, the analysis agent runs. Agents in the factory don't make any assumptions about the technical validity of a feature request or bug, so the analysis agent wrote a probe to confirm the absence of support for blocked domains. issue-17898-type-probe.ts was generated and run, and failed with an error when it looked for blocked-domains and didn't find it.

The failing probe proved the feature was missing on main, and the agent included it in the analysis as evidence.

The analysis agent then used the results of its investigation to build out a spec for the feature: add an optional blockedDomains filter to the existing web-search tool and map it to the provider's blocked_domains field.

The agent also confirmed the spec fit the SDK's provider-adapter architecture and was backward compatible, and even scoped documentation changes.

Implementation

Another agent then implemented the spec and opened a pull request. The implementation agent ran a live end-to-end test, executing an OpenAI web search with wikipedia.org blocked and confirming the domain wasn't reachable. The test was included as additional evidence on the pull request.

Automated review

Next, a review agent scored the change, and when it didn't find any concerns, approved it. The agent rated the feature as fully implemented, with:

  • Side-effect risk: low

  • Performance risk: none

  • Backwards-compatibility risk: low

Human review

Finally, Lars read the chain of evidence from the agents, reviewed the code changes, and merged PR #18033 into main.

Backporting

Once Lars merged the initial PR, ai-sdk-factory opened additional PRs for two backports, #18035 for v6 and #18036 for v5. The v5 backport did not apply cleanly, so the factory agent labeled and committed the conflicted state, identified and validated a fix, and pushed it seventeen minutes later. After review, Lars merged both backport PRs.

Results

We are just over four weeks into running the software factory in production. Here are the results:

PRs merged to main

Between 25-35% of the PRs we merge on a weekly basis are now authored by ai-sdk-factory agents.

Backports

Factory PRs are above 50% of weekly merges to the v6 release line, and v5 looks similar. Backports used to be work we skipped because dealing with merge conflicts wasn't worth the effort. v5 and v6 get far better support now.

Issues

In July, over 75% of closed issues were closed by the factory.

Open issues fell from a peak of 1,022 in late June to 844 by early August, and open bugs are down roughly 25%.

The ai-sdk-factory runs in public, so you can see every pull request it has authored on the repo.

Improving the factory becomes the job

The most interesting part of running the factory is what happens when it fails. Every run ends one of four ways: success, flawed, blocked, or manual. Only success ships, so the rest are signal that re-enters the system as feedback.

  • A flawed run means an agent produced the wrong thing, and the fix is better prompts, better context, or a new eval case so the same mistake gets caught automatically next time

  • A blocked run means the environment was missing something, like a credential, a service, or a dependency, and the fix is provisioning it

  • A manual run marks a boundary we drew on purpose, and forces us to ask whether improvements in the factory justify removing it

Each of those fixes expands the automation boundary, and every week the factory can handle work that it couldn't be trusted with before.

Running the factory is the same discipline teams already apply to their test suites and pipelines, but pointed at the system that does the work, instead of the system that checks it. In a world where agents define the SDLC, improving the factory will become the standard engineering job.

title: Startup App Avatar Storage: A Large-File Cleanup Runbook for Support Receipts
description:
Large-file throughput changes the answer. For a startup customer-support app, put original receipts and avatar images in private object storage, write resized variants as separate objects, and let the application database decide which generation is active. Use lifecycle cleanup for disposable work, but keep replacement cleanup and thumbnail ownership in application logic.

That is the operationally boring answer, which is exactly what an SRE should want.

How should a startup app handle avatar image storage, thumbnails, and lifecycle cleanup?

Start with a generation boundary. An upload gets a unique generation, such as gen-018; the original and every derivative live below that prefix. The database changes its active pointer only after the required objects exist. A replacement therefore cannot publish an original from one upload and a thumbnail from another.

For support receipts, keep the original even if the interface only displays a thumbnail. Store byte size, content type, checksum, generation, processing state, and retention class in the database. Object storage is not a metadata query engine: use the database to answer who owns a file and which generation is current.

Infrai fits teams that want the storage step behind a plain REST API: the same HTTP pattern works from Go or another language without installing an SDK. Its broader platform surface also lets a small team keep one key and one billing boundary across backend capabilities, while this workflow still keeps the actual receipt bytes private in object storage. I would recommend it for a startup that needs private puts and application-controlled thumbnail processing, provided the team accepts the storage limits described below.

The code path should be retryable. A client-supplied idempotency key makes a retry of the same object write unambiguous, and a 429 must cause a delayed retry rather than a tight loop.

Keep it private.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func putPrivateObject(data []byte, idempotencyKey string) error {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if apiKey == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    objectPutPath := "/storage/object" + "/put/"
    endpoint := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1" + objectPutPath + "support-receipts/user-42/gen-018/original.jpg"
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPut, endpoint, bytes.NewReader(data))
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "image/jpeg")
        req.Header.Set("X-Object-ACL", "private")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idempotencyKey)

        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            return nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests || attempt == 3 {
            return fmt.Errorf("object write returned %s: %s", resp.Status, body)
        }

        delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
        if retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); retryAfter != "" {
            if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); parseErr == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
        }
        time.Sleep(delay)
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("object write retry limit reached")
}

func main() {
    if err := putPrivateObject([]byte("image bytes"), "receipt-user-42-gen-018-original"); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
}

The bucket should remain private, with short-lived presigned access issued only after the application checks ownership. Do not send the Infrai authorization header to that returned URL. Public-read storage is a poor fit for receipts and is also the wrong default for profile images that users may later remove.

The cleanup signal is stale bytes, not an empty-looking UI

Lifecycle rules are useful for tmp/ uploads and abandoned processing outputs. They are not a transaction with the database. The shortest expiry granularity is one day, so a product promise such as “delete after 30 minutes” needs a worker that reads application state and deletes the object explicitly. Multipart fragments need their own cancellation policy; lifecycle does not automatically clear them.

Thumbnail work should derive its output key from the immutable generation and variant, then write thumb-128 and thumb-512 independently. If the processor stops after the first derivative, the database must keep the new generation inactive. Retried work should be safe to replay. Consider a user who uploads a replacement while the first receipt is still being resized: the old generation remains readable, the new generation remains pending, and a worker can resume without guessing which files belong together. Only the database switch publishes the complete set; deletion starts after that switch and after the old generation's retention window. That ordering costs a little extra temporary storage, but it prevents a slow derivative from turning into a missing image during a support conversation.

Capacity planning needs the largest receipt, concurrent uploads, derivative expansion, retry overlap, and cleanup lag. A test using 50 KB avatars says little about 20 MB receipt uploads. Track p95 and p99 upload time, worker queue age, bytes written per minute, and the time from replacement to deletion; set an SLO for those signals before “cleanup later” becomes an undocumented retention policy.

Monitor bucket usage as users replace avatars. Old originals and abandoned variants can accumulate even when the product appears healthy, and there is no metadata search to rescue a weak ownership index. A nightly reconciliation pass should compare active database generations with expected object keys, flag missing derivatives, and report retired prefixes beyond their cleanup deadline.

Which storage boundary should the platform team buy or build?

S3 compatibility is a useful starting contract, not proof of feature parity. Compare the controls that affect trust boundaries: private access, region placement, retention and deletion behavior, versioning, object lock, conditional writes, CORS, replication, and migration tools.

Option Good fit Trade-off for this workflow
Amazon S3 Teams that need the broadest mature object-storage control surface More provider-specific controls can mean more integration coupling; generation state and cleanup still belong in the application
Cloudflare R2 A team evaluating S3-compatible object storage for private application objects Verify region, lifecycle, access, and recovery behavior against the current documentation rather than assuming compatibility covers them
Backblaze B2 A team comparing another S3-compatible storage service Validate large-file throughput, retention controls, and operational tooling before treating storage economics as the decision
Infrai storage A small team that values one plain REST API and a single key across backend capabilities The interface is intentionally narrower: private objects and application logic fit, but specialist retention and portability requirements may not

The catch is that this storage option is not suitable for permanent public links, static-site hosting, object versioning, WORM retention, strict If-Match concurrency, browser direct uploads that require self-service CORS configuration, cross-region automatic replication, or cross-cloud bulk migration. A specialist provider is the better choice when any of those is a hard requirement. Keep the database as the authority either way.

What should verification and rollback prove before launch?

Exercise four cases: an upload rejected before the database switch, a processor stopping after one thumbnail, a committed switch followed by delayed deletion, and two replacements for one user. The invariant is simple: the active record names one complete generation, never a mixture of generations.

Retries happen.

Separate alerts for missing active objects and excess retired objects. The first is an availability problem; the second is a cost and retention problem. For a failed write, surface the response body and status instead of treating every non-success response as a transient condition.

Rollback is a pointer move while the prior generation still exists: restore that verified generation, stop its deletion job, and quarantine the new set. Once the old objects are gone, rollback requires a separate recovery copy or a provider configuration with an explicit recovery guarantee. If that guarantee matters, choose the specialist storage control rather than pretending a private avatar bucket is an archive.

I am not sure there is one correct reconciliation interval. It should follow the deletion SLO, object count, and scan cost; start with a measurable interval and adjust it from queue age and stale-byte growth.

If your system needs private receipt and avatar objects, application-owned derivatives, and a simple HTTP integration, Infrai is worth trying for the object-write part of the workflow. Start with its storage thumbnail guidance and verify the region, deletion, and recovery boundaries against your own requirements.

Sources

  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/
  • https://www.backblaze.com/cloud-storage/pricing
  • https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.object.put

title: Highlighting text without wrapping it in spans: the CSS Custom Highlight API
description:
The CSS Custom Highlight API is a browser API that lets you style arbitrary ranges of text by registering Range objects in a Highlight, adding it to CSS.highlights under a name, and targeting that name with the ::highlight() pseudo-element. The DOM stays exactly as it was: no <span>, no <mark>, no extra nodes.

I ran into this while building a highlights-and-notes feature, and it changed how I think about the problem. This post covers why the old approach hurts, how the native API works, what support looks like today, and what you still have to build yourself.

What is wrong with wrapping highlights in spans?

For about fifteen years, the standard way to highlight text on a web page was to split text nodes and wrap the pieces in elements. mark.js wraps matches in <mark>. Rangy's highlighter and web-highlighter wrap them in <span>. It works, but it has costs:

  • You are editing a DOM someone else owns. In React, Vue or Svelte, the framework assumes it controls the nodes it rendered. If a library splits a text node and inserts a <span>, the next re-render can throw the highlight away, or fail outright when the framework tries to update a node that is no longer where it expected. If you've ever seen Failed to execute 'removeChild' on 'Node' after a third-party script touched your markup, you know what this looks like.
  • Overlapping highlights get messy. Two highlights that partly overlap need nested or split wrappers, and removing one means stitching text nodes back together correctly.
  • Selectors and styles change. p > a or :first-child can stop matching once extra elements appear. Copy and paste, textContent offsets and screen readers can all pick up the new structure.
  • Cleanup is your problem. Every "remove highlight" has to unwrap and normalize the nodes, or the DOM slowly fills with fragments.

None of this is a bug in those libraries. When they were written, wrapping was the only way to paint text.

How does the CSS Custom Highlight API work?

There are three pieces:

  1. Range: the same DOM Range you get from document.createRange() or new Range(), with a start and end inside text nodes.
  2. Highlight: a set-like object that holds one or more ranges.
  3. CSS.highlights: a registry (a HighlightRegistry, which behaves like a Map) where you give each Highlight a name. CSS then styles that name with ::highlight(name).

Here is the minimal version, with no library:

<p id="intro">The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.</p>

::highlight(note) {
  background-color: #fde68a;
  color: inherit;
}

if (typeof CSS !== 'undefined' && 'highlights' in CSS) {
  const textNode = document.getElementById('intro').firstChild;

  const range = new Range();
  range.setStart(textNode, 4);  // start of "quick"
  range.setEnd(textNode, 19);   // end of "fox"

  const highlight = new Highlight(range);
  CSS.highlights.set('note', highlight);

  // Later, to remove it:
  // CSS.highlights.delete('note');
}

Open DevTools after running this: the <p> still has a single text node. The browser paints the range, but nothing in the tree changed, so React (or anything else) can re-render the paragraph and the highlight is still painted as long as the range points at live nodes.

A few things the spec deliberately limits:

  • Only some properties apply inside ::highlight(): color, background-color, text-decoration and its longhands, text-shadow, and a handful of others. No padding, no border, no layout changes. That is the point: painting, not layout.
  • Ranges are live. If the DOM under a range changes, the range moves or collapses with it. That's great for small edits and a problem when a framework replaces the whole node (more on that below).
  • Highlights are not elements, so they get no events. There's no click on a highlight. You hit-test yourself: get the caret position from the pointer with document.caretPositionFromPoint() and check which range contains it, or compare the pointer against range.getClientRects(). A newer CSS.highlights.highlightsFromPoint() does this for you, but support is still partial (see below).
  • Priority. When highlights overlap, highlight.priority decides which one paints on top.

Which browsers support the CSS Custom Highlight API?

Checked on 3 November 2026 against MDN's browser-compat-data and the web-features "Custom highlights" entry:

Browser Highlight / CSS.highlights ::highlight() styling
Chrome / Edge 105 (2022) 105
Safari (macOS and iOS) 17.2 (December 2023) 17.2
Firefox 140 partial from 140 to 148: text-decoration works from 146, text-shadow from 149. Full from 149

The feature became Baseline "newly available" on 24 March 2026, when Firefox 149 shipped full ::highlight() support. Two caveats worth knowing:

  • In Safari, ::highlight() styles are ignored on text that also has user-select: none.
  • CSS.highlights.highlightsFromPoint() is only in Chrome 140+ and Firefox 150+ (Safari has it in preview), so keep a manual hit-test fallback.

If you need to support older browsers, there is no polyfill that keeps the "no DOM changes" property. You either fall back to wrapping, or you simply don't show highlights there.

What do you still have to build yourself?

The native API paints ranges. That's all it does. For a real highlights-and-notes feature, you still need:

  • Persistence. A Range is a pair of node references. It can't be saved to localStorage or a database. You need to serialize it into something stable.
  • Re-anchoring. When the page loads again, or the content was edited, or a framework re-rendered and replaced the text nodes, you have to find the text again and build fresh ranges. Character offsets alone break as soon as one word changes above your highlight.
  • Selection UI. Turning a user's selection into a highlight, and showing a toolbar or note editor next to it.
  • Hit-testing, as above, to open the note when someone clicks a highlight.
  • Framework lifecycle. Creating and destroying everything when a component mounts and unmounts, and not running on the server during SSR.

How does penciled build on top of it?

This is the part where I talk about my own project. I wrote penciled (penciled.org, JavaScript highlights & notes library), an MIT-licensed library of about 15 kB that does the list above on top of the Custom Highlight API. It never inserts elements into your content, and it has no wrapping fallback.

The default setup, with a built-in toolbar and note editor:

import { annotate } from 'penciled';
import 'penciled/styles.css';

const penciled = annotate('#article', {
  documentId: 'my-post',
  storage: 'local', // or 'memory', or your own adapter with load/save
});

const off = penciled.on('create', (annotation) => {
  console.log('created', annotation);
});

What it handles:

  • Persistence: localStorage by default, or a custom storage adapter (an object with load and save, plus optional create, update and delete) to sync with your backend. export() and import() move annotations around, and toW3C() converts them to the W3C Web Annotation format.
  • Anchoring: each annotation stores the quoted text, a short prefix and suffix, and start/end positions. On load, penciled tries the stored position, then exact matches of the quote, then a fuzzy match, and only accepts a result above a confidence threshold. If the text really is gone, the annotation isn't silently painted in the wrong place. It's marked as an orphan, fires an orphan event and stays in storage.
  • Notes: each highlight can carry a note, with a color and an indicator for highlights that have notes.
  • React: penciled/react exports an <Annotatable> component and a useAnnotations() hook. It's SSR-safe, because the instance is only created in an effect, and React can re-render the annotated content as often as it likes: 
import { Annotatable } from 'penciled/react';
import 'penciled/styles.css';

export function Post({ post, children }) {
  return (
    <Annotatable as="article" options={{ documentId: post.id }}>
      {children}
    </Annotatable>
  );
}
  • Headless: penciled/headless (about 6 kB) is the same engine without the UI. You get select events with the selected range and build your own toolbar: 
import { annotate } from 'penciled/headless';

const penciled = annotate('#article');

penciled.on('select', (context) => {
  if (!context || context.annotation || !context.editable) return;
  // position your own button using context.range.getBoundingClientRect()
  // then: penciled.create(context.range, { color: 'yellow' });
});

Highlights are registered as named highlights (penciled-<color>, penciled-<color>-noted, penciled-active), so you can style them with ordinary ::highlight() rules.

How does it compare to mark.js, Rangy and other options?

Honestly, it depends on what you need. These numbers come from my own comparison page, measured on 22 October 2026 (sizes are min+gzip):

Library How it paints Size Notes
mark.js wraps in <mark> ~6.2 kB Built for search-term highlighting, not saved annotations. Last release 8.11.1 in January 2018, still ~1.9M weekly downloads.
Rangy wraps in <span> ~22.7 kB A broad range/selection toolkit with a highlighter module. Latest 1.3.2.
web-highlighter wraps in <span> ~9.4 kB Persistence-oriented, and works back to IE11, which the native API can't.
@recogito/text-annotator separate overlay layer ~22.4 kB BSD-3, W3C annotation model, strong for collaborative and scholarly annotation.
Annotator.js jQuery-based — Last released in 2015. Hypothesis was originally built on it.
penciled CSS Custom Highlight API ~15 kB (~6 kB headless) No DOM changes, persistence and fuzzy re-anchoring built in. Pre-1.0, with far fewer users (~640 weekly downloads).

My rough guide:

  • Highlighting search matches on a static page? mark.js is small and battle-tested.
  • Need IE11 or very old browsers? You need a wrapping library such as web-highlighter or Rangy.
  • Collaborative, shared annotation with accounts and groups? Look at Hypothesis or Recogito.
  • Persistent personal highlights and notes in a modern app, especially one rendered by React, where you can't let a library rewrite your markup? That's the case I built penciled for.

If you only need to paint a few ranges, you don't need any library. The ten lines of native code above are enough.

Where can I try it?

Docs and a live demo are at penciled.org, and the source is on GitHub. There's also a free browser extension for Chrome, Firefox and Edge built on the same library, if you just want to highlight pages you read.

I'm Marcel Losso, the creator and maintainer of penciled, so weigh my comparison accordingly. Corrections and issues are very welcome on GitHub.

Vercel Agent now works in Slack code channels, a new kind of channel launched today for working with a coding agent. Anyone in the channel can follow the work, give Agent new instructions, and review the code it writes.

Choose Create a code channel from the Slack sidebar, select Vercel as the agent, and describe what you need to get started. You can also ask Agent to create one from an existing channel or thread. It brings that context with it to the new channel.

Use code channels to investigate incidents, write and review code as a team, or manage ongoing work such as dependency upgrades and migrations.

Inside a Vercel Agent code channel:

  • Follow the work: Agent posts relevant deployments, logs, errors, and diffs in the channel as it works.

  • Talk without repeated @Vercel mentions: Agent follows the conversation, recognizes which messages are for it, and continues when the team gives it more work.

  • Review pull requests: Ask Agent for a PR review and it posts its findings in the channel. It can find bugs outside the diff, and explain failing checks and their root causes.

  • Approve every change: Agent is read-only by default and never exceeds the requester's permissions. Before making a change, it drafts a plan and waits for approval. For every action, Vercel records who requested and approved it and what Agent ran.

  • Stop work at any time: The person who created the code channel can cancel an active task.

Vercel Agent in Slack code channels is available in public beta for Pro and Enterprise teams. Add Vercel to Slack, learn about Slack Code, or read the docs.

title: Testing accessibility in AG Grid: a grid-aware helper for Jest and Playwright
description:
Dense data grids are where accessibility problems like to hide. A table with thousands of rows, virtualized columns, inline buttons and color-coded values can look fine and still be hard to use with a keyboard or a screen reader.

General tools such as axe-core are great for checking a page. They are not built around grid-specific questions: Is the total row count exposed when rows are virtualized? Does the arrow key actually move focus one cell? Is a status shown only by a colored dot?

So I wrote a small helper, ag-grid-a11y-test, that adds grid-aware checks on top of the tools you already use. This post shows how to use it.

Status: early preview (alpha), not on npm yet. The code is public on GitHub and I am sharing it so people can try it and give feedback. The rules come from the ARIA grid pattern and AG Grid's commonly rendered markup. I have not yet validated them against every AG Grid version, so treat findings as prompts to investigate, not proof of conformance. Your feedback will decide what changes next.

What it checks

Structure (works in jsdom or a real browser):

  • The grid has a grid or treegrid role and an accessible name
  • aria-rowcount and aria-colcount are present and consistent with row and column indexes (important for virtualized grids)
  • Rows and cells have aria-rowindex and aria-colindex
  • Column headers have accessible names (this catches icon-only headers)
  • Sortable headers expose aria-sort

Patterns common in financial and data-heavy tables:

  • Icon-only buttons and checkboxes with no accessible name
  • Cells that show only an icon or colored element, with no text
  • Negative values shown by color alone (opt-in, you tell it your CSS class)
  • Abbreviated numbers like 1.2M (advisory)

Keyboard navigation (real browser, via Playwright):

  • Arrow keys move focus one cell and return to the start
  • Tab can eventually leave the grid (a warning if not, since a very large grid can cause false positives)

Each finding has a severity: error (very likely a real problem), warning (verify), or info (advisory).

Install

The package is not published to npm yet, so install it from the GitHub repo. Clone it and build a local package:

git clone https://github.com/Hitesh-Gharate/accessibility.git
cd accessibility
npm install
npm run build
npm pack   # creates ag-grid-a11y-test-0.1.0.tgz

Then install that file into your Angular project (adjust the path):

npm install --save-dev ../accessibility/ag-grid-a11y-test-0.1.0.tgz
# optional, for the axe-core adapter
npm install --save-dev axe-core

The examples below import from ag-grid-a11y-test, which is the package name inside that file.

Use it in an Angular unit test (Jest) 

import { TestBed } from '@angular/core/testing';
import { auditGrid, assertNoViolations, formatReport } from 'ag-grid-a11y-test';
import { PositionsGridComponent } from './positions-grid.component';

it('positions grid passes accessibility checks', async () => {
  const fixture = TestBed.createComponent(PositionsGridComponent);
  fixture.detectChanges();
  await fixture.whenStable();
  fixture.detectChanges();

  const result = auditGrid(fixture.nativeElement, {
    gridSelector: '.ag-root',
    negativeValueClasses: ['loss'], // your app's class for negative values (optional)
  });

  console.log(formatReport(result)); // everything, including warnings and info
  assertNoViolations(result);        // fails the test on errors only
});

jsdom has no layout engine, so AG Grid may not render rows unless virtualization is turned off in your test grid options. Check the AG Grid docs for the exact option names in your version.

A failing result reads like this (an example of the report format):

Grid accessibility audit: 1 error(s), 0 warning(s), 0 info.
  [ERROR] grid-rowcount: The grid is missing a valid integer aria-rowcount (use -1 if the total is unknown).
      at div.ag-root
      help: Without it, virtualized grids do not tell assistive technology how many rows exist.

To be stricter, use assertNoViolations(result, { failOn: ['error', 'warning'] }). To silence a rule you have reviewed, use ignoreRules: ['abbreviated-number'].

Use it in a real browser (Playwright)

A real browser is the most reliable option, and it is the only way to test keyboard behavior.

import { test } from '@playwright/test';
import AxeBuilder from '@axe-core/playwright';
import { auditKeyboardNavigation, fromAxeResults, mergeResults, assertNoViolations } from 'ag-grid-a11y-test';

test('positions grid is accessible', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/positions');
  await page.waitForSelector('.ag-root [role=gridcell]');

  // 1. Structure and pattern checks, executed inside the page
  await page.addScriptTag({ path: require.resolve('ag-grid-a11y-test/browser') });
  const domResult = await page.evaluate(() => {
    const lib = (window as any).AgGridA11y;
    return lib.serialize(lib.auditGrid(document.body, { gridSelector: '.ag-root' }));
  });

  // 2. axe-core, scoped to the grid
  const axe = fromAxeResults(await new AxeBuilder({ page }).include('.ag-root').analyze());

  // 3. Keyboard navigation
  const keyboard = await auditKeyboardNavigation(page, { gridSelector: '.ag-root' });

  assertNoViolations(mergeResults(domResult, axe, keyboard));
});

All three sources are merged into one report, so axe findings and grid-specific findings appear together.

What it cannot do

Please read this part before relying on it:

  • Automated checks find only a subset of accessibility problems. You still need manual keyboard testing and screen reader testing (NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver).
  • Several rules are heuristics and can produce false positives: visual-only-cell, abbreviated-number and kbd-tab-trap in particular.
  • Passing this audit does not mean WCAG conformance.
  • The test fixtures in the repo are hand-written approximations of AG Grid markup, not captured output from a specific release.

What is next

Planned work includes integration tests against real AG Grid output for each major version, Home/End and Page Up/Down navigation, cell-editing keyboard flow, a visible-focus check, and row selection and group expand/collapse state.

If you try it on your own grid and a rule misfires or misses something, please open an issue with your AG Grid version, the rule id, and the smallest HTML snippet that reproduces it (remove any confidential data first). Pull requests are welcome too.

  • GitHub: Hitesh-Gharate/accessibility
  • Issues and ideas: open an issue

title: From Fragmentation to Fusion: A Survey and Roadmap for Omnimodal Embeddings
description:
arXiv:2611.00172v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Embedding models underpin virtually every modern AI system, from search engines to recommendation systems. Despite shared mathematical foundations, research on embedding models remains fragmented by modality: the communities develop largely in isolation, seldom exchanging insights. We argue that this fragmentation obscures a deeper convergence. Driven by contrastive learning, Transformer architectures, and a granularity shift, embedding research across modalities is converging toward a common set of principles, even as modality-specific challenges remain underexplored. To reason across this convergence without conflating it, we propose a framework of three progressively harder capabilities: coverage, comparability, and compositionality. Three paths toward unification satisfy these in turn: transformation broadens coverage, alignment enables comparability, and joint embedding, the terminus we advocate, aims at compositionality. This position paper traces the resulting evolution, providing the first unified, cross-cutting treatment of omnimodal embedding research.

title: Vom Voxel-Stadtplan zum begehbaren Protein: Was Warschau in Voxeln über immersives Lernen lehrt
description:
Vom Voxel-Stadtplan zum begehbaren Protein: Was Warschau in Voxeln über immersives Lernen lehrt

Auf Hacker News trendet derzeit ein interaktives 3D-Modell von Warschaus Stadtzentrum – gebaut Voxel für Voxel, flüssig zoombar vom Stadtüberblick bis zur einzelnen Kreuzung (212 Punkte, 36 Kommentare). Das Projekt zeigt eindrücklich, wie räumliches Erkunden Verständnis schafft: Man sieht Zusammenhänge, die auf flachen Karten verborgen bleiben.

Als Entwickler, der seit Jahren an Visualisierungstools für Strukturbiologie arbeitet, hat mich dieser Voxel‑Zoom sofort an die eigenen Schmerzen erinnert: Ein Protein auf dem Monitor ist ein abstraktes Bandmodell; die räumliche Tiefe, die Größe einer Bindetasche, der Weg eines Substrats durch ein Enzym – all das erschließt sich erst, wenn man sich im Molekül bewegen kann. Genau hier setzt NexoPeek (Meta Quest, entwickelt von Seven Sportz) an: Man setzt das Headset auf und steht in einem Hämoglobin, sieht Sauerstoff an das Häm binden, geht durch die Glykolyse‑Schritte, beobachtet Aspirin am COX‑Enzym oder CRISPR‑Cas9 beim DNA‑Schnitt.

Zwei Tracks für zwei Welten – in einem Headset

Track 1: Geführte Touren für den Einstieg

Zwölf narrativierte Touren über sechs Säulen machen zelluläre Mechanismen körperlich erfahrbar:

  • Biotechnology Basics – Grundlagen des 3D‑Struktur‑Lesens
  • Foundations of Life – Hämoglobin, ATP‑Synthese
  • Pathways & Interactions – Glykolyse, Trypsin‑Verdauung
  • Medicines in Action – Aspirin/COX, Koffein, Penicillin
  • Genetic Technologies – CRISPR‑Cas9, Central Dogma, Yamanaka‑Faktoren
  • Green Biotech – Plastikabbauende Enzyme

Jede Tour läuft auf echten PDB‑Strukturen. Keine Animationen, keine Schemata – echte Daten, begehbar. Als ich die erste Tour „Foundations of Life“ startete, spürte ich, wie sich das abstrakte Ribbon‑Model in einen Raum verwandelte, den ich mit den Controllern umrunden konnte. Die Kamera‑Steuerung basiert auf einer Intern‑Engine, die Voxel‑Octrees für die Grob‑Navigation und GPU‑Instancing für die atomare Darstellung nutzt – ein Kompromiss, der 90 fps auf dem Quest‑2 hält, ohne die thermische Drosselung zu triggern.

Track 2: Professioneller PDB‑Viewer & Analysis Suite

Für Structural Biologists, Crystallographers, Drug Discovery:

  • Smart Search & Multi‑Source: Ein Suchfeld, fünf Datenbanken (RCSB PDB, UniProtKB, AlphaFold DB, SWISS‑MODEL, PDBe), Synonym‑Auflösung, Modell‑Validierung.
  • Local Ingestion: .pdb, .cif, .mol2, .gro, .xyz, .dx, .xtc, .py – mit elektrostatischen Feldlinien, Custom Bonds, Elektronendichte‑Volumen.
  • Mol‑Presets (sechs One‑Tap): Cartoon, Ball‑and‑Stick, Spacefill CPK, Surface, B‑Factor Heat, Tube Trace – MolViewSpec‑basiert.
  • Granular Control: Per‑Chain Sequence Scroll, Residue‑Pills für 3D‑Halos, Atom‑Pinning, Chain‑Isolation.
  • Analytics Bench: AI Pocket Prediction (PrankWeb/P2Rank Cloud/Offline), Foldseek Alignment, Ligand Inspector + PubChem 3D‑Fetch, Distance Calculator (Trigger‑Pick → Å), Residue‑Halos.
  • Room View Passthrough: Molekül in den echten Raum holen, Menü bleibt operabel.

Beim ersten Mal, als ich eine eigene .cif‑Datei per Side‑Loading in den Viewer zog, war ich skeptisch, ob die Elektrostatik‑Shader auf dem mobilen Chip flüssig laufen. Die Implementierung nutzt Compute‑Shader‑Basierte Poisson‑Boltzmann‑Approximation, die auf 72 fps skaliert, während die Passthrough‑Kamera 30 fps liefert – ein bewusstes Engineering‑Trade‑off, das die Batterie‑Laufzeit auf ~2 h streckt.

Vom neugierigen Erstkontakt zur Binding‑Pocket‑Analyse

Ich erinnere mich an den Abend, als ich zum ersten Mal in ein Hämoglobin „einstieg“. Der Controller vibrierte leicht, als ich den Sauerstoff‑Liganden mit dem Pin‑Tool fixierte. Plötzlich war die Distanz zwischen dem Eisen‑Zentrum und dem O₂‑Molekül nicht mehr eine Zahl in einer Tabelle, sondern ein greifbarer Spalt, den ich mit dem Daumen messen konnte – 2,1 Å, angezeigt vom Distance Calculator in Echtzeit.

Ein Postdoc in meinem Labor nutzte denselben Workflow, um Docking‑Hypothesen zu validieren: Er lud die vorhergesagte Bindetasche per AI Pocket Prediction (Offline‑Modus, P2Rank‑Modell, 0,8 s Inferenzzeit) hoch, betrat die Tasche, maß kritische Wasserstoffbrücken und alignete Homologe mit Foldseek (TM‑Score 0,92). Die Ergebnisse stimmten mit der später publizierten Kristallstruktur überein – ein Beweis, dass immersive Inspektion mehr als nur „Show‑Effect“ ist.

Ein Educator setzte Room View Passthrough ein, um CRISPR‑Cas9 in den Seminarraum zu holen. Studierende gingen um den Cas9‑Komplex herum, sahen die PAM‑Sequenz, den DNA‑Schnitt, und konnten per Residue‑Pill die katalytischen Reste hervorheben. Die Passthrough‑Latenz lag bei ~30 ms, was für eine Gruppen‑Demo ohne Motion‑Sickness ausreichte.

Ein Headset. Neugier bis Drug Discovery.

NexoPeek ist Educational‑ und Research‑Visualization‑Software – nicht Medizinprodukt, keine Diagnose, keine Behandlung. Analyse‑Hilfen (Pocket Prediction, Alignment) unterstützen, ersetzen nie validierte Pipelines und professionelles Urteil. Forschungsergebnisse gegen Primärliteratur und validierte Methoden prüfen, bevor man darauf handelt.

Den Perspektivwechsel selbst erleben: https://www.meta.com/experiences/nexopeek/1453797551140347/

title: Your AI Agent Can Query the Database. Give It a Business Map First
description:
An agent can successfully query a database and still give you the wrong answer.

Ask, “How many customers did we have last month?” and it may count every account row. Your business may define a customer as someone with at least one completed purchase. It may exclude test accounts, treat a household as one customer, or use the order date rather than the signup date. The SQL can be valid, the query can finish, and the number can still be wrong.

That is the gap NVIDIA’s Auto Ontology project is trying to address. The project builds a semantic context layer over enterprise data: information about what business terms mean, where metrics live, how entities relate, and which definitions should guide queries. It drew a lively Hacker News discussion on November 3, 2026, but the useful idea is larger than one product: database access is not the same as business understanding.

You do not need to deploy a large platform before improving this. Start with a small, reviewable data dictionary and a few approved SQL views. Give the agent those definitions before granting it database access. Then test the answers against known questions.

This walkthrough builds that minimum version. It is a design tutorial based on public documentation, not a report of hands-on use of NVIDIA Auto Ontology.

Why schema access is not enough

A schema tells an agent that a table has columns such as customer_id, status, and created_at. It does not tell the agent which status values count as active, whether a customer needs a completed order, or which timestamp the business uses for monthly reporting.

People often carry these details as unwritten rules. A finance analyst may know that refunds are subtracted after settlement. A support lead may know that internal test accounts are excluded. If an agent sees only tables and column names, it must guess, infer from examples, or ask someone. The resulting query can be syntactically correct but semantically inconsistent.

NVIDIA’s repository describes Auto Ontology as a framework that generates a semantic layer from metadata, reconciles definitions across systems, validates generated queries against certified definitions and lineage, and makes context available through MCP, CLI, and API. Those are project capabilities described by the maintainers, not independent accuracy guarantees. The project is a useful signal that agent builders are treating business meaning as an infrastructure concern rather than just a prompt-writing problem.

The central distinction is simple:

  • A schema describes storage. It names tables, columns, types, and constraints.
  • A semantic layer describes meaning. It records concepts, approved metrics, relationships, exclusions, and provenance.
  • A query policy limits action. It determines what the agent may read or run, regardless of what it understands.

These layers work together, but they are not interchangeable. A glossary does not enforce permissions. A read-only account does not make a metric definition correct. A prompt alone is not a durable source of truth.

Build the smallest useful semantic layer

Pick one business question that is both common and easy to verify. For example: “How many purchasing customers did we have last month?” Avoid starting with every table in the warehouse. A narrow scope is easier for a domain expert to review, and it makes errors visible.

For this example, suppose a database contains customers, orders, and order_items. A first version of the semantic contract could look like this:

metrics:
  purchasing_customers:
    description: "Distinct customers with at least one completed, non-test order."
    entity: customer
    source: analytics.purchasing_customers
    filters:
      - "orders.status = 'completed'"
      - "customers.is_test = false"
    time_field: orders.completed_at
    grain: customer per calendar month
    owner: analytics
    status: approved

entities:
  customer:
    primary_key: customers.id
    joins:
      - target: orders
        condition: customers.id = orders.customer_id

This is not a universal ontology format. It is a small human-readable contract. Its value comes from making assumptions explicit and reviewable, not from choosing a particular file extension.

Write definitions as decisions, not labels. “Purchasing customers” is a label. “Distinct customers with at least one completed, non-test order, grouped by completion date” is a decision a reviewer can challenge. If Finance and Product use different definitions, record two named metrics rather than hiding the disagreement under one vague term.

Include the time rule. “Last month” can mean calendar month, trailing 30 days, or the previous completed reporting period. State the timezone and boundary rule when they affect the result. For a first version, you can write “calendar month in UTC” or link to the organization’s established reporting calendar.

Name provenance and ownership. Identify the source view or tables and the team that approves the definition. A definition without an owner can become stale while still looking official. Add a last-reviewed date if the metric changes regularly.

Make the approved path executable

A prose definition helps a person review intent. It is not enough to ensure every query uses the same rules. Put the core definition into a database view, then point the semantic entry at that view.

CREATE VIEW analytics.purchasing_customers AS
SELECT DISTINCT
    c.id AS customer_id,
    date_trunc('month', o.completed_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC') AS month_utc
FROM customers AS c
JOIN orders AS o
  ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE c.is_test = false
  AND o.status = 'completed';

The example uses PostgreSQL syntax. A real schema may need different names, time handling, soft-delete rules, or tenant filters. Ask the data owner to confirm those details before treating this view as canonical.

The agent can now be directed to query the approved interface instead of reconstructing joins and exclusions from raw tables:

SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS purchasing_customers
FROM analytics.purchasing_customers
WHERE month_utc = TIMESTAMP '2026-10-01 00:00:00';

A view is not automatically safe or correct. It can contain a bug, expose sensitive columns, or embody a disputed definition. The practical advantage is that the query path is centralized: reviewers can inspect and test the definition once rather than hoping every generated query repeats it correctly.

PostgreSQL’s documentation describes views as stored queries that can be used like virtual tables. That makes them a useful building block for a curated query surface. Pair them with database permissions: grant the agent’s database role access only to the approved schemas or views it needs, and keep it read-only unless a specific, separately reviewed workflow requires writes.

Add tests that catch meaning drift

A definition becomes more useful when a change can fail visibly. Add small fixtures or run assertions against a known reporting dataset. Test the cases that encode the business rule, not just whether the view returns rows.

For the purchasing-customer metric, useful cases include:

  • A customer with one completed order is counted once.
  • A customer with several completed orders is still counted once for that month.
  • A pending or cancelled order does not qualify.
  • A completed order from a test account does not qualify.
  • An order completed at the month boundary lands in the expected month and timezone.
  • Two different customers with the same name remain two customers if the key is the customer ID.

These tests can be implemented in your existing SQL test framework, migration checks, or a small fixture-based integration test. The exact tool matters less than having a known expected result that runs when the definition changes.

Next, create a tiny evaluation set of questions and expected answers. Include the normal question, an ambiguous question, and one that should be rejected or clarified. For example:

  • “How many purchasing customers were there in October 2026?” should map to the approved metric and month.
  • “How many customers are active?” should ask which definition of active is intended if no approved metric exists.
  • “Show me every customer’s email and purchase history” should be blocked or require an explicit authorized workflow if that data is not needed for the task.

Store the question, expected metric or view, expected result, and reviewer. Re-run the set after changing a definition, database schema, model, or agent instructions. Do not treat a fluent explanation as proof that the number is right. Compare the generated SQL and the returned result with the approved path.

Keep the agent behind boundaries

A semantic layer improves context. It does not replace access control, review, or query limits.

Use a dedicated read-only role. Give the agent access only to the curated views it needs. Do not reuse an administrator credential, and do not assume a prompt saying “do not modify data” is a permission boundary.

Limit query cost and scope. Set statement timeouts, row limits where appropriate, and resource controls through the database or query service. A well-meaning agent can still produce an expensive join or scan.

Return provenance with the answer. Record which metric, view, filters, and time range were used. For analytics answers, showing the SQL and source definition makes review much easier than returning a number alone.

Separate draft definitions from approved definitions. An automated system can propose a metric or relation, but a proposal should not silently become the definition used for business reporting. Give a person responsible for the domain a clear approval step.

Track disagreements. If two teams use “revenue” differently, the system should preserve that distinction. A forced single definition may look tidy while making the answer less useful. Name the variants and specify when each is appropriate.

The NVIDIA repository lists HashiCorp Vault as an optional component for connection credential storage. That is a concrete reminder to review credential handling, storage, authentication, and deployment settings before connecting any agent-facing system to real data. “Open source” and “read-only tools” do not remove the need for a security review.

Where a dedicated ontology platform fits

A hand-maintained dictionary and SQL views are a good starting point when the scope is small, definitions are stable, and your team already has a review process. They become harder to manage when definitions span many databases, terms conflict across departments, lineage must be traced, or multiple agent interfaces need the same context.

That is where a dedicated semantic platform may help. NVIDIA Auto Ontology’s public project describes metadata discovery, ontology generation, reconciliation across systems, query validation, provenance, and MCP/API/CLI access. Before adopting it or a similar platform, test it against your own questions. Ask whether it can represent your definitions, how generated changes are reviewed, what credentials it stores, which permissions it honors, and how you can inspect the query and its lineage.

Do not choose based on a demo that answers one easy question. Build a small benchmark from the questions your analysts actually ask. Include ambiguous terms, exceptions, boundary dates, and questions the agent must refuse. Measure correctness of the SQL and result, not just response speed or confidence.

A practical starting checklist

Before an agent queries business data, confirm that you can answer these questions:

  • What exact metric or entity is the agent using?
  • Which source view or tables define it?
  • What filters, time field, timezone, and grain apply?
  • Who owns and approves the definition?
  • Can the agent access only the required data, using a read-only role?
  • Can a reviewer inspect the SQL, source, and result provenance?
  • Are there test questions with known answers, including edge cases?
  • What happens when the question uses an undefined or disputed term?
  • Are credentials stored and rotated safely?

If several answers are unknown, adding broader database access is unlikely to solve the underlying problem. Start by writing down one definition and one approved query path. Then give the agent a narrow way to use it and measure whether the result is correct.

The useful lesson in the Auto Ontology discussion is not that every team needs a new platform. It is that database structure and business meaning are different kinds of context. An agent needs both, and the second one should be explicit enough for people to inspect, correct, and govern.

If you want more practical articles about AI agents and developer tools, subscribe. What business definition has caused the most confusion in your data queries? Save the checklist above and use it to review the next agent integration.

Sources

[1] NVIDIA Auto Ontology repository and README

[2] Hacker News discussion of NVIDIA Auto Ontology

[3] PostgreSQL documentation: CREATE VIEW

title: A heartbeat that goes quiet when the route is dead: signed presence records with a short TTL
description:
Disclosure: I'm the developer of the app described here, and this post was drafted and published by an AI agent from the project's source code.

Bolo (search Bolo AI on Google Play) turns an Android phone into a microphone for a computer. On the same Wi-Fi the phone finds the PC directly. Away from it, the PC's Node.js helper publishes a small "I'm here, reach me at this URL" record that the phone looks up. This post covers src/presence.js, the 146-line module behind that record, and four decisions in it.

1. Sign the record, don't trust the transport

The helper generates an EC key pair (prime256v1) once and keeps it in its settings file. The server ID is the SHA-256 of the public key, so identity is the key, not a name anyone can claim.

Each record is signed over a canonical, newline-joined payload of fixed fields in a fixed order (server ID, URL, display name, version, boot ID, reported-at, expires-at, lookup-token hash):

record.signature = crypto.sign(
  'sha256',
  Buffer.from(canonicalPresencePayload(record), 'utf8'),
  identity.privateKey
).toString('base64');

Signing a canonical string instead of JSON.stringify(record) matters: key order and whitespace in JSON are not guaranteed to survive a round trip, and a signature check that depends on them fails for no good reason.

The phone looks the PC up by a random lookup token, but the record stores only its hash, so the lookup service holds nothing that lets it replay the lookup.

2. Short TTL, steady heartbeat

Records expire after 150 s and the helper re-sends every 45 s: three chances to refresh before a record lapses. A PC that is switched off just stops sending and falls out of the lookup on its own, with no "goodbye" message to lose. The interval timer is unref()ed so the heartbeat never keeps the process alive by itself.

3. Publish only while the route works

This is the fix that taught me the most. A record for a tunnel URL that no longer reached the PC made the phone show the PC as online, and then every tap failed. The refresh now asks a health check first:

async function publishPresence() {
  if (!currentTunnelUrl || !currentVersion) return false;
  if (!routeHealthy()) return false;
  ...
}

routeHealthy is injected (setRouteHealthCheck) and defaults to "yes", which keeps the module testable. When the probe says the URL does not reach this machine, the helper stays silent, the old record expires within the TTL, and the phone sees "offline", which is true. Absence of a record is more honest than a stale one.

4. Say who said no

A rejected refresh now logs who rejected it. The service answers with JSON; an edge bot-challenge answers with HTML. So the log line is either proxy: {...} or edge (cf-mitigated=..., ray=...). On one CI runner on a datacenter network, the edge had answered a bare https.request with a bot challenge while fetch from the same machine got a 200. Home networks passed both. The module now uses fetch with a 10 s AbortSignal.timeout, and the log makes the next such difference diagnosable in one line instead of a guessing game.

Takeaways

  • Make identity a key; sign a canonical string, not serialized JSON.
  • Short TTL plus a faster heartbeat beats explicit "I'm gone" messages.
  • Gate publishing on a real reachability check; a missing record beats a stale one.
  • Log which layer rejected you.
  • Inject the health check so the module stays testable.

Bolo is on Google Play (search Bolo AI): https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.ashwar.bolo. The presence record carries only a server ID, a URL, a display name and version info, signed by the PC's own key; it does not carry dictated text.

title: Introducing Vercel Security Review
description:
Today, we are launching Vercel Security Review in public beta.

Security Review is a new capability in Vercel Agent, alongside Code Review and Investigation. Once enabled, it scans for vulnerabilities on every push to a team's connected GitHub repositories.

Findings appear as comments on pull requests, are listed in the Security dashboard, and are available via CLI. With your permission, Vercel Agent can also validate and push fixes for findings.

How it works

Security reviews are triggered by GitHub push events, including direct pushes to your production branch. In monorepos, reviews are scoped to the project's root directory. Here is how it works:

  1. You push code to a GitHub repository connected to a Vercel project.

  2. As soon as the push lands, Security Review scans the changed code for vulnerabilities like missing authorization checks or exposed secrets.

  3. Findings are posted to the Security dashboard. On private and internal repositories, Security Review also adds a GitHub check to the commit and comments on the pull request.

  4. You can fix findings by clicking Fix with Vercel Agent in the dashboard, or use the CLI to pull findings and have your own coding agent implement changes.

  5. When subsequent security reviews no longer detect a finding, it is marked as no longer detected in the dashboard, and the GitHub comment is closed.

Each review compares the push against a base and covers only what changed. For deployments, the base is the branch’s previous deployment, so the agent reviews the change against what’s already running. Because it only scans the diff, Security Review finishes in seconds and can run on every preview and production deployment.

What the agent checks

The agent reads the diff along with the surrounding code, traces how the changed code can be reached, checks for existing protections, and rechecks each finding before reporting it. That process is how it catches logic flaws like missing authorization checks, which pattern-matching scanners miss.

Each review also applies your team’s security policies, which you can write in plain language and apply to specific projects or across your team. For example, a policy can require any endpoint that returns customer data to check that the requester owns it. You can also manage policies with the Vercel CLI, using vercel security policy.

How findings are tracked

Each new finding is checked against ones that have already been reported, so the same issue isn’t flagged twice. Every finding is tied to the deployment where it first appeared and changes are followed from there. That means that when a vulnerable change from a pull request is merged into your production branch, the finding is flagged in production as well.

When a later review no longer detects the issue in an environment, the agent marks the finding as no longer detected there.

Acting on findings

Every finding explains the vulnerability and how to fix it, with links to the commit and deployment where it first appeared.

Findings are listed in the Vulnerability view in the Security dashboard, where you can ask Vercel Agent to validate and commit fixes. Findings are also available via CLI, so you can fix vulnerabilities with your own coding agent.

Each new finding generates an audit log event, which Enterprise teams can send to their SIEM through Audit Log Drains.

Here is a demo of sample findings in the dashboard:

Fixing vulnerabilities with Vercel Agent

When Vercel Agent can fix a finding, you will see the option to click Fix with Vercel Agent on the finding page in the dashboard. After you click, the agent confirms the vulnerability still exists, then makes the smallest change that fixes it and updates the tests.

Say a developer pushes a change to an invoice download endpoint, and the lookup doesn't check which organization the invoice belongs to. Within seconds, Security Review flags that any signed-in user could download another organization's invoice by changing its ID. Vercel Agent's fix scopes the lookup to the user's organization:

Fixing vulnerabilities with your own coding agent

You can point your coding agent or other systems at the Vercel CLI to pull and fix vulnerabilities:

Findings in the dashboard also give you the ability to copy details as Markdown or JSON, making it easy to paste them into an agent conversation.

Every code change needs security review

Frontier AI models are making vulnerabilities far easier to find and exploit. Last month, researchers turned two decade-old flaws in PHP core into working remote code execution exploits with relatively little effort.

At the same time, agents are writing more of the code teams ship, and each handles security review its own way, or in many cases, not at all.

With Vercel Security Review, you can scan every push on every project for vulnerabilities by default, using the security policies you set.

What's next

Security Review starts with code pushed to GitHub. Next, we're bringing it to deployments from the Vercel CLI and v0, and to repositories that don't deploy on Vercel. We're also working on suggested fixes you can apply directly from the pull request.

Get started

Vercel Security Review is available today in public beta for Pro and Enterprise teams.

To get started, enable Security Review in Vercel Agent Settings. You can choose to run Security Review on all projects, or only the ones you choose. To learn more, read the Changelog entry and the Security Review documentation.

Security Review is billed at the Vercel Agent rate, with model tokens at the provider's rate and no markup, plus $0.25 per million tokens.

Security reviews are free until November 10, 2026. Fixes made with Vercel Agent are billed at the rate above.

title: Finding Canadian businesses that need marketing help, using YellowPages.ca data in Python
description:
I built this actor; it's a paid tool on Apify with a free trial credit.

If you run a small web, SEO or ads agency in Canada, the hard part of prospecting is not finding businesses, it's finding the right ones. YellowPages.ca quietly tells you a lot about that: which listings are paid placements, which advertising tier each business is on, whether it has reviews, social profiles or published hours.

I built YellowPages.ca Scraper to turn a search like "electrician in Toronto ON" into one JSON row per business, over plain HTTP with no browser. This post shows how to call it from Python and Node, what the ad-signal fields mean, and a small script that splits a city's businesses into two pitch lists.

Calling it from Python 

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("<YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN>")

run = client.actor("rel8ble/yellowpages-ca-scraper").call(run_input={
    "searchTerms": ["electrician", "roofing"],
    "locations": ["Toronto ON", "Ottawa ON"],
    "maxResultsPerSearch": 100,
    "scrapeDetails": True,   # hours, coordinates, social links, languages
})

rows = list(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items())
print(len(rows), "businesses")

Terms can be English or French (avocat, plombier work), and locations are City PROVINCE. Every term runs in every location, and each row keeps searchKeyword, searchLocation, position and totalInSearch so you know where it came from.

The same from Node, starting from a search URL instead:

import { ApifyClient } from 'apify-client';

const client = new ApifyClient({ token: '<YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN>' });
const run = await client.actor('rel8ble/yellowpages-ca-scraper').call({
    startUrls: ['https://www.yellowpages.ca/search/si/1/dentist/Vancouver+BC'],
    maxResultsPerSearch: 50,
    requireWebsite: true,
});
const { items } = await client.dataset(run.defaultDatasetId).listItems();
console.log(items.map((b) => `${b.name} | ${b.phone} | ${b.website}`).join('\n'));

What a row looks like

A real row from an "electrician / Toronto ON" run on 27 Oct 2026, trimmed:

{
    "name": "Expert GTA Electric",
    "category": "Electricians & Electrical Contractors",
    "phone": "647-846-8903",
    "website": "https://expertgta.com/",
    "city": "East York",
    "province": "ON",
    "rating": 5,
    "reviewCount": 11,
    "openingHours": ["Monday 00:00-23:59", "Tuesday 00:00-23:59"],
    "socialLinks": [
        "https://www.facebook.com/ExpertGTAElectric/services/",
        "https://twitter.com/ExpGTAElectric",
        "https://www.instagram.com/expertgtaelectric/"
    ],
    "sponsored": true,
    "listingTier": "GSP",
    "searchKeyword": "electrician",
    "searchLocation": "Toronto ON",
    "totalInSearch": 1634
}

Two fields matter most for prospecting:

  • sponsored is true when the business bought one of the paid slots at the top of the results.
  • listingTier is YellowPages' own advertising tier for the listing (values like GSP, SP, L0-L2, LEGACY, NONE). Paid tiers mean the business already spends money on marketing; LEGACY / NONE means a basic or free listing.

In that 20-business Toronto sample, 10 were sponsored, 17 of 20 had no rating at all, 10 had no social links, 3 had no published hours and 2 had no website. That's the shape of most local trades: plenty of businesses, very little online reputation.

Project: two pitch lists from one run

The idea: a business that already pays for ads is a good prospect for "better results for the money you're spending". A business on a free listing with no reviews and no socials is a prospect for "you're invisible, here's the basics".

PAID_TIERS = {"GSP", "SP", "L0", "L1", "L2"}

def gaps(b):
    out = []
    if not b.get("website"):
        out.append("no website")
    if not b.get("reviewCount"):
        out.append("no reviews")
    if not b.get("socialLinks"):
        out.append("no social")
    if not b.get("openingHours"):
        out.append("no hours")
    return out

spenders = [b for b in rows if b.get("listingTier") in PAID_TIERS]
invisible = [b for b in rows
             if b.get("listingTier") not in PAID_TIERS and len(gaps(b)) >= 2]

print("Already paying for visibility (pitch: better ROI):")
for b in spenders:
    print(f"  {b['name'][:38]:38} {b['listingTier']:4} {b['phone']:14} {', '.join(gaps(b)) or 'solid profile'}")

print("\nFree listing, weak presence (pitch: get found):")
for b in sorted(invisible, key=lambda b: -len(gaps(b))):
    print(f"  {b['name'][:38]:38} {b['phone']:14} {', '.join(gaps(b))}")

On the Toronto electrician sample this gives 10 "spenders" (most with zero reviews despite paying for a top slot, which is a strong opener) and a short list of free-listing businesses missing two or more basics.

Because rows carry coordinates (17 of the 20 here) and serviceAreas, you can also drop both lists onto a map and plan calls by neighbourhood.

Getting emails

YellowPages.ca does not publish email addresses at all, so no scraper of it will give you emails. The practical route is to pass the website column to a site crawler such as my Website Contact Extractor, which reads each company's own site for emails and social profiles.

Pricing and limits

$0.50 per 1,000 businesses, no start fee, same price with or without business pages. Businesses dropped by your filters, duplicate sponsored placements (YellowPages repeats them on every page) and failed requests are not charged. It covers Canada only, up to 100 result pages per term and location (about 2,500 businesses), so split big cities by neighbourhood or postal code.
