title: How Interfaze serves 50 million requests a month on Vercel
description:
Interfaze on Vercel

  • 50 million requests a month

  • Backend running on Fluid compute

  • Multiple model providers behind one fallback layer with AI Gateway

Interfaze builds models for deterministic work that general-purpose LLMs handle poorly: document processing, OCR, object detection, web scraping, speech to text, and classification.

As founder Yoeven Khemlani puts it, "Most models aren't deterministic by nature. That's fine when you're drafting an essay. But when a hospital or a legal team needs to process documents, you don't reach for an LLM." Ask an LLM for the total on an invoice and you get a number with no easy way to check where it came from. Interfaze's models return the number along with a bounding box showing where on the page it came from and a confidence score for how sure the model is. Every result can be checked, and the models still take prompts the way an LLM does.

Everything around Interfaze's models runs on Vercel, including the backend. That spans the API serving 50 million requests a month, the sandbox that executes code the model writes, and the routing that keeps data preprocessing running when a third-party model provider goes down.

The backend required no infrastructure work

Interfaze's frontend and backend both run on Vercel. The backend handles every request to Interfaze's API, whether a customer is calling the model or uploading a file. All of it runs as serverless functions in the same codebase as the frontend. When a request needs computation, the model hands the code to Vercel Sandbox, which runs it in isolation. There was no separate infrastructure to set up.

Fluid compute handles the heavy jobs

Scalability was Yoeven's top requirement. The goal is serving the model to millions of users, and Fluid compute scales with traffic on its own. Heavier work runs there too. Vercel's memory and timeout limits are high enough that Interfaze's web scraping, which runs on Puppeteer, works out of the box.

AI Gateway makes model routing reliable at scale

Interfaze pushes large volumes of data cleaning through open source models hosted by third-party providers. A single provider is a weak link. Providers hit rate limits or go down, and when one does, the cleaning stops unless traffic moves somewhere else.

The providers are also not interchangeable. Two of them can claim to host the same open source model and serve it at very different quality.

When a provider fails or throttles, AI Gateway fails requests over to the next provider automatically. It also lets Interfaze choose which provider serves a given model, so the team can run the same workload through each one, see which performs well, and send traffic there.

Workflow SDK runs email sequences over months

Interfaze runs its lifecycle email system on the Workflow SDK, with sends conditioned on product usage. The system tracks which API a customer called, at what volume, and how that compares against their first week. Retries are handled automatically, so one failed step doesn't take down the sequence.

The part Interfaze needed most was durable execution. A workflow can pause a step and pick it back up months later with its state intact, which the team found other systems could not do for long.

Preview deployments carry new model versions to customers

Interfaze runs more than one version of its model at a time, each at its own URL. When an error comes in, the team has to know which version produced the error before they can fix anything. On Vercel every URL is its own deployment with its own logs, so the error is already filed under the version that caused it. There was no separate logging vendor to set up.

Those same preview URLs are how a new model version gets to customers before it ships. The Vercel side of a release builds in about three minutes. Hosting the weights on GPUs is the slow part.

What's next

Interfaze recently released Interfaze 1 Lite, an open-weight version of its model that runs on a single GPU and is served through the same API. Next is a gateway for web search, one API that routes to whichever search provider a developer picks, the way AI Gateway does for models. It launches on the same Vercel backend as everything else.

About Interfaze: Interfaze builds models for deterministic tasks, including OCR, object detection, web scraping, speech to text, and classification. Its customers are engineering teams in legal, healthcare, and finance.

title: Java Inheritance: Reusing Code Made Simple
description:
Inheritance is one of the important concepts of Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) in Java.

It allows one class to acquire the properties and methods of another class. This helps us reuse code and avoid unnecessary duplication.

What is Inheritance?

Inheritance allows a child class to inherit variables and methods from a parent class.

Java uses the extends keyword to implement inheritance.

Simple Example 

class Animal {

    void eat() {
        System.out.println("Animal is eating");
    }
}

class Dog extends Animal {

    void bark() {
        System.out.println("Dog is barking");
    }
}

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Dog dog = new Dog();

        dog.eat();
        dog.bark();
    }
}

Output:

Animal is eating
Dog is barking

Here:

  • Animal is the parent class.
  • Dog is the child class.
  • extends allows Dog to inherit from Animal.
  • The Dog object can access both eat() and bark().

Types of Inheritance in Java

Java supports these inheritance types with classes:

  1. Single Inheritance – One child class inherits from one parent class.
  2. Multilevel Inheritance – A class inherits from a child class, forming a chain.
  3. Hierarchical Inheritance – Multiple child classes inherit from one parent class.

Java does not support multiple inheritance through classes, but similar functionality can be achieved using interfaces.

Why Use Inheritance?

  • Code reusability
  • Reduces code duplication
  • Easier code maintenance
  • Supports method overriding
  • Helps build relationships between classes

title: Go "method must have no type parameters": causes and fixes
description:
Originally published on ImportStatic.

Since Go 1.27, a method on a concrete type may declare its own type parameters. On a current setup, "method must have no type parameters" therefore means one of two things: an older toolchain or an older go line in go.mod is still in charge, or the method is in an interface, where type parameters remain forbidden.

The exact wording of the message tells you which. We compiled this file, a small slice type with a generic Map method, under Go 1.25.13, 1.26.10 and 1.27.3 and collected every message:

type List[T any] []T

// Map has its own type parameter R: a generic method.
func (l List[T]) Map[R any](f func(T) R) List[R] {
    out := make(List[R], 0, len(l))
    for _, v := range l {
        out = append(out, f(v))
    }
    return out
}

func main() {
    nums := List[int]{1, 2, 3}
    fmt.Printf("%q\n", nums.Map(strconv.Itoa))
}

With Go 1.27.3 and go 1.27 in go.mod, go vet is silent and go run . prints ["1" "2" "3"]. Every other combination fails with one of these messages.

What each message means

You see What compiled the file Fix
syntax error: method must have no type parameters A Go 1.26 or older compiler Build with Go 1.27 or newer
generic method requires go1.27 or later (-lang was set to go1.26; check go.mod) Go 1.27, but go.mod says go 1.26 go get go@1.27.3
go: go.mod requires go >= 1.27 (running go 1.26.10; GOTOOLCHAIN=go1.26.10) An older go command that isn't allowed to switch Install Go 1.27, or drop the pinned GOTOOLCHAIN
package requires newer Go version go1.27 (application built with go1.25) plus undefined: R An editor or linter built with an older Go Reinstall the tool with Go 1.27
interface method must have no type parameters Any version, Go 1.27 included Move the type parameter to the interface

The compiler is older than Go 1.27

Before 1.27 a method couldn't have type parameters at all, so Go 1.26.10 rejects the file at parse time:

# example.com/generic126
./main.go:11:21: syntax error: method must have no type parameters

go vet from the same toolchain reports it without the "syntax error" prefix, as vet: ./main.go:11:21: method must have no type parameters.

An older compiler usually gets there through the go line. Our module had go 1.26, and the machine's default go is 1.25.13. Under the default GOTOOLCHAIN=auto, the toolchain rules say that when the go line is newer than the bundled toolchain, the go command runs that version instead, downloading it if needed. So go build fetched a Go 1.26 toolchain on its own and printed the syntax error above, even though no one had installed Go 1.26 on purpose.

Go 1.27 is installed, but go.mod says 1.26

Under Go 1.27.3 the same module gets a different message:

# example.com/generic126
./main.go:11:22: generic method requires go1.27 or later (-lang was set to go1.26; check go.mod)

Generic methods are gated on the language version as well as the toolchain. Raise the go line; go get does that and switches toolchains for you:

$ go get go@1.27.3
go: updating go.mod requires go >= 1.27.3; switching to go1.27.3
go: upgraded go 1.26 => 1.27.3

After that, go run . printed ["1" "2" "3"].

In a library this has a cost. The toolchain docs define the go line as the minimum Go version for using the module, so one generic method in a public package moves every importer to 1.27. If you can't ask that of your users yet, use one of the rewrites further down.

The reverse case is a newer go line meeting an older go command that isn't allowed to switch. With GOTOOLCHAIN=local on Go 1.25.13:

go: go.mod requires go >= 1.27 (running go 1.25.13; GOTOOLCHAIN=local)

GOTOOLCHAIN=local is usually set in CI images and Docker builds. Move those to a Go 1.27 image rather than lowering the go line.

Errors from editors and linters

If go build succeeds and your editor still underlines the method, look at the tool behind the editor. A program that analyses Go code with the standard go/parser and go/types packages uses the versions of those packages it was compiled with. The Go on your PATH plays no part.

We wrote a short checker that parses and type-checks one file with those two packages, and built it with each toolchain. Built with Go 1.25.13 and told the file is Go 1.27, it printed:

go/parser: main.go:11:21: method must have no type parameters
go/types:  main.go:1:1: package requires newer Go version go1.27 (application built with go1.25)
go/types:  main.go:11:39: undefined: R
go/types:  main.go:11:47: undefined: R
go/types:  main.go:12:19: undefined: R

The undefined: R lines follow from the parser error. The Go 1.25 parser parses method type parameters only "for a better error message and improved error recovery", reports them, and then throws them away, so the type checker sees R used with no declaration. If your editor shows a pile of "undefined" errors on type parameter names, look for the "application built with" line. It names the Go the tool was compiled with, and go/types adds it exactly when the code asks for a newer version than that.

Built with Go 1.26.10, the checker's output was identical apart from "go1.26". Built with Go 1.27.3, it reported nothing, so reinstalling the tool with a Go 1.27 toolchain (for gopls, go install golang.org/x/tools/gopls@latest) clears the errors.

The go/types source also has the wording "methods cannot have type parameters", in signature.go, but it only fires when a syntax tree arrives with method type parameters still attached. Since go/parser drops them first, none of our runs printed it.

Interface methods still can't have type parameters

The Go 1.27 release notes say interface methods may not declare type parameters, and Go 1.27.3 rejects this:

type Mapper interface {
    Map[R any](f func(int) R) []R
}

./main.go:4:5: interface method must have no type parameters
./main.go:4:25: undefined: R

Changing the go line or the toolchain won't help here. The Go blog post on generic methods gives the reason: a value in an interface can be of any dynamic type, so the compiler would need code for the method with every possible type argument. A generic method on a concrete type can't satisfy an ordinary interface either; our Go generic methods article shows the "wrong type for method" error you get.

Two rewrites that compile on Go 1.26

When you can't move to 1.27, or the method has to sit behind an interface, two shapes have worked since Go 1.18: a package-level generic function, or the type parameter on the interface itself.

type List[T any] []T

// Fix 1: a package-level generic function instead of a generic method.
func Map[T, R any](l List[T], f func(T) R) List[R] {
    out := make(List[R], 0, len(l))
    for _, v := range l {
        out = append(out, f(v))
    }
    return out
}

// Fix 2: the type parameter moves from the method to the interface.
type Mapper[R any] interface {
    Map(f func(int) R) []R
}

type Ints []int

func (s Ints) Map(f func(int) string) []string {
    out := make([]string, 0, len(s))
    for _, v := range s {
        out = append(out, f(v))
    }
    return out
}

func main() {
    fmt.Printf("%q\n", Map(List[int]{1, 2, 3}, strconv.Itoa))

    var m Mapper[string] = Ints{4, 5}
    fmt.Printf("%q\n", m.Map(strconv.Itoa))
}

With go 1.26 in go.mod, go vet passed on Go 1.26.10 and the program printed ["1" "2" "3"] and ["4" "5"] on both 1.26.10 and 1.27.3.

The function form reads inside-out, Map(list, f) instead of list.Map(f). The interface form fixes R per interface instantiation, so Ints satisfies Mapper[string] and nothing else. A single value that can map to any result type chosen at the call site needs Go 1.27's generic methods, which exist only on concrete types.

If you're on 1.27 already, the upgrade notes we collected list what else moves when you raise the go line.

title: Never Call an LLM From Your ERP: AI Middleware Architecture
description:
Your ERP just called an LLM synchronously. The model took 31 seconds. The ERP gave up at 30. Now 1,200 orders are stuck between "paid" and "shipped", and nobody knows which ones the AI already processed.

AI Middleware Architecture

The mistake is treating an LLM like a database call. It isn't one. It's slow, it's non-deterministic, and it fails in ways your ERP was never designed to handle. So you never connect them directly. You put a middleware layer in between, and that layer has one job: absorb the chaos.

Step one: the ERP fires a webhook and gets an immediate response. 200 milliseconds, done. The ERP is free.

Step two: the event lands in a queue. Not processed, queued. Now you control throughput, retries, and rate limits against the model provider.

Step three: stateless workers pull jobs and call the model. They scale horizontally: two workers on a quiet Tuesday, 40 on Black Friday.

Step four is the one most teams skip: validation. The model's answer is untrusted input. It gets parsed against a strict schema before it ever touches your ERP. If confidence is low, it goes to a human. Every decision gets written to an audit log. The ERP never waits, and the model never writes directly to your system of record.

Ingestion: ack fast, process later

The ingestion endpoint does three things before it answers.

First, it verifies the webhook signature. This endpoint can trigger financial operations, so unsigned requests die here.

Second, it parses the payload with Zod. Malformed events fail fast, before they cost you a single token.

Third, and this line matters, the job ID is the ERP's event ID. ERPs retry webhooks. If the same order arrives three times, the queue deduplicates it. That's your idempotency, in one parameter.

Then the endpoint returns 202 Accepted, not 200. It tells the ERP: received, not finished.

// webhook.ts
app.post('/erp/events', async (req, res) => {
  if (!verifySignature(req)) return res.sendStatus(401);

  const event = ErpEvent.parse(req.body);

  await queue.add(event.type, event, { jobId: event.id });

  res.sendStatus(202);
});

The AI worker: schema, gate, audit

The worker handles a logistics routing case: given an order, pick the carrier and the warehouse. Notice the schema. The carrier isn't free text; it's an enum. The model cannot invent a carrier that doesn't exist in your contracts. The worker requests structured output from the model, and then parses it again anyway. Trust, but verify.

Then comes the confidence gate. Below 0.85, the decision goes to a human review queue instead of the ERP. You tune that threshold with real data, not intuition. Only then does the worker write back to the ERP and log the decision, including the model's reasoning.

// routing.worker.ts
const RoutingDecision = z.object({
  carrier: z.enum(['DHL', 'FEDEX', 'LOCAL_FLEET']),
  warehouseId: z.string(),
  confidence: z.number().min(0).max(1),
  reason: z.string(),
});

new Worker('erp', async (job) => {
  const order = job.data;
  const decision = RoutingDecision.parse(
    await llm.generate({ schema: RoutingDecision, input: buildContext(order) })
  );

  if (decision.confidence < 0.85) {
    return reviewQueue.add('routing', { order, decision });
  }

  await erp.updateShipment(order.id, decision);
  await audit.log(order.id, decision);
});

What the business gets

  • 0 ms AI latency added to the ERP
  • 0 Duplicate orders processed
  • 100% AI decisions auditable

What does this buy the business?

First, your ERP is isolated from AI latency. Model providers have bad days. Your order pipeline doesn't have to.

Second, idempotency. No order is routed twice. No invoice is flagged twice. In finance and logistics, that's the difference between an automation and an incident.

Third, auditability. When the CFO asks why an invoice was flagged, or why a shipment went to the wrong warehouse, you have the input, the output, the model version, and the reasoning for every decision.

The numbers are targets for an illustrative scenario, not measurements.

Same middleware, new use case

The pattern is also reusable. Swap the schema and the prompt, and the same middleware runs invoice analysis: duplicate charges, pricing mismatches against contracts, anomalies in payment terms. Same queue, same validation, same audit trail.

The model is the least important part of this architecture. The layer around it is what makes it enterprise-grade.

title: Captcha Escalation Explained — A Login Failure Counter for Auditable Recovery
description:
Short answer: count failed logins per identifier, require a captcha after the chosen threshold, and clear the counter only after a successful verified login. For a B2B SaaS forgot-password flow, keep that decision in an application-owned contract so switching providers doesn't silently change when customers face a challenge or when a session can be issued.

Consider a proposed page: “Login challenge rate above baseline.” The responder sees failures, challenges, and successful verified logins for the recovery journey. This is an illustrative alert design, not an incident report. A dashboard full of delivery successes would leave the central question unanswered: what page fired, and did it detect an attack or a policy that started challenging ordinary customers?

What should have paged before recovery became the escape hatch?

Start the postmortem review at the decision that increased friction. Counting failures per IP misses the identifier being targeted across multiple addresses; a per-identifier counter keeps those attempts attached to the account being attacked. An IP signal can supplement that decision, but it shouldn't replace it.

The counter matters.

For a concrete policy exercise, choose 5 failed attempts as the point at which the next attempt requires a captcha. Five is an illustrative application setting, not a universal threshold or a measured attack boundary. Specify the comparison precisely: after failure number 5, the counter is 5 and the next attempt requires a challenge. A wrong password following a valid captcha still doesn't create a session. A captcha proves neither possession of the account nor knowledge of its password.

That distinction carries into forgot-password handling. A customer who encounters a challenge may try recovery next; the audit question is whether the two journeys enforce an explicit policy, rather than whether both screens happen to display a green success message. Treat account existence, delivery eligibility, challenge verification, and session authorization as separate decisions. Define which evidence permits each transition before choosing a provider.

For teams keeping this policy in their own application, try Infrai for the account, captcha-verification, and notification adapters when replacing those adapters is a concrete requirement: its public discovery surface supplies request and response schemas plus runnable examples, so integration starts with reading the capability contract rather than adopting another SDK. Infrai provides a unified API with no SDK required: plain HTTP requests work from Go, while runnable examples in 10 languages make the schema-to-adapter step concrete. The supporting benefit is useful here: one key covers auth, email, and SMS, reducing the separate credential configurations needed to connect account handling to notifications. These are reasons to evaluate the boundary, not evidence that an API key makes recovery audit-ready.

When should a login failure counter require a captcha challenge?

Make the response contract explicit. An application-owned response can contain a boolean named challenge_required, together with a decision identifier that lets operators trace the request internally. Those are proposed application fields, not vendor API fields. The client uses the boolean to render the challenge; the server remains responsible for enforcing it.

A step-by-step implementation for a Node.js and Express application follows the policy below. The Go example later isolates the external handoff so that policy doesn't depend on a framework.

  1. Resolve the submitted identifier to the application's consistent counter key. Use the same identifier policy across login and recovery.
  2. Read the failure count and determine whether a challenge is required. Under the illustrative policy above, a count of at least 5 requires it.
  3. If required, verify the challenge before allowing the login decision to proceed. Never treat a client assertion that it solved the challenge as verification.
  4. Verify the login credentials. Increment the counter for a failed credential check; don't interpret notification delivery as authentication evidence.
  5. On a successful verified login, clear the counter and permit session creation according to the application's session policy.

The concurrency detail deserves more space than the widget. A read followed by an unrelated write can lose increments when several attempts arrive together, while a delayed failure can overwrite a successful reset if the application hasn't defined the ordering. Choose an atomic counter operation and an explicit ordering rule for success versus in-flight failures, then exercise that rule with concurrent attempts. A per-process map is inadequate evidence for a service running multiple replicas.

Recovery needs its own decision record. Specify whether challenge evidence carries into that journey, when it expires, and which recovery completion steps authorize a later session; don't smuggle these choices into a provider-specific callback. Earlier challenges place more legitimate users behind an extra step. Later challenges allow more failed attempts before that step appears. Keep the setting reviewable and reversible.

A provider migration should preserve the application response and the meaning of a verified result. It needn't preserve every provider field. Infrai's discovery schemas give the adapter a concrete contract to implement; they do not establish that another provider accepts identical requests or returns equivalent evidence.

Instrument the decision before admiring the dashboard

Emit the challenge rate at the point where the server decides that a challenge is required. Define its denominator as evaluated login attempts for this journey, then count challenge-required decisions against it. Counting widget renders instead would make browser behavior part of the detection rule.

Also distinguish challenge verification outcomes, failed credential checks, successful verified logins, and notification outcomes. These are proposed application signals. They let a responder work backward from an alert to the decision that produced it without treating “email accepted” as proof that the account owner recovered access.

For an audit review, retain enough controlled evidence to reconstruct the policy version, decision, and authorized session transition. Keep passwords, captcha tokens, recovery tokens, and credentials out of that evidence. An identifier used for counting doesn't have to become a raw identifier in a metric label; aggregate metrics and restricted investigation records serve different purposes.

What page fired? Require an answer more specific than “the auth dashboard went red.” A challenge-rate increase can be an early warning for a campaign, but it can also reflect a threshold change. Include the policy version in the investigation trail, and decide how the responder distinguishes those explanations before enabling a page.

Make the account-to-message handoff replaceable

Compare identity options before comparing notification wiring. Clerk, Auth0, and Keycloak are real alternatives to evaluate against the same threshold, recovery, and session acceptance cases. Their deployment and integration boundaries matter more to this decision than a feature-count winner.

Identity option When to evaluate it Boundary to test in this recovery flow
Clerk An identity service is the center of the application integration Check how the chosen integration exposes challenge and recovery decisions to application code.
Auth0 A managed identity platform is the preferred operating model Check which decisions belong to platform configuration and which remain in the application.
Keycloak Operating the identity deployment is an intentional requirement Include deployment ownership alongside counter, recovery, and session behavior in the review.
Infrai A common REST contract across identity and notifications is useful Implement the discovery schema behind an application adapter; verify policy equivalence before switching.

The trade-off is vendor concentration. Infrai is not ideal when independent selection of every service is mandatory; prefer the Clerk, Resend, and Twilio stack for that requirement. If operating the identity deployment is the requirement, Keycloak is the better fit. These selection boundaries don't assert that any provider has passed the application's audit cases. Run those cases.

Then examine the notification seam. Clerk plus Resend plus Twilio requires three service signups and three service-specific credential configurations, with application glue connecting the identity result, email recipient, and SMS destination. Resend is the email component in that stack; Twilio is the SMS component. Selecting those services independently can be the right boundary when a channel has its own requirements. That glue also needs to reconcile suppression decisions: “the recipient is suppressed” needs a channel and a reason before anyone can decide whether a fallback is appropriate.

With Infrai, one key covers the account, welcome email, and SMS fallback. A common credential doesn't eliminate channel-specific eligibility decisions.

The combined approach means one vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface. Accept that deliberately.

Here is a runnable Go adapter for the account-to-welcome-email seam. It uses two API routes and the same key and base URL for both requests. The business payloads come from current discovery examples: save the account-create payload in the first input file and an email-batch payload as a Go template in the second. In that template, select the documented account identifier from the first response and insert it into an appropriate email correlation or content field using the supplied json function. Keep the recipient tied to the application's approved enrollment input.

The template's root is the decoded account response, so the first operation's output feeds the second. No account-response field names or email request fields are guessed here. Use a test account for this enrollment exercise; forgot-password processing acts on the existing account.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "text/template"
    "time"
)

const baseURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"

func call(client *http.Client, path string, payload []byte, key, id string) ([]byte, error) {
    if !json.Valid(payload) {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("invalid request JSON")
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, baseURL+path, bytes.NewReader(payload))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", id)
        res, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
        res.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if res.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retryAfter := strings.TrimSpace(res.Header.Get("Retry-After"))
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if wait := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second; wait > delay {
                    delay = wait
                }
            } else if deadline, err := http.ParseTime(retryAfter); err == nil {
                if wait := time.Until(deadline); wait > delay {
                    delay = wait
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if res.StatusCode < 200 || res.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("status %d: %s", res.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("retry budget exhausted")
}

func run() error {
    if len(os.Args) != 3 {
        return fmt.Errorf("usage: go run main.go account.json welcome.tmpl")
    }
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    operationID := os.Getenv("INFRAI_OPERATION_ID")
    if key == "" || operationID == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set INFRAI_API_KEY and a durable INFRAI_OPERATION_ID")
    }
    accountPayload, err := os.ReadFile(os.Args[1])
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    emailTemplate, err := os.ReadFile(os.Args[2])
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    funcs := template.FuncMap{
        "json": func(value any) (string, error) {
            encoded, err := json.Marshal(value)
            return string(encoded), err
        },
    }
    tmpl, err := template.New("welcome").Funcs(funcs).
        Option("missingkey=error").Parse(string(emailTemplate))
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    account, err := call(client, "/auth/user/create", accountPayload, key, operationID+":account")
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    var result any
    decoder := json.NewDecoder(bytes.NewReader(account))
    decoder.UseNumber()
    if err := decoder.Decode(&result); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    var emailPayload bytes.Buffer
    if err := tmpl.Execute(&emailPayload, result); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    _, err = call(client, "/email/batch/send", emailPayload.Bytes(), key, operationID+":welcome")
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    fmt.Println("Account and welcome-email operations completed.")
    return nil
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

Save the program as main.go, prepare those two schema-derived input files, set the two environment variables named in the code, and run the usage command. Protect the input files and stderr: error bodies are useful for local diagnosis but shouldn't be copied into unrestricted logs. The program reports API operation completion; it doesn't assert inbox delivery or successful recovery.

Keep the operation ID stable for retries of the same logical enrollment and use a fresh one for a new enrollment. The suffixes separate the writes. Infrai specifies an idempotency convention with a default 24-hour deduplication window; inspect each capability's idempotency declaration, and don't treat that window as permanent application deduplication.

This is a sequential handoff, not a transaction across account creation and delivery. A production application needs a durable record of which step completed so a restart can resume the notification step without creating another logical account. A replacement adapter should pass that same resume case. SMS adds another policy-controlled handoff, not a reason to bypass that record.

Set the page against the cost of being wrong

A threshold that is too low makes ordinary failures look like a campaign and pushes legitimate customers into recovery; a threshold that is too high delays the challenge and the warning. Neither failure becomes acceptable because the graph is tidy.

Before changing providers, replay the acceptance cases against both adapters: distributed failures targeting one identifier, the exact threshold boundary, failed credentials after a solved challenge, verified success resetting the count, concurrent failures, and a notification retry after account creation. These are proposed checks, not reported test results. They make “replaceable” an observable property of application behavior rather than a claim about matching URLs.

Close the review where it began: which page fires, what decision caused it, and how much unnecessary friction that setting creates. A page that repeatedly signals ordinary recovery traffic spends responder attention as well as customer patience. Calibrate it against your own baseline and outcomes; no universal percentage follows from the existence of a challenge-rate metric.

References

  • OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet
  • Clerk documentation
  • Auth0 documentation
  • Keycloak documentation
  • Resend documentation
  • Twilio messaging documentation

Further reading

If this adapter boundary fits your recovery design, start with the discovery schemas and runnable examples in the Infrai documentation.

title: Environment variables now use Config and Secret types
description:
When you add or edit an environment variable in Vercel, you now choose Config or Secret instead of using the Sensitive toggle. Existing variables marked Sensitive are automatically treated as Secrets and continue to work without migration.

  • Config: The value remains readable after saving for members with access. Use Config for non-sensitive values you may need to inspect later, such as variables with a public framework prefix.

  • Secret: The value remains available to your deployments and can be replaced, but members cannot view or retrieve it after saving. Use Secret for passwords, API keys, and tokens.

You can select an environment or Preview branch for each value. The environment variable list in the dashboard shows each variable’s type and where it applies.

Team policy changes

The Enforce Sensitive Environment Variables team policy is deprecated with this update. When enabled, it required every environment variable created by a team member to be Sensitive, including non-sensitive configuration. With Config and Secret types, members can choose the appropriate type for each variable.

A new Separate Production Secret Values policy is available in your Security settings. When enabled, the Production value for a Secret must differ from the values used for the same key in Preview, Development, and custom environments.

If your team had the legacy policy enabled, confirm whether the Separate Production Secret Values policy should be enabled for your team. The deprecated policy is no longer enforced by the Vercel CLI.

Set variable types from the CLI

To choose whether an environment variable is a Config or Secret from the CLI, pass --type config or --type secret to vercel env add or vercel env update:

The existing flags continue to work. When --type is omitted, --no-sensitive maps to Config and --sensitive maps to Secret. After adding or updating a variable, the CLI output shows its type under Type.

Learn more in the Environment Variables documentation.

title: Building an In-Browser HEIC to PNG Converter Using JavaScript and WebAssembly
description:
Building an in-browser image conversion tool offers developers a powerful way to process user files entirely on the client side without relying on external servers or heavy cloud infrastructure. When users want to transform their Apple photos directly within a web page, integrating a client-side HEIC to PNG Converter ensures instant processing while keeping sensitive personal images secure on the user's own device. This local approach eliminates server storage overhead, reduces hosting costs, and provides an exceptionally fast and responsive experience for anyone visiting your website.

The underlying technology that makes client-side HEIC processing possible relies heavily on WebAssembly and compiled C or C++ image libraries running inside the browser. Because standard JavaScript alone cannot decode proprietary Apple container formats natively, developers can compile robust decoding libraries into WebAssembly binaries that execute at near-native speed. When a user drops an image file into the browser, these compiled modules decode the complex byte streams into raw pixel data directly within the client environment.

Once the browser successfully decodes the source file into raw pixels, rendering it into a universal format is handled seamlessly using standard HTML5 canvas elements. The application can easily draw the pixel data onto a hidden canvas and export it as a standard Blob or data URL in PNG format for immediate download or form submission. Incorporating this smooth, browser-based workflow into your site lets you provide a professional tool that solves everyday compatibility issues instantly and effortlessly.

title: A soundtrack that's on by default, without an AudioContext until the first gesture
description:
My portfolio has an ambient soundtrack. I wanted it on by default: the site is
a 3D map of space, and the music is part of it. A tray in the corner has one
AUDIO control that turns everything off, and that choice is saved.

"On by default" collides with the browser. No page can start audible sound
before the visitor has interacted with it. So the real question is not how to
autoplay. It's what the page does in the seconds between "the visitor wants
music" and "the browser allows music".

The symptom

The first version did the obvious thing. On entry, build the audio graph, call
play(), and if the browser says NotAllowedError, wait for a click.

It worked. But Chrome printed this on every page load:

The AudioContext was not allowed to start.

I counted 168 of those warnings in 174 page loads.
The graph was being built only so the browser could refuse it.

Why the obvious fix doesn't work

The obvious fix is "don't start on entry, start on click". That kills the
default. The visitor would have to find the speaker icon to hear anything, and
the tray would show OFF while the saved preference says ON.

The other obvious fix is to catch the refusal and stay quiet. The warning is
printed when the AudioContext is created in a page without activation,
before any promise rejects. There is nothing to catch.

What I did: an armed state

The player has six states. One of them is new:

/** `armed`: on by default, waiting for the browser's first user gesture. */
type Playback = "off" | "loading" | "playing" | "armed" | "paused" | "error";

armed means "the visitor wants sound, and the browser hasn't allowed it yet".
The tray shows it as ON, because what it shows is the intent, not the wait.

The browser can tell you whether a gesture has happened, through
navigator.userActivation. If it says no, the player goes straight to armed
and doesn't touch Web Audio at all:

startDefault() {
  // ...the saved "off" returns early...
  this.wanted = true;
  if (this.mustWaitForGesture()) {
    this.update({ playback: "armed" });
    return;
  }
  void this.play(false);
}

/** True while the browser says no gesture has happened yet and no graph exists. */
private mustWaitForGesture(): boolean {
  return this.context === null && typeof navigator !== "undefined" && navigator.userActivation?.hasBeenActive === false;
}

The AudioContext is only created inside play(), and play() runs from the
first gesture. So the graph is built inside the activation, as a click handler
would do it:

this.prepare(); // new AudioContext(), new Audio(), gain at 0
// Both calls happen within the click's user activation, including iOS.
await Promise.all([this.context!.resume(), this.media!.play()]);

The gain starts at 0 and ramps to the visitor's volume over 1.2 seconds, so
the first gesture never produces a jump.

The unit test checks the thing I actually care about: no graph before the
gesture, one graph after it.

it("before any gesture it arms itself without building an AudioContext (no console warning)", async () => {
  vi.stubGlobal("navigator", { ...navigator, userActivation: { hasBeenActive: false, isActive: false } });
  player.startDefault();
  await Promise.resolve(); await Promise.resolve();
  expect(player.getSnapshot().playback).toBe("armed");
  expect(AudioContext).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
  expect(Audio).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
  // The first real gesture builds the graph inside the activation and plays.
  vi.stubGlobal("navigator", { ...navigator, userActivation: { hasBeenActive: true, isActive: true } });
  player.resumeWanted();
  await Promise.resolve(); await Promise.resolve();
  expect(AudioContext).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);
  expect(player.getSnapshot().playback).toBe("playing");
});

There was one more door. pageshow fires right after load, and its handler
also called play(). Same warning, through a different path. It now asks the
same mustWaitForGesture() first.

My mistake: the first tap was lost

The control listened for pointerdown and keydown. On a desktop that's
fine. On a phone, the music only started on the second tap.

A touch doesn't activate the page on pointerdown. It activates on
pointerup or touchend. So the first tap called play() too early, got
refused, and the player went back to armed. The second tap's pointerdown
came after the first tap's activation, so it worked.

The fix listens to every event that can be the activating one, in the capture
phase on window, so no other handler can swallow it:

const UNLOCK_EVENTS = ["pointerdown", "pointerup", "touchend", "keydown", "click"] as const;

for (const type of UNLOCK_EVENTS) window.addEventListener(type, unlock, { capture: true, passive: true });

unlock only calls resumeWanted(), which does nothing once the music is
really playing. Wheel and pointer movement are not in the list: they never
count as activation, so no code can make them sound. Someone who reads the
page by scrolling with the wheel stays armed until their first click or key.

The quiet bug behind it

While testing that, I found a worse case. Sometimes the <audio> element
fired playing, but the AudioContext was still suspended. Sound was
flowing into a stopped graph. That's silence, and the old code marked it as
playing. The tray said ON, nothing sounded, and the next gesture thought
there was nothing to do.

Now playing only counts when the context is running:

media.onplaying = () => {
  if (!this.wanted || this.hidden) { media.pause(); return; }
  // Frames flowing into a suspended graph make no sound: still waiting.
  if (context.state !== "running") { this.update({ playback: "armed" }); return; }
  this.update({ playback: "playing" });
  this.level(1.2);
};

And resumeWanted() retries when the state says playing but the context
doesn't:

resumeWanted() {
  if (!this.wanted || this.hidden) return;
  const silent = this.context !== null && this.context.state !== "running";
  if (this.state.playback !== "playing" || silent) void this.play(false);
}

Making the wait visible

armed showing ON had its own problem. People saw ON, heard nothing, and
assumed it was broken. So while the player is armed, the tray says "Click to
listen" ("Tap to listen" on touch screens) and the ON label pulses softly. It
goes away as soon as the music plays or the panel opens.

What isn't solved

A new visitor always needs one gesture. That's the browser's rule and it's a
good one. The only way to hear the music without a click is for the visitor to
allow sound for the site in their browser settings.

Where navigator.userActivation isn't available, mustWaitForGesture()
returns false and the old path runs: try to play, get refused, go to
armed. It still works, but the warning can come back there.

And the site still has two AudioContexts: one for the soundtrack and one for
the sound effects bus. One control drives both, but it's two graphs to keep in
sync.

A question

How do you show "sound is on, but waiting for you" without it looking broken?
A pulsing label is my answer for now, and I'm not sure it's the best one.

You can hear it (after one click) at
jonasjavier.dev.

I'm Jonás Javier Encarnación, a full-stack developer in Santo Domingo,
Dominican Republic. I wrote this post with help from an AI assistant; the code,
the bug and the decisions are from my project.

title: Cap agent React refactors to one tree layer per PR
description:
I asked an agent to “clean up the Checkout folder” once. It came back with a PR that touched the page, three child forms, a shared hook two levels up, and a utility used by Settings. Reviewing it felt like reviewing four PRs stapled together.

Green CI. Unreadable blast radius.

So I stopped saying “refactor the feature.” I cap the agent to one tree layer per PR.

What “one tree layer” means

In a typical React tree:

CheckoutPage
  ├── ShippingForm
  ├── PaymentForm
  └── OrderSummary
        └── LineItemRow

One layer means: change ShippingForm or CheckoutPage or LineItemRow — not all of them in the same diff. Sibling components at the same depth can share a PR only if the change is the same mechanical rename and the prompt says so.

Hooks and utils count as their own layer. If the agent needs a new useShippingAddress extracted from ShippingForm, that extraction is PR 1; wiring it into a sibling is PR 2.

Why unbounded refactors go sideways

Agents are good at local pattern matching and bad at your mental model of ownership. Give them a whole folder and they will:

  • “helpfully” rename props across parents and children in one go
  • move shared state up “for cleanliness” while changing leaf UI
  • rewrite a utility used by unrelated routes because the types looked similar
  • collapse three tiny components into one mega-file because the prompt said “simplify”

Each of those might be fine alone. Together they make bisect useless and force reviewers to trust the model instead of reading the diff.

I’ve also seen agents “finish” a layer by rewriting the parent’s error boundary “while they were there.” That while-they-were-there clause is how one-layer work becomes a rewrite.

How I prompt it

I name the exact file (or folder of siblings) and ban climbing the tree:

Refactor only `src/checkout/ShippingForm.tsx` and files it exclusively owns
(styles / tests colocated under the same folder).

Do not edit:
- parent `CheckoutPage`
- siblings `PaymentForm`, `OrderSummary`
- shared hooks under `src/hooks/`
- anything under `src/settings/`

If a change truly requires a parent or shared hook, stop and list the follow-up PR instead of editing it now.
Max ~200 lines of net change. Prefer extract + thin wrapper over rewrite.

If I’m using a ownership map (one file → one owner component), I paste the relevant rows and say “stay inside these paths.”

What I accept vs reject in review

Accept

  • Prop rename inside one component + its colocated test
  • Extracting a private helper used only by that file
  • Splitting a bloated leaf into two leaves without changing the parent’s public API in the same PR

Reject / split

  • Parent layout change + child form rewrite in one PR
  • New shared hook + adoption in three features
  • “Also fixed Settings while matching the pattern”
  • Deleting a prop from a shared type that other trees still need

When the agent stops and proposes PR 2 for the parent, that’s success — not incompleteness.

Tiny checklist before I hit merge

  1. git diff --stat — mostly one directory?
  2. Does the commit message name one component or layer?
  3. Could I revert this without breaking a half-migrated parent?
  4. Did shared modules change? If yes, was that the whole point of this PR, or drive-by?

If (3) is no, the layer cap failed.

Prompt snippet I reuse 

One tree layer only. Target: <ComponentOrPath>.
Edit that layer’s files only. No parent/sibling/shared climbs.
If blocked by a parent or shared API, output a short “PR 2 proposal” and stop.
Do not rewrite unrelated utilities to match style.

Tiny habit

Next time you ask an agent to refactor React, don’t hand it a feature folder. Hand it one node in the tree.

Smaller PRs merge faster, bisect cleaner, and keep the agent from turning “tidy ShippingForm” into “accidentally redesign Checkout.”

title: Is Your Old Computer Still Safe? What Unsupported Windows Versions Mean for Your Business
description:
The Windows box in the corner that runs the legacy app. The PC wired to the lab instrument. The machine that hosts a script nobody wants to migrate because "it just works".

It boots every morning. Nobody complains. And that's exactly why it's dangerous.

"It still works" and "it's still safe" are two very different statements.

What "end of support" actually means

When Microsoft ends support for a Windows version, nothing visibly happens. No shutdown, no banner, no countdown. The machine just stops receiving security patches.

Here's where the common versions stand:

Version Support ended
Windows 7 January 2020
Windows 8.1 January 2023
Windows 10 October 14, 2025

Windows 10 has a paid Extended Security Updates (ESU) programme as a bridge. It's per-device, time-limited, and gets pricier over time, so think of it as a way to buy time rather than a plan.

Why unpatched Windows is a real problem

If you've read a CVE advisory, you know how this goes:

  1. A flaw is found and patched on supported versions.
  2. The patch and advisory make the flaw public.
  3. Attackers build exploits and scan for machines that never got the fix.

Supported systems are covered after step 1. Unsupported ones stay exposed to everything from step 2 onward, forever.

And the machine doesn't have to be valuable to be dangerous. It just has to be reachable. A single unpatched endpoint is a classic foothold for ransomware to move toward file servers, credentials, and backups.

Antivirus and EDR can detect and respond. They can't patch a vulnerable OS component.

Find what you actually have

You can't secure what you don't know about. For domain-joined machines:

Get-ADComputer -Filter 'OperatingSystem -like "*Windows*"' `
  -Properties OperatingSystem, OperatingSystemVersion, LastLogonDate |
  Select-Object Name, OperatingSystem, OperatingSystemVersion, LastLogonDate |
  Sort-Object OperatingSystem |
  Export-Csv .\windows-inventory.csv -NoTypeInformation

For a single machine:

Get-CimInstance Win32_OperatingSystem |
  Select-Object Caption, Version, BuildNumber

Then go looking for the machines AD can't see: standalone PCs, kiosks, point-of-sale terminals, and anything attached to specialized equipment. The ones with a LastLogonDate from months ago are usually the forgotten ones, and the forgotten ones are the risky ones.

Can it run Windows 11?

Windows 11 needs TPM 2.0, Secure Boot, and a supported CPU. A quick local check:

Get-Tpm | Select-Object TpmPresent, TpmReady
Confirm-SecureBootUEFI

On legacy BIOS systems, it throws an error, which tells you something on its own. For the full answer, including CPU support, use Microsoft's PC Health Check app or your endpoint tool's readiness report.

Then sort every machine into one of three buckets:

  • Upgrade: meets the requirements, so upgrade in place
  • Replace: hardware can't run Windows 11, so budget for a new device.
  • Special case: tied to a legacy app or device, so contain it and plan

Contain what you can't replace yet

Some machines genuinely can't move today. Proprietary drivers, vendor lock-in, a tool that only runs on an old OS. If that's you, shrink the blast radius:

  • Put it on an isolated VLAN with strict ACLs.
  • Block outbound internet unless there's a documented need
  • No email, no browsing on that machine
  • Remove everyday admin rights and restrict logins
  • Keep backups offline or immutable.
  • Ship its logs somewhere central and alert on weird traffic

⚠️ This reduces risk. It doesn't remove it. Treat it as a seatbelt on a car with bad brakes: better than nothing, not a long-term plan.

Don't let "temporary" become "forever".

My favourite low-tech fix is an exception register. A simple table in your repo or wiki:

Hostname OS Why it can't move Owner Controls Review date
LAB-PC-01 Windows 7 Vendor driver J. Doe VLAN 40, no internet 2027-01-31

Every exception gets an owner and a review date. Without those, "we'll fix it next quarter" quietly turns into five years.

The non-technical argument (for when you need budget)

If you're making the case to management, these usually land:

  • Compliance: PCI DSS, HIPAA, and GDPR all expect reasonable patching.
  • Insurance: cyber insurers increasingly ask about unsupported systems.
  • Support drift: browsers and business apps eventually drop old Windows versions.
  • Productivity: old hardware crashes and lags, and the lost minutes add up.

A ransomware incident costs far more than a replacement cycle spread over a few quarters.

TL;DR

  1. Inventory everything, including the forgotten machines.
  2. Sort into Upgrade / Replace / Special Case
  3. Isolate what can't move, and write down who owns it.
  4. Replace on a schedule, starting with the most exposed machines.

Unsupported machines don't fail loudly. They sit there working while the risk grows. The fix is boring, and that's a good thing.

Have you dealt with a stubborn legacy Windows dependency? How did you handle it? Let me know in the comments. 👇

title: Updating Rustup 1.29.3 while keeping the compiler fixed
description:
The toolchain manager and the compiler have separate version numbers. I updated an isolated Rustup installation from 1.29.2 to 1.29.3, kept its linked compiler at 1.99.1, then compiled and ran a small program through that same toolchain.

That gives me a useful way to handle this patch: update the manager that selects the tools, then check which compiler a project actually uses.

Recorded versions from the isolated update and the compiled sample. Image by the author.

What the patch changes

The Rustup team reports two regression fixes in 1.29.3: an illegal-instruction failure on certain x86_64 CPUs without SSE4.1, and an unsupported-lock error on Solaris. Those are upstream release claims; this walkthrough does not reproduce either hardware-specific failure. [1]

If you already have Rustup, the release instructions say to stop programs using it and run:

rustup self update

The word self matters. This updates Rustup itself. It is different from asking Rustup to update installed Rust toolchains with rustup update. That broader command can also update the manager. [1]

Check both sides of the selection

I used separate CARGO_HOME and RUSTUP_HOME directories for the trial, with shell startup files left alone. Rustup documents these locations as configurable. [2] I linked an existing compiler under the custom name pinned-local; I did not download a fresh compiler or replace the usual installation.

Here is the version ledger:

Component Before After
Rustup 1.29.2 1.29.3
Linked Rust compiler 1.99.1 1.99.1

To check the selection in that shell, I ran:

rustup --version
rustup show active-toolchain
rustc --version

The active toolchain was pinned-local (default). Keep the complete version output when troubleshooting; the table above extracts the version fields so the two components are easy to compare.

Rustup's rustc and cargo commands are proxies: they pass the invocation to a selected toolchain. Updating that routing program does not, by itself, request a different compiler. [3]

There is one practical prerequisite here: the shell must be reaching those proxies. A rustc supplied by another installation can produce a perfectly valid version line while bypassing the Rustup selection you intended. Mayur Kumbhar's environment setup walkthrough makes the related point that verifying the compiler and Cargo in a fresh shell is part of installation, rather than an optional last step. [4]

Compile through the named toolchain

For a small end-to-end check, I saved this as demo.rs:

fn main() {
    let values = [2_u32, 3, 5];
    println!("sum={}", values.iter().sum::<u32>());
}

Then I selected the linked toolchain explicitly:

rustup run pinned-local rustc demo.rs -o demo
./demo

The executable printed:

sum=10

pinned-local is the custom name from this trial, not a toolchain Rustup ships. Use a toolchain you have actually installed or linked when adapting the command.

This is a narrow update check: manager version, compiler selection, compilation and program output. It does not test all Cargo dependencies or establish that a project will build on every target. For a real project, keep its selected compiler visible alongside the manager version. “Rust updated” hides a distinction that the tools themselves already let you inspect.

References and resources

  1. The Rustup Team, Rustup 1.29.3 release announcement.
  2. The Rustup Book, installation locations and environment variables.
  3. The Rustup Book, how Rustup and its proxies work.
  4. Mayur Kumbhar, Rust Essentials: How to Set Up Your Development Environment.

Asset credits

Original version-track diagram from the recorded update and compile check. No third-party image assets.

title: CompSkill: Compiling Execution Experience for Skill Retrieval
description:
arXiv:2611.01115v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on skill documents, yet most retrievers rank them by description alone and ignore what earlier executions revealed, even though a relevant skill can hurt execution. We present CompSkill, which indexes skills with learned 512-d keys and compiles matched same-task comparisons into skill offsets and capped key residuals (KeyOpt), so experience changes which document the executor receives, never its text. Under a logistic outcome model with unknown task difficulty, matched comparisons cancel that difficulty and only discordant ones carry information; on support executions, predictions improve with each discordant task. An experience hypergraph keeps each comparison with its executor and document versions, recalls missed skills and grounds a cited review. Compact keys raise SkillRet NDCG@10 from 64.0 to 70.9 at one eighth of the dimension. With one document, CompSkill completes 256 and 260 of 332 ToolQA tasks with GPT-5.6-luna and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, respectively, more than every baseline, and stays on par with the strongest baselines on AppWorld and ALFWorld. On 332 newly generated ToolQA tasks, it completes 256 with GPT-5.6-luna, significantly more than BM25, SkillRet-8B, Tool2Vec and RankGPT; over all 844 ToolQA tasks, it completes 24 more than the strongest baseline. Selection matters beyond relevance: pairing the right guide with a same-database sibling instead of another database's guide costs 8 of 96 tasks. Code, models and support data: https://github.com/satoshinji2992/CompSkill

title: Do AI crawlers read llms.txt? What three days of server logs show
description:
Originally published by the AI Visibility Census at aivisibilitycensus.com/do-ai-crawlers-read-llms-txt. Data free to reuse under CC BY 4.0.

Short answer: some do. In the first three days of our brand-new site, three crawlers checked against their company’s published IP ranges asked for llms.txt or llms-full.txt: Googlebot 5 times, GoogleOther 4 times and ClaudeBot once. Bingbot and Applebot never asked, and no verified request came from an OpenAI or Perplexity crawler. The same crawlers fetched our Markdown page copies 77 times, so the files llms.txt points to got far more attention than llms.txt itself.

What is llms.txt?

llms.txt is a Markdown file at the root of a site: a title, a short summary of the site and lists of links to its key pages, each with an optional note. It was proposed on 3 September 2024 as a way to give language models a short, clean map of a site (llmstxt.org). Many sites also publish llms-full.txt, a longer file with the full text of their pages; that is a common convention, not part of the proposal. llms.txt itself is a proposal, not a standard that search engines or AI companies have signed up to, so the useful question is whether their crawlers fetch it at all.

Our site has both files, generated automatically from every published page, plus a Markdown copy of every page at the same address with .md on the end. The full setup is in Lab note 001.

What our logs show

The window is our first logged request at 10:23 UTC on 29 October 2026 to 13:00 UTC on 1 November 2026, about 75 hours. The table counts only requests whose IP address matched the crawler company’s published ranges.

Crawler (company) Verified requests llms.txt llms-full.txt Markdown copies (.md)
Googlebot (Google) 230 3 2 42
ClaudeBot (Anthropic) 101 1 0 14
GoogleOther (Google) 72 2 2 21
Bingbot (Microsoft) 13 0 0 0
Applebot (Apple) 12 0 0 0
Google-InspectionTool (Google) 12 0 0 0
OpenAI crawlers 0 0 0 0
PerplexityBot 0 0 0 0
Total 440 6 4 77

Source: AI Visibility Census bot log, 29 October 10:23 UTC to 1 November 13:00 UTC 2026. Requests over http and https are counted together. Ten requests that used a crawler’s name (Googlebot 6, ClaudeBot 2, GPTBot 2) came from addresses outside that company’s published ranges and are excluded. They came from the same addresses as our own testing.

That is 10 llms file requests out of 440 verified crawler requests, about 2%. Markdown copies made up 77, or 17.5%.

ClaudeBot was the first verified crawler to ask for llms.txt, at 15:38 UTC on 29 October, about five hours after launch. GoogleOther followed at 21:07 UTC the same evening, and Googlebot at 18:45 UTC on 30 October.

Crawlers found the Markdown copies before they read llms.txt

All three crawlers that read llms.txt had already fetched a Markdown copy first. ClaudeBot’s first .md request came at 15:37 UTC, about a minute before its llms.txt request. GoogleOther fetched Markdown from 17:59 UTC and llms.txt at 21:07 UTC. Googlebot fetched Markdown from 21:27 UTC on 29 October, about 21 hours before it asked for llms.txt.

So llms.txt was not how they found the Markdown pages. Every HTML page on our site also points to its Markdown copy with a Link: rel="alternate"; type="text/markdown" header, and that is one route they could have used. Our log shows what was fetched and when, not why.

Bing was told about llms.txt and never fetched it

Every time we publish or update a page, our site submits the page, its Markdown copy and llms.txt to IndexNow, which passes them to Bing and the other engines that take part. llms.txt was in dozens of those submissions, each answered with response code 200. In the same 75 hours Bingbot made 13 verified requests, none for llms.txt, llms-full.txt or a Markdown copy.

Should you create an llms.txt file?

On this evidence, it costs little and some crawlers do fetch it. Two cautions. A fetch is not use: our log shows a crawler downloaded the file, not that any AI answer drew on it. And on our site the Markdown copies of pages drew about eight times as many verified requests as the llms files, so if you can only do one, clean Markdown versions of your pages look like the bigger draw.

This is one new site over three days. Treat it as a dated example, not an average. In Lab note 001 we predicted that no verified AI crawler would request llms.txt in the first 30 days. ClaudeBot proved that wrong within five hours.

What we are testing next

We have registered a follow-up for the rest of November, LL-001, on our experiments page. It asks whether verified AI crawlers are any more likely, within an hour of reading llms.txt or llms-full.txt than within an hour of reading robots.txt or our sitemap, to fetch a page they had not requested since our log began on 29 October. The result is due on 1 December 2026, whatever it shows.

Whether a site serves llms.txt and Markdown is one of the things the CensusIndex™ looks at in its monthly check of how ready the leading sites in each software category are for AI search. Whether AI answers then name a brand is what the Census100™ counts for software buyers, and our Editions count for professional services firms, starting with Ireland. To check crawler visits on your own server logs, the free AI crawler log check skill is on our Tools page.

Frequently asked questions

Does Google read llms.txt?

Google’s crawlers fetched it on our site: Googlebot asked for llms.txt or llms-full.txt 5 times and GoogleOther 4 times in our first three days, all from Google’s published IP ranges. Fetching a file does not show that Google uses it in search results or AI answers.

Does ChatGPT read llms.txt?

We cannot tell yet. In the first three days, no request identifying as an OpenAI crawler came from OpenAI’s published IP ranges, for llms.txt or anything else.

Where does llms.txt go?

At the root of the domain, so it loads at yoursite.com/llms.txt, the same place as robots.txt.

How can I see if AI crawlers fetch my llms.txt?

Search your server or CDN logs for requests to /llms.txt, then check each request’s IP address against the ranges the crawler’s company publishes. A user agent name on its own proves nothing, because any client can send it.

About this article

Lab note 002 in our series on a brand-new domain. Counts come from our own bot log, which checks each request against the IP ranges that Google, Microsoft, Apple, Anthropic, OpenAI and Perplexity publish. Requests from Claude-User, Anthropic’s user-triggered fetcher, came from our own testing and are left out, as in Lab note 001. How we count is set out in the methodology, and the launch-day numbers, with a CSV, are on the new site crawl and indexing statistics page. Data in this article is free to reuse under CC BY 4.0.

Sources

  • llmstxt.org: The /llms.txt file, the proposal and format.
  • AI Visibility Census bot log and IndexNow log, 29 October to 1 November 2026.
