title: The Ultimate Guide to Modern Infrastructure, Architecture, and Cloud Storage
description:
In the modern digital era, data and computing infrastructure have become the lifeblood of both personal productivity and enterprise operations. Gone are the days when we were entirely dependent on physical local hard drives, fragile legacy storage, or easily misplaced USB flash drives to store our important documents, photos, music, and videos. Today, a revolutionary technology keeps our digital lives running seamlessly behind the scenes: Cloud Computing.
Whether you are a student keeping your assignments safe, a developer deploying an application, or a global enterprise managing a complex microservices architecture, cloud technology has transformed the way we interact with data. This comprehensive guide breaks down everything you need to know about cloud computing, exploring its primary service models (IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS), its profound deployment benefits, and the top platforms available to get you started.
**

What is Cloud Computing and Cloud Storage?

**
At its core, cloud computing is the delivery of computing services over the internet. These services include servers, databases, networking, software, analytics, and intelligence. Instead of buying, owning, and maintaining physical data centers and servers, individuals and businesses rent access to storage and computing power from a cloud provider.
A vital and highly practical branch of this technology is Cloud Storage. This is an incredibly useful facility that allows you to save and store your essential files—such as documents, photographs, music tracks, and videos—not just on your local computer's physical drive, but also on secure, remote servers accessible via the internet.
When you store your data in the cloud, it is generally managed in two distinct ways depending on your architecture and privacy needs:
**

1. Personal Storage (Private / Restricted Access)

**
When you save files under a personal setting, the data is entirely private to you. No one else has the authorization to view, edit, or tamper with your files. It acts as your private digital vault, ensuring high confidentiality and security for sensitive information like personal financial ocuments, private photos, or official credentials.

2. Shared Storage (Collaborative / Multi-User Access)

If you are working with others, cloud storage provides the facility to convert files into shared assets for friends, family, or professional groups. This offers a massive advantage for collaborative environments. If you are executing a project with a team, you can easily share documents in real-time. Team members can view, comment on, and edit the files simultaneously from their respective locations, eliminating the hassle of emailing multiple versions of the same file back and forth.
Furthermore, cloud storage offers the flexibility of managing files both online and offline. You can choose to keep a synchronized copy locally on your device for offline access, which automatically backs up and syncs to the internet the moment your device reconnects to a network.

**

**### The Three Pillars of Cloud Computing:

IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS

To truly understand cloud computing beyond simple storage, you must understand the three core service models that dictate how cloud resources are provisioned and managed. These models exist on a spectrum of control, ranging from maximum user management to complete provider management.
Feature / Model Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) Platform as a Service (PaaS) Software as a Service (SaaS)
Definition Raw computing infrastructure rented over the internet. A complete development and deployment environment in the cloud. On-demand, ready-to-use software applications hosted by a provider.
What You Manage Applications, Data, Runtime, Middleware, OS. Applications, Data. Nothing. The provider manages everything.
What the Provider Manages Virtualization, Servers, Storage, Networking. OS, Middleware, Runtime, Virtualization, Servers, Storage. Applications, Data, OS, Hardware, Infrastructure.
Best Used For Migrating workloads, hosting websites, networking. Building APIs, deploying code quickly, DevOps pipelines. Day-to-day productivity, CRM, collaborative tools.
Real-World Examples AWS (EC2), Google Compute Engine, Microsoft Azure VMs. Heroku, Google App Engine, AWS Elastic Beanstalk. Google Drive, Microsoft 365, Dropbox, Slack.

**

1. Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)

**
IaaS provides the fundamental building blocks of computing. With IaaS, you rent raw hardware capabilities from a cloud vendor, including physical or virtual machines, storage blocks, and networking tools.
The Benefit: It offers the highest level of flexibility and architectural control over your cloud resources. You can install any operating system (OS), manage firewalls, and configure complex networking environments.
The Trade-off: It requires significant technical expertise. You are entirely responsible for OS updates, security patching, and middleware configurations.
**

2. Platform as a Service (PaaS)

**
PaaS removes the burden of managing underlying hardware and operating systems. The cloud provider delivers a fully managed platform equipped with operating systems, databases, runtime environments, and development tools.
The Benefit: Developers can focus entirely on writing code and building applications without worrying about server provisioning, load balancing, or infrastructure scaling.
The Trade-off: You have less control over the underlying infrastructure. If your application requires highly customized OS tweaks, PaaS might limit your options.

**

3. Software as a Service (SaaS)

**
SaaS is a complete, fully functioning software solution that you access over the internet, typically through a web browser or a mobile application. The vendor hosts, updates, secures, and maintains the entire product.

The Benefit: It requires zero technical maintenance from the user. You simply log in and start working. This is exactly where services like consumer cloud storage fit into the picture.

The Trade-off: You have minimal customizability over how the application runs under the hood, and you are entirely dependent on the vendor’s uptime and data security practices.
**

The Transformative Benefits of Cloud Computing

**
The shift from localized physical hardware to cloud infrastructure brings a massive array of benefits that enhance security, scalability, and convenience.

Here are the primary advantages of utilizing cloud computing and storage:

Dual Online and Offline Backup: Your files remain permanently secure because the system maintains synchronized backups, keeping data safe even if your internet connection drops temporarily.
Location Independence: You can open, edit, and manage your files from absolutely any geographical location in the world, provided you have an internet-enabled device.

Effortless Multi-Location Sharing: A single file or an entire folder can be shared simultaneously with multiple people across different regions with just a few clicks.

Instant Disaster Recovery: If your physical computer crashes, gets stolen, or suffers hardware failure, you lose nothing. You can easily log into a brand-new computer and restore or access all your files instantly.

Seamless Cross-Device Accessibility: Your data is accessible concurrently across an array of ecosystems, allowing you to switch smoothly between your mobile smartphone, desktop computer, laptop, and tablet.

Cost-Free Entry Point: Most major cloud providers offer this facility completely free of charge for a generous base amount of storage, allowing anyone to leverage the technology without an upfront financial commitment.

Zero Additional Hardware Required: You do not need to purchase expensive external hard drives, network-attached storage (NAS) bays, or physical servers. The cloud provider handles all hardware infrastructure.

User-Friendly Interface: Cloud applications are designed to be highly intuitive. They appear and operate exactly like your standard computer file manager or Windows Explorer, making them incredibly easy to use.

Real-Time Online Editing: Many platforms embed cloud-based productivity suites, allowing you to edit documents, spreadsheets, and presentations directly within your web browser without downloading them.

No File Size Sharing Limits:

Traditional emails restrict file attachments (often limiting them to 10 MB or 25 MB). Cloud storage removes this barrier, allowing you to share files of virtually any size simply by sending a web link.
Travel Flexibility: You can travel light anywhere in the world without carrying physical storage media or heavy laptops, knowing your vital travel documents, tickets, and portfolios are securely waiting for you in the cloud.
Generous Free Storage Capacity: Standard free tiers across popular services offer anywhere from 5 GB to 25 GB of free online data storage, which is more than sufficient for everyday personal documentation.
**

How to Use Cloud Computing and Storage Services

**
Getting started with cloud computing is incredibly straightforward and requires no technical expertise. The entire onboarding process can be completed in just a few minutes. Follow these simple steps to begin leveraging the cloud:

Select a Provider:

Choose a reputable cloud storage service that aligns with your operating system and preferences (such as Google Drive for Android/Google users or OneDrive for Windows users).
Create an Account: Visit the official website or download the mobile app of the service provider. Register for a free account using your email address.
Set Up Security: Choose a strong, unique password and enable Two-Factor Authentication (2FA) to ensure your private files remain completely secure.

Upload Files:

Drag and drop your files into the browser window, or use the "Upload" button to select files from your local device.
Organize and Share: Create folders to categorize your data just like you do on your local PC. Right-click on any file or folder to generate a shareable link for your peers or family.
**

Top Platforms Providing Cloud Services

**
The cloud ecosystem features several highly reliable platforms that cater to billions of users globally. Depending on whether you need a simple SaaS storage tool or a broader computing ecosystem, here are the top services:

Google Drive (Google Cloud Workspace)

Developed by Google, this is one of the most widely used SaaS cloud services in the world. It integrates seamlessly with Android devices and Google Workspace (Docs, Sheets, Slides). Google Drive offers a highly generous 15 GB of free storage upon account creation, making it an excellent starting point for storing documents, photos, and collaborative team projects. On an enterprise scale, it is backed by Google Cloud Platform (GCP).

Microsoft OneDrive (Microsoft 365)

Baked directly into the Windows operating system architecture, Microsoft's cloud platform is ideal for users who rely heavily on Microsoft Office applications like Word, Excel, and PowerPoint. It allows flawless synchronization between your local desktop environment and the cloud, offering a highly polished, professional interface for both personal and enterprise files. It is backed by Microsoft's enterprise-grade Azure infrastructure.

Dropbox

As one of the pioneers of consumer cloud storage, Dropbox is celebrated for its incredibly fast and reliable file-synchronization engine. It acts as a seamless folder on your computer. Whenever you drop a file inside it, it instantly uploads to the web. Dropbox is favored by creative professionals for its simplicity, robust app integrations, and clean user experience.

Yandex.Disk

Provided by the web services company Yandex, Yandex.Disk is a reliable and highly secure cloud storage service. It provides user-friendly cross-platform applications for Windows, macOS, Android, and iOS. It features automatic photo uploads from smartphones, integrated document editing tools, and an easy-to-use interface modeled after classic desktop file environments.

4Sync

4Sync is a specialized cloud storage service designed with a heavy focus on media synchronization and sharing. It allows users to easily store, zip, access, and share files like audio tracks, videos, and large zip archives. It is a fantastic tool for users who need straightforward, file-hosting capabilities alongside standard cross-device syncing features.

Cloud Security and Data Encryption FAQ
When migrating to modern infrastructure, security is paramount. Below are answers to the most critical questions regarding data safety in the cloud.
**

How is data encrypted in cloud computing?

**
Cloud computing providers secure data using two distinct types of data encryption:
Encryption at Rest: This protects your data while it is physically stored on the cloud provider's hard drives or solid-state servers. Advanced encryption standards, such as AES-256, scramble the data so that even if someone physically accesses the hard drive, they cannot read it.
Encryption in Transit: This protects your data as it travels across the internet between your personal device and the cloud server. This is typically handled by secure protocols like HTTPS and TLS, preventing interception by bad actors during the upload or download process.
**

Can cloud providers see my private files?

**
By default, major cloud computing vendors possess the master keys to decrypt data for indexing, file previews, and compliance checks. However, many services offer End-to-End Encryption (E2EE) or Zero-Knowledge architectures. With E2EE, your data is encrypted on your local device before it ever reaches the cloud. Because only you hold the unique decryption keys, the cloud provider cannot view or access your files under any circumstances.
**

Is my data safe if the cloud provider suffers a server crash?

**
Yes. Unlike a local hard drive, cloud computing architecture relies on a principle called redundancy. When you upload a file, the cloud provider automatically creates multiple exact copies and distributes them across completely separate, geodistributed data centers. If one server facility suffers a hardware failure, natural disaster, or power failure, another data center instantly takes over, guaranteeing that your data remains intact and available without interruption.
What steps can I take to maximize my personal cloud security?
While providers manage infrastructure security, you must secure your individual access points. Always execute the following best practices:
Use a robust, complex password manager to avoid repeating credentials across websites.
Mandatory activation of Two-Factor Authentication (2FA) or Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) via an authenticator app.
Audit your shared file links periodically to revoke access permissions when public collaboration concludes.
**

Conclusion

**
Cloud computing and cloud storage are no longer futuristic concepts; they are essential pillars of modern technological architecture. Whether you are using IaaS to launch virtual machines, PaaS to build apps, or simple SaaS tools like cloud storage to keep your personal files safe, migrating to the cloud protects you from physical hardware failures, unlocks the freedom to work from anywhere in the world, and makes teamwork completely effortless. With multiple premier platforms offering massive amounts of storage entirely for free, there is no better time to secure your digital world. Create an account with a trusted cloud provider today and experience the ultimate convenience of modern data management.
Disclaimer: The information provided in this article is for general informational and educational purposes only. While we strive to present accurate, up-to-date details regarding cloud computing models, infrastructure security, and storage architectures, individual service configurations, free storage tiers, policy structures, and data encryption implementations vary by provider and change over time. Readers should independently review the Terms of Service, Privacy Policies, and Security Agreements of individual cloud vendors before uploading sensitive personal or corporate data.

title: Configure Queue Rate-Limiting for HTTP-Based Webhook Reconciliation — Migration Boundaries
description:
Short answer: configure a queue for rate-limiting webhook processing from an HTTP-based cron handler, and keep the worker behind an adapter so the nightly reconciliation can move between providers. The deciding constraint is latency versus cost: a short trigger keeps the scheduler responsive, while a rate-limited worker absorbs the provider's pace.

Nightly payment reconciliation should start with an HTTP cron handler that enqueues bounded work, not with a long request that tries to drain a provider. The application owns the business result; the queue owns delivery pressure.

The invariants are more important than the queue brand. Every reconciliation unit needs a stable idempotency key, an audit record of enqueue, attempt, acknowledgement, and outcome, and a clear expiration policy. Standard queues are at-least-once, so exactly-once is a processing mindset rather than a delivery promise: the consumer must make a duplicate harmless. A cron execution is limited to 900 seconds, which is a useful boundary for the trigger, not a reason to pretend a large reconciliation is synchronous.

For this boundary, Infrai is a plausible fit before the competitor details: its public discovery surface exposes request schemas and runnable examples without a key, while its queue and cron capabilities stay behind a plain REST contract. I would consider it for the trigger-and-queue adapter, provided the ledger remains the authority for idempotency and audit.

Keep it boring.

No shortcut.

Still.

How should I configure a queue for rate-limiting webhook processing from an HTTP-based cron?

The trigger owns schedule validation, partition selection, and publication. It should not own provider calls that can run past the execution limit. For a nightly run, I would partition by merchant, settlement date, or another domain key that can be replayed independently, then publish one message per bounded unit. A separate queue for each webhook destination is warranted when their rate limits differ; otherwise the slowest destination becomes everybody's backpressure.

Delay support belongs in this design as a control, not as a substitute for a scheduler. A retry can carry a delay when a destination asks the worker to wait, but the documented ceiling is 604800 seconds. Message bodies are limited to 256 KB, retention is at most 30 days, and acknowledgement deletes the message. Those limits make the message an instruction plus retry data, not a durable ledger or a Kafka-style replay log.

A compact worker boundary makes migration possible. The monitoring call below is intentionally small: it reads the live cron capability schema, handles rate limits, and leaves provider-specific reconciliation logic in the application. In a real adapter, the same boundary would feed queue-depth and attempt-age measurements into the rate policy; the scheduler contract should remain inspectable even when the worker implementation changes, because a migration is safest when the business job, delivery attempt, and provider response remain separate records rather than one opaque request.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    url := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/cron.create"
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(context.Background(), http.MethodGet, url, nil)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            wait := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); retryAfter != "" {
                if seconds, parseErr := time.ParseDuration(retryAfter + "s"); parseErr == nil {
                    wait = seconds
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(wait)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("queue stats failed: %s: %s", resp.Status, strings.TrimSpace(string(body))))
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return
    }
    panic("queue stats remained rate-limited after retries")
}

The Claim operation is the important line. It must be backed by a uniqueness guarantee and an audit trail, and the provider call must be chosen so that a retry cannot create a second financial effect. A timeout is not evidence that the provider did nothing. Marking a job successful before recording the provider result creates a reconciliation hole; recording a result without a durable claim allows duplicate work. Neither is acceptable for a payment ledger.

Which queue boundary survives a vendor change?

A queue provider should sit behind the small contract above: publish a job, consume it, acknowledge it, reject or retry it, and expose enough statistics to tune the rate limit. The application should own the job identity, destination policy, retry metadata, and ledger state. That division lets a replacement preserve the business contract even when delivery semantics differ.

Option Useful fit for this reconciliation Boundary or limitation
AWS SQS A managed queue with explicit dead-letter handling and a familiar operational model Delivery is still at-least-once; visibility, retention, and redrive settings must match the ledger's retry policy.
RabbitMQ Teams that need broker-level routing and richer consumer controls Its routing flexibility increases the number of broker decisions the application must document and test.
Apache Kafka High-volume event history and multiple independent consumers A replayable log is a different operating model from a bounded nightly work queue; partitioning and offset ownership add weight here.
Inngest Event-driven functions with durable steps and orchestration Its workflow model is more useful when the unit of work spans steps; this reconciliation still needs an application-owned ledger.
Trigger.dev Long-running background jobs with a developer-oriented execution model It suits job execution better than a minimal queue adapter when the team wants hosted task runs and workflow controls.
Temporal Durable workflows whose state and retries are the primary concern It is the stronger choice for orchestration, but heavier than a queue for independent webhook deliveries.
Infrai scheduling A REST-shaped queue and cron surface when discovery and migration simplicity matter It is not a workflow engine, has no DAG or join primitive, and does not provide topic-style one-to-many delivery; separate queues are needed to simulate fan-out.

The comparison is deliberately uneven because the workload is uneven. SQS is a reasonable default for a team already standardized on AWS. RabbitMQ is stronger when routing topology is the central requirement. Kafka is the better choice when retaining and replaying a multi-consumer event history is the product requirement. A REST queue is attractive when the integration surface itself is the migration cost: Infrai's public discovery endpoint exposes request schemas and runnable examples, and the documented capabilities include Go examples, so a new capability can be inspected without first adopting a proprietary SDK.

I would try Infrai for the cron-triggered queue portion when a plain, self-describing REST contract reduces integration work and the application already owns idempotency and audit state; that choice matters because it keeps the queue adapter narrow enough to replace later. Its consistent idempotency convention is a supporting benefit for write retries, but it does not remove the need to make the consumer idempotent. The discovery surface is useful for checking the contract before implementation, not for outsourcing the architecture.

There is a second practical advantage for a small platform team: Infrai provides one key and one bill across the broader backend surface, currently 295 routes across 20 modules, so the reconciliation service does not need a separate credential and billing workflow for every adjacent capability it adopts. That reduces operational coordination around the queue, while the adapter still preserves the option to move the queue itself.

How do retries and rate limits avoid a feedback loop?

Start with a conservative per-destination limit, then watch queue depth, attempt age, response timeouts, and provider responses. Adjust the limit from observed webhook behavior. Frequent timeouts justify default retries with exponential backoff and a dead-letter path, not an immediate increase in concurrency. A retry record should include the destination, original job identity, attempt number, next eligible time, and enough response data for an operator or later worker to understand the failure.

The consumer should distinguish a transient response from a permanent validation failure. A transient failure is delayed and retried; a permanent one is acknowledged only after durable failure recording, or moved to a dead-letter queue according to the provider's semantics. AWS's dead-letter guidance is a useful operational reference here, although the same principle applies elsewhere: redrive is an explicit recovery action, not an invisible second chance.

Do not confuse FIFO deduplication with ledger idempotency. The FIFO deduplication window is only five minutes, while a reconciliation can be retried much later. Also, there is no native debounce or throttle primitive, so rate control belongs in the queue configuration and worker policy. The monitoring loop is part of the design.

The rejected design and its proper use

I would reject a single cron request that calls every webhook destination serially. It couples scheduler runtime to downstream latency, makes a timeout ambiguous, and forces the next run to compete with unfinished work. It is acceptable only for a deliberately tiny, bounded probe whose completion fits comfortably inside 900 seconds and whose side effects are idempotent. That is a narrow exception, not a reconciliation architecture.

I would also reject using this queue as a workflow orchestrator. There is no DAG execution, no fan-out/join primitive, no Kafka-style multi-consumer replay, and no catch-up for cron triggers missed while paused. Public HTTP targets are required for cron tasks, and push subscription targets must be public HTTPS endpoints, so a private worker should consume through an application-controlled boundary rather than being assumed reachable by the scheduler.

The final decision rule is straightforward: keep the nightly trigger short, partition work by a replayable business key, isolate destinations whose limits differ, and make the ledger the authority for exactly-once effects. Choose the broker for the delivery and operating model you actually need. Keep the adapter replaceable.

If that boundary fits the system, start by inspecting the scheduling contract at the cron capability discovery endpoint, then verify queue limits and retry behavior against the live schema before wiring the adapter.

References

  • AWS SQS dead-letter queues
  • RabbitMQ documentation
  • Apache Kafka documentation
  • Cron capability discovery

title: AWS S3 Bucket Versioning: Protect Your Data from Accidental Deletes and Overwrites
description:
A hands-on guide to enabling S3 versioning, recovering deleted files, and keeping costs under control with lifecycle rules."

tags: aws, s3, cloud, beginners

Overwriting the wrong file or deleting an important object in S3 is easy to do, and by default it is permanent. S3 Versioning fixes this. It keeps every version of every object in your bucket, so you can recover from mistakes and from application failures. In this post I enable versioning, test it, and recover a deleted file.

vishalcloudjourney

📦 What is S3 Versioning?

Versioning is a bucket-level feature that keeps multiple variants of an object in the same bucket. Every upload of the same key creates a new version with its own unique Version ID.

A bucket is always in one of three states:

  • Unversioned (the default)
  • Versioning-enabled
  • Versioning-suspended

⚠️ Once you enable versioning, you cannot go back to unversioned. You can only suspend it, and existing versions are kept.

✅ Why use it?

  • Recover from accidental deletion: a delete only adds a delete marker, and the data stays.
  • Recover from accidental overwrites: older versions are still there.
  • Keep a history: useful for audits and rollbacks.
  • Safer backups: a good protection layer against human error and some application bugs.

🖱️ Hands-on: Enable versioning in the console

Step 1: Create a bucket

  1. Open the S3 console and click Create bucket.
  2. Enter a globally unique bucket name, such as vishal-versioning-demo-123.
  3. Choose your region and keep Block all public access on.
  4. Click Create bucket.

Step 2: Enable versioning

  1. Open your bucket and go to the Properties tab.
  2. Find Bucket Versioning and click Edit.
  3. Select Enable and click Save changes.

Step 3: Upload and overwrite a file

  1. Create a file demo.txt containing Version 1 and upload it.
  2. Change the content to Version 2 and upload it again with the same name.
  3. Open the Objects tab and turn on the List versions toggle.

You will see two versions of demo.txt, each with its own Version ID. The latest one is the current version, and the other is a noncurrent version.

Step 4: Delete and recover

  1. Turn List versions off, select demo.txt and click Delete.
  2. The file seems to disappear. Turn List versions back on.
  3. You will see a Delete marker on top of your versions. Your data is safe.
  4. Select the delete marker and delete it. demo.txt comes back.

To remove a version permanently, delete it by its specific Version ID.

⌨️ Hands-on: Using the AWS CLI 

# Enable versioning
aws s3api put-bucket-versioning \
  --bucket vishal-versioning-demo-123 \
  --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled

# Check the status
aws s3api get-bucket-versioning --bucket vishal-versioning-demo-123

# List all versions and delete markers
aws s3api list-object-versions --bucket vishal-versioning-demo-123

# Download a specific version
aws s3api get-object \
  --bucket vishal-versioning-demo-123 \
  --key demo.txt \
  --version-id <VERSION_ID> demo-old.txt

# Permanently delete one specific version
aws s3api delete-object \
  --bucket vishal-versioning-demo-123 \
  --key demo.txt \
  --version-id <VERSION_ID>

💡 Things to know

  • Cost: every version is stored and billed as a separate object, so storage grows with each update.
  • Lifecycle rules: use them to expire noncurrent versions after N days, or move them to a cheaper storage class. This keeps costs under control.
  • Objects uploaded before versioning: they get the Version ID null.
  • MFA Delete: an optional extra protection that requires MFA to permanently delete a version or change the versioning state. Only the bucket owner's root account can enable it, and only through the CLI or API.
  • Replication: Cross-Region Replication requires versioning on both buckets.

🏆 Best practices

  1. Turn versioning on for buckets that hold important or hard-to-recreate data.
  2. Add a lifecycle rule to clean up old noncurrent versions.
  3. Restrict who can permanently delete versions with IAM and bucket policies.
  4. Consider MFA Delete for critical buckets.
  5. Monitor storage growth in the S3 console and in billing.

🧹 Cleanup

A versioned bucket is not empty until all versions and delete markers are removed. Use Empty in the console, then delete the bucket, so you don't pay for leftover data.

📚 Key learnings

  • Versioning turns a permanent delete into a recoverable one.
  • A delete on a versioned bucket adds a delete marker, and the data stays in the bucket.
  • Lifecycle rules are the best way to keep versioning affordable.

🤝 Connect with me

  • LinkedIn: Vishal Patil
  • GitHub: VishalPatil-DevOps-AWS
  • dev.to: @vishal_patil_aws

If this helped you, drop a ❤️ and tell me how you use S3 versioning in the comments!

title: Not Every Slow Query Needs a New Index
description:
What a SQL review taught me about assumptions, AI-written queries, and common-sense tuning

A development team asked me to review the SQL behind a change-data publishing job before they moved it from once a day to once an hour. In QA, one full run took 10 to 12 minutes. After the review, the same run took under 30 seconds. In production, most of its queries now finish in under a millisecond.

Almost none of that came from adding indexes. It came from reading the queries, asking what the job actually needed, and checking each assumption against real data. This post walks through what we found, in the order we found it, and what I would tell any team (or any AI assistant) writing SQL against a busy production database.

The short version:

  • You don't always need to tune the database. Often you need to understand the use case and explain how the database behaves.
  • Functions on indexed columns and "this column might be null" assumptions are the most common silent performance killers.
  • What is harmless in QA can be dangerous in production, because the data is shaped differently.
  • An index can make a query slower. Measure after every change.

The setup

The job polls a PostgreSQL read replica for rows that changed since its last run and publishes them as events. It is a classic checkpoint pattern:

  1. Read a ceiling: the newest change timestamp in the source tables.
  2. Count the rows changed between the last checkpoint and that ceiling.
  3. Page through them with keyset pagination, 500 rows at a time.
  4. Store the ceiling as the next checkpoint.

I'll use a generic schema for the examples:

Table Rows (largest) What it holds
accounts ~1M Users, organizations and partners, with an account_type column
contracts ~1,100 Partner contracts, keyed by the owning account
memberships ~650k Which accounts belong to which organization, with a membership_type
org_members ~9M Account-to-location assignments
locations ~hundreds of k Organization addresses

Every table has created_at and updated_at. The source system also maintains updated_at_num, a numeric YYYYMMDDHHMISS copy of updated_at, and that column is indexed on every table. Keep that last detail in mind.

Lesson 1: A function on an indexed column throws the index away

Every change-window filter in the job looked like this:

WHERE COALESCE(a.updated_at, a.created_at) >  :checkpoint
  AND COALESCE(a.updated_at, a.created_at) <= :snapshot

The intent is reasonable: if a row was never updated, fall back to its creation time. But PostgreSQL can only use a B-tree index when the predicate matches the indexed expression. Wrap the column in COALESCE, and the index on updated_at (or updated_at_num) is no longer a candidate. Every window query became a sequential scan of the whole table.

The COALESCE also encoded an assumption: that updated_at can be null. So before changing anything, we checked:

SELECT count(*) FROM accounts WHERE updated_at IS NULL;      -- 0
SELECT count(*) FROM accounts WHERE updated_at_num IS NULL;  -- 0

Zero on every table. The source system sets both timestamps when a row is created, so the fallback could never fire. The fix was to drop the function and filter on the indexed column directly:

WHERE a.updated_at_num >  :checkpoint
  AND a.updated_at_num <= :snapshot

That one change turned every window query into an index range scan.

Two things to take from it:

  • Don't defend against a condition until you've checked whether it exists. A one-line count(*) settled a question the code had been paying for on every run.
  • If you really do need the fallback, write it so it can use an index. Either (updated_at > x AND updated_at <= y) OR (updated_at IS NULL AND created_at > x AND created_at <= y), or an expression index on exactly COALESCE(updated_at, created_at).

Lesson 2: What is fine in QA can bite in production

The COALESCE wasn't the only defensive habit. One query filtered on TRIM(a.account_type) = 'STAFF'. In QA that is harmless: small tables, fast scans, correct results. In production it does two quiet things:

  • It stops any index on account_type from being used.
  • It hints that some values might be padded with spaces. If that were true, every other query that compares account_type without TRIM would silently miss those rows.

Again, the answer was in the data:

SELECT count(*) FROM accounts WHERE account_type <> TRIM(account_type);  -- 0

No padded values, so the TRIM came out, and the queries became consistent with each other.

I want to be clear about where this comes from. The developers I work with write good SQL. But we are now in an era where a lot of SQL is drafted by AI assistants, and they are very good at producing queries that return the right answer. They are much less good at knowing your data. A model will happily add COALESCE, TRIM, LOWER or DISTINCT "just in case", because in the abstract each one is safer. On a 10,000-row QA table you'll never notice. On a 10-million-row production table, each one can turn an index lookup into a full scan.

The result being correct does not mean the assumptions behind it are. Before a query ships, check it against the data's real shape: null counts, value distributions, duplicates, and how skewed the busiest keys are. Or ask a database engineer to review it. It never hurts.

Lesson 3: Carry every filter you know into the subquery

The partner-count query looked like this:

SELECT count(*)
FROM contracts c
JOIN accounts a ON a.account_id = c.account_id
WHERE c.org_id = :org
  AND a.updated_at_num > :checkpoint AND a.updated_at_num <= :snapshot
  AND c.account_id IN (
        SELECT DISTINCT m.parent_account_id
        FROM memberships m
        WHERE m.membership_type = 'PRIMARY'
          AND m.is_deleted = false
          AND (m.end_date IS NULL OR m.end_date >= :as_of));

The outer query was narrowed to one organization and a one-hour window: 59 candidate rows. The subquery wasn't narrowed at all. PostgreSQL read 1.77 million membership rows, built a distinct list of 831 IDs, then matched that list against the 59 candidates. That was 31,395 buffers and 83 ms to return a count of zero.

Two changes fixed it:

  AND EXISTS (
        SELECT 1
        FROM memberships m
        WHERE m.parent_account_id = c.account_id   -- correlate to the outer row
          AND m.org_id = :org                      -- the filter the outer query already had
          AND m.membership_type = 'PRIMARY'
          AND m.is_deleted = false
          AND (m.end_date IS NULL OR m.end_date >= :as_of));
IN (SELECT DISTINCT …) Correlated EXISTS with filters
Execution time 83 ms 0.8 ms
Buffers 31,395 181
Memberships access Parallel sequential scan Index lookup per candidate

A note on IN versus EXISTS: PostgreSQL already turns IN (subquery) into a semi-join, so the two often plan the same way. The DISTINCT adds nothing, since a semi-join never returns a row twice, and it can push the planner toward building the full list first. Switching to EXISTS helps. The bigger win is adding the filter. If the outer query is limited to something you also know about the subquery's rows, say so in the subquery too. Don't rely on the planner to infer it.

Lesson 4: Ask what a query is for before you tune it

The slowest query in the job didn't return any data. It computed the run's ceiling:

SELECT max(ts) FROM (
    SELECT max(updated_at_num) AS ts FROM accounts WHERE account_type IN (...)
    UNION ALL
    SELECT to_char(max(password_changed_at), 'YYYYMMDDHH24MISS')::numeric FROM accounts WHERE account_type IN (...)
    UNION ALL
    SELECT max(updated_at_num) FROM org_members
    UNION ALL
    SELECT max(s.updated_at_num)
    FROM staff_links s JOIN accounts a ON a.account_id = s.account_id AND a.account_type = 'STAFF'
) x;

It took 853 ms and about 1 million buffers to return one number. The plan showed three different behaviours:

Branch How PostgreSQL ran it Cost
max(updated_at_num) on one table Backward index scan, stops at the first row 0.2 ms
max(password_changed_at) Sequential scan; the column has no index ~590 ms
max(...) over a join Full join of every staff account, then aggregate ~270 ms

PostgreSQL has a neat shortcut here. As the CREATE AGGREGATE documentation explains, a MIN- or MAX-like aggregate can be answered from an index, because SELECT max(col) FROM tab is equivalent to SELECT col FROM tab ORDER BY col DESC LIMIT 1. The planner walks the index backward and takes the first non-null value. It also works on partitioned tables and UNION ALL views, by merging each child's index. It does not work through a join. The planner source (planagg.c) limits the shortcut to queries that reference exactly one table, so the join branch had to build the whole join just to find its largest value.

That is where understanding the use case matters more than tuning. This value is an upper bound for the next change window. It doesn't have to be the exact newest staff row; it only has to be at least as high. Dropping the join and taking max(updated_at_num) over all of staff_links gives a bound that is never lower, and costs a single index probe. The join filter still applies in the query that reads the window.

The same review turned up a second easy win. The ceiling was global, but the job ran it once per scope, inside a loop, so it returned the same value several times per run. Computing it once per run cost nothing to change.

The password_changed_at branch I left alone. More on that in Lesson 6.

Lesson 5: A test that returns zero rows proves nothing

My first round of EXPLAIN ANALYZE used a one-hour window, the job's steady state. Most queries looked great: under a millisecond. Then I noticed how often the plans said (never executed). In that hour, no organization had changed, so every join after the first step was skipped. The plan was cheap because there was no work, not because the work was cheap.

Widening the window to 30 days told a different story. One query that ran in 0.7 ms on the hourly window chose a completely different plan:

  • It started from the membership table instead of the changed rows.
  • It read every one of the 15,368 primary memberships, then probed accounts for each.
  • It found 31 changed rows, after 72,522 buffers.

The cause was a row estimate. The planner expected 188 primary memberships and got 15,368, about 80 times more. With 188, starting from memberships looks cheap. A likely reason is how PostgreSQL combines filters: by default it multiplies each condition's selectivity as if they were independent, so correlated filters (type, deleted flag, end date) can be badly underestimated. Check that statistics are fresh with ANALYZE first. If the columns really are correlated, CREATE STATISTICS can tell the planner how they relate.

So I now test every change-data query with three windows:

Window What it tells you
Normal (one hour) Steady-state cost
Wide (30 days) What happens after an outage or a missed run
Full history The very first run, when the checkpoint is empty

The first run is easy to forget. Here it was fine: page one of the full-history query took about 20 ms, because the planner could stop as soon as it had 500 rows. But you only know that by running it.

Lesson 6: "Good enough" is a valid result. Index only what doesn't scale

After the rewrites, I had a list of index candidates that would have made every remaining query near-instant: one on password_changed_at, a partial index for a rare account type, and a few more. Before building any of them, I added up what an hourly run actually cost without them:

Part of the run Cost
Ceiling queries, once per run ~1.5–1.8 s
Change-window queries, per scope ~1.2 s for the largest
Whole run ~6–7 s, every buffer from cache

The slowest single statement was under a second, far from any timeout. Every index you add costs writes, storage and maintenance forever, and here the database was a replication target that would pay for each one on every write. So most of the candidates were dropped. That is a fine outcome. Not every slow-looking query needs an index; sometimes it needs nothing.

One query was different, because its cost multiplied. It loaded full account details in chunks of 100 IDs, and each chunk joined org_members on account_id, a column with no index. Every chunk scanned a 9-million-row table: about 0.7 s.

Scenario Accounts to load Chunks Time
Hourly ~50 1 ~0.7 s
30-day catch-up ~20,000 ~200 ~2.5 min
First run ~870,000 ~8,700 ~1.7 hours

That is the test I use now: don't ask whether a query is slow, ask whether its cost grows with the data or the backlog. Fixed costs can usually be tolerated. Costs that multiply need an index. We added exactly one: org_members (account_id).

Lesson 7: A new index can make a query slower

The new index worked exactly as planned: the org_members step went from scanning 5.4 million rows to reading 2,217 buffers. Then I looked at the total for the chunk query. It had gone from 723 ms to 26.9 seconds.

Before the index After the index
org_members Parallel sequential scan, 174k buffers Index scan, 2,217 buffers
memberships One scan of the 15k primary rows, hashed 7,191 index probes, each discarding ~14,000 rows
Total 723 ms, 243k buffers 26,872 ms, 22.7M buffers

With org_members suddenly cheap, the planner switched to a nested loop and probed memberships once per organization row through an index on org_id. That index holds every membership in the organization, one per member account. The accounts in this chunk belonged to very large organizations, so each probe walked about 14,000 entries to find the one primary membership it needed.

The planner expected roughly one row per probe. When it knows a value in advance, PostgreSQL can look it up in its most-common-values statistics. Here each probe's value came from the outer row at run time, so the planner estimated an average number of rows per organization. The handful of very large organizations didn't fit that average, and re-running ANALYZE doesn't change how the estimate is made.

The fix was another index, but a very small one: a partial index containing only the rows the query asks for.

CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY memberships_primary_org_idx
    ON memberships (org_id) INCLUDE (parent_account_id, end_date)
    WHERE membership_type = 'PRIMARY' AND is_deleted = false;

It holds about 15,000 rows instead of 650,000, so it is small and cheap to maintain, and each probe now lands directly on the row it needs. PostgreSQL uses a partial index only when it can prove, at planning time, that the query's WHERE clause implies the index predicate. The docs point out that a bind parameter such as membership_type = $1 can't prove that. Because this query uses membership_type = 'PRIMARY' AND is_deleted = false as literal values, the planner can match the partial index without any code change.

The lesson isn't "avoid indexes". It's that an index changes the plan around it, not just the step it targets. Re-run the full EXPLAIN ANALYZE after every index, and read the total, not just the line you were fixing.

Building the indexes online

Both indexes went in with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, so writes kept flowing. A few things I check every time:

1. Look for old transactions first. Per the CREATE INDEX docs, a concurrent build waits before each table scan for transactions that have modified the table, and after the second scan for any transaction holding a snapshot older than that scan. My pre-check found 65 sessions from a replication tool sitting idle in transaction for 28 days. Before cancelling anything, check whether they actually matter:

SELECT count(*) AS sessions,
       count(backend_xmin) AS holding_snapshot,
       count(backend_xid)  AS holding_xid
FROM   pg_stat_activity
WHERE  state = 'idle in transaction'
  AND  now() - xact_start > interval '1 day';

Ours held no snapshot, no transaction ID and no locks on the target tables, so they couldn't block the build or hold back vacuum. That's a cleanup item, not a blocker.

2. Run with autocommit on. CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction block, and some SQL clients wrap scripts in one.

3. Decide on lock_timeout deliberately. It lets a build fail fast instead of queueing behind a long transaction, but a build that fails partway leaves an invalid index behind. I left it unset and watched the progress view instead.

4. Check for invalid indexes afterwards. CREATE INDEX ... IF NOT EXISTS sees an invalid leftover's name and skips it with only a NOTICE. Drop it with DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY and build again, or rebuild it with REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY.

SELECT indexrelid::regclass FROM pg_index WHERE NOT indisvalid;

5. Build smallest to largest, and watch replication lag during the big ones.

A review checklist

This is what I now run through for any SQL headed to a large production table, whether a person or an AI wrote it.

Predicates

  • No functions wrapped around indexed columns in WHERE or JOIN (COALESCE, TRIM, LOWER, casts, date math).
  • Every "defensive" expression is backed by a data check: null counts, padded values, duplicate keys.
  • Filters the outer query knows are repeated inside subqueries and on every joined table.
  • IN (SELECT DISTINCT ...) replaced with a correlated EXISTS, or at least the DISTINCT dropped.
  • Partial-index conditions written as literals, not bind parameters, so the planner can match them.

Purpose

  • For each query, what is it for? A ceiling, a count or a page may not need the precision it was written with.
  • Values that don't change within a run are computed once per run, not inside a loop.
  • Keyset pagination sorts on a unique key, or ends with a unique tie-breaker.

Evidence

  • EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on production-sized data, for normal, wide and first-run windows.
  • No (never executed) hiding the parts you care about.
  • Estimated versus actual rows compared; a gap of 10x or more is worth chasing.
  • Costs that multiply (per chunk, per page, per backlog hour) indexed; fixed costs judged against the schedule.
  • The full plan re-run after every new index.

Closing: tuning is mostly a conversation

Looking back, the biggest gains came from questions, not configuration:

  • "Can this column actually be null?" No, so the COALESCE went, and the existing index started working.
  • "What is this MAX used for?" An upper bound, so it didn't need the expensive join.
  • "Does this cost grow with the backlog?" Only in one place, so we added one index instead of six.

None of that needed database expertise the developers couldn't learn. It needed someone to explain how the planner reads a predicate, why a function hides an index, and why QA data isn't evidence for production. Once that was clear, the developer rewrote the queries himself, and the run time in QA went from 30–50 minutes to under 30 seconds.

Some tuning really is just common sense and basic troubleshooting: read the plan, check the data, and ask what the query is for. If your team writes SQL, especially with an AI assistant drafting it, get a database engineer to look at it before it meets production data. It never hurts, and sometimes it saves you an hour-long first run, or a 27-second query you didn't know you had.

References

  • CREATE AGGREGATE: how MIN/MAX-like aggregates use an index
  • planagg.c: the MIN/MAX optimization and its single-table restriction
  • Indexes on Expressions
  • Partial Indexes
  • Index-Only Scans and Covering Indexes
  • Row Estimation Examples: MCV lists, averages and combining conditions
  • Statistics Used by the Planner: including extended statistics
  • Using EXPLAIN
  • CREATE INDEX: Building Indexes Concurrently

title: What is Mounting in React?
description:
Mounting is the first phase of a React component's lifecycle.
When a component is created and displayed on the screen for the first time, it is called Mounting.

  1. Mounting steps
  2. Component Function Runs – React executes the component.
  3. DOM Creation – React prepares the UI.
  4. DOM Update – React displays the UI on the screen.
  5. useEffect Runs – The effect runs after the component is displayed.

Example:

import React, { useEffect } from 'react';

function App() {

useEffect(() => {
    console.log("Component Mounted");
}, []);

return (
    <h1>Hello React!</h1>
);

}

export default App;

Output:

Hello React!

Console:

Component Mounted

title: If You Think React Is Free to Use, You Are Wrong.
description:
React Is Not Free. Let’s Clarify This.

When you use an abstraction over a complex task, it gives you convenience by moving complexity into a framework, which you learn through another mental model present in your mind.

This adds more concepts, like React mental model complexity, component/state complexity, and reconciliation/runtime complexity.

That’s why I say it: you move complexity into the mental model that is present in the mind.

Another trade-off is control.

You get maximum control when you work directly with DOM manipulation.

But in the case of React, control is given to React.

React manages all the operations, like insertion and deletion of DOM elements and updates to the DOM.

Now, you don’t have direct access to the DOM.

You exchange control for complexity.

If you lose control, then you lose ownership.

Now React becomes the owner of the rendering process.

It becomes a middleman between your application and the browser.

It creates the necessity to understand React’s rules.

That’s it.

Ummmm, really, don’t.

Another big trade-off is runtime overhead and memory.

Assume that React has some work pending to do.

Now, the question is: does React directly hand over this work to the browser?

Really, don’t.

It creates a virtual DOM, then uses reconciliation and updates the Fiber tree before reflecting the updates.

This can make the application slower due to runtime overhead.

Maintaining the React Fiber tree requires additional memory, which is not required in a vanilla JavaScript application due to its limited framework state.

In the case of React, it is not free to use.

You pay the cost through these trade-offs and mental models.

title: AI Gateway now supports asynchronous video generation
description:
Video generation on AI Gateway can now run asynchronously.

By default, generateVideo keeps one HTTP request to AI Gateway open until the result is ready. Because video generation can take seconds or minutes, that request can exceed request timeouts.

With asynchronous generation, your application can receive a webhook, poll for completion, or start a generation and retrieve the result in a later request.

Choose an option based on whether your process can keep running and whether your application can receive webhooks:

Existing generateVideo calls continue to work as before. All four options support text-to-video, image-to-video, reference-to-video, and other video inputs.

Upgrade the SDK

Install the latest versions of the AI SDK and AI Gateway provider:

Use asynchronous video generation

Wait for completion in a Workflow

An easy way to consume the completion webhook is a Workflow SDK. The workflow creates its own webhook URL, passes it to startVideo, and suspends until AI Gateway delivers the completion event. Install the Workflow SDK alongside the AI SDK:

While the video renders, the workflow run is suspended and resumes when AI Gateway delivers the terminal event.

Use a webhook with generateVideo

Pass webhook to generateVideo to wait for a completion event without polling. AI Gateway sends an event when the job completes or fails. The SDK waits for that event, fetches the generated videos, and resolves the original generateVideo call.

The calling process and webhook handler need a shared token and store so the delivery can be matched to the correct generation. generateVideo does not expose the signing secret for this job. See the webhook verification documentation for the complete receiver pattern.

Both the polling and webhook options for generateVideo return result.videos as GeneratedFile objects. The SDK downloads provider-hosted videos, making uint8Array, base64, and mediaType available in either job.

Poll with generateVideo

Add poll to an existing generateVideo call:

AI Gateway starts an asynchronous job, and the SDK sends a short status request at each interval until the job finishes. The calling process must remain running until generateVideo resolves, but no individual request to AI Gateway stays open for the full generation.

Start a job and retrieve it later

startVideo returns an operation as soon as AI Gateway accepts the job, without waiting for rendering to finish. Store that operation and pass it to getVideoStatus later from the same process or another one:

The operation is JSON-serializable, so it can be stored in a database or passed through a queue. Your application controls how long to keep checking the job because it has no built-in timeout.

You can also pass webhookUrl to startVideo to receive a completion event instead of checking the status. The start response includes the signing secret needed to verify the webhook.

Unlike generateVideo, getVideoStatus does not download hosted videos. It returns provider URLs or inline bytes. Hosted URLs can expire, so download any videos you need to keep.

Monitor asynchronous jobs

Every asynchronous generation appears on the AI Gateway Logs page as soon as it starts. Jobs show as Running while generation is in progress and update when they complete or fail.

Under Request Mode, select Async to show only asynchronous jobs. Opening an entry shows the job ID and the request details.

Only asynchronous requests create jobs. A standard generateVideo call appears as a single completed request after the video is ready.

For size limits, idempotency for retried job starts, webhook delivery retries, and other operational details, read the asynchronous video generation documentation or browse all video models.

Read more
