title: The intrusion-detection rule that could never fire
description:
I have been building CNDS, a home-network intrusion detector, for a while. It captures packets with Scapy, scores each flow with five engines (a supervised FT-Transformer, an Isolation Forest, an LSTM autoencoder, a rules engine and a baseline that trains on my own traffic), and maps what it finds to MITRE ATT&CK. This month I put it on a Raspberry Pi 5 and let it run. This is what I learned, including the parts that are not flattering.

Week one: the alerts were all wrong

On day one the detector produced about 45 alerts an hour. On 30 and 31 October the database had 195 and 362 alerts, and I ended up labelling almost all of them as false positives (178 and 336).

The first cause was embarrassing and easy to find. The Isolation Forest and the LSTM that ship with the project are demo models trained on synthetic N(0, 1) data. On real traffic the LSTM scored 1.0 on 300 of 300 alerts I looked at. It was not detecting anything; it was saturating. I set its weight to zero.

The second cause was the rules. All 54 critical alerts came from payload regexes (XSS, SQL injection, command injection) matching TLS and binary traffic: CloudFront downloads and an S3 service on my own network. The supervised model had called those flows benign, but a critical rule overrides the blend and forces a score of 1.0. The fix was to skip payload regexes on encrypted or high-entropy payloads.

The third cause was a monitoring probe. Two flows (my Pi talking to a proxy, and a blackbox exporter probing its neighbours) made up 89 % of the remaining alerts. I replaced IP-wide suppression with narrow rules: source, destination and port.

There was also a logging trap. The detector wrote the [ALERT] line before suppression rules ran, so 243 [ALERT] lines in ten hours meant about three real alerts. I now log [SUPPRESSED] separately.

After all that, daily alerts fell to 63, 48 and 37, with none rated high or critical. That is a quieter system. It is not proof the system works.

The test: can it detect a SYN flood?

False positives are only half of the question. To measure the other half I built a small red-team tool, cnds-red-team. It has an allowlist, a hard-coded list of hosts it can never touch, a duration and packet budget for every run, and a kill switch. I pointed it at the Pi from another Pi.

The first scenarios, a port scan and a burst of DNS queries, detected nothing. The DNS result was expected: CNDS has no DNS rule, and my "expected signal" for that scenario had been a guess. The port scan result sent me to read the code.

CNDS has a syn_scan rule. It fires when a flow has more than 20 SYN flags and fewer than 5 forward packets. Read that again. Every SYN is itself a forward packet, so a flow with more than 20 SYNs has more than 20 forward packets. The two conditions can never be true together. Using git log -L, I confirmed the condition had been like that since the very first implementation, and a later refactor that renamed magic numbers into constants copied it forward unchanged.

The rule's own comment says "high SYN count with low data". The second clause was meant to look at payload, not packet count. The fix was one line (use the count of packets that carry data), plus a test.

The second bug was in my own configuration

With the rule fixed, the SYN flood still produced no alert. The reason: on my Pi the rules engine weighs 5 % of the ensemble. A perfect rule hit adds 0.05 to a score that has to cross 0.55. I made syn_scan a critical rule, which bypasses the blend, as unambiguous signatures like SQL injection already did.

The part I have not solved

I then confirmed that every packet leaves the sender's network card and reaches the Pi (a sniffer on the target matched the timestamps), and that feeding the same packets straight into the deployed detector code produces a score of 1.0 and syn_scan. A normal request containing a literal UNION SELECT generates an alert through the live detector. But the raw-socket SYN flood does not, and I do not yet know why. I ruled out the logic, the feature indices, the port state and a stuck process. What is left is somewhere between the capture queue and the flow dispatcher, and I have not instrumented it yet.

I am telling you this because the result of this project is not "it works". It is a list of things I now know do not work, found by testing instead of reading my own code with kind eyes.

What I'd do differently

Test with real traffic from day one. Two of the bugs above had unit tests that passed, and neither test could have caught them, because the tests built the same flows the code expected. If a model's score is always 1.0, it isn't a detector, whatever its F1 says on the test split. And log what you drop: my alert counter counted before suppression, so for a week it told me the system was noisier than it was.

I also wrote the limits into the README before cutting the release. CNDS 2.0.0-rc.1 says that recall hasn't been measured. A pre-release that lists what it can't do yet is easier to trust than one that doesn't.

The code is AGPL-3.0, release v2.0.0-rc.1: https://github.com/RobertoDeLaCamara/Cognitive-Intrusion-Detection-System

If you have an idea why a raw-socket SYN-only flow reaches the NIC but never reaches the flow dispatcher in a Scapy-based sniffer, I'm all ears.

title: Play Minecraft in Rust - Open Source Engine
description:
TL;DR: Horizon implements Minecraft Java Edition from scratch in Rust, sitting on top of modern graphics APIs like Vulkan and Wgpu while relying on a custom launcher to prepare game assets from an existing user installation.
Best for: Rust developers and Minecraft enthusiasts wanting native performance and programmatic agent control.
Repository snapshot: ⭐ 6 226 stars · 🍴 854 forks · Rust · MIT
Daily picks: Follow GitHub Open Source on Telegram

What it is

Horizon is an independent implementation of Minecraft Java Edition written from scratch in Rust. It bypasses the Java virtual machine to deliver native performance, advanced rendering features, and a programmatic control interface.

How it works

The engine relies on modern graphics stacks like Vulkan and Wgpu for rendering. It uses a custom launcher to prepare game assets from an existing user installation and employs 281 differential harnesses to check parity against the vanilla game.

Key features

  • Run vanilla world generation, mobs, redstone, and commands without Java
  • Render distant terrain up to 1024 chunks using modern graphics APIs
  • Control the game programmatically or over control interfaces using horizon-ctl
  • Import CurseForge and Modrinth modpacks containing content and data packs
  • Manage and host servers locally or on a VPS without Java dependencies

Getting started

Clone the repository from GitHub, ensure you have a Rust toolchain installed, and use the Horizon launcher to prepare your game assets from an existing legitimate installation.

When not to use it

Do not use this if you expect complete zero-bug compatibility today, as the project is still tracking hundreds of open parity gaps with the original Java release.

title: Dark Mode in 12 Lines of CSS (No Library, No Framework)
description:
Most dark-mode tutorials reach for a library or a theme provider. You don't need one. CSS variables already do the whole job: define your colours once, swap the values when a toggle flips, and let every element follow.

Here is the complete theme from a working demo page I built:

:root{
  --bg:#ffffff;
  --text:#16202e;
  --card:#eef2f7;
  --accent:#c9a227;
}
body.dark{
  --bg:#0b1220;
  --text:#f5f0e1;
  --card:#16223a;
  --accent:#e7c34a;
}

That's the theme itself. Everything else on the page just uses the variables:

body{
  background:var(--bg);
  color:var(--text);
  transition:background .3s, color .3s;
}
.card{ background:var(--card); }
button{ background:var(--accent); }

The toggle

One button, one class on <body>, and localStorage so the visitor's choice survives the next visit:

const b = document.body;
if (localStorage.getItem('demo-theme') === 'dark') b.classList.add('dark');

document.getElementById('t').onclick = () => {
  b.classList.toggle('dark');
  localStorage.setItem('demo-theme', b.classList.contains('dark') ? 'dark' : 'light');
};

Why this works so well

  • One source of truth. Backgrounds, text, cards and buttons all read the same few variables, so the dark theme can't drift out of sync with the light one.
  • No flash of the wrong theme is handled by applying the saved class before the page settles — the check runs immediately.
  • Zero dependencies. Nothing to install, nothing to break on the next framework update. It works in a static HTML file, a WordPress theme, or inside any framework's stylesheet.

Dark mode isn't just a trend — visitors stay longer on pages that are easy on their eyes at night. With variables, adding it is an afternoon's small change, not a project.

I'm Mamad Mirza, a full-stack developer in the UK. I build a small working project every day — follow along here, or work with me on LaborX.

title: SQL Injection Explained for Beginners: How It Works and How to Prevent It
description:
SQL Injection Explained for Beginners: How It Works and How to Prevent It

SQL injection (SQLi) is one of the oldest and most dangerous attacks against web applications that handle databases. Despite its long history, it remains a frequent threat because many developers build dynamic queries without properly validating user input. In this article you will discover, in a practical and straightforward way, what SQL injection is, how it is carried out, and, most importantly, what measures you can apply today to protect your projects.

What Is SQL Injection and Why Is It Dangerous?

An SQL injection occurs when an application inserts user‑provided data directly into an SQL statement without sanitizing it. The attacker exploits this lack of control to alter the query logic and, thereby, bypass authentication, extract confidential information, or even modify and delete data.

“SQL injection is an attack that manipulates dynamic SQL statements to bypass authentication or expose data, taking advantage of web applications that generate queries from unvalidated user data.” (Guru99)¹

The consequences can be severe: from leaking customer data to taking full control of the database server. That’s why understanding the attack mechanism is the first step toward preventing it.

How SQL Injection Works: Step‑by‑Step Process

  1. Unvalidated input The application receives data from the user (for example, a login field) and inserts it directly into an SQL string. 
   SELECT * FROM usuarios WHERE usuario = '$_POST[usuario]' AND clave = '$_POST[clave]';

  1. Payload injection

    The attacker supplies a value that closes the original string and appends their own SQL code.

    • Typical input: admin' --
    • Resulting query: 
     SELECT * FROM usuarios WHERE usuario = 'admin' --' AND clave = '';

The -- comments out the rest of the statement, causing the password condition to be ignored and the attacker to log in as admin.

  1. Execution and exploitation The database executes the altered query and returns data the attacker should not see. Depending on the payload, the attacker may also:
    • Union‑Based: combine results from other tables (UNION SELECT …).
    • Error‑Based: force errors that reveal the database schema.
    • Blind: infer data through true/false responses when direct output is hidden.

These are some of the injection types described in specialized guides (DataCamp, Nurbak)².

Main Prevention Techniques

1. Parameterized Queries and Prepared Statements

The most recommended way to avoid injection is to never concatenate values directly into the query. Instead, use parameters that the database treats as data, not code.

$stmt = $pdo->prepare('SELECT * FROM usuarios WHERE usuario = :usuario AND clave = :clave');
$stmt->execute(['usuario' => $inputUsuario, 'clave' => $inputClave]);

Parameters are substituted safely, preventing any special character from altering the SQL logic. This practice is highlighted in Victor Hugo Solís’s guide as an essential step for any project³.

2. Input Validation and Sanitization

Although parameterized queries are the primary defense, validating input further strengthens security:

  • Data type: ensure a field that should be numeric receives only numbers.
  • Length: limit the number of characters to prevent overly long payloads.
  • Whitelist: accept only expected values (e.g., “admin”, “user”) and reject everything else.

3. Principle of Least Privilege

Configure the database account used by the application with only the permissions it strictly needs. If the account only needs to read data, do not grant write or administrative privileges. This way, even if an attacker manages to inject code, the potential damage is reduced.

4. Careful Use of ORMs and Frameworks

Object‑Relational Mappers (ORMs) simplify database access, but they are not an automatic shield against injection. Some implementations can generate dynamic queries that still accept values without parameterization. Nurbak’s guide notes that “ORM pitfalls still catch experienced teams,” so it’s vital to review the documentation and ensure the ORM always uses prepared statements⁴.

5. Scanning and Security Testing

Incorporate static and dynamic analysis tools that detect vulnerable queries. Conduct regular penetration tests, focusing on data entry points (forms, APIs, URL parameters). Early detection allows you to fix vulnerabilities before they are exploited⁵.

Practical Example: From Vulnerable Code to Secure Code

Vulnerable code (PHP):

$user = $_GET['user'];
$pass = $_GET['pass'];
$query = "SELECT * FROM usuarios WHERE usuario = '$user' AND clave = '$pass'";
$result = mysqli_query($conn, $query);

Secure code with parameters (PHP + PDO):

$user = $_GET['user'];
$pass = $_GET['pass'];
$stmt = $pdo->prepare('SELECT * FROM usuarios WHERE usuario = :user AND clave = :pass');
$stmt->execute(['user' => $user, 'pass' => $pass]);
$result = $stmt->fetchAll();

In the first case, an attacker could send admin' -- as the user value and bypass password verification. In the second case, the value is treated as data and the query can never be altered.

Conclusion and Call to Action

SQL injection remains a real threat because the root problem – mixing code and data – is easy to overlook in rushed projects. With a few solid practices (parameterized queries, strict validation, least‑privilege accounts, and continuous testing) you can virtually eliminate the risk.

Your next step: review your application’s code today. Identify any query built by concatenating values and replace it with a prepared statement. If you use an ORM, verify that all read and write operations employ the secure mechanisms the framework provides. Finally, schedule an internal penetration‑testing session to confirm that the vulnerabilities have been fixed.

Protect your data and your users’ data: security starts with simple yet decisive choices in every line of code. Act now and keep your application safe from SQL injection!

¹ Guru99, “Tutorial de inyección SQL: aprenda con el ejemplo”.

² DataCamp, “Inyección SQL: Cómo funciona y cómo prevenirlo”.

³ Victor Hugo Solís, “Inyección SQL: Cómo Funciona y Cómo Prevenirla”.

⁴ Nurbak, “Inyección SQL: Ejemplos y Cómo Prevenirla”.

⁵ Avast, “¿Qué es la inyección de SQL? | Explicación y protección”.

Sources and references

  • Tutorial de inyección SQL: aprenda con el ejemplo - Guru99
  • Inyección SQL: Cómo funciona y cómo prevenirlo - DataCamp
  • Inyección SQL: Cómo Funciona y Cómo Prevenirla – Victor Hugo Solís
  • Inyección SQL: Ejemplos y Cómo Prevenirla (Guía 2026) – Nurbak
  • ¿Qué es la inyección de SQL? | Explicación y protección – Avast

title: ChatGPT Recommends Your Shopify Product. Can the Customer Choose and Buy It Correctly?
description:
A customer asks ChatGPT for help upgrading home Wi-Fi, compares a few options and arrives at your Shopify store. That visit is useful, but the buying decision is not finished. They may still be unsure whether the item is an access point or a router, how it is powered, and what the package includes.

A page promising fast, stable coverage does not resolve those questions. The work after product discovery is to make the offer understandable, selectable and purchasable.

This guide uses the UniFi U7 Pro as a technical example. Hardware details come from Ubiquiti; the store, customer situation and merchant-created package arrangements are hypothetical. No live recommendation or conversion experiment was performed.

Start with the actual customer journey

Shopify currently describes its ChatGPT channel as a product-discovery referral channel. Customers continue to the merchant's online store checkout. Eligibility depends on the store, products, market and relevant terms and policies; using Shopify does not by itself establish that every product is eligible. Check Sales channels → Agentic for the actual store. ChatGPT channel guidance

Eligible products can be made discoverable through Shopify Catalog, but inclusion does not guarantee a recommendation for any particular question. Work through eligibility, the product record and the purchase journey in that order. If the admin displays an ineligibility reason, address that reason instead of repeatedly changing the title. If eligibility details are temporarily unavailable, preserve that status and check later or contact support. Catalog requirements

Translate specifications into buying conditions

The U7 Pro specification lists Wi-Fi 7, a 2.5 GbE uplink, PoE+ power and UniFi Network version 8.0.28 or later. Experienced network buyers may understand those terms immediately. A first-time customer may not know what they need to prepare. Official specifications

Official Ubiquiti product illustration. Manufacturer coverage and client-count figures are not promises for a particular home. Source.

Suppose the customer says the home already has Ethernet cabling. That does not establish suitable power. An ordinary network port, an appropriate powered switch and a separate power device are different situations. The page should help the customer check the actual hardware and power requirements.

Present the information in three layers. First explain the role of the device: this is an access point, so a customer replacing an entire home network must also consider routing, the internet connection and management. Next explain the preparations: power, uplink and software requirements, with installation documentation. Finally describe the offer: what this actual sales package contains and what needs to be purchased separately. Do not imply that every device in a marketing image comes in the box.

These are buying conditions, not decorative technical details. When compatibility remains unknown, give the customer a route to check documentation or ask a question before ordering.

Put product facts in the right Shopify records

The product page, the information available to AI channels and the cart should work from consistent business records. Start at Products → the relevant product and review its title, description, images, price, stock and publishing status.

Where important information lives in custom fields, inspect the Catalog source and available mapping under Sales channels → Agentic → Sources → Shopify Catalog. Shopify provides Channel mapping for custom data sources; do not assume that every field you created will automatically be distributed with the meaning you intended. Product data and mapping

For this example, prepare an internal fact sheet with the exact model, device type, power requirements, interfaces, management conditions, package contents, sales market and source of each fact. This is a team document, not a claim that Shopify includes those exact field names.

Repeated specifications and documentation links can be maintained in suitable product or variant Metafields, then displayed by the theme. Entering a field value and connecting it to the storefront are separate jobs. Using metafields

Also distinguish a variant from an accessory. If a single device and a merchant-assembled package have different prices, inventory or fulfilment contents, choose an appropriate product, variant or bundle implementation first. A dropdown labelled “includes accessory” does not automatically implement inventory or fulfilment. Variant management

Use ChatGPT to find unanswered questions

Once reliable facts are available, AI can help identify what a customer would still need to know. A product name alone leaves too much room for unsupported assumptions. Supply official specification excerpts and the merchant's confirmed package information, then ask:

Use only the information below. Review it for a first-time wireless access point buyer. Separate confirmed facts, missing information and proposed buying guidance. Mark unspecified accessories, device compatibility, coverage outcomes and after-sales conditions as unconfirmed. Do not fill them in. End with three checks the customer should make before ordering.

Compare every affirmative statement in the response with the supplied sources. Claims such as “no extra equipment required,” “works with every router” or “covers the whole house” need evidence before publication.

This is an information review and drafting task. An ordinary chat does not update Shopify inventory, match accessories or test an order. Even with an authorized connected tool, review the actual object and fields being changed and check the saved result. An instruction written by AI is not evidence that a backend change has happened.

Design the page around decisions and maintenance

A visitor arriving from a recommendation needs to confirm the exact item, suitability and offer before reading the broader brand story. Explain the product's role and key prerequisites near the purchase area. Make the selected configuration and included contents clear, then support the decision with interface images, compatibility information and installation references. Delivery and return conditions should be accessible before purchase.

Official Ubiquiti product image. Read interface and power details against the exact model and installation documentation. Source.

In custom storefront design and development, this is a content and interaction problem together. Use the theme's existing specification or collapsible sections when they suffice. Connect reusable specifications to fields and components. Evaluate an app or custom logic when the business genuinely needs compatibility filtering, restrictions on unsuitable combinations or complex package relationships.

Acceptance should cover maintenance as well as appearance. Can an operator find the place to change a specification? Do related modules update? Does the purchase button submit the current selection? Will the next launch require editing the same fact in many places? Those questions determine whether the site remains usable after handover.

Test three customer situations, then observe real evidence

Start with one product rather than a whole-store rewrite. Test a customer who already has suitable power and management arrangements, one who lacks supporting equipment, and one who has not identified the existing hardware.

For each, record whether the page provides a clear answer, which item or configuration was selected, and whether the cart's name, quantity, price and image match. When necessary information is missing, the journey should support further checking rather than silently selecting an accessory and claiming compatibility is solved.

Use the Catalog search preview in Sales channels → Agentic as a directional check of product information and query relevance. AI channels may reorder results, so the preview is not a guaranteed ChatGPT placement. The same area provides channel-performance entry points where available; compare sessions, orders and sales over a consistent period. Agentic management and reporting

If you also use Analytics → Reports, distinguish acquisition sessions from sales. One ChatGPT-referred visit does not establish an incremental order, and it cannot substantiate a claimed conversion uplift from a redesign. Acquisition reporting

The next operator should be able to find the source, update the right field and check the actual item in the cart without guessing. ChatGPT can change where discovery starts. The storefront still needs to help customers make the remaining decisions accurately.

Sources checked November 4, 2026. This is a documented teaching workflow, not a completed merchant implementation or measured conversion result.

title: Is Heroku shutting down? What sustaining engineering means
description:
TL;DR

  • What you get: a plain answer to "is Heroku going away?", what changed on 6 February 2026, a 10-question checklist to decide whether to stay or move, and a dated price table for the same app on 5 platforms.
  • Who it's for: anyone running a production app on Heroku who saw the news and isn't sure whether to act.
  • Time needed: 10 minutes to read, 20 minutes to run the checklist against your own app.
  • Short answer: Heroku is not shutting down. Nothing is forcing you to move this year. But if you're on the heroku-22 stack, you have a real deadline in April 2027 either way.

Your app has run on Heroku for years. Then a headline says Heroku is in "maintenance mode", and your team chat fills up with "do we need to migrate?". Moving a production app is risky and expensive. Moving too late, in a panic, is worse.

This guide helps you decide calmly. You'll learn exactly what Heroku announced, what it does and doesn't change, how to score your own app's risk in 20 minutes, and what the same app costs on Heroku and four alternatives, with prices read on 4 November 2026. If the answer is "move", you'll also see the cheapest safe way to try it first.

Try it on Hubfly space: the free tier gives you 360 compute hours a month with no card, enough to run a copy of your app next to Heroku before you decide anything.

What Heroku announced, in plain words

On 6 February 2026, Heroku published An Update on Heroku. It said three things:

  1. Heroku is moving to a "sustaining engineering model". The focus is stability, security, reliability and support, "rather than introducing new features".
  2. Nothing changes for card-paying customers. Pricing, billing, service and day-to-day use stay the same, for existing and new customers who pay by card. Apps, pipelines, teams and add-ons keep working.
  3. Enterprise Account contracts are no longer offered to new customers. Existing Enterprise contracts are honoured and can renew.

The reason given: Heroku is putting its investment into other areas, including helping organisations build enterprise AI securely.

What "sustaining engineering" means in practice

Think of a car model that's still sold and serviced, but won't get a redesign. You still get oil changes, recalls and safety fixes. You don't get a new dashboard.

For your app, that means:

  • Security patches and OS updates keep coming. The Heroku stack page lists the newest stack, heroku-26, as supported until April 2031.
  • Your bill doesn't change. The Heroku pricing page still shows Eco at $5, Basic at $7 and Standard-1X at $25 a month.
  • Fewer big new features. The roadmap is about keeping things running, not chasing what newer platforms ship.

What it does not mean

It's not a shutdown, and nobody announced an end date. To be fair to Heroku, it's also not a freeze. Heroku's own October 2026 update lists Heroku Postgres Advanced (a new database tier), Cloud Native Buildpacks for Cedar apps, and Postgres 18 as the default on every database tier. The pace is slower and more focused, but work continues.

So the honest summary is: Heroku is a stable, slower-moving platform now. For many apps, that's fine. For some, it's a reason to plan an exit on your own schedule.

The one deadline that matters either way

Before you debate staying or leaving, run this:

heroku stack -a your-app

If the active stack is heroku-22, note the date. The stack page lists heroku-22 as deprecated, end of life April 2027. You'll need to upgrade to heroku-24 or heroku-26 before then, which can mean code and dependency changes.

That's useful for planning. An upgrade is already a chunk of work that touches your build. If you were going to move platforms within a year, it may be cheaper to do it once, instead of upgrading the stack now and migrating later.

Stay or move? A 10-question checklist

Score each question for your app. Give yourself 2 points for each "yes" and 0 for each "no". A "yes" points toward moving. Be honest; nobody else sees this.

# Question Why it matters
1 Is the app on heroku-22 (or older)? You must touch the build before April 2027 anyway.
2 Are you waiting on a feature Heroku doesn't have (more regions, GPUs, bigger dynos for less money)? Under sustaining engineering, don't plan around it arriving.
3 Is your Heroku bill a noticeable share of your costs? Same-size apps cost less elsewhere (see the table below).
4 Were you hoping to sign a new Enterprise contract? New Enterprise contracts are no longer offered.
5 Is your app containerised already (Dockerfile, or easy to add)? Moving is mostly config work then, not a rewrite.
6 Do you have fewer than 5 add-ons? Each add-on is something to replace or re-wire.
7 Is your database under 10 GB? pg_dump and restore in minutes, not hours.
8 Can you accept a short maintenance window (10–30 min)? A planned cutover is far simpler than zero-downtime.
9 Does someone on the team have a free week in the next quarter? Migrations fail when they're squeezed between other work.
10 Is your app not tied to Salesforce (Heroku Connect, Salesforce data sync)? Those integrations are Heroku's real moat. Leave them alone if you depend on them.

How to read your score:

  • 0–6: stay. Heroku still works, your bill is stable, and moving would cost more in time than it saves. Upgrade your stack, set a calendar reminder to rerun this in 6 months, and get on with your product.
  • 8–12: plan, don't rush. Run a copy of your app on one alternative this quarter. Compare cost, deploys and logs side by side. Move when it's boring, not when it's urgent.
  • 14–20: move this quarter. You're paying for a platform that won't grow with you, and the move is cheap for your app's shape. Pick a quiet week and do it.

If question 10 is a "no" for you (you depend on Heroku Connect), take 4 points off your total. Replacing that integration is a project of its own, and it's where Heroku is strongest.

What the same app costs on 5 platforms (November 2026 snapshot)

Here's a typical small production app: one web process, one background worker, and a small Postgres database, all always on. Prices were read on each platform's official pricing page on 4 November 2026.

Platform Web Worker Postgres Monthly total
Heroku (dynos, Postgres) Basic, 0.5 GB: $7 Basic, 0.5 GB: $7 Essential-0, 1 GB: $5 $19.00
Render (pricing) 512 MB instance: $7 512 MB instance: $7 256 MB, 1 GB storage: $6 $20.00
Railway (pricing) usage-based usage-based usage-based + 1 GB volume ≈ $10.81 (see assumptions)
Fly.io (pricing) shared-cpu-1x 512 MB: $3.69 shared-cpu-1x 512 MB: $3.69 Managed Postgres Basic: $38 + 1 GB at $0.28 $45.66
Hubfly space (pricing) 0.5 vCPU / 512 MB: $2.23 0.5 vCPU / 512 MB: $2.23 Managed PostgreSQL Nano (0.25 vCPU / 512 MiB / 10 GiB): $2.02 $6.48

How the totals are worked out:

  • Heroku: $7 + $7 + $5 = $19.00.
  • Render: $7 + $7 + $6 = $20.00 on the free Hobby workspace. Render's background workers use the same instance prices as web services.
  • Railway: Railway bills what you actually use: $0.00000772 per vCPU-second ($20.29 per vCPU for a 730-hour month), $0.00000386 per GB-second of RAM ($10.14 per GB-month), and $0.00000006 per GB-second for volumes ($0.16 per GB-month). Assume each of the 3 services averages 0.05 vCPU and 0.25 GB of RAM: (0.05 × $20.29) + (0.25 × $10.14) = $3.55 per service, × 3 = $10.65, plus a 1 GB volume at $0.16 = $10.81. The Hobby plan's $5 a month includes $5 of usage, so the bill is $10.81. A busier app costs more; a quieter one less.
  • Fly.io: $3.69 × 2 + $38 + $0.28 = $45.66. Fly's own example notes that Managed Postgres is most of a small app's bill. You can run Postgres on a plain Machine for less, but then backups and upgrades are your job.
  • Hubfly space: compute is $0.004 per vCPU-hour and $0.002 per GB-hour of RAM, over 730 hours. One 0.5 vCPU / 512 MB service with 4 GB of disk: (0.5 × 0.004 × 730) + (0.5 × 0.002 × 730) + (4 × 0.00001536 × 730) = $1.46 + $0.73 + $0.04 = $2.23. Two of them plus Managed PostgreSQL Nano at $2.02: $2.23 + $2.23 + $2.02 = $6.48.

Where each platform wins

Price isn't everything, so here's the fair version:

  • Heroku wins on maturity and ecosystem: the add-on marketplace, pipelines, Heroku Scheduler for cron-style jobs, and deep Salesforce integration. If those carry your app, staying is reasonable.
  • Render wins if you want something that feels most like Heroku, with point-in-time recovery on Postgres (3 days on Hobby, 7 days on paid plans) and up to $10K in migration credits, per its pricing page.
  • Railway wins for spiky or mostly idle apps, because you pay for real usage, not reserved size.
  • Fly.io wins when you need your app close to users in many regions.
  • Hubfly space wins on price for always-on small services, and you can run apps, databases, file storage and email from one account. Be clear on the trade-offs: for Managed PostgreSQL, automatic backups are still marked "coming soon", and there's no built-in scheduler like Heroku Scheduler yet. If you need automatic database backups on day one, Render or Heroku is the safer choice for the database today.

For a deeper side-by-side, see Best Heroku alternatives in 2026: 7 options and what they cost and Heroku vs Render vs Railway vs Hubfly space: 4 prices for one app + Postgres. If you can't decide between fixed and usage-based billing, Fixed vs pay-as-you-go hosting: find your break-even point does the maths.

If you decide to move: the low-risk way

Don't migrate in one go. Run both side by side first. For the full walkthrough with commands, see Migrate from Heroku without losing jobs.

  1. Freeze the app's shape. Write down every process in your Procfile (web, worker, release), every add-on, and every config var. Run heroku config -a your-app --shell > heroku.env to export the config vars. That file holds secrets, so keep it out of Git.
  2. Containerise it. If you don't have a Dockerfile yet, add one now. It removes the biggest difference between platforms. A Dockerfile in the repo root is picked up automatically on Hubfly space.
  3. Rebuild the Procfile as a Compose file. Each process becomes a service. The release command becomes a one-off job that must finish before web starts. On Hubfly space, a service with restart: "no" imports as a Job, and depends_on with service_completed_successfully makes web wait for it.
  4. Copy the database. Take a fresh backup with heroku pg:backups:capture, download it with heroku pg:backups:download, and restore it into the new database with pg_restore (Heroku's import and export guide shows the exact flags). Do a dry run first and check row counts on your biggest tables.
  5. Run the copy for a week. Point a staging domain at the new app. Compare deploy time, logs and the real bill.
  6. Cut over in a quiet window. Put the Heroku app in maintenance mode, take a final backup, restore it, switch DNS, and keep the Heroku app around for a few days in case you need to roll back.

What can go wrong

1. You treat "sustaining engineering" as "shutting down" and rush. A rushed migration is how data gets lost. Fix: run the checklist, and if your score is under 8, stay and revisit in 6 months. Nothing in the announcement forces a date on you.

2. You forget the stack deadline. You decide to stay, then heroku-22 reaches end of life in April 2027 and builds start failing. Fix: run heroku stack -a your-app today and put the upgrade on the calendar.

3. Workers lose jobs during the cutover. If an old worker on Heroku and a new worker elsewhere both read from the same queue, or the old one is killed mid-job, jobs vanish. Fix: maintenance mode on Heroku doesn't stop worker dynos, so scale them to zero after the queue is drained (heroku ps:scale worker=0 -a your-app), then start workers on the new platform.

Takeaway

Heroku isn't going anywhere soon. It's a stable platform that's stopped racing. That's a fine place to run an app that doesn't need new features. Your real decisions are smaller and more concrete: upgrade off heroku-22 before April 2027, and use the 10-question checklist to decide whether that upgrade is also the moment to move.

If you score high, try the move on your own schedule. Run a copy for a week, compare the bills, and only then switch DNS.

Next step: price your own app. In the Hubfly space dashboard, Create Container shows the monthly cost live as you move the CPU and RAM sliders. Start with 0.5 vCPU and 512 MB per process, add a Nano database from the pricing page, and compare the total to your last Heroku invoice. To run a copy for free, create a Hubfly space account; the free tier needs no card.

Go further on Hubfly space

  • Get a managed database for about $2 a month: How to get a managed PostgreSQL database for about $2 a month.
  • Bring your whole Compose file: Deploy a docker-compose.yml as-is: 8 platforms compared.
  • Deploy automatically on every push: How to deploy on every push with GitHub Actions and a webhook.

title: Self-Refining Prompt Induction for Streaming Text-to-SQL
description:
arXiv:2611.00960v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Text-to-SQL assistants for streaming engines must handle dialect-specific types, windowing rules, and temporal semantics, including constructs poorly handled by generic prompts. We present Self-Refining Prompt Induction (SRPI), an offline method that converts generation failures into reusable dialect instructions while keeping model weights fixed. A Refiner revises the Generator's prompt using reference-conditioned feedback from three LLM judges; a sampled regression guard checks earlier successes, and a separate Compressor reduces prompt length. Inference uses the frozen prompt without retrieval or query repair. We evaluate cross-domain and cross-model transfer on Confluent Cloud Flink SQL using a controlled synthetic workload seeded by 30 expert-written examples, with 335 induction examples and 257 questions from held-out domains. The same induced prompt improves mean judge scores across seven Generators by 7.1-19.2 percentage points, including an increase from 85.3% to 97.5% for the induction model. A separate compression study reduces prompt length by 52.7% with a 0.19-percentage-point score decrease. An assistant using the induced prompt is in early access, with initial user feedback to inform subsequent refinement.

title: Best Employee Monitoring Software: A Four-Week Test Plan You Can Score on One Page
description:
Every "best employee monitoring software" list is secretly the same list. Vendors, features, a star rating. What is missing is the part engineers would insist on in any other purchase: a test plan. This post gives you one. It is a short evaluation harness for employee monitoring software that you can run in four weeks and score on a single page.

The test plan at a glance

Phase Duration Question it answers
Baseline Week 0 What do we believe today?
Smoke test Week 1 Does it install and report correctly?
Soak test Weeks 2-3 Is the data stable and trusted?
Review Week 4 Did it change a decision?

Phase 0: write your assumptions down

Before installing anything, record what you believe: who is overloaded, where time goes, which projects slip. These are your expected values. A tool is only useful if it can confirm or correct them.

Phase 1: smoke test

Install on a volunteer team of five to eight. Check the basics:

[ ] Installs on every OS in the team
[ ] Reports appear within a day
[ ] Idle time is not flagged for calls and reading
[ ] Categories can be changed per role
[ ] Employees can open their own dashboard

Any failure here is a deal breaker, not a bug to wait on.

Phase 2: soak test

Leave it running for two weeks and watch for false positives. If a designer in a long review looks idle, tune the settings and see whether the tool copes. Data you cannot trust after tuning is data you will not use.

Phase 3: review against assumptions

Compare the report with your Phase 0 notes. Score each tool:

  • Accuracy: did it match reality after tuning?
  • Clarity: can a manager read it in five minutes?
  • Fairness: would the team be comfortable if the dashboard were public?
  • Actionability: did it change at least one decision?
  • Effort: how much admin did it need?

Below 18 out of 25 means it does not ship.

title: datapatch Fails in sqlpatch.pm: Fixing a Corrupted PDB$SEED Tempfile in Oracle 19c
description:
The symptom

datapatch -verbose stopped with:

Unsupported named object type for bind parameter at $ORACLE_HOME/sqlpatch/sqlpatch.pm line 6153.

That message says very little. The useful clue was in the database alert log at the same time:

Read of datafile '/u01/oradata/CDB1/pdbseed/temp01<timestamp>.dbf' (fno 202) header failed with ORA-01206
ORA-01122: database file 202 failed verification check
ORA-01206: file is not part of this database - wrong database id
PDB$SEED(2): Cannot re-create tempfile /u01/oradata/CDB1/pdbseed/temp01<timestamp>.dbf, the same name file exists

What the alert log is telling you

  • ORA-01206 (wrong database id): the header of the PDB$SEED tempfile belongs to a different database.
  • "Cannot re-create tempfile... the same name file exists": when PDB$SEED opened, Oracle tried to rebuild the bad tempfile on its own. It couldn't, because a file with that name was already on disk.
  • The datapatch error: datapatch needs a working temporary tablespace in every container, including the seed. With none available, it hit an unhandled exception in sqlpatch.pm.

Likely cause

The tempfile name carries a timestamp from 2024, but PDB$SEED had already been patched successfully in an earlier cycle, so the header problem probably appeared after that, for example following a storage-level copy or a refresh of the database files between patch cycles. I can't prove when or how it happened, so treat this as the most likely explanation, not a confirmed one.

This is a useful lesson in itself: a seed that patched fine once can still break later.

The fix

I replaced the bad tempfile in PDB$SEED with a new one. This uses a hidden parameter, so read the cautions below first.

sqlplus / as sysdba

-- allow changes to the seed (session level only)
ALTER SESSION SET "_oracle_script" = TRUE;

ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE PDB$SEED CLOSE IMMEDIATE;
ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE PDB$SEED OPEN READ WRITE;

ALTER SESSION SET CONTAINER = PDB$SEED;

-- remove the corrupted tempfile
ALTER DATABASE TEMPFILE '/u01/oradata/CDB1/pdbseed/temp01<timestamp>.dbf' DROP INCLUDING DATAFILES;

-- add a clean one
ALTER TABLESPACE TEMP ADD TEMPFILE '/u01/oradata/CDB1/pdbseed/temp01.dbf'
  SIZE 100M AUTOEXTEND ON NEXT 10M MAXSIZE 2G;

-- put the seed back as it was
ALTER SESSION SET CONTAINER = CDB$ROOT;
ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE PDB$SEED CLOSE IMMEDIATE;
ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE PDB$SEED OPEN READ ONLY;

EXIT;

Then rerun datapatch:

$ORACLE_HOME/OPatch/datapatch -verbose

Verify

After the fix, the rerun patched all three containers, including the seed:

$ORACLE_HOME/OPatch/datapatch -verbose
SQL Patching tool version 19.32.0.0.0 Production

Installation queue:
  For the following PDBs: CDB$ROOT PDB$SEED <PDB_NAME>
    The following interim patches will be rolled back:
      37847857 (OJVM RELEASE UPDATE: 19.28.0.0.250715)
    Patch 39472050 (Database Release Update : 19.32.0.0.260721):
      Apply from 19.28.0.0.0 to 19.32.0.0.0
    The following interim patches will be applied:
      39222882 (OJVM RELEASE UPDATE: 19.32.0.0.260721)

Patch installation complete.  Total patches installed: 9

Patch 37847857 rollback (pdb CDB$ROOT): SUCCESS
Patch 39472050 apply (pdb CDB$ROOT): SUCCESS
Patch 39222882 apply (pdb CDB$ROOT): SUCCESS
Patch 37847857 rollback (pdb PDB$SEED): SUCCESS
Patch 39472050 apply (pdb PDB$SEED): SUCCESS
Patch 39222882 apply (pdb PDB$SEED): SUCCESS
Patch 37847857 rollback (pdb <PDB_NAME>): SUCCESS
Patch 39472050 apply (pdb <PDB_NAME>): SUCCESS
Patch 39222882 apply (pdb <PDB_NAME>): SUCCESS

Then check the tempfiles across all containers:

SELECT con_id, file_id, file_name, tablespace_name, status
FROM cdb_temp_files ORDER BY con_id;

CON_ID 2 (the seed) should show the new temp01.dbf. Confirm the seed is back in its normal state:

SELECT name, open_mode, restricted FROM v$pdbs;

Finally, check that the patch was recorded:

SELECT patch_id, action, status, description
FROM dba_registry_sqlpatch ORDER BY action_time;

Cautions

  • _oracle_script is an underscore parameter. Oracle's own scripts use it, but using it by hand to change the seed is not something I'd do without a backup and a check of the relevant My Oracle Support note. In production, I'd raise a Service Request first.
  • I set it at session level only. ALTER SESSION means it was gone when I exited and never touched the spfile.
  • Take a backup first and try this in a non-production database.
  • Read-only afterwards. Always put PDB$SEED back in READ ONLY once you're done.

What I learned

  • A Perl-level error can hide a storage problem. When datapatch fails inside sqlpatch.pm, read the alert log at the same moment.
  • Check the seed's tempfile, not just the root. A bad tempfile in PDB$SEED can block patching even when everything else looks healthy.
  • Open your PDBs before running datapatch. It only patches PDBs that are open, and it skips closed ones.
  • Files can change between patch cycles. A seed that patched fine before can still break after copies or refreshes, so it's worth checking tempfile headers before a patching window.

Have you seen this error after patching a cloned or refreshed CDB? I'd like to hear whether the cause matched.

Kumaran Murugan is an Oracle Apps DBA and OCI Cloud Administrator with 5+ years of experience in Oracle E-Business Suite, database migrations, and OCI infrastructure. Connect on LinkedIn.

title: My journey down the database rabbit hole is complete, and it completely changed how I think about building software.
description:
It started with a simple question: Can a database handle a customer buying 1.5 kg of sugar?

What followed was a masterclass in software tradeoffs. I went from discovering a critical hardware flaw, to trying two clever workarounds, to finally understanding the gold standard used by major financial systems.

Here is the exact journey of what I learned:

Step 1: The Binary Flaw (Why floats fail)
I discovered that computers think in 0s and 1s (Binary), while humans think in decimals (Base-10). Because of this, standard computer memory cannot cleanly save numbers like 0.1 or 0.2. They turn into endless repeating fractions. If you add 0.1 three times and subtract 0.3, a computer doesn't give you 0.0. It gives you a bizarre micro-error like 5.55111512312578e-17. Over time, these errors compound and break your systems.

Step 2: The Text Bridge (My first workaround)
Since SQLite doesn't have an exact decimal type, my first idea was to save the stock numbers as TEXT (like "1.5") to freeze the characters in place, and use a SQL CAST statement to convert them to numbers when doing math.

I tested this live in a database browser and immediately hit two massive traps. First, text sorts alphabetically, not numerically. A query looking for items with stock "less than 30" will falsely include "100" because the character "1" comes before "3". Second, using CAST forces the database to open every single row and convert the data on the fly, which completely destroys database indexing and slows your app to a crawl.

Step 3: The Rounding Trick (My second workaround)
Then I noticed SQLite has a NUMERIC label and a ROUND() function. It feels like a fix because it cleans up the screen. But under the hood, SQLite's NUMERIC is just a mask - it secretly turns decimals right back into binary floats. Using ROUND() just slaps a band-aid over a broken number after the damage is done. Plus, if you or a teammate forget to write ROUND() in just one single reporting query, those hidden micro-errors leak into your code and cause invisible bugs.

Step 4: The Enterprise Database Illusion
I thought, "Fine, I will just upgrade to an enterprise database like PostgreSQL later, because Postgres has a native, exact Base-10 decimal engine."

But as I dug deeper, I learned that senior developers across the industry avoid using decimal data types altogether, even in advanced databases like Postgres.

Why? Because of four hidden bottlenecks:

  1. Performance: Pure whole numbers (Integers) are processed directly by computer hardware almost instantly. Software-defined decimal types require complex algorithms that calculate math digit-by-digit, creating a massive CPU bottleneck for systems processing millions of transactions.

  2. The API and Code Trap: Even if your database stores a perfect decimal, the moment that number leaves the database via an API or into JavaScript, languages often force it right back into a standard binary float, instantly corrupting it.

  3. Portability: If your code relies on one database's unique decimal engine, your code will break if you ever have to migrate to another system.

  4. Storage: Integers take up a small, fixed amount of space. Complex decimals are variable-length and take up significantly more hard drive space and memory.

The Elegant Ultimate Solution: Integer Scaling
The ultimate breakthrough was realizing that the best way to handle decimals is to eliminate them completely from your data layer.
Instead of tracking 1.5 Kilograms, you multiply by 1,000 and track 1500 Grams as a pure INTEGER. Instead of tracking 14.50 dollars, you track 1450 Cents.

Integers never suffer from binary float distortion. They remain perfect integers inside the database, perfect integers when traveling through a JSON API, and perfect integers inside your frontend code.

The golden rule of engineering is simple: Keep the absolute truth as a whole integer through your entire system, and only insert the decimal point at the very last microsecond right before showing it on the user's screen.

title: A college notice board in React: a first project for web design students
description:
If you're a student learning web design and you've just finished HTML, CSS and some JavaScript, React can feel like a big jump. The best way across is a small project that you'd actually use. Here's one we give students: a college notice board.

What it does

  • Shows a list of notices (title, department, date).
  • Lets you filter by department.
  • Lets you add a notice through a form.
  • Saves notices in localStorage so they survive a refresh.

That's enough to touch components, props, state, events, forms, lists and effects, without a backend.

Step 1: Set up 

npm create vite@latest notice-board -- --template react
cd notice-board
npm install
npm run dev

Step 2: Model the data 

const starter = [
  { id: 1, title: "Mid-sem exams start 18 Nov", dept: "CSE", date: "2026-11-04" },
  { id: 2, title: "Placement talk in Seminar Hall", dept: "All", date: "2026-11-05" },
];

Step 3: State that persists 

import { useEffect, useState } from "react";

function useNotices() {
  const [notices, setNotices] = useState(() => {
    const saved = localStorage.getItem("notices");
    return saved ? JSON.parse(saved) : starter;
  });
  useEffect(() => {
    localStorage.setItem("notices", JSON.stringify(notices));
  }, [notices]);
  return [notices, setNotices];
}

Step 4: Components

Split it into NoticeList, NoticeCard, DeptFilter and NoticeForm. Pass data down as props, and pass functions like onAdd down so the form can update the list.

function NoticeCard({ notice }) {
  return (
    <article className="card">
      <h3>{notice.title}</h3>
      <p>{notice.dept} · {notice.date}</p>
    </article>
  );
}

Step 5: The filter 

const visible = dept === "All"
  ? notices
  : notices.filter(n => n.dept === dept || n.dept === "All");

Step 6: Make it look good

Use CSS Grid for the card layout and a single media query for mobile. Check it on your phone. Most people who view your portfolio will.

Stretch goals

  • Sort by date, newest first.
  • Mark notices as "important" with a badge.
  • Deploy it and put the live link on your CV.
  • Later, replace localStorage with a small API.

What this teaches

By the end you have used every core React idea a junior interview asks about, and you have something finished to show. That matters more than a long list of half-done tutorials.

We teach this project in the React module of our web designing course for students in Mohali and Chandigarh. The full module list is on the Dzimark Training course page.

title: Is my Supabase database open for anyone to read?
description:
Is my Supabase database open for anyone to read?

Is my Supabase database open for anyone to read? It can be, if an AI coding tool built your app and Row Level Security (RLS) was never turned on for your tables. You can check in a few minutes, and the fix is usually small.

What you’re seeing

Most owners see nothing wrong. The app works. Users sign in, data shows up, and you ship it.

That’s the trap. An open database looks just like a working one. No error, no warning banner, nothing breaks.

UpGuard scanned about 300,000 Supabase domains and found 16,326 databases with tables readable from the public internet with no authentication. Over half showed signs of personal data.

A smaller case shows what this looks like in one app. In February 2026, The Register reported on an education app built with Lovable. It had 16 vulnerabilities, 6 of them critical, and exposed 18,697 user records, including 14,928 unique email addresses. The causes were missing RLS and inverted auth guards, which means the login checks were working the wrong way round.

If your app stores emails, names, orders or messages, you’re in the group that should check.

Why it happens

Your app can look finished while the database is still wide open. That gap usually comes from how the tables were made.

Tables made in the Supabase dashboard get Row Level Security turned on by default. Tables made through the API or raw SQL — the route most AI coding tools take — don’t.

So your app can pass every screen test and still leave its tables readable by anyone who knows how to ask.

A quick way to check this is to look in Supabase at whether RLS is on for each table, then test that table from a logged-out browser session.

Is my Supabase database open for anyone to read? The minimum fix

You don’t need to rebuild the app. Start with this list, in order.

  1. Open Supabase and list every table in your app.
  2. Turn on RLS for each table — no exceptions.
  3. Add one policy per table that says who can read it and who can write to it.
  4. Log out, then try to read each table without signing in. Nothing should come back.
  5. Fix any table that still returns data before you move on.

Don’t just add a policy and assume it’s safe. A policy with the wrong condition can leave a table open while looking protected.

Don’t hide behind a secret key in your app code, either. Anyone who can read that code can use the key — and then your RLS rules don’t matter.

Don’t rely on the app hiding a screen or a button. If the table is readable, the screen is only hiding it, not protecting it.

When to get help instead

If you don’t know which tables hold personal data, or which policies your app actually needs, stop there.

Guessing at policies can lock out real users or leave a gap open. Get someone who has fixed this before to check the tables and policies with you.

If this is your app, contact me through https://israr-kundi.web.app

title: Planning a Corporate Website: Structure, Features, and Content
description:
A company website has to serve more than one visitor. A prospective customer may need to understand a service, an existing client may be looking for support, a partner may want a contact, and a job seeker may need current openings. A navigation menu is useful only when it helps those people complete their tasks.

This guide explains how to plan the pages, functions and ownership behind a corporate website. It uses a fictional B2B supplier as an example; it does not prescribe a fixed set of pages for every business.

Start with visitor journeys

List the site's business goals and the visitor's questions separately. A company may want quote requests, but a buyer might first need to know whether the service fits their equipment, location and timing. A form alone cannot answer those questions.

Visitor Typical question Useful destination
Prospective customer What does the company offer, and how do I get an estimate? Relevant product or service page and a clear contact route
Existing customer Where can I get help or find documentation? Support information, instructions or the responsible team
Partner Who handles cooperation? A partnership page or specific contact
Job seeker Are there suitable roles, and how do I apply? Current openings and an application method

Interview sales and support staff, review recurring questions and use existing site data where you have access. Choose a few priority actions to test. Do not add a portal or a complex catalog just because another company has one: every feature needs accurate data, an owner and maintenance.

Decide which pages deserve their own place

A small company may need only a handful of pages. A larger organization may have several business lines, support routes, locations and document collections. Create a separate page when it answers a distinct question and has enough reliable content to do so.

Home page

Explain what the company does, for whom and where visitors can learn more. Link to the main services or product groups and provide a clear way to reach the right team. Replace broad claims with concrete, verified descriptions.

For example, a fictional equipment supplier could describe the types of equipment it handles, the regions it serves and how a business can request an assessment. It should not promise a response time that its team cannot meet.

Services and products

Give each distinct service enough room to explain its purpose, process, limitations and next step. If a quote depends on several factors, say which information is needed for an estimate instead of inventing a fixed price.

For a product catalog, define who maintains specifications, documents and availability. Test search and filters only if visitors have enough products and attributes to make those features useful. Confirm product claims and technical documents with the people responsible for them.

Company and experience

Describe the organization's work and relevant expertise. A case study should explain the problem, the work performed and a result that can be supported. Obtain permission before publishing a customer's name, images or figures. If a project cannot be named, a carefully labeled description of the process may be more useful than a fabricated testimonial.

Contact, support and careers

Make it clear which channel reaches sales, support or another department. Include current contact details and working hours when relevant. A careers section is helpful when someone owns the process of updating vacancies and handling applications; an empty, abandoned page does little for applicants.

Add news, resources, frequently asked questions or documents when they support a real task and can be maintained. Requirements for particular disclosures vary by organization and jurisdiction; confirm them with the responsible specialist.

An example sitemap

Imagine a fictional company that supplies and services equipment for businesses. A first version might include:

Section Purpose Next step
Home Explain the main offerings and audience Choose equipment or service
Equipment Show categories, verified specifications and documents Ask about fit or request a proposal
Service Explain diagnosis, maintenance and limitations Contact the service team
Projects Share approved examples of completed work Explore a relevant offering
About Explain the company's profile and experience Find partnership information
Contact Separate sales, service and general inquiries Select the right channel

If support receives repeated questions, add useful instructions or a support form. If the company has no active hiring process, a careers page can wait. Test the proposed map with people who represent the audiences, and check whether internal department names make sense to outsiders.

Plan forms as operational processes

A request form is not finished when a visitor clicks “send.” Map what happens next: where the message goes, who owns the queue, what the visitor sees on success or failure, and how the team handles an outage.

Ask only for information needed to respond, such as a name, contact and description of the request. Offer an alternative contact method. With the owner's permission, submit a test inquiry and verify that it reaches the right person; handle test data according to the team's process.

Validate input on the server, limit unwanted submissions and avoid writing secrets or unnecessary personal data into open logs. Have the responsible specialist review the data-handling text and process for the applicable context.

Treat integrations as dependencies

A CRM, accounting service or email integration can save manual work, but it adds another failure path. Test the whole journey: submission, receipt, assignment, error handling and safe recovery without accidental duplicates. Confirm the actual capabilities and configuration of the products in use instead of assuming any two systems connect automatically.

For an early launch with a small volume of inquiries, a documented manual process may be more reliable than an untested integration. Add automation when the workflow and its owner are clear.

Assign ownership to content

For each important page, record its audience, purpose, content owner, source of facts and review date. Separate drafting, subject-matter review and publishing. A specification or support contact that has become outdated can frustrate customers even when the design looks polished.

Gather inputs from the people who know the service: common questions, real limitations, approved documents and permitted photographs. Keep a way for staff to report outdated information and a process for removing or revising it promptly. Publish news only if the team can maintain it.

Check navigation and accessibility

Use labels your visitors understand rather than internal department names. Ask a new user to find a service, contact the appropriate team and return to the section they came from. On a larger site, a sensible hierarchy, breadcrumbs and search may help; they should reflect the actual content structure.

Test representative pages on a phone and a desktop. Check text readability, keyboard operation, form labels, visible errors and text alternatives for meaningful images. Tables and menus should remain usable on small screens. These tests improve the experience, but one test or a sitemap alone does not guarantee search indexing or rankings.

A practical launch sequence

  1. Define audiences, priority tasks and the measures the team can observe.
  2. Give every proposed page a purpose, audience and content owner.
  3. Map each form and integration from input through failure handling.
  4. Verify facts, media permissions, contacts and planned translations.
  5. Ask representative users to complete key journeys on different devices.
  6. Check access, backups, links, forms, test-environment restrictions and a plan for fixing issues.
  7. Record who owns the domain, infrastructure and ongoing page reviews.

A corporate site is a service that needs care after launch. A smaller map with accurate content and clear owners is easier to maintain and extend as the organization grows.

title: I used to think React updates the entire page whenever the state changes. But that's not exactly how it works.
description:
When I started learning React, I came across something called useState().

At first, I only knew how to use it.

For example:

const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

Click a button, increase the count, and React updates the screen.

Pretty simple, right?

But then I started wondering...

What actually happens when I call setCount()?

I learned that React doesn't reload the entire webpage.

Instead, something interesting happens:

React receives the state update.

The component runs again with the new state.

React compares the previous UI with the new UI.

It updates the necessary parts of the actual DOM.

For example, if only the counter value changes, React doesn't need to recreate the entire page.

That made me understand one important thing:

Learning React isn't just about knowing components, props, and hooks.

It's also about understanding what React does behind the scenes.

I'm still exploring these concepts, and honestly, every small discovery makes React more interesting.

title: What is CLS in Core Web Vitals? How to stop your page jumping
description:
Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) is a Core Web Vitals metric that measures how much visible content unexpectedly shifts around on a screen while a page loads. If you have ever tried to tap a button on your phone only to have a banner load at the last millisecond and cause you to tap an ad instead, you have experienced a poor CLS score firsthand.

Google treats visual stability as a key indicator of user experience. Pages that jump around irritate visitors, increase bounce rates, and lead to accidental clicks that frustrate potential customers.

Google measures CLS on a scale starting at zero, calculated by multiplying how far unstable elements move by the percentage of the screen they affect. A good CLS score is 0.1 or lower. A score between 0.1 and 0.25 needs improvement, and anything above 0.25 is considered poor. In my client work, keeping this number under 0.1 is essential for passing Google's real-user page experience assessments, as outlined in my guide on Core Web Vitals explained.

Why web pages shift while loading

Browsers build web pages incrementally. When someone requests your URL, the browser starts reading the HTML document from top to bottom, rendering text and basic structural elements immediately before all media files and external scripts finish downloading.

When an image, script, or custom font arrives a fraction of a second later, the browser must adjust the layout to fit that new asset. If your code did not tell the browser how much room to reserve ahead of time, existing text and buttons get pushed downward or sideways.

Layout shifts do not just happen during the initial page load. Any delayed action—such as an automated newsletter pop-up, an accordion expanding without smooth transitions, or a cookie consent banner loading late—contributes to your overall CLS score if it moves visible elements without direct user interaction.

The three most common causes of high CLS

In almost every website audit I perform, high layout shift scores come down to three specific technical oversights. Fixing these issues usually resolves the majority of page stability problems immediately.

  • Images, videos, and iframes without dimensions: When media tags lack explicit width and height attributes in the HTML, the browser allocates zero vertical pixels until the file downloads, suddenly shoving down everything beneath it when the image renders.
  • Dynamically injected banners and ads: Third-party scripts often insert cookie notices, chat widgets, marketing notification bars, or ads at the very top of the page after the initial layout has rendered.
  • Custom web fonts: When custom web fonts load slowly, the browser displays a temporary fallback font. If the custom font has different letter widths or line heights than the fallback, the entire text block reflows and shifts once the font arrives.

How to find which elements are shifting

Before changing your code, you need to identify exactly which elements are moving. You can start by running your page through Google PageSpeed Insights or using a free website speed test to see your current laboratory and field metrics.

Under the Diagnostics section in PageSpeed Insights, locate the audit titled 'Avoid large layout shifts'. Expanding this section reveals the exact HTML elements responsible for the highest shift scores, alongside screenshots showing the page before and after the shift occurred.

For a more granular view, open Chrome DevTools on your computer, navigate to the Performance tab, and record a page reload. DevTools creates an 'Experience' row that flags every individual layout shift with a red bar, listing the exact element and shift contribution when clicked.

How to fix CLS and keep your layout stable

Once you know which elements are causing the movement, the technical fixes are straightforward to implement in production code.

Always define explicit width and height attributes on your image and video elements. Modern browsers use these attributes to calculate the aspect ratio automatically, reserving the exact box space before the image file even downloads. If you build with modern frameworks like Next.js, the built-in Image component handles this automatically by requiring dimensions or an explicit layout fill strategy.

For dynamic elements like cookie banners or promotional headers, reserve space in your CSS using min-height or skeleton loaders. By reserving the height upfront, the container simply fills in when the script executes, preventing the main navigation and hero copy from dropping down.

To solve font shifting, use modern CSS font-display properties like 'optional' or adjust fallback font metrics to match your custom font dimensions. If you are struggling to resolve shifting across complex templates, bringing in a targeted speed and Core Web Vitals fix helps isolate script conflicts and stabilizes critical rendering paths.

Practical takeaways for a stable website

Eliminating layout shifts requires adopting consistent layout habits during development and marketing updates. Keeping these simple rules in mind protects your user experience and keeps your Core Web Vitals in the green.

  • Aim for a CLS score under 0.1 across both mobile and desktop visitors.
  • Never add an image, video, or iframe without explicit dimensions or an aspect-ratio rule in CSS.
  • Reserve vertical container space for third-party scripts, cookie notices, and marketing banners.
  • Preload key web fonts and align fallback font metrics to prevent text reflows.
  • Test your pages on throttled mobile connections before launching new components.
