title: Delayed User Reminders: Common Python Cron Trust-Boundary Failures
description:
A delayed renewal notice is usually a boundary failure, not a mysterious cron failure. For a healthtech system, I would keep the scheduler responsible for reaching a small public callback, move any work that can approach 900 seconds into a worker queue, and keep sensitive reminder content inside the specialist notification provider. That split makes recovery observable while limiting what crosses each processor boundary.

Short answer: the common causes are a paused or badly resumed cron job, an unavailable public HTTP endpoint, and a task that runs past the 900-second execution limit. Missed triggers are not automatically backfilled after a pause. A reminder system also becomes harder to trust when it sends protected data through a scheduler that only needs to know when to wake up.

The practical test is not “did cron fire?” It is “can I prove which boundary failed, retry the right unit, and avoid sending the same renewal notice twice?”

For this narrow trigger-to-worker boundary, Infrai is worth testing because it exposes a plain REST API without an SDK to install, and one key can cover the scheduling and queue capabilities in the same backend surface. Its public, self-describing discovery response is also useful during an evaluation: a Python team can inspect request and response schemas before committing to a client wrapper. Those conveniences reduce integration friction; they do not answer regional residency or processor-contract questions.

What are common causes of delayed or missed user reminders?

Start with a timeline, not a vendor dashboard. A renewal notice normally has at least four transitions: a business deadline is calculated, a scheduled trigger occurs, a callback accepts the work, and a notification provider delivers it. Each transition has a different owner. Treating all four as one cron task turns an operational recovery problem into a blind retry problem.

A paused job is the first boring cause, and it is common enough to deserve a deliberate check. An operator may pause a schedule during a migration and resume it later, but the missed trigger does not come back automatically. A bad resume can have the same visible result as a bad expression: no callback, no queue message, no reminder. The run history tells you that nothing happened, which is useful, but it cannot reconstruct the event by itself.

The second cause is the callback boundary. Cron tasks that rely on an HTTP callback need a publicly reachable URL. An internal hostname, a private network address, a certificate problem, or an endpoint that is unavailable during deployment can interrupt execution before application code has a chance to enqueue anything. The scheduler is not a tunnel into a private service.

The third is the hard runtime ceiling. A cron execution may start correctly and still fail because its work exceeds 900 seconds. This is especially easy to do when the callback performs database scans, calls a notification provider, waits on a rate limit, and tries to write a detailed audit record in one request. The cure is architectural: let cron trigger a short enqueue operation, then let a worker perform the longer job.

There is a fourth failure mode that belongs to the application rather than cron: at-least-once delivery. A retry can create two worker attempts. The consumer must make the renewal event idempotent, using a stable business key such as account ID plus renewal deadline, before it calls the notification provider. Exactly-once language is comforting; a durable deduplication decision is useful.

That distinction matters.

Imagine a renewal deadline at 09:00. The schedule is paused from 08:55 to 09:10, then resumed. A system that silently assumes the missed 09:00 trigger will be replayed can leave the account untouched; a system that immediately sends every late reminder can create an inappropriate notice after the business deadline has changed. The safer recovery path records the missed deadline, checks current account state in the worker, applies the product’s late-notice rule, and emits one idempotent decision. None of those choices belongs in a cron expression. They belong in code that can be tested with a clock and a small set of account states.

Why do trust boundaries change the scheduler design?

The data question comes before the product question. A scheduler may need a timestamp and an opaque reminder ID. It does not need a diagnosis, a full patient record, or the text of a protected message. In a healthtech flow, the safest callback payload is a reference that lets a controlled worker fetch the minimum data required for the next step.

That gives the system a clean division of responsibility:

Boundary Smallest useful responsibility Recovery question
Scheduler Wake up at the business deadline and call a public endpoint Was the job active, and did the callback respond?
Queue and worker Claim the reminder reference and perform bounded retries Was the message accepted, retried, or dead-lettered?
Specialist notification provider Apply delivery policy and send the approved content What delivery status and retention policy apply?

The scheduler can handle the trigger and the public HTTP handoff. It does not establish audio residency, contractual processing terms, or a regional deletion guarantee for a downstream specialist. Those questions remain with the provider that handles the actual notification data and with the contracts governing the deployment.

This is where a broad backend surface can be useful, but only in a narrow role. Its scheduling and queue capabilities can cover the trigger-to-worker part, while the specialist provider remains responsible for the sensitive notification operation. I would try Infrai for that orchestration boundary when the team wants one HTTP integration and can verify the required region, retention, deletion, and processor terms separately. The no-SDK boundary removes one integration concern; it does not turn a general backend API into a compliance contract.

The same distinction prevents a common design mistake: placing the protected message body in a delayed queue just because the queue accepts it. Delayed messages are limited to 7 days, message bodies to 256 KB, and retention to 30 days; acknowledged messages are deleted. Those limits may be fine for a reminder reference and an expiration timestamp. They are a poor substitute for a notification system’s regulated record policy.

Which Python scheduler fits the recovery boundary?

The familiar tools solve different problems, so a fair comparison needs a failure model.

Celery is a strong fit when the application already has a broker and worker fleet. Its task model, retries, and worker execution are natural for the long-running half of this design. It also creates more infrastructure to operate: broker behavior, result handling, task visibility, and consumer idempotency become part of the service. Celery is the better choice when the team already owns that operational surface and needs deep worker control.

APScheduler is a useful in-process scheduler for a single service or a deliberately small deployment. It is approachable in a Python codebase, but process restarts, multiple scheduler instances, persistence, and coordination need explicit decisions. I would use it for local or tightly bounded scheduling, not as the only recovery record for business-critical renewal notices across several replicas.

Airflow is designed for DAGs, dependencies, and scheduled data workflows. That is valuable for reconciliation pipelines, but it is a wide tool for one deadline-triggered reminder. Its model becomes attractive when the reminder is one stage in a larger dependency graph. A simple trigger-plus-worker design is easier to reason about when there is no workflow join to coordinate.

Temporal is the specialist option when durable workflow state, timers, retries, and long-lived orchestration are the central requirement. It earns its operational complexity for multi-step processes that must resume through failures and wait for external events. It is a better boundary than a basic cron system when the renewal process has approvals, compensating actions, or several human pauses.

A REST-first scheduling layer sits in a different part of this comparison. It can reduce client-library coupling and centralize a trigger and queue interface, but it is not a replacement for Airflow or Temporal’s workflow semantics. It has no DAG or workflow orchestration and no fan-out aggregation primitive. If the domain needs those, use the specialist.

A small Python boundary I can test

The most valuable code in the first experiment is the part that makes recovery decisions deterministic. This example keeps the scheduler payload free of message content, records the business idempotency key, and separates a short callback decision from worker work. It is local Python on purpose: the policy is testable before any backend integration is selected.

import json
import os
import time
from urllib.error import HTTPError, URLError
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen


def get_queue_schema() -> dict:
    request = Request(
        "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/queue.create",
        method="GET",
        headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}"},
    )

    for attempt in range(4):
        try:
            with urlopen(request, timeout=15) as response:
                if response.status != 200:
                    raise RuntimeError(f"discovery failed: HTTP {response.status}")
                return json.load(response)
        except HTTPError as error:
            if error.code != 429 or attempt == 3:
                detail = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
                raise RuntimeError(f"discovery failed: HTTP {error.code}: {detail}")
            retry_after = error.headers.get("Retry-After")
            delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt
            time.sleep(delay)
        except URLError as error:
            raise RuntimeError(f"network failure: {error.reason}") from error


schema = get_queue_schema()
print(schema["id"], schema["method"], schema["path"])

The discovery call is intentionally small. It reads the live schema before the integration code is written, uses an environment-provided key, checks the status, and honors Retry-After on a rate limit. It does not send reminder content anywhere.

In production, the callback should persist or publish the decision quickly and return an error when it cannot do so. The worker then fetches the minimum permitted data, checks a stable business idempotency key, calls the specialist notification provider, and records the provider result. A standard queue is at-least-once, so the idempotency check belongs at the consumer boundary, not in a comment beside the cron expression.

The scheduler-side recovery controls should be equally explicit. A pause is an operational state change; it is not a backfill policy. A resume restores future triggers, while missed deadlines need a separate reconciliation query or business rule. Keep that rule visible in the application, where the team can decide whether a late renewal notice is still appropriate.

What should I measure before copying this design?

I would run a small evaluation harness before committing to a platform. Create cases for an active schedule, a paused schedule, a resume after a missed deadline, an unavailable callback, a 899-second worker handoff, and a deliberately duplicated queue delivery. For each case, assert the expected state transition rather than only checking that an HTTP request returned successfully.

The important measurements are recovery evidence and data exposure: time from deadline to accepted enqueue, count of missed triggers requiring reconciliation, duplicate notification attempts, callback error classification, and the fields crossing each provider boundary. Also test deletion and retention behavior with the actual notification provider. A scheduler’s successful run does not prove that downstream data was deleted under the required policy.

If the system only needs a public callback, a queue reference, and a worker with clear idempotency, a plain REST scheduling layer can be a reasonable fit. Infrai is the option I would test for that narrow trigger-and-queue boundary because its API avoids an SDK installation and its self-describing discovery surface reduces schema guesswork. If the required guarantee is regional residency, contractual processor coverage, durable workflow history, or a specialist notification record, choose the provider and workflow system that explicitly supplies that guarantee instead. For a concrete next step, inspect the user-reminder queue pattern and validate its data boundary against your own provider terms.

The best reminder system is not the one with the most cron features. It is the one that can answer, for one account and one deadline, what crossed the boundary, what was retried, what data was retained, and what action is safe now.

References

  • Celery introduction
  • Airflow documentation
  • Temporal documentation
  • APScheduler user guide
  • Infrai capability discovery

title: Reformulation and Equivalence of Bock's Algorithm for Exact Dependency Parsing
description:
arXiv:2611.00939v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Bock's algorithm provides a matrix-based alternative to Chu--Liu/Edmonds (CL/E) for exact dependency parsing. We present a reformulation that retains original node and arc identities through component labels, column adjustments, and star-and-bar transfers. In exact arithmetic, we prove operational equivalence to original Bock under matching scan and tie rules, and establish correspondence with corrected Tarjan under a prescribed component schedule. A separate analysis establishes optimal-value equivalence with Dozat-derived CL/E under the stated score and single-root conventions. We integrate reformulated Bock into a biaffine dependency parser and evaluate decoding and structured training on the Penn Treebank and Chinese Treebank. These results establish Bock as an alternative exact oracle for dependency parsing and structured training, while distinguishing equality of optimal values from identity of returned trees and training trajectories.

title: Handling Fatal Errors in Production: Lessons from Incident Investigation Protocols
description:
Handling Fatal Errors in Production: Lessons from Incident Investigation Protocols

When Systems Fail: Building Resilience Into Critical Workflows

The recent investigation into an on-field medical incident reminds us that some failures demand immediate, thorough response protocols. While the context is sports medicine, the operational lesson applies directly to fintech and payment systems: when a critical transaction or event fails, your investigation and recovery process can determine whether trust survives.

In payment systems, a "fatal error" isn't death—it's a failed ACH transfer, a reversed payout, or a settlement that never completed. Like a medical investigation, a payment incident requires:

  1. Immediate detection – Did the system know failure occurred?
  2. Root cause analysis – Which component failed, and why?
  3. Stakeholder notification – Who needs to know, and when?
  4. Recovery procedure – What's the next valid state?

ACH Return Codes as Incident Signals

When an ACH payout fails, NACHA return codes (R01–R85) are your incident classification system. Each code signals a specific failure mode:

Code Meaning Recovery Action
R01 Insufficient funds Retry after balance check; notify user
R03 No account/unable to locate Route to alternate payment method
R10 Unauthorized Verify authorization; escalate to compliance
R29 Corporate account closed Update account status; halt future attempts

Unlike a manual investigation, your code must detect and classify these codes automatically. A developer who treats all ACH returns as identical failures will lose customer trust faster than any single transaction.

Building an Incident Response Flow

Here's a production pattern for handling ACH returns without breaking your payout engine:

def handle_ach_return(return_code, payout_id, recipient_id):
    """
    Classify ACH return and route to appropriate recovery.
    """

    # Permanent failure: no recovery possible
    permanent_codes = ['R03', 'R04', 'R29', 'R31']

    # Temporary failure: safe to retry
    retryable_codes = ['R01', 'R09', 'R16', 'R20']

    # Requires manual review
    escalation_codes = ['R10', 'R37', 'R51']

    if return_code in permanent_codes:
        # Mark recipient account as invalid
        mark_account_invalid(recipient_id)
        notify_user(payout_id, "Account no longer valid. Please update.")
        return 'FAILED_PERMANENT'

    elif return_code in retryable_codes:
        # Schedule retry after 2 business days
        schedule_retry(payout_id, delay_days=2, max_attempts=3)
        return 'SCHEDULED_RETRY'

    elif return_code in escalation_codes:
        # Flag for compliance review
        escalate_to_support(payout_id, reason=return_code)
        return 'ESCALATED'

    else:
        # Unknown code: safe default is escalation
        log_unknown_return(payout_id, return_code)
        escalate_to_support(payout_id, reason=f"Unknown: {return_code}")
        return 'ESCALATED'

Timing and Notification

ACH returns arrive 1–5 business days after the original transfer attempt. Your system must:

  • Poll or subscribe to return notifications from your ACH provider (most offer webhooks or SFTP feeds)
  • Correlate returns to original payouts using trace numbers
  • Notify affected users within 24 hours of detecting the return
  • Avoid double-processing if a retry is scheduled

A developer who waits for a user to report a failed payout has already failed the incident response test.

The Broader Pattern

Whether investigating a medical incident or an ACH return, the principle is identical:

  1. Detect the failure signal immediately
  2. Classify it into a known category
  3. Route to the appropriate handler (retry, escalate, or terminal fail)
  4. Notify all stakeholders
  5. Log for audit and learning

In payment systems, this discipline isn't optional—it's the difference between a payout platform customers trust and one they abandon.

Decoding ACH return codes programmatically? The ACH Return Codes API returns the full Nacha R01–R85 set with plain-language descriptions and handling guidance.

title: Save Now, Scrape Later
description:
You don't always know what data you'll need from a webpage until later. By then, the page might have changed, been taken down, or moved behind a login. And while the Wayback Machine can sometimes help, it won't always have the exact version of the page you saw, or the parts of it you actually care about. With Gaffa, you don't have to guess ahead of time what you'll extract. With capture_snapshot, you can save a static copy of a page the moment you see it, then decide later exactly what to pull out and in what format.

What capture_snapshot actually gives you

capture_snapshot returns a single HTML file that captures the page as it looked at the moment of the request, with images and CSS embedded. It opens offline, on any machine, with no connection to the original site required. The saved file disables JavaScript, so anything interactive is frozen exactly as it was when you captured it.

That last part matters for what comes next. Because the output is a normal HTML file with a URL of its own, you can feed that URL straight back into Gaffa as the target of a brand new request, and run any extraction action against it whenever you're ready.

Gaffa has a demo article page you can use to try this yourself, one that generates a fresh set of paragraphs and images on every visit, so it's a decent stand-in for a page you know is going to look different by the time you come back to it. Here's a request that saves a snapshot of it:

Capturing a Snapshot

{
  "url": "https://demo.gaffa.dev/simulate/article?loadTime=0&showModal=false&modalDelay=0&paragraphs=10&images=3",
  "settings": {
    "record_request": false,
    "actions": [
      {
        "type": "capture_snapshot"
      }
    ]
  }
}

Running that returns a URL pointing to the saved HTML file, something like this:

Output from Capturing a Snapshot

{
    "data": {
        "id": "brq_VxrdoBT94ySC5ENidUz9f4Y4LMmNGb",
        "url": "https://demo.gaffa.dev/simulate/article?loadTime=0&showModal=false&modalDelay=0&paragraphs=10&images=3",
        "state": "completed",
        "credit_usage": 0,
        "http_status_code": 200,
        "from_cache": false,
        "data_deleted": false,
        "started_at": "2026-09-25T13:43:27.7740162Z",
        "completed_at": "2026-09-25T13:43:33.3222277Z",
        "running_time": "00:00:05.5482115",
        "page_load_time": "00:00:00.4860422",
        "actions": [
            {
                "id": "act_VxrdoCezW7TBmHfE8XEjv95Xf124D8",
                "type": "capture_snapshot",
                "timestamp": "2026-09-25T13:43:33.3222063Z",
                "output": "https://storage.gaffa.dev/static/blog/save-now-scrape-later/snapshot.html"
            }
        ]
    }
}

Save that URL; it's what makes everything below possible.

Also note: How long the URL stays accessible depends on your plan's data retention period, so if you plan to come back to a snapshot weeks or months later, check that your plan covers it before you rely on it.

Decide how to extract the data later

Imagine you're tracking product pages, articles, or listings you might want structured data from eventually, but you're not sure yet what that structure should look like. Instead of building a schema before you've seen the full picture, you can snapshot pages as you come across them and work out the extraction later, without needing the original page to still exist or look the same.

When you're ready, pass the snapshot's URL as the URL of a new request and run parse_json against it, the same way you would against a live page:

Parsing a Saved Snapshot Into JSON

{
  "url": "https://storage.gaffa.dev/static/blog/save-now-scrape-later/snapshot.html",
  "settings": {
    "record_request": false,
    "actions": [
      {
        "type": "parse_json",
        "data_schema": {
          "name": "ArticleInfo",
          "description": "Extract the title from the article page",
          "fields": [
            {
              "type": "string",
              "name": "title",
              "description": "The article's title"
            }
          ]
        }
      }
    ]
  }
}

parse_json runs on the gpt-4o-mini model by default, and it doesn't care whether the page you're pointing it at is live on the web or sitting in a snapshot file; it reads the content either way.

Change your extraction format without revisiting the page

The same snapshot URL isn't locked to one action either. If you parse a batch of pages into JSON and later realise you actually want the readable text instead, you don't need to go back to the original site to fix it. Feed the same URL into a new request with generate_markdown instead:

Converting a Saved Snapshot to Markdown

{
  "url": "https://storage.gaffa.dev/static/blog/save-now-scrape-later/snapshot.html",
  "settings": {
    "record_request": false,
    "actions": [
      {
        "type": "generate_markdown"
      }
    ]
  }
}

Because you're loading a lightweight static file rather than the live page, there's no navigation, ads, or third-party scripts for Gaffa to load first, so these requests tend to complete faster than the original capture did, and typically use fewer credits too, since there's far less for the browser to fetch and render.

What kinds of actions work on a snapshot URL

parse_json and generate_markdown aren't special cases here. Any action that just reads the page content already sitting in front of it works the same way against a snapshot. parse_table finds a table in the saved HTML exactly as it would on a live page, capture_screenshot renders the static file and takes the shot, print exports it to PDF the same way it would export any other page, and capture_dom and generate_simplified_dom both work too, since they're only reading and reshaping the DOM that's already there.

What doesn't work are actions that need to interact with a live, running page, things like scroll, click, or type. JavaScript is switched off in a saved snapshot, so nothing is left to trigger. If a page needs interaction, that has to happen before you capture it, not after.

Load everything before you capture

capture_snapshot saves the page exactly as it appears when you take the shot, which means anything that hasn't loaded yet simply won't be there. Gaffa's demo storefront can be configured to load its product listings as you scroll, using the loadingMode, itemCount, and itemLoadTime parameters in its URL. If you captured a snapshot without reaching the bottom of the page, those later products wouldn't be in the saved file, and no amount of waiting in place would load them, since they load only in response to scrolling.

Adding a wait for the first product to render, followed by a scroll action, takes care of this: the wait makes sure the grid has actually mounted before anything tries to move the page, and the scroll then takes you to the bottom and keeps going for as long as new items keep appearing, so you don't need to guess how many there'll be.

Scrolling to Load Every Product Before Capturing

{
  "url": "https://demo.gaffa.dev/simulate/ecommerce?loadTime=2&showModal=false&modalDelay=0&loadingMode=infinite&itemCount=500&itemLoadTime=0&isVirtualScroll=false",
  "proxy_location": null,
  "async": false,
  "max_cache_age": 0,
  "settings": {
    "record_request": false,
    "actions": [
      {
        "type": "wait",
        "selector": "[data-testid^=\"product-1\"]"
      },
      {
        "type": "scroll",
        "percentage": 100,
        "timeout": 5000,
        "wait_time": 1000,
        "max_scroll_time": 25000
      },
      {
        "type": "capture_snapshot"
      }
    ]
  }
}

The wait step waits for the first product card to appear, so the scroll action never runs against an empty, unrendered page. From there, percentage: 100 sends the browser to the bottom; timeout: 5000 gives Gaffa up to 5 seconds to treat the page as scrollable rather than giving up the instant it checks; and wait_time: 1000 does the lazy-loading work. After each arrival at the bottom, Gaffa watches for a second, and if the page has grown, it keeps scrolling and the wait resets. max_scroll_time caps the whole thing at 25 seconds, so a page that never stops loading (as this one can, with itemCount=infinite) doesn't run the action forever; it just stops cleanly rather than failing.

Since JavaScript doesn't run inside the saved file, this is also your only chance to expand collapsed sections, open tabs, or dismiss cookie banners using an action like click before you capture. Anything you don't open beforehand stays closed in the snapshot.

Other things you can do with a snapshot

Extraction is only one use for a saved page. A snapshot is also a straightforward way to keep proof of what a page looked like on a given date, whether that's for a pricing dispute, a compliance record, or just your own reference before a competitor's site inevitably redesigns itself. Since the file opens offline in any browser, you can hand it to someone else, store it alongside other records, or drop it into a shared drive without requiring a Gaffa account.

Capturing a page doesn't have to mean deciding on the spot what you'll do with it. With capture_snapshot, you can save the page now and work out the extraction, schema, or format later, without needing the original site to still be there. If you haven't already, sign up at gaffa.dev and try it in the API Playground.

Frequently asked questions

What does capture_snapshot actually save?

It saves a single offline HTML file of the page as it looked at capture time, with all images and CSS embedded. JavaScript is disabled, so anything interactive stays frozen as it was.

Can I run parse_json against a saved snapshot instead of the live page?

Yes. Pass the snapshot's URL as the URL in a new request and run parse_json against it exactly as you would a live page or online PDF, with your schema defined the same way.

Can I convert a saved snapshot to markdown instead of JSON?

Yes, use generate_markdown with the snapshot's URL as the request's URL. You can run either action, or both, against the same saved snapshot at any time.

What other actions can I run against a saved snapshot?

Any action that just reads the rendered page works, including parse_table, capture_screenshot, print, capture_dom, and generate_simplified_dom. Actions that need to interact with a live page, like scroll or click, won't do anything.

Why is content missing from a snapshot?

The page probably loads that content dynamically, after a delay or as the user scrolls. Add a wait or scroll before capture_snapshot so everything has rendered before the capture happens.

How long does a snapshot's URL stay accessible?

That depends on your plan's data retention period, for example, 7 days on the Starter plan, 30 days on Startup, or 3 months on Growth. Extract what you need from it before that window runs out.

Can I use capture_snapshot just to archive a page, without extracting anything?

Yes. The saved HTML file opens offline on any machine, which makes it useful for keeping a record of how a page looked on a given date, independent of any extraction step.

title: Sign JWTs from your Functions without managing private keys
description:
Vercel KMS lets you sign JWTs and arbitrary messages from your Vercel Functions using managed asymmetric signing keys, so private keys never live in your code or environment variables. Your function authenticates with its Vercel OIDC token, and the private key stays inside Vercel's key management service while verifiers use only the public key.

With Vercel KMS you can:

  • Create and rotate issuers and signing keys (RSA and ECDSA) from the CLI and dashboard.

  • Sign JWTs with custom claims and a configurable TTL, or sign raw bytes, using the @vercel/kms package.

  • Grant a project signing access per environment, including production, preview, development, and custom environments.

  • Constrain the claims a project can request per grant, and validate token claims against a JSON Schema.

  • Verify signed tokens anywhere. Each issuer publishes a public OpenID Connect Discovery document at https://kms.vercel.com/<issuerId>/.well-known/openid-configuration and a JWK set at https://kms.vercel.com/<issuerId>/jwks.json, so any standard OIDC or JOSE library can validate tokens without Vercel-specific code.

Sign a token inside a function:

Verify a token anywhere with a standard JOSE library, using the issuer's public JWKS:

Set up an issuer and grant a project access from the CLI:

As a best practice, create a separate issuer per project and environment. Isolating issuers keeps each token audience distinct, scopes signing access to exactly one project and environment, and lets you rotate or revoke keys for one without affecting the others.

To get started, read the docs or open Key Management in your team's dashboard.

title: A Vitest test that fails when anyone types one of our prices
description:
We run BaseAcross, a site for founders outside the US forming US companies. A price on a site like ours shows up in more places than you'd guess: the landing page, the pricing table, the checkout total, guides, FAQ answers, glossary entries, emails, JSON-LD offers and the llms.txt file. On 29 October 2026 our founder said our pricing didn't look consistent across pages.

So we audited it. We fetched all 516 URLs in the sitemap and checked 16,540 dollar amounts against the catalogue. No page printed a wrong number for a product we were selling. The inconsistency he saw was real, and it came from three other places:

  1. Plans we no longer sold still had prices on the site, including JSON-LD offers on three pages. A reader who clicked through would find a different plan at a different price on the order form.
  2. An add-on that was switched off was still priced in one guide.
  3. One state charges an LLC and a corporation different yearly amounts. Both totals were correct, and different pages showed different ones without saying which was which.

The audit also counted state fees typed by hand into prose: 69 Wyoming and Delaware fee figures across 16 files, each one right on the day it was typed. Each of them would stay put the next time the state changed its fee.

What follows is the setup we built after it: one home for every figure, tokens for prose, and a test that walks every string in src/ looking for a price somebody typed.

The catalogue is the only place a price may live

Plans, add-ons and the state fees we pass on live in src/lib/data/catalog-picks.ts and a short list of product modules beside it. Public pages read plansOnSale, a filtered view of the catalogue, and a page that names one plan goes through a helper that throws for a retired one:

export const plansOnSale: PlanPick[] = planPicks.filter((plan) => plan.onSale);

/** A plan by key, for a page that names one: throws for a retired plan. */
export function planOnSale(key: PlanKey): PlanPick {
  const plan = plansOnSale.find((p) => p.key === key);
  if (!plan) throw new Error(`Plan ${key} is not on sale.`);
  return plan;
}

The arithmetic gets the same treatment. Whether a plan includes the state's filing fee is decided in one function, and everything that adds a state fee to a plan price calls it:

/**
 * Everything that adds a state fee to a plan price goes through here, so the
 * figure on the pricing table, the one in the wizard's running total, the one
 * on the review and the one Stripe charges cannot disagree again.
 */
export function stateFeeFor(plan: Pick<PlanPick, "coversStateFee">, state: { stateFee: number }) {
  return plan.coversStateFee ? 0 : state.stateFee;
}

Formatting has one home too. money() prints whole amounts without cents and keeps cents only when an amount has them, because a page showing a rounded figure next to a card charge with cents looks like a mistake even when it's a rounding choice:

export function money(value: number, options: Intl.NumberFormatOptions = {}) {
  const places = Number.isInteger(value) ? 0 : 2;
  return new Intl.NumberFormat("en-US", {
    style: "currency", currency: "USD",
    minimumFractionDigits: places, maximumFractionDigits: places,
    ...options,
  }).format(value);
}

Prose gets tokens instead of template literals

Code was already reading the catalogue. The 69 typed fees were all in prose, and they were typed for a plain reason: writing ${money(DE.annualCost)} in the middle of a long guide paragraph is clumsy, so people typed the number. The fix had to keep plain strings for the people writing them.

So prose now writes a token, and prices() swaps it for the catalogue's figure when the module that holds the text loads:

const TOKEN = /\{((?:price|fee|addon|total)\.[A-Za-z0-9.]+)\}/g;

export function prices(text: string): string {
  return text.replace(TOKEN, (_, name: string) => {
    const amount = PRICE_TOKENS[name];
    if (amount === undefined) throw new Error(`Unknown price token {${name}}`);
    return money(amount);
  });
}

A sentence in a guide reads like this (an illustration in the shape our data files use):

a: prices("Launch is {price.launch} a year, and Delaware then charges {fee.DE.annual.llc} for an LLC."),

PRICE_TOKENS is built from the catalogue: plan prices, add-ons, every state fee field, and a few totals such as a plan plus the state's filing fee. Three properties fall out of that.

  • A typo like {fee.DE.anual.llc} throws when the module loads, so it fails the build and never reaches a reader.
  • A retired plan has no token, so its price can't be written into a page. prices("{price.build}") is a test case that must throw.
  • The regex only matches the four token families, so the add-on blurbs' own {state} and {turnaround} placeholders pass through for their own filler.

The test reads every string in src/

Tokens only help if people use them. src/lib/price-literals.test.ts checks that they do. It builds the set of every amount the catalogue charges or passes on, formatted by money(), then parses every .ts and .tsx file with the TypeScript compiler API and looks at string literals, template literals and JSX text:

if (ts.isStringLiteral(node) || ts.isNoSubstitutionTemplateLiteral(node)) {
  words = node.text;
  context = words;
} else if (ts.isJsxText(node)) {
  words = node.text;
  context = node.parent.getText();
}
// … template expressions are read with their ${} holes blanked out

for (const m of words.matchAll(AMOUNT)) {
  if (!guarded.has(m[0])) continue;   // not one of our figures
  if (!OURS.test(context)) continue;  // not next to our words
  // … allow-list check, then report file:line and the words around it
}

We parse instead of grepping so that comments are never read. A comment can explain where a figure came from without failing the build. Code that computes a figure from the catalogue isn't text, so it passes too.

A failure prints file:line $X | the 80 characters either side, so it shows the sentence as well as the line.

Keeping false positives down

A site about company formation is full of dollar figures that aren't ours: other providers' prices, other states' fees, worked examples of a payment. The test filters in layers.

  • AMOUNT matches a whole figure, so a larger amount that starts with the same digits isn't read as one of ours.
  • Only figures equal to one we charge or pass on count.
  • Only figures in a string that also contains one of our words count: a state we form in, a plan name, "state fee", or "we" and "our".
  • The catalogue modules themselves are exempt, along with the token resolver.
  • Anything left goes on an allow-list, and the allow-list is held to its own rules: 
const ALLOW: { file?: RegExp; near?: RegExp; amounts?: string[]; reason: string }[] = [
  { file: /^lib\/site\/data\/competitors\.ts$/, reason: "Rivals' prices, as each publishes them." },
  { file: /^lib\/site\/sources\.ts$/, reason: "The source's own words, which the source check looks for." },
  { near: /authori[sz]ed shares|…/, amounts: ["$…"], reason: "Delaware's authorised-shares franchise tax, not a certificate fee." },
  // …
];

it("keeps the allow-list small, each entry with its reason", () => {
  expect(ALLOW.length).toBeLessThanOrEqual(12);
  for (const a of ALLOW) {
    expect(a.reason.length).toBeGreaterThan(10);
    if (a.near) expect(a.amounts?.length, a.reason).toBeGreaterThan(0);
  }
});

The last rule matters most. An entry matched by nearby words has to name the exact amounts it lets through, so a second figure typed into the same sentence still fails.

What it doesn't catch

The guarded set is today's catalogue. If a price changes and an old figure is still typed somewhere, that old figure no longer matches anything and the test passes. The test catches a literal at the moment it's written, while it still equals a real price. The literals that were already there had to be found by the audit and converted by hand.

Retired plans needed their own tests for the same reason. One asserts that only the two plans on sale are on sale. One checks that structured data offers only those plans. One serialises the add-on pages, guides, glossary and FAQ and fails on a retired plan's name or price. That last matcher needed care, because one retired plan was called "Build", which is also a verb, so it only matches the name in plan-shaped phrases like "on Build" or "Build plan".

Beyond that, the test only knows dollar-sign figures, and "we" and "our" are a blunt way to decide whose number it is. We'd rather take the occasional allow-list entry than miss a real one. The audit found 69 typed fees, each right on the day it was typed; the test's own header says it exists so the 70th is caught when it's written.

Drafted with AI assistance and checked against our code and the sources it cites.

title: Pitch Correction Under the Hood: Pitch Detection, Shifting and Why Auto-Tune Sounds the Way It Does
description:
By Tania Alwan

Pitch correction is everywhere in modern music, from subtle tuning on ballads to the hard, robotic effect in pop and rap. Under the hood it's a neat chain of signal processing: detect the pitch, decide the target, shift the audio, and do it without making the voice sound like a chipmunk.

This post walks through each stage with small Python examples, explains where artefacts come from, and covers how pitch correction fits into AI vocal workflows.

The pipeline in four stages

Almost every pitch corrector, hardware or software, follows the same steps:

  1. Pitch detection: estimate the fundamental frequency (f0) of the voice over time.
  2. Target selection: map each detected pitch to the nearest allowed note in a scale.
  3. Correction curve: decide how fast and how strongly to move toward the target.
  4. Pitch shifting: resynthesise the audio at the new pitch while preserving timing and, ideally, timbre.

Stage 1: detecting pitch

Monophonic pitch detection is a well-studied problem. Common algorithms include:

  • Autocorrelation: find the lag at which the signal best matches a shifted copy of itself.
  • YIN and pYIN: refinements of autocorrelation that reduce octave errors; pYIN adds a probabilistic model to track pitch over time.
  • Neural pitch trackers: models like CREPE, trained on audio to predict f0 directly.

With librosa, pYIN is one call:

import librosa, numpy as np

y, sr = librosa.load("vocal.wav", sr=None, mono=True)
f0, voiced_flag, voiced_prob = librosa.pyin(
    y, fmin=librosa.note_to_hz("C2"), fmax=librosa.note_to_hz("C6"), sr=sr
)

f0 is an array of frequencies in Hz (NaN where unvoiced). Clean input matters: reverb, noise and backing-track bleed all confuse detectors, causing octave jumps or flicker.

Stage 2: snapping to a scale

Converting frequency to MIDI note numbers makes the maths easy:

midi = librosa.hz_to_midi(f0)
target = np.round(midi)                       # chromatic: nearest semitone

# restrict to C major
scale = np.array([0, 2, 4, 5, 7, 9, 11])
def snap(m):
    if np.isnan(m): return m
    octave, pc = divmod(m, 12)
    nearest = scale[np.argmin(np.abs(scale - pc))]
    return octave * 12 + nearest
target_scale = np.array([snap(m) for m in midi])

Real products add a lot on top: key detection, note-level segmentation, and handling notes that sit exactly between two targets.

Stage 3: the correction curve (the "Auto-Tune effect")

The famous robotic sound isn't caused by pitch shifting itself. It comes from correction speed.

  • Slow correction: pitch glides gently toward the target, preserving vibrato and scoops. This is transparent tuning.
  • Instant correction: pitch jumps immediately to the target note. Natural transitions between notes become hard steps, and vibrato disappears. That's the "hard-tune" effect.

A simple smoothing model:

def correct(midi, target, speed=0.2):
    out = np.copy(midi)
    for i in range(1, len(midi)):
        if np.isnan(midi[i]): continue
        error = target[i] - midi[i]
        out[i] = midi[i] + error * speed   # speed=1.0 -> hard tune
    return out

Most plugins expose this as a "retune speed" or "humanize" control.

Stage 4: shifting the pitch

Once you know how many semitones to move each frame, you need to shift the audio. Options:

  • Resampling: simplest, but it changes duration and timbre together (the chipmunk effect).
  • Phase vocoder: works on the STFT; changes pitch independently of time, but can sound smeared.
  • PSOLA (pitch-synchronous overlap-add): cuts the signal into pitch periods and re-spaces them. Very good for monophonic voice, the basis of many classic correctors.
  • Formant-preserving shifting: keeps the vocal tract resonances in place so large shifts don't change the perceived "size" of the singer.

For a quick global shift, librosa is enough:

shifted = librosa.effects.pitch_shift(y, sr=sr, n_steps=-2)  # down 2 semitones

Time-varying correction (different shift per frame) needs a PSOLA or vocoder implementation, such as those in Praat via the parselmouth package or the WORLD vocoder via pyworld.

Where the artefacts come from

  • Octave errors in detection cause sudden, wrong jumps.
  • Unvoiced sounds like "s" and "t" have no pitch; correcting them produces glitches if not gated.
  • Breathy or noisy takes reduce detection confidence.
  • Large shifts without formant preservation change the character of the voice.

Pitch correction in AI vocal pipelines

Pitch matters in AI voice work too. In voice conversion pipelines such as RVC, a pitch track is extracted from the source vocal and passed to the model, and a transpose setting shifts it, for example when converting a male vocal for a higher target voice. Errors in that pitch track show up directly in the output.

That's why a typical cover workflow looks like:

  1. Separate the vocal from the mix (e.g. Demucs, or a hosted stems tool).
  2. Clean it: reduce reverb and noise so the pitch tracker isn't confused.
  3. Tune lightly if the source is off-pitch.
  4. Convert with the voice model.

Hosted tools bundle some of these steps. Voicestars, for example, has a reverb remover and noise remover alongside its voice conversion, while open-source users can chain the same steps in Python. I covered the separation and conversion part in more depth in Vocal Isolation and Voice Conversion.

Practical settings for natural tuning

If you just want a vocal to sound in tune rather than robotic, these habits help:

  • Set the correct key first. Most bad tuning comes from snapping to the wrong scale.
  • Use a slower retune speed on sustained notes and ballads.
  • Leave vibrato alone where possible; many tools have a separate vibrato or "flex" control.
  • Tune phrase by phrase instead of applying one setting to the whole track.
  • Bypass often and compare with the original to avoid over-processing.

Free tools to experiment with

  • Graillon (free edition) and MAutoPitch are free pitch-correction plugins for DAWs.
  • librosa, parselmouth and pyworld cover detection and shifting in Python.
  • Audacity offers pitch changes for whole clips.

Try it

Record a short sung phrase, run pYIN on it, plot f0 against the nearest semitones, and see how far off you really are. If you're preparing vocals for AI conversion, clean them first; you can do that locally or with the Voicestars reverb remover.

Disclosure: this article was written in partnership with Voicestars.

title: Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) is now supported on Vercel CDN
description:
Vercel CDN now supports Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) for domains managed by Vercel DNS. ECH encrypts the Server Name Indication (SNI) in the TLS handshake, the last part of an HTTPS connection that revealed which hostname a client was connecting to. With ECH, network observers see a connection to Vercel's shared ECH hostname, vercel-ech.com.

ECH is managed at the platform level and automatically enabled selectively where supported, starting in the US for a limited number of TLDs, and expanding to more TLDs and regions over time.

Recent versions of Chrome, Edge, and Firefox support Encrypted Client Hello.

Learn more about ECH and how Vercel CDN protects your application in the CDN encryption documentation.

title: How to Build an Express Middleware Setup for Error Tracking: 2026 Property Costs
description:
Short answer: use one Express error-tracking middleware setup that emits a normalized JSON event with run_id, property_id, stage, and error_code; retain the compact event longer than its raw payload so nightly property-pipeline costs can be attributed without storing every request body.

A nightly property-management pipeline usually does not need a bigger error platform. It needs one error record that answers three questions: which run failed, which property or tenant cohort was affected, and what retention decision created the bill. Put that context into structured logs at the Express boundary, propagate a request or job identifier, and keep verbose payloads on a short retention schedule.

The least complex useful implementation is an error-handling middleware that emits one normalized event per failed request, while the pipeline worker emits the same shape for scheduled jobs. The middleware should preserve the original error for local diagnostics, remove secrets before serialization, and let the process-level policy decide whether the request can continue.

What is the bill actually made of?

For a property operator, the useful unit is rarely an individual log line. It is a nightly run: 8,000 leases imported, 312 address records rejected, three downstream calls retried, and one reconciliation step marked incomplete. If every debug payload and stack trace survives for 30 days, storage and indexing grow with the number of records even though the operator mostly searches by run_id, property_id, stage, and error_code.

Start by measuring those terms in your own pipeline. Count records per run, bytes per record, retry attempts, and the percentage of failures that lead to a support investigation. Do not use an assumed vendor price as the model; retention, indexing, and query volume vary by deployment. The decision is still concrete: keep compact failure summaries long enough for reconciliation, and keep raw input samples only long enough to diagnose a malformed record.

Here is a small Python calculation for the planning worksheet. It does not predict a bill. It exposes which field is driving retained volume.

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class RunVolume:
    runs: int
    records_per_run: int
    bytes_per_record: int
    retention_days: int

    def retained_gib(self) -> float:
        total_bytes = (
            self.runs
            * self.records_per_run
            * self.bytes_per_record
            * self.retention_days
        )
        return total_bytes / (1024 ** 3)


volume = RunVolume(
    runs=30,
    records_per_run=8000,
    bytes_per_record=1200,
    retention_days=30,
)
print(f"{volume.retained_gib():.2f} GiB before indexes and replicas")

The change that usually matters is boring: emit one summary event for each rejected record and attach the detailed input only to a sampled or explicitly quarantined record. That makes the search path predictable and gives cost attribution a stable key. The trade-off is real. After the raw sample expires, reconstructing the exact malformed input may require returning to the source system or rerunning the job.

The record is the unit of search, but the run is the unit of accountability.

That distinction changes the retention design in a useful way. A property manager investigating a missed lease import needs to identify the run, isolate the affected property, see whether the record failed validation or exhausted retries, and find the next system responsible for correction. They do not need every successful row, every request header, or a permanent copy of an upstream response. Keeping those details forever makes a later query noisier and expands the data that must be protected. Keeping only an opaque error code makes the event cheap but leaves support with no path back to the source. The compact summary and expiring detail reference are the middle ground: enough context for attribution, with a deliberate escape hatch for diagnosis.

How should Express middleware preserve the failure context?

Express error middleware has four arguments and must be registered after the routes. That placement matters more than the logger choice. The handler should classify the error, select a safe public response, and write a structured event with fields that a nightly job uses too. It should not dump the entire request object into a log record.

This example uses only Node.js interfaces and a JSON writer. The writer could send to a file, a collector, or a self-hosted log service; the middleware does not need to know which. That is the setup boundary: the application chooses fields and severity, while the transport chooses where records are retained.

import crypto from "node:crypto";
import express from "express";

const app = express();
app.use(express.json({ limit: "256kb" }));

function requestId(req) {
  return req.get("x-request-id") || crypto.randomUUID();
}

function classify(error) {
  if (error.code === "PROPERTY_NOT_FOUND") {
    return { status: 404, error_code: error.code };
  }
  if (error.code === "UPSTREAM_TIMEOUT") {
    return { status: 503, error_code: error.code };
  }
  return { status: 500, error_code: "INTERNAL_ERROR" };
}

function writeEvent(event) {
  process.stdout.write(JSON.stringify(event) + "\n");
}

app.get("/properties/:propertyId/ledger", async (req, res, next) => {
  try {
    const ledger = await loadLedger(req.params.propertyId);
    res.json(ledger);
  } catch (error) {
    error.propertyId = req.params.propertyId;
    next(error);
  }
});

app.use((error, req, res, next) => {
  const id = requestId(req);
  const result = classify(error);

  writeEvent({
    timestamp: new Date().toISOString(),
    signal: "log",
    severity: result.status >= 500 ? "ERROR" : "WARN",
    event_name: "http_request_failed",
    request_id: id,
    run_id: req.get("x-run-id") || null,
    property_id: error.propertyId || null,
    stage: "ledger_lookup",
    error_code: result.error_code,
    http_method: req.method,
    route: req.route?.path || "unknown",
    status_code: result.status,
    retryable: result.status === 503,
    exception_type: error.name,
  });

  res.status(result.status).json({
    error: result.error_code,
    request_id: id,
  });
});

There are two details worth defending. First, request_id is returned to the caller, so an operator can connect a tenant report to the server-side event without exposing a stack trace. Second, run_id remains nullable because interactive traffic and scheduled work have different origins. A fake run identifier would make cost attribution look precise while silently joining unrelated events.

In a real application, loadLedger would be defined elsewhere. The example is about the boundary contract, not a complete property ledger implementation. The process must also handle rejected promises and uncaught exceptions according to its runtime policy; an HTTP middleware cannot observe failures that occur outside an Express request.

That is the whole setup. Keep it small.

Which fields make a nightly run searchable?

Use a small, stable event schema. OpenTelemetry describes logs as a signal that can carry timestamped records and shared context, including trace-related correlation fields. You do not need to adopt every field on day one, but aligning names and semantics with an established model prevents a private schema from becoming an integration tax later.

For this pipeline, I would make run_id, property_id, stage, error_code, attempt, and source_system searchable. Put the tenant's email address, lease text, and full upstream response in a quarantined detail record instead. Those values increase privacy exposure and make cardinality expensive.

A useful event might look like this: single-line JSON, no embedded request body.

{
  "timestamp": "2026-10-28T02:14:07.431Z",
  "signal": "log",
  "event_name": "pipeline_record_rejected",
  "run_id": "pm-2026-10-28-02",
  "property_id": "property-184",
  "stage": "lease_import",
  "source_system": "rent_feed",
  "record_key_hash": "sha256:...",
  "attempt": 2,
  "error_code": "MISSING_MOVE_IN_DATE",
  "retryable": false,
  "detail_ref": "quarantine/pm-2026-10-28-02/record-91"
}

record_key_hash supports repeated-failure analysis without making a personal identifier the query key. Hashing is not anonymization by itself, especially when the input space is small, so access control and deletion policy still matter. The detail reference should expire independently from the summary event, and its retention should be justified by the support workflow.

What happens when retries create false cost signals?

A retry is an operational action, not a new business failure. If the same source record times out three times, emit three attempt events but one final outcome event, or include an explicit outcome field that makes the distinction queryable. Otherwise a dashboard may charge the property for three failures when the pipeline eventually succeeded. This distinction is the difference between error tracking and failure counting: tracking preserves the execution path, while attribution needs the final business result.

I use these decision rules: a validation error is terminal and points to the source record; a timeout is retryable and points to the dependency; a duplicate import is a business outcome and should not page the on-call engineer. The exact codes belong to the domain, but the separation should be deliberate.

Test the middleware with a real error matrix, including an error without a code, a missing x-run-id, a route that throws after a promise rejection, and a request containing a secret header. Assert the public response and the emitted fields separately. A passing HTTP test that accidentally serializes an authorization token is still a failed observability test.

The retention rule I would ship

Keep compact run summaries and terminal error events for the period needed to reconcile property statements. Keep verbose payloads and stack traces for a shorter, access-controlled window. Sample successful records aggressively; retain failures according to their diagnostic value, not because storage made indefinite retention easy.

The final check is a query rehearsal: given run_id and property_id, can an engineer find the affected stage, distinguish retry from final failure, locate the safe detail reference, and explain why that data still exists? If the answer is no, adding another dashboard will not fix the schema. Cost attribution is an observability design problem before it is a storage problem.

Further reading

  • OpenTelemetry, “Logs signal concepts”: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/logs/
  • Express, “Writing middleware for use in Express apps”: https://expressjs.com/en/guide/writing-middleware.html
  • Node.js, “Process events”: https://nodejs.org/api/process.html
  • OpenTelemetry, “Semantic conventions”: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/

title: I was sure it was a memory leak. It was a glowing border using 131 % of a CPU core
description:
My app is an Electron desktop for Claude Code: glass windows with backdrop-filter blur, a WebGL rain background, a few terminals. One day I wrote in my own bug list: "If I leave it running for a while, it gets really slow."

"Slow after a while" sounds like a memory leak. I was so sure that I nearly went looking for one. Then I measured first.

The measurement

One Claude Code session working in a terminal, the app in front. Numbers are CPU time per process, as a percentage of one core:

Version GPU process Renderer
installed 1.9 131 % 30 %

Memory was flat. Main process around 110 MB, renderer heap around 20 MB, no growth. No leak.

What actually happened: the laptop (integrated Intel graphics) got hot and throttled after a few minutes. "Slow after a while" was thermals, not memory.

So what was burning a core and a third on the GPU process while I was just watching a terminal?

Suspect 1: the glow

When Claude is working, its window gets a soft, breathing glow:

.gwin.claude-working {
  animation: claude-glow 2.8s ease-in-out infinite;
}
@keyframes claude-glow {
  50% { box-shadow: 0 0 0 1px rgba(159,184,255,.3), 0 0 40px rgba(124,156,255,.26); }
}

Pretty, harmless, right? Not with glass around it.

A smooth infinite animation means the compositor has to produce a new frame 60 times a second. And every new frame recomputes the big backdrop-filter blurs of every glass panel on screen. My rain shader was carefully throttled to 15–30 FPS. One CSS animation quietly overrode that and pushed everything to 60.

Two things surprised me:

  • Size doesn't matter. An 8-pixel equalizer icon in the dock cost the same as the big window glow. Any animated pixel means a new frame, and the blur gets recomputed.
  • transform instead of box-shadow didn't help either. The usual "animate only transform and opacity" advice is about layout and paint cost. Here the expensive part was the frame itself.

The fix is one word:

.gwin.claude-working {
  animation: claude-glow 2.8s steps(5) infinite;
}

steps(5) makes the glow breathe in five visible stages instead of a smooth curve. Between the steps nothing changes, so no new frames are produced. At normal viewing distance it still reads as "breathing". I moved every long-running infinite animation to steps(): the waiting dot (which can sit there for hours), the equalizer, a live indicator. Short loading spinners stay smooth, because they disappear after a second.

Suspect 2: the rain that wasn't raining

The WebGL rain has an intensity slider. At 0 % you see a still background. But the shader kept rendering 15–30 frames a second of zero raindrops, because the "paused" flag was never passed down.

Now the frame scheduler returns "no frames" at 0 %:

export function frameInterval(s: FrameState): number | null {
  if (s.paused || (s.rain !== undefined && s.rain <= 0)) return null
  if (s.idle) return 1000 / FPS_IDLE
  return 1000 / (s.saver ? FPS_SAVER : FPS_FOCUS)
}

Suspect 3: every line of terminal output

This one I can't fully fix. A terminal that's streaming output changes pixels all the time, and every change under a glass panel recomputes its blur. For battery mode the glass now turns into plain, nearly opaque panels:

.app.saver .gwin, .app.saver .dock { backdrop-filter: none; background: rgba(13,17,25,.9); }

After

Step GPU process Renderer
1.9 (smooth glow) 131 % 30 %
glow on steps() ~26 % ~14 %
rain off really means off ~20 % ~12 %
battery saver without live blur ~11 % ~11 %

From 131 % to about 11 %, mostly by deleting frames nobody needed.

How I measured (and two traps)

  • I started a second, isolated copy with Playwright's _electron, a copy of my real settings and its own user-data folder, so the measurement didn't touch my working setup.
  • Trap 1: app.getAppMetrics() reports CPU divided by the number of cores. On 8 cores, "16 %" is actually more than a full core. I switched to measuring the difference in CPU seconds per process from the OS.
  • Trap 2: a hidden or covered Electron window stops requestAnimationFrame. My first measurement showed almost 0 % GPU because the test window was behind another one. Bring it to the front (setAlwaysOnTop, focus) before you measure.

What this doesn't prove

It's one app on one laptop with integrated graphics. On a desktop GPU you'd likely never notice the glow. But if your Electron or web app combines backdrop-filter with any infinite animation, it's worth five minutes with the profiler.

Question

Have you ever chased a "leak" that turned out to be something else? What was it?

A) thermals / throttling

B) a runaway animation or render loop

C) a cache doing its job

D) an actual leak, finally

(The app is VibeDesk, open source, so all of the CSS above is in the repo.)

title: My app passed 1,100 tests. Six minutes on a real phone found five bugs.
description:
I'm building a budgeting app called Budget Lover. It is a personal project, written in Flutter with Firebase behind it, and it tries to answer one question: how much can I spend today? At its heart is a single "Safe to Spend" number, worked out from the balance, the bills that are coming and the person's typical spending. It speaks 15 languages, and it isn't released yet: so far it lives on an emulator and on my own phone.

A few days ago I installed the latest build on that phone, ran it in Greek, and spent six minutes tapping through it while taking screenshots and recording the screen. The screenshots and the recording showed five bugs. The test suite, more than 1,100 tests, had passed earlier that day.

Two of the app's six tabs: Insights, where the "Safe to Spend" number lives, and Savings.

This isn't an argument against automated tests. Every bug below now has one. It's a record of what my tests were blind to, because I suspect many apps share the same blind spots.

What the tests covered

The suite includes layout tests that open every screen and bottom sheet in all 15 languages, at a normal and an enlarged text size and on a small 320 dp screen, and fail on any overflow. That net had already caught plenty of long German and Greek labels. It did not catch these.

1. A word that didn't fit

The Home screen has four quick actions with a short caption under each. In English the captions are short. In Greek, "Add savings" is Προσθήκη αποταμίευσης, and its last word is wider than a quarter of the screen, so the app showed "αποταμίευσ…".

My layout tests fail on overflow, but a caption cut short with an ellipsis is not an overflow: Flutter did exactly what I had asked it to do. The caption now shrinks until its longest word fits, and a new test checks whether any caption was truncated, in every language.

The same four quick actions in four languages. The long Greek and German captions now fit.

2. English inside a Greek screen

The same screenshot showed a sentence in English on the trip card. In the app, the English text is the key to its translation, and a script scans the code for those keys and complains about any that a language table is missing. This sentence was picked by a condition (isEmpty ? 'a' : 'b'), which the script can't see.

There are now two defences: a second scanner for exactly that pattern, which found eight texts hiding the same way, and a test that opens every screen in Greek and fails if any text is missing from the table.

3. A dialog nobody opened

On Sundays the app offers a short weekly review in a dialog with an icon and a title. In Greek the title, Κυριακάτικη ανασκόπηση, ran out of the dialog on the right. No test had ever opened that dialog, because it only appears on Sundays. It is now part of the layout tests like every other sheet, and in Greek it overflowed by 96 pixels the first time it was asked.

The lesson: whatever appears conditionally (on Sundays, for one kind of account, on first launch) needs a deliberate way to be reached from a test.

4. The screen that kept reloading

This one was my own doing, and only the recording showed it. Every time the keyboard opened on the sign-in screen, the loading screen flashed over the form and the text I had typed disappeared.

I had just added a soft cross-fade between the loading, sign-in and app screens. The gate behind them asked Firebase "who is signed in?" inside its build method, which creates a new stream on every rebuild, and a new stream starts out as "waiting", which the app shows as the loading screen. The keyboard animation triggered a rebuild on every frame, and the new cross-fade made each of those moments visible.

// Before: a new stream every time the screen rebuilds
StreamBuilder<User?>(stream: FirebaseAuth.instance.authStateChanges(), ...)

// After: asked once, kept for the life of the screen
late final _auth = FirebaseAuth.instance.authStateChanges();
...
StreamBuilder<User?>(stream: _auth, ...)

The more useful change was the test. It types into the form, moves the keyboard frame by frame, rebuilds the parent, and checks that the loading screen never appears and the text stays. Then I put the old code back for a minute to make sure the test fails against it. It did.

The sign-in screen in English and Greek, in the app's brand colours.

5. A login that only failed in the real build

Not a language problem, but the same lesson. The Google sign-in button failed on my phone with an error about a missing server client id. The Google plugin looks that value up in a string resource by name, and the release build's resource shrinker removes strings that look unused. My debug builds carry the string; the release build did not. The app now passes the id explicitly, and a test checks it against the Firebase configuration file.

And a sixth, while writing this

While taking the screenshots for this article I found one more. Arabic reads right to left, so the first tab sits on the right of the tab strip. Its highlight stayed on the left, under the wrong tab. It was a one-word fix (a direction-aware alignment instead of a fixed one), and a test now checks the highlight under every tab in both directions.

One screen in six of the 15 languages, including Arabic, which reads right to left.

What I changed in how I work

  • Tests mirror what a user sees. Every screen, every language, three screen and text-size combinations.
  • Every bug leaves a test behind, and where I can, I check that the test fails on the old code before I trust it.
  • A real-device pass stays in the loop, and it is a recording, not just screenshots. The flicker was invisible in a still image.
  • Translated text is product code. The English string is the key, and a script refuses any language table with a missing key or mismatched placeholders.

Questions I'm still thinking about

Translation quality is the part I can judge least. I read Greek and English; for the other thirteen languages the checks tell me the text is complete and that it fits, not that it sounds natural. If you speak one of them, I'd be curious whether the wording feels like a native app or like a translation.

The number on that orange card is the heart of the app, and I keep wondering what makes a person trust a figure like that. If you've ever tried to budget, what would you want to see behind it?

And on the engineering side: when did a real device last prove your test suite wrong, and what did you add afterwards?

The app is still in testing, so none of these decisions is final.

Disclosure: I drafted this article with the help of an AI assistant and edited it myself.

title: Two prompts took an untested Express API to a passing suite
description:
Two prompts and three manual npm test runs took an untested Express API from 0 tests to a passing node:test suite, and the source diff review was the check that mattered.

agentshipped / notes-api

Agent Shipped demo repo (notes-api): the public playground used in the channel's videos.

notes-api

A tiny Express notes API. This is a public demo repo for the Agent Shipped YouTube channel: techniques from real projects are shown here, on code anyone can clone.

npm install
npm start          # http://localhost:3000/notes
npm test           # node:test (no tests yet - that is on purpose)

Endpoints: GET /health, GET /notes, GET /notes/:id, POST /notes {title, body}, DELETE /notes/:id.

Shown in

Videos on the Agent Shipped channel that use this repo:

  • One git hook blocked a fake GitHub token, so no secret hit history #Shorts · E002 · 2026-11-02
  • Claude Code invented one endpoint shape. A 3-line rule fixed it #Shorts · E001 · 2026-11-03

View on GitHub


The demo is notes-api, a small Express notes API. The technique is a prompt that treats the README as the contract, plus a review routine that does not trust a green run on its own.

The untested API

The repo has two source files, five endpoints and no tests. The README says so on purpose. package.json already has a test script, and the Node built-in test runner is available, so there is no framework to install. Fewer moving parts make it easier to tell a bad test from bad code.

ls && cat package.json && wc -l src/*.js && git log --oneline | head -n 5

The git log is short, so the final diff shows exactly what the agent touched. The plan is two prompts: the first asks for tests based on the documented behavior, the second makes the agent triage whatever the first run exposes.

Read the store

Before the agent writes anything, I read src/store.js myself. It holds the notes and decides how ids are created and what a lookup returns. When a test fails later, I need to tell quickly whether the test or the code is wrong. That is easier to judge now, while nothing is broken.

Read the routes

Next is src/index.js: health, list, get by id, create, delete. Two things to watch.

First, how the server starts. If the app begins listening as soon as the file loads, a test cannot import it cleanly. The agent may need one small change for that. I allow exactly that and nothing more.

Second, the validation on create and what happens with an unknown id. The README is the contract: a title and a body go in, a note comes out, and an unknown id should not blow up. The tests must check that, not what the code happens to do today.

Baseline run

Record a baseline before the agent touches the repo:

npm install && npm test

With no test files the runner has nothing to report. Without this starting point you cannot say later what the agent changed.


The baseline: the test command works but there are no tests to report yet. · watch this step

Prompt one: write tests

The first prompt opens like this:

Write a test suite for this Express API using only the built-in node:test runner and node:assert, no new dependencies. Put it in test/api.test.js. Base the tests on the contract in README.md, not on what the code currently does.

The rest of the prompt covers:

  • one task: write the tests
  • cases that include the unhappy paths, such as an unknown id, because agents like to test only the sunny day
  • a rule about state, so tests do not depend on each other
  • one narrow permission to make the app importable, and a ban on changing anything else
  • an acceptance criterion: run it and show the output

The agent reads the repo, writes the file and runs it. It checks its own result, and that is the habit worth copying.

First honest run

Then I run the suite myself, because the agent's summary can misread its own output:

npm test 2>&1 | tail -n 45


Read the summary lines at the bottom: tests, passes and failures from my own run. · watch this step

If anything fails, the question is always the same: is the test wrong or the code? A test that fails because the agent guessed a status code is a bad test. A test that fails because the code breaks its own documented contract is a bug found. Decide whose fault it is before fixing anything.

Prompt two: the review rule

The second prompt starts:

Run npm test in this repo. For every failing test in test/api.test.js, decide whether the test or the source is wrong by checking it against the contract in README.md. If the source breaks the documented contract, fix the source with the smallest possible change.

It continues with the guardrail I care about most: never weaken, skip or delete a test to get green. Without that sentence, an agent under pressure can make the test easier instead of fixing the code. It is not malice, just the shortest path to a passing run.

Here the first run was already green, so there was nothing to triage. The rule still earned its place, because the agent has to report what it did not change. It flagged two things: the test script it edited in package.json, and a README line that is now out of date. I compare that report against the diff. If they disagree, I stop and look closer.

Second run 

npm test 2>&1 | tail -n 30

Green alone proves little, because a green run can hide a test that was quietly made weaker. Compare the totals with the first run: the test count should have grown or stayed the same. A drop means something was deleted, even when nothing fails.

Review the diff 

git status --short && git diff --stat && git diff -- src

The status shows which files are new or changed, the stat shows the size of the change, and the last command shows only the diff in the source folder. That last one I never skip.


Check the source diff at the end: nothing printed means no source file changed. · watch this step

Here it is empty. The agent changed no source file, only the test script in package.json, and the test folder is new and untracked. When the diff is not empty, I read every line: does it match the reported failure, is it the smallest change the README justifies, did anything else sneak in?

Final measurement 

git diff --stat; npm test 2>&1 | grep -E "(tests|pass|fail|duration_ms) [0-9]"

The filter reads straight from the runner: the number of tests, passes, failures and the duration of the whole suite.


The final numbers read straight from the runner: tests, pass, fail, duration_ms. · watch this step

The measured result: 2 prompts and 3 manual npm test runs took notes-api from 0 tests to a passing node:test suite.

What to copy

  • Write the prompt against the written contract (the README), not against the current code.
  • Put the acceptance command inside the prompt, and name the runner so no dependency sneaks in.
  • Run the tests yourself and compare the totals between runs.
  • Forbid weakening, skipping or deleting tests, and ask the agent to report what it did not change.
  • Run git diff -- src and read it line by line. The judgment about whose bug it is stays with you.

Not just JavaScript

The same technique works on other stacks: pytest instead of node --test, or go test with Go's testing package. Both are driven by the written contract and a no-weakening rule.

Video with the full run: https://youtu.be/vjfrORiDoG0
