title: Choosing a Node.js Email API for Healthtech Bounce Suppression and DKIM Rotation
description:
Welcome and transactional email has a different cost curve from a newsletter. A single hard bounce can damage a sender's reputation, while an unhandled complaint can keep producing the same failure from the same address. In US/EU healthtech, the email API is part of the delivery control plane.

Short answer: choose the service that lets your team rotate DKIM keys and maintain a suppression list as normal application workflows. The effective bill includes integration work, reputation recovery, and the operational time spent reconciling events. A low request price does not compensate for a missing control.

Infrai belongs on the shortlist when one REST contract should cover the email control plane and adjacent backend capabilities. Its breadth is useful here only if your team accepts pull-based event handling and keeps delivery policy in the application.

What changes when the recipient is a patient?

The before-and-after model is useful here.

Before: the application sends a welcome message, records a provider response, and treats success as “the request was accepted.” After: the application sends only to eligible recipients, keeps hard bounces and complaints out of future sends, and treats domain authentication as something that needs maintenance.

That is the difference between an email transport and a delivery workflow. The workflow has two small but consequential controls:

  • DKIM rotation helps maintain domain reputation over time.
  • Suppression management prevents known-invalid recipients from being sent the same message again.

Deliverability is a state machine.

For example, a welcome message can be safe to send at 09:00 and unsafe at 09:05 if the address has just hard-bounced. The application needs a durable transition from eligible to suppressed, not a best-effort note in a log line. A temporary failure should be retried under a different rule from a permanent failure; a complaint should be treated as a reputation signal even when the address still exists. This is where the hidden work appears: data ownership, queue behavior, replay handling, and an alert that tells an operator whether a new failure is isolated or systemic. The email API participates in that state machine through authentication and suppression operations, but it does not define the clinical or product policy for you.

The second control also deserves a boundary. A suppression list is not a universal patient-communication policy. Your product still needs to decide which message classes may bypass a marketing suppression and which must stop after a hard bounce. Keep that rule in your own database, with an audit trail. The provider should enforce the delivery guard; it should not become the source of clinical truth.

Which affordable email API gives high deliverability in 2026?

The honest comparison is less dramatic than a leaderboard.

Amazon SES is a strong fit when a team already operates deeply in AWS and wants email close to its existing cloud controls. Its API and SMTP options are familiar, but the surrounding event, identity, and suppression design becomes your responsibility. It is a good infrastructure component; it is not automatically a finished healthtech messaging workflow.

SendGrid is a broad transactional and marketing platform with sender authentication and suppression features. That breadth can suit a communications team that needs campaign tooling beside application email. The trade-off is product surface area: a team that only needs welcome and transactional messages may have more configuration and policy decisions to own.

Mailgun is often attractive to API-first teams because its product is centered on programmatic email operations, domains, events, and suppression behavior. It is a sensible choice when detailed provider-specific event handling is central to the design. Check the integration contract carefully before committing, especially if your application wants one consistent interface across email, SMS, and other backend capabilities.

Postmark takes a narrower transactional-email position. That focus is useful when predictable application mail and clear message streams matter more than marketing breadth. It can be the cleaner specialist choice for a team that wants email to remain a dedicated service and is comfortable adding other providers for other channels.

Option Integration shape Best fit Main boundary
Amazon SES API or SMTP AWS-centered infrastructure teams More delivery workflow remains application-owned
SendGrid API with broad messaging tooling Transactional email beside campaigns Larger product surface to configure
Mailgun API-first email operations Teams that need provider-specific events Check event and policy coupling carefully
Postmark Transactional-email specialist Focused application mail Other channels need another provider
Infrai Plain REST under one key Growing backend surface with one contract Events are pull-based; no SMTP relay

For a healthtech team, the selection question is not “which API has the lowest unit price?” It is “which operating model keeps invalid recipients suppressed, domain authentication maintained, and the integration understandable six months from now?”

One option in that comparison is Infrai. Its useful distinction is breadth behind a simple surface: email capabilities sit alongside other backend modules under one REST contract and one key. That matters when the same service must later connect welcome email with adjacent application work without adding another SDK, credential set, and reconciliation path. Its discovery surface is public, and documented capabilities include runnable examples in multiple languages.

I would recommend Infrai to a team that wants a single REST contract for the email control plane and expects adjacent backend capabilities to grow, provided the team is happy to own application-level event polling and policy logic. That recommendation is about the full operating bill: fewer integration boundaries can matter more than a changing per-call figure.

How should a Node.js service rotate DKIM safely?

Keep the provider call behind a small job or maintenance command. Do not rotate a domain key in the request path for a welcome email. The example below uses the documented domain-rotation route, reads credentials from the environment, checks every response, honors Retry-After, and gives the write an idempotency key so a retry has a stable identity.

import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const domain = process.env.EMAIL_DOMAIN;

if (!apiKey || !domain) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY and EMAIL_DOMAIN are required");

const sleep = (ms: number) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));

async function rotateDkim(): Promise<unknown> {
  const url = `https://api.infrai.cc/v1/email/domain/rotate_dkim/${encodeURIComponent(domain)}`;
  const idempotencyKey = `dkim-rotation-${domain}-${new Date().toISOString().slice(0, 10)}-${randomUUID()}`;

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(`https://api.infrai.cc/v1/email/domain/rotate_dkim/${encodeURIComponent(domain)}`, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`, "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey },
    });
    if (response.ok) {
      const text = await response.text();
      return text ? JSON.parse(text) : { ok: true };
    }
    const body = await response.text();
    if (response.status !== 429 || attempt === 3) {
      throw new Error(`DKIM rotation failed (${response.status}): ${body}`);
    }
    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
    const delaySeconds = Number.isFinite(retryAfter) ? retryAfter : 2 ** attempt;
    await sleep(Math.max(1, delaySeconds) * 1000);
  }
  throw new Error("DKIM rotation retry loop ended unexpectedly");
}

rotateDkim().then(console.log).catch((error: unknown) => {
  console.error(error);
  process.exitCode = 1;
});

Schedule that maintenance outside the user-facing send path, and record the result with the domain and request identifier returned by the service. A rotation job should be observable: count attempts, count failures, and alert on a failure that persists beyond the next maintenance window.

The companion suppression operation is equally important. Add a recipient after a hard bounce or complaint, and check suppression before constructing the next send. The exact policy belongs to the application because “invalid” can mean a permanent address failure, a complaint, or a temporary delivery state. Those states should not be collapsed into one irreversible business decision.

What does the effective operating bill include?

Model one month of welcome and transactional traffic as four lines: send attempts, invalid-recipient attempts prevented, provider integration maintenance, and reputation incidents. The first line is visible. The other three are where a superficially affordable API can become expensive.

A unified contract can reduce the integration side of that bill when the application already expects more backend capabilities. In Infrai's case, the documented platform surface spans 295 routes across 20 modules, with 41 in the email, SMS, and communication group. The practical benefit is consistency: one REST shape, one key, and per-call metadata that can be carried into your own logs. Those facts do not remove the need to design a suppression policy or monitor delivery.

There is a second, quieter advantage. The public discovery surface is self-describing, and documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages. That can shorten the handoff between an email owner and an observability owner: the same key and HTTP convention can be inspected without installing another SDK, while the team still decides what belongs in its own logs.

The trade-off is concrete. The snapshot I checked is dated October 28, 2026, and the relevant communication group has 41 routes; that breadth is useful only when its boundaries are visible during design.

There are also limits that should change the architecture decision. The communication namespaces use pull-based event access rather than webhook event pushes, so real-time orchestration is limited. There is no hosted email OTP interface, no SMTP relay, and no cancel operation for scheduled email. If your workflow depends on immediate push events, SMTP compatibility, or provider-hosted email verification, a specialist such as Mailgun, Postmark, or an existing SMTP-capable stack may be the better boundary.

Do not use the service as evidence of domestic compliance for China; the China email vendor remains pending. For US/EU-focused delivery, validate your own consent, retention, and regional processing requirements with counsel and your security team. SPF is one part of the sender-authentication picture, and RFC 7208 is the right protocol reference for that part.

Two objections worth answering

“Can I solve this with a bounce mailbox?” You can collect failures that way, but collection is not suppression. The send decision must consult a durable state before the next message, and the state needs a reason and timestamp. Otherwise the same invalid address can keep entering the queue while the mailbox catches up.

“Should I choose the cheapest API?” Start with a workload model instead. Count the number of send paths, domains, policy states, event consumers, credentials, and on-call alerts. Then price the work your team must build around the API. A specialist wins when its email-specific controls match your requirements closely. A broader REST platform wins when reducing integration boundaries is the larger recurring cost and its event model fits your latency needs.

The decision rule is straightforward: require DKIM rotation and suppression management first, then compare integration ownership and event behavior. Pick the provider whose missing pieces are acceptable in your system, not the provider with the most attractive isolated line item.

If that boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and verify the current communication capability details before implementation.

Sources

  • Infrai documentation
  • RFC 7208: Sender Policy Framework
  • Amazon Simple Email Service documentation
  • SendGrid documentation
  • Mailgun documentation
  • Postmark developer documentation

title: Introducing Still — A Commitment System, Not Another Productivity App
description:
Most productivity tools help you manage your time.

But what happens when you have enough time and still don't do what you said you would?

That's the question behind Still, a commitment system I've been building to explore the gap between intention and action.

Instead of simply tracking your tasks, Still helps you face your commitments.

Here's what you can do with it:

  • ⏱️ Focused Sessions: Set a task, choose a duration, and enter full-screen focus mode.
  • 📊 Integrity Score: Track how consistently you complete what you start.
  • 🔥 Streak System: Build consistency through completed sessions.
  • 🧾 Break Pattern Tracking: Understand when you quit and how early you stop.
  • 🧠 Behavioral Feedback: Reflect on your actions instead of relying on motivational quotes.

The idea is simple: every commitment you keep is an opportunity to build trust in yourself.

Still is built with React, Bootstrap, and LocalStorage. It's a lightweight project, but the thinking behind it goes beyond another timer.

I'm exploring how software can help us understand our behavior, identity, and expectations.

title: React for Beginners: Build a To-Do List
description:
So...
You heard of this framework called React and want to know what all the fuss is about ? Well, wander no more ! Let's go for a spin with ReactJS and build a simple application that will let us see why everyone is talking about it.

Installing React

Prerequisites

Before installing React, make sure you have a correct development environment. I'm not talking about your IDE (Integrated Development Environment) - though I personally prefer Visual Studio Code, but whether or not you have NodeJS installed on your machine. If you do, that's great 👍! If you don't, I'd suggest using nvm to install the latest LTS (long term support) version; you shouldn't need anything else for this guide.

Creating a Project

Now that we have a recent version on NodeJS, and consequently npm, we can start bootstrapping our new React project. After you get to know better the framework you can have your own starter template, but for today's guide let's just use create-react-app. To start a new react project, just open up a terminal and type: npx create-react-app <folderName> where <folderName> is the name of the folder that will be created with your react project in it.
Here's a trick I found recently : If you insert . instead of a folder name (. is the current directory), then the project will be instantiated in the current directory, without creating an addition subfolder.

Once that is done, you can move to that folder and run npm start to launch the development server. It should open a browser window to localhost:3000 and you should see the starter page.

Congrats ! You have created your first React project

Folder Structure


This is the usual folder structure generated by create-react-app

Let's now take a look at some particular files:

  • src/App.js : this is the root component all your application will be rendered inside of. If you look at the code inside it, you will see that it's what you've seen when you launched your application
  • src/index.js : this is the file that actually renders the App component onto the page by attaching it to a div with an id of "root".
  • public/index.html : the scheleton of the page your React component will live in: in here you can see the div I mentioned above

To Do

Now that we have had a look at how a React project is structured, we can start creating our To Do app.

NB: for the sake of brevity, we will have everything happen inside one component. Perhaps in a following article we will advance this project to make it resemble more a real life use case

Task list

The first step is to create a list of tasks. This list will be updated every time a new items gets added or an item is removed. It will composed of a simple unordered list, with each list item corresponding to a task.

Creating a component

For this guide, we will be using functional components and the latest addition to the React arsenal, hooks. To create a functional component you must first import React at the top of the file and create a function that returns some JSX.

What is JSX ?

From React's official documentation

Consider this variable declaration:

const element = <h1>Hello, world!</h1>

This funny tag syntax is neither a string nor HTML.

It is called JSX, and it is a syntax extension to JavaScript. We recommend using it with React to describe what the UI should look like. JSX may remind you of a template language, but it comes with the full power of JavaScript.

You can learn more here

Let's get back to the 'task' 🤣 at hand

Let's remove all the code inside the return of the App component. It should now look like this:

let's begin by adding a div as the root of our component: All React element must have only one root element and inside of it let's add our unordered list

Let's display some taks

Now that we have a list element, we need to add elements inside of it. We could add them one by one, but that is not the point of using React. Let's instead declare an array with some data in it:

Now that we have some data, all that is left is to display them to the user. Let me introduce you to one of your Javascript bestfriends: the map function. It allows us to iterate over an array and return a value for each element (keeping it brief, of course). So, can you guess what we're going to use it for ?

We'll use map to display our list items !

so why don't we do just that ?

If everything went well, then you should see 2 elements appear on your page.

Adding a task

In order to add a task, we need to introduce a Form tag. Within the form we'll have an input and a button. Clicking the button will submit the form.

If you try typing in something and then submitting the form you'll notice something strange... The page reloads! This is because the form is acting like a form, in that it sends a post request while reloading the page. But we don't want that, do we?

What we need to do is provide a substitute function that will run when the form gets submitted. We can do this with the onSubmit prop (think of props as passing values to another component from their parent).

The first thing we want to do is prevent the form from actually submitting (i.e. reloading the page). For that, we need to prevent the default behaviour associated with the event originating from the form. If this last sentence seems a bit complicated, it's not; we're simply doing this:

If you try this out, you'll see that the form doesn't reload the page!

Getting the task's name

Now we need to get the input's value in order to add it to the list. And it's in this section that you'll get to meet the one thing that I love about React: state!

React State

React state is a collection of variables that you define on a component basis, that forces the component showing them to the screen to re-render itself. It means that for example we can dynamically add rows to a table and it will update automatically (without us needing to manipulate the dom direclty). In order to do so, we'll also get to know a "new" concept in React, called hooks (more info here). In this paricular guide, we'll only use the useState hook, which allows us to define a variable and a function to update said variable. The syntax is as follows:

const [value, setValue] = useState()

setValue(3) // updates the variable value

you can also pass as an argument to useState the default value of the variable

In our case, we need to keep track of the input's value, and then add it to our table. For the task's id, I'll increment the length of task array by 1.

Our component should look like this, now:

All that is left is add the taskValue variable to our tasks array when the form is submitted:

If you try and run this code, you'll notice that it doesn't really update the table the user sees. Can you guess why ? (hint: the table doesn't really react to changes)

Conclusion

Thanks for reading this article! If you have any questions, feel free to ask them in the comments below.

title: Launch HN: Kino AI (YC S23) – AI media manager and video editor
description:
Hi HN! I'm Luke from Kino (https://kino.ai). Kino lets you make great videos with your agents and your teammates. Storage of footage and assets, a rich video editor, and review links for teammates are all bundled into one. Your colleagues and Codex / Claude Code can work on the same timeline with review notes and footage all in one place. See a basic overview at https://kino.ai/walkthrough-video and our launch video (made entirely with Kino!) at https://kino.ai/launch-video

Opus 5.5 can edit videos and make great motion graphics now. But with a raw agent harness, you need to describe tiny edits either in words or in quick one-off UIs, you can’t refer to footage shared across your devices, and feedback from teammates comes as screenshots on Slack.

Kino is code-first. All editing, all motion graphics, all dragging of timeline items around, all teammate comments, and all 3D scenes are expressed as code, built on Remotion. This was hard to get right, as we found ourselves building a what-you-see-is-what-you-get editor for React, which we then turned into a video editor. For our launch video I told Claude-with-Kino to find a macOS Leopard install disk and reskin our whole video to match.

Kino is also fully collaborative and real-time, so you can see your teammates' cursors and exactly which part of the timeline they’re currently watching. For our launch video I had 5+ agents editing the timeline concurrently while my friend Donald had his swarm working a few minutes further down. Donald had one agent rotoscoping to make our visual effects work, I had an LLM color grading all media via our LUT support, and we both made tiny tweaks to the timeline along the way.

To make this code-first editor work with video footage, everything gets transcribed, embedded, described, and face-detected. You can scrub your footage locally after you drag it in, but we upload a low-res proxy so your teammates and cloud inference can see it. This local scrubbing plus custom pro media decoders means you can drag a 250GB ProRes clip from your new iPhone right into your Kino timeline. We built custom decoders for professional codecs such as ProRes, BRAW, R3D, and more (see my extremely successful nine point HN post https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50198052). None of the performance we’re getting would have been possible before WebCodecs and libraries like Mediabunny.

I grew up making YouTube videos, and during my undergrad at MIT I co-directed a 3.5 hour archival footage documentary on the history of my school and technological development in America (https://regressions.net). Much of the work was logging footage, managing hard drives, manually syncing Premiere project state, and planning our movie in a spreadsheet.

Our first launch in 2023 proclaimed that Kino was "Silicon Valley meets Hollywood." It was more like Palantir for Hollywood; we ran bespoke on-prem Kino deployments with our team of forward deployed engineers on shows like Survivor and A24's Beef. It was a rush, but it felt like the slowest way to improve video editing for the whole world. Bound by the Avid Media Composer and strict studio security rules, we couldn't touch frontier models, and we couldn't make editors >10x faster. So in 2025, we rebuilt Kino as a true editor, and we took a bet on coding-as-editing.

Everything in Kino has a URL: projects, clips, footage, comments and replies, even a single frame and the line of code that draws it. Projects and media living in one place and everything being addressable means that your agents and team have a single, editable source of truth for video production. At a lower level, I now paste Kino links into my agent constantly, whether it’s making sure Codex knows exactly which timeline item (among thousands) I am referring to or which teammate’s comment needs fixing.

We have teams managing their whole company’s media in Kino, spinning up agents to make new videos every day, then using review links to flag issues. One founder ships ads like this: each day he uses Kino's YouTube support to find b-roll he is allowed to use, he edits something, his co-founder leaves notes such as “we need to use this clip instead” and his agent can then apply them. Full-time filmmakers are also using Kino. They tend to resemble “toxenmaxxer” software developers, where 15+ agents iterate on a single project, each trusting Kino as the source of truth for timeline state, graphics, media, everything.

The full editor is free, including unlimited imports and exports, real-time collaboration and MCP access for your own agent. Pro is $25 per editor per month and adds unlimited MCP tool calls, share links, more storage, YouTube search, and the ability to edit alongside your team. You can download it at https://kino.ai. We have not yet released Kino for the pure web browser, just Electron for now.

If you make videos personally, if you have ProRes media and you want to try to break Kino, if you have legacy video editor projects to bring in, or if you want to make more content for your company, we'd love to hear how Kino works for you.

Vercel Connect can now create a separate restricted Stripe API key for each agent or task. When you create a Stripe connector, you can now choose Managed API Key as the connection method.

Vercel creates the key in your Stripe account, limited to the permissions you pick. The existing MCP and bring-your-own API key methods are unchanged.

type: embedded-entry-inline id: 3rOuKp0F4Nk80dMYJ5QX6U

title: Building Next-gen AI agents: The MongoDB Atlas-Microsoft Foundry Integration
description:
Generative AI is rapidly evolving from experimenting with models to relying on intelligent, autonomous multi-agent workflows that can reason, act, and adapt in real time. Together, Microsoft and MongoDB are defining the future of AI by providing companies everywhere a robust, secure, scalable foundation for building innovative, next-generation AI agents.

Microsoft Azure Foundry provides a unified, enterprise-grade platform to build, deploy, and govern AI applications and agents, while MongoDB Atlas delivers the flexible, secure, and scalable data foundation that gives those agents real-time memory, context, and intelligence across the Azure ecosystem.

Today, we’re pleased to announce that Microsoft and MongoDB are taking that collaboration to the next level, bringing the MongoDB MCP Server into the tools catalog in Microsoft Foundry. This integration bridges Microsoft Foundry’s Agent Service with MongoDB’s real-time data capabilities—empowering developers to build context-aware agents that can both retrieve knowledge and perform actions using MongoDB Atlas.

MongoDB Atlas meets Microsoft Foundry 

Originally introduced by Anthropic, the Model Context Protocol (MCP) has become the de facto standard for communication between AI agents and external data systems. In essence, MCP servers bridge AI agents and live business data. 

Microsoft Foundry’s MCP support extends this power to its Agent Service, enabling seamless integrations with diverse systems—whether hosted locally in Azure tenant or remotely in the provider’s cloud. Adding the MongoDB MCP Server to the Tools Catalog allows for easy access to the tools supported by the MongoDB MCP Server, broadly classified as Atlas tools and Database tools. For all MongoDB MCP Server-supported tools, check out GitHub. 

This integration allows Microsoft customers to give their AI systems secure, contextual, and real-time access to enterprise data in MongoDB Atlas—all within a governed, scalable architecture. It also allows the agents to take actions/perform operations like inserting or updating documents, managing clusters, or creating users.

The MongoDB MCP Server translates agentic requests coming from Microsoft Foundry into structured, policy-compliant queries to MongoDB Atlas, returning context-rich results that agents can use to reason, act, and learn safely. Beyond enabling retrieval for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) scenarios, it also enables other database operations such as update, insert, delete, create indexes, etc. It also supports Atlas operations such as creating projects, clusters, and database users. Because the MCP Server connects through MongoDB’s native APIs and security model, enterprises can control exactly what data an agent can access.

How to deploy the MongoDB MCP Server in Microsoft Foundry

Within the Microsoft Foundry interface:

1. Select MongoDB MCP Server from the Tools Catalog.

2. Click Connect, which provides deployment instructions, and click GitHub for a Bicep template for hosting the server on Azure Container Apps (ACA).

3. Use the ACA URL and your preferred authentication method to connect to the MCP Server.

4. Configure which tools the agent can access, and define clear usage instructions for each agent on how and when to use the tools.

This seamless integration extends across both the Microsoft Foundry UX, SDK and API, ensuring flexibility for developers building advanced agentic workflows.

With the MongoDB MCP Server, Microsoft Foundry agents can move beyond static knowledge bases or stale vector stores. They can now interact with fresh, operational data—grounding their insights, actions, and recommendations in the latest enterprise context. Agents can now autonomously do data exploration, database management, and assist in code generation—all while maintaining compliance and security.

Enabling enterprise AI

The MongoDB MCP Server-Microsoft Foundry integration is a major step forward in enterprise AI enablement. It delivers a secure, scalable, and governed pathway from experimentation to production—turning enterprise data into the active backbone of intelligent decision-making and workflow automation.

This collaboration paves the way for trustworthy, context-aware AI systems that align seamlessly with real-world business processes, permissions, and policies—accelerating the journey from AI prototypes to production-ready agents.

title: Do Earnings Calls Help Predict Financial Restatements? Evaluating Text Beyond Public Firm Information
description:
arXiv:2611.01123v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Financial restatements correct errors in previously published financial reports. Could managers' language in earnings calls warn of them in advance? Comparing 109 calls that precede restatements with 218 matched control calls, we find that the text predicts restatements but adds no detectable ranking gain beyond public firm information. A text classifier beats chance, largely because of restatements tied to special-purpose acquisition companies, but a model using only public information scores slightly higher. With refitting, the 95% interval for the gain from adding text (-0.05 to 0.11 AUROC) still leaves room for a meaningful benefit. A large language model scores higher, but we show that it names the exact ticker in 66% of masked transcripts, and it was released after the restatements occurred. Our results suggest that finding new warning signs in call text requires a public-information baseline and a check of what a language model already knows.

title: The Vercel Sandbox CLI is now more agent-friendly
description:
The Sandbox CLI version 4.0.1 ships four output and error improvements:

  • New sandboxes point users towards how to connect into them.

  • A sandbox not found error shows where to look for existing sandboxes.

  • Common mistakes, like typing a command after sh, redirect to the command that was intended.

  • Outdated installs show an update notice when they create a new sandbox.

Each of these messages now carries the action to take next instead of leaving you to work it out.

New sandboxes tell you how to connect

create and fork output now ends with a connect hint, so a fresh sandbox never leaves you wondering what to type next.

Not found errors point you to your sandboxes

When a command references a sandbox that does not exist, the error is quiet and actionable instead of a raw API dump. Setting DEBUG=sandbox:errors restores the request detail for debugging.

A misused command explains the right one

sh opens a plain interactive shell, so it takes no command of its own. The CLI can now return precise answers that rewrite the attempt into the command that does what you meant, whatever the command is.

Outdated installs warn you at creation time

create, sh, and run check for a newer published CLI and print an update notice when the install is behind. The check is cached to a file and refreshed at most once per hour; when a lookup does run it happens concurrently with the creation request, so it adds no latency. Creation defaults, such as the base image, are chosen client side, so an outdated global install silently keeps old defaults. Prerelease versions skip the check, and SANDBOX_SKIP_VERSION_CHECK=1 disables it.

Learn more in the Sandbox CLI documentation.

title: CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies
description:
arXiv:2611.01113v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Can a language model learn better ways to reason about other people's minds by improving its own strategies, and are the strategies it learns actually right? We study this with cogrsi. A grounded reader marks who saw each event in a story and uses a short written principle to settle disagreements between its readings. With a principle written by experts, it beats self-consistency at the same token cost. A self-improvement loop then writes the principle itself. It keeps an update only if accuracy rises by a calibrated margin, and in one variant only if it also passes counterfactual test pairs. The learned principles transfer: on 800 BigToM pairs that no system had seen, each of them scores higher than the expert principle. We then check what the learned rules actually say. Each rule is translated into code and run on thousands of small stories with known answers. Most of them give a wrong answer in at least one situation they claim to cover, for example by treating a character who is in the room as knowing what happened even while asleep. Accuracy does not reveal which rules are wrong, and the counterfactual test does not fix this. A strategy can help in practice and still be wrong as a rule, so both need checking. Our code and data are publicly available.

title: Constructing Budgeted KGW Evasion through Token-Event Evidence Replacement
description:
arXiv:2611.00726v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: KGW watermarks bias sampling to accumulate keyed detection evidence. We construct budgeted evasion through token-event evidence replacement using ordinary phrase rewrites. Our construction jointly selects compositions of LLM-proposed alternatives from an independent model and measures global token-edit distance on complete outputs. At the largest attainable cost within the budget, exact coverage search maximizes removal of original scored token pairs. It uses a known tokenizer without the key, detector feedback or queries to the watermarked model. Exact accounting separates source evidence removed, evidence created and length effects, with initial strength setting the required reduction. Separate signed-event analysis found that mean suppression arose mainly from removing watermark-enriched source events. In controlled, occurrence-counted, one-token-context KGW tests on short passages, 39 of 82 qualified, initially detected sources yielded rewrites with terminal detector score Z < 4 that passed blinded source-relative model review, at a mean actual token-edit cost of 16.0% under a 20% allowance. To examine whether this initial requirement can be inferred, a separate historical 95-passage study estimated initial detector score Z0 from generation traces with correlation 0.793 and an in-sample association beyond length. This aggregate information did not establish improved allocation, and the separate no-trace stopping test did not reliably exploit cheaper reviewed crossings in the candidate bank. Comparisons did not establish an advantage over simpler selection and ordinary constrained rewriting. The construction makes budgeted evidence replacement executable while exposing limits in signed reduction and recognition of sufficient editing.

title: How I structure a Java test automation project (and the free template I made from it)
description:
Keep assertions only in tests. Give every parallel test its own browser. Mock APIs for logic checks. Tag tests as smoke or regression. I turned all of this into a free GitHub template you can clone today.

Every time I started a new test automation project, the first weeks went to the same chores: choosing library versions, deciding on folders, wiring reports, writing a pipeline.

After the fifth time, I turned my setup into a template. This post explains the structure and the rules behind it, so you can use them even if you never clone the repo.

🧭 The one rule that keeps projects clean

Tests assert. Everything else acts.

Layer What it does Assertions?
Page objects Click and type Never
API clients Send requests and return the response Never
Repositories Run SQL Never
Tests Check the result Always

Because only tests contain assertions, you can reuse every page, client and query in any test without surprises. Here is a page object from the template:

public class LoginPage extends BasePage {
    @Step("Login as {username}")
    public LoginPage loginAs(String username, String password) {
        locator("#username").fill(username);
        locator("#password").fill(password);
        locator("button[type='submit']").click();
        return this;
    }

    public String flashMessage() {
        return locator("#flash").innerText();
    }
}

And the test that uses it:

@Test
@Tag("smoke")
void validLogin() {
    LoginPage page = new LoginPage().open().loginAs("tomsmith", "SuperSecretPassword!");

    assertThat(page.flashMessage()).contains("You logged into a secure area!");
    assertThat(page.currentUrl()).endsWith("/secure");
}

There is no sleep and no wait code. Playwright waits for each element to be ready before it acts.

⚡ Parallel runs without flaky chaos

Fast suites run tests in parallel, and that breaks anything that shares a browser.

The template gives every test its own isolated browser session. A small manager stores one session per thread, and a JUnit extension starts and closes it around each test. When a test fails, the same extension attaches a screenshot and a Playwright trace to the report.

The trace is the feature I would not give up. You replay the failed run step by step, with page snapshots and network calls, instead of guessing from a stack trace.

🧪 Mock-first API tests

Tests against a public test API fail when that API is slow or down. For logic checks I stub the service with WireMock and keep only a few tests against the real one:

wm.stubFor(get(urlEqualTo("/api/users/2")).willReturn(okJson(body)));

client.getUser("2").then()
        .statusCode(200)
        .body(matchesJsonSchemaInClasspath("schemas/user-response.json"));

The JSON schema check turns the response into a contract, so a renamed field fails the test even if the status code is still 200.

🔎 Queues and log search without hand-written JSON

If your system uses RabbitMQ or Elasticsearch, tests need small helpers or they turn into copy-pasted boilerplate. A fluent query builder keeps Elasticsearch requests readable:

ElasticQueryBuilder query = ElasticQueryBuilder.create()
        .filterTerm("service.keyword", "payments")
        .filterRange("@timestamp", "now-1h", null)
        .sortBy("@timestamp", false)
        .size(20);

SearchResult result = elastic.waitForHits(index, query, 1, Duration.ofSeconds(15));

The waiting method polls, because Elasticsearch needs about a second before a new document becomes searchable. That is a place where a fixed sleep always ends up wrong.

🏷️ Smoke and regression with tags

Every test carries a layer tag (ui, api, db, integration) and a level tag (smoke or regression). Pull requests run only smoke, and the nightly run does everything:

mvn clean test -Dgroups=smoke
mvn clean test -Dgroups="api & regression"

Failed tests retry once with -Drerun.count=1, and the report marks them as flaky, so retries never hide a problem.

🚀 Try the template

The whole structure is available as a free GitHub template with:

  • Playwright UI tests with screenshots and traces on failure
  • REST Assured + WireMock for API tests
  • Database, RabbitMQ and Elasticsearch helpers
  • Allure reports and a GitHub Actions pipeline
  • Secrets read from environment variables
  • A script that renames everything to your own package 
git clone https://github.com/edwardmrdoian/qa-enterprise-template
./scripts/new-project.sh com.acme.qa acme-qa-tests
mvn clean test -Dgroups=smoke

edwardmrdoian / qa-enterprise-template

Production-ready QA automation template in Java: Playwright UI, REST Assured + WireMock API, JDBI database, RabbitMQ and Elasticsearch/ELK helpers. JUnit 5 parallel runs, Allure reports with failure traces, GitHub Actions CI. Clone, rename with one script, and start writing tests.

QA Enterprise Template

A Java 25 starter for maintainable UI, API, database, RabbitMQ and Elasticsearch tests The default suite checks the framework using real local infrastructure or isolated mocks Chromium against a local HTTP fixture, REST Assured against WireMock, and JDBI against H2. Public demo services and Docker-backed examples are explicitly opt-in.

Stack: Maven Wrapper 3.9.9, JUnit 5, Playwright, REST Assured, WireMock, AssertJ, Awaitility, Jackson, JDBI/HikariCP, Owner, Datafaker/Instancio, Allure and Spotless.

1. Create your project

Install JDK 25 and set JAVA_HOME; no global Maven installation is needed. Use GitHub's Use this template button when enabled, or clone into a new repository. Keep the MIT license notice when redistributing template code.

From the project root, initialize the Java package, Maven coordinates and display name:

# Windows (also works in PowerShell on Linux/macOS)
.\scripts\new-project.ps1 com.acme.qa acme-qa-tests "Acme QA Tests"
# Linux/macOS or Git
…
View on GitHub

If it saves you time, a ⭐ on GitHub helps other testers find it.

What would you add to a template like this? Tell me in the comments.

title: Better Release PRs with brel
description:
I really like release-plz for my Rust projects (balzac uses it); it's easy to configure, it automatically updates the relevant version fields (in cargo.toml) and can even update the CHANGELOG.md of your repo. There's only one problem: it only works with Rust. So I decided to make my own.

Better Releases

better releases is a tool that works on any Github repo, with any language and any stack. It uses a simple-ysh brel.toml file and:

  • reads the commit from the previous tag (if it exists)
  • figures out the next tag based on conventional commits
  • opens/updates a release pr

Once the pr is merged, it can optionally publish the detected tag to potentially trigger other workflows; in the drizzle-sluggable repo, this is what I use to trigger publishing the package to npm.

Getting Started

To get started, you need to install brel (better-releases' main tool); if you don't want to, you can also run it with

npx brel@latest init

The init command will ask some question to setup the base config and will generate the base workflow for Github Actions. Here's what the config file might look like

default_branch = "main"

But we can do so much better than that.

Note:
When modifying the config, you will need to rerun the init command to update
the workflow file

Bumping Package versions

Honestly, this feature is why I decided to build this tool: I wanted to be able to update versions across toml and json files (Rust, Javascript, PHP) with a single tool. Let's see how we can do this.

For a package.json file, we might want to bump the version field; with Brel, you can just do:

[release_pr.version_updates]
"package.json" = ["version"]

But that's not all! Imagine you want to update the version inside a lock file (though you probably shouldn't do this in CI), you can also pass selectors when selecting an array:

[release_pr.version_updates]
"Cargo.toml" = ["package.version"]
"Cargo.lock" = ["package[name=brel].version"]

You might notice there's a .lock file in there; you can override the filetype like this:

[release_pr.format_overrides]
"Cargo.lock" = "toml"

Pushing a Tag

Let's say we want to add automatic tag creation when merging the release branch; we can do so with a few config changes

[release_pr.tagging]
enabled = true
tag_template = "{version}"

With this setup, merging the branch will create a tag corresponding to the version, like 0.7.0

Warning:
To actually enable release tagging, you need to provide a token allowed to do
so under the secret name BREL_TAG_PUSH_TOKEN

Generating/Updating a Changelog

When enabled, Brel integrates with Git Cliff to automatically update a CHANGELOG.MD file. Here's how you might configure this:

[release_pr.changelog]
enabled = true
output_file = "CHANGELOG.md"

This will automatically update the CHANGELOG.md file using Git Cliff

There's more

I will not bore you with everything Brel can do (you can even customize the template used for the pr body), but if you want to give it a try here's the official website and the github repo; do try it out if you have need of a tool like this and let me know what you think!

title: GKE Workspaces: Your notebook, on Google's AI infrastructure
description:
by Siyuan Zhang & Antonio Ojea, Google Cloud

If you're an ML engineer or researcher, the GPUs and TPUs you need increasingly live on Kubernetes, but Kubernetes should be an invisible layer. While your platform team sets up the GKE cluster and manages accelerator capacity and reservations, your job is to train and ship models—not to manage Kubernetes infrastructure.

Today we're introducing GKE Workspaces, a self-hosted AI/ML development platform for Google Kubernetes Engine, built on the open source Kubeflow Workspaces project. Deployed on your team's GKE cluster, it provides a dedicated web dashboard where you can pick an IDE and a machine, and start coding on cloud accelerators in minutes.

Why Kubeflow Workspaces

Kubeflow Workspaces gives every researcher a personal, persistent development environment on shared cluster hardware.

  • Self-service, in a few clicks. Sign in to your team's Workspaces web UI, choose JupyterLab or in-browser VS Code, pick an environment, and select a hardware size such as "Small CPU", "GPU", or "TPU". Researchers don't need Google Cloud Console access, YAML, or command-line setup.
  • Your work persists. Each workspace mounts its own home directory on a dedicated, encrypted Persistent Disk in your Google Cloud project—isolated to that workspace, so your files, notebooks, and installed packages stay safe across restarts, pauses, and machine changes.
  • Guardrails set by your platform team. Admins curate the approved images and hardware options, and decide which machines, reservations, and capacity types (such as on-demand or Spot) back them. Researchers only see choices that work.
  • Open source and portable. Workspaces is part of the Kubeflow community, empowering you with the freedom and flexibility of a fully open source notebook ecosystem.
  • Upstream integration and open licensing. GKE Workspaces builds directly on Kubeflow Workspaces with key enhancements for GKE environments—including standalone deployment without Istio dependencies, integrated authentication token flows, and stateful GPU/CPU pause and resume capabilities. Both GKE Workspaces and upstream Kubeflow Workspaces are released under the Apache 2.0 open source license, and we are actively working with the Kubeflow community to upstream these features.

What's unique about GKE Workspaces

GKE Workspaces brings Kubeflow Workspaces together with capabilities that are only available on Google Cloud.

1. Pause and resume—without losing your state

You've spent an hour loading a large model into GPU memory and building up results across notebook cells. Now it's time to go home. Normally you have two bad options: shut down and lose everything, or leave it running and pay for an idle GPU overnight.

With GKE Workspaces, you just pause by clicking a button from the Workspaces Dashboard. Built on Pod Snapshots, GKE takes a snapshot of your running notebook—including variables in memory and models loaded on the GPU—saves it to Cloud Storage, and releases the hardware so you stop paying. When you resume, you pick up exactly where you left off. Workspaces can also be paused automatically after a period of inactivity.

2. An easy on-ramp to Cloud TPUs

Moving from a quick experiment to large-scale training on TPUs used to mean switching tools at every step. GKE Workspaces keeps you in the same notebook the whole way, with both JAX and PyTorch:

  1. Prototype on a single TPU chip, just like you would on a GPU.
  2. Scale to multiple chips on one machine by choosing a bigger hardware option.
  3. Scale out to multi-host TPU slices by sending the same training function from your notebook to a larger slice. Logs stream back to your notebook, and the TPUs are released as soon as the job finishes.

3. Use your local coding agents with cloud accelerators

Prefer using your own AI coding agents and editors locally? You can easily bridge them to cloud compute. In the Workspaces web UI, generate a short-lived, revocable link to run your notebooks and agent-generated code on a remote GPU or TPU. Traffic is secured over HTTPS via Google Identity-Aware Proxy and the cluster's access proxy, checking permissions on every request—so no SSH keys, local tunnels, or cluster credentials ever sit on your laptop.

4. A launchpad for distributed work

Your workspace doesn't have to be big to drive big jobs. From a small, inexpensive CPU notebook you can process data with Spark, launch multi-host training, serve your model, and scale Ray clusters—all from Python. Built-in Cloud Storage access, with no keys to manage, makes it easy to pass data between each step.

5. A portal to safe elastic sandboxes for coding subagents

Running a fleet of coding agents directly on your local machine can drain your battery, expose sensitive files or credentials to agent-executed code, and halt progress as soon as you close your laptop. From a standard GKE Workspace, you can safely task your favorite coding agent to hand off parallel work—such as resolving failing tests across a repository—to background subagents. Crucially, while your primary workspace operates as a full-featured environment, these subagents are isolated within lightweight, in-cluster sandboxes using providers like Agent Substrate, requiring zero local setup. Each subagent executes independently in its own sandbox on shared cluster nodes, continues running even when you log off, snapshots to Cloud Storage at zero compute cost while idle, and outputs a clean patch for your review and merge.

6. Lightweight and secure by default

GKE Workspaces runs on its own on GKE Standard or Autopilot—you don't need to install the full Kubeflow platform. Users sign in with their Google accounts, traffic is encrypted with Google-managed certificates, and each team's work is isolated from the others.

Get started

GKE Workspaces lets ML teams focus on models, not infrastructure: one-click development environments, stateful pause and resume, a smooth path to Cloud TPUs, and the power of GKE behind every notebook.

Ask your platform team to deploy it using the GKE deployment guide, and learn more about the upstream project at Kubeflow Workspaces. We welcome feedback and contributions for both Apache 2.0-licensed projects.

title: Transactional Outbox and Inbox in Spring Boot
description:
A polling-based transactional outbox and inbox for Spring Boot, taken apart: how events leave the database, why the polling delay adapts, why each event type gets its own settings, and the three clocks that decide how long a duplicate is remembered.

The write that has two destinations

I wrote a transactional outbox for two of my own projects. The existing options did not fit, and log-based CDC with Debezium felt too heavy for a simple requirement: save an event together with the data, and send it later. oncebox is what that outbox grew into.

The requirement exists because a service that changes its database and then publishes a message is writing to two systems, and a database transaction covers only one of them. If the process dies between the commit and the publish, the data has changed and nobody was told. Reverse the order and a message goes out for a change that never happened.

The outbox pattern closes the gap by making the event part of the transaction. Instead of publishing straight to the broker, the service writes the event into a table next to its business data, and a separate step delivers it later.

In the outbox variant the event is a row committed with the business data. Publishing becomes a separate, retryable step that cannot lose the event, because the event is already durable.*

The outbox: one transaction, two rows

Publishing is one of two calls. The manual one takes an event type and a payload, or a list of payloads for a batch. The declarative one is an annotation on the method that already holds the transaction:

@Transactional
@OutboxPublish(eventType = "create-example-event")
public ExampleDto save(ExampleCreateDto dto) {
    ExampleEntity entity = repository.save(mapper.toEntity(dto));
    return mapper.toDto(entity);
}

Both write to outbox_events through methods annotated @Transactional(propagation = MANDATORY). The library never opens the transaction itself. It joins yours, and that is the whole guarantee: the event row commits or rolls back together with the business row. With the annotation, the payload is the method result by default (#result) and can be pointed at a parameter with a SpEL expression.

Every event also gets a UUIDv7 id. Time-ordered ids make inserts land at the tail of the primary key index instead of scattering across it, which matters for a table that takes a write for every event. The same id travels in the oncebox_event_id header and later becomes the deduplication key on the consumer side.

Once the row is in the table, it moves through a small set of states. Four background jobs drive it forward, and the diagram shows who does what.

The poller moves events forward, stuck-event recovery rescues a batch whose publisher died, the DLQ transfer moves exhausted events across in a single transaction (lock, insert into target, delete from source, commit), and clean-up removes processed rows.*

The IN_PROCESS state is the reason a crashed publisher does not lose events. The poller marks a batch the moment it locks it. If the instance dies before the broker confirms, those rows stay IN_PROCESS. A recovery worker finds rows that have sat there longer than max-batch-processing-time and returns them to PENDING without counting a failed attempt, since the event never had a chance to fail.

Delivery on this side is at-least-once. The poller waits for the broker acknowledgement before marking an event processed, so a lost acknowledgement means a second send, never a missing one. Removing that duplicate is the inbox's job, which comes later in this article.

Polling: how events leave the table

Each event type is polled on its own schedule. A library-managed thread pool runs one poller per type next to a few background jobs: stuck-event recovery and clean-up, plus three more when the DLQ is on. The sizing rule is 2 + n threads without the DLQ and 5 + n with it, where n is the number of event types.

Several application instances can poll the same table at once. The query that takes a batch uses FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED (on PostgreSQL inside a CTE that also moves the rows to IN_PROCESS in the same statement), so each instance locks a different slice of the pending rows instead of waiting on the instance in front of it.

Instances do not elect a leader or talk to each other. The database row locks are the only coordination, and they hand out disjoint batches. Events are ordered by next_retry_at inside a type, which is the creation time until a first failure.*

MySQL note. Run the outbox datasource at READ COMMITTED. Under InnoDB's default REPEATABLE READ, the polling query takes next-key (gap) locks, so several instances polling the same table deadlock instead of each taking a disjoint batch. PostgreSQL and Oracle are unaffected.

That leaves one question, and it is the one that decides how the library behaves in production: how often should each poller ask the database whether there is anything to send?

Adaptive polling

A fixed delay forces a trade. A short one gets events out quickly and queries an empty table around the clock. A long one is cheap and makes every event wait. Most outboxes spend most of their time with nothing to send, so the short delay is paid for mostly in empty answers.

The adaptive strategy removes the trade by letting the delay follow the workload. After each poll, the poller sets the delay for the next one with a single rule:

The poll returned a full batch (as many events as batch-size): more are probably waiting, so the delay resets to min-fixed-delay.

The poll returned less than a full batch, or nothing: the backlog is drained, so the delay is multiplied by multiplier, up to max-fixed-delay.

With the defaults (250ms minimum, multiplier 1.5, maximum 1m), consecutive empty polls stretch the delay like this:

It takes 14 empty polls, a little over three minutes of idleness, to reach the one-minute ceiling. Computed from the scheduling rule in AdaptiveOnceboxScheduleStrategy.*

To see what that is worth, count the polls one event type makes against an idle table in an hour, on one instance, using the same rule:

A fixed 250 ms delay asks the database 14,400 times; adaptive with default settings asks about 70 times, the ramp included. Same configured minimum, roughly 200 times fewer empty answers.*

The reset rule is what keeps this safe under load. A burst fills batches completely, every full batch resets the delay to the minimum, and the poller drains the backlog at the fastest cadence the type is configured for. Once a poll comes back short, it starts backing off again.

Eight empty polls, a burst of five full batches, one short batch, then idle again. The scenario is illustrative; the delays follow the library's rule exactly.*

The delay ceiling doubles as a latency budget. An event that lands just after a poll waits at most one current delay, so max-fixed-delay is the longest an idle type can make an event wait for pickup. That number is a setting, and every event type has its own.

Per-event-type settings

Events in one service rarely share the same urgency. A payment confirmation should leave within a fraction of a second. A nightly report can wait minutes. One global polling setting forces both onto the same cadence, so a service has to choose between a database that is queried constantly and critical events that wait.

oncebox keeps one defaults block and lets every event type override any part of it: polling strategy and delays, batch size, retry count and backoff. Unset values are inherited, so an event type states only what makes it different.

oncebox:
  outbox:
    defaults:
      batch-size: 200
      polling:
        type: adaptive
        min-fixed-delay: 250ms
        max-fixed-delay: 1m
        multiplier: 1.5
      max-retries: 3
      backoff:
        enabled: true
        delay: 10s
        multiplier: 3.0

    events:
      high-priority:
        topic: events
        polling:
          min-fixed-delay: 250ms      # inherits everything else

      low-priority:
        topic: events
        polling:
          min-fixed-delay: 10s
          max-fixed-delay: 5m
          multiplier: 2.0
        backoff:
          enabled: false

The two profiles behave very differently on the same idle table:

The high-priority type is back at the one-minute ceiling after about three and a half minutes. The low-priority type climbs to five minutes. Computed from the two configurations above.*

Event type Polls per idle hour Longest pickup wait when idle
high-priority 70 1 min
low-priority 15 5 min

Retries are per type as well. The delay before a retry is delay × multiplier^n, so the defaults give 10 s, 30 s, 90 s. A type that is cheap to repeat can retry quickly; a type that hits a fragile downstream can back off hard or stop after two attempts. Once retries run out, an event of any type moves to the same DLQ.

Because every type has its own poller, a slow type does not hold up a fast one. A burst on create-order shortens only that type's delay; the other pollers keep their own pace.

The inbox

Everything so far was about getting an event out reliably. Reliable delivery has a price on the receiving side: at-least-once means the same event can reach a consumer twice, because of a lost broker acknowledgement, a stuck-event recovery, or a consumer group restart. The outbox cannot prevent that, so the consumer has to tolerate it.

oncebox's inbox is a table of processed event ids. It does not store messages and does not process anything asynchronously. An event whose id is already recorded is skipped. Everything is keyed on the UUIDv7 that the outbox assigned when the event was created, which the consumer reads from the oncebox_event_id header.

public ExampleKafkaListener(@TransactionalConsumer IdempotentConsumer idempotentConsumer) { ... }

@KafkaListener(topics = "example-events", groupId = "example-group",
               containerFactory = "inboxKafkaListenerContainerFactory")
public void listen(Message<ExampleDto> message) {
    idempotentConsumer.consume(
        message,
        OnceboxHeadersUtils::extractId,
        m -> handlers.get(OnceboxHeadersUtils.extractEventType(m)).accept(m.getPayload())
    );
}

There are two implementations, and the choice is a statement about what a duplicate costs you:

Qualifier Order of steps If the operation throws
@TransactionalConsumer (effectively-once) one transaction: record the id, run the operation, commit the id rolls back with the operation, the redelivery runs it again
@NonTransactionalConsumer (at-most-once) record the id and commit, then run the operation the id stays, the redelivery is skipped

Use the transactional one when the effect is a write to the same database: the id and the effect commit together or not at all, so a redelivered event never changes data twice. Use the non-transactional one for effects that cannot be undone, such as sending an email, where a repeated side effect is worse than a missed one. The README calls this effectively-once rather than exactly-once, because the library cannot deduplicate inside the broker itself.

The cache sits in front of the database check. It is written only after the wrapped consumer returns, so it never claims an event that was not processed.*

Batches use the same inbox. When a listener receives a list, ids that were already consumed are filtered out and the operation receives only the new ones, so a partly redelivered batch does the right thing without any code in the handler.

One rule keeps the bookkeeping honest: within a service, one event is handled by one consumer. The inbox records an event by its id alone, whichever consumer recorded it. Two listeners in the same service that both want the same event would split it, so the second one skips it. Give each effect its own event type, or its own service.

The cache: what it does for the inbox

Without a cache, every delivery checks the database: a lookup of the id, and for the transactional consumer an insert inside the business transaction. For a stream where redeliveries are rare, that lookup is paid on every message just to catch the occasional duplicate.

The optional cache moves repeated lookups out of the database. It plugs into Spring's CacheManager, so Redis or any other cache you already run works. On a hit, the consumer returns before it touches the database. On a miss it falls through to the inbox as usual and, after the consumer succeeds, puts the id into the cache.

oncebox:
  inbox:
    cache:
      enabled: true
      cache-name: "orders-service:oncebox:inbox"

Three details decide whether it behaves:

  • The cache name is per service. The key is the event id alone. Two services that consume the same event and share one Redis under one name would mark each other's events as seen. Prefix the name with the service name, or give each service its own key prefix.
  • You own the expiry. The library hands the cache an id and nothing else. How long it lives is a property of the CacheManager bean you configure, which brings the cache into the retention story below.
  • The cache is an accelerator. A cache that loses an entry costs one database lookup; the inbox table is still the source of truth. Single-event consume calls go through the cache, and batch calls go straight to the inbox table.

Three clocks

An inbox only deduplicates what it still remembers. Ids are kept until clean-up removes them (oncebox.inbox.clean-up.ttl), so a redelivery that arrives later than that is treated as a new event. How long that window needs to be depends on how long a duplicate can still be on its way, and three separate systems each run a clock that answers a part of that question.

1. The broker: how long a message can come back

oncebox does not configure the broker. Kafka keeps messages for its retention period, whatever consumers have read; a consumer group reset or a replay can deliver any message still inside that period. Kafka's own default is seven days. RabbitMQ holds an unacknowledged message until it is acknowledged or expires through a queue or message TTL you set, and an unacknowledged message is requeued when the listener throws.

Acknowledgement itself is on your side of the fence, and the defaults are right for the inbox. Spring Kafka commits offsets after the listener returns, and RabbitMQ's AUTO mode acknowledges after the listener returns. enable.auto.commit=true breaks that, and the starter logs a warning when it sees it.

2. The inbox table: how long an id is remembered

The inbox clean-up job deletes ids older than its ttl, 24 hours by default, in batches, on one instance at a time under a distributed lock. Its polling is adaptive like everything else, so rows live slightly longer than the ttl: the job removes them on its next pass, not at the exact second of expiry.

3. The cache: how long the shortcut lasts

The cache entry expires on your CacheManager's schedule. The README's rule is that inbox clean-up happens after the cache entry has gone. In other words, the cache lifetime must not exceed the inbox ttl. The cache then only ever shortens the path to an answer the table would give, and the inbox ttl stays the single number that defines the deduplication window.

The inbox ttl has to reach as far as a duplicate can still arrive. The cache sits inside it. Bars for oncebox settings show the library defaults; the broker bar shows Kafka's own default retention and moves with your cluster; the cache bar is an example length, and any value up to the inbox ttl is valid.*

Two rules follow from this:

cache TTL ≤ inbox ttl, so a cached id never outlives the row that backs it.

inbox ttl ≥ the longest time a duplicate can still arrive: the time the outbox can republish an event (retry backoff, plus the max-batch-processing-time of 300 s after which a stuck event is re-sent) and, when you replay or reset consumer offsets, the broker's retention.

The defaults make this concrete. A 24-hour inbox ttl covers every republish the outbox itself can produce, which happens within minutes. It also covers ordinary redelivery after a consumer restart. A replay from a Kafka topic that keeps seven days of history reaches further back than 24 hours, so a service that replays old offsets sets the inbox ttl to match the retention it replays from.

The outbox has a clean-up ttl of its own, also 24 hours by default, but it belongs to a different table. It removes PROCESSED rows from outbox_events and has no effect on deduplication. Neither does the DLQ's RESOLVED clean-up.

Setting Where Default Decides
Topic retention / queue TTL broker Kafka: 7 days how old a message can be when it is redelivered or replayed
oncebox.inbox.clean-up.ttl inbox table 24h how long an id blocks a duplicate
cache expiry in CacheManager Redis or other cache yours how long a duplicate is answered without the database
oncebox.outbox.clean-up.ttl outbox table 24h how long PROCESSED rows stay for inspection
max-batch-processing-time outbox recovery 300s when a stuck batch is sent again

The whole thing in one file

A service with an outbox and an inbox needs the starter, exactly one database dialect module and one broker module. Everything else has a default, so a working configuration stays short:

oncebox:
  thread-pool-size: 5
  outbox:
    sender:
      type: kafka
    defaults:
      batch-size: 200
      polling:
        type: adaptive
        min-fixed-delay: 250ms
        max-fixed-delay: 1m
        multiplier: 1.5
    events:
      create-order:
        topic: orders
      daily-report:
        topic: reports
        polling:
          min-fixed-delay: 10s
          max-fixed-delay: 5m
    dlq:
      enabled: true
  inbox:
    source:
      type: kafka
    clean-up:
      ttl: 24h
    cache:
      enabled: true
      cache-name: "orders-service:oncebox:inbox"

Beyond the parts covered here, the library also ships a REST API for working through the dead letter queue (inspect, retry, resolve, delete), Micrometer metrics with cached gauges, and a fully containerized example project with a traffic generator.

Repository: github.com/dmitriy-iliyov/oncebox
Maven Central: io.github.dmitriy-iliyov:oncebox-starter
Example project: oncebox-example

Charts in this post are computed from the library's scheduling rule and its documented defaults. They do not show measurements from a running system.

title: Best Chart Components for Medical Patient Monitoring Systems
description:
Smoothness and interactions on data visualizations instantly provide trust in medical settings. To achieve this, you want both the rendering and the UI to function and look slick, powered by a rendering engine and data visualization layer purpose built for real-time, smooth interactions. You also don't want these to lag or stutter regardless of the hardware. To help you choose the best chart components for medical patient monitoring systems, we’re sharing the architecture, performance and features that really make a difference.

Are you looking to standardize on lower-cost hardware and don't want the UI, memory, or CPU usage to be a blocker or cost barrier? Whether you’re working with multi-lead ECGs, plethysmograms, or capnograms, this breakdown isolates the engineering trade-offs and pros of each data visualization option.

What’s the Risk of Underperforming Data Visualization in Clinical Settings?

A delayed draw call or an unhandled garbage collection pause could compromise patient care. The challenge for engineers of an ICU telemetry console, for instance, is how to handle continuous, multi-channel streams of high-frequency data.

If a rendering engine cannot keep pace with incoming telemetry, the system experiences frame drops, erratic waveform scrolling, and interface freezes.

Resolving these bottlenecks requires a better understanding of the low-level rendering mechanics of specialized chart components for medical monitoring systems.

What Are the Best Chart Components for Medical Patient Monitoring Systems?

The best chart components for medical monitoring systems with telemetry displays are ones that reliably offer real-time digital signal processing pipelines.

Consistency Across Hardware & Platforms

A consistent UI in terms of look and feel is often crucial to medical device developers who may have mobile devices, tablets, web portals, embedded hardware and desktop applications in their ecosystem. SciChart is the only product that provides a consistent look and feel across all supported platforms, through its shared C++ rendering engine.

High-Performance Rendering Engines

Standard charting tools rely on the CPU for geometry computation and use vector-based rendering primitives, such as SVG or Canvas 2D contexts. Under heavy data loads, this approach results in immediate performance degradation. Advanced medical instrumentation typically benefits from GPU acceleration through graphics APIs such as DirectX, Metal, WebGL, or WebGPU. This shifts rendering workloads to the GPU, reducing visual processing overhead and helping maintain responsive user interfaces under demanding real-time conditions.

Real-Time Update Capabilities

To avoid garbage collection pauses, medical dashboards must bypass standard object allocation patterns. The chart component should implement highly efficient memory management structures, such as continuous ring buffers, that append new coordinate matrices while discarding aged samples instantaneously. True real-time components execute these operations with a flat O(1) time complexity, maintaining a stable 60 Hz or higher refresh rate under demanding conditions.

Customization & Flexibility

Medical hardware configurations frequently feature unconventional ultra-wide or vertical aspect ratios. Combine this with strict clinical design mandates and out-of-the-box UI templates quickly become insufficient.

What you require instead is granular control over rendering behaviors, specialized sweeping/scrolling modes, and custom pixel-shader effects.

Technical Support & Compliance

Even if you have access to the best chart components and customizations, that doesn’t mean you want to wait weeks or even months to get technical support when it’s needed.

Direct developer access to software engineers and responsive technical support can make all the difference. This is especially true when handling complex device certification and compliance cycles. Even better, we recommend choosing a chart library that has a successful track record of working with companies that secured HIPAA or FDA compliance for their monitoring systems. For instance, the ANNE® One neonatal monitoring platform received FDA-clearance.

What Are the Best Chart Libraries for Medical Patient Monitoring Systems?

Selecting the optimal visualization framework involves assessing the trade-offs between native execution speed, web portability, and architectural constraints.

Highcharts

Pros: Highcharts is widely recognized in web development for its clean API design and accelerated initial prototyping phases.

Cons: Despite its effectiveness in standard business intelligence applications, it struggles under the demands of real-time clinical telemetry. Highcharts relies on SVG, WebGL, and standard browser layout engines. When forced to stream multiple high-frequency channels simultaneously, rendering latency increases sharply, causing stuttering during live waveform animations.

Qt Graphs

Pros: Qt Graphs serves as a common option for native desktop application development, particularly within embedded medical devices running specialized Linux or Windows configurations. It integrates directly with the broader Qt framework, facilitating clear communication with hardware abstraction layers.

Cons: While highly effective at basic vector operations, developers often find themselves writing extensive custom rendering code to achieve fluid real-time performance.

D3.js

Pros: D3.js is a flexible choice for custom web-based data manipulation. It gives developers control over the structural mapping of data to visual primitives, making it popular for academic and custom research applications.

Cons: The major drawback involves its rendering performance. D3.js updates the browser Document Object Model directly. When dealing with complex, fast-changing medical datasets, the resulting DOM overhead can stall the main thread, making it unsuitable for live patient alarms.

SciChart

SciChart offers advanced chart library support for MedTech chart developers.

The Visual Xccelerator™ engine serves as a high-performance cross-platform bridge, translating drawing instructions directly into native graphics APIs. This includes DirectX, Metal, and WebGL. SciChart.js v6 added support for WebGPU, a more modern graphics API, alongside the existing WebGL renderer.

SciChart can perform complex rendering on the GPU while selectively employing the CPU for coordinate calculations. This preserves 64-bit precision, while maximizing rendering performance.

Our technology stack leverages WebAssembly and Memory64 to plot 1 billion points in the browser on JavaScript, and 100 billion on desktop.

Lossless data resampling, powered by SciChart's proprietary algorithms, is useful for multi-stream rendering in real time. They preserve peaks and troughs, while enabling overlays, annotations, and smooth interactions even on low-cost hardware.

The framework delivers a compelling combination of high-speed execution, deep layout customization, and direct access to an expert engineering support team backed by an integrated AI assistant.

Performance Comparison Table for Medical Telemetry Chart Libraries

The following table contrasts how these libraries manage the technical demands of intensive chart components for medical monitoring systems.
