Try SciChart Today

Developing medical patient monitoring systems requires a graphics infrastructure that eliminates performance volatility. Relying on unoptimized graphics pipelines creates risks for your telemetry displays.

Want to see how SciChart’s specialized medical data charting solutions handle extreme data throughput for yourself? Download SciChart’s open-source chart benchmark on GitHub to review and stress-test raw rendering performance across your target hardware configurations.

Ready to build your next clinical dashboard? You can get started with SciChart.js today to integrate responsive, stable charting components directly into your medical monitoring application.

Get Started With SciChart

Frequently Asked Questions

Why do open-source charting libraries fail in medical patient monitoring systems?

Most open-source charting frameworks rely heavily on high-level web vectors or direct browser DOM manipulation. While these architectures are perfectly adequate for standard business dashboards, they lack the memory layout and allocation structures required for high-frequency telemetry. When forced to stream and redraw multiple continuous waveforms simultaneously, they trigger frequent CPU garbage collection and layout calculations, causing visible application lag.

What is the benefit of a GPU-accelerated rendering engine in MedTech software?

A hardware-accelerated engine offloads vertex processing and pixel calculations from the system CPU directly to the graphics card. This clear separation ensures that your application UI thread remains entirely unblocked, allowing operations, such as alarm processing, user inputs, and background data analysis, to run smoothly even while rendering millions of live data points.

Can JavaScript-based charts safely run inside intensive medical monitors?

Yes, provided that the underlying visualization library bypasses standard browser layout engine constraints. Frameworks that use advanced WebGL configurations deliver native rendering speeds and stable, real-time performance for JavaScript charts.

Fixed

Fixed in this release

Bug ID Description
578314600 Fixed an issue where apigee-connect-agent ignored HTTPS_PROXY and failed to establish a tether in clusters that require an HTTP forward proxy for egress; the agent now uses HTTP/2 keepalive pings on the control-plane connection while honoring HTTPS_PROXY (including proxy credentials).
576707253 Removed the compromised emSign roots and the cross-signing Comodo AAA Services root from the system and Java (cacerts) trust stores across containers.
573622417 Fixed an issue where apigee-ingressgateway forwarded the x-envoy-decorator-operation header to upstream runtime and target backends.
572025634 Fixed an issue where responses with a compressed text/event-stream body to a proxy with an EventFlow returned a corrupted body; compressed text/event-stream responses now skip EventFlow processing and pass through intact.
571378258 The apigee-redis container now uses the Valkey engine (version 8.1.10). The RESP2 wire protocol and redis-server and redis-cli binary names are unchanged.
568860869 Fixed an issue in the RegularExpressionProtection policy where patterns starting and ending with .* whose middle section contained regular expression syntax were matched as literal text instead of regular expressions.
560272924 Apigee hybrid now supports continuous-scan bidirectional gRPC streaming for the SanitizeModelResponse policy over Server-Sent Events (SSE) streams, preserving native LLM provider SSE JSON envelopes and event framing.
555332621 Fixed an issue where Model Armor policies did not honor HTTPClient.managementplane.skip.proxy: when set, Model Armor callouts now bypass the forward proxy like other googleapis traffic, while streaming (ContinuousScan) Model Armor traffic uses the forward proxy.
554114419 Fixed an issue where an AssignMessage, HTTPModifier, or RaiseFault policy that creates a new request (createNew="true") in an HTTP/2 flow could not set the :path and :authority pseudo-headers and failed with an invalid-header error.
549779897 Apigee analytics now reports the Model Armor template, verdict, and matched filters for each request on both the prompt and model-response directions.
546141116 The SemanticCacheLookup policy now reports the cache key and cache name to analytics in the ai_semantic_cache_key and ai_semantic_cache_name fields.
535395491 Extension Processor (ext_proc) denials now return the status and body that the policy or FaultRule produced, instead of always returning HTTP 500.
524115876 Fixed an intermittent HTTP 400 error in the OASValidation policy's strict parameter validation that rejected valid requests under load.
502231886 Fixed an issue where the SanitizeUserPrompt and SanitizeModelResponse policies failed to extract content using default source templates when the <Source> element was omitted and <IgnoreUnresolvedVariables> was set to false.
492041991 Fixed an issue where VerifyAPIKey and VerifyAccessToken set the apiproduct.operation.llmTokenQuota.* flow variables from unmatched LLM operations; they are now set only from the LLM operations that matched the request.
449228485 Fixed an issue where podDisruptionBudget overrides configured in the Helm charts were dropped by the Kubernetes API server.

Cloud Profiler

Security

The Cloud Profiler Java agent is updated with a new Certification Authority (CA) certificate bundle, in response to security bulletin GCP-2026-071. Google Cloud infrastructure and the Cloud Profiler backend service are not affected.

If you use the Cloud Profiler Java agent, take one of the following actions:

  • Upgrade the Java agent to cloud-profiler-java-agent_20261026_RC00 (GitHub release v0.5.0) or later, and then rebuild and redeploy your applications. Download the updated archive, https://storage.googleapis.com/cloud-profiler/java/cloud-profiler-java-agent_20261026_RC00.tar.gz, or, for musl-based Alpine Linux containers, https://storage.googleapis.com/cloud-profiler/java/cloud-profiler-java-agent_20261026_RC00_alpine.tar.gz.
  • If you can't immediately upgrade or rebuild, update your host or container operating system's CA certificate store as described in GCP-2026-071, and then set the GRPC_DEFAULT_SSL_ROOTS_FILE_PATH environment variable to point to the updated PEM bundle.

For more information about installing the agent, see Profiling Java applications.

Dataflow

Feature

Dataflow has added the following features to tune horizontal autoscaling for Streaming Engine jobs:

  • Latency tiers: You can configure the backlog threshold by choosing a latency tier (low_latency, medium_latency, or high_latency), allowing you to configure the autoscaler's sensitivity to backlog duration and balance latency requirements with resource costs. For more information, see Set the latency tier.
  • Autoscaling schedules: You can configure recurring autoscaling schedules to automatically apply parameter overrides—such as minimum and maximum workers, worker utilization hints, or latency tiers—during specific time windows. For more information, see Schedule autoscaling changes.

You can configure these features when you create a job or update them while the job is running.

Dialogflow

Security

Dialogflow ES: The Dialogflow ES LINE integration validates the X-Line-Signature HTTP header on incoming webhook requests using your LINE channel secret and rejects requests with missing, duplicate, or invalid signatures with an HTTP 400 Bad Request error. Make sure your configured channel secret matches your LINE Messaging API channel and that any intermediate proxy forwards the X-Line-Signature header and raw request body unmodified.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Feature

Managed OpenTelemetry for GKE is generally available (GA) on clusters running GKE version 1.37.1-gke.1697000 or later. You can collect OpenTelemetry Protocol (OTLP) traces, metrics, and logs from your workloads with a Google-managed collector instead of a self-managed OpenTelemetry Collector deployment:

  • Configure otlp_grpc in the Instrumentation custom resource (GKE version 1.37.1-gke.1697000 or later), or send telemetry directly to the in-cluster collector's gRPC endpoint on port 4317 in addition to HTTP on port 4318.
  • The managed collector routes logs alongside traces and metrics through the Cloud Telemetry API (telemetry.googleapis.com), with improved per-signal queueing and autoscaling for high-throughput clusters. (Logs ingested through telemetry.googleapis.com default to the otlp log name instead of gke-managed-otel-collector.)
  • Multimodal prompts and responses collection for LangGraph ReAct and Agent Development Kit (ADK) agents, the --managed-otel-scope flag in the gcloud CLI (version 576.0.0 or later), and managed_opentelemetry_config in terraform-provider-google (v8.8.0 or later) are generally available.

To use the GA collector and features, upgrade clusters from earlier Preview versions to 1.37.1-gke.1697000 or later. For architecture details and setup instructions, see Managed OpenTelemetry for GKE and Deploy Managed OpenTelemetry for GKE.

Identity and Access Management

Feature

The Admin (roles/admin), Writer (roles/writer), and Reader (roles/reader) basic roles are generally available (GA). For more information, see Basic roles.

The legacy basic roles—Owner (roles/owner), Editor (roles/editor), and Viewer (roles/viewer)—are still available for use and are being actively maintained. However, if you need to grant a basic role, we recommend granting the Admin, Writer, or Reader role instead of a legacy basic role. This is because the newer roles support additional features, such as the use of IAM Conditions.

Looker

Announcement

Beginning October 26, 2026, the following features will be automatically enabled for Looker (original) and Looker (Google Cloud core) instances running Looker 26.20.

Feature

The ability to generate a summary of an Explore by using Gemini assistance is now generally available.

Feature

The bullet chart visualization type is now generally available. Bullet charts let you evaluate a single primary metric's performance as one or more bars and mark your goal with a target line. You can plot both against shaded background ranges that represent performance thresholds, such as "poor," "satisfactory," and "good." For more information, see Bullet chart options.

Feature

Looker now includes network diagnostics to help you troubleshoot database connectivity issues. When a database connection test fails, Looker automatically tests DNS resolution and TCP connectivity for the connection's endpoints and appends the results to the error message. To test network reachability to any hostname and port without creating a connection, Looker administrators can click Test Reachability on the Connections page.

Note: This item was added on October 30, 2026.

Feature

The Table Row Grouping feature and the Grouping menu options are now generally available. The Grouping menu options let you display and customize the appearance of table chart data hierarchically in groups.

Feature

The Visualization Assistant is now generally available.

Feature

Looker Continuous Integration (CI) now supports hub-and-spoke projects. If your Looker project uses local project imports to import files from an upstream hub project on the same Looker instance, then you can use CI to automatically test downstream spoke projects. Testing runs whenever a pull request is opened or updated on the hub project. This capability lets you catch breaking changes in downstream Explores, content, or data tests before upstream LookML changes are merged. For more information, see Creating a Continuous Integration suite.

Feature

Two new legacy features, Use Legacy Explore and Merge Query Experience and Use Legacy Explore and Merge Query Experience for Embed, are now available for Looker (original) and Looker (Google Cloud core) instances. These features let administrators configure Explores and merged queries to open in the classic experience by default across an instance or in embedded contexts. For more information, see Legacy feature schedule.

Feature

Looker now includes a new histogram chart visualization option. A histogram chart is a graphical representation of the data distribution of an attribute. A histogram creates intervals (bins) and counts how many values fall into each bin.

Feature

The KPI (Single Value) chart type is now generally available. The KPI (Single Value) chart type replaces the Single Value chart type.

Feature

The new Looker Explore and merge query experience is now generally available and is the default interface for Explores and for joining data from multiple queries.

Feature

When you enter values in a string filter on dashboards, Looks, or Explores, clicking Done or clicking outside the input field no longer creates a filter chip from uncommitted text. To create a filter chip, press Enter, enter a comma (,), or paste values into the input field.

Feature

The new Dashboard Tile Groups preview feature lets you organize related tiles into collapsible containers for improved visual organization. You can move, duplicate, or delete multiple tiles as a single unit on dashboards that use the newspaper layout. This update also adds LookML support for programmatically managing tile groups.

Feature

Now available in preview, the Release Changelog gives Looker users and administrators real-time visibility into the features, behavioral changes, and bug fixes that are available for their instance.

Feature

The Legacy features page is now available in the Admin panel for Looker (Google Cloud core) instances. Legacy features that appear on the Looker (Google Cloud core) Legacy features page might differ from those that are available on Looker (original) instances. For more information, see Looker (Google Cloud core) admin settings.

Announcement

The latest versions in the Looker (Google Cloud core) release channels are beginning deployment as follows:

  • Latest version in the Rapid channel: Looker 26.22
  • Latest version in the No Channel channel: Looker 26.22

The latest version in the Regular channel remains Looker 26.18.

Breaking

Some elements of the Conversational Analytics System Activity dashboard have been renamed. The dashboard layout and capabilities remain the same.

On the Token usage tab, the Conversational Analytics API value in the Feature column and the Feature Name filter has been renamed to Looker API. This value refers to the Conversational Analytics methods for the Looker API.

This rename might cause a breaking change if you built custom dashboards that reference the former Feature column or Feature Name filter value.

Change

The Use Legacy Connections Page legacy feature and the legacy database connection workflow have been removed. All database connections now use the connection workflow that is described in Connecting Looker to your database.

Feature

description:
Why a text editor?

In March I started a new project to keep experimenting with Claude Code. I wanted something real, not a toy: something I would actually use, and something hard enough to show me how far (and how well) you can go writing software with an AI agent.

The answer was easy. The tool I spend most of my day in is my editor. I've used Vim and then Neovim for many years, to the point where I just can't use anything that isn't modal. I'd also been curious for a long time about the Kakoune and Helix approach, where you select first and then act.

So I decided to be bold and write my own modal editor. I called it HUME, as in "HUME's Unfinished Modal Editor" (because who doesn't like recursive acronyms?).

It was a chance to build my dream editor, and it also turned out to be a great benchmark, because under the hood an editor is full of hard problems: UTF-8 everywhere, undo trees, rendering, terminal quirks, LSP, plugins.

The irony: I stopped using my editor

About a month in, I realized something: all the code I was producing was written by an agent. I was building a text editor, and I was basically no longer using one.

That could have been the end of the project. Why build the perfect tool for a job you no longer do? I have two reasons:

The first one: checking the diff, reviewing the code and doing small edits here and there are definitely better with a full-featured editor (HUME has a live inline diff and LSP-backed navigation and diagnostics for precisely this reason).

The second one took me a few months to figure out. I understand HUME well at a high level, but reviewing code means catching the small, hard details, and that skill fades if you don’t practice it. Writing code myself is how I keep it sharp, so I plan to keep doing it, even if only on a small side project. And for that, I still want a good editor.

So I kept going, and today HUME is my daily editor.

What HUME is today

HUME is a pragmatic, extensible modal editor. It has all the bells and whistles a modern editor should have, it reuses what I think works well in Vim, Kakoune and Helix, and adds a few ideas of its own:

  • Scheme as the embedded scripting language (I've always been fascinated by Lisp...).
  • Most of the big features are written as plugins, so you can turn them on or off, customize them, or replace them with your own.
  • A "smart" paste that does what you most likely meant, with multiple registers and a kill ring.

Oh, and it supports the Helix theme format: why reinvent the wheel?

Lesson 1: how do you review code you can't read?

One thing I find exhilarating about agentic coding is that it lets you write a program in a language you don't know. I've worked for many years with Ruby, JavaScript and then TypeScript, plus SQL, bash and so on. But Rust? Never.

I know what a struct or an array is, and what an if or a for loop does. I think I get the idea behind the borrow checker (traits, less so). But I think that's not enough to properly review the code Claude writes.

So how do you review code you don't understand? You can ask the agent to review it, but then you're trusting the same LLM that wrote it in the first place. It's almost a philosophical problem.

Learning some Rust along the way certainly helps, and so does pushing back on the agent every time something doesn’t fully convince me. But that alone isn’t enough: I also want a workflow that works, and rules that are enforced automatically. I don’t have a perfect answer, but I found a few things that help.

The basic workflow

The first thing you learn is the basic workflow: plan, implement, review. These are the basics for a reason: they work.

The real lesson here is that asking the LLM to review the code it just wrote works better than trying to get it perfect on the first pass. And since the LLM is fast at writing code, iterating is the way to go.

Let the machine check what I can't

If I can't reliably judge the code by reading it, I want as many rules as possible enforced mechanically. In Rust, one way is to use newtypes everywhere a plain integer could be confused with another (a byte offset is not a char offset is not a line number). On top of that, I added strict clippy rules and architecture lints that stop modules from reaching where they shouldn't. Last but not least, CI runs on macOS, Windows and Linux.

Review only works when it's grounded

This lesson took me longer to learn: agent code review works well only when the agent can see the real thing it's reviewing against.

An example: say you build a generic API meant to serve two different kinds of consumers, but you only write one of them. Ask the agent to review that API and it will keep finding "bugs" for the second consumer. It doesn't know what that consumer looks like, so it guesses, and every guess produces a new hypothetical problem. You end up chasing ghosts.

The fix is boring: don't build for consumers that don't exist yet. Write the real second consumer, or drop the generality until you need it. Once the code is grounded in concrete use, the reviews get much shorter and much more useful.

Lesson 2: notice the pattern, fix it once

The most valuable habit I built wasn't about prompting. It was about watching.

Agents have tendencies, and the same bad move shows up again and again. For example, I noticed Claude widening the visibility of a method, or relaxing a restriction, just to get a test to green faster. The test passed, but the design got a little worse every time.

Correcting it in the moment fixes one diff. Writing it down fixes every future one. So every time I spot a pattern like this, I add a rule to my global CLAUDE.md so it doesn't happen again.

Another example: Claude would skip an architectural fix because it was "not worth the churn". So I tried to teach it that correct code (or a correct algorithm) is always worth the churn, even when it doesn't seem to buy you anything.

**Cost is not a verdict on correctness.** "One call site", "not worth the churn", "non-trivial for now" never license a known-wrong design. Either fix it, or measure the cost and report the number — never assert it. A wrong pattern at N=1 is the template for N=2, and the site may itself grow before anyone revisits it.

I've caught and fixed many other patterns this way. If you're curious, my dotfiles repo is here.

The rest of the journey

HUME is already usable (and, dare I say, powerful), but there are still many features I plan to add, and probably a few bugs to fix (what software doesn't have bugs?).

In the next post I’ll dig into what makes HUME different: select-then-act, smart paste, and writing a plugin in Scheme.

If you're curious to try it, here are a few links to get started. Feedback and contributions will be highly appreciated!

Prebuilt binaries

Currently available for macOS (Apple Silicon), Windows and x86_64 Linux:

  • Releases

It works best in a terminal that supports the kitty keyboard protocol (such as iTerm2, WezTerm, Ghostty, foot, etc.).

title: Humanized but Still True? Auditing Facts and Detection in AI-Text Humanizers
description:
arXiv:2611.00359v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI "humanizers" rewrite machine-generated text so that detectors classify it as human-written. Public leaderboards score evasion and embedding similarity, but not whether checkable details survive. We check whether numbers, dates, person and organization names, and quoted spans survive each rewrite, using a rule-based checker validated by two AI annotators (precision 0.84-1.00, recall 0.93-0.95; no human annotation). In the October 2026 cycle of a public humanizer leaderboard, all 11 commercial tools changed or dropped at least one of these units in 35-65% of the documents that contained one. Most changes were to quoted spans; counting numbers and names alone, 10 of the 11 tools still altered at least one in 20% or more of the documents. The September 2026 cycle was similar (19-50%). An open 12B humanizer kept at least 97% of numbers and names in fact-dense U.S. federal agency text, but reworded 67-78% of the quoted spans, against its own prompt. Unit retention and detector evasion were not clearly related across tools (Spearman rho = -0.46, 95% CI -0.65 to 0.08), and the open model's four released files (two of them quantization-aware low-bit files) did not show the pre-registered monotone trade-off. On federal texts with matched human, AI-styled and humanized versions, a general-purpose decision model, Jev, asked a single zero-shot question, separated human originals from humanized rewrites with AUROC 0.864 (0.827-0.902), 0.18-0.22 higher than Binoculars, Fast-DetectGPT and the adversarially trained RADAR, while calling 24% of the human originals AI at a 0.5 threshold. On the AI-styled rewrites by 2026 models, both perplexity-based detectors scored below chance (AUROC 0.37 and 0.39), also with line breaks removed. Hypotheses, data rules and analyses were frozen before the main runs; two earlier data contacts are disclosed. We release the checker and the per-item results.

title: Advanced Cloud Networking: PrivateLink, Hybrid & DNS
description:
⚡ TL;DR: Go past the basic VPC: connect privately to services with PrivateLink, choose peering versus Transit Gateway, link on-prem over VPN or Direct Connect, and make DNS actually resolve across the boundary.

Contents

  • The wall you hit after the VPC works
  • One idea: connectivity is plumbing, not magic
  • The picture: services, VPCs, and on-prem
  • Private connectivity to services (PrivateLink / PSC)
  • VPC peering vs Transit Gateway
  • Hybrid connectivity (VPN / Direct Connect / ExpressRoute)
  • Build it: a PrivateLink endpoint + private DNS zone
  • How DNS actually resolves across the boundary
  • Common mistakes that cost hours
  • Takeaways
  • Where to go next

The wall you hit after the VPC works

You built a VPC. Subnets are carved up, route tables are clean, the NAT gateway works, and your app reaches the internet. Then a real requirement lands: "Reach the managed database, but never over the public internet." "Connect this VPC to four others without a tangle of peerings." "Let the on-prem payroll system call our internal API." "Make db.internal.acme.com resolve the same from a Lambda, an EC2 box, and a server in the data center." Suddenly the basic VPC mental model runs out of road.

This is the layer where cloud networking stops being about one VPC and starts being about connectivity between things, services, VPCs, and your own data center, plus the DNS that ties them together. Get it right and traffic stays private, predictable, and cheap. Get it wrong and you either expose internal systems to the internet or spend a day staring at a name that won't resolve.

📌 Who this is for: Engineers who already understand a single VPC (subnets, route tables, security groups) and now need private service access, multi-VPC topologies, hybrid links to on-prem, and DNS that works across all of it. New to VPCs? Start with Cloud Networking Fundamentals: How a VPC Actually Works first.

One idea: connectivity is plumbing, not magic

Advanced cloud networking is just deciding which pipes connect which buildings, and making sure every building uses the same phone book.

The whole article in one line

Every option below is a different shape of pipe, and DNS is the shared phone book. Before the cloud-specific names overwhelm you, anchor on the physical picture:

In the real world In tech
A private hallway between two adjacent offices VPC peering, direct, 1:1, non-transitive
A central transit hub every office connects to once Transit Gateway, hub-and-spoke for many VPCs
A service window into a shop, no street access PrivateLink / Private Service Connect, reach one service privately
An armored tunnel to your old headquarters VPN / Direct Connect / ExpressRoute, hybrid to on-prem
The shared phone book every building trusts Private DNS zones, internal names that resolve everywhere

Cloud networking primitives mapped to a city of buildings.

The picture: services, VPCs, and on-prem

Here is the topology most senior cloud engineers end up building. An application VPC reaches a managed service privately through PrivateLink, connects to other VPCs through a Transit Gateway, and reaches the on-prem data center over Direct Connect or a VPN, while a private DNS resolver makes internal names resolve from every side.

App VPC reaches a service via PrivateLink, peers VPCs through a Transit Gateway, links on-prem via Direct Connect/VPN, and resolves internal names via a private resolver.

  1. App makes a request to db.internal.acme.com: The app does not know or care whether the target is a managed service, another VPC, or on-prem. It just resolves a name.
  2. The private resolver answers: A private hosted zone returns a private IP, the PrivateLink endpoint's ENI, a peer VPC address, or (via a forwarding rule) an on-prem record.
  3. Traffic takes a private pipe: PrivateLink for a single service, the Transit Gateway for VPC-to-VPC, or Direct Connect/VPN for on-prem. Nothing crosses the public internet.
  4. Return path mirrors it: Route tables on both ends must point back the right way. Asymmetric routing, out one pipe, back another, is the silent killer here.

Private connectivity to services (PrivateLink / PSC)

PrivateLink (AWS) and Private Service Connect (GCP) solve one precise problem: reach a single service over private IP space without peering whole networks together. The provider exposes the service behind a load balancer; you create an endpoint in your VPC that materializes as a network interface (an ENI) with a private IP in your own subnet. Your traffic to that IP is tunneled to the service, no internet gateway, no public IP, no route changes between networks.

The win over peering is isolation and scale. Peering joins entire address spaces and forces you to manage overlapping CIDRs and bidirectional trust. PrivateLink exposes only the one service and is one-directional, the consumer reaches the provider, never the reverse. It is how you consume a SaaS vendor, another team's internal API, or an AWS service (S3, Secrets Manager) without your packets ever touching public routes. The trade-off: it is per-service, so it does not replace VPC-to-VPC routing for general traffic.

VPC peering vs Transit Gateway

VPC peering is a direct, point-to-point link between two VPCs. It is cheap and low-latency, but it is non-transitive: if A peers with B and B peers with C, A still cannot reach C. With N VPCs that all need to talk, you face N·(N-1)/2 peerings, a full mesh that becomes unmanageable past a handful.

Transit Gateway (AWS) / Cloud Router + VPC peering hubs (GCP) is a hub-and-spoke router. Each VPC attaches once to the hub, and the hub routes between all of them, and to on-prem over the same attachment model. It costs more (per-attachment and per-GB) and adds a hop, but it turns an O(N²) mesh into O(N) attachments and gives you one place to apply route tables and segmentation. Rule of thumb: 2-3 VPCs that rarely change, use peering; a growing fleet or anything hybrid, use a Transit Gateway.

Pattern Joins Transitive? Best when Watch out for
VPC Peering Two VPCs, full CIDRs No 2-3 stable VPCs, lowest cost/latency Mesh explosion; overlapping CIDRs block it
Transit Gateway Many VPCs + on-prem via a hub Yes (per route table) Growing fleet, central segmentation, hybrid Per-attachment + data cost; extra hop
PrivateLink / PSC Consumer → one service N/A Consume a SaaS/internal API/AWS service privately Per-service only; one-directional
VPN / Direct Connect Cloud ↔ on-prem Via TGW/router Reaching the data center VPN = internet-dependent; DX = lead time + cost

Pick the connectivity pattern by what you are actually joining.

Hybrid connectivity (VPN / Direct Connect / ExpressRoute)

Hybrid means joining your cloud network to your physical data center. Two grades exist. A site-to-site VPN runs an encrypted IPsec tunnel over the public internet, fast to stand up, cheap, but latency and throughput ride on the open internet, so it varies. Direct Connect (AWS) / ExpressRoute (Azure) / Cloud Interconnect (GCP) is a dedicated private circuit from a carrier into the cloud provider, consistent latency, higher bandwidth, lower per-GB cost at scale, but weeks of lead time and a monthly port fee.

The common production pattern is both: Direct Connect as the primary path for predictable performance, with a VPN as automatic failover if the circuit drops. Routes are usually exchanged via BGP, so each side learns the other's prefixes dynamically, which is exactly why your CIDR planning has to be disjoint from day one (more on that in mistakes).

Build it: a PrivateLink endpoint + private DNS zone

Here is a minimal Terraform setup: an interface endpoint (PrivateLink) for a service, plus a private hosted zone so a friendly internal name resolves to it. Scope this to your VPC and private subnets.

privatelink.tf

# Interface VPC endpoint (PrivateLink) into the provider's service
resource "aws_vpc_endpoint" "svc" {
  vpc_id              = aws_vpc.app.id
  service_name        = "com.amazonaws.vpce.eu-west-1.vpce-svc-0abc123"
  vpc_endpoint_type   = "Interface"
  subnet_ids          = aws_subnet.private[*].id
  security_group_ids  = [aws_security_group.endpoint.id]
  private_dns_enabled = true # service's own DNS name now resolves to the ENI

  tags = { Name = "svc-privatelink" }
}

# Lock the endpoint down: only the app tier may reach it on 443
resource "aws_security_group" "endpoint" {
  name   = "privatelink-endpoint"
  vpc_id = aws_vpc.app.id

  ingress {
    from_port       = 443
    to_port         = 443
    protocol        = "tcp"
    security_groups = [aws_security_group.app.id]
  }
}

private-dns.tf

# Private hosted zone, internal names that never leak to public DNS
resource "aws_route53_zone" "internal" {
  name = "internal.acme.com"

  vpc {
    vpc_id = aws_vpc.app.id # zone is only visible inside this VPC
  }
}

# Friendly alias pointing at the PrivateLink endpoint
resource "aws_route53_record" "db" {
  zone_id = aws_route53_zone.internal.zone_id
  name    = "db.internal.acme.com"
  type    = "A"

  alias {
    name                   = aws_vpc_endpoint.svc.dns_entry[0]["dns_name"]
    zone_id                = aws_vpc_endpoint.svc.dns_entry[0]["hosted_zone_id"]
    evaluate_target_health = true
  }
}

💡 Verify before you trust it: From an instance inside the VPC, run dig db.internal.acme.com, it must return a private (RFC 1918) address, not a public one. Then nc -vz db.internal.acme.com 443. If dig returns a public IP, your private DNS or private_dns_enabled isn't wired up.

How DNS actually resolves across the boundary

DNS is where hybrid setups quietly fall apart, because there are three name spaces, cloud private zones, on-prem internal zones, and the public internet, and every resolver has to know which one to ask for a given name.

Private hosted zones

A private zone (Route 53 private hosted zone / Cloud DNS private zone) is a DNS zone visible only inside the VPCs you associate with it. db.internal.acme.com resolves to a private IP for anything in the VPC and does not exist on the public internet. This is how you give services stable internal names without ever exposing them.

Split-horizon (split-brain) DNS

Split-horizon means the same name returns different answers depending on who asks. api.acme.com resolves to a private endpoint when queried from inside the VPC, and to a public load balancer when queried from the internet. You achieve it by running a public zone and a private zone for the same domain; the private zone wins for in-VPC queries. It is powerful, one hostname everywhere, but it is the single most confusing failure mode when someone debugs from the wrong network and gets the "other" answer.

Resolution across hybrid

For cloud and on-prem to resolve each other's names you need a resolver with forwarding rules: an inbound endpoint so on-prem can query cloud names, and an outbound endpoint with a conditional forwarder that says "send *.corp.local queries to the on-prem DNS server at 10.10.0.53." Without these, an instance in AWS asking for an on-prem hostname gets NXDOMAIN even though the network path is wide open.

Common mistakes that cost hours

  1. Overlapping CIDRs. Two VPCs (or a VPC and on-prem) using 10.0.0.0/16 cannot be peered or routed together, routing is ambiguous. Plan a disjoint IP address scheme across every VPC and data center before you build anything. This is the #1 retrofit nightmare.
  2. Exposing internal services publicly. Reaching for a public load balancer or a 0.0.0.0/0 security-group rule because "it was faster than PrivateLink." Internal APIs and databases should only ever be reachable over private paths, PrivateLink, peering, or the Transit Gateway.
  3. DNS works in cloud, fails to on-prem (or vice versa). Network path is open but names won't resolve, because there is no conditional forwarder / resolver endpoint bridging the two name spaces. Always test resolution from both sides.
  4. Split-horizon confusion. Debugging api.acme.com from your laptop (public answer) while the app inside the VPC gets the private answer, and concluding the app is broken. Always check which network the failing query came from.
  5. Asymmetric routing. Traffic leaves over the Transit Gateway and tries to return over a VPN, or the return route table never got the peer's CIDR. Stateful firewalls drop the reply. Confirm route tables point back symmetrically on both ends.
  6. Peering mesh sprawl. Adding the fifth, sixth, seventh peering by hand until nobody can reason about the topology. Move to a Transit Gateway hub the moment you outgrow a handful of VPCs.

Takeaways

The whole article in seven lines

  • Advanced networking = choosing pipes between services, VPCs, and on-prem, plus a shared DNS phone book.
  • PrivateLink / PSC: reach one service privately, one-directional, no CIDR entanglement.
  • Peering: cheap, direct, 1:1, non-transitive, fine for 2-3 stable VPCs.
  • Transit Gateway: hub-and-spoke that scales VPC-to-VPC and hybrid; turns O(N²) into O(N).
  • VPN = quick internet-based tunnel; Direct Connect/ExpressRoute = dedicated private circuit. Often both, with VPN as failover.
  • Private zones hide internal names; split-horizon serves the same name differently per network; forwarding rules bridge cloud and on-prem.
  • Plan disjoint CIDRs first, keep internal services off public paths, and test DNS from both sides.

Where to go next

Build the muscle memory hands-on, then zoom out to how this fits a real multi-account organization.

  • Practice routing, endpoints, and resolution in the Networking lab and the DNS lab.
  • Solidify the basics first if any of this felt shaky: Cloud Networking Fundamentals: How a VPC Actually Works.
  • See where these VPCs and connectivity live in a real org: Multi-Account / Landing Zone Strategy & Governance.
  • Map the full journey on the Cloud Engineer career path.

Originally published on TheSimplifiedTech, where this guide is interactive, with in-browser terminal labs and diagrams. Learn cloud and DevOps by doing, no videos.

title: Quick Start: C# and MongoDB - Starting and Setup
description:
In the first of the C# Quick Start series, I'll show how to set up connections between C# and MongoDB.

In future parts we'll move on and work through:

  • Database Create, Read, Update, and Delete (CRUD) operations
  • Map MongoDB to C# objects
  • Look at MongoDB aggregation
  • How to use LINQ with MongoDB

As you already know, C# is a general-purpose language and MongoDB is a general-purpose data platform. Together, C# and MongoDB are a powerful combination.

To follow along, I'll be using Visual Studio 2019 on Windows 10 and we will be connecting to a MongoDB Atlas cluster.

If you're using a different OS, IDE, or text editor, the walkthrough might be slightly different, but the code itself should be fairly similar. Let's jump in and take a look at how nicely C# and MongoDB work together.

Getting Setup

For this demonstration, I’ve chosen to create a Console App (.NET Core), and I’ve named it MongoDBConnectionDemo.

Next, we need to install the MongoDB Driver for C#/.NET for a Solution. We can do that quite easily with NuGet. Inside Visual Studio for Windows, by going to Tools -> NuGet Package Manager -> Manage NuGet Packages for Solution..._

We can browse for MongoDB.Driver. Then click on our Project and select the driver version we want. In this case, the latest stable version is 2.9.1. Then click on Install. Accept any license agreements that pop up and head back to Program.cs to get started.

Putting the Driver to Work

To use the MongoDB.Driver we need to add a directive.

Inside the Main() method we’ll establish a connection to MongoDB Atlas with a connection string and to test the connection we’ll print out a list of the databases on the server. The Atlas cluster to which we’ll be connecting has the MongoDB Atlas Sample Dataset installed, so we’ll be able to see a nice database list.

The first step is to pass in the MongoDB Atlas connection string into a MongoClient object, then we can get the list of databases and print them out.

When we run the program, we get the following out showing the list of databases:

The whole program comes in at just over 20 lines of code:

C# and MongoDB

By developing with C# and MongoDB together one opens up a world of possibilities. Console, window, and web applications are all possible. As are cross-platform mobile applications using the Xamarin framework. Join me in this Quick Start series and learn how to perform CRUD operations with C# and MongoDB.

title: Chat memory as a 41.9 MB file: building on MemT-1.0-Nano's save and reload
description:
Most chat backends resend the whole transcript to the model on every turn. MemT-1.0-Nano, an open model from MemTensor whose base model is the Qwen team's Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, works on a different contract. Turns you flag are folded into a block of numbers that never grows, and that block can be written to disk. In the test, a saved memory was loaded into a new session holding zero messages, and the model got all nine recall questions right. Every saved file weighed 41,944,024 bytes.

The tables and setup are in the full MemT-1.0-Nano memory file write-up on inferencekey.com; here is what you would build around it.

Your code chooses what the model keeps

The session API in MemTensor's modeling_memt.py treats remembering as an explicit call. Pass enable_memory=True and that turn is committed into the memory state and its text discarded. Other turns stay in the session as ordinary text. Shortened from the model card:

session.chat("<facts to remember>", enable_memory=True, enable_thinking=False)
session.save_state("dana.safetensors")
restored = model.create_session(tokenizer, state="dana.safetensors")
print(len(restored.messages))  # 0

Which turns deserve the flag is product logic you write. Tokens are the word pieces a model reads, and in the restored session the input for each question went from 27 tokens to 210 over four questions, because the questions themselves were never flagged and piled up as text. Flag nothing and the transcript is back.

By default save_state will not overwrite an existing file, so plan your naming.

Disk gets worse, rereading gets better

As text on disk, the made-up bakery owner's history in the test was 107 tokens, a few hundred bytes. The memory file is 41.9 MB no matter what.

It competes instead with the working memory a regular model rebuilds from the whole history and holds on the GPU while the session is open. According to the storage arithmetic in the MemT-1.0-Nano research post, the fixed file only beats it once the history passes roughly 2,000 tokens, and at 128K tokens it is about 64 times smaller. For speed, MemTensor's paper has Nano losing on short histories, breaking even near 32,000 tokens and pulling ahead by about 1.86 times at 128K. The test measured neither.

On one A100 80 GB, loading took 1.35 to 1.99 seconds and saving 0.66 to 1.02. Generating was slow: answering a "remember" turn with 128 tokens took about 13 seconds on the stock Hugging Face code, without the optional faster GPU components and with no tuning.

Two traps worth knowing first

Compressing to 8 bits does not get you onto a smaller GPU. The weights normally run in bf16, a 16-bit number format. With the A100 limited to what a 48 GB card offers, the 8-bit load ran out of memory after asking for about 64 GiB. With the limit removed it loaded, and the first "remember" call then died with a dtype (number type) mismatch. The cause is in the architecture. Each layer holds 256 experts (sub-networks the model picks between per token), stored as fused 3D parameters rather than nn.Linear layers, so the bitsandbytes 8-bit library skips them and the saving is about 2 GiB. The 48 GB case was emulated with a cap, and no other shrinking method was tried. With no official compressed release, budget for an 80 GB GPU.

Load by repo id, not from the Hugging Face cache folder. trust_remote_code lets Transformers, the Hugging Face Python library, run the model's own Python files. Pointing it at the downloaded snapshot directory fails with "file not found": Transformers follows the modeling_memt.py symlink into blobs/ and looks for the relative import there. Loading by repo id with a pinned revision avoids it.

Behind an API, the state file will not fit a result payload capped at 8 MB. In the InferenceKey backend it stays on the worker's disk (the worker is the program running the model on the GPU machine), and the API returns its size and sha256.

Two licenses, two answers

The Nano weights carry Apache-2.0, which permits commercial use. MemTensor's own code on GitHub, the two-GPU memt-sglang server included, is under PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0. The test ran the Apache-2.0 code from the Hugging Face repo, the slow path.

What a pilot should measure

Every recall question in the test asked for a short fact given to the model moments earlier. That shows the round trip works, not memory over months. MemTensor is open about this: text-based memory systems still lead, above all on long histories where a precise detail has to be found. On the LongMemEval-S benchmark the paper puts Nano at 32.6, while sending the whole conversation scores 76.8. On your own data, check:

  • Exact details from early in long histories, compared with a text store.
  • Whether many memory writes over time push older facts out. Nobody has tested it.
  • Behavior with several sessions at once. The test sent one request at a time.

The hosted InferenceKey endpoint was not tested either: the run used a local test copy of InferenceKey and a worker on a GPU on our cloud.

Credit goes to MemTensor for the model, the trained memory block, the session API and the MemT-1.0 paper, to the Qwen team for the base model, and to Hugging Face Transformers for running the custom code. We found the model through the AI Search news video and an r/LocalLLaMA thread. We wrote the custom backend, found the load fix and ran the tests. To repeat the round trip on your own NVIDIA machine, the SDK example for the MemT-1.0-Nano backend runs it end to end.

The GPU memory results, every timing, the paper's benchmark numbers and the open issues are in the MemT-1.0-Nano research article on inferencekey.com.

title: I built a bot that plays my Unreal game and files the bugs
description:
I'm making an indie game in Unreal Engine 5.8, and like most solo developers I have a testing problem: nobody walks the whole game after every change. I do it for ten minutes, see nothing wrong, and ship the build. So I wrote a bot to do the boring part, and I'm releasing it as open source. It is called PlayGoblin, and it is pre-release (0.1.0-dev), so please read the limits section before you get excited.

A real 150 s run on my game, shown as a 3x time-lapse of seconds 19 to 52 (overlay added by me). The full run walked 251 m and reached 19 waypoints, but covered only 12.0% of the 1137 walkable cells; it logged 1 confirmed and 12 unconfirmed stuck spots. Coverage in the overlay is derived from sampled positions. The goblin is not a speedrunner yet.

The problem

Unit tests check what you thought to assert. Recorded input replays only cover the path you recorded and break when the level changes. Manual QA is great, but it does not run at 3 a.m. after every commit. The gap I care about is "nobody walked there": a stuck spot behind a prop, a fall through a missing collision, a menu button wired to nothing, a TODO that made it into a title screen.

What PlayGoblin is

An engine-side component walks the game and writes a plain run folder: events.jsonl plus a summary. A Python CLI reads that folder and produces findings, an HTML report, and optionally GitHub issues. Each finding has evidence, meaning an event, a frame, or a log line. If the bot cannot show it, it does not report it.

There are engine sides for Unity (6000.4 tested) and Unreal (5.8.3 Win64 tested). Any other engine that can write the run-folder format (documented in docs/PROTOCOL.md) gets the same checks and reports. I tested that with a fake Godot-style run, not a real Godot game.

The bugs it found on my game

I ran it on my Unreal game this week. Three results are worth telling honestly.

The player could not move. The game had no input bound to move the pawn. The bot, which reads the game's own key and axis bindings and presses the keys that should move the player, never left the spawn point and reported "The player never moved" as critical.

A bug in the bot, found by the game. My game has a level-sized invisible blocking volume. It hid the ground from every floor probe, so the bot saw nothing walkable. That was a bug in PlayGoblin, not in the game, and the fix is that the bot now skips actors it starts inside and logs them. Real games are weirder than sample projects, and this is why I am asking for run folders from yours.

Grey-box look. It lists visible actors still using /Engine/BasicShapes meshes or the engine grid material and reports each as "Prototype look". It is a cheap way to see how much of a level is still placeholder art.

On the Unreal sample project, which has bugs I planted, it also finds a UMG "Options" button that does nothing and menu text reading "TODO: title". Another false positive taught me something: it flagged a pastel-pink game as missing-material pink. Now only pure magenta counts.

How it works

It plays through real input. In key mode (-PlayGoblinKeys) it presses the game's bound keys, turns with simulated mouse movement rather than setting the camera, taps action keys at irregular intervals, and tries a jump when stuck. If nothing moves the player, or the mouse does nothing after repeated probes, that is itself a finding (dead_input).

It crawls UMG menus. About every two seconds it finds visible widgets, reports placeholder text, and clicks each enabled button once. A button is dead if nothing observable changed within a second.

It explores on purpose. Instead of random destinations it heads for the nearest unvisited ground next to what it has already seen. On the sample project, same seed and 150 seconds, coverage went from 34% to 73% on one level and from 48% to 93% on the other. Every report prints coverage.

The checks have no LLM in them. Each check is a pure function: run folder in, findings out. The same events give the same findings every time, and there are 62 Python tests. A stuck spot only counts as confirmed once it repeats, so one unlucky run does not file a fake bug. An LLM can optionally write a summary paragraph, labelled as such.

Agents can drive it. There is an MCP server (playgoblin mcp) with five tools: status, run, report, findings and file_issues. The repo is also a Claude Code plugin with a skill that teaches an agent when to run it and how to read confidence. Filing GitHub issues is a dry run unless you explicitly confirm.


The HTML report: each finding links to its evidence.

Quickstart 

pip install "git+https://github.com/grloper/playgoblin#subdirectory=cli"   # Python 3.11+

Unreal: copy unreal/PlayGoblin into your project's Plugins/ and launch the game with the flag:

UnrealEditor-Cmd.exe MyGame.uproject -game -playgoblin -PlayGoblinSeconds=300 -PlayGoblinSeed=1 -PlayGoblinOut=D:/runs -PlayGoblinExit
playgoblin report D:/runs/<run id>     # report.html, report.md, findings.json

Unity: add the package from https://github.com/grloper/playgoblin.git?path=/unity, put the PlayGoblin Player component on your player, press Play, then playgoblin run --minutes 10 --runs 3.

The plugin does nothing unless -playgoblin is on the command line, so shipping with it enabled is harmless.

Honest limits

  • It is pre-release. Unity 6000.4 and Unreal 5.8.3 on Win64 are the only tested combinations.
  • Accuracy on real games is not measured. My samples were written by the people who wrote the checks, so treat them as regression tests. The Unreal plugin passed its sample (all 5 planted bugs, nothing on the clean twin) on one seed and one machine.
  • UMG buttons are clicked by broadcasting OnClicked, so Slate hit testing is not exercised; Enhanced-Input-driven and CommonUI-only menus are not covered.
  • It walks and clicks. It does not judge fun, balance, visuals or audio, and "no findings" never means bug free.

Try it, and help

The most useful contribution right now is running it on a game and telling me what it missed or got wrong, with the run folder attached. Open an issue at https://github.com/grloper/playgoblin. Roadmap items: more real-game runs with published precision numbers, other Unreal versions and Enhanced Input, Unity UI Toolkit and player builds, and a GitHub Action. If you build for another engine, the run-folder format is short; a writer for it is a good first contribution.

title: Three CSS rules for Arabic RTL: one was a no-op, one reversed the reversal
description:
When I added Arabic to my app, I did what the tutorials tell you to do: flip dir, add a couple of rules for inputs, mirror the tab bar, done. Ten lines of CSS in a 258-line stylesheet. I shipped it, looked at a screenshot, saw the text sitting on the right side of the screen, and called RTL "supported".

Months later I sat down to audit it properly. The audit started with the three rules in that block. Two of them do not do what I thought they did.

This post is what I measured, how I measured it, and the checklist I ended up with. It applies to any app that ships an RTL locale, not just mine.

The ten lines

Here is the entire RTL section of my stylesheet, comments included:

/* direction:rtl makes text right-align and reverses flex rows automatically.
   Do not add text-align:right to h1/p/button — it breaks centered elements. */
[dir="rtl"] {
  direction: rtl;
}
[dir="rtl"] input,
[dir="rtl"] textarea {
  text-align: right;
}
[dir="rtl"] .tab-bar {
  flex-direction: row-reverse;
}

Three rules, three declarations: direction, text-align, flex-direction. The switch itself is one line in React:

useEffect(() => {
  document.documentElement.lang = language;
  document.documentElement.dir = language === 'ar' ? 'rtl' : 'ltr';
}, [language]);

If you have written RTL support before, you already noticed the contradiction: my own comment says direction:rtl reverses flex rows automatically, and then the third rule reverses them again.

How I measured it

I did not want to reason from the spec and hope. I built a throwaway probe page, opened it in the browser I actually ship in (Chrome 156), and read the layout back with offsetLeft:

function build(dirCss, flex) {
  const w = document.createElement('div');
  w.style.cssText = `width:320px;display:flex;flex-direction:${flex};direction:${dirCss}`;
  for (const n of ['A', 'B', 'C']) {
    const s = document.createElement('span');
    s.textContent = n;
    w.appendChild(s);
  }
  document.body.appendChild(w);
  return w;
}
const order = w =>
  [...w.children].sort((a, b) => a.offsetLeft - b.offsetLeft).map(e => e.textContent).join('');

Four configurations, four answers, in the order children were appended as A B C:

configuration visual order, left to right
direction: ltr + row ABC
direction: rtl + row CBA
direction: rtl + row-reverse ABC
direction: ltr + row-reverse CBA

Row 2 is the behaviour my comment describes correctly. Row 3 is what my stylesheet actually applies to the tab bar. row follows the inline base direction, so under RTL row already lays children right-to-left; row-reverse means "opposite of the inline direction", which under RTL is left-to-right. Stacking them gives you back the LTR order.

So the third rule does not mirror my tab bar. It un-mirrors it. My four tabs — Create, My Names, Daily Fortune, Profile — sit in exactly the same left-to-right order in Arabic as they do in English. If the intent was "Arabic users get a mirrored bar", the rule delivered the opposite; if the intent was "the bar should look like the English one", then the rule is redundant, because the browser was going to draw it mirrored and I had to actively cancel that.

Either way, the fix is the same one-liner: delete the rule.

The second rule was a no-op

text-align: right on inputs. I added it because the first screenshot showed typed text sitting against the wrong edge... except it could not have, because direction on an ancestor already does this.

I checked instead of arguing with myself:

const d = document.createElement('div'); d.dir = 'rtl'; d.textContent = 'نص';
getComputedStyle(d).textAlign;          // "start"

const inp = document.createElement('input'); inp.dir = 'rtl';
getComputedStyle(inp).textAlign;        // "start"

Computed value is start, in both cases. start is a direction-relative keyword: it resolves to the right under RTL and to the left under LTR. The initial value of text-align is already start, so under direction: rtl a text block or an input is already right-aligned before I touch it. My rule sets a value that is, by definition, where the text already was.

Delete it. Three rules become one.

I want to be precise about why this matters, because "harmless dead CSS" is not the interesting part. The interesting part is that I wrote this block by pattern-matching tutorials, and the two rules that felt most load-bearing were the two that did nothing. The single line that actually carries RTL — direction: rtl — is the one I would have written from first principles in thirty seconds. The rest was ceremony that made the diff look like work.

The real problem was outside that file

Once the block was reduced to one line, I went looking for the directional assumptions that actually ship. I scanned the src tree (excluding generated data) for physical declarations. React inline styles are where all my layout lives, so this is where the answer is:

declaration count
textAlign: 'left' 15
textAlign: 'right' 1
paddingLeft 8
borderLeft 8
left / right 9
marginLeft / marginRight 3
translateX 2
total physical 46
marginInline / paddingInline / insetInline / InlineStart / InlineEnd 2

Two. Both are insetInlineEnd on absolutely positioned badges. So the ratio is 46 to 2, and — this is the part that stings — the two prove that the logical syntax works fine in React. insetInlineEnd is just a camelCase property. There was never a tooling reason to write the other 46 the physical way. It was habit.

In the stylesheet the number is smaller but the ratio is the same: 2 physical declarations, 0 logical ones.

Note that not every physical value is a bug. Eight of my nine left/right values are direction-agnostic: four left: 50% with a negative margin-left to center an element, and two left: 0; right: 0 pairs that stretch a bar across the full width. Only one is asymmetric — a single left: 64% keyframe waypoint inside a decorative animation. This is why I prefer counting over grepping: the count gives you the surface area, the inspection tells you which entries matter.

What the quote bars look like in Arabic

The eight borderLeft + paddingLeft pairs are the ones I actually saw on screen. They are all the same pattern:

<div style={{ borderLeft: '2px solid rgba(212,168,67,0.4)', paddingLeft: 12 }}>

Seven in one long-read screen, one more on a name detail card. In English this draws the familiar quote bar: a gold rule on the left, 12px of breathing room, text to the right of it. In Arabic the text starts at the right edge, so the gold rule ends up on the far side of the paragraph — visually detached from the thing it is supposed to anchor, and the 12px gap is now on the wrong side of the text as well. The block still reads; it just looks like a mistake, because the one element that carries "this is a quote" is pointing away from the reading edge.

The fix is two tokens:

<div style={{ borderInlineStart: '2px solid rgba(212,168,67,0.4)', paddingInlineStart: 12 }}>

Same pixels in ten locales, correct edge in the eleventh. borderInlineStart has been in every engine I target for years; there is no excuse left except that I typed borderLeft out of muscle memory seven times.

Of 67 textAlign declarations, 16 are physical (15 left, 1 right) and 50 are center, which is direction-neutral. So roughly a quarter of my alignment decisions hard-code a side. Some of those are inside deliberately LTR blocks — a pinyin line, a numeric stat row — and are correct as written. The rest are just untranslated assumptions.

RTL also lives in the strings, not only in the CSS

The part that no amount of CSS fixes: the text itself. My Arabic locale file holds 202 translated strings and 5,361 Arabic characters, and here is what the same scan found in it:

  • 0 strings use Arabic-Indic digits (٠١٢٣). 35 strings contain ASCII digits.
  • 18 strings mix Latin letters into Arabic sentences — brand names, Apple ID, product nouns.
  • 23 strings use the Arabic comma ،. 2 still use ASCII , ; : ? !.
  • 3 strings contain →, which does not mirror.

The digit choice is a product decision, and Western digits are the common choice in modern Gulf and Egyptian interfaces, so having zero Arabic-Indic digits is defensible. What is not defensible is that it is a decision nobody made: it fell out of what the translator typed. Pick one convention, write it in the style guide, and audit against it — otherwise you will ship a screen with ٠١٢ next to 012 two releases from now.

The arrow is a subtler one. → is U+2192, which is bidi class ON (other neutral), and — unlike matched brackets — it has no mirrored counterpart in Unicode's bidi mirroring table. Browsers do not flip it for you. So a string like:

أدر اشتراكك في الإعدادات → Apple ID → الاشتراكات

reads right-to-left ("manage your subscription in Settings, then Apple ID, then Subscriptions") while every arrow points right, which in RTL is backwards along the reading direction. The sentence tells you to go left, the punctuation says right. Either reverse the arrow in the Arabic string (←), or replace it with a non-directional separator like · or > wrapped in a <bdi>.

Same family of problem, one level down: in one string I interpolate a rank as المرتبة #${rank}. # is also neutral, so it takes its direction from context, and depending on what surrounds it you get #96 or 96#. The fix is boring and reliable — wrap the number:

<span dir="ltr">{rank}</span>

The suspicious thing that turned out to be fine

I had flagged 29 letterSpacing declarations as an Arabic risk. Arabic is a cursive script: letters join, and in some engines letter-spacing is applied between joined letters, which visually tears words apart. It is a real phenomenon and I have seen it in the wild.

So I measured it instead of assuming, with a 28px system font:

text letter-spacing: normal letter-spacing: 1px delta
محمد (4 letters) 65.46px 65.46px 0.00px
mmmm (Latin control) 91.49px 95.49px +4.00px

Chrome applies letter-spacing to the Latin run and drops it on the cursive Arabic run — the width is identical to two decimal places, which means no extra advance was inserted between any of the four joined letters. Shaping is untouched. The 29 declarations cost me nothing.

I am keeping this in the post because it is the most useful result in the audit: I had a plausible theory, I could have spent an afternoon migrating 29 style objects to a conditional letterSpacing, and measurement said the entire refactor was unnecessary. It also gives me a baseline: if a future engine version starts applying spacing there, the width probe will catch it in one line.

What I have now

The block that started this is one line:

[dir="rtl"] { direction: rtl; }

Everything else moved to logical properties in the components that needed them, and the remaining work is a list, not a vibe:

  1. Grep for textAlign: 'left' | 'right', paddingLeft, paddingRight, marginLeft, marginRight, borderLeft, borderRight, left:, right:, translateX — in the stylesheet and in inline style objects.
  2. For each hit, decide: symmetric (center, 0/0 inset) → leave it; asymmetric → logical property.
  3. Delete any [dir=rtl] override for something the browser already handles (direction covers alignment, flex order, and inline-start insets).
  4. Audit the locale file: digit convention, punctuation convention, and every non-mirrored glyph (→ ← ▸ •) inside translated sentences.
  5. Wrap numbers interpolated into RTL sentences in dir="ltr".
  6. Declare an Arabic-capable font stack instead of inheriting the Latin one.

That last item is still open in my app. My --font-sans is five Latin-first families (-apple-system, SF Pro Text, Helvetica Neue, …) and my --font-cn is a Chinese chain (PingFang, Microsoft YaHei). Neither lists a single Arabic face, and the only @font-face I ship is a Chinese brush font. Arabic therefore renders in whatever the operating system substitutes — fine on iOS, different metrics on Android, and I have never measured it. My plan is an explicit Naskh/Kufi fallback in the stack plus, if the metrics drift too far, one self-hosted Arabic face; both are measurable before and after with the same width probe I used above.

The broader lesson is the one I keep relearning: "it looks right in the screenshot" is not a test. I looked at a screenshot in Arabic, saw the text on the right, and concluded RTL was done. Ten lines of CSS, two of them inert, one of them actively cancelling the browser. The screenshot could not tell me any of that, and offsetLeft told me all of it in under a minute.

I build NameSoul, a Chinese-name app whose past-life stories ship in 10 languages, Arabic included — which is how this audit happened in the first place.

Wan 3.0 from Alibaba is now available on AI Gateway as alibaba/wan-v3.0-video.

Wan 3.0 combines text-to-video, image-to-video, first- and last-frame conditioning, and reference-based generation in one model. References can include images, video, and audio. It generates clips up to 30 seconds at 30 fps in 480p, 720p, or 1080p, with synchronized audio.

Generate a video

Wan 3.0 supports asynchronous generation, so no HTTP request needs to remain open for the entire render.

Pass a webhook to receive an event when the generation finishes:

Learn about asynchronous generation options in the docs, including how to verify webhook deliveries.

Add references

Pass image, video, or audio references through inputReferences, including the source and media type for each one. Images accept hosted URLs or base64. Video and audio references require hosted URLs.

First- and last-frame conditioning accepts one image for each frame and can't be combined with other references.

title: Paste the failing Network panel into the agent, not a vague “API broken”
description:
I used to type “the API is broken” into the agent and watch it invent three wrong theories: CORS, a stale token, a missing header that was never missing. Then it rewrote the fetch wrapper “just in case.”

The bug was usually sitting in DevTools the whole time — a red row in the Network panel with a status, a request URL, and a response body I never pasted.

So I stopped narrating. I paste the failing request.

What I actually paste

Not a screenshot. Text the model can grep.

From the failed request in Network:

  1. Method + URL (full path, query string included)
  2. Status (and status text if useful)
  3. Request headers that matter — Authorization redacted to Bearer ***, Content-Type, any custom X-* the API cares about
  4. Request payload (trimmed if huge)
  5. Response body (or the first ~2KB if it’s a wall of HTML)
  6. Timing note — “fails only after hard refresh” / “only on the second click” / “only in the deployed preview”

Example of what goes in the prompt:

Failed request (Chrome Network → Copy as fetch, then edited):

POST https://api.example.com/v1/orders?include=line_items
Status: 422 Unprocessable Entity

Request headers:
  Content-Type: application/json
  Authorization: Bearer ***
  X-Idempotency-Key: ord_9f3a…

Request body:
  {"sku":"tee-blue","qty":2,"promo":"SPRING"}

Response body:
  {"error":"promo_expired","message":"SPRING ended 2026-03-01","code":42201}

Repro: fails every time from the cart Checkout button; same payload works in curl from my machine against staging.

That’s enough for the agent to aim at promo validation instead of “rewrite the client.”

Why “API broken” wastes a whole turn

Vague prompts invite architecture fanfic. The model doesn’t know if:

  • the browser never sent the request
  • the request left and got 401
  • you got 200 with an empty array
  • the UI ignored a successful response

Each of those is a different fix. Without the Network row, the agent picks a story and starts editing the wrong file.

I’ve also seen it “fix” client code that was fine while the real issue was a 307 to the wrong host after a env typo. The Network panel would’ve ended that in ten seconds.

Tiny workflow I reuse

  1. Reproduce once with Network open (Preserve log on).
  2. Right-click the red/failed row → Copy → Copy as fetch (or copy URL + response).
  3. Paste into the agent prompt before any “please fix” prose.
  4. Add one sentence of expected vs actual: “expected 201 + order id; got 422 promo_expired.”
  5. Ban drive-by refactors: “Do not rewrite the fetch client unless the response proves the client is wrong.”

If I’m in a hurry I still paste status + URL + response JSON. Headers and body are the upgrade when that isn’t enough.

What I reject from the agent

  • “Maybe it’s CORS” with no OPTIONS / ACAO evidence in what I pasted
  • A new retry/backoff layer when the server returned a clear 422 business error
  • Silent swaps of the base URL “to match docs” without showing the failing host
  • Deleting the idempotency header because “it might confuse the API”

If the pasted response already names the bug (promo_expired), the patch should touch promo handling — not the transport layer.

Prompt add-on that keeps it honest 

Use only the Network evidence below. List: (1) failing hop, (2) status meaning, (3) smallest client or server change that matches the response body.
If evidence is missing (no status / no URL / no body), ask for it — do not invent a root cause.
Do not refactor unrelated fetch utilities.

Tiny habit

Next time a UI call “just fails,” don’t describe the feeling. Copy the failing Network row into the agent: method, URL, status, payload, response.

Agents are decent at reading HTTP. They’re terrible at reading your mind when all you said was “API broken.”

title: React Hot Toast: Simple Notifications for React Apps
description:
Every React developer eventually runs into the same problem: something happens in the application, and the user needs to know about it.

A form gets submitted successfully. An API request fails. A record gets deleted. A file finishes uploading. These are small interactions, but they make a real difference to how an application feels.

The obvious solution is to display a message. But building a good notification system from scratch means dealing with positioning, animations, dismiss behavior, stacking multiple messages, loading states, and accessibility. Using browser alerts is easier, but they interrupt the user and don't fit naturally into a modern interface.

This is where React Hot Toastcomes in.

React Hot Toast is a lightweight notification library for React that lets developers display success messages, errors, loading indicators, and custom notifications with minimal code. Instead of building the entire notification system yourself, you can install the library, add a single component, and trigger notifications wherever they're needed.

In this article, we'll explore how React Hot Toast works, how to integrate it into a React application, how to handle asynchronous API requests, and how to use notifications without making the user experience noisy or confusing.
We'll focus on practical implementation and the decisions developers make in real projects, rather than spending time on unnecessary UI boilerplate.

"Simplicity is the ultimate sophistication." - Leonardo da Vinci

Why Notifications Matter in React Applications

Imagine submitting a form to create a new customer. The button spins for a moment, the request completes, and the form clears. But nothing tells the user whether the operation actually succeeded.

Now imagine the same interaction with a notification saying, "Customer created successfully."

The second experience is clearer because the application communicates what happened.

Notifications are especially useful for actions that don't require a full page transition. They provide immediate feedback while allowing users to continue working without navigating away from their current screen.

Common examples include form submissions, CRUD operations, authentication feedback, file uploads, clipboard actions, background processes, and failed API requests.

However, notifications should be used thoughtfully. A toast is appropriate for a brief confirmation, but it isn't a replacement for inline form validation, a persistent error message, or a confirmation dialog before a destructive action.

The goal is not to show a message after every interaction. The goal is to give users the information they need at the right moment.

Why React Hot Toast?

React Hot Toast keeps the implementation simple while providing useful features out of the box. Its official documentation highlights customizable notifications, promise-based notifications, accessibility support, and custom rendering.

Some of its most useful capabilities include:

  • Simple API:Display a notification with a single function call.
  • Built-in notification types:Handle success, error, loading, and regular messages.
  • Promise support:Automatically update a notification as an asynchronous operation progresses.
  • Custom styling:Adjust placement, duration, appearance, and content.
  • Centralized rendering:Manage notifications through a shared component.
  • Custom components:Render richer notification content when a plain message isn't enough.

These features make React Hot Toast useful for dashboards, admin panels, SaaS applications, e-commerce interfaces, and other React-based products.

The biggest advantage is not simply that the notifications look good. It is that developers can add consistent feedback without creating another collection of custom components and state-management logic.

Key Takeaways

  • React Hot Toast provides a straightforward way to add notifications to React applications.
  • The component provides the notification rendering layer, while toast()triggers messages.
  • Built-in methods such as toast.success(), toast.error(), and toast.loading()cover common use cases.
  • toast.promise()simplifies feedback for asynchronous operations such as API requests.
  • Global configuration helps maintain consistent notification placement, styling, and duration.
  • Notifications should complement form validation and error handling, not replace them.
  • Good notification design means communicating meaningful changes without overwhelming users.
