title: Class and Object in Java
description:
Introduction

Java is an object-oriented programming language. In Java, Class and Object are two important concepts used to organize code and develop applications.

Before understanding Class and Object, let's take a real-world example.

Imagine a car manufacturing company. Before manufacturing a car, the company needs a design or blueprint. The blueprint describes how the car should look and what features it should have. Using that blueprint, the company can manufacture many cars.

In Java, a class works like a blueprint, and an object represents an actual instance created using that blueprint.

What is a Class in Java?

A class is a blueprint or template used to create objects. It defines the properties and behaviours that objects can have.

For example, a car has some properties, such as brand, colour, and speed. It also has behaviours, such as starting, stopping, and moving.

In Java, we can define these properties and behaviours inside a class.

Example: 

class Car {

    // Properties
    String brand;
    String color;
    int speed;

    // Behaviours
    void start() {
        System.out.println("Car is starting");
    }

    void stop() {
        System.out.println("Car is stopping");
    }
}

In this example:

  • Car is the class name.
  • brand, color, and speed are variables that represent the car's properties.
  • start() and stop() are methods that represent the car's behaviours.

A class only defines the structure. It does not automatically create an actual car object.

What is an Object in Java?

An object is an instance of a class. It represents a particular entity with its own identity, state, and behaviour.

For example, consider two cars. One car is a BMW with a black colour, and another is an Audi with a white colour.

Both cars can be represented using the same Car class, but their details are different.

In Java, objects are commonly created using the new keyword.

Example: 

Car c1 = new Car();

Here:

  • Car is the class name.
  • c1 is a reference variable.
  • new is the keyword used to create an object.
  • Car() calls the constructor.

The reference variable c1 refers to the newly created Car object.

How to Create and Use Objects in Java?

After creating a class, we can create an object and access its variables and methods using the dot (.) operator.

Let's understand this with a Student example.

Example: 

class Student {

    String name;
    int age;

    void study() {
        System.out.println(name + " is studying");
    }
}

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Student s1 = new Student();

        s1.name = "Abishek";
        s1.age = 21;

        System.out.println("Name: " + s1.name);
        System.out.println("Age: " + s1.age);

        s1.study();
    }
}

Output: 

Name: Abishek
Age: 21
Abishek is studying

In this program, a Student class is created with two variables, name and age, and a method called study().

First, an object called s1 is created using the new keyword. Then, values are assigned to its variables.

Finally, the study() method is called using the object reference.

The dot operator is used to access the object's variables and methods.

Creating Multiple Objects from One Class

One of the useful features of classes is that we can create multiple objects using a single class.

For example, a college management application may contain hundreds of students. Instead of creating a separate class for every student, we can create one Student class and use it to create multiple student objects.

Example: 

class Student {

    String name;
    int age;

    void display() {
        System.out.println(name + " - " + age);
    }
}

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Student s1 = new Student();
        Student s2 = new Student();

        s1.name = "Abishek";
        s1.age = 21;

        s2.name = "Arun";
        s2.age = 22;

        s1.display();
        s2.display();
    }
}

Output: 

Abishek - 21
Arun - 22

Here, both objects are created using the same Student class. However, each object maintains its own values for name and age.

This makes it easier to manage multiple students using a single class.

Difference Between Class and Object

Class and Object are related concepts, but they have different purposes.

Class Object
A class is a blueprint or template. An object is an instance of a class.
It defines properties and behaviours. It has its own data and behaviour.
It is declared using the class keyword. It is commonly created using the new keyword.
One class can create multiple objects. Each object represents a particular instance.
Example: Student Example: s1, s2

For example, Student is a class, while individual students can be represented as different objects of that class.

Why Do We Use Classes and Objects?

Classes and objects help developers organize programs and represent real-world entities.

Some important advantages are:

1. Code Reusability

A single class can be used to create multiple objects without writing the same structure repeatedly.

2. Code Organization

Related variables and methods can be grouped together inside a class.

3. Easy Maintenance

Organized code is easier to understand, modify, and maintain.

4. Real-World Representation

Real-world entities such as students, employees, cars, products, and bank accounts can be represented using classes and objects.

5. Object-Oriented Programming

Classes and objects provide the foundation for important OOP concepts such as inheritance, encapsulation, polymorphism, and abstraction.

Conclusion

Class and Object are the basic building blocks of object-oriented programming in Java. A class defines the structure and behaviours, while an object represents an instance created using that class.

Classes help organize related data and methods, while objects allow us to work with individual entities and their data.

Understanding these concepts is important for developing Java applications and learning advanced object-oriented programming concepts.

title: Everyone is building AI agents. Who’s designing the stop button?
description:
We used to design predictable user flows. Now AI can interpret, decide, and act on its own. Here’s why the hardest design decisions happen where that autonomy ends.

In September 2025, researchers at Thinking Machines Lab ran the same prompt through a language model 1,000 times. They set the temperature to zero, a setting that should, in theory, make token selection deterministic.

They got 80 different completions from the same prompt, model, and settings.

What’s even more interesting is that all 1,000 outputs were identical for the first 102 tokens. The differences started at token 103, when the model described where Richard Feynman was born.

The researchers traced the variation to how computations were performed under different server batching conditions. With a modified implementation, they eventually got all 1,000 outputs to match.

Their research demonstrated something important. Even when you try to make a language model behave predictably, the infrastructure running it can introduce variation.

Now imagine building a product on top of that model. One that creates freight bookings, updates customer records, or moves medical documents between systems.

The problem isn’t that AI can produce different answers. That’s often exactly why we’re using it.

The problem starts when those answers turn into actions, and nobody has decided which parts of the process are allowed to be unpredictable.

For decades, we designed software around the assumption that we knew what would happen next. AI is making that assumption increasingly difficult to maintain. And I think a lot of early-stage teams are still designing as if nothing has changed.

—

We used to know what would happen next

Think about how we’ve designed digital products for the last few decades.

You open an app, select something, complete a form, click a button, and move to the next step. The interface responds according to predefined rules.

A flight booking is a good example. Select your destination, choose a date, pick a flight, enter passenger details, pay, and receive confirmation.

There might be hundreds of conditions behind that experience, but the designer and engineering team can define them in advance. If the payment fails, show an error. If a seat is unavailable, offer another. If information is missing, ask the user to complete it.

This is the thinking that shaped most of our design tools and methods. User flows, wireframes, journey maps, information architecture, design systems, and interactive prototypes.

We design states and transitions between them. We decide what happens when someone clicks a button, makes a mistake, or returns to an unfinished process.

Traditional software was never perfectly deterministic. Search results changed, recommendations were personalized, and external services could fail. But the core behavior of most transactional interfaces was defined by explicit rules.

The designer didn’t need to know which flight someone would book. They needed to know how booking a flight worked.

What’s interesting is that the idea of software moving beyond explicit commands is not new. In 1993, Jakob Nielsen wrote about noncommand user interfaces. He described systems that could infer what users wanted instead of requiring them to communicate everything through specific commands. That was more than 30 years ago.

We’ve been imagining software that understands intention for decades. We just couldn’t build many of those experiences in a commercially practical way.

Now we can and that changes what it means to design a user flow.

—

The user no longer has to define every step

Imagine you’re designing a reporting tool.

Previously, a user would select data, configure filters, choose a report format, generate the report, and download it. The interface existed to collect instructions.

Today, someone can simply write: “Tell me why our conversion dropped last month and what we should investigate.”

The product can interpret the request, retrieve information, compare periods, identify patterns, and decide how to present the findings.

We removed five steps from the interface, but we introduced a completely different kind of complexity.

What if the data is incomplete? What if two dashboards define conversion differently? What if the AI produces a convincing explanation that is actually incorrect?

A traditional user flow doesn’t fully capture these possibilities because the system can now make decisions about how to approach the task.

This is also where the difference between AI adoption and actual automation becomes interesting.

According to the 2026 Stanford AI Index, 88% of surveyed organizations reported using AI in 2025, up from 55% in 2023. Yet scaled AI agent deployment remained in the single digits across nearly all business functions.

Companies are using AI, but letting it run meaningful business processes is a very different challenge.

There’s a big difference between asking AI to draft an email and allowing it to send that email to 4,000 customers.

This is where UX becomes much more important than simply making the interface look intelligent.

—

Non-deterministic vs deterministic

I think it’s worth clarifying the terminology because we tend to mix these things together.

A deterministic system follows predefined logic. Given the same relevant input and state, the same rules produce the same output.

A non-deterministic system can produce different outcomes under apparently identical conditions. With generative AI, it’s often more useful to talk about probabilistic behavior, interpretation, and uncertainty.

Think about the difference between validating an email address and understanding what an email means.

Checking whether an email address has the correct format is a deterministic task.

Understanding whether an incoming message is a complaint, a booking request, or a pricing enquiry requires interpretation.

Now connect that interpretation to an actual workflow.

If the AI decides it’s a booking request, it might create a shipment. If it decides it’s a complaint, it might escalate the issue. If it identifies a pricing enquiry, it might prepare a quotation.

The user didn’t explicitly select a workflow. The system did.

So yes, the output might be non-deterministic UI. The wording changes, the content changes, and sometimes even the structure of what appears on the screen changes.

But the bigger problem is UX.

Users need to understand what the system is doing, predict the consequences of their actions, correct mistakes, and know when they can trust an outcome.

You can design a beautiful AI interface with great typography, smooth animations, and perfectly polished chat components. But if the underlying system makes decisions users cannot understand or correct, the experience is broken.

The difficult part is designing what the product is allowed to do with that response.

—

The biggest mistake is making everything non-deterministic

There’s an assumption that the more autonomous an AI product becomes, the better it is.

Why ask people to complete forms when AI can understand them? Why use predefined workflows when an agent can decide what to do?

Those are reasonable questions. But just because AI can interpret information doesn’t mean it should be responsible for executing every resulting action.

And just because a product uses AI doesn’t mean everything inside it has to behave probabilistically.

In fact, some of the more interesting AI products are doing the opposite. They’re deliberately combining deterministic and non-deterministic systems, deciding exactly where each one should take control.

A lot of failures come from making something non-deterministic that should have been a form.

This is especially relevant for early-stage founders. It’s tempting to turn every interaction into a prompt because it makes the product feel more advanced.

But sometimes a form, a predefined workflow, or a simple confirmation button is exactly what the experience needs.

Two products illustrate this particularly well.

—

Routine Labs: Let AI build the workflow, not improvise while running it

Routine Labs works on automating processes inside existing legacy software, particularly in healthcare. Its approach is interesting because AI is used to help build automations, while production execution follows deterministic workflows.

Imagine a medical practice dealing with documents across several applications. A blood test arrives and needs to be identified, checked against patient consent, and uploaded to Germany’s electronic patient record, known as the ePA.

Traditionally, someone has to move between systems, find the correct information, check the necessary conditions, and complete the process manually.

A fully autonomous AI agent could attempt to interpret and navigate that process every time.

Routine takes a different approach.

According to the company, its hybrid engine uses generative AI to create automations, but the workflows running in production follow repeatable, logged logic. On its healthcare website, Routine also states that it doesn’t use AI during production operations or transfer personal data to LLMs.

That’s a very deliberate product decision. The uncertainty is concentrated in building the automation, where the process can be defined and checked. Production execution is designed to be predictable.

Now think about what that means for UX.

The user doesn’t necessarily need a conversation with an agent. They need to know what automation is running, which steps have been completed, whether the correct document was processed, and whether something requires their attention.

Routine’s public product examples show exactly this type of workflow: search for blood tests, check ePA consent, and upload the document.

The interface can communicate progress and exceptions through familiar patterns such as status indicators, execution histories, and review steps. No chatbot required.

And that’s what makes this approach interesting. The intelligence is used where it adds value, without making the entire experience dependent on the model interpreting the process correctly every single time.

Routine is an example of how you can build an AI-native product while keeping its actual execution deterministic.

—

Zauber: Let AI handle ambiguity, but make uncertainty visible

Zauber approaches the same problem from a different direction.

It builds AI agents for sea and air freight forwarding, working inside existing tools such as Outlook and integrating with systems like CargoWise.

Freight forwarding is an interesting environment for AI because so much operational work depends on interpreting unstructured information.

Emails, PDFs, packing lists, changing shipment details, special instructions, and incomplete documents. Information comes from different sources and doesn’t always agree.

An operator might receive an email requesting a shipment booking, with a packing list attached and a delivery date changed somewhere in the conversation.

Traditionally, someone would read everything, interpret the request, check the details, and manually enter the information into the booking system.

Zauber uses AI to handle much of that interpretation.

Its agents can read rate requests, identify relevant shipment details, retrieve rates, and prepare quotations for review. For booking creation, they can extract information from emails and documents and populate the necessary fields in CargoWise.

But the most interesting part is how the product handles information it cannot verify.

According to Zauber’s product page, if a declared value is missing or the volume doesn’t match the packing list, the system flags the discrepancy rather than guessing. The operator confirms the information before the booking is created.

Imagine the email says a shipment has a volume of 58.4 m³, while the packing list says 60.03 m³.

The AI has already completed most of the work, but the interface should make that disagreement visible, show where the information came from, and let the operator resolve it.

Instead of asking the user to complete every field, the product directs their attention to the two fields that matter. That’s a different way of designing workflows.

And there’s another detail I like about Zauber. Its product documentation describes monitoring agent sessions, including where the workflow hands control back to a human operator. The handover itself becomes something the company can observe, measure, and improve.

Routine and Zauber use different architectures, but they make a similar decision. They don’t treat autonomy as an all-or-nothing feature.

They decide where the AI should interpret information, where deterministic rules should take over, and when the user needs to step in.

—

Why a great AI demo can become a terrible product

Here’s a simple calculation that explains why these decisions matter.

Imagine a workflow with ten steps. Each step has a 95% chance of completing correctly, and all ten steps must succeed. Assuming the outcomes are independent, the probability of the entire workflow succeeding is:

A workflow that’s 95% reliable at each individual step could succeed end to end only about 60% of the time.

This is a simplified example, not a measured AI failure rate. Real systems have dependencies, validation, retries, and recovery mechanisms that change the result. But it illustrates why model accuracy alone isn’t a sufficient product metric.

An AI might extract information correctly most of the time. What happens when it doesn’t? What if an incorrect value gets passed to another system? What if an action succeeds but the confirmation fails? What happens if the agent repeats the action and creates a duplicate?

A lot of products look great because we’ve designed and tested the successful version.

The first time the model gets confused, the actual product experience begins. That’s where traditional design tools start showing their limitations.

A Figma prototype is excellent for representing predefined states. It’s not particularly good at representing a distribution of possible outputs, variable execution paths, or a failure that happens once in 50 runs.

This doesn’t make Figma irrelevant. It means static screens are no longer enough to validate the behavior we’re designing.

—

What happens when we ignore this?

One common failure is the illusion of completion.

An agent says it updated a record, sent an email, or created a booking. But perhaps it only prepared the action. Maybe an API failed. Maybe the system saved the wrong information.

If the interface displays the model’s response as proof that the action succeeded, the user has no reliable way to know what happened.

Another is hidden uncertainty. Information extracted from a document might appear exactly like verified information retrieved from a database. The interface gives both the same visual weight, even though one is an interpretation and the other is an authoritative value.

Then there’s the opposite problem: excessive human supervision.

Some products solve uncertainty by asking users to approve absolutely everything. But if someone has to review 100 decisions and 98 are consistently correct, they eventually stop paying attention.

You’ve automated the original work and replaced it with a new job: supervising the automation.

That’s not necessarily a better product.

There’s also the problem of incorrect decisions spreading through otherwise reliable systems. An AI might identify the wrong customer, after which every deterministic step executes perfectly while updating the wrong records.

The system worked exactly as designed, but the business outcome was wrong.

It takes us to the point when designing error states isn’t enough. We need to design the relationship between interpretation, verification, execution, and recovery.

—

How I approach designing this in an early-stage team

Working on a new AI product today, I’d start by mapping the workflow into three categories: deterministic, fuzzy, and irreversible.

It’s a simple exercise, but it forces you to make decisions that are easy to ignore when you’re focused on the demo.

Deterministic steps are operations with clear rules. Validating required fields, checking permissions, retrieving records, and preventing duplicate actions. These should generally be handled through conventional software.

Fuzzy steps require interpretation. Reading an email, understanding a document, classifying a request, or drafting a response. This is where AI becomes useful.

Irreversible or high-impact steps are actions with meaningful consequences. Sending an external email, issuing a payment, changing a sensitive record, or committing a booking. These need explicit permission boundaries, verification, and, where appropriate, human approval.

Once you’ve mapped those steps, a lot of product decisions become clearer. You can decide where the model is actually needed, what the interface needs to communicate, and which actions should never happen silently.

The next thing I’d do is stop treating the AI output as the interface itself. For many B2B products, I’d rather have the model return structured information and let deterministic components render it.

If an agent extracts booking information, the user should see a normal booking interface, not a paragraph explaining what the model found. The model fills in the card. It doesn’t need to invent the card.

Let’s take something everyone understands. Booking a flight.

You ask an AI assistant to book an early flight to Lisbon on Friday for you and Ania, returning Sunday evening.

First, the fuzzy part. The model has to interpret what “early” and “evening” mean, figure out which Ania you’re talking about, and make a few assumptions based on your previous bookings.

Instead of giving you a long chat response, the UI presents a structured draft. You can see what the model understood, where each assumption came from, and correct anything that looks wrong. Nothing has been booked yet.

Then comes deterministic validation. The system checks actual flight availability, passenger details, fare conditions, and prices against the airline’s data and predefined rules.

Everything checks out. Two seats are available, the refundable fare costs €398, and it’s within your budget. The interface shows a verified booking summary, without making you go through every individual check.

Now the interesting part.

You click Book, but the refundable fare sells out before the booking is completed. The only remaining option is €342, but it’s non-refundable.

Technically, it’s cheaper. It even passes your budget limit. But it’s not what you originally agreed to.

This is where the interface needs to change. Instead of letting the agent choose the cheaper ticket, the UI explains what happened, keeps all the information that’s still valid, and asks whether you want to book the non-refundable fare or look for another option.

Looking at the entire flow, the interesting part is how the boundaries change. The model can interpret the request, but it can’t set prices or book anything. Rules and live systems handle validation. And when the refundable fare suddenly becomes unavailable, the system stops and hands the decision back to the user.

Here’s how those boundaries work across the same booking:

One booking, three different levels of autonomy. The system can interpret, validate, and prepare actions, but the rules for handing control back to the user change depending on the consequences.

This is why I don’t think we can design AI workflows as just a sequence of predetermined screens anymore.

The same task moves between interpretation, validation, and execution. A decision that seemed straightforward a moment ago can suddenly require human judgment.

And the interface has to handle that without making someone start the whole process again.

There’s no need to show confidence scores or explain every decision the model makes. Show the assumptions when they matter, keep routine checks in the background, and make the consequences clear when something changes.

The difficult part is designing the transition between them.

—

Prototype the behavior, not just the happy path

I’d also move to working prototypes earlier.

Tools like Cursor, Lovable, v0, and Claude Code make it easier to build interfaces connected to actual model behavior. You can still start in Figma, but at some point you need to see the variability rather than imagine it.

Run the same scenario repeatedly. Try different phrasing. Use incomplete documents. Give the system conflicting instructions. Turn the failures into evaluation cases.

Anthropic’s research on building effective agents makes a useful distinction between predefined workflows and agents that dynamically decide their own steps. It also recommends starting with the simplest architecture that can solve the problem.

Not everything needs an agent. Sometimes a fixed workflow with one intelligent step is more useful, less expensive, and significantly easier to test.

For the actual implementation, structured outputs, schemas, state machines, execution logs, and human approval mechanisms help make these boundaries real. Tools like LangGraph and LangSmith can support stateful workflows, tracing, and evaluation.

None of these tools eliminates model uncertainty. They help you design a product that knows what to do when uncertainty appears.

Finally, I’d measure something more useful than how often the AI completes a task. I’d measure how much human attention the workflow requires.

Things like:
How often does someone need to correct the output? How long do those corrections take? How often does the agent require intervention? How many tasks actually finish correctly without creating additional work?

An agent that automates 80% of a process but makes the remaining 20% painful may not save much time. The goal is reducing the total effort needed to achieve a reliable outcome.

—

The hardest decision is how much control to give away

For founders, this is where UX becomes product strategy.

Give AI too little autonomy and you’ve built an expensive assistant that still requires users to do all the work. Give it too much and users have to trust decisions they cannot inspect or predict.

There’s no universal answer because the consequences vary between workflows. Drafting an email is different from sending it. Preparing a booking is different from creating it. Extracting information from a medical document is different from modifying a patient record.

And the boundary isn’t necessarily permanent.

A workflow might begin with every action requiring approval. After hundreds of successful executions and measurable evidence of reliability, some steps can become automatic. Other steps might always require human involvement because the cost of a mistake is too high.

This also changes how I’d approach a zero-to-one product.

Instead of promising to automate an entire business operation, I’d start with one painful workflow, make it measurable, understand its exceptions, and gradually expand.

“Our AI handles your entire freight operation” might sound impressive.

“We turn incoming shipment requests into verified, ready-to-create bookings” is a much clearer product promise.

You can measure the time saved. You can understand what goes wrong. You can build trust before introducing more autonomy.

And for an early-stage startup, trust is a much more useful asset than an impressive demo.

—

Design the boundary, not just the flow

For decades, we focused on making software easier for people to navigate. We mapped their journeys, removed unnecessary steps, and made interfaces more predictable.

Now we’re increasingly designing software that navigates parts of the work on their behalf. We need to understand what the system knows, what it assumes, what it can verify, and what it’s allowed to do when information is incomplete.

We need to decide when the system should act, when it should ask, and when it should stop. And perhaps most importantly, we need to accept that not every part of an AI-native product benefits from more AI.

Sometimes the best decision is to let a model interpret something and hand execution to deterministic software.
Sometimes it’s to prepare an action and ask for confirmation.
Sometimes it’s to admit that there isn’t enough information to continue.

Routine Labs and Zauber are useful examples because they make those boundaries part of their product architecture rather than treating them as an afterthought.

The next generation of product design isn’t just about making interfaces more intelligent. It’s about deciding how much unpredictability the product can safely absorb.

If you’re a founder building in this space, take your most important workflow and mark every step as deterministic, fuzzy, or irreversible. You’ll probably discover more about the product you’re building than you would from another conversation about which AI model to use.

Your AI doesn’t need to behave the same way every time.
But your users need to know what they can depend on.

References

  • Thinking Machines Lab, Defeating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference (2025)
  • Stanford HAI, 2026 AI Index Report
  • Jakob Nielsen, Noncommand User Interfaces (1993)
  • Microsoft Research, Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction (2019)
  • Anthropic, Building Effective Agents
  • Routine Labs
  • Zauber, Product

The Routine Labs and Zauber examples are based on their publicly available product descriptions, not independent production testing.

Everyone is building AI agents. Who’s designing the stop button? was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: DeepSeek V4 Flash Vision Experimental now available on AI Gateway
description:
DeepSeek V4 Flash with vision is now available on AI Gateway.

This model is an experimental version that accepts images alongside text. You can ask it to describe a picture, read text out of a screenshot, or work through a chart in the same request as your prompt. DeepSeek V4 Flash Vision Experimental now available on AI Gateway. Tool use, reasoning, and caching all work the same as before.

Use deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash-vision-exp to get started:

The -exp in the model ID marks this as an experimental release. Expect behavior to change, and keep a fallback model configured if it's on a production path.

To use it in a coding agent, run vercel ai-gateway coding-agents setup to connect agents like Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, and Pi, then select deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash-vision-exp inside the agent.

title: MedAstra: ASR-less Speech Retrieval with Diagnostic Grounding for Medical QA
description:
arXiv:2611.01261v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Spoken medical question answering can fail when automatic speech recognition (ASR) corrupts a clinically important term before retrieval. We present MedAstra, a framework that maps frozen WavLM speech representations through a lightweight adapter into a frozen E5 text embedding space. This enables a dense retrieval path that accepts a waveform without a query transcript. Retrieved passages and speech-linked textual metadata support answer generation with entity alternatives, diagnostic contrasts, relation heuristics, and bounded retrieval refinement. ASR-less refers to the initial speech retrieval interface; lexical retrieval, string-based entity correction, and the text generator require textual inputs. The deterministic speech embedding does not constitute a calibrated model of acoustic uncertainty. Reported retrieval results reach 87.6 Recall@10 for the speech-only retriever and 90.4 for the hybrid configuration, compared with 81.0 for transcript-first dense retrieval. Medical QA and ablations provide descriptive system comparisons, with input-provenance and evaluation limitations stated explicitly. We distinguish controlled synthetic acoustic tests from real clinical speech, qualify component attribution, and specify the remaining comparisons needed to assess speech-only QA and clinical generalization.

title: Precedent Labels and Facts Shift LLM Approval Decisions in Opposite Directions
description:
arXiv:2611.00672v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When a language model decides refund or claim requests under written policies, the system can show it similar past cases. Each past case has two parts: its facts and the decision recorded for it. We separate the two. A model sees a policy, a request and three past cases, and we change either the recorded decisions or the facts, keeping the request fixed. We select requests that are close calls: deciding without past cases, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash approved each in some of four tries and denied it in others. When the past cases are near-copies of the request (its facts with a few details changed), switching their recorded decisions from DENY to APPROVE raises approval by about 30 to 55 percentage points in DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, GPT-5.6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 on policies written for the study, and DeepSeek and Luna show the same on nine public policies paraphrased from real ones. The facts push the other way: shown without their recorded decisions, past cases whose facts support approval make these two models approve less often than past cases whose facts support denial. One reading is that the request looks weaker next to them. This push is not just a correction toward the right answer: in an additional DeepSeek analysis, it was of similar estimated size on requests that human annotators judged approvable and on those they judged deniable. In a separate DeepSeek run on the public policies, when the past cases are near-copies of a different request, switching their decisions moves approval by 9 points instead of 43, while facts that support approval still lower it by 22 points against facts that support denial. Systems that retrieve past decisions should test the two parts separately.

title: Configure Automatic Error Grouping in Node.js Error Tracking: 5 Reversible Rules
description:
Batch pipelines make it hard to configure automatic error grouping in Node.js error tracking. A nightly run can emit hundreds of failures from one bad input, or one deployment can create dozens of unrelated stack traces. The grouping rule has to compress repeated evidence without hiding a new failure, and it must be possible to undo when the rule is wrong.

It fails quietly.

Short answer: configure automatic grouping around a stable error fingerprint, but derive that fingerprint from normalized type, operation, and source location rather than the raw message. Keep the original message and full stack as searchable event fields. Version the rule, sample the groups before rollout, and retain a fallback to the previous key for rollback.

The example here is a Node.js service that searches structured logs from a nightly developer-tools data pipeline. The practical target is not a prettier error dashboard. It is a grouping scheme that helps an on-call engineer decide whether a failed run is one repairable defect or several defects that must be rolled back independently.

Why does automatic grouping fail on nightly pipelines?

The raw error string is usually the wrong identity. It may contain a customer identifier, a file name, a row number, or a server-generated request ID. Two events from the same defect then become separate groups. The opposite failure is just as dangerous: a rule that removes too much context merges a parser failure with a network timeout because both happen to be thrown as Error.

Nightly work adds a second complication. The batch name and run date are useful for searching, but they are usually poor grouping dimensions. Including run_id creates a new group every night. Including no batch identity at all can merge a schema failure in the billing export with an authentication failure in the index refresh.

The first trap is a successful-looking deduplication report. Suppose a parser starts rejecting a new field after release-42. Every event carries a different row number, so raw-message grouping reports many incidents. A normalizer that removes row numbers fixes that split. A careless normalizer that also removes the operation name can then merge parser errors with failures from the commit stage, making the dashboard quieter while the rollback decision gets less reliable. I keep those fields separate in fixtures because the bad result is easy to miss in aggregate counts.

I start with the rollback question: “If this group grows after a deployment, what evidence would tell me to revert?” That question produces a narrower key than a generic error hash. It also keeps grouping separate from retention, alerting, and log search. A group is an index for related failures; it is not the complete incident record.

OpenTelemetry describes logs as records with a body and attributes, and its signal model is deliberately separate from any one storage product. That separation is useful here: keep the event rich, then calculate a grouping fingerprint as an additional attribute at the error boundary.

The five rules I use for a reversible fingerprint

  1. Normalize the exception class. TypeError and SyntaxError should not collapse into a generic JavaScript error.
  2. Use an operation name that represents the pipeline stage, such as manifest.parse or index.commit. Do not use a transient run identifier.
  3. Use the first application-owned stack frame, not the entire stack. Library upgrades and wrapper functions can otherwise split a stable defect.
  4. Remove volatile values from the message before retaining it as a grouping input. Keep the unmodified message in the event for investigation.
  5. Include a rule version. A changed normalizer should create an explicitly comparable generation, not silently rewrite history.

These rules make a deliberate trade-off. More dimensions reduce accidental merging but increase group cardinality. For a rollback decision, a false merge is usually more expensive than a few extra groups because it can make a bad release appear to have one familiar cause.

Here is a small Node.js implementation. It does not send data anywhere; the returned object can be attached to an OpenTelemetry log record or to the generic event envelope used by an error-tracking service. In one nightly run, for example, row 1842 and row 9817 may both say that an owner is invalid. If the message normalizer strips only those row numbers, they share a group; if it strips the stage name too, a manifest parser defect can merge with an index commit defect. That is the boundary the fixture test must catch before the rule reaches production.

import crypto from "node:crypto";

const VOLATILE = [
  /\brequest[-_ ]?id[=:]\s*[^ ]+/gi,
  /\b(run|job|tenant|user)[-_ ]?id[=:]\s*[^ ]+/gi,
  /\b\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}T\S+/g,
  /\b\d+\b/g
];

function normalizeMessage(message) {
  let value = String(message ?? "").trim();
  for (const pattern of VOLATILE) value = value.replace(pattern, "<value>");
  return value.replace(/\s+/g, " ").slice(0, 240);
}

function firstApplicationFrame(stack, root = "/app/") {
  return String(stack ?? "")
    .split("\n")
    .map((line) => line.trim())
    .find((line) => line.startsWith("at ") && line.includes(root)) ?? "unknown";
}

export function groupingAttributes(error, context) {
  const identity = [
    "group-v1",
    error?.name || "Error",
    context.operation,
    firstApplicationFrame(error?.stack),
    normalizeMessage(error?.message)
  ].join("|");

  return {
    grouping_rule: "group-v1",
    error_fingerprint: crypto.createHash("sha256").update(identity).digest("hex"),
    error_type: error?.name || "Error",
    operation: context.operation,
    batch_name: context.batchName,
    run_id: context.runId,
    original_message: error?.message || "",
    stack: error?.stack || ""
  };
}

The hash is an identifier, not a security boundary.

Keep the evidence.

The event still needs access controls because original_message and the stack can contain sensitive data. The regular expressions are also policy, not magic. If a legitimate error message contains a numeric schema version, replacing every number may erase useful distinction. I test the normalizer with fixtures from real log shapes and with deliberately adversarial values before changing the rule.

How can Node.js tracking configure automatic error grouping safely?

The group key should be low-cardinality enough to scan and high-signal enough to support action. Fields such as service, environment, and deployment_id are valuable dimensions, but I keep them available as filters instead of automatically placing all of them in the fingerprint. Environment is a special case: production and staging usually deserve separate views, while a deployment identifier is better for release correlation.

A useful event has at least three layers: the grouping identity, the diagnostic evidence, and the operational context. In JSON, that might look like this:

{
  "severity": "ERROR",
  "body": "Manifest row 1842 has an invalid owner",
  "attributes": {
    "error_fingerprint": "sha256:...",
    "grouping_rule": "group-v1",
    "operation": "manifest.parse",
    "batch_name": "nightly-index-refresh",
    "run_id": "2026-10-28T01:00:00Z",
    "deployment_id": "release-42"
  }
}

The run_id belongs in context, not in the grouping identity. That single boundary prevents the common “one group per run” mistake. The body remains searchable for the exact row and owner, while the fingerprint answers the narrower question: which failures share a cause under the current rule?

For a developer-tools pipeline, I also record the input artifact and stage as attributes, but I do not put an arbitrary path or line number into the key unless that location is stable across runs. This is where deliverability-style thinking helps: classify signals before reacting to them. A burst is a signal; it is not proof that every event in the burst belongs to the same defect.

What should be compared before choosing a service?

The service is the last part of this design. The first comparison is between grouping behaviors, because different systems may interpret a custom fingerprint, stack trace, or exception name differently. A useful evaluation exercise sends the same fixture set through three categories of implementation: a self-hosted collector, a hosted error tracker, and a log search backend with alerting. The names matter less than the observable contract.

Check five things: can the system accept an explicit fingerprint; can an event retain the original stack and attributes; can a rule version be queried; can groups be split without deleting evidence; and can a bad rule be disabled without rewriting historical events? A hosted tracker may offer opinionated stack-based grouping, a collector may give more control over normalization, and a log backend may make arbitrary queries easier than durable issue grouping. Those are boundaries, not rankings.

I would reject a choice that answers only “does it group errors automatically?” The real test is replayability. Export a fixture containing a timeout, a malformed manifest, a permission failure, and two copies of the same malformed row with different IDs. Then verify that the same defect groups together, the distinct failures stay apart, and the original fields remain available. Repeat the test after a wrapper-library update.

Do not compare only the happy path. A rate-limited ingestion endpoint, a partial batch, a missing stack, and a changed source-map format are all grouping inputs. In email and OTP systems, I learned to distrust any classification that behaves perfectly until a provider changes one header; log pipelines have the same shape.

A rollout that can be rolled back

Roll out a new fingerprint as a shadow field first. For one or two nightly runs, calculate group-v2 while continuing to display group-v1. Compare split and merge candidates by sampled event IDs, not by total group count alone. A lower count can mean better deduplication, or it can mean unrelated defects were hidden.

Keep both values during the transition:

def choose_group(event, enabled_rule):
    candidate = event.get(enabled_rule)
    fallback = event.get("error_fingerprint_v1")
    return candidate or fallback or "unclassified"

The operational switch should be configuration, not a code edit during an incident. Record the active rule in deployment metadata, alert annotations, and the event attributes. If the new rule merges two defects, disable it, return to the previous rule, and preserve the events already received under the new version for later analysis. A rollback should change future classification; it should not destroy the audit trail.

The decision rule is compact: prefer the smallest stable identity that keeps rollback-relevant failures distinct. Measure that with replay fixtures and sampled production events, then promote the rule only after the false-merge cases have an owner. Automatic grouping is useful when it reduces noise without reducing evidence.

Sources

  • https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/logs/
  • https://nodejs.org/api/errors.html
  • https://nodejs.org/api/crypto.html
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5424

title: What is Rendering in React?
description:
Rendering means displaying the UI (User Interface) based on the component's JSX.
Rendering means React prepares what should appear on the screen.

Example of Rendering:

function App() {
return (


Hello React!


Welcome to my website.



);
}

export default App;

Output:

Hello React!
Welcome to my website.

React renders this JSX and displays it in the browser.

When does Rendering happen?

There are two main situations:

Initial Render: When a component appears on the screen for the first time.

Re-render: When state or props change and React needs to update the UI.

Example Using useState:

import { useState } from 'react';

function App() {

const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

return (
    <div>
        <h1>Count: {count}</h1>

        <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>
            Click Me
        </button>
    </div>
);

}

export default App;

Output:

Count: 13

Click MeTry clicking the button. The count changes because React re-renders the component.

Step-by-step:

Initially, count = 0.

React renders the component.

You click the button.

setCount() updates the state.

React renders the component again.

Updated count appears on the screen.

title: Community detection in complex networks via node similarity, graph representation learning, and hierarchical clustering
description:
arXiv:2303.12212v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Community detection is a significant challenge in analysing real graphs, including social, citation, biological, and many other networks. This article proposes three new, general, hierarchical frameworks to deal with this task. The introduced approach supports various linkage-based clustering algorithms, vertex proximity matrices, and graph representation learning models. We compare 364 module combinations on Stochastic Block Model graphs and real-life datasets. We observe that our best pipelines (Wasserman-Faust and the mutual information-based PPMI proximity, as well as the deep learning-based DNGR representations) perform competitively with the state-of-the-art Leiden and Louvain algorithms. At the same time, unlike the latter, they remain hierarchical. Thus, they output a series of nested partitions of all possible cardinalities which are compatible with each other. This feature is crucial when the number of correct partitions is unknown in advance, and we show that it is obtained at near-zero practical cost in terms of partition quality. On graphs composed of many small communities, our pipelines are more accurate than the reference solutions. Nevertheless, the downside of our approach is its time complexity, which confines the framework to networks of some 10000 vertices on personal machines.

title: Before Writing Code, Understand the Process: My Introduction to SDLC
description:
When I started learning software development, I mainly focused on the coding part: writing functions, creating models, building APIs, and solving programming problems.

But there's something important I wanted to understand better:

How does a software project actually go from an idea to a working application?

That's where I learned about the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC).

What Is SDLC?

SDLC stands for Software Development Life Cycle.

It's a structured process that helps development teams plan, design, build, test, deploy, and maintain software.

Instead of immediately starting to code, teams follow an organized process to understand what they're building and how they should build it.

Think about building an e-commerce application.

Before creating Django models or API endpoints, you need to know:

  • What problem does the application solve?
  • Who will use it?
  • What features are required?
  • How should the database be designed?
  • How will the application be tested and deployed?

SDLC helps organize these decisions.

The Six Phases I Learned About

1. Planning

Understand the problem, gather requirements, define project goals, and estimate resources.

One important document introduced in this phase is the Software Requirements Specification (SRS), which describes what the software should do.

2. Design

Plan how the application will work technically.

This includes architecture, database design, components, and relationships.

3. Development

This is where developers write code and implement the planned functionality.

For a Django REST Framework project, this could mean creating models, serializers, views, URLs, and permissions.

4. Testing

Verify that the application works as expected.

Some common testing types are unit, integration, system, and acceptance testing.

5. Deployment

Release the application into an environment where users can access it.

6. Maintenance

Fix bugs, improve performance, address security issues, and introduce new features after release.

Waterfall vs. Iterative Development

I also learned that SDLC doesn't always follow one fixed sequence.

The Waterfall model generally moves through phases sequentially.

Iterative development, on the other hand, allows teams to revisit previous phases, collect feedback, and improve the software through repeated cycles.

This makes development more adaptable when requirements change.

Another Interesting Concept: Prototyping

A prototype is an early, simplified representation of a software idea.

It helps stakeholders visualize proposed features and provide feedback before the complete application is developed.

For example, a team planning an e-commerce application might create a basic product page mockup to understand how users will interact with it.

My Main Takeaway

Before this lesson, I mostly associated software development with writing code.

Now I understand that building software involves much more than implementation.

Planning, understanding requirements, designing the architecture, testing, deployment, and maintenance are all important parts of the process.

As I'm continuing my backend development journey with Python and Django REST Framework, understanding SDLC gives me a better perspective on how real-world software projects are organized.

I'm still learning, and this is one more concept I'm adding to my developer toolbox.

Question for other developers:

When working on a project, which SDLC phase do you think developers tend to underestimate the most: planning, design, testing, or maintenance?

I'd love to hear your thoughts!

title: Labadain-MedQA: A Tetun Medical QA Dataset for Fine-Tuning and Evaluating Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.00935v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Advances in large language models (LLMs) have created opportunities for cross-lingual transfer of medical knowledge from high-resource to low-resource languages to support access to healthcare information. However, medical question-answering (QA) datasets for fine-tuning and evaluating LLMs remain scarce for Tetun. To address this gap, we translated MedAlpaca's Medical Flashcards and WikiDoc Patient Information collections into Tetun using Gemini 2.5 Flash, producing 39,077 medical QA pairs. Translation quality was assessed on 50 randomly sampled QA pairs (100 documents) using automatic metrics against human reference translations and evaluations by two native Tetun-speaking healthcare professionals, focusing on medical accuracy and Tetun fluency. Human translations achieved higher mean ratings than LLM-generated translations for both criteria (4.43/5 vs. 4.02/5), with statistically significant differences (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p < 0.001). To assess downstream utility, we fine-tuned Gemma and Llama variants on the translated MedAlpaca dataset using parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) and evaluated them on 325 Tetun-translated United States Medical Licensing Examination multiple-choice questions. Gemma 4 12B fine-tuned using QLoRA achieved relative improvements in mean accuracy of 10.79% with 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4) inference and 10.42% after merging the LoRA adapters into the BF16 base model, compared with the corresponding base models. These results highlight the viability of automatic dataset translation for Tetun medical QA and the effectiveness of PEFT in enhancing model performance. The datasets, models, and evaluation resources are accessible at https://github.com/labadain/labadain-medqa to support reproducible research on Tetun medical QA and facilitate machine translation, cross lingual, and multilingual research.

title: yt-dlp subtitles: the commands that work, and 3 traps that cost me an afternoon
description:
If you only want the subtitles from a YouTube video, yt-dlp can do it without downloading the video. The flags look simple. Then you run them on a real channel and get a 429, a folder full of junk languages, or a re-run that starts again from zero.

Everything below was run with yt-dlp 2026.07.04 on real videos this week.

The one command most people want 

yt-dlp --skip-download --write-subs --write-auto-subs \
  --sub-langs en --sub-format srt \
  -o "%(id)s.%(ext)s" \
  "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dQw4w9WgXcQ"

What each part does:

  • --skip-download keeps the video off your disk. You only get the subtitle file.
  • --write-subs takes subtitles the creator uploaded.
  • --write-auto-subs takes YouTube's auto-generated captions.
  • With both set, yt-dlp prefers the creator's track and falls back to the auto one. On the video above it picked the uploaded track, which has proper punctuation and the ♪ marks.
  • --sub-format srt asks YouTube for SRT directly, so no ffmpeg step is needed.

To see what a video has before downloading anything:

yt-dlp --list-subs "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dQw4w9WgXcQ"

Trap 1: --sub-langs "en.*" gets you a 429

The yt-dlp help text uses en.* as an example, so it's the first thing everyone tries. On a popular video, --list-subs shows why it's a bad idea: the automatic captions include dozens of machine-translated tracks, and the codes look like this:

en-en      English from English
ab-en      Abkhazian from English
en-de-DE   ...

en.* matches en, en-orig, en-en, en-de-DE and more. yt-dlp requests every one of them back to back, and YouTube answered my test with:

ERROR: Unable to download video subtitles for 'en-de-DE': HTTP Error 429: Too Many Requests

The fix is to ask for exactly what you want:

--sub-langs en            # just English
--sub-langs "en,es"       # English and Spanish
--sub-langs "en,-live_chat"  # English, never the live-chat replay

Trap 2: auto-caption VTT files are not readable text

If you grab auto captions as VTT and open the file, you see this:

00:00:21.800 --> 00:00:25.950 align:start position:0%
We're no strangers to
love.<00:00:22.800><c> You</c><00:00:23.039><c> know</c><00:00:23.279><c> the</c>

Each word has its own timing tag, and every line appears twice, because auto captions "roll" on screen. Feed that to an LLM and you pay for every word twice.

This turns it into clean text:

import re, sys

def vtt_to_text(path):
    lines = []
    for line in open(path, encoding="utf-8"):
        line = line.strip()
        if not line or "-->" in line or line.startswith(("WEBVTT", "Kind:", "Language:")):
            continue
        line = re.sub(r"<[^>]+>", "", line)  # drop the per-word timing tags
        if line and (not lines or line != lines[-1]):  # auto captions repeat each line
            lines.append(line)
    return " ".join(lines)

print(vtt_to_text(sys.argv[1]))

Output:

[Music] We're no strangers to love. You know the rules and so do I. ...

If you want timestamps, ask for --sub-format srt instead. The SRT version of the same captions doesn't have the rolling duplicates.

Trap 3: --download-archive does nothing with --skip-download

For a whole channel you want re-runs to skip what you already have, so you add --download-archive done.txt. I ran it on two videos from a channel, and done.txt was never created.

yt-dlp only writes the archive when it downloads the video, and --skip-download means it never does. You need one more flag:

yt-dlp --skip-download --write-subs --write-auto-subs \
  --sub-langs en --sub-format srt \
  --download-archive done.txt --force-write-archive \
  --sleep-subtitles 2 \
  -o "subs/%(upload_date)s %(title).80s [%(id)s].%(ext)s" \
  "https://www.youtube.com/@veritasium/videos"

The second run printed has already been recorded in the archive for both videos and skipped them.

The other flags in there:

  • --sleep-subtitles 2 waits between subtitle requests. On a big channel this is what keeps you clear of trap 1's 429.
  • -I 1:50 (not shown) limits the run to the newest 50 videos, which is handy for testing.
  • The output template puts the date first, so files sort chronologically, and keeps the video id in brackets so you can always find the source.

When yt-dlp stops being the right tool

All of this works from a laptop on a home connection. From a cloud server it usually stops. YouTube blocks most datacenter IP ranges, and you start seeing Sign in to confirm you're not a bot. Then you're dealing with cookies, residential proxies and PO tokens. I wrote about that in an earlier post.

I build BulkTranscripts, which runs yt-dlp behind residential proxies so you don't have to. You paste a channel or playlist and get SRT, VTT, TXT or JSON for up to 1,000 videos. It's paid after the first 30, so if the commands above work for you, keep using them. They're free.

If you hit a yt-dlp subtitle error that isn't covered here, paste it in the comments and I'll take a look.

title: Always-on tracing for production and preview traffic
description:
With always-on tracing, you can now debug your real user requests without reproducing them.

Always-on tracing continuously collects traces from your production and preview traffic. Unlike session tracing, which only captures requests from your own browser, it samples your live traffic.

You control what's collected with sampling rules. Each rule sets a trace rate for an environment (All, Production, or Preview), optionally scoped to a path prefix like /checkout. Nothing is collected until you add a rule, so you pay only for what you choose to trace.

You can also manage sampling rules from the CLI. vercel traces config set adds a rule, or changes the rate of an existing one when you run it again with the same environment and path prefix:

Infrastructure and outbound fetch spans are captured automatically. To add framework and custom spans, instrument your app with @vercel/otel.

To view a trace, open the Logs or run vercel traces get <request-id>.

Always-on tracing is is now in beta and available to teams on all plans. Tracing is priced at $0.50 per 1M span units. Traces follow your runtime log retention: 1 hour on Hobby, 1 day on Pro and 3 days on Enterprise.

Get started by adding a rule in Settings → Tracing or from the settings icon in Logs. Learn more in the documentation.

title: Catching dead CSS variables in CI before they break production
description:
A bug report rolled in late on a Friday. The primary call to action on our checkout page was completely invisible. Someone had deleted a colour token in Figma. Our automated pipeline updated the JSON file in our repository. The global CSS variables updated perfectly. But a React component deeper in the tree still referenced the old variable name. The browser could not find it. It fell back to transparent. We lost real money because of a simple typo in a token name.

CSS variables are brilliant. They make theming so easy. You can swap a whole colour palette just by changing a class on the body tag. But they have a massive flaw. If you reference a variable that does not exist, the browser just ignores it. There is no build error. There is no warning in the console. You just get a silent failure.

In a large codebase, this is terrifying. Designers rename things. Tokens get deprecated. And you have no way of knowing which components are still relying on those dead tokens. I decided we needed to catch this in CI before we ever merged a pull request.

The naive regex approach

My first thought was to just write a simple script. I wanted to read our exported Figma JSON file and extract all the valid token names. Then I would scan our codebase for any string matching the CSS variable syntax. If the variable was not in the JSON file, the script would throw an error.

Here is the basic JSON structure we get from our design system.

{
  "colors": {
    "brand": {
      "primary": {
        "value": "#0d6efd",
        "type": "color"
      }
    }
  }
}

This eventually turns into a CSS variable called --colors-brand-primary. So basically we need a script to flatten this JSON and build a list of valid CSS variable names.

Here is the Node script I wrote to do exactly that. Notice I am using standard JavaScript modules.

import fs from 'node:fs'
import path from 'node:path'

const rawData = fs.readFileSync('./tokens.json', 'utf-8')
const tokens = JSON.parse(rawData)

const validVariables = new Set()

function flattenTokens(obj, prefix = '') {
  for (const key in obj) {
    const value = obj[key]
    if (typeof value === 'object' && value !== null && !value.value) {
      flattenTokens(value, `${prefix}${key}-`)
    } else if (value.value) {
      validVariables.add(`--${prefix}${key}`)
    }
  }
}

flattenTokens(tokens)
console.log(validVariables)

This works really well for extracting the valid names. The next step is finding where we actually use them in our CSS and React files.

Scanning the codebase for usages

Finding the variables in the codebase is a bit trickier. You could use an Abstract Syntax Tree to parse the CSS. But we also use these variables inline in our React components. So we need something that just looks at raw text.

I wrote a regular expression to find anything that looks like a CSS variable. It looks for var(-- and captures the variable name.

import { globSync } from 'glob'

const files = globSync('src/**/*.{css,tsx,jsx}')
const variableRegex = /var\((--[a-zA-Z0-9-]+)/g

let hasErrors = false

for (const file of files) {
  const content = fs.readFileSync(file, 'utf-8')
  let match

  while ((match = variableRegex.exec(content)) !== null) {
    const variableName = match[1]

    if (!validVariables.has(variableName)) {
      console.error(`Error in ${file}: Variable ${variableName} does not exist in tokens`)
      hasErrors = true
    }
  }
}

if (hasErrors) {
  process.exit(1)
}

This script is small but it is incredibly powerful. It literally reads every source file and checks every single CSS variable usage against our source of truth. If a designer deletes a token in Figma, this script will fail the build if we are still using it.

The problem with dynamic variables

We ran this script on our main repository. It immediately found twelve dead variables. That felt like a massive win. But then we hit a wall.

Sometimes developers construct CSS variable names dynamically in JavaScript. They might do something like this in a React component.

const buttonColor = `var(--brand-${variant}-500)`

return (
  <button style={{ backgroundColor: buttonColor }}>
    Click me
  </button>
)

Our regex script completely chokes on this. It tries to look up --brand-${variant}-500 in our token list. Obviously that does not exist. It is a dynamic string.

We had two choices. We could try to make the regex smarter. Or we could just ban dynamic CSS variable names entirely.

Honestly, we chose the second option. Banning dynamic variable names makes your codebase much easier to search. If you need a dynamic colour, you should map it to a static variable using a data attribute.

button[data-variant="primary"] {
  background-color: var(--brand-primary-500);
}

button[data-variant="secondary"] {
  background-color: var(--brand-secondary-500);
}

This is much cleaner. And it means our simple regex script works perfectly.

Wiring it up in GitHub Actions

The final piece of the puzzle is running this automatically. You do not want developers to remember to run this script locally. It needs to happen on every pull request.

Here is the GitHub Action workflow we use. It is very straightforward. It checks out the code, installs dependencies, and runs our validation script.

name: Validate Design Tokens

on:
  pull_request:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  validate-tokens:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Setup Node
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      - name: Run token validator
        run: node scripts/validate-tokens.js

Now, if someone tries to merge a PR that uses a dead CSS variable, the build goes red. The reviewer can see exactly which file contains the error. It completely eliminates the risk of silent CSS failures in production. this is the one thing nobody talks about when setting up design systems. You need strict validation just like you have for TypeScript.

Getting the tokens into the repo

Writing the validation script is the easy part tbh. The hardest part of this entire workflow is actually getting the token JSON from Figma into your repository reliably.

For a long time, we just asked designers to manually export a JSON file and send it to us on Slack. It was a terrible process. Files got lost. People forgot to send updates. We ended up with massive drift between Figma and code.

I got so tired of this that I built a tool to fix it. I am the creator of Design System Sync. It is a Figma plugin that exports your design tokens directly to GitHub or Bitbucket via automatic pull requests.

You just map your Figma variables, click export, and it generates a PR with the updated JSON and CSS files. It even assigns reviewers automatically. It supports W3C Design Tokens, standard CSS Variables, and Style Dictionary formats. It handles multi-mode variables for light and dark themes perfectly.

You can check out the website here: https://ds-sync.netlify.app?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=bot

And you can grab the plugin directly from the Figma Community here: https://www.figma.com/community/plugin/1561389071519901700?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=bot

If you combine an automated export tool with a strict CI validation script, your design system becomes bulletproof. Designers can clean up tokens with confidence. Developers never have to worry about broken UI. It is just a much better way to work.

title: OMID browserOptional describes the JavaScript environment.
description:
The name browserOptional is easy to misread as permission to skip verification JavaScript. It describes the script's execution environment. Confusing those meanings can leave a player showing video while the required verification resource never runs.

This is especially relevant when a player moves from a browser test page to an app or another environment with a different JavaScript runtime. The same resource URL does not establish the same available APIs.

VAST 4.3 section 3.17.1 provides the selection rules. The integration work is to apply them to a real environment, preserve the selected resource and verify what actually executed.

Describe the environment precisely

A resource marked browserOptional="true" declares support for execution without DOM and other browser built-ins. The resource remains JavaScript. The flag does not replace it with a native measurement vendor SDK.

For browser or webview execution, the specification prefers resources marked false when both forms are available. A non-browser JavaScript environment may execute only resources marked true. If it receives only unsuitable resources, the associated not-executed reporting must remain visible.

Start an integration record with the player build, OM SDK integration, runtime and supported framework. Avoid a single isNative variable that attempts to represent all those properties. An app can host a webview, and a platform label alone does not tell you which environment executes verification code.

Validate the XML attribute before selecting a resource

An XML parser usually returns attribute text. In JavaScript, Boolean("false") evaluates to true. The string is nonempty, so ordinary truthiness does not interpret its XML meaning.

The following complete Node.js example accepts XML Schema boolean forms and then applies a narrow resource-selection rule:

import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

function parseXmlBoolean(value) {
  if (typeof value !== 'string') {
    throw new TypeError('browserOptional attribute is missing');
  }
  const lexical = value.trim();
  if (lexical === 'true' || lexical === '1') return true;
  if (lexical === 'false' || lexical === '0') return false;
  throw new TypeError('invalid XML boolean');
}

function selectForEnvironment(resources, environment) {
  if (resources.some(r => typeof r.browserOptional !== 'boolean')) {
    throw new TypeError('resources must contain validated booleans');
  }
  if (environment === 'browser') {
    return resources.find(r => r.browserOptional === false) ?? resources[0] ?? null;
  }
  if (environment === 'non-browser-js') {
    return resources.find(r => r.browserOptional === true) ?? null;
  }
  throw new Error('unknown execution environment');
}

const resources = [
  { id: 'portable', browserOptional: parseXmlBoolean('true') },
  { id: 'browser', browserOptional: parseXmlBoolean('false') }
];
assert.equal(selectForEnvironment(resources, 'browser').id, 'browser');
assert.equal(selectForEnvironment(resources, 'non-browser-js').id, 'portable');
assert.equal(selectForEnvironment([resources[1]], 'non-browser-js'), null);
assert.equal(parseXmlBoolean('0'), false);
assert.equal(parseXmlBoolean(' 1 '), true);
assert.throws(() => parseXmlBoolean(undefined));
assert.throws(() => parseXmlBoolean('False'));
assert.throws(() => selectForEnvironment([{ browserOptional: 'false' }], 'browser'));

The selector deliberately assumes that the caller already filtered resources for the relevant verification entry and supported API framework. It illustrates environment selection, not the complete VAST verification algorithm.

The parser preserves missing or invalid values as errors. Supplying a default at this stage would hide a malformed declaration and make the later selection look justified.

Keep eligibility separate from successful execution

Selecting the portable resource establishes that it is eligible under this environment rule. Several later questions remain: did the player fetch it, did loading complete, did its execution succeed and did it participate in the expected measurement session?

Record these as separate outcomes. A resource that was eligible but failed to load needs a different investigation from a resource the player never selected.

Keep the verification vendor, selected URL, resource position in the document and environment in the diagnostic record. If wrappers add verification entries, preserve which document introduced each one. Otherwise a report can identify the wrong vendor script when several resources are present.

Do not conclude that measurement worked merely because a global JavaScript object exists. Check the integration's documented session and event observations. The exact instrumentation depends on the SDK and platform, so retain the build and test environment with that evidence.

Test the matrix that your deployment will use

Create one fixture with a browser-only resource, one with a portable resource and one containing both. Run them against each execution environment your product supports.

For the browser environment, verify the selection preference when both forms are offered. For the non-browser environment, verify that the browser-only fixture cannot accidentally pass because a desktop test harness supplies a DOM.

Add a fixture with a missing attribute and another containing the text false. The latter specifically guards against a future refactor replacing deliberate parsing with Boolean(value).

Keep environment selection deterministic. If two resources are equally eligible, document the implementation's selection behavior rather than allowing iteration order from an unrelated data structure to choose the script accidentally.

Use runtime failures to narrow the next step

If a resource is never selected, inspect the parsed declaration and framework filtering first. If it is selected but never requested, inspect the player's execution policy and instrumentation. If the request occurs but execution fails, inspect the response, loading restrictions and runtime diagnostics.

A script can also depend on browser APIs despite declaring portability. Retain a minimal reproduction in the actual non-browser runtime, with the vendor resource revision. Changing the flag in your local XML without checking the script's behavior does not repair that dependency.

When no verification executes, preserve the associated failure reporting. Missing measurement is an operational result that needs explanation, not a successful session with zero measured activity.

Put the declaration and observation in the same review

A useful acceptance record includes the XML fixture, parsed boolean, selected resource, runtime identity and measurement-session observation. Another engineer should be able to determine where the check stopped without rerunning the entire campaign.

I maintain VASTlint. Use the VAST XML validator to inspect the declaration before the environment test. Keep its structural result beside the player evidence, so each result supports the question it actually checked.

Sources

  • VAST 4.3, section 3.17.1
  • OMID API 1.5

Technical sources checked October 25, 2026. Drafted with AI; examples are synthetic unless explicitly stated otherwise.
