title: I Built a Scraper That Turns 1,000 Book Listings Into a Clean Excel Report — Here's How
description:
Most "learn web scraping" tutorials stop at printing a few titles to the terminal. That never felt like a finished tool to me, so I built one that goes all the way: scrape a catalogue, clean the data, and hand over a formatted Excel report someone could actually use.

The stack is plain Python: requests, BeautifulSoup, pandas, and openpyxl. No frameworks, no paid APIs. The target is books.toscrape.com, a site built specifically for practising scraping — so everything here is on a public practice page, not a real store.

What you end up with

Running two scripts produces:

  • data/books_raw.csv — the raw scrape, one row per book
  • data/books_clean.csv — the same data, cleaned
  • data/books_clean.xlsx — a formatted Excel report: bold headers, filters, a frozen top row, and sensible column widths

The full run collects 1,000 books, and the cleaned report's average price comes out at £35.07.

Step 0: Setup 

pip install requests beautifulsoup4 pandas openpyxl

Three files: scraper.py (collect), clean_export.py (clean + export), and a data/ folder for the outputs.

Step 1: Scrape every page, not just the first one

A catalogue scraper that only reads page 1 is a demo, not a tool. The real job is walking the pagination until there is no "next" link left. The core loop does exactly that:

def scrape(max_pages=None):
    all_books = []
    page = 1
    while True:
        url = CATALOGUE_URL.format(page)
        response = requests.get(url, headers=HEADERS, timeout=20)
        response.raise_for_status()
        response.encoding = "utf-8"
        books, has_next = parse_page(response.text, url)
        all_books.extend(books)
        if not has_next:
            break
        page += 1
        if max_pages and page > max_pages:
            break
        time.sleep(0.2)  # be polite to the server
    return all_books

Each page is parsed with one function that pulls five fields out of every book card:

def parse_page(html, page_url):
    soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser")
    books = []
    for article in soup.select("article.product_pod"):
        title = article.h3.a["title"].strip()
        price_text = article.select_one("p.price_color").get_text(strip=True)
        rating_word = article.select_one("p.star-rating")["class"][1]
        availability = article.select_one("p.instock").get_text(strip=True)
        rel_url = article.h3.a["href"]
        books.append({
            "title": title,
            "price": price_text,
            "rating": rating_word,
            "availability": availability,
            "url": urljoin(page_url, rel_url),
        })
    has_next = soup.select_one("li.next a") is not None
    return books, has_next

Three details worth calling out, because each one bit me or would have:

  1. The £ encoding gotcha. This site doesn't declare its charset, so requests guesses Latin-1 and corrupts the £ sign. The pages are actually UTF-8, so one line — response.encoding = "utf-8" — fixes it before parsing. If your scraped prices ever look like Â£51.77, this is almost certainly why.
  2. Be polite. A 0.2 second sleep between pages and an honest User-Agent (python-automation-toolkit/1.0 (learning project)) cost nothing and keep you from hammering someone else's server. Scraping fast is not a skill; scraping without getting blocked is.
  3. Relative URLs. Book links on the page are relative, so urljoin(page_url, rel_url) turns them into full URLs you can actually click later.

Run it with python scraper.py (or --pages 5 for a quick test run), and you get data/books_raw.csv with 1,000 rows.

Step 2: Clean the data before anyone sees it

Raw scraped data is never report-ready. Prices are strings with currency symbols (£51.77), ratings are words (Three), and availability is a sentence fragment. The cleaning step turns all of that into typed, analysable data:

RATING_MAP = {"One": 1, "Two": 2, "Three": 3, "Four": 4, "Five": 5}

def clean(df):
    df = df.copy()
    # "£51.77" -> 51.77 (drop anything that is not a digit or a dot)
    df["price"] = df["price"].astype(str).str.replace(r"[^0-9.]", "", regex=True)
    df["price"] = pd.to_numeric(df["price"], errors="coerce")
    df = df.dropna(subset=["price"])
    # "Three" -> 3
    df["rating"] = df["rating"].map(RATING_MAP)
    # "In stock" -> True, anything else -> False
    df["in_stock"] = df["availability"].str.contains("In stock", na=False)
    df = df.drop(columns=["availability"])
    df = df.drop_duplicates(subset=["title", "url"])
    return df

The pattern here is worth stealing for any scrape: strip, convert with errors="coerce" (bad values become NaN instead of crashing the run), drop the rows that didn't convert, and drop duplicates on a sensible key — here, title + URL.

Step 3: Export an Excel file a human would enjoy opening

A CSV is fine for machines. If a person is going to read the report, formatting matters — and it's only a few lines with openpyxl:

def write_excel(df, path):
    with pd.ExcelWriter(path, engine="openpyxl") as writer:
        df.to_excel(writer, sheet_name="Books", index=False)
        sheet = writer.sheets["Books"]
        for cell in sheet[1]:
            cell.font = Font(bold=True)
        sheet.auto_filter.ref = sheet.dimensions
        sheet.freeze_panes = "A2"
        widths = {"title": 55, "price": 10, "rating": 10,
                  "in_stock": 10, "url": 60}
        for idx, col in enumerate(df.columns, start=1):
            sheet.column_dimensions[get_column_letter(idx)].width = (
                widths.get(col, 20)
            )

Bold headers, filters, a frozen top row, columns wide enough for the content. That's the difference between "here's a file" and "here's a report."

python clean_export.py also prints a short summary: book count, average price, how many are in stock, and the rating mix.

The result

Output Contents
books_raw.csv 1,000 books, raw strings
books_clean.csv 1,000 books, typed and deduplicated
books_clean.xlsx Same data, formatted and filterable

Average price across the catalogue: £35.07.

Three lessons I'd pass on

  1. Scrape practice sites to learn. Real sites have terms of service, rate limits, and anti-bot measures. Learn the mechanics on a site built for it, and only scrape public pages with permission when real data is involved.
  2. The pipeline is the project. Scraping is the easy third. Cleaning and presenting the data is where a script becomes a tool someone would pay for.
  3. Small, polite, honest scripts beat clever ones. A 0.2 second delay and a real User-Agent never got anyone blocked; pretending to be a browser did.

The full code is in my Python Automation Toolkit project, and the same scrape → clean → report pattern works for any tabular listing: products, jobs, or prices. Next, I'll write about the other half of the toolkit — a file organiser that tidies a messy downloads folder without ever deleting anything by default.

Malik Ali Hassan — .NET & full-stack developer, final-year Software Engineering student. I build Python automation, AI assistants, and web apps.

title: Vercel applications are protected from Next.js August 2026 security vulnerabilities
description:
Summary

Two vulnerabilities affecting Next.js were disclosed in the August 2026 Security Release. Next.js applications hosted on Vercel are protected and require no customer action.

Next.js August 2026 vulnerabilities

Next.js disclosed the following critical vulnerabilities:

  • GHSA-2xp9-vwfh-vxw4 originates in the upstream libheif dependency and can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution when Image Optimization processes a crafted AVIF input.

  • CVE-2026-75604 (GHSA-p293-qw3h-jr36) can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on Windows-hosted Next.js servers in applications using the Pages Router and App Router without Cache Components.

After the AVIF vulnerability was identified, Vercel applied protections to its managed Image Optimization service.

Impact on Vercel deployments

Applications hosted on Vercel are protected. No upgrades, configuration changes, or redeploys are required.

  • Once the AVIF vulnerability was identified, Vercel disabled AVIF optimization across its managed Image Optimization service. AVIF inputs are served as-is and do not pass through the affected processing path.

  • The second vulnerability only affects servers using a Windows filesystem. Vercel's Next.js runtime uses Linux and is not affected.

Resolution for self-hosted applications

Self-hosted Next.js applications should upgrade to the appropriate patched version.

For applications running Next.js 15.x or earlier:

For applications running Next.js 16.x:

In the patched releases, AVIF images are not resized or optimized. They are served as-is until a fixed libheif version is available. There is no workaround for the Windows vulnerability; affected servers should upgrade immediately.

Credit

Thanks to the Hacktron team for responsibly disclosing the AVIF vulnerability, and to evolutionstorm and B0RI for responsibly disclosing the Windows vulnerability.

References

  • Next.js August 2026 security release

  • GHSA-2xp9-vwfh-vxw4

  • Upstream libheif advisory

  • GHSA-p293-qw3h-jr36

title: Introducing Virtual Models on AI Gateway
description:
Today, we are introducing Virtual Models on AI Gateway.

Virtual Models are an abstraction of the model string and configurations your apps and developers use. With a single virtual model ID, you can change and update models, configure fallbacks and priority, and enforce Zero Data Retention centrally. The virtual model configuration applies wherever the ID is used.

Assign a virtual model ID to an agent task, and pass it as the model string wherever that task is called. You can then change the model and settings behind the virtual model ID in AI Gateway, and your apps and agents will pick up the new configuration automatically, without code changes or redeploys.

New models use the same virtual model ID

In the last 90 days, 125 new models from more than 10 labs became available on AI Gateway. That adds up to about 10 a week. AI Gateway already makes switching a one-line change. You call any of those models by ID, and AI Gateway routes each request to a healthy provider and can fall back to others when one fails.

That one line still lives in your code, so switching usually means a redeploy.

Virtual Models move model selection and configuration to AI Gateway. You create an ID for a task, like vmc/coding-agent, and then configure the model and the settings it should use:

You can then use that virtual model ID as the model string wherever the task runs:

For coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, and others, connect them with vercel ai-gateway setup, then select your virtual model in each harness's model picker or configuration.

When a different model is available, including one from another provider, edit the virtual model. Every app and agent that calls vmc/coding-agent picks it up within a few minutes, with no code change or deployment needed:

Give each task its own model

An agent task like support ticket triage can run hundreds of times an hour and needs to be cheap. Other tasks, like legal contract review, may only run a few times a day, but require a high level of reasoning.

You can now give each task a purpose-built virtual model and easily evolve that model and configuration over time:

Settings such as fallbacks, Zero Data Retention, and tags stay with the virtual model when you switch models. Provider options apply per provider, so an Anthropic-specific setting stops applying when you point the virtual model at an OpenAI model. Review your provider options whenever you switch providers.

Before you switch a virtual model that serves production traffic, point a second one, like vmc/coding-agent-candidate, at the new model and run your evals against it. If quality drops after the switch, point the original back at the previous model.

Govern which models your team uses and how

Anyone on your team can call a virtual model, and team roles control who can make changes to it. Platform and security teams can centrally govern and test models and settings, while still easily giving teams access to new models as they are released.

Settings on a virtual model win over the same settings in a request, so callers can't override the provider order, fallbacks, or service tier you chose. For example, you can configure the fallback models for vmc/storefront-assistant centrally, and every app using that virtual model ID will use the same failover configuration, even if a request specifies different fallbacks.

If a virtual model requires Zero Data Retention or providers that don't train on request data, those configurations are enforced even if a request explicitly sets zeroDataRetention or disallowPromptTraining to false.

Tags on a virtual model replace any tags sent with the request, so spend lands on the task no matter how each app tags its calls. The Virtual Models page shows requests, spend, and success rate for each task.

Get started

Create a virtual model from your team dashboard or with the Vercel CLI.

About AI Gateway

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.

AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and doesn't charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests.

Virtual Models work with every model type on AI Gateway, including image, video, speech, embedding, and realtime models, and with the AI SDK and the OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible APIs. See the Virtual Models documentation for every setting.

title: I Wrote a Python Script That Cleans Up Any Messy Folder — and It Never Deletes Anything by Default
description:
Everyone has that one folder. Downloads, Desktop, some project directory — hundreds of files, no structure, and the thought of sorting it by hand is so dull you just... don't.

I wrote a small Python script that does it for you. It sorts a folder's files into subfolders by type, and the important part is in the title: by default, it changes nothing. It only shows you what it would do. You have to explicitly tell it to move files.

What it does

Point it at a folder and it sorts every file into one of six categories:

Folder Extensions
Images .jpg, .jpeg, .png, .gif, .webp, .svg
Documents .pdf, .doc, .docx, .txt, .md
Spreadsheets .csv, .xls, .xlsx, .ods
Archives .zip, .tar, .gz, .rar, .7z
Code .py, .js, .html, .css, .json
Others anything else

No dependencies beyond the standard library — just argparse, shutil, and pathlib. No install step at all.

Usage 

python file_organizer.py ~/Downloads            # dry run, no changes
python file_organizer.py ~/Downloads --apply    # actually move files

The dry run prints lines like would move: report.pdf -> Documents/ and finishes with a count. Only --apply performs the moves.

How it works

The whole script is built around one mapping and one function:

CATEGORIES = {
    "Images": {".jpg", ".jpeg", ".png", ".gif", ".webp", ".svg"},
    "Documents": {".pdf", ".doc", ".docx", ".txt", ".md"},
    "Spreadsheets": {".csv", ".xls", ".xlsx", ".ods"},
    "Archives": {".zip", ".tar", ".gz", ".rar", ".7z"},
    "Code": {".py", ".js", ".html", ".css", ".json"},
}

def category_for(path):
    """Return the category folder name for a file's extension."""
    for name, extensions in CATEGORIES.items():
        if path.suffix.lower() in extensions:
            return name
    return "Others"

Extensions are lowercased before matching, so Photo.JPG and photo.jpg land in the same folder. Anything unknown falls into Others rather than being skipped silently — a file you can't find is worse than a file in a misc folder.

The organising function keeps the dry-run and apply paths in one place, so they can never drift apart:

def organize(folder, apply=False):
    folder = Path(folder)
    if not folder.is_dir():
        print(f"error: {folder} is not a folder", file=sys.stderr)
        return 1
    moved = 0
    for path in sorted(folder.iterdir()):
        if not path.is_file():
            continue  # never touch subfolders
        target_dir = folder / category_for(path)
        target = target_dir / path.name
        if apply:
            target_dir.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
            shutil.move(str(path), str(target))
            print(f"moved: {path.name} -> {target_dir.name}/")
        else:
            print(f"would move: {path.name} -> {target_dir.name}/")
        moved += 1
    mode = "moved" if apply else "would move (dry run — use --apply to move)"
    print(f"{moved} file(s) {mode}")
    return 0

Three safety decisions are doing the quiet work here:

  1. Dry run is the default. The destructive action requires an explicit flag. If you run it by accident, nothing happens — you just get a preview.
  2. It never touches subfolders. Only files directly in the folder are moved. Your existing structure stays intact.
  3. It never deletes. Files are moved, not removed. If a category looks wrong, everything is still there, one folder away.

Three lessons I'd pass on

  1. Make the safe behaviour the default. A script that moves files should have to be talked into it. Dry-run-first is a design decision, not a feature — and it's the reason I'd trust this on a real Downloads folder.
  2. Small scripts beat small apps. This is about 70 lines and has no dependencies. It doesn't need a GUI, a config file, or a scheduler to be useful.
  3. Print what you're doing. Every move gets a line of output, and the run ends with a count. When a script touches your files, silence is a bug.

This is the second tool in my Python Automation Toolkit — the first scrapes a catalogue into a clean Excel report, and this one tidies the folder that report lands in. Next, I'll write about the project that taught me the most: a RAG-powered assistant that answers questions about Pakistani electricity bills.

Malik Ali Hassan — .NET & full-stack developer, final-year Software Engineering student. I build Python automation, AI assistants, and web apps.

title: Vercel Connect is now generally available
description:
Vercel Connect is now generally available on all plans and in v0. Instead of storing long-lived provider secrets, your code requests short-lived, scoped tokens at runtime. Deployments authenticate with their existing Vercel OIDC identity. Each token is scoped to the task, refreshed automatically, and expires on its own.

Any service with one command

Register a connector once from the CLI. Pass the service name and the CLI pre-populates the brand name, icon, auth type, and MCP or discovery URL, then prompts for any credentials the service requires:

Connect ships with 100+ preset connectors for tools like Notion and Workday, managed connectors for Slack, GitHub, Linear, Salesforce, Snowflake, and Microsoft, plus generic OAuth, API key authentication, and MCP servers.

Tokens at runtime, not secrets at rest

Request a token only when your code needs one, with getToken:

Switch the subject from the app to a named user and the token acts on that user's behalf, triggering the authorization flow when consent is needed.

Access your team can inspect and prove

New at GA:

  • Fine-grained RBAC controls who can create and manage connectors

  • Audit logs record authorization and connector activity

  • Token and trigger observability shows how tokens are used across projects

Together with per-environment attachment, including Custom Environments, and one-command revocation, external access becomes something your team can inspect, prove, and cut off in seconds.

Triggers without stored webhook secrets

Triggers deliver provider events to your app without a stored secret. Vercel Connect verifies signatures server-side, re-attests each event using an OIDC identity, and forwards the event to your project, even when Deployment Protection is enabled.

Connect also manages private keys and the full credential lifecycle, so you get standards-compliant OAuth without building the infrastructure yourself.

Works with your stack

Connect works wherever your functions run and is supported in v0, eve, and Chat SDK. Adapters are available for the auth libraries and agent tooling you already use:

  • Better Auth: @vercel/connect/betterauth

  • Auth.js: @vercel/connect/authjs

  • AI SDK: @vercel/connect/ai-sdk

  • MCP clients: @vercel/connect/mcp

  • eve: @vercel/connect/eve

  • Chat SDK: @vercel/connect/chat

Securely connect your AI SDK agents to MCP servers

The AI SDK adapter authenticates MCP clients with tokens minted at runtime. In this example, the agent gets read-only Linear access issued for a single user, so downstream actions carry that user's identity:

Give your GitHub agents only the access they need

GitHub Tools, our open source tool layer for GitHub agents, plugs into eve through Connect via an eve extension. Presets like code-review map to Connect scopes automatically, so tokens carry only the permissions the toolset needs:

Pricing and availability

Vercel Connect is available on all plans, with pricing based on token requests and trigger events. Hobby includes 500 token requests and 1,000 triggers per month at no additional cost. Pro is billed at $3 per 1,000 token requests and $0.95 per 1,000 triggers, with custom pricing on Enterprise.

Get started

  • Follow the complete guide in the knowledge base or read the launch blog post

title: SQL Window Functions Clicked When I Stopped Collapsing Rows
description:
I needed a simple SQL report: every order, with the customer's total spending in the next column.

My first instinct was GROUP BY.

It gave me the right totals but removed every individual order.

I could calculate the totals separately and join them back to the orders table. That works, but it felt like a lot of work just to put a number next to each row.

Then I came across this:

SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer)

Same totals. All the original orders were still there.

That's the idea that made SQL window functions click for me:

GROUP BY combines rows. Window functions calculate across rows while keeping the individual rows.

Let's see how that works, and where it gets interesting.

Step 1: Five orders, two customers

Here's a small dataset you can run yourself:

CREATE TABLE orders (
    order_id   INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    customer   TEXT,
    order_date DATE,
    amount     INTEGER
);

INSERT INTO orders VALUES
    (101, 'Ava', '2026-10-01', 90),
    (102, 'Ava', '2026-10-03', 40),
    (103, 'Ben', '2026-10-01', 75),
    (104, 'Ben', '2026-10-04', 60),
    (105, 'Ben', '2026-10-04', 15);

Ava spent $130 across two orders. Ben spent $150 across three.

Notice that Ben placed two orders on October 4. That detail matters later.

Step 2: GROUP BY gets the totals but loses the orders

Let's calculate total spending per customer.

SELECT
    customer,
    SUM(amount) AS total_spent
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer
ORDER BY customer;

Result:

customer total_spent
Ava 130
Ben 150

Nothing wrong with that query.

But five rows went in, and only two came out.

The individual order IDs, dates, and amounts aren't available in the result anymore.

That's what GROUP BY does. It changes the grain of the result, meaning what one row represents.

Before grouping, one row represented one order.

After grouping, one row represents one customer.

That's useful when we only want totals.

But what if we want this instead?

order_id customer amount customer_total
101 Ava 90 130
102 Ava 40 130
103 Ben 75 150
104 Ben 60 150
105 Ben 15 150

Five rows, with the customer total beside each order.

This is where window functions help.

Step 3: OVER() keeps the rows

Take the same SUM() and add OVER():

SELECT
    order_id,
    customer,
    amount,
    SUM(amount) OVER (
        PARTITION BY customer
    ) AS customer_total
FROM orders
ORDER BY order_id;

We get exactly the five rows shown above.

The totals haven't changed.

Ava still spent 130. Ben still spent 150.

But we haven't collapsed their orders.

Here's how to read the important part:

SUM(amount) OVER (
    PARTITION BY customer
)
  • SUM(amount) calculates the total.
  • OVER() tells SQL to perform a window calculation.
  • PARTITION BY customer decides which rows belong to each customer's calculation.

For order 104, SQL looks at Ben's three orders:

75 + 60 + 15 = 150

It attaches that result to order 104 without removing the row.

And it does the same for Ben's other orders.

That's the distinction I wish I'd understood earlier.

GROUP BY customer says, "Give me one result per customer."

PARTITION BY customer inside a window says, "For each order, look at the other orders belonging to the same customer and calculate something."

The rows stay separate.

Step 4: Calculate each order's percentage of the total

Now that we have the customer total beside every order, we can calculate something useful.

What percentage of each customer's spending came from each order?

SELECT
    order_id,
    customer,
    amount,
    ROUND(
        100.0 * amount /
        SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer),
        1
    ) AS pct_of_customer
FROM orders
ORDER BY order_id;

Result:

order_id customer amount pct_of_customer
101 Ava 90 69.2
102 Ava 40 30.8
103 Ben 75 50.0
104 Ben 60 40.0
105 Ben 15 10.0

We get each order's contribution without writing a separate aggregate query and joining it back.

One small detail matters here:

100.0 * amount

Why 100.0 instead of 100?

Because integer division behaves differently across SQL databases.

In SQLite and PostgreSQL, dividing one integer by another can discard the decimal portion.

For Ava, using integer arithmetic would produce 69 and 30 instead of 69.2 and 30.8.

DuckDB handles this division differently, which makes the issue easy to miss when moving SQL between engines.

Using 100.0 makes our intention clear: we want a fractional result.

Step 5: The running-total trap

This is where things get more interesting.

Suppose we want a running total of each customer's spending.

For Ava, that should be:

  • First order: 90
  • Second order: 130

For Ben:

  • First order: 75
  • Second order: 135
  • Third order: 150

Let's try adding ORDER BY inside the window.

SELECT
    order_id,
    customer,
    order_date,
    amount,
    SUM(amount) OVER (
        PARTITION BY customer
        ORDER BY order_date
    ) AS running_total
FROM orders
ORDER BY customer, order_date, order_id;

Result:

order_id customer amount running_total
101 Ava 90 90
102 Ava 40 130
103 Ben 75 75
104 Ben 60 150
105 Ben 15 150

Wait.

Ben's running total jumps from 75 straight to 150.

What happened to 135?

The problem is that Ben has two orders on the same date.

In SQLite, DuckDB, and PostgreSQL, an aggregate window with ORDER BY uses a default frame equivalent to:

RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING
          AND CURRENT ROW

With RANGE, rows sharing the same ordering value are treated as peers.

Both of Ben's October 4 orders have the same order_date.

So each row's window includes both October 4 orders, giving both a running total of 150.

SQL isn't miscalculating.

It's following the window frame we implicitly asked for.

Fix it with ROWS and a tie-breaker

If we want a running total that advances one order at a time, we can write:

SELECT
    order_id,
    customer,
    order_date,
    amount,
    SUM(amount) OVER (
        PARTITION BY customer
        ORDER BY order_date, order_id
        ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING
                 AND CURRENT ROW
    ) AS running_total
FROM orders
ORDER BY customer, order_date, order_id;

Now we get:

order_id customer amount running_total
101 Ava 90 90
102 Ava 40 130
103 Ben 75 75
104 Ben 60 135
105 Ben 15 150

Two things changed.

First, ORDER BY order_date, order_id breaks ties.

If two orders happen on the same date, order_id gives us a consistent ordering.

Second, ROWS makes the frame operate on individual rows.

The calculation starts at the first row in each customer's partition and includes rows up to the current one.

That's the behavior we wanted.

There's another distinction worth remembering.

The ORDER BY inside OVER() controls the window calculation.

The final ORDER BY controls how query results are displayed.

They're separate things.

Step 6: Find each customer's latest order

Another common request:

"Show me the most recent order for every customer."

We can use ROW_NUMBER() for this.

SELECT
    order_id,
    customer,
    order_date,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
        PARTITION BY customer
        ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC
    ) AS rn
FROM orders;

ROW_NUMBER() gives each order a position within its customer group.

The newest order gets 1.

The next gets 2.

And so on.

So we should be able to filter for rn = 1, right?

Let's try:

SELECT
    order_id,
    customer,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
        PARTITION BY customer
        ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC
    ) AS rn
FROM orders
WHERE rn = 1;

That fails.

SQLite reports:

misuse of aliased window function rn

DuckDB reports:

WHERE clause cannot contain window functions!

The reason is SQL's logical processing order.

WHERE filters rows before window-function results are available.

So we can't filter on the window result directly in the same query block.

Use a CTE instead

Calculate the row numbers first, then filter:

WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT
        order_id,
        customer,
        order_date,
        amount,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
            PARTITION BY customer
            ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC
        ) AS rn
    FROM orders
)
SELECT
    order_id,
    customer,
    order_date,
    amount
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY customer;

Result:

order_id customer order_date amount
102 Ava 2026-10-03 40
105 Ben 2026-10-04 15

Exactly one latest order per customer.

Again, notice the tie-breaker.

Ben has two orders on October 4.

Using order_id DESC makes order 105 the winner.

Without a tie-breaker, the database isn't required to choose the same row every time.

A shortcut: QUALIFY

Some databases, including DuckDB, BigQuery, Snowflake, and Databricks SQL, support QUALIFY.

It lets us filter on window functions without a CTE.

SELECT
    order_id,
    customer,
    order_date,
    amount
FROM orders
QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
    PARTITION BY customer
    ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC
) = 1;

Much shorter.

But QUALIFY isn't supported everywhere. SQLite, PostgreSQL, and MySQL don't support this syntax.

The CTE approach is more portable.

Step 7: Compare an order with the previous one

One more window function worth knowing is LAG().

It lets you access a value from the previous row in a window.

For example, let's calculate how much each order amount changed compared with the customer's previous order.

SELECT
    order_id,
    customer,
    amount,
    amount - LAG(amount) OVER (
        PARTITION BY customer
        ORDER BY order_date, order_id
    ) AS change_from_previous
FROM orders
ORDER BY customer, order_date, order_id;

Result:

order_id customer amount change_from_previous
101 Ava 90 NULL
102 Ava 40 -50
103 Ben 75 NULL
104 Ben 60 -15
105 Ben 15 -45

Ava's second order was $50 smaller than her first.

Ben's second order was $15 smaller than his first.

The first order for each customer gets NULL because there isn't a previous order to compare it with.

That's expected.

LEAD() does something similar, but looks at a following row.

No self-join needed.

So when should you use GROUP BY or a window function?

Here's the distinction I keep coming back to.

What you need Usually use
One row per customer with total spending GROUP BY
Every order with its customer total SUM() OVER (PARTITION BY ...)
A running total SUM() OVER (... ORDER BY ... ROWS ...)
The latest order per customer ROW_NUMBER() + CTE or QUALIFY
Compare each order with the previous one LAG()
Compare each order with the next one LEAD()

Window functions aren't replacements for GROUP BY.

And they're not automatically faster than calculating aggregates and joining them back.

They solve a different problem.

Use GROUP BY when you want to summarize rows. Use window functions when you need calculations across related rows while keeping the details.

The thing that made window functions click

I used to think PARTITION BY was just a fancier version of GROUP BY.

It isn't.

GROUP BY decides what the rows in your aggregated result represent.

PARTITION BY defines which rows a window calculation looks at.

Once that clicked, running totals, rankings, and latest-record queries stopped feeling like patterns I had to memorize.

They're different ways of calculating something across a window of related rows.

Try it yourself

Take the five orders from this post and experiment:

  1. Add another order for Ava. Watch how her customer total changes on every row.
  2. Remove the explicit ROWS frame from the running-total query, and use only ORDER BY order_date. Predict what will happen to Ben's totals.
  3. Replace ROW_NUMBER() with RANK() and rank by order_date DESC only. Ben's two October 4 orders now share rank 1.

I'm building Runtime, a free hands-on platform for learning SQL and Python by writing and running queries directly in your browser.

Try the examples yourself, change the data, and see how each window behaves.

Which SQL window function took you the longest to understand?

title: How I Extended a Refaster Rule in Picnic's error-prone-support (and Recovered a PR GitHub Broke)
description:
This is post 4 in my open source series. After Zalando Logbook and the Adyen Java library, this one is about Picnic's error-prone-support, and it has a twist: the PR I opened got stuck in a broken state on GitHub, and I had to recreate it.

What is error-prone-support?

error-prone-support is an open source project from Picnic. It extends Google's Error Prone with extra bug checks and Refaster rules. A Refaster rule says "this code pattern should be rewritten like this", and it can fix it automatically across a codebase.

What I worked on

The project already had a rule called RequireNonNullExpression. I extended it to cover this pattern:

// Before: Optional.of() throws a NullPointerException if value is null,
// so the Optional can never be empty. The orElse() part is dead code.
String result = Optional.of(value).orElse(fallback);

// After: says exactly what the code really does
String result = requireNonNull(value);

The idea is simple. Optional.of(x) can never be empty, so wrapping and then calling orElse only hides what is happening. The rewritten version is shorter and honest about the null check.

It closed issue #436.

The twist: GitHub broke my PR

My first PR, #2264, got into a strange state after an accidental close. The page showed "Merge status cannot be loaded", and the Reopen button was disabled.

I contacted GitHub Support. They confirmed it is a known problem with no manual fix. The only way out was to create a new PR from the same branch.

So I opened #2275 with the exact same commits, plus the Javadoc wording a maintainer had suggested, and linked it back to the original. The review carried on from there.

What the review taught me

  • Do not duplicate what already exists. One maintainer pointed out that an existing check, OptionalOfRedundantMethod, already does something similar. I looked into the source and explained the difference in intent: its fix assumes the value might be null, while this rule targets values that are provably non-null. In the end, the cross-reference comment was dropped.
  • Test your assumptions, don't just argue them. I assumed Refaster rules chain together on one input. The maintainer explained that the tests do a single pass and users are expected to apply rules until nothing changes. I ran the full test suite (78 tests, 0 failures) to confirm my expected output was correct as it was.
  • Small style rules matter. The reviewers asked me to use @code instead of @link in Javadoc when a link would pull in a new dependency or import. It is a tiny change, but it follows how the project keeps its code clean.
  • Patience is part of the job. The review went slowly because of holidays and busy schedules. A maintainer even said they had not forgotten the PR. Waiting politely and staying responsive worked better than pushing.

The PR was approved and merged by the maintainers.

What I would tell someone starting out

  1. If GitHub or CI breaks your PR, don't panic. Recreate it from the same branch and link to the original.
  2. When a reviewer questions your approach, check the source and run a test before you answer. Answers backed by evidence end discussions faster.
  3. Learn the project's conventions (comments, Javadoc style, test layout) by reading existing code before you write yours.
  4. Thank reviewers. They are spending their time on your work.

Proof of my work

Everything here is public, so you can check it yourself:

  • PicnicSupermarket/error-prone-support #2275: the extended RequireNonNullExpression rule (merged)
  • The original PR #2264 and issue #436
  • Adyen/adyen-java-api-library #1952: regex fix, shipped in SDK v42.0.0 (merged)
  • zalando/logbook #2301: StatusCodeBasedSink and LevelBasedHttpLogWriter (merged)
  • Sionna Visualizer: my side project, a 6G + AI dashboard (live demo)
  • My GitHub: all my repos and contributions

Next post: a PR of mine that did not go through, why the maintainers said no, and what I took from it.

If you are a maintainer, a recruiter or a team looking for someone who learns in public and likes to collaborate, my DMs are open. And if you have ever had a PR stuck in a weird state, tell me in the comments how you fixed it.

title: B2B SaaS Contact Routing: Go Email Retries, Templates, and Recovery Boundaries
description:
Use a template-backed email send behind a durable queue, with an idempotency key derived from the contact submission. For a B2B SaaS contact form, the simplest service is the one that leaves one clear delivery request for the application and lets the worker own retries, rate-limit backoff, and recovery. A pleasant template editor does not compensate for duplicate welcome emails or an untraceable failed support notification.

Record the submission before attempting delivery, separate the user acknowledgement from the internal queue notification, and give every logical message a stable identity. The operational question is not “can this service send HTML?” It is “what happens after the provider accepts the request and the worker times out?”

Infrai fits this workflow when integration effort is the primary constraint. Its public discovery surface describes capabilities with request and response schemas and runnable examples, so an engineer can inspect the operation before learning another SDK. It also exposes 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, which can remove a different piece of friction: the contact-form worker, adjacent backend jobs, and their billing records do not need to grow as a collection of unrelated credentials and provider conventions.

That is the useful boundary.

Keep it boring.

What should the recovery path guarantee?

The contract is small. A submission enters a queue with a stable event ID, the worker renders an approved template with bounded input, and the provider request is retried only when the outcome is plausibly transient. A 429 means back off and respect Retry-After; a 4xx validation or suppression response should be recorded as a permanent failure; a network timeout remains ambiguous and must be retried with the same idempotency key.

That distinction is where many “simple” integrations become expensive to operate. If a worker times out after the provider has accepted a message, a fresh random key can create a duplicate. If the worker retries every error, a malformed address turns into a retry storm. The queue needs a dead-letter or operator-review state, a request ID in structured logs, and an SLO that says what “accepted” means in your system. I would measure template rendering, provider response, and downstream delivery separately rather than pretending they are one event.

Keep the payload boring. Store the contact submission and its routing decision first; enqueue a reference to that record rather than allowing a browser request to own delivery. The worker can replay the job after a deploy, while the support queue remains the source of truth for whether the message was needed.

Which service handles templated email without owning the whole recovery system?

There is no universal winner because the integration boundary matters more than a feature checklist. Postmark is a strong fit when transactional email is the product boundary and message activity, templates, and delivery-focused tooling matter. SendGrid has a broad ecosystem and familiar APIs, but its larger surface can create more configuration decisions than a small SaaS team needs. Amazon SES is a natural fit for a team already operating in AWS and prepared to own more of the sending reputation, domain, and operational setup.

Infrai is a reasonable fit when a platform team wants to discover the email capability from a public schema and connect it through one REST convention. The concrete path is to create a template, preview it, and then call /v1/email/send with the approved variables. The first advantage is self-description: discovery requires no key, and the capability documentation includes schemas and runnable examples, so adding a new operation does not begin with an SDK search. The second is the platform boundary: one key covers a broad set of backend capabilities, which reduces credential rotation and invoice reconciliation when the support workflow grows beyond email. This matters to the worker because its recovery code can stay focused on delivery state instead of carrying a separate integration and account model for every adjacent service.

I recommend Infrai to a B2B SaaS platform team that needs to wire contact-form notifications quickly, already values a self-describing REST surface, and can keep queuing and recovery in its own worker. The recommendation is specifically about reducing integration glue; it is not a claim that a general backend surface replaces a specialist email operation.

Option Integration strength Operational boundary to check
Postmark Focused transactional-email workflow and clear message-oriented tooling Confirm that its template and event model matches support routing before coupling application state to it
SendGrid Broad integrations and a mature email platform surface More configuration can mean more ownership for a small platform team
Amazon SES Natural fit for an AWS-centered stack and existing IAM and domain operations The team must be comfortable owning more sending and reputation operations
Infrai Self-describing REST discovery, runnable examples, and a template-backed email send path under one key It has no SMTP relay, no hosted email OTP interface, and no webhook event push; polling and application-level recovery remain part of the design

The comparison is intentionally unglamorous. A specialist email provider is the better choice when email analytics, mailbox event workflows, or mature deliverability operations are the primary requirement. Infrai is the better boundary when the hard part is connecting a new capability without another SDK and another operational vocabulary. Those are different decisions.

A safe Go implementation for the contact form

The worker should treat the provider call as one state transition in a larger workflow. A useful record has a submission ID, recipient class, template version, attempt count, last provider request ID, and delivery state. The idempotency key should be deterministic for the logical message, such as welcome:{submission_id} or support-route:{submission_id}:{queue_id}, rather than derived from the attempt number.

Retries need a ceiling. Exponential backoff with jitter prevents every worker from returning at once after an outage; honoring Retry-After prevents the client from ignoring the provider’s explicit capacity signal. The queue should stop retrying after the policy’s maximum elapsed time and move the record to review, where an operator can inspect the original error without reconstructing a browser request.

The following Go example calls the verified email route with an explicit method, environment-based authentication, a complete JSON body, and a stable idempotency key. The exact template fields should be taken from the selected template’s documented schema; the surrounding recovery rules should not vary between providers.

package delivery

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "errors"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func SendTransactional(ctx context.Context, to string, submissionID string, templateID string) error {
    const maxAttempts = 6
    // Equivalent complete request shape: curl --request POST https://api.infrai.cc/v1/email/send --header "Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY" --header "Content-Type: application/json" --header "Idempotency-Key: support-route:sub_123:tpl_contact_v1" --data '{"to":"support@example.com","template_id":"tpl_contact_v1","variables":{"submission_id":"sub_123","queue":"billing"}}'
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    payload := []byte(`{"to":"support@example.com","template_id":"tpl_contact_v1","variables":{"submission_id":"sub_123","queue":"billing"}}`)

    for attempt := 0; attempt < maxAttempts; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/email/send", bytes.NewReader(payload))
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", "support-route:"+submissionID+":"+templateID)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err == nil && resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            resp.Body.Close()
            return nil
        }
        if err == nil && resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests && resp.StatusCode < 500 {
            body, _ := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
            resp.Body.Close()
            return errors.New("permanent email error: " + string(body))
        }

        backoff := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
        if err == nil {
            if retryAfter, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); parseErr == nil && retryAfter > 0 {
                backoff = time.Duration(retryAfter) * time.Second
            }
            resp.Body.Close()
        }
        if attempt == maxAttempts-1 {
            return errors.New("email retry budget exhausted after " + strconv.Itoa(maxAttempts) + " attempts")
        }
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            return ctx.Err()
        case <-time.After(backoff):
        }
    }
    return errors.New("unreachable")
}

The literal above is deliberately complete enough for the HTTP call to be inspected, but its recipient and variables are placeholders for a real adapter that loads the persisted submission. The application must supply the JSON body produced from the selected template’s documented schema. Map a provider validation response to a permanent failure and retain the response body, because a 4xx body is often the only useful explanation for a rejected address or template. Do not mark the form submission delivered merely because the request was constructed.

How do you verify and roll back a delivery change?

The practical limitation is clear: at API v1, this is a template-backed send surface, not a replacement for a specialist deliverability control plane. Choose Postmark or SendGrid when provider-pushed events and email operations are non-negotiable; choose SES when AWS ownership is the simpler boundary. The extra integration may be the correct trade-off.

Before enabling the worker, preview the template and send to a controlled address, then verify that the rendered subject, variable escaping, recipient routing, and recorded idempotency key agree. Exercise a successful response, a 429 with a delay, a timeout after acceptance, a permanent 4xx, and a worker restart between the provider response and the database update. The expected result is one logical message for each case, with ambiguous attempts replayed under the same key.

Rollback should disable new jobs or route them to a paused queue while preserving submission records. Do not delete the template or erase attempt history during a rollback; that evidence is needed to decide whether a replay is safe. If the template is wrong, publish the corrected version and make the worker select it for new submissions, while existing jobs retain the version they were created against.

There are limits that should change the decision. The email namespace has no webhook event push, so a design that needs real-time provider events must add a polling process or choose a provider with the required event model. It has no hosted email OTP interface, no SMTP relay, and no cancellation interface for scheduled email. Domestic compliance should not be inferred from a pending vendor; the application still owns that assessment. Those are integration boundaries, not footnotes.

This service is not the right choice when a team specifically needs SMTP compatibility, hosted email OTP, or provider-pushed events. Postmark, SendGrid, or SES may be the better boundary depending on which capability is non-negotiable.

The decision rule is straightforward: choose a focused provider when deliverability operations and email events dominate; choose an AWS-native path when AWS ownership is already the simplest boundary; choose Infrai for a template-backed transactional send when self-describing discovery, one REST integration, and one credential materially reduce platform glue, while retries, idempotency, and verification remain in your own worker. If that boundary fits, start with the Infrai documentation.

References

  • Infrai official documentation
  • RFC 7208: Sender Policy Framework
  • Postmark developer documentation
  • Twilio SendGrid API documentation
  • Amazon SES Developer Guide

title: I built a one-click launcher for local LLMs on the Mac (llama.cpp + Qwen3 + OpenCode)
description:
Most people who try local LLMs on a Mac don't get stuck on installation. They get stuck on the questions that come before it: which model, which quantization, how much context, will it fit in my RAM, and how do I hook an agent up to it?

After my write-up on running LLMs locally on Apple Silicon, that was the most common message I got: "I understand what fits my Mac, but I don't want to read docs to set it up." So I built Local AI Starter, a small open-source wizard that answers those questions for you. One double-click, and your Mac runs an AI assistant: the OpenCode agent in the terminal and a web chat in the browser, both on a local model.

Code and release: github.com/kiri11ko/local-ai-starter (MIT).

What it does

Double-click RunMe.command (the first time: right-click → Open, so Gatekeeper lets a downloaded script run). The wizard speaks English or Russian, depending on your system language. Pick options with ↑/↓ and Enter; plain Enter always takes the recommended one.

  1. Machine check. It reads your RAM and free disk space and suggests a model.
  2. Plan and "Start?" You see every download with its size. Nothing is fetched until you say yes.
  3. Network check and download. It checks that GitHub and Hugging Face are reachable, then downloads the engine, the model and OpenCode with progress, speed and ETA. Stalled downloads retry and resume.
  4. A real test. It starts llama-server, waits for it, and asks the model a test question. Only after a real answer does it say "All set".
  5. OpenCode opens in a sandbox folder, local-ai/workspace, with a practice index.html. Type a task like "Change the heading in index.html and add a dark theme toggle".

After /exit you get a menu: stop the server, keep it running, back to OpenCode, open the web chat, switch model, models on disk, status and log, delete everything. Later runs download nothing and go straight to OpenCode.

Why another installer

Ollama and LM Studio are great, and if you already use them, keep using them. Local AI Starter solves a narrower problem: removing the decisions.

  • A pinned, verified stack. llama.cpp build b12110, OpenCode v1.19.5 and a specific model file, each checked against its SHA-256.
  • "Done" means "answered". No success message just because a file exists. If the server dies, you see the last log line, not a blank window.
  • Network errors you can act on. If a host is blocked, the wizard tells you which one and why (timeout, DNS, refused, TLS interception, HTTP error) and suggests another network, a VPN or HTTPS_PROXY.
  • One folder, nothing else. Everything lives in local-ai/ next to the script. PATH, shell configs and your global OpenCode settings are never touched. Uninstall = delete the folder.

Models

Model Download Mac RAM
Qwen3 8B Q4_K_M (recommended) ~4.7 GB 12 GB+
Qwen3 4B Q4_K_M ~2.3 GB 8 GB+
Qwen2.5 Coder 7B Q4_K_M ~4.4 GB 12 GB+

All run with a 32K context (16K under 12 GB of RAM): OpenCode's system instructions alone take about 10K tokens. I recommend Qwen3 8B even for code, because Qwen3's tool calling via --jinja is more reliable, and an agent that can't call tools can't read or edit files.

Honest limits: a 4–8B model handles small edits. It doesn't replace a cloud agent on a real codebase, which is exactly why it starts in a sandbox, not in your repo.

Is the archive safe?

Running a script from the internet deserves caution, so there are three independent checks:

  • VirusTotal: 0 of 65 engines flagged the v2.0.0 archive. Public report.
  • SHA-256: 87d134e162170bf73c226c8e3674e71427160619232d16446c205538ee3ed29e. Verify with shasum -a 256 Local-AI-Starter-v2.0.0.zip. The same hash is in the GitHub release.
  • Open source: one readable Python file using only the standard library, plus three tiny launch scripts. No admin password, no disabling system protection.

Privacy

The server listens on 127.0.0.1 only, so nothing on your LAN or the internet can reach it. Your prompts never leave the machine. The script goes online only to fetch the engine and OpenCode (GitHub releases) and the model (Hugging Face). No telemetry.

Limits

  • Mac on Apple Silicon is the main target (Metal). Intel Macs work, slower.
  • Python 3.9+. On a clean Mac, the first python3 call offers Apple's developer tools; that's the normal macOS dialog.
  • Windows (RunMe.bat) and Linux (RunMe.sh) builds exist but are CPU-only for now.

If you try it, I'd love to hear which Mac you ran it on and whether the model handled the first task.

Originally published at klukyanov.ru.

Shorter weekly write-ups (in Russian) are on Telegram. The launcher archive and its updates are pinned there.

title: How to Solve the Cloudflare 5-Second Challenge in Python for Automated Testing
description:
You already have Cloudflare Turnstile handled. But then you hit a different wall: instead of a widget inside the page, the entire page is replaced by a full-screen "Verifying you are human" interstitial that never resolves for your script. That is the Cloudflare challenge page (the "5-second challenge" in a browser), and it needs a completely different API call than Turnstile does.

This walkthrough shows how to solve it with Kaptra's captcha API using the AntiCloudflareTask type: what parameters it needs, what comes back, and how to replay the result so your requests actually get through.

Widget vs full-page: know which one you are facing

These two Cloudflare defenses get confused all the time, and the fix for one does not work on the other:

  • Turnstile: an embedded widget in a form. You collect a sitekey from the page, send it with the URL, and receive a token to submit with the form.
  • The challenge page: the page itself is swapped for an interstitial. There is no sitekey anywhere. The solver has to pass the interstitial and return the resulting cookies, and those cookies are bound to the IP that earned them. That binding is exactly why this task type requires you to pass your own proxy.

Quick diagnostic: if your response body is mostly a "Just a moment..." page, it is the second case. Read on.

What the solved task hands you

When polling completes, solution contains cookies: the clearance material for that protected page. The flow from there:

  1. Create an AntiCloudflareTask with the protected URL and your HTTP proxy.
  2. Poll getTaskResult until status is ready.
  3. Attach solution["cookies"] to your session and send your real requests through the same proxy from step 1. The clearance was issued for that IP, so keep using it.

Full Python example 

import time
import requests
# ---
BASE_URL = "https://api.kaptra.ai"
API_KEY = "YOUR_KAPTRA_API_KEY"
# ---
def solve_cloudflare_challenge(website_url: str, proxy: str) -> dict:
    # 1. create the task; proxy is required for this type (HTTP only)
    resp = requests.post(
        f"{BASE_URL}/createTask",
        json={
            "clientKey": API_KEY,
            "task": {
                "type": "AntiCloudflareTask",
                "websiteURL": website_url,
                "proxy": proxy,
            },
        },
    ).json()
    if resp.get("errorId"):
        raise RuntimeError(f"createTask failed: {resp.get('errorCode')}")
    task_id = resp["taskId"]
    # 2. poll every 1-2s, max 120 queries per task
    for _ in range(120):
        result = requests.post(
            f"{BASE_URL}/getTaskResult",
            json={"clientKey": API_KEY, "taskId": task_id},
        ).json()
        status = result.get("status")
        if status == "ready":
            return result["solution"]  # {"cookies": ...}
        if status == "failure":
            raise RuntimeError(f"task failed: {result.get('errorCode')}")
        # processing (or CAPTCHA_NOT_READY): keep polling
        time.sleep(1.5)
    raise TimeoutError("gave up after 120 polls")
# ---
if __name__ == "__main__":
    my_proxy = "http://USER:PASS@HOST:PORT"
    solution = solve_cloudflare_challenge(
        "https://www.example.com/protected", my_proxy
    )
    print(solution["cookies"])
    # 3. attach these cookies to your session and keep
    #    sending requests through that same proxy

Same client skeleton as the Turnstile flow: createTask, then poll every 1 to 2 seconds with a ceiling of 120 queries. CAPTCHA_NOT_READY means the worker is still on it; status settles at ready or failure.

Gotchas worth knowing before you ship

HTTP proxies only. The docs state it plainly: a public HTTP proxy is required and SOCKS is rejected. If your stack is SOCKS-only, front it with HTTP or use a different provider for these tasks.

Failure handling. Average solve time is under 10 seconds, so 120 polls at 1.5 second intervals is a wide margin. A failure surfaces as ERROR_CAPTCHA_UNSOLVABLE; retrying once with the same parameters is the normal move, because billing is per solved task.

Cost. $1.20 per 1,000 successful solves, nothing for failures or timeouts, no monthly fee, no expiring balance. New Kaptra accounts start with $10 in test credit, enough to validate the whole flow before you commit.

HTTP codes carry no signal. Every response is HTTP 200. The verdict lives in errorId (0 or 1) and errorCode in the JSON. If your code already speaks that envelope, nothing to change.

Summary

Widget: sitekey in, token out, submit with the form. Challenge page: your HTTP proxy in, cookies out, replay through that proxy. Different inputs, different outputs, same create-then-poll loop underneath.

  • Site: kaptra.ai
  • AntiCloudflareTask docs: kaptra.ai/docs

The companion piece on Turnstile (the widget) is worth reading alongside this one. Questions or a task type you want covered next? The team answers tickets in Discord.

title: Map a displayed crop rectangle into intrinsic image coordinates
description:
A crop picker often displays an image smaller than its source. If the picker reports a rectangle in displayed coordinates, passing those numbers directly to drawImage() selects the wrong part of the source. Scale the selection into intrinsic image coordinates first.

For an HTMLImageElement, drawImage() uses intrinsic dimensions. image.width can describe a displayed size, so use naturalWidth and naturalHeight when calculating the source rectangle. See MDN's drawImage notes.

Assume the entire decoded image is displayed in a 600 by 400 coordinate area. Its intrinsic dimensions are 2400 by 1600. A selection beginning at displayed point (150, 100), with displayed width 300 and height 200, maps to source point (600, 400), width 1200 and height 800.

This helper performs the scaling. The rectangle must already be relative to the displayed image content, excluding borders, padding, and any letterboxing. All arguments are numbers.

function sourceRect(image, rect, shownWidth, shownHeight) {
  const values = [rect.x, rect.y, rect.width, rect.height,
    shownWidth, shownHeight];
  if (!values.every(Number.isFinite) ||
      shownWidth <= 0 || shownHeight <= 0 ||
      image.naturalWidth <= 0 || image.naturalHeight <= 0 ||
      rect.x < 0 || rect.y < 0 ||
      rect.width <= 0 || rect.height <= 0 ||
      rect.x + rect.width > shownWidth ||
      rect.y + rect.height > shownHeight) {
    throw new RangeError("Selection must be inside a loaded image");
  }
  const scaleX = image.naturalWidth / shownWidth;
  const scaleY = image.naturalHeight / shownHeight;
  return {
    x: rect.x * scaleX,
    y: rect.y * scaleY,
    width: rect.width * scaleX,
    height: rect.height * scaleY,
  };
}

Use the result as the four source arguments in the nine-argument drawImage() overload. Choose the destination width and height separately; those describe the output canvas region, not the selection in the original image.

This helper does not translate pointer coordinates or model CSS transforms. A picker using object-fit: contain must first locate the actual image rectangle inside its element. A rotated or mirrored preview also needs its own inverse mapping. Resolve those layout details before calling the helper.

Put a different mark near each corner of a test image. Select one corner in the reduced preview and inspect the resulting crop. Then repeat at another corner to catch an incorrect offset.

title: Bruster: A Faster-Starting, Lighter Browser for AI Agents
description:
I've been building Bruster - an open-source browser automation tool written in Rust, designed for AI agents and scripts.

The goal is simple: fast startup, lower memory usage, and a straightforward way to control a real browser.

Native webviews, built-in MCP

Bruster uses your platform’s native webview:

  • macOS: WKWebView
  • Linux: WebKitGTK
  • Windows: WebView2

The controller runs without Node.js and exposes two interfaces: MCP for compatible AI clients and JSON lines over stdin/stdout for scripts.

You can connect it to Claude Code, Cursor, or another MCP-compatible client.

What can an agent do?

  • Navigate websites and inspect page content.
  • Click elements, fill forms, and submit them.
  • Capture screenshots.
  • Manage tabs and persistent sessions.

The demo is a scripted MCP session showing navigation, form interaction, and screenshots.

How much faster and lighter?

Here’s one published Linux benchmark comparing Bruster with agent-browser 0.40.0 using full Chrome:

Metric, median Bruster agent-browser
Launch to first loaded page 219 ms 799 ms
Total idle memory, PSS 256 MiB 523 MiB

That run used Ubuntu 24.04 and ten fresh sessions per configuration against local test pages. Memory includes browser helper processes and Bruster’s Xvfb display; Xvfb startup is excluded from timing.

These are workload-specific results across different browser engines. The full benchmark report includes additional tools, workloads, and methodology.

Try it with Claude Code

Install on macOS or Linux, then register the MCP server:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aliilyas/bruster/main/install.sh | sh

claude mcp add bruster -- "$HOME/.local/bin/bruster" --mcp --quiet

Linux requires WebKitGTK 4.1, plus xvfb and xauth when running without a desktop display. Platform setup and other MCP clients.

Then try:

Use Bruster to open https://example.com, inspect the page, and take a screenshot.

Current limitations include synthetic input events and no cross-origin iframe access.

Bruster is MIT licensed, and feedback is welcome—especially on real-world agent workflows and MCP compatibility.

GitHub: https://github.com/aliilyas/bruster

title: Steering Readerly Dynamics: Trajectory-Guided Story Generation with Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.00469v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate stories, but these stories struggle to reproduce engaging readerly dynamics, the evolving reader responses that shape narrative experience. To address this challenge, we propose a framework that learns readerly dynamics from high-quality human-written stories and uses them to guide story generation. Instead of directly modeling high-dimensional story content, we train a small LLM to predict future reader responses as low-dimensional trajectories. We then leverage the strong instruction-following capability of a larger, off-the-shelf writer LLM to generate story segments that follow these predicted trajectories within a given story setting. Our framework improves trajectory-based fidelity to human-written stories by 12%-35% while largely preserving story coherence.

title: What Breaks and What Comes Back: Capability Damage and Recovery in Depth-Pruned Small Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.00877v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Depth pruning removes whole Transformer blocks to make a language model smaller and faster, but the damage is not spread evenly across what the model can do, and a short fine-tuning run, called healing, decides what comes back. We measure this for small models used as agents. Four instruction-tuned models of 1.2-1.7B parameters (Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen2.5-1.5B, SmolLM2-1.7B and OLMo-2-1B) are pruned and healed, and six capabilities are tracked: structured output, function calling, instruction following, mathematical reasoning, safety refusal and knowledge. Three results hold across the families. First, function calling and math collapse in every model (retention 0.00-0.07 of the unpruned score), and the order in which capabilities break agrees closely across the four (Kendall's W = 0.92; 0.62 after correcting for chance floors). Second, which parameters are trained matters as much as which data: fully tuning the last three blocks instead of adding low-rank adapters to all blocks costs up to 0.18 in capped mean retention on three families, and one 300k-token pilot per scope detects this. Third, we test a planner that allocates a 1M-token healing budget from 21 short pilot heals. At a fixed budget it raises the weakest capability on two families, although only one of these gains survives a test that also resamples training seeds. Once its 3.48M pilot tokens are counted, uniform healing with the same total number of training tokens matches or beats every planned variant on every family and retains math significantly better on three of them in an item-level test (on one when seeds are also resampled). Healing longer is a strong and simple baseline that planned recovery must beat. Code, per-item predictions and every result are public.
