title: Checkout Refresh Token Rotation: 3 Controls for Sliding Expiry With Absolute Caps
description:
A bot doesn't become a shopper because it keeps a session busy. For an existing e-commerce app adding phone one-time-code login, that operational constraint changes the refresh policy: activity can extend a session's idle deadline, but it must never move the original absolute deadline.

TL;DR: Refresh on activity, rotate the session on every successful refresh, and calculate the next expiry as the earlier of the sliding deadline and the original lifetime cap. In a Node.js application using Express, enforce this decision behind the refresh handler in shared session state. The Go examples below separate the local policy from inspecting an integration contract, without inventing provider request fields.

The three controls are an idle timeout, credential rotation, and an absolute lifetime cap. Rotation limits the value of a captured session; the cap prevents repeated activity from keeping it alive indefinitely. Neither replaces protection against automated phone-code requests.

What page fired when refresh traffic kept a session alive?

For a hypothetical production review, I would start with a bounded checkout scenario: a shopper signs in with a phone code, browses, leaves the cart open, and returns while an automated client keeps submitting refreshes against a captured credential. This is a thought experiment, not a reported incident. Give the session a 20-minute idle window and an 8-hour absolute cap, both illustrative policy choices rather than service defaults. At hour seven, activity may extend the idle deadline. At hour eight, it cannot.

Ask what page fired.

A dashboard showing successful refreshes can look reassuring while concealing the failure that matters: old credentials continue to work, the original login time gets overwritten, or refresh traffic counts as activity without any distinction between shopper behavior and a script. The postmortem question is whether the enforcement path rejected an expired or superseded credential, and whether the evidence lets an on-call engineer reconstruct that decision. A green request counter can't answer it.

The invariant is small enough to write on the incident timeline: the absolute deadline belongs to the original session family and survives every rotation. Treating each rotated credential as a fresh login destroys that invariant. So does creating a new family automatically when an old one reaches its cap. Require authentication again at that boundary.

For a team adding this policy to an existing commerce backend, I recommend trying Infrai for the session API integration when plain HTTP fits: its REST API needs no SDK to install or client library version to maintain. Infrai offers one key, one wallet, one bill across backend services; a single key and consolidated billing reduce credential administration and invoice reconciliation when the login workflow draws on authentication and messaging. Its unified API spans 295 routes across 20 modules, a broad capability surface with a consistent interface for teams integrating several backend functions. Those are integration and operating benefits; the application still needs to define and enforce its session lifetime policy.

Count the workload before calling the integration cheap

Consider an explicitly hypothetical planning worksheet with 10,000 daily login sessions and six refresh attempts per session. That's 60,000 refresh attempts to account for, before phone-code sends, verification attempts, rejected replays, and authentication after the absolute cap. It is arithmetic, not a benchmark or a prediction of real shopper behavior. The missing input is the distribution: six attempts spread across a day have different operational implications from six attempts arriving together for one credential.

Count attempts separately.

The useful operating bill includes provider usage, SMS triggered by fresh authentication, application work to serialize rotations, support effort when concurrent browser tabs collide, and incident response time when logs can't explain why an account stayed signed in. A shorter cap can increase fresh authentication and downstream messaging; a longer cap allows more elapsed time before authentication is required again. Choose that trade-off against checkout risk and the team's tolerance for interruption, then measure it on the actual workload. No unit-price leaderboard can settle it.

A retry trap deserves its own place in that worksheet. If a refresh succeeds but its response is lost, the client may retry with the previous credential. That retry needs a deliberate, bounded treatment tied to the same logical operation; accepting the previous credential as an unrestricted second session defeats rotation. Browser concurrency produces a similar symptom without requiring an attacker. Count these cases before labeling every rejected refresh an account takeover.

Routine rotations belong in low-level logs. A burst is a signal worth retaining, but an alert should identify the affected session family or account pattern, what was rejected, and what the responder should inspect. Keep raw credentials and phone codes out of those records.

Compare the operating boundary, not a vendor score

Auth0, Amazon Cognito, and Firebase Authentication are real alternatives to evaluate for this login change. Their documentation gives three different starting points: Auth0 documents refresh-token rotation, Cognito documents user-pool refresh tokens, and Firebase documents phone authentication. The job contains both a phone-code entry point and a session lifetime policy; evidence that a product addresses one doesn't establish how the application should implement the other.

Option Concrete evaluation starting point Boundary to verify for this app
Auth0 Its refresh-token rotation documentation Check rotation and expiry semantics against the existing session model; prefer a dedicated identity platform when that is the operating boundary the team wants.
Amazon Cognito Its user-pool refresh-token documentation Evaluate it when user pools already anchor account management; check how the application preserves its original lifetime cap across refreshes.
Firebase Authentication Its phone-authentication documentation Evaluate phone sign-in directly; separately establish which credential controls the commerce backend's session lifetime.
Infrai Plain REST access and public schema discovery Evaluate it for an HTTP-oriented backend; inspect the session contract before mapping application policy to provider fields.

These are review targets, not a claim that all four offer identical rotation behavior. A route named refresh isn't proof of a particular replay policy, idle-time default, or absolute-cap setting. Those details need a documented contract before adoption.

A dedicated identity provider is the better choice when the team wants the provider's documented session model to own this boundary and it matches the required policy. An existing Cognito or Firebase integration may outweigh introducing another service merely to avoid an SDK. Conversely, a backend that already centralizes session decisions has a reason to evaluate direct HTTP integration. Compare ongoing responsibility, including who handles a lost rotation response, rather than awarding points for feature names.

How should refresh token rotation enforce sliding session expiry and an absolute cap?

This complete Go program models one session in memory, using illustrative durations. Save it as main.go and run it with Go. It demonstrates the deadline calculation and rejection of an old credential; it doesn't issue browser cookies or constitute a deployable authentication server.

package main

import (
    "crypto/rand"
    "encoding/hex"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "sync"
    "time"
)

type Session struct {
    mu sync.Mutex
    credential string
    idleDeadline time.Time
    absoluteDeadline time.Time
}

func credential() (string, error) {
    var b [32]byte
    if _, err := rand.Read(b[:]); err != nil {
        return "", err
    }
    return hex.EncodeToString(b[:]), nil
}

func (s *Session) refresh(presented string, now time.Time, idle time.Duration) (string, error) {
    s.mu.Lock()
    defer s.mu.Unlock()
    if idle <= 0 {
        return "", errors.New("idle lifetime must be positive")
    }
    if !now.Before(s.absoluteDeadline) || !now.Before(s.idleDeadline) {
        return "", errors.New("authentication required")
    }
    if presented != s.credential {
        return "", errors.New("credential is no longer current")
    }
    next, err := credential()
    if err != nil {
        return "", err
    }
    deadline := now.Add(idle)
    if deadline.After(s.absoluteDeadline) {
        deadline = s.absoluteDeadline
    }
    s.credential = next
    s.idleDeadline = deadline
    return next, nil
}

func main() {
    now := time.Date(2026, time.November, 4, 0, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC)
    original, err := credential()
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    s := &Session{
        credential: original,
        idleDeadline: now.Add(20*time.Minute),
        absoluteDeadline: now.Add(8*time.Hour),
    }
    current := original
    for minute := 10; minute < 480; minute += 10 {
        current, err = s.refresh(current, now.Add(time.Duration(minute)*time.Minute), 20*time.Minute)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
    }
    _, err = s.refresh(original, now.Add(471*time.Minute), 20*time.Minute)
    fmt.Println("old credential rejected:", err != nil)
    _, err = s.refresh(current, now.Add(480*time.Minute), 20*time.Minute)
    fmt.Println("absolute cap enforced:", err != nil)
}

The mutex ends at one process. For a distributed Express deployment, move the comparison and replacement into a shared-store transaction or equivalent atomic conditional update. Otherwise two workers can each accept the old value, issue different successors, and leave the shopper holding whichever response loses the storage race. Preserve the original absolute deadline in that same authoritative record. Use server time; don't accept a client-supplied original login time.

The loop keeps the illustrative session active until ten minutes before its cap. At the cap, rejection is mandatory, including equality at the deadline. A production validation plan must also cover simultaneous refreshes and a lost successful response; the example deliberately rejects the previous credential and provides no retry-recovery mechanism.

Before implementing the provider adapter, inspect its published contract. Infrai's discovery surface is public and self-describing. The separate, runnable Go program below fetches that catalog with an explicit GET, bounded retries for rate limiting, and status checking. It performs no session write, so it requires no write-idempotency mechanism. Set INFRAI_API_KEY in the environment for the Bearer header; no credential belongs in source control.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func run() error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set INFRAI_API_KEY")
    }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 8<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retry := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retry); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if wait := time.Duration(seconds)*time.Second; wait > delay {
                    delay = wait
                }
            } else if date, err := http.ParseTime(retry); err == nil {
                if wait := time.Until(date); wait > delay {
                    delay = wait
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        _, err = os.Stdout.Write(body)
        return err
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

This is a contract-inspection step, not a refresh implementation. Read the session capability's schema before binding actual fields in the Express handler. Keep the local lifetime invariant independent of field naming, and require the adapter to preserve it. A plausible field name is still an integration error.

Where this policy stops helping

A bot that can request unlimited phone codes can cause downstream messaging work before any refresh policy runs. Add abuse controls at code issuance and verification, then treat refresh bursts as another observable signal. An absolute cap is a lifetime boundary, not a bot detector, and rotation doesn't establish that the current actor is the legitimate shopper.

If the primary requirement is a managed abuse-detection program or provider-owned identity lifecycle, select a specialist whose documented controls and operating model fit it. If the existing app owns the policy, evaluate the REST integration against the total workload and keep the cap invariant visible in code review and incident evidence.

Sources

References for evaluating the authentication and session boundaries:

  • OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet
  • Auth0 refresh-token rotation
  • Amazon Cognito refresh tokens
  • Firebase phone authentication

If this HTTP integration boundary fits your existing app, start with the schemas and examples in the Infrai documentation.

title: NestJS vs Hono vs Fastify (2026): Benchmarked on Node.js 26
description:
Cross-posted from my blog. The original, with any updates, lives on fabwaseem.com.

"NestJS vs Hono vs Fastify" is one of the most common backend questions I see from TypeScript developers in 2026, and most answers are either opinion or benchmarks from 2023. So I ran my own: the same three routes on Express 5.3, Fastify 5.12, Hono 4.13, NestJS 12.3 on Express and NestJS 12.3 on Fastify, all on Node.js 26.13 (the current LTS), on the same machine, with the same load generator.

This post gives you the numbers, the exact code, and a straight answer on which one to pick for an API, a SaaS backend or an edge function.

The test setup

  • Machine: one 8-vCPU Intel Xeon Linux VM. The server was pinned to one CPU core with taskset -c 0 (Node runs your JavaScript on one thread, so this is a fair per-process number). The load generator, autocannon 8, ran on 6 other cores.
  • Runtime: Node.js v26.13.0.
  • Versions: express 5.3.0, fastify 5.12.8, hono 4.13.16 with @hono/node-server 2.1.6, @nestjs/core 12.3.3 with @nestjs/platform-express and @nestjs/platform-fastify 12.3.3. NestJS was compiled with TypeScript 5.9.3.
  • Load: 100 connections, no pipelining, 3-second warm-up, then 8 seconds per route.
  • Rounds: 3 full rounds, run one framework after another (interleaved), and I report the median of the 3.
  • Routes:
    • GET /json returns {"hello":"world"}
    • GET /users/:id returns the route parameter as JSON
    • POST /echo parses a small JSON body and sends it back

No logging, no validation, no database. This measures framework overhead only. Every request returned 2xx.

The code

Express 5:

import express from 'express';
const app = express();
app.use(express.json());
app.get('/json', (req, res) => res.json({ hello: 'world' }));
app.get('/users/:id', (req, res) => res.json({ id: req.params.id }));
app.post('/echo', (req, res) => res.json(req.body));
app.listen(3000);

Fastify 5:

import Fastify from 'fastify';
const app = Fastify({ logger: false });
app.get('/json', async () => ({ hello: 'world' }));
app.get('/users/:id', async (req) => ({ id: req.params.id }));
app.post('/echo', async (req) => req.body);
await app.listen({ port: 3000 });

Hono 4 on Node.js:

import { Hono } from 'hono';
import { serve } from '@hono/node-server';
const app = new Hono();
app.get('/json', (c) => c.json({ hello: 'world' }));
app.get('/users/:id', (c) => c.json({ id: c.req.param('id') }));
app.post('/echo', async (c) => c.json(await c.req.json()));
serve({ fetch: app.fetch, port: 3000 });

NestJS 12 (one file, the adapter is picked by an env variable):

import 'reflect-metadata';
import { Body, Controller, Get, Module, Param, Post } from '@nestjs/common';
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { FastifyAdapter } from '@nestjs/platform-fastify';

@Controller()
class AppController {
  @Get('json') json() { return { hello: 'world' }; }
  @Get('users/:id') user(@Param('id') id: string) { return { id }; }
  @Post('echo') echo(@Body() body: unknown) { return body; }
}

@Module({ controllers: [AppController] })
class AppModule {}

async function bootstrap() {
  const app = process.env.ADAPTER === 'fastify'
    ? await NestFactory.create(AppModule, new FastifyAdapter(), { logger: false })
    : await NestFactory.create(AppModule, { logger: false });
  await app.listen(3000);
}
bootstrap();

Results: requests per second (one core, higher is better)

Framework GET /json GET /users/:id POST /echo
Fastify 5.12 85,448 82,040 59,746
Hono 4.13 (Node) 83,184 80,728 51,192
NestJS 12 + Fastify 70,082 69,010 48,596
Express 5.3 48,564 45,476 32,969
NestJS 12 + Express 43,844 39,340 29,563

Median of 3 rounds. Latency was low for all of them at this load: p50 was 1-3 ms and p99 was 2-11 ms. The highest p99 (11 ms) was NestJS on Express for POST /echo.

Results: startup time and memory

Framework Start to first 200 RSS idle RSS after load
Hono 4.13 90 ms 65.6 MB 110.5 MB
Express 5.3 115 ms 66.9 MB 115.7 MB
Fastify 5.12 158 ms 73.8 MB 116.5 MB
NestJS 12 + Fastify 404 ms 104.9 MB 136.2 MB
NestJS 12 + Express 486 ms 105.2 MB 149.9 MB

"Start" is the time from spawning the process to the first successful response, polled every 5 ms.

What the numbers say

1. Fastify and Hono are close; Express is roughly half as fast. On simple GET routes Fastify and Hono were within 3% of each other. Both did about 1.7-1.8x the requests of Express 5. Express 5 is a big cleanup (async errors, better path matching), but it did not change the performance picture.

2. Fastify wins on JSON bodies. On POST /echo, Fastify did 17% more requests than Hono (59,746 vs 51,192). Fastify has its own body parser and a compiled serializer path. Hono on Node goes through the Web Request adapter in @hono/node-server, and c.req.json() pays for that.

3. NestJS costs you about 16-19% on Fastify, and the adapter matters more than the framework. NestJS on Fastify kept 81-84% of raw Fastify's throughput on every route. NestJS on Express kept 87-90% of raw Express. But NestJS + Fastify was 60-75% faster than NestJS + Express on GET routes. If you already run NestJS, switching the adapter is the cheapest performance win you have.

4. NestJS starts 3-5x slower and uses ~40 MB more memory. That's the DI container, the module scan and reflect-metadata. It does not matter for a long-running API. It does matter for serverless cold starts and for scale-to-zero containers.

5. Hono starts fastest and uses the least memory. 90 ms and 65.6 MB idle. Add the fact that the same Hono app runs on Cloudflare Workers, Bun, Deno and Vercel, and it is the best default for small services and edge functions.

Caveats (read these before quoting the numbers)

  • This is framework overhead with trivial handlers. A real handler that hits Postgres for 2-5 ms will flatten these differences. At 30,000+ requests per second per core, the framework is rarely your bottleneck.
  • One VM, one core per server, 100 connections. Your hardware will give different absolute numbers; the ranking is what to take away.
  • Express used express.json(); Fastify and Nest used their default parsers. No schemas, so Fastify's schema-based serialization was not used. Fastify can serialize faster with a response schema; I did not test that here.
  • Hono was tested on Node.js through @hono/node-server. Hono on Bun or Workers is a different test.

Which one should you choose?

If you are building... Pick Why
A large team API with modules, DI, guards, OpenAPI NestJS on the Fastify adapter Structure and conventions; the Fastify adapter kept 81-84% of raw Fastify speed here
A high-throughput Node.js JSON API Fastify Fastest here, especially on POST bodies; mature plugin ecosystem
Edge functions, Workers, multi-runtime code, small services Hono Near-Fastify speed on Node, fastest startup, smallest memory, runs everywhere
An existing Express app Stay on Express 5 unless you have a measured performance problem Migration cost is real; the gap only matters at high load

My own default: Hono for small services and anything that might run on the edge, NestJS with Fastify when a SaaS backend needs structure and several developers. I covered the Express side in more depth in Hono vs Express, and what changed in NestJS itself in NestJS 12.

How to reproduce

Install the same versions, start each server pinned to one core, and run autocannon:

npm i hono@4.13.16 @hono/node-server@2.1.6 fastify@5.12.8 express@5.3.0 \
  @nestjs/core@12.3.3 @nestjs/common@12.3.3 @nestjs/platform-express@12.3.3 \
  @nestjs/platform-fastify@12.3.3 reflect-metadata rxjs autocannon@8

taskset -c 0 node fastify.mjs &
npx autocannon -c 100 -d 8 http://127.0.0.1:3000/json
npx autocannon -c 100 -d 8 -m POST -H content-type=application/json \
  -b '{"name":"Waseem","tags":["a","b","c"],"n":7}' http://127.0.0.1:3000/echo

Run each framework a few times, alternate the order, and use the median.

FAQ

Is Hono faster than Fastify?

Not on Node.js in my test. On simple GET routes they were within 3% (Fastify 85,448 vs Hono 83,184 requests per second on one core). On a JSON POST body Fastify was 17% faster. Hono started faster (90 ms vs 158 ms) and used less memory.

Is NestJS slower than Express?

NestJS adds overhead on top of whatever adapter it uses. NestJS on Express did about 10% fewer requests than plain Express on GET /json. NestJS on the Fastify adapter was faster than plain Express by about 44% on the same route.

Should I use the Fastify adapter in NestJS?

If you don't depend on Express-only middleware, yes. In this benchmark NestJS on Fastify served 60-75% more GET requests per second than NestJS on Express, started faster (404 ms vs 486 ms) and used less memory under load.

Is Express 5 faster than Express 4?

I did not benchmark Express 4 in this test. Express 5 focuses on modern behaviour (promise-aware error handling, updated path matching) rather than speed, and in this test it was still about 43% behind Fastify on GET routes.

Which is best for a SaaS backend in 2026?

For a team project with auth, modules and many endpoints, NestJS on the Fastify adapter gives you structure without giving up much speed. For a small API or one that needs to run on Cloudflare Workers or Bun too, Hono is the simpler choice.

Originally published on fabwaseem.com.

title: 2026 · Week 44
description:
Hello! This week’s reading keeps circling back to a question: when software gets cheaper to produce, what becomes expensive?

There’s plenty here about AI and engineering, a look at where CSS could go next, and a bird-sticker collection for a change of scenery.

Blogs & essays

The compiler was supposed to end programming too · Hatim Rih

In 1954, IBM suggested FORTRAN would virtually eliminate coding and debugging. Debugging appears to have missed the memo.

Hatim traces that promise through successive generations of programming tools. His argument is that cheaper software makes more problems worth solving, including the ones nobody could previously justify spending a team’s time on.

The useful tension is between adoption and trust. Developers can rely on AI tools while remaining frustrated by output that is almost correct. The article’s imagined developer workday in 2031 brings that into focus: agents handle implementation, while a person has to decide what a refund policy should do when the customer’s original card has expired. Someone still has to answer the question before the code can be right.

The internet is in its guano years · Hatim Rih

The title takes a little explaining. Bird droppings accumulated for centuries before becoming a valuable commodity. Hatim uses that history to examine the posts, answers, and conversations that accumulated on internet platforms before becoming valuable training data.

The parallel gives the essay its shape, but the question of ownership is what stays with you. People contribute the writing; platform owners control access and negotiate its value.

One passage in the week’s saved notes captures the concern:

“If your words only live on someone else’s platform, they’re part of someone else’s deposit, and the owner decides what they’re worth and who gets to read them.”

The practical suggestion is modest: keep an export of your work somewhere you control. You don’t have to abandon every platform to want a copy of your own words.

Every architecture is a receipt · Hatim Rih

An architecture records what its designers were short of: memory, machine time, coordination, or attention. The trouble starts when we copy the solution without checking whether we have the same constraint.

Hatim opens with his own agent-assisted project. Agents write most of the code, but he has to review it, so his architecture is deliberately small enough to keep that review manageable.

That makes the historical examples useful beyond nostalgia. A decision can have been sensible at the time and still deserve revisiting once its costs change.

The article ends with a small addition to architecture decision records: write down what is scarce and when to reconsider the decision. That would give the next person considerably more to work with than “this is how we’ve always done it.”

The Future of CSS ✨ · Josh W. Comeau

Josh walks through his ten picks for Interop 2027, including CSS functions and new ways to shape corners and borders. These are his requested focus areas, not a promise that every feature will become universally available next year.

The examples make this worth opening in a browser. With corner-shape, for instance, the altered shape can be reflected in borders, outlines, and shadows, which makes it more useful than simply clipping a rectangle into something interesting.

Josh also makes a point that connects neatly with the earlier engineering reads: knowing modern CSS still matters when you work with coding agents. You need enough familiarity with the platform to recognise when an agent reaches for an old workaround that the browser no longer needs.

Resources

Developing taste · AI for UI

A learning resource saved alongside this line:

“In a world of scarcity, we treasure tools. In a world of abundance, we treasure taste.”

It belongs beside this week’s engineering essays: once producing another variation becomes easy, choosing which variation deserves to survive takes more of the work.

Huashu bird stickers · Huashu / alchaincyf

A collection of bird illustrations covering the 11,064 living species in the project’s chosen taxonomy, accompanied by structured species data and names in up to 43 languages.

There’s more here than a folder of pictures. The repository includes taxonomy and cross-database identifiers, making it worth exploring for visual projects that need the information behind the illustration too.

One detail to check before reusing it: the data and artwork have different licensing terms. The stickers restrict competing birding products, and the README flags additional questions around reference-photo rights. A public repository is not the same thing as unrestricted artwork.

title: Introducing the MongoDB Google ADK Integration: Durable Memory for Agent State
description:
We’re excited to announce the MongoDB Google ADK Integration, which provides developers with the building blocks they need to create durable memory for agent state.

As agents move from prototypes to real-world applications, they need secure, dependable access to data and the ability to retain context over a long time. However, developers still need to build their own tooling for a data store that provides durable agent memory for agent state. 

This integration gives developers a cohesive, ADK-native experience for using MongoDB as the data platform for agents.

What is the Google ADK?

The Google Agent Development Kit (ADK) is an open source agent development framework that lets you build, debug, and deploy reliable AI agents at enterprise scale. It is available in Python, TypeScript, Go, Java, and Kotlin.

Google ADK offers developers an extensive set of tools for creating, deploying, assessing, and scaling agents, enabling developers to build anything from personal AI assistants to mission-critical business workflows.

How does the MongoDB Google ADK Integration help?

Developers can prototype an agent that searches a product catalog or knowledge base, then evolve it into a production experience that preserves user context across conversations and recalls relevant prior interactions. With MongoDB as the data layer, developers can keep the data their agents search over, the conversation state that needs to survive a restart or a scaled-out instance, and the memories agents build over time, all in the same place as the rest of their application data. That means no separate database to stand up for retrieval, no pipeline syncing app data into a different memory index, and no added latency pulling context from another system before the agent can respond.

ADK supplies the agent framework and tool interface; this integration provides the data and persistence layer beneath it, so developers can easily take an agent from prototype to production. These agents can maintain conversation and session memory independent of any single machine, and carry a user's history across sessions.

Providing a unified agent architecture

At the core of this integration is Google ADK 2.0, which serves as the code-first orchestration layer for multi-agent systems. ADK 2.0 provides the deployment framework, while MongoDB provides session and memory storage for agents.

Integrating directly with the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, ADK 2.0 eliminates the need for custom routing logic by providing standardized tool-calling interfaces, native telemetry, and enterprise access controls out of the box. Developers can use Gemini 4 Argon for multi-step reasoning and Gemini 3.8 Flash for low-latency execution.

Figure 1. The MongoDB Google ADK Integration adds session and memory storage for single or multi-agent workflows.

How do Sessions and Memory storage work?

Great agent experiences improve with context. This integration introduces MongoDbSessionService to persist sessions, events, and application-, user-, and session-scoped state to MongoDB.

This means developers can build agents that retain the context needed for longer-running and multi-turn interactions. The session service includes optimistic concurrency control to help applications safely manage concurrent updates, while configurable collections make it easier to fit the service into existing data architectures.

The following Python code shows how you can add MongoDbSessionService to your agent:

For agents that need memory beyond a single session, MongoDBMemoryService ingests session events into MongoDB collections and recalls relevant memories through keyword matching. Memory ingestion is idempotent, which prevents duplicates when a session is added again.

Together, these services help agents become more useful over time without requiring developers to stitch together separate systems for retrieval, state, and memory.

How does MongoDB Search help agents with data retrieval?

Having memory for agent state is essential, but agents also need fast access to the operational data they search over, the same product catalogs, documents, and records your application already queries. This is where MongoDB's built-in search capabilities come in. MongoDB Vector Search leverages Voyage AI's embedding models, which are the same engine backing MemoryService's semantic retrieval in this integration.

Developers can also perform hybrid search by combining vector search with full-text search using the $rankFusion aggregation stage.

This gives agents access to the right information and context at the right time, delivering better responses in production. Whether you are building product discovery, knowledge assistants, support experiences, or domain-specific copilots, agents can automatically leverage semantic and hybrid retrieval to ground their responses in your data.

The application owns the database connection, database name, and search configuration. The agent gets focused tools to call, without exposing those operational details in its context.

Using MongoDB as the operational data store, the memory layer for agent state, and the search engine over both, developers get one platform instead of three, on whatever deployment they run it on. title: 4 mistakes I made building a Claude Code security hook (and how to avoid them)
description:
Claude Code can run a command of yours before every tool call: a PreToolUse hook. It’s a great place for guardrails, but it’s easy to get subtly wrong. I built one that blocks secrets, and these are the lessons. (Check the current Claude Code hooks docs for exact field names, since they can change.)

How a hook works, in 30 seconds

Claude Code sends the tool call to your command as JSON on stdin, containing the tool name and its input. For a file write that includes the path and the content. Your command either lets it through or denies it.

Registering a hook looks like this in .claude/settings.json:

json

{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Write|Edit|MultiEdit|NotebookEdit|Bash",
        "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "your-hook" }]
      }
    ]
  }
}

The matcher decides which tools trigger it. Include Bash, or the agent can bypass your file checks with echo "KEY=..." > file.

Mistake 1: Emitting “allow” when everything looks fine
My first version printed an “allow” decision for clean calls. That sounds harmless, but an explicit allow can skip the user’s normal permission prompts. A guardrail should only ever remove permission, never grant it.

Fix: for a clean call, print nothing and exit 0. Only speak up to deny.

Mistake 2: Assuming any non-zero exit blocks

In Claude Code, exit code 2 blocks the call, but exit code 1 is treated as a non-blocking error. If your hook crashes on bad input and exits 1, the tool call goes ahead. Decide deliberately:

Can’t parse the input → exit 1 (non-blocking), with a message on stderr.
Found a problem → deny, either with a JSON permissionDecision: "deny" or exit 2.

Mistake 3: Letting the agent exempt itself

Many scanners support a comment like # allow to ignore a line. That’s fine for humans, but an agent can just write the comment next to its own secret. In agent mode I ignore inline allow comments and only honor the allowlist in the config file, which the human controls.

Mistake 4: Failing open on big input

If the input is too large to scan, the easy choice is to let it through. Then a huge file becomes a free bypass. I cap input at 16 MiB and block anything larger, telling the agent to split the content. A check that silently covers only part of the content reports a false “clean”.

And most critical what not to put in the deny message

When you block, the message goes back to the model. Don’t include the real secret. I show only a masked form like AKIA************WZVB, so the credential never enters the model’s context a second time.

The project

I turned all of this into a free, local, open-source tool called StagedSec, and the hook is one command: stagedsec agent-hook --print-config prints the settings snippet. It’s early (v0.1), and I list its limits in the README, including that split or encoded secrets aren’t detected yet.

If you’ve built Claude Code hooks, what surprised you? I’m especially curious about edge cases around multi-edit calls.

title: A Token Is Not a Unit of Difficulty: Segmentation Controls Where Adaptive Computation Goes Inside a Word
description:
arXiv:2611.00983v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Early-exit language models decide for each token how much computation to spend, usually by stopping once the prediction is confident. Yet a token is not a fixed unit: tokenizers cut words into different numbers of pieces in different languages. We ask where inside a word such a policy spends its budget. In Qwen3, along two adaptive axes (the timesteps of a spiking conversion and the layers of the original Transformer), confidence stopping gives the continuation pieces of a word less computation than its first piece in English, German, and Turkish, but more in Bangla. Segmentation drives this. Re-segmenting the same parallel passages with BPE-dropout shifts the gap by up to eight exits on both axes, small models trained under two tokenizers shift Bangla's gap by six exits, and BLOOM and mGPT, which split Bangla less finely, give it the English pattern. Characters per token do not predict the gap across languages; within-word surprisal explains 75% of its variance. A learned stopping head beats confidence stopping by 7 to 8 points, but gains less than one point over the best mix of fixed exits at equal cost, and sometimes loses. All results come from offline analysis, not measured speedups.

title: useContext in React
description:
Imagine we are building a website with a dark mode feature. Multiple components may need to know whether dark mode is enabled or disabled.

One way to share this data is through props. But passing props through many components can become difficult.

React provides a hook called useContext to solve this problem.

1. What is useContext?

useContext is a React Hook that allows us to access shared data from different components without passing props manually through every level.

In simple words, useContext helps components share data easily.

2. Why do we need useContext?

Let's understand with an example.

Imagine we have three components:

  • App
  • Profile
  • User

The App component has a username that the User component needs.

We can pass the username through props:

function App() {
  const username = "Lokesh";

  return <Profile username={username} />;
}

function Profile({ username }) {
  return <User username={username} />;
}

function User({ username }) {
  return <h2>Hello, {username}</h2>;
}

Here, Profile does not need the username for its own work. It only passes it to User.

When we pass props through components like this, it is called prop drilling.

For deeply nested components, prop drilling can make code difficult to manage.

This is where useContext becomes useful.

3. How does useContext work?

To use useContext, we generally follow three steps:

  1. Create a context.
  2. Provide a value using the Context Provider.
  3. Access that value using useContext.

Let's understand each step.

Step 1: Create a Context

First, import createContext from React and create a context.

import { createContext } from "react";

const UserContext = createContext();

Here:

  • createContext() creates a context object.
  • UserContext is the context we will use to share data.

Step 2: Provide a Value

Now, we need to make the data available to the components that need it.

import { createContext } from "react";

const UserContext = createContext();

function App() {
  const username = "Lokesh";

  return (
    <UserContext.Provider value={username}>
      <Profile />
    </UserContext.Provider>
  );
}

Let's understand this:

  • UserContext.Provider makes the context value available to its child components.
  • value={username} is the data we want to share.
  • Profile is inside the Provider, so it can access the shared value.

Step 3: Access the Value Using useContext

Now, let's access the username inside the Profile component.

import { useContext } from "react";

function Profile() {
  const username = useContext(UserContext);

  return <h2>Hello, {username}</h2>;
}

Here, useContext(UserContext) reads the value provided by UserContext.Provider.

We don't need to pass the username through props anymore.

4. Complete Example

Here is the complete code:

import { createContext, useContext } from "react";

// Creating a context
const UserContext = createContext();

function App() {
  const username = "Lokesh";

  return (
    // Providing the username to child components
    <UserContext.Provider value={username}>
      <Profile />
    </UserContext.Provider>
  );
}

function Profile() {
  return (
    <div>
      <h2>Profile Component</h2>
      <User />
    </div>
  );
}

function User() {
  // Accessing the shared username
  const username = useContext(UserContext);

  return <h3>Welcome, {username}</h3>;
}

export default App;

Output:

Profile Component

Welcome, Lokesh

Notice that the User component can access the username even though the Profile component does not pass it as a prop.

That's the main advantage of useContext.

5. Where is useContext Used?

useContext is useful when multiple components need access to the same data.

Some common examples are:

  • Dark Mode: Share the selected theme across components.
  • Authentication: Share the logged-in user's information.
  • Language Settings: Share the selected language.
  • Shopping Cart: Share cart information across different components.

6. Important Points to Remember

  • createContext() is used to create a context.
  • The Provider makes a value available to its child components.
  • useContext() is used to access the context value.
  • Components must be inside the appropriate Provider to receive its value.
  • useContext helps avoid unnecessary prop drilling.

title: Responsive Iframes in Chrome 154: Auto-Height in 3 Steps
description:
Originally published on ExtensionBooster.

Responsive iframes are finally a platform feature: since Chrome 154 hit Stable on September 22, 2026, an iframe can grow to fit its content with no script in the parent page. The WHATWG request for this has been open since January 2016, and the classic Stack Overflow question about auto-height iframes has passed 1.5 million views. Here is the three-step setup, what you can delete, and how to ship it without breaking Firefox and Safari.

Why this matters

An iframe is a fixed viewport (300×150 px unless you size it). Taller content means a second scrollbar inside your page. For a decade the fix has been a two-sided protocol: the child measures itself, postMessage()s the height, and the parent sets style.height.

Chrome 154 replaces that with a double opt-in: a CSS property on the embedding side and a meta tag on the embedded side. It ships on desktop, Android and WebView, and the spec lives in the CSS Sizing Level 4 working draft.

The 3 steps

1. Embedder: set frame-sizing.

.embed {
  width: 100%;
  frame-sizing: content-height;
  max-height: 80vh; /* optional guard against runaway embeds */
}

Available values: auto (default, old behavior), content-height, content-width, and the logical content-block-size / content-inline-size. For horizontal writing modes, content-height is the one you will use.

2. Embedded document: agree to share its size.

<meta name="responsive-embedded-sizing"
      content="allow-origins=https://publisher1.example https://publisher2.example">

This tag must be in the HTML the server delivers. Google is explicit that it can't be injected after load, so a React head manager won't cut it. Use allow-origins=* only if any site may embed you.

3. Call requestResize() when content changes.

Sizing happens once, at load. That one-shot model is deliberate: it prevents the resize → reflow → resize loop. After you load more comments or expand an accordion, ask for a re-measure:

function render(items) {
  list.replaceChildren(...items.map(toListItem));
  if ('requestResize' in window) window.requestResize();
}

Call it once after the DOM update finishes. Don't wire it to a ResizeObserver that fires every frame.

What you can delete (and what you can't)

Concern postMessage resizer frame-sizing
Parent code Listener + height logic One CSS declaration
Child code Measure + postMessage Meta tag + requestResize()
Origin checks Manual, easy to botch Declarative allow-origins
Jitter / loops You debounce it Avoided by design
Support Every browser Chrome 154+

One more reason to look at this: iframe-resizer v5 moved to GPL v3 or a paid commercial license (4.x was MIT), so closed-source teams have been pinning old versions or writing their own.

What you can't delete yet: Firefox and Safari haven't published a position. Keep the fallback and gate both paths:

.widget { width: 100%; height: 500px; }

@supports (frame-sizing: content-height) {
  .widget { height: auto; frame-sizing: content-height; }
}

if (!CSS.supports('frame-sizing', 'content-height')) {
  window.addEventListener('message', onHeightMessage); // legacy path
}

Also watch Core Web Vitals. Google warns the late resize can shift content, so give embeds a realistic min-height and avoid auto-sized embeds above the fold.

The extension angle

Browser extensions often inject an extension page as an iframe from a content script so the host page can't restyle or read the UI. Height was always the pain point. Now the pattern is:

  1. List panel.html in web_accessible_resources with matches limited to the sites where the panel actually appears.
  2. Put the meta tag in the panel's static HTML entry (not a component, whether you use WXT, Plasmo or CRXJS). The embedder origin is the website, not your extension.
  3. From the content script, set frame-sizing with !important (the iframe lives in the host DOM, so page CSS can target it), and fall back to a fixed height elsewhere: 
const frame = document.createElement('iframe');
frame.src = chrome.runtime.getURL('panel.html');
if (CSS.supports('frame-sizing', 'content-height')) {
  frame.style.setProperty('frame-sizing', 'content-height', 'important');
  frame.style.setProperty('max-height', '80vh', 'important');
} else {
  frame.style.setProperty('height', '420px', 'important');
}
document.body.append(frame);
  1. Call requestResize() inside the panel after each render.

Chrome hasn't documented any special case for chrome-extension:// documents, so test on a real target site in Chrome 154+ before removing your old resizer.

Security note: height is data. The explainer warns that a page observing an iframe's laid-out size can learn things about the cross-origin document. If your panel's height depends on login state or result counts, any allowed embedder can read that. Scope allow-origins tightly, keep matches narrow, add frame-ancestors CSP on regular sites, and don't let a sensitive panel's size reflect private data before the user interacts.

Key takeaways

  • frame-sizing: content-height + a server-rendered meta tag = auto-height iframes in Chrome 154+.
  • Sizing is one-shot; call window.requestResize() after dynamic updates.
  • Firefox and Safari have no signal yet, so ship behind @supports and keep your resizer.
  • Reserve min-height to limit layout shift.
  • For extensions, treat iframe height as leakable state and scope origins narrowly.

The original article also covers iframe vs Shadow DOM trade-offs and other Chrome 154/155 changes, so read the full guide to responsive iframes and frame-sizing in Chrome 154 for the details. If you build extensions, ExtensionBooster's growth tools for Chrome extension developers can help after you ship.

Are you keeping your postMessage resizer as a fallback, or has iframe-resizer's license change already pushed you to roll your own? Tell me in the comments.

title: Designing a Birth-Time Form That Does Not Invent an Astrology Chart
description:
A birth-chart form appears to need only three inputs: date, time, and place. But those fields contain several decisions that can change the result. If the interface hides those decisions, it can produce a confident-looking chart from an incorrectly interpreted birth record.

Keep the local time and the place together

“04:10” is a clock reading, not a universal timestamp. The same instant may appear as 04:10 in Jakarta and 05:10 in Singapore. If someone was born in Jakarta, they should be able to enter the time recorded there and select Jakarta as the birthplace. The application should handle the time-zone conversion.

Asking users to convert their birth time to another city first creates an easy mistake: they may enter the converted time while still selecting their original birthplace, causing the application to convert it again.

A useful data model keeps the original local date and time, the birthplace, and the resolved time zone separate. That also makes it possible to show users which assumptions were used.

Use the rules from the birth date

A place's current UTC offset may not be the offset it used decades ago. Daylight saving rules have changed, sometimes more than once. A birth-chart calculator needs the time-zone rules that applied at the birthplace on the birth date.

The interface should also handle uncertainty honestly. If a historical local time cannot be resolved unambiguously, ask for clarification or show the uncertainty. Silently choosing an offset makes the chart look more certain than the input allows.

Unknown is a valid input state

Many people do not know their birth hour. Replacing a blank field with noon or midnight may make a form easier to process, but it changes the chart.

For BaZi, the year, month, and day pillars can still be shown while the hour pillar remains unknown. For Zi Wei Dou Shu, the missing hour affects the palace layout more substantially. In either case, the UI should explain what can be calculated and leave the rest unresolved.

Make calendar boundaries visible

Time zones are only one source of disagreement between calculators. In BaZi, the year pillar changes at Li Chun, around the beginning of February, rather than on January 1 or necessarily on Lunar New Year. The month pillar follows solar terms.

For a birth close to one of these boundaries, a short note beside the result can explain which rule the calculator used. That is more useful than presenting two different charts as though one must be a software error.

We apply these principles in the fatequery BaZi calculator: the chart is calculated from the birth details first, and an AI-assisted reading explains the chart shown on screen. A follow-up question does not need to generate a new chart.

The broader design lesson applies beyond astrology. When an application turns local time into a rule-based result, preserve the original input, expose consequential assumptions, and allow unknown information to remain unknown.

title: Character-Name Concentration in LLM Fiction: Measuring Displacement and Mitigating Repetition
description:
arXiv:2611.01284v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Character names in large language model (LLM) fiction concentrate on a handful of recurrent names such as 'Elara' and 'Elias', a measurable face of AI slop. Existing fixes either require logit access or retraining, or operate per request and cannot control concentration across a corpus. How much prompt-level strategies reduce concentration, and at what cost to name naturalness, has not been systematically measured. We present an empirical study of name-concentration control across eight strategies and introduce speculative naming, a fine-tuning-free method that adapts the draft-verify-reject paradigm of speculative decoding from tokens to names. The method requests candidate name-sets through verbalized sampling, scores them against a SlopTracker that combines a per-model fingerprint with a runtime counter, and selects through a temperature-controlled rule or its strict variant (HARD). We use 20 LLMs to generate 44,782 stories in four languages from text and visual stimuli (88,919 named characters), and measure concentration with a list-free collision metric (Slop Ratio, SR) decomposed into known and emergent components. List-based strategies do not remove slop: static banlists displace concentration to emergent names and more than halve the share of attested real names. Speculative naming removes it: the sampling scaffold alone cuts SR by 89% on average, the dynamic tracker brings the total reduction to 95%, mean collision probability falls from 7.3% to 0.4%, and known-name collisions hold at zero while naturalness stays close to baseline (42-69% attested by language) and within-story collisions drop from 4.3% to 0.2%. The strategy ranking is stable across languages, model families, and name-counting conventions. Name concentration is thus controllable at the corpus level without logit access or retraining; broader creative diversity beyond naming remains open.

title: A map that doesn't need colour: our embed in Windows forced-colors mode
description:
We're the team behind Regime Map, a country-by-country register of gambling regulation. Our embeddable map colours each country by its regulatory status. A few days ago we wrote about making that embed survive any host page. Under that post, a reader asked something we hadn't tested: what happens to the map in Windows forced-colors mode?

The honest answer was that it broke. This post is how we fixed it.

What a contrast theme does to a map

In a Windows contrast theme the browser repaints every page with a small palette of about eight system colours: one for the background, one for text, one for links, one for buttons, and so on. For text, that is exactly what a reader with low vision or light sensitivity wants.

Our map has six statuses, each with its own fill: licensed regime, state monopoly, varies by region, prohibited, no licensing regime and not assessed, plus "not covered yet" for countries we haven't checked. The legend under the map is the key.

In forced colours the legend lost its key: every swatch went blank, so the map was still coloured but nothing said which colour meant which status. And the map ignored the reader's theme: with the default embed code, in a dark contrast theme it sat on the page as a bright block of our own colours, exactly the glare the reader had switched the theme on to avoid. (An embed set to its dark theme kept its dark palette instead; its legend was just as blank.)

Both have one cause. The browser repaints CSS backgrounds, so the swatches lost their colours. Chromium doesn't repaint SVG fills, so the map kept ours.

Who sees it, and who turns it on

Not us. A reader turns it on in Windows 10 or 11 (Settings → Accessibility → Contrast themes), and Edge, Chrome and Firefox all follow it. Firefox can also be set to override the colours a page specifies. macOS "Increase contrast" doesn't trigger it.

The page sees a single media feature:

@media (forced-colors: active) {
  /* … */
}

So there's no option in the embed code and nothing for a host site to configure. The script form and the iframe form behave the same: the embed follows the reader's system.

Textures instead of colours

The fix had to work inside the reader's theme: no colours of our own, only the system's handful, and that isn't enough for six statuses. So something other than colour has to carry the status. Each status got its own texture:

status texture
Licensed regime solid
State monopoly dots
Varies by region diagonal hatch
Prohibited cross-hatch
No licensing regime horizontal lines
Not assessed vertical lines
Not covered yet empty, dashed outline

On the map they're SVG <pattern>s drawn in CanvasText on Canvas, so they invert correctly between dark and light themes. In the swatches, the same textures are CSS gradients. A lawful exception, such as pachinko halls in Japan's land-based gambling, keeps the asterisk pattern it already had, and it's spelled out in words in the tooltip, the table and the card.

Here is the "prohibited" pattern, slightly simplified (the renderer builds this markup as a JavaScript string and writes the transform at draw time). Two crossing bars, rotated 45°, give diagonal lines both ways:

<pattern id="rmefc-pro" width="6" height="6" patternUnits="userSpaceOnUse"
         patternTransform="rotate(45)">
  <rect width="6" height="6" fill="Canvas"/>
  <rect width="1.25" height="6" fill="CanvasText"/>
  <rect width="6" height="1.25" fill="CanvasText"/>
</pattern>

The system colours sit in presentation attributes, and one rule in the forced-colors block points each country at its pattern:

@media (forced-colors: active) {
  .map [data-s=prohibited] { fill: url(#rmefc-pro) !important; }
}

System colour keywords, and nothing else

Inside the forced-colors block there are no hex values at all, only CSS system colour keywords:

@media (forced-colors: active) {
  /* Canvas, CanvasText, GrayText, Highlight,
     LinkText, ButtonFace, ButtonText. No hex. */
}

The reader's theme decides what those look like. In Chromium's dark emulated palette, GrayText comes out green and links yellow; in the light one, GrayText is dark red. We don't need to know. There is one such block per stylesheet: the map's, the card's, and the <link> fallback for browsers without constructable stylesheets.

Opting out, only where it's needed

In forced-colors mode the browser takes over every colour by default, and for almost everything that's what we want: text, buttons, links, borders, the tooltip. We leave those alone.

Two things opt out: the map's SVG, and the status swatch, one small element reused in the legend, the table, the tooltip, the bottom sheet, the search list and the card. These are the real rules, trimmed (sizes dropped, one of the six swatch textures shown; .xsw is the legend's small asterisk key):

@media (forced-colors: active) {
  .stage svg.map, .rme .xsw { forced-color-adjust: none; }
  .rme .sw { forced-color-adjust: none; border: 1px solid CanvasText; background: Canvas; }
  .rme .sw--prohibited { background:
    repeating-linear-gradient(45deg, CanvasText 0 1.25px, transparent 1.25px 6px),
    repeating-linear-gradient(135deg, CanvasText 0 1.25px, transparent 1.25px 6px), Canvas; }
}

The swatches are tiny CSS boxes whose textures are background gradients, and forced colours removes background images, so without opting out they go blank. The map's SVG opts out too; in Chromium that turned out to be only a safeguard (its pattern fills survive either way), but other browsers treat SVG differently.

Having opted out, they do the browser's job themselves: they draw only in system colours. Opting out and then painting in your own brand colours would undo the reader's theme.

The rule from the first post still holds: there is no style="" attribute anywhere, so a host with a strict style-src-attr still renders the map. Sizes go through the CSSOM or SVG attributes, never a style attribute, and the pattern tiles are rescaled at every zoom level so they stay 6 × 6 pixels on screen. This is the real line (ES5); S is screen pixels per map unit:

x.setAttribute('patternTransform', 'scale(' + (1 / S).toFixed(5) + ')' + (r ? ' rotate(' + r + ')' : ''));

Bigger dots, focus in Highlight

Under forced colours only, the small-state dots grow from a radius of 4 to 6 at world scale and get a Canvas halo, so they stand out from the sea. Keyboard focus and the selected country are drawn in Highlight, the colour the reader's theme uses for "this one".

If the reader switches a theme on or off with the page open, a matchMedia('(forced-colors: active)') listener redraws the map.

Two browser quirks

  • A transparent border is forced visible. Our inactive product tabs had transparent bottom borders. In forced colours every tab grew an underline, and you couldn't tell which one was active. The inactive tabs now use a Canvas border, which blends into the background as intended.
  • Chromium paints a "backplate" behind text. In "Find a country", the active match had a filled background, and the backplate hid its own label. The active option is now an outline instead of a fill.

Testing without a Windows machine

We tested in Chromium's forced-colours emulation, light and dark palettes. In Playwright:

await page.emulateMedia({ forcedColors: 'active', colorScheme: 'dark' });

and the same with colorScheme: 'light'. By hand, in Chrome: DevTools → Rendering → "Emulate CSS media feature forced-colors". Chromium's two emulated palettes are those of Windows' classic "High Contrast Black" and "High Contrast White"; the dark one is close to Windows 11's "Night sky".

We went through 21 states in both palettes: the world map for two products, Europe with the small-state dots, zoomed in once and twice, the narrow product menu, search, a tooltip with an exception, the bottom sheet on a phone, keyboard focus on a country and on a dot, the table view, the credit bar, the country cards, and the iframe forms.

The other half of the test mattered as much: had we changed the normal look? We screenshotted the same 21 states, light and dark, with the old renderer and the new one, both on the same production data, and compared them pixel by pixel. 38 of the 42 pairs were identical. The four keyboard-focus states differed by 1,710 to 2,570 pixels of anti-aliasing along borders, and the old renderer compared with itself differs by the same amounts.

What it cost

1.7 KB gzipped for the map renderer and 0.4 KB for the card. The whole map (loader, renderer and data) is now about 47 KB gzipped, and a country card about 8.5 KB.

What we haven't done yet

  • A real Windows machine. Everything above is emulation. Windows 11's other contrast themes (Aquatic, Desert, Dusk) use other colours. The textures, layout and wording stay the same, but we haven't seen them on the real thing. Nor have we tested Firefox's own "override the page's colours" setting.
  • The closest calls. At world scale, a state-monopoly dot and a prohibited dot are four dots in a ring against an X in a ring: distinct, but small. A country only a few pixels across, like Luxembourg or Cyprus, has no room for a 5–6 px texture until you zoom in, as in the normal look. And "not covered yet" differs from the sea only by its outline.

If you use a contrast theme, we'd like to hear what you see: in the comments, or at support@regimemap.com.

Try it

The configurator, with a live preview of the map and the country cards, is at regimemap.com/data-api. The Hugging Face demo loads the live embed, so it already shows all of this: open it, turn on forced-colors emulation in DevTools and look.

Last time we promised a post on counting embeds without logging the people who read them. That one comes next.

title: Three Correlations Passed Validation. The Matrix Was Impossible.
description:
A risk dashboard can look completely convincing while displaying numbers from a model that should never have accepted its inputs.

Imagine a UI with three correlation sliders:

  • Asset A and asset B: +0.90
  • Asset A and asset C: +0.90
  • Asset B and asset C: -0.90 Every input fits the permitted range. The diagonal of the resulting matrix is 1. The matrix is symmetric. A naïve form validator gives it a green checkmark.

And yet no three random variables can have all three of those pairwise correlations at once.

This isn't a report of a production failure. It's a failure mode we explicitly designed against while building a browser-based portfolio-risk visualization. The surprising part is that the bug can live entirely in the inputs, before any rendering code runs.
The matrix that looks valid

Our three sliders produce:

A      B      C

A [ 1.00, 0.90, 0.90 ]
B [ 0.90, 1.00, -0.90 ]
C [ 0.90, -0.90, 1.00 ]

The following check is necessary, but insufficient:

const correlations = [0.9, 0.9, -0.9];
const inRange = correlations.every(
  value => Number.isFinite(value) && value >= -1 && value <= 1
);

It returns true. That proves only that individual cells are in range.

A correlation matrix has to describe a jointly possible system. Its entries are constrained by one another.

There is a geometric intuition: if B closely follows A, and C also closely follows A, then B and C cannot simultaneously behave as almost exact opposites. The three statements conflict.

Why the determinant exposes the contradiction

For a symmetric three-asset correlation matrix with off-diagonal entries a, b, and c, its determinant is:

det(R) = 1 + 2abc - a² - b² - c²

In this example, a = 0.9, b = 0.9, and c = -0.9, so:

det(R) = 1 + 2(0.9)(0.9)(-0.9) - 3(0.9²)
= -2.888

A real correlation matrix must be positive semidefinite (PSD): for every vector x, the quadratic form xᵀRx must be nonnegative. That is what makes it possible to interpret the matrix as correlations coming from a covariance matrix.

This particular matrix has eigenvalues -0.8, 1.9, and 1.9. A negative eigenvalue is enough to show it is not PSD.

Here's another way to see it. Take x = [-1, 1, 1]. Then xᵀRx = -2.4. If R were a covariance matrix of unit-variance variables, that would claim a linear combination has negative variance. That's impossible.

One nuance: a bad correlation matrix does not necessarily produce a negative variance for every long-only portfolio. It is invalid globally, even if one portfolio happens to produce a nonnegative result. That's why validating only the final variance is not enough.

You can also derive the allowable third correlation when the first two are fixed:

ab - sqrt((1 - a²)(1 - b²))
   ≤ c ≤
ab + sqrt((1 - a²)(1 - b²))

For a = b = 0.9, the range is 0.62 ≤ c ≤ 1.00. A value of -0.9 is nowhere near feasible.

Changing c to +0.8 creates a valid matrix with determinant +0.036. But an application should not silently change a user's assumption. Fixing or projecting a matrix is a modeling choice that deserves an explanation.

A tiny JavaScript engine you can run

The example below deliberately has three assets so the PSD test fits in one formula. It is a self-contained teaching implementation, not a copy of our production module and not a generic validator for matrices of any size.

It also demonstrates a second engineering invariant: the sum of Euler volatility contributions must equal portfolio volatility whenever that quantity is defined.

Create risk-matrix.mjs:

// Standalone educational example for the DEV article.
// Three assets, decimal inputs, no dependencies, no price feed.
import { fileURLToPath } from 'node:url';
import { resolve } from 'node:path';

const EPS = 1e-10;

export function validateCorrelation3(R) {
  if (!Array.isArray(R) || R.length !== 3 ||
      R.some(row => !Array.isArray(row) || row.length !== 3)) {
    throw new RangeError('Expected a 3 x 3 matrix');
  }

  for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) {
      const r = R[i][j];
      if (!Number.isFinite(r) || r < -1 || r > 1) {
        throw new RangeError('Correlations must be finite and in [-1, 1]');
      }
      if (i === j && Math.abs(r - 1) > EPS) {
        throw new RangeError('Diagonal entries must be 1');
      }
      if (Math.abs(r - R[j][i]) > EPS) {
        throw new RangeError('Matrix must be symmetric');
      }
    }
  }

  const a = R[0][1], b = R[0][2], c = R[1][2];
  // For a symmetric 3x3 unit-diagonal matrix, with |a|,|b|,|c| <= 1,
  // all principal minors are nonnegative iff this determinant is >= 0.
  const determinant = 1 + 2 * a * b * c - a*a - b*b - c*c;
  if (determinant < -EPS) {
    throw new RangeError(`Not positive semidefinite; det=${determinant.toFixed(3)}`);
  }
  return determinant;
}

export function portfolioRisk3({ weights, vols, correlations }) {
  validateCorrelation3(correlations);
  if (!Array.isArray(weights) || weights.length !== 3 ||
      weights.some(w => !Number.isFinite(w) || w < 0 || w > 1) ||
      Math.abs(weights.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) - 1) > EPS) {
    throw new RangeError('Long-only weights must sum to 1');
  }
  if (!Array.isArray(vols) || vols.length !== 3 ||
      vols.some(v => !Number.isFinite(v) || v < 0)) {
    throw new RangeError('Volatilities must be nonnegative decimals');
  }

  const cov = correlations.map((row, i) =>
    row.map((rho, j) => vols[i] * rho * vols[j]));
  const sigmaW = cov.map(row =>
    row.reduce((sum, element, j) => sum + element * weights[j], 0));
  const variance = weights.reduce((sum, w, i) => sum + w * sigmaW[i], 0);
  if (variance < -EPS) throw new RangeError('Negative portfolio variance');

  const volatility = Math.sqrt(Math.max(0, variance));
  // The Euler attribution is undefined at zero volatility; don't fake shares.
  const contributions = volatility > 0
    ? weights.map((w, i) => w * sigmaW[i] / volatility)
    : null;
  return { volatility, contributions };
}

export const IMPOSSIBLE = [
  [ 1,   0.9,  0.9 ],
  [ 0.9, 1,   -0.9 ],
  [ 0.9,-0.9,  1   ],
];

export const POSSIBLE = [
  [ 1,   0.9, 0.9 ],
  [ 0.9, 1,   0.8 ],
  [ 0.9, 0.8, 1   ],
];

if (process.argv[1] && fileURLToPath(import.meta.url) === resolve(process.argv[1])) {
  try {
    validateCorrelation3(IMPOSSIBLE);
  } catch (error) {
    console.log('Rejected:', error.message);
  }
  const out = portfolioRisk3({
    weights: [0.4, 0.35, 0.25],
    vols: [0.3, 0.2, 0.15],
    correlations: POSSIBLE,
  });
  console.log('Portfolio volatility:', `${(100 * out.volatility).toFixed(3)}%`);
  console.log('Risk contributions:', out.contributions.map(x => `${(100 * x).toFixed(3)}pp`));
  console.log('Sum:', `${(100 * out.contributions.reduce((s, x) => s + x, 0)).toFixed(3)}pp`);
}

Run it with Node.js (tested with Node 22.16.0):

node risk-matrix.mjs

Expected output (rounded for display):

Rejected: Not positive semidefinite; det=-2.888
Portfolio volatility: 21.938%
Risk contributions: [ '11.856pp', '6.637pp', '3.444pp' ]
Sum: 21.938pp

Nothing here calls an API or downloads price data. The weights, volatilities, and correlations are hypothetical decimals, not historical estimates or investment recommendations.
The important part is what we test
For risk software, a nice-looking result isn't an acceptance test. We want a handful of invariants that can fail loudly:

  • The impossible matrix is rejected before pricing or rendering.
  • A valid matrix is accepted with its determinant unchanged.
  • Risk contributions sum to the same volatility computed by the covariance model.
  • Singular PSD matrices can be valid, but zero-volatility risk shares are undefined rather than an invented 0% / 0% / 0% chart.
  • Unnormalized long-only portfolio weights are rejected.
  • A negative individual Euler risk contribution can be legitimate when an asset hedges the rest. Don't automatically clip it to zero. Create risk-matrix.test.mjs: 
import test from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import {
  validateCorrelation3, portfolioRisk3, IMPOSSIBLE, POSSIBLE,
} from './risk-matrix.mjs';

const close = (actual, expected, tolerance = 1e-12) =>
  assert.ok(Math.abs(actual - expected) < tolerance,
    `Expected ${actual} ≈ ${expected}`);

test('rejects pairwise-valid but jointly impossible correlations', () => {
  assert.throws(() => validateCorrelation3(IMPOSSIBLE), /Not positive semidefinite/);
});

test('accepts a valid 3-asset correlation matrix', () => {
  close(validateCorrelation3(POSSIBLE), 0.036);
});

test('risk contributions add up to portfolio volatility', () => {
  const out = portfolioRisk3({
    weights: [0.4, 0.35, 0.25],
    vols: [0.3, 0.2, 0.15],
    correlations: POSSIBLE,
  });
  close(out.volatility, 0.2193769586807147);
  close(out.contributions.reduce((s, x) => s + x, 0), out.volatility);
});

test('accepts singular PSD matrices but does not invent zero-risk shares', () => {
  const perfectOpposites = [
    [1, -1, 0],
    [-1, 1, 0],
    [0, 0, 1],
  ];
  const out = portfolioRisk3({
    weights: [0.5, 0.5, 0],
    vols: [0.2, 0.2, 0.2],
    correlations: perfectOpposites,
  });
  close(out.volatility, 0);
  assert.equal(out.contributions, null);
});

test('invalid weights never reach the model', () => {
  assert.throws(() => portfolioRisk3({
    weights: [0.5, 0.5, 0.5],
    vols: [0.2, 0.2, 0.2],
    correlations: POSSIBLE,
  }), /weights must sum to 1/);
});

test('negative Euler contributions can be legitimate', () => {
  const hedge = [
    [1, -0.9, 0],
    [-0.9, 1, 0],
    [0, 0, 1],
  ];
  const out = portfolioRisk3({
    weights: [0.05, 0.8, 0.15],
    vols: [0.2, 0.2, 0.2],
    correlations: hedge,
  });
  assert.ok(out.contributions[0] < 0);
  close(out.contributions.reduce((s, x) => s + x, 0), out.volatility);
});

Then run:

node --test risk-matrix.test.mjs

Result: six tests pass on the code above. The valid example uses weights 40% / 35% / 25%, individual annualized volatilities 30% / 20% / 15%, and pairwise correlations 0.9 / 0.9 / 0.8. It calculates 21.938% modeled portfolio volatility. Its contributions are 11.856, 6.637, and 3.444 volatility percentage points—not three independent asset volatilities.

The units matter: 0.20 means 20% annualized volatility; 0.20 is not 0.20 percentage points. Errors here can be just as misleading as a bad matrix.
This is a UI architecture problem, too
In MarketDeck's Risk Constellation, the live public educational lab models four fictional assets. It calculates covariance, portfolio volatility, and Euler risk contributions in a numerical engine rather than inferring them from how far a line stretches on screen. Its public equal-correlation slider is constrained to a safe 0...1 range; you cannot paste the impossible three-asset matrix into that public UI.

The engineering lesson is still useful for any application that accepts independently edited pairwise assumptions:

  1. Validate the complete mathematical object, not individual form fields. For bigger matrices, use a tested PSD eigenvalue or factorization method, with an explicit numerical tolerance.
  2. Don't let a renderer own the answer. The chart, table, tooltip, and accessible text should all read the same verified result.
  3. Reject or explain invalid edits. If you choose a nearest-correlation-matrix repair, show the changed assumptions. Don't silently manufacture a different experiment.
  4. Make undefined states explicit. Zero portfolio volatility doesn't produce meaningful proportional risk shares.
  5. Test identities, not screenshots alone. The equality sum(risk contributions) ≈ portfolio volatility is a stronger regression check than a beautiful SVG. The nearest-correlation-matrix problem is a serious numerical-analysis problem in its own right; Nicholas Higham's paper is a good starting point if you want to investigate careful projection algorithms rather than simply rejecting an input. One last challenge Try replacing the valid matrix's third correlation, 0.8, with 0.61. The entry is still between -1 and 1, yet the complete matrix should fail the PSD test. Then try 0.62, the singular boundary, and see why a zero determinant does not automatically mean an invalid correlation matrix.

It's a small experiment, but it carries a general engineering lesson:
A set of individually plausible inputs is not necessarily a mathematically possible system.

That's true in finance, numerical simulation, ML feature engineering, and many applications where relationships are entered pair by pair.

References: Higham, Computing the Nearest Correlation Matrix, Node.js built-in test runner.

Disclosure: This article and its illustrative code were drafted with substantial AI assistance. The mathematical definitions were checked against the MarketDeck model and numerical references, and the included JavaScript example was executed with six passing tests. A human publisher should review the final text before releasing it. The example is educational only.
