title: Seven passes on one guidance arrow, and what each pass fixed
description:
Development covered 25 Sep 2026 to 26 Sep 2026 (commit dates).

In Myriad Immortal Sect you can light a Wayfinding Lamp to find your current quest target. Until this week the lamp showed you the way in two places: a highlighted diamond on the minimap and a line of text with a direction and a step count. Both worked. Both also meant looking away from your character to find out which way to walk.

So I added a third: a small gold arrow at the player's feet, pointing at the target, with the distance beside it. It took seven passes in two days, and almost none of them were about whether the arrow pointed the right way. They were about where it sits, how big it is and how it moves.

Pass one: agree with the other two

The first rule was not visual. The arrow, the minimap diamond and the text row all had to point at the same thing, so they all read from one place that decides what the lamp is leading you to. Three indicators that can disagree are worse than one, because the moment they split the player trusts none of them.

Passes two and three: a circle on the bearing

The first arrow circled the feet on a small flattened ellipse, which is the obvious way to draw something "on the ground". It looked right and behaved wrong. On an ellipse the arrow's position does not lie on the true bearing to the target, so it pointed one way and sat slightly in another.

It now orbits a true circle, 150 to 200 pixels out from the player in screen terms, and sits exactly on the line to the target. That had a nice side effect: clicking the arrow walks you towards the target, because the arrow is literally on the path. The step count moved directly under the arrow so the two never overlap.

When the target is closer than the orbit, an arrow circling at 150 pixels would point past it. Instead it glides in to just short of the target and points straight at it.

Passes four and five: smaller, then quieter

The arrow needed to read as "go this way" rather than as a static decoration, so it slides forward and eases back every 0.9 seconds. I kept that motion on even for players who ask for reduced motion, because that preference is about flashes and shaking, and a slow slide is neither.

Then I watched it for a while and it was too much. The arrow and its label came down by forty percent, the label rendered at high resolution so it stays sharp under the map zoom. The nudge got shorter. Then shorter again, from sixteen pixels to under six. Every one of those numbers came from looking at it during actual play, not from a mockup, because the right size for an indicator depends on everything else on screen at that moment.

Passes six and seven: depth, and room for the head

A flat arrow sliding back and forth is easy to stop seeing. Every five seconds it now rolls once around its long axis, a short flip that reads as three-dimensional without changing the direction it points. It is enough to catch the eye again without demanding it.

The last fix was about the player's own sprite. The character and their health bar stand above the point on the ground where they are anchored, so an arrow pointing upward at the normal radius crowded into the head. The orbit now widens by up to thirty percent as the arrow swings towards straight up.

The same idea applied to whole screens

A guidance arrow answers "where do I go?" without making you read. In the same window a handful of screens learned to answer "what is this page for?" in one line. The alchemy hall used to open with a piece of atmosphere, "One cauldron burns without rest", which told a first-time player nothing. It now opens with "Turn herbs into pills here. Each pill needs its recipe first." The Scripture Library, the Destiny page and the Treasures screen each gained a single plain sentence above their first card, and a recipe's description now says "Lets you brew X in the Alchemy Pavilion. It is never used up."

The codex of recipes lists every brewing and forging recipe that line now describes, and the guide to resources you find on the map covers what the lamp tends to lead you to.

What I took from it

Guidance elements are judged in context or not at all. On a blank canvas my first arrow was fine. On a busy map, next to a health bar, over a river, during a fight, it needed seven rounds of watching. Budget for that. And when you can, put the pointer where the player is already looking.

Light a lamp and follow it: play free in the browser, no download.

title: ASP.net Resting!
description:
In this post we're cooking up two apps that work together:

  1. FoodMenuApi, a REST API over a small restaurant database of dishes, their cuisines and categories, and which restaurants have them on the menu.
  2. FoodMenuClient, an https://www.google.com/url?q=http://ASP.NET&source=gmail&ust=1793897479914000&sa=E Core MVC website that calls the API with HttpClient, so users can browse, search, add, edit and remove dishes through normal web forms.

Along the way we'll cover EF Core scaffolding, keeping controllers skinny with a repository, DTOs, CORS, proper HTTP status codes (including a 409 Conflict when you try to delete a dish that's still on a restaurant's menu), and a tiny JavaScript page that calls the API directly.

Here's the API we're building:

Method URL What it does
GET /api/dishes All dishes, sorted by name
GET /api/dishes/5 One dish
GET /api/dishes?name=pad Dishes whose name starts with "pad", any case
POST /api/dishes Add a dish (data in the body)
PUT /api/dishes/5 Update a dish (data in the body)
DELETE /api/dishes/5 Delete a dish, or 409 if it's on a menu

The API runs on http://localhost:5050 and the MVC site on http://localhost:5060.

The finished project

Files marked ★ are ones we write or edit. Files marked ⚙ are generated by EF Core scaffolding.

FoodMenuSolution/
├── FoodMenu.sql ★ (database script)
│
├── FoodMenuApi/ ← Part 1: the REST API

│ │ └── DishesController.cs ★

│ │ ├── DishDTO.cs ★

│

Part 1: The REST API

Step 1: Create the database

Our database has five tables. menu_items is the link table that says which restaurant serves which dish, and it's the reason some deletes will be refused later.

cuisines (cuisine_id PK, cuisine_name)
categories (category_id PK, category_name)
dishes (dish_id PK, dish_name, cuisine_id FK, category_id FK, calories, price)
restaurants (restaurant_id PK, restaurant_name, phone, city)
menu_items (restaurant_id PK/FK, dish_id PK/FK, daily_portions) ← links dishes to restaurants

Step 2: Create the Web API project

In Visual Studio: Create a new project → https://www.google.com/url?q=http://ASP.NET&source=gmail&ust=1793897479915000&sa=E Core Web API. Name the project FoodMenuApi and the solution FoodMenuSolution, and keep Use controllers checked.

Then install these four NuGet packages (right-click the project → Manage NuGet Packages), all published by Microsoft:

Delete the template's WeatherForecast.cs and Controllers/WeatherForecastController.cs, since we won't need them.

Step 3: Add the connection string

Step 4: Let EF Core write the models for us

Step 6: DTOs, the public face of a dish

It's tempting to return the Dish entity straight from the API, but that causes problems:

  • It exposes database details like navigation properties and foreign keys the client doesn't care about.
  • Navigation properties can create loops when serialized.
  • If you accept Dish in a POST, [ApiController] validation complains that "The Cuisine field is required", because the navigation properties are non-nullable.

The fix is DTOs (Data Transfer Objects): small classes shaped for the outside world. Create a DTOs folder with two of them.

DTOs/DishDTO.cs is what the API sends out. It swaps unhelpful ids for readable names:

namespace FoodMenuApi.DTOs
{
public class DishDTO
{
public int DishId { get; set; }
public string DishName { get; set; } = string.Empty;
public int CuisineId { get; set; }
public string? CuisineName { get; set; }
public int CategoryId { get; set; }
public string? CategoryName { get; set; }
public int Calories { get; set; }
public decimal Price { get; set; }
}
}

DTOs/DishInputDTO.cs is what the API accepts for POST and PUT. There's no id because the database generates it:

Step 7: A repository to keep the controller skinny

If you scaffold an API controller, Visual Studio stuffs all the EF Core code right inside it, which makes a "fat" controller. A cleaner approach is a repository: one class that owns all the data access, so the controller only deals with HTTP.

Create a Repositories folder. First the interface, Repositories/IDishRepository.cs:

using FoodMenuApi.DTOs;

namespace FoodMenuApi.Repositories
{
public enum DeleteResult { Deleted, NotFound, Conflict }

public interface IDishRepository
{
Task<List<DishDTO>> GetAllAsync(string? name);
Task<DishDTO?> GetByIdAsync(int id);
Task<DishDTO> AddAsync(DishInputDTO input);
Task<bool> UpdateAsync(int id, DishInputDTO input); // false = not found
Task<DeleteResult> DeleteAsync(int id);
}
}

Then the implementation, Repositories/DishRepository.cs:

using FoodMenuApi.DTOs;
using FoodMenuApi.Models;
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;

namespace FoodMenuApi.Repositories
{
public class DishRepository : IDishRepository
{
private readonly FoodMenuContext _context;

public DishRepository(FoodMenuContext context)
{
_context = context;
}

// Entity -> DTO (manual mapping)
private static DishDTO ToDto(Dish d) => new DishDTO
{
DishId = d.DishId,
DishName = d.DishName,
CuisineId = d.CuisineId,
CuisineName = d.Cuisine?.CuisineName,
CategoryId = d.CategoryId,
CategoryName = d.Category?.CategoryName,
Calories = d.Calories,
Price = d.Price
};

// All dishes, or only those whose name starts with `name` (any case), sorted by name
public async Task<List<DishDTO>> GetAllAsync(string? name)
{
IQueryable<Dish> query = _context.Dishes
.Include(d => d.Cuisine)
.Include(d => d.Category);

if (!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(name))
{
string lower = name.Trim().ToLower();
query = query.Where(d => d.DishName.ToLower().StartsWith(lower));
}

List<Dish> dishes = await query
.OrderBy(d => d.DishName)
.ToListAsync();

return dishes.Select(ToDto).ToList();
}

public async Task<DishDTO?> GetByIdAsync(int id)
{
Dish? dish = await _context.Dishes
.Include(d => d.Cuisine)
.Include(d => d.Category)
.FirstOrDefaultAsync(d => d.DishId == id);

return dish == null ? null : ToDto(dish);
}

public async Task<DishDTO> AddAsync(DishInputDTO input)
{
var dish = new Dish
{
DishName = input.DishName,
CuisineId = input.CuisineId,
CategoryId = input.CategoryId,
Calories = input.Calories,
Price = input.Price
};

_context.Dishes.Add(dish);
await _context.SaveChangesAsync(); // the database generates DishId here

return (await GetByIdAsync(dish.DishId))!;
}

public async Task<bool> UpdateAsync(int id, DishInputDTO input)
{
Dish? dish = await _context.Dishes.FindAsync(id); // find it first
if (dish == null) return false;

dish.DishName = input.DishName;
dish.CuisineId = input.CuisineId;
dish.CategoryId = input.CategoryId;
dish.Calories = input.Calories;
dish.Price = input.Price;

await _context.SaveChangesAsync();
return true;
}

public async Task<DeleteResult> DeleteAsync(int id)
{
Dish? dish = await _context.Dishes.FindAsync(id);
if (dish == null) return DeleteResult.NotFound;

// Referential integrity: a dish on a restaurant's menu can't be deleted
bool onAMenu = await _context.MenuItems.AnyAsync(m => m.DishId == id);
if (onAMenu) return DeleteResult.Conflict;

_context.Dishes.Remove(dish);
try
{
await _context.SaveChangesAsync();
}
catch (DbUpdateException)
{
return DeleteResult.Conflict; // any other foreign key problem
}
return DeleteResult.Deleted;
}
}
}

The search uses ToLower() on both sides plus StartsWith, so pad, PAD and pAd all find "Pad Thai".

Step 8: Wire it all up in Program.cs

Now we register the DbContext and the repository, and turn on CORS. Browsers block JavaScript from calling an API on a different origin (a different port counts) unless the API explicitly allows it. CORS is that permission.

using FoodMenuApi.Models;
using FoodMenuApi.Repositories;
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

// Database
builder.Services.AddDbContext<FoodMenuContext>(options =>
options.UseSqlServer(builder.Configuration.GetConnectionString("FoodMenu")));

// Repository
builder.Services.AddScoped<IDishRepository, DishRepository>();

// CORS: allow JavaScript from other origins to call this API
builder.Services.AddCors(options =>
{
options.AddPolicy("AllowAll", policy =>
policy.AllowAnyOrigin()
.AllowAnyHeader()
.AllowAnyMethod());
});

builder.Services.AddControllers();
builder.Services.AddOpenApi(); // .NET 9+ template default; older templates use AddSwaggerGen()

var app = builder.Build();

if (app.Environment.IsDevelopment())
{
app.MapOpenApi();
}

// app.UseHttpsRedirection(); // off: we're using plain https://www.google.com/url?q=http://localhost:5050&source=gmail&ust=1793897479915000&sa=E

app.UseDefaultFiles(); // "/" serves wwwroot/index.html
app.UseStaticFiles(); // serves files from wwwroot

app.UseCors("AllowAll"); // must come BEFORE MapControllers

app.UseAuthorization();

app.MapControllers();

app.Run();

Step 9: The (skinny) API controller

Right-click Controllers → Add → Controller → API → API Controller with actions, using Entity Framework. Pick model Dish, context FoodMenuContext, and name it DishesController (plural, which makes the route api/dishes). Then replace the generated code with this version, which only handles HTTP and leaves the data work to the repository:

using FoodMenuApi.DTOs;
using FoodMenuApi.Repositories;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc;
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;

namespace FoodMenuApi.Controllers
{
[Route("api/[controller]")] // → api/dishes
[ApiController]
public class DishesController : ControllerBase
{
private readonly IDishRepository _repo;

public DishesController(IDishRepository repo)
{
_repo = repo;
}

// GET api/dishes → all dishes, sorted
// GET api/dishes?name=pad → dishes starting with "pad"
[HttpGet]
public async Task<ActionResult<IEnumerable<DishDTO>>> GetDishes([FromQuery] string? name)
{
List<DishDTO> dishes = await _repo.GetAllAsync(name);

if (!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(name) && dishes.Count == 0)
return NotFound($"No dishes start with '{name}'.");

return Ok(dishes);
}

// GET api/dishes/5
[HttpGet("{id}")]
public async Task<ActionResult<DishDTO>> GetDish(int id)
{
DishDTO? dish = await _repo.GetByIdAsync(id);
if (dish == null)
return NotFound($"Dish {id} not found.");

return Ok(dish);
}

// POST api/dishes (dish in the body)
[HttpPost]
public async Task<ActionResult<DishDTO>> PostDish(DishInputDTO input)
{
try
{
DishDTO created = await _repo.AddAsync(input);
// 201 Created, with a Location header pointing at GetDish
return CreatedAtAction(nameof(GetDish), new { id = created.DishId }, created);
}
catch (DbUpdateException)
{
return BadRequest("Could not add the dish. Check that CuisineId and CategoryId exist.");
}
}

// PUT api/dishes/5 (dish in the body)
[HttpPut("{id}")]
public async Task<IActionResult> PutDish(int id, DishInputDTO input)
{
try
{
bool updated = await _repo.UpdateAsync(id, input);
if (!updated)
return NotFound($"Dish {id} not found.");

return NoContent(); // 204
}
catch (DbUpdateException)
{
return BadRequest("Could not update the dish. Check that CuisineId and CategoryId exist.");
}
}

// DELETE api/dishes/5
[HttpDelete("{id}")]
public async Task<IActionResult> DeleteDish(int id)
{
DeleteResult result = await _repo.DeleteAsync(id);

return result switch
{
DeleteResult.NotFound => NotFound($"Dish {id} not found."),
DeleteResult.Conflict => Conflict($"Dish {id} is on a restaurant's menu and can't be deleted."), // 409
_ => NoContent() // 204
};
}
}
}

A quick cheat sheet of the status codes we're returning:

Helper Code When
Ok(x) 200 GET worked
CreatedAtAction(...) 201 POST worked
NoContent() 204 PUT or DELETE worked
BadRequest(msg) 400 Bad data or a missing foreign key
NotFound(msg) 404 No such dish
Conflict(msg) 409 Dish is still on a menu

Step 15: One class for all the HTTP calls

Just like the repository on the API side, we'll keep HttpClient code out of the controller. Create a Services folder and add DishApiClient.cs:

`csharp
using System.Net.Http.Headers;
using System.Runtime.Serialization.Json;
using System.Text;
using FoodMenuClient.Models;

namespace FoodMenuClient.Services
{
public class DishApiClient
{
private readonly string _baseUrl;

public DishApiClient(IConfiguration config)
{
_baseUrl = config["DishesApi:BaseUrl"]
?? throw new InvalidOperationException("DishesApi:BaseUrl is missing from appsettings.json");
}

// Steps 2-4: create the client, clear headers, accept JSON
private static HttpClient CreateClient()
{
var client = new HttpClient();
client.DefaultRequestHeaders.Accept.Clear();
client.DefaultRequestHeaders.Accept.Add(new MediaTypeWithQualityHeaderValue("application/json"));
return client;
}

// Steps 6, 10 and 11: stream → DataContractJsonSerializer → object
private static async Task Read(HttpResponseMessage response)
{
using Stream stream = await response.Content.ReadAsStreamAsync();
var serializer = new DataContractJsonSerializer(typeof(T));
return (T)serializer.ReadObject(stream)!;
}

// Object → JSON request body (for POST and PUT)
private static StringContent ToJson(Dish dish)
{
var serializer = new DataContractJsonSerializer(typeof(Dish));
using var ms = new MemoryStream();
serializer.WriteObject(ms, dish);
string json = Encoding.UTF8.GetString(ms.ToArray());
return new StringContent(json, Encoding.UTF8, "application/json");
}

private static ApiResult Fail(HttpResponseMessage response, string body) => new ApiResult
{
StatusCode = (int)response.StatusCode,
Success = false,
Message = string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(body) ? response.ReasonPhrase : body
};

private static ApiResult Unreachable(Exception ex) => new ApiResult
{
StatusCode = 0,
Success = false,
Message = "Could not reach the API. Is FoodMenuApi running? " + ex.Message
};

// GET api/dishes or api/dishes?name=xxx
public async Task>> GetAllAsync(string? name)
{
using HttpClient client = CreateClient();
string uri = string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(name)
? _baseUrl
: $"{_baseUrl}?name={Uri.EscapeDataString(name)}"; // step 5

try
{
HttpResponseMessage response = await client.GetAsync(uri);
if (!response.IsSuccessStatusCode)
return Fail>(response, await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync());

return new ApiResult>
{
Data = await Read>(response),
StatusCode = (int)response.StatusCode,
Success = true
};
}
catch (HttpRequestException ex) { return Unreachable>(ex); }
}

// GET api/dishes/5
public async Task> GetByIdAsync(int id)
{
using HttpClient client = CreateClient();
try
{
HttpResponseMessage response = await client.GetAsync($"{_baseUrl}/{id}");
if (!response.IsSuccessStatusCode)
return Fail(response, await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync());

return new ApiResult
{
Data = await Read(response),
StatusCode = (int)response.StatusCode,
Success = true
};
}
catch (HttpRequestException ex) { return Unreachable(ex); }
}

// POST api/dishes
public async Task> CreateAsync(Dish dish)
{
using HttpClient client = CreateClient();
try
{
HttpResponseMessage response = await client.PostAsync(_baseUrl, ToJson(dish));
if (!response.IsSuccessStatusCode)
return Fail(response, await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync());

return new ApiResult
{
Data = await Read(response), // the API sends back the new dish
StatusCode = (int)response.StatusCode,
Success = true,
Message = "Dish added."
};
}
catch (HttpRequestException ex) { return Unreachable(ex); }
}

// PUT api/dishes/5
public async Task> UpdateAsync(int id, Dish dish)
{
using HttpClient client = CreateClient();
try
{
HttpResponseMessage response = await client.PutAsync($"{_baseUrl}/{id}", ToJson(dish));
if (!response.IsSuccessStatusCode)
return Fail(response, await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync());

return new ApiResult
{
Data = true,
StatusCode = (int)response.StatusCode,
Success = true,
Message = $"Dish {id} updated."
};
}
catch (HttpRequestException ex) { return Unreachable(ex); }
}

// DELETE api/dishes/5
public async Task> DeleteAsync(int id)
{
using HttpClient client = CreateClient();
try
{
HttpResponseMessage response = await client.DeleteAsync($"{_baseUrl}/{id}");
if (!response.IsSuccessStatusCode)
return Fail(response, await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync());

return new ApiResult
{
Data = true,
StatusCode = (int)response.StatusCode,
Success = true,
Message = $"Dish {id} deleted."
};
}
catch (HttpRequestException ex) { return Unreachable(ex); }
}
}
}
`

Two things worth knowing about DataContractJsonSerializer:

  • A single object deserializes as Read<Dish>, and an array as Read<List<Dish>>.
  • It can't parse ISO date strings like "2026-11-04T12:00:00" into DateTime. If an API you're calling returns dates, make those properties string.

Step 17: The MVC controller

Right-click Controllers → Add → Controller → MVC Controller - Empty → DishesController. Each action calls the API client and decides which view or message to show:

`csharp
using FoodMenuClient.Models;
using FoodMenuClient.Services;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc;

namespace FoodMenuClient.Controllers
{
public class DishesController : Controller
{
private readonly DishApiClient _api;

public DishesController(DishApiClient api)
{
_api = api;
}

// GET /Dishes or /Dishes?name=pad
public async Task Index(string? name)
{
ApiResult> result = await _api.GetAllAsync(name);

ViewBag.Search = name;
ViewBag.Status = result.StatusCode;
ViewBag.Error = result.Success ? null : result.Message;

return View(result.Data ?? new List()); // step 12
}

// GET /Dishes/Details/5
public async Task Details(int id)
{
ApiResult result = await _api.GetByIdAsync(id);
if (!result.Success)
{
TempData["Error"] = $"({result.StatusCode}) {result.Message}";
return RedirectToAction(nameof(Index));
}
ViewBag.Status = result.StatusCode;
return View(result.Data);
}

// GET /Dishes/Create
[HttpGet]
public IActionResult Create()
{
return View(new Dish());
}

// POST /Dishes/Create
[HttpPost]
[ValidateAntiForgeryToken]
public async Task Create(Dish dish)
{
if (!ModelState.IsValid) return View(dish);

ApiResult result = await _api.CreateAsync(dish);
if (!result.Success)
{
ViewBag.Error = $"({result.StatusCode}) {result.Message}";
return View(dish);
}

TempData["Message"] = $"({result.StatusCode}) Dish added with id {result.Data!.DishId}.";
return RedirectToAction(nameof(Details), new { id = result.Data.DishId });
}

// GET /Dishes/Edit/5 → form pre-filled with the current values
[HttpGet]
public async Task Edit(int id)
{
ApiResult result = await _api.GetByIdAsync(id);
if (!result.Success)
{
TempData["Error"] = $"({result.StatusCode}) {result.Message}";
return RedirectToAction(nameof(Index));
}
return View(result.Data);
}

// POST /Dishes/Edit/5
[HttpPost]
[ValidateAntiForgeryToken]
public async Task Edit(int id, Dish dish)
{
if (!ModelState.IsValid) return View(dish);

ApiResult result = await _api.UpdateAsync(id, dish);
if (!result.Success)
{
ViewBag.Error = $"({result.StatusCode}) {result.Message}";
return View(dish);
}

TempData["Message"] = $"({result.StatusCode}) {result.Message}";
return RedirectToAction(nameof(Details), new { id });
}

// GET /Dishes/Delete/5 → "are you sure?" page
[HttpGet]
public async Task Delete(int id)
{
ApiResult result = await _api.GetByIdAsync(id);
if (!result.Success)
{
TempData["Error"] = $"({result.StatusCode}) {result.Message}";
return RedirectToAction(nameof(Index));
}
return View(result.Data);
}

// POST /Dishes/Delete/5
[HttpPost, ActionName("Delete")]
[ValidateAntiForgeryToken]
public async Task DeleteConfirmed(int id)
{
ApiResult result = await _api.DeleteAsync(id);

if (result.Success)
TempData["Message"] = $"({result.StatusCode}) {result.Message}";
else if (result.StatusCode == 409)
TempData["Error"] = $"(409) Dish {id} is on a restaurant's menu, so it can't be deleted.";
else
TempData["Error"] = $"({result.StatusCode}) {result.Message}";

return RedirectToAction(nameof(Index));
}
}
}

Troubleshooting

  • "The Cuisine field is required" on POST. The API is accepting the Dish entity instead of DishInputDTO.
  • "blocked by CORS policy" in the browser console. AddCors/UseCors is missing, or UseCors comes after MapControllers.
  • "Could not reach the API" in the website. The API isn't running, or the port in the client's appsettings.json doesn't match the API's launchSettings.json.
  • Blank values in the website. A [DataMember(Name = "...")] doesn't match the JSON key exactly. Compare against the JSON in Postman.
  • Search is case sensitive. You forgot ToLower() on one side of the comparison.

Reusing this for other APIs

  • Calling someone else's API: open it in Postman, build a [DataContract] class that matches its JSON, change BaseUrl, and copy DishApiClient with your class swapped in.
  • Building an API over a different database: scaffold it, write DTOs, add a repository and its interface, register them in Program.cs, and keep the controller focused on HTTP.

Wrapping up

We built a REST API with EF Core, kept the controller lean with a repository, shaped responses with DTOs, returned meaningful status codes, opened it to JavaScript with CORS, and then built an MVC site that calls it through HttpClient. The recipe is the same whatever's on the menu. 🍕
